It is commonly regarded as one of the best puzzle games of all time due to its precise design and carefully considered gameplay. It has no fat on it to trim and the fluff was never there to begin with. It needed no balance patches, and to go along with it, that one, continuous song that became etched into the minds of a generation. It was a real life Polybius, and many people called it the perfect game.

35 years later, Balatro was released.

Balatro is a special kind of game. It's a game where the success of the player isn't determined by how fast they can act, like tetris, how precise their inputs, like mario, or even how much they know, like pokemon. It's instead about how they use their head to navigate simple systems that play off each other perfectly. A player need not even tab out of the game to access all the information about what could appear in the shop, what cards they might draw, or how much their hand may score. But there's ambiguity there, there's uncertainty. It's the ability to have enough control and information to make an informed decision, like chess, but enough randomness to bring additional excitement that is absent in games with less ambiguity. And so you sit at your computer, hitting that reset shop button, eyes glued to the screen, waiting for that one piece so that your build can all fall into place. 50 gold becomes 45. 45 becomes 39. 32. 25. This next shop needs the card you want if you want to be able to afford it. You hover your mouse over the reroll button. The one, infectious melody playing over and over in your head. And you've travelled back to 1989, you're sitting on the carpet too close to the screen in your pyjamas, it's past your bedtime. Boom. Tetris.

Donated said money to orphanage for kids without fathers—hopefully they'll learn how to play Poker some day too.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 187, "timestamp_created": 1762702780}, {"review_text": "[b]Balatro[/b] is a roguelite deckbuilder pretending to be a pixel-art poker game.  I know everyone's at least heard of it at this point, [i]but[/i] I've 100%'d it 2.5 times on mobile and wrote this to figure out where my life went wrong.  

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
[b]Balatro[/b] eases you into madness: You start with a basic deck of 54 cards, score points on traditional poker hands, and earn money.   Spend that money on upgrades: joker cards that alter scoring, "tarot cards" that upgrade your deck, and "celestial" cards that increase point yields.  It seems so simple.  

And then it goes off the rails.

You're constantly unlocking new decks that behave in unique ways, new jokers that add crazy nuance and multipliers, new ways to score, etc.  "Spectral" cards tempt you to risk everything in exchange for massive gains.  New difficulties force you to level up faster.  Before you know it, you've spent an entire overnight flight trying to score a hand with five gold sevens of clubs, and have yet to sleep a wink.

[h3]What Works For Me[/h3]
✅ I actually love the artwork.  It's so dumb and so simple, but some of the jokers are just… the best.

✅ I did not understand poker or poker hands before [b]Balatro[/b], but "Run Info" includes a simple visual guide that makes more sense than any video I've ever watched.

✅ The card synergies!  The absolute insanity you can create with some Magicians and a Lucky Cat, or a King, a Mime, and a lot of chariots, red seals, and demonic deer!  

✅ Players that stumble across particularly cool combinations can share "seeds" for others to enjoy too, or use their own seeds to conduct post-mortems on rounds that didn't quite work.   Seeded games do not count toward victories or achievements.  If you're still in relatively early game, this was in my most recent play-through and is hilariously OP; I have never hit the billions so quickly: DWDV2JTN

[h3]What Doesn't Work For Me[/h3]
🟥 The Steam version is less intuitive than the mobile app (but does work well on Steamdeck).  On mobile, you drag and drop cards to buy, sell, use, etc.  On desktop, the cards sprout little tabs that you have to click to buy, sell, use, etc.  It's less tactile and a little more… fiddly.

🟥 The mobile version is a battery vampire.  I recently flew from the USA to Italy and back again, and despite having my Switch and a half-dozen reports to write, played [b]Balatro[/b] the entire time.  The battery pack that powered my husband's and my phones through a week-long blackout last year was fully depleted by the time I returned home. 

🟥 Endless mode ramps up too quickly, especially on lower stakes.  You want to refine an interesting deck, but the game gives you a few extra antes before saying, "Okay, now score 300 million."   Well, fuck you too. 

🟥 No one will read this review because this little indie game that the dev reportedly made for his friends has taken off like [i]Stardew Valley[/i].   I am so late to this party that it isn't even fashionable. 

[h3]Final Thoughts + Recommendation[/h3]
If you haven't played [b]Balatro[/b], or if you have but don't understand the hype (like me at first):  it starts off pretending to be poker, but it's not poker.  It is a tricky, RNG-driven roguelike with some [i]insanely[/i] cool engine-building and so much variety that you will never play the same game twice.  

In a weird way, I think it reminds me more of engine-building board games like [i]Terraforming Mars[/i], [i]Race for the Galaxy[/i], and [i]Splendor[/i] than any particular card game.  I love a good puzzle and building a good foundation, and that's what [b]Balatro[/b] is about.  It's also super easy to play in waiting rooms, lounges, in front of the TV, and so on.

If you enjoy [b]Balatro[/b], then I'd suggest checking out [i][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1404850/Luck_be_a_Landlord/?curator_clanid=45365863]Luck Be A Landlord[/url][/i], [i][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/646570/Slay_the_Spire/]Slay the Spire[/url][/i], and [i][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/3211750/Neongarten/?curator_clanid=45365863]Neongarten[/url][/i] for similar-but-different games.

It can't be as simple as "haha gambling but without losing real life money". And after playing the game for 400+ hours, seeing tons of Balatro videos, and comments around the game, I think I maybe know what's the secret formula behind Balatro's astronomic success.

It has to do with how majority of items, be it Jokers or tarot/planet cards are all build around snowballing effect and deck fixing. In other roguelikes, like Binding of Isaac, there are far more items that are simply a positive for almost any run, just flat dmg or flat tear up, you can just find mom's knife in first treasure room of Isaac, and just win the run here and there, Balatro doesnt have that many items like that. It has cavendish, but you can only buy it after Gros Michel expires from your joker slot, and even Cadendish has small chance to expire too and doesnt even have the biggest flat xmult in the game.

Same story goes for deck fixing, and how, unlike in other roguelikes, you're pushed the most in Balatro to master deck fixing for certain builds, say you get early blackboard, now unless you get super lucky to find other xmult joker for late game, you're encourages by the game to start deck fixing for spades/clubs to get the blackboards x3 mult, because like I said, most Jokers/items are situational, so the game requires you to create said situations more and more. 

Which in turn creates addictive loop of wanting to master deck fixing, because if you dont, you most likely lose. But because of how fast the game is(you can speed up card dealing in options menu plus you dont need to backtrack, like how you need to in say Isaac), even failures dont feel punishing, so you want to master it more and more, in order to either 100% the game(like me) or chase those crazy endless high scores.

I sit atop my father's knee, watching as he plays the version of Spider Solitaire that came pre-installed on the family computer. I watch cards move across the screen and stack on top of each other as they make a satisfying sound akin to a deck of cards being shuffled. Some twenty-odd years and dozens of different card games played later and I now have Balatro, a game whose developer names Solitaire as its most important inspiration. It's almost as if Balatro was made for me... is what I would say if I had a delusional level of self-importance.

The aim of Balatro is simple: play a combination of poker hands in order to score enough points to meet an ever-increasing threshold each round. The reward for beating a round is some $$$ and the chance to shop for packs, tarot cards, planet cards, and the famous Jokers which you can purchase to empower your run. Each run is comprised of 8 levels or 'Antes' each with ending with a 'Boss Blind', a high scoring round with an additional  stipulation such as "all heart cards are de-buffed". This all culminates in one final boss blind that you must complete to win the run. From there, you can keep going in endless mode to get high scores or play again with a new deck or at a higher difficulty or 'Stake'.

Balatro achieves the singleplayer experience of Solitaire that inspired it but it also feels like a hybrid of a card game and an autobattler at times. Both Balatro and Teamfight Tactics, for example, require the player to manage their economy, take direction from what appears in the shop, use currency to reroll the shop, and know how and when to pivot their build. Just imagine that you replace all the units with cards and the PvP rounds in TFT with a Hearthstone lethal puzzle and you basically have Balatro.

Balatro invokes in me the experience that the critic from Pixar's Ratatouille has when he sits down at Gusteau's and takes that first bite. He is served a common peasant's dish, one that reminds him of his earliest years, and yet it is executed on so masterfully that the dish, to him, feels fresh and new. This game serves me something that is familiar on the surface; a standard deck of 52 cards accompanied by a series of snaps and clicks that throw me back to sitting atop my father's knee. Beneath the top layer lies a court of jesters and fools that breathe life into the humble playing card and I am invited to taste and savour all of the game's possible combinations. What I am left with every time I put Balatro down is a feeling of satisfaction yet a yearning for more. This game is what any hungry card game enjoyer's palate ought to crave. It is, for me, a game that I will always come back to. The one you boot up when there's nothing else to play, or on a rainy Saturday afternoon in early 2025. It is endlessly replayable with so many card and Joker combinations, unlockables, challenges, and difficulties. It can be as relaxing or demanding as you like; as simple or difficult as you require.

It was the year 2000.
I was six years old — too young to understand strategy, too young to understand competition — but somehow just the right age to fall in love with chaos.
That day, my cousin showed me a dusty PC in a smoky internet café.
A CRT monitor flickered. A mouse too big for my hand.
But it wasn’t just a game.
It was my first battle.

He loaded up de_dust, and suddenly, the world outside — the noise, the crowds, the slow passage of real life — faded into nothing.
There were no big cutscenes, no heroes.
Just me, a Desert Eagle, and an objective I barely understood.
I wasn’t just playing.
I was fighting.

And then came the countless hours.
Headphones crackling with radio commands.
My heart racing with every corner I peeked.
Maps that became burned into my brain — the feel of them, not just the look.
I didn’t need tutorials.
We learned by losing.
By fumbling flashbangs and mistiming bomb plants.
By laughing at every terrible mistake and swearing we’d get it right next time.

Sometimes my father would peek into the room,
watching me shout at a screen filled with pixelated soldiers.
He didn’t understand why I cared so much about a digital bomb ticking down.
But he let me have that world.
A place where mistakes had a "restart" button.
Where battles could be won with practice, not just luck.

Now, two decades later, I still come back.
The graphics are ancient.
The servers mostly abandoned.
The hitboxes feel like ghosts compared to what games are now.

But something inside Counter-Strike still breathes.
Every footstep on old concrete.
Every panicked spray of bullets.
Every dusty corridor, whispering memories from a time when everything felt new and impossible and alive.

Counter-Strike isn’t just a shooter.
It’s a fossil from a younger Earth.
It’s a monument to when games weren’t about battle passes or daily challenges—
just pure, raw, imperfect competition.

And as I buy armor and a defusal kit one more time,
as I run through the same broken hallways I knew before I even knew what nostalgia was,
I remain there.
Hand on the mouse...
And a tear I cannot quite name—
whether it’s loss, or gratitude.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1745704445}, {"review_text": "This game is fire. When Valve made the fatal decision to replace CS:GO with CS2, it exposed a years-long movement away from making great games for the players.  You see, Valve had been working on this Source 2 engine for years.  And now that they finally "Finished" it, they needed a game to test it out on, to see if the playerbase would react positively.  For this they chose the age-old classic CS:GO.  To Valve, CS:GO had proven itself to be a hardy and everlasting popular game.  It would make a great candidate, they thought.  But for some horrendous reason they chose to REPLACE CS:GO with CS2, rendering online play in the former completely impossible.

But why would they do this?  This decision stems back to around a year before CS2 came into existence.  It goes back to a terrible company called Blizzard.  They had this game called Overwatch which was a tremendous success.  In 2022 they put out Overwatch 2, which would REPLACE the first Overwatch.  To my knowledge this is the first major game to have this done to it.  Overwatch 2 was also one of the first games, to my knowledge, put out by a major studio to have initial Overwhelmingly Negative reviews on Steam.  But even with this backlash, people couldn't put their money where their mouth was and still continued on playing Overwatch 2.  It's like Call of Duty syndrome.  People complain year-in and year-out that each new Call of Duty is basically the same game (which it is).  Yet they gladly plunk down 7 Hamiltons a year to play it, 14 if they play on Xbox.

The following year, 2023, Valve knew the time was right and followed in Blizzard's footsteps.  They made the decision to replace CS:GO with CS2.  First off we need to establish why Valve saw it necessary to update the game to Source 2 in general.  They did this because A: they had already been working on Source 2 for years and B: they wanted to pump new life into CS:GO.  Hopefully they won't do this with TF2 because that game has nothing wrong with it in terms of the engine it runs on.  Anyways, that's the reason they moved it to Source 2.  But why replace the game??

The reason they replaced it stems from the Item Economy that CS:GO had.  That's right.  Valve once and for all dispelled all rumours to the contrary.  They place the item collectors and the skin hunters over the actual players of the game.  They had to replace the game due to the difficulty and uncertainty of appID inventory migration.  Would our great community of skin hunters and gamblers appreciate having their items stuck in an old installment of the series, or worse, deleted due to a potential unforeseen migration bug???  Of course not, so we must replace the game.

All of the people, like me, that enjoyed the old CS:GO system of gameplay are now forever condemned to offline or community servers.  Me, I haven't booted up CS2 ever.  And I won't because I despise what Valve did to their greatest game.  All to keep the cash cow running.

So I vow never to play the game again and move on.  But hundreds of hours of CS:GO sort of gives you this itch that needs to be scratched every so often.  At first I can ignore it but eventually I have a deep desire to play CS:GO.  But I can't!  So next I try the ways of the old school.  I give CS:S another shot and, as evidenced in my review for that game, it still stands up as a masterpiece of FPS games.  Best part too is that you can still play it!

And then I try the original Counter-Strike, the game which this review is for.  And lo and behold it too stands up as a masterpiece of the FPS genre, only this game has infinitely more classic appeal than even CS:S.  Counter-Strike somehow knows exactly when and where to reward you for your efforts, and it makes you want to play more even when you're getting owned.  Each time you die, you think you know exactly how to win next time and you want to try again.  Even if you get owned again, you still think this until one day you figure out how and you become Skilled.

This game comes from a bygone era in software and video game development.   By todays "Standards" this game would be blasted.  Graphics aren't good enough! No skin customization! No ranking system!  This simplicity is what I absolutely love about this game.  Back in the 90's, when this game was being created as a mod offshoot of Half-Life, this kind of thing absolutely blew people away.  How the hell could a computer do this? - people would think.  And to think it was made and conceived by such a small group of people.  To captivate the genius minds of the gaming public today, at least a medium-sized gaming studio is required, with some rare exceptions.  And to captivate the majority of gamers, a Triple A studio is needed.  Back when Counter-Strike came out, a few college students could make a game that ruled the Internet.

This kind of thing simply does not happen anymore.  Innovation in gaming is dead.  Now we have companies focusing on hyper-realism and replacing amazing video games with subpar imitations, all to keep a skin economy running.  There will be no more Dooms or Counter-Strikes anymore.  By this I mean games that revolutionize genres.  It simply won't happen.  The almighty Dollar has taken over the world of video game development and companies realize it is more profitable to make stupid loot boxes than it is to make a great game.  This is because the average gamer has the brain of a chimpanzee, and will drool at fancy golden guns and rare Legendary outfits, and will stop at nothing to get them, even wasting away their savings opening random loot boxes.  It disgusts me and it should disgust you.

This is why I will heap as much praise as I can onto a game like Counter-Strike.  There are no loot boxes.  There are no skins, no item economy.  There is nothing in this game that makes Valve money with the sole exception of you buying it.  And this means that Valve isn't going to tamper with the game and ruin it for eternity, so you get to enjoy the game until the very last community server shuts down.  And that is exactly what I plan to do, because Counter-Strike is a relic of a game.

The granddaddy of clutch shooters. If you haven’t raged at a CRT monitor over a one-tap headshot on Dust2, did you even game in the 2000s? Valve basically took a Half-Life mod and accidentally (or maybe on purpose, who knows) dropped the blueprint for every sweaty, team-based shooter that’s come out since. No respawns, no cheap killstreaks, no “press F to pay respects.” Just you, your squad, and a whole lotta nerves.

The rules? Simple as hell. Terrorists, counter-terrorists. One round, one life. Screw up, and you’re watching your teammates for the next two minutes. Every round’s got that gut-churning tension, even if you’re just creeping around a corner praying nobody’s holding the angle. You clutch a 1v3 on Inferno? That’s not just a highlight, that’s bragging rights for the next year.

The gunplay? Brutal. You either learn to control that AK spray, or you’re cannon fodder. The AWP, meanwhile, makes its own rules, one shot one kill, and a sound that’s basically a trauma response for anyone who’s ever peeked mid. Honestly, every gun’s got its own flavor, and none of them forgive sloppy play.

And the maps, man, the maps are legends. Dust2 isn’t just a battleground, it’s a rite of passage. Mirage, Nuke, Train, by the time you’ve learned all the callouts, you’ve probably lost a few friendships over “who the hell didn’t smoke cross?” These aren’t just places you play, they’re places you live in. And every time you think you’ve mastered something, someone comes along and wallbangs you through a box you didn’t even know existed.

Graphically? Yeah, it looks ancient now. But honestly, that’s part of the charm. No busy clutter, no neon skins, just crisp lines and a HUD that actually tells you what’s up. You hear a footstep, you know where it’s coming from. You hear a grenade, better duck. It’s all gameplay, zero fluff.

Story? Ha. The story is “get good or get out.” No lore, no drawn-out campaign, just pure, unfiltered competition. You either adapt, or you spend a lot of time spectating.

But here’s what gets you hooked: those moments. The 1v5 clutch, the ninja defuse, the round-winning flashbang. It’s sweaty palms and heart-in-throat suspense, and when you finally pull it off, you feel like a god. Lose? You’ll want to smash your keyboard, but you’ll queue up again anyway.

Multiplayer is the whole deal. Whether you’re stacking with friends or getting yelled at by strangers in a pub, it’s all about outsmarting the other team. Teamwork isn’t a suggestion, it’s the difference between winning and getting stomped. Lone wolves get eaten alive.

Counter-Strike 1.6 didn’t just set the bar, it [b]is[/b] the bar. Every tactical shooter since has been chasing its shadow. Decades on, it’s still a masterclass, tight, intense, and never forgiving. [{"review_text": "[b] This negative review can be summed up in 1 only line:  [/b]

[h1] GREEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEED [/h1]

 [b] But here's the elaborated version:  [/b]

After spending ~1000h ingame on the EA platform, and additionally ~600h on steam, 
and playing all previous titles of this franchise (on EA platform), and basically growing up with the franchise,
I just have to write a bad review about TS4. 

The game is fun mind you, but I just cannot recommend it anymore due to the greediness of the franchise. 
The game has almost 1500€ of DLC's! 

Of course there are also other games with a lot of DLC's, 
but what bothers me is that compared to previous sims titles, 
it feels like [b] with each sequel, they split up the DLC's more and more and by that, asking more money from the players.  [/b]

Like, why does TS4 need 2 separate expansion packs of 40€ each for school related things? (university + highschool)
Why does the TS4 need 2 separate dlc's of 40€ each for having a business? (business & hobbies + get to work)
Why does it need a separate DLC game pack to own a restaurant that you can manage? 

I can buy at least 2 separate simulator games that are a lot more in depth in owning / managing a restaurant for that amount of money... 

They could have easily combined the dine out game pack + business & hobbies + get to work, in 1 dlc! 
But no, they split it up and ask 100€ in total for it.
and there are many more examples of their greediness...
 [b]
Sims 1 had 7 expansion packs
Sims 2 had 8 expansion packs + 10 stuff packs
Sims 3 had 11 expansion packs + 9 stuff packs + 11 world packs
Sims 4: has 19 expansion packs, 12 game packs, 21 stuff packs and 46 kits  [/b]

Do you see the list getting longer with each sequel?

There is even this feature, you had standard in previous sims titles, 
which is having a burglar that comes to your house to steal your stuff. 
In sims 4, they didn't implement that "at first", and how long did we have to wait for them to finally grant the players their request to have it in the TS4? We waited 10years!!! 10 LONG DAMN YEARS.
But hey! On the bright side, I was very baffled, it was a small & free update, and that they didn't ask 40€ for it as a DLC...

I hope people can agree that the previous titles of the game were in many ways a lot better and less money grabby.
[list]
   [*]We had open world in TS3; In TS4 everywhere we go, we have a loading screen.
   [*]We had a color wheel to adjust each peace of furniture, hair,... 
In TS4 we only have a small set amount of predefined colours. 
   [*] We don't even have cars we can drive & own, except for miniature decorative cars, 
that you scale up to make it look like you own a very pixelated car and just pretend it's the same as the feature we had in TS3..
And so on...

But hey! Who knows, maybe we will get all those features back, later in 3 separate DLC's for 40€ each!

[/list]
Thank goodness there is a mod community, because without that, I think the game would have died ages ago.

Anyway, I just had to get these frustrations out of the way. 
I guess I just had enough of it, and decided to write a bad review for the TS4, right after another certain game in the life-sim genre, had very recently released a huge DLC, with a lot of & more modern features and many new items FOR FREE!

I just can't wait for a competitor of TS franchise to come out with a similar game, 
or to refine their currently released game, so that TS4 can die out, 
and in a perfect world, EA decides to be less greedy in the future.

But I guess if ever a next sims title will be released, they will only bring out the double amount of DLC's that TS4 has....

I'll still play the game from time to time, with the content that I have, 
but I am just done spending money and supporting this franchise in this way.

[b] I'm not against DLC's of games, and I think It's nice of them to have made the base game Free to play, 
after having people paying for it all those years, but I am against the greediness
and the fact they could have easily combined DLC's instead of splitting them up more and more into separate, expensive DLC's. [/b]

i started playing the sims around seven years ago now, starting with this game. never played any sims games that came before, to me this was enough. for this, the game sits in a place in my heart for the sake of nostalgia. for a while i didn't touch it, except when it was to make some stupid joke household, but around a year ago i picked it up and dumped the majority of the playtime you see on my record in. by this point i was mostly out, i could say with pride i was a girl, and the sims has my thanks for helping me just disappear into a world of my own for a while, forget all the documents and medical procedures and just play in a body i was happy with.

I ended up installing mods, some for affirming stuff, as well as stuff i felt should just be in the game, but i'm not gonna talk about mods, not yet. we're staying on the base game for now.

EA has always been famous for not doing the best job at, well, anything other than devouring people's wallets, and i'm gonna admit, i've probably given EA more money than ANY other games company, i knew EA was greedy for cash, but i kept feeding it. Why? because the basegame felt pretty lifeless.

The sims 4 without DLCs consists of three worlds: Willow creek, Oasis Springs, and Newcrest, if you are curious what they consist of, here's a summary of each:

-willow creek: from what i understand this area is inspired mostly by Lousiana, in the USA. it's your basic neighborhood, and yeah, that's how i'd describe it, as basic. not in a bad way, it just kinda is your stereotypical american neighborhood, i say this as a non-american, and will admit my references for this are mostly cartoons and other random pieces of media, sorry if i'm wrong and that this is an outdated stereotype of middle-class americans. it consists of what i'll call an amenities chain (for lack of a better word) which consists of a gym, a library, a museum, and a club. There is also a park, which is standard for most if not all worlds in the sims, dlc or not, and consists of 13 homes that have already been built, 4 of which are inhabited. also the other statements won't be as long this is hurting my fingers.

-oasis springs: okay, imagine willow creek, but get this, DESERT. But in all seriousness, the two starter worlds function in a very similar way. you have some beginner homes, which are small with very little room for expansion most of the time (unless you are willing to build a multi-stage bunker or a skyscraper), some decent homes and finally the kinds of houses that keep the american nightmare going. Oasis springs also has an amenities chain, except instead of a library there is a bar and instead of a club there's a lounge (if you don't know what the difference between a club and a lounge is, i don't know either) as well as a park, as well as, like willow creek, 13 prebuilt residential homes, 4 of which are inhabited.

-Newcrest: contains nothing, it's your's to create. it has no amenities, no park, no houses, it's up to you what happens to it. can't complain about it, i'm not a massive builder myself but it's there for anybody who is.

[{"review_text": "A lot of things to like about this game, but a few annoying ticks as well.

The Good:

- Very solid RPG. Dialogue is genuinely interesting, entertaining, and well-written. I was immersed the whole way through Chapter 1.
- Feels like Oblivion meets Hyperlight Drifter meets Dark Souls.
- Zero bugs and glitches. The game is seamless.
- There is replayability. The first map comes with two major factions, and joining one locks you out of the other. Likewise, there's no way you can cover all the weapon builds in just one playthrough.
- Mobs/bosses/etc are genuinely hard. I died 6x to the Bear boss alone. Felt like a kid playing Dark Souls again.
- Music is really solid.
- Aesthetic is fantastic.

The Great:

- You can beat up/attack most NPCs and loot them for their stuff. It's a very viable way to get gear, but they're tough as nails. You genuinely have to consider how to talk to people because 9/10ths of the NPCs in this game are built different. If you are rude to someone in a conversation, they might just beat your a** for it and take all your stuff.

The Funny:

- I slept in a gladiator's bed, so they woke me up, knocked me unconscious, stole all my money, and 9hrs later, I returned, kicked the sh** out of them and stole their hat.

The Not-so Great:

- Difficulty, at times, comes from the mobs and bosses simply not knowing when to stop. 
- Unlike you, they have no stamina/focus bar.
- So if you fight a guy in the arena, he will spam special attacks over... and over... and over.
- There is no actual ebb and flow to some fights. You just get railed on with magic/shouts/special stuns, and that's... that. You just sort of have to roll with it.

The Annoying:

- Some of the NPCs you can fight have power levels that don't make sense.
- I was playing a new Hardcore playthrough and decided to beat up a kitchen wench because she denied me a quest reward. She hit me with iron daggers, at first, then got tired of that and changed to a high-level sling; which one shot me, totally breaking my immersion.
- This lets down an otherwise great mechanic, because you are never really sure who you can start on and who you can't.... despite it being an integral gameplay feature.

As far as a role-playing game goes, it is great. But you occasionally run into those awkward (?) moments that make you feel awkward and like your time isn't being respected. I feel like the developers should go back and tighten up a few screws on the NPCs. Non-fighters probably shouldn't hit like The Terminator.

Edit: I saw that this review blew up. I should add:

The Dev team for this game is beyond excellent. If you check out their Discord, you'll notice they're active with the community. Likewise, this game feels like one of those early PS1 titles that you grow up with. If you were to boot up this game, and it was one of your first ever games, you would get absolutely lost in it. I'm biased because I've played through 800+ titles in my life, which leads me to compare it to everything else (the shtick of old age). Enjoy!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762429836}, {"review_text": "Akin to Stygian and Iron Tower before them, Just2D have shown us that a CRPG can be made on a budget. This can't be overstated, for we almost lost my beloved genre to the AAA vulgarisation. It's about to bloom instead. Alas, Drova: Forsaken Kin is an unfortunate title. At least 3 people I know called it Foreskin. Well then, let's pull it back to see what's under the hood. A c#cking good CRPG with twin-stick combat and a hard emphasis on Zelda-esque exploration! Not a game to take the world by storm, yet the one whose little world you could take to heart. Much like Gothic that inspired it. Not being its bleak parody, Drova takes Gothic's unique features and capably integrates them on a deeper level.

[h3]Exploration[/h3]
You begin by following a couple of druids from your village who decide to use a mysterious magic crystal for trans-dimensional travel. Things go awry, they die. Now, you're alone in Drova with the stone in one hand and your dong in another. Then the story gets lost in the shuffle for such a long ass time you'll forget the game had one. Let's do the same and talk presentation. Drova is a love child, evident through its polish, diligent animation, and spritework. The lively pastoral views of the countryside idyll make way for gloomy forests and bogs enveloped in thick fog. The leaves are in motion, bushes and canes sway when you move through as the raindrops ripple in the water, while extremely cute piglets skitter about to the sound of wistful ambience and fitting fantasy instrumentals.

The world of Drova makes you wanna linger. There's always something off the beaten path. Tracks to follow, a treasure in the ruins, a sprawling cave system full of traps. After roaming about for a few minutes, you may find a stone that bestows learning points or a concealed dungeon. Then get ambushed by bandits and loot a powerful rare axe. The rewarding nature of exploration is almost overwhelming. The perks of being inquisitive and perceptive are evident right from the start, getting you excited for the rest of the game. Another great feature is what I'd call impractical interactivity. It isn't Ultima or even Gothic, but there's a drop of it here and there. Little things like being able to start a fight with almost anyone, sit in a chair, play a lyra, or dance at a tavern add a drop of flavour that pertains to immersion.

I also loved how you have to examine some stuff for a sec before using it. It makes for detective hunts where you need to identify what happened to a person by the traces left or find a button on a wall. A fun mechanic that adds up to the overall superb map design. The world of Drova is full of prominent landmarks and you got a handy map with the ability to denote places of interest with stamps of your choice. You'll need it for the lack of objective markers or even fast travel. A diegetic form of it appears later, but it's limited and costly. I applaud, except backtracking can feel tedious. While map verticality adds depth and there are shortcuts, prepare for long detours around ledges, taking you to dead ends. You have the means to raise your running speed, however, it would be nice if bigger buffs applied for longer than a minute. See, Gothic was technologically advanced for its time, so running around the place had an element of spectacle to it. Here, not so much.

[h3]Combat[/h3]
There's no character creator, you create yours in the process of playing. Just like in you know where. Similarly, you get learning points upon level-up, then find instructors to raise attributes and master various combat or crafting skills. It's not that big a hassle. Stats have an incremental effect, albeit, improving your combat skills or obtaining new gear feels impactful. The gear typically isn't too interesting, though, usually only providing droves of said stats. To compensate, Drova has complementary systems at work. Expansive crafting makes it so even the lamest cave has something for you. I used the system to create super-potions and stack up on consumables, which would've bankrupted me otherwise. The economy is pretty harsh. It took me a long time to get rich. I consider it a merit in a genre where balance has always been an afterthought. In Drova, one has to be resourceful to stay alive.

The enemy roster is diverse, from bears roaming across the flower fields to Dwarf-Huluds and swamp cronenbergs. Because enemies are tanky and hit hard, they force you to respect their patterns. Especially bosses who remain a reasonable challenge no matter how hard you munchkin. Save a few magic nukes for those. Speaking of magic, you don't get to have spells outside of finite scrolls until much later in the game. For the most part, you'll have to get down and dirty by engaging in snappy twin-stick combat. Drova is a proper Medieval hack-and-slash rather than your typical hit-or-miss. It isn't Dark Souls, in case you wondered, stamina only expends on dodge, block, or enemy stance strikes. It's a loose system where you can spam attacks. It starts off simple, then becomes more interesting as you build up your skillset, getting access to more options. It's pleasant to grow and see how yesterday's threats die in one hit.

Some complain there's no level-scaling, so you're free to wander where you don't belong to do little damage and perish. Such fights are optional challenges for people who like getting ahead of the curve. To win a battle out of your league grants a sense of accomplishment like no other. It motivates players to get stronger and more inventive, to learn and appreciate all of the tools at their disposal. Use it as a chance to take another look at your loot. Sometimes it leads to a discovery of something like a scroll that does 750 damage in the area, collecting dust in your backpack. Set up traps or make enemies in-fight for your benefit. All to lay your hands on the treasures you "aren't supposed" to have! Even if you can't succeed now, you can always come back later with a satisfactory vengeance. Level-scaling would've taken it all away.

[h3]Role-Play[/h3]
I expected an ARPG, then got blindsided by the humorous branching dialogues that force you to take sides all the time. Sure, that stuff comes to binary choices and fetch quests, but there's more to it. Although you don't get to know anyone that well, you can talk to most NPCs, and they don't come off as caricatures. The snippets of their pasts provide insights into the kind of hard lives people live in Drova. Its world does its best to be sandboxy and reactive. A character may acknowledge your achievements, notice you're wearing a thing stolen from them, or give you a stat boost after a hearty exchange. When someone says they go somewhere, they really run all the way there! Coupled with couriers and bandits skulking about, it gives the world a lived-in feel. Instead of killing you, said bandits just knock you out and rob you. You can do the same to most people, preferably without witnesses.

All of the above gives a reason to get invested in the world. There are several forces at play, but the choice between 2 camps, Remnants and Nemeton, is what propels the plot forward. Despite the hints, it's a blind choice that locks you up into following their leader's ambition. The consequences might upset you. As a cop-out, you can achieve a good ending anyway. On a smaller scale, the game gives you multiple ways to get favours with people or access places. Lots of extortion, blackmailing, swindling involved. Day and night cycles during which people follow their schedules help with your shady business. The freedom to be a jerk is the sign of a true CRPG. Here, being a greedy cheat pays while ethics usually cost you, which is a good lesson. What's in benevolence if you don't sacrifice for it? Drova places these petty things on your conscience while leaving the final word to you.

The combat is very dynamic, the quests are fun, exploration is rewarding, leveling up feels amazing, and the gameplay "loop" -- of fighting, crafting, cooking, upgrading, etc. -- is both very accessible at a conceptual level but endlessly complex at a strategy level. The writing is good; it's not incredible, but it never annoyed me. It was exactly what it needed to be for this type of game. I'm a slow player who is probably about an 80% completionist on most games, and this was almost 100 hours of fun. Support the devs and get it with or without discount.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1734735084}, {"review_text": "[h3]The Repetitive Gameplay Drova Me Away[/h3]
Drova has all the ingredients of the sort of game I would normally love. It's got amazing pixel art, souls-lite action rpg combat, a crafting system, and character customization. But it suffers from issues of repetitiveness in all the above areas. I realize this is a small indie game, from a small indie team, so I have chosen to omit my more minor points, and just include the major points. Ultimately, I found myself having less and less fun, the more I played.

[b]Repetitive Combat[/b]
[list]
    [*]Get ready to hit the same random monster upwards of 30-50 times before it dies. I am not including all the necessary dodging, blocking, and movement in this metric. Monster health bars are insanely large, even for what are supposed to be minor foes, and your damage dealt is very low by comparison. A single hit will take off [i]maybe[/i] 1-5% from the healthbar. 
    [*]They offer an Explorer difficulty setting, where you can increase your damage dealt to an additional 100%. Even at this highest setting, combat with small minions felt far too drawn out.
    [*]There is not enough variety in monster attack patterns or in weapon attack patterns and combos. This means that the sequence of button presses felt far too steady. The timing for combos, dodging, blocking, all fell into very similar pacing.
[/list]

[b]Repetitive Character Models[/b]
[list]
    [*]Gorgeous pixel art, with a very consistent art style
    [*]ALL human characters are based on a single basic male model. There is no female character model. Creating a female avatar only adds a tube top to your character's chest. The model proportions are still very clearly male-presenting, such as wide shoulders, narrow hips, thick neck.
    [*]This means that there are also no variant models to represent different character silhouettes. While I appreciate how incredibly efficient they were with their limited resources, it would have been nice to at least created one other base model, such as a female model.
    [*]Some of the tilesets for areas got to be very samey as well, particularly the Caverns tileset (there are a lot of caverns). One of the qualities that makes a tileset great is variety. A tileset with enough design variation allows the devs to create more unique and memorable moments for the player to experience. I found most of the level tilesets did accomplish this goal, but some, like the cavern set, were lacking.
[/list]

Ultimately, this game will still be deeply memorable to many fans of pixel-art games, souls-like combat, and gothic worlds. But the flat pacing of combat and the repetitive art assets, though beautifully crafted, ended up sullying an otherwise unique game. 

I hope to come back to this game after some period of time to see if my opinion has changed. If so, I'll update this review.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1736270992}, {"review_text": "I bought this game based only on the fact that the developer marketed this as a Gothic 1 inspired 2D rpg. The dark theme does indeed feel like a 2D Gothic 1 game, but that's about it. There are 3 things that made Gothic 1 awesome and this game failed to implement. 
Also i see that after the game got released the developer removed every single mention of it being inspired by Gothic 1. Was this a choice knowing they failed at the implementation or did they get served with a cease and desist by THQ? Who knows...


[h3]The world[/h3] 
Has hard blockers that stop you from accessing every corner of the map. In Gothic 1 if i wanted i could go and visit every single part of the map, yeah i would get completely demolished by enemies but i could visit those areas if i wanted. In this game there are 2 types of blockers, the flame and some rubble in the middle of the road.
Either don't boast that you are inspired by Gothic 1 or actually give me free roam.
Another thing about the world is i was still in act 1 and i saw 95% of the map and killed most things. As i got to act 2 the monsters didn't respawn or get replaced by harder monsters, again don't boast about being inspired if you aren't going to use the mechanics. I did see a handful respawned monsters in act 4 but that was dust int he wind compared to how Gothic 1 and 2 respawned or added new monsters between chapters. Another thing is the world feels kinda small.


[h3]The story[/h3] 
Is really boring and cliche. I could see the 'backstabs' at the end of the quest from the start of said quest. In act 3 you get a choice to warn the people in the forest about what you are about to do, they say yeah yeah it's ok. Then in act 4 they get mad with you for what you did. My brother in Christ, don't boast about being inspired by Gothic 1 if you aren't going to keep track of my decisions and make the NPCs act like i didn't do a certain action to try and prevent bad things from happening.


[h3]The combat[/h3] 
Was a huge miss. It's really repetitive since you do the same exact attack over and over again with some 'special attacks' when you build the focus meter. If you say you were inspired by Gothic 1 then show me how the protagonist actually improves combat wise, not just some new stats or a new learned technique in the character sheet. It Gothic 1 if you are untrained you hold the 1 handed weapon with two hands and with each level reached your stance chances to show that you are mastering the 1 handed sword combat. Here on the other hand if you have 1 level or max level you attack the same, there is no stance change or how you hold the sword or how you move with it. Again, don't boast about this game being inspired from Gothic 1 if you can't implemented what made the game what it is.


These three things really pissed me off especially when the devs really pushed with the 'inspired by Gothic 1' thing and they didn't deliver. Also what's up with the spitting? It felt like some characters were spitting every other sentence. Does somebody in the dev thing have a fetish about spit? Because it sure feels like that since it's as present in the game as the cliches in the story, way too much.

Don't recommend this game full price. I got this on a 25% sale during the steam summer sale and i feel like it's not worth that much. 1. The color palette is very muddy and washed out, which leads to a poor level of contrast between interactive and background elements. This lack of contrast makes it difficult for my eyes to determine what I should be focusing on, causing them to feel strained.

2. The movement of the character feels too quick for the very limited field of view presented to you. This makes the game feel disorienting to play.

3. The camera system does not keep your character centered on the screen. For those that have no clue what the "Gothic" reference means besides the game title, then let me explain. The game experience is difficult initially as you're treated as an outsider and most things are pretty tough. You will have to earn the trust of most NPC you encounter and those that appear "too" friendly usually want to lure you into an alley, beat you up and steal your items.
The world is lively and NPC walk around with a daily schedule that can be affected by you and also how the story moves on. A lot of your choices have an impact and will even be "revisited" during the ending.

The combat in Drova takes on a bit of souls-like with a Stamina bar, however only for dodging, heavy attacks and blocking. You're free to attack with basic attacks leading into combos, but button mashing punishes you. Time your attacks right for quicker attacks and new attacks as you level up your weapon abilities. You're also capable of using various ranged attacks and spells.
Leveling up gives you learning points and is another reference to Gothic, where you need to find trainers in order to learn new skills. Certain skills require a collected amount of Prowess, which is your attributes, so you may have to train more attributes to learn higher level skills. Trainers may also require payment to even be willing to teach you, require a trust to be earned or beat the trainer to show you're not a weakling.

The world in Drova isn't very large, but it's dense and will change in areas as you continue your story. It rewards exploration as well, as some areas won't be found through quests. Drova also keeps navigation "oldschool", meaning you have no minimap and maps have to be bought my NPC to see various landmarks. Ink can be bought to make your own map markers.
Quests will not be marked on the map, so they require your attention reading what the NPC say, although the Journal is well described regarding where to go.

The game is always a slog, even if you're doing things in the right order, you never get to the point where you feel more powerful than you used to be. The game throws legions of unfair enemies at you, making you do things like kite enemies, get them trapped around corners, or inch close enough to only aggro 1 at a single time so you can manage the fights.

Every single combat encounter is like this.

The factions are both extremly unlikeable in their own ways. The Remenants want to escape back to the real world, but are basically a dog eat dog crime syndicate. The Nemeton by contrast are deluded and a bunch of holier than thou types who will kick anyone out at the drop of a hat, oh and do wickerman style sacrifices.

There is a lot of attention to detail and nice small mechanics, like having to actually get a map to be able to use it, or not knowing the name of the npcs until they tell you. 
This isn't a huge game, but it makes it up with density and a fair sense of difficulty, making every fight and choice you make a stretch.

[{"review_text": "Well Captains, where to begin...

Decided to pick up this game after stalking it on Youtube for months. I knew it had a reputation for micro-transactions (*) but decided what the heck, I am an adult (mostly) with a job (sorta) and the ability to budget (ha! this guy).

Lets start with the good:

The core of this game is fantastic. Sail ship, see enemy, shoot enemy, neuron activation. A+ gameplay loop. There are many many types of ship to choose from. From carriers to destroyers to battleships and cruisers, there is something for everyone's play style and skill. 
I had fun learning the various classes of ship as well as the characteristics of each nations Navy.
Ships are modeled well, especially the older ships are a real treat to play an admire if you are a naval history nerd. It rapidly became my most played game on Steam.
I found some great people to play with and even joined a few clans.

But, like a week of shore leave in a rough port, the experience can sour with time ...

Now on to the bad:

The game has taken a steady decline in the almost 3 years I have played it.  The war in Europe has distinctly affected this game as a large part of the original Dev team was Russian and had to split from the overall company. 
Since then, quality of the game has suffered noticeably, though the new Dev. team has in fairness been consistent with new updates.

However, real world pressures notwithstanding, the game has also become a giant money sink. It feels that the game that used to be free to play with the option to pay has morphed into a giant ship based gambling simulator.
I know for a fact there are some brilliant, hardworking, passionate people working at the studio who really want to make a great game. Sadly, I feel these folk are completely held hostage by a corporate structure so bent on short term profit at any cost it would make EA blush in sheer embarrassment. It is now obvious the leadership is incompetent and has no idea why people play this game to begin with. I wish the design, gameplay, creative and art teams good fortune and I hope they make incredible things somewhere else.

What's more is the playerbase. To be clear I am an average player who played this game mainly to relax after work. I was not a competitive player, though I did try my best not to drag down my team. I mention this to clarify I am not trying to say I am better than most players or even the average player, far from it.

With those caveats out of the way... I have never encountered a game with such a miserable playerbase. Chat is constantly salty, which is sometimes part of the fun, but sometimes you just wish idiots would quit if they can't sail straight and shoot at the same time.

The good players (Unicums in WoWs parlance) are no better. People spend so much time berating bad play in chat it is a wonder why they loose so often. Some really good players just suck it up and play but they are rare. Other than a few Youtube heros, few good players will actually teach people the advanced tactics in this surprisingly complex arcade game. 

Additionally, the Youtube and Reddit hiveminds are completely at war with the Developer. To be clear the Devs are no saints and do get a lot wrong, but the community at large is still inconsolable about Carriers, Submarines, balance changes etc. It's ridiculous.  Carriers for example are in fact harder to play than they look, but the hivemind thinks they are cheating hax and with hound anybody who enjoys them to death in chat or in foums.

The hivemind in one breath decries the declining playerbase and blames it all on the Developer (**) while at the same time being hostile to new players learning the ropes, shaming people who like to play the "wrong ships" and endlessly whining about Whales (***) despite the fact many of them keep this free (****) game paid for.

This has become a rant, my apologies dear reader.

To sum up, World of Warships is a sad saga of a beautiful game killed both by the incompetent disconnectedness of it's parent studio and the mind-numbing lunacy of it's man child player base.  Perhaps one day I will return when my sanity does, but until then I must depart for greener shores.

Until we meet again, thank you for spending some time with this review. I hope it helps you make good choices.

Fair winds and following seas!

(*)  If you can call between $50-$200 USD a "micro" transaction.
(**) WG has made it's fair share of mistake to drive players away too. Raising costs for thing that were free, etc.
(***) Whales are players that buy all the new ships, cosmetics and battlepasses instead of "honorably" grinding. To be fair to the hivemind, they are locked in a captive relationship to WG. If you have already spent hundreds to thousands of dollars on a game, sunk cost fallacy is hard to get out of your head.
(****) It is still, in all fairness, completely FREE. IF ... (big if) ... you are very disciplined and don't mind missing premium content.

The game allows you to take command of some of history's most iconic warships, from battleships to aircraft carriers, each offering a unique playstyle and set of challenges.

The action is intense, with massive explosions, precise aiming, and tactical decision-making. Whether you prefer staying at long range with a battleship or engaging in close-quarters combat with a destroyer, there’s a playstyle for everyone.

The game also offers a strong sense of progression, as you unlock new ships, upgrades, and skills that improve your naval prowess. The progression system is rewarding, allowing you to customize your ships and adapt your strategy as you rise through the ranks.

Visually, the game is stunning, with beautifully rendered ships, realistic water effects, and vast ocean maps that add to the immersion. The sound design also adds to the atmosphere, with realistic gunfire, ship engines, and the roar of waves crashing.

If you’re a fan of tactical combat games or enjoy naval warfare, World of Warships is a game that offers hours of fun and strategy. WG should fix this", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1741619538}, {"review_text": "At the moment, I do not recommend the game.
I would only recommend it if you genuinely enjoy naval combat, ships, and the WWII aesthetic and you have no intention of falling into the gacha loop or the pressure of “playing to win.”
If your goal is simply to enjoy the battles, take the game lightly, and play free-to-play because you like the ships or the era, then yes — you can still have fun.
I’ve been a player for over eight years, even before the Steam release, and I’ve witnessed many stages of the game: its evolution… and its degeneration.

➤ The main issue: the gacha model

A few years ago, the game introduced a business model based on loot boxes, random rolls, and probability systems.
This completely changed the experience:

It’s no longer just paying for a ship.
Now it introduces anxiety, bundles, odds, and the illusion of obtaining something valuable.
Ships have become excuses to generate spending, more than actual content.

While there is some generosity toward free-to-play players, that generosity is completely tied to profit.
They cannot be “too generous” unless revenue stays high — and it shows.

➤ The rarity system reinforces the gacha feeling

The game also added a rarity-based ship classification system, depending on how frequently ships appear or how difficult they are to obtain. The categories go from Common to Legendary:

Common (gray): standard tech-tree ships
Uncommon (green): often premium or shop ships
Rare (blue): usually Research Bureau ships or ships obtained with coal or steel
Epic (orange): time-limited ships; very difficult or expensive to obtain
Legendary (yellow): extremely rare; I own none, and the Captain’s Logbook only shows two legendary ships in total

This system shifts the focus from gameplay to collection pressure, encouraging investment based on scarcity more than value.

➤ Game balance: certain ships dominate ranked

The variety of ships and playstyles has always been one of the game’s strongest points.
However, lately I’ve noticed bad players performing well simply because the ships they use are overly strong, especially:

Pan-American battleships
German alternate cruisers

In Random Battles, the balance is still somewhat acceptable due to larger team sizes (12 vs 12).
But in Ranked Battles, any ship from these lines heavily tilts the match, and if a skilled player is behind them, the difference becomes overwhelming.

➤ The deeper issue: the psychology of PvP

In any PvP game, players ultimately want to win.
So when a ship becomes S-tier — whether premium, special, epic, or part of a tech tree — many players choose it simply because it increases their chances of victory.

But when everyone gravitates toward the same S-tier ships, the game stops being about skill and becomes a race to pick the strongest tool.
This creates a meta where diversity disappears and the experience becomes unbalanced and predictable.

The dangerous part is that players often don’t even realize this is happening.
They think they are “just playing to win,” while the entire environment is being shaped around a handful of overtuned ships that distort the whole match experience.

And the developers likely understand this dynamic.
If an overpowered ship generates revenue, the cycle repeats:

A new strong ship appears
Players rush to get it
The meta breaks
The next strong ship is released
The loop continues
This self-reinforcing cycle benefits monetization at the expense of balance.

There are also other game modes that can be enjoyable for casual play, farming missions, or playing with friends, such as Operations and the occasional Asymmetric Battles. These modes still offer some fun and variety outside the main gameplay loop.

➤ Naval variety: its biggest strength… with a big “but”

The game includes real historical ships, prototypes, and ships that never existed.
Each nation has its own mechanics and identity, and some hybrid concepts are genuinely interesting.

But one thing ruins part of the experience:
it doesn’t feel good to play a real historical ship and get destroyed by a design that never existed, especially when that fictional ship is clearly superior for commercial reasons.

Yes, many ships are free-to-play friendly and obtainable with steel or coal — and that remains one of the best aspects of the game.
But even this gets overshadowed by the greed behind bundles and the gacha system.

➤ Gameplay mechanics that no longer maintain even the illusion of realism

The game was never fully realistic, but it used to maintain a coherent naval atmosphere.
That illusion breaks when mechanics such as these appear:

Cruisers and destroyers launching bomber planes
Abilities that contradict traditional naval logic

These mechanics completely break immersion.

➤ FOMO and psychological pressure

Many events and limited ships rely heavily on FOMO (fear of missing out).
This encourages quick purchases, impulsive decisions, and the constant feeling that you’re always “missing” something important.
Ship collectors are especially vulnerable.

For this reason, I do not recommend spending money on a game that relies more on illusions and psychological pressure than genuine value.

➤ In the end, what matters is not what the game offers, but what you expect from it.
The experience depends less on the game and more on what you seek inside it.

[{"review_text": "Rhythm Doctor is a transcendental experience. This game is loosely modeled after Nintendo's Rhythm Heaven series but goes so much further in both premise, gameplay, and accessibility than Nintendo has to date. The premise is simple: you use one button to follow the rhythm cues, but the cues get more complicated and layer on top of each other over time... pretty much until you're a music theory god.

While the minute-to-minute gameplay is addictive, the character writing, chart design and set pieces are what truly make this game shine. The game is subdivided into "acts", and in each one are 4-5 levels with front and back sides to enjoy. However, you also are introduced to a new pair of characters and experience the game through a series of cutscenes--many of which are weaved into the gameplay itself. Crazy, I know, but in that time you really do start to feel for and care for the characters introduced.

While the final act of the game isn't out at the time of this review. I'm counting down the days to the 1.0 release and what I can only assume is the conclusion of the story.

Rhythm Doctor is a must-play for rhythm game fans, but its accessibility and gradual introduction to rhythm concepts make this an apt pick for those who maybe haven't gotten into rhythm games before too. Other reviews mention that you can probably play the game blind, and I tend to agree.

On top of all of this, Rhythm Doctor features a level editor and extensive community support through custom levels. I'm not a charter, but the few levels I downloaded through Steam Workshop were insane testaments to how powerful this editor is.

On a personal note, I picked this game up due to its rave reviews without watching trailers or much previous research at all. I don't regret going in blind and I think this is probably the best way to go into this game.

If you're on the fence, this game is well worth your time and money. I loved this game so much I bought it two more times for friends. unless you have epilepsy. flashing lights and colors is a very big aspect of this game. sorry. genuinely.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1753253735}, {"review_text": "Rhythm Doctor is one of those rare rhythm games that feels both deeply intuitive and astonishingly innovative, offering a musical experience that’s as emotionally resonant as it is mechanically precise. Developed by 7th Beat Games, this indie title sets itself apart from the rhythm game crowd by embracing simplicity on the surface while subtly layering in complexity and narrative depth. At its core, the game asks you to press a single button — just one — on the seventh beat of each bar. That sounds laughably simple, and for the first few minutes, it is. But very quickly, Rhythm Doctor morphs into something much more intricate, introducing syncopated rhythms, shifting time signatures, visual distortions, and even deceptive audio cues that turn each level into a test of focus, intuition, and raw musicality.

The brilliance of Rhythm Doctor lies in how it teaches rhythm through gameplay rather than instruction. Traditional rhythm games often rely on visual prompts, but this game challenges players to listen, to feel the beat — which is exactly what makes it so engaging and, at times, brutally difficult. The timing windows are extremely tight, which can be frustrating for those accustomed to more forgiving mechanics. However, the game mitigates this with a forgiving grading system and a true emphasis on progression over perfection. Each new mechanic is introduced through cleverly designed stages that double as character-driven narrative beats. You don’t just play levels — you experience the emotional arcs of doctors, patients, and relationships that evolve through the music itself.

The story, surprisingly heartfelt, is conveyed in a style reminiscent of visual novels, using dialogue and stylized character portraits to create bonds between the player and the characters they’re helping. Each patient in the hospital has a unique theme, rhythm, and ailment, and each stage is tailored to reflect their emotional or physical struggles. For instance, one patient may have a heartbeat that stutters due to anxiety, and the accompanying track reflects that in unpredictable syncopation and jittery time signatures. Another level may simulate two characters falling in love, with rhythms overlapping and harmonizing as their stories intertwine. These storytelling techniques are not just clever — they’re deeply affecting. The combination of audio design, rhythm mechanics, and narrative context creates a kind of synesthesia where gameplay and story are inseparable.

Aesthetically, Rhythm Doctor is a love letter to pixel art and dynamic visual design. Despite its retro look, the game constantly surprises with inventive visual effects that alter the playfield — flashing lights, screen glitches, perspective shifts — all timed perfectly to the music and narrative stakes. These aren’t just for flair; they challenge the player by disrupting visual reliance and forcing deeper musical intuition. The soundtrack is exceptional — a genre-hopping mix of lo-fi, chiptune, pop, EDM, and even orchestral elements. Each track is tightly composed to support both the gameplay and the emotional tone of the level. It's no exaggeration to say that the music in Rhythm Doctor carries as much weight as the gameplay itself. Some levels feel like playable music videos, others like interactive emotional vignettes.

Perhaps the most commendable aspect of Rhythm Doctor is its bold commitment to accessibility and inclusivity, both in theme and design. The developers have created a system that allows for assistive features like visual beat indicators and adjustable difficulty options, without compromising the integrity of the experience. Additionally, the game showcases a cast that’s diverse in ethnicity, gender identity, and personality — and it does so naturally, without drawing excessive attention to itself. Representation is treated as a given, not a selling point, which makes the game's world feel refreshingly real and grounded despite its surreal visual flair.

Despite its near brilliance, Rhythm Doctor isn’t without flaws. The game is still technically in Early Access (as of this writing), and though it already boasts dozens of handcrafted levels, the full story has yet to be completed. Some players may find the difficulty spikes abrupt, especially in boss levels, where visual distractions and timing shifts can feel overwhelming rather than challenging. And while the game offers a level editor and a vibrant custom song community, the UI for creating and browsing user-generated content still feels clunky and underdeveloped compared to more polished rhythm games. However, none of these issues significantly diminish the core experience, which remains one of the most inventive and emotionally engaging rhythm games in years.

In summary, Rhythm Doctor is a masterclass in rhythm game design that dares to challenge not just your reflexes, but your musical perception and emotional connection. Its one-button mechanic belies an intricate system of musical storytelling that is rarely seen in the genre. With its heartfelt narrative, diverse characters, stunning audio-visual design, and ingenious level mechanics, Rhythm Doctor stands tall as both a work of art and an addictive game. Whether you're a rhythm game veteran or a newcomer looking for something unique and meaningful, this is a title that deserves your time, your patience, and your ears.

1) There are too many annoying bugs.  Nothing game breaking that I've found, but there's a couple in particular that irritate me.  Like occasionally you'll get a customer delivery order with no notification.  In this scenario, bringing up the bag shows the incorrect number of delivery orders in progress.  You can still fill the order, but you need to be constantly checking to make sure one didn't slip in.  Also, there's a bug with the car where about 2/3 of the time, putting a box in the trunk also causes you to enter the car, which is *really* annoying when you're trying to load up a bunch of boxes, which you'll have to do because......

2) The game gets *very* tedious about 10 hours in.  Once you unlock a vehicle, you'll realize that you effectively *need* to get your products from the other stores around town, because they all sell goods at half their market value.  This is the only realistic way to make money after a certain point because your employee and bill costs get too high to manage on the margins afforded by ordering your goods online.  The problem is, getting goods from these stores is insanely time-inefficient.  There's no way to create a meaningful shopping list to take with you (you *can* use the product scanner to sorta create one, but it doesn't work at the other stores so you're constantly flipping to and from it just to look at whatever you added to it).  It effectively becomes a memory game for what you need to get, and beyond that, the vehicles only fit so much, so you end up spending 10-15 minutes at the start of every day driving back and forth to these stores, which completely invalidates the product scanner, which was one of the best things they added to the release game.

3) The game forces you to automate away your agency.  I know a lot of people are gonna say "well, just don't do that then" and you'd be right, if it weren't for the delivery orders that only you can do.  None of the other jobs (save cleaning) can be left unattended when you're doing multiple deliveries per day.  You will need, at the bare minimum, one cashier, one assistant, one security guard, and every restocker the game will let you unlock.  Otherwise your store will cease to function while you're away.  I think a good fix for this, ironically, is to add another automated employee: the delivery driver who can do deliveries for you.  Then, rather than allowing the player to unlock as many employees as they want, instead have a max employee count that scales with level, and it's up to you to decide how to allocate those slots among the different employee types, leaving whatever task(s) the player finds most enjoyable for themselves.  More customization is more good.

4) Restockers are still really annoying sometimes.  I hate how you'll be trying to reorganize a shelf, and they'll come in and restock it before you can remove the tag, or fill a shelf before you can put stolen goods back onto it.  There needs to be a grace period after the player interacts with a shelf, or some way to temporarily lock a shelf, that will prevent restockers from getting in your way.

5) XP and money gain are way out of whack with one another.  You'll spend most of the game having a crazy excess of one while being severely bottlenecked by the other, creating long periods of mindless grinding before you can unlock new content, at which point the bottleneck will flip to the other resource, and the whole process will start anew.  Some progression smoothing is needed, or some kind of system that lets you turn XP gain into money gain, or vice versa.  Maybe some special kiosks around the store.  Like, maybe a lottery scratcher machine that takes some of the money customers would otherwise spend on products (meaning you don't get it), but gives you bonus XP when they buy scratchers.  Or an arcade cabinet that does the opposite, bonus money at the cost of XP.  Just something that would let the player customize their resource gains in some way.

6) The game is begging for a talent tree of some kind. Visual variety of staff – Restockers, cashiers, etc., all look the same; more visual diversity would add immersion.

Personal shopper & delivery driver roles – Assign staff to fulfil and deliver online orders.

Interactive staff – Currently only the boost option exists. More ways to interact with staff (e.g., feedback, training, scheduling) would improve immersion.

Janitor behaviour – Even if there’s nothing to clean, have janitors wander and carry out small maintenance actions (e.g., polishing floors).

Staff break system – Introduce a break room and staff rotations, with sick days and holiday leave included.

Staff wage customisation – Allow wage adjustments that affect morale and efficiency.

Natural interactions – Customers and staff could say basic phrases like “hello”, “thanks”, “come again” to enhance atmosphere.

Gameplay Features

Auto restock from web – Let players set restock thresholds that trigger automatic online orders if funds are available once you unlock that tool or option, or staff skill.

Auto loan repayment – Just like with bills, allow auto-pay options for loans.

Income-based loan access – Base interest rates and available loan sizes on player income and financial health.

More loan options – Greater variety of loan types and terms would improve flexibility.

Time rebalancing – Either slow down time or speed up work rates, particularly restocking. Address the “infinite free time” before 8am or after 9pm – perhaps by introducing overtime pay or sending workers home at 9:30pm.

Progression & Economy

Product unlock pacing – Product licence unlocks feel too fast, especially in early-mid game. Slower progression or rebalancing is needed.

Price management assistant – Have staff managers that can auto-adjust prices based on target margins, manage loan/bill payments, forecast income, and organise staff breaks – since the player is more like a business owner than a floor manager.

User Interface & Tools

Pricing interface improvements – Replace awkward sliders with percentage inputs. Add a double-click option to match market prices quickly.

Furniture tab improvements – Add categories and item descriptions. Expand warehousing tools like waste disposal, forklifts, pallet networking.

Decorations tab – Combine paints, floors, and decorations. Add details like how much area a paint pot covers, and allow decorative items to boost morale and attractiveness of the store for customers.

Expand tools category – Include items like delivery rucksacks, palm pilots for order picking, mobile phones for staff management, wholesale orders and customer service.

Immersion Enhancements

Interactive customers – Have them react to long queues, missing items, instead of just saying it. Some could leave the store in protest, or leave negative feedback based on poor service or supply.

Customer review/complaint system – Track satisfaction with a review or complaints feature that has gameplay consequences, with ways to fix them and have reviews change based on your actions.

Different city options – Offer a variety of cities with different demographics, demand, and challenges.

Mini-games on the computer – Add small diversions like  Solitair, Snake, Asteroids etc.

CCTV system – Enable viewing and switching cameras from the in-game computer.

Delivery van/lorry system – Add delivery vans for local deliveries and lorries for wholesale pickups.
