Developed by DotEmu and published by Ubisoft, this remastered version of the original 1999 classic brings back the turn-based tactics, empire-building, and hero-led warfare that made Heroes III a benchmark for the genre. The HD Edition revitalizes the game's graphics with updated resolutions and sharper sprites, making it visually compatible with modern displays while preserving the charming art style and distinct faction aesthetics that defined the original. The hand-drawn environments, town screens, and unit animations remain as iconic as ever, now presented with a cleaner, crisper look that respects the game's roots.

At its core, Heroes III remains a deeply strategic and rewarding experience. Players control powerful heroes who explore richly detailed maps, gather resources, capture towns, and command fantastical armies composed of dragons, undead, angels, and more. Each faction, from the necromantic stronghold of Necropolis to the magic-rich Tower, offers distinct playstyles, units, and strengths. Strategic planning—both on the battlefield and in resource management—is crucial. The turn-based combat system, played on a tactical hex grid, is as compelling today as it was decades ago, requiring players to balance unit synergy, positioning, and spellcasting to gain the upper hand. The game also retains its addictive loop of exploration, upgrading, and confrontation that keeps players returning for “just one more turn.”

Where the HD Edition succeeds best is in preserving the tight, meticulously balanced gameplay of the original. The single-player campaigns are intact and just as engaging, with a mix of well-written storylines and challenging mission objectives that span dozens of hours. The skirmish mode and hot-seat multiplayer also return, allowing for local competitive or cooperative play that remains a hallmark of the Heroes series. Additionally, Steam integration brings achievements and a more modern multiplayer experience through online support, though it’s not without its limitations.

However, the HD Edition is not without shortcomings. Perhaps the most notable disappointment is the exclusion of the two official expansions, Armageddon’s Blade and The Shadow of Death, due to the loss of original source code—a significant omission, as those expansions introduced critical quality-of-life improvements, extra content, and fan-favorite factions like the Conflux. Longtime fans may also notice that the remaster does not include mod support or compatibility with fan-made content, which has become essential to the Heroes III experience in recent years through platforms like the Heroes III: Complete GOG edition or the Hota (Horn of the Abyss) mod. While the HD visuals are a welcome improvement, they may not justify the price for those who already own more complete versions of the game.

In conclusion, Heroes® of Might & Magic® III - HD Edition is a love letter to a genre-defining strategy classic, providing a cleaner, more modern visual presentation and maintaining the core gameplay that made it legendary. For newcomers or nostalgic players wanting a polished, accessible way to revisit Erathia’s magical battlefields, the HD Edition offers a streamlined entry point. However, for purists and dedicated fans, its lack of expansion content and mod support may leave it feeling like a missed opportunity rather than a definitive version. Nonetheless, the brilliance of Heroes III still shines through, offering one of the most compelling and timeless turn-based strategy experiences ever made.

A certain memetic shopkeeper had the internet hooked for years for a reason: He's extremely funny, yet somehow has a Mariana Trench of writing associated with him, moreso than any other character in, I argue, the Undertale-Deltarune franchise. Despite that, he isn't very omnipresent. The hidden route associated with this chapter gives Undertale's Genocide Route a run for its money in its haunting nature as well, and the way it is built on later shows boundless potential. I think most people can enjoy this one.

I really like what Chapter 3 has. The boss ties up loose ends with Chapter 2 in a very natural way, producing a continuous, coherent world. I like what goes on. The enemies are all very fun to fight, and said boss's slow unravelling is fun to watch. The minigames and dialogue are extremely fun, and I found myself laughing a lot. The final fight is phenomenally enjoyable and by far my favourite part of the game so far. Well-placed, absolutely shocking intro, all with an excellent challenge to enjoy. Brilliant. Coupled with the amazing music you've come to expect, it's just a chef's kiss. 

However, Chapter 3 also feels very half-baked. The Zelda-like sequences (both regular and "Sword Route") are frankly very painful to go through; they're slow and devolve into autoscrollers occasionally. I see the vision, but not the execution. These make up the bulk of Chapter 3's length, much more than anything else. It brings the chapter down a lot. It's a Legend of Zelda parody but in all the ways that make it fail in modern-day rather than its actual good parts. If intentional, I call it bad game design. When I experienced an actual crash (which is now fixed) 2/3 into one segment I dreaded going through it a second time. I also think the chapter is missing a bit of that sauce. The TV World isn't very big compared to other Dark Worlds, there's extremely little to explore. There's also the awkward release schedule causing the hidden route to feel extremely disjointed, though in a complete product it would probably be fine. I strongly feel that a "Genocide" element needed to be in this chapter that isn't there - with or without the hidden route. There's the hallmarks of a troubled development cycle here. 

Chapter 4 is where Deltarune begins hitting its stride. You see a strong narrative building up, with some worldbuilding involving a sort of religion around the Deltarune prophecy. The theme is great and not what I expected at all. You're intentionally left with more questions than answers. Climbing mechanic was a very fun addition, with just enough depth for me to enjoy it thoroughly; I hope it is built on later. I think the narrative buildup around Noelle deserves particular note. You could have a red herring or a huge lead here. The interaction with Kris in either route is extremely strong. Callbacks to Chapter 2 are abound and amazing.

However, the minibosses of this Chapter are extremely boring and not fun to engage with; their characterisation, though, are brilliant. The final boss of the Chapter has amazing music and makes for a decent climax to the "first half", though I find the sequence leading up to it and the fight itself to feel a little easy, possibly even weak. The hidden boss is long and far the best part, and will not be what anyone expects. He saves the boss lineup from being a general "quality drop". I didn't enjoy the dark segments of Chapter 4 one bit, though this is likely a disagreement in game design principles more than anything.

Overall, a fantastic game that is absolutely worth the money. Yes, just... Let your soul connect with it. You will not regret it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1750831487}, {"review_text": "With the cultural phenomenon UNDERTALE as it's spiritual predecessor, for a long time it felt like DELTARUNE had impossibly big shoes to fill. With the release of Chapter 3 and 4, I can now confidently say that DELTARUNE not only meets these expectations, but it some cases even manages to exceed them.

Starting with the art style, it is what you've come to expect from Toby Fox and the team behind DELTARUNE. 
The 16-Bit artstyle is plain beautiful, the sprites + their animations are gorgeous and hand-made, the setpieces are varied and the small details show the love that has been put into even the smallest text box.

Despite having (close to) no voice acting, the game manages to be astonishingly expressive, for example making the letters of a character's dialogue shake subtly to suggest fear. Little details such as this, the aforementioned gorgeous sprites and the charming dialogue are where DELTARUNE truly manages to immerse and engage the player.

As to story and overall lore of the game, it's hard to give a definitive rating here as the game and therefore the story aren't finished yet. Without going into spoilers, a lot of things still remain unanswered after Chapter 4 that leave me interested as to how it'll all fit together in the end.
Judging from what is available now, DELTARUNE's writing really excels on a moment-to-moment basis in the different situations the group finds themselves in. As for the whole story long term, the writing so far is pretty good and I'm excited to see how it continues.

When it comes to gameplay, I'll have to admit I was doubtful whether DELTARUNE would be able to keep the "Touhou-esque" JRPG combat fresh enough after the creativity that UNDERTALE displayed.
Again, I was wrong. Though Chapter 1 and 2 already always found a way to keep the different enemies and combat in general fresh, Ch. 3 and 4 manage to exceed even that. Without exaggeration, EVERY SINGLE different enemy fight's completely differently, requiring you to do completely different things.
It's hard to describe it further without getting into mild spoilers, so I'll leave it at that.

Regarding the OST and Music of the game, I don't think anything needs to be said. The Soundtrack is an absolute masterpiece and almost every track WILL manage to burn itself into your frontal cortex.

Overall, Chapters 1-4 of DELTARUNE convinced me that the game isn't barely a sequel or spin-off with a similar scope to UNDERTALE but a LOT bigger, not only in terms of game length but also gameplay variety. The clever (and sometimes hilariously dry) writing still works just as good as it did in UNDERTALE and similar to it's predecessor, DELTARUNE perfectly balances the humor against the serious bits of story.

In conclusion, the only reason I can give not to recommend DELTARUNE would be if you don't enjoy the artstyle or combat system at all, which of course is completely fine, Though I suggest you at least try UNDERTALE or the DELTARUNE Demo if you haven't already. I too was sceptical whether I'd like this style of combat before playing, turns out I like every bit of it.

For me personally, DELTARUNE is arguably already the best gaming experience I've had in my life, and it's crazy to think there are still (at least) three Chapters coming. If the first four chapters are any indication to the quality of the remaining three, DELTARUNE will easily be my game of the decade.

Thanks Tobias Foxington, good soup", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 34, "timestamp_created": 1749052701}, {"review_text": "Deltarune is a great game I would recommend to almost anyone, but I wanted to give it a proper review that actually explains why it's good to people who haven't heard of it before, so here we go!

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Deltarune is half turn based RPG, and half bullet hell. You choose your actions on your turn, then the enemy will unleash their own unique bullet patterns that you have to dodge to avoid taking damage. You also obviously have the option to either fight enemies with violence to beat them, or use various acts to either convince or subdue them into defeat, each of which is rewarding in its own way. Strategising how to beat enemies using acts efficiently is a treat the first time you play, as many of the acts will launch you into a unique QTE that determines how effective it will be, and there's no harm in experimenting since you'll pick up how to dodge most enemy attacks pretty quickly. Fighting enemies with violence is less interesting but arguably more fun, since it always launches you into a QTE but that which never changes between enemies.
The TP mechanic complements this well because it incentivises you to play dangerous and get close to bullets to gather more TP once you already know how to dodge the attack normally, which can speed up battles if you manage your turns well. Dodging bullets never gets boring, as even the regular enemies have multiple adaptive patterns you can learn to dodge, and bosses ramp this up massively with a huge selection of attacks that you need to learn quickly to beat them.
Deltarune also has many overworld puzzles which I find to be quite overlooked despite being well designed, as they introduce their various concepts intuitively then increase in difficulty in a way that will never be frustrating for the player. 
It also has gimmick minigames and battles which mix up how you play the game in a fun and interesting way, and I like these as they are designed to be easy to learn but hard to master, and they never feel like they overshadow the main gameplay loop of battles. Chapter 1 has basically none of these (makes sense, you're still learning how to play the base game at this point), Chapter 2 has a few gimmick battles, Chapter 3 is chock-full of minigames and gimmicks (it's very fun), and Chapter 4 has some gimmicks but they don't really impede on the main gameplay.

[h1]Story[/h1]
It's no secret that Deltarune's story is incredibly well written, as it's masterful in using the fact that it's a video game (like Undertale did) and there are already some incredibly emotional moments even though only 4 out of the 7 chapters are released right now. Every major character really does feel real and every bit of dialogue is just as endearing as the next. You can feel that the game benefits from a much longer runtime, as characters are allowed to have their own arcs that feel natural without getting in the way of gameplay or the wider story. Once you start looking between the lines, it's not hard to realise that the whole game is leading up to a story that will tie everything together once the final 3 chapters are out, and being along for the ride is so worth it. I will say though, if you're one of those people that absolutely hate it when games have a large focus on story, this game might not be for you since there's a LOT of dialogue, but for pretty much everyone else you'll likely love it.
Deltarune is also really funny in general,the writing is so quirky and fun in most cases that you'll always be looking forward to the next cutscene or interaction. It's also really good at separating the funny parts from the serious parts, at no point will you find tone shifts to be jarring at all despite the fact it really does change drastically over the 4 chapters.
As for the negatives, you may find that the story is kind of insignificant around the start and middle of Chapter 1, since all the game is doing at that point is setting up characters, but it REALLY starts to ramp up in Chapter 3 onwards. If you even remotely enjoy the writing or gameplay in Chapter 1, the rest of the chapters are well worth your time, I can guarantee.
Despite the game telling you otherwise, your choices do matter, though not in a drastic way as of yet (mostly...). It shouldn't need to be said that your choice to defeat enemies either with violence or mercy is diegetic and has impacts on the story, though it is hard to say exactly how much they will matter in the end, since we don't have the final chapters yet.
Going in blind and making the choices that you want is by far the most important thing you should do when playing this game.

[h1]Difficulty[/h1]
This is kind of subjective depending on how much you have played video games before, but Deltarune is not a difficult game as of right now. Generally, each chapter increases its difficulty from the last, so we can expect that Chapters 5, 6 and 7 will present more of a challenge, but the challenge currently doesn't really show itself off apart from optional content. If you're already generally good at games, it's likely that you won't lose a single time during your playthrough of Chapters 1-4 if you don't engage with any secret encounters, as the game has a gradual difficulty curve that means you likely will be pretty skilled at the game's mechanics before it throws any remotely difficult fight at you. If you are looking for a challenge, then the secret fights are your saviour, since it's unlikely that you beat any of them on your first try unless you're already a big fan of hard bullet hell games.
Apart from secrets, Chapter 1 is very easy, Chapter 2 is harder but it's not that noticeable if you've already got to grips with the game, Chapter 3 might surprise you with the difficulty on some fights on your first playthrough, and Chapter 4 will test to see if you really pay attention to the game's mechanics.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
This aspect of the game varies quite a bit between each chapter, Chapter 1's pixel art is quite simplistic but by no means ugly, but by Chapter 3 the game starts looking incredibly good and animated, as the pixel art improves and characters generally move a lot more fluidly and with more detail in cutscenes. Character design is top notch, everyone is incredibly memorable no matter what chapter. The design and feel of the environments becomes amazing by Chapter 2, every place you visit nails the tone exactly. Overall, the visuals of the game are very consistent despite spanning a very wide range of set pieces and tones, except when there's a funny reason otherwise...

[h1]Soundtrack[/h1]
Music is something that Toby Fox is well known for, and it shows in his game. The music brings every environment, battle and character to life in a way I haven't seen before, and it's always incorporated in a way that enhances the tone of every scene. You WILL find yourself searching up the track name of a song you realised was an absolute banger while playing the game, there are so many memorable tracks which really resonate with you. Every chapter has its own selection of amazing tracks, you won't be forgetting the songs from this game for a very long time. Apart from the music tracks, sound design is also unique and memorable to this game, it always is used in a way that fits the tone and enhances gameplay.

[h1]Is it worth the price?[/h1]
Deltarune has plenty of content despite only being the first 4 chapters as of now, though I think it's hard to put a reasonable estimate as to how long your experience will last due to just how many interactions are optional. On top of that it has plenty of replayability, since your choices do have effect on cutscenes and gameplay, and is generally fun to play all around. So yes, it is most definitely worth the price, and you will even get the remaining chapters for free once they release if you do pay for it. There's so many mechanics and aspects I didn't mention here so that you can learn them yourself!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1757695976}, {"review_text": "Admittedly, the whole releasing chapters one by one thing created a lot of theories and discourse online, which is cool.

But at the same time, it bothers me I can't play this game in one go, because it's fantastic. Worth a replay once all the chaps are out anyway

[{"review_text": "I said I would write a review on Valheim once I reached 1000Hrs, so here I am.

I fully recommend everyone buy this game to play and judge for yourself, This game is great playing by yourself but, Valheim is one of if not the best Co-op game I've ever played. Nigh Perfect.
If you're a new playing thinking about buying this game just remember it might start off slow, boring for some, to progress but boy does it speed up.
When it was first shown to me all I wanted was a PC to play it, I bought my PC just to play Valheim on. My friend and I have a world we have played since we started, and it’s got over 1500 days recorded on it. He builds massive castles and fortified townships whilst I stick to a more Viking Longhouse village type build set, the mix of both in my opinion is perfect. I have built lit up roads connecting all our Towns/Villages. I love this game so much I got a full back tattoo of Eikthyr’s bust and a river scenery underneath it, pain was worth it.
I could write many novels of my friend and my adventures we've had in this game.

Pros:
•	The Scenery of this game is beautiful in all ways; the graphical choice I find it to be simplistic yet perfect. From the fog, rain, wind, and waves, and to the blinding sunrises and glowing sunsets. 
•	One of my favourite aspects of the game is the sailing from island to island looking for loot and expanding our locations, the long rides on the ships are perfect for conversing about our days. Turning on PVP on the boat rides to punch each other to level up blocking and whatnot. We enjoy going out on oceans at night to intentionally hunt down serpents for food and revenge.
•	The building in this game is one of the best things the game has to offer, each player you meet has a different build style and technique which expands beautifully in this game, from Castles to Villages to simple shack designs, the possibilities are endless.
•	The crafting progression in Valheim is how I think a lot of survival games should be, don’t tell me what I’m missing, let me figure that out myself. Each boss killed, each item picked up is all newly discovered crafting recipes. I find that to be perfect.
•	The cooking is very thought out, I like the many different options for food items and the many different perks that come with them.
•	Boss fights are always fun to do no matter how much you’ve played. We had another friend join and we made him kill all the bosses up to Moder himself, my friend and I just stood around blocking and watching.
•	The lore is really in depth and rather large when you get into reading the Lore Stones
•	Great selection of weapon types to choose from, perfect for each players preferred playstyle.


Cons/Improvements/Things I would like added:
I’ll start by saying that it is very hard for me to find cons for this game as I don’t really think of many things in the game as a con, for some people it might have cons, but for me and my friend to few to mention.
•	Oceans are lacking content, I really hope the devs make the oceans plentiful. More sea creatures to fight would be great and rival Vikings on boats that will attack you.
•	This one is from my friend; He wants more interior adornments. Larger selection of rug shapes and sizes, more hangable objects for walls, and custom banners for each faction/settlement you make.
•	Stronger support beams for building, like a blackmetal beam.
•	NPC Vikings to populate our empty settlements, give them jobs to do. So our places don’t look barren.
•	Carts for Loxes would be a great addition, I have many Lox in a farmstead but not much to do with them. I’d love to take them into the Black Forest and fill carts with ore to cart back. If I want to move my storage rooms from settlement to settlement Id like to use loxes instead of portals.
•	I would really like a 64* beam/roof pieces, (1m base 2m high) for more of a barn shape of roofs, and when I build longhouses, I would like them to be the wall supports.
•	Ship customisation, colour of sail, more storage, being about to have a workbench on it would be good and have an option of the sail to become transparent when sailing.

I have read many reviews of the game and a lot of them mention the slow release of updates of content and it has never bothered my friend and I. The game is fun no matter what, we just continue to improve our characters and build more and more. Like I said at the start this game is Nigh Perfect.

If you've read this far down, sorry for the blabber but its hard to write down what I'm thinking. I have a lot more to say but don't want to bore. Brother, what? You paid $15 and got a thousand hours out of the game and there's more coming at some point. Just play something else until the next update.

Coziest game I've played in years; possibly ever. Super fun to play solo, even moreso with friends.
Combat is simple, you have basic attack, block, and weapon-specific strong attacks. Different weapons for different enemies e.g mace against skeleton, frost arrows against wet enemies etc.
The pacing feels like classic WoW in the sense of having a "quest" (goal) and then wandering off into the wilderness for a couple hours until the goal is complete.

There's a really interesting dynamic in that the map is enormous, ore is heavy, and you can't take it through portals. This means if you're in a new biome farming the ore, it's probably a really long way from your initial base. And so you'll build a smaller secondary base in the new biome to repair your tools and store your metals while you go get more. Running back and fourth to transport 20 ore at a time isn't super efficient, so instead you'd build a cart, load it with ore, and pull it all to your base in 1 go. But the cart gets damaged by falling / hitting bumps / being attacked by monsters. So it can be efficient in the long run to build a road. But then you unlock boats and sail to new islands and now you're building docks and moving ore overseas and moving livestock overseas. It makes it super gratifying to go off on a mining expedition and bring back a literal boatload of resources all at once. 

The building mechanics are also immaculate.The structural integrity mechanic keeps your buildings grounded because you can't just build an infinitely tall tower, or break the foundation for a floating house. Instead you're building pillars and rafters not just because they're cool but because if you don't your stone roof will fall down. You can only dig into or raise the ground 6 meters below the original terrain of the map, which limits how much you can landscape an area to suit the house you have in mind. This, combined with the ore transporting, means there's a lot of thought going into where you're going to build your base but also makes it really satisfying when you find an ideal spot.

Super fun game, highly recommend, if you don't have a lot of time to play I'd recommend using mods/map modifiers/console commands for speeding up the gathering/building processes. The game plays well on both systems, but of course if you have a good PC you can really take this game to the next level on presentation and performance.  Whether you're a controller or KBM player, this game has you covered and it even plays well on Steam Deck (which I have).  One of the benefits of such a small game install that punches above it's weight.

What sets Valheim apart is how balanced and streamlined its survival mechanics are. You won’t spend hours babysitting hunger bars or suffering from overwhelming penalties. Instead, the game rewards you for eating a variety of foods by increasing your health and stamina, allowing you to focus on the fun parts of exploration, combat, and building.

They all feel fun to progress through and explore and the upgrades to your equipment feel rewarding.  However, the entire second half of this game ranges from boring to borderline unplayable.
  The Plains is a boring, wide open field with next to nothing of interest to discover or explore.  99% of the Plains is empty nothingness and the remaining 1% is goblin camps.  This biome feels vacant and lifeless.  The Mistlands is an absolute chore to play through.  It's an endless labyrinth of cliffs with little to no visibility.  The combat is very clunky in this biome due to the nature of the terrain and the hitboxes of the enemies.  I've lost count of the amount of times that I've been hit by an enemy that I cannot hit because they are either lower or higher up than I am.  Finally, the Ashlands abandons all other forms of gameplay and devolves into endless fighting.  Want to explore, mine, or build?  Too bad, because 99% of your time in this biome will be spent fighting the constantly spawning, endless hordes of enemies.  This game does not have the combat or the movement system to be Dark Souls, yet the developers made a biome that's just that.  If the sheer volume of enemies isn't bad enough, this biome has some of the most annoying enemies in the game.  There are two flying enemies with wonky hitboxes that are difficult to hit with melee weapons, there are skeletons that sit back and throw rocks and shoot arrows at you constantly and run away if you try to attack them, and there are giant lizards that will send you flying with how much knockback they have.
  The difficulty of this game is simply due to it being unfair.  The combat is wonky, the hitboxes are bad, and the enemy density is ridiculous.  This wasn't as much of an issue in the earlier stages of the game because the game focused more on exploration, but when the second half of the game focuses more on combat, the issues become apparent.
  I truly wish I could recommend this game, because it has a lot of potential and I very much enjoyed the earlier stages, but when half of the game is a tedious slog, I simply cannot.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1743280932}, {"review_text": "Playing Valheim is very refreshing. It's a very difficult game, sometimes feels brutal...

But it's just WILD. You go around and fight storms, enemies, cold and learn to survive. The environment and music is quite charming. You get good rewards for exploring and traveling, sometime trying very dangerous things.

The union between gear, food and buildings is really great. Bosses that feels like invincible once you understand what type of gear, potions you need and how to use structures to your advantage become doable.

This is fun in solo!  But in a group it's where it really shines, going around in a group of friends is really a marvelous game!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1739615871}, {"review_text": "i first bought this just as something to stop my boredom but now i cant stop playing, im even trying to convince my BF to buy it so we can play a game together for once.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761675297}, {"review_text": "The game is beautiful, and some of the music is absolutely phenomenal. The feeling when you first set sail on your karve and reach top speed --I don't think any other game has ever given the same experience for me. I could almost [i]feel[/i] the wind in my hair, the salt water droplets on my chin, and the absolute thrill of setting off to the unknown.

It does get old eventually, when you're hauling your fifth load of iron back to your base because you just need [i]so much of it[/i], but even then? It's a nice, relaxing experience. Until the sea serpent attacks your small boat in the middle of the ocean and you realize losing it means losing your entire haul of iron, that is. If you can't outsail it, you need to kill it. Hopefully there's land nearby so you can repair your ship before it breaks apart, or at least it breaks in the shallows where you have some chance of recovering your items.

The combat is... passable. There are optimal weapons for all monster types, and it feels kind of necessary to keep your gear up to date especially in the latter biomes. Bosses are typically not very hard once you know what you are doing, but the fight can definitely spiral fast if you aren't prepared enough. The gods may be merciful, but repeatedly dying still eats up a lot of food and potions, so you should always make tons of them in advance. [i]"Surely this is enough"[/i] turns to [i]"Oh[/i] shit[i], I ran out"[/i] real fast when you die 30 seconds after recovering your first corpse and have to re-rest and re-eat again just to repeat the run of shame again. And again... and again.

You can [b]never[/b] have too many poison, ice, and fire resistance potions. Just trust me on this.

Preparing your gear takes a lot of resources, and it's truly a grind. I definitely recommend setting material rates to 2x resources or even more to speed it up a bit. Once you are more familiar with the monster types and know the tricks to surviving, you can skip gear tiers, but as a new player you should probably just accept the speed penalty of heavy armor sooner rather than later. The allure of running fast and being agile vanes in the tight corridors unless you have a tanky friend between you and the monsters.

The absolute best part of the game, though?

Building, no question about it. It's simple, but flexible. It makes you think about smoke and structural integrity. At first you are stuck building small wooden houses, but then you unlock stone. Once you unlock iron, you can build higher and wider with iron supports, and you are free to experiment.

Resource gathering for building is pain, though. But you can set the game the to Hammer mode to just let your creativity fly. There are also a ton of mods to finetune and adjust the game, to add quality of life features, and new building pieces and furniture, so you can make your own fun. Challenge runs are also a thing, like going mapless or without portals.

All in all, Valheim is not a perfect game, but it is definitely a perfect game [i]for me[/i]. It set the standard for survival games for me, and no other game has come close to matching it.

Here's to waiting for Deep North. The retro aesthetic and freeform procgen fully modifiable game world draw comparisons to minecraft, but with decidedly more progressive, biome-based gameplay, creating a more hardcore and drawn out experience.

The creativity the game does give you, mostly to do with building, farming and shaping the terrain, is more than enough to flex your artistic side while still keeping your attention on gameplay and survival. The warmth, weather and comfort systems are just enough to encourage innovative and convenient structures that are fully functional.

The food and hunting/farming systems are likewise enough to make extra effort worth it, but never completely necessary. The game has a remarkable ability to avoid tedium while still necessitating constant effort and attention to its varied mechanics. The very real threat of death and progression loss makes the safety of early biomes and resources relevant even in the late game.

Rushmore" of games. It's a game that I've sunk countless hours into, and told anyone and everyone how much I love it and cherish it. The game has a fun, magical charm to it - and it truly encapsulates the beginning of the survival-game genre boom right after Covid.

As others have mentioned, the development of this game is abysmally slow. In the 4.5 years it's been in early access, they've only released two new biomes (which are the main sources of new content and progression) - and they are not the most balanced or fleshed-out pieces of content. I've personally defended the game and its devs up and down to myself for quite some time, but I think it's impossible to prevent it from causing a sour taste in my mouth about the game any more. They had a wild level of success with EA and have not had a passion to efficiently get it to full release. I highly doubt they have any plans to support it much afterwards either.

Overall: amazing, magical game that I would have recommended wholeheartedly if you were in the market for a survival game a couple of years ago. Unless you plan on taking advantage of the great work that the modding community has done (essentially taking over for the devs), I unfortunately would say to pass on this game and instead grab one of the more recent games that builds upon the gameplay style that Valheim created.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 19, "timestamp_created": 1751344490}, {"review_text": "[h1] A Viking Adventure Worth Every Minute [/h1]
[b] Valheim is an incredible game in every way - challenging, creative, and absolutely rewarding. [/b]

Starting out can feel a bit tough at first, especially if you're new to survival games. But the beauty of Valheim is that it doesn't take long to "click." After just a few hours, the learning curve flattens and you're fully immersed in the world.

[h2] Boss Fights and Progression [/h2]
The boss fights are a real highlight - each one feels epic and offers just the right level of challenge. Every victory feels earned, and progressing through biomes gives a strong sense of purpose and excitement.

[h2] Build, Create, Conquer [/h2]
One of the best parts of Valheim is building your own base. Seeing your own creation come to life is incredibly satisfying, and the building system is flexible enough to let you create anything from a simple hut to a sprawling fortress.

[h2] Stunning in Its Own Way [/h2]
The graphics may not be high-end, but Valheim still looks beautiful in its own style. The atmosphere, lighting, and world design more than make up for the low-poly look. And once you're in the game, you barely even think about it - you're too busy surviving, exploring, and building.

[h2] Final Thoughts [/h2]
If you enjoy survival, crafting, and exploration with a strong sense of progression and creativity, Valheim is a must-play. It’s a game where your time and effort feel truly meaningful.

Valheim is a solid single or co-op game experience in which players acquire resources to build and unlock other blueprints or items. For those seeking an open-world game where crafting is possible anywhere, along with progressive difficulty, this might be worth a second look!

Valheim's [b]gameplay[/b] is solid. The premise is the player's customized/created character is dropped in by a giant bird somewhere on the map (the middle, always). The maps are randomly seeded and are varied game to game, depending on the seed. The map itself contains different zones that the player explores. The further out from the Meadows the player goes from, the harder the enemies. Biomes will also have "caves" or "dungeons" that the player can explore to gather resources further needed to expand their base. Some of these dungeons are decently difficult and can cause the player a headache, especially if they die in them. Players are able to pick up their items from their fallen body (and thanks to the map for marking it), but they will respawn with absolutely nothing and must go back to that location to get their items back. Again, each area that the player visits will offer different challenges, whether its the enemies or traversing the biome itself. In addition to challenges new resources are available and can be harvested with the right tools. Sometimes, a raft is needed to get to other distant lands; they can be crafted by the player.

The [b]combat[/b] in the game was done well, but I feel it could've been better. There were a few missed opportunities (such as heavy hits or alternative dodging maneuvers) that could've taken the game to the next level, or at least some sort of alternate attacks. Same with dodging; it's included in the game with only one variation of how it works. Blocking, same idea - one action for them all. It's not necessarily a bad thing, but again feels a little limiting. I'm glad to say that the ability has been at least included, but a lot more could've been done in this realm to further immerse the player into the game, rather than move/attack/move/attack/dodge/attack/move etc... Blocking does mix that formula up a little, but would've been another reason to get the game. [b]Combat[/b] is a little bland, but can be fun throughout different moments. The variation in enemies is certainly welcomed (randomly found a troll exploring levels), but dealing with them can sometimes be a bit of a headache. There are some areas that contain spawn points in which the player needs to destroy in order to control the amount of enemies. Wait too long and good luck taking that zone out.

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] were done well. They're not exactly fine or high detailed graphics, and some pixel/voxel animations seem to show up, but some parts of the levels are visually appealing. (especially from a distance). The balance between performance and visuals were well done to the point where particle effects don't necessarily slow or lag the game. There was a recent update where everything is a little smoother and particle affects have a little more sparkle to them. Zooming in closer to characters and such players will notice some Play Station 1/2 polygon graphics. The good news is - is that it doesn't impede on the [b]gameplay[/b] or atmosphere. The [b]sounds and music[/b] were well done, although a little more is left to be desired. The [b]music[/b] certainly ramps up when the player nears danger and changes quite well according to whatever the player is doing. Soundtrack was pleasant to listen to and didn't feel at any point that any particular song was a nuisance. The [b]sounds[/b] themselves were moderately well done. I feel as though this realm could've been done a little better. The monsters in the game make appropriate sounds, but it's nothing where it makes the player feel like they should be booking it away from that area.

Overall, pretty decent game. There is a LOT to explore, there is lots of room to build, and there certainly is no shortages of enemies or things to discover. Some nuances in the game can become annoying to players such as enemies spawning constantly, enemies spawning too quickly while trying to take down a spawn point, lack of specific save states (the "oh crap big enemy save now in case I die" doesn't work), and generally how the game works. The game's rating significantly rises when there are more players contributing and playing at the same time, this is where Valheim certainly shines. Players will have to eat throughout the game and food does give a bonus to characters. Farming and other sort of ventures are available later in the game as the player discovers new material. Would highly recommend a purchase on sale and for friends who enjoy crafting, exploring, and some minor combat in games.

[{"review_text": "Let's face it, Hi-Rez is not doing well. Restructurings, layoffs, pulling the plug on essentially all their games and barely keeping them alive to scrap some leftover pennies from sporadic new players - it doesn't sound good.

They decided to go all in on Smite 2, but for some reason, they thought having anti-cosumer practices that insult your intelligence was the way to go.

These guys pulled an Overwatch and killed their first game under the pretense they'd bring a new, more polished version of it. They didn't. This game, while somewhat visually more appealing, has been tweaked in the worst ways possible. And the best? It's the greediest, most revolting, insulting and obnoxious cash grab ever that makes AI generated hentai gacha games seem dignified triple A games.

These are the guys selling you 3 different version of their game, with the difference between the $29,99 and the $99,99 version (yes, there's a $100 version for a crappier version of SMITE 1, which in itself was a crappier version of LoL) are two skins and a boost for God passes. That's it. Two skins, and a boost, for dumb little you. No need to thank them! They do it from the goodness of their heart. <3

And you read that right - PASSES. These guys have BATTLE PASSES for each individual CHAMPION, each costing $10 each, in a rooster of 50 gods, the vast majority of which are just HD versions of SMITE 1 gods, for which you have no skins even if you played SMITE 1. And it doesn't end here. Now there's the WaNdErInG MaRkEt which are basically CLUSTERS OF BATTLEPASSES each costing $10 as well. Don't you get the hint, you stubby ball of lard? GIVE THEM YOUR MONEY. God. You're so dense!

There's not 1 or 2 battle passes, but about 6, offering MINIMAL content. They broke down ONE battlepass into SIX, and charged $10 for each piece. Like ordering a carbonara, and being charged the price of the dish for each component - $10 for the spaghetti, $10 for the bacon, $10 for the cheese, etc. in what's a capitalist's explosive wet dream. And hey, be happy there's no minimum-wage service associated! At least here you don't need to give a compulsory +350% tip to your gaming-waitress!

And it doesn't end here. Progress is AWFUL. YOU WON'T MAKE IT WITHOUT LEVEL AND WORSHIPPER BOOSTS WHICH, you guessed it, you can buy by unit with real money as well. You'll be shoving an extra $10-$15 just to actually get somewhere. Just GIVE THEM MONEY, TIMMY, GOD. Throw your wallet against the screen or something, but HURRY up.

"B-but you can play the base game for free!!!" my guy there are SO many player-friendly games out there that offer you SO MUCH MORE hard-worked and polished content for free. Even the dreaded Overwatch 2 currently does. Hi-Rez is trying to push the boundaries of consumerism and lack of critical thinking from buyers to try and desperately suck up to their stockholders. No, I wouldn't. Unless I really dislike them. It's a bad game optimised worse. They took a game that was kind of dying, due to poor choices, they made a worse game with less options, more bugs and all the same poor choices that were killing the game to begin with. To that, they've added more bad choices. The game is riddled with bugs, it barely works, they remove items saying "we're working on a fix because this item is too strong/too weak" and after a week or two they add the item back in. Exactly as it was when they removed it. They keep disabling gods, usually The Morrigan, saying they have to fix some bug, yet after doing this over 20 times they still need to "fix some bug". In my personal experience you get little to no help from anyone working with them and asking the people closest to me, including my significant other, you actually get absolutely no help. Even when the issue is caused by something they did wrong. You're still the one being punished by their poor behaviour or their poor choices. I've spent almost 2000 hours on this game and I regret every second of it. So, if you want an honest opinion, the game is interesting. It's a fresh take on mobas, a smart idea worth investing in. But it's handled terribly and in the hands of a company who clearly does not know what they're doing and how to stay afloat. It's not like me to wish bad things to others, I also don't really care, but I doubt they'll manage to go forward much longer. If HiRez is called by the entire playerbase "lowrez".. There's a reason. I suggest you stay clear of this, save your time, save your money, save your sanity and save yourself some big disappointment.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1745594280}, {"review_text": "I want to start with the negatives of the game. 

1. MOBAS are difficult and are inherently toxic. Since the game is lacking in player count, content creators who make genuine educational content are not present. You will deal with toxic players. 

2. "+1s" are additions to a characters kit from their SMITE 1 counter part. For example, Khepri can cast his ultimate while using his first ability on an enemy. This allows him to have much more versatility. How could I consider these negative?
 
I would argue several of the additions to SMITE 1 kits that have been ported over so far feel based on preference or what the developers could find to add to the character. For example, Anhur (one of the most iconic carries) had two changes that I know of: His first ability goes on cool-down upon casting (more of a buff) and his ult was changed to look more cool but it's essentially a nerf. Anhur feels more like a -1 than a +1 regardless of what statistics could be presented about win/pick rates of the god. An example of a god that god several +1s is another god in the carry tab: Jing Wei. Jing Wei's first ability does not need her to be hit by it to gain its buffs, her second ability can have up to 12 charges vs her smite 1 counter part, her third ability has more ways for the user to manuever it and her ult does more damage and can be refired for more damage/repositioning. I don't want to waste too much time, but Jing Wei in comparison to her SMITE 1 counter part feels like she got a +25 versus one or some minor changes to her kit. I should mention she actually has a real early game in this game as well. 

+1s are good in practice, but I fear in the long term that a lot of dev time will be wasted either adding things not needed, overpowered, or nothing really at all. 

3.  Aspects are part of a new game-play design feature in SMITE 2. Aspects are similar to facets from DOTA II, but differ in one way, you are not forced to choose them. Aspects change parts of a gods abilities to allow a different play-style to happen (i.e glass cannons can be come tanks but with less damage). Why can this be negative as well? 

Aspects are good, but also have some issues. For example, Mordred aspect (upon release) as infinitely better than his base kit to the point where the devs fully reworked him to have it as normal and created another aspect you can use. Khepri aspect simply adds more damage to his kit while having very little downsides. Again, this feels very forced in some instances and have lead to reworks, toxic game-play loops, or nothing burger aspects (Loki). AS WELL, some aspects in combination with certain +1s feel incredibly strong (Sol). In total, these additions lead to several balance problems over time. 

4. Bugs. This critique is a part of the game just being in beta but some issues have been present since long in the Alpha. Mercury released 3 patch cycles ago (~6 weeks) and he still has several bugs that have been acknowledged, but not fixed.  Achilles still has issues with his executes going through gods and he has been out for several months. The Morrigan still has several bugs and should have been one of the characters that have been release last as to have her game-play mechanics fine tuned and not buggy. This god is really cool (please nerf her trading pattern it is really toxic), but has several issues that make her feel unrewarding to play. This is just to list a few. 

5. Monetization. My issue with monetization is very short. It was initially advertised that any SMITE 1 skin ported over to the new game you would not have to pay for. You will use legacy gems (this amount is based on how much in-game currency you purchased in smite 1) to purchase them. This is still the case currently, but there are caveats to it. A SMITE skin is released and it is behind a paywall for 6 weeks generally, but within this paywalls are Chromas (skin recolors) in a mini battle-pass system. I genuinely do enjoy waiting six weeks to get a skin and not to mention some of these passes have actual skins pay-walled behind them as well. I get that this is a live service game and this is how you pay for salaries, hit certain projections, etc.. Just be forward with consumers. You would be surprised the response you get. 

6. UE5 games tend to just run like shit if you aren't inclined economically with your PC set up. Do not be surprised if you are not getting the frames you could get in other games. 

Genuine positives for this game.

1. Of the community members still playing, making content etc., this game has one of the best communities out there. It's really positive. I would think of it like New York Knicks fans who just love the team for the romance of the team sport of basketball: There are a few, but they are passionate and loving. 

2. If you are interested in attempting to try out the MOBA genre, SMITE 2 is one of the best ways to try it out. It lacks a few of the prevalent mechanics in other MOBAs such as creep score and wave management. However, it excels at rewarding players for counter building, positioning correctly, match-up spreads, and having excellent team-play. At the end of the day, this is what is generally important in these style of games. Additionally, execution is a big part of this game whereas other MOBAs rely much more on drafting to win games at high levels because they have optimized so much the game-play so much. This game has so much more to optimize even as the devs change the map and game play loops. 

3. I believe the Founder's Edition/Ultimate God pack is still one of the most valuable DLCs you can buy for any games. You can have multiple tiers. Increasing the tiers increase the cosmetics you get. The base tier (the most bang for your buck) allows you to have all gods and all FUTURE releases of gods. If you like this game, this is genuinely a no brainer. 

4. The upgrade to UE5 has been rocky, but has been positive. It will continue to become more so as the game's life span progresses. Some of the character models and skins are so stunning even on low graphics. Even the base game visuals from objectives like the Fire Giant are so cool.

5. The current meta (September 2025) has had tanks been the healthiest they have ever been in a long time. They legitmately feel very tanky outside of extremely late game carries nuking you, but that is supposed to happen. Additionally, they actually do a healthy amount of damage and can punish those who miss-play.  Hopefully, they can create a system in which bruisers can be strong and not the best archetype of character.

6. One of the coolest aspects of this game is the HUD Editor. It is so much more customize able.  I would add the SMITE 1 "New" HUD Friendly team level-up system. You can see yours and every elses levels without using tab. I had it instead of my god portrait. Also, please add grids and snapping (i understand this is probably a 1.0 feature).

7. While they are not in "they rescued this game" category, the devs genuinely have patched this game into a state where they are almost close to having it in a decent spot..

8. The non-SMITE 1 gods release so far have really tested the new tech they can use in UE5 and they all have been so awesome. Alladdin is the coolest character in the game and he is not even a god. He's just a guy with a really powerful lamp. 


The devs have got me from "full doomer" (layoffs and no fully sponsored sports league) to "I do not know what will happen". I still think a larger company buying this IP and giving it the much deserved dollars it needs is so important and will likely help with this games long term success. More god releases and more time is needed for me to really give my best review. For now, 6/10 and I will recommend for now as it still is one of my favorite games. I want to revisit this in a year and see if my opinion changes.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1756960559}, {"review_text": "After learning how Stewart Chisam (the ceo of hirez) has grossly mismanaged the studio/game resulting in them having lay off over half of their devs, I'm uninstalling the game and standing with the workers. [{"review_text": "It's been a while since I last actually chilled playing a game and never regretted it. Or maybe I'm just growing old. Doesn't matter anyway. Aight imma cast my ol' maple rod.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 9, "timestamp_created": 1762244564}, {"review_text": "Give a man a fish, and you feed him for a day. Teach a man to Cast n Chill, and he'll chill for a lifetime.

Beautiful art, a relaxed atmosphere, and gameplay that's engaging with the option to idle n chill. It feels like you're fishing inside of a Bierstadt painting. The amount of work it must've taken to add this much detail both above and below the water is incredible. It's relaxing to watch day turn to night and get lost in the pixels.

I've been playing since the demo came out last month and the devs clearly listened to the feedback. You can tell a lot of love went into this game and it's well worth your time.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 28, "timestamp_created": 1750097806}, {"review_text": "My recently widowed 55yr Mother-in-Law, a couple of weeks ago, received a diagnosis of around a 10% 90-day mortality rate. 
She’s been wanting to go fishing while she can, but she has a lot of fatigue and concerns that make that difficult or impossible. 

I’ve been waiting for this game for her since seeing its demo. I bought it as soon as I saw it was available, figuring it would be good at least on the go for long Dr appointments or upcoming hospital stays. She’s also been taking a liking to our house cats — She said she’d have loved a Maine coon if she could have had one in her life. I saw the supporter DLC and had to have it for her (I usually don’t grab stuff like this, but the coincidence made it impossible to pass up).

She’s absolutely loved it. She hasn’t played games in decades, since Mario brothers. It’s really helping her mind’s sharpness. She’s been so happy and excited with all of the different fishing options, fish types, the pretty pixel art that she’s never really seen before. It’s gorgeous art and day/night cycles, too! (I haven’t played that much myself for a review from me personally).

She’s gonna be playing more soon! She’s hooked (ha-ha). The dev(s) have made her so very happy with this product. Thank you. 
The memories made here are priceless, and the starting value (with initial discount) an incredible deal.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1750126433}, {"review_text": "I'm a budget gamer, I value my time vs what i'm able to spend which is rarely much, and reading some other reviews and seeing price being such big focus. I get it, I do, I rarely have the budget to buy games and I've been fortunate to be a part of a very generous group of friends or back in the day Humble Bundle or Game Pass, Epic etc etc. A LOT of free to play games. 

This I bought for myself. I bought it the moment I saw the trailer.

Best $20 AUD I've spent on myself in a long time. 

The Graphics, Stunning and Beautiful, but playful.

The Mechanics, whilst not exactly hand holding, it's rather intuitive, far from taxing and still somehow engaging. Especially when chasing trophies or just exploring new fish and working out what works, where they are, the time of day they might feed (unsure if that is a mechanic, however I've seen fish ignore their preferred bait until the evening etc. I could be imagining it)

The Fish Diversity, For the current state of the game, As someone who doesn't have an exceptional amount of time to play games there's a lot to do and it doesn't feel overwhelming. I'm expecting this to potentially include other interpretations of other places around the world.. Id absolutely love to see this game show off Australia or anywhere in Europe. Even Ocean. it would be sick to be landing Flatties or Bream or Mullet, Barramundi... SHARKS.

The Idle, I'm not a massive fan of idlers, Rev Idle being my last dabble. but this just hits different, its basically no commitment if you just want it to Idle. wonderfully enough this game managed to really hit the mark, it captures what I imagine fishing is actually like to those who dream of peaceful moments in between their catches in the boat with mates or alone. This game in my opinion manages to really hit the point between immersion, background or casually picking it up occasionally.

if this game continues to grow and do the things it does. I'll play this for a very long time, I'll try to 100 the Achievements. 

It make sense if this isn't your thing and fair call. but as someone who usually questions what i'd spend on something purely because of budget, this has been well worth my dollar and more importantly, my time.

Pay the man at the counter, He tells good stories.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1750422968}, {"review_text": "Cast N Chill is exactly what the name promises; a beautifully crafted, laid-back pixel art fishing adventure that nails the cozy vibe better than most games in the genre. The graphics are absolutely gorgeous in their simplicity, and the environments are full of charm and peaceful ambiance. It's one of those rare games where you can just exist in the world and enjoy the flow of things. The light banjo tune when you catch a fish, the birds chirping, the sound effects, chef's kiss. 

I beat the game and earned every achievement in just under 20 hours, and honestly, I loved every minute of it. It doesn’t try to be something it’s not. It’s a chill, focused experience that doesn’t overstay its welcome. It’s not difficult, but there is a technique to it.

There’s a logbook of all the fish and where to catch them. There are many rods, lures, boats (upgradable!) and fishing licenses you can purchase with the money you earn from your catches. Each fishing license unlocks a new location to fish. The concept is simple and satisfying. You and your dog catch your bag limit, return to the dock, sell your fish, and save up for your next upgrade. It’s a loop that just works. For me, time absolutely flew by while playing.

It’s one of those games where you say, “Just one more cast,” and next thing you know, it’s 45 minutes later. Or you tell yourself, “I’m just going to catch these last two fish and hop off,” but now you have enough money to unlock the next location… and if you're like me, there’s no way you're going to bed without seeing what it looks like.

Also, having the dog companion was such a nice touch. I found myself petting him constantly without even thinking about it. It sounds silly, but if you play the game, you’ll get it. And yes, there’s a cat companion in the DLC if that’s more your thing.

Worth mentioning, I played the game on the SteamDeck (mostly docked), and it runs beautifully.

Now, about the people leaving bad reviews. Let’s be real, most of them barely gave the game a chance or were expecting a deep open-world RPG disguised as a fishing sim. That’s on them, not the game. Downplaying something this charming and well-made because it’s “too simple” or “not enough content” completely misses the point. Not every game needs to be 100+ hours long and overly complex to be worth playing.

If you're even remotely into pixel art, cozy vibes, or just need a break from your usual library, Cast N Chill is an absolute win.

10/10 would cast and chill again.


If you've read this far, just buy it. 


Devs, if I could make a suggestion: please add a volume and SFX slider option in the menu to control the audio. I would like the ability to turn the reeling audio and SFX up a couple notches. I found the audio in general to be a tad quiet. (Could also be because it was played docked 98% of the time). Still would be a nice option. 

Happy fishing! And don't forget to tip the gentleman in the shop!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1750599266}, {"review_text": "Ideas that would make this game better:
1. Have us right click bait and rods so we have the ability to stop the idle from changing it.

The idle mode lets the AI do the work, which is just as varied as real fishing. Sometimes it will catch fish one after another and other times it just sits there casting for absolutely nothing until the AI gets fed up and moves on to another spot. It will even change lures and rods to use what it thinks best for those areas. This is also a mixed bag with varying results. So what about the player? Yes, you can take control and do the fishing yourself, but the best part of this game is just sitting back and enjoying the audio of water and nature sounds while the computer does the fishing. This may not be for everyone, but I enjoyed it quite a lot. At 51 hours played I'm about half way through the steam achievements and plan to work on collecting a trophy size catch for every species, but it will be a slow process to complete. I recommend this game especially for those of us that don't necessarily need our gaming experience to be a constant button smashing, action packed, thrill ride... This game is a screen saver you can occasionally pop into and catch a few fish manually and then pop out of without fuss. There's no expectation, no timer, no nothing. I adore it. It's also lightweight as hell so you can have just about anything up and keep this on the side while you play and it doesn't matter.

Superb ambiance, owing to fantastic pixel art and amazing music loops. There could be a few more customization options, sure, fine. But for what it is? Love it. 

Just having it open and glancing over truly does give me a small boost of serotonin.

Atmosphere and Presentation

The strongest aspect of the game is its visual and audio identity. The graphics are beautiful, calm, and detailed. The soundscape is soft and restrained, reinforcing the peaceful fishing mood. Small moments, like when a fish breaks the surface or when you finally reel it in, are well executed.

Accessibility and Controls

The game is easy to understand from the start. The mechanics are intuitive and accessible. Both mouse and keyboard work naturally together, and the controls never get in the way.

Gameplay, Difficulty, and Tension

The game is relaxing and simple to learn, but also very easy to complete. For players looking for challenge, unpredictability, or progression depth, the current design may feel too light. It becomes more of a checklist than excitement and unexpected anticipation and struggle.

Underwater View and Loss of Mystery

The ability to look under the water removes a significant amount of tension. When you see exactly what is down there, fishing becomes a predictable “aim and retrieve” action rather than an experience built on anticipation.

When fishing from the surface camera, the occasional jump of a fish breaking through the water is a wonderful moment. Without the underwater camera, this detail would become even more meaningful. The underwater view reduces the sense of discovery and undermines the surface-level atmosphere.

Progression and Economy Imbalance

The in-game economy is too basic. It is straightforward to buy everything in the shop long before the game asks you to complete important tasks. Once everything is purchased, money loses all meaning. This removes progression tension and undermines long-term motivation.

Boat System and Lack of Impact

Boats are visually appealing but have little practical impact on fishing mechanics. Different models do not significantly change strategy, risk, or access to new areas. They feel more like cosmetic swaps than systems connected to gameplay decisions.

Suggestions for Future Development
Make the World More Dynamic
Seasons and weather

Introduce seasonal and weather changes that influence fish behavior. Spring, summer, autumn, and winter could each create unique fishing opportunities. Weather conditions like strong winds, heavy rain, snow, fog, or thunderstorms could affect bite rates, boat control, and travel speed. This adds unpredictability and encourages adaptation.

Terrain accessibility through boat upgrades

Let boats determine where the player can travel. Larger or more advanced boats could access deep water, offshore zones, remote islands, or hidden coves. Progression becomes tied to exploration rather than only shop purchases.

Deepen Boat Mechanics and Upgrades
Boat impact on fishing

Small boats could tilt, drift, or get dragged away when hooking larger fish. Bigger boats could offer stability but come with slower travel or higher cost. This introduces meaningful gameplay choices and tension.

Practical equipment and utilities

Expand the toolset available on the boat. Examples include sonar, echo sounders, limited underwater windows, radios for hints or weather updates, and drones for scouting.

Add classic fishing tools such as nets, hooks, or bells. A landing net could secure large fish near the surface. Different hooks could affect which fish are attracted. A bell on the rod could signal unexpected bites. These items would strengthen the feeling of operating a real fishing vessel.

Give the Dog and Player More Character
Dog behavior

The dog could sleep, nap, bark, react to weather, jump in the water, or show excitement during big catches. Feeding the dog fish could trigger animations or sound reactions. These interactions add life and personality.

Naming options

Allowing the player to name the boat and the dog increases emotional attachment and personal identity.

Player actions

Whistling, toggling a radio, or reacting to weather could deepen immersion without complicating controls.

Emergent Events and Surprises

Unexpected events can make each session unique. Sudden weather shifts, lightning strikes, radio broadcasts with rumors or location tips, birds attempting to steal caught fish, fishing lines snapping, or the dog jumping into the water all create opportunities for surprise. These events also support creative achievements and new story moments.

Social Layer and NPC Interaction

Introduce NPC fishermen in nearby boats or along the shore. They can comment on bait, weather, or locations. The player can cooperate, share advice, mislead them, or fish side-by-side. Even minimal interactions add a sense of community and variety.

Progression, Economy, and Late-Game Purpose

Stretching out the economy and introducing high-cost optional upgrades would prevent early saturation. Rare fish, event-based requirements, and cosmetic customizations can keep money relevant throughout the game.

Cosmetic options for rods, boats, colors, or the dog’s appearance provide progression without disrupting balance.

Conclusion

My final rating is 5 out of 10. This reflects the game in its current form, not its potential. The game has excellent atmosphere, beautiful art direction, and intuitive controls. However, it lacks depth in progression, tension, and long-term engagement.

For that simplicity, though, they tended to be very fun, something you don't always get in a modern game.

BallxPit asks the question, what if Old School, but designed to run on modern systems?  The result is something that may well be the single most fun game I've purchased in years.  The demo convinced me to buy on release, a decision I have not regretted.  BP styles itself as a modern take on the Atari classic Brickout.  But there are elements of Space Invaders and Pong.  The end result is a fast paced game with remarkable depth and variation.    There's also a base-building element, giving a goal to the battles rather than merely battling.

And because its a modern game, while simple in idea, there's a lot of complexity; almost everything is can be combined to form new things; Brood Mother + Bleed turns into a cloud of mosquitoes, which can be merged with a toxic ball for a cloud of poisonous mosquitoes.  Each character alters the way the game is played slightly, but build the right building in your base, and you can play the character that launches the balls and the one that makes them act like there's gravity at the top of the field.

Even better, it doesn't require large blocks of time; a give battle is in the neighborhood of 15 minutes.  And because it's indy, some finance bro doesn't think we're willing to pay 80 bucks for it.  I bought full price, I've gotten more than my money's worth already.

The graphics are simple, but well designed, and sound is well done; a lot is going on, but nothing runs over anything else in the soundscape.  So far, I've only encountered a single bug, two characters froze while trying to catch twin baby balls coming in from either direction.  But only once, and it didn't set me back very far, in terms of game progression.
