The gameplay is fun. Skating around really does feel great, the new animations are really nice and smooth, there's a decent selection of options to really fine-tune your experience how you want, etc.  Everything surrounding the gameplay is a positive. 
If you liked the old games or skateboarding in general, [b]you should try this game.[/b]
The problem is basically everything else.

-People have commented on the artstyle being unappealing for over a year. I do not want to buy clothes for these ugly Sims Mobile looking people. 
-The replay editor barely works, stuttering and lacking even basic features like keyframes. This is something that Skate has understood the importance of since 2007. It is unbelievable to launch without this.
-Many spots in the city are strangely obstructed. Ledges blocked by vending machines, benches blocked by trashcans. In Skate 3, you could move these items out of the way. Now you can only add more clutter. This means some spots are simply bad and cannot be improved by the player.
-Because its a live service treadmill, you will play the same missions dozens if not hundreds of times eventually. Could they add more? Sure, and they probably will, but I've been doing some of these missions for years now and expect they won't be going anywhere.
-There are no communication features. This makes collaboration when building spots basically impossible. I guess that's why they stopped calling them "Collabo Zones".
-There are tricks missing that were in Skate 3 (darkcatches, fingerflips) that will come eventually, but it's still unfortunate.

Personally, I wouldn't recommend playing NIOH1 and NIOH2 back-to-back in one sitting, as the two games share significant repetition. Playing for extended periods straight can lead to severe fatigue. If you only plan to play through the game once casually, focusing primarily on the story and combat, then it's not a major issue. However, if you intend to thoroughly explore every detail, play through at least four times, and ultimately unlock all achievements, the weariness and frustration from playing both back-to-back will become increasingly apparent.

From a gameplay perspective, NIOH2 does offer a richer experience than NIOH1. It builds upon its predecessor by introducing several interesting new gameplay mechanics and systems, while also refining and improving numerous details from the predecessor. This allows it to maintain a familiar feel while delivering some genuinely fresh gameplay experiences. However, this is largely thanks to NIOH1 establishing such a solid foundation for its gameplay mechanics, enabling NIOH2 to expand upon it. Second, NIOH2 fundamentally retains the gameplay systems of NIOH1. Consequently, despite the new additions, this sense of novelty doesn't last long. Take my experience as an example: I just finished replaying NIOH1 and unlocked all achievements, then dove straight into NIOH2. The freshness and enthusiasm it offered faded almost completely within 20 hours. Instead, an increasingly palpable sense of frustration and fatigue took hold. After all, NIOH2 essentially amounts to a copy-paste of its predecessor—whether in its action mechanics, combat system, map design, or core gameplay, it remains virtually identical to the original. Third, in my view, not all of NIOH2's adjustments and changes to the predecessor deliver a better experience. For certain gameplay elements, I personally still prefer the settings of the NIOH1.

From a narrative standpoint, I find NIOH1's story more compelling. NIOH2's plot unfolds before the events of the first game, functioning as a prequel. NIOH1, however, is set during the late Sengoku period of Japan, weaving a rich ensemble tale through the eyes of William Adams (Miura Anjin). This era of Japanese history gave birth to numerous legendary figures. NIOH1 masterfully weaves these elements into a fantastical saga of the late Sengoku period's warlords. In contrast, NIOH2's historical backdrop feels comparatively muted. It adopts anime-inspired tropes and JRPG narrative techniques, focusing its storytelling on a core group led by the protagonist to reflect the era through intimate details. While this narrative style differs from its predecessor and has its own merits, its overly familiar tropes inevitably feel tiresome. Furthermore, the game repeatedly emphasizes themes commonplace in Japanese anime by its later stages: mutual understanding, harmonious coexistence, and letting go of hatred. While NIOH1 touched upon similar themes, it did so subtly and integrated them seamlessly into the plot. Personally, I preferred NIOH1's ensemble-driven narrative, which delivered a sense of grandeur and epic storytelling. In NIOH2, the plot truly began to feel compelling only towards the end of the main story, when William's return brought all the nostalgia and memories from the first game flooding back. Unfortunately, by this point, the game was essentially over. As for the DLC content, it objectively fills in some gaps in the game's lore and setting, making certain elements more logically consistent. But ultimately, it devolves into a rather melodramatic family saga—the legendary arch-villain turns out to be the protagonist's mother's brother, and all the fighting boils down to familial grudges and fated enmity...


In summary, NIOH2 is objectively a masterpiece not to be missed, and I highly recommend it. Subjectively, however, my prolonged marathon playthrough of both games left me fatigued, affecting my enjoyment of NIOH2. That said, purely in terms of unlocking all achievements, NIOH2 is considerably easier than NIOH1. Consequently, I only played through NIOH2 once with serious dedication, then unlocked all achievements as quickly as possible, and then decided to take a break. I won't be revisiting NIOH2 for quite some time. Therefore, I personally recommend that if you've just finished playing NIOH1 and played it very seriously, you might want to take a break before starting NIOH2. This approach will give you more freshness and sustain your enthusiasm for longer, making it less likely to burn out quickly. Play this game, and play it with your friends too.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1747500437}, {"review_text": "some of the enemies have really nice boobies, which throws me off in battle, its a huge distraction", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 27, "timestamp_created": 1755506735}, {"review_text": "In my opinion, what’s really lacking in today’s video game market is respect for the player’s abilities and intelligence. Maybe there’s some specific, unexplainable charm when a game plays itself - where you don’t put in any actual effort - but I can’t say that I’m a fan of this type of approach. Sure, who wants to be stressed out or filtered by some random NPC enemy, especially when one of the main points of playing a game is getting a genuine dose of fun?

But isn’t it good when you’re going through that real, unfiltered experience which provides a moderate amount of joy through a real but at the same time fair challenge? Nioh 2 is about that.

Unlike Dark Souls, which tends to take a much more conservative approach in its gameplay foundation, Nioh 2 is an unchained bastard that will screw you up immediately if you don’t learn every layer, tech, or ability in its stash. Yes, you will be dead in a matter of seconds - just like your opponents. You are playing by the same rules as any foe. To deal with them, you’ve got a very flexible combat system, which creates remarkable freedom of choice in what EXACT type of style fits you the most. The number of possibilities and tools in dealing with enemies is astonishing in its own way.

Going through the main campaign, I never once said to myself, “This is complete bullshit, this game isn’t fair to me.” Only the wrong approaches and occasional quirks - from my point of view - that’s what failed me. Nioh 2 hits that sweet spot of being on the edge of risk, where basically every battle is a milestone skill check, and even a little threat can play a cruel joke on you.

Why glazing about something that you really adore is pretty cool, but I do think that competent reward is nonexistent in Nioh 2. You get a huge amount of loot for accomplishments like killing low-grade enemies or finding some distant chest - only to receive low-grade loot with some insane level of bullshitery represented by stats. Bet you’ll love getting a new yellow-rarity katana with Quick Attack Ki Consumption -7.5%, or a purple-grade tonfa with Yokai Close Combat Damage +2.5%. Pretty cool, right?

But there’s one major upside to all of this - gratification through gameplay is priority number one, not the rarest loot in the game. The uncommon weapon won’t help you on your first runs by any means. Only an understanding of the combat system and at least a minimal grasp of its uniqueness will earn you the finest reward: unspoiled in its purity experience.

While this review doesn’t really touch in detail on the basis of the game, which can be a crucial factor for some people - I still really want you to check out the game blindly, without looking at detailed reviews about features, mechanics, or skills. While I will understand if it’s not going to grip you with some questionable RPG elements, I believe that this game brings that feel of why exactly I - or even we - play games in the first place.

Nioh 2 is about improvement.
Nioh 2 is about learning.
Nioh 2 respects you.

There's also yokai abilities you can obtain from defeated bosses, who drop Yokai Cores. Equipping these cores will raise several attributes of your character's stats, and/or add additional perks, while also allowing you to use the boss' special attack. You can equip two of these, and there are melee types and ranged types.

There's also magical spells you can cast, which replenish after resting at a shrine (a la Dark Souls' bonfires), as well as ninjutsu weapons that also replenish the same way. (Shurikens, caltrops, etc)

As you earn amrita (the game's version of 'souls' as currency), you can level up your character's stats, which will bolster the effectiveness of spells, weapons, items, bolster health, ki (stamina) and more.

There are also gear sets that can have set bonuses, and by default, buying the Nioh 2 complete edition starts you off with set gear and powerful weapons. (They are level 1 but can be boosted when you find higher level gear later).

The game also features a character transmog system, which allows you to play as several NPCs, once unlocked.

The game takes place before Nioh 1, and doesn't require you play Nioh 1 at all, as the only shared elements are the setting of feudal Japan, and the presence of Yokai. Each game does their own thing with story and don't play off each other.

Nioh 2 also features more weapons and abilities than the first game had, so is a technical upgrade.

Ally phantoms require Ochoko Cups to summon, with the higher the NPC player's level than you, the more cups required. (Reminiscent of Dragon's Dogma's pawn summon system).

Beware of anomalies, monsters, and armed bandits.

It feels like a mix of Lethal Company/R.E.P.O. but with base building mechanics - don't worry, enemies can't get to your base (Yet!! Who knows, they might add it as a feature!)

I highly recommend giving this game a go because I didn't expect to love it as much as I do!

I'll explain it in a short-as-possible way:

- You (and friends) load in and have 60 seconds to collect as much loot from your house as possible and get to your bunker before the timer runs out and a nuke goes off.

- Once you're ready, you can venture into the wasteland which is a randomly generated map you can explore, scavenge for supplies, fight enemies (to begin with mostly humans with knives, maybe a gun and the occasional angry deer/boar.

- During the time out of the bunker you'll want to find food, water, medicine etc. weapons, storage containers, equipment like weapons, clothes with pockets and weapons.

- After some time it will be time to return to the bunker as a new emission is about to hit and will kill you if you don't make it back in time. (Pressing Q will show your compass and the bunker is on the northern wall of the map (which is the left side of the compass - a little confusing, but, you get used to it quickly).

- Once the new emission passes you'll have a quick load screen and it'll be time to go back out, the map will have generated a new layout, enemies, anomalies, loot to search for etc.

This is generally the overall gameplay loop, over time increasing the size of your bunker and upgrading your gear, what you can craft and as you get further into the game enemies will become tougher will more radiated areas so you'll need the right equipment to survive. 

Again, I can't say this enough but I absolutely am in-love with this game and what the Dev has created and I can't wait to see where they go with it in the future. I really hope they succeed! 

Those of you expecting perfection, there are of course some bugs, game lagging due to memory loss (a quick save and reload fixes), hotbar slots unavailable to put items in. One time, my friends having an empty, unloaded invisible map with invisible enemies, buildings etc. (everything was fine for me, just an issue for them)... So there are bugs that'll no doubt be worked on and ironed out over time.


Thank you again to the Dev for producing such an amazing game, I cannot wait to see where it goes!

Now for the cons:

- Performance is the BIGGEST issue of this game right now. Not gonna lie it's not that bad in general but at random times your FPS reduces 3X ! I've a very powerful pc with RTX 5080 + RYZEN 9950X3D and i'm getting 40-30 FPS if i haven't died in a long time not only that game looks like GMOD LIDAR when FPS drops down to those scales. I am enjoying the core gameplay of Battlefield 6, but the current weapon and attachment unlock system is actively sucking the fun out of the game.

The challenges required to unlock basic and essential weapon attachments are excessively tedious and demanding, often requiring thousands of kills per weapon. This isn't a challenge; it's a punitive, soul-crushing grind that forces players to ignore the objective and focus on senseless metrics. It feels like the requirements were generated by an algorithm, not a team that actually plays the game.

To make matters worse, the developers have decided to target the only viable workaround: nerfing progression in Bot matches. Players were using bot matches to bypass the impossible grind in the main multiplayer modes, and instead of addressing the root problem—the ridiculous challenge requirements—the developers simply punished the players for trying to catch up.

This decision sends a clear message: "Play our game our way, even if it's not fun."

The only result of this will be player burnout. No one wants to spend dozens of hours unlocking the basic components for a single weapon. This current system is:

Anti-casual: It completely locks out players who don't have infinite time to grind.

Anti-teamplay: It encourages players to farm specific stats rather than playing the objective.

Anti-fun: The process is boring and repetitive.

DICE, you must revisit these challenges. Dial back the required numbers significantly. Stop trying to force a ludicrous grind for attachments. If the goal is player retention, this system is a spectacular failure. Right now, it feels less like a game and more like a second job, and that is not what Battlefield should be.

Do better, please.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 232, "timestamp_created": 1761103470}, {"review_text": "I played the beta and loved every second of it. When it ended, I could not think of anything else -it was just me and other Battlefield diehards, living the dream.

The campaign is not bad, but it is nowhere near the immersion of Battlefield 3 or 4. The character designs feel a bit off; the skins lack detail, and no one really stands out as an iconic figure worth remembering. Often rigged with bugs or just distracting assets disappearing in thin air, like a vehicle you just blew up might disappear shortly after, same with corpses from your enemies. I also fell through the map after getting out of a military vehicle. The AI feels very brain-dead; they often stand there, doing nothing. Same with friendly AI. They are not coded to kill enemies for you unless you order them to. So, a lot of the time, I was getting flanked by the enemy when I thought everything was clear, because my teammates were not reacting to anything. But they were ignoring an enemy standing right where I wanted to take cover, and they had a clear view of it the whole time. Happens a lot.

The multiplayer, though… oh boy. Gameplay feels great, but the netcode is still awful at times. You can empty half a mag into someone’s skull and they just shrug it off, then two-tap you without a single muzzle flash. Maybe it depends on the time of day or the servers, who knows.

My biggest gripe? They broke the class system. Letting everyone pick any weapon turned the entire game into Supportfield. Nobody plays their role anymore - they hoard ammo, refuse to revive, and chase their precious K/D. The teamwork spirit that made Battlefield special is gone. Thankfully, some of those wannabe lone wolves are quitting little by little; constant deaths tend to humble people who never learned how to play as a team.

I have always played Support class the right way - reviving, resupplying, and swapping to Engineer or Recon when needed. But these days, teammates respawn before I can revive them, wasting tickets and making the effort pointless. It is infuriating.

Overall, the game is fun, feels snappy at night when less people are playing, looks great, and the soundtrack is top-notch. There is a solid weapon variety too, no stupid skins (like in Call of Duty), no complaints there. But the community? It is a mess. At this point, I would rather play with bots who actually understand the assignment.

Anyway, I hope this review was helpful!

It's really, really good", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1639, "timestamp_created": 1757126328}, {"review_text": "Completed 100% achievements today after around four playthroughs — what a ride! All of this for just €19.50 is insane compared to overpriced AAA games. I'll break down my thoughts by different aspects. For context, I've completed Hollow Knight multiple times, got 100% achievements, and even finished Path of Pain.

[h2]Art[/h2]
The art is improved. HK was really dark and gray, while Silksong is much more colorful. Zone
designs are magnificent, and the enemies are equally impressive. I don't think there's another Metroidvania that can compete visually besides the original Hollow Knight.

[h2]Map[/h2] 
The map is HUGE compared to the first game. HK had 16, Silksong has 28 — almost double. Every zone has its own charm. 
Some areas remind me of the first game but they are still unique enough to stand on their own.

[h2]Music[/h2] 
I've listened to Christopher Larkin's soundtrack from the first game a lot - enough that he's in my Spotify top 10. Silksong's OST is on the same level as HK. 

[h2]Story[/h2] 
The story is the most important aspect of the game, but I can't say much about it since I've only understood part of it. I'll probably wait for Mossbag to release a video explaining it fully. The atmosphere is still that "haunting"/"infection" type from the first game, with most enemies appearing in a kind of zombie-like state. I loved the cutscenes and the dialogue with NPCs. Another major win is that Hornet can talk, unlike the Knight — it adds a lot of personality and depth.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
HK had 168 (counting bosses + DLCs). Silksong has 235 in the base game, which is impressive. The design of enemies and 
bosses is excellent, and their attack patterns are interesting - each feels distinct. There are a few downsides that many players (myself included) have noticed:

1. Too many flying enemies. They're often tanky, ranged, and frustrating to deal with. You spend time waiting for them to come 
close, only for them to dash backward and attack from a distance.
2. Double Damage. Around 90% of players (myself included) complained about this early on. After a few playthroughs, I've gotten used to it, but I still think
it's unfair to throw double damage enemies at you right from the start. Overall, I'd say double damage feels unfair for some enemies, but fair for others.
3. Environmental damage. This one's a mixed bag for me. I'm used to it now, but some zones were very frustrating at first.
4. Arena / Trials lack meaningful rewards. Usually, completing a trial just opens a new path instead of giving something worthwhile

Bosses 
I consider some fights excellent([spoiler]First Sinner, Cogwork/Clover Dancers, Phantom, Second Sentinel, all Lace fights[/spoiler]), challenging, fair, and memorable. Others, like [spoiler]The Unravelled, Groal the Great, and Moorwing[/spoiler], feel poorly designed or frustrating rather than fun. Bosses in general are a bit of a coin flip. Some
runbacks are awful.

[h2]Platforming[/h2]
Exploration comes with plenty of platforming challenges. A lot of people criticize the diagonal pogo, but I've gotten used to it over time. That said, my view might be a bit biased since I usually play with the [spoiler]Wanderer crest[/spoiler] - its pogo and attack style feel very similar to the Knight's in the first game. Overall, platforming in Silksong is faster-paced and more varied than in HK, thanks to the different skills you gain along the way. Personally, I find it 
really fun.

[h2]Combat and Skills[/h2]
Combat is faster than in the first game. Crests give unique playstyles with different attacks.
I tried most of them, but Wanderer stuck with me the most. Each crest has its own attack style
and sometimes even a unique way of healing, with clear upsides and downsides. 

In HK, you had 3 skills - here you get double that, and each skill feels useful for different encounters. My personal favourite is the parry - it's good in every game, and Silksong is no exception. Movement skills are unlocked gradually, with some returning like dash, wall climb and double jump. There are also new ones, such as sprint, float, a different type of dash, and a super jump (similar to super dash from HK, but only works upward).

[h2]Tool System / Charms[/h2]
Honestly, I think the charm system in HK was better, simply because it allowed for more varied builds and creativity. In Silksong, tools are tied to the crest you're using, which is both a W and an L depending on how you look at it. Personally, I find the red tools the most fun, and usually they make the biggest impact. Some tools are very situational, shining in specific boss fights or areas.

[h2]Quests[/h2]
I liked most of the quests, especially since in HK the only real quest we had was the White Flower. The only ones I genuinely disliked were the courier quests. As for the standard quests, most are needed for completion percentage and for progressing into Act 3, so at least they feel more connected to the main game.

[h2]Progression[/h2]
The game is divided into 3 acts, with Act 3 being somewhat of a secret. Unfortunately, the pacing often feels ahead of the player. Upgraded your mask? Congrats — now you can die in 3 hits... again. Most of the time, you're stressed about dying or which enemy will hit for double damage.

As I've mentioned, the difficulty is high from the start and the learning curve is punishing. Many encounters feel downright unfair, which led to some players
to quit or use the popular 1x damage mod. I get why - they own their game and can play how they want - but unfortunately, the Hollow Knight community 
has become somewhat toxic, often mocking players who struggle with the infamous "git gud" ragebait. Silksong seems designed specifically for hardcore HK fans 
who enjoy extreme challenges like "fireb0rn" - not for casual players.

[h2]Game Currency / Economy[/h2]
The game has two types of currency:

[b]1.Shell Shards[/b] - These drop from most enemies, especially beast-like ones, and are used to recharge tools and for certain quests. I often run out of Shell Shards, and farming them can be annoying. In Steel Soul mode, you get a semi-infinite supply... kind of. I haven't tried a proper farming method besides just  killing everything in the way. 

[b]2.Rosaries[/b] – The main currency, used to buy most items. They drop from some enemies in small amounts, so farming is often necessary. Rosaries can be converted to strings to prevent losing money on death, but even with strings, money can be scarce. Farming typically requires repeatedly killing the same enemies. You also need to pay Rosaries for benches and travel stations, sometimes at high prices.  Overall, the economy could use better balance.

[h2]Extras[/h2]
I really enjoyed the minigames, though there aren't many- around five in total. There's a dice game, a race game, and three minigames with the fleas: Pogo, Dodge and Juggle.  I'd love to see more content of this kind added in the future. I was also hoping for something like a Godhome or an area to practice bosses.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
I've really enjoyed Silksong, but at the same time, it's been frustrating. Some parts of the game feel unfair and time-consuming. It feels like the game doesn't respect your time.  Rewards for trials and bosses are rare and usually underwhelming, which can be frustrating if you only have a few hours to play. I had the free time to adapt, but not everyone will. In terms of improvements it surpasses the first game in about 90% of aspects. The game still deserves all the praise it gets - it's phenomenal for the price,  especially considering it was mostly made by a team of three. 1. Very, or even extremely good at this kind of game
2. Immensely patient/Have too much time on your hands

TL:DR: Game very hard.

With that out of the way, this game is GORGEOUS to look at, the soundtrack puts that of the original Hollow Knight to shame, I found myself healthily challenged by most, if not all of the bosses in the game, and much of the exploration genuinely felt more natural than in many games I've seen exploraiton as a central mechanic in.

Took about 16 hours to beat the game, anticipating another 10-20 to 100% it. Gonna take a very long time to beat the game in steel soul mode. 

Hornet's movement is different from the knight. not good, not bad, just different. takes some time to get used to, and can lead to frustration early on in some areas (pogo'ing isn't the easiest thing at the start of the game)

The game is significantly more difficult, making fights like Nightmare King Grimm look easy by comparison. Silksong is just fun, that's how I'd summarize it. This is my GOTY for this year.

Well I want to start off by saying that the price tag is fantastic. In an age where 8-14 hour games (Doom dark ages, Silent hill f, MGS3 delta, etc) are being released for 80 euros/dollars, team cherry provided us with a full game with tons of well-polished content for only 20 bucks.

As for the gameplay itself, the combat is nice and fluid, the movement is fast and satisfying, the story/lore is nice, the quests are nice, the bosses are challenging but incredibly fun to fight, the map is really well-made (except for some areas), the visuals and the sound design + the art direction are all great too.

I honestly don't get the complaints about the difficulty, I can understand the complaints about some areas being annoying to traverse, or about some random enemies being a bit too annoying/damage dealing, but as for bosses, I don't get it, sure, some were a bit challenging but nothing too crazy imo.

Anyway, Silksong is more of what we already had with the OG hollow knight, but expanded upon and even more polished, It's a 10/10 for me.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1760356159}, {"review_text": "One of the best games I have ever played. The story is very well done, the locations are excellent, which is twice as long as the first game, and the soundtracks are really well done. I also really like the bosses and the combat mechanics as well.

Personally, I consider this game to be a strong contender for the GOTY, since I really enjoyed playing it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1759392871}, {"review_text": "It has the soul of the first game (ambience, cute bugs living in a very dark world, soundtrack) while keeping things fresh and interesting by making the main character play and fight very differently. One of the best sequels ever made in my opinion.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1757789267}, {"review_text": "After 7 years in development, hopefully it will have been worth the wait.

Silksong is a very tight and punishing experience, and is certainly not for everyone. If you're expecting something like Hollow Knight with relaxing exploration, a lot of slow shambling enemies, and all of the emphasis put on bosses, you're gonna be disappointed--if you remember the 'flow state' you'd get from the Mantis Lords, Silksong expects that of you in over half of all combat encounters, including regular enemies.

For the people looking for what is in effect "Dark Souls mixed with IWBTG if they made it a cartoon metroidvania", there is no better game than Silksong, and there will likely never be one. The controls are consistent and responsive, the enemies are varied and have great attack variety, I'm still finding new ways to customize my build 25 hours in, and the scope of the world just *keeps getting bigger*.

For what you get, the $20 price tag feels like robbery. They made a world the size of 3 Hallownests and sold it for only $5 more.

Personally, it's a 10/10 experience polished to a mirror finish. But this game will make you *mad.*", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1757421931}, {"review_text": "This game is already gorgeous. Well worth the price and wait.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 19, "timestamp_created": 1756997453}, {"review_text": "Amazing game, but I’m not sure I can call it better than Hollow Knight—at least not yet.
The gameplay is fun, the world is fantastic, and the music is simply sublime. However, the 2–4 minute trek between a bench and a boss fight, combined with a fairly difficult platforming challenge, feels more tedious than enjoyable. The fact that many enemies deal double damage doesn’t help the experience either.
And about the currency system… just let every unit drop rosaries. Simple fix.
I’ve seen a lot of players complain about the diagonal pogo mechanic, and I kind of get it. But after 20–30 minutes of practice, it starts to feel natural, fun, and full of potential.

Overall, if they tone down the double damage on some mobs and tweak the currency system a bit, I could easily say it’s even better than Hollow Knight. Definitely a Game of the Year contender in my book—and I’m not even finished yet.

Thank you, Team Cherry, for yet another banger!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1757277918}]

To be honest, I wasn’t expecting this game to be [b][i]as good and astonishing as it turned out to be[/i][/b]. When I bought it, I thought it was just another story about a god-killer. In reality, it turned out to be an amazing reboot of the series, offering more emotional depth than any of the previous games — and, frankly, more than most games overall.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3369330496
[b]This God of War takes a very different approach compared to its predecessors.[/b] While the earlier games focused on Kratos destroying everything and everyone in his path, this installment delves into themes of remorse, redemption and reckoning with the past. Instead of merely slaying another god (or gods), the story revolves around the father-son dynamic, and the developers handled it masterfully, or at least to a very high standard. The main storyline kept me hooked throughout, and at no point did I feel the urge to stop playing or just drop the game.

[b]The graphics are stunning,[/b] even when compared to newer titles, and [b]the gameplay holds its own.[/b] While [i]I can’t say the gameplay is entirely without flaws[/i], these minor drawbacks don’t detract from the overall experience. I particularly appreciated how Santa Monica Studio crafted a combat system that’s simple yet engaging, epic without feeling overwhelming. I would also like to [i]point out a sense of cyclicality that some players might notice[/i]. There aren’t that many enemy types in the game (aside from the main bosses), and while certain elements are varied in some ways, the core remains the same. [b][i]However, the game manages to counterbalance this repetition effectively, which is quite satisfying and ensures it doesn’t become a significant drawback for the majority of players[/i][/b].
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2925853587
In conclusion, I’d say this game is absolutely worth everyone’s attention. God of War has rightfully earned its accolades (though I wouldn’t rank it above RDR2 in terms of Game of the Year). [h2][b]Here's The Breakdown[/b][/h2]
[h3]A new journey for two began, one ridden with a past that haunts[/h3]
God of War starts off on a surprisingly quiet note. No epic boss fights or gods getting tossed through buildings. Just Kratos, grieving, and chopping wood. It’s a different kind of opening, but one that immediately sets the tone for what kind of story the Santa Monica Studio is going for.

The story takes its time, but in the best way possible. You’re not just rushing to the next objective. You’re uncovering the past, learning about the world, and watching both characters slowly open up. The hack-and-slash element is still there, sure, but the focus is clearly on his role as a grieving father, trying to raise his son while wrestling with his past which he tries to bury and refuses to share with his son. And Atreus? He starts off as a curious, and slightly annoying kid who just wants to make his father proud. But as you progress into the story, you’ll get to see his moments of growth as a person,  from the tantrums and doubts to the realization of who he truly is. Long story short, watching their relationship shift as the journey progresses is one of the most rewarding parts of the game.

Now, not everything lands perfectly. The final boss fight, while narratively satisfying, doesn’t quite hit the “holy crap” and mind-blowing level of hype you'd expect from a game like this. I mean it’s okay, but it could’ve been better. And once the story wraps, that’s it. No post-game plot or extra cutscenes to look forward to. You still have plenty to do, sure, but don’t expect any new twists after the credits roll.

[h3]Unveil the hidden lore scattered across the nine realms[/h3]
Santa Monica studio really nailed the visual aspect of this game. This reimagined vast norse landscape is a marvelous feast for the eyes. With the addition of bifrost, you’ll be able explore some of the nine realms where each of them has its own unique identity and wonders. From the vibrant and colorful land of Alfheim to the haunting atmosphere of Helheim where the dead lingers and barr our way. And as we traverse these realms you’ll uncover tons of optional content that’s actually worth your time. Whether it’s uncovering ancient texts, diving into the backstories of the realms, or just listening to your companion tell absurd-yet-surprisingly-deep myths.

The game world isn’t open-world in the traditional sense, but it gives you plenty of freedom to poke around — which you should. Side quests (or “favors,” as they call them) aren't your typical fetch quests. Some tie beautifully into the lore, others build out the side characters, and a few even carry emotional weight that adds depth to the main narrative. Plus, clearing them affects some scenes in subtle but satisfying ways.

Now for some of the disappointing bits. While exploring the vast and beautiful landscape of the reimagined Norse world is exhilarating and rewarding on its own, the lack of fast travel — which only becomes available very late into the journey — makes revisiting old spots a bit of a chore. Collectible hunting turns into a tedious backtracking session, and that can definitely wear you down. In addition to that, the post-game content, well... if you’re into perfecting builds and hunting rare drops, there’s plenty to grind. The catch? Most of it relies heavily on RNG — and honestly, I’m not much of a fan of that. On top of that, there’s barely any new content after the main story ends, and even New Game+ doesn’t offer much outside of tougher enemies and better loot. In other words there’s minimum replayability. 

[h3]Mashing your way through simply won’t cut it[/h3]
Combat starts off a little basic, but instead of the ol’ and dear partner Kratos used throughout the previous games, we begin with an axe — the Leviathan Axe. Its ice element and Mjolnir-like properties add flair to his new fighting style — and yes, you can fling and recall the bloody thing.
While it’s different from the usual weapon Kratos swings around, every hit with the axe feels heavy and damn right satisfying. Later on, you’ll unlock another weapon (you know the one) and runic skills that completely flip how combat flows. And once swapping between the tools you’ve got becomes second nature? You’re in for a treat.

As I said, combat might start off basic, but don’t be fooled — there’s depth hiding just beneath the surface, and it doesn’t take long before you’re knee-deep in systems that demand real timing, awareness, and control. Plus, Atreus isn’t just tagging along; his support attacks and abilities are surprisingly useful.

Enemy variety can feel a little dull at times — a few are just reskinned versions of earlier fights, which gets old fast. And some fights can feel spongy and down right tedious. But! The game still throws in enough mini-bosses and unique enemy types to keep things interesting. Especially the hidden ones — and honestly, I’d argue some of them are even better than the main bosses.

Additionally, the RPG elements here are solid. You can lean into Runic for flashy special attacks or pump your Strength stat for raw, heavy-hitting chaos. Each armor set offers unique boons and sockets you can fill with gems — found through exploration or side quests — that add even more unique bonuses to mix and match to your liking. It’s not super deep like a full-blown RPG, but it’s more than enough to keep things interesting, especially on harder difficulties.

Yes, you should buy Hitman WoA. It's one of the greatest stealth games of all time and an absolute steal even at $70. And yes, if you're new to the series, this is a good starting point. All you need to know is that you play as the most inconspicuous 6'2 bald man ever created, spend most of the game wearing other peoples' clothes to great effect, and set up traps that would make Kevin McCallister give you a high five. It's amazing. For best results ignore the Mission Stories at first, pay attention to everything you hear and read, and let your heart guide you to your methods of choice. But just to be 100% clear: 

[h1]DO NOT BUY "PART ONE".[/h1]

Nobody knows why the part one edition exists, and most people agree that it shouldn't. All it does is confuse people, and in most cases you just end up spending more money than you needed to. Whatever your justification may be for wanting it, just save yourself some hassle. These are the only things you need (assuming you aren't buying the Deluxe edition, which includes these already):

HITMAN World of Assassination (the standard edition; this sometimes gets moved beneath the Deluxe Edition in the list if only Deluxe is on sale)
HITMAN 3 Access Pass: HITMAN 2 Expansion (accessible individually within the Hitman 3 deluxe bundle)

The Expansion Pass gives you the extra two maps that were in Hitman 2's season pass, as well as a few item packs, and everything in it is worth the $10, but its review score is "Mostly Negative" anyways because of 300 people who bought Part One and thought it would give them all of Hitman 2. It doesn't. Don't be like these people.

There are a few other stray DLCs here and there, like the Celebrity target packs and the rest of the deluxe edition, but I would avoid buying these at first (unless there's a target pack you just really want, like the cool new Casino Royale pack, in which case go for it), for two reasons. The first is that a lot of the side DLCs vary wildly in quality once you get out of the elusive target packs. The second one is less subjective, and more just a factual observation: You will probably never finish everything the base game has to offer.

Just finishing the three campaigns' missions once can easily last you upwards of 30-40 hours, and if you dive back in to see all the possibilities you missed the first time (which you really should!) and unlock the various mastery rewards for each map it will very likely soar past 100. Then there's Hitman 1's Patient Zero mini-campaign, various individual special assignments that revamp existing maps, and seasonal themed maps for various holidays. There's a whole swathe of "Escalation Contracts", silly side contracts that ask you to kill various other NPCs in the existing maps with increasingly constrictive requirements (not all of which are created equally, but a lot of them are extremely funny). There's a roguelike-inspired mode called Freelancer that some people sink hundreds of hours into on its own, and a Contracts mode where people can make and share player-made contracts. There's even a co-op mode coming soon. And if you somehow manage to exhaust all of that, you can load up Hitman 2's Sniper Assassin mode and play the world's deadliest game of Where's Waldo.

What, you thought that was it? No such luck, because now we're gonna talk about Elusive Targets. These were the star of the show back in the Hitman 2016 days; elusive targets are special assassinations that add new NPCs to the existing maps, tasking you with finding and eliminating them. They don't get marked on your minimap or otherwise identified by the game, so you have to explore the map and find them yourself. Sometimes it's as easy as matching them to their photographs, while other times you might have to wait and observe to tell which waiter is your target (most ETs come with a fair amount of new dialogue), and sometimes you don't get a photo to work from at all. But that's not what makes them "elusive" -- it's that they only show up for a few weeks at a time, and you only get one shot at them. There's no saving or loading, no retrying if you fail, and as soon as you complete any objective of the contract, you're locked in. These were a little polarizing in the beginning before people started to see the vision, but personally they've always been my favorite part of the game. They're really tense, in a way that you don't always get from the main game.

Or at least, that's how it worked back then. These days a lot of the Elusive Targets tend to rerun at later points, so they're rarely truly missable, and even then, most of them have been added to a new mode called the Elusive Target Arcade. This mode lets you play a pretty wide selection of elusive targets any time you want (though there is a 12 hour cooldown, to preserve a little bit of the tension), and while it does have a separate reward track from the real things it ensures that you can't truly "miss" the content they add.

In that regard, there are only a few things that have been left by the wayside. The Gary Busey elusive target is seemingly never coming back (but don't worry, I got the bastard for you), Conor McGregor's DLC and its fine fur coat couldn't beat the allegations, and Hitman 2's Ghost Mode, a hilarious and tragically underplayed competitive assassination mode, is now only playable through modded servers. But for the most part, it's actually pretty impressive how much stuff has piled up over the years. Hitman WoA has regular content "seasons", but rather than being heavy on FOMO, the majority of what each season adds just gets permanently added to the game, and outside of those few exceptions you haven't really missed anything important. There are also a few items that were only accessible to legacy players who own Hitman 2016 and Hitman 2, but don't let anyone try to convince you that you missed out on the Black Winter Suit or Outstanding Performance Coin. You did kind of miss out on the Travel Briefcase, but the Executive Briefcase Mk.II replaces it in late game anyways.

When each part first released individually, all three of them were standout titles, but none of them were without quirks. Added when the game was rebranded, this is a Roguelite mode in which you must execute sets of missions (known as campaigns) without dying, and can only bring in limited items. If you fail, you lose everything you brought with you or earned through the campaign. You take on these missions from a customizable Safehouse, gaining access to more items and unlockables based on your progress in the mode. Eventually, it can be a sprawling building with many rooms and decor. Plus, the challenge in this mode can get extremely high depending on the campaigns you undertake.

In terms of graphics, Hitman: World of Assassination is still one of the best-looking games. It's recommended to play it without ray tracing, as RT was added later in development. If you do turn it on, you'll find that it's usually very gorgeous, but the FPS drop from it is immense: not even an RTX 4090 can currently run this game at 60 FPS at 4K with RT on in every situation, even with DLSS. IOI has always done their research when it comes to rendering technologies and implemented extremely good-looking shadows and reflections even without RT. To be honest, if you turn it off, you will likely not even notice much of a difference -- the normal, non-ray-traced graphics are masterful.

In terms of audio, the game sounds overall good, and positional audio is well-implemented. One remarkable weakness is the gun sounds, which often come off a bit weak, poorly thought-out, and too consistent between different guns despite huge weapon variety. As well, there aren't many accents for the NPCs, which may feel strange when NPCs in Japan are speaking to you in a British accent. In lore, 47 is fluent in most languages, so maybe we're supposed to assume that we're getting the translated version. However, it's jarring at first.

Controls are well-made and easy to use, and the game can be played almost as well on a gamepad as keyboard & mouse, outside of headshot aim. You can rebind almost, but NOT QUITE everything. However, outside of "Which key do I press to skip this?" and some menus always being bound to F-keys, etc, this isn't a huge problem; very few keys are blocked. As someone who uses a mouse left-handed, I often run into trouble with this from other titles, but here, there is no issue.

This was my first Hitman title. I was terrible at this game, but in time I worked my way up as far as "SASO" enjoyably. This trilogy, through its three games worth of missions, tells you enough about 47 and his handler Diana to get you by without ever making past games obsolete in their storytelling. It only hints at things revealed in past stories, enough to get you curious, without making you feel left in the dark. It's a great place to start. At first, 47 may seem an entirely cold and uncaring character, and at base levels, he is -- but it's fascinating the true depths he has, which you'll discover.

I would strongly recommend this game to any Hitman fan on the fence, as well as anyone stealth-curious. [{"review_text": "The Castlevania Advance Collection brings together three classic Game Boy Advance titles: Castlevania: Circle of the Moon, Castlevania: Harmony of Dissonance, and Castlevania: Aria of Sorrow. While each game offers a unique experience, the collection as a whole provides a compelling look at the evolution of the Castlevania franchise during this era.

Circle of the Moon: This game stands out for its innovative DSS (Dimensional Shift System), allowing players to combine different cards to create powerful attacks. The difficulty curve is relatively steep, but the rewarding combat and exploration make it a worthwhile challenge. The graphics are simple but charming, fitting the GBA's limitations well.

Harmony of Dissonance: A direct sequel to Circle of the Moon, Harmony of Dissonance features a more linear structure. The DSS is gone, replaced by a more traditional approach to abilities. The game still offers satisfying combat and exploration, but the linearity might feel limiting to some players accustomed to the open world of Circle of the Moon. The graphics and sound are improved over Circle of the Moon, although still characteristic of the GBA era.

Aria of Sorrow: Often considered the best of the three, Aria of Sorrow introduces the Tactical Soul system, allowing players to absorb enemy abilities. This adds a layer of strategic depth to the combat, encouraging experimentation and diverse playstyles. The game also features a larger world map and a more refined gameplay experience compared to its predecessors. The graphics are noticeably improved, with more detailed sprites and backgrounds.

The Collection's Extras: The collection isn't just a simple port. It includes several quality-of-life improvements, such as save states, rewind functionality, and various display options (including the ability to play in their original aspect ratios or widescreen). These features enhance the overall experience significantly, making these older games more accessible to modern players. There is also a gallery of concept art and music, offering a nice touch for fans.

Overall: The Castlevania Advance Collection is a must-have for fans of the franchise and anyone interested in classic action-adventure games. While the individual games have their own strengths and weaknesses, the collection as a whole provides a comprehensive and enjoyable journey through a pivotal period in Castlevania's history. The inclusion of modern conveniences makes these older titles more accessible and enjoyable than ever before.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1752748909}, {"review_text": "Great games, specially Aria.

But got them to tell Konami we need a 3D Collection with Castlevania Curse of Darkness, both versions of Castlevania 64, Lament of Innocence, Castlevania Judgment (the fighting game), Harmony of Despair, and if you throw in Symphony of the Night the community will forever love you.

Like this to make Konami aware.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1742323879}, {"review_text": "A solid collection of the Game Boy Advance titles, all of which are strong in their own right. It was an experimental time, and the experimentation between each of these titles is keenly seen and felt.

[b]Circle of the Moon[/b] is the earliest title of the three. While it has the RPG elements of a modern Metroidvania, it gestures back to the classic Castlevania titles: your movement is deliberate if clunky and enemy damage is high. The story and its characters serve as a means to propel you forward throughout the castle - it is perfectly serviceable. Personally, I most fondly remember Circle of the Moon for its magic system (cards you combine to create effects) and its distribution of optional rewards; progressing along the critical path will reveal to you a number of optional goodies that reward altering your journey even just slightly, such as raising a bridge to snag an item underneath it.

[b]Harmony of Dissonance[/b] is a frenetic blur of motion that catches a lot of flak for its aesthetic presentation. Juste has a garish blue outline that no longer feels necessary on modern technology (the original Game Boy Advance had no backlit screen), and the soundtrack is incredibly divisive with its intentional inclusion of dissonant melodies. I enjoyed only one or two tracks from the game myself. As for gameplay, you are immediately given a forward and back dash that allows you to cross massive spans of the castle in a fraction of the time that it would take in the early stages of Circle of the Moon; later on, your slide is ruthlessly powerful and efficient. However, the momentum is not preserved when you jump, requiring a bit of a learning phase. In terms of exploration, the game offers an enormous experience, but most of its optional areas only offer you a background cosmetic for a specific room in the castle. Exploring the castle is mandatory for a true ending, but its rewards often feel lacking. All in all, Harmony of Dissonance demonstrates some serious growing pains in the franchise, but there's enjoyment to be found here.

[b]Aria of Sorrow[/b] is widely regarded as the most beloved of the three GBA titles on display here, as it has the benefit of learning from all of the titles that come before it. Movement is responsive, you are given more air control akin to other platforming games (and less like classic Castlevania titles), and you obtain a backdash very early on that has some slick combat and movement applications (including some speedrun tech). Its magic system is a promise from the game to the player that every enemy will have a unique soul or ability, which does well to generate an early curiosity! Beware: drop rates vary from enemy to enemy and can quickly result in lots of grinding for a completionist. The soundtrack is comprised of mostly new tracks with the occasional throwback to a classic theme; this, coupled with the game's more modern setting and spry teenage protagonist (not a Belmont!), helps the game to feel like a passing of the torch. Aria of Sorrow is a game I find myself revisiting over and over, be it for a fresh playthrough, challenge runs (e.g. Silver Handgun only), or randomizer mod experiences. Final note: Soma's also kind of a huge dweeb despite his fashion sense and he loves his girlfriend. I love him.

The collection has a bunch of expected functionality, like save states, rewind, galleries, and the like. However, for whatever reason, it lacks a built-in borderless fullscreen option, so - if you're like me - you'll often need to use your computer's shortcut when booting the game up. If you're a fan of the genre and you haven't touched these games yet, you'll get a lot out of the experience - even if only if you treat it like a time capsule.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1757085304}, {"review_text": "just finished Aria of Sorrow and god this game might be one of my favorite games of all time. Super grateful for this collection making these games available on modern platforms, even if half the included games aren't ones I personally care for at all. That doesn't mean they shouldn't be preserved, and I'm glad to see that here. My only real nitpick with this collection is that it never remembers my window size settings, and I wish the gadgets for Circle of the Moon and Aria of Sorrow didn't appear every. Single. Time. I hit an enemy. Limit it to one popup per enemy at a time!

Anyway, my quick thoughts on each game:

[b]Circle of the Moon[/b] - A very important game in the series' history, bringing a SotN-like experience to handhelds, but ultimately one I find too dull and frustrating. The castle design is boring, controlling Nathan is clunky, and there are no tangible rewards for exploring besides life/MP/heart max increases. The DSS system is very cool on paper! But in practice is just a chore of a grind.

[b]Harmony of Dissonance[/b] - Definitely the weakest musically, and Juste is a bit floaty, but I still find this one fun to play. I feel its own central mechanic is a bit underbaked and its castle design can also come off uninspired, but for what it is, it's worth a playthrough. Plus, you get to decorate your own room!

[b]Aria of Sorrow[/b] - A masterpiece and one of my favorite games, period. Soma controls excellently and the soul system is a brilliant way to encourage experimentation and even potentially make each playthrough feel unique. The castle design is superb with an excellent sense of flow, save for maybe one area. There's [i]some[/i] usage of soul swapping that can get a little tedious, but I otherwise have very little to complain about with this one.

[b]Dracula X[/b] - A baffling inclusion, especially with it being a Classicvania, but at least it's available somewhere. This is actually one of my least-favorites in the series for being an obnoxious revision of Rondo of Blood, full of irritating enemy placements and frustrating platforming. The musical conversions and graphics are excellent, but those are the only positives I can think of. And no, it's not an aversion to Classicvanias; I [i]love[/i] CV1, CV3, and Bloodlines!

Overall, if you've never played Castlevania before, and you pick this up and enjoy your time with it, I highly recommend getting the Dominus Collection as well!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1762846969}, {"review_text": "[h1][b]Review[/b][/h1]

[b][i]Castlevania Advance Collection[/i][/b] includes 4 games: 2 of them are disappointing to say the least, 1 is alright, and 1 is great. The collection has [u]substantial quality of life features[/u]. I will not review the collection as a whole; each individual game will be reviewed and scored. I only used the save/load feature in the first two games. Chronological release order:

[hr][/hr]
[h1][b][i]Dracula X[/i][/b][/h1]

[b][u]Playtime: 2 hours, 35 min[/u][/b]

[h3][b]The Highlights[/b][/h3]

[list]
[*]For a reimagination of a 1993 game, the pixel art is still highly appealing. I don't have anything bad to say about the aesthetics.
[/list]

[h3][b]The Drawbacks[/b][/h3]

[list]
[*]The controls SUCK. It's really bad, and I know that this is a mark of an era, but [b]Super Castlevania IV[/b] had much better controls, and it came out 4 YEARS before [b]Dracula X[/b]!

[*]The instant kill abysses are terrible. Again, I understand that this was a thing back then, but it still sucks.

[*]As a result of the controls being awful, the combat is also awful. It's highly imprecise, highly difficult, and unfun.

[*]I was going to only save once per stage at first, but I quickly changed my mind.
[/list]

[h3][b]Conclusion:[/b][/h3]

[b][i]Dracula X[/i][/b] stinks. It's bad from the beginning to the end; aside from the nice Castlevania aesthetics, there isn't anything good about this game. It's not fun at all, and the only thing that makes it "bearable" is the fact that it is kind of part of the Castlevania series.

[h2][b]2/10[/b][/h2]

[hr][/hr]
[h1][b][i]Castlevania: Circle of the Moon[/i][/b][/h1]

[b][u]Playtime: 17 hours, 36 min[/u][/b]

[h3][b]The Highlights[/b][/h3]

[list]
[*]The aesthetics are fine. The sprites aren't as pretty as [b]Symphony of the Night[/b], but it's good enough.

[*]The [b]DSS[/b] is pretty nice. It has many variations of cards that you can combine and evoke. The only bad thing is that... it's kinda rough to make cards drop.

[*]The QOL features help a lot. Being able to see which monsters drop cards or the overall encyclopedia. Although these features are not part of the original game, and without them, the game would be EVEN worse than it is.
[/list]

[h3][b]The Drawbacks[/b][/h3]

[list]
[*]The movement is super stiff. It's the major drawback in this game; it really stinks. Even after you get more abilities that improve your movement, it still feels bad to play.

[*]Combat feels pretty bad because you can't move the way you wish to; it's a huge disservice and gets even worse because of the difficulty spikes.

[*]The game is rather difficult; it gets more difficult with time, and I love challenging games, but when the movement itself feels so sluggish, then the difficulty drifts from being fun to being a painful torment.
[/list]

[h3][b]Conclusion:[/b][/h3]

[b][i]Castlevania: Circle of the Moon[/i][/b] is a bad Metroidvania, not just a bad MV but a [b][u]BAD GAME[/u][/b]; the DSS is a nice feature, but the movement gets in the way of everything else; it's utterly the worst. If it weren't for the save/load, I wouldn't have finished this; I do not recommend.

[h2][b]3/10[/b][/h2]

[hr][/hr]
[h1][b][i]Castlevania: Harmony of Dissonance[/i][/b][/h1]

[b][u]Playtime: 14 hours, 26 min[/u][/b]
[b][u]Misc: 200% Map[/u][/b]

[h3][b]The Highlights[/b][/h3]

The multiplayer (the core of the game) is really really good.  Most of the time it's fairly clean racing.  The MP is truly the reason this game is popular.  No other sim has this level of competition and matchmaking.  Lot's of racing classes and a license level system to ease you into new racing series.  It encourages you to stay in one class for an entire season which is about 12 weeks.

The reason I can't recommend this game is the pricing model.  It absolutely destroys any chance of making this usable.  Paying a (steep) monthly subscription fee, plus $12 per car and $15 per track is insane.  Buying all the content for this game would run you north of $2000.  Buying just the content you will need to get your A license in the racing type of your choice (road, oval, or dirt) will be hundreds.  I am simply not will to pay that kind of money.  I have a life.  That's not ok.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1759457234}, {"review_text": "I created this account to try iRacing one last time, since I had already tried it for 1 month in my main account.
This game is straight up not worth it, you're paying a premium for the illusion of feeling like you're part of an elite cult.

[h1]The positive[/h1]
iRacing sports an incredible amount of variety when it comes to tracks and cars, no game even comes close to it and likely never will.

The cars are beautifully modeled, tons of detail on the interior and exterior of the cars. The setup pages also look believably realistic, with each car sporting very different options for each part you can fine tune.
Not many other games go this far with detail, especially on the setup menus.

There are always people playing this game, I don't think I've ever seen the online player count be below 10k, regardless of the time. Again, no other game in the same genre gets even close, and probably none will ever.
However, this doesn't necessarily mean all races are populated. I'll talk about it in the negative part.

Sadly, that's about it. There are many other positive points but they get so heavily overshadowed by the negative part that they will need to be addressed in the next part. Also, there is one big problem with this game that essentially renders all these good things pointless anyways.

[h1]The negative[/h1]
Even though there's a lot of variety, a lot of series will see a very small attendance number. I think part of this is because many events have a lot of waiting time between races, forcing people who want to race more often to the series that do run more often.
Most players will be doing sports car racing, oval and formula run rather similar numbers at a glance. The dirt racing stuff is kind of a wasteland, I'm pretty sure you'll be seeing the same names for a long time if you decide to race those series.
Some series run tons of events with only 10 players at most, sometimes there may be a spike at a certain hour but that's the one time during the day that series sees multiple splits.
Most people will be doing MX5s or GT3s, but GT3s only run every two hours although enough events cross over for constant racing. I don't know about Oval or Formula, but I'm sure it works the same way but with less people.

Most tracks are still missing properly modeled rumble strips, they just play sound and have slightly less grip but that's about it. They don't bump the car up and down, it's very easy to just drive over the curbs without the car really protesting.  Granted, even on the tracks with proper collisions on the curbs the cars still behave nice, but the difference is noticeable and you have to be more careful to not make a mistake when driving over them.
Trackside objects range from okay to 2008. More recent tracks, or tracks that had been revamped recently, look fine, but there are a lot of tracks that look very dated. At least the driving surface is nice and detailed, but they really look a generation old.

The car collisions and general netcode doesn't feel great either. Sometimes the smallest contact gives you tons of damage, sometimes a pretty hard hit does nothing.
Their lag compensation stuff is pretty inconsistent, but sadly people don't play with that in mind...
Most of my races I've just sandbagged quali and just took the scraps during the race. If you're trying to go through the licenses to unlock the races for the content you purchased, be prepared to avoid racing because it's far too dangerous to go close to other cars.

Then of course, the big iRacing tyre debacle.
It is as you've heard, these tyres cannot go over the limit without throwing a fit. You have to under drive the car to be on the limit, the tyres will be screeching and screaming but your inputs are like if you're driving grandma to church.
It's very counterintuitive, but honestly, once you get the hang of it it's pretty nice.
The low speed grip is nice and the cars do feel very darty and planted, a big contrast when compared to many newer sims that have a very sloppy and delayed initial bite to the tyre. But this comes at the cost of the tyres just turning off the moment you press the throttle a bit too hard, or trailbraked a bit too well.
It's very easy to tell when you go over the limit, but once you notice that it's almost always too late. To be fair, it's easy enough to stay under the limit, but of course you have to push the limits of the tyres to go fast and the game punishes you very harshly when you go over.
Even the updated GT3 tyres have this issue, and this was the main reason I wanted to try iRacing. If this is worlds better than what they had before, I honestly feel bad for whoever was driving GT3s before. The car will just wipe out on you when the tyres are on the colder side and even when up to temp it's very easy to just have the car die on you.
The MX5s are absolute hell to drive, these cars are thrashed around the track in real life, but in iRacing you need to drive them with clinical precision. You're still doing 4 wheel slides through the turns, but your inputs really don't match what the car is doing. It's very, very awkward.

[h1]The worst part[/h1]
This would all be acceptable if it wasn't for the insane premium you have to pay.
Steam is the cheapest way to get into this game, I bought 1 year of iRacing for ~20 euro (yes, after tax). I also bought two GT3s because I wanted to have those so I could compare the driving with other games.
However, once this subscription is over I'll have to pay ~80 euros to renew it, and that is on Black Friday which is the cheapest discount they offer for renewals.

But the subscription is just the beginning, then there's a fee of ~14 euros per car and ~17 per track. The final price will depend on your country or state's VAT, but it won't be too far from that.
If you decide to get into a series that doesn't run a lot of free content, you'll be paying around 150 euros to be able to race it. And that will only work for that season which changes every quarter. They'll keep making you buy new tracks if you want to do all the races in your series of choice.
There's a discount if you buy stuff on bulk, but it's such a small amount that won't really make a dent unless you're spending thousands on getting all the content in the game.
THOUSANDS to have everything in this game, not hundreds.
This is how they lock you into their game. You spend thousands on the content, so what's another $200 every 2 years to keep using it.

Maybe it's my luck, but this doesn't help with the quality of the racing anyways. You'd think that people who get into this game and pay hundreds every year for the content and the game would take it more seriously and avoid dumb moves, especially with how this game's netcode can be pretty bad. 
Top split, bottom split, doesn't matter, a lot of people just don't know how to drive and they just ruin everything. Again, this would be fine if it wasn't for the cost.
On the topic of the netcode, a lot of people say the price of the subscription is justified since they need to keep the service running, but other games are doing a better job while being a fraction of the price.

Yeah and unfortunately this game isnt playable offline without a subscription even for tracks and cars you have bought. So unless you plan on committing $120 a year + $$$ for cars and tracks long-term its HIGHLY Non Recommended.

I have been playing Le Mans Ultimate which is the same boat (subscription based) but offers free ranked races without one and also gives you an option to buy the dlcs and pay the cheaper subscription (even the more expensive one is $40-50 less than iracing) or with the full subscription gives you all the DLC tracks and cars so I can sub for a month when I have extra money and still do free races on months im not!", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1750908049}, {"review_text": "Most people consider iRacing THE sim-racing title, warts and all. There isn't anything like iRacing within the sim-racing sphere. At almot any time of the day, you'll find a race somewhere being ran. Drivers celebrating every victory like it is their last. Others relishing in the agony of defeat. 

It's what made me finally take the jump. After 10+ years of sim-racing, it was more or less what I expected (which is a bit disappointing).

It's practically an MMO given the purchasing model and rather open-ended content structure. If there's a series you want to run, you'll be paying hand over fist for every track and car. If you want truly everything, it'll be thousands of dollars in addition to your standard subscription fee every month by the way..

If you're anything like me, you'll finally dip a toe in. Pick a few series you want to run based off of your real-life motorsport tastes..but grow annoyed with the uninutitive physics model.
While improved from previous iterations, it still has several massive issues. To keep it somewhat brief
- Tyres insanely sensitive to oversteer, tyre slip 
- Cars having too much aero relative to IRL counterparts
- ABS & hybrid engine systems functioning unlike they do in real life
Not to mention even larger issues that plague niche licenses like dirt road & dirt oval. (Don't even get me started on the plague that is the idea of a setup shop having a bloody subscription service when you are already paying a subscription for the service in the first place. How about a subscription for better overlays than the dated ones in-game too! Might as well make a five-layer lasagna out of all these money-milking services!)

Don't get me wrong, the matchmaking system iRacing uses to populate their service is nearly 1/1 but it has its own flaws.

You start your journey with a rookie safety license which grants you access to beginner-friendly cars to help you figure out the basics of race procedure and racecraft. 

 Even as you get into higher safety rating classes and higher splits, the racing standards don't improve. Of course this varies from license to license but generally is pretty hit or miss. If anything, they get worse as drivers get faster & faster; and more daring and reckless with their offensive driving manuvers. For example, when a B-class sportscar race with a average iRating (iRacing's ELO system) of 2.2k is filled with more dangerous drivers than a comparable lobby in C-class with a average rating of 1.5k, then surely there is something wrong right? I can't imagine putting in the effort to get a fairly high iRating in your favorite class only for the racing standards to improve marginally or even get worse in some cases.

 I've seen people chalk most of this up to the growth of sim racing since the pandemic (the more apples you pick, the more rotten you'll find) but I think it's two-fold. iRacing's flawed, no-fault safety rating system contributes to this too. Using the same hand to punish someone avoiding an incident or getting caught up in another racer's reckless mess as you do if they are wrecking people just didn't make sense to me. It's a complicated issue that I don't really know if it has any answer. Maybe it's me getting burnt out and disappointed with the overall experience with the service but the general lack of a racing standard, particuarly across the road racing licenses is what shocked me. 

Not to mention the hivemind of a community who will sycophantically praise iRacing for its feature list (which is already being replicated for a much cheaper cost for other devs or community members of other titles) while deflecting any and all  critique back at frustrated users.


(I'm no world-beater, for what it's worth. My iR across sportscar sits around 1.8k and 1.7k in open-wheelers. Oval, dirt oval and dirt road are there or even higher. I know I've raced way too much and won often enough in the six months I've been on iRacing to know that I don't completely suck.)

Nevertheless, if you have the patience, time and most importantly, money to pay the costs to truly get everything you'd want out of iRacing (it being your main hobby of choice), then I'd say go for it.

If you're a average or above average sim racer who wants to actually enjoy the hobby and not waste a bunch of money, then stick with titles like Automoblista 2 and Assetto Corsa. Not to forget older titles like rFactor 2, GTR2, NR2003, or even older titles like the fantastic Grand Prix Series or the underrated IndyCar Racing II.

There's plenty of ways to enjoy this hobby in a fun & healthy way; I think for most people, iRacing doesn't factor into that. In short - this game requires kernel level anticheat (Easy Anti Cheat) but you only find out about it after you violate refund policy for subscription based games.

Full story - this game has requirement which is not mentioned anywhere, neither on the store page, nor when you click "launch" in steam, nor there any mentions during downloading/installation phases. Initially it launches sort of *manager* client where you browse in-game shop, race schedule etc. , then once you found an event you'd like to take part in you click "race" button, that's when the *simulation* client is being launched which is where you actually drive and which happily throws an error at you "easy anti cheat not found". After googling you find out that there are Easy Anti Cheat installion files buried somewhere inside game files and that you have to manually go there and install this anticheat. The trick is that this game is subscription based and steam has different refund rules for such, namely you can only refund your subscription in 48hrs period and only if you haven't *used the service* after subscription period became active. Since I've been shown the error message after launching the *manager* client I've technically used their service even though I wasn't able to take part in a single race and thus my refund request was rejected.
