Marvel Rivals uses engagement-optimized matchmaking (EOMM), which means the game doesn't prioritize giving you fair matches but matches that are most likely to keep you playing. The result of that are massive winstreaks and massive losestreaks. Every game is a steamroll for one side and your actions feel useless. You could be the best player on the game but if you are on a lose streak it won't matter how good you are. The opposite is also true, you could run off the map and contribute nothing to your team, but if you are on a win streak you are gonna win. As long as Marvel Rivals keeps  this matchmaking system in place I can not recommend this game to anyone. The first few matches are fun but when you realize how it works it just makes you not want to turn the game on(which you can see if you look at steam charts).", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 15, "timestamp_created": 1752442337}, {"review_text": "I love the game but, The community and its fan base sucks.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 13, "timestamp_created": 1759606866}, {"review_text": "If you are not interested in playing this game in Ranked mode, I do recommend this game. But if you are, then I don't recommend it, and here's the reasons why:

Competitive Matchmaking is not skill based, and it shows.

Every match is a curbstomp, and you are either giving it, or receiving it. EOMM (Engagement Optimized Match Making) is not geared towards fair games, it's geared towards player engagement, and one of its main criteria is played time, not rating. Once I learned of this, I decided to try some things.

So, some experiments that yielded consistent results (that is, happened five times in a row for each): if you keep playing on a losing streak, the algorithm will just think your engagement is not affected with losing, so it will use you as fodder to feed winning streaks for others (tested with two separate 10-match losing streaks after a single win, one after the other. Enough to knock me down from Celestial II to Grandmaster II). If you quit the game after two or three losses, you will guarantee a win on your next login (five out of five tries). If your winning streak makes you climb a rank, you will start a losing streak two wins into that rank (five out of five tries).

Take it with a grain of salt, of course, but I don't think it's luck.

The goal of this EOMM system is to keep you engaged in a psychological hamster wheel. Once you start winning, you ride that dopamine high hard, until the game serves you a loss. And then the game keeps serving losses, trying to get you to chase that high again, testing your limits, but it will only realize it pushed too hard when you quit the game out of frustration. So, to placate you it will give you a win or two when you return, then a loss or two, keep you playing, keeping it tame.

And eventually a streak will begin, either winning or losing, rinse and repeat. The end result is that too many players are boosted by the artificial wins the algorithm serves. I'm writing this review after a match in Grandmaster II where none of my teammates made KOs, while the other team had 10-20 each. This is something I have never seen in 30 years of gaming, not even in bot matches.

As I said, every match is a curbstomp one way or the other. Fair matchmaking means the matches should be close, should be intense victories, but that only happens on 1/20 matches. What we have here is people that climb the rankings because they only play a couple of hours a day, get their couple of wins, and when they log off, the algorithm takes it as "no engagement", and keeps serving wins to people who clearly shouldn't get them in a competitive setting, just to keep them coming back.

Me, I'm not a particularly good player. I dabble, and I can aim and play reasonably well, and that got me to Celestial II. But I've been through massive 10 match losing streaks multiple times, and those losing streaks aren't against incredibly good players, it's just having really bad teams one after the other. You could argue this review is a huge amount of copium, but the evidence is so egregious that it comes to a point where you truly wonder what's going on, with no ego. One thing is "I played terribly, we lost because of that, but my ego won't let me accept it, so I'll blame the healers", and another is having the entire team play terribly against a team that plays flawlessly. It simply is not fair.

In any case, this system is very documented. It is patented, and Netease devs have published papers about it. Here's the disclarimer that there's no direct confirmation that Marvel Rivals uses it, but skill-based matchmaking never felt like this, both in win-ratios, and in match quality.

It's a shame. The game is fun, the mechanics are really good, it really is what Overwatch should have been. But with this type of matchmaking, chasing the competitive grind is simply not worth it. I'll keep coming back for the Quick Play and battlepass, but the matchmaking ruined any prospects of seriously devoting any more time to this.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 103, "timestamp_created": 1747018240}, {"review_text": "Jarvis, solo ult the Rocket Racoon.

The art style and graphics in general are awesome and fortunately the performance is also working flawlessly even when considering how good it looks and due to dealing with the amount of crazy transitions and huge amount of effects on screen (both in-game and UI/Menus).

This system is designed to keep players playing as much as possible, without necessarily concerning itself with keeping matchmaking balanced or giving you fair, skill-based matches. It does not reward consistency or skill alone, and manipulates your matches based on play habits and predicted emotions.

You gotta be f***ing kidding me I hope learn a valuable lesson behind this.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 45, "timestamp_created": 1753572459}, {"review_text": "Overall, an enjoyable game. But, before I get into why I like it, I'll explain what's going on with its review score first.

[h2]Why is it reviewed so poorly?[/h2]

There are a few reasons. There were apparently some pricing issues in China. Some people felt the game was too punishing. Then it was updated and some people felt it became too forgiving. But I'm going to focus on what I think are the biggest reasons.

Edit: A comment was added that explains things a bit more. I'll add it to the bottom of this review for more visibility.

[h3]Performance[/h3]

Many people were hit by performance issues. Honestly, I feel like the minimum and recommended specs are too optimistic. Instead of just trusting them, I'd recommend doing some research to see how your setup will perform.

[h3]Censorship[/h3]

Yup. This game takes place during the downfall of the Ming dynasty. You fight historical figures, and you can also get attacked by civilians. Turns out some people were offended that you could kill Han Chinese from the Ming dynasty. To handle this, the game was censored in a post-release patch. And, honestly, the censorship just sucks. The censorship changes the story, as characters who died now live on. And it was just so clumsy and awkward. After the censorship, when you defeat a historical character, instead of falling to the ground they just... stop. It looks like a bug, not a feature. It looks like what happens when someone's internet breaks in a multiplayer game. It ruins the moral choices and tragic tone of the game. Before, when civilians attack you by throwing rocks (which barely do damage), you could choose to fight back, or show them mercy by leaving them alone. But now that choice is made for you, since they don't attack you and you can't attack them.

[b]The censorship significantly affected [i]an entire gameplay section.[/i][/b] There was a whole part that was originally a 3-way fight between you, soldiers, and monsters. The censorship made those soldiers unkillable, and they no longer attack you, so now it's a 2v1 with you and soldiers fighting monsters, and just makes that whole area so trivial.

[hr][/hr]

Alright, with that out of the way, here's what I think about the game itself.

[h2]Gameplay mechanics[/h2]

I [i]loved[/i] the gameplay mechanics. I don't play many souls-like games, so forgive me if I gush over something that's pretty standard.

First, there's Skyborn Might. Might are points that you can spend to cast spells, use weapon class skills (called Disciplines), or unique skills for each weapon. Gaining Might is so satisfying. The basic way to gain Might is to execute perfect dodges. Basically, you get rewarded for using the I-frames in a dodge. After a few upgrades, you can also gain might from attack combos or parrying. I just loved this risk and reward system, and I got to play this game fast and aggressively, which I like.

Speaking about risk and reward, there's also the Madness system. When your Madness is high, you deal more damage, and also some of your moves get stronger. But you also take more damage at high Madness. If you die while your Madness is too high, then it will spawn the Inner Demon where you last died, which will fight you (or other enemies).

The variety of moves is also great. Like I said, there are Disciplines, and weapon skills. The basic Disciplines are like blocking while using an axe or an evasive kick while using a sword. But you can unlock and equip new ones for weapons in a matching class. And the weapon skills are great. For example, with Skyborn Might, you can make a whip sword extend and hit enemies that are far away. There isn't a lot of weapon variety, but each weapon feels special, thanks to these skills. Some Disciplines and weapon skills can also be mixed into a combo, allowing you to do things like perform the strongest move in a light attack chain in 3 moves instead of 5. There's also a lot of magic with interesting animations and effects. The magic isn't your basic "shoot fire out of your hands" stuff.

And while I'm speaking about variety, I have to mention the armor. Armor sets are divided into head, chest, arm, and leg armor. You can mix and match, but you can also alter any piece of armor [i]to look like any other piece of armor,[/i] so stats don't limit your style and vice-versa. Nearly every time you beat a boss, you get the chance to get their armor, too, and steal their look.

[h2]Exploration[/h2]

I also loved exploration. Each time you enter a new area, it feels like a maze. But once you open up a few shortcuts, every area turns out to be simple and interconnected. There's just something satisfying about fighting through a tough area, then opening up a shortcut that lets you rest at a shrine before going back. And there are a lot of secrets to look for. Funnily enough, some great secrets are found by falling for traps, like grabbing an item on a breakable platform.

[h2]Visuals[/h2]

Medieval China with a horror twist looks really cool. Sometimes the game looks beautiful, and sometimes really gruesome. I'll often stop just to admire the scenery. A temple under siege at sunset. A field of flowers in the moonlight. An underground torture chamber with monsters hanging from the walls and ceilings. The art direction is just great. What I like is that they always choose the best lighting for the environment, even if it isn't realistic. You can walk out of a bright and sunny forest and into an autumnal scene, and watch the lighting rapidly change from white to a deep orange. The sun and moon don't follow the rules of time, but instead do whatever looks the most pretty, which was a great decision.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3548997012

[h2]Challenge[/h2]

I played about half the game before version 1.5, and half after, so this is a bit tough to judge. But it seems like the game is the most difficult in the beginning, before you have access to a variety of moves and magic. I died a lot to early-game bosses, but the final few bosses rarely took many tries. Some moves are absolutely broken against certain bosses, and will make them trivial.

[hr][/hr]

That's mostly what I have to say. I was tempted to give a negative review to voice my complaints about the censorship, but I wanted to be honest. And, honestly, even with the flaws and disappointment, I still liked this game. At first, it might seem like a generic souls clone, but it gets a lot more interesting after a few hours.

Wuchang honestly took me by surprise in many ways that we will discuss in the pros and cons. 

PROS:

Graphics - This game is absolutely gorgeous in every way. The detail in the game is insane. The Chinese architecture really shines here in many moments throughout the game and I caught myself stopping to take a lot of screen shots. Wuchang herself is highly detailed and the enemy bosses will blow you away with some of their abilitiies and how awesome it looks with the particle effects etc. Overall this game looks beautiful and is one of the better looking soulslike games. 

Game play - The game play is Wuchang really surprised me. At first, I thought it to be simplistic but immediately I was proven wrong. As i upgraded Wuchang and went through the skill tree, my strategies began to change. Before I knew it, there was dozens of play styles to explore and options to choose from, multiple buffing effects that you can upgrade in different ways, temperance and Benediction stones to customize your play style and "clash" / Swift draw which allows you to further enhance your play. Overall from a game play perspective you WILL be satisfied as a souls player because there is a lot of skill and strategy here to find and build maxing.

Difficulty - This game is extremely difficult. There is literally no moment of rest or reprieve. Even when you feel like you can let your guard down...well...I wont spoil it, but theres a really messed up mechanic in this game that will most likely get 99% of souls players the first time it happens. If you are looking for a challenge, this is it. This is one of the most challenging souls like games I have played and I have played way too many. It will be rage inducing, but rewarding. Challenging, but fun. I loved it personally.

Gear Customization - This game features insane amounts of customization that actually matter. Between the weapon times, gear you can find/loot, upgrades in your skill trees and the temperance / benediction stone slots, this game has it all. You will be min maxing all the time and its super fun to figure out best builds for the situation (no piece of gear is best for all situations)

World Design - This game is TOP TIER world design. So many short cuts, so many caves to explore, so many places to see. It is truly insane some of the levels. When you eventually unlock the jungle / forest, you will know exactly what I mean. This is when I realized "holy crap this is insane" moment. They did a really great job putting together the world and making it ALL connect. Exploration in this game is just too dam fun. 

Boss Battles / Design - This game features really full and cool looking boss fights. There's no where near as much bosses as say Black Myth Wukong, but every boss feels fun and impactful. There are side bosses / hidden bosses / quest line bosses that you can fight, which give you that feeling of exploration. 

NPC Design - The NPC's in this game are pretty interesting. Each with their own story and why they are there. Multiple quest lines (some more important than others) but still impactful. Plenty of items to give them to further quest lines and explore more dialogue. They all look vastly different as well.

Ambient Sound / Music - This game features incredible ambient sound. It is seriously so good. The music is mainly saved for bosses and the music HITS. They did a great job with setting the tone and feeling of whatever you are experiencing in the music you are hearing.

Value - This game offers tremendous value. The replayability, the overall length of the game and all of this for $50 retail? This is another $50 victory in the year of 2025 with many $50 victories over the increasingly demanding $80 industry. 

CONS:

Stability issues - This game ran perfect for me since the start, even before the patches. I will say that, however; this game has a ton of issues at launch. Stability and performance issues through the roof, that thankfully the developers quickly addressed, but still is unacceptable to release a game in that state for many people. It's a good thing the developers are trying to fix it quickly, because there's a incredible game here to find, BUT, it is still something to note and mention because it did happen and is not something that should happen. 

Repeating Enemy NPC's - The enemy NPC's you will fight, outside of bosses, are very repetitive. There are moments where it does vary pretty nicely in some areas but after a while, youll feel like your fighting the same enemies most of the time. 

EVERY LEVEL IS BLIGHT TOWN FROM DARK SOULS - Okay so this is a personal issue for me. I love the world design, love the graphics, super fun to explore and all that...But I couldn't shake the feeling that almost every dam level in this game was modeled after Blight Town in Dark Souls. It is absolutely infuriating sometimes. I understand the desire for difficulty and I am okay with that, but dam does everything really need to be blight town? Eventually you start to escape that feeling towards the end...Only to end up in some other totally messed up situation. Regardless, I couldn't escape that feeling of "the developers saw blight town and wanted to make an entire game of it". You can make a difficult game without making it all feel like one area people notoriously hated in another game lol. 

Emotionless Wuchang - Wuchang is not a character you create like in a souls like game. Shes her own characters whos journey you explore. When I tell you Wuchang is lifeless I mean it. This is no eve from stellar blade with her own personality. Wuchang barely does anything other than stare lifeless and look good while doing it. I expected a little more from Wuchang to be honest. 

Animation Lock - This game has some of the worst animation lock I've seen. Not only that, when Wuchang is knocked down, unless you get very lucky you are exposed for an extremely long time where you cant do anything and also still take damage. It's insane. Couple this with one of the LONGEST healing times I've ever seen in a souls like game and you will find yourself locked to no end. This becomes less apparent as the game progresses and you unlock more abilities (clash especially helps with this when used properly) but still overall it's insane. They really need to speed up the healing animation at minimum.

[h2] Positives - [/h2]

- Level design is well done. - Boss design so far has been pretty cool (except a certain woman in a water area who was rather dull).
- I like the madness mechanic, it's fun.
- Funny dancing guy.
- Outfits are pretty cool.

[h2] Performance/Optimization [/h2]

This game isn't graphically any more impressive than other games larger in scope and that have released before it, yet, it has forced up-scaling, and performs worse than those other better looking games. (not including MHW lmao).
If you don't mind ghosting and grainy artifacts, then up-scaling/FG will make this game playable for anyone with a mid range set-up. 
I didn't really have any issues with performance consistency, and found it perfectly playable at mostly stable 90+ FPS, but I just think that there isn't really any justification for the lack of optimization that requires up-scaling to get decent and stable frames, and I'm really tired of games relying so heavily on DLSS/FSR.
The recommended/minimum specs should NEVER be tested and listed with up-scaling on. 
Up-scaling tech is fantastic, but it's a monkeys paw, because while it should allow us to get more frames at higher resolutions with heavy tech like ray-tracing, instead, it's used in place of good optimization, and we end up with a net zero gain overall, or even worse than where we were before up-scaling was around.

[h2] Story [/h2]

I found the narrative to be overall a bit... Directionless? 
I understand that Souls games are very vague and the narrative is mostly optional, but they always make sure that from the jump, you understand the big, overarching goals (Kill these four dudes and use their souls, burn the tree, link the flame etc etc).

[h2] Combat [/h2]

[h3] Animations [/h3]

The animations in this game are all quite flashy, you do spins, and jumps and flips, and during all of that, you might get a hit-box out two or three times, meanwhile, while you're spinning around before your attack actually comes out, you're wide open to getting hit. 
Flashy animations are awesome in character action games, DMC, Bayonetta, MGRR, Nier etc, they're amazing games with flashy combat. 
Flashy animations are just kinda frustrating in a souls game though most of the time, I mostly don't use weapon arts with long animations in Elden Ring unless I'm OP'd. 
I want to get a hit out, and be able to back off. That's the point of a souls game right? Taking hits bad, enemies do a heap of damage and can stun-lock you, you don't want to risk dying and having to run back.
They have this "Clash" system there, to mitigate this a bit, so you can do a flashy combo, but it feels like a band-aid on something that doesn't feel like it fits. 
Pulling a combo string and hoping the move with the clash is timed when the enemy decides to attack, and not in between, just feels cumbersome when you can just poke with a spear instead and reliably avoid the risk.

[h3] Fights [/h3]

I have a few issues with the combat itself in this game, first, you can get hit during your get-up animation, which is ridiculous.
Sometimes you'll perfect dodge an attack, but end up still within a lingering hit-box, so you'll take damage anyway.
Weapons and hit reactions feel a bit lackluster.

[h3] Progression [/h3]

Progression in this feels really underwhelming. I don't feel like I have a lot of fine control over my build, and leveling up doesn't feel all that impactful. 
The skill tree is an interesting idea, but I feel like tying the skills directly to specific weapons, and having us allocate stats individually like other souls games would have both made the weapons feel more important, and given us more of a sense of accountability and ownership over our game-play. 

[h2] Gooner Stuff [/h2]

I don't really get the hype man, it's there I guess, but SB did it much better. Aside from that, I think a lot of the costumes I've found so far look pretty cool, so ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

[h2] Summary [/h2]

This game isn't BAD, I just don't find myself having a lot of fun while playing it, and when there are SO many good games to play right now, I don't feel like it's a time sink that I can recommend personally.
For me, I need good loot/progression, really satisfying combat, a really engaging story, or the holy grail of all three... This game just doesn't quite hit the mark on any of these for me.
I'm sure there are plenty of people who will really enjoy it, and I hope these devs are able to make more stuff, and refine their product.

I had a great time with it.

The level design is one of its standout features. The world feels thoughtfully interconnected, with areas linked both horizontally and vertically in a way that really reminded me of Dark Souls 1. That satisfying moment of realization “Wait, I ended up here without a loading screen?” happens often. It’s impressive. That said, it can get confusing. The paths sometimes fork unexpectedly, and you might find yourself completely lost only to stumble onto a hidden secret or shortcut. It’s a little chaotic, but it works.

Combat is fast-paced and packed with depth. There are a lot of unique systems at play "Skyborn Might" gives you flashy, weapon specific skills, while "Discipline" adds extra movesets. There’s also "Temperance" for flexible builds and a massive skill tree to experiment with. One thing I appreciated you don’t have to upgrade each weapon individually, refinement levels apply across all weapons of the same type. There’s also a precise parry/counter mechanic, a stun system called Obliterate, and a Madness mechanic that raises both your damage and the damage you take if you die or kill human enemies. It’s a lot to take in, but once you get the hang of it, it really freshens up the formula.

Bosses are tough. Their move sets are long, aggressive, and sometimes frustrating especially their unpredictable movement but they deliver those classic high-stakes fights fans of the genre live for.

As for the world and lore, it’s atmospheric and rooted in Chinese mythology, but to be honest, I didn’t pay a ton of attention to the story. Like most Soulslikes, the lore is fragmented hidden in item descriptions or buried in obscure NPC questlines. One thing worth noting is that there have been some post-launch plot changes due to censorship in mainland China, which might impact how the narrative is received after recent patches.

In the end, Wuchang offers top-tier exploration, intense combat, and plenty of memorable moments. It might not be the most polished game in the genre, but it brings fresh ideas to the table. [{"review_text": "Let me begin by saying this: if you're a fan of the Avatar universe, love open-world exploration, and want an immersive solo adventure—GET THIS GAME. The campaign is solid, the world feels rich and alive, and the pacing avoids the usual open-world bloat. It's a surprisingly well-crafted experience that hits especially hard for fans of science fiction or cinematic worldbuilding.

But if you're hoping to play multiplayer?
[b]DON’T.[/b]

My wife, a lifelong Avatar fan, picked up the game at launch and loved it. I joined her a few months later, and we dove into co-op—and it was magical. It quickly became one of my favorite shared gaming experiences of all time. The gunplay, traversal, and co-op fluidity made every session feel like a movie we were starring in together.

Then, in April, mid-playthrough and deep into Act 3, a patch dropped that effectively destroyed that joy.

As of the update, [b]guest players in co-op no longer receive progression for collectibles, power-ups, or stat upgrades.[/b] While quest progression is still saved—so yes, you can still play the campaign together—any meaningful character progression must now be earned in your own world, solo. This means you’ll have to revisit and re-collect every Sapling, Bellsprig, and upgrade node just to keep up.

In a genre already flirting with grind, this update turned co-op from joyful into punishing. The magic we had—sprinting through the trees, soaring on our Ikrans, discovering new lands together—was undercut by the knowledge that only one of us was really progressing anymore.

And worst of all?
[b]There is no valid reason for this change.[/b]
If it was to prevent some form of duplication or stat inflation—let players make that choice. This isn’t a competitive or PvP experience. It's a chill, story-rich RPG meant to be shared. This update didn’t solve a problem. It created one.

I want to love this game. And in many ways, I still do. It’s unfairly criticized as a “Far Cry reskin” when it’s actually something far more interesting. Think Far Cry Primal with a sci-fi lens and a Halo-style assault rifle. When it works, it works beautifully and does some cool things that no other RPG has done as well.

But I can’t recommend a game that broke our shared adventure mid-journey.

[b][h1]PROS.[/h1][/b]
[b]•Fun exploration that feels fresh and rewarding.[/b]
[b]•Satisfying, simple gunplay that keeps combat fun.[/b]
[b]•Traversal and climbing are incredibly smooth.[/b]
[b]•Story and pacing are better than expected.[/b]
[b]•Mount system is fluid and engaging.[/b]
[b]•Price is fair* for how much content you get.[/b]
[b]•Customization is intuitive and surprisingly robust.[/b]
[b]•30+ hours of content for story; 60+ for completionists.[/b]
[b]•Two out of three major zones are jaw-dropping.[/b]

[b][h1]CONS.[/h1][/b]
[b]•Bugs and technical hiccups are still present.[/b]
[b]•Post-patch multiplayer removes guest upgrade progression.[/b]
[b]•That multiplayer nerf is bad enough to deserve a second bullet point.[/b]
[b]•A key story character is genuinely hard to listen to.[/b]
[b]•Crafting feels pointless for most of the game—looting is better.[/b]
[b]•Enemy AI often behaves like it’s in a comedy sketch.[/b]
[b]•Stealth mechanics are far too forgiving.[/b]
[b]•Hacking minigame grows stale fast.[/b]
[b]•Male player voice sounds like an edgy anime cliché.[/b]
[b]•Requires strong hardware and MUST be installed on an SSD.[/b]
[b]•One of the three main biomes is clearly less polished.[/b]

[b][h1]TL;DR.[/h1][/b]
If you're here for a powerful single-player journey—[b]buy it and enjoy it.[/b] It’s a love letter to Pandora and a joy to explore.

If you're here to play with someone else—[b]you’ll still get story progression in co-op, but all meaningful upgrades must now be earned solo.[/b] That change turned a beautiful experience into a frustrating one.
[b]Skip it for co-op. It’ll waste your time—or worse, break your heart.[/b]

I am in the final unlockable area of the game, level 19, solo playing. Making this spoiler-free as possible.
------
PROS
------
- Honestly, beautiful game. It's been a lot of fun. 

- In fighting back the RDA, there are multiple base types. It doesn't feel like a repeated "go here and do the mission" (even though that's what it is) because 'the mission' is always changing.

- A lot of customization for my Na'vi and Ikran, without spending any money on the Ubisoft crap. The clothes and weapons actually look amazing. 

- The three clans you meet in this game, and the respective areas, are really unique and stand out a lot. They make the game feel more alive and special. I love walking around and coming across random Na'vi who are like "hey you want this super awesome item??"

- The story is amazing so far. There's been maybe 2-3 times so far where I've gotten the usual "tragedy war music", which kind of pulls me out of the immersion because I Know it's a theme song of war. Outside of that, music has been beautiful, story has been beautiful and sad and emotional, I wish people were nicer. Also I love that when you're sneaking around, and you fire off a shot, the music always naturally kicks up. You go from suspense to a "jumpscare" sound effect, but YOU'RE the jumpscare.

- Lesbians. 

- Took me 20-25 hours just to get my Ikran. I'm putting this as a pro because 1) I wound up doing a LOT of side quests instead of gunning for it, so maybe it only took this long because of the way I played; 2) fast travel is pretty much immediately available if you have a lot of food to do it, so this wasn't tedious for me; 3) I tried to run around as much as possible in the first level and this really got me familiar with the environment. 

- THE PARKOUR. The running, the climbing, the jumping, the falling: it's all beautiful and strategic. I haven't had a single movement bug. If it's a branch that LOOKS like it can support me, it probably can. I loved Mirror's Edge and this gave me similar vibes. Similarly, there's the option to change your jump on the controller to a trigger if you want to do that. 

- Though I only got to experience it for a few hours (see below), I loved playing with the controller. I loved the pressure-sensitive controls. Though, to be fair, I am way better at aiming with a mouse. 

- I GOT THIS GAME FOR $20. ON SALE. WORTH.
------
CONS
------
- There's a few known bugs about this game that just never got fixed. One of them is that if your controller is connected, and the game is open, and your controller times out/disconnects while the game is open, you will never be able to connect your controller to the game again. This really sucked because there IS pressure-sensitivity enabled in the trigger for gathering materials and working with the hacking tool. 

- Some RDA Bases are story-specific and won't activate/trigger unless you're at that point in the storyline. Kinda sucks when I am already snuck inside and I realize this, I wish it was more obvious.

- I just tried to harvest Radar Mushrooms. Apparently if you go through the method too fast, they don't open to let you harvest. Sadge.

- Took a lot of playing and messing around to get up to ~130-150 fps. The fps also drops to around 50-80 when you load into an area, but it quickly bounces back. (Or if you're like me and don't notice these things, just know that Game Look Good but Stats Bros Say It Could Be Better.)

- Taking up over 100 gb on my hard drive while I'm playing. I will be uninstalling this game when I'm done lol

- Apparently, you can make Eywa mad. I fvked up a quest, still trying to figure out how to fix said quest. Anyway, don't go shooting around animals you aren't sure you absolutely need to or should be. If you fuck up too many times, you get a semi-permanent debuff; I've only gotten the warning once, because as soon as I got it, I looked it up. Otherwise I've been fine.
------
RESPONSE TO REVIEWS I SAW BEFORE PLAYING
------
- "This game is a Far Cry ripoff!" Okay, as someone who's never played Far Cry, this game was fantastic. So, there's that. 

- "The second two areas are worse than the first!" No, no they're not. The first level is just what we're used to seeing from the movies, crowded and full of lush forest. The second area looks exactly as it is meant to, and the third area is the return of a forest aesthetic that I'm very much enjoying.

Those were the two that had me on the fence about this game. Hopefully they sway other folks.

After buying and playing both DLCs, and 100% achievement-ing this game, I still recommend it. It is a LARGE game requiring FANTASTIC computers to run and run smoothly, I have a relatively new almost top of the line computer and have never experienced lag or bugs that other people have but it still takes up most of my graphics card. PLS PLS PLS do NOT get it if you aren't confident in your computer's performance.

This game was very obviously made for console, and some controls are clunky. There are options to set hard to do stuff to automatic, but I tend to keep a controller on hand because I like to do it myself. 

It is an extremely linear story, no options to be made by you other than where to go next, but I honestly don't mind it. Most game story's tend to be linear with illusions of choice that actually don't effect the story at all, and personally I would prefer no choices to ones that don't matter. The story is pretty standard, if you have watched the movies the message is pretty much the same, but I find it interesting enough to continue. 

I think people got a little spoiled from bg3 and expect all open world games to have as many choices, modes of quest-lines, and exploration as humanly possible. This game mildly reminds me of how skyrim worked and I personally have no issues whatsoever with it.

Now for some of my own takes: 

Navigation is kind of a bitch and constantly holding down the na'vi senses to try and figure out where you're going gets so ungodly tiring, I've found putting a waypoint on the map to where you're going helps a lot with it but I wish there was a simpler method. 

With the game as expensive as it is, I think there is no need for it to have purchasable story dlcs... like be so fr 20/15 dollars for extra story for a 70 dollar game is insane, for that price we should have the entire game. But I get it, thats the game economy we have today sigh. I still think the amount of stuff to do without the dlcs is worth the price, albeit but a small margin.

The combat isn't hard, and as someone who doesn't play many shooters or any similar games, I found it enjoyable. It was easy enough that I was able to clear through camps, and hard enough I still had to fight for my life. If you like more cod style combat, this ain't it. I've also not had issues with stealth, so idk why people are complaining about it.

So in conclusion:

This game isn't as bad as people make it out to be, and even though there are improvements to be made, I would still recommend this game (but maybe during a steam sale). I haven't had a game keep me absolutely locked into exploration like this one has in a long time and if given the choice knowing what I know now, I'd buy it again. But, so far, those are my ONLY complaints about the game. And, honestly, the grinding part isn't even a complaint. I'm someone who's put 3k hours into Red Dead 2/Online JUST doing grinding stuff like collecting. It's how I decompress. But anyway.

This was worth the money I dropped on it. Absolutely worth it. The world is rich with both active and passing story-telling, the design of each clan and how it reflects their environment being the highlight of those things for me. Quests weren't just your usual go-and-fetch, you have to use resources, plan ahead, gear up. And for the RDA-related quests, there's different ways of doing things depending on your play style.

I had a few minor visual bugs, like ground textures sometimes not rendering in certain squares, but it was fixed just by re-booting the game (this happened most often in the Kinglor Forest). Sometimes, loincloths would whip about like the funky balloon guys outside a car dealership, and this did ruin the first time I got to the Skybreaker opening scene (one of the few times we get to see our PC), but it's no real biggie. Our bond with the world is 100% the net that caught my proverbial fish brain (because I only have 2 active brain cells at one time and they're both focused on this game right now). Helping and soothing animals, clearing the atmosphere, connecting to Tarsyu Flowers just felt so raw, I wish we had so much more of it. And the ikrans... Oh god, do I love my ikran. The game is beautiful, fun, intuitive, and immersive, and while it does have its fair share of flaws (as most Ubisoft games do) they're not as game breaking as everyone makes them out to be. Plus, in my opinion, the gameplay more than makes up for it.

A majority of people who made negative reviews talking about how buggy and unplayable the game is have probably installed it on an HDD. Like the system requirements say it requires an SSD - an HDD cannot run it properly.
If you've run into problems like:
* clipping through walls and falling through the map
* noticeable input lag when moving, interacting with items and npcs, opening inventory, etc.
* finding yourself in rooms that are entirely unrendered, or in rooms you're otherwise obviously not supposed to see/access in normal gameplay
* not being able to break the vent covers in the opening tutorial
* action prompts not showing up when they should and/or cutscenes not triggering when they should
* bugged ai behavior (scripted rda soldiers in the opening tutorial having broken pathfinding, not turning hostile when they see you, straight up not being where they should be, etc.)
* low (<20) framerates when you meet system requirements
* excessive graphical/rendering bugs (low quality textures on high graphics settings, patchy terrain, models not loading correctly, etc.)
* very slow (~10+ minute) load times
* frequent CTD. I'm not talking about a crash every half hour or so (this is Ubisoft we're talking about), but crashes so frequent that it's a struggle to progress
* any other unusual issues that I may not have heard of or personally seen

... then you've probably installed the game on an HDD. The only way to fix this is by installing the game on an SSD. If you're not sure which one you have, you can check in the Perfomance tab of Task Manager.

If you're 100% sure you installed the game on an SSD and are still seeing patchy terrain, open the graphics config file (Documents\My Games\AFOP\graphic settings.cfg or something similar) and make sure lines 7 and 8 look like this:

bloom = true,
		["bloom dirt"] = false 

If that doesn't fix it or if you're having any of the other graphical issues I mentioned above, open the same graphics settings config file and edit the following:

near the top, change ["character detail"] = 1 to ["character detail"] =2. [strike] higher values may have better results, but I haven't tested it [/strike] 2 seems to be the max. going any higher causes the setting to revert back to 1

near the bottom, change ["streamer dedicated budget"] = 64 to AT LEAST ["streamer dedicated budget"] = 512. this is the amount of memory that will be allocated for texture rendering, in MB. the more memory you allocate the sharper the textures will be, but the lower your performance will be. 1024 is a good middle ground, but if you can afford to you can also do 2048 or 4096. make sure you actually have the memory you're allocating or you're going to run into crashes

a bit underneath that, change scaleQuality = 1 to scaleQuality = 2. this will increase texture quality at a moderate performance cost and the textures may still occasionally drop in quality, but will correct themselves after a few seconds of being within your render. if you've been having issues with textures suddenly dropping in quality only after opening photo mode, this may fix that too. [strike] feel free to input higher values to see what it does - I can't be bothered [/strike] max is 3, quality improvement is marginal. higher values cause the setting to revert back to 1

If you're having significant framerate issues, try disabling the vignette, framerate cap, and/or reduceLatency options in the config file, along with lowering the settings ingame if you need to.

So much potential here, but it's unfortunately squandered by a remarkably unimaginative application of Ubisoft's tired and reductive open world formula.

Let's start with what's good. The game looks amazing and runs really well (make sure you meet the hardware requirements!). It fulfills the fantasy of visiting a gorgeous planet full of alien flora and fauna. The different biomes have distinct flavors and there's just so much stuff and color and sound through which you can walk, gallop, and fly. I especially loved the thunderstorms: The first time lightning struck a "tree" beside me my jaw dropped. The HDR implementation is very good, especially during the daytime in which the alien sun washes the landscape in an adoring glow. As for gameplay, combat is fairly satisfying if simplistic. There isn't much variety in enemies, but the set pieces offer a lot of opportunity for infiltration strategy and tactics.

Unfortunately, everything else is ... sigh. The main quest is OK, but not great. What bogs it down is that it's structured in a plodding, awkward, and mechanically linear manner. You are told exactly where to go and what to do and really don't have to think about it at all. Still, it has its moments with a handful of set pieces and thrilling action. The story itself is a [I]very[/I] on-the-nose retelling of how Europeans treated Native Americans and other displaced peoples, and oh yes don't forget to save the environment. So, on brand. And unlike the 2009 [I]Avatar[/I] game, you are [I]not[/I] given the choice to side with the humans against the Na'vi. Actually you can only play a Na'vi. Unfortunately you will have to look elsewhere to fulfill your colonial and/or white savior fantasies. "Is our children learning?"

However. There are the side quests, which are what should be the meat in an open world game. Here they are very many, very repetitive, and too often very dumb. Like, incredibly dumb. It's as if the devs blew the whole budget on licensing the [I]Avatar[/I] IP and could only afford interns to write these. There are only a handful of quest types, but they are repeated again and again and again. Cookie cutter. Filler. Padding. Bloat. And virtually all are "find this fruit" or "my brother went fishing and got lost". I'm not opposed to grind when the gameplay loop is satisfying and rewarding. I enjoyed the first few iterations of these. By the twentieth time I was bored. By the fiftieth time I was angry. The design team must truly believe this is what gamers consider fun. Folks, let me tell you: we play your games [I]in spite[/I] of this mind-numbing routine, not because of it.

The reward economy is also quite broken. I maxed out all skills before the endgame, which removed any material reason to pursue boring side quests. Extra skill points are useless for the main game, though they can be used in the DLC. I also saw no reason to try to get the special "coin" used to buy items, nor find rare materials to craft them, because what I already looted was better. And even if you don't aim to acquire the best gear, you'll be fine. The default level of difficulty is quite manageable. Maybe higher levels of difficulty would require more involvement with this economy, but I assume most players would stick to the defaults.

And collectibles. There are, I believe, about eleventy billion of them. Finding them is a slog, even with online guides.

There is also a variety of mini-games. I didn't hate them and thought they were a nice change of pace, but I think some people would find some of them frustrating because they depend on precision movement.

All the above is pretty much what I expect from a Ubisoft game, but what really bummed me out is how often [I]Avatar[/I] punishes you for exploring. I love going off on a whim and messing with the supposed order of the plot. It's part of the joy of open world games: they should let you find your own story. But in [I]Avatar[/I] your own story will be about locked doors, inactive terminals, unclimbable hills, and seemingly abandoned bases, which only "activate" later when you hit the right quest checkpoint. And this is not indicated to you. Again and again I tried to make sense of intriguing locations only to find out later that the game simply disabled them. My curiosity and problem-solving skills were "rewarded" by a pointless waste of my time.

In summary, [I]Avatar[/I] will let you visit Pandora. And that's cool. Unfortunately, in this rendition it's too rarely an a exciting place.

Want to have adventures in an open alien world? You'll have a much more satisfying experience with [I]Outcast: Second Contact[/I] and its sequel.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 41, "timestamp_created": 1736412230}, {"review_text": "Great visuals, solid gameplay – but co-op restrictions ruin it for me

I really wanted to love Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora, and in many ways I do. The world is beautiful, the movement and combat feel great, and it’s clear a lot of passion went into making this game.

But the co-op experience is extremely limited, and that ruins the fun for me and my friends. As a guest in someone else’s game, your progress is heavily restricted — you can’t contribute to faction progress, collectibles don’t count, and a lot of world interactions simply don’t carry over. Only story missions, XP, and some loot are saved.

This feels like a major design flaw, especially in a game that markets itself as having full co-op. If Ubisoft improves or reworks the co-op system to properly support guest progression, I would happily repurchase the game in the future.

I have not yet played Station to Station, so this is the first time I've played a game from Galaxy Grove, but I'm blown away! What a beautiful and elegant game. The pixel artwork is so well done, and even the smallest details are added. For example, there are different color flowers, and you can choose the color, but it is also possible to just select them randomly to create a more "natural" effect. And as if that wasn't enough, you can also use those flowers in different ways; you can place them on the ground, hang them on buildings, or hang them under a window. Each option shows them in a different way while using the same "item" from the building menu. 

I am also very impressed with how the different people look, and how they really add to the bustling feeling of the city you're building. They walk around in the city, enjoying the view over the water, or at the flowers in a park. and the music is lovely as well, especially the tune when you upgrade your city level. 

Town to City also gives you a lot of tools to check the status of your city, it splits it in the different class of people, but you can also see it when clicking on a house, or in an overview where with colors it will show where there isn't enough of something. It will reward you for using different type of buildings, so keep building the same food market stall will not do as much as having different ones. Balancing between having enough to fulfill one of the needs of the people in your city, but adding more people to the town will give a shortage of another need, was an addictive balance. I couldn't find a way to do it perfectly, but it was possible to fulfill them " good enough" so that they are happy. 

Another thing I highly appreciated is that the game asks you to decorate your town and gives you a ton of options. An example is when using lights, which turn on during the evening and night, giving Town to City an extra cozy feel and they will count toward the beautiful score of your town. Sometimes a family demands a little extra, you can turn them away, but sometimes it is better to accept them because it is easy, like placing a bit more lanterns around a house, or a bit more plants is easily done. Need them close to a mountain but have already used those houses on other families? You can move those families and then add those new people to this house. 

None of the achievements are missable, and most of them you'll do while building your city. I highly recommend building at least one building of every type, and 5 of each small decoration item to make sure you trigger all the mayor requests questlines. I wouldn't worry about the fence achievement until after unlocking all the others, as it is easiest done on a sandbox map, but if you wait till you done the rest, you might have already placed some meters of fences, and it is the total amount that counts. 

I give Town to City 4,5 out of 5 stars. This game made me extra curious to try out Station to Station in the future.

What I want to make clear here is that this is not a game for me, not that it is a bad game. 

I expected this game to be a city builder, but it is closer to a diorama builder. The maps are tiny, cramped, even the full flat map feels too small. I absolutely love beautybuilding in city builders, but for some reason developers of all city builders besides Cities Skylines (and technically them too) have this urge to limit the size of their map. Why? What compells all developers to make maps so small? It's not performance I tell you, because all they'd need to do is limit the size and allow you to build over the limit by ticking some box in options, Rimworld does this perfectly for instance. They even warn you there about increasing size having big impact on performance, but they give you a choice. The implications are massive. Everything you can build will feel like a miniature city. I don't want miniature, I want full scale. I want to build whole countryside, not a fraction of it. Give me kilometers of farmlands, woodlands, I love scale.

It's not about the urban target of the game's theme that has to limit the size. In fact the game isn't much of a town to city as it is village to town, so it should feel much larger than it is. While detailing is awesome and I absolutely love it, the building selection further proves that the game is meant to look good as a miniature. Signature buildings look too distinct to blend well, at least some of them and their inclusion also makes little sense since the map is so small and you really aren't going to find most towns of such size to have as huge buildings. Just look at the fountain and this little castle/masnion/chateau thing among some others. Or how large the train station gets by the end. There are exceptions of course, but most towns of such size should feel less grandeur. To me city building is about trying to build something both unique and realistic. For that you need huge building variety, detailing, and scale. This game to me offers the best detailing experience I have ever seen, but not the other two things. In fact scale is probably among the worst and building variety is fair for an indie title at this price, fair doesn't mean good, it means, acceptable.

Another thing that bothers me to no end and that wasn't fixed since demo, the clothing store, and likely many other buildings, still enforce a partial perimeter of grass around them, meaning even if you want to have it near a plaza, you will have to suffer a patch of grass that looks totally out of place. You can't build over it either. For some reason only Cities Skylines allows anarchy. I don't care about overlap, let me overlap, let me clip. But no, I will have to be forbidden from doing this rather than given a choice. Just highlight it in yellow to indicate clipping. So if this bug wasn't fixed for a couple of months, it's not a good sign, what else will I find broken while playing naturally? Such things are my pet peeve, if you give me a game about detailing and make it impossible and glaring, I will suffer.

To me this is a real shame, because this game put tons of love and care into detailing, the models look great, the atmosphere is amazing, you can really feel the heart was poured into this, but what good is that when it's so small. I'd rather play Anno or Cities Skylines. Not because of the simulation or theme or other mechanics, purely from the perspective of building something nice. Scale matters in city builders, correct distance between certain areas does matter. Even the rular areas need correct size, bigger is better always.

The game is going to be updated over time, but I doubt my concerns are going to get any attention from the looks of the roadmap, and that's fine, the game is simply meant for a different audience than me. And that's why I in particular can't recommend this in good faith despite game likely ending with 95%+ positive reviews. That's the core audience, not me. It is an early access title, but it's not going to go in a direction I need, and that's fine again, just not for me in particular.

What I can tell you is that if you are okay with this scale, if you like the particular style they went for, go for it, it's an amazing game for you. But if like me, you feel like all city builders lack something important, this game lacks it more than others, despite appearing at first like it holds some hidden potential.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1758157879}]

If this is not enough to convince you to avoid this game, you seriously need to raise your standards. There are better games out there, trust me.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 13, "timestamp_created": 1752305134}, {"review_text": "Destiny 2  The Light That Burned Too Long

I was twelve when Destiny came out. Fifteen when Destiny 2 launched. I’m twenty-three now and for almost half my life, this universe has been a constant companion. Across thousands of nights, thousands of hours, and 4,200 on Steam alone, I’ve fought gods, built fireteams, cleared raids, and watched the stars over the Tower more times than I can count. This game shaped the way I see stories, friendships, and Art.

But after all that, I can’t recommend it.
Not because I hate it, because I don’t.
But because I don’t care anymore.

That’s the hardest part to admit. It’s not pain or anger that finally broke me, it’s apathy. The quiet realization that I’ve run out of reasons to log in, that the spark that once burned so bright has simply gone out. Destiny 2 hasn’t betrayed me. It’s exhausted me.

---

The community gets called toxic a lot. Negative. Impossible to please. You’ll hear that complaint under almost every official post. And yes, there are always people who lash out, but overwhelmingly, the frustration isn’t born from hatred it’s born from grief. It’s the kind of collective exhaustion that only comes from caring too much for too long.

For years, this community did more for Destiny than any studio could ask of its fans. They built websites, crafted lore archives, tracked data, created art, composed music, wrote entire essays trying to explain why this world mattered. Even through the content droughts and controversies, players carried the game with their love. Bungie made the universe but the players gave it life.

And for a long time, that relationship worked. Destiny wasn’t perfect, but it felt alive. Every login felt like an adventure, every exotic weapon had a story behind it, and every strike or raid was a memory made with friends. The game wasn’t just about loot or grind it was about discovery, mystery, and awe. When you stood before Oryx or finally cleared Last Wish, you didn’t just get gear. You got a story of you and your friends.

There was something sacred about that.

That era The Taken King, Forsaken, the early years of D2 felt like lightning in a bottle. Bungie had created something truly special, something that felt new even when it repeated itself. You didn’t play Destiny because you felt obligated to; you played because it captured your imagination. Every sound, every skybox, every tiny detail reminded you that someone cared deeply about crafting this world.

But somewhere along the way, that changed. Not in a single update or with one bad decision (though some decisions could be argued) but slowly, quietly, over time. Destiny became less about wonder and more about maintenance. The joy of discovery turned into a to-do list. You stopped exploring, because you already knew what was waiting: another seasonal currency, another rep grind, another limited-time armor set that would mean nothing in six months.

It’s not even that the game got worse it just stopped evolving. The same loop, over and over, dressed in slightly different colors. The same promises of change, the same resets, the same “this time it’ll be different.” The gunplay is still perfect. The art direction is still among the best in gaming. The soundtrack still hits harder than almost anything else out there. But all of that brilliance is buried under systems that don’t respect the player’s time or passion.

And that’s where the heartbreak really lies. Because the players never stopped trying. We kept hoping that next season, next expansion, next big reveal would be the one to reignite the feeling that Bungie would remember what D2 used to be. But it never quite came.

Now, D2 feels like a monument to potential. A game that was once about fighting back against the darkness now feels consumed by it not in theme as such, but in spirit. You can feel the fatigue in the community. The once-buzzing excitement before every new release is gone, replaced by weary skepticism. Content creators sound tired. Fireteams drift apart. And when you finally do log in, it feels more like visiting a ghost town than returning home.

The worst part is that the world around Destiny hasn’t stood still. We’re in a golden era for games where passion projects are thriving, where studios are putting out bold, creative work that reminds us why we fell in love with gaming in the first place. Games like Baldur’s Gate 3, Balatro, Cyberpunk 2077’s redemption arc, you could keep going and going, they prove that ambition and care can still redefine the medium. And standing next to them, Destiny looks… tired. Beautiful, yes, but tired. Like an old god still standing, long after the faith has faded.

When I think back to what Destiny meant to me, to all of us really,  I don’t regret the years I spent with it. It gave me friends I’ll never forget. Moments that felt real. Music that still gives me chills. It’s a part of who I am, for better or worse. But I can’t pretend that what’s left now is the same game I fell in love with. The magic’s gone, replaced by obligation. And no matter how good the gunplay still feels, that’s not enough anymore.

So no, I can’t recommend Destiny 2.
Not because it’s terrible it’s still capable of brilliance. But because it’s hollow. A game that once stood for discovery, hope, and light has become routine. Predictable. Cold.

The Light didn’t die really. It just faded quietly, over years, until there was nothing left to chase but the memory of what it used to be.

TLDR
Destiny 2 is a masterpiece turned mausoleum. I’ll always love what it was. But I can’t pretend to love what it’s become.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 22, "timestamp_created": 1760383387}, {"review_text": "The real Final Shape was the FOMO we experienced along the way.

This game has been carved up and stitched back together in so many ways and reinvented itself so many times since launch, sometimes for better, and sometimes for worse.  Two things are constant: It is pretending to be a free to play game with perhaps the most abysmally shallow free-to-play component ever, and the price to get into this game is getting higher with more and more ways of monetization being added.  Sure, you can buy the Legacy Pack to give you an "affordable" Destiny 2 experience, but do you know what's missing from that? It's missing over half of the game! 

For context, between expansions, Destiny 2 has seasonal content to serve as smaller, usually self-contained story drops that tie into the overarching narrative. Sometimes this involves tying up loose ends from the expansion they were introduced in, and sometimes they create a way to lead into the next one. These seasonal drops would contain new weapons, a new activity/mission type, lore, armor, sometimes a dungeon, and new exotic gear to chase from missions that unlock later in the season. Oh, and a battlepass with its own shallow rewards that I won't touch on.

But since the Beyond Light era, following the release of a new expansion, all existing seasonal content from the last expansion - save the dungeons - are "vaulted to return at a later time." This means they'll probably bring the seasonal armor and guns back, but all that story you could experience for yourself? Poof. Gone. You had to be there!

This is also why the new player experience is so awful: Because the original campaign of the game and almost everything leading up to the Shadowkeep expansion is just gone! It never returned after they vaulted it! You can't play the vanilla story of Destiny 2 anymore! If you are free to play, there is no story to experience past the first mission and lore tabs for the small amount of gear you can use! ...But you can watch a video, or read the wiki to get the story you're missing! 

Edit: I forgot they made Shadowkeep and Beyond Light's campaign free to play, so there is something more to the f2p  experience now. You still have to pay for the Shadowkeep and Beyond Light packs to get access to the exotic gear + raids, and strikes though. When you're out of story content to do there? Fork up the cash. 

On a different note: It looks like Bungie wants to walk back weapon crafting that The Witch Queen era introduced as a form of bad luck protection, and way to get players to try new weapons and perk combinations. The system was not perfect, it had a few iterations before it was truly right ... but it was perhaps the BEST thing Witch Queen did. Grind out a weapon's crafting pattern, and you are rewarded with a weapon blueprint that would then let you craft the weapon, and modify the perks on it as you see fit. Crafted guns had their own progression to level them up to get better and more powerful perks, and a kill tracker to show how much you used the weapon. I spent hours collecting every pattern from every season up to the Final Shape. It got me to try new guns since I could get a good perk combination as long as I unlocked the craftable weapon!

I don't see why they'd remove such a player-friendly feature, it feels like something they are only doing because they want higher player retention. Remove the way to get a guaranteed good roll on a gun, and supposedly you have more players farming for drops of that gun in playlists... but this just makes me want to not even bother. Collecting the blueprints was the goal. Like collecting loot, collecting blueprints was fun. I could still get the amazing 5/5 roll with rng, just I was guaranteed to get it with the crafted version after a slight grind for it.

But that is far from the only change they're making in the coming expansion, though. The seasonal power grind is only going to get worse from what they've shown. Weapon tiers and reworked armor essentially means it's another soft-reset where existing and crafted gear seems like it will be worse than what you can get normally. Plus a seasonal currency for infusion that disappears at the end of the season... so everyone will be at square one again a few months down the line when the next season comes out and resets everyone to 0 again. Ten years of a power grind, and yet it only ever mattered in deltas of 5 or 10... 

It sucks to really enjoy this game and the universe built around it, and it sucks to WANT to recommend it to your friends, but can't because of the asking price. It sucks this game seems to be stuck in the cyclical nature of wanting to reinvent itself, to the point where this game has a highly predictable cycle of "It's so over" and "we're so back" depending on if the expansion was good or not and if Bungie wants to wring more money out of their playerbase for less effort. 

EDIT 2: To touch on existing monetization for those curious:
-One legacy pack ($70, at the time of writing there is a sale to make it way more affordable)
-One expansion ($40) OR the Yearly bundle with dungeon keys + battlepass reward tracks ($80) OR the premium Yearly bundle with additional cosmetic things ($100) 
-Premium shop with associated premium currency
-Dungeon keys in said premium shop ($20 of the premium currency for one pack, $60 total for all of them) These used to be free with expansions btw :)
-Event passes for holiday events ($10 of premium currency, $15 if you want additional cosmetics and a faster progression track)

I love this game, and I hate this game. It was beautiful and it was awful. You had to be there, and I wish you were. Unfortunately what was "there" is no longer "here."", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 29, "timestamp_created": 1752244241}, {"review_text": "Destiny 2 is a very complicated game to review as it's one of the most polarizing experiences i've ever had to undergo in recent memory; i've been playing D2 almost exclusively for the past 3-4 months and throughout all that time i've had my opinions on it dramatically switch from one extreme to the other over & over until the newness finally wore off and the few amazing highs could no longer cover for all the frequent, terrible & extreme lows the game seems to go through every couple of weeks/months.

On one hand, the gunplay & the way the "shooting" feels here is simply unrivaled; the core gameplay of D2 truly is one of a kind, BUT on the other hand everything else about it is either mediocre at best or just plain BAD.

I don't even know where to start with this one, i guess i'll try to recap my experience so far?
- Stage 01: The new player experience: probably D2's biggest flaw, i don't know about the general population but 7 out of 8 of my friends permanently quit D2 less than 10 hours in because of how overwhelmed/confused they felt, it's genuinely baffling how bad the onboarding experience is, nothing is properly explained beyond the most basic stuff, you're instantly bombarded with countless quests, currencies, a dozen different upgrade materials, a new different DLC cutscene every time you launch the game before you even finish the tutorial, often out of order making you question WTF is going on, by the time you finally get to said DLC the corresponding cutscene is long forgotten, i could go on and on but you get the idea.

- Stage 02: Working through (what's left of) the story & all the different campaigns; this was the time i first fell in love with D2, some of the best stories & lore in a shooter period, and is well worth experiencing especially if you get the legacy collection on sale; an 8/10 in this aspect. (you'll still NEED to watch 1-3h YouTube essays to fill in the massive gaps left by all the vaulted content so maybe not?)

- Stage 03: Power leveling: (currently the reason why i'm done with the game but more on that later), truly one of the most pointless aspects of D2 & only serves to time-gate the fun stuff & heavily inflate playtime for shareholders.
I remember it actively discouraging me from doing anything worthwhile since it felt as if i'm wasting good drops at a lower power, up until i thankfully found out about the free (mediocre) 2020 max power loot Bungie gracefully offered as part of the rite of the nine event (i used to believe we'd get something similar every season, oh how wrong i was..), with which i was finally able to start to freely enjoy the game, my experience would've been very different had i been forced to level from 1650 to 2020.

- Stage 04: Trying all the different strikes and nightfalls, discovering the awesome dares of eternity mode (it's like a game show), some of the most fun i had with D2 as the content felt endless & even had the quality to back it up, with max power level i had access to everything i wanted & was never penalized for playing my way and not bungie's way, oh how the tables have turned.. but more on that later.

- Stage 05: finally trying to engage with the loot system, what's good? what's bad? by now i already had my vault filled with all kinds of guns but mostly used the same 10 weapons for over 200h, they weren't the best but it didn't matter as they were still fun to use, tried to figure it out myself, nope, too complicated for me, 100 different stats and perks and traits.. etc, tried to feel by hand, got discouraged with how many i had to try, tried to google it, found lists but i didn't have god rolls and didn't even know where to start to chase em (neither did i care if i'm to be honest), tried to see the source for good armor, mostly hardest content or (conveniently) PAID seasonal vendors, i didn't have The Final Shape DLC nor did i have any paid seasons so that was that & i just gave up and kept using the same mediocre RoTN armor i got earlier. *shrugs*

- Stage 06: finding an active clan & finally engaging with dungeons (my current favorite D2 content, never raided though :( ) starting with matchmade RoTN dungeons on explorer (the best idea B ever had, adding matchmaking to dungeons, ofc they scrapped it all after having the feature be universally praised) and then with clanmates, this reignited my love for the game right when i was contemplating quitting for the first time after having finished all strikes & campaigns at least once.
i would've probably spent at least a 100h more in had they just not removed explorer mode & matchmaking even if i didn't get any loot, dungeons were THAT fun.
This was also the time i found out i had to pay 20$ per dungeon key if i wanted to play them, and that they NEVER go on sale, ever, which guaranteed i'll never buy any that didn't already come with the DLCs i had, way to go Bungo!

07- Edge of Fate DLC: The current state of the game, the reason why i'll never recommend D2 to anyone ever again..

With the EoF DLC, Bungie have made some massive changes that completely killed any semblance of what Destiny 2 used to be.

[h2]THE BAD:[/h2]
YEARS of mismanagement have sullied it in the eyes of many with the outright removal of previous campaigns which people paid for. Back then, it was a $60 game and having the content that was paid for taken away and never able to be experienced again SUCKED.

Now, its F2P, but that comes with caveats in and of itself. You can expect a lot of popups asking you to purchase various content. Even for someone like me who owns all the DLC, I still get popups to purchase things on Bungie's merch store, which can be annoying. There are a lot of activities which are paywalled, such as a lot of dungeons, raids, and even subclasses. If you're playing with people who have had the game for a while, you likely won't be able to do those activities (personally the most annoying one is the DLC-gated Nightfall strikes, getting blocked out of a ritual activity sucks).

As well as that, the new player experience is a SLOG. The questlines to get to anything resembling freedom to play the game how you want takes a few hours alone. It's personally turned away several of my friends from the game and even for me when I make a new character, it is boring as all hell.

[h2]THE GOOD:[/h2]
The game is free, and the amount of content you get as a F2P player is enough to sustain you forever. You get all the PvP activities, Gambit, (most) Vanguard activities, several dungeons and raids, and a fair amount of exotic armors and weapons, most of which are still relevant in the game's current landscape. If you understand the fact that you won't have access to some things, you can still have a damn good experience on the game in your daily playing.

Almost all of the game's DLCs are worth the money in my opinion. Even ones that I consider lackluster, I don't regret purchasing, such as Lightfall. You get a breadth of content that opens up countless hours of activities, and given the state of microtranscations in gaming right now, the prices aren't insane. The DLCs often go on sale, and a friend of mine who is new to the game purchased all of them for roughly $45 a couple months ago. Wait for a sale and you'll get more content than most AAA titles for less than the cost of a full game.

On the topic of microtransactions, the Eververse store is limited to cosmetics only with a F2P currency rotating shop option which can get you these cosmetics without having to spend a dime, granted it will take a while.

[h3]THE WEIRD:[/h3]
Destiny does have a seasonal battle pass, it has both a paid and F2P branch, which features cosmetics, exotics, and some helpful currencies. That being said, Exotics are easily obtainable without the battle pass, and these currencies are featured in lesser quantities on the free pass, and only serve to expedite the process of crafting certain weapons. It's not a perfect system, but given it's price I don't hate it. It's certainly not as generous as the battle pass for a game like Fortnite, which gives you enough currency to purchase itself again, but it's there whether you love or hate the system.

Bungie is also working on their new game, Marathon, which has had the community concerned for a while that Destiny will be on the backburner and not receive enough attention. This latest season personally has dissuaded my fears, as Marathon is closer than ever to launch, and Destiny feels like its in a pretty good place for an 8 year old game. New expansions and system reworks are coming very soon, and new ritual activities for all players. It is still something to note and keep in mind when looking at the future of the game. It's also worth mentioning that Destiny 1 is still up even now, and has maintenance done regularly. Destiny 2 should be fine for a while.

[h1]CONCLUSION:[/h1]
Destiny's F2P and new player experience isn't great unless you put in a few hours or have someone there to play through it with you. THE F2P content you get is expansive enough in my opinion, and the cost of DLC and seasonal passes is pretty inoffensive given the current gaming landscape. If you like FPS and MMOs Destiny is a great game, and given its age I believe its still quite enjoyable and well loved by both its community and Dev team.

I look forward to the next expansion and another 1000 hours.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1745340158}]

The game hit me so hard that I couldn’t imagine my life without video games anymore. And when the twentieth anniversary update came out, it felt like the perfect reason to return to it and hear the familiar line again. “Rise and shine, Mister Freeman. Rise and shine.”

Coming back to Half-Life 2, I was surprised by how well it has aged. I still feel a bit of dissonance when I remember that it came out in 2004. I spend my time surrounded by titles built with modern technology and at some point I forgot that a game doesn’t need realistic lighting or giant textures to stay memorable.

The physics make that even clearer. They remain a big part of the whole experience. Not many titles let you experiment with the world in the same way. I spent most of my playthrough with the gravity gun because throwing objects at Combine soldiers was simply fun.

When I stepped off the train and wandered into City 17 again, I could feel how naturally the game builds the mood of an Eastern European city. And soon after that you start to notice the people who live in confinement and have no idea what waits for them. Their quiet conversations and the propaganda announcements and the city broadcasts build a sharp sense of dystopia.

But what I love most about Half-Life 2 is the characters. They feel real and simple and honest. Alyx always shows up when things get rough. Doctor Kleiner finds a way out of tough situations with this quiet mix of charm and confidence. Barney softens the world with humor and treats everything with straightforward honesty. Each of them has a rhythm and a personality of their own and even though they are digital you can still learn something from them.

Thinking about all this reminded me of something Marc Laidlaw once said. He hoped that Half-Life would inspire people to create something new instead of copying what already exists. And it really did. It inspired a whole generation of players and pushed the industry forward. It feels good to be part of this community and to share these feelings with so many people around the world.

Score: 10/10 🌟
