Valve dropped it back in 2004, and yeah, people lost their minds. It’s one of those sequels that actually lives up to the hype, which, let’s be real, almost never happens. Instead of just riding on the first game’s coattails, HL2 basically grabbed the whole first-person shooter genre by the collar and shouted, “You can do better!”

So, City 17. Not exactly a vacation spot. The Combine’s in charge, everyone looks miserable, there’s this constant feeling of “Big Brother is watching,” and you, Gordon Freeman, the dude who never, ever talks, like, seriously, not a peep, are somehow the hero. That whole silent protagonist thing? Oddly, it works. You feel more like you’re actually in the story, not just playing some bloke with witty one-liners. Valve nailed it by ditching the usual cutscenes and letting everything play out in real time. NPCs just… talk, stuff happens around you, and the world tells the story if you bother to look around. Kinda wild for its time.

Now, the real party trick: physics. The Source engine was a game-changer. The Gravity Gun? Absolute legend. People still geek out over it. You could just mess around, picking up saw blades, toilets, random junk, launching it at headcrabs or whatever. It wasn’t just a gimmick, either. Solving puzzles or fighting, the physics always felt spot-on. Even now, it holds up. Some modern games can’t even pull that off.

Level design? No dead air. One minute you’re creeping through tight, creepy hallways, next you’re in a shootout, then you’re running from zombies in Ravenholm (ugh), or zooming across the map in a buggy. The pacing’s tight, there’s always something messing with you, and the enemies aren’t dumb, they’ll flank you, flush you out, make you sweat.

And the characters! Alyx Vance is a total standout. Not just there to dump exposition, she’s smart, funny, and probably the only reason you don’t lose it in that grim universe. Dr. Kleiner, Eli, Dog… they all feel like actual people, not just plot devices. You end up caring about them, which is rare for games, honestly.

On the tech side, HL2 was a beast. The facial animations were bonkers for 2004. Lighting, sound, the whole package, just dripping with atmosphere. Even the soundtrack sneaks up on you, kicking in at just the right moment or fading away to let the world do the talking.

Two decades later and people still talk about this thing. Devs reference it, fans mod it, it’s basically the blueprint for how to do a story-driven shooter. It’s not just nostalgia, either, it’s actually that good.

Half-Life 2’s more than a classic. It’s the gold standard. If you haven’t played it, what are you even doing? PRO

- Graphics: The game looks great, running on a custom-designed graphics engine which has surprisingly moderate system requirements
- There are many different tanks to research
- WoT features lots of community events; there's something new almost every week
- Games can be entered quickly, and servers are generally quite stable

CON

- Strong pay-to-win aspects. Some examples: new premium tanks are mostly stronger than researchable tech tree tanks (used to be different btw), playing high tier matches is hardly an option unless you invest money, premium ammunition and other consumables that provide a distinct advantage cost a lot of credits (which again are difficult to afford without paying real money) ... etc.

- Premium tanks are very expensive, with a single tank often costing 30 Euros and more (To be fair, it is not really necessary to buy too many, though)

- The WoT community is probably among the most toxic among all online games - certainly the worst I know, by a mile. So toxic, in fact, that there is a series of YouTube videos dedicated to demonstrate just how destructive players sometimes are

- Poor map designs: Many maps are one-sided (i.e. favour spawn points), offer little variation or are really too small for the capabilities of the tank tiers that can play on them. Note that this is not true for all of them, of course; some are really great, but notably the more recent ones are mostly really poor

- Extremely poor game balancing: This is the easily worst aspect of the game, and it comes in many shapes. Some examples:

* Although there are exceptions in every tech tree, it is an open secret that certain nations are quite consistently better than others in the game. Not that Wargaming would ever admit that, of course.
* Wargaming has a policy of rewarding the strongest players with the strongest tanks, so in high tier matches inexperienced players are put at an extra disadvantage
* Some tank classes are extremely difficult to counter (artilleries, wheeled tanks with an absurd auto-aim while moving).
* Due to the nature of matchmaking you will frequently find yourself in matches where you can do next to nothing
* The disparities in strength between tanks of the same Tier are often hair-raising. On Tier VIII, for example, a handful of tanks (mostly premium, of course) are so utterly dominant that the rest might as well not be in the game.

and and and ...

All in all, I would not recommend WoT to any new players anymore. It really isn't a particularly good game now; Wargaming have made too many poor design decisions over the past few years - the introduction of the stupefyingly idiotic wheeled tanks was just one example among many. It is true that it still has no equal in its niche, so if somebody wants to play a fast-paced tank shooter, it's probably this or nothing. This is the highest skill ceiling "shooter" I've ever played. I say "shooter" in air quotes because, if you play it like a traditional shooter, you will get your ass handed to you in a mess tin. Twitch shooting is not a useful skill in this game, because the tank defines how quickly and accurately you can shoot, not your reflexes. It is a game where success is not so much defined by raw mechanical skill, but how you apply those mechanical skills with your specific team lineup against the specific team lineup your opponents have to win.

As a direct result of that, no tank in a team (apart from maybe artillery) is dispensable. Subsequently, the pressure to perform to or above your potential is [i]immense[/i]. I have sat down in front of traditional twitch shooters after playing this game and it has felt like relaxing holiday compared to the absolute forehead-vein-bulging pressure to perform in World of Tanks. There are no respawns and no healing in this game - damage and death is permanent in match, so there is no way to patch up for your mistakes after the fact, or try again if you fail. The community in this game has a ridiculously low tolerance for people trying to learn how a tank works, and pretty much expect you to perform at or above potential straight out of the garage. Play a tank wrong or make a dumb mistake and your team will make sure you remember it for the rest of your life.

Many times, this game is an exercise in futility and frustration as a battle feels more like 1v29 instead of the 15v15 format it has. You're sometimes battling not only the enemy, but also the tidal wave of absurdity from your own team. In its default incarnation, this game has no skill-based matchmaking (SBMM), which means that not infrequently you will end up on teams that look like they're trying to actively figure out the controls as they roll out of base - doubly so now that signing in or up after the 2.0 update granted you 1-2 tech trees, up until tier 10, sight unseen. This, when combined with no SBMM, can have you left on teams where you feel like you're the only one who's even figured out what end the bullets come out of.

The advantages that can be gained by paying in this game are also not-insignificant. I would estimate that it is possible to gain about a 25-30% performance advantage by paying, and more than that, you also opt out of the most frustrating aspects of the tech tree and economy grind by doing so. This is not something that everyone appreciates and the monetisation in this game has been getting worse and worse over the years. The premium tank spam is relentless and power creep is reaching Destiny 2 levels of problematic.

The learning curve in this game isn't a curve, it's a flat wall that you will bang your head against for hundreds of hours until you learn to scale it and then start to do well. I have taught a friend to play this game, in addition to learning myself. Provided your friend(s) even have the patience and/or masochism to last past tier 6, it's all uphill from there. The amount of cool game mechanics is mind blowing, must play for anyone)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1741655656}, {"review_text": "[h1]Hazelight Delivers Again[/h1]

Hazelight is number 1 at co-op gameplay, and Split Fiction proves it. The game expands It Takes Two mechanics to present a fresh and enjoyable interactive cooperative experience. Just like It Takes Two, every section of the game introduces something new, keeping things fresh from start to finish. The level design is awesome. The gameplay is incredibly polished, and all the immensely various mechanics feel satisfying to play. Truly a peak game design showcase.

[h3]The Story – The Weakest Part of the Game[/h3]

The gameplay elements of the game outshine everything else because like It Takes Two, the narrative is the weakest part of the experience. Hazelight nailed this better in A Way Out and in Brothers, A Tale of Two Sons, which was a game that used no words to tell its story. The storytelling attempts from Split Fiction fall short because it tries too hard with emotional moments that don’t really land. It also is not goofy like It Takes Two. Split Fiction takes its story too seriously. The dialogue, the characters, they are just too predictable, too one-dimensional. After playing It Takes Two, and other Hazelight games, I was sure of what was gonna happen at the end 100%. And when that's the case, you can't really connect with the story since the writing is also kind of cliche and boring. The story stands as Split Fiction's main weakness though it does not reach unacceptable levels. To be honest, I just wanted to jump back into the gameplay.

[h3]Pacing Issues[/h3]

The pacing in It Takes Two was handled better than Split Fiction. In Split Fiction, some levels go on for way too long. The monkey and Groot level is an example of that. It just keeps going and going. The side stories in this game end at about 60-70% of the game but It Takes Two balanced its additional content across the entire game. Split Fiction doesn't have minigames (except the snow riding part) which is a negative, but there are side stories that were pretty insane in creativity. This issue is also to be seen in the later sections of the game, where you are presented with puzzles or puzzle-ish levels back-to-back, slowing down the game.

[h3]Graphics & Optimization – This is How UE5 Should Be Used[/h3]

Unlike many modern Unreal Engine 5 titles that are full of performance issues, Split Fiction runs amazingly. It doesn't have the disgusting render distance fog, no anti-color horrible filters, and remains a steady and high FPS at all times while looking amazing at all times. The art design is phenomenal. Every level is creatively mesmerizing and gorgeous without relying on Unreal Engine 5's lazy photorealism. And the game runs very well unlike the 20FPS UE5 slop we're seeing too often these days. Take notes, game devs!

[h3]A GOTY Contender, But Not the Winner[/h3]

Even though it's still too early to talk about Game of The Year in March, I think Split Fiction should and will be a nominee in The Game Awards this year. However, it's also It Takes Two 2.0, a refined, better version, but not something completely new like it was in It Takes Two. Which is why I think It Takes Two completely deserved the win in 2021. So that's why I don't think it should be Game of The Year since it's not going to be mine. My Game of The Year 2025 will probably be Death Stranding 2: On The Beach, or Grand Theft Auto VI if it releases this year, or Hollow Knight: Silksong? Who am I kidding? Silksong is not releasing this year :(

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]

I would love to play another one of these but I hope they will use their expertise to develop a fresh experience that revolutionizes another genre like they did with the co-op games. Hazelight is one of the few studios still doing great things in modern gaming and huge respect for EA for supporting them and giving them full creative freedom. The Friends Pass System is an amazing consumer-friendly move. Thank you, EA. I definitely recommend this at full price, since you can pay half with your friend.

I've been a fan of Hazelight's work ever since A Way Out wowed me and my closest friend back in 2018. Its mixture of varied gameplay, ample use of its co-op mechanics, and a well-written story featuring a great twist at the end, all made for my favorite co-op game I've ever played (at least in terms of two players since Left 4 Dead will always be my baby). It Takes Two didn't wow me quite as much, especially around its weird messaging surrounding divorce and marital issues, but it was fun in its own right.

So when I tell you that Split Fiction is the peak of Hazelight's efforts (albeit with the occasional rough edge), I mean it. This is some of the best-looking work the team has ever produced, and the gameplay is arguably the new benchmark for how these sorts of games should be approached. Even the writing, while imperfect, was relatable and nicely interwoven with gameplay in a way that felt natural.

Certain aspects of the story hit on a personal level for me. The two central characters, Mio and Zoey, adore sci-fi and fantasy respectively but abhor the other for one reason or another. The gameplay is a direct reflection of that, alternating between technological marvels and mystical worlds for each chapter. But it's the way the two of them begin to appreciate that other genre that resonated with me so much. I've always been a diehard fan of sci-fi with Mass Effect being my favorite series ever (we don't talk about Andromeda), but only recently through games like Enderal: Forgotten Stories and Dark Souls have I started to truly appreciate fantasy settings more for their strengths. Split Fiction acting as a reflection of that growth and appreciation was awesome to see, along with the central plot focusing on a topic I have a lot of thoughts about (extra points for the accurate depiction of most CEOs).

Admittedly though, the character development could've been delivered a little better. Across the game's eight chapters and roughly 12-hour length, the entire first half is dedicated to Mio with only the occasional mention of Zoey's inner turmoil. Then, after fully wrapping up Mio's story around the end of the fourth chapter, Zoey gets the spotlight for the rest of the game. The issue here is how little they allude to Zoey's turmoil early in the experience, leading Mio to seem like an asshole while Zoey comes across as prim and perfect until halfway through, she suddenly shifts. I'm pleased with the individual backstories of each character and how they're resolved, but it can't help but feel almost artificial in its delivery.

Outside of the story though, gameplay is damn near perfect. My friend can attest to this, but I can't count the number of times I said "this is so damn cool" out loud, because Split Fiction just *is* that exciting. Each of the eight chapters is handled with such care and attention to detail for its core mechanics that it manages to hit that sweet spot of never feeling overdone, while simultaneously never feeling underappreciated. Every chapter is not just memorable but endlessly refreshing, from an exciting motorcycle escape sequence to a dance-off with a Monkey King (I'm not joking about that one). The amount of care and passion put into the variety is virtually unmatched, something I haven't felt since playing through Titanfall 2, my favorite FPS campaign ever.

And even if you don't gel with a particular level, four of the eight chapters include three Side Stories. These are optional levels that take a fraction of the time to complete, but feature mechanics that are better for the shorter length and take place in the opposite setting (a train heist in the middle of a fantasy level, for example). It's a super unique way to approach side quests, both working in the context of the experience while offering equally memorable gameplay to the game's other levels.

Almost everything about it is just pitch-perfect. The level design, the mechanics themselves, and the way co-op is utilized while giving space for each individual to breathe. They even include a few hilarious nods in secret areas for those who have played past games or other well-known video games. One of my favorites involved being able to rest at a certain sword embedded in the ground that was barely lit up. I'll let you put that one together yourself.

Like I said, however, it's *almost* perfect. While all these mechanics and levels are perfectly fine-tuned, the controls can be mediocre at the best of times. I recall one particular moment where I had to awkwardly rotate certain discs to let my friend cross, but the rotation randomly inverted on the final cylinder, forcing us to redo that little section. It was never a huge deal, but those sorts of issues were enough to piss us off at times.

And the best thing is there's literally no chapter/level that feels the same as others, every time you experience something new", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1743368263}, {"review_text": "I think that in terms of Hazelight's library, Split Fiction is probably my least favorite of them to date. But for a studio like this, that's like naming your least favorite item on the menu of a five-star restaurant; either way, you're still getting good food. This is still some of the best co-op gaming on the market, and Josef Fares and his team still haven't lost their magic touch. 

Like their previous works, when Split Fiction is going great it repeatedly does things you've probably never seen in a game before, and when it's at its best it pulls stunts you might not have even thought were possible in a multiplayer context. There are some incredible stages and setpieces throughout the game, and those moments alone are worth the price of a ticket for two (which only requires one copy of the game, thanks to the usual friend pass system). The two protagonists' stories tend to start out pretty threadbare, but they do eventually build up to the obligatory heart-tugging drama that dares you to cry in front of a friend, and while the villain main is as cartoonish as it gets he's at least simple in an extremely funny way if you don't try to take it too seriously. 

When it isn't going great, though, the core problem is its inconsistency, especially early on. Where Brothers, A Way Out, and It Takes Two rarely had dull moments, Split Fiction occasionally gets bogged down in ideas that just aren't working very well. A lot of the early cyberpunk-inspired stages from Mio's side of things tend to just be an hour or so of fairly straightforward action platforming with few diversions, or a lengthy section where the only gimmick is that both players have laser guns that are mostly used for opening doors, and frankly the visual style for a lot of them hovers between "fake video game on a tv show" and "car insurance commercial". They're never bad enough to make you want to quit, but they sometimes feel too scripted and simple to feel genuinely exciting, and I think that's a shame in its own right. To me a large part of what made Hazelight's previous games so special was how seamlessly and frequently they moved between narrative gameplay, puzzles, action, and interactive diversions, and used a mix of their goofy gameplay gimmicks and competitive minigames to foster a very loose sense of cooperation that left the door wide open for all kinds of player-driven shenanigans. Split Fiction doesn't really have that; there are little crumbs of it every now and then, and the game does have brief side stories every now and then that give you a break from whichever half of the two flavors of stage you're currently in, but most of the parts that have that exceptional Hazelight spark are backloaded into the second half of the game. The silver lining is that they are more than worth the wait.

The other thing that surprised me is how much the story takes backseat most of the game, considering its concept. The premise of the game is that each stage is based on one of the protagonists' ideas for a novel, but the stages themselves rarely feel like something that would actually stem from that. I'm not saying I need the game to be Alan Wake, but in a lot of segments you're lucky if you have a story concept at all, and when you do it's rarely more than "we need to stop this bad guy", which is usually accomplished by just platforming your way forward and then killing them. For the first half of the game my partner and I genuinely couldn't tell if we were supposed to believe that either of the protagonists were even good at writing or if the point was supposed to be that there's a reason neither of them had been able to secure a publishing deal from anyone that wasn't trying to harvest their ideas into ChatGPT, and frankly even if the villain's plan had worked I think most of these story ideas would have just poisoned the dataset if anything. And while once again it's never a dealbreaker, I think that part of why the low points of the games end up being low points is because of this. It's understandable that in a co-op game you want the story to be light enough to not slow the gameplay down, but a lot of the standout moments in all three of their previous games were standout moments because of the way the story context amplified the meaning of what you were doing. A lot of the early stages have fancy setpieces like climbing a skyscraper or jumping along flying cars in a floating highway that end up feeling a little mundane because there's just no context to ground them in or give you a reason to care about anything more than Mio and Zoe moving forward and leaving, because the game's plot effectively starts at the halfway point.

None of this is to say that you shouldn't buy the game, because you absolutely should! It's fantastic. The only reason I'm nitpicking is because both my partner and I agreed that the amount of perfect score reviews this game has received set our expectations a bit higher than we maybe should have, and while it didn't sour our experience I think it's worth avoiding any sort of disappointment to focus on the things this game does really great instead. In my eyes, this is less a 10/10 masterpiece and more a very solid 8/10 game with individual bursts of 10/10 moments and rare 7/10 dips. If you've played their previous works and love them then maybe slightly adjust your expectations, but if this is your first Hazelight game, you might not even believe that it can get even better than this.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1742879428}, {"review_text": "I don't think it's possible to describe this game in one word because it's just out of this world. [{"review_text": "The game is actually nice in some sense, and I feel sorry to not recommend it at a time. The issue is, I felt like I bought early access disguised as a full release. 
The questionable controls on pc, reproducible bugs, unbalanced progression, unused content (full furniture sets with no purpose), lack of pretty obvious features like any kind of inventory sorting, or dismantling the items we don't need - all that creates the feeling the game is still actively in development. I also had plenty of black screens instead of cut scenes, still not sure if it's a bug or placeholders for the future content. And all this is the kind of thing I'd liked to be aware of BEFORE buying something.
So, while I enjoyed the game for what it could become, if I'd knew all this beforehand I wouldn't buy it right away", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763222362}, {"review_text": "Great visuals, very pleasant music and sounds, cute characters and it definitely gives you the cozy vibes you bought it for. But a game cannot 100% rely on cozy and I am very disappointed since I wanted to love Winter Burrow. You'll beat it in less than 10 hours and it's got zero-replayability, which I could have accepted if not for:

Decorating the burrow feels pointless

In such a short game, you'll hardly want to replace your bed with a different one if there's no benefit, just different looks. And still you get so many (too many) furniture alternatives, while there's no option to dismantle the "old" ones (nor old tools) and you actually need nothing but a bed and a container. Which is already there when you arrive. Why bother building a wardrobe if old clothing can go with rocks and sticks in the pre-existent box?

You unlock a ton of decorations at the very end of the game, and there's no late game at all: you won't care about crafting it unless you're a completionist and want the achievements. Quality of life is also not great, but given how effortless the game was, I honestly did not mind. 

You will unlock the possibility to grow mushrooms in the cellar, which is just boring and unnecessary you'll probably do it once then forget you can. You find a ton of mushrooms outside and there's no reason at all to plant, water them and go through the process. 

Gameplay

I am all for cozy, but there's no challenge at all and it gets boring once you're done taking in the beautiful visuals. It's also frustrating at the beginning because your inventory starts way too small and what actually makes the hours played go up is going back and forth to the burrow to deposit resources.

The sense of progression you get at the beginning, while upgrading your clothing, will fade away fast. The last quests give "find object, give object, find second object, deliver object" and DEFINITELY made me feel like I spent almost 20 euros on an early access game disguised as a full release.

Some characters will deliver new lines if spoken to again, which you won't spontaneously do once done with their questline. What will happen is, you'll talk to them for the final quest and have multiple conversations all at once, completely wasted, just like the decorations you'll unlock.

Therefore...

I could not wait to play the full game after playing the demo, and now I would refund it if I could. It's not worth the full price at all, so wait for patches and a big discount. So disappointed.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763304585}, {"review_text": "Ok I’m 2.5 hours in, in the game itself is not bad. Here’s what I like and dislike.

Dislike: 
Map- there’s no map
linear- too linear (can’t really explore much outside of current quests/can’t craft much outside of current quests)
Backtracking- I would say half of my playtime has been spent back tracking (going back home) either to store things bcuz the inventory is too small, even after my first inventory upgrade (only +4 more) I’m constantly having to backtrack home (no fast travel ) to get rid of full inventory. 
Heat meter- the heat meter wears down too quickly, it’s not the biggest deal in the world especially since there’s food that can up the heat meter but it’s a bit of a hassle

What I like-
The art: art speaks for itself
No bugs (so far)


Forgot to mention but with the 2.5 I already have a third of the achievements so now I’m worried the game will be too short.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1762978526}, {"review_text": "Yes, it is a cute game. Yes, it is cozy and visually pleasing. But, that set aside, the story is extremely short and the remainder of the game is just gather stuff and create the same things you already have but slightly better. Half, if not more, of the game is played running back to your home either because your backpack is full or because it is night and/or you are cold. Actually thoroughly disappointed.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1763040863}, {"review_text": "This game had the potential to be my GOTY. Instead, I ended up so frustrated with the lack of even basic QoL that I barely had enough motivation to finish the story. I'm leaning towards a negative review to send a stronger signal, but I'd gladly update it after some adjustments. I don't know if this game could still be fixed enough to be GOTY material for me, but it could be much more fun. 
It does have a lot going for it. The visuals are obviously nice and cute. The sound design and music are just right. The little mouse noises are adorable. I found the characters well-written with a lot of funny and heart-warming lines. 
The rest is more complicated, let's go through it systematically: 

[b]The "Cozy"[/b]
Your mouse has a tragic back story. Literally every character you meet has a tragic story. You find corpses... I didn't find it too grim personally, especially because you can make things better. Spoiler for those who are wondering about the outcome and NPCs: [spoiler]All the NPCs you talk to will be fine(ish), though you do find a dead partner and have to break the news. The ending is hopeful.[/spoiler]
The importance of berry pies and knitting by the fireplace is probably the most adorable thing, other than being a mouse. There are recipes using bug and spider meat, but they are fully optional. 
Combat can be completely avoided by running and hiding, but you can't get all achievements without killing lots of small animals. The option to turn off spiders is very welcome. Running from bugs wasn't much of a challenge, but it became annoying with the more aggressive ones later in the game. It doesn't make or break the game by itself, but another toggle for bugs seems easily possible and would have made the game more enjoyable for me. 

[b]The "Survival"[/b]
You can't die, only pass out (drop your items and wake up at home) if your health drops to 0 from cold, hunger, or bug/spider bites (?). The only challenging one is the cold. There's a nice sense of progression from unlocking helpful clothing and consumables that let you venture further. I found this aspect interesting and not too hard, but I shamelessly took advantage of a bug that caused excessive item drops and that's now being fixed... Others have commented that your warmth drops too quickly. 

[b]The QoL[/b]
Pretty much absent and by far my biggest issue. Your little forest mouse having a terrible quality of life may be realistic, but it's not very fun. This game desperately needs a map, and either a bigger inventory much sooner or the ability to establish small bases outside of your burrow. As it is now, I found it way too tedious and frustrating. 

Too many smaller annoyances to list them all, the first that came to mind: You can't divide stacks or auto-sort. The crafting menu won't tell you if or how many of an item you already own. You can't craft multiple items at once without using up your resource entirely, and you'll need lots of some items. 
In many cases you have to walk to places to see which resources they require; you can track at least one of those, but that will take up an annoying chunk of your screen and can't be hidden unless you go to the same place again and untrack it. The quest tab is almost useless, with hardly any explanations. And without a map, good luck remembering every NPC's name and location - especially if you come back after taking a break from the game. 
I feel like I spent most of my play time backtracking, running from bugs, getting lost, or checking what to drop because
Your inventory is full
Your inventory is full
Your inventory is full 

[b]The controls[/b]
Actually very playable with mouse and keyboard, despite the warning. The only thing that was a real pain was navigating through the crafting menu and storage. 

[b]Pacing and balance[/b]
Often felt off. Biggest examples I can think of: 
There's a dramatic story arc that seemed to me like it would lead to the climax and conclude the game after tying up a few loose ends. But instead, the most dramatic thing is shown in some drawings and text instead of giving you at least an illusion of agency, and then the game just goes on and on with what felt like minor side quests to me. 
By the time you finally get the resources to unlock the mushroom cellar, it's completely useless. Not that it would have been very useful in the first place, considering you only get one harvest and have to chop down lots of wild mushrooms for the very low drop rate of spores. 

[b]Decorating your burrow[/b]
Quite lackluster, though there is a bunch of cute stuff. Most furnishings are square shaped, they can only be flipped or turned 90 degrees, and you have to use a grid to place them. So the entire system assumes straight walls and corners, while your home is... round. 
I had issues with placing objects in some places, and with background objects clipping into foreground ones. 
By the time you get the nicest decorations, you're mostly done and can't get much of that satisfying and Cozy effect of returning to your nicely decorated home from a day of questing. 

[b]Bugs[/b]
Too many for my taste of both the 6-legged and the virtual variety. Some achievements don't pop, especially for people continuing from the demo. Some quests had reported issues that might be solved now. I didn't experience anything major, just a lot of small annoyances that made for an unpolished feel. 


[b]UPDATE:[/b] I just finished the story after taking in the beautiful visuals and appreciating the dialogues some more. I love how all the characters have their own way of speaking and their own idioms that reflect their environment and culture. It's a shame that the rest felt like a chore a lot of the time. The ending was... fine, I guess? Added to my impression that the game just isn't really finished tbh. Just a simple credits roll, maybe with some concept art, would have gone a long way. 

Most of these issues seem like they should have been caught by decent playtesters. Maybe the devs bit off more than they could chew? I guess my recommendation is to wait for updates. 

A "cozy survival" game that I enjoyed much more is Wildmender. It also feels a bit unfinished and you have to go through some very easy combat, but other than that you can fine-tune your experience from unforgiving to harmless. You can't be a mouse, though. 

* * * 

If you like chill and story-driven games, check out my curator [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/35872486]Peaceful Adventures and Stories[/url]. You're also welcome to join the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/chilladventures]group[/url].", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1763220697}, {"review_text": "I saw this game on a twitch streamer's live stream, and I thought the game was adorable. It was the fact that I could knit that sold me on it. But after playing, the game just feels like an early release, making it seem like an overpriced game.

PC controls aren't the best and are bit janky. Other than the story, there's not too much to do.  Respawn rates increase as you progress so stock piling food becomes ridiculously easy, I could gather over 40 elder berries in one go for example. Stats such as hunger (which barely goes down) and warmth (just blocked the screen and did barely any damage) didn't really matter because you could just eat something. Making the fire pit and kindle instantly obsolete before you get it.  

The food bonuses don't really matter because the bonuses are so similar in time limits and don't increase a lot for each skill, thus not making a huge impact in playing.  Cooking also becomes quickly useless, because in the end you could dig up cooked foods and drinks all through out the map. A way to fix this would be doing something similar to Valheim, and have lower stats that increase with better food items for a time and remove the cooked food from the map and let players cook basic items at campfires. The temp buffs just seemed unnecessary.

 I also wished you didn't get all of your recipes at once, we had a small amount of cooking recipes given to us. The back packs all around the map could have had a recipe and an example of said food item. Making backpacks a more desirable hunting item than they were in the end. Maybe upgrading the stove could soft lock some of the recipes as well, giving players something more to upgrade other than your tools.

One thing that drove me mad was the chest system, no sorting what so ever and you quickly create a stock pile of stuff in there that is a nightmare to look through. I would've preferred just having chests have various spaces so I could ort it myself. Scrolling up or down took forever, making it even more annoying. nor could you get rid of repeat/obsolete items you didn't need, such as the silk hat we get from moss after receiving the silk clothe set first.  Getting things to your quick bar also was a bit weird and slow, maybe just add a button so you can swap an item in your hot bar with one in your backpack inventory would help a lot and make decorating less of an annoyance. I did really appreciate that when in the house I didn't need to fetch an item in a chest to use it, so mad respect for that.

Decorating your burrow has no bonuses, only just a simple achievement.  They could've done so much more with that, such as a rested bonus the better furnished your home is, buffing some of your stats for a little bit. You also had a few items that were un-moveable, which made how I could designed the space felt very limited to me. 

Clothing also had issues, rather than make each set more cold resistant, make each set better for some gathering related task (when you wear it all the pieces together) and let players upgrade the sets to make them more cold resistant. Having a set for chopping, another for mining, and the last one for combat or digging for an increase in drops/speed makes the clothes seem less one and done. Knitting needs a spinning wheel/spindle for making yarn, something to process the raw item into yarn like with the stove or workbench that you can upgrade.

 The same complaint for the tools, they should've let the player upgrade up from your pebble tools, rather than have your old tools sit taking up space in the inventory. The acorn lantern is a specific item that could have been an upgradable item, increasing light radius, which is kind've needed to be honest.

Next, some map designs have too much. For example Bufo's oak area is hard to navigate because of the color palette is too similar, making it difficult for the player to find where they need to go for quests. The tall plants (clovers for example) are cool, but really saturate the area and seem like you can walk through, when you actually can't, adding to the confusion. Took me hours to realize I need to go south and break down those rocks because they blend in really well, which was a common issue in that zone. The oak had the same issue in Bufo's zone, hard to tell if you could cut some logs or that it was there at all, that clearing with the mushrooms and weavil is a prime example of that. It took several run throughs of the area for me to find what I could go through and not go through. Willow's area, I found it hard to find the next area again. This was less the color palette and more of the surrounding area looking un-crossable around the edges. I got stuck several times on hills and thinking this was the edge of the area when it wasn't. It was so open compared to the rest of the map, that I kept thinking I reached the edge when I hadn't. 

The combat was actually really good, from weaving and dodging the enemies as you attack. But some bugs had way too much population compared to others. The beatles/june bugs were just everywhere and weavils felt almost non-existent. I felt like having some bugs get trapped in the webs or the spider actively attacking other bugs would have made the spiders feel more like a threat than they were in the end. You could totally add poison for ants and spiders. If poison is added, lower the spiders health a bit. It would also help give healing items more weight, varieties, and quests/recipes you could get from Gnarltusk.

The characters are well designed and their stories have different impacts that hit deep, but some weren't long enough I think. Willow's could've had a bit more too it. It felt anti climatic and lacking in the emotional depth of being the last mole in the forest. I also wished that Willow could've appeared around the map, making the artifact hunting quest and digging up burrows more than just a one and done quest. Another wish I had was that she wasn't reduced to a gossiping mole who rewards you with furniture. 

One giant issue I realized, was digging up mounds. You didn't know what you'd get, but the amount of cooked foods and teas made no sense and broke the cooking aspect of the game, which I mentioned before. I would have stacks of items sitting next to the mounds because I either didn't need the item, I had dug up something better, or it wasn't worth it due to limited inventory space. Digging up the occasional berries, nuts, rock, and wood made sense but it would be cool to find something else, like root plants to cook with instead of cooked food. Making cooking a better. Digging was just too over powered for the survival aspect

My last complaint lies with the big bad of the game's story: the owl. Other than the cut scenes, the owl isn't a threat as the characters make it seem. You could have the owl fly around and the character would have to hide after Betulinda is taken, giving the game a better survival aspect as was implied in the opening cut scene. You could let the players adjust game difficulty via actual survival and exploration this way. The game feels way too easy for the atmosphere the lore hints at.

Over all the game feels so incomplete. There is way to much left desired after playing the game through, that I feel like the devs should have either made a single linear adventure game with a bit more characters and plot, or a proper survival game, they did not mash both very well and it shows. I hope they update the game and maybe take some of my suggestions into consideration. I loved the game concept and design, but what it lacks shines way too much over the positive. Potion Permit, which is very similar to multiple aspects of Winter Burrow, had the same issues. It took a little bit of updates after a brief hiatus, but they fixed the game, making it worth the price they charged originally.

I hope one day I can comeback and rewrite this review.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1763750636}, {"review_text": "Yes I gave it a thumbs up….HOWEVER

It’s another game where I wish steam had a neutral button to push. For as many good things I have to say about it I have equally bad things to say about it.

Honestly, it was just lacking IMO. It’s like the devs decided to try and do too many genres at once and thus each of them was lacking. It feels like it’s 20 percent survival, 20 percent cozy, 20 percent adventure etc.

None of them are super satisfying, all of them blend together and overall it was just lacking in a lot of regards. 

I give it a thumbs up because I think the game is stable, affordable, and average. But it’s not some great game or anything.

The combat is boring, bland and awkward. Controls on the PC are awkward. Navigating the UI has some mechanical issues. The story and plot is unoriginal as is the idea of being animals in a wild world. 

And I think the cozy and survival tags are just add ons to the games actual main genre which is adventure. The gist of the game is going from one key figure to do quests to unlock a path just so you can go on to the next key figure rinse and repeat. With no weapons, puzzles, unique or variating paths or engaging combat or problems to solve. It’s got some balance and pacing issues as well. The cold will kill you if you're out too long, and with no map or fast travel system you’ll find yourself desperate to find a randomly placed campfire to save yourself. Good luck with that though as I could never find one. And if you run out of kindle then the only place to make more is all the way back at the beginning of your journey at your home which serves not much else purpose than a place to sleep and craft things. There’s no animations for most things you do, there’s nothing to do inside your home other than crafting and only one of those craftings gives you animations. 

I could go on and on and on about the things I didn’t like, but all in all the game wasn’t bad either. It was just painfully average. But I still think the price tag is appropriate so if it still looks and sounds interesting to you, give it a shot I guess. But I didn’t really like it.

If you’d like more information with gameplay I encourage you to check out the review on my YouTube Channel (link below).

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bCndQoidiJQ

Otherwise, thanks so much for reading and I hope I managed to help some of you out there spend your money wisely.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1762977397}, {"review_text": "Very cute game, my progress from demo got carried over into the game too", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1762969013}, {"review_text": "This is one of those games where I really wish that I could post a "middle of the road" type of review. This is not a bad experiance, and the music and art are lovely. The game, itself, however, leaves a lot to be desired. There's just not a lot to do or explore right now and the gameplay gets repetitive really quickly. The combat is also just not very fun. I do, however, love being able to turn off spiders. Big thank you to the devs for that!

This game is still very cute and charming, and I'm going to come back to it someday, I think. But for now I'm going to uninstall and shelve it until some more updates come along. I may change this to a recommend eventually, but I don't feel that I can do so fully right at this moment.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1763044980}, {"review_text": "I love this game but I do have some problems 

Bugs

-sometimes when the mouse goes to sleep the dark screen doesn't go away and I have to exit the game 

Other issues 

There is no map
Difficult to locate characters 
Quests don't have much information and I have to look up everything 
Please add a compass and map


This game is amazing but the navigation is hard and I get lost many times and pass out", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763587246}, {"review_text": "Please....more content, I am in love this game. The storytelling, the characters, and the environment. Omg, I love Gnawtusk. That beautiful, beautiful squirrel😭", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764103841}, {"review_text": "Winter Burrow provided a nice break from typical survival games. Sure you still have to manage your vitals but it never felt tedious or overwhelming.

Performance: Game ran at a stable 180 FPS with no crashes or other performance issues for me (RTX 4090/I913900K).

Game Length: It took me a little over 9 hours to 100% the game.

What I Liked: Craft from storage, no gear durability, the warmth mechanic, no map and the game felt just the right length.

What I Disliked: Combat was pretty basic, can't rebind keys and backpack space felt a little to limited early on.

Overall Winter Burrow was a fun experience and nice diversion from your typical survival game. It is a complete experience at launch, where nearly every survival game launches in early access, and I recommend checking it out if you enjoy survival games.

Here's my full review if you are interested in hearing more: https://youtu.be/Huj0WmMRiMk", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1762967650}, {"review_text": "$20 for a game you can beat in under 12 hours is going to be off putting for some. It would've been nice if there was more content. But, as of writing this; this game has no re-play ability once completed. While I do like the game, I think it has a lot of potential; but I can't call it a great game as it currently is. 
Unique? Yes. 
Cute? Indeed. The storybook design really shines through. 
Cozy? kind of?? If searching the woods while trying to not freeze to death and kill bugs is your idea of cozy then yep, sure is. 
It gets tedious quickly due to the inventory limits. While yes, you can get more space by finding the random expansion out in the woods. The backpack upgrades are spaced too far apart. It's very easy to get lost and wonder where am I supposed to go? because there are parts of the map that don't look like you can go there, when in fact, you can and are supposed to. 
While my tracks in the snow is a nice detail; it would be nice if they went away, or at least faster than they currently do. Like by the next day they're gone, or when it's a blizzard(?) there are no tracks and you don't leave any. 
When you have tracks everywhere, because you're wandering around wondering where do I go? Add in the fact there isn't a map or mini-map at all. It's all the more easy to get lost. 
I would love to see an expansion to this game going forward and I think this game would truly benefit from one. Such as playing the other 3 seasons. Ex: Spring expansion where you need to settle down and have little mice of your own and protect your new family from the owls.
TLDR: Wait for a good sale. And wait and see where the game hopefully goes from here.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1763179280}, {"review_text": "Need a maybe button lol - overall: 5,5/10, achievements: 4/10

Winter Burrow has an absolutely gorgeous art style that deserves a lot of praise. The visuals are so so cozy. Unfortunately, the rest of the game doesn’t feel quite as polished or fully thought out.

The story itself is very simple, but genuinely cute, and the NPCs are all adorable with sweet little backstories. However, the game is missing some important quality-of-life features. Things like item sorting, being able to rotate furniture in all directions, or tracking multiple quests at once would have made a big difference.

The biggest issues, though, are the lack of a map and the extremely small starting inventory. The game often feels like one big running simulator — especially in the beginning, when you don’t know the layout yet and end up running the same paths ten times just to find your way around. On top of that, your inventory fills up insanely fast, forcing you to micromanage what you carry in a way that clashes with the otherwise relaxed vibe.

Overall, it’s a sweet little game for in between. I finished the full story and all achievements in about 10 hours. The achievements are fine — not hard, just a tiny bit grindy in places, but mostly very easy.

For €20, though, it feels too expensive. It’s cute, the art style is absolutely wonderful, but the game is too short and too unpolished for full price. Get it on sale or if you find it cheaper somewhere — then you’ll have a lovely 10-hour experience without feeling disappointed.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763771268}, {"review_text": "This is a very cozy, melancholy take on survival games, which I really enjoyed. The gameplay is about 10 hours, maybe 11-12 if you like to complete all achievements. I loved the story, thought the pace for tool improvements and inventory growth fit the size of the map and the game, and appreciated that it was story that drove your ability to acquire new recipes, but definitely wished for a bit more story at the end as the last couple hours of the game felt more focused on decoration hunting than anything. 

Other pros: Well balanced for the game size, good story, Cute as heck, you can decorate the burrow, fun map exploration, and great emotional atmosphere set by the art, music, and narrative scenes. Cooking and knitting are also absolutely adorable crafting options. 

Cons: I wanted more clothing options to customize appearance w/o sacrificing warmth. A map would have been helpful by mid-game or later (even a very general one). More story would help pad the grind for furniture recipes at the end of the game.

Overall this was a good game and I enjoyed the experience. Good job!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764446740}, {"review_text": "The visuals and music are very cozy and appealing. Love the characters that you meet along the way. With that in mind I really wanted to like this game since it fits perfectly with the type of gameplay I enjoy, however the game does have a few issues and definitely has space for improvement. 
First of all, the games story line is all over the place and it was, for me at least, very difficult to figure out at a certain point exactly where I had to go.  When it comes to the recipes and upgrades, they are very all over the place and some you get with the story and others you find on your own. On top of everything, the game is extremely glitchy and for me personally I was unable to finish the game due to one of the quests freezing on one of the interactions. This game has a lot of potential but I feel like it should not have been fully released yet.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1763406047}, {"review_text": "I enjoyed my time with Winter Burrow. An exploration game with light crafting elements and a home base to decorate. One distinct feature of this game is a cold mechanic. Needing be near a fire after a certain amount of time that can be extended by crafting warmer clothes and eating food. It adds some nice urgency in the early game and tension as you explore new areas.

The main story is ~5-9hrs of gameplay, so don't come into this expecting a forever game like Minecraft, Don't Starve, or Terraria.

Pros:
*Strong art style that ties very well into the theming of the game.
* The progression of the game ties into the theming. The confidence you feel navigating the world as your equipment and knowledge improve reflect the PC's own development.
*Each NPC and their questline felt distinct.
*Each NPC is tied to a different area and each area is distinct enough to navigate without a map. Impressive considering everything is woods, streams, and snow.
*Solid spider design. I was mildly puzzled at the option to turn off spiders in the menu, but after encountering them I see why. Nicely chunky and hairy and big in a way that startled me the first time. As a spider monster appreciator, A+.

Neutral:
* While you can navigate just fine without a map and having one would change the gameplay experience, I still missed having a map. The longing is part completionist 'what if i missed something' and part wanting it as a comfort object.
*The ending, while set up well and fitting for the story, feels abrupt. A little more fanfare or something to extend the celebratory feeling of the climax would have been nice. The conclusion to the NPC sidequests felt better paced in comparison. 
* Unless you want to forage for furniture designs you might have missed or make furniture to get those final achievements, there really isn't anything to do after getting the ending.

Cons: 
* No way to delete or dismantle non-consumable items. They can only be dropped or put in the storage box. Storage is infinite, but it bugged me to have multiple things I was never going to use again there.

Get a cup of hot coco and enjoy the game", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1762970180}, {"review_text": "Liked the style but for a cozy crafting game, this was one of the more tedious ones. Have to constantly go back and forth back and forth for every little task.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1763487665}, {"review_text": "This is a short, cozy game with a pleasant aesthetic and a charming art style, with some lovely artwork interspersed throughout. You play as a mouse returning to a dilapidated former home, and are tasked with rebuilding it while surviving the harsh winter weather.

Mechanically it's your bog-standard "health/food/endurance" (the latter in the form of how warm you are) survival game. Eat food to recover those, rest to recover health, find sources of heat so you don't freeze. There's basic crafting for tools, furniture, and food. Very simplistic combat. The music and look is nice. The story's first real swerve is a family member being snatched by an owl, and the adventure kicks off from there. Throughout your adventure you can spruce up your burrow with crafted furniture, cooking/sewing/crafting things you need, planting/growing other materials, and more.

Unfortunately, I can't really recommend this game in its current state. I've completed it under 10 hours with all achievements. Not quite 100% (there's some stuff I know I haven't found yet). The brevity of the game isn't what's holding me back from recommending it, however. With a price point of $20 the game feels unfinished in a few too many aspects. (And I am taking into account that this isn't a game with a massive production / development budget).

The game does have a few bugs, some more noticeable than others. Nothing game-breaking, but ones you wouldn't expect to see in a released title. There's more than a few typos, beyond what I would call reasonable. While the game is primarily text-focused, there's not a massive volume of words by any means, yet typos were a regular occurrence. 

The story,[spoiler]after kicking off, doesn't really do a whole lot else. The main antagonist presented (the owl) is dealt with off-screen in a cutscene indirectly and never shows up again. The story then, while I do appreciate its simplicity in "finding friends around the burrow and helping them out", doesn't really have any more hooks, and ends rather abruptly with a "thanks for playing!" title card.[/spoiler]

The writing isn't too great, in terms of what little the game has to offer (characters + interaction). The main character is a nameless mouse, who barely says anything (and they aren't a silent protagonist) beyond what's absolutely needed to further the plot along. Most of the time they don't say anything with other characters making one-sided conversations with themselves. For a game that primarily conveys the story through text/conversation, this makes what little story there is, drag.

The combat is barebones (click to swipe weapon until enemy is dead; enemy infrequently attacks for minimal damage). The crafting is alright, though inventory management will leave you frustrated as there's no mechanism for sorting anything, and you have one main storage chest. Interacting with pick-ups can be frustrating, especially when you're out of inventory space (this will happen a lot), and you just want to consume the item on the floor. But to do that you have to drop/swap/eat/pick up in a tedious dance. The interface overall can lead to frustrating moments of things like "accidentally consume an item" or lacking clarity in where things will end up when taking an action in menus, etc.

Navigation can feel repetitive as you have to backtrack to your burrow to do anything (craft/cook/access storage), and the small map means lots of backtracking. Personally though, I don't mind the backtracking as much (the point of the game is exploration), but having to run back to the burrow all the time was not desired. A lot of folks are asking for a mini-map, but I actually liked not having one, insomuch that it was left to me, the player, to navigate or remember where things were, using landmarks, etc. (Or whip out a pencil/paper to roughly map out where to go.) that being said, the art style, while nice, can sometimes mislead you into thinking you can go certain places only to bump into the map's barriers. There's not too much that "hints" towards paths you can traverse on. Which is part of the appeal of exploration, but in my opinion this game leans a little too hard in the "discover it yourself" direction.

---

All of the above means I can't really recommend folks to pick this one up as-is. I commend any team for getting something out the door, but this one definitely needs more time in the oven before I can recommend anyone buy this for $20. It's earnest in its efforts but leaves you wanting.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764288448}, {"review_text": "Really cute game! I had a lot of fun and really enjoyed the story. The game could really have been improved if one of the characters gave us a map at some point. There was way too much backtracking and wandering without any idea how to progress. An hour or two of my playtime was probably spent lost trying to remember how to get to a location I went to once before. Still a great game", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763185650}, {"review_text": "Absolute treasure! This will be a yearly replay game during cozy winter times.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763361671}, {"review_text": "This is a yes, provided you get it on sale. I do really like it, but there isn't a lot of bang for your buck in terms of content.

The music is really good, the art is stunning, the game play loop is enjoyable, and I find the characters to be really charming. The story is very short, though, and even taking your time, you might get 10 hours out of the game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763152391}, {"review_text": "Winter Burrow is a beautiful, cozy little adventure and it's the perfect game to curl up with under a blanket and a warm cup of tea on a winter weekend. It’s gentle, charming, and easy to sink into for an entire day (or two, in my case). I especially loved the storylines of the neighbors; they add so much warmth and personality to the world. 

In my experience it ran perfectly on my Steam Deck.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764330386}, {"review_text": "“But it looks like Don't Starve!” Well... yes, but no.

For its proud claim to be a "survival game," it definitely lacks the teeth and temper. Winter Burrow is way too cute and reminds of a good old fairy tale, this one where relatives die painful deaths and the main characters risk their lives for basic necessities. You know, an average Tuesday in the good old days. Overall, you really have to try hard and use all your skill and gaming experience to die. The game forgives everything, like those toxic relationships you keep telling yourself you’ll escape from. A few enemies are nothing to fear, as they are usually slow, do little damage, and in the time between their attacks, any self-respecting ADHD gamer can watch a couple of videos. Even the weather conditions are predictable and can be countered with a hat and warm underwear. For a hardcore survivalist, this just isn’t enough, as there is simply no challenge in the game. Quests are simple, straightforward, and very, very monotonous (which didn't prevent my great survivalist genius from challenging the system and getting stuck in the middle of an area, not understanding where to go or what to do next). However, for a tired brain, this is just what you need, when the story just calls for the usual "fetch and carry" and "find someone", especially with its gorgeous visuals and matching music.

Winter Burrow would be perfect for mobile platforms, with all its naivety, simplicity, and unobtrusiveness. For a relaxing pastime, on sale or as a survival game for the little ones, it’s a good purchase. However, for other platforms, the price tag is quite high, considering the game's length and overall level.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764876275}, {"review_text": "Winter Burrow is a survival game that felt perfectly my pace. I thought the characters were incredibly well written, the level of crafting was excellent, and the art and music are fantastic. I struggled at times with clarity in some of the story quests but I would recommend this game to so many people. I really enjoyed a cozier survival experience.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1762970090}, {"review_text": "Getting really tired of unfinished, very short, early access games getting a “finished” price.

The art is really nice, the controls feel good. 

But for 9-10 hours of playtime, $25 after the 10% discount is ridiculous. The gameplay is basically spoon fed to you. When anything exciting feels like it’s about to happen, you get treated with cutscenes instead and then you continue playing in the aftermath. 

It says I’ve played 50+ hours of this, that’s because it froze multiple times on the main menu and I turned everything off in frustration and forgot about it. 

It’s not a difficult game by any means but it’s also missing a lot of what makes a game fun to play. The rewards never feel worth it, you don’t need half the healing items or food you come across, the furniture isn’t necessary but the items you do need (wool for warmer clothes) are incredibly difficult to find and I usually turn the game off after a half hour of playing cause the constant walking back and forth to my home and the next objective gets old quick. I also can’t understand the devs decision on not adding a compass or map from day 1. Feels like Gaming 101.

It’s a cute game, it’s an admirable effort. But  given the bugs, lack of content, and unenjoyable re-playability…it should be a $15.99 game.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763661912}]

column13: Become the custodian of a store dealing in occult antiquities. Explore the quaint and gloomy town of Undermere, where strange goings-on and dark mysteries abound. Find and identify arcane artefacts, use your collection to aid the townsfolk with their unusual problems — and remember to pet your cat!
