[{"review_text": "A jeweller’s kind of game. You sit alone, hunched over your table, magnifying glass in hand, [i]Parva Naturalia[/i] and [i]Corpus Hermeticum[/i] beside you, and try to shed a dim, flickering light on the grim dark world around you, bring a little order to the ever-disturbing chaos of existence, one little strange artifact at a time.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758370999}, {"review_text": "After playing and loving Strange Horticulture I knew I had to get this one on day one! In fact I was so excited, that for 2 hours this afternoon I checked Steam every 5 minutes to see if it was finally out. 
Only 1 1/2 hours in and I can already tell it will be one of my new favourites.
I love the dark yet cozy atmosphere the devs managed to capture. It's perfect for cuddling up with a blanket and big mug of hot chocolate (which is exactly what I did when I started the game for the first time today). 
The riddles are a bit more challenging than in Strange Horticulture, but I personally enjoy that a lot.
There is a lot of mythology embedded into this game which makes it incredibly engaging. 
I can't wait to figure out every ending and find out how the story will unfold. 

I also enjoy how the UI improved compared to Strange Horticulture. Exploring your tiny Antiquities store is so much more fun now. I can't wait to absolutely most certainly 10000% not touch anything at all while Eli is gone 🤫

Thank you to the devs for the work you put into this game. You can really feel all the love, thought and hard work that was put into this game.

Also there is Jupiter. Need I say more??

Edit after finishing my first playthrough: 10/10 as expected", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1758131875}, {"review_text": "The puzzles are much improved from the Horticulture (on account of not just the plants) + managing and sorting collection is much more convenient. The next game should be about a library.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762785635}, {"review_text": "I feel like this game is DEFINITELY more challenging than Strange Horticulture. There are far more resources you need to cross-reference in order to identify items, and luckily the quality-of-life improvements like the index at the back of the book were incredibly helpful for flipping through the DOZENS of artifacts and entries. While it's challenging, it's also forgiving. The minigame that you play to resume your attempt after too many failures doesn't reset the whole day, it simply brings you back to the last encounter you were on before you went insane, which is incredibly merciful, and the minigame itself isn't too hard. I also made liberal use of the hint button, which was very helpful, I especially appreciated the progressive hints, going from a more general "put you in the right direction" type of hint, to eventually directly telling you the answer if you were really struggling. It is a very fun and worthwhile puzzle game experience, and do highly recommend. Though, if you feel like you might need a bit of a more entry-level introduction to a game like this, I honestly think Strange Horticulture might be a better start!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758437229}, {"review_text": "I have been eagerly awaiting this game and I can truthfully say... IT WAS WORTH THE WAIT! If they make a hundred more, I will play them all. Strange Literature, Strange Beasts, gimme all of them! If you loved Strange Horticulture then you'll love Strange Antiquities. It plays so similarly but they've added elements to make it feel fresh without changing its identity. The atmosphere is cozy and calming. The sound of the rain and Jupiter purring is enough to put anyone in the mood to solve a mystery in the ominous, gloomy town. The characters are interesting, the oddities are fascinating and the story keeps me hooked. Oh and the music! The music is scrumptious. I can't sing its praises enough. Just buy this game already! 

PS. You better pet the cat. Always. Hellebore will know if you neglect his friend.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758164073}, {"review_text": "Super fun, I'm really enjoying it. Most hints are appropriate in terms of difficulty, only a few have been problematic. I give it a 9.5/10. If you loved the first game, or story-driven games in general, I recommend giving it a try. The demo is an accurate representation of the gameplay.

I'm deducting .5 points because of two things:
- The aforementioned occasional hint that is just not adequate or is easy to interpret incorrectly (like one of the map hints really should say north, not northwest). 
- In circumstances where the next thing you need to do involves finding some secret within the shop, the game's hint system gives you a generic "you haven't fully explored the shop yet" type message, and then doesn't give you anything else. Good luck clicking everywhere and waving potentially-activating items around until you give up and google it. I think the generic hint is fine if the player hasn't viewed a hint for it yet, but if they have, the next hint should give *something* more helpful, at least the general area of the shop or the mechanism for the missing thing.

Those are really minor gripes, but they did negatively impact my experience a bit.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758230898}, {"review_text": "Clues! Labelling things! Arranging them on shelves! Maps! 

If you like deductive games where you work things out by consulting multiple sources of information, you will quite probably like this. If you liked the first game, you will definitely like this. 

I haven't even finished this one yet and am pining for more of these games. Maybe next time we will get Strange Aviary? Strange Entomology? Strange Fishery? Give me more cool looking things to label, it soothes my soul!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758137679}, {"review_text": "Strange Antiquities takes what made Strange Horticulture fun and then goes a step further with the study of occult objects and themes.  This is the type of material I personally enjoy.  A good mystery, a nice rainy atmosphere, a purring cat, and some spooky objects with mysterious uses and symbolism.  There are some great puzzles here.  I found myself clicking around and seeing what would happen.  There could be some quality of life improvements such as being able to write notes, bookmark pages, and perhaps the ability to have more than 1 book or map open and able to review the contents together.  I found clicking on the book would turn the page when I was simply trying to put two books side by side on the desk, which was slightly annoying.  I did enjoy the multiple resources needing to be consulted, however, I began just making notes in my own 'book of shadows' to keep track of the clues from the shop visitors.  Regardless of those small nuisances, there's plenty to label and sort in this installment, and while I'm not quite finished with it, I am already hoping there's more to come.  Perhaps a strange apothecary/alchemist or potion making/spell casting will be in the future?  

Praise the Dendrew.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1759938647}, {"review_text": "Strange Antiquities is the long-awaited "sequel" to Strange Horticulture and it does not disappoint! If you enjoyed Strange Horticulture you will undoubtedly enjoy Strange Antiquities. So go on, stop reading the reviews and immerse yourself once again in the gloomy world of Undermere! Even if you liked the concept of Strange Horticulture but felt a few things were lacking, there's a good chance you will like Strange Antiquities, as it has improved upon the concept. But no worries if you haven't played Strange Horticulture as you can definitely play this masterful narrative-driven, puzzle-solving mystery on its own. 

Set in the gloomy town of Undermere, you work in a "shop" selling "strange antiquities". Customers will come to you with their troubles and ask for help in finding the correct object. Sometimes they know what they want and you just have to identify the correct object. Sometimes they don't know what object they are looking for and it's up to you to figure out what would be the right item for them. And sometimes they know what they want, but maybe you don't want to give it to them. Your actions do have consequences though, as the game also likes to remind you that the citizens of Undermere don't forget (and neither will you).

During the game you collect several books which will help you in identifying the objects. Don't forget to label them once you've done so, or you can turn on the auto-labelling feature. Not all objects are what they seem and the clues and identifying features vary, keeping the game exciting and fresh. You also get a new card every day which might lead you to more antiquities, if you manage to solve it. Aside from the day-to-day dealings of artifact collecting and helping customers, there is something brewing under that dark cloud that is Undermere. A story in which you play a big role in how it will end. Who do you trust? Which path will you take and where does it lead? Or will you try them all? And if you haven't had enough mysteries yet, there are even more mysteries lying in the store itself. 

This game is perfect if you're looking for something with that dark, gloomy atmosphere, without being too scary or horror. It manages to fit into the cozy category, without being cute. Perfectly fitting for the Fall season and Halloween, but I honestly would play it any time of the year. And when you feel like your sanity needs a little something, you can always pet your cat (or can you?). And don't forget to try placing some objects next to your furry friend and see if he'll react!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1760888463}, {"review_text": "Strange Horticulture was my favorite game of 2022. It was dark, moody, brilliant, relaxing and enthralling with its plots and deduction loop. Strange Antiquities is that, but more. It's an expansion of the concept first explored in its predecessor.

It's not quite the exponential growth, more like a curious wave, slowly but steadily getting bigger as it hits the cliff, testing the effects of the erosion it causes, taking more from it, leaving only the salt and the spaces, and then deciding that it was to hit faster, stronger, meaner. When Strange Antiquities decides that you've had enough time to learn, it hits you with everything it's got and then some.

The gameplay loop remains the same. You're in charge of a store, it's mysterious objects instead of plants this time, and have to give clients whatever they ask you for. For that, you'll have to follow the clues in one or more books to know which object is which, and then go out to find more of these antiquities following the lead of obscure riddles with too many layers sometimes. And then, on top of that, you've got some decision making here and there, because it's up to you to decide whether to give whatsherface and whatshisname something that might aid them.

Or something that might end them.

Undermere is still the home of weird happenings. Its inhabitants too tempted by the whispers of the unknown, or following traditions older than the sea. And the story itself is contained enough that you don't need to tahe played Horticulture to submerge yourself in these pages and our ever comforting Jupiter's company. But why wouldn't you? You're doing yourself a disservice by passing on that chance.

Brilliant, easily my GOTY of 2025.

For more reviews of games that are cute, or creepy, or both, please check my curator page: https://store.steampowered.com/curator/44079361/", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1759091993}, {"review_text": "I haven't played the predecessor yet (I'll catch up on that, I already had it in my library somehow), but somehow  the antique setting appealed to me more than the plants. The game manages to captivate you, because finding the items and locations is really fun...and you can pet the cat. :3
Since I like it so much, I'll definitely play the first part right after this.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762538280}, {"review_text": "You don't need to have played Strange Horticulture (SH) to play this, but there are returning characters and some references to SH.

[b]The Verdict:[/b] Vibes on point. The story, characters, and every secondary mechanic improved, in exchange for the core gameplay mechanic getting worse. 

[b]The Good:[/b]
- Preserves the overall Brit fantasy, cozy mystery, tea and rain on the windowpanes vibe of the first game. 
- Story and characters are deep enough to be interesting, light enough to not drag on the pacing, and you feel more like a participant in the story this time (SH sometimes felt like the story was happening around you more than to you). 
- The exploration/map-puzzle part of the game has expanded and is LOTS of fun. Maybe the next game should be Strange Cartography?
- No more exploration energy meter. You just have a longer sanity meter now. Useful or neutral exploration doesn't cost you anything, dead-end or risky exploration costs sanity. Much tidier than the two separate meters from SH. 
- The game automatically creates multiple saves, making it easier to replay if you want to try to get all the endings. 
- Some features for speeding up looking at reference materials (e.g., a book having clickable keywords that link to an index).
- If you were mad at only having three options for labeling stuff in SH, guess what: you now have multiple colors, shapes, and symbols to choose from.
- Cat. 

[b]The Bad:[/b]
Compared to SH, the core gameplay mechanic -- investigating, sorting, and IDing your items -- is more complex, but not in a good way. It's less about deductive reasoning and research skills, and more about your willingness to tediously click through every possibility on every screen. 

SH had one book, a couple of tools, and one description for each item. Here you will eventually have multiple books, several tools, and every item can be investigated for up to 12 different details. In many cases, you'll need to check over a lot of stuff to ID your item. But you can only look at one thing at a time: You can't bookmark the books, you can't have multiple books open at once, you can't examine two items at once, and you can't look at an item and a book at the same time. Those last two are really bizarre considering that when you're looking at an item, the screen is mostly empty... and when you're exploring, you CAN have a book open over a map, and easily flip back and forth between the two.

Multiple times, rather than "researching" the item the way I was supposed to, I just tried every item I had and playing the sanity minigame when I got it wrong too many times -- it was faster and less of a headache. (The sanity game is now a dice game, which is fine, I guess. It's not bad, it just doesn't match the vibe or the theme IMO.)

Worst of all, most of the late game IDs depend on using a specific tool, which is embedded on a separate screen from where you keep the items. So to use it, you have to drag each item one at a time over to an entirely different screen. If your other clues are vague, this could easily mean dragging 10+ objects across two screens (and back) to check each one with the tool. This finally broke me and I just started using guides to cheat on item ID. 

[b]The Bottom Line:[/b] Buy on sale.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1758599864}, {"review_text": "Strange Horticulture was one of my fav games the last few years, which always creates slight trepidation for if a new offering can live up to the original. 
Thankfully Strange Antiquities is just as good as the original, if not even more substantial. Both games do an absolutely amazing job of making you feel like a genius puzzling out and categorising all the objects [i]all on your own[/i], even tho it is in reality all expertly planned to give you the exact info you need to puzzle out the relevant customer requests and nothing else.

I have some tiny nit-picks that could have made it even better - 
- I wish the map-based puzzles were slightly more friendly for ppl who're directionally challenged
- I wish some of the late game items had one more clue making them less of a guessing game
- and I wish the thaumic fields were actually noted down somewhere after you discover them, as it's awkward that is the only clue not noted down on a piece of paper/in a book. I resorted to a notebook and pen, but it is strange to have to do that for this one puzzle element and none of the others.

But none of those nitpicks affected my experience enough to leave me feeling anything other than extremely satisfied and happy after finishing the game.

The world building continues on Strange Horticulture, and presents another engaging and dark mystery, with changes depending on how you solved the "pick one of two options" customer requests, that can lock you out of endings alltogether.

I hope we keep learning more about the town of Undermere and the world of the Strange universe, and I am eagerly awaiting the next game from Bad Viking", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758348971}, {"review_text": "Pure vibes honestly, a worthy successor to Strange Horticulture 

The general gameplay is much more engaging whether its toying around in the shop, exploring Undermere's places of interest or just trying to identify which artefact is which using all the tools you have at your disposal from the composition, the weight or if it just makes you *feel* anything. its great

definitely a buy", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758124630}, {"review_text": "Fantastic game. Great story throughout and interesting puzzles/ detective style tasks. 
I love the atmosphere, the music and the characters. I like how you get decisions to make sometimes and enjoy the investigative side - Loving the three maps this time and the several books you have to look through. 
Loved it!! Being greedy - would love another game. Really enjoyed Horticulture and this one. One with beasts / animals - a Bestiary would be wicked!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1759301373}, {"review_text": "I love the puzzles. The shop is even more interactive than Strange Horticulture and that makes it even more challenging and fun. Glad to have a released OST for this one too!!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758609669}, {"review_text": "This is great follow up to the first game Strange horticulture but just be warned: they definitely increased the difficulty in this game! Instead of 1 map, you now have 3. Instead of 1 book for references you now will have a total of 4. On top of maps and books you will have additional tools to help you solve riddles and identify items. I will confess I still needed to use the hint system 3 times but otherwise I found all the new additions, although overwhelming at first, worked together great once you get into the groove.

It's a lot tho and it might be overwhelming for newbies, so just be warned! Some puzzles took me almost 10mins to solve as I needed to consult several books and utilize tools as well. BUT if uou thought the first game was too easy or you're looking for a challenge: this is the game for you!

I had a lot of fun and I'm looking forward to the next game by the devs!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758790563}, {"review_text": "Incredible story and atmosphere. The subtle world building you learn through the descriptions of items you find is incredibly enthralling.
In comparison to the prequel, Strange Horticulture, Strange Antiques improves on the formula and overall a better game in most areas:
- The art is cleaner.
- New and returning characters are written well despite minimal dialogue.
- Decoding which item is which is much more difficult than Horticulture, yet more rewarding including feedback to learn the "systems" that trinkets are built within.
- I especially enjoy the enhanced "closer look" mechanic, now including multiple ways to interact with items than Horticulture, including ways you wouldn't expect to try.
- My only gripe is the Game Over minigame is by far the most significant downgrade in the series. Instead of being a simple, cozy puzzle to resume gameplay, it's a game of chance. Sure, this improves the idea that you're on the brink of disaster, building upon your characters inner tension of "will I win my mind back or will it shatter in two?" But no matter how good you are at the dice game, in which I can usually win very quickly, you're still down to the whims of chance. But, please, don't let this single part detract from you buying the game. It's just my opinion of the change in game design that I personally find more gripe than kudos to give.

Overall, again, Strange Antiques is a phenomenal game for the scope it's looking to fill, and those "Aha!" moments you have while playing make this a great puzzle game for people of all difficulty levels.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1759025225}, {"review_text": "It's a good puzzler that rewards careful observation and clues. My only critique is that some of the later clues are *very* opaque. All told, the puzzles are fun and the narrative makes the puzzle solving more engaging.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763229554}, {"review_text": "Had fun until I didn't. The idea is good, and it's mostly well developed, but the puzzle design has flaws. Games like this rely on satisfaction of a clever solve, and the puzzles got less and less satisfying as it went on. The number of details you’re expected to either remember or reference is too high in the late game, it becomes tedious to mouse over dozens of objects multiple times to reference information. 

QOL issues: Takes too long to page through books, which is most of the game. Can't view vital pieces of information alongside other vital pieces of information. The game asks you to remember details of items from hours previous, or spend time re-learning every bit of information about previous items. 

Suggestions - Page turns should be instant. Allow "pinning" of an item/note/card to screen. Allow text-searching for labeled items (a-la control-f). Add an in-game notes feature to prevent me from alt-tabbing to notepad. Auto-sort feature for identified items (alphabetical or otherwise) would be nice. Don't reveal total number of days in the game, I shouldn't be constantly aware what % of the game I'm through. Don't tell players to "slow down" every time they make an error, disregarding the possibly immense time they spend on the decision. The dice game to recover after "loss of life" is too easy, and honestly just shouldn't exist in this game. Add a “failure counter” to endgame. 99% of players are playing this exactly once, don't force re-solve of puzzles, it's a waste of time, not a consequence (which might lead to growth). 

Despite all this, I like the game a lot, and would gladly pay the game's price again for the same experience. I almost never write critical reviews, and only give a thumbs down here because I love this genre, and hope the devs see this feedback. I'm so grateful for the love put into this game, and I hope Bad Viking can continue to learn and grow, and keep making puzzle games in the future. Peak.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758157813}, {"review_text": "An extremely compelling puzzle game. I don't think I have yet encountered a puzzle that when I finally figured it out didn't have me slapping my head and going "how could I have missed that". The story elements are also very nice, and having this weird world steeped in mystery and bizarre occurrences in the background is lovely.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1759719553}, {"review_text": "Fantastic and fun puzzle game with an eerie/cozy atmosphere. I am excited to revisit this game in a few years!!!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758589829}, {"review_text": "Even better than the first game - perfect mixture of cozy and creepy atmosphere, with improved UI and puzzles.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758138601}, {"review_text": "Fiendishly difficult in places, this builds upon the foundation of Strange Horticulture to several more layers of complexity. If I had one criticism, it's that the map puzzles that depend on matching or following directions depend a bit too much on vague rather than precise appearance. This can lead to a bunch of brute-forcing to explore. Additionally, the extra complexity for the items has not kept pace with the tagging system. Nevertheless, I find myself very immersed.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1759871860}, {"review_text": "Has a cat you can pet ... if anything else needs adding then it's a solid puzzle game, just long enough so the gameplay loop doesn't become boring, pleasing art, eerie vibes.
Not sure it captivated me enough to want to replay it for the rest of the endings, but overall thoroughly enjoyable, and its prompted me to dust off it's predecessor from the deep depths of my un-played games.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1764930011}, {"review_text": "a neat little sequel to the already perfect "strange horticulture", expanding on the original ideas, adding a couple of new mechanics, it charms you like a morgan's folly and doesn't let you go until you finish it. perfect for rainy autumn evenings.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1759590885}, {"review_text": "A brilliant follow up to Strange Horticulture. They've expanded on how you identify objects in really satisfying way which feels a lot more immersive. I also like that they swapped your energy meter for travel to just a small penalty if you identify a clue card location wrong. I was waiting for this to drop cause I loved the first game so much so I am biased but even if the first game wasn't quite your thing I would recommend trying this game out still as everything is a lot more polished. I've only just started playing so will update my review once I've finished but I'm really loving it so far 10/10 spooky cozy mystery dark academia vibes!!!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758125576}, {"review_text": "It's a ~6 hour deductive reasoning game with a darker atmosphere.

Gameplay-wise, you're asked to identify mystical objects based on vague descriptions, and associative imagery. The puzzles here are better than I expected; not everything is spoon-fed to you. You'll often have to make an educated guess based on multiple pieces of information spread across different sources. 

Narrative-wise, it's fine. It has some minor branching paths based on how you solve certain requests, but it's pretty much linear. There's darker elements, but it's not an overt horror game. Didn't hate it. Didn't love it. There are some returning characters from the previous game, but the story is completely separate.

Overall, it's a direct upgrade over Strange Horticulture, and I'd recommend just playing this instead. The puzzles are better; the objects are better; and the QoL is much better.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763644204}, {"review_text": "Did you enjoy Strange Horticulture? There is *chance* that you may not enjoy this one as much.

To get right to the point, Antiquities iterates on Horticulture in a few frustrating ways: Gone are the hidden messages, in place are additional texts for referencing and a clunky new tool to detect "fields" around objects which is disconnected from your main shelf view. Imagine if, in Horticulture, you had to swap completely over to a different window and try and drag several plants with you in order to use a tool that was the ONLY WAY you could identify species in the late game; That's what happens in Antiquities, the late game is mostly detecting these fields using a tool that is not only inelegant to use, it's not fun to use either.

Antiquities also gives a couple new "maps", in addition to one for the town of Undermere (rather than the county, as in Horiculture) but for me all of these maps seems a little less fun to navigate than the previous game. True, the grid system was probably a bit unrealistically simple, whereas Antiquities you really have to thing around how buildings are shaped and named to figure out clues, in that regard it is HARDER, but not in a fun way, if that makes sense? The game requires a lot more studying than logic at a certain point, and really stumbles over that dangerous line between a game of research and feeling like homework.

A complete improvement is in the "failure" game, this time a dice matching game much like Yahtzee, really making failing a less frustrating possibility.

Regarding the story, I found myself less interested in these peoples' lives than I was in Horticulture, the 'threat' to Undermere felt a little less intriguing this time around, and I didn't feel like I made as much use of my Antiquities in this one as I did the plants in the previous game. Additionally, I really didn't like how you the player are presented as this sort of dumb little shop assisstant, a real step down from taking over the shop as the owner of Strange Horticulture.

Overall this was missing the immersion into the story as well as the level of fun in the puzzle solving from the previous game; There are more variables to consider with the Antiquities, which again makes it strictly harder if that's what you're looking for, but it is unwieldly and not fun to access all the tools you need between Sight, Perception, Touch, Fields, and the litany of symbology included to familiarize yourself with, it became such a chore that I just ended up using a guide for the Antiquities by the last few says of the story, something I never did for Horticulture. If you are a BIG BIG Horticulture fan you'll probably try this anyway, but if you're looking to save a bit of money I might suggest that this could frustrate you more than fulfill you, and rather fill you with a desire to go back to the previous game instead of replaying this one.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758650678}, {"review_text": "i played the first game, strange horticulture, and it was interesting, this one seems to be just a copy of it, so i found it boring. I don't suggest to buy it.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1762313320}, {"review_text": "It's more Strange Horticulture, but with creepy artifacts. I enjoyed the first game thoroughly and have been anticipating this one's release for quite some time. Let me tell you: the wait was absolutely worth it.
Both Strange Horticultute (which you totally should check out in case you haven't yet!!!) and Strange Antiquities capture the atmospere of cozy and interesting, yet misterious and mildly unsettling atmosphere of occult Britain. I find it genuinely enjoyable to sort through items and puzzles one by one, and the main plotline you get to experience via talking to a handful of characterts only adds to the satisfaction.
The desings and the attention to detail is simply great, however I do have to note. I still recommend the game 100% and hope to see new creations from the developers in the future!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1760405530}, {"review_text": "I really really really wanted to love this game, because I enjoyed Strange Horticulture so much. The gameplay mechanics were definitely improved from Strange Horticulture - really enjoyed the Index function included in this one. Maybe I'll pick it up again when I have more patience. For now, time to replay Strange Horticulture!", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1760076575}, {"review_text": "This game and strange horticulture are a blast. go in as blind as you can!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1759025397}]

10/10 would buy it again", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 54, "timestamp_created": 1762789811}, {"review_text": "Love this game but, there are some major flaws that need to be addressed. Now this is gonna be a major yapfest, but that's only because I love this game and want it to be better than it currently is.

Too Many Currencies: This game early on was originally planned to be a gacha game and many elements of that still remain. There are so many different currencies and different stores to buy different things, such as equipment, kits, special moves, etc. Getting most of them is RNG and none of the ingame stores have everything so you will HAVE to farm tokens to get those special moves you want. Crazy Idea, but what if... We just had one currency for each gamemode? I can't be expected to try for a random chance at 8 riceballs for some shoes when I gotta equip my whole team. It honestly felt like they were planning to have a paid currency that applied for everything, but since they canned the idea of this being a full on gacha game they scrapped that idea but the garbage token system remained.

[strike]Chronicle Mode: It's exhausting to play. You may not feel it in the beginning, but eventually you realize, "Oh. I gotta do every match TWICE to continue." The idea is you first play as the original team the scenario had, heavily scripted. After beating that you then use your own team to do the same match except now it's not scripted. Now I used to flip flop between Story and Chronicle mode to avoid fatigue if I got too tired of one. But I've since beaten story and now I sometimes turn my brain off in some Chronicle matches which is not a good thing. Possible solution? Have us only needing to do Chronicle Battle to unlock the next match and unlock ALL the difficulties of the match we just beat. I'm gonna go back to farm anyway. Just don't make it mandatory for us to do 2 of the same match for every match just to progress.[/strike]
They've made it so if you score enough points in the first half you can skip the remaining game. Good change.

Bond Stars: Bond Stars are the currency for the Gacha. The currency itself is fine, but getting them is the issue. The only way to consistently get them is via online matches which gives 5 per match(5 Bond stars let you run the Gacha once which gives you 12 characters each). In Chronicle mode doing the max difficulty option, Hero Battle only has a CHANCE at giving you like 2 Bond Stars. This is terrible. Do they not realize that some people on Console don't have online subscriptions? Those people have no consistent way of farming the Gacha currency. Make 5 Bond stars the minimum reward for completing max difficulty matches so that everyone has a way to farm.

Keshins/Hyper Skills not accessible: In order to purchase Keshins like Lancelot or Maestro you need to fully complete Inazuma Eleven Go's Chronicle route. That is way too long to be able to obtain them. Now some Keshins are available in the marketplace, but those are mostly Special and Movie Keshins. The chronicle mode let's you play the story of the og games, with Go Galaxy, Ares and Orion releasing at a later point. You can switch between dub and sub names which shows they are aware of their fanbase.

There's different ways to unlock characters. You can unlock players through a gacha, which you unlock the tokens for through PvP. There's multiple groups/banners with players, so you can decide who you want to pull for. You can also just play chronicle mode and then unlock players and abilities through there. Chronicle mode let's you play the key matches of the anime and og games stories and then gives you a chance to unlock the players and abilities from those teams. If you have trouble unlocking players there is a shop that allows you to use spirits of other players and merge them into your preferred player or abilites. For example: Legendary Burn + Gazel + Aphrody = Chaos Break or IE2 Shawn/Aiden x4 gives you IE3 Fused Shawn. Spirits are basically players, you can keep them as spirits as exp to boost another player to a higher tier, or use the spirit to unlock the player itself. 

PvP is actually pretty balanced, any character can become great through the abilearn board (skilltree). However there isn't a level cap in competitive. This can still be daunting but players do have different tiers (common, rare, advanced, top, legendary, hero). With these tiers levels aren't as important. The higher tier a player, the slower they level up but the stronger they get. So if you have lvl 50 legendaries, you could still compete against level 80 commons. As such, it will not adress basic gameplay that is inherent in all Total War games, such as turn based production and real time battling, but rather will compare Empire: Total War with other Total War titles.

As a Total War fan, my personal preference goes to this title, Empire. I like most Total War games, but Empire stands out to me. For one, I enjoy the historic time period. For two, it plays the most 'different' from the other titles.

Older titles, such as the first Rome: Total War game and Medieval II, heavily favour an agressive play style, with a lot of chaotic melees. Later games, such as Rome II and Shogun II, lean more towards a balanced stance between agression and response, depending on how superior your battlefield position and force is.

Empire: Total War, in contrast, is a game of patience. Instead of charging into melee, the gameplay entails meticulously positioning lines of infantry and laying down volleys of fire. Mirorring the idea of the age, it is the 'gentleman's edition' of Total War. The Fall of the Samurai expansion to Shogun II comes closest to the Empire style of play, with rifle armed infantry and gatling guns, and keeps the option to go into melee samurai charge mode, but Empire remain the only edition (excluding Napoleon: Total War) to favour a line to line exchange of fire.

Another difference is the naval battles. Granted, later editions in the Total War series incorporate these as well, but Romans or Edo era Japanese boats firing on one another with arrows pale next to the awesome power of a multiple deck ships of the line wailing away at one another. Again, Fall of Samurai introduces ironclad ships that approach this somewhat.

Of course, later titles have more recent, better developed versions of some of the aspects of Empire, and there are some other downsides to Empire. As usual with a Total War title, Creative Assembly has a tendency to leaving things not as smooth as they could have been. Most bugs have been smoothed out after release, as they usually are, but some small problems remain here and there (such as batteries of cannon simply not firing unless directed to do so in a very specific way).

Additionally, while the battles themselves offer some of the most unique Total War battle experiences, the map campaign improves little on previous editions. Not that this is necessary, because the region based resources and capture cities work well for the entire series. However, there is one significant improvement to me here, and that is that the map spans the most territory of any Total War game. Where Rome II limits itself to Europe and North Africa, and Shogun II is set in Japan, Empire scopes the entire Western dominated world of the Elizabethan age: Europe, North America, Africa and the Indies. The later release Napoleon: Total War does not nearly reach the score Empire does, and its campaigns are focused on smaller scale conquest rather than the world theatre of Empire.

As for the research system, it seems that the Empire title marks the start of an overhaul, where the series starts mimicing the more traditional 'tech tree' idea that prevails in many strategy games. This is not a bad thing, but it is an addition that was perhaps not entirely necessary. All the more so because sometimes it seems like a shoehorn to introduce the game's traditional late game obstacle. Every Total War game has some sort of hindering mechanic that makes the game prgressively more difficult as time advances. In Empire, research (which you need to keep up with your modernizing rivals) introduces squalor, which makes for an unhappy populace, which makes you either have to sink money into keeping them happy or have to deal with rebellions.

If you prefer a more agressive slugfest in a game, I would suggest Rome II, Shogun II, or if you don't mind some more antiquated aestethics and graphics, Medieval II.
If you like your games new and crisp, the more recent titles are sure to be your thing as well. If you want a more modern game that still uses line infantry and gun batteries, Shogun II's Fall of the Samurai expansion is your ticket.

But if you want a true, professional standing army of line infantry that knows how to hold under fire as well as deliver it, if you want to be a gentleman general of standing, if you want an 18th century battlefield, then this, my friend, this is the game for you.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763583960}, {"review_text": "THE best 18th century RTS ever made. I say this is still a worthy entry to the Total War series.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758507202}, {"review_text": "Total War: EMPIRE – Definitive Edition is a comprehensive and polished update to one of the most ambitious entries in the Total War series, blending grand strategy with epic real-time battles set during the volatile 18th century. Covering a period of intense geopolitical upheaval, colonization, and technological advancement, the game immerses players in a sprawling campaign where diplomacy, military might, and economic management all play crucial roles. The Definitive Edition refines the experience with improved visuals, UI enhancements, and all previously released content, making it the ultimate way to experience this classic.

At the heart of Empire lies the dual gameplay loop: the strategic campaign map where you govern your empire, manage diplomacy, research technology, and expand your influence; and the real-time tactical battles that bring historical warfare to life. The scale is impressive, with dozens of playable factions spanning Europe, Asia, and the Americas, each with unique units, challenges, and strategic positions. Naval warfare, a major highlight of the game, is detailed and rewarding, adding an extra dimension to both combat and empire-building.

The Definitive Edition smooths many rough edges from the original release, offering a more user-friendly interface and better AI, which makes diplomacy and combat feel more engaging and less frustrating. The game’s complexity can be daunting at first, but the depth is what fans of grand strategy cherish. Managing supply lines, balancing budgets, and navigating alliances or betrayals create a rich tapestry of decisions that shape your path to dominance—or ruin.

Visually, the update enhances the detailed units, sprawling battlefields, and vibrant cities, breathing new life into the 18th-century setting. The soundtrack and sound effects evoke the era’s tension and drama, from the thunder of cannon fire to the subtle ambient sounds of bustling ports and forests. These elements contribute to an immersive historical experience that both educates and entertains.

In summary, Total War: EMPIRE – Definitive Edition stands as a definitive package for strategy enthusiasts seeking a complex, historically grounded, and visually improved Total War title. Its vast scope, combined with engaging tactical battles and deep strategic layers, offers countless hours of gameplay. Whether you’re reliving the Age of Enlightenment’s conflicts or forging your own empire, this edition is a worthy revisit for longtime fans and a strong recommendation for newcomers to the series.

(edit) i hate this game

genuinely only play this game if you want to hate the human species.

on a real note though, this game has serious issues. the community is appalling. you will either get toxic killers that slug and tunnel all game and then nod their head like theyre amazing at the game or that theyre funny, or on the other hand you will get toxic survivors that tbag the killer needlessly or sandbag and troll other survivors to ruin their experience. or lastly - you'll get people like the infamous annieilusion_ttv, who are just so oblivious to their own delusion and will do everything except take responsibility for being a complete ass. usually its easy to not let the community of a game influence your opinion on it, but with this game, its so in your face that you cannot avoid it. and the thing i hate most about this community problem, is that when you get in a game with either of these types of people, your natural instinct is to dc. but OHH NO you will get a dc penalty/ban that prevents you from playing. its like the devs DONT want you to play their game. I understand that dc'ing was a big issue in dbd, and so i respect that they made it harder for sore losers to stop disconnecting the second the game isnt going the way they want, but with such a toxic playerbase, its hard not to dc sometimes - especially when faced with players who want to make the experience miserable.

next is the problem with balancing. you will either go against killers that have no kind of cooldown or punishment for misusing their abilities - like the ghoul or legion for example that can use their ability to gain distance on survivors and cancel it to get quick and easy downs without any kind of punishment for cancelling their ability, or they will be using the most obnoxious perks that make it impossible for you to make any progress in the match. or you will go against a 4 man swf with perk builds that are solely purposed to making your experience as difficult and as painful as possible. and the problem with both sides is that some people will say the game is killer sided, while some will say its survivor sided. there is a severe divide in the community. my opinion? as someone who plays alot of both killer and survivor, i just say that the game is overall unbalanced on both sides. its just a mess.

next is map rng/randomness. some maps will have an insane amount of vaults and pallets that make it torture to play on as killer, but other maps will have dead zones everywhere with no vaults or pallets within a 32m+ range - making it nearly impossible for survivors to have a chance on.

then you will get problems with bugs and glitches and cheaters. i will admit that ive not had many issues with cheaters or glitches - so w anticheat i suppose, but the game is still spaghetti coded, and that often leads to odd issues arising when new content is added like new characters and perks.

i just hope some major changes can be made to this game, because i play it so much and love it. im addicted, but i also hate 3/4's of the time i spend on it, because the game is unbalanced, the community is abysmal, and players will exploit every unbalanced thing in the game to make your experience as either killer or survivor as miserable as possible.

not only that, but i miss the old vibe that the game had. it was darker and grittier, and had a watercolour/oil painting aesthetic that me and alot of people miss. now unfortunately i didnt play dbd back then, i started playing in the fnaf chapter, but ive still played well enough to know where the game's flaws are - and i understand that dbd is a more competitive game now, and if it had the same level of darkness and aesthetics that it did back then, it would be even more of a miserable experience.

i think the one of the most annoying things is when you get teammates that blame everything on you when they were throwing the game or doing nothing all game.

[EDIT] i felt the need to add this little segment in to complain about how broken killers like the legion are. i just went against a complete failure of society who was using legion to gain distance and block pallets and get easy downs. they were using spirit fury and gen pop perks to waste as much of our time and resources as possible while also making it impossible to progress. I HATE THIS GAME.

anyway;
despite all of this, i still love the game for some reason, i just want it to improve.

First things first: the game’s concept is excellent for casual players. It’s constantly updated, with new content every few weeks. You can treat it as a quick pick-up-and-play experience, or sink thousands of hours into it - it’s as shallow or as addictive as your preferences allow.

That said, the learning curve is steep. While the core gameplay is simple and there aren't many interactable elements, the depth comes from its variety. As of writing this, there are over 40 killers and 127 killer perks, which means learning dozens of playstyles and counterplay strategies.

On the flip side, there are 46 survivors with around 150 perks. Again, lots of combinations to experiment with or master.

Most perks can be unlocked through play or purchase. But don’t expect a quick grind. Even after 1000 hours, you may not unlock everything. Some perks are also locked behind paid DLCs(not a complaint, just a fact).

Here’s the twist: despite the wide variety, once you climb the matchmaking ranks, you'll notice a pattern. Only a few killers dominate the meta, and only a handful of survivor perks are commonly used.

And the community? It’s the full internet zoo. You’ll meet incredibly kind, wholesome players—but they’re the minority. Most matches involve someone sandbagging, throwing the game, or verbally melting down over a single mistake.

You’ll see people building their real-life identities around this game.
You’ll see how deeply some crave digital victory.
You’ll see content creators whose "amazing" fans may harass you.
You'll see that some players seem to log in purely to annoy others.
And yes, you’ll see both blatant and subtle cheaters—and it might take BHVR a while to act.

Now I mainly play it because I hate myself and I deserve the suffering :)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 108, "timestamp_created": 1746996260}, {"review_text": "This game.

This game is like a methed out stripper with the world's most prime example of a 'butter face'.
You pop seven honey packs while she tugs at your shirt to bring you behind the building where the prettiest sight is the dumpster with handlebars for her to grab onto.

You're thinking to yourself, "Fuck, anything is better than nothing"

No. You're wrong. You wake up with a burning, itching nutsack and heroin needles stuck in your arm.

I have played Dead by Daylight long enough to know that this is not a game. This is a curse. A loop of anguish disguised as a multiplayer horror experience. If hell had patch notes, they’d look exactly like DBD’s.

It is a psychological torture chamber duct-taped together with piss, rust, and false hope. It’s the gaming equivalent of someone whispering “trust me” right before pushing you down a flight of stairs, then charging you for cosmetics on the way down.

At first glance, it seems harmless. Spooky, even fun. Fix some generators, run from a killer, escape. How hard could it be?

That’s how it gets you.

Dead by Daylight is a poisoned apple. It looks shiny. Crisp. You take a bite, and before you know it, you’re foaming at the mouth, crawling through a nightmare landscape of camping Bubbas and teammates who couldn’t outsmart a Roomba.

That feeling dies faster than a Meg running in a straight line.

This game doesn’t play you, it gaslights you. It convinces you that if you just try harder, you’ll enjoy it. That next game will be different. It won’t be. DBD is Sisyphus with a skill check, and the boulder is on fire.

The gameplay loop is a hamster wheel from Hell, greased with survivor blood and killer tears. Every match feels like waking up in a Saw trap where the only way to escape is to play the same four maps against the same four meta perks while being chased by the same three killers who play like it’s a job and you're the unpaid intern.

Want to play killer? Hope you enjoy being flashlight-blinded by a SWF squad with comms sharper than a military operation, tea-bagging you at every pallet like you owe them money. Want to play survivor? Get ready to be tunneled like the killer spotted you in a dream once and took it personally. You'll spend 80% of the match crouching in a bush, praying your teammates weren’t spawned directly from a YouTube comment section.

The matchmaking system was forged in the deepest pits of digital hell. It doesn’t care. You could be new, hopeful, full of light. The Entity does not care. It will match you with a Prestige 100 Blight main who treats your existence like a personal offense.

This game is a slot machine designed by a drunk Cenobite. Everything is RNG. Spawns? RNG. Skill checks? RNG. Killer powers? RNG wrapped in lag. You’ll get hit around corners, downed through pallets, and blamed for it by a game engine held together with bubble gum and trauma.

Playing Dead by Daylight is like being stuck in an elevator playing clown music while someone slaps you every 30 seconds and occasionally throws bloodpoints at your face as a reward. And you’ll thank them. You’ll thank them because you’ve been conditioned to think this is normal.

It is not normal.

This game is an abusive loop of dopamine spikes and absolute despair. It’s like getting back together with an ex because they said they’ve changed — and they have. They’ve gotten worse. And they brought friends. Named “Deadlock” and “Pain Resonance.”

You don’t play DBD because it’s fun. You play it because it’s personal now. You’re in too deep. The grind has you. Your brain is mush. You’ve screamed at the screen more than you’ve spoken to your friends. You ARE the Wraith now.

And yet you queue up again.
Because maybe this time it’ll be different.
It won’t be.
It never is.

Dead by Daylight is a haunted casino where the only thing you gamble is your sanity.

Then I switched to killer. Yeah. Nevermind.

Suddenly every match was a parade of flashlight clicking, teabagging at every corner, whether it is behind the pallets or at the exit gates, hook dancing like it’s a school talent show, and then the cherry on top: endgame chat filled with angry essays and threats to report me because I committed the ultimate crime of... playing the game.

You can’t tunnel, you can’t camp, you can’t slug, you can’t hook the same person twice unless you’ve asked for permission and sent a handwritten apology. Forgive me masters! Who am I to defy you? You waited near hook while three of them were circling it like mosquitoes? That’s camping.
You left someone on the ground to chase someone else? Slugging.
You dared to down someone in under 15 seconds? How dare you. Reported.

Winning isn't allowed, or it is allowed but only in spesific conditions, those are? I don't know either, maybe true winning was the friends we made along the way...

You so much as exhale at the wrong moment and it's "wow, toxic killer."
You blink before they do? Reported for harassment.
You play without letting them 99 every gen, unhook their friends, heal under your nose and spam emotes at every pallet? You’ve crossed a moral line, my friend. You’re the problem.

I've been accused of tunneling in matches where I barely remembered who I hooked once. But apparently that guy with four meta perks, voice comms, a flashlight, and 3 resets somehow has the moral high ground. Incredible.

And don’t think Reddit is any better. That place is a sandbox for people to roleplay as philosophers. "Here's a 900-word post on why killers shouldn't pressure gens too hard because it makes me anxious." These people are writing ethics dissertations about a horror game while teabagging you at the gate and flashblinding you mid-pickup.

The hypocrisy is astonishing.

They’ll use every dirty trick in the book, abuse every exploit, spam every mechanic, and then cry about "toxic behavior" because you tunneled their friend after he ran into you three times in a row like it was a social experiment.

The only way to survive this game as a killer is to mute chat, never open Reddit, and treat every survivor like they’re one step away from writing a twitlonger about you.

This community is toxic, delusional, and self-righteous.

I cannot advocate more against playing this game than anything I have ever played. Dead by Daylight is likely one of the worst multiplayer games to try to pick up and play in modern gaming due to the sheer amount of complexity that is involved in learning this game. I have accumulated 1600+ hours over around a year and a half, and I can confidently say that I have a firm grasp of this game and its various mechanics, perks, killers, and techs. There is some fun to be had in this game for sure, but some fun is all you will get as it will quickly sour and turn into one of the most frustrating games you will ever play. Both sides of this asymmetrical game are extremely infuriating due to how terrible the DBD community has become and due to how incompetent Behaviour Interactive is at maintaining their biggest game with no competition.

[h2]How it feels to play killer [/h2]
While playing killer, you will feel powerless and survivors will often have perks builds that intentionally torture you the entire match. A group of survivors queued together is a very common reason your matches as killer will be so insufferable due to the match becoming almost impossible to win if the survivors are good enough. Personally, I do enjoy going against high skill survivors and trying my best to outsmart them and use my own personal skill to win the match, but more than likely you will not win against these kinds of players. This makes playing killer feel almost hopeless at times because you just can’t catch a single break as you lose match after match. Trying to play fair will often result in you losing so you will almost be forced into using meta perks and “toxic” gameplay to enjoy any of your matches. As a killer player, you will have to be aware of the “Survivor Rulebook” where you prioritize their fun over your own. If you want to win the match as a killer it’s “toxic” or try-harding but when survivors want to win it’s fair for them to use every means necessary. It’s a very hard balance to maintain as you want to enjoy your match but also want to make the match fun for the survivors as I think it’s important to remember that the survivors are people who are playing the game just the same as you are. Killer gameplay can be very rewarding and satisfying at times, yet it ends up getting more and more stressful as you get less and less gameplay when you prioritize fun over winning because generators will get finished very quickly without constant babysitting.

[h2]How it feels to play survivor [/h2]
While playing survivor, you will come across many toxic killers that make the game absolute hell for your team. This can be fixed by queuing with friends and working together to skew the match heavily in your favor as this game becomes extremely survivor sided once there is direct communication between the survivors. There are also many perks that can drastically improve your chances at winning as a survivor. Some of these perks have been practically unchanged from their initial release such as Dead Hard being a meta perk since it was released back in 2017 and maintaining its place as one of the best perks in the game till the modern day. This makes survivor gameplay pretty stale because you have to use perks that give you as much advantage to try and survive against killers using meta perks as well. Playing survivor can end up feeling quite good after a while, but your general experience will end up being unpleasant due to the large amount of killers and perks you have to learn to play around.


[h2]Items, Add-ons, Map Offerings [/h2]
Both sides fall into this meta hell of using the best things the game allows you to use so that your matches feel less frustrating and left up to chance. Adding any sort of variety to the perks you pick increases the risk of you having no fun in your matches significantly. There are also plenty of items for survivors and killer add-ons to use as well to increase your chances of winning. These can feel necessary sometimes because of how good survivor items can be and how bad your killer's basekit can be without certain add-ons. There are also map offerings which will end up being used in many of your matches because certain maps in this game give an extreme advantage to one side or the other according to their perks or their killer. This is one of the worst parts of the game because you essentially lose the match before it even starts. They are addressing this issue, but it’s much too late.

[h2]Personal Experience/Rant [/h2]
My personal experience with this game has been easily negative as it has been one of the most unfun, stressful, and anxiety filling games I have ever played. Despite my utter [b]hate[/b] for this game, I kept playing it somehow. There’s something severely addicting about this game where it feels like you spin a slot machine to try and have fun in each match. I typically prefer playing killer because survivor solo queue is extremely unfun/inconsistent (also cause Wesker is very fun), yet I have around equal time playing killer and survivor. Even when I win a match as a killer, it feels like I haven’t won because of how unfun and stressful the typical match can end up being or it was so easy to win that it feels unsatisfying. I typically don’t even expect to win my survivor matches because I feel like when you pick survivor you shouldn’t expect to survive. The entire lore of DBD is that the survivors are supposed to be under-powered and tortured by the entity, but they end up being the ones dictating the flow of the match the higher elo you get. It feels as if the main goal of this game has become solely to win rather than enjoy the match on your own terms and that is obvious the more you play against better players. Many DBD players are chronically online and end up being some of the worst people you can interact with as they cannot take a single bit of criticism or negativity without it becoming a personal attack on them. There’s certainly some good cookies out there, but if you play this game enough you will end up playing against or with these entitled DBD addicts. They take the game much too seriously and ruin the experience for others. There’s also the competitive scene of this game which I think is a joke (no offense to the people who partake in it). DBD has to be one of the most competitively unviable games I have ever played and the majority of the games I have the most time in have been competitive games. It’s extremely unbalanced and even when played at the highest level it has to have so many rules to make it viable as a competitive game. There is also the issue of Behaviour Interactive being some of the worst developers for an extremely popular game that is constantly getting bigger and bigger media licenses for their game that they seemingly cannot fix. It feels as if there is another game breaking issue every other update or even more frequently than that. I’m not gonna sit here and pretend game development is easy, but I’m not going to let Behaviour try to convince people that the bugs and glitches they allow in the game aren’t a problem. They’ve also removed certain features of killers that had increased the skill ceiling of those killers such as Blight Hugtech being removed. This gives the implication of other skillful mechanics that weren’t intended being removed like Wesker Hugtech or Hillbilly/Oni 180 Flicks which slowly makes the game even less fun for skillful play. Wesker Hugtechs and his general gameplay have been the main reason I stuck around this game. I’m around my limit of playing this game consistently because it just isn’t fun anymore. I have no incentive to continue improving past the point I have reached because the game just isn’t worth it. 

[h1]I regret playing this game. [/h1]", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 74, "timestamp_created": 1741761649}, {"review_text": "This game has to many problems to make it recommandabele for new players. You are going to spend the first couple of hundred hours getting absolutely destroyed. You could seriously fill a college degree with the amount of esotheric knowledge within Dead by Daylight. Practially none of which the game will actually explain to you. Meanwhile you are playing against people who have condensed this game down into a science, instead of a fun party game.

If you play as a survivor you will have to learn how every one of the 40 killers work. With some being much more complex than others. Some killers are basically several killers worth of mechanics rolled into one, while others just try and throw an axe at you. 
On top of that some 180 different perks that greatly affect the killers abilities, of which they could be running any four. And finally up to 2 different add-ons that can fundamentally alter how a killers core mechanics work. And if you want to get good at the game, you need to know at least most of them.


Then there are some 220 perks you could get as a survivor that you also need to learn and understand  Of course you dont get any of these at the start, you'll have to grind for them and 'Prestige' characters. It'll easily be several hundred hours before you even have access to most of the good ones.
You'll also have to learn to do chases and all the intricate mechanics, which often also means becomming familiar with all the different maps and their variations. This is a game where you can actively get better by just watching other people play, just because of how heavy it is on all the little details that amount to a big deal in a match. So be prepared to get dunked on for a long while

If you're killer the game is a lot easier because solo-queue is very killer sided, but you're still going to spend hundreds of hours just to get some perks. And you will occasionally go up against a Survive With Friends (SWF), that is basically a premade group, and they absolutely clown on you. Why? Because the game is balanced around survivors lacking a lot of important information. You even have a lot of perks you can use as a survivor that are just designed to give you some small amount of information. The game itself has no voicechat, or even an ingame chat function.

So a group together on 3rd party voicechat is basically bypassing all that, and the access to information survivors wouldn't normally have flips the games balance on its head. And your favourite killer might be practically useless as you go from the hunter to basically being the play thing.

But why would you be facing such big range of skill in survivors or killers? Because Dead by Daylight has one of the worst matchmaking i have ever witnessed in a multiplayer game. 
It will happily put very new players with just a couple dozen so hours against players with thousands of hours. Do not be fooled by claims that it is skillbased matchmaking, as the outcomes go exactly as you would expect when some fresh killer tries to catch some survivor with 6000hours and every meta perk. Or if some rookie survivor with less than a hundred hours catches the attention of a killer who is pushing 2000 hours.

To compound further, the netcode is terrible, just aweful. I've played games that can to a pretty good degree track even individual bullets with dozens of players in the same match. Dead by Daylight cannot even accurately track entire player entities, and there are at most 5. Even the slightest bit of latency can drastically throw off the game, and a ping of over 100 already produces some real bullshit.
On top of that there is such a huge array of bugs, that in such a thightly 'balanced' game can make a big impact. Such as being unable to hear sounds properly, or entire attacks simply failing to register even if they connected. Yet these bug can go months or even years without ever getting fixed. In some cases they simply became a part of the game as a 'feature', with the community calling them 'techs'.


Also we cannot ignore that the game is certainly to a degree pay-to-win, as you need to buy survivors/killers in order to get access to their perks. While it is not essential to play the game, 
 as some very good perks are available in the base game. Having access to a wider range will undeniably be an advantage as perks make up essentially most of your 'power' as a survivor (and also to a large degree as killer).

Lastly the community certainly leaves much to be desired. Trolling, outright leaving are very common occurances, trying to get themselves killed fast so they can leave. This isn't as common anymore with recent changes and survivors can no longer kill themselves when they get put on their first hook, but it is an ongoing issue of unsportmanlike behavior.

If despite this you still really want to play an asymetrical multiplayer game that is essentially a game of tag, with or against cool monsters and experience the high when you lose a killer in a chase, or outplay a survivor and get that kill. Then i dont believe there is really anything better on the market right now. 
It does get better after the first 200 - 300 hours. I just cannot recommend a game that requires such a massive time investment and comes with so much potential frustration. before it becomes 'good'. The community will typically regard anyone with less than quadruple digit hours of playtime as pretty new.

Also, like most games, it's more fun with friends.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1737301854}]

At its best, it feels like you're playing with a living, breathing ant farm—but the ants have weapons, personalities, and the terrifying ability to form kingdoms, go to war, and start rebellions while you’re trying to just grow a mushroom forest in peace.

The charm of the game lies in how free it is. You can drop meteors, raise mountains, flood entire continents, or just zoom in and watch a random villager named Greg survive against impossible odds and somehow become king. The pixel art is clean, the sound design is surprisingly atmospheric, and the simulation depth can get pretty impressive when everything starts interacting.

But—there’s a “but”—sometimes that freedom turns into chaos you can’t really steer. The simulation is fun, but also feels a bit too hands-off at times. Kingdoms rise and fall so fast that it’s hard to actually follow a story unless you’re constantly pausing and checking menus. And once things spiral out of control, it’s like the world melts into a soup of fire, acid, and tiny pixel screams.

Also, the UI can feel a little clunky when you want to be precise, and some god powers could definitely use a little tweaking or better feedback. Like, when I smite someone, I wanna feel that divine judgment, not just see a puff of smoke and guess if it worked.

That said, Wordbox scratches a very specific itch—playing god in a sandbox full of tiny dramas. It’s chaotic, it’s messy, and sometimes it doesn’t make much sense... but that’s also part of the fun. If you like world-building, breaking, and watching unexpected stories unfold, it’s definitely worth a try.

The open beta has amazed me way beyond what the mobile game already has. It's amazing game for idle play or direct play. It's a game for any creatives that love world-building and want to create their own lore for DnD or fiction writing. You can customize and create your own maps, kingdoms, villages, cultures, clans, religions, languages and subspecies.

The religions and languages, part of the "Beta Monolith" update seem to go so deep in their customization and how they play out in the entire world. And I'm really happy that you can trace back parental and child relationships through the genealogy tab. You can actually track how traits are passed down and their patterns, and manipulate them if you want. 

The Gene Loci is crazy, I ignored it for the first 8 hours because I didn't look up a guide for it....it was overwhelming at first and then it clicked for me how to use it - it's like a puzzle, you can put different genes anywhere in the Loci but they need to have matching ATCG color-coded links.

There are so many races and species you can choose from, I can barely fit all of them on the biggest sized map. There's the typical Elves, Dwarves, Humans, Orcs. Yet there's humanoid versions of lemons (unacceptable!!! - Lemongrab), cats, dogs, lizards, frogs, armadillos, goats, rhinos, buffalos, sheep, foxes, snakes, penguins, CAPYBARAS, monkeys, LLAMAS, bunnies, .....garlic.....and more. They have animal and humanoid versions of these animals, some that create kingdoms and civilizations and can speak languages and others that are simply animals - you get to choose.

You can make an evil candy kingdom of evil gingerbread men and a psychotic paranoid kingdom of lemon people. You can make pacifist buffalos be forced to go at war with bunnies with bloodlust. Different species can join the same kingdoms, villages, religions, clans. The only thing species can't do together is procreate with each other. But you can even customize how each species reproduces, whether they require male and female, or even two parents, or if they give birth through eggs or by actual birth.

This game just seemed extremely detailed.

This game can be simple and played without much input, yet you can also customize every single thing and follow your favorites and be playing more directly.

I highly recommend this game to people who love procedural generation or colony sims. If you've already tried the mobile game, I would recommend getting the early access beta PC game over the Premium mobile game.

Have you ever played a game and just been overwhelmed by the possibilities within that have yet to be realized?  Worldbox, for me, was one of those games.  Operative word is "was".  I'd have called this game "GOAT God Game Potential: The Game" before the recent beta update.  In fact, I removed it from my wishlist (I played mobile for a long time) assuming the game was dead.  My heart just couldn't take it waiting so very long for something to be done with the game.  I didn't buy it...  There wasn't 20 dollars worth of material in the game to buy it on top of the mobile version.

Boy was I mistaken.  Worldbox is the No Man's Sky of god games.  It never was bad, though.  It was just frustrating to see what the game could be versus what it was.  Little did I know that they'd layer on a whole new game on top of the sim they built.  Before, I was overwhelmed with disappointment that there wasn't more meat on the bone, but now I'm overwhelmed with the sheer number of additions and features.

For the uninitiated, Worldbox, is a god game sandbox in the vein of old Bullfrog games like Populous, letting you interact with the world in any way you want and to any degree.  It's for kids who liked watching ant farms and enjoy emergent stories and situations.  It even comes complete with a series of challenges hidden inside the achievement system, where you can unlock and control a series of powerful aspects by which to modify both the world and its inhabitants.  It's a game where you can just watch things happen or you can meddle with the world's population all the way down to neuron activation and genetics.  

The part that blew me away was that all of this chemistry set is there to give you options.  For example, I found a race of candy creatures in a special biome that were just milling about.  I bestowed a prefrontal cortex and an advanced hippocampus and now those candy creatures established a colony in their candy land, somehow got the "evil" trait, and threatened to take over my world.  The last alliance of elves and humans held them off but I had to interfere with a well-placed volcano, to keep King Candy with his full set of legendary armor and a flame sword from wiping out the elves with his counterattack.

Stuff like this is commonplace in this game and the butterfly effect is very real.  Had I not messed around with the natural order, King Candy would have never risen to power and laid waste to most of my world.  

In short, 10/10... best god game ever without the Peter Molyneux bravado and over-promising.  Well done.
