Alright, that was the simple review, time for my detailed one. 
Ahem I'd recommend grabbing a snack. 

(This review is mainly for people looking to buy the game.)
(Some details are omitted for spoiler purposes)

Graphics: I personally adore the graphic style, it is not at all "realistic" if that is the style of games you're looking for. It's a game that has a "cartoony" vibe with dark undertones. Think, 2d platformer smashed with a 3d dungeon crawler then add some gore. It's a stylized look, as I'm sure you can tell from the pictures. There isn't much to say about the graphics besides they are awesome if you love tarot cards.

Gameplay: Personally I dont give a rats ass if the game is repetitive, if you dislike repetitive games DO NOT GET THIS GAME. I've seen reviews of people talking about how they HATE the gameplay loop. Allow me to describe the game loop to you quickly. 

Lamb (You) has a cult (Think animal crossing village), and to get materials, they need to leave the cult. Which is where the dungeon crawler comes in. 

You go through an area, get your materials, come back to the cult, build shit, then leave. 

Seems repetitive, which it is. However there are some things I glossed over like the fact you can leave the dungeon anytime (If you have the cloak for it, a cloak upgrade is basically when you defeat a big boss you get something to get a new cloak, and an ability of one of those cloaks is you can teleport out of the dungeon whenever you want with a short windup). So you're not "forced" to go through the full dungeon. Plus, I've actually seen people completely skip over the dungeon crawler portion, which I find kinda insane. The dungeon crawler is a key component of the game, but you CAN avoid it, HOWEVER it is SIGNIFICANTLY more difficult to deal with your cult.

 Basically what I'm stating here is: If you don't like dungeon crawlers this isn't the game for you, but if you love the game enough (stubborn enough) you could avoid that part of the game. You will be missing the story however so it's not recommended. 

Alright lets talk about the difficulty of the dungeon crawler itself now that everyone who hates dungeon crawlers has left. 

The difficulty of the dungeon crawler itself is player focused/skill. There are things that can assist, or make it more difficult for players either looking for a challenge or simplicity, which I will not get into much as that leads to spoilers. But lets simplify it, lets say you're just using vanilla lamb (basic/starter kit). Here's the basic dungeon rundown:

When you go into a dungeon, the dungeon will show multiple types of rooms. A dungeon run is called a CRUSADE. There's 14 total types of rooms. I would highly recommend searching “Cult Of The Lamb: Level Types” if you're a visual learner. I'll list all the rooms you'll come across keeping one out for spoiler purposes. If not, I'll try to explain here. The brackets are the symbols you'll see

Normal fight (Sword Symbol), Hearts (Heart), Coins (Coin), Food (The Food of that Dungeon), Lumber (Chopped Wood), Stone (Rocks), Bones (Crossbones), Tarot (Card), Shop (Shop), Event (Question Mark), New follower (Stick Figure Kneeling, Holding Hands upward), Miniboss (Skull and Crossbones). 

Okay Now ill briefly explain what each room actually IS;

Normal Fight: I will come back to this one to not confuse you

Hearts: You get Health

Coins: You get Money

Food: You get Food for your Cult

Lumber: You get Wood for your Cult

Stone: You get Stone for your Cult

Bones: You get Bones for your Cult 

Tarot: You get an NPC that gives you a temporary bonus ability ONLY for that run

Shop: You can buy shit there. Do you not know what a store is? Touch grass.

Event: This one basically has a chance of a few different rooms and I will avoid stating because of spoilers.


New Follower: You get the CHANCE to free a NPC to join your cult

Miniboss: This one will ONLY EVER appear at the end of the dungeon run. It is exactly as it's said. It's a miniboss. 

Alright now you know what rooms are congrats. Let's go back to the Normal Fight room. You will ALWAYS start a Crusade in a Normal Fight Room. A normal fight room is basically where you go through multiple smaller rooms freeroam (you get a minimap) and you fight shit. Make sure you explore everywhere because most of the time you have the chance of running into a Tarot type room, or an NPC, or Treasure. What's Treasure? Treasure can vary. Coins, Materials, or Weapons to use in the dungeon. During the start of the Crusade when you enter the Normal Fight Room you will get 2 weapons. A physical one, and a ranged one, and yes you carry this weapon throughout your entire crusade.

If your fucking confused. Think of a Russian nesting doll. There are the General levels, which I mentioned. Then the Normal Fight Rooms.

Okay enough about the gameplay, if you really need to know more search up a video stupid. 

Audio: The audio is heavenly, you just gotta hear it for yourself. Sadly the person who made the original music passed away. RIP your music was beautiful. 

PC Requirements: It's pretty average. You don't need a super computer, but you still have a decent computer. The size is workable, there really isn't much to talk about here, idk what computer you have. Figure it out yourself.

Grind: There isn't a grind. UNLESS you care about achievements. If you do, Well… have fun. 

Story: I will not go into the story at all as this is mostly a spoiler free review. However, the story is good, and the Final Boss Fight is awesome. Highly recommended.

Game Time: It gets repetitive, the game will go as long as you can go. 

Price: For me it's highly worth the price, and if you don't think so, just wait for it to go on sale. It goes on sale very often. I bought it full price, with every possible DLC. (Jumping on Woolhaven the second its OFFICIALLY out).

Bugs: Very Minor Bugs, If you do find any, report to the discord. They deal with it pretty quickly.

For me? 10/10 I love being a psychopathic lamb that runs a cult.

[{"review_text": "Toby Fox probably did not expect the amount of love and tears this game would bring to the players, since his own description to advertise the game is unserious; joking about dating skeletons and dogs appearances. Yet the simplicity of his production reached millions of hearts in a way few games ever do.

At first glance, Undertale seems like a quirky, retro-style puzzle game . But it quickly becomes something more; a story about kindness, choice, and the consequences of your actions. It doesn’t just let you spare your enemies; it makes you wonder why you would want to hurt them in the first place. And somehow, in its quietest moments, it reaches your heart in the gentlest way.

Soundtracks are fun, super fun, a little sad, heartwarming, nostalgic to many, and so much more. I have a hard time not getting mist-eyed over ost 071 of this game, simply titled “Undertale”. This simple melodious and heartfelt ost is how Undertale feels, and what Undertale is. I retreat my words from earlier, probably Toby DID know how moving this experience would be, it just seems right to assume so, why would the most soul-stirring ost that you cant just simply ignore the tears building up as you listen, share the name of the game? 

I can’t believe this game is turning 10 years old this year, it takes me back so long ago, the old memes, the gameplays of many youtubers, people getting mad that Sans was hard to beat, the Amv’s, the AU’s, the AU’s soundtracks, the cringe OC’s that we used to meme about; you couldn’t escape the fandoms best and worst moments, I wonder if we were too judgmental on this cringey phase some in the fandom shared, we were younger, and much were just kids being kids that shared the same passion as the others. 

Now we look back with a nostalgic feeling, and i intend to always remember this game for what it was, for what it meant to many and to me, for what it offered and delivered, a fun, heartwarming, inspiring, engaging and beautiful experience, that brought me laughter and tears equally, rage too for many hehe.

Ten years of history and an unforgettable game that will be in our hearts as long as time goes by. Thank you Toby Fox, forever.❤️", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1747674742}, {"review_text": "[h1][b]Undertale...[/b][/h1] 

[i]Where do I even start with this game?*[/i] I feel like this is the type of game that everyone who loves video games has heard about, but not everyone has truly played. Sure, you might’ve seen the memes, the fan art, the endless discussions about the “pacifist” route vs. the “genocide” route, but [b][i]it’s the experience of actually playing it that hits you in a way that no amount of spoilers or reviews ever could[/i][/b]. Like, yeah, it’s a game, but [b]it’s also way more than that[/b]. [b][i][u]Undertale is a journey[/u][/i][/b]. [i]And a damn good one at that[/i].
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3443430778
Look, I’ve played my fair share of games. I’ve had my emotional moments. The highs, the lows, the victory, the defeat. But [i]Undertale did something[/i] that no other game has ever done for me: [b][i]it made me feel like my actions actually mattered[/i][/b]. I’ve never been forced to think so much about my choices in a game. Do I spare this monster? Do I show them kindness, even if it’s just a few words? Or do I give in to my darker impulses and kill them? The fact that [b]the game forces you to live with those choices[/b], that no matter what path you take, [b]the consequences hit home[/b]… it’s just something that so many other games miss. [i]Most games don’t ask you to actually feel the impact of your actions. [u]Undertale does[/u]. And that’s what makes it stand out.[/i]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3517859518
[b]It’s not trying to WOOOW you with high-end graphics or flashy cutscenes[/b]. Hell, the visuals are super basic, the characters are pixelated, but it doesn’t need all that. [b][i]The real strength of this game lies in how it uses the medium of video games to tell its story[/i][/b]. You’re not just a passive observer. You’re the one pulling the strings. The characters aren’t just there to look pretty or be generic NPCs — they have personalities, desires, fears, and they react to you. [i]The whole game feels like it’s speaking directly to you[/i], and that’s a rare thing to find in modern gaming.

[i]The humor, the heartache, the twists[/i] — [b]it’s all woven together so perfectly[/b] that I was laughing one moment and then tearing up the next. [i][u]Undertale knows how to balance its tones[/u][/i], something a lot of games can’t pull off. [i]It’s not just about having a good story [/i]— [b]it’s about how the story makes you feel[/b], and Undertale nails that in a way that very few games do.

[i]And the best part?*[/i] [b]You don’t need to play this game with any kind of guide or prior knowledge[/b]. Just dive in and let it take you wherever it wants to go. Every playthrough is different, and no matter how you approach it — pacifist, neutral, genocide — there’s something valuable to learn, something profound to experience. It’s not just a game. [i][b][u]It’s an experience that stays with you long after you’ve turned off the console[/u][/b][/i].
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3450456815
If you’ve somehow never played this game, do yourself a favor. Play it. Go in blind, with no expectations other than to see what unfolds. I promise you, this is a game that’s going to leave a mark on you. It’s the kind of game that makes you think about what it means to be human, to have choices, to live with the consequences. [b][i]A true masterpiece in every sense. 10/10[/i][/b], and I wouldn’t change a thing.

I've made some memories for sure", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1749224181}, {"review_text": "[h2][i]Monster Hunter: World - From Fear to Fatalis: My Hunter’s Journey[/i][/h2]

Monster Hunter: World is a [b]very special game[/b] to me, it was my first experience with the Monster Hunter series and my introduction to the franchise. I first started playing back in 2018 on PS4 as part of the [b]new 5th Generation of Hunters[/b], completely new to the series.  

At its core, [b]this game isn’t special in the traditional sense[/b], [b]no standout characters[/b], and [b]no emotionally rich NPCs[/b]. But for me, it became a [b]second home[/b], a world filled with [b]countless memories and unforgettable experiences[/b]. It's easily one of the [b]best games I’ve ever had the opportunity to play[/b].  

This game is exactly what its name suggests, you [b]hunt monsters[/b]. You [b]study their behaviors[/b], [b]trap them[/b], [b]exploit their weaknesses[/b], and [b]adapt to their strengths[/b] in order to take them down. You use [b]various weapons, tools, and strategies[/b] to hunt these massive, catastrophic creatures, and it’s an absolute blast, especially with friends.  

I still remember [b]being terrified of my first Anjanath[/b], running for my life, screaming and here I am about to [b]solo my first Fatalis[/b](a super boss) though I’m pretty sure I’ll fail. But that journey from clueless rookie to seasoned hunter is what makes this game so special. This game has a unique, indescribable charm to it. It constantly [b]pushes you to improve[/b], giving you that [i]butterflies-in-your-stomach[/i] feeling every time you hit a wall that seems impossible to overcome, until, suddenly, [b]everything clicks[/b] it's pure magic.

[h3]The "World" Aspect[/h3]
The name Monster Hunter: [i]World[/i] couldn’t be more fitting. The environment is absolutely mesmerizing teeming with small critters, towering monsters, and breathtaking landscapes that feel alive. Getting all the achievements in this game led me to discover hidden caves, secret traversal paths, and entire areas I never even knew existed. And even now, I’m certain I’ve only scratched the surface.

Every time I play, I learn something new not just about monsters or weapons, but about the world itself. Whether it's a hidden mechanic of a weapon, a subtle environmental detail, or an unexpected monster interaction, this game constantly surprises me. The sheer amount of content showcases the love and dedication of the developers, and it’s incredible to see how much thought went into every detail.

One of the most immersive aspects is how monsters interact with their environment. They claim territories, warn you when you get too close, and engage in brutal turf wars when another predator enters their domain. Witnessing these battles unfold feels like watching one of the most cinematic moments in gaming history. I could probably write an entire essay about all the incredible things I’ve experienced in this world.

[h3]Base Game & Iceborne Expansion[/h3]
The game is split into two parts:  
- [b]Monster Hunter: World (Base Game)[/b] – This was my [b]introduction[/b] to the series, and I already liked it.  
- [b]Iceborne (DLC Expansion)[/b] – This is where I [b]fell in love[/b] with the game.  

Iceborne [b]forced me to "Git Gud"[/b] Master Rank hunts are no joke, especially post-Iceborne content like [b]Tempered Furious Rajang[/b] and [b]Arch-Tempered Velkhana[/b] are relentless. No matter how much I improve, I still can’t beat them, but teaming up with random players it is always a chaotic good time.

The game is [b]easy to pick up but hard to master[/b]. The difficulty spikes can be [b]brutal and abrupt[/b], so take your time, be patient, and adapt you’re a hunter, and finding a way to take down the monster is part of the challenge.  

This game [b]isn’t for everyone[/b]—some might even hate it and never want to touch it again. But give it a shot—who knows? You might end up loving it just as much as I did.  

I loved this game so much that I bought it a second time on Steam, along with the Iceborne DLC when it went on sale. The DLC is locked behind the main game, so you need to reach a certain point before accessing it, but it’s 100% worth it. It actually [b]provides more content than the base game itself but only buy it after completing the base game.
 
[h3]Fatalis boss Fight - Spoiler[/h3]
This fight was really well put together as the final boss of this journey. I have mixed feelings about it, but it’s a battle I’ll never forget. It forced me to engage with aspects of the game I had never fully explored before. At first, I struggled - attempting it multiple times over several days with no success. Eventually, I caved and looked up a guide, something I had never done before in this game.

I ended up using a Bowgun strategy to chip away at Fatalis, slowly crafting two pieces of its armour. It was my first time using a Bowgun, and the game even gave me a short tutorial, which was hilarious given the hundreds of hours I had already spent in the game. The sheer amount of preparation and optimization required for this fight was insane smoke bombs, perfect evade timing, baiting its cone flame attacks, wall-banging it at the right moment, and learning how to position myself just right to maximize damage. There were so many micro-adjustments and strategies I picked up along the way.

It felt somewhat forced, as I had to play in a very specific way to even stand a chance, but at the same time, I loved the challenge of mastering Fatalis. And the best part? After finally defeating it, the game sends you back to Astera. The familiar music plays, and suddenly, I was taken back to 2018 when I first started this journey. That moment hit me hard I couldn’t stop myself from tearing up. It was such a fitting, emotional conclusion to an incredible game - an experience that made me feel things I haven’t felt in a while.

[h3]❌Cons & Performance Issues[/h3]
This game [b]isn’t perfect[/b], and there are some [b]performance issues[/b], but they can be improved:  
[list]
[*] [b]Unoptimized engine[/b] causes random performance drops.
 → Fix: Install the [b]“Performance Booster and Plugin Extender”[/b] mod from NexusMods.
 → [i]Achievements are unaffected by mods, so completionists don’t need to worry.[/i]

[*] [b]Turn off Volumetric Fog[/b] if you’re experiencing performance issues. 
[/list]

[h3] Final Thoughts [/h3]
This isn’t a game for everyone, some people will bounce off the difficulty or the grind. But if it clicks, [b]it might become something deeply personal[/b], like it did for me.
I even bought it a second time on Steam, with Iceborne, and I have zero regrets. I’m planning to buy [b]Monster Hunter: Wilds[/b] when it launches. I played the open beta, and it was already a blast.
I might update this review if I manage to beat Fatalis, get 100% achievements, and finally [b]wrap up this game[/b].", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1740475385}, {"review_text": "You fail and fail again but then it clicks and becomes like a dance where its just a rhythm game, in the end its just two nobodies fighting over nothing at the end of the world

You won't regret it :)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1740710519}, {"review_text": "it`s still a great game if your pc can`t run MHWild, still has a lot of content and fun monster that isn`t in Wild.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1745741882}, {"review_text": "I started playing the monster hunter franchise through MH Wilds so there are a lot of nice QoL features that were felt when going to an older title. However, this game is just so ahead of its time when it comes to a lot of what it offers.

The main strong point for it is the sheer amount of content this game has, especially with Iceborne DLC. You could easily spend hundreds of hours in the game farming and killing monsters for their gear and just getting stronger and stronger, especially with the guiding lands being introduced that adds almost infinite replayability even though it came out years ago. The addition of the clutch claw in Iceborne also had some controversy due to it being almost mandatory in Iceborne (especially in the later assignments), but I think it's really fun to use and I am glad it's introduced from the very start of the game to help with fighting monsters in the low/high rank.

The different systems with decorations and the augmentations are really interesting although I believe Wilds has a better decoration system. In Wilds, a tier 3 decoration gives the level 3 effect of the decoration, but in World it doesn't, which is a bit confusing when coming up with builds. That being said, it's still very well done and there are a lot of good ways to farm decorations (guiding lands especially with tempered farming).

The event quests that came out (which can be accessed with mods if they aren't around) are all very fun and unique and I feel like they should keep this trend in Wilds because there are some really cool monsters that we fight in World such as the Behemoth for the FFXIV event and the Leshen for The Witcher 3 event. There are more events, but these are some of the larger ones and they are really cool.

Some other great additions (which I think is personally quite nice) are the custom rooms. I would love this in Wilds but the fact you can completely customise your room to your liking and can share it with people is a nice side thing to work on while progressing. The steamwork in Iceborne is also a really nice way to get some meld materials and some other general items just by playing passively.

The modding potential for World (same with other titles) is really cool as well. There are a lot of ways for you to make the game feel personalised and certain features that make the game a lot better for your progression without being considered cheats is also really nice, such as having a mod for the item drops to have highlights on them or having the monster's weakness element easier to find. Just small changes like this are really helpful, and although this is credited to the mod developers and the community, it's still something that I wanted to mention since this game does have mod support which is super nice. I hope they keep mods around.

The only thing I somewhat dislike about World is the stun effects (although in late MR this is negated by armour sets). The stun lasts absolutely ages even if you try to spam the input for it, which often can just kill you or make you vulnerable for such a long time. It isn't an issue in the later grind but early on it became super frustrating especially in the High rank and early Master rank when monsters do a lot of stunning. It felt mandatory to build against stuns before having the armour set that completely negates stun effects. It could also be skill issue because of getting hit by the attacks, but you're gonna get hit when learning a monster for the first time, but it feels like a cop out to get hit by a stun and then hit again when I should only get hit the one time and be able to recover.

That being said, despite the age of this game it still holds well currently and is definitely worth the pickup. It is a very difficult game compared to Wilds especially in the later MR assignments such as Fatalis (who is probably the hardest thing I've fought in any game so far). This game has so much replayability to it and will probably continue to be one of the best Monster Hunter titles in the franchise.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1742598374}, {"review_text": "Ride monster,

I’d never played a Monster Hunter game before, but he was super excited to introduce me to it, and I was ready to dive in. At first, I was absolutely set on getting all the achievements—big goals, right? But due to the grindy nature of them and the game itself, I ended up taking a break from it in 2023. Before my long hiatus, we were so close to the end. We only had four monsters left: Furious Rajang, Raging Brachydios, Alatreon, and Fatalis. That was it! We were so close. Getting through those last four monsters was rough, but we finally did it, and I’m so proud we saw it through together.

Now, three years later, I’ve finally finished the game. No, I didn’t get all the achievements (and honestly, I have no desire to try). I’ll definitely be playing Monster Hunter: Rise and Wilds eventually—and of course, I’ll be playing with the husband again. Anyway, I highly recommend World if you like action-y co-op games and don’t mind a bit (or a lot) of grinding. It was a great experience, even if it took me a few years to finish.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1748518056}, {"review_text": "So... Now, I know Rise and Wilds exist, and I do own both, but Rise puts you too close to anime powerhouse and pretty much flying for me to like it more than this game for some reason (still a good game, go play it, it's beautiful and does play real well just not my style) and Wilds uh... the game is TOO easy. Not like I can stop y'all anyways, but I figured I should say something at least. Later!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1751029778}, {"review_text": "Things you should know about playing MH:World (+ Iceborne!)

Soft-ish spoilers in here, really just Monster names. (If you don't want to know the names for some reason, avoid this?)

Out of all the "modern" Monster Hunter games, this is the one that shines the most, you're not going to get the performance issues of Wilds, or the baby'd-down combat of Rise.

If you're interested in a story for some reason, this game has one, but you're probably going to be mentally checked out until the end of the base-game, then back to checking out until Iceborne where the combat is shining and the gaps between story beats are a little longer.

I would absolutely under all circumstances recommend you DO NOT start with the Defender Armor or weapons, it was designed for people wanting to skip to high rank on new characters, not for first time playthroughs, it circumvents the armor and weapon system and prevents you from learning the gearing loop.

All of low-rank is your tutorial, they're going to gloss over a lot of systems and hand the reins over to you a bit but you're going to be closing a lot of dialogues that do and don't explain everything you need to know.
The intro is extremely hand-holdy and if you have functioning brain cells during the tutorial section of the game it is going to try to turn them off, it's really really slow.

The systems in the game won't baby as much you once you're getting into high-rank, you're going to slowly taper off off the in-game tutorials and guides and reach a point where you need to become self sufficient and either play extremely well solo or be extremely communicative in groups.

Difficulty across the game is very subjective, personally before getting deep into the combat systems I could get away with soloing literally everything [u]without clutch claw[/u] up until mid-Iceborne (Around Rajang, Zinogre, etc.). The skill floor starts rising once you hit that point, monsters are going to stop pulling their punches and you're going to have to start learning monster mechanics and double down on practicing some runs instead of first time clearing everything.

Iceborne is a double edged blade for most people who play this game, a lot of the traditional hunters do not like clutch claw, a lot of people who [u]aren't[/u] traditional hunters don't like clutch claw.
The introduction of the claw saw all of the game being rebalanced with the claw in mind, meaning if you don't own Iceborne, you still have to deal with monsters that have Iceborne health, if you do own it, you're incentivised to use it at almost every point possible, with how it was designed, this can completely break low/high-rank content.

However, Iceborne's slight gameplay additions, in the form of new attacks and the clutch claw, added some dynamic elements to the fight and multiplayer increased both tension and excitement. Overall, the base game was better but still not a huge amount.

Iceborne is where the switch flipped for me. It took a few hunts but most of the new monsters were fantastic. Coming out of base game with improved experience of our weapons, my friends and I were confronted with challenge after challenge, pushing our game knowledge and skill set to new heights while we fought off unique and engaging monster designs that the base game sorely lacked. The monster music finally found its footing with rhythmic and exciting tracks, combat was riveting and intense with each new monster being a monster to overcome as a collective, and the tedious gameplay systems either fell into muscle memory or obscurity. After my experience, I would love to call Iceborne and World as a whole perfect but I can't do that.

Base game still carries a great many issues that bog down the game. The Guiding Lands post-game in Iceborne, while cool in concept, ended up being and absolute slog alongside raising our level to get access to gear augments. This slowed down my group's pace to a crawl. The story is still forgettable. A number of hitboxes in both the base game and expansion felt utterly unfair.

Despite these issues, Monster Hunter: World (WITH Iceborne) was a fantastic experience. If you like rich action games with depth to both player and enemy move set, an engaging and growing difficulty curve that relies more on the player skill than gear, and just fighting big dinosaurs and dragons, this game is an easy recommendation, especially with some friends by your side.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1745750663}, {"review_text": "My first monter hunter game and it turn out to be very addictive", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1744722047}, {"review_text": "Amazing game! Whether you're a longtime fan or new to the series, this is the definitive way to experience Half-Life.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1746816407}, {"review_text": "Black Mesa is a true labour of love. In development for more or less 15 years, a mod team (Crowbar Collective) set out to remake Half-Life, the classic and iconic title that influenced an entire generation of games, using the Source engine. When funds and manpower were short, it was literally passion that kept the project going. Valve eventually even gave them their blessing. 

The story remains the same, as players take the role as Gordon Freeman in the Black Mesa Research Facility. An experiment goes awry and a rift opens up, allowing creatures from another world to infiltrate and cause havoc. The military is sent in to contain the situation, and eliminate ANY witnesses that are present, including the science team and facility staff. Gordon finds himself on a journey to close the rift, while battling both aliens and soldiers, and has multiple interactions with the enigmatic G-man along the way. 

The gameplay is faithful to the original, but with improvements to elevate it to modern day standards. Enemy AI is vastly improved, creating more dynamic situations. Of course the visuals have received a complete overhaul. Textures and models are beautifully rendered. The use of light and shadows is amplified thanks to the Source engine. Half-Life was known for its impressive level design and Black Mesa builds on this foundation. Many levels retain their iconic look and feel but have more expansive functionality. The levels are quintessential to the environmental storytelling experience, and are atmospheric and immersive. The Xen levels are the most drastic change in design compared to the original. In what was previously a barren and disjointed final act, Black Mesa has reworked Xen to feel alive with its stunning environments and textures. 

Black Mesa is a homage to everything that made Half-Life great, with updated mechanics, design and polish. The dedication shown by the developers is nothing short of inspiring. This is the remake we had been hoping for.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1743101026}, {"review_text": "Big fan of the HL series, this remake of HL is a work of art! fantastic gameplay and graphics!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1753516820}, {"review_text": "AMAZING masterpice of a game.

Brilliant remake, at times even beats the original.

The big highlights for me are the combat and the improved level design, making the Black Mesa Research Facility feel as real as ever, removing some of the more nonsensical aspects of the original and allowing the level design to flow at a much more breakneck pace.

The combat is fast-paced and constantly keeping you on your toes, the reduced ammo values encourages you to constantly switch between your many different weapons, giving each part of your arsenal a unique role for each enemy you face. The HECU grunts are always a welcome challenge and definitely my favourite enemy to face in the entire game.

Xen was excellent, besides the conveyor belt section which admittedly went on a little too long but that doesn't detract from the rest of the experience too heavily in my opinion. The Gonarch and Nihilanth boss fights are done so well, both serving as very exciting multi-phase fights. A definite improvement over the original in every aspect.

I would argue that this is the best entry point to the series, with almost 20 years of hindsight Crowbar Collective were able to create an experience that not only brings Half-Life to the modern age, but even improves on it in many aspects, while staying faithful to the the original 1998 release that revolutionised the First-Person Shooter genre when necessary.

I played HL1 back in the days like 25 years ago. I was a kid with zero knowledge of English. I genuinely thought the game is bugged because I couldn't stop a tram nor leave it. I was like "what on the Earth is wrong with this game?". Restarted it several times and the "bug" kept showing but once in my afk I got to a destination point and finally could touch gameplay. Nevertheless it made no difference because of the same reason - I was absolutely clueless and naturally got soft-locked at one of the initial locations. Should I tell what impression of the so-called GREAT HALF-LIFE SERIES I carried through the years?

My friend advised me to play Black Mesa not long ago and I decided to give it a second chance. Now I know what the fuss is all about. This game has elegant harmony of storytelling and gameplay which most of modern games lack. No pretentious "deepness" - just solid and straightforward but engaging plot. It's all due to Valve although Collective Crowbar added no lesser value.

This is an absolutely fantastic remaster. Visuals look good even in 2024. Xen is beautiful. Music is nice but a bit loud. Fights are cool and movement... I usually love all that movement thing and unfortunately I discovered interesting mechanic too late. It would make my journey even more enjoyable. 
Here is the mechanic: when you got to Xen you obtain a Jetpack allowing you to double-jump with high velocity. So after double-jump you need to hold crouch and you will be sliding on the ground with high speed. Moreover if you jump again then your speed will be kept.  In other words you can do something like bhop without strafe.

The highest difficulty as always allows you to get full experience so it's my permanent recommendation. Unless you do rerun for Hat&Pizza achievements. You can but why. 

The first time I completed the game and looked through achievements to understand what's left I was unpleasantly surprised that you need to bring two objects to the end of the game. It seemed stupid. But I wanted to get them all so I started a new game. There is no challenge to carry one thing (either hat or pizza) it's just boring and time-consuming. But if you decide to carry both of them I assure you'll have so much fun. The whole gameplay had changed for me. I was very sceptical and irritated at the beginning but eventually I loved it. I could bring them to the place with 8 jump pads, there I spent two hours trying a lot of ideas but gave up, made a save and proceeded further with one thing. What a run was it, a puzzle after a puzzle, what a pleasure to solve them. Don't google how if you stuck, just think and try.

In conclusion I wanted to talk about expansions. As of now - 21 December 2024 - a different team is working on the mod Blue Shift. And it needs Black Mesa to run. I know Valve allowed to earn money for Crowbar Collective and I would be so happy if all of them somehow resolve situation to the point where Blue Shift could be published as an official DLC for Black Mesa or as a separate game. I am not into mods and in addition I love steam's game progression system with all these achievements, playtime and cards. I hope I am not alone in my infantile desire. 

Anyway, enjoy the game, enjoy the achievements and don't forget GALANGA and GALALANG.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1734813209}, {"review_text": "Really cool re-imagining of the original Half-Life game. I like the more modern graphics, additional maps, and how the zombies are inspired more by Half-Life 2 and are more articulated. Personally I love the addition of achievements since it will give me satisfaction when I eventually "100%" the game. I also really enjoyed how lots of the NPC dialogue carried over, it made it feel like it was another installation of the original franchise. 
I also very much liked the direction On a Rail was taken in. It was a lot more straightforward in progression and barely required any going around in circles or getting lost. 

Popular opinion, though, the Xen and Interloper portions are killing me. Currently they amass about 5 hours of my play time (~1/3). It is much longer than the original. More than just a remake, Black Mesa is a testament to fan devotion and creative vision, meticulously rebuilding the world of Gordon Freeman with modern technology while preserving the essence that made the original so beloved. Released in full in 2020 after years in early access, the game offers both longtime fans and newcomers a deeply polished, atmospheric, and narrative-driven FPS experience that stands tall on its own merits.

From the outset, Black Mesa impresses with its visual fidelity and attention to environmental detail. The Black Mesa Research Facility has been completely overhauled with high-resolution textures, dynamic lighting, and more expansive and immersive level design. Gone are the blocky, low-polygon corridors of 1998; in their place are sprawling, believable industrial and scientific complexes that feel like functional spaces rather than simple backdrops for gunfights. The game’s visual storytelling is subtle and powerful, evoking a sense of realism and dread as players witness the slow unraveling of the facility after the infamous resonance cascade. Every lab, tunnel, and security checkpoint is infused with the eerie quiet of a disaster in progress, amplifying the game's sense of isolation and tension.

The core gameplay remains faithful to Half-Life’s pioneering blend of combat, exploration, and environmental puzzle-solving, but Black Mesa enhances it with refined AI, tighter gunplay, and smoother platforming. Enemy soldiers and alien creatures are far more challenging than in the original, employing smarter tactics and more aggressive flanking maneuvers, which keeps the player constantly on edge. The weaponry, though largely unchanged in its roster, feels punchier and more satisfying to use, especially classics like the shotgun, revolver, and the experimental Tau Cannon. The crowbar, of course, still reigns supreme as Freeman’s iconic blunt instrument of survival.

One of Black Mesa’s most notable achievements lies in its reimagining of the controversial Xen chapters, which in the original game were widely criticized for being rushed, repetitive, and disorienting. Crowbar Collective chose to expand Xen into a sprawling, visually stunning, multi-hour experience that transforms what was once a low point into a narrative and gameplay high. The alien world is richly textured and imaginative, with bizarre flora, treacherous platforming, and some genuinely awe-inspiring scenery. New gameplay mechanics are introduced here, including elements of low-gravity movement and environmental interaction, which keep the final act feeling fresh and otherworldly without deviating too far from the game’s established tone.

On the audio front, Black Mesa excels with a powerful and atmospheric soundtrack that underscores the game’s tension, mystery, and moments of chaos. The music swells at key moments, reinforcing the pacing and emotional beats of the story. Sound design is equally commendable—every alien screech, weapon discharge, and ambient machinery hum contributes to the immersive soundscape. Voice acting, although limited mostly to incidental dialogue from scientists and security guards, maintains the dry wit and nervous energy that defined the original characters, further grounding the game in its darkly humorous tone.

Performance-wise, Black Mesa runs smoothly on a wide range of hardware, with the Source engine’s modifications offering modern rendering features without sacrificing optimization. Occasional bugs and glitches do appear, particularly in complex AI encounters or during physics-heavy sequences, but they are infrequent and rarely game-breaking. Crowbar Collective has shown a strong commitment to patching and supporting the game post-release, reinforcing the sense that Black Mesa is a labor of love, not just a nostalgia cash-in.

In terms of narrative, Black Mesa doesn’t rewrite Half-Life’s story so much as it enriches it. The story of Gordon Freeman—a silent MIT physicist thrown into a nightmarish alien invasion—is told through the world rather than cutscenes, and Black Mesa excels at environmental storytelling. The game expands and deepens the original’s pacing and mood, taking its time to build tension before plunging the player into high-stakes action. Despite knowing the beats of the plot, returning players will find themselves captivated again by the sense of dread, wonder, and escalating catastrophe.

Ultimately, Black Mesa succeeds not just as a remake but as a fully realized reimagining that brings Half-Life into the modern era with reverence and creativity. It honors the past while improving on nearly every aspect of the original—gameplay, graphics, level design, and atmosphere—making it both a perfect entry point for newcomers and a worthy tribute for veterans. It is a rare example of a fan-made project reaching—and arguably surpassing—the standards of the official source material. Black Mesa is not only a love letter to one of gaming’s most influential titles, but a masterpiece in its own right.

[b]The Good:[/b]
[list]
[*] The NPC behavior is reactive, making them more human-like than artificial;
[*] Engaging puzzle sections that introduce variety to the gameplay i.e. less monotomy and more mind-bending;
[*] Great and melodic soundtrack that perfectly reflects every situation that happens within the game;
[*] Mesmerizing visuals that do a good job at creating a good immersion for the player;
[*] Re-imagined maps that offer far more content than the original game ever did. For those who played the original before, they will instantly recognize most of the maps at a first glance, but be welcomed with a completely different flow and scale, which benefits the game greatly;
[*] The last few chapters were remade from scratch thus making them a vastly different and superior experience compared to the original.
[/list]

[b]The Bad:[/b]
[list]
[*] Enemies are far too precise with their shots forcing the player to be as quick as possible, which is not always a good thing;
[*] Some puzzle sections can get too repetitive for their own good;
[*] Some traps are really mean and hard to dodge from. Expect a significant loss of armor and HP whilst escaping from them;
[*] Tends to crash a lot during intense scripted sequences, making it impossible to finish the game. Saving during those sequences is not advised. Either save before or after.
[/list]

[b]Highlights:[/b]
[list]
[*] Boss fights tend to be legendary. They are much harder unlike the original but more interesting to be part of thanks to their presentation and variety;
[*] The game creates a good sense of emergency for the player. Unlike the original, this game keeps reminding the player of the urgency of the mission they’re carrying out, thanks to a bigger presence of NPCs in the story. It no longer feels like the player does everything for their own survival but for the sake of everyone caught in that situation.
[/list]

[b]Performance Notes:[/b]
Runs astonishingly bad when using native Linux build. Especially noticeable when traversing through the open areas. Windows build with Proton on top is a must.

The experience team gained during development of Black Mesa half showed really well in the second half.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Core gameplay based on [b]co-op exploration across 30+ backrooms levels[/b], including puzzles, navigation, and [strike]trash talking friends[/strike] running from [i]entities[/i]. Each level draws from creepypasta lore, featuring unique layouts like endless yellow rooms, electrical stations, cave systems, or flooded areas (poolrooms, thalassophobia). Puzzles vary: aligning electrical panels, searching for needed code in area, combining environmental items (e.g., keys, levers, tv's), or timing sequences under pressure.
There are no tons of mechanics, one of them is useless: leaning left/right. Also there's type of mechanics as sanity, which will go down over time, and go faster if you see something scary. You can restore it by consuming items like almond water, juice, energy bar, moth jelly [strike]or liquid death[/strike].

[h2]Graphics[/h2]
[i][b]Perfectly serviceable horror visuals[/b][/i], way sharper after 1.0 and now genuinely impressive for an indie backrooms game that doesn’t try to melt your GPU.
Classic mono-yellow hell is spot-on: endless damp carpets that look like they’ve never been cleaned, wallpaper peeling like it’s trying to escape, and those buzzing fluorescent lights flickering in the exact rhythm that makes your eye twitch. The volumetric fog is thick enough to cut with a knife, legitimately hides corners and turns every hallway into a coin-flip between “safe” and “random jumpscare”
[b][i]Entities[/i][/b] look properly unsettling: 
[list]
    [*][b]Smilers[/b] glow like discount neon signs from hell
    [*]These dog-like [b]Hounds[/b] look worse than my drunk uncle
    [*]Comically wired [b]Bacteria[/b] with long odd arms
    [*][b]Partygoers[/b] whose appearance and 7ft height genuinely scare shit outta you
    [*]Forgot 'bout [b]Skinstealers[/b] - entities which can [i]change[/i] their appearance to regular player, then turn into giant bulk monster and demolish you with single smash
[/list]
[b][i]Animations[/i][/b] are [i]smooth[/i] as butter, chases feel fast and scary, and ragdoll deaths occasionally produce accidental comedy gold. You literally explode and then your body lays on the floor without legs and arms like starfish.
Textures hold up close, post-processing is tasteful (light bloom, subtle vignette, just enough chromatic aberration to make everything feel “off”).
Doesn’t chase photorealism and doesn’t need to. Does [b]exactly[/b] what it has to do, nothing more, nothing less.

[h2]SFX[/h2]
[b][i]Exemplary spatial audio[/i][/b]. 3D sound positions footsteps, water splashes, and breaths directionally — headphones are [u][b]REQUIRED[/b][/u]. No cheesy music, just subtle drones that creep under your skin like existential dread.
[i][b]Entity SFX not the best[/b][/i], but it does its function perfectly - [i]inspires fear[/i]. Hound's wet snarls of rabid dog, Skinstealers mimic warped voices as [i]"Hello?"[/i] which turns into a growl after few seconds, same with Partygoers, but they're ain't greeting you.
[i][b]Proximity VC[/b][/i] integrates seamlessly, with entities detecting raised voices for added risk. In group play, hearing teammate's panic heightens realism and sustain paranoia. 

[h2]Optimization[/h2]
[b][i]It is quite good[/i][/b], 'cause on my ancient pc (i7 920, 6gb ram, 1050ti) everything was great except few levels.
If your pc's better than mine, you can play on high settings without thinking about lags or freezes.

[quote=Michael] Pretty good if playing not alone (7/10) [/quote]

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Sanity-draining exploration, clever puzzles, and entity chases that demand real teamwork via proximity chat. Great SFX and atmospheric visuals turn endless hallways into pure dread. Buttery optimization means your weak PC squad joins the panic without lag.
[i]Solo?[/i] It's playable but feels like wandering a party alone — functional, yet missing the screams and chaos that makes it legendary.

[b]Final verdict: [u][i]HIGHLY RECOMMENDED[/i][/u] — but grab the squad first, or stay a solo psycho forever[/b]

[{"review_text": "Portal 1 is lightning in a bottle. Apart from maybe some dated graphics etc, its the perfect game.

I got so tired of hearing my dad talk about how mind-blowing this game was that I finally asked him to let me try it. It was all true. There's so much to love: No timer, no cut-scenes, and the ability to make you feel like a genius after solving each chamber.

I played Portal for the first time when I was in grade 4 with my brother who was in grade 3. Just imagine a 10 year old and an 8 year old trying desperately to play this really complex and hard puzzle game 24/7 for about a month. I remember we would ask our dad to translate every pice of dialogue (or monologue) because we couldn't understand any English yet (we are from Greece). Many years later it is still my favorite game ever and we have been playing it almost every summer just for the nostalgia. I am so sad that we won't get a Portal 3... you have no idea.

Portal 1 is lonely and isolated to the point where you form a strong attachment to a simple thing like a cube with a heart on it. I loved the melancholic, lonely feel of the game. Something about its eerie atmosphere just resonated with me. And the darker tone of the game made it feel more real. I can't even fully explain it but it's just a ton of little things, such as the empty offices, the huge white rooms filled with artificial light, the way they impliment the soundtrack in this game, the ratman stuff you find later on, the behind the scenes feeling of the lab feeling like you shouldn't be there... I can go on and on but in my first playthrough there would be times where all of these things added up and I got tense almost as if I was in a psychological horror game. I definetly might be the only guy who felt that way to that extent about this game, but I really do think that's something that isn't said enough about Portal 1.

I also typically don't like games that I can finish in one sitting but Portal 1 is that rare exception. Not only that, it's one of my favorite games of all time, probably because it made you WANT to complete it to the very end. There's a reason I don't beat very many games; I have no reason to at all. What do I acheive other than bragging rights and completionism? Sure the story is something to drive you but most games IMO simply don't compel you enough to finish them for the story. I play games for their unique experience, so for this game to wrap so much depth and entertainment into roughly (for me) 5 hours of gameplay is something marvelous.

Portal 1 is basically video game perfection, literally nothing about it should be changed. Nothing is wasted, and nothing is unnecessary. The difficulty curve flawlessly keeps puzzles from being frustrating while still making you feel clever for solving them, the writing is clever and subtle, the story never hinders the gameplay, and the runtime keeps it from outstaying its welcome. To conclude, Portal 1 is just one of the best-made games I’ve ever experienced, and if by any chance you still haven’t tried it to this day… what the  hell are you waiting for?

📜 Overview
Portal is a first-person puzzle-platform video game developed by Valve and released in 2007 as part of the The Orange Box compilation. It quickly gained acclaim for its innovative gameplay mechanics, minimalist design, and dark humor. The game revolves around the use of a "portal gun," a device that allows the player to create linked portals on flat surfaces. The goal is to navigate through increasingly complex test chambers by creating portals to move objects, avoid hazards, and reach the exit. The game’s main protagonist, Chell, is guided (or rather taunted) by an AI named GLaDOS, whose quirky and sinister commentary adds an extra layer of intrigue to the experience.

🌟 Pros
✅ Innovative Gameplay – The portal mechanic is incredibly unique and offers creative puzzle-solving opportunities, providing a fresh take on traditional puzzle-platform games.
✅ Challenging Puzzles – Each level introduces new complexities, keeping the puzzles engaging and rewarding as players master the portal mechanics.
✅ Memorable Characters – GLaDOS, the game's sarcastic and often chilling AI, is one of gaming's most iconic characters, adding humor and tension throughout the story.
✅ Atmospheric Design – The sterile, clinical environment of Aperture Science combined with minimalist visuals creates an atmospheric and immersive experience.
✅ Brevity and Polish – The game is concise, with a perfect length that ensures it doesn’t overstay its welcome. The levels are designed to gradually ramp up in difficulty without feeling frustrating.

⚠️ Cons
❌ Limited Replayability – While the puzzles are satisfying to solve, the game's relatively short length and the lack of alternate gameplay modes may limit replay value for some players.
❌ Simplicity for Some – Although the puzzles can be tricky, some experienced players may find the game's difficulty to be on the easier side compared to other puzzle games.
❌ Lack of Deep Storyline – While GLaDOS's commentary is entertaining, the overall story is more of an atmospheric backdrop rather than an in-depth narrative.

💬 Player Sentiment
Positive Reviews: Players appreciate the game’s innovation, design, and unique puzzle mechanics. The integration of humor with GLaDOS’s commentary has been widely praised. It’s also considered one of the best examples of a short, polished game that doesn’t waste the player’s time.

Negative Reviews: Criticisms mostly focus on the game’s short length and lack of additional content beyond the main story, which leaves little incentive for replaying once the puzzles are solved.

Fans of puzzle games who enjoy unique mechanics and strategic thinking.
Players who enjoy a humorous, dark narrative experience.

The plot is essentially that you're in a lab as a research subject learning to use various in order to solve puzzles and make it to the exit of each test chamber. You'll slowly learn how room elements work such as boxes, pressure switches, and of course portals. This main mechanic of the game consists of two portals, a blue one and an orange one. Early on you'll be given a blue portal gun to work with alongside fixed orange portal placements to learn how this works. Essentially, entering either portal will have you exit the other portal. Once you've had enough testing time to familiarize yourself with this concept, the game will give you the dual portal gun which will allow you to create both blue and orange portals. Only one of each color can exist at a time. They can only be placed on white surfaces and if the surfaces moves then the portal will disappear. The goal is simple: solve all of the puzzles to complete every test chamber and you'll be reward with cake!

While using the portals to solve puzzles is the main goal, you'll need to manipulate other objects along the way. There are companion cubes that can be picked up, placed, and dropped. Often these will need to be placed on pressure switches in order to open the exit. You may need to reach buttons to spawn the boxes in the first place or to activate other mechanisms in the room. Some mechanisms will require power. To supply it you'll need to get an energy orb from a shooter and get it to the power node. You'll also start to have obstacles and hazards to impede your progress. Barriers exist that will destroy all items the pass through them and also remove all existing portals if you yourself pass through them. Stationary turret robots with machine guns will gun you down if you get within their line of sight. You'll need to find a way around them or knock them down to deactivate them. Water is the most dangerous hazard of all as it will kill you very quickly upon contact. Death results in respawning at the last checkpoint. There is no real fail-state in the game. Complete all 19 test chambers to conclude the research the computer requires of you.

GLaDOS the computer has some funny lines yet also some unsettling ones as well. The atmosphere of the game is very good at being ambiguous as to if you should trust these experiments or not. You're often left to wonder what exactly you're doing here and what this testing is in service of. The mechanics are fantastic. The concept of using portals can be difficult to wrap your head around at first, but it's used in so many different ways along with the other test chamber elements. I really appreciate that the game really makes the most out of the simple portal mechanic. It never feels like moving from gimmick room to gimmick room because anything new is always adding to the main mechanics of using the portals. I'm sure it's a technical marvel to make this work in terms of programming as well, but even just taking that for granted the concept is so unique and executed incredibly well.

That's not to say the game is flawless, though. For one thing, it's a bit on the short side. It's also a bit on the clunky side when it comes to action segments. Platforming is difficult due to very poor jumping ability. If you jump too soon you won't make it and jumping too late will just end up in you falling instead. It can also be difficult to line up portals to increase your momentum. There are multiple instances where you need to create a portal to fall into, one to fall out of, and then shoot again while falling to create enough momentum to launch yourself somewhere. This can be hard to do on the fly when the portal width is so narrow. You often just get caught on the sides and ruin the momentum. Worse yet is that if you make an infinite loop to fall through with portals without very particular placement, you'll be twisting around as you fall out of them and trying to aim to where the next portal needs to go while still falling will put you just enough out of alignment to catch the edge of the portal and stop your necessary loop.

So overall, the action sections are a pain, but the puzzles sections are excellent. This game is still quite unique and well-regarded for a reason. I did try a bit of the bonus levels but I'll admit I didn't do too many of them. There are extra stages that are harder variants of the normal test chambers, but I quit as soon as one had a hard action section. And the challenge stages are doing the main levels in a limited amount of time, steps, or portal placements. I'll also admit that this game was probably much more jaw-dropping to play when it originally released many years ago, but even so I still think it's a great experience. I'm very happy to have finally played it for myself. And the good news is that it goes for fairly low prices on basically all platforms these days. Personally I played it on my Steam Deck and loved it, but no matter where you play it, Portal is Portal. Now if you'll excuse me, I have some cake to go eat. Is it just me or is it getting kind of warm in here? Huh.

So, how was my first [i]Portal[/i] experience?

[h1]Puzzles for the non-puzzler[/h1]

Well, first order of business: what, exactly, [b]is[/b] [i]Portal[/i]?

Yes, it's a puzzle game, but unlike many puzzle games, this game doesn't expect you to use science/math logic, at least not beyond common sense logic that everyone should have. I always did really well in school but it has been a while and even in spite of that, I hated math (and advanced science); I've never been one to think with cold logic and numbers, I've always been more of a "see the paths ahead of you" sort of guy and I can safely say that [i]Portal[/i] is that kind of game.

You are expected to get from one end of the map to the other, and you have to do so by evaluating the layout, knowing how the mechanics work, and sometimes you need good timing as well. A good example of this is a sequence where you have to open a portal on a platform, drop down a deep pit and open a second portal there. This flings you up into the air and while you're mid-air, you want to switch out the pit portal for a new portal on a higher platform. You continue this onward until the end of the sequence, which requires some good timing and continued momentum in addition to the logic.

It also justifies these puzzles with story, stating that you're a test subject for Aperture Science, a company who developed wormhole technology and you're a tester for that tech. This justification is a huge part of what makes [i]Portal[/i] compelling to people like me, who usually play games for the story.

[h1]Sci-fi intrigue and comedic goofiness[/h1]

Speaking of the story, this game's plot is actually very interesting, though you wouldn't assume that from looking at it. You start off as the test subject, locked in a doorless cell with a bed, toilet, radio, coffee mug and notepad. This subtle setup does a great job at environmental storytelling, showing you your first hint as to what Aperture Science is like. This, combined with a female robotic voice you'll begin hearing, begins to subtly unravel story about Aperture, your role with them, and the world at large outside of the facility.

It also has loads of environmental storytelling, starting with a few areas where you can go a little outside of the normal testing chamber grounds. In these offset areas, you'll encounter clues that show you that you're not the first subject, and that your precursor(s) may have been fleeing from something. This comes to a head when you reach the end of the test chambers: [spoiler]while that robotic voice is trying to kill you off, you have the opportunity to flee and this ends up taking you through loads of 'unapproved' areas of the Aperture facility[/spoiler].

What's funny is that all of this leads to a real sense of adventure and even a bit of a pulse-pounding adrenaline rush in some segments. All the while, as you're trying to progress, you begin to uncover more and more that really starts to paint a clear picture of what's going on. I won't spoil that, though; all I'll say is that if you're a Valve fan, you're going to like the story of these games.

[h1]Timeless art[/h1]

Despite releasing in 2007, this game still looks fantastic, even without the ray tracing version (a free DLC). The Source Engine still holds up quite well today. It's very difficult to have a realistic, sci-fi art style that doesn't age poorly as graphic tech advances but [i]Portal[/i] had no such difficulties. Sure, it doesn't look [b]new[/b], by any means, but it still looks appealing.

I think part of this has to do with the fact that you never see any sort of human characters, aside from brief reflections of your character that you might see if the portals line up just right. Character design tends to age the worst in game graphics, so this worked out great in retrospect. However, the overall art design, color palette and graphics tech work together to give you a very, very good-looking game even in the 2020s.

The funniest thing, though, is how it starts off deceptively monochrome. [/h1] 

 

[i]The Sims 2[/i] is an iconic game, known for pushing the boundaries of what the life simulation genre could do and being so rich in gameplay that it would be hard to follow even decades after its release. Some would say it is the best entry into [i]The Sims[/i] franchise, and I think that is for good reason. This game is so full of nostalgia for many players, myself included. And for those players, you can now experience the classic [i]The Sims 2[/i] experience all over again – for better, and for worse.  
 
This is the classic [i]Sims 2[/i] experience from 2004, complete with bugs, crashes and pink soup. The bugs in this game are not negligible. Having played both [i]The Ultimate Collection [/i] and [i]Legacy Collection,[/i] I think this most recent iteration is much buggier even still. To the developer’s credit, they are working on making it better and each patch I do believe they have made progress. However, these kinks should have been ironed out before being sold – asking for $30+ for a game that was already given away for free ten years ago with less bugs and more content at that is asking a lot. The least you could do would be to release it in a functioning state. So, despite them working on it still and releasing patches it is hard to commend them for it since that should have been done already.  
 
There were times early on in my time with this game that it really rarely crashed. Granted, that was after a few patches already rolled out. Then as I played more and more, the crashes started happening a lot more frequently and where at the start I could get an hour or two of gameplay in before crashing, I can now get maybe 20 minutes. This game makes [i]The Sims 3[/i] look stable, and that is saying something.  
 
On an aside, EA “stole” old mods that the community made to fix the game and put them in without asking or even crediting the creators they took from. Yeah, all of the property modders work with belongs to EA, but it still is very underhanded and lazy. At that point, why not have some of those modders help you with fixing the stuff up before releasing the game in the first place?  
 
The upside to this version is that it’s more convenient and is allegedly still receiving support. I don’t necessarily regret my purchase, because just for the convenience this version gives, to me it is worth it. I hope that they will continue to work on the kinks that need fixing. I love the game, and I spent many hours with [i] The Ultimate Collection[/i] with a lot less issues. Now I’m ready to play this in a way that I can just focus on enjoying it.  
 
TL;DR – If you really want to play [i]The Sims 2[/i] in a convenient way and have it through Steam and all the boons that come with that, then it will probably be worthwhile to you. And make no mistake, even despite the bugs and crashes, I’ve really enjoyed this game. I just couldn’t ever in good conscience with how they rolled the game out recommend it to anyone firstly, and secondly in its current state it is inexcusably buggy. At the end of the day, it really makes me happy to see TS2 get some love again, and finally get a proper digital release on Steam, with all the expansions (except the Ikea Stuff Pack) included, all for a reasonable price, but I wish EA had given it a bit more of the respect it deserves.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1738347602}, {"review_text": "I've played this game for 20 hours, and I’d like to share my experience to help others decide whether it’s worth purchasing.

[h3] Pros [/h3]
 
It’s essentially The Sims 2, rereleased and made playable on modern devices—no remaster or remake. This can be great if you’re a returning player looking to relive the experience.

Now that the game is for sale, EA is giving support for it. Expect more updates and patch notes from now on.

The game has received a few fixes, and in my experience, it runs buttery smooth—better than the Ultimate Collection, may I add. My Ultimate Collection used to stutter a lot, and FPS drops were too prominent to ignore, even with community patches like Graphics Rules Maker and the RPC Launcher from Lazy Duchess.

Since its rerelease, the game has received even more updates (things that should've been added from the beginning, but that's not the focus). The game now automatically recognizes your device and applies the correct graphical settings, instead of defaulting everything to low. It's not surprising that the majority of Simmers aren't very tech-savvy. I couldn’t stand seeing comments blaming the devs for the rerelease supposedly disabling shadows, when you could simply toggle the option on and off by loading a lot and adjusting the settings. The stupidity amuses me. On a positive note, the voices are no longer robotic and low-quality, and the custom skintone window now works properly—issues that used to bother me but have been fixed. 

[h3] Cons [/h3]
ㅤ
There is absolutely NO REASON to rerelease this game in its current state. Half the comments are from people complaining that the game won’t even launch. While I understand the pressure of strict deadlines and the reality of post-launch fixes, there’s no excuse for a game to fail at simply launching. That’s stupid.

It has been a week, and there’s still no fix for the absurdly small UI when playing at higher resolutions. When I heard the news about the rerelease, my first thought was: surely they’ll fix the UI and stretch the loading screens—but no. Even just... scaling it with AI would’ve been less humiliating than doing nothing at all. And no, the game automatically setting your screen to a lower resolution just to make the UI larger is NOT a fix. The UI becomes blurry and looks unappealing to look at. Shame on EA.
 
LOL. No BodyShop? One of the core reasons The Sims 2 is so beloved is the ability to create genuinely unique and attractive Sims using BodyShop. Yet, this rerelease doesn’t include it. I can understand leaving out something like the IKEA Stuff Pack, but removing BodyShop is baffling.

[h2] Should you buy this? [/h2]


It depends. If you already own the game on the EA app or through... other methods, then no. With community patches, you already have a functional version of the game. There’s no need to spend money on this rerelease.

However, if you don’t own the game yet, go for it. As I mentioned, the game is receiving official support now, so patches and updates are on the way.

At the end of the day, the rerelease brings more people into the Sims 2 community, which is a good thing. Whether you buy the new version or stick with your Ultimate Collection, just enjoy the game and have fun. Dag Dag.

[{"review_text": "Very early days, but there's already a lot to love here. Many people have already made the comparisons to 7 Days to Die and Project Zomboid, and those are entirely accurate. The pace is exceptionally and intentionally slow - this seems like a game that's less about surviving the zombie apocalypse and more about the rebuilding society while incidentally dealing with zombies. There's a massive amount of details in the crafting and world interaction options - if you can see it, you can affect it, and it's a lot of fun to pull working parts out of one car to install in another to make a working option. Or lowering the blinds all through your safehouse so that you can turn the lights on, from time to time.

It's the development direction that bears watching, because that's sort of where the Fun Pimps went wrong - by making a game that was more accessible to more people, they stripped out most of the really good, crunchy parts of the game. And by contract, PZ is a masterpiece, but is hard to pull people into, graphically, and has a depth of detail so overwhelming that the learning curve bucks a lot of folks off. Right now, Vein is riding the line between those two really well - you're willing to learn the deep functioning because the world is vibrant and interactive. I keep finding fun surprises that keep me playing, and I'm excited to get a chance to play with my friends. 

Don't lose sight of the fact that this is still very much in dev, and only has a team of two working on it. Even if that changes, this has a ways to go before launch, so if you're picky about 100 percent complete games, keep it on your wishlist for now. 11/10 game, not sure if that scene intentionally triggers a horde but it got me good, GG devs.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 103, "timestamp_created": 1762130306}, {"review_text": "**Try the demo before buying. It’s the same as base game but with a limited map area and capped skill leveling. It’s a great way to see if the game in its current state is for you.**

I have watched this game be built from the ground up for over 3 years now. And what can I say? It’s exactly what people are seeking when they think of a “3D Project Zomboid.”

With just two developers at the helm, VEIN has the potential to be one of the best survival sim titles to come into the market, and I have full confidence the developers will deliver on this, however long it may take. For years I have seen a very rare consistency seen in gaming — constant git submissions, feedback aggregation, and really a resounding focus on building a foundation for a game that is both in-depth and enjoyable to play. The game features an absolute plethora of depth throughout the world, with interactivity at nearly every turn and survival systems that you simply don’t see in other games at this stage. There’s a reason it’s conflated with Zomboid at nearly every turn - it’s very much a simulation game at its core.

This isn’t to say Vein doesn’t have the issues of an early access title. A good bit of animations are placeholder, which is a chief complaint among a lot of players. Networking still needs some passes, so for now, I’d stick to singleplayer or run a private game with 2-3 friends, as it’s the most stable networking-wise. Placeholder assets are present across the game as well, but I’ve seen VEIN evolve from 0.001, and I feel like I can confidently say the developers got this in the bag. Now that they’re in EA, they can work on the game more consistently, and bring on whatever talent they need to better flesh out assets / mechanics / etc.

I’m very happy and proud of the developers for getting to this stage, and I can’t wait to see what they create over the next few years in VEIN. 🙌", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1761496630}, {"review_text": "I decided to write this review after I lit a cigarette in game near a propane tank that said "no smoking" - They've included so many systems and features that I was genuinely nervous that the tank was going to explode and promptly moved away from it.

Crossing my fingers that this game gets the support it deserves so it can grow.

Impressive highlights so far;
- Shot a zombie from a car. Drove by a zombie on a motorcycle and smacked him with a baton.
- Got ambushed by a boar that scared me more than any zombie did. Still put 4 rounds into it.
- Found a functional police car, which fits my Police background choice and lets me wee-woo around.
- Didn't know how I could fit a Generator into inventory so I loaded it into the bed of a pickup. 10/10
- Finding DVDs around the world that I can put on to play in the background while I work.
- Made myself some tea after a little trial and error and was significantly rewarded with CONFIDENCE.
- Made some soup and got a 'nice smell' buff. 
- Smoked some cannabis and savored my victory soup.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 48, "timestamp_created": 1761663157}, {"review_text": "At first glance, it looks like every other zombie asset flip. But I am impressed how much it goes deeper. Things that would simply be cosmetic in other games have functionality here. I was surprised to find a functional washer/dryer for clothing that uses detergent and needs to be connected to water and power. Sinks can be filled with water, and the water gets dirty if you wash yourself in it. If your friend hasn't washed in a while, you will actually get a whiff of their stink anytime they come near you. 

The vehicles all have parts that can be replaced. They have air conditioning, working radios, and even a dome light. If you forget to engage the e-brake, it may roll away. I think there is a way to tow things, but I haven't figured that part out yet. You even have to change the oil on your car when it gets dirty.

Electricity and water isn't just magically in a house. There are actual distribution sites around the map that provide services to regions, and you can shut off an entire region. I don't know why you'd want to do that, but you can. The grid stuff looks very promising already.

There are already some interesting medical features in the game, like insulin for diabetics and a framework for different types of wounds and diseases (even tuberculosis!). 

The level design is also very good. Initially when I looting around houses, most homes were just copy pasta. Then I found some of the darker locations like mass burial sites. Yes, every zombie game has those "FEMA' camps, but this one does a good job making it creepy. 

I realistically expect this game to be in early access for a few years. For a very early access game, this is already quite amazing! The attention to detail is superb. There are even working TVs with DVD players and you can watch Night of the Living Dead...which is crazy! 

You can drive ANY vehicle you find, either via key or hotwiring. RVs, trucks, quads, motorcycles, golf carts, sports cars...so many choices.

What needs to get better:

1) Combat is kinda janky, but an in-game setting makes it better as far as head bobbing. Still needs to be smoother out a bit, but is currently "acceptable".

2) A lot of graphical glitches like bodies and objects clipping through walls and doors. Hair is crazy and doesn't follow physics, lol. Things LOOK nice as in details, but the clipping is unimmersive.

3) Arrows weigh approximately 600% more than real life, so carrying 30 arrows will be 15 pounds of backpack weight (30 medieval iron-tipped arrows would weight about 2-3 pounds IRL). There are quite a few other weight issues that make no sense, which, with limited capacity, really adds up. 

4) Food satiety is REALLY weird. You gain weight and get fatter by staying satiated. The game wants you to stay "peckish" 24/7 to stay trim. I'd rather be able to eat more and not have to eat as often. It's tedious.

5) There are currently bugs with saving the game. You might have issues reloading, or lose items. Part of the issue seems to be a save taking 30 seconds to happen, and people quitting before it fully saves. So save times need to speed up.

6) Also, I get a tinge of feeling that the devs want the game to be too tedious. I don't want more Fun Pimps and their constant nerfing in 7 Days to Die.
