While there's lots to improve on and I'm confident the developers know that, the biggest stand-out right now is how janky, weird, and unreliable melee feels. I'm sure this is mentioned by other reviews, but I'm going to focus on this since it's my #1 complaint about the game:
 - Reach/range on melee attacks feels universally too short, playing in first person and coming from a background of decades of FPS games that have either a melee focus or incidental melee, I  would say the reach the character has feels like it's about 20% too short at a minimum.
Right now, weapons have different stats, but they largely operate in the same ways. Ie, spears don't feel like they give you range, they more 'slash' than stab, etc. I'm assuming this is just a matter of time/effort/assets. 

Ideally different weapons will have different ranges, swings, etc, in addition to just having a swing speed, damage type, and damage values, which is how it seems to stand now. It'd also be "nice to have" more specialized melee skill trees eventually, in some capacity.

Thankfully 'dying' is not as nearly as brutal as zomboid - if it was 100% loss of all progress, the current gameplay would not be satisfying or fun at all.

The slow zombies give pretty good/sufficient audio cues and hints they are around (groaning, footsteps, etc), but like many games that fall into this same trap, the fast zombies effectively end up as magical often-silent ninja zombies that sprint at your back.

In-game explanations and tutorialization could be better, but it's definitely playable, especially with a few extra google searches or questions asked of the players if you're on a server. 

Some things are very unclear in the game itself, like on a PvE server, it seems like the 'claim' system (such as it is) thatr involves utility cabinets or whatever they're called seem to protect against breaking/building/etc, but aren't inherently secured or locked, relying on you actually locking them (keys or otherwise).

It was clunky, there were hardly any zombies around, but it had promise. For a game made by just two people, it was a very solid tech demo.

[{"review_text": "EDIT: After doing some more math and interacting with park chest rewards I no longer think the income would be that awful if they just allowed us to melt 2nd dupe or gave us full melt freedom back. The primary factor causing economic problems is resources getting stuck in stacks of 3 golds/legendaries you don't even want to use. We need dupe requirement to drop to 1 or 0.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

I greatly enjoyed the first Shadowverse and was happy to support it by buying cosmetics since it was quite possible for normal players to craft their preferred deck by melting down cards they did not wish to use. In this sequel, the income is DRASTICALLY nerfed (packs now cost 500 gold, gold income is ~200-400 per day compared to almost always getting enough coins for 1-2 pack buys from dailies in SV1) and you cannot melt cards unless you keep 3 or more copies, even if you don't want to play them. The free daily pack does not sufficiently offset this, since the income from melting silver rarity cards is greatly nerfed and legendaries still cost 3500 to craft. Even if it did, forcing people to open the game every day to have a hope of affording their list is cringe.

The economics of Worlds Beyond are abysmal, even with all the preregistration bonuses and tutorial income I was not able to assemble ONE deck without skimping on literal gold rarity utility cards. Whales with 10+ legendaries in their list will run over anything you can scrape together as a new player no matter how skilled you are, and this issue will only become more pronounced as expansions come out. All the other mechanical and visual polish is meaningless if f2p players cannot reasonably create an optimized deck. Do better, Cygames. I'll not be changing my review until something is done about it.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1750206993}, {"review_text": "As a player with 2000 hours in Shadowverse, I wish I could write something positive but I simply can't.

I'm a long time player of the first Shadowverse game and one of the reasons why I fell in love with it is because of the leaders in game. The animations are pretty and they're one of the eye catchers in the game. I was delighted that you can farm out the pity of a single expansion during its course due to its smooth economy meaning you can get the leader you want as long as you play the game.

The main reason I'm giving this game a negative review right now is because of how stingy the game has become with its poor economy, notably the event rewards. I'm mostly disappointed with the events we recently got and how garbage the rewards were. You cannot just x5 the price of a card pack and not adjust the event rewards accordingly. Keep in mind, I have no issues with vials or crafting decks... it's just the event rewards are a whole lot less compared to the original Shadowverse and I don't know why.

Here are some comparisons from the original Shadowverse:

Shadowverse: 
- 1 card pack costs 100 rupies
- Dailies gave you 100-120 rupies in total, enough for a single card pack. Sometimes a daily gives out a card pack for 7 wins
- You can liquefy any cards you do not want and turn them into vials. You are not locked to 3 copies.
- Legendaries are not guaranteed every 10 packs
- Treasure Trove of Rupees (Rupees Galore in WB) gave plenty of rewards that allowed multiple pack openings
- Grand Prix gave you 50 Rupies simply by entering and quitting. You get a free entry daily. Getting wins in the Grand Prix either gave you card packs or generous amount of rupies per day (100-300)
- The Daily Treasure Chest event (the one that appears randomly every day with 0/5) gave you card packs and generous amount of rupies
- Battlepass went up to level 100, with more rupies rewarded if you pay for it. You also get "Future card packs" so you can start opening some packs when the new expansion comes out.
- Expansion pity is set to 400
- Getting the leader from opening the packs straight out gave you the alternate card artwork, the lobby background, the emblem, and the card sleeves along with the leader

Shadowverse: Worlds Beyond:
- 1 card pack costs 500 rupies

Currently in game player doesn't have to manage soil hydration and animal husbandry is so bland. Farms use animals to fit niches and this game dose not implement that at all. Great game regardless of bugs ETC", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1744403498}, {"review_text": "The Farming Simulator series, once seen as a refreshing niche experience for fans of agriculture and simulation, has increasingly become a glaring example of a franchise coasting on brand loyalty while offering little genuine innovation. The latest installment, released on November 24, continues this unfortunate trend, recycling the same core engine and mechanics with only minor, often cosmetic, tweaks - changes that could easily have been delivered through a patch or DLC for previous versions.

What makes the situation worse is that these marginal updates are marketed as full-priced new entries, effectively turning the series into a cashgrab. Players are paying top dollar for what is, in essence, a lightly modified version of the same game they've already purchased one or more times before. The developers, GIANTS Software, seem to rely on the loyal modding community to fill the gaps in creativity and depth, while delivering the bare minimum in terms of technical or gameplay evolution themselves.

At its core, Farming Simulator fails to live up to its genre’s potential. Despite its name, the game lacks the intricate depth that one would expect from a true simulation. Crop management, soil chemistry, equipment wear and tear, dynamic weather systems - elements that should add meaningful layers of realism - are either simplified to the point of irrelevance or entirely absent. Farming in the real world is a complex, constantly evolving process, but Farming Simulator presents it as a rinse-and-repeat grind with little nuance or challenge.

Even worse, many longstanding bugs persist despite years of feedback. Issues with AI workers getting stuck, poor pathfinding, clipping problems, janky vehicle physics, and multiplayer desyncs remain unresolved, making the experience feel unpolished and frustrating—especially given how long the series has been around. These aren't minor quirks; they're quality-of-life issues that have been present since multiple earlier titles and simply should not still exist.

In a gaming landscape where simulation titles are pushing boundaries—look at what titles like SnowRunner or DCS World are doing - Farming Simulator feels stuck in neutral. It's content to play it safe, releasing just enough to justify a new number on the box but not enough to warrant the purchase.

Until GIANTS Software starts addressing these core problems and rethinks their business model, Farming Simulator will remain a series with untapped potential, diluted by complacency and commercial opportunism.

FS25 was the first game in the series I decided to pre order. With 910 hours clocked across FS15, FS17, FS19 and FS22, last of which completely revolutionized my FS experience, I decided to support the developer. The launch was less than smooth…

First and foremost - it ran like crap, I barely managed to squeeze out consistent 60 frames. And there were a lot of bugs initially, many of which are still present three months after launch, albeit to a lesser degree. Using any kind of loader with a pallet fork or a bucket is still bound to get sucked in the abyssal depths of the bug realm for no apparent reason. Same goes for being hatefucked out of the map boundaries at fractional mach, with your combine (that you cannot recover unless you revert to a previous save) for no apparent reason. The vehicle fleet available on launch, even with the MacDon pack which I got for preordering the game, is insultingly small compared to the previous titles. Precision Farming was not featured (credit where it is due, they never claimed it would be) and is only now being worked on, and I fear it may be locked behind a paywall when it releases. [{"review_text": "I got this game on a sale for 1.49 EUR and it was the best deal ever, it turned out to be amazing. It's not for everyone however, as it's quite long, you need to pay attention to the story and get used to the clunky combat - you'll either love it or give up in the first few hours.

I started the game to see what it's like, struggled with the fighting, played half an hour until it suddenly crashed and I realised I didn't save the game. I didn't really like what I saw first, but I decided to give it another chance. Fortunately, the dialogues are skippable, so I could continue almost immediately and this time I read the tutorial more attentively and managed to find out how to properly kill enemies. As the story progressed, I got more and more into it and started to enjoy the game very much.


[u][h1]Graphics[/h1][/u]
Even though the game came out in 2007, it's beautiful. The environments are detailed, colourful and interesting, most places are not just visually but aesthetically pleasing. Heck, even some dark crypts and caves look exquisite here and there due to the nice colours and great lighting.


[u][h1]Gameplay[/h1][/u]
When you start the game, you have to choose a style you want to play it in, and you still have the opportunity to change this anytime. You can have an isometric camera or OTS, so you can play point and click style, and also in third person if you want to (I chose the latter). Being inexperienced with RPGs, I played on easy. My character became pretty strong eventually (maybe too strong for this difficulty), yet there still were a few challenging parts to balance that out.

As you play, you gain XP and level up. While meditating, you can access the skill tree, which looked a bit complicated at first, but it makes perfect sense. Alchemy is pretty useful, especially for bigger fights, I haven't used any bombs though.

The gameplay is not particularly interesting on its own, the story is what makes it special. Sometimes there's a lot of running back and forth, collecting things, which gets boring after a while. I was very grateful for the few fast travel options we got.

On the other hand, there are lots of side quests to keep you busy. Some of them are of the general [i]collect-this-and-I-reward-you[/i] tpye, and there are more important ones as well. Some side quests enrich the story [i]a lot[/i] and have an overall impact on how you experience it, so it's definitely worth completing those.


[u][h1]Combat[/h1][/u]
It's doubtless that this is the low point of the game. The first time I saw Geralt grabbing a sword and swinging it around above his head like an idiot, I laughed out loud, I thought it was a bug. (Later though as I applied more talents on the swords, he became a much better fighter.) To evade attacks you need to dodge by pressing one of the direction buttons twice or more times, depending on how responsive it wants to be in the current situation, I had some trouble sometimes when Geralt got cornered. To attack, you need to click on the enemy and do not click again immediately, doing so will cancel the attack. Only click again when the cursor changes, allowing you to do combos if you click in time. It definitely takes some getting used to.

Collect as much information as you can on the enemies you have to face, it's important to read the Journal, especially the pages on Monsters to learn what they're immune to, where they can be found, which fighting styles are efficient against them. It helps you a great deal. The Signs are very useful and fun, too.

The controls during combat are pretty awkward sometimes, even if I had the right fighting style selected, I couldn't attack or hurt the enemies. I had to switch to another style and then back for it to decide to work again.


[u][h1]Story[/h1][/u]
After the low point, here comes the best part. The story in this game is [b]incredible[/b]. It's very detailed, very deep and exciting. The dialogues are filled with humour and deep philosophical thoughts here and there.

The world is consistent, the characters are likeable and unique, after a while you find yourself caring about many of them. They all respond to your actions and choices. There's quite a number of decisions you have to make that (sometimes pretty heavily) affect the story and your relationship to certain characters. I loved the amount of freedom I had in the game, I was never forced to get in an intimate relationship with any character or play dice, etc. - it's entirely up to the player.

The way women were portrayed though - boobs, boobs and more boobs. I've seen more boobs in this game than my own. :P Jokes aside, I simply had to play very carefully when others were in the same room with me, because almost every woman you can interact with is um... underdressed. Good for Geralt I guess. ;)

As you play more and more, the story just drags you in - even if you don't like the combat or the gameplay, it's definitely worth to play this through just for the story alone.


[u][h1]Animation and voices[/h1][/u]
This is something I wasn't entirely pleased with. Yes, it's not a game from today, but the characters often looked very stiff, which is not a good thing when there's a lot of dialogue. Another thing which detracts from the experience is the mediocre voice acting. First I found it very awkward, but got used to it eventually and after a certain point it simply didn't bother me anymore.
(I kept finding the same character models throughout the game though, now that did annoy me a bit.)


[u][h1]Music and atmosphere[/h1][/u]
The music was pretty great, fast paced and dark when needed, beautiful and calming while exploring beautiful areas. It really spiced some great moments up. Same with the atmosphere, the time of day really sets the mood of some locations, as well as the occasional rain and storms.
I also loved the art style, there's some gorgeous artwork during storytelling parts.


[u][h1]Summary:[/h1][/u]
+ nice visuals
+ amazing story with brilliant dialogues
+ great music and atmosphere

- combat might be hard to get used to
- bad animations


It took me 46 hours to finish the adventure and it's become one of my all-time favourite games. If you can get used to the combat and want to take a break from no-brainers, I highly recommend The Witcher, it's going to be an amazing and unforgettable experience.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 83, "timestamp_created": 1430412540}, {"review_text": "[h1] Should you still play the Witcher 1 in 2020? [/h1]
That’s a fair question to ask, considering that this game is now 13 years old with its release in October 2007. 

[h1] Cons [/h1]
With a game that is 13 years old, it’s clear that its age will show in some aspects. One of these is the outdated [b] graphics [/b] . (Especially if you play without any mods, like I did). Also, there aren't a lot of different character models for the NPC’s, so you will encounter a lot of clones. Personally, this didn’t bother me that much, but it may be distracting for some players. 

The game has a [b] slow start [/b] . In the beginning, you may find yourself annoyed by the point and click combat or the slow start to the story. But I will promise you, the game really does get better the further you get. After some time, I even found myself enjoying the combat, I just needed to get used to it.

The [b]Navigation [/b] was a bit frustrating. It’s really annoying how often the direct way is blocked so you have to walk all the way around, even though you can already see your destination.

[b] There is no fast traveling. [/b] During some parts of the game, you can teleport to certain locations, but that doesn’t change the fact that 40% of your play time will just be walking around from one place to another, which can feel a bit annoying at times, especially considering the amount of backtracking needed if you really want to finish all side quests and contracts.

[b] Fighting feels very clunky.  [/b] There is no active dodging, and if you get stunned when fighting more than two enemies, you can proceed to grab a cup of tea while watching said enemies slowly beat Geralt to death because no matter how frantically you press your keys, you will not get out of that situation.

[b] There is no animation cancelling.  [/b] Animations have to finish before you can start doing something else. After you drink a potion or eat something, Geralt has to stand still for the whole duration of the animation before you can move or drink another potion. This may be intended but feels unnatural and a bit clunky. Every normal person can move while drinking, especially while being chased by monsters. But our Geralt here is different. He likes to drink his potions in peace of mind, as if he has all the time in the world, not minding the monsters attacking him while doing so. 

If you play on normal difficulty,  [b] the game will be too easy  [/b] , especially later on. The only boss fight that felt challenging to me was the Chapter 1 boss fight, because I hadn’t levelled my Aard sign at all (note that with levelled Aard sign, it is also very easy). But the later boss fights, especially the final ones in Chapter 5 and the epilogue, are way too easy if you know how to use alchemy and signs. Because of that, I recommend playing the game on the hardest difficulty and not on normal difficulty.
Also, you can’t pick up loot during combat. The game makes you wait around 3 seconds after combat finishes before you are allowed to pick something up.

[b] In conclusion  [/b] , the negative points mostly concern the lack of convenience we are used to from newer games. Most of these points only caused me minor frustration and didn’t stop me from playing and enjoying the game. 

[h1]Pros[/h1]
It’s worth discovering how [b] the story [/b] of the Witcher games started, because it’s a great, immersive story. For someone who read all the books and already played Witcher 3, it was a great experience to discover how the games continue to develop the story from the books. 

[b] The world [/b] . The world of the Witcher is grey and cruel, but it’s also rich in lovable and humorous characters and filled with a lot of lore to discover. Most characters are layered and have good reasons for their actions; almost no one is just evil for the sake of being evil but rather convinced that what they are doing is the right thing. 

 [b] The choices  [/b] you make affect the story. A lot of times, there are various outcomes to a quest based on your decisions. The world isn’t simply black and white. The developers stayed true to Andrzej Sapkowski’s notion of “Choosing the lesser evil” from the books. Even though the most canon choice is to stay neutral in the conflict presented in the game, it is up to the player if he wants to side with one of the two factions (Sco’iatel or Order of the Flaming Rose) or not. 

[b] The soundtrack [/b] : This game has one of the best video game soundtracks imo, the music helps creating an immersive atmosphere.

[b] The levelling system [/b] : You can personalize the combat by putting skills in magic signs, alchemy, bombs or the different sword styles. 

[b] Combat tactics [/b]: I love the fact that you have be tactical in combat and that alchemy and signs actually matter. In order to deal damage, it is crucial to pick the right sword (silver for monsters and steel for humans), the right style and to use the right potions. You can’t just mindlessly slice through enemies 

[b] play time [/b] : There are a lot of things to do in the Witcher, there are a lot of side quests, contracts and trophies. If you don’t plan on rushing the main story, you have around 50 hours of content. 

[b] Price: [/b] I picked it up for like 1-2 Euro on sale, and the amount of content you get for the price is amazing.

 [h1] Conclusion  [/h1]
The worst part of this game is definitely its controls and the general inconvenience, which may make it feel like a slog to some players. But if you manage to get used to that, it’s still a very good game with a great world and story. I recommend the game to everyone who isn't too bothered by aged controls and I think it's still worth your time to play this game in 2020.

This is the first game in the Witcher Series. 

The gameplay in Witcher a split between focusing on the hack and slash, and the other on the heavy dialogue scenes. The game can be played in one of three camera angles, there are two top down angels, and one over the shoulder view – I mainly used the third person view as it suited the gameplay more than the others.  Combat in this game is something that sometimes receives criticism but I found it to be a nice change from the regular combat you see in RPGs – you have three different styles of attack, a quick, heavy and group attack – each of these attacks have three stages of attack and you have to click at the right time in order to continue your combo of attack. This does feel a little like a QTE, but for me it is disguised well enough that you don’t really notice it. The Witcher also comes equipped with two different main weapons – one sword which deals more damage to monsters, but is less effective against humans, and another weapon which is the opposite. Another major portion of the gameplay is based on alchemy, you will be spending a lot time collecting herbs in order to make an assortment of potions in order to help you progress.  This is one of the first games I have played that your actions really do have a massive impact on how the story flows and concludes. A lot of the dialogue options when conversing with other characters will also affect the story and how that character in particular interacts with the player.  

This game is eight years old now, so you would expect the graphics to be a little on the dated side, however when wracking the resolution up to 4k, the game still has a current gen look to it; whilst some of the textures may be on the lower quality scale still, the open worldness of the game means that you can’t really expect mind blowing graphics at the time of its development.  The game also has some very nice looking special effects, such as water effects. 

On release of Witcher, the game’s voice acting was supposedly one of the worst that has been seen, however the Enhanced Edition of the game, which everyone got who purchased the original version, greatly improves the voice acting to acceptable levels – whilst it is still not the best by today’s standards, every single character in the game is catered for and has a voice to be heard.  The game has a couple of sound tracks that are really iconic too, and the sound effects are all really on par. 

Witcher’s plot is one of my all-time favourites – it is very rare that a game is able to completely suck me into the story right from the word go. The game is split in to various chapters, which allows the game to create sub plots whilst also progressing the overall main story line at an acceptable pace. A lot of the quests in Witcher will bear no importance to the main story, and often are there to add an extra layer of depth to the world in which you are in. The immersion levels are sky high in this game as you will find yourself caring greatly for the characters.

This game comes with three levels of difficulties; Easy, Medium and Hard. I was playing on medium on my run through the game and was still challenged to the point where I had to replay a few parts due to death. Hard mode is seriously for the hard-core RPGers out there; you will need to take full advantage of the alchemy system in the game as most of the more advanced fights will 100% require the use of multiple potions. Your average Joe gamer will get a great amount of enjoyment and challenge from the medium settings though.

This version represents the developers' final thoughts and ideas on the game, and it differs considerably from any other version.

In this game, the player takes the role of Geralt of Rivia, a witcher or a professional monster-slayer. There is no character-build menu, no fancy options about hair-colour or the width of your eyebrows. You are Geralt of Rivia, you are a Witcher. And to put it simple: the game is so utterly brilliant since it manages to let you believe that, almost from the start. Seldom have I felt so deeply connected to the character I was playing: after a couple of in-game hours, I started to think as Geralt, react to my surroundings as Geralt, even feel like Geralt: I was completely involved, the game got deep under my skin, I was bewitched. It's not that I played the game for hours and hours on end, or that I played through the night, no: it's more like I felt Geralt had become part of my life, not only while in-game, but also while not playing. I started to look for articles and websites to read about [i]The Witcher[/i] and its world, and I even dreamt a couple of times about the game and its characters...

[h1]The game's greatest strengths: the world, the story, the choices[/h1]

As is commonly known by now, the Polish developer CD Project Red started working on [i]The Witcher[/i] – actually their first game – out of love for the books, novels and stories by the Polish writer Andrzej Sapkowski. Sapkowksi is the author of The Witcher-universe: a collection of books and stories about a fictional, fantasy-world with a profound background and a history all of its own. Sapkowski has often been called "The Polish Tolkien", and while that might be too big a compliment, I often felt like I was part of a world that could hold its own against Tolkiens incredible rich universe. And I suppose that explains why I felt so connected to the game and so deeply involved: the world of The Witcher did already exist before the game, and is completely coherent and believable by itself.

It is one thing to have an interesting world to build a game in, it's another to write and develop a story within this world that works well for a role-playing game. The story of [i]The Witcher[/i] however succeeds brilliantly in keeping the player's interest. It is ambitious, full of twists and unexpected turns, but it stays believable right up to the end. The different characters, both Geralt and his main protagonists, are complex and multi-layered: hardly anyone in this world is just "good" or "evil": most of the time, its a mix of both, often with one or several other characteristics  added. The game does a fantastic job in introducing the player (Geralt) to this world, using an old trick: after having lost his memory, Geralt has to rediscover not only the places, the stories and the people, but he has to rediscover himself: he has to give himself a place in the dark, conflict-ridden world he lives in.

The main way to do this, is by making choices: the game's strongest point by far is the feeling you get that the decisions you make actually matter, and do influence the flow and even the outcome of the story. This is especially impressive since almost every choice, from minor to very important, is difficult and hardly clear-cut. The games offers tons of dialogues, more than 5000 lines of text to be read and/or said, but very seldom did I feel like doing the "good thing". It was more like "trying to do my best, and hoping for the best", since often decisions or roads taken early in the game, proved to have unexpected consequences (much) later on. The way in which this game manages to make me think about good and evil, about morality and consequences, is utterly and completely brilliant.

[h1]The game's problem: it tries too hard to be the best rpg in the world[/h1]

From whatever angle you look at it, it is obvious that [i]The Witcher[/i] is a very, very ambitious game. The developers made no secret of it that, even back in 2007 when they were almost unknown, they wanted to make "the best rpg ever". Ambition definitely is a good thing for any developer, it can also be a trap. While CD Project Red succeeded brilliantly with everything story- and character-related, they paid dearly in some other departments. The actual gameplay, the movement and combat, form the game's biggest downfalls. As a matter of fact, lots of people have tried the game, only to leave it after running into frustration with the combat system. Combat is an exercise in rythmical feeling: by clicking at the right moment, Geralt can chain attacks together so that they become much stronger. Fast clicking is of no use whatsoever, as is blocking or parrying since the game takes care of that.

Moreover, Geralt has two different swords (steel for humans and animals, silver for monsters) and three differend combat styles (strong, fast and group style) at his disposal, so choosing the right weapon and the right sword for any fight is an important issue. Still, when one is prepared to play the game slow, with lots of attention to the myriad of entries in the journal (on quests, people, monsters, alchemical ingredients, recipes or locations), the sense of fulfillment can be enormous. This is most of all true of the alchemy, which is a very important part of the game. It takes a time to get the hang of it, when once mastered, it proves very rewarding.

[h1]Final thoughts[/h1]

Playing and mastering [i]The Witcher[/i] felt like climbing a mountain: it takes time, patience and commitment, even preparation, but once everything gets going, the long way to the summit becomes a joy by itself. In the case of the first game in the series, the mountain definitely is not Mount Everest nor even Mont Blanc, and the path is littered with dangerous spots and possible downfalls, but the scenery is gorgeous nonetheless, and the journey towards the summit proved one I won't ever forget.

Steam integration: 7/10 (like any older game, it comes without cards or achievements)
Game for the money: 9/10 (it's a very long game, but it's not an open-world sandbox)
Personal appreciation: 10/10

[h1]INTRODUCTION:[/h1]
The Witcher (1) is a critically acclaimed 2007 action role-playing game by polish developer CD Projekt RED. The game was based on the novel series by Andrzej Sapkowski with the same title. An “enhanced edition” was released on 2008 and a “director’s cut” edition on 2009.

[h1]PLOT (No Spoilers):[/h1]
The game follows the story of Geralt of Rivia – a genetically modified professional monster slayer otherwise known as a Witcher. Having recently lost his long-term memory due to amnesia, Geralt must embark on a journey of self-discovery while at the same time, recover the stolen secrets on how to make Witchers and bring those responsible to justice. The world, the people, the events, and the overall story will change depending on the player’s choices and actions.

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
+ Good graphics and art style despite its age;
+ Great voice acting, music and sound design;
+ Unique and fun combat mechanics but…(see Con #1);
+ Unique gameplay mechanics such as (but not limited to): alchemy and potion crafting; skill distribution system; monster hunting and trophy system; and ingredient gathering;
+ Great main story with branching storylines depending on player action;
+ Interesting side quests;
+ Great world building with a solid lore backing it up;
+ Fun mini games;
+ Day and night cycle that changes the game’s atmosphere (night time being more dangerous);
+ Adequately sized maps with room for exploration;
+ Interesting supporting characters;
+ Lengthy (but not boring) game time;
+ Good level and chapter designs; and
+ D-Cups everywhere.

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
- The game is way too easy even on the hardest difficulty;
- FPS drops in certain areas (especially in the later chapters);
- Most weapons look the same (even the unique and rare weapons look like the standard starting Witcher’s sword);
- Very limited armor choices; and
- Limited NPC model variation (most of them look alike).

[h1]NEUTRAL:[/h1]
+/- Some side quests are easy to miss
+/- Some players may find the UI ugly and too cluttered

[h1]CONCLUSION:[/h1]
[b]GREAT GAME[/b] and I [b]HIGHLY RECOMMEND[/b] it to any RPG fan out there. The Witcher delivers a fantastic story, set in a great fantasy world, and merges it with an interesting and fun gameplay mechanic that makes for a truly immersive gaming experience. This game demonstrates how good story telling, great visuals, and fun gameplay can be rolled into one package.

[h1]WORTH IT?[/h1]
I can easily recommend this title at [b]full price[/b], but for the best value for your money, try purchasing the [url= http://store.steampowered.com/bundle/727/The_Witcher_Trilogy/ ]Witcher Trilogy Bundle[/url].

[h1]FINAL NOTES:[/h1]
Your save games in the final chapter of this title can be carried over to the sequel ([url= http://store.steampowered.com/app/20920/The_Witcher_2_Assassins_of_Kings_Enhanced_Edition/ ]The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings[/url])

[h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Writing & Worldbuilding[/h3]
The world is only a shell of its former self, ravaged by madness and purposelessness after the Shattering of the Elden Ring. Born as one of many Tarnished, you too would be destined to roam this endless limbo; however, that was not meant to be. Gifted with the ability to see the elusive remnants of divine Grace, you’re set on a journey to follow them through a broken world, with the ultimate goal of mending the Elden Ring, restoring the world to what it once was, or mold it into something different. 

It’s an obscure narrative, that doesn’t get more clear as you progress, unless you spend time reading all the fine print on items you acquire, exhaust all optional dialogues, and figure things out on your own. As cloudy as it might be, there’s a surprising depth and meaning in each character, friendly or otherwise, that you may encounter, as there is in each perilous fortress, dungeon or ruin you may venture into. Such obscurity may feel unwarranted, but it’s rewarding in its own way, as it allows players to piece together the story, motives and lore bit by bit instead of dumping it linearly as most games do. It’s written extremely well, and gives a new dimension to the exploration component, where items aren’t only tools, but also a source of understanding.

The world is nothing short of spectacular, both visually and artistically. From vast plains and labyrinthine cities to dark dungeons and putrid swamps, there’s enough variety to keep exploration fresh for more than a hundred hours, and that’s certainly something. Each location feels coherent in its characters, ambience and visual style, perfectly matching the background lore and events that may have occurred there. 

[h3]Exploration & Secrets[/h3]
You’ll explore the world on either foot or horseback, your summonable steed an essential tool to traverse the large swathes of land between each dungeon, fortress or point of interest. Other than offering convenient functions like crafting, leveling and weapon ability swapping, Grace sites also act as fast travel beacons, and are conveniently placed all over the world. Of course, using them also means respawning all enemies except bosses. Unlike other Souls, there’s a map, with custom markers even, but nothing more than that. 

You’ll have to find places on your own, with nothing hinting that a hidden dungeon, cave or whole parts of the world may be hidden past the most remote crevices and corners. Despite that, the superb map design always gives you hints and landmarks to figure out if there’s still something left to find. It’s supremely rewarding to comb every tidbit of land, because when you least expect it, you’ll always find a unique item, a hidden NPC, a portal to a secret location; it’s the definition of organically rewarding exploration. 

[h3]Combat System & Bosses[/h3]
Given the hundreds of available weapons, spells, and armor sets available, you’ll be able to shape your character into whatever most suits your playstyle. Be a powerful mage and destroy your foes from a distance, a swift rogue banking it all on attack speed and critical strikes after a parry, or a mighty warrior hitting foes hard enough to break their poise, exposing them to a deadly finisher. Or why not, a mix of all of the above and more; there isn’t a right or wrong build, as everything is equally viable if used correctly. 

Combat is, above all, based on individual skill, precise dodges, learning enemy patterns and picking your fights wisely. It’s a learning process, where each death makes you stronger in experience, despite the Runes (souls) you might have lost. More than in any other Souls however, Elden Ring puts emphasis on builds, giving you passive tools like talismans, interchangeable weapon skills and a wide variety of buffs and utilities to find the perfect combination to overcome your foes.

Enemies are deadly and merciless at all times. Those who recklessly rush, or button mash, will be demolished even by common trash mobs. Elden Ring is almost never unfair, but it’s impossibly difficult if you don’t approach it in the correct way and refuse to play by its rules. That only is more true for bosses, most of which have evolving movesets and even double phases, so that once you think you have mastered their moveset and found a strategy, a higher challenge presents itself. A wide array of status effects, damage types, resistances and weaknesses you’ll have to figure out on your own are present to make some fights much easier, and only through trying and failing many times will you be able to find the right strategy. 

[h3]Character Progression[/h3]
As you level up with Runes gathered from defeating enemies and using certain items, your attributes will allow you to use more powerful weapons, many of which having unique special abilities, and even normal ones can be customized with the skills you like the most, through a simple yet deep crafting system. Elden Ring isn’t as gear-dependent as classic RPGs may be, but unless you’re a tryharder masochist, having good gear to complement your build definitely makes all the difference in not getting one-shot by everything and not taking forever in killing bosses.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 29, "timestamp_created": 1741374349}, {"review_text": "Elden Ring is an incredible action RPG that I loved from start to finish. [b]Replayability:[/b] With multiple possible endings, new game plus, dozens of secrets, hundreds of bosses, and insane build variety, there’s plenty to explore in the Lands Between. And then just when you think you’ve seen it all, [i]Elden Ring[/i] whispers, “Have you tried dual-wielding great hammers?” ★★★★★

[b]Final Thoughts:[/b] Like any souls-like game, expect to rage nonstop. The difference? This time, you get to decide whether to die miserably on foot, on horseback, or with your equally doomed friend by your side. Would I recommend [i]Elden Ring[/i]? Only if you're ready for a stunning but punishing adventure—and the chance to put a ring on a lunar princess, even if she immediately ghosts you.

I have repeatedly told all of my friends that Skyrim is now my #2 favorite game of all time. This is the game that dethroned it.

There isn't a single aspect of this game that is lacking, in my opinion. It has some of the best gameplay you could ever ask for. It has hundreds of weapons to choose from. There's something to fill almost every niche you could think of. Multiple play styles are all perfectly viable and it includes the ability to respec your character after the second major boss, so you could potentially make use of literally any of them in a single run. But you can also have multiple characters. You can even play it with your friends without downloading a mod. (But if you want to have a better experience, the Seamless Multiplayer mod is safe and carefully designed so you won't get banned from the core game.) The unmodded multiplayer is the only minor problem I could list about the game.

Aesthetically, it is incredibly impressive. I can't think of a single game that has blown me away this much from just a visual perspective. The landscapes, the atmosphere, the music, the character and enemy designs, every tiny polygon of this game has been lovingly crafted. It doesn't have the absolute most high resolution textures or the most stunning raytracing, but you won't notice any of that because you'll be too busy drooling at the art direction.

The environmental storytelling is second to none. Where many games are content to just throw items at you for no reason that makes sense, Elden Ring continues the tradition that From Software started with Demon's Souls. Anyways, it's still a fun game, even if I feel a bit cheated.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1740234878}, {"review_text": "As an engineer and physics teacher, I find it a pleasure to write a review for "Oxygen Not Included." This game has captivated me for over 600 hours, and for good reason. It’s one of those rare titles that can make you lose track of time, often at the expense of a good night’s sleep, thanks to its deep and engaging base-building and management mechanics.

The gameplay and art are top-notch, as expected from the creators of "Don’t Starve." The game’s incorporation of real-world physics, chemistry, and even a hint of biology sets it apart from typical base-building titles. Concepts like denser gases sinking, thermal conductivity of materials, and gas flow mechanics aren’t just visual flourishes—they’re crucial to mastering the game’s systems. I’ve even recommended it to some of my students as a fun way to engage with these scientific ideas in a practical context.

One area that feels like a missed opportunity, however, is the game’s approach to electricity. While it introduces the concept of transformers to manage potential differences, it falls short of incorporating more sophisticated concepts like series and parallel circuits. Given the game’s 2D aesthetic, I believe the addition of more realistic electrical systems could have been a natural and engaging fit for players to experiment with.

Make no mistake, this is a challenging game. Your duplicants (the characters you manage) will suffer and perish in various ways—hunger, heat, and oxygen shortages, to name a few—until you master the balancing act required for survival. Problems often reveal themselves too late, forcing you to start over from scratch. But therein lies the charm of "Oxygen Not Included": every failure is a lesson learned. The experience of rebuilding from scratch, armed with newfound knowledge, makes for an incredibly rewarding gameplay loop.

For those who enjoy base-building games, I wholeheartedly recommend "Oxygen Not Included." It’s not always a smooth ride, and losing a base after dozens of hours can be disheartening, but the lessons learned with each restart make every new base a little smarter and more efficient than the last.

The expansions are promising, though I’ve only scratched the surface of the newer ones. Mods, on the other hand, are a mixed bag. There’s a rich modding community offering everything from quality-of-life improvements to full gameplay overhauls. Personally, I’m a bit of a purist, preferring cosmetic mods over those that make the game easier. The only caveat is that mods often break after updates and require patching to work again.

All in all, "Oxygen Not Included" is a meticulously crafted, mentally stimulating, and sometimes brutally unforgiving game. If you’re up for the challenge, it’s well worth your time—just don’t be surprised if it ends up taking more of it than you expected.

1000/10 would recommend", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1748312856}, {"review_text": "If you're the kind of player who thrives on depth, complexity, and the thrill of solving problems with increasingly elegant systems, Oxygen Not Included might be your next obsession. After 1700 hours, I can say without hesitation: this game has earned every minute.

Depth That Never Runs Dry
What looks like a quirky space-colony sim quickly reveals itself as a brutally intricate simulation of thermodynamics, fluid dynamics, gas exchange, agriculture, industrial automation, psychology, and even rocket science. And yet, it’s all packed into a charming, side-scrolling aesthetic with expressive Duplicants and satisfying sound design.

Even after thousands of cycles across multiple colonies, I'm still refining my designs, optimizing layouts, and discovering new strategies. There's no “one solution” — just more refined ones.

Engineering Playground
You’re not just surviving; you’re building systems. Water loops, oxygen production, heat management, food chains, power grids, automation, and late-game interplanetary logistics — this is a game where planning matters, and poor choices 100 cycles ago can come back to melt your base.

Mistakes teach. Recovery is a puzzle. Mastery is satisfying.

Endless Replayability
Every asteroid type demands new thinking. Traits, biomes, geysers — all randomized. You’re never playing the same game twice. Want a relaxed experience? Play Terra and build at your own pace. Want a challenge? Start on Rime and deal with the cold. Or try modded asteroids and explore community-curated chaos.

Systems Nerd Heaven
If you enjoy games like Factorio, Dwarf Fortress, or RimWorld, but crave more simulation and fewer guns, this is your game. ONI is about processes. It’s a colony sim where how you do something is often more important than what you do. That’s a rare design choice — and it's beautifully executed.

Minor Critiques
The early game can feel like a trap for new players who don’t understand heat, gas stratification, or resource scarcity.

Performance can drop in large colonies with lots of automation and piping.

There’s no hand-holding — but the Wiki and community are incredibly helpful.

Final Verdict: 10/10
Oxygen Not Included isn't a game you play. It's a game you inhabit. It's a slow-burn obsession for systems thinkers, tinkerers, and masochists who enjoy watching colonies implode because they forgot to vent CO₂. It’s also one of the most rewarding games I’ve ever touched.

With its vibrant art style, quirky characters, and focus on strategic teamplay, TF2 stands out in the crowded multiplayer shooter genre. The game’s charm lies in its simplicity and accessibility, making it enjoyable for both newcomers and veteran players.

The game is built around nine distinct classes, each with its own unique abilities and playstyle, from the all-around Soldier to the support-heavy Medic. These classes encourage teamwork, as each one plays a specific role in achieving objectives, whether it’s defending a point, pushing a cart, or capturing a flag. The balance between offense, defense, and support creates a dynamic experience that demands coordination and strategy.

One of Team Fortress 2’s standout features is its art style. The game adopts a colorful, cartoonish look that not only makes it visually distinctive but also keeps the tone lighthearted and fun, even amidst chaotic firefights. This art direction, combined with the comedic voice lines and quirky character designs, gives the game an enduring charm that still resonates with players today.

The weapons, for the most part, are well-balanced and strong, and it is SO satisfying to land a clean shot with them. And don't get me started on the visual style - the dusky watercolour feel of those rocky Midwest mountains and the spytech-loaded secret bases reminiscent of 60s action flicks stands out among the recycled, lifeless feel of more modern titles with a similar nature. And the characters are some of the most iconic faces in gaming. Our beloved 9 mercenaries have been ingrained into pop culture to the point where it feels wrong without them, and they are loaded with more personality than anything any AAA studio of this day can push out. And this couldn't have been possible without years of trial and error from a team that genuinely cared about delivering the best possible experience. And I think they damn well succeeded - overall, TF2 has earned its place as one of the greatest games of all time, and it's easy to see why so many people fell in love with it, myself included.

But, if I love the game so much, why am I leaving a negative review? Well, notice how I said, "in its base form" earlier. That's because it has strayed very far from it. And I'll admit, I do want to give it that big blue thumbs-up... but I can't. It would be a crying shame to do so. Becuase TF2 might be the most mistreated game in history.

Once the old dev team got booted out or moved to other projects, Valve started to use the game as a testing ground for predatory monetisation schemes. They did make content themselves, but over time relied more and more on the community to do the work for them - and the paychecks offered for doing so led to not-great things happening (I'll get to that).
Cosmetics, fancy effects, weapon skins, kill trackers: all paid-for items. TF2 became seen as a money printer to Valve and nothing more - especially after becoming free-to-play, even if it introduced so many more players to the battlefield (like me). As a wise zesty man once said, "If you have a successful casino, why charge a fee for entry?"

Valve's lazy, half-baked attempt at turning TF2 into an esport led to the replacement of the high-speed, hassle-free Quickplay system with the fundamentally-flawed Casual Matchmaking system still used today. Unbalanced teams, one-sided steamrolls, increased downtime between map changes, ridiculously long queue times and more all stem from this horrible excuse for a matchmaker. Another major issue is the content we've gotten in recent years - and who's been making them.
Ever since Valve stopped making items for the game, a small, closed-off group of workshoppers have been largely responsible for the items included in the seasonal updates TF2 still gets. And when I say "largely", I mean an OVERWHELMING majority. This is because Valve likes to pick items from specific creators because they know it won't crash the game. And the TF2 Emporium knows this - they're behind the piles of unbalanced/gimmicky maps and ugly cosmetics we've gotten since MYM (Smissmas 2020 be damned forever), almost as if they're trying to turn the game into a completely different one.

Store and Casual map pool, with absolute garbage barely befitting of TF2 - and all for stuffing their pockets a little bit more. The love of money is indeed the root of all evil.

And I won't even mention the ultra-toxic, gambling-addicted, rewards-obsessed culture of Mann vs. Machine, which is why I'll happily stay away from Mann Up and stick to Boot Camp. I'd much rather focus on blasting some robots than getting a golden gun for doing so.

I will forever love this game, but it has been fucked over so many times by the developers and community... and that is depressing to think about. There isn't much I can do about it, but the least I can do is share my frustrations, and not give the blue thumbs-up.

It’s a free-to-play, team-based shooter, but calling it “just” that doesn’t really do it justice. This game oozes style and sarcasm, with a dash of that old-school, Saturday-morning-cartoon vibe. If you haven’t heard of it by now, congrats on waking from your coma.

The whole thing boils down to two squads (RED and BLU) duking it out in modes like Capture the Flag, Payload (push the dang cart, people!), and King of the Hill. You’ve got nine classes to pick from, and they’re all their own brand of chaos. Wanna go full Rambo with rockets as the Soldier? Go for it. Or maybe you’re in the mood to cosplay as a French jerk and backstab everyone as the Spy. There’s even the Heavy, who’s basically a human tank with a minigun and a sandwich obsession. Teamwork is king here, even if your team is mostly yelling at you to “get on the point.”

Visually, TF2 is basically the Pixar of shooters. The cartoon graphics never really age, and those goofy voice lines? Chef’s kiss. Even the hats are legendary, seriously, people will spend real money on headwear for their digital dudes. And the game lets you deck out your characters with all kinds of wacky cosmetics and weapon skins. Most of it’s just for laughs, but hey, sometimes you need a flaming hat to feel alive.

And the community? Still kicking. Mods, custom maps, endless memes, TF2’s player base is like the internet’s fun uncle who refuses to quit. [{"review_text": "220 hours in (most of which were probably spent theorycrafting, building my castle or farming), I've finished everything the game has to offer to a solo player on normal difficulty. I took my time and loved every minute. I've known about the devs since their Battlerite days, and V Rising feels like a spiritual successor to its combat system, with a few caveats after recent updates (nerfed player mobility, bosses still doing parkour).

I dove headfirst without any prior knowledge and pretended it was 2005; no wiki, guides, reviews or speedrunning. It was great as a mainstay game for the duration. More below:

[hr][/hr]
[h2]1. Pros:[/h2]

🟢 One of the most intuitive and hassle-free crafting/building systems I've interacted with. Rooftop generation is automated after you enclose a room. The only downsides are that a) you can only rotate everything 90 degrees, and b) snapping cannot be toggled off. Placement requirements are sensical and balanced in terms of costs. Castle architecture is where the real end-game is at, so the possibilities are aplenty.

🟢 The power fantasy is gradual and done right. You start off as a scrawny vampire fledgling, and you slowly move up to defeating Dracula himself. The layers of complexity that come with progression are served to you with a piecemeal approach, and you have complete freedom over how slow or fast you go. There are a few main quests that serve as railguards and guide you throughout the entire run, but there is no hand-holding involved; you awaken into a world with a mind of its own and are forced to thrive or die. 

🟢 You can freely change between different playstyles (melee, ranged, caster) on the go by equipping different item sets and ability jewels; nothing is set in stone, so you don't spec into one niche at the beginning of the game and then stay pigeonholed forever after. 

🟢 Skills and tooltips have an accessible level of complexity; there are no hidden interactions or shenanigans. What you see is all there is. 

🟢 No P2W. Microtransactions are purely cosmetical. 

🟢 The soundtrack. It's available on most streaming platforms under the artist Migova. You also have a pretty little music box as a prop for your castle, unlocking more music as you progress. You can exclude tracks from the rotation if you'd rather not listen to combat music while idling. "Dawn Comes" is a standout. The sound design overall is memorable as well.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]2. Mixed bag:[/h2]

🟡 Gear, skill and playstyle diversity is insufficiently encouraged. I soldiered my way through with nothing but my bow, shortsword/claws, and the same spells on repeat (veil of storm, bloodrage, sanguine coil, crimson beam), with very few exceptions. If you're the lazier armchair gamer type, this is great news, but brutal difficulty is a different story. Overall, V Rising is ultimately a skill-based arena brawler type of game wherein combat is the only solution; you can't play economic wars or take the non-lethal route. 

🟡 Some boss encounters can be exasperating (Simon and Megara especially). If you're into souls-like fights, rejoice. For the more casual players like myself though, this resulted in frustration. This is especially true as their AI has a tendency to anticipate your skillshots and dodge as soon as you cast. On the other hand, summoning minions tends to mess with their aggro meter, so you can cheese them to an extent. 

🟡 Most server settings can be tweaked via rulesets you can customize yourself or import predefined ones. However, they are set in stone once you start the playthrough; other than the difficulty, you can't modify them later (at least not in-game; you can alter the JSON file though). For PvP this is great, as it ensures a more consistent experience for everyone; for solo PvE players it can feel restricting, especially if it's your first time playing. Most of the jargon from the rulesets only makes sense after you have already invested a few hours into the game, so it'd be best to stick to vanilla settings if you're soloing PvE and have no clue what the parameters mean. 

🟡 Every once in a while you will run into stacked encounters that are pure chaos. You're following the blood trail of a boss, but you get ganked halfway through; then, your initial target somehow finds you instead, multiple bosses summon adds, the sun rises, the environment provides no shade, you run out of potions or defensive cooldowns, so you end up getting sandwiched on every possible front. This is not a frequent occurrence, but it does tend to happen with roaming bosses like Vincent, Jade, Jakhira or Bane. It can be fun if you enjoy surprises; I acknowledge the potential for entropy to keep things fresh, as the majority of bosses are in set locations, but this just wasn't for me.  

🟡 Rift incursions are the only recurrent event. V Rising doesn't try to be an MMO, but I would've liked to have more side-content other than fishing, building or min-maxxing servants and prisoner blood quality. There's not much else to do after you defeat Dracula as a solo player; you either give brutal a try, or join a PvP server. The game doesn't branch out in any other direction; it is built from the ground up to culminate with you killing the immortal king, or being the top dog if playing PvP.

🟡 This is a Unity game. Don't expect it to have a visual style like that of No Rest for the Wicked or Pathfinder WOTR. It sits somewhere between Original Sin 2 and Magicka 2 in terms of graphics and geometry, and it has a mild voxel flavor. Serviceable, but not outstanding. 

🟡 Steam achievements are there (49 in total), but there's definitely room for more.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]3. Cons:[/h2]

🔴 [b]The damage you take from sun exposure[/b] is one the most consistently punishing mechanics, even with sun resistance potions or blood key amulets. ✅ Massive Open World – Explore diverse biomes and encounter a variety of creatures and settlements.

✅ Incredibly Fun Multiplayer with Friends – Team up to take on challenges and build together for a more engaging experience.

✅ Difficulty Options and Customisable World Settings – Adjust resource yields, crafting speeds, and other settings to tailor gameplay.

✅ Great Music (Mostly) – The soundtrack fits the gothic tone well, though some boss themes repeat.

✅ Smooth Performance on High-End Machines – No bugs or performance issues encountered during play.

✅ Gear and Spells Encourage Many Playstyles – Plenty of options for tailoring your combat and survival strategies.

✅ Great DLC for Builders – Adds more building options and features, especially enjoyable if you love castle construction.

[b][u]The Downsides:[/u][/b]

❌ Repetitive Boss Music – Many bosses share similar music tracks, which can get monotonous over time.

❌ Early Movement Feels Slow – Movement speed can be sluggish at the start before unlocking more abilities.

❌ Forced Building Snap Can Be Frustrating – Snapping mechanics sometimes make precise placement difficult.

❌ Mostly Top-Down Isometric Camera – You can angle it slightly, but it doesn’t offer full third-person or over-the-shoulder views, which might not appeal to everyone.

❌ Very Small and Unofficial Modding Community – Few up-to-date mods exist, and there is no official mod support.

❌ Limited Replayability After Completion – Once the main content is done, replay mainly involves starting a new save on a different difficulty.

[b][u]Final Verdict[/u][/b]

V Rising is a richly atmospheric vampire survival game that offers a compelling mix of crafting, exploration, and combat. Its stylish visuals and fluid gameplay make it a joy to play, especially with friends. While it has a few minor frustrations like repetitive music and building snap issues, the solid performance and depth of systems provide hours of satisfying play. The DLC enhances the experience for builders, but even without it, V Rising is well worth your time.

⭐ Highly Recommended for fans of survival games, gothic fantasy, and castle building! ⭐", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1754812401}]

I consider myself a staunch defender of Age of Empires IV. In fact, I think it is one of the finest RTS games ever made, and it deserves far more recognition than it gets. For me, this is not just another installment in the series, this is the perfect spiritual successor to Age of Empires II, built with modern design principles and an incredible attention to detail.

AoE4 takes the core magic of AoE2 and turns the depth dial up to eleven. Every single civilization is truly unique. Not just slightly different bonuses or tech trees, but entirely different playstyles, mechanics, and strategies. Playing the French feels nothing like playing the Mongols, which feels nothing like playing the Chinese, which feels nothing like playing the Malians. The variety is staggering, and it fundamentally changes how you approach the game depending on your faction.

Even the presentation is outstanding. Civilizations are not only visually distinct, they are culturally alive. Your units speak in their own historical languages, their architecture evolves through the ages in a way that reflects their heritage, and the attention to detail in animations, unit design, and map variety makes the world feel authentic and vibrant. Few RTS games have ever achieved this level of immersion.

The gameplay itself is razor sharp. It keeps the accessibility that makes AoE approachable while adding layers of complexity and asymmetry that reward mastery. This is a game where learning a new civilization feels like learning a whole new game, and that is a rare achievement in the RTS genre.

If there is one problem, it is not in the game design itself, but in the amount of post-launch content it receives. Compared to Age of Empires II Definitive Edition, which gets new civilizations, campaigns, and maps at an incredible pace, AoE4 feels like it is only receiving a fraction of that love. That is a shame, because if the developers poured the same amount of attention and expansions into AoE4 as they do with AoE2, I genuinely believe it would become the greatest Age of Empires game ever made, no contest.

As it stands, it is already a masterpiece in my eyes. It is a game with immense potential, already delivering a fantastic experience, and capable of becoming the definitive RTS of our era if given the support it deserves. I will keep playing it, I will keep recommending it, and I will keep defending it, because AoE4 is not just good, it is the future of the franchise!

I think players newer to the series would prefer this one.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1760512506}, {"review_text": "Fantastic game, can spend hundreds of hours learning the intricacies of different civs. Super competetive, fun campaign, and a good price.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1741629266}, {"review_text": "When I heard about Age of Empires IV (AoEIV) I couldn't wait to play it, since playing all of the previous entries had gave me one of the most memorable experiences I had ever had in gaming. And here is what I have to say:

I love how AoEIV had taken the time and effort to bring us a historically-accurate stories that are tied to the gameplay. I really enjoyed the aesthetic of it; it certainly makes the game so unique with their colors, their sound design and the way you can experience the gameplay and the cinematics. I think this is the part that I love the most.

Each of the civilizations feel unique, although not as unique as in Age of Empires III (AoEIII), in my opinion, with exceptions, naturally. I think it a bit as a combination between Age of empires II (AoEII) and AoEIII, leaning a little bit towards AoEII, which, by the way, is my favorite Age of Empires due to several reasons. The strategies and battles are surely good and I enjoy having different kinds of the same group of units, each with different functions. The walls' mechanics are also a good addition and adds a lot in terms of strategies and siege.

I know for a fact that many of the updates have solved many of the issues that player the player base have experienced by now and I applaud this; it was actually the bugs that led me to abandon the game some time ago, hoping for it to get better after some updates. And it really happened, even releasing a DLC. Reading this DLC's reviews, which I won't buy at least for now, shows me that AoEIV may be in a limbo where instead of taking advantage of what it is, it is just a bit nervous about the steps they need to follow to earn new and old fans of the series.

One of the things I don't like at all is that there's too little focus on the single-player experience. What I loved about AoEII was the different heroes, scenarios and setting of the campaigns, and that is also one of the things that made AoEII so memorable for many people; the amount of content that you could experience on your own was tremendous and adding the multiplayer was just perfect for all types of players. AoEIV is lacking heavily on this side: there's only half the campaigns for each of the civilizations that you can play. This is, you can't have a designed single-player experience focused on each civilization, which I find upsetting. Even more: I believe that releasing a DLC with single-player DLC-civ's campaigns before having the base game civ's ones is unforgivable.

The game really wants to push you into multiplayer, which, of course, is a big part —maybe even the most important part— of these types of game. And even though I understand why this has been done, I think that leaving the single-player experience ins such a small featuring is something that takes too big a hit on the experience.

Finally, I want to say that I played all the campaigns but I was not able to get one of the achievements due to a long-known bug. The game has been out for years by now and I think that having this bug, something so small, still lingering in the game after all the feedback is so embarrassing. 

With that being said, I think that the game is a good one and for the time I played it I had fun. It obviously had a new and good idea of what to do and what it wanted to be, but I think that the execution is a half-baked product that leaves aside a great portion of the players. I think that the game can continue with this fresh appearance and twist on the series, which I think is amazing, but it also has to take into consideration all of the accomplishments made by previous games to be better that the sum of its parts.

Solid game, but it still needs some work.

Microsoft has lost their ways, The Developers do not care about the game or the players", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1750962500}, {"review_text": "I've spent longer thinking about AOE IV than playing AOE IV at this point, mostly in trying to deduce why it is that I'm just not enjoying it despite my heavy involvement in RTS games since they got started. Not only that, but as one of many thousands of players who hold AOE II as their favourite game of all time, I was long looking forward to the next generation after AOE III. And while this is technically is that game, there's more to delivering a sequel than simply incrementing the title's numeral.

In reality, it's now clear that although I was looking for a sequel to AOE III, I was evidently specifically looking for a sequel to AOE III by Ensemble Studios. The more I play IV, the more painfully the reminder that Ensemble is no longer here and that Microsoft, after cannibalising them, continues to try to wear their skin as a hat and capitalise on their good reputation.

There are several things that IV does right, especially in terms of concepts that old Age of Empires manuals hinted as being mechanical goals in future games, such as being able to station archers onto walls and move flawlessly on and off of them through access points which also serve as tower segments. Some innovations from older games have also been carried forward, such as auto scouting and infinite resource generation sources which makes longer games more viable. 

At the same time, there have been some changes which have felt very regressive. It's somewhat reminiscent of Age of Mythology, both in terms that each major civilization (not counting the cheap variants) play and even advance differently. For the same reason, because of this larger set of mechanics and unit types, they don't appear to be as balanced as they could be. The user interface is also less intuitive and user-friendly than previous instalments, especially when there's such a strong push for a specific style and condensed colour scheme. 

For example: it's pretty impossible to look at the map selection at a glance and tell what's going on. There's black, blue, and gold; the black tends to be land and blue tends to be water, but determining what's going on in the gold pictographs requires some visual scrutiny to interpret, whereas the previous games straight up had close to model mini-maps with full colour, making it instantly clear what was land, resource, cliff and sea.

The building and unit style also somewhat bothers me. Although it's not totally out of character from the 3d models of AOM, this game which was released nineteen years later has an almost Disney-Pixar cartoon-like element that seems to cheapen the atmosphere. Likewise, the campaigns which used to be narrative character-based roleplays are now done from an American History Channel and or BBC infotainment style that both expects their audience to have no attention span or general education, while simultaneously speaking with a delivery that suggests they believe their every sentence will drop your jaw to the floor in wonder.

Ultimately the bottom line is that it doesn't feel fun or engaging to play. I can point to specific things I didn't care for and things that I don't feel measure up to the previous games like I have above, yet I don't think those properly capture why I don't have a good time with this and why even victories don't feel rewarding. [{"review_text": "One of the best sim racing experiences you can get, even years later.

Assetto Corsa might be getting old, but it’s aged like fine wine - especially once you dive into the modding scene. The base game alone is solid but a bit barebones by today’s standards. The real magic happens once you install Content Manager and Custom Shaders Patch (CSP). Those two completely transform the game -better lighting, weather, physics tweaks, smoother performance, and tons of quality-of-life features. It honestly feels like a new title after that.

Then you’ve got the mods - cars, tracks, visuals, sound packs, everything you can imagine. The community support is insane, and there’s something for every kind of driver, from casual track day enthusiasts to full-on sim racers. You can go from drifting in Japan to racing GT3s at Spa, or even just cruising through city maps at sunset.

If you’re playing on a controller, don’t worry - there are some amazing Gamepad FX scripts that completely change how Assetto Corsa feels without a wheel.

For grip racing, there’s Advanced Gamepad Assist, which smooths out steering, reduces twitchiness, and gives you way more precision when braking and cornering. It makes racing with a controller feel natural and consistent.

For drifting, there’s a different script called A7 Assist, designed specifically for smoother countersteering. It makes it much easier to catch slides and hold long drifts without the car snapping or feeling unpredictable.

Both are absolute game-changers depending on your driving style.

Performance-wise, it runs great on most modern PCs, and the visuals can look stunning once you tune everything with CSP and a good graphics preset (would definitely check out Pure if I were you)

All in all, Assetto Corsa is one of those games that grows with you - the deeper you go, the better it gets. It’s not perfect out of the box, but with the right setup, it’s easily one of the best and most flexible sim racing platforms ever made.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1762949551}, {"review_text": "---{ Graphics }---

[b]P.P.S. Supergiant has reworked the ending from its previous four-car pileup to a more gentle, screaming six-g U-turn. While I don't think the gist of the review is invalidated, it'll probably not reflect the views of a new player. I leave it as an important historical document.[/b]

Overall the game is good, fun and accessible. Supergiant can still deal out a mean action game, and it's still beyond its peers regarding art and sound direction. [i]ok time to nit piiiiiick[/i]

So, mechanics-wise: more moves than original Hades, to the point it gets a little complicated to use your whole arsenal effectively and you'll likely favor two or three moves on each play -- and that's probably how it was intended. The boons and other gifts are a bit over-balanced: a lot of boons amount to the same flat damage bonus to a different move or set of moves, maybe with a little condiment on top.

Funny that it does a Silksong and innovates the gameplay loop by adding a mechanic that's over a decade old and maybe two decades old by this point (quests in silksong and crafting recipes here)

Story-wise: Hades 2 tries to be the inverse of Hades 1. Instead of a cynical layabout, the protagonist is a naïve child soldier. The "home base" is not a house, but a refugee camp. The problem is situational, instead of structural, which makes Melinoe an agent of the status quo instead of a revolutionary. And while Hades was a tormented figure who hid his issues with a broken system behind a duty to the same broken system, Chronos is a scenery-chewing deposed king, whose internal conflict amounts to whether to kill the gods or enslave humanity first.

So this is the anti-Hades I. But the story of Hades I was not just a story of gods; it was carefully tailored to the roguelike genre. You have permadeath, you have a story that carries across loops, you need a way to make the gameplay loop continue after the cutscene, and it all needs to be within budget. That means you can't ever shake the story up enough that gameplay would be altered.

This works in Hades I, whose moral is more or less "a system that incorporates rebellion can remain functional and even improve itself". This does [i]not[/i] work in Hades II. There is no way to end the story and keep it aligned to the roguelike loop without descending into farce. And that's exactly what Hades II does.

Hades 1 was a demonstration of how far you could push storytelling in a roguelike: Hades 2 may be a demonstration of its limits.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1759064315}, {"review_text": "i take it all back. this game is a masterpiece the likes of which i have never experienced. i played early in early access, and i was hasty.
