I love it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 44, "timestamp_created": 1762367221}, {"review_text": "This game seemed like it would be made for me. I grew up playing diner dash and the sims and as an adult my favorite social hobby is d&d. Somehow, Greenheart Games has managed to create the perfect game (for me). It has a little bit of everything:
-As a tavern keeper, you can hire, fire, manage, and schedule your own staff. Every hospitality job I have had, I ended up being in charge of the schedule because I'm good at it and I enjoy it. I get to micromanage these silly little workers to no end. Employees have skill bars for the four positions they can hold at the tavern and they all have little quirks that make managing them slightly more difficult or that make them somewhat more useful at one position or another. Some only like to work at night. Some are slow. Some are famous chefs. Anyway, if you like to micromanage and over-schedule your life, or if you own an expensive Office Depot planner, you should buy and play this game just for that feature.
-You get to design your own menu (literally make your own recipes) and buy your own stock. All of the alcohol have hilarious names (my favorite is mudweiser) and various benefits/flavor profiles.
-You get to build the rooms and set them up. Most of the taverns come with a couple of things to get you started, but everything is movable and removable. There's a ton of options of things to purchase to decorate your tavern and even a custom design option. I was never much of a design shark, so I haven't played around much with that feature, but you do earn satisfaction points based on decor so if that's your thing you can go wild. The rooms also have their own individual settings, so different rooms in your tavern can literally have different operating hours.
-There are clear checklists that are paced very well. Some of my favorite games suck at having checklists that help you feel like you're progressing a story--this game does not do that. Instead, each location for a tavern has its own story to progress and you feel like a meaningful member of the local community. Plus, you make some great friends along the way.
-The little storybooks help you feel like you have even more autonomy, especially in progressing those stories. They have wholesome responses and f**k you responses and everything in between. 
I know I have to be forgetting plenty of features that bring me so much joy in this game, but I've lost so much sleep since this game came out 48 hours ago that if I don't stop myself now I will keep typing forever (plus, I want to go back to playing!). I had a countdown to when it would release, and boy it didn't disappoint. This game would earn the perfect game achievement in Game Dev Tycoon because they mastered their genre/topic/audience/platform combo like no one else this year. 10/10, I can't wait for a sequel :)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1762402016}, {"review_text": "Absolutely cozy, casual tavern RPG. I've been playing Greenheart's first game -- Game Dev Tycoon -- since it released in 2013 and could not wait for their next title. Now that it's out, neither my spouse or I have been able to put it down.

The most important thing to me about this game is the dev response and communication. They have been releasing several patches per day since release. They respond to their Discord messages as tickets directly to your email with a quick update about when they expect it to be fixed. For example, I had an issue completing a quest and simply asked a question about it in Greenheart's Discord channel. Within 24 hours I had an email from them telling me it would be updated, and within 48 hours of the original Discord message, it was fixed.

GHG has a roadmap with plenty of new content for 2026 and I can't wait to get my hands on it.

It's cute and complicated enough to keep you engaged but not so complicated you want to tear your hair out. The narration and voice acting are fantastic. I could listen to the soundtrack for hours (especially the Orc rendition of Ode to Joy).

There are only three maps currently, but every time I play one of the maps I wind up learning a ton and restarting so I can run a more efficient and friendly tavern. And the random events are sufficient enough that no new playthrough is precisely the same as the last.

You can tell GHG poured their heart and soul into this game and it shows in every corner of your pub. I'd recommend this game at full price and even moreso during the launch sale.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762619365}, {"review_text": "It's so nice to see this developer again after so many years, Game Dev Tycoon was such a classic title and they've come back strong with their second game. It's a very colorful and amusing romp through a casual management sim, with plenty of room for higher effort optimizing. Reminiscent of the Two Point series in some ways as well.

Admittedly, the price is a little steep for what isn't a terribly deep experience, though a nice launch sale is bringing that down a bit. I have high hopes for the continued development of this game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762235741}, {"review_text": "I enjoy it, but I'm worried that the reviews are so good that the devs will get a bit complacent. I'm not experienced in manager games to explain the faults well, but this game is definitely far from a finished product. I suggest more people give honest criticism for the game so it can be an even more enjoyable experience. 

Needs dozens of quality of life updates, worker ai/pathing is questionable at best, information is poorly explained...I often have no idea when something is going to catch on fire or why, I'm sure I'm doing something wrong but the info for why is normally convoluted. The map layouts need some work, they are unnecessarily wonky and cramped, making it hard to even utilize the hundreds of decorations you give us that the player often won't give a shit about. LESS DECORATIONS, OR MAKE THE MENU FOR IT MUCH BETTER. THERE IS TOO MANY AND THE VALUE OF THEM IS NEGLIGIBLE. GIVE US MORE THINGS THAT CHANGE HOW THE MAP INTERACTS OR IMPROVE DECORATION SYSTEM. This is a glaring flaw that will need to be addressed, it's bloating and I think less is more would be VERY good here.

I could sit here and name a bunch of other issues that may or may not just me being bad problem, but they stick out. 

With that being said, game is super fun. I just love the coziness and art style. I want this game to reach it's potential though, so I will help and be critical. Cheers guys, keep it up.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1762684828}, {"review_text": "With how the comments currently stand, I feel that there should be at least one fly in the ointment - so here's my buzzing on the matter....

Everyone who've said how this game is incredibly cozy & beautiful, how funny it is and how you can see love & attention to even little details are spot on - it's indeed a labour of love for the developers and you can see it everywhere!

HOWEVER, there are certain gameplay elements that make the game unplayable for me personally:

1. First glaring issue is an obvious flawed logic in your employees AI: you'll constantly see how your janitors will be spending 90% of their worktime moving around different parts of the tavern to clear random dirt spots instead of starting out in one place and gradually move throughout the room, or seeing how your chef will be following your hauler outside to get water only to start going back to the kitchen once the hauler got the bucket full, thus wasting precious work time (many other games handle this with reservations of job assignments to avoid such cases). 

2. Next up is the fact that your servers & cooks can't do multitasking, as in the Server cannot be taking more than one order or carrying more than one glass/plate to a Customer, and your Chef can't cook more than one item on a  grill despite it being so goddamn wide. This is neither -- and actually, really, honestly represents a great game in this niche.  Lots of good feels and clearly being made with care.  Older gamers that enjoyed Tycoons and feels that seem lost to time will find stuff to enjoy here; and it's very exciting to see the early hints of what is clearly to come. 

The question at this point really is... can they maintain the Overwhelmingly Positive start that they have shown and proven they can do?  I hope so, and this especially on-sale is a stupid easy purchase to play now and later.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763059201}, {"review_text": "I havent finished the game yet, but!! I have gotten a good way into the story and honestly? This game is super fun. I havent really hit any bugs that I could tell. The game runs well on linux. I am honestly kind of addicted (which is a problem).
Anyway, if anything happens further into the game I'll update my review, but this seriously does not feel like your average early access game

Edit: I have now finished the early access story (which looks to be half the story chapters that will exist by the time full release happens) and omg I had so much fun!! I am going to keep playing in free play mode definitely (and am sadly still addicted).", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762278383}, {"review_text": "i'm on the fence with how i'd like to review this, because it's almost there worthy of a thumbs up.

for me personally the game feels too scripted. slightly too easy on normal mode, and 'the tavern' starts slightly too poor on the difficult setting. 

i have 10 hours in game so far, yet, and i still have no clue whether or not my staff gain XP or not, or if the skills they start with remain the same the entire playthrough. i'd like to see a bit more variety in staff, either more traits, or the ability to "train" skills. the backstories are cute, but are they relevant at all?

i think the tutorial section is well put together and sets you up nicely for Halfington, where juggling all the expenses becomes much more micromanagy. and i've got an itch to min/max the layout and prices to really get my tavern profitable right from the beginning, so the groundwork of an addiction is being laid nicely. but i'm not sure if there's enough content and variety to really sink my teeth into yet.

i love the narrator, and i love the way a lot of the game mechanics blend together. and i think the game has a lot of potential. yet it does seem like something is missing. i know the devs don't want to be compared to stardew, and it's not fair to them. But i want that level of "game" in my cozy town. i want more.. more surprises, more RPG elements 'somehow' - i understand "the tavern" is my playable character, but i want more. 

right now i'm not super happy with the price to content ratio, but i do look forward to changing this review to positive in the future as more content and polish gets added and the price feels more justified.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1762538215}, {"review_text": "On the surface the game looks nice, but inside it feels unimaginative and hollow. The basic loop is quite simple: You make sure there's enough food and drinks to serve, hire people and manage their timetabling, and respond to events every once in a while; when you have money to spare, you expand, but honestly it feels more like an idle game rather than one belonging in the simulation/management genre.

There seems to be a serious lack of options on what I can actually do with what is supposed to be my tavern; Scenarios start to feel quite dull very early on whenever you figure out the newest features; progressing from one tavern to the next certainly refreshes the gameplay, but that excitement does not last for long. I'll try to ramp up the difficulty and see if that solves it, but I don't think this type of game should be dependent on fine tuning settings.

Overall, many of the design elements (starting from the UI) feel more like they were influenced by Sims rather than games in the supposed genre; while this isn't bad in and on itself, it means the game leans more on narrative design. Unfortunately, I think it's done quite poorly. Sure, the narrator has a charming voice, but the actual dialogue and character design are very generic and sometimes outright cheesy. There's a lot of dialogue/narration to go through, but what's actually said there feels more like a student scrolling through a thesaurus in order to hit a specific word count for their essay rather than saying something meaningful. The two exceptions to this are Dorothy and the skeleton employee from the demo, who at least feel like their own personas. And while it isn't a bad thing per se, straight up copypasting The Shire, to me, speaks to lengths about not knowing what type of world you actually want to introduce to us.

UX often pulls you away from the moment. It's unfortunate, and this happened with Frostpunk 2 as well, where you are constantly reminded by the fact that you are actually playing a game rather than allowing you to immerse yourself in a fantasy world.

Perhaps the game reaches its full potential when I've got all the features unlocked, but I would have liked to enjoy the story along the way. At its current state, I do not.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1762440327}, {"review_text": "An early access game that doesn't feel like early access.
- great voice acting
- creative story
- fun game mechanics
- lots of creative design
- Developers constantly push updates to improve the game (+7 updates in the past 24 hours to fix minor bugs or give QoL updates from community feedback)


Other than not having steam workshop for custom items, or ability to make custom maps, i'm very happy with the game so far! 100% worth the price", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762710187}, {"review_text": "Bought the game because of Worth a Buys recommendation and was welcomed with a thank you for buying their last game. These guys deserve all the money unlike AAA slop.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762769273}, {"review_text": "There are two major drawbacks in this game currently.
First: as it's only an early access, only 3 scenarios are available so far. Maybe it's not really a drawback cause...
Second: you login to check your tavern, pass a (game) day or two maybe. PAUSE. Why is it 5 am already????

This game is fantastic (including the fan speed as my laptop is below the mininal requirements)! It's literally filled with humor, I felt like sending each dialogue to my friend cause they are all superb! And cause they somehow manage to have Rimworld vibes (feel free to explore stories, there are no wrong or right answers). 
The style is adobrable. The ability to design our own objects is cool but as it's not what I am good at, I am going to enjoy others templates!
Got few bugs but nothing that could lock me out of the progression. Had to restart last scenario as my tavern ended up burning to hell. But that only added some spices to the fun I got from playing. Thank you!
PS. The amount of small details is crazy, they all add up to a really fun game!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763679311}, {"review_text": "Hmm. This is a tough one. Cause it sure ain't bad. But the more I played the more meh I became on the systems.
And that's the crux of it - I just didn't feel like I wanted to play any more.

Even though the developer is clear on their page about the intents for the game, I am still surprised at how on-rails the experience of the scenarios has felt.

I get that the idea here was to create highly curated scenarios to play through, but the extremely limited options for deciding how to utilize the taverns just about killed my interest. I couldn't bring myself to start the third campaign when I saw the layout. Limitation breeds creativity, I'm a huge proponent of this concept in general - but at the same time this experience has felt pretty much on-rails to the extreme. You WILL pretty much use area X for staff and area Y for the tap room unless you really go out of your way to.

On the flipside, the decoration aspect of the taverns I find a massive disappointment as well.

Most of the options to actually pretty up your tavern are functionally useless and basically free, including massive scaling options and no real collision detection. I remember placing a 400 foot tall rabbit and fox outside a tavern cause wee why not. This is fun for a little bit but runs the risk of being entirely ignorable - and it is. I recall having a similar experience with housing in EverQuest II - once I could scale and rotate and do whatever with any item all incentive to be creative with it left. There's no game behind it, and honestly it's a bit of a pain to constantly scale or anchor things that you do want. I'll give it realism points there cause it's a pain to literally decorate an entire house, and it is here too. The benefit of such a system is that if you DO take the time you can really make some really great designs.

But that's only part of the decoration. The other includes the *actual* decorative pieces the game requires for your tavern stats that do cost money and take up some space. Unfortunately as far as I could tell there doesn't seem to be much beyond them but buy tons of them and spam them around rooms - particularly ones that go on walls that can be overlapped with one another. The extremely limited floor space ended up meaning that I'd end up wanting to resort to whatever is the most efficient, small piece and toss em all over. Perhaps this is not truly the case although it is what I've seen echoed in some posts - spam decorations without any real thought behind them cause it's all just a point counter.

I could go on about the campaigns or the frankly pretty bad AI decision process, but ultimately I think I needed a little more space to feel like I had SOME degree of freedom with these taverns. They're pretty much all laid out for you, and the management systems in place didn't quite do it for me at the moment.

Part of me feels like this game was designed to be played on a speed of 1 especially if the developer states that the campaign takes people around 20-25 hours at present, and that you are expected to micromanage quite a few tasks. If so, the UI for micro managing is pretty clunky and discourages me from really wanting to engage with it much.

I also believe it's a swing and a miss to disallow basements and/or second floors. I understand why the developer says they did it, but with how limited the play space is to begin with I disagree with the decision and do not feel it is at all necessary to always be able to see the entire tavern.

I knew this wasn't going to be a classic Tycoon game (I miss Pizza Tycoon) but I really was hoping for a little more on the layout side of the game. And goodness, I could create scheduled purchase orders back in DOS games, is there really no system for that here or am I just a buffoon?", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1763006521}, {"review_text": "⭐ 9/10

Tavern Keeper is honestly a really cozy, engaging, and well-made tavern sim. The narrator gives the whole thing a kind of Hearthstone vibe, and there’s an actual story with quests that make progress feel meaningful — not just “scale the spreadsheets.” For Early Access, there’s already a solid amount of features working, and I definitely feel like I got my money’s worth.

The AI staff is actually smart for this type of games. You assign rooms, shifts, and roles — and they just work. They’ll get tired, complain, or make mistakes, but they generally behave like you’d expect. You spend your time designing and managing your tavern instead of micromanaging every individual action. It’s refreshing.

The in-game feedback tool is also extremely well done. I had a couple of crashes early on, submitted reports with screenshots, and the devs emailed me back and fixed the issues quickly. That level of communication is rare and deserves respect.

Things that could be improved:
- More QoL tools (hotkeys for map modes, quick hide/show walls, etc.)
- The RPG/dialogue side is still shallow — skill checks exist, but don’t impact much.
- Decorations feel a bit too much, like Parkitect “decorate for the sake of decorating”.
- Late-game gets repetitive with guest planning, musician booking and food managment.

Food management needs smoothing — it’s easy to leave a dish on the menu with no ingredients and forget about it. Fires also occur a bit too often (though it’s configurable).

Overall: Really charming, enjoyable, and clearly made with care. If the team keeps polishing and expanding the QoL + RPG depth, this could turn into something genuinely special.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762627193}, {"review_text": "Just the tutorial section on it's own revealed to me how much effort and heart was put into this game, haven't had this much love for a game in years. The art direction is charming, the gameplay is engaging, the amount of decorative freedom it gives you makes me blush, and there's so much content that if you sold me this as a non-early access game I'd gobble it right up.

Also my favorite character in the game is definitely the swamp delivery boy (not the travelling boat merchant). I WILL obtain it's collectible card and learn it's name.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762258858}, {"review_text": "played for 9 hours straight. genie in the beer bottle kept telling me each hour i should probably take a break. best reverse psychology ever. nah but seriously, game is hooked with fun", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1762479737}, {"review_text": "An Incredible Indie Gem!

This indie game is absolutely amazing, and the developers are constantly rolling out updates and bug fixes — their dedication is truly impressive.

If you’re only picking up one management sim this year, make it this one. You can feel the love, time, and effort poured into every part of it. The devs genuinely care about their community and are clearly striving to make this game the best it can be. It’s easily one of my best purchases this year.

This game deserves to be on Steam’s front page — and I’m confident it’ll get there soon. From the very first moment, you can tell it’s a labor of love: the charming opening cutscene, the engaging tutorial, and the wonderful narrator all set the tone perfectly.

The voice acting is fantastic, the atmosphere is spot-on, and the overall vibe is pure joy. It’s smooth, frustration-free, and overflowing with charm — even when things start to go off the rails.

The art style is unique, the music delightful, and the visuals captivating.

Honestly, it’s hard to rate this game with just a number — it’s something everyone should experience. It’s a game that radiates happiness, and it’s a shame it isn’t more well-known yet. But I’m sure that will change soon.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762875894}, {"review_text": "Greenheart Games has an absolute gem in the making here. The features that are already present have me excited, engaged, and constantly trying to optimize and beautify my tavern. Not to mention the story scenarios are very fun and engaging, and the narrator is absolutely hilarious.

Looking at the roadmap has me EVEN MORE excited, which I didn't think was possible. I absolutely can't wait to see how this game looks when it's at full release, because it's already more than worth the price. Sure, there are some minor QoL changes needed such as more readily accessible sales info, but I have every bit of confidence in Greenheart Games to add everything it needs to shine even brighter.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763760052}, {"review_text": "TLDR: The best Tavern game out there without a doubt, overflowing with attention to detail and passion. 

The campaign so far (3 "levels") has taken me around 20h to beat, it was well written, entertaining and funny the whole way through, and I'm going to start over again immediately, this time making different story choices and trying a different tavern layout for each region. Theres even a bunch of skillchecks and dice rolls involved that you can reroll at the cost of slightly increasing random events (both good and bad) which imo is a very good way of doing things. I even kept most failed rolls just to see what would happen and the outcomes were never something that would prompt me to load the game, despite me being a habitual F5 F9 abuser, which was a pleasant surprise.
And the best part: It's fully voiced, in high quality, from start to finish, including every little random event that happens, with the exception of letters in your mailbox.

The management part of the game lets you micromanage things to a quite detailed degree, playing on normal difficulty its not that necessary though, and there's plenty of difficulty settings to make it as relaxed or demanding as you want. Things to manage start at what and where you order from on the world map, creating your own dishes, reacting to events and surges of patrons, picking staff (with an abundance of unique properties and perks) as well as their time tables, supply chain and price fluctuations, and most importantly maximising satisfaction by tailoring everything to your local audience needs. This also leads me straight to my next point, all of it is integrated very well with the fantasy worldbuilding.

Whether youre serving e.g. Halflings or Orcs makes a big difference in what they like, and where you order on the map has a big impact on delivery times (3h to 2+ days), and express delivery costs extra so planning ahead pays off. Maybe your very popular cheap (and importantly local orcish) beer is out of stock for the next couple of days and now you have to fill that gap with cheap human swill imported from the swamps far away, because its still better than whatever pansy drinks the Halflings enjoy. While it is a pretty vanilla fantasy setting that is going to be immediately familiar to most people, its also made with loving whimsy and fully embraces all the clichés of those familiar fantasy races and tropes. Which brings me to the next point, the world map is made in a beautiful minimalist style and wherever you move your camera the music theme switches seamlessly to the same song but themed to the region youre looking at, so now that cosy little jingle you heard looking at the Halfling part of the map is now being sung by drunk Orcs accompanied by drums. 

The game is absolutely filled to the brim with such polish and details. Almost every UI element is "tactile" and very well animated, to a degree i would have never expected. Creating a meal has all the ingredients being physically tossed into the bowl (or onto a skewer) and cooked as you add stuff, fully animated. Animations of characters are also very detailed, with lots of variations, including seeing people take bites from their food (and the food changing as they do), or people doing funny and slightly over the top flourishes when serving/cooking/eating etc.
The art style is minimalist but good looking, cohesive, and most importantly has good visual clarity when there's a lot going on on the screen. Even the story books through which most of the narration happens has a little living ink drop jump onto the page and form the words, sometimes poking its head out and blinking at you when the page stays open for a while. Each page also comes with a "3D" picture to illustrate the scene, all carefully crafted still images made from the huge amount of in-game assets, which we can also use ourselves.

The game has a very big library of decorations to place, but unlike in other similar games where you put down something from the "table" category on a table, locked to a single slot in the center, here you can place whatever you want wherever you want. But even better than that, there's a very in depth asset editor that lets you completely overwrite the looks of even any functional furniture by cobbling together your own from a myriad of options that all perfectly fit into the games art style, or just make fancy looking furniture to place as decoration. All of it can be easily saved and shared online from within the game.

I really like the "Tavern" genre and this is the best entry so far (by far). Looking at the sheer quality it has already I can't wait to see how this is going to turn out at 1.0", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762793376}, {"review_text": "This is the tavern keeping game I have been looking for. No silly quests that take you away from that. No busy work that isn't part of KEEPING MY TAVERN. I love everything about this game and can't wait for General Release, new content and all the things that may come. No other "Tavern Management" game is better than this one. NONE. But it. Play it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764335785}]

[{"review_text": "Amazing how the people behind this game listen to the community!

I already enjoyed the game when it launched, even though it was obviously flawed in some regards. Over the last 2 years the game received numerous updates, and today I got recommended a video about update 2.0 launching, and it literally fixed EVERY SINGLE FLAW the game had. And even though I already own the game I really respect the game being on a 67% discount for 2 weeks right after the update drops, instead of making people pay the standard price of 60€ for it after upgrading its value this much.

I really hope this game will receive the love it deserves!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 14, "timestamp_created": 1744925479}, {"review_text": "After playing Demon's Souls, all the Dark Souls games, Elden Ring, Mortal Shell, Nioh (1 and 2), Lies of P, and even the goofy charm of Another Crab's Treasure, I finally got around to Lords of the Fallen 2.0 and I reaaaally loved it. I finished the game twice on my xbox series X with regular and adyr ending ng+, yet to finish it here. 

The combat is really polished. It feels a lot better than the original Lords of the Fallen which I also have finished on xbox, You’ve got a dedicated jump button now, which is honestly unnecessary but I think it's something some people asked and that's another point I liked, CI Games proved they listen us, and the many complaints people did at launch. The game also have some of that Elden Ring smoothness, but don’t expect the same level of freedom. And while the lock-on system is definitely improved, it’s still not as buttery as Dark Souls 3. Some weapons hit hard and feel super satisfying, kinda like Mortal Shell’s heavy crunch. I used radiance build in my first run and inferno build in my 2nd run, but I feel inferno is the most powerful one. 

Now the co-op mode share progression, and they’ve got this Friend Pass thing that lets your friends join in even if they don’t own the game. Again, CI GAMES proving they care and listen to us. 

There are two realms—the regular one and this creepy Umbral realm, which gives me goosebumps sometimes. The lamp system that helps with navigation is pretty neat. 

Character customization is better now. It’s not on the same level as Nioh 2, but it's also great. And the visuals are amazing, Unreal Engine 5 makes everything look great, and I love the photo mode and the 3d photos, the gothic vibe and the energy the landscape gives me. 
  
I personally enjoyed Lords of the Fallen 2 just as much as I enjoyed Elden Ring and Dark Souls, you must at least try it, you will not regret If you’re into Soulslike games.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1745140207}, {"review_text": "Absolutely yes !! This game, and the love its devs are constantly putting into it deserves atleast Mostly positive, if not Very positive ratings. There are many worse souls-likes out there with better ratings. This game isn't flawless, but I think the rating is yet to move past the horrible launch this one had, because trust me, the game is well past it. 

The world building and the story are good, the combat takes a minute to get used to (you do get generous i-frames, which was a surprise to me), the level designs are a little confusing, you get lost very easily on some levels, you can parry almost all bosses and mobs, the soulflay technique is amazing, the incorporation of the two worlds concept (umbral and axiom) into the world-building is well done in my opinion, the music is good and bosses are good too, albeit on the easier side for souls-veterans (provided you pick a build, any build, because the game punishes bad levelling). Technically, the performance was really good, no crashes, minor glitches and bugs. NG+ unlocks modifiers to increase difficulties and some major changes to the gameplay as well for those seeking challenge. The one complaint I have is the enemy variety, you'll get used to the mobs very quickly and you'll keep seeing them throughout the game.

Overall, this game is a solid 7.5/10. Give it a try, if in a doubt wait for sales, you might be surprised by how much you like this. Cheers!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1742843413}, {"review_text": "They keep updating and improving the game, deserved purchase.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1744924221}, {"review_text": "I came into this game wary from all the negative reviews and feedback I'd heard since launch, but in it's current state? Man, this game deserves so much more praise. The devs have been consistently updating with player feedback since launch and have really turned this into one of the most visually impressive and technically ambitious offerings in the 'Soulslike' genre. Forget any impressions you may have from launch discussions or from the previous game if you played it. The world is expansive, darkly beautiful and interconnected in a way that hasn't been done since the original Dark Souls. The combat, while admittedly unbalanced (magic and status effects can be hilariously broken with the right gear and stats), is decently paced and rewarding, with a wide variety of weapon types and combinations. If the 'Soulslike' genre is one of your favorites, or if you just enjoy dark fantasy action rpgs, there is SO much to love and appreciate here, and I honestly hope the devs get a chance to take the lessons they learned and create a proper sequel.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1742842620}, {"review_text": "I was hesitant to buy Lords of the Fallen due to the mixed reviews on Steam, but after watching gameplay and feeling the itch for another soulslike after Elden Ring, I decided to give it a shot. Now, after spending time in the game, while there are some things I don’t like, I can confidently say I’m enjoying it and can’t wait to play through the rest. If you’re into soulslikes, I’d say it’s worth checking out.

Performance
The devs have addressed most of the initial issues, and as of January 2025, the game runs smoothly. I’m playing on an old GTX 1650 with low settings and FSR3, and while there are occasional frame drops, I don’t blame the game—my hardware is definitely showing its age.

Combat
The combat is satisfying, with weighty, well-animated attacks and a solid variety of weapons for each class. However, one thing that could be improved is the hyper armor for grand weapons—even a simple arrow can stagger you mid-attack, which can be frustrating. On the bright side, ranged combat is finally viable in a soulslike and doesn’t feel like an afterthought.

Weapons & Armor Variety
There’s plenty of variety when it comes to weapons and armor, and the designs are cool af. And let’s be real—fashion is just as important as stats!

Boss Fights & Mobs
The bosses I’ve faced so far are well-designed, both visually and mechanically, with modest difficulty. Each fight felt unique, requiring different strategies. However, enemy variety in the open world is lacking. The same mobs appear repeatedly, making some areas feel repetitive. The Umbral world, despite its eerie aesthetic, only features about 4-5 enemy types, which is a bit underwhelming.

World & Exploration
The map is huge, and exploring is a joy. The world is eerie yet beautiful, and I’ve caught myself taking screenshots constantly. There are some surprises along the way, and I’ve had a fair share of unexpected deaths. However, one major downside is the Vestige Seed checkpoint system—these are not permanent and have to be purchased at a high cost, which feels unnecessarily restrictive.

Quests & Lore
As expected in a soulslike, quests are cryptic, and NPC encounters feel completely random. You never really know what’s happening or where you’ll meet an NPC next, which adds to the mystery but can also be frustrating.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1738559858}, {"review_text": "Right, look - this game deserves better than the kicking it's been getting. The devs have actually bothered to fix their mess, which is more than you can say for most studios who just take your money and bugger off to make NFTs or whatever.

The launch? Absolute disaster. Crashed more than my uncle at Christmas dinner. But here's the thing - they've actually fixed it. I know, shocking isn't it? A developer that doesn't just abandon ship when things go tits up. CI Games have been listening, making changes, and generally not treating their customers like idiots. Revolutionary stuff.

The combat's genuinely good now. Feels miles better than the original Lords of the Fallen, which to be fair, wasn't difficult', that game played like you were swinging a cricket bat through treacle. You've got a jump button now, completely pointless, but apparently some people got very upset about not being able to hop about like idiots, so there you go. Happy now?

It's borrowed some smoothness from Elden Ring (because everyone's nicking from FromSoft these days, aren't they?), but don't expect the same freedom to wander off and get murdered by a random tree. Lock-on's better, though still not Dark Souls 3 levels of buttery. Some weapons absolutely crunch when they connect – very satisfying, bit like Mortal Shell if you played that.
I went Inferno build, and honestly, it's absolutely mental. Proper overpowered.

You get surprisingly generous invincibility frames when dodging, which was unexpected. Usually these games want you to suffer more than a vegan at a barbecue, but no, they've been reasonable about it. Takes a minute to adjust, especially if you can parry most things (and you can – bosses, mobs, your nan).

The world-building's solid. Two realms, normal boring one and the Umbral realm, which is properly creepy. Sometimes genuinely unsettling, which is nice. They've woven this lamp navigation system through it all, and the whole Axiom/Umbral concept actually works. The Soulflay technique is brilliant, really adds something fresh to the genre, which is impressive given how many of these games are just copying homework at this point.

Music's good, story's decent, and Unreal Engine 5 makes everything look gorgeous. Proper gothic atmosphere, the kind of visuals that make you want to use photo mode even though you'll never look at those screenshots again. The 3D photos are a nice touch, bit gimmicky, but whatever.

Despite the game’s occasionally striking character and environment design, I [i]wish[/i] I had something genuinely positive to say - but I just can’t.

I understand this game has a rather... specific fanbase. If someone doesn’t enjoy it, they’re often dismissed as being "not good enough" and told to go play something easier. Well then, let my platinum trophies in all souls-likes made by From Software speak for me: I love this genre, and played more than my fair share of other entries in the genre. I know what I’m doing — and precisely because of that, I consider this game a weak entry in the souls-like family.

[b]The dual-realm mechanic[/b] may have sounded promising on paper, but in practice, most of the game takes place in the Umbral realm only. That’s where the bulk of shortcuts, secret paths, and progression are found. The result? The world quickly loses any sense of atmosphere or variety. Every area in Umbral ends up looking the same, and you’re constantly fighting the same five Umbral enemy types. It doesn't matter if you’re in a castle or a swamp - it all blends together.

It becomes especially ridiculous when you, for example, activate a shortcut only visible in Umbral, then immediately find a Emergence Effigy to leave Umbral, only for you to have to switch back into Umbral again just around the next corner to activate the another shortcut. [i]Why?[/i]

[b]Level design[/b] is another problem. Large portions of the game are spent trudging through swamps, caves, mines, and other uninspired environments. After one swamp, you find yourself in a cave, then a mine, then... another cave. It’s repetitive and uninspired. Interesting areas are few and far between.

What’s worse is how confusing and unnecessarily convoluted the level design is. Many paths and tunnels lead nowhere of interest - maybe a hidden item, maybe just a loop. It feels like the developers wanted to avoid linearity at all costs, but their only solution was to throw in endless forks and detours. And of course, you’re stuck doing most of this in Umbral, so you don’t miss yet another obscure hidden path - that, again, often leads nowhere.

[b]Gameplay-wise[/b], the developers seemed to borrow mechanics from every other souls-like, but misunderstood how to implement most of them. For example, they’ve reused the guard regain system from Lies of P - but here, [i]even perfect parries deal damage. Why?[/i] Worse still, parrying doesn’t always stagger enemies on the first try. You often have to parry several times, still taking damage, and even when you finally land a riposte, you barely recover any of the lost health.

So the more you parry, the greater the risk, with very little reward. Meanwhile, if you’re hit by a stray AoE attack - which bosses use constantly - you lose all the health you’ve been trying to recover. If the devs wanted to discourage parrying, mission accomplished. But dodging isn’t reliable either. Especially when a boss overwhelms you with endless attack combos or massive AoEs that you can’t avoid because you often don't have enough stamina. And if you parry... right, you still take damage. That’s just dumb, isn’t it?

Pair that with the fact that you can’t cancel most animations - a basic feature in most modern souls-likes (like cancelling an attack with a dodge roll) - and the game punishes you for any minor timing error. Add in pitiful health scaling with level-ups, and it all feels needlessly punishing in a clunky, outdated way.

It’s as if the developers wanted to make the game "hardcore" by stacking difficulty mechanics on top of each other, without ensuring any of them actually worked together well. And the pacing in this game isn’t even too fast - it's just your character is very sluggish and unresponsive.

As for [b]enemy variety[/b] - it’s simple: there isn’t any. As mentioned, the Umbral realm recycles the same five enemies for most of the game. Add around five more per faction (Radiant and Inferno), and that’s your complete roster. Bosses are the only real highlight - until they get demoted to mini-bosses or regular enemies later. Sometimes the reuse is laughable. You’ll beat a boss, walk for two minutes, and suddenly be fighting the same boss again, now as a basic mob. And when it happens for the tenth time, it’s hard to feel anything but exhaustion.

And finally, a few words about [b]multiplayer[/b]. It took the developers over two years to add level-based matchmaking. Until then - and I’m not joking - a level 500 invader could drop into the world of a level 15 player who just stepped out of the hub. That alone speaks volumes about the questionable decisions made during development. But hey, at least they (somewhat) fixed the seamless coop! 2 years later.

In the end, this is a faceless souls-like that even happened to copy-paste the style of Mortal Shell in many places, yet fails to leave any lasting impression. The initial release was packed with technical and design issues - poor performance, frequent crashes, clunky movement, overwhelming enemy placement, and some truly frustrating questlines. Performance still isn’t perfect, but it’s far better than it used to be. After lowering reflection and global illumination to medium, I was able to play smoothly - and I haven’t had a single crash in over 66 hours of gameplay.

Co-op guests are unable to upgrade their healing item and lantern, and they cannot get boss gear/weapons.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1745372799}, {"review_text": "Oh boy, this was a hard one to review, but overall, due to the sheer love and effort put into this game for its 2.0 launch, I had to give a thumbs up.
[b]This recommendation comes with some notable caveats though.[/b]

For the record:
- I am an avid Souls-like fan. 
- I haven't played this game prior to the 2.0 release. 
- I was playing in the much welcomed new co-op mode with my partner.
- I am aware that I'll be making the cardinal sin of comparing LotF to Elden Ring/Dark Souls, but I feel the points are justified nonetheless.

We started the game quite impressed with the visuals and sound design. I would have given the game a solid 7 out of 10 right there - which, in my books, is still a game definitely worth playing.

Though, there are some glaring issues that began to creep through the cracks the longer we played.

1. The biggest issue? The weapons. 

See, the multitude of various weapons you will find give an [i]illusion[/i] of variety, but in reality, each weapon of a type will attack the exact same way as any other weapon of that type.
Perhaps I have been spoiled by the massive variety presented in Elden Ring and Dark Souls, but it made finding new weapons extremely uninteresting as, apart from visual appeal and stat scaling, the move-sets are all [b]exactly[/b] the same.
Find a really cool looking short sword? Well, it will essentially operate the same as the one you're currently carrying. The only reason to change is whether the new one matches your stats/attributes more effectively.

I'll expound upon this point shortly, but it ties into point number two.

2. Gear (apart from armour)

Namely rings and pendants. There's very little in the way of variety here. 
Increase Holy defence. Increase Fire defence. Increase Poison Resistance. Increase Str. Increase Vit. Etc. You get the gist.
Essentially, all the basic-type talismans you'd find in Elden Ring are copy and pasted here. Except, none of the interesting ones that can change your build in fun ways.

Now, combining the aforementioned points, this is where I found my biggest source of frustration/boredom with LotF; there really isn't a lot of [b]true[/b] build variety.
Sure, you technically [i]could[/i] play as a pure Str mage, but it won't work out as you hope. It'll just be weak and sub-optimal.
The game almost expects you to use a very select few options of weapons/gear for your chosen attributes/stats. There's no effective way to change this (besides one niche end-game thing - for a single weapon - and not all types).

It was extremely disappointing, as I even had the benefit of having my partner able to drop me unique weapons so that I could dual wield them, but alas, there was really no point. Nothing was unique. No weapon operated any differently from it's genre-specific counterparts.
So, we settled on Great hammers. And whichever one matched our stats.

Note: There [b]are[/b] boss weapons that you get access to, from their remembrances (much like Elden Ring). And while they'll also have the exact same move-sets, [i]some[/i] of them have a ridiculously convoluted way of giving them a [i]slightly[/i] different attack. But I ask you, wouldn't it have just been better to have these moves operate differently from the outset? Otherwise, they simply aren't worth the time. We didn't even bother.
Which brings me to point number 3.

3. Boss rewards (especially from remembrances) 

...Pretty much useless, unless they had a specific spell you needed, or a specific armour set you thought looked cool. But mostly, you'll overlook the boss rewards as there isn't a lot worth taking.

4. Input reading

Some bosses and enemies have some of the most egregious input reading examples I have seen in a souls-like game.
I don't simply mean "They dodged two of my arrows", I mean "They are literally dodging, back-to-back, both my partner and I spamming ranged attacks."
It was literally that bad at times.

5. Over-use of branching paths

I appreciate, and quite enjoy the thoughtful and creative use of branching paths that create an intertwined world. Dark Souls 1 did this very well.
But LotF has an absolute metric f**k tonne of moments where you are given a choice of 'Left or right'. Then, when taking a path, there's another 'left or right' and so on.
Now, I can't quite articulate why, but it wasn't creating a sense of fun exploration for us. It was creating no small amount of tedium. Perhaps because we knew that any reward we found would be lacklustre anyway?
Either way, at around 80% completion of the game, we eventually just decided to ignore most branching paths just to streamline game-play.
And as a minor ancillary point to this, the game gives very poor direction as to what you're expected to do to proceed the story. NPC quests are constantly expecting you to randomly backtrack to random (and unintuitive) places, to proceed their arc. This aspect simply wasn't planned very well.

6. Exploration (for loot) is disincentivised.

Once you have your build organised, which can be sorted out quite early on once you realise weapons are all functionally identical, there really is no reason to explore for cool items and weapons. You simply wont find some cool sword that makes your character do amazing things.
And the best spells are easily purchased. You're better off just sticking to the path that gets you through the story.

7. Bugs and Glitches

Throughout our playtime, we probably had to restart the game around 4 times due to glitching through the floor and being stuck. It wasn't a huge inconvenience, but it was still frustrating when it happened.

Now, all that being said, LotF does do some things well. Credit where it's due.

- The story isn't bad. It's not [i]outstanding[/i] but it's serviceable.

- LotF is also one of the very few souls-like games that does ranged combat well. In fact, it makes it a viable option as a main strategy (if you build it right, and manage to have a backup for the worst input-reading offenders). The ranged system works similarly to the way magic works - but they simply substitute mana for ammunition, and mana stones for ammunition pouches. It's simple, but effective.

- The 'Shadow realm' gimmick is interesting. It can be annoying at times, sure, but it's an interesting approach.

- Co-op works very well.

- As mentioned above, the visuals are genuinely very nice.


Overall, by the end of our play-through, we became quite tired of a game that began to feel like a chore. So much so that we ended up putting the game aside, indefinitely - not even wanting to finish. And I found myself thinking "I think I'd much rather just play Elden Ring with a co-op mod. It'll feel more fulfilling."
And that just sucks, because I had some high hopes for LotF at the start.

As of now, I don't know what I'd score LotF. Definitely not a 7 out of 10, as I found too many frustrations by the end. However, I can also see that the game deserves to be rewarded for the dev's willingness to improve upon the game with the 2.0 release.
So that being said, I guess I don't have a final score. I wish I could enjoy it because the actual game part is brilliant. It quite the first of its kind, but it definitely defined and popularized it, and it's easy to see why. They took the fun of hero characters in RTS games, amplified it tenfold, and then built a whole game around it. Every match you have a lot of decisions to make that vary drastically based on the state of the game, team compositions, economy, individual player builds and playstyles, etc. Even the characters themselves are so diverse, and I think this is the biggest leg up it has over the competition. Gameplay itself can shift so much from character to character that it's almost understandable why some sickos pick one flavor and the eat nothing but that for thousands of hours.

It's also an almost paradoxical game where both hero and system overall enable a great amount of skill expression, yet proper teamwork and coordination are still important to an extent that you rarely actually see in team based multiplayer games. It's also one game where "nobody is broken when everyone is" really does feel accurate. In the right hands and with the right items, pretty much every character can do things that will make you think "well, that's some bull****," yet there is often a powerful counter to it, a way to play around it, or something equally bull that every other character can pull off. Dota 2 *feels* loose in every element of its design, yet when you look closer at any of those elements, you start seeing thin but unbreakable connection that weave the fabric that Dota is made of.

Even in terms of visuals and storytelling I like more about it than I would expect from a MOBA. There's a lot of lore to explore, and while much of it is lacking, and Valve is sort of just sitting on it, it feels like whoever is responsible for putting it all together still cares deeply about the universe that this game is set it, and Crownfall is hopefully first of many examples of what can be done with it. 

The only caveat here is that Valve also has some of the soulless, greediest monetization practices, and very low standards for maintaining the visual integrity of the games they created. All the fine craftsmanship that was put into creating the art style of TF2 was smeared with crap once lootbox money started rolling in. CS mostly resisted this, because cosmetics used to be limited to only weapons, but Dota 2 art style also went down the drain. Anything is permitted, and the more offensively tasteless it looks, the more rare and expensive it is. 

The base characters all have their charm in some way. I understand that they aren't to everyone's taste. Many of them lack maybe one or two features that would make them feel like a "main character," which is something that I feel a lot of hero based games chase after. All of them are just a bit too plain or simple to fit that role. You have dozens of dudes in armor of various colors and sizes, but it weirdly appeals to me that no individual character feels too "special" I guess? 

That was all thrown out the moment Valve smelled money. Now you can spend an unreasonable amount of money in order to turn your unremarkable mook into a high level MU Online whale. It's funny because Valve still has those brilliant cosmetics guidelines for people who want to make something, but they haven't cares about what is said there for years. Silhouettes? Who cares. Glance value? Dude, just remember that this pile of pixels is Sniper. The arcanas are especially offensive, because they advertise extra crap as a selling point. Most Dota 2 chars emit zero lights or particles, some sets will give you clouds, glowing gems, arcs of lightning, buzzling flies or orbiting stars, excess is the goal over something coherent or appealing, and the community happily eats it up. Perhaps they don't even care about the look, since all of this is connected to the real money marketplace that enables gambling addicts, whales, and kids who think they can make money by playing their favorite video game.

Anyway, Valve happily enabling gambling aside, one of the main things that makes this game harder to enjoy is the quality of matchmaking and moderation. I have a succesful griefing report for pretty much every single day that I played, and to give you an idea, that doesn't even include a case where we had a willow that stood AFK in the fountain and sent our her courier to die, I guess that didn't count or something. Griefers would be one thing, but there's also so many accounts that are merely days old but obviously aren't remotely new to Dota. If it all it takes to avoid smurf que is to occasionally throw a game, then I'm not sure Valve understands the point of smurf que. Finally even ignoring these two points that already ruin 90% of my matches, the game loves to put new and old players together. I don't care if MMR is similar, a Zeus with 12k wins will be stronger than (non-smurfing) Zeus qith 20 games under their belt, it makes no sense to not take player count into account.

Maybe ranked would've resolved some of my woes, but you need 100 in-game hours to even gain access to that. It took me well over 150 matches to get to that point. I'm not sure if Dota players understand this, but the point of ranked isn't just to stroke your ego and to achieve the highest number/icon possible. It's there to enable fair matches between equally matched opponents. If someone is new and bad, they will be put up against other new and bad players, that's good.

"But it keeps smurfs out" please reconsider even attempting to think that this makes sense. More dedicated smurfs are buying accounts and paying boosters to get whatever they want, Valve is exceptionally bad at handling that too. More stingy ones are then thrown into unranked with players who could've been playing ranked, and I'm not sure too many of them are willing to endure low quality matches for 100 hours before they are allowed to experience something more tolerable. It's really a shame. I'm glad that the resident returned from action/shooter to horror.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1741050055}, {"review_text": "Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is the jolt of adrenaline the franchise desperately needed. After a few action-heavy missteps, Capcom takes a bold pivot back to its horror roots—and it’s nothing short of brilliant.

Trading in global bioterrorism for claustrophobic dread, the game places you in the shoes of Ethan Winters, an everyman searching for his missing wife. His journey leads him to the decaying estate of the Baker family, deep in the Louisiana bayou, where something has gone horribly, unnaturally wrong. From the first creaking door to the final grotesque showdown, RE7 immerses you in an atmosphere dripping with menace.

The biggest change is the shift to first-person perspective. It's a gamble that pays off. Every hallway becomes a tunnel of anxiety, every sound a potential threat. The intimacy of the view heightens the horror—when Jack Baker bursts through a wall with a shovel, you don’t just see it. You feel it.

What sets Biohazard apart is its pacing. It knows when to dial up the terror and when to give you a moment to breathe. The puzzles are satisfyingly old-school, and the resource management is classic survival horror—limited ammo, tight inventory, and tense decision-making.

The Bakers themselves are unforgettable antagonists: grotesque, charismatic, and terrifying. They’re not just monsters; they’re characters. Each member of the family offers a distinct brand of horror—from Jack’s relentless pursuit to Marguerite’s insect-infested madness.

Graphically, the game is stunning in a disgusting sort of way. The RE Engine delivers uncanny realism, from mold-caked walls to glistening entrails. Sound design, too, deserves praise—groans, whispers, and footsteps constantly gnaw at your nerves.

If there’s a drawback, it’s in the final act, where the narrative takes a more conventional turn, slightly pulling you out of the suffocating tension that defined the earlier hours. Still, it's a minor blemish on an otherwise masterful experience.

Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is a triumphant resurrection of the series’ core identity. It’s brutal, unnerving, and deeply atmospheric—everything survival horror fans crave. Not just a great Resident Evil game, but one of the best horror titles of the last decade.

It has really good jumpscares, amazing graphics and the story is very interesting. 9.5/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1750111719}, {"review_text": "Resident Evil 7 went back to its roots with it being a survival-horror adventure - full of exploration and item hunting - compared to its early predecessors. The atmosphere was extremely frightening, eerie and hair-raising and kept me on the edge of my seat throughout the entire game. It takes place on the mysterious Dulvey plantation, in which Ethan desperately searches for his missing wife, Mia, after being summoned by a cryptic email by her. Compared to the cold, medieval interior of the Spencer mansion, which felt like a huge maze, the household of the Baker family feels like home, in which a normal middle class family could live in, which is a great change of scenery of something this series has never fully explored before.

Something this game has really failed are the far-to-simple and rare puzzles the players have to solve in order to progress further. Instead of resorting to have to find codes and passwords hidden in certain notes spread across the map or written on the side of various safes, the only thing you need to do is to find a certain item (which you only have to do once, as you don't have to pick up anything else the following times) and line it up to a certain form on a painting and press the "ok" button. That's already it. Not much exploring to do, which would immerse you even more in this game, no you just have to spin a weird looking object and align it with something shown on a painting and that's it. That's a huge shame. Proper exploring and thus discovering more about the history of the respective places, as in the predecessors or in the Last of Us games would've been million times more interesting and better.

Onto the good stuff: The Baker family, in whose home Ethan wake up in after being abducted by Jack Baker, are the first enemies you encounter and are, by a mile, the most interesting ones. The first fight with Jack forces you to have to make quick decisions in regards to whether you make use of your handgun with its limited ammo or find another way to fend him off. If you actually unload your gun on him, this will come back to haunt you. It was also a really threat and reminded you that you're not safe, even if you think you are. At one point, he burst through a wall just like Mr.X in RE 2.

RE 7 has no hiding or heavily stealth-focused gameplay, contrary to what its first-person horror style might lead one to believe. You need to shoot your enemies to kill or else they'll continue to road around the area, until they get the opportunity to unalive you. You can't really rely on the safety of load screen doors to keep your opponents out. Instead, you better not forget to close the doors behind you. All of which massively increases the tension, especially when your on low health or low ammo.

While the Bakers are the best enemies, the only other prominent and worth-to-be-remembered baddie are the hulking, oil-black creatures called the Molded. They come in a few varieties: The standard Molded; the ones with a giant, warped arm reminiscent of classic tyrant designs, ones that crawl around; ones who vomit acid. Although they're visually quite shocking, they very quickly lose their ability to scare the crap out of one, mainly because the scenarios you encounter them in are so similar (i.e. them tearing themselves out of a wall with a distinctly slimy sound and only in areas overtaken by mounds of black mold). That's the total opposite of the moments, during which you encountered Hunters and Crimson Head in past games.

Micromanagement is still a thing in this game, as in all other RE games obviously. Only this time, conserving your items and managing them was, for some reason, way to easy. Maybe it was the lack of various herbs and herb combinations compared to RE 4, in which you had so many different ones, which might've lead to someone losing his overview of them. Who knows. However, the introduction of psychostimulants, which helped the player in tracking down well-hidden items, was a welcome idea and brought something new to the table.

Thanks to compelling pace that ensured I always knew what to do next. Most of the times wandering hallways, searching rooms for possible useful items and unlocking secret passageways and shortcurts around the Dulvey property was very, very well-spent, especially as the story keep progressing with each file and phone call I received. The objectives are made extremely clear thanks to the great story direction. Albeit to obvious at times, which removed some of the confusion, tension and horror (which is something that makes such a game fantastic in the first place), it's almost impossible to hit a frustrating and time-consuming dead-end, which would take a bit of fun out.

Resident Evil 7 was just another fanastic sequel of this legendary series and the first modern original release of it giving it a new flair after RE 6, which came out in 2012 and was already extremely outdated compared to 2017 games. Admittedly, I absolutely hated it early on, just like the Resident Evil 4 remake, but as the time went on and I progressed further and further, this sequel just grew on me more and more. The whole game feels quality from top to bottom, from the visuals to the audio to the gameplay itself, nothing felt rushed, and it all came together to make a brilliant game that I can't recommend enough", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1752655320}, {"review_text": "A return to form and done right.
No notes on the story at all, it is just right, though maybe it could have used lesser parts of the ship section.
It definitely overstayed its welcome.

The replay value is just amazing. 
Madhouse difficulty is should be a textbook example of how to up the game's difficulty.
They did not just inflate every enemies' HP, they made changes to item placements, made resources even more scarce (this one's a staple in RE's franchise hardest difficulty) and even added more antique coins while also changing their placements.

[spoiler] The encounter with Jack in the garage having you to rush for the lockpick since the car key is locked inside the toolbox [/spoiler] is such a nice, twisted change on the devs' part. I remember being so confused and panicked since I couldn't get the key immediately after the cop cutscene happened. Madhouse was not only challenging, but also makes an already-scary game much more scary. I had to look in between objects just to find 3 handgun bullets while playing this.

I also really love how you're incentivised to hit for headshots, since the molded takes literal tons of bullets if you are not aiming for their head. At the same time, they twitch so much so you really got to take your time while managing your distance so they won't mess you up.

For this entry in the franchise, it involved the live inventory system which basically means if you're getting jumped, you cannot "pause" the game as usual to briefly escape the chaos. This also means that timing your key items usage is vital. I cannot stress this enough, it was so stressful when I was trying to use the hatch key when I was chased by Jack during my Madhouse playthrough. It's so good. That induces fear. I love it.

The DLCs are fine, I really loved Bedroom & Nightmare especially. 
Not really a big fan of Jack's 55th Birthday & 21 though. Especially the latter when I had to sit down for hours trying to pass through Survival+. Luck was not really a big of a factor if you knew what you were doing through the game, but unfortunately it still was a factor. 10/10.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1759075241}, {"review_text": "RE7 impresses with a good story and stylish graphics; the good staging and effects come across well. This game is an outlier in the Resident Evil series, as it deviates from the usual successful formula and focuses more on storytelling and horror. It's not entirely my taste, but I still enjoyed playing through it and had fun.

Unfortunately, some levels towards the end felt recycled, and it felt like they were trying to stretch the time, as you had to go into the same rooms over and over again.

The horror element was played out at every turn, and very well in my opinion. It's very dark at times, the enemies are hungry, and every now and then there's a jump scare in your face, and the disturbing sounds do the rest.

All in all, it's a solid game. I think the majority of players don't have a problem with this title, but they do have a problem with it being called Resident Evil, even though it isn't.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1756763320}, {"review_text": "As a longtime fan of the Resident Evil franchise, I’ve seen it evolve in many directions—some great, others a little more divisive. But Resident Evil 7... this one hit differently. Honestly, this was probably my favorite entry in the newer generation of Resident Evil games. Capcom did an incredible job bringing the horror back to its roots, while still innovating enough to make it feel fresh and terrifying in the best way possible.

The shift to first-person perspective was bold, and at first, I was skeptical—especially since I usually resist new characters being introduced into a series I already love. But Ethan Winters completely won me over. His journey through the Baker estate was absolutely chilling, immersive, and genuinely stressful (in a good way). The atmosphere was claustrophobic, unsettling, and beautifully detailed—from the creaking floorboards to the grotesque yet unforgettable design of the Molded.

What really surprised me, though, was how rich the story was. It never felt like a drag or like filler. Every moment pushed things forward, and the pacing was tight and rewarding. And the villains—my God, the Bakers! Each one felt like a boss out of a twisted nightmare. Jack Baker in particular left a lasting impression. He was menacing, unpredictable, and strangely tragic in the end. They weren't just "bad guys," they were characters—with depth, mystery, and emotional weight.

RE7 felt like a love letter to fans of classic survival horror, while also being accessible enough for newcomers. The blend of old-school tension and modern gameplay mechanics was pitch-perfect. I can’t praise it enough.

10/10. Truly unforgettable. Resident Evil 7 didn't just revive my love for the series—it reminded me why I fell in love with it in the first place.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1748873427}, {"review_text": "THE Resident Evil that revived the entire survival horror series. THE scariest RE game in the entire series. I enjoyed every second of it. 
*I wish they made Marguerite hotter though", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 11, "timestamp_created": 1752071462}, {"review_text": "[h1]Growing Pains[/h1]

Resident Evil 7 marks a return to survival horror after the action-focused RE5 and RE6, but I still think it could have been much better. As the first mainline FPS entry in the series, that shift is obvious from the start. The level and environmental design feels a bit too restrictive for my taste. I get that the game aims to create a claustrophobic, immersive experience by adopting a first-person perspective, but I believe it sacrifices some of the most beloved aspects of the Resident Evil formula.

The puzzles are among the simplest in the series. You never feel the fear of getting lost or find yourself scratching your head over a solution. It's all very straightforward and focused, which isn't necessarily a bad thing but in my view, good survival horror demands more from the player.

On a new save, the game offers just two difficulty options: easy and normal. Games that cap at normal difficulty are often challenging, finely tuned for that magical first playthrough. Unfortunately, I can't say the same for RE7. It quickly becomes too easy to navigate its shallow level and enemy design, and that’s my biggest criticism of the game by far.

Overall, RE7 is a very different experience from the holy trinity of RE2, RE3, and RE4, and not in a particularly good way. Many consider it the scariest entry in the series, but due to its lack of intricacy, challenge, and depth, it didn’t strike me the way those survival horror masterpieces did. For some, the first-person perspective and photorealism are enough to evoke fear, but for me, that effect is a fine line that only a few survival horror games have managed to walk in the last decade.

That said, RE7 is still a good game. Holding it to a high standard may make it seem underwhelming, but it manages to scratch the survival horror itch with passing grades. Maybe they fully realized the new formula with RE Village, and what we see here are just growing pains. I’ll be solving that puzzle very soon.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1749562453}, {"review_text": "This is my first horror game that i’ve played solo (not co-oping with someone), and it has successfully kept me on the edge of my seat every time i load it. After surviving a major encounter early in the game, i thought i could get over my initial fear and start to feel somewhat at ease for the rest of the game, but nope. Every corner of the house is filled with a constant sense of dread, even the safe room doesn’t truly feel secure. The game has a way of keeping you tense through the atmosphere of the Baker family’s home — deafening silence, spreading mold, rotting foods, flickering lights, rattling windows, etc. Overall 10/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1751692917}, {"review_text": "While not as much of a polished action game as 8, RE7 absolutely stomps it in the horror department, and a lot of the comparatively basic gameplay is intentional in that regard.

For example, having a currency not earned by defeating enemies, but be a very finite collectable that can only buy a very small number of upgrades is amazing. Newer RE games, 8 included, will often have SOME way of replenishing a TON of ammo, but 7 is very stingy on higher difficulties and the ammo, or the means to craft it, will always be in the exact same place in the exact same quantity. This is not an oversight, this encourages (or forces on Madhouse) players to play smart with what they have, spend wisely, and avoid enemies instead of attacking all of them. 

Crafting items, using items, even swapping between weapons only being possible while the game is moving similarly is seen by some as some kind of shortsighted thing, but again, it has a purpose. You cannot simply stop in middle of a fight to craft 12 First Aid items and 200 rounds of ammo, you need to be ready at all times. You can still pause for a breather, but only a breather as the pause menu otherwise only has the games' options, a restart button, and a quit button. 

The atmosphere is immaculate, with each leg of the game being scary in its own unique way. 

Even the swap to mold instead of a virus really improves upon old RE. Mold is a product of decay, an inherent part of death, something that spreads disease not only through blood like the various Viruses of RE, but simply through proximity. It changes the environment itself, being a visual warning of "This place is dead and you will be too if you get close". It's inherently disgusting looking, instinctually you will never want to approach mold, while a virus is often invisible aside from its symptoms. 

Though to that end, I feel that is where RE7 falls short most: The connections to old RE. They feel a little shoehorned at times, and before RE8 elaborated (making it a little worse imo) it was as if the connections (heh) to the older games were just coincidence and only there to establish that this entirely new type of game with a new type of threat is indeed still Resident Evil. 

The only other qualm I have with the game is how easy it gets after the first half of the game. Again, not as bad as 8 or the remakes, but once you get the double-barrel shotgun, grenade launcher, and/or 50. cal, the game becomes more of a shooter than a horror experience. The last two chapters, without spoiling much, seem to double down on this intentionally by giving you multiple new powerful weapons and a ton of ammo in a really short period. 

Subsequent playthroughs of course will further this feeling, though thankfully this time around, most of the NG+ stuff is easily avoided simply by... not touching it. RE8 didn't even do that. Most of that sentiment will come from understanding the game itself, from the mechanics to the scares, so it isn't as impactful as when it was new. 

Aside from all that, it is a stellar game. Most of the DLC is really fun (God please give me a multiplayer 21), and if you ever in your life thought RE should be scarier, I would say that this game is better than the rest of the series on that front. Absolutely amazing.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1753645713}, {"review_text": "Resident Evil 7: Biohazard is nothing short of a masterpiece in the survival horror genre, a thrilling return to the roots of the series while introducing new innovations that elevate it to new heights. The game brilliantly dials up the tension, immersing you in its world with its first-person perspective, making every creak of floorboards and distant noise an unnerving experience.

The eerie and grotesque Baker family, the central antagonists, are both terrifying and deeply fascinating, each encounter leaving you breathless. The game brilliantly combines psychological horror with traditional elements of survival, from managing limited resources to solving mind-bending puzzles. What truly sets RE7 apart, however, is its incredible atmosphere—it's a haunting, relentless tension that lingers with you long after you've put down the controller / Keyboard & mouse.

The story, while tied to the Resident Evil lore, also stands on its own with a gripping mystery that keeps you hooked from start to finish. Ethan Winters, our protagonist, is an ordinary man caught in an extraordinary and nightmarish situation, making his journey deeply personal and incredibly engaging.
