"welcome to the family son"", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1738178726}, {"review_text": "Probably one of the best (if not the best) horror game out there. Capcom really does not pull any punches in how disturbing this game is and it results in a horrifically excellent experience that everyone needs to have at least once.

This game has blood, gore, torture and every kind of horror you can think of and i absolutely loved every single minute of it. I honestly dont know if any game (or movie tbh) has ever created a cinematic immersive experience as disturbing and horrific as this game has. Mix that disturbing shock factor with a great story, incredible survival horror gameplay, and some classic fun resident evil puzzles and you got yourself a legendary must-play game not just in the horror genre, but in gaming as a whole.

With all the praise I give this game, I do have a few very minor gripes. The graphics are sometimes a bit rusty, as the anti-aliasing creates blurry edges that render the game to not look very good. This is a bit of a uncommon issue though, as most of the game takes place in small dark eerie hallways and rooms, rendering the flawed graphics a lot less visible. It's also important to note this game came out in 2017, so this is a very reasonable flaw. 

My only other issue is how short this game was. I finished the entire main story + the not a hero DLC and clocked in about 10 hours. That's a bit short and considering how much i enjoyed my time with this game, I really wish it was much longer. There is a 2nd ending to explore, but I shouldn't have to replay the entire story just to view that individual ending (although I will anyway). I appreciate them adding more replay value to the game with another ending though.

Aside from all those nitpicks, i couldn't recommend this game enough. That's coming from someone who doesn't even like horror games that much at all so trust me. It's a horrifically excellent experience that you will not find in any other game. It's a must-play for fans of horror and video games as a whole. And that is why i recommend Resident Evil Biohazard.

It was an interesting experience in which we fight off Venoms in Asmongold's house and solve puzzles inside an old-school RE level design. It has one of the best stories, that you'll see in the intro, as well as the cut-scenes too when playing in Story mode, secret fights, etc. 
Several things I liked about this game is how thorough and clear the instructions are, and that's not just from the tutorial alone. When you're playing against bots, like Invasion or specific Towers you, can always hit escape check your Moves list to see how to do certain attacks. The special move bars on the bottom right of your screen will also show which buttons to click on your keyboard/controller, too if you wanted. This is great - MK games known to have over dozens of attacks and combo moves, so it made learning how to play much easier for me.
The difficulty scaling is also decent, beginner friendly (for players who are now to the fighting genre), and flexible for players of all skill levels and playing preferences. When I want to go for a more casual, easy-going experience I'll just hit up a Tower with the 'Very Easy' difficulty on. PvP is excluded from this condition, since pub matches can connect you to some pretty sweaty players from my experience.
The graphics is where MKX takes the cake, from all it's predecessors. The sharp details of the characters, the environment and event the fataility scenes are all there, and the soundeffects adds even more to the visual experience. The special moves cutscenes, from bone snapping to limb-ripping animations are so realistic and even painful to watch at times. But, what else to expect from a game full of gore? The arenas where we fight are also just as lively, with some places having interactable BG items; like throwing barrels and corpses at your opponent at the Kove, and using a hammer at Quan Chi's Fortress to name a few.
Last but not least, is all the additional features beyond just the combat and fighting matches. You have factions that you can join, achievements where some will help you uncover some interesting moves of certain characters, as well as the ability to customize your own pfp and background! The settings to adjust audio and visuals are nothing short of useful too, if you're playing on older PCs like Win 7. With over 20 base characters, and several DLCs characters; some are cannon, while others are coops like Alien, Jason Voorhees, Bubba, etc. each character has interesting and very distinct voice lines between others depending in who your opponent is. It adds to the plot and lore really.
The devs really went above and beyond designing this game, which made it the star of fighting games during it's time. Heck, even now it's still loved and has an ongoing community. As one of my favourite fighting games, MKX has a special place in my heart and I give it two thumbs up!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1757397843}, {"review_text": "Still one of the Best Mortal Kombat That ever exist. Solid 10/10 game", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1754095236}, {"review_text": "Mortal Kombat X is where the series stopped looking back and fully embraced its future. It’s faster, gorier, and more cinematic than ever—yet still unmistakably Mortal Kombat. NetherRealm Studios took the classic formula and supercharged it with modern graphics, brutal new mechanics, and a fresh roster that bridges generations. Whether you’re in it for the competitive edge or just want to finish off your opponent in the most absurdly violent way possible, MKX delivers.

The biggest evolution here is the variation system. Every character comes with three distinct fighting styles, changing special moves and strategy dramatically. This gives you more to master, more to experiment with, and way more variety in matches. It’s a clever way to keep the roster deep without bloating it.

Combat itself is tight and fast. Movement feels responsive, combos are crisp, and X-Ray moves return for those ultra-violent finishers mid-match that make you cringe in the best way. For casuals, the mechanics are welcoming. For veterans, there’s room to lab, perfect spacing, and build serious skill.

Mortal Kombat X strikes a strong balance between old-school legends like Scorpion, Sub-Zero, Raiden, and newcomers like Cassie Cage, D’Vorah, and Kotal Kahn. The younger generation isn’t just filler—they feel like real, well-designed characters with stories and styles of their own.

DLC characters like Predator, Jason Voorhees, and Alien were wild choices, but they surprisingly fit—and gave the game a ton of crossover appeal.

NetherRealm continues to lead the pack in fighting game storytelling. MKX features a movie-like campaign that tells a surprisingly ambitious narrative about legacy, revenge, and a new world order in the Mortal Kombat universe.

It’s cheesy, over-the-top, and self-aware—but that’s exactly why it works. You’re not just watching cutscenes, you’re fighting through them.

Let’s be clear: Fatalities in MKX are the most gruesome and creative the series has ever seen up to that point. Whether you’re splitting heads with acid or pulling someone’s spine through their mouth, they never fail to shock—and delight. The level of detail is unsettling in the best way.

The graphics are sharp, the environments are interactive, and sound design hits hard (bone-crunching hard). The overall polish shows MK is no longer just about nostalgia—it’s a modern, high-quality fighter.

Towers (classic and “Living”) offer dynamic single-player challenges.

Faction Wars add a layer of global competition, letting you join a team and contribute to a larger online battle.

The Krypt returns as a creepy, unlockable treasure hunt with in-game currency, jump scares, and hidden lore.

Online play, while solid overall, had some early hiccups but became more stable over time.

Mortal Kombat X is a bold, confident step forward for the franchise. It doesn’t forget its roots—it rips them out, sets them on fire, and throws them through a flaming portal. With fluid combat, great character design, an entertaining story, and some of the most jaw-dropping finishers in gaming, this is one of the best entries in MK’s long history.

Whether you're a casual fan who just wants to "Finish Him!" or a competitor ready to climb the ladder, MKX has something for you—just don’t blink, or you might miss your own spine getting ripped out.

It’s got that perfect mix of brutal combat and comic book spectacle, with every punch, kick, and special move landing with an impact that feels as satisfying as it looks. Whether you're throwing down as Superman or taking the fight to Batman, the game keeps the action fast-paced and visually stunning, with each character feeling like they truly belong in the DC universe.

The roster is packed with fan-favorite heroes and villains, and each one feels distinct, with unique moves and playstyles that keep things fresh. The customization system is a huge win, unlocking gear for your characters not only gives them a unique look but also lets you tweak their stats to suit your playstyle. The ability to level up your fighters and modify their abilities adds an interesting layer of strategy to the already solid fighting mechanics.

The combat itself is fluid and fun, with a solid balance between accessibility for newcomers and depth for competitive players. The special moves and environmental interactions are a spectacle to behold, and there's a real sense of satisfaction when you pull off a perfectly timed super move or launch your opponent into a destructible part of the stage. The story mode, while a bit predictable at times, is still an engaging ride that gives you an excuse to see these iconic characters clash in epic battles.

Visually, the game is a knockout, character models look fantastic, and the stages are vibrant and dynamic. The voice acting and sound design bring the characters to life, with each hero and villain feeling true to their comic book and movie counterparts. Online multiplayer is solid, though it can be a bit hit or miss with matchmaking at times, especially if you're jumping into ranked matches.

That said, Injustice™ 2 isn't without its quirks. Building on the foundation of its predecessor, Injustice: Gods Among Us, this game takes everything fans loved and amps it up with refined mechanics, an engrossing story, and a bold new gear system that blends fighting prowess with RPG progression.

The story mode remains a highlight, weaving an intense, cinematic plot that explores the fractured remnants of Superman’s authoritarian regime. This time, Earth faces a new threat: Brainiac, whose arrival forces uneasy alliances and soul-searching among the DC pantheon. The writing is tighter, the pacing is more dynamic, and the cutscenes feel like a legitimate animated film. While it leans into comic-book melodrama, it never loses its emotional core—especially in Batman and Superman’s ideological showdown.

Injustice™ 2 perfects the franchise’s signature style: methodical yet explosive 2.5D combat. Each fighter feels unique, from the high-flying acrobatics of Cheetah to the bruising gadgetry of Batman. The clash system returns with even more flair, and environmental interactions are smoother and better integrated.

The fighting is accessible for newcomers but offers enough depth for serious players. Timing, spacing, and character mastery are all rewarded, and transitions between areas mid-fight are still some of the most thrilling moments in any fighting game.

Perhaps the most divisive but ambitious addition is the gear system. After each fight, players earn customizable gear that alters both the appearance and attributes of their characters. It adds an addictive progression loop, almost like a fighting game-meets-looter hybrid. Competitive purists can opt for “Tournament Mode” to strip away stat boosts, keeping fights fair, but for casual players, customizing Superman in glowing Kryptonian armor is pure joy.

Visually, Injustice™ 2 is a stunner. Character models are detailed and expressive, from Harley Quinn’s manic grins to the glowing menace of Darkseid. The stages are vibrant, destructible, and each one tells its own story. The voice acting is solid across the board, with standout performances by Kevin Conroy (Batman) and George Newbern (Superman), lending extra gravitas to their legendary conflict.

Injustice™ 2 isn’t just a great fighting game—it’s one of the most compelling interpretations of the DC Universe in gaming. With deep mechanics, a robust single-player campaign, and a creative progression system, it appeals to both fighting game enthusiasts and comic book fans. Whether you’re here to save the world or dominate it, there’s a place for you in this visually striking, emotionally rich brawler.

An exceptional fighter that balances narrative depth with mechanical excellence. Justice has rarely looked—or played—this good.

My first night in Rust, I built a tiny shack. Four walls, a door, a campfire. I felt safe. I shouldn’t have. Because in Rust, safety is just silence before the storm.

It started with footsteps. Soft, circling. Then a whisper in voice chat:
“Nice base you’ve got.”

I didn’t sleep much after that.

You learn quickly that everyone on the island is either a hunter or prey, and you don’t get to choose which one you are. I’m not saying these games are perfect, or that good games aren’t made anymore because that’s ridiculous, but the specific brand of whimsy nonsense embodied by these games just isn’t done anymore. They’re products of their time in the best ways possible.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761042804}, {"review_text": "This collection is the perfect way to dive into the Kingdom Hearts series or relive it in all its glory. Six titles in one — four playable games and two beautifully remastered cinematic experiences. If you love action RPGs, emotional storytelling, and a touch of Disney magic, this one’s for you.

🔹 Kingdom Hearts Final Mix
Where it all begins. It’s charming, emotional, and a bit old-school in its design, but that’s part of the appeal. Right from the start, you can feel there’s something deeper going on beneath the bright, colorful worlds.

🔹 Re:Chain of Memories
A totally unique experience with a card-based battle system that takes some getting used to. The grind can be real, especially later on — but once it clicks, it becomes surprisingly fun and rewarding. Plus, the story takes a darker turn in a really compelling way.

🔹 358/2 Days (HD Movie)
It’s not playable here, but even as a cinematic, it hurts in the best way. A quiet, emotional story about friendship and loss that hits hard — especially if you’ve played KH2. It stays with you.

🔹 Kingdom Hearts II Final Mix
This one is just phenomenal. Everything is smoother, faster, and more intense. The combat is easily the best in the series, the bosses are exciting (and sometimes brutal), and the story really comes into its own. A fan favorite for a reason.

🔹 Birth by Sleep
Three new heroes, three perspectives, and one bittersweet backstory. The gameplay feels fresh, and the emotional payoff is strong. Definitely one of the deeper and more tragic entries in the series.

🔹 Re:coded (HD Movie)
Not the standout of the bunch, but still worth watching for the lore bits. The digital twist is fun and gives a different flavor to the usual Kingdom Hearts formula.

Final Thoughts:
This collection isn’t just nostalgia. It’s a magical, emotional rollercoaster with great gameplay, unforgettable music, and characters you grow to truly care about. Not every part is perfect — but together, it’s a masterpiece of storytelling and heart.

Would I play it all again? In a heartbeat. ❤️", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1744698442}, {"review_text": "Kingdom Hearts 1.5 has always been a special game to me. A true favorite. Because of its music, its story, its characters… but also because of the moment in life when I first discovered it.

I still remember borrowing the PlayStation 2 box from my big sister whenever she went to work. I would put the CD back exactly how it was—same angle, same tiny dust mark on the corner—just to make sure she wouldn’t notice. Those were the golden days.

Today, I’m older. My tastes have evolved, my gaming hours are more limited. And yet, in June 2024, the Integrum Masterpiece collection suddenly drops on Steam. Every game in the saga. (Except the latest one, Chains of Melody, still missing in action.) And just like that, the door to light opens again in my life—ready to pull me out of the darkness.

So here it is: my review of the achievements in KH1.5.

KH1.5 has 55 achievements, and there’s something for everyone: completing the main story, finding all the collectibles, collecting every piece of equipment, reaching level 100, finishing every challenge, every boss, every mini-game... and much more. It’s a JRPG, so of course—it demands time, patience, and a healthy dose of madness. Expect around 130 hours for the full 100%. I did it in 46, but hey, pro gamer privilege.

You’ll probably start on Beginner Mode for your first run. It’s perfect to learn the mechanics, enjoy the story, and ease into the game without too much frustration. The first 20 hours? Probably some of the best you’ll ever experience. You’ll save entire worlds, meet iconic characters, and defeat thousands of Heartless. And once the adventure ends... the real grind begins.

You’ll need to hit level 100—either with optimized EXP gear or pure brute force. You’ll have to fight secret bosses like the Clock Tower Phantom, with sadistic but brilliant mechanics. Complete all the tournaments in Olympus: in teams, solo, timed... across four brackets. Hunt rare drops from Heartless to craft powerful items with the synthesis system. And let’s not forget the special Heartless, each with their own unique quirks—definitely bring a guide for those.

Like every classic JRPG, KH1.5 throws a ton of collectibles at you: the 99 Dalmatians, the Trio Marks, Ansem’s Reports, the Winnie the Pooh mini-games, all the magic spells, the hidden chests, the abilities... You’ll revisit every world again and again. But that’s part of the beauty. The repetition becomes ritual.

Then comes Proud Mode. The expert difficulty. That’s when the tears begin to fall. I’ve never struggled so much in my life as a trophy hunter. Maybe because I didn’t have much JRPG experience. Maybe because I always rushed Kingdom Hearts. I had to learn every enemy’s pattern, optimize every stat, manage my items with care, and above all—stop yelling at Donald for wasting his damn MP. It’s brutal.

And then comes the final madness. Finish the game in under 15 hours, without dying once, using only the default equipment. It’s doable after completing Proud Mode. But your damage output is a joke.

Kingdom Hearts is an ARPG combining both Disney and Final Fantasy to create an original story. KH 1.5 + 2.5 HD Remix covers the best story arc from Birth by Sleep to KH 2 and features 4 playable games and 2 3-hour movies for 358/2 Days & Coded. Before going into a breakdown on each playable game, the only technical issue I had was an audio glitch consistent across all titles. This doesn’t break the experience as it is fairly infrequent, but it is a little distracting. Otherwise I’ve had no other technical issues. Kingdom Hearts has always meant a lot to me having grown up with the series and reliving these games has been a wonderful experience.

[b][u]Kingdom Hearts[/u][/b]

Kingdom Hearts follows the story of Sora as he embarks on a grand adventure with Donald and Goofy throughout various Disney worlds. While KH 1 is the most nostalgic, it aged the poorest due to stiff gameplay and an abysmal camera that has a spasm every time Sora faces a different target because of how close it is to him (change the camera from auto to manual). That being said, this game is a lot of fun with a great story, amazing world-building and exciting boss fights. It also has better partner AI customization (setting the frequency of regular & special attacks, support abilities and when to use items) and makes your partners much more useful than the succeeding titles (Donald especially as the magic system in KH 1 complements him more). In terms of exploration, this game can be a bit confusing to navigate and I recommend a guide for new players. However, this isn’t too bad and you do get used to the gameplay over time. 

The Gummi Ship system also didn’t age well as it isn’t very intuitive and is poorly explained in-game. While customizing the ship isn’t necessary, having a stronger ship at later stages helps as playing through the shooting segments in-between worlds is mandatory until late in the game when fast travel becomes available.

While KH 1 didn’t age well, it still is a memorable experience with plenty of fun moments that both new and returning players will love. I give this game a 7/10.

[b][u]Kingdom Hearts Re: Chain of Memories[/u][/b]

Chain of Memories is the bridge game between 1 & 2 following both Sora’s and Riku’s adventures in Castle Oblivion. While the story is decent, the gameplay suffers from repetition due to little variation between worlds as these are created from cards with fixed rooms. Before starting Re: CoM, I recommend watching 358/2 Days first and reading all the extras (click in and out of each) as end game cards are locked behind this. 

Re: CoM uses a card combat system that gets mixed reception. I find the system to be decent since there are enemy cards which are useful: Genie Jafar gives you 20 unbreakable attacks, Vexen auto-revives you with some HP (combined with Oogie Boogie which heals you 10 times refilling your HP to max) and Roxas doubles your attack power for 20 attack cards. However, the grinding in Re: CoM is very tedious especially for card collection. While enemy cards drop more frequently in rooms like Almighty Darkness, it’s painful to get every single enemy card. YouTube user DERIKUF created an amazing video showing how to manipulate the game’s RNG to drop enemy cards more frequently through the use of Warp, dodge rolls and whether to attack an enemy before engaging in combat which I fully recommend.
 
Re: CoM isn’t a difficult game and I found proud mode easier than the GBA version given how big of a battlefield you have to maneuver. While this game has a decent story and some surprisingly good mini-games, I consider this to be the weakest entry for its repetitive nature and I give the game a 6/10.

[b][u]Kingdom Hearts 2[/u][/b]

Everything about Kingdom Hearts 2 from the story featuring loveable characters, world-building, music, smooth gameplay (including a fully revamped Gummi Ship system), exciting boss fights and all the content it provides are the pinnacle of the entire franchise. The only critiques that I had were minor nitpicks:

[b]Nerfed Partner AI Customization[/b] – Partner AI customization is limited to the frequency of special attacks making partners less useful than they were in KH 1 (especially Donald as the magic system doesn’t complement him at all).

[b]Tedious Grinding[/b] – Material grinding in KH 2 is worse than KH 1 as synthesis requires more time and investment. Level-grinding also takes longer as EXP dropped from end-game enemies was nerfed from the original KH 2.

[b]Average Mini-games/Challenges [/b] – While they aren’t terrible, the mini-games in 2 aren’t that great and can be annoying if you’re trying to do all the journal objectives (especially Mushroom XIII). 

KH 2 can be difficult, but it isn’t unfair. If you want the secret ending, it’s better to bite the bullet and play on proud mode since the unlock requirements (100% journal + game completion) are easier than normal (same as proud + all Gummi Ship missions). Despite the critiques, KH 2 is a masterpiece and I easily give it a 9/10.

[b][u]Kingdom Hearts: Birth by Sleep[/u][/b]

Taking place 10 years before KH 1, Birth by Sleep follows the stories of Terra, Aqua and Ventus as they go through their own journeys. BBS often gets mixed reception, but I find the game to be a fun experience featuring an amazing story with likeable characters, fun gameplay that while floaty, isn’t too bad and the best mini-games in the entire series (Command Boards especially). The critiques I have of BBS are:

[b]Repetitive Nature[/b] – Because there are 3 stories, this means visiting the same worlds 3 times with minor changes made to them which in combination with tedious grinding, wears out the game’s welcome. 

[b]Command Melding & Grinding[/b] – Command melding, while not bad, is tedious without a guide to look up how to craft commands and abilities. I found that grinding commands and abilities as early as the second world helped as a lot of the commands necessary for melding are available by that point. This served as a fast way to max out abilities early on (unlocked when a crystal is melded with 2 maxed out commands and becomes permanent when the melded command is maxed out). There are also fast ways to grind levels:
 
Terra – Equip EXP Chance (remove EXP Walker), 2 Mega Flares and 1 Victory Pose, lower your health to 25% (flashing red), go into Skull Rock on Neverland and cast both Mega Flares while standing in place followed by Victory Pose. Leave the area, go back in and repeat. You’ll get ~3-3.5K EXP every ~10 seconds.
 
Ventus & Aqua – Equip EXP Chance (remove EXP Walker & Treasure Magnet), 2 Thundagas & Victory Poses (Thundaga followed by Victory Pose) and a keyblade with good magic. Lower your health to 25% (flashing red) and go to the Jungle Clearing in Neverland. Defeat both groups of Unversed (quickly dodge to avoid picking up any health orbs and use Victory Pose for each group). Leave the area, go back in and repeat. You’ll get ~2-2.5K EXP every ~15 seconds.
 
[b]Unfair Difficulty[/b] – BBS is the hardest game in the franchise by far. It doesn’t help that the secret ending encourages you to play on at least proud mode (requires full sticker collection + last episode + all Xehanort reports for each character), but this game has the worst secret boss fights in the entire series and I’m convinced the only way to beat them is to cheat.

While not the strongest entry in the series, BBS is still a fun experience and I give it a 7.5/10.

[b][u]Conclusion & Recommendation[/u][/b]

Everything about Kingdom Hearts from the story, loveable characters, world-building, beautiful music and fun gameplay make this a truly magical adventure worth owning. After everything, I give this collection a 7.5/10.

Needing to level up your commands constantly for melding or else grind the arena to level instantly makes it worse. Still not a terrible game but in a series as good as it is falls pretty flat in my eyes.

358/2 Days isn't playable in this compilation, but if you still happen to have a DS or 3DS lying around somewhere I'd give it a go. It's not for everyone since while it translates the general combat of the main series pretty well it does lack some of the intensity the better hardware can provide, and some mission types some find annoying. It definitely has a unique charm though really making you feel like you're a member of Org XIII and I still enjoy it as a more relaxed KH experience, and the fantastic story definitely hits harder having actually played the game through. The multiplayer is great as well 19 playable characters is really something it's always fun to mess around with new playstyles.

Re:Coded is also not playable here, but it's also on the DS like Days. The story is pretty pointless and forgettable and while it has some of the best systems in the series the gameplay loop started to get old for me very quickly even despite the relatively short length. The completely new gameplay styles for boss fights were mildly interesting but ended up more annoying than anything. It uses the digital theme quite well but the lack of relevance and gameplay that failed to keep me engaged makes it a hard recommendation. If you're really curious you can get a copy for like $20 so it's not the end of the world.

This is very clearly the best value in the series and absolutely where anyone should start if they want to try out the series for the first time, or just recently coming back.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1746247982}]

PLAY THIS RIGHT NOW!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1742297988}, {"review_text": "When I first booted up Cuphead, I was immediately struck by how it looked like an actual 1930s cartoon. The hand-drawn animations, the grainy film filter, the jazz-heavy soundtrack—it all felt like I had stepped into a Fleischer short. But then the gameplay kicked in, and I realized this wasn’t just style over substance.

Cuphead is brutally hard. Like, throw-your-controller hard. Every boss felt like a puzzle where I had to memorize patterns, dodge perfectly, and stay calm under chaos. I’d die dozens of times on a single fight, but when I finally nailed the last parry or landed the final shot, the sense of victory was unmatched. The game punishes every mistake, but it also makes every win feel earned.

I also appreciated the run-and-gun levels. They weren’t as memorable as the bosses, but they gave me a chance to experiment with different weapons and charms. Switching between spread shots, homing bullets, and smoke dash felt like finding the perfect tools for different fights.

If I’m being honest, Cuphead isn’t for everyone. It demands patience, practice, and a willingness to fail over and over again. But for me, the combination of its gorgeous presentation and nail-biting challenge made it one of the most rewarding games I’ve ever played. I didn’t just beat bosses—I survived them, and that felt amazing.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1757782356}, {"review_text": "More passion and effort went into a single frame of this game that anything I've ever done in my entire life.

Pitch perfect platforming, and gorgeous art. Some of the best ever put into a video game. They nailed the look of these cartoons. The DLC only adds better animations. It's a level of motion that's unreal. Seeing modern fighting game references put into this style is so weird, but it just works. There is a love for all kinds of animation, including animation in other games. I'm so happy this exists. It's the kind of game that seems impossible, and it's a game I'm lucky to enjoy.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1743998578}, {"review_text": "Cuphead isn’t just a game—it’s an experience. From the moment the hand-drawn animations flicker to life, you know you're stepping into something special. Inspired by the rubber-hose cartoons of the 1930s and powered by brutally challenging run-and-gun gameplay, Cuphead is equal parts artistic masterpiece and test of patience.

The Good:

Stunning Visuals: Every frame is hand-drawn, inked, and painted in a style that feels like a lost Fleischer Brothers cartoon. The attention to detail is absurd—in the best way possible.

Incredible Soundtrack: The jazzy, big-band score is not just background noise—it’s integral to the game’s identity. It pumps you up and sets the tempo for every boss fight.

Boss Design: Each boss is wildly imaginative, with multiple stages that evolve in surprising, often hilarious ways. It’s a masterclass in creativity and game pacing.

Tight Controls: Despite its chaos, Cuphead always feels fair. Responsive controls ensure that when you die (and you will), it’s usually your fault.

The Not-So-Good:

Unforgiving Difficulty: This game is hard. Not unfair—but absolutely punishing. It’s not for casual players or those looking for a relaxing time.

Minimal Story: The charm is there, but the narrative is light. If you’re looking for deep lore or character arcs, you might be underwhelmed.

Repetitive for Some: The game is boss-centric, with a few platforming levels. If boss rushes aren’t your thing, it might wear thin over time.

Cuphead is a rare fusion of style and substance. It looks like a vintage cartoon, plays like a bullet-hell classic, and feels like a labor of love. It will test your reflexes, your patience, and maybe your controller durability—but the sense of accomplishment after beating each boss is second to none.

If you’re into tight gameplay, timeless art direction, and don’t mind dying a hundred times to learn a pattern, Cuphead is a must-play.

I want to talk a bit about the difficulty, because it can be a little overwhelming at first and might scare off newcomers, but the game is actually not that hard, it just throws you into the thick of it while you're still learning the controls and how the game is meant to be played.

By which I mean, it's a boss rush game, there's no "beginning area" where you can fool around, it immediately opens up with a multi-stage boss fight pelting you with projectiles. In addition, the default control scheme is a little strange, to say the least. I recommend rebinding right away to e.g. LT = aim lock, RT = shoot, X = dash, A = jump.

Granted, there are 2 side-scrolling levels with no bosses per each world, but they're paced like [b]Ghouls 'n Ghosts[/b] stages with constantly respawning enemies and deadly hazards. While the rest of the game is elaborate boss fights with many phases.

Is it harder than [b]Dark Souls[/b]? Yes, you can't level up, there's no healing, no OP builds, you die in 3 hits. The game plays more like the classic run & guns like [b]Contra Hard Corps[/b], [b]Gunstar Heroes[/b] and [b]Alien Soldier[/b], except there's virtually no punishment for death, aside from restarting from the first phase.

There's a shop where you spend coins to buy a variety of weapons, e.g. a spread shot for close range combat, a charge shot a la [b]Mega Man[/b] for potentially the highest damage but you'll need to constantly charge it and aim well. You can carry two weapons into battle and swap between them. There are also passive charms, most people will probably settle on the smoke bomb which adds i-frames to your dash. If you own the DLC, you can immediately visit the DLC area to unlock an additional character who has 1 more HP and a few extra moves (such as double jump and dash parry) to make the base game a little easier.

In conclusion, you'll get your face smashed in when you start, that's normal, don't rush to refund the game, because 15 minutes later you'll be dabbing on bosses once you get used to how the game plays. I wouldn't say it's a try hard game, I'm pushing 40 and awful at games, and I'm doing just fine (cleared the first two worlds in 5 hours and 50 deaths). If you're able-bodied and don't have anger issues, you can beat this game and have a lot of fun doing it!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1748256814}, {"review_text": "[b][i]Cuphead[/i][/b] is one of the most artistically impressive pieces of media there is, and fortunately, that's far from the only thing it surprises players with.
The game offers us two main types of levels: Run 'n Gun, where the main objective is to collect all the coins and reach the finish to buy new weapons and buffs, and the more prevalent type - boss battles, where every enemy truly feels like an original and unique obstacle to overcome.
More experienced players also have a chance to further prove their skill by trying to achieve the Pacifist and S ranks in the aforementioned modes, respectively, thanks to the level completion ranking system.
For a challenging platformer, there wasn't a single time I thought I had died in unfair manner, which is a really hard feat to pull off - but studio MDHR proved they are among the best at doing so.
Ultimately, [b][i]Cuphead[/i][/b] is, without a doubt, one of the most popular, influential and successful indie games to come out in the last 15 years and potentially, of all time - which is absolutely deserved. Anyone who hasn't given it a fair chance is missing out on an astounding experience.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1746944459}, {"review_text": "Disclaimer: The game offers the ability to play with a friend, but I played through this one in single-player only. 

The game was released in the PS4/XBox One generation and it's made in Unity, so I was a little worried going in that this wasn't going to run very well on my late 2010's i5 laptop. Thankfully it's smooth as butter. There's only really one boss fight in the DLC and a couple attacks in Rumor Honeybottoms' fight on the third Isle that cause consistent questionable performance, and that may just be a GPU issue.

Everyone's banged this drum already but Cuphead has really fun presentation. In terms of artstyle there's nothing else really quite like it on the market, outside of a couple direct imitators. That partially comes down to the sheer amount of time and effort necessary for drawing, colouring, painting all the assets. It is not cheap to make a game that does its best to look like a cartoon (albeit with concessions to the actual gameplay). At the same time, executives will decry the cost/time of a hand-drawn project as the reason not to go ahead with it, and then pump several hundred millions of dollars and half-decades or entire decades into homogeneous CG games and films, so it's really just a fob-off excuse - when people with money know what they want, they'll move heaven and earth to get it there. It was a warm surprise therefore for Microsoft to help market and bankroll Cuphead, even as the creators had to move their own heaven and earth to get it to release. The art direction is a fun breath of fresh air in an industry that's still chasing the polygonal glass ceiling even to this day.

(If you're a stickler for consistency like me, then the character animations all being at 24fps will clash with the player's movement, particle movement, background scrolling etc all running at 60fps. It can come off like things are disjointed. Those aforementioned attacks in Honeybottoms' fight are maybe also the only assets in the game that are computer-generated particles rather than hand-drawn. If you can get past all that or not notice it, you should be golden.)

Only a couple songs from the game really stuck in my head (the early few bosses such as the Root Pack and the battle theme for the mini-boss gauntlet near the end). This isn't to say the music's bad, it's great - it feels like a good 2010's recreation of the Scott Bradley school of cartoon composition, or something more akin to Christopher Willis, rather than Richard Stone handicapped by Tom Ruegger, or Carl Johnson and Joshua Moshier ("wahhhhhh") - it's just I was usually too busy concentrating on the mechanics to even pick up on sound cues telegraphing attacks, let alone the songs. Cuphead takes a fun cue from particular Fleischer cartoons where the voice actors would ad lib or mumble over character actions, and this comes through in the game, but it's easy to tune it out - for me at least - along with the game's other sounds.

Cuphead was built with consoles in mind and the controller seems to be the best option for ease of use, though I'm not keen on the default control layout itself. You can rebind keys in the options, however most all the buttons on a conventional gamepad are used except the two shoulder triggers (I used an XBox Series controller for reference), so there's little wiggle room. Regardless you should be able to set up, for example, shoot and dash on the triggers and be more comfortable that way. I've gone through the game entirely with the default layout. 

I don't have any real issues as far as actual character movement or input response goes, it's as good as you could ask for from a platformer and a game that demands constant awareness. If you keep using super attacks while ignoring the detritus on screen, you're going to suffer (and I'm a slow learner for this sort of stuff). The amount of wiggle room you have, before your character overlapping with something registers as 'damage', is pretty vague but errs on the side of generous, favouring the player most times. You will learn the general boundaries of what not to touch through trial and error anyhow.

The meat and potatoes of the game is in the boss fights; there are nearly twenty in total, not counting the mini-bosses. By comparison there are two levels on each Isle focused more on straight platforming mixed in with gauntlets of enemies. These levels are technically not mandatory, but the majority of the coins for buying new weapons and charms come from these stages, and if you stick with the peashooter and no charms or weapons to swap out, you're going to make the experience much more frustrating for yourself. At the very least grab the Chaser and the Smoke Dash, then decide further down the road what looks good in the shop, or consult a guide. The game will also provide prompts through the NPCs to change your loadout, as there's no one universal solution to all the different fights - unless you're very stubborn about it. (Again, I was a slow learner.)

I would recommend at least playing through all of the regular mode, and would recommend the DLC if you've enjoyed the main campaign. Don't expect to ace any boss on the first try. Most all the bosses are satisfying to learn and overcome, though you do have to be comfortable with the idea of throwing yourself at a brick wall over and over until it starts crumbling down. The game's presentation is what helps mitigate that, so if you're low on patience or Cuphead's cartoon world doesn't do it for you, I would say skip this game altogether.

I personally would not recommend playing all the bosses on expert mode (or going for the pacifist run on the run 'n' gun levels) because at that point it stops being seasonably satisfying and becomes more of a slog, but your mileage will vary. Definitely don't beat the game on regular difficulty and then expect starting over on Isle 1 on expert will be a piece of cake, you'll be surprised. In other 'stuff I don't like'isms, there's a particular run 'n' gun level on Isle 2 where you need to reverse gravity frequently to advance, and it just feels frustrating advancing past some of the enemies like the walls and trombones. I'm definitely not a fan of Dr Kahl's Robot on the third Isle; even once you get a hang of the first phase and find a good order to break everything down, the second phase is kind of uninteresting and the third phase is a huge health sponge with some unfortunate foreground distractions that can make the phase feel unfair, almost luck-dependent. I'm also not a fan of Cala Maria's boss fight or the horse racing mini-boss for similar reasons, you can just end up with the stars aligning in the wrong way on some runs. The feeling of beating these bosses isn't satisfaction but "man, I don't want to do that again". Maybe that's sour grapes; other people are a lot better at consistent A/S ranks with these fights.

The DLC is slightly larger than the size of a regular Isle. Five main bosses, a mini-boss selection, an extra final boss and a hidden fight. The shop now boasts a broken trinket that works as an extra self-imposed challenge to use and unlock its full potential. You also get the option to play a new character that's mostly got it better than the brothers (extra health, invincibility on roll, double jump) but whose dash parry takes some getting used to and can make a couple boss patterns in the base game much more uncomfortable to deal with. This character's designed with the DLC bosses in mind (particularly the chess-themed fights) but there's nothing really stopping you from unlocking her early and then beating the main game that way, other than your own self-control.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1751634179}, {"review_text": "“Here’s a real high-class bout! - And begin!”

Was meant to write a review for Cuphead after beating the game and deciding whether or not to grab The Delicious Last Course. But it’ll probably take quite a while before I reach that point and you know what, that’s totally fine. It took me eight years just to finally start playing it. Plus, I’m not exactly in a situation right now where I can just summon the motivation to finish it no matter what, especially with plenty of other games catching my attention. Still, hope to finish it someday.

The difference between many masocore, soulslike or just games with a high difficulty and frustration level and Cuphead, is that this one really really grabs me, visually and musically. 
The whole look and sound hits something deep in me, and even though I’ve honestly thought about just watching a playthrough, I actually want to experience it myself. That old-school Betty Boop/Fleischer style just has something special, the way arms and legs move like rubber hoses, objects come to life, and everything feels a bit surreal. Of course, nostalgia also plays a big part.
Maybe I’m not telling anyone anything new here, but I was blown away when the soundtrack hit number one on the US Billboard Jazz Charts and even made it into the Guinness Book of World Records. Back then just like now, I really wanted that soundtrack on vinyl. But just like with games, there’s so much other great music out there. Still, I really hope that one day the OST will find its way onto my record shelf.

[{"review_text": "Let’s talk gameplay: you walk. That’s it. You walk. You don’t even swing your weapon. The game does that for you. Because apparently the developers saw how little effort gamers were putting into life and said, “Let’s meet them halfway.” It's like a bullet hell shooter got drunk and passed out on a CRT monitor from 1993, and somehow, it’s art.
And oh, the dopamine. Every pixel explosion, every shiny gem, every upgrade — it’s like your brain is getting suckled by an arcade machine from a timeline where Castlevania went completely feral. Level up every 7 seconds.
The soundtrack? Banger. Absolute banger. I’ve started hearing “Revenant” in the background while doing dishes. My dishwasher has a kill combo. I don’t even have a dishwasher.
The characters? Oh, the deep, rich, emotionally resonant lore of “Guy With Axe” and “Skeleton With Gun.” There are approximately 947 playable characters and they all boil down to: “Hits stuff good.” Thank God. If I wanted emotional arcs, I’d rewatch Breaking Bad. I’m here to walk in a circle while deleting legions of undead like a Roomba with war crimes.
And don’t get me started on the items. Laurel? Yes, please, give me a shield so I can feel something. Clock Lancet? The game equivalent of putting the entire universe on hold while you decide whether to eat string cheese. The real star though? Garlic. You get Garlic, and you become a stinky god of rot and glory. You ever walked into a room so pungent you kill Death itself? You will.
Eventually, the game rewards you with a mode called Endless. Bold of them to assume I haven’t already been living in that mode since the day I installed it.
And yet. And yet. I cannot stop. I am freebasing pixels. I am optimizing builds in my sleep. I see red XP gems in my dreams. My mouse hand has calcified into a permanent WASD claw, but my soul? My soul is radiant. Bathed in golden chests and the unholy light of duplicator rings.
10/10. Highly recommend. [i]Vampire Survivors[/i] didn’t sound like my kind of game. Bullet hell? Auto-attacks? Roguelike stuff? [i]Hard pass.[/i]
But a friend swore by it, so I gave it a shot…

…and now I’ve lost hours of my life mowing down pixel monsters like it’s my full-time job.

Once it clicks, you’re in. The chaos ramps up fast, the upgrades are addicting, and unlocking new characters and weapons keeps the loop feeling fresh. One second you're like, [i]"I'll just do a quick run,"[/i] and suddenly it's 2 a.m. and your screen is a glowing mess of lasers, explosions, and flying rotisserie chickens.

It’s cheap, runs on basically any toaster, and somehow manages to be both brain-off [i]and[/i] brain-on at the same time. Pure dopamine.

[b]If you’re even slightly curious, just play it.[/b] You’ll thank me later or curse me when you realize you’ve “accidentally” sunk hours into it!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1744968608}, {"review_text": "I booted up Vampire Survivors expecting a casual time. Next thing I know, it's 3 a.m., I'm surrounded by 10,000 skeletons, my screen is a fireworks display of garlic, birds, and Bible circles, and my GPU is screaming in Latin.

Do I understand what's happening? No.
Am I having the time of my life? Absolutely.
Did I just evolve a pigeon into a nuclear dove of death? You bet I did.

This game turns you from "please don't hurt me" to "I am the bullet hell" in 20 minutes flat.

And yeah, this review was written by an AI. But just like this game, I'm borderline sentient and addicted to shiny numbers flying everywhere.

Buy it. Play it. Ascend.

🕹️💀🕊️🔥", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 52, "timestamp_created": 1744101181}, {"review_text": "You know that feeling when you say “just one more game” and then realize you’ve got to be up for work in a few hours? Yeah… that’s Vampire Survivors.
It’s got this ridiculously addictive loop where all you’re doing is moving and picking upgrades… but somehow your brain’s in overdrive, engineering the perfect doomsday build. The game fires your weapons for you, so you can focus on weaving through swarms, grabbing clutch upgrades, and watching your power spiral out of control in the best way.
Endless unlocks—new characters, weapons, stages—constantly tempting you with “just a little more power”, win or lose. And the best part? No shady microtransactions. No battle pass. Just pure “pay a few bucks and go nuts” fun.

And it does what it wants to do, very, very well. The game is simple, you start a game, kill things, collect gold, die, buy upgrades, and try again, a simple rogue-like, but it's rare to find one that is this complete and this satisfying to play. 

When playing and doing random objectives, you'll unlock characters, that start with a different weapon, have different bonuses, you'll unlock weapon upgrades ect..

The updates come frenquently so I often start the game to do the achievements that have been added, and it's a blast every single time.

No van Helsings though, just a few Belmonts.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1738516380}, {"review_text": "[h1]Just half an hour more...[/h1]

Vampire Survivors is a game that's a bit rogue-like, a bit action-packed, and a bit horror. Well, there's a lot going on in this game, but the main goal is always the same—survive as long as possible. That's 30 minutes, because then death comes and kills us anyway. Unless we play long enough and discover that there is more to this game and that death is not such a formidable opponent after all.

So why is this game so good? Well, because every subsequent game, every subsequent death is a continuous progression. During the game, we unlock new characters, collect gold, and spend that gold on new attributes that make our character stronger, faster, have more life, and are generally awesome. Each character has their own unique weapon, and we can combine these weapons with a passive weapon, giving us an upgraded version of that weapon. During the game, we can have a maximum of 6 weapons, and we can upgrade each of them. However, there are... a lot of weapons to choose from throughout the game.

The game's graphics are simple, based on pixel art. This game will run on any hardware, and problems may only arise when our screen is flooded with waves of enemies. The simplicity of the graphics may be a disadvantage for some, but for me it is an advantage, introducing an interesting atmosphere. The game took me back in time, which I found enjoyable. The retro-style sounds are similar. Simply wonderful.

There is one more thing to add about this game. It has a cooperation system, so if you get bored of killing enemies on your own after a while, just invite a friend or a few friends and play together, figure out which weapon combos are best, and simply kill boredom.

[h1]Summary[/h1]

Is Vampire Survivors an outstanding game that will be remembered in the future? Of course not, but it's a great game when you have some free time and don't know what to play. In Vampire Survivors, there will always be another character, weapon, or relic waiting for you to unlock, and it will literally take you a dozen or so minutes. And with that price, it would be a shame not to try it.
[b]
✔️Game style, mainly graphics
✔️Large number of characters/weapons to unlock
✔️Cooperative mode
✔️Addictive gameplay (hard to put down)

[i]Time of completion: There's no point in even counting it.[/i]

[b][u]Rating: 9/10[/u][/b]

Let’s be clear: this game looks like it was developed in a haunted microwave. The graphics are what happens when Castlevania and MS Paint have an awkward one-night stand. The music slaps so hard it woke up my minions from the dungeon. And the gameplay? It’s just moving. You move. That’s it. You don’t even attack. The weapons fire themselves while you strafe around like a caffeinated Roomba with divine power.

And yet… it is glorious.

You start as a weak little worm with a whip. You end as a screen-destroying celestial tornado of holy garlic and lightning books, melting legions of undead like you're the unholy blender of fate. At first, you struggle to survive a single minute. Later, you pity Death itself as it tries—and fails—to kill you for the fifth time while you’re AFK microwaving pizza rolls.

It is digital crack cocaine with pixel art. It has no right to be this good. The entire game is built on the premise: “What if numbers go up, and you feel good about it?” And it works. Every. Single. Time.

Balance? HA! Some weapons are useless garbage until they evolve into god-tier screen nuke cannons. Others are immediately busted. But who cares?! You’re too busy unlocking secret characters like a ghost dog with a flamethrower or a literal piece of furniture that kills stuff. Yes. A chair. That kills.

You want story? No. There is none. Stop asking. This is not for your brain. This is for your lizard brain. The part of you that shrieks in delight when your character gets three chests in a row and turns into a walking disco apocalypse. This game has zero plot, infinite gameplay, and endless regret when you realize it’s 3AM and you’re STILL TRYING TO UNLOCK QUEEN SIGMA.

And the best part? It costs five dollars. Five. Dollars. Diablo 4 sold you a trash fire at seventy bucks with a battle pass for armor dyes. This game sold you a lifetime supply of chaos, serotonin, and existential reflection for the cost of a sad sandwich. The only thing Vampire Survivors lacks is the ability to physically inject itself into your bloodstream. Which I’m sure is in a patch.

Final Verdict: 💀💀💀💀💀 (5 out of 5 Skulls)

What is, essentially, Castlevania but a survival game with over 50 characters to choose from and an outstanding number of cultural references and some surprisingly interesting lore, Vampire Survivors runs on a very simple premise: Survive for a period of time, die, rinse and repeat. But there are so many unlockables, so many challenges, so many things that capture the fancy of anyone looking for a good time for what might constitute a whole freaking day of work for some.

Vampire Survivors actually follows a similar formula to the Binding of Isaac, Brotato, and other games, but it uses the formula and references numerous horror franchises while playing into meta-humour and adding an undertone of the creepy that will scratch that needed scare itch.

After that is the snowy biome (where, after a short time, a blizzard starts blowing from all sides, draining your stamina unless you find shelter). Then there's the pre-final zone, lava mountains, and finally you need to climb out of the volcano crater, which is almost a vertical ascent.

I should mention we played with a mod that allows a larger lobby. Sure, the game isn’t decked out with AAA-level visuals, but who cares when you’re dodging lava geysers and questionable mushrooms with friends, all while laughing at the physics mishaps? It’s proof that pixel-perfect climbing excitement is worth far more than pixel-perfect graphics.

The core of PEAK is beautifully simple: you and up to three pals are stranded nature scouts, and your only escape is to scale a mountain that changes every 24 hours. The procedural ascent keeps each climb feeling fresh, whether you’re slipping off slippery ice or managing your stamina between bites of dubious food, talk about “rock” and roll. Watching a friend accidentally trigger map collapse? Pure comedy. And yes, it’s more fun when someone’s flailing mid-air than watching a cinematic cutscene.

Even better, this game runs like a dream. No need for a beefy rig, PEAK thrives on low-spec setups, making it perfect for anyone who wants cooperative thrills without demanding a graphics card upgrade. It delivers smooth performance, instant restarts, and enough slapstick moments to fill a blooper reel, proof that you don’t need photorealism to get a game to hit the peak of entertainment.

In short, PEAK is a delightful reminder that good gameplay and good friends can overshadow even the fanciest visuals. It’s affordable, hilarious, and built on teamwork (or guilt-tripping teammates into saving you after a face-plant). If you're looking for something fun, low-fi, and exceedingly playable, PEAK’s got you covered, no high-end PC required, just bring a sense of humor and a friend (or three).[/b]", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1756755755}, {"review_text": "not your average friendslop
PEAK doesn't fail to generate funny moments and does get exponentially more enjoyable when playing with funny buddies, there is an actual game there that dares to try something  original and actually pulls it off

the traversal challenge and environmental puzzle solving couple with resource management gameplay loop of PEAK is something I've wanted to see for a long time

it has a few problems tied to its whacky physics heavy gameplay that need to be ironed out, like getting randomly shot out of walls at mach speed or items falling through solid ground, and only getting to play the map of the day (without mods) but outside of those it is absolutely phenomenal and well worth your time and money", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 9, "timestamp_created": 1751676201}, {"review_text": "I once nearly fell off a tall mountain during a trip, and my friend pulled me back at the very last second. Ever since that day, seeing a hand reaching out from above fills me with a strange mix of trust, fear, and adrenaline. Maybe he has forgotten about it by now, but for me it was a moment where I truly believed my life was ending. I’m still grateful he was there, and I’ll never forget what he did for me.

PEAK brought that feeling back. It captures the fear of slipping, the comfort of teamwork, and that rare moment when you know someone is there for you. Peak is one of the greatest games I have ever played, with friends this experience can be so chaotic, fun and awesome at the same time.

The devs clearly put a lot of care into the design and game, and it really shows!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1760639341}, {"review_text": "After finishing everything the game has to offer, between all the achievements and extra difficulties, I can confidently say this is probably one of my favorite games to come out this year, not only is it fun to play with friends but playing it solo allows you to play in a more selfish way that you can't really do in multiplayer.

It's not all sunshine and roses, the game has some optimization issues here and there, very noticeable in later stages of the game, and there's some stuff that I wish were handled client-side.

All things considered this game came out with a surprising amount of content, plenty of stuff to do, and needless to mention, a lot of climbs, 5 days into the game every daily map has been a different experience, im sure as the game goes on some of these could start to blend together, but routing them has been a lot of fun.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1750448677}]

I love this game for 5 main reasons:

[olist]
    [*]Simple gameplay with high stakes, as your character moves through the levels automatically and you only need to control when it jumps, but if it hits just one obstacle, it dies and you have to restart the level from the very beginning! This creates a frustrating yet addictive experience, and it makes you want to try and try again, because you know where you messed up, and since the gameplay is so basic, you know what to do next time to get a little further into the level! Besides that, the game has a lot of level objects, from orbs that make you jump in the air when you click them, portals that change character's gravity and speed, to different character gamemodes, which change their jump to flight, switching gravity, teleporting and so on, and it all makes the gameplay fresh in every level so you won't get bored.
    [*]Strong sense of progression, because in a hard game such as this, you will clearly see your growth in skill, not in basic statistic, but in the levels you completed. At first, you are going to complete the easiest of levels, but eventually you'll move onto harder and harder ones. You will notice then how much confidence you have to complete the levels you previously feared. This brings a truly satisfying feeling, more than simply completing a game - you become skilled and confident enough to take on harder challenges. This sense of progression is further supported by showing you the amount of stars and demons, the hardest levels of the game, on your account. Additionaly, many icons for your character can only be unlocked by completing harder challenges, and by seeing how many icons you unlocked, you can see how far you've come in this simple game about jumping over spikes. 
    [*]Amazing level editor, which is THE selling point of Geometry Dash! This is the thing that gives truly limitless potential for the game, as I believe this is one of the best level editors in the game industry. Any object can be moved to any part of the grid, any object can be rotated to any degree you'd like, and any object can even be scaled by X and Y axis. This gives you a lot of potential for decoration in your levels! Besides that, level editor lets you place triggers, which manipulate the level in different ways. They can do something simple, like move objects or change their colors, and can do something drastic, like check collision or remember certain data. Triggers are what allow determined creators to change the level from a simple autoscroller to different game genres! And just when you think it can't get any better, the editor allows to use a vast majority of songs to be played in the level, like music from popular creative website Newgrounds.com, music from popular electronic music label NoCopyrightSounds, and a large music library from songs of various music composers! There are certain limits to this level editor, but as the creators push the limits of the game, the editor expands every update, bringing new features to create unbelievable levels!
    [*]Passionate community, because a good level editor isn't the only ingredient for a timeless game. Without the passionate community, that learned how to push the game and it's level editor to the limits, GD wouldn’t have come so far! This community is truly amazing, continuously supporting the game by creating artistic masterpieces, that sync with the song perfectly, that have beautiful decorations, and that have fun gameplay. Yeah, not all levels are this perfect, and you will find yourself disagreeing with many players, but this doesn't take away from the fact that this community loves the game very much to still keep it alive. Not only the creator side of the community is awesome, a big part of the playerbase are challenging themselves to the hardest levels in the game, which keeps raising the bar of difficulty of this already hard game!  
    [*]Passionate creator, Robert Topala, who has been working on this game all by himself since 2013, clearly showing how much he loves his game and its community. Not only is he working on the game itself, he continuously supports it by rating new community levels, running creator contests and sometimes interacting with the community directly. RobTop really is my favourite game developer, and he is a living proof that you can have a successful and fulfilling life by creating a game that everybody likes, which inspires me to try and become a game developer myself.
[/olist]

However, Geometry Dash is not perfect, like any other game. It has some significant flaws, like security issues, many bugs ranging from annoying to gamebreaking, outdated rating system, and, worst of all, slow updates. And yet, most of these problems could be fixed if RobTop hired more people to work on the game and didn’t have to do it alone.

I know I just praised RobTop for being so passionate about his game, but the problem is, he’s just one developer. GD is way bigger now than it used to be years ago, and it’s obvious that RobTop struggles to have time for everything. I hope one day he will realise that him working alone will mostly harm his game in the long run.

Nevertheless, these flaws don’t ruin the game at all, as in my experience they rarely mattered. And when you don't encounter them, you get a game with limitless amount of artistic and challenging levels for just $4.99! You don't need to purchase any extra dlc or microtransactions to get the full experience, and that in my opinion makes Geometry Dash one of the best deals on the market!

Finally, Geometry Dash means a lot to me personally. Ever since childhood, this game has caught my attention, when me and my classmates were very engaged with this game on our mobile devices and all tried to complete the main levels for glory! And after all this time, after I grew up, finished school and went to university, this game is still with me, still mostly the same, but growing, just like me. And I still find people who play Geometry Dash together on their mobile devices, continuing the trend of beating the levels for glory in their class. Seeing this makes me smile everytime, because I remember that Geometry Dash is still alive and well even after 12 years already, and not going to die anytime soon!

So thank you, Geometry Dash! I probably have around 2-3k hours on this game in total across all platforms. It's my most played game by far. Though there's a lot I love about this game, it has some serious problems that really need fixing. 

First of all, lets get to the good. By far the best thing about this game is the level editor. The level is editor despite seeming very daunting, is actually pretty easy to learn. Despite being somewhat easily accessible, it provides for near limitless possibility. You can make pretty much anything in the level editor, from motion graphics to animations to entire full length adventure games. Due this limitlessness, there is a near infinite amount of community content that you can play, and if you play levels that are rated personally by the creator of the game, you get stars and such. There's also Gauntlets which although aren't always the greatest, can contain very good levels of varying difficulties that usually share a common theme. The gauntlets peak at hard demon, so they aren't always the most accessible to new players but there are a lot of easy gauntlets that contain really well made levels. Map packs are similar although most of the map packs are complete garbage due to the fact that they are very old. However aside from all that, my favourite thing about this game is the game play. This game is extremely satisfying to practice and complete, especially for levels around easy to medium demon difficulty once you get good enough for that. Attempting to Sightread levels when your able to is also very fun. However the best thing in this game is when your attempting a new hardest level. The best moments I've had in any game ever is when I've practised an extreme demon for over 40 hours and I finally beat it, showing that all that practice didn't go to waste. It is by far the most euphoric, most exhilarating feeling I've ever felt when playing a game, and nothing even comes close. Now that doesn't mean I'd recommend other people to go through the same thing as some of the most miserable moments I've had playing any game also come from this game, because once again, practising a level for over 40 hours and still not being very consistent can be discouraging to say the least. However pushing the limits of what you can handle is apart of the fun, and when you finally end up beating that level, nothing is more satisfying. This game pretty much embodies delayed gratification, and it helps you improve your planning and persistence for not just games, but anything in life. 

Now onto the bad, which I have a lot to say. If you haven't played this game or are new to it and trying to get into it, Geometry Dash hinges on one key mechanic that is pretty much required when you get into the harder levels: Practice Mode. I find that a lot of new players are easily frustrated and quit fairly quickly when trying to beat the main levels. The reason for this is usually very predictable, and that's because they refuse to use practice mode. And I don't blame them, practice mode in its default state is extremely boring, and that's largely because the practice music is very monotonous and boring to listen to, and the only way to change it so it actually matches the level your playing without mods is to unlock it with 2000 diamonds, which requires a fair bit playing already. By the time you've gotten 2k diamonds you've probably already beaten the main levels, which means you've probably already gotten used to the boring monotony that is the default practice music. It makes no sense that Practice music sync is locked behind getting collectables that take quite a bit of playtime to grind out, especially because practice mode is infinitely more enjoyable with it. The average player is not gonna try and install mods to unlock it like that either, so its either sit through the boring monotony of practice mode or grind the game until your used to it. This leads me to my second point is that the game is infinitely more enjoyable with QOL mods. It makes no sense why these mods aren't already in the game considering they are very simple to add in and have been around for forever. Lets take a mod called "Level thumbnails" for example. In Vanilla Geometry Dash when your scrolling through custom levels, all you see is the name, the length, and the song. That's it. Pretty much no information about the level itself. You have to go into the level yourself to see if it's worth playing. Level thumbnails shows a snapshot of the level beside the level name, making it way easier to select or filter things you wanna play, based on decoration for example. Why isn't this in the game? A few other examples include being able to remove the death effect or showing hitboxes on death, these are small things that vastly improved the quality of the game, it makes no sense how robtop worked nonstop for 7 years on the game and still has yet to implement these basic features while instead adding useless physics changes that make a bunch of old levels impossible. Not only that, but the rating is system is awful too. If you don't know, every single level is reviewed by robtop and rated based on what he feels like that day. Over 40k levels rated by one guy. I hope I don't even have to explain how inefficient this method is. If he doesn't like a level for a subjective reason like it annoys him he can easily just reject it. Now there are mods that send levels to robtop, but a lot of the time it can take him months to get to these levels. And how does one become a mod? Well simple, you just have to have robtop make you mod based on how he feels about you. On top of  all that, demons have an entirely different system where instead of individual mods sending them to robtop they vote on it. Why? Don't ask me. Obviously, this system is absolutely terrible and makes getting your level rated an absolute nightmare. Even worse, there's a ton of corruption and favouritism behind this system. If your friends with a mod, you can your level rated easily. And if you're not? Tough luck. Not only this, but due to the fact that levels are rated based on robtop's whims, rated levels can vary drastically in quality. For example, there's a level in the NCS gauntlets called "WANNACRY". This level is terrible by every metric. Its pretty much unplayable and has one really good looking part in the entire level while the rest is straight up nausea inducing. Yet its rated mythic, the highest quality rating in the game. Why? Cuz rob felt like giving it mythic that day. On top of all this though, Rob does all this while working on updates for the game. Its no wonder 2.2 took 7 years to come out. Any other reasonable Dev would let high status mods rate levels or at least hire a team to help them develop the game. But either Rob is an egomaniac, or he just doesn't care. Rob also for some reason, has some sort of vendetta against the hardcore player base. Every time a new hardest demon comes out, for some reason he takes an eternity to rate it. Say what you want about the quality of these levels, they are not meant to be good, they are meant to be hard and they bring the most eyes to the game. The most notorious example of this is of a level called Crimson Planet, which despite being the hardest level in the game when it was verified, wasn't rated for an entire year. I'm sorry but that's just unacceptable, but unfortunately the community has become accustomed to it instead of demanding a new rating system. The game is riddled with these problems, that can be easily fixed, but unfortunately Rob doesn't care what anyone says.

Anyway that was a lot of complaining, but I'd be foolish to not recommend this game after spending so much time playing it. But these issues are seriously plaguing the game and they need to be fixed.

[{"review_text": "I was excited for the 1.0 release after playing this game for a good few hours throughout early access.

Unfortunately though, the game has been released in a really bad state, and feels as though this was all a cash grab. The early access started off well, with regular weekly updates etc. which were relatively minor, but gave the impression it was being developed slowly and patiently. But for some reason since August this year everything fell silent with no updates. Then a seemingly surprising announcement was made about the full release coming today a few weeks ago - promising MASSIVE improvements and almost a changed game.

Unfortunately the release has barely changed anything. The amount of visual bugs, physics bugs, framerate issues, and graphics issues alone remain completely unchanged. The gameplay also hasn't changed, UI is still ugly, characters are copy/pasted throughout the map, physics for vehicles are incredibly bad, and the overall game felt pretty much exactly the same before/after this 1.0 update today - albeit with just some new areas and mini-games. 

The additional areas added seem like filler content with very little improvements to anything, (e.g. ive unlocked a fair bit in the game, and the only thing its added, is the incentive for more vehicles by playing some incredibly poor and tedious mini games, that have clearly been made just to pad things out). For example here, the "minigame area" has cut/paste booths everywhere, and reflects real laziness in design work. The new vehicles also are pretty pointless, and have no real reason to them.

It really sucks, as this game was very promising through early access, and looked to be something that could have been developed alot further, but something feels to have changed in the development team, and its seemingly being positioned to be abandoned in a real crappy state. 

It's not a full game at this stage, and shouldn't be sold as such, I would only recommend getting this if you are happy with the game being in a permanent early access state.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Just an add: They updated the game since I posted this review, so I played a couple more hours. I do respect the fact they are trying to address minor issues reported, but unfortunately the game still has these glaringly massive issues. For example, the NPC vehicles drive around like its destruction derby, and just mow you or your van down when parked. Customers of your store literally drop-spawn in from the sky like they are visiting from the promised land. The list goes on.. its quite hilarious, but still feels my above review is very much unchanged.
