[h1]The way you bid, the amount by which you do it and the manner in which you try to outbid the competition has >>NO EFFECT WHATSOEVER<< on your final price. [/h1]

Bidding is extremely unrealistic and might as well not exist at all in its current form. There is no game mechanic, there is no way to 'win'. You get to either pay the predetermined price or walk away, you have no influence or any way to lower this reserve price. No bidding strategy will let you have it for less than what the game decides you should pay the moment you step into the green circle.

Detailed rant below
---------------------------------
Level 5 auctions really shows the key weakness in this game, as do blind ones. It is very clear that every container you open has a reserve price under which your opponents will [b]always[/b] outbid you, no matter what. For this test, I chose a Lvl 5 auction and saved right before enrolling, to try different strats.

I tried bidding in low increments, in large increments (to 'scare others off'), and I tried to get others to bid against each other and snipe with last minute bids - it won't matter. Every single time, the bidding would continue to somewhere well into the 10k$. This is what it comes down to every single time:

[list]
    [*]Bidding starts, multiple participants
    [*]Above a certain price, one 'nemesis' remains that will keep outbidding you
    [*]Waiting until the very last moment to bid proves that nobody else wants to outbid, so the 'nemesis' will get it for whatever that price is
    [*]Bidding / sniping at the very last moment does nothing, the 'nemesis' will simply bid again
    [*]The 'nemesis' will only stop bidding above some certain pre-set price, which for all different auction levels usually is around some set multiple of the starting price. For lvl 5's, it's in the 10k$ range.

[/list]

Method a): letting others bid against each other. I'd just wait, and around 4-5k$, the bar would go to almost zero. I snipe it at the very latest moment, meaning that the NPC would have gotten the container for that price. However, this NPC will outbid me all the way up to ~10k, where at some point he will let me have it.

Method b): getting a bid in early, letting the others bid against each other until the container would go, and then sniping it myself. Again, the 'nemesis' will take over. I'd try to scare them with a few maximum bids of +400 and +800 - it doesn't matter. He will outbid me with 80-160 until the price is over 10k. 

Methoc c) [SUPERSNIPER]: getting a bid in early, and then trying to go to the 'nemesis' stage as early as possible. Usually happens when I outbid someone anywhere within the period where the auctioneer starts counting down. From this point on, I'd [b]only and exclusively bid on the very last moment with the lowest amount possible[/b]. The 'nemesis' would outbid me literally every time. 

[b][u]This auction lasted literally til 09:38PM ingame because it took so comically long.[/u][/b] Lol. 

Blind auctions: super clear that you're supposed to bid triple the starting price. You can bid slow, fast, whatever, right now I just speedrun them by bidding above 1500$ as quickly as I can, and then my next 80$ bid always gets it.

You can even turn on "hard" mode, which basically adds the risk of the AI bidders trying to bait you into paying exorbitant amounts for a locker, but you can easily spot it and walk away, because there is always another auction just around the corner.

Adding to this, the roster of items in the game is truly staggering, even after my full ~50hr playthrough, winning hundreds of auctions, buying every pawn shop, house and truck currently in game with a fully decorated and decked out mansion, there were still auctions at the end where I was finding items I hadn't seen before. It was early in its release, the controls felt like they were held together with duct tape, and I bounced off it hard. A few months later, I decided to give it another shot — and to my surprise, I actually had some fun... for a few hours.

Then the repetition set in. Fast. Like, “wait, didn’t I just do this?” fast. By the 10-hour mark, things were already feeling samey; by 30 hours, it was downright unbearable. I finally put the game on the shelf permanently at 36 hours — partly out of mercy for myself, and partly because I was starting to play it in my dreams (and not in a good way).

The tutorials? Practically nonexistent. You’ll end up Googling things you didn’t even know you needed to Google. I don’t mind figuring things out, but when I need an internet degree just to understand a core mechanic, it stops being immersive and starts feeling like homework.

And don’t even get me started on the auction system. During higher-level auctions (like level 5), NPCs will snipe your bid at the last second — over and over — until you question your life choices. I once spent 10 real-life minutes (3 in-game hours) fighting the AI over items that weren’t even worth half of what they bid them up to. I eventually gave up and assumed this was the game’s way of teaching me the valuable life lesson of “you can’t win them all.” Very philosophical. Not very fun.

Achievements? Half of them might as well be encrypted. Even the internet has collectively shrugged in defeat trying to figure out how to unlock some of them.

In short: I was honestly torn between giving this a positive or negative review. There is some fun to be had early on, and I can see the potential underneath. But ultimately, the negatives outweigh the positives. The repetition sets in fast, the mechanics overstay their welcome, and the fun eventually grinds to a halt.

If you can grab it on sale and want a few evenings of light entertainment, it might be worth a spin. Unfortunately, that rarely happens.

Even the Normal difficulty is straight-up unplayable:
1. Auction start prices are insanely high for no reason, often higher than the combined value of all items inside.
2. NPCs ramp prices into the stratosphere like they're billionaires with nothing better to do regularly drive bids to double the actual item value.

Since unlocking Tier 2 and 3, this problem has become extreme. It makes absolutely no sense to participate in an auction when the starting price is already above the total worth, or an NPC instantly rockets the price into absurd territory. We had to cancel around 70% of all auctions, and the ones we finished often ended with a small payout of about 0$ - 100$. Sometimes we made $600–$700 losses. That completely kills the flow and fun of the game.


The grind is enormous:
1. Tool upgrades cost ridiculous amounts of money if you consider the the amount of money you get in auctions.
2. There are no small rewards to keep you motivated. We have never found an item with a slightly higher value in a lower-level auction to boost morale and our progress. It’s just a long, exhausting uphill battle.


Then there's the prototype Multiplayer: (A lot of frustrating bugs)
1. Sometimes no items spawn at all during auctions. (Reload required)
2. FPS can drop to around 6 because the game can’t handle a box full of junk on your truck while driving. (You have to come to a full stop every few 100 meters)
3. We lost $700 after reloading a save thanks to a lovely little bug.
4. Items can get stuck after selling a box that contained them. (They despawn after reloading the save, all money lost)
5. Sometimes the truck can't drive faster than 16km/h. (Reload required)


The graphics are… UE5 standard I quess. Not completely terrible, but definitely not good. There’s ghosting without TSR, and an overall smearing and dithering look that really brings the experience down.
Performance is good, but not impressive. (Better than a lot of other UE5 games)

To be fair: searching the map was fun, and you can find some genuinely cool stuff. But that tiny spark of fun doesn’t make up for the mountain of problems.


But right now?
The systems don’t work together, the economy is completely broken, and the bugs make it worse.

Storage Hunter Simulator is a game that will definitely appeal to fans of simulation games, especially those who enjoy a grindy experience. The premise is simple yet satisfying: you bid on abandoned storage units, then rummage through them to find valuable items you can sell for a profit. It’s an addictive loop of buying, digging through, and selling, which makes it a lot of fun if you’re into this type of simulation. The grind is rewarding and provides a sense of progression that keeps me hooked.

🎮 Gameplay
The gameplay mechanics are straightforward. You bid on storage units, find valuable items hidden inside, and sell them for a profit. The grind aspect adds depth to the gameplay, making it incredibly satisfying as you work towards earning money to bid on bigger units. The graphics are decent—not groundbreaking, but they create a solid experience. The environments and items are well-designed, and the overall presentation is polished for the type of game it is. Though repetitive, the loop of bidding, rummaging, and selling never gets old and keeps me engaged.

🔑 Conclusion
In conclusion, Storage Hunter Simulator is a fun and satisfying game, especially for fans of grindy simulation experiences. The core mechanics are simple yet engaging, and the progression system keeps things rewarding. The demo/prologue is a nice way to test out the game, but be aware that it doesn’t showcase everything the full version has to offer. If you're a fan of simulation games with a grind, it's definitely worth a try.

For the most part, any coop horror game I've played seemed like it would simply be better as a solo experience. That was before Lethal Company dropped. 

Lethal Company took what looked to be a repetitive, formulaic extraction coop game and blew me away. It works beautifully solo, and only gets better playing with friends.

This is true *survival horror*. So much so I half expected to find a pair of bolt cutters somewhere. You are not just a fly on the wall experiencing a scripted jump scare or traveling down a series of spooks "on rails" to reach your objective. Your knowledge of the game, it's design, enemy mechanics, and use of tools are essential to success. It's anything but RNG (though you will get fucked by seeds once in a while). Every game plays out differently, and each scare feels unique to that game.  

This is the only coop survival game that can go from hilarious to terrifying in seconds. You'll be talking with your friends over proximity chat through a maze, laughing about the dumbas that got squashed by a trap when some jackal pulls the apparatus early and the lights go out. You're both still laughing, though, until there's a crack, thump and silence. You'll call their name out and be met with darkness. Now you're alone, and you don't remember exactly how you made it this deep into the map anyway.

The sound design alone is a huge part of what makes LC scary, and it's done really well. Great example being the dial tone on the phone; that shit has no right sounding that way, especially if the rest of your crew is dead and you can still hear footsteps outside the ship.

At first glance, it looks like a simple indie horror game, but after a few sessions with friends, it became one of the most entertaining co-op games I’ve played in a long time.

The game thrives on teamwork. Whether you’re scavenging deep inside an eerie industrial complex or guiding your crew from the ship, success depends on communication and coordination. It’s not just about surviving—it's about how you and your friends react under pressure, and those moments lead to some of the most genuinely funny and chaotic gameplay I've experienced.

The tone walks a fine line between tension and absurdity. While the atmosphere can get genuinely creepy, it never feels overly serious. Monsters are terrifying, but it's the unpredictability of your team that makes things really fun. One second you’re sneaking through a dark hallway, and the next you’re sprinting back to the ship while everything falls apart. Somehow, even the failures are entertaining.

It’s also incredibly easy to pick up. The controls are straightforward, and the game doesn’t overwhelm you with complicated systems. But there’s just enough strategy to make each run feel meaningful—whether it’s deciding what equipment to bring, when to cut your losses, or how to maximize your earnings before the ship takes off.

The randomized maps, shifting enemy behavior, and different weather conditions keep things fresh. Every mission feels a little different, and the tension never completely fades, even after dozens of hours. On top of that, the developers are clearly invested in improving the game, and the community is active and full of creative energy.

I recommend Lethal Company because it captures something a lot of games miss—it’s genuinely fun to fail. It turns panic into laughter and chaos into memorable stories. Whether you’re playing with close friends or jumping into a game with strangers, it delivers an experience that feels unpredictable, alive, and worth coming back to. alot of the dlcs should just be added as updates instead", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1756455563}, {"review_text": "Assuming you have no DLC packs, the game starts out slow. You begin as a level 1 hunter with a measly .243 rifle, only the best placed shots can take down medium sized game. You might spend a lot of time wrapping your head around the game mechanics as well as track a bunch of wounded animals at first, but soon you will start making some money and filling out your perk trees. I was left with a bad impression of the progression system at first but the strength you feel during the mid and late game definitely pays off. 

At the writing of this review, I have 170 hours of play time. I only have 1 / 19 maps completely explored. I chose to do the Layton Lake District map first (soon I will explain why I regret this decision)  and I have that map 100% explored and about 90% of the missions completed, so there is still more work to nickel and dime there as well. I hope this gives an accurate representation of just how much playtime you can get out of one map. I am currently working on exploring the Hirschfelden map and I have it ~60% completed with many missions left to go. At this rate, each of the 19 maps is offering me around 100-150 hours of gameplay, and even if I complete every mission there is nothing stopping me from continuing to hunt on the map.

I want to use this last bit here to share a few tips to anyone going into the game fresh. Earlier I stated I played the Layton Lake District map first. In hindsight, I would have much rather done Hirschfelden first because the map has more game animals that can be taken down by your free starting rifle and ammo, as well as many birds that can be hunted with the base shotgun (although this will come at a cost of the weapon itself and ammo). So in my experience, I started off on the harder of the two base maps which lead to me leveling up more slowly but also working harder. If you are playing a new vanilla game with no DLCs, please do yourself a favor and start off with hunting a bunch of Roe Buck and Red Fox on Hirschfelden Reserve. If you are willing to buy DLC weapons and maps, then by all means go crazy and start wherever you wish. My last piece of advice, there are two very powerful perks you want to acquire asap, which is Zeroing and Sight Spotting. Zeroing allows you to change the range your scope is zeroed in at with the press of a button. For example, for rifles it can be cycled between 75 m, 150 m, and 300 m, allowing you to take very precise shots at three preset distances. Sight Spotting allows you to mark and leave an outline on animals temporarily, especially useful when hunting at night. This mechanic can always be achieved with your binoculars, but this perk allows you to avoid the hassle of rotating between your binoculars and firearm, saving precious seconds. 

So yeah, I like this game a lot. I got a very good vanilla experience from the game before spending about $150 USD on DLC for this game during the summer sale. I would not be surprised if I accumulate 1,000 hours of playtime in the future. I grew up playing Cabela's hunting games on my PS2, then Hunting Unlimited for PC when I was older, and now playing Call of the Wild as an adult feels like the perfect way to progress this hobby.

The reason I'm saying this is because of the grind mechanic that becoming more and more prevalent with each new updated.

The game is absolutely beautiful. The animals look good enough and they're challenging enough to track and hunt to make it a fun game. My absolute favorite way to play is to go into a park and walk around to see what I find. I favor things with antlers, like deer and elk, so it is always exciting to see a red deer with an impressive rack walk by.

Now here is the issue; animal spawns are RNG based and set in such a way "rare" spawns (like albino and melanistic) are... well, very rare. You might be under the impression that, if you walk around for long enough, you will see these rare spawns, but the reality is that there is no guarantee that there is a single special animal in your population files at all. Your park could have not a single rare spawn at all, so you will spend hours walking around, seeing the same basic colored animals over and over again.

The only way to make the game spawn rare animals is to remove animals from the population so it has to spawn a new animal, and if you get lucky, it might be one of the 0.051% chance of getting an albino wolf, with the odds for Great Ones being likely even lower. People have gone on literal grinds of THOUSANDS of animals trying to get a Great One to spawn. There are 8 species in the game that can spawn a Great One, and 5 of these have multiple colors, 6 in the case of moose, 8 in pheasants, 7 in red fox and so on.

The way efficient grinding works is to set up tents near drink zones, teleport to the tent, cull certain leveled maled, reset time, got to another drink zone and repeat the whole process over and over and over again. It's tedious, to the point yesterday I realized I wasn't enjoying the game any more. I wasn't doing what I loved about the game, I was lost in a repetitive, boring task that made it feel like a job, not a leisurely game to disconnect and have some fun. There is something very wrong when a game makes you feel like you're working.

Not only that, but in a game that's basically a hunting simulator, a grind mechanic as the one describes completely destroys any immersion. To me, walking around the park and encountering that rare spawn without expecting it has always had far more value and been more exciting than grinding my way until the albino wolf appears. In the first case, seeing the rare spawn was awe-inspiring. In the second, it was more as relief. "Finally the thing has spawned!". No awe, no wonder, just relief that I was able to move on and do something else instead of the boring, repetitive grind. In my opinion, immersion is everything in a game like this.

Spawns should be common enough to be rare, but not unicorn rare, and they should appear in normal gameplay, not spawn after a tedious grind, or not at all (since the chance of them naturally spawning is VERY, VERY LOW). I understand making the game challenging, but challenging would be giving the Great One enhanced detection skills to the point it'd require a very skilled stalker to even approach to shooting range. Perhaps making it move all over the map so it's harder to track. Lowering the spawn rate so it forces you to shoot 5,000 whitetails while you camp their need zones is not challenging, it's just time-consuming and tedious.

Lets not forget something, these are games. We play these to disconnect from real life, to do the things we can't do in real life, to live a fantasy. Most hunters will never encounter an exceptionally colored animal in the wild, but that's precisely where games come in to play, to give you the chance to live that fantasy. Games should be challenging, but not mimic real life. Nobody plays Skyrim to have their same 8 to 5 accountant job.

I love the game, but I honestly think they need to take a step back and stop using mindless grinding and exaggerated rare spawns to boost game engagement. A game should NEVER expect its players a dedication akin to having a job just to have a chance at triggering the spawn of a rare animal. You walk through the early morning fog, hear the distant call of a deer, and the entire experience feels almost meditative. Unfortunately, the moment you progress into the endgame and encounter the Great One grind mechanic, that atmosphere completely dissolves. What begins as a hunting game slowly turns into systematic map resetting and mechanical herd elimination. Not because it’s enjoyable, but because the game has no other meaningful way to reward your time.

Yes... The Great One is not the pinnacle of hunting mastery. It is merely the outcome of statistics. It does not matter how skilled you are, all that matters is how many times you repeat the same action. In practice, this is not hunting. It is an endless loop of teleporting from tent to tent, skipping time forward, and repeatedly shooting the same spot at a lake. The immersive hunting experience turns into a logistics routine. You are just resetting the world and waiting for RNG to finally give in.

It feels like a mechanic imported from an entirely different genre more fitting for titles like Diablo, Path of Exile, WoW or Lineage II, where spending hundreds of hours farming for a rare drop is part of the core identity of the game. The difference is that those games are built around that grind and openly embrace it. But this presents itself as a hunting game. In this context, the grind doesn’t feel like a challenge. It feels like a design flaw. A system that punishes players for trying to play authentically and forces them into repetitive behavior that goes against the spirit of the genre.

And that is the real disappointment. There should be a better way. It should not be the result of how efficiently you can teleport around a lake. I think that this mechanic needs to be reworked so rare animals can be somehow discovered through organic gameplay rather than pure statistical repetition (And NO. I do not accept a 0.00001% chance as meaningful game design). Until that happens, this will stand as a symbol of how a visually stunning and atmospheric game can undermine itself by replacing immersion with routine.

[{"review_text": "Sparking zero could easily be the best Dragon Ball game ever made, if only the developers had taken more care and fully embraced its potential.

I’ve been waiting this game for years, probably over a decade. 
My favorite Dragon Ball game is Budokai Tenkaichi 3 and I played it a lot. This new game feels like BT3 with Super characters, some minor gameplay changes and unfortunately a few missing characters that really should’ve been added as DLC by now.
The story mode was fine, it included some what if scenarios that I really enjoyed. Honestly, I wish the game focused entirely on this direction, because replaying the same story over and over in every game is boring, at least for me. Still, it’s better than nothing.
Custom Battle is amazing. I knew right away I’d spend a lot of hours into it, recreating the what ifs I used to watch on YouTube, imagining in my head or discussing with friends. It could definitely be improved, but even as it is, it gives the game infinite replay value for me.

Now for the negatives.
Online was ridiculously unbalanced at launch and the developers took way too long to fix it, which drove away 90% of the player base. The game desperately needs more gamemodes (like Survival, Mission 100 or additional what if stories) as well as new outfits and accessories for all characters. The customization potential would be incredible: imagine Goku in old Saiyan armor or Frieza dressed as Goku with a saiyan tail. Some characters don’t even have a second outfit, which is unacceptable considering even BT3 gave everyone at least one alternate color.
The DLC situation is also very bad. The release time is way too slow. By now, we should’ve had most GT characters, full Daima, and maybe even some unique what if fighters like Gohan Black or Gohkan.

Do I recommend this game?
Yes but only on sale. It’s still a great Dragon Ball experience and it has the potential to become probably the best. 
But unless the developers do something, mods are the only way to experience the game’s true potential.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1757187085}, {"review_text": "Historically bad post launch support. It *shouldn't be* a live service game. imo the only reason it *has* online is because fans would bitch and moan if it didn't. But it's built upon a foundation that cares much more about delivering a fun Dragon Ball experience to play alone or with friends than it does about ranked ladders.

And it's more of an Action RPG / fighter hybrid, whereas this is an Arena fighter. I'm glad that both exist, and we even have FighterZ for that classic 2d fighting feel. tl;dr: This is a Dragon Ball fanservice sandbox, as it should be, not an online competitive fighting game. If that's what you want then you'll have a great time and I 100% recommend it. The biggest issue ailing this game is expectations. Many people bought into the hype too much and ended up disappointed as a result. So let me tell you what I expected: A fun single player offline anime arena fighter with a large cast of characters. And Sparking Zero delivers perfectly on that front! It's got so many characters (180ish in the base roster and 200+ with DLC) covering so many aspects of this great series. Z, Super, GT, Daima, and a little bit of OG DB as well! Basically every important and iconic character is in here and they look beautiful. Their animations are gorgeous and they feel great to play!

Something I think that gets overlooked now is just how high quality the animations are in this game. Not only is the roster massive, but every character has unique Super and Ultimate attack animations! Even when two characters share a technique (like Super Kamehameha), it's animated slightly differently. It's a great bit of attention to detail that separates Sparking Zero from games like BT3 and XV2 where animations are copy/pasted in their entirety. (And that isn't a bad thing at all! But it's nice that this game doesn't do that.)

I'm someone who grew up playing Raging Blast 2 and Tenkaichi Tag Team. My favorite thing to do was to go into an offline battle, select my characters and my opponent's characters, and fight against the CPU. It's what I've come to love about this series. Sparking Zero lets me do that but with a LOT more characters.

I never really cared for online play. It's not my thing. But that's where many fans are disappointed, specifically regarding Ranked Mode. Ranked Matches set up the expectations that there will be some amount of balancing so that both players are fighting at an equal level. But that's not what Tenkaichi is. Tenkaichi is built to be a game about power levels and the disparity between a weak character and a strong one. And that's what Sparking Zero is, too. The Ranked Mode in Sparking Zero isn't a balanced environment where both players are given the same tools for victory. If you want that then you should look into Dragon Ball FighterZ. Sparking Zero's Ranked Mode is tacked on in comparison. It isn't a balanced ranked experience. It's a ranked mode for an unbalanced game. This is what leads players to call for nerfs to system mechanics. They expect this game to conform to their expectations of Sparking Zero being a balanced competitive game rather than accepting that this game was never intended to be competitive.

So don't come to this game expecting it to be balanced. It isn't. It was never intended to be. That's what the draw of the Tenkaichi series is. But do expect a pick up and play casual game that's great solo or with friends. column30:
[{"review_text": "GRIDLESS BUILDING
Not many gridless village builders.  This one is one of the best especially with the new customization options and sandbox settings.  
Generate your own maps as well.

TRY IT BEFORE YOU BUY IT
Oh and there is a demo.  Devs who include demos for their games deserve extra kudos IMO. 

8 thumbs up.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1738339669}, {"review_text": "Ok, so.

The game is good, but it COULD be great. I'm hesitating to recommend or not-recommend the game, but while I enjoyed my time on it, I'll likely not play before the next update(s), because of the frustration it induces... and still recommend it.

The obvious pros: the game is cute, it's a city builder, with organic behavior of the citizens. Sound design is excellent. Modular buildings are a GREAT mechanism.  Unlock tree is ok even if the system feels a bit artificial (I end up placing like a hundred bushes near the right type of building to unlock things).

After a while unlocking new stuff, seeing my pops and buildings have more requirements, I started to feel something like the fun I felt when I played Caesar III, decades ago... but at a smaller scale, as the game does not seem well optimized, and struggles to run a few hundred citizens.

Aaaand now, here is the issue. 

Just like in old games and any good city builder, the mechanisms require you to optimize some stuff, so that your peasant can satisfy their needs, but here it gives you almost no tool to do it properly. The logistics issues are hard to understand and impossible to debug because you can't really control where people will store stuff, where people will sell stuff, you can't prioritize jobs, you can't really steer people to given neighbourhoods when areas lack workers when others don't and people will do 15 km to fetch food, which prevents them to go to work...

People are unhappy because they don't have access to basic stuff that are on sale 15m from them, and FINDING what's wrong is inexplicably hard. My houses are degrading, why? no way to know. Wheat does not go from storage to mill, why? no way to know. My bailiff always quits the city even when happy, why ? no way to know. Can I prioritize stone for road paving over house rerererererebuilding ? Not that I can see...

There are also quite a lot of bugs which are not all game breaking but still give an impression of an unfinished or unpolished game, but really my main remark would be this : *if you want me to build a nice city with hundreds of citizens and knights and monks with needs, give me tools to do it properly. I cannot click on individuals and buildings in the whole map, so at some scale of city I'll need to have an map overview of who does not have water, service, or whatever, of which buildings lacks what and why (is it production ? logistics ? can I fix it with more storage ? hiring more people ? where ?) Where are people going to get their food ? their clothes ? How much time does it take them that they don't use to work, and why can't I compensate that by hiring more people in that underutilized building ? People tell me they can't find a home, but all the homes around have lots of empty room, what exactly are you looking for and where ? and so on and so forth*

Basically, QoL for big cities is not there (yet ?).

Ah, and the other bad UX thing for me which gets me to eye roll is the "click on something happening at some precise point on the map before a timer" aspects, which really reminds me of bad mobile games and, imo, has nothing to do on a PC city builder. I'm *designing a city*, so I don't want to move all over the map to welcome three new citizens, just find yourself a home already, yes I need you or I would have specified it in an immigration policy. Emissary of abbess/king/whatever ? Just show me the event or show up on the side of the screen, I was *busy* trying to sort out wood logistics 30 seconds of map scrolling to the west, please. Also, having to micro my three main people who do the missions to get progress and new people, why ? just get on a loop of $mission and give me mental time to plan quarries; and having to micro the lvlup of citizens to optimize jobs, please nooo ... I have money, just auto-upgrade whoever works as a tax collector or whatever, auto-upgrade a random monk when I have 5 books, auto-upgrade soldiers, etc. 

For me, the ultimate goal of a cute city-builder is to get to the point of being able to just visit the map and look around, and the city Works. See logistics flows, money gets in, people get around, go in, take free jobs and live their lives. All microgestion prevents that, and knowing the game will never let me just "enjoy what I built without having anything to click on to get it to run" is a frustration.

Overall, yes, it's a good cute city builder. You can build small villages. But for now, the lack of QoL and the forced microgestion of pops means it cannot reach the "zen" point of truly great citybuilders where you can just stop, look at your megalopolis, and enjoy looking at details of your creation or do building micro-adjustments for hours.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1745618558}, {"review_text": "So, uh, they removed the weather system and there is no natural day/night cycle. 

Fun game, but whyyyyyyy remove such little things that create immersion?", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1763173497}, {"review_text": "This is a tough review because I really like the game. Unfortunately, the game's current state is abysmal. If this game was still in early access, I would be able to recommend it based on where it is now. However, I am concerned about this games future given the Dev's decision to launch this "1.0" build.

The game-play is fun but all the systems and supply chains are very shallow. Each movie only has 4 levels and they don't really feel as fleshed out as other Lego games. The plots for each movie are super abridged to accommodate for the short length of the campaign, neutering the story in favour of most of the plot taking place in the open world. About 60-70% of the story takes place in the open world, not in levels. Most of the 'gameplay' in the open world is walking through empty locations following objective markers to get to the next plot point, and that also suffers from a lot of backtracking and time wasting. The game is bloated and padded to hell and back to hide how little variation there is in the game.

The new additions to the game such as the enhanced combat feel unnecessary with how bland the level design is. Most enemies barely pose a threat to you, and that's not even considering the fact that death is pointless in Lego games as you instantly respawn with a few less studs.

Despite how this is meant to be a love letter to classic Lego games like The Complete Saga, they still don't capture the spirit of the originals since most of the cutscenes are just 1-1 recreations of their respective movie scenes but with Lego Minifigures, whereas fans of Complete saga enjoy it for the non-spoken slapstick comedy storytelling. They added the "mumble mode" extra but that doesn't address the root problem as the cutscenes are still 80% dialogue but the characters are just gagged now and make noises instead.

The game's development was plagued with tight work schedules and crunch culture, leading to a lot of scrapped content and the game being a buggy mess on launch, which it still is as the game barely got any bugfix patches in favour of adding several waves of DLC characters that aren't even voice acted, instead resorting to generic grunting noises.

Theres not really replayability to the open hub worlds, they mostly feel kind of empty. It's neither noticeably interconnected, nor clearly separated - both approaches having their respective advantage. A strange in-between. I don't understand why you would cut the bread and butter part of LEGO Star Wars games (missions) so much, only to give us huge hubs with little to fill them.

I don't really like the bossfights being so scripted, forcing you into repetitive QTE's. They are creative, but it feels like you just work your way through preconceived patterns where you don't really have any freedom or choice. The camera lock adds to that. Either give us camera lock outside of bossfights or have it the old school way: only on transitions. I found the camera a pretty big downside of the game in general, it's way too close for me and it can get very messy/clippy in certain puzzle situations (stacking orange boxes for example). I think the old LEGO game style camera was better, including co-op mode without a split screen. It's cool that player two can go miles away on their own, but why would I want to do that. It feels way less cooperative in my opinion.

The game looks great, the audio seems quiet to me in comparison to other games.

Having no main hub area in the game is criminal, especially after what the old games did with Mos Eisley. Your unlocked characters just moving around in the area, starting fights or searching for your favourite figure was so much fun, you often didn't even have to play missions to have a great time.

Also, not being able to create your own unique character out of unlocked LEGO parts really feels like a loss here. I don't get this decision.

Lastly, the menu system is a mess. You have multiple types of menus, sub menus, sub-sub menus, it's very unintuitive (e.g. you have to press Select again to close the map instead of the B-button, which only brings you back one layer) and bloated - there is just way too much stuff.

having clone wars, rebels, mandalorian and even solo series characters but not even their side quests? I mean it might be so greedy to ask for an entire gamemode (story line? idk) for each of these DLCs but we would appreciate at least some side quests or some maps for these characters.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1757347893}, {"review_text": "Terrible game, an absolute shadow of its former self in the older Lego Star Wars game (The Complete Saga), due to switching to an open world theme over the actual levels. Don't get me wrong, open world is great and all, but it should never overshadow the rightful place of the levels being the main theme in the game. 
My issue with this game is: The levels are FAR too short! 5-10 minutes each, seriously???????? And the worst part is, the levels don't even take you through the whole story line, like the Complete Saga did, instead, these tiny levels only happen at certain parts in the story, with the majority of the story playing out in cut-scenes. When it was doing a cut-scene of Amidala and her troops storming the city, I was sitting there, thinking, "Come on, let me in, I want to play as them now, doing this, when can I participate, already?!" :D But, nah...instead, it rudely held me captive in the cut-scene, only letting me play when Darth Maul stepped in. Grrrrr.....boooo :P 

Rather than actually being able to play the game in the story-line, I spent the majority of the time travelling great distances in the open world to get to the location to start the levels, only to find, it just lasted a tiny 5-10 minutes....then, after that tiny window, had to run a marathon to get the next level location again. Nope, sorry, didn't even finish the Star Wars 2 chapter, and already threw in the towel in this game. Because, if the rest of the game is clearly gonna be like this, favouring open world over the levels, then count me out. I'm going back to the classic older games, like Star Wars the Complete Saga, or really any of the older Lego games that don't neglect the levels in a way that would make it be unequal with the amount of open world exploration.

The problem with making open world the main theme of the game, over the levels, is: So, you finish the game, got all collectibles in the open world, and the levels. Then what? What does the open world now have to offer? Nothing, just scenery, with no objectives, giving no incentive to keep playing. Whereas, with the levels, when you have the opportunity to play them again and again in free play mode as many times as you want -  playing as the characters yourself, I would specifically add, not be pulled or sped through in cut-scenes - that provides the appeal that makes you want to come back for more. 
Except, since the levels in this game are in such as a poor state, by being too short for you to actually enjoy the game, or process what is going on in the game, because it skips the majority of important events, it's not even worth playing again, in free play mode. No one wants to sit through the majority of the game watching cut-scenes, when you could otherwise spend it playing. 

If you want to have an enjoyable experience in Lego games, I strongly advise not to get any Lego games like this, that focus so much on an open world experience, that they neglect the importance of the levels. The levels in any lego game should always remain the top priority of the Lego games, because at the end of the day, that's what you will have left to engage in, at the end of the game, when everything is done. The levels should, at minimum, be 20 minutes long, and happen at all points in the story-line, otherwise, it feels like things are going too fast. The cut-scenes should only take up a small fraction of this game, only triggering at the conclusion of the levels, not playing through the majority of it....I want to take the wheel myself, and be able to play as these characters, don't need the cut scenes to skip ahead and automatically do the job for me, thank you :D

I'd strongly recommend the older Lego games, such as Star Wars the Complete Saga, Pirates of the Caribbean, Lord of the Rings, Marvel Superheroes 1, because these all provide a far more enjoyable experiences. Especially the Superheroes one, because it offers just as much fun in the levels as it does with the open world. Something's gone very wrong with this one, sheesh.....too much open world, not enough time for levels. 
This game seriously reminds me of 'strike rushers' in Destiny 2....people who just rush past all the enemies in a multiplayer mode called Strikes, speeding through all the story and fun, to complete the game as soon as possible. Just like that ruins their teammates' experience, who want to take the time to actually enjoy the game, this game achieves the same result: Speeding through the story-line in the form of automatic cut-scenes is not just fair or fun to the people out there who actually want to take the time to enjoy the game, in the levels. But this game does not allow that, unfortunately. 

My advice to the devs of any future Lego games: Just move back to the classics, please. Include open world, if you will, because that in itself is a great change, but don't focus on it so much that it completely discards the levels. To provide the best experience in any Lego game, the amount of time levels and open world take up in the game should always be equal with each other, otherwise, it just feels too unbalanced on either side.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1739927942}, {"review_text": "The Skywalker Saga is easily the most ambitious and technically impressive LEGO game to date. The sheer scope of its open-world design is staggering, featuring a vast array of explorable planets, detailed environments, and a level of polish that surpasses any previous entry in the series. The combat is deeper, the visuals are stunning, the voice acting is well-done, and the game’s structure is a massive step up in terms of presentation and storytelling.

That said, the shift toward open-world gameplay comes at a cost. While the exploration is fun and filled with side content, the classic linear levels that made The Complete Saga so memorable take a backseat. Missions feel shorter and less structured, making the experience feel unfocused compared to the tight, replayable design of the older games. It’s clear why they leaned into open-world design, it’s a modern trend, and the amount of work poured into it is impressive... but in doing so, they lost part of what made LEGO Star Wars so fun in the first place.

I wish The Skywalker Saga had struck a better balance between open-world exploration and structured linear levels. As it stands, I feel like I need to play this, The Complete Saga, and LEGO Star Wars III: The Clone Wars just to get the full experience. A hybrid approach, with more dedicated linear levels alongside the open-world hubs, could have made this the definitive LEGO Star Wars game.

Just the fact that you can finish The Phantom Menace and have only fought about 15 battle droids perfectly encapsulates my issue with this game.  For example, it’s great that you can revisit Naboo during The Clone Wars as Anakin and Padmé to help Captain Panaka clear out remnant battle droids... those kinds of ideas for side content are fantastic. They make each movie feel like a mid-sized RPG if you engage with the side content as it unlocks. But because everything has to take place in open-world areas, the combat encounters are never more than a small group of battle droids shooting in the middle of a town square... there are no handcrafted combat scenarios. Hell, I'd even be happy just to have Complete Sagas levels directly ripped out and plopped into this game alongside the hubs. As it stands, it feels like a game that’s only hubs.

Overall, it's an incredible technical achievement with tons of content, but the lack of classic linear levels leaves a gap that previous games still fill better.  I want to stress that I do recommend this game, what's on offer here is awesome, it's SO MUCH FUN flying around the galaxy, exploring the ridiculous number of planets they recreated, but having played many of the other Lego games, it really leaves a lot to be desired for someone like me, who appreciated single player games ability to have tight linear design.  

Think Skyrim, without the linear dungeons, that's what this game feels like to me, and it's a problem I have with the vast Majority of open world games, even masterpieces like Witcher 3 still suffer from the same problem. Breath of the Wild, a game I have put an easy thousand hours into, has the same problem.  Too much focus on the open world, not enough focus on linear areas. Before you buy the game on sale, consider the following.
First of all, the game: 6/10.
Worth playing despite a negative review?
Answer: Yes.
___________
However, consider these thing. Starting with the negatives: 
1. Story
Like other reviewers have said, I feel the same. If you liked the old Lego Star Wars games — especially on PS2, or even Star Wars III — then Disney's/Lego’s version is laughably bad in comparison, both to the games and the movies. It feels like the devs didn’t bother watching the films or playing the old games. Instead, it’s like they skimmed some TL;DR on Reddit written by someone with major memory gaps. No, the story doesn’t follow the old Lego games. That’s fine — Disney wants their own take. Totally fair.
But not sticking to the movie scripts? Skipping scenes? Making stuff up? That’s not okay. Examples? Sure. Some scenes are just cut — like the little black trunk guy who calls in stormtroopers when Solo, Ben, Luke, Chewie, R2 and 3PO leave Mos Eisley. JUST GONE??!
Other times the plot is just wrong — like Solo and another soldier finding Luke in the Wampa cave. That never happens in the movie. Bottom line: If you’ve played the old games or seen the movies, the story will annoy you — especially anything from Episodes I–VI.

2. length of chapters
Also, like others have said, each chapter is really short — around 5 to 10 minutes. Personally, I don’t mind that much. I think each level still does its job, and the game is interactive enough that it doesn’t feel too annoying.But I get why others think it’s too short, especially with all the long cutscenes. In the old games, a chapter could last anywhere from 20 minutes to an hour, depending on how fast you were. What does bother me is how hard it is to get True Jedi in this game.Studs — which have always been a core part of LEGO games — are way too hard to collect now. You basically have to break everything in the level to get True Jedi, which just feels annoying instead of fun like in the older games.

3. PG3
Alright, listen. Am I complaining that the game is made for kids? No, not at all. The old games were also rated PG3 — easy to play, fun for both kids and adults. Great. But if this game is PG3, then I don’t even know what rating the old ones should’ve had… 7+ maybe? Disney removes anything that looks like real danger or violence — even when that’s literally what the story is about. Why not handled in a similar way as the old games did — still kid-friendly, but kept at a good level. Some scenes are made so kid-friendly it’s almost embarrassing to watch. Even the shooting mechanics and lightsaber duels feel weirdly simplified.
Yes, there are more moves and better animations — but the feel just isn’t the same as the old games. IDK, maybe that’s just me being stuck in nostalgia.

4. The humor:
Last bit of criticism: the humor. Man, the humor in this game… I don’t even know where to start. I’m probably different from a lot of people here, since many actually liked it — and I did too, to a point. But that point is when literally every single cutscene has to include a joke. I’m not kidding. Every scene has some dragged-out joke or a gag just to cover something Disney didn’t want to show from the original story. And after a while, it just stops being funny — especially because all the jokes are basically the same.
I swear the devs must’ve laughed just as hard at every single one while making the chapters... Why not just do it like the old games? They had jokes too — but just enough, without taking away from the story. This version doesn’t feel like Star Wars.
_________________
If you’ve read all this and wonder how someone with this much criticism still thinks the game is worth buying and playing — yeah, I get you. But here’s the thing: the negative stuff is actually balanced out by a lot of positives.
Take the graphics, for example. They’re absolutely stunning, and work really well with the open world concept Disney added (which I honestly don’t mind). Way better than expected — even on my system, which is decent but nowhere near a 4090.
The voice lines also fit well, even if they’re a bit simplified. And I really like that you can access the upgrade and character menus from anywhere in the galaxy. Yeah, it’s a bit weird compared to the old cantina bar setup, where you bought everything. But here, having everything in one place is just… convenient.

Final words: I like Star Wars. I especially like the old Lego games. That’s probably why I still think this one’s worth playing.
Will it be the most amazing experience of your life? No. Will parts of it annoy you? YES, most likely. But is it still fun to have a full, modern Lego Star Wars game?
YES — hell yes it is.

Think it through. Then buy it.
// Glenn", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1742939246}, {"review_text": "Its a grind to 100% and get all the steam achievements, but overall fun game and I enjoyed it. Not because I don't know what to say about the game, but because I want these words to honour its excellence, without being hyperbolic but saying what I honestly think this game really is.

For years I heard this is the game with which gaming reached its adulthood. 
And it is true.

Sometimes it feels like being in a classic movie, such as Unforgiven. 
Also true.

I constantly felt I was comparing it to certain Cormac McCarthy's novels, specifically [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Border_Trilogy]The Border Trilogy[/url].
In fact one of the main themes of the game reminds me a lot of the ending of Cities on a Plain: how civilisation has no place for those who don't adapt to industrialism. It also felt many a time like [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_Meridian]Blood Meridian[/url], with all its cruelty.

But not only that. 
I constantly felt like being inside a Ken Burns documentary. From [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_West_(miniseries)]The West[/url] to [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_American_Buffalo]The American Buffalo[/url].

It goes without saying that RDR2 is a flawless representation of that period in history.
A true Academic document.

But there is more.
You can play the game and perceive a layer, let's say an action western or a movie.
But you can play it and fall into the study of nature, on a deeper level.
Or play it and pay attention to the small details, such as the conversations at the bonfire, or the journal...
and then you realise you stand before one of the most impressive accomplishments in the history of gaming.

Because just like a great novel can transform you after reading it, this "game" can have the same effect on you.

Which is why, after constraining my words for weeks, I think it is fair to say this is, in my humble opinion, 
the best videogame ever made.

I don't mean the one you, or me, or anyone, have to like it the most. 
I mean it in the sense that I don't think there is going to be something similar for a very long time, and we are very lucky for having it.

All of it makes the game feel strangely uplifting despite a lot of genuine tragedy within and the bittersweet nature of its ending.

The game is still an absolutely unbeaten marvel regardless. There is so much detail in here it's crazy. It solves the years-long "lovable characters turn into robotic NPCs outside of the campaign" problem by sheer brute force. Every last who-cares "collect ?/30" activity has a dedicated fully mocapped cutscene and some kind of story payoff.

Ah, Call of Duty. The game franchise that somehow manages to release the same game every single year, slap a different name on it, and still charge full price like it’s the second coming of gaming innovation.

Gameplay? Copy + Paste.
Every year it's:

Sprint → Slide → Jump → Die to some 12-year-old halfway across the world bunny-hopping with an MP5.

Respawn → Get killed by a camper in the corner → Rage.

That’s the real Call of Duty cycle. Forget skill — this game rewards whoever can mount their gun on a window ledge faster than you can say "broken hitboxes."

Maps? Recycled Garbage.
Remember that one map you liked from 10 years ago? Surprise, it's back! Only now it’s somehow worse. Either it's littered with a million objects that block movement or wide open fields where snipers thrive like mosquitoes in summer.

Skill-Based Matchmaking (SBMM) — aka SweatFest 3000
Trying to have fun? Not in this economy. The game sees you do well for ONE match and suddenly throws you into lobbies with professional esports wannabes rocking headsets more expensive than your console.

Microtransactions — The Real MVP
Want a cool skin? $20. Want that same skin but in a slightly different color? Another $20. Want to actually feel like content isn’t locked behind a paywall? Too bad.

It’s like they sat in a meeting and said, "How can we charge players for basic fun?"

Warzone? More like Bugzone.
Cheaters, invisible skins, broken guns, game crashes — it’s like a free-to-play FPS mixed with a beta test nobody asked for. Every patch fixes 1 bug and adds 3 new ones.

Final Verdict:
Call of Duty isn’t a game anymore — it’s a $70 annual subscription to rage, sweat, and disappointment. But somehow... we all keep playing it. The older Call of Dutys? Miles better. Black Ops 2, MW2, hell even Ghosts — they all feel like Michelin-star gourmet meals compared to this reheated gas station burrito of a game. Back then, you got smooth gameplay, working hit detection, and lobbies that didn’t implode mid-match. Now? The game crashes harder than the stock market in ‘29 and lags like I’m playing on a potato Wi-Fi signal from Mars.

You know it’s bad when I can smoke a whole ass bowl, clear my head, and STILL play older Call of Duty games like they’re brand new. I could literally get high enough to see Jesus, hop on MW2 from 2009, and have a smoother, more polished experience than this $70 war crime.

And the bugs? It’s like Activision went back to the Book of Exodus and took notes: plague of frame drops, plague of sound glitches, plague of invisible guns, plague of “Oops, you got booted to desktop for no reason.”

The social media team? Professional copy-pasters. “We hear you.” “We’re working on it.” “Stay tuned for updates.” Bro, the only thing you’re updating is my blood pressure. And support? Calling Activision support is like praying to the gaming gods during a hurricane — technically you can do it, but nothing’s going to happen.

AI is taking over, corporate greed is at an all time high, and now COD is shifting gears completely and mimicking Fortnite with the intention of bringing in the new generation of gamers while ostracizing the OG playerbase.

I won't lie, I don't have enough stake to talk about COD. My first COD game was Advanced Warfare. I never owned a PS3 or Xbox 360, so I never got to experience the Godsends like BO1/BO2, the MW trilogy. I went from AW, to Ghosts, to BO3 and so on. My opinion isn't completely valid and I understand that. 

However, it is undeniable that COD is completely dead in the water, and the fact that they are now completely catering to children, especially with them now requiring you to enter your DOB before playing to make sure you're not underage (an M rated game, mind you) is confirmation that the devs no longer care, and they want to make as much instant-gratification money as possible, instead of thinking long-term.

You guys are dirty.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1748688285}, {"review_text": "When I first played Mafia II, it was the original release, and it absolutely floored me. The storytelling hit hard, the cinematics were on point, and the whole presentation felt like sitting through a full Hollywood crime drama where I actually cared about everyone involved. It was stylish, emotional, polished, and honestly one of the most impressive narrative experiences of that generation. Then the Definitive Edition showed up like a long-lost cousin who says he’s here to help, but somehow steals your wallet and eats all your snacks.

For a remaster that was supposed to preserve and enhance the original, it manages to introduce issues that simply did not exist before. It is almost impressive in a chaotic, scientific way, like someone took the clean original code, shook it around like a snow globe, dumped half of it, then said, “Ship it.”

Starting in Chapter 3, during the stealth section where you infiltrate a government building to steal gas stamps, there’s a guard sitting in the lobby who apparently has supernatural powers. Every time I tried to stealth takedown this man, he pulled an alarm even as he was actively being strangled. Not after. Not before. During. As if his final act on Earth was to ruin your mission out of spite. The only real solution was to pretend he didn’t exist and move on.

Then Chapter 8 arrives, and suddenly the game decides it wants to be a slideshow. You show up at a rival gang’s meeting spot, ready to shoot the place up like a normal gangster, and the framerate drops harder than a car with bricks tied to it. It is the only part of the game that suffers this horribly, so it feels like PhysX just gave up and walked off the job.

By Chapter 10, Vito begins repeating his lines like he’s stuck in an existential loop, sometimes saying the same thing two or three times right after a cutscene. By Chapter 14, things escalate into full chaos when both Vito and Joe talk over each other during gameplay, like two actors whose microphones turned on at the same time and nobody bothered to fix it. It feels like half the dialogue triggers are firing out of sync, and no one made it back to clean them up before release.

Somewhere around Chapter 16, there is a cutscene involving Vito and another character I won’t spoil. What I will spoil is that this man’s eyes are permanently glued to the left for the entire scene. He never looks at Vito once. It is like he spotted a ghost and refused to acknowledge anything else happening around him. It completely derails the moment because you’re too busy wondering if he’s okay or if his face rig ran away.

Then there is the hat situation. If Vito wears a hat in some cutscenes, it will occasionally phase into his skull and reveal the glorious alpha hole inside, the one meant to prevent clipping. Instead, the hat clips, the head clips, and suddenly your smooth cinematic scene turns into a horror film about scalp mesh exposure. Half gangster drama, half biology lesson.

And then there is the rain. In the original game, tunnels protected you from the rain, because that is how tunnels work. In the Definitive Edition, rain now passes through concrete like it is made of sponge. You drive into a tunnel, and the rain just follows you in. The road stays wet the entire time, as if the tunnel roof is purely decorative. An immersion-breaking choice if I ever saw one.

The game still plays well, and the core story is just as strong as ever, but these issues pile up and constantly remind you that this is not the version anyone asked for. The inclusion of the Samson Drifter from Mafia III only adds to the confusion. The interior is low-resolution, clearly ported in without adjustments, and for a 1970’s muscle car, it handles like it is missing half its horsepower. It looks wrong, feels wrong, and drives worse than cars in the actual 1940s setting of the game.

So here is the honest truth: Mafia II is still fantastic, but the Definitive Edition is like watching a remastered movie where they redid the audio by recording it in a bathroom. But overall, I don't recommend.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1754411772}, {"review_text": "Mafia II is considered the best entry of the trilogy by many fans, yet ironically it's also the most straightforward and basic. In a landscape dominated by Grand Theft Auto and Saint's Row, Mafia II delivers arguably the finest crime story ever told in video game form. This is more than enough to overcome a standard gameplay loop and an open-world without much to do. It's a case of backdrop over sandbox, and context over player freedom. 

Vito Scaletta is an immigrant who yearns for the American Dream; a big house, fancy cars, comfortable living, the whole nine yards. He turns to a life of crime in the late 1940s and early 1950s, only to be used and exploited by just about everyone he comes across. There's this constant sense that he and his best friend Joe Barbarro never really get anywhere and this is reinforced by a careful structure and creative choices that reflect the protagonist's changing position. Across fifteen well directed chapters, the overall design puts you right in Vito's shoes; he is showered with money at one moment, only to lose it all the next.

Mafia II is far more gritty and unflinching than the original, a tale of loss, stagnation and grim consequences; something that runs counter to every other open-world game out there. The trifecta of third-person shooting, driving and stealth is present and accounted for. Once again it gets the job done with the plot being the main draw. You can buy clothes and guns, crush cars and take on wanted posters for some extra money, but the game always keeps you on task, waiting to drop the next big twist. When you're done, some extra DLC packs and collectables extend the game's length with Joe's Adventures being the best of the bunch, adding some extra detail to the narrative.

As for the Definitive Edition? It runs well enough, but there are some irritating glitches that dampen the immersion a bit. The environmental pop-in is the most glaring flaw, but I also encountered dialogue playing multiple times, strange looking facial expressions and a tailing mission that bugged out a couple of times when the target refused to move. Hanger 13 really should have remastered this game alongside its predecessor. You may want to stick to the 2010 original to experience Mafia II at its best, but if you're a fan of story-driven games, this title is a must-own.

My video retrospective on the Mafia trilogy can be viewed here: https://youtu.be/l7B123JuNZI?si=O1TARK0JWoP7rAoR", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1738790993}]

Assetto Corsa Competizione had promise. Initially, it delivered a reasonably authentic GT racing experience with solid physics and decent car handling. The version 1.9 update showed the developers could still produce meaningful improvements to the simulation aspects that made the game worthwhile for serious racing enthusiasts.

The Bad (Everything Since)
Unfortunately, Kunos Simulazioni have completely bollocked what was once a respectable racing simulator. The developers made the catastrophic decision to pivot away from their core audience—actual racing enthusiasts—and instead pandered to streamers and influencers who prioritise flashy content over authentic simulation.

Major Issues:
Abandoned Development: The last meaningful update was over a year ago. For a live-service racing game, this is absolutely unacceptable
Misguided Priorities: Streamers whined about realistic tyre wear being "too hard" because they couldn't flat-out thrash the car for entire races without consequences. So the developers neutered the tyre model to let content creators produce more "exciting" footage rather than maintain authentic racing strategy
Community Neglect: Long-standing issues reported by the racing community remain unaddressed whilst developers chased mainstream appeal

The Verdict
What was once a promising GT racing simulator has become a cautionary tale about developers losing sight of their purpose. The shift towards appealing to content creators rather than racing enthusiasts has resulted in a game that satisfies neither demographic effectively.
The extended development silence suggests Kunos have either moved on entirely or are planning some sort of reboot, but given their recent track record, neither prospect inspires confidence.
Do not recommend. Save your money and stick with other racing sims that still respect their core audience. Like Le Mans Ultimate or iRacing. Truly a MOBA experience of all time.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1756853673}, {"review_text": "I really wish to I could recommend this game, but with the state it's in and the direction (if there even is a direction) it's heading I think it's time to just move on to something else. 
I played the shit out of this game when the EGS gave away the early access for free and loved absolutly everything about it. It was clearly missing a whole bunch of stuff, it's early access after all, but they had a really solid base to build on.

But here we are now, over a year since the lukewarm release of 1.0 and the game is clearly having an identity crisis with deciding whether it wants to appeal to the MOBA crowd or the more casual hero shooter crowd.

The constant changes to the game's speed and attempts to lower match times is slowly killing the little bits left of the MOBA feeling this game had. It's as if the devs watched the success of marvel rivals and wanted to cannibalise their game into becoming a clone of that instead. 

The map has been a major complaint from the majority of the early access players, and the only thing we got was a few tiny changes that only serve to speed up the game further without addressing the problem. The map is tiny and cramped, it already allowed for rotations to go unpunished constantly, laning is barely a thing anymore with how badly you're punished if you don't follow and counter every enemy rotation , how fast they can get back from base after a recall, and how short early death timers are, you'll be lucky to shove a wave under their tower before they comeback in time. Constant team fights are pretty much just the standard now, by the 5 minute mark you'll be throwing the match if you're team isn't gathered going from lane to lane trying to get as many kills as they could after the 5 minute mark.

Even the art direction of the game went on a massive downward spiral after for whatever reason after 1.0 . The new hero designs are...fine I guess, they're pretty uninspired save for a few are passable. The skin design on the other hand is laughably generic, repetitive, and kind of embarrassing with how clearly the artists think that adding a cartoonishly massive ass crack and side flaps to every character gets the job done,  Not to mention how insane the prices are for just how low the quality is. I actually won't be surprised if the art department is just one guy throwing prompts into stable diffusion for 'inspiration'. Not to mention the item art is still placeholders from early access, and they're still adding more placeholders for items, and now even the new objectives are just store bought assets. 

Usually this would be a none issue to me, small studios gotta use their resources carefully. But where the hell are those resources even going? The game is getting constantly hit with barely thought out changes to the gameplay, the art direction is practically none-existent, the map is getting changes that try to work around an inherently flawed structure, and seemingly everything is planned to be worked on but is not a priority. And that's my current biggest problem: what even is the priority right now? [h3][Positives][/h3]
- Mostly faithful remake. It’s pretty neat to see all the iconic scenes are areas recreated.
- Solid story which has been expanded from the original. Most of the additions are really good.
- Good characters.
- Decent gameplay.
- Good pacing.
- Memorable missions.
- Tons of vehicles and solid driving mechanics.
- Great graphics and art style.
- Much more polished than the original game.
- A lot of padding was cut that was in the original.
- Cars are stored in an infinite garage now, so you don’t need to sacrifice cars when you unlock new ones.
- Paulie and Sam are more present in this game compared to the original, which helps flesh their characters out more. Other characters are expanded upon as well.

[h3][Mixed][/h3]
- Some missions were shortened from the original game, but also some missions were expanded.
- Some story details were changed. You may or may not like the changes, but I think they’re mostly fine.
-The game does a better job at directing the player compared to the original game, but sometimes this goes a little too far and makes the game feel too linear and hand holding.
- The open world is neat, but it’s pretty shallow. This isn’t a deal-breaker given that the game is mostly linear.
- The stealth mechanics are a bit better, but now they’re fairly generic. There’s no more hitting enemies with baseball bats from behind to knock them out. Now you just have a typical ‘Press B from behind’ takedown system.
- Cover mechanics in the combat are a questionable inclusion.
- The shooting while driving mechanics are still a bit clunky, so it’s a bit of a sidegrade.
- The Lucas Bertore sub-quests from the original games story were exchanged for free roam side missions instead.

[h3][Negatives][/h3]
- Combat and gunplay feel more generic compared to the original game. Most weapons feel worse than the original. The Tommy Gun being one of the most noticeable downgrades.
- The game was made significantly easier compared to the original. I’d recommend playing on Hard or Classic.
- The racing mission is notoriously difficult, especially on Classic difficulty.
- Some of the chase sequences are pretty scripted.
- Some of the collectibles are neat, but there’s too many of them and the in-game methods of tracking them are incredibly lacking.
- Various downgrades from the original. The city is a bit less interactive, being able to freely ride public transport was removed, car damage isn’t as impressive, some of the immersion feels weaker. The original game also felt fairly advanced for it’s time, this remake feels a bit too safe and generic in some ways.
- It's a bit of a movie game. Not much replayability.

[h3][Conclusion][/h3]
Mafia: Definitive Edition isn’t without it’s faults, but overall it’s a solid remake. I'd consider it to be (mostly) an improvement over the original. It’s not very replayable, but it’s worth a shot for the story alone.
7.5/10

This is a story driven action game, "story driven" meaning very cutscenes-driven here.

Gameplay consists of generic action-type stuff as well, you'd drive around, you'd punch some guys at times, you'd shoot some guys at times, and you'd yet again drive, quite a lot, all separated by many cutscenes. Visually, the remake shines. Lighting, textures, and environmental details all work in harmony to recreate the 1930s atmosphere with remarkable fidelity. Minor technical hiccups, such as occasional frame drops or slightly rigid NPC animations, are present but rarely detract from the experience.
