[{"review_text": "Madden NFL 26 Review

A step forward in presentation, a stumble in fundamentals.

Madden NFL 26 is, on paper, the most ambitious Madden in years. Franchise mode has been overhauled with new systems, the presentation finally feels like a true NFL broadcast, and even weather adds more variety to immersion. But while the game looks and sounds better than ever, the same old gameplay issues drag everything down. Until EA addresses these year-over-year problems, no amount of new features can make Madden feel like real football.

✅ Strengths

Franchise Mode Adds Depth
Franchise is the clear highlight this year. Wear-and-tear adds long-term roster considerations, coordinator skill trees bring variety to staff building, and weekly playsheets allow for better preparation. On paper, this is the deepest Franchise has been in a decade and a genuine step forward.

Better Salary Management With Edge Classification
A subtle but important change is the new edge classification for pass rushers. In the past, a 3–4 outside linebacker and a 4–3 off-ball linebacker were valued the same, which broke contract logic. Now, elite sack artists are grouped and paid properly, while role players are valued more realistically. It’s a small tweak that makes salary cap and roster management feel much more authentic.

Presentation Is a Huge Step Forward
Madden 26 finally nails the NFL atmosphere. Team-specific field art, jumbotron graphics, dynamic lighting, and broadcast-style commentary make every game feel like a true Sunday showcase. It’s easily the biggest leap in presentation the series has made in over a decade.

Dynamic Weather Brings Variety
Weather effects add personality to games, with rain, snow, and shifting conditions keeping Franchise matchups fresh. When tuned properly, it’s a strong addition to immersion — though not without flaws.

Pre-Snap Adjustments Add Real Depth
On both sides of the ball, Madden offers an impressive range of pre-snap options: hot routes, audibles, blocking shifts, coverage shells, line shifts, shading, and more. This toolset gives players tremendous control over tailoring their strategy, reacting to defenses, and disguising their looks. In terms of customization and flexibility, Madden provides one of the most robust pre-snap systems in sports gaming.

Passing Rewards Skill (When Using Placement & Accuracy)
The placement-and-accuracy passing mechanic isn’t new, but it remains Madden’s best way to throw. It rewards timing, ball placement, and decision-making in ways that legacy controls don’t. At its best, it makes passing genuinely satisfying and shows the kind of skill gap the series should lean into.

❌ Weaknesses

Wear-and-Tear Doesn’t Apply Fairly
The wear-and-tear system adds depth for the user, but CPU teams don’t appear to be affected in the same way. Opposing stars rarely wear down over a season, which undermines realism and creates an uneven playing field.

Blocking and Pass Protection Remain Broken
Offensive linemen still abandon their assignments, chasing defenders who pose no threat and leaving huge gaps unprotected. Sliding protection, meanwhile, often fails to pick up blitzers even when you’ve set it correctly. These issues make running inconsistent and pass protection unreliable.

Quarterback AI Is Nonsensical
Quarterbacks scramble far too often, even pocket passers who shouldn’t. They also take repeated hits without fumbling or getting injured, breaking immersion and balance. Instead of playing to their strengths, QBs often behave like glitchy hybrids.

Coach ID & Team Identity Fall Flat
Coach ID was supposed to bring unique tendencies to coordinators and head coaches, but in practice it doesn’t feel impactful. Run-first teams almost never commit to the ground game — outside of Baltimore, the AI rarely leans on it. The lack of team identity makes every opponent feel the same.

Reach Mechanic Hurts Power Backs
The new reach-for-extra-yards mechanic makes power runners a liability. Instead of triggering a truck, backs often attempt a reach animation that leads to unnecessary fumbles. EA should have tied this to a modifier (like LT) instead of making it override trucking by default.

Kicking System Feels Awful
The revamped kicking and punting controls are clunky and lack feedback. While designed to reward skill, they feel unpredictable, leaving you unsure where the ball will land. Special teams play is worse off because of it.

Pre-Snap Options Are Poorly Explained
For all its depth, Madden does a terrible job teaching players how to use pre-snap mechanics. That’s a huge issue because many of these tools are core counters to other systems. Sliding protection, for example, is designed to stop blitzes — but if players don’t know how it works, they’ll assume blocking is broken. By failing to explain its own mechanics, Madden wastes one of its biggest strengths.

General AI Awareness Issues
Across the board, AI awareness is poor. Linemen ignore assignments, quarterbacks make nonsensical decisions, and coaches call games without identity. Too often, outcomes hinge not on user skill but on AI errors that break football logic.

⚖️ Verdict

Madden 26 makes meaningful strides off the field. Franchise is deeper and smarter, the new edge classification improves roster management, and the presentation finally captures the look and feel of the NFL. When the gameplay works as intended — threading a perfect pass with placement and accuracy, disguising a blitz, or locking down a drive with smart defense — Madden shines. The problem is those moments are too few and far between.

The on-field issues remain the same year after year: broken blocking, clueless AI, unrealistic quarterback behavior, and now a frustrating new kicking system. Until EA addresses these fundamentals, every new feature will feel like window dressing.

Madden 26 is an improvement over recent titles, but it still isn’t the Madden fans deserve.

Score: 6/10 — Outstanding presentation, deeper Franchise, but still broken where it matters most.

Edited Update

Since my original review, a recent patch and some personal adjustments have noticeably improved my experience with Madden 26. One of the biggest changes was switching Franchise Mode from Simulation to Competitive. In Competitive, outcomes are tied more directly to player ratings, which makes plays feel a little more consistent and predictable compared to Sim. This shift, along with slider tweaks to balance QB accuracy, pass coverage, and tackling, has helped smooth out a lot of the gameplay’s rough edges.

That said, the game’s AI remains a major weak point. Defensive backs controlled by the AI routinely come down with contested 50/50 balls in ways that feel scripted, while your own receivers often don’t get the same treatment. These outcomes highlight how heavily the game leans on predetermined results, rather than dynamic, skill-based interactions. Even in Competitive mode, where ratings are supposed to drive outcomes, it can feel like the system is stacked in the AI’s favor at critical moments.

So while the updates and adjustments do make Madden 26 more enjoyable, the core problems with AI logic and scripted gameplay remain. The game is better than it was at launch, but it still struggles to deliver a truly authentic football experience without player-side tinkering.

I really hope Konami allows Bloober Team to do more remakes or at least port the other classic Silent Hill games.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1742712740}, {"review_text": "[h1] Maximum Immersion Guide after 27 trips to Silent Hill [/h1]

Silent Hill 2 is in my Top 3 games of all time. I just finished my 27th playtrough including my runs in vanilla on PS2, Directors Cut on PC, the "not so HD" collection on PS3 and the Remake on PS5. I got 100% on all of those platforms, 75% on PC while writing this. The game is excellent on all levels so all I wanna do here is give you my top 5 tips for your ultimate "first-time" experience with the best horror game ever made. Follow these and you'll never forget this trip, promise.

1. Turn off the lights or even better, play alone in an abandoned hospital. Or just at home at night, thats fine as well. [b] Turn up your headphones [/b] (Akira Yamaoka is perfection).

2. Watch and listen. SH2 was made and intended to play slowly. Explore the town when outside. Walk instead of running around, especially indoors. [b] Check your map constantly. [/b] Take your time - read everything, question what you see, listen to the sounds of the city. Soak everything up. There is only one first playtrough, after that its gone, forever.

3. Start on both normal combat / riddle difficulty. Its the balance the devs have intended, imo its the perfect balance. Her animations alone add layers of subtext that were impossible to express in the PS2 era.

The monsters, grotesque manifestations of James’s internal struggles, look disturbingly organic. Their movements are erratic but purposeful. Their designs are faithful to the original but refined, more grounded yet more symbolic. They feel like half-living sculptures of guilt, fear, and suppressed desire.

Every environment tells a story. Hallways are lit with flickering lights that seem to tremble under the weight of the air. Walls decay in patterns that resemble bruises or burns. Abandoned rooms feel like memories left to rot. The level of detail invites close inspection, yet at the same time something inside you wants to look away.

The result is a world that feels less like a place and more like a psychological pressure chamber.

⭐ Gameplay — Imperfect, and Perfectly So

Silent Hill 2 Remake doesn’t chase fluid combat or power fantasy. Instead, it designs systems that reflect vulnerability, clumsy fear, and the uncomfortable truth that James is not a trained fighter, but a damaged human being stumbling into situations he is wholly unprepared for.

Combat is heavier. Weapons have weight and delay. Every swing is a commitment. Enemies don’t behave like scripted obstacles — their movements reflect animalistic confusion and malicious curiosity. They react to sound, to light, and to your hesitation.

You don’t just finish Silent Hill 2 Remake.
You recover from it.

Silent Hill 2 Remake is respectful of its legacy while enhancing it with modern storytelling tools. It never feels like a cash grab. It never feels like an imitation. It feels like a passionate restoration of a timeless piece of psychological art.

Worth the price?

[h1]In-Depth[/h1]
[h3]Writing & Worldbuilding[/h3]
First and foremost, Silent Hill 2 is a psychological horror centered on the mind of its protagonist, James Sunderland. After receiving a mysterious letter from his supposedly dead wife, he sets for the remote town of Silent Hill, where he first met his now lost love, hoping to find her again. 

The psychological aspect is very prominent, and every location has plenty of details that reflect how the events that transpired there are interpreted by James’ mind. How the line between reality and fiction blurs the more you progress, in a subtle but steady way, gives the narration a sense of mystery and uncertainty perfect for this kind of story. The few NPCs encountered are peculiar and well-characterized, and linked to James himself in more subtle ways than one would expect. Overall, the story of Silent Hill 2 is involving and well-written, and will stay interesting for the whole run. 

Despite the iconic fog masking most of the layout of Silent Hill’s exterior, solid attention to detail can be seen in the making of most locales and areas. There are subtle elements of environmental storytelling that reinforce what’s already present in the lore files, or known by progressing in the story. The atmosphere is dark and oppressive, as it should be in survival horror, and will never make you feel like you’re safe anywhere, in a city infested by monsters and horrors; even “safe rooms” will not feel as safe as they could in other titles of this genre, and that’s an intentional choice to keep the tension high.

[h3]Exploration & Secrets[/h3]
You’ll explore Silent Hill and its environs solely on foot, through maps that, generally, have a good degree of openness and aren’t entirely linear, but also couldn’t be defined as ‘open-world’. In fact, aside from optional areas you’re free to explore if you stumble upon them at all, most other sections of each level are barred behind critical items tied to story progression. There’s usually a precise, formulaic order in which you’ll acquire them and gain access to further parts of that map. There are no outright ‘secret’ areas or items to find, but there are many secondary locations that often house missable weapons, interactions and lore items that can make your run more interesting, and in some cases, less troublesome, if acquired. 

As with most survival horrors, being attentive, opening all containers and looking behind every corner is essential to scavenge enough ammo and healing to survive the frequent enemy encounters, and also collect notes, diaries and puzzle-related items. Exploration is interesting and compelling, given that you won’t know what to expect next, in a world where reality and figments of James’ mind intertwine the more you press forward. Other than always showing your position in a well-made layout, your map will automatically mark locked doors, important devices and landmarks; getting lost won’t ever be an issue.

[h3]Combat System & Bosses[/h3]
You’ll fight several kinds of monsters, each representing a specific trauma from James’ past, during your travels in Silent Hill. On the Hard difficulty at least, each of them is a serious threat: just a few attacks can kill you, and earlier on these creatures are tough to defeat, and can also revive if you don’t make sure they stay dead by hitting their corpses. Most of the enemy moveset is melee, although some of them also have ranged attacks; dodging with near-perfect timing is an essential mechanic, as is learning each monster’s attack patterns to know when to strike in melee without risking a painful retaliation. Using ranged weapons gives you a decisive advantage, but ammo is scarce for most of the adventure, and should be saved for bosses and more demanding combat sections with multiple enemies. 

Unfortunately, the enemy variety is low, and soon enough you’ll be tired of fighting the same three or four archetypes recycled over and over. Story:

Characters:

Gameplay:

There are games you play, games you finish, and then there is Age of Empires II — a game you casually install “for nostalgia,” only to wake up three weeks later arguing with strangers on the internet about whether Franks or Britons have the superior late-game. Spoiler: it’s always situational, but good luck telling that to anyone.😅

What makes AoE2 one of the rare immortals of gaming? It’s simple, and also not simple at all — just like trying to quickwall while your villagers loudly ignore you.🧱👀

📜-A History Lesson That Somehow Isn’t Boring ---❤️"As a Persian, I love history — and this game even lets me play my own civilization." 

AoE2 takes historical figures — Joan of Arc, Saladin, Genghis Khan — and instead of burying them in dusty textbooks, lets you live their stories in beautifully crafted campaigns. The narrative is simplified enough to be digestible, but rich enough to spark real curiosity. I’ve learned more world history from this game than from actual classes, and I’m not ashamed to admit it.🏺✨

⚔️🌍-Civilization Balance: Diversity Without Chaos

Each civilization feels distinct, flavorful, and strategically meaningful. Whether it’s the Mongols racing across the map like medieval motorcyclists or the Byzantines out-tanking your entire existence🛡️,AoE2 somehow manages to keep everything competitive.


-Gameplay Depth That Ages Like Wine 🍷 (or a Well-Boomed Economy 🐑💰)

The brilliance of AoE2 lies in how every tiny decision matters.
Do you rush? Do you boom? Do you tower rush and lose all your friends?
Economy management, map control, scouting, micro, macro — the game has layers upon layers of strategy that have kept both casual players and pros addicted for 25 years. You don’t just “play” AoE2 — you develop a lifestyle.⚒️🔥

🎨🎶-Graphics & Sound: Nostalgia Meets Modern Polish🎨🎶

The Definitive Edition somehow preserves the warmth of the original pixel art while making everything crisp, vivid, and animate in ways we never thought possible on modern screens.
And the soundtrack? Still one of the greatest blends of ambient calm and battle anticipation.
You could put it on during a road trip and no one would question it.

🌐🔥A Community That Never Sleeps

If AoE2 were a city, it would be one of those places that’s always awake, always alive, always yelling “GG” whether you deserve it or not.
From Steam Workshop mods to wild custom scenarios, to massively competitive tournaments like Red Bull Wololo and Hidden Cup, the community keeps the game thriving like it’s permanently 1999 plus HD plus DE plus infinite expansion packs.

😇😈-Accessibility: Beginner-Friendly, Expert-Cruel

-AoE2 has this magical flexibility:

New players can jump in, build some houses(or Towers for Rushing..), make some knights, and have a great time.

⏱️💣Experts, meanwhile, are calculating build orders down to the millisecond like they’re defusing a bomb.
The same game. Two very different emotional experiences.

-Definitive Edition Improvements🔧✨

The Definitive Edition is the perfect example of “if it ain’t broke, polish it anyway.”
New campaigns, new civs, quality-of-life improvements, smarter AI (usually), and a smoother interface all help the game feel completely modern without losing its soul.

-Imperfections? Sure — but Charming Ones🤏😄

Sometimes the AI still sends a single militia to die proudly under your Town Center.⚰️
Sometimes new players still get overwhelmed by the depth.😵‍💫
And sometimes Mongol scouts still act like caffeinated toddlers.🐎⚡
But honestly? These tiny flaws are part of the game’s identity — they’re as familiar as the “wololo” we all secretly fear.✨

⭐- Final Verdict

Age of Empires II is not just a real-time strategy game — it’s a generational masterpiece that refuses to die, refuses to age, and refuses to stop being relevant.
It’s emotional, competitive, educational, hilarious, frustrating, and unforgettable, all at the same time.
If you give it enough time, it becomes less of a game and more of a friend.🤝💙

Since Dynasties of India, the only normal DLC with civilizations and campaigns as we used to get back when is Mountain Royals, whereas the rest aren't.

Return of Rome had attempted to bring back AoE1 up to par with AoE2, but the devs again failed to develop its civs or (original) campaigns to the level of AoE2. This review is my first impression for each)

TLDR: These games are MANDATORY for any Hack n' Slash enthusiast. They are the best on the market, and I only hope 4 and 5 can compare. 

DMC1 is a literal proof of concept: It was the original Resident Evil 4, but was given the greenlight to be an independent game; its built on the foundation of another, scrapped, game. For the time of its release, it was akin to God of War: A veritable king that has since defined an entire genre. It did a lot of good, for absolute sure, and I do not actively hate the game. I respect what it did. However, more than 20 years later, the gameplay itself does not hold up. The game is incredibly jank, held back by an extremely terrible camera (In a fixed position that swaps during combat and changes directional inputs), an awful save/checkpoint system, a poor lock on system for aiming, few combos and weapons, and overall boring combat. There is no tutorial or introduction to anything (other than the water level controls a quarter of the way through), no ability to replay missions, random one off gimmicks thrown in, poor item management (Game limits your items, despite there not being a cap. You're just not allowed to buy more than one), and no player direction. I did not enjoy actually playing the game and found it very frustrating. I did enjoy the aesthetics, music, enemy design (They have their own movesets rather than single attacks)... Quite literally everything in the game is SSS+ except the combat. It even has NG+ and carries all of your stuff, with new enemy placements. I beat it purely for the sake of getting a better understanding of how far the franchise has come and developed itself as a part of Hack-and-Slash / Action Game Royalty. I would not skip this one, as its more unique than the rest of the franchise. Additionally, it allows you to see where the core of the series originated. However, I do not recommend playing it more than once due to the other games just being better and for most people, the jank will frustration you. Though, despite everything I've said, I think it'd be my favorite if it got a proper Remaster to further flesh this rendition of a Resident-May-Cry.

DMC2: Universally acclaimed to be the worst in the series... this is true. From the beginning, it was destined to fail. The director and team behind DMC1 were not called upon to work on the sequel and as such, the game was a total failure. Nobody making the game understood what to do, and they only began working in the final 6 months before release, with a new team. The game fails at too many things to properly list, however, here is a short list of what absolutely ruins this game and makes it unworthy of being a good game: Comically easy enemies (Which often stand still), lack of puzzles and secrets, Dante having no personality, poor map design and layout, fewer weapons than the first game, weapons having no identity or variation (Never call iconic weapons by name, and all melees are identical), every boss in the game is easily exploited (Standing next to some of them renders them unable to hit you) and the bosses themselves are boring, uninspired, or copy/pasted from DMC1 (Despite there being no lore for their return or lack of voices?), overtuned firearms which trivialize the game, and half of your armory isn't usable due to the aforementioned guns taking precedent (You're expected to use guns for almost everything and get punished for melee). I didn't understand what was going on, as Dante doesn't even speak until Chapter 7, which is 45% through the story. There's an absolute disconnect between the player and the characters... HeII, you can't even pick the legacy control scheme from DMC1. Now, the game does do SOME good. I enjoy the advanced mobility via wallrunning, shooting downwards, having extra air attacks, being able to carry more items, as well as chapter select. However, the list of positives is very small, and since the game is so uninteresting, I never attempted to play the game as the other two characters: Lucia and Trish (Which uses DMC1 Dante as a base) There's technically three, with DMC1 Dante if you beat the game on DMD, but you'd have to pay me to open DMC2 after this first impression. I recommend skipping DMC2 in its entirety. You will not lose anything from doing so. 

DMC3: Wow, "this party's getting crazy!". DMC3 is the absolute definitive triumph and return to form DMC needed and has since given us. While DMC2 was challenged in many places, it had pieces to the ultimate hack and slash game. The team behind DMC2 asked for another chance to develop another DMC, though this time, with proper time and research dedicated to the cast, their personalities, style, and tone for the new game. While they hastily began work for DMC3 almost immediately after DMC2 released and failed, this speed was precise. They knew what they wanted, and had more than a few years of backed up feedback from players. DMC3, and both its Special and HD editions, have done nothing but impress and improve, every iteration. DMC3 has, with no exaggeration, earned its title as 'One of the Best Video Games Ever Made'. The formula is damn near perfect. So much so, that every game after it has basically copy/pasted it, with more and more and more... Dante has SO much character and personality. He's cocky, witty, likes to have fun, and can be very serious. Dante has genuine character growth: Going from not caring about the plot other than fighting Vergil again, to going out of his way to help a stranger with their family issues, and coming to terms with personally witnessing the end to his family, culminating with him crying (Hence where the name of his business and game comes from). Its all over the top and badass, but in a cool MGS way. Its a 'HELL YEAH' kind of game. The art style returns to something akin to DMC1, for better or worse with some map tiles (Leviathan was not great), and the gameplay itself is actually similar to DMC2. Specifically the formula and layout of having extra buttons to press for combos, different combo branches, and the addition of specialized movements ala Gunslinger  'Style', such as gun spinning, shooting more enemies, charged shots, etc. Speaking of 'Styles', they are a new addition to the franchise which lets you modify Dante's moveset to accommodate how you like to play. As aforementioned, Gunslinger plays more like a DMC2 Dante, while Swordmaster introduces new combos and attacks for all melee weapons. Trickster gives Dante special dodges on the ground and in the air, as well as a teleport feature. There are 5 to start, and you can unlock 2 more through fighting special bosses. In regards to enemies... I hate to say, but this had some of the weaker enemy design I've seen so far. There are enemies I just found frustrating, or annoying, thought they felt out of place when lined up to other enemy types. The Fallen were worse versions of Death Scissors from DMC1, having armored wings to protect them, long range, multi-hit melee attacks, and could fly through walls. The Enigma is probably the worst, as it is a ranged enemy which knocks you back, stuns you, has multiple dashes it can use while firing at you, and is very evasive. I don't mind a ranged enemy, but when these are present, the entire fight becomes much worse. The Dullahan, Soul Eater, and Leviathan are also fairly weak in design. But other than a few weak links, the enemy/boss design are absolutely 10/10. Vergil II is my favorite, by far. A close second would be Agni and Rudra (Such good weapons too, top 3 so far). The game also lets you play as Vergil and has... CO-OP MODE (Accessible via Doppelganger Style or with DMC3 Crimson Mod). This game truly does do it all... I've actually spent so much time I got through Easy/Normal/Hard/Very Hard and over 1000 floors of the ENDLESS MODE (Bloody Palace)... I have so much to say that I ran out of review space!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1747002929}, {"review_text": "🎭 Devil May Cry (2001)
The one that started it all. Originally directed by Hideki Kamiya under Capcom’s supervision (and initially planned as a Resident Evil title), this game revolutionized the action genre by introducing fast-paced combat, stylish rankings, and a charismatic anti-hero: Dante.

With its gothic atmosphere, punishing boss battles, and now-iconic cutscenes, DMC1 is rough around the edges but dripping with charm and originality. The controls may feel stiff compared to modern standards, but once you get used to it, the satisfaction is real.

🕶️ Devil May Cry 2 (2003)
Let’s be honest — this is the black sheep of the franchise. Dante’s personality is muted, the gameplay is oddly slow, and the level design is uninspired. But is it unplayable? Not at all. In fact, with the right expectations, it offers a chill, almost meditative hack & slash experience.

On the bright side, it introduced Lucia as a playable character and gave us some cool dodging mechanics and wall-running. Think of it as a breather between two chaos-filled storms.

[h3][i]DMC[/i][/h3]
This is the game that made me a fan of this franchise and Capcom games in general, so my opinion on DMC will naturally have some form of bias, but personally speaking, I do not think this game has aged anywhere near as badly as what some people make it out to be.

The premise itself is fairly basic: main character Dante gets attacked by a mysterious woman named Trish at his office as a test and is then requested by her to enter a castle on Mallet Island to fight against the demon emperor Mundus, who is responsible for killing Dante’s brother and mother. There isn’t much plot in the game; it is mainly there to establish the setting and tone, but what’s there in the game does work. It’s simplistic and enjoyable for what it is.

The gameplay is rewarding and unique for its age. You slash down enemies with Dante’s sword and juggle enemies with your guns so you can increase your stylish rank. You are ranked based on your performance in each mission, so you’re encouraged to play better as you gain more red orbs, which act as a currency to buy items and moves for Dante. You can unlock Devil Trigger, which is a special transformation that lets Dante deal more effective attacks at lightning speed. DT is a very fun mechanic, and it will aid you the most during the game’s more difficult moments, so you’ll want to take advantage of it.

Unlike most of the games in the franchise, DMC is fundamentally designed with knowledge checks in mind. Certain attacks and weapons will deal more effective damage to specific enemies. If you’re familiar with any of the mainline Mega Man games and how they’re designed, you’ll have an idea of what to do in this game, but if you’re not willing to put in the time to figure out how the game works mechanically, then you likely won’t have the greatest time, especially on harder difficulties.

As for the camera, it is very similar to the use of fixed camera angles found in older Capcom titles. I do not mind how it functions in this game, but this will likely turn off some people who are particularly more used to camera control found in more modern games.

This game oozes atmosphere with its gothic environments, which stem from the game’s Resident Evil roots. The non-diegetic soundtrack helps the player settle into DMC’s dark world, and it really fits the mood of the game. 'Anarchy in the U.W.' and 'Flock Off!' are tracks I vibe with a lot.

While DMC is still very much an enjoyable classic, I feel that it unfortunately gets overshadowed by most of the games directed by Hideaki Itsuno. Hideki Kamiya’s vision of DMC is worth your time, and it’s still a fascinating experience that holds up today. Do not sleep on this game.
 
[h3][i]DMC2[/i][/h3]
DMC2 is a rushed abomination that Capcom somehow managed to release, with Itsuno being forced into the director’s chair last minute to finish up work on the game.

In this game, you play as two protagonists, Dante and Lucia. Dante controls like a slow tank with how he swings his sword around, and his guns deal far more effective damage than his sword, which straight up goes against what made his gameplay fun and interesting from the first game. As for Lucia, her gameplay is not much different from Dante’s. Her blades attack faster than Dante’s sword, and her selection of projectiles feels slow to use. New to this game is the ability to run on walls, but it really isn’t all that helpful to do for the most part.

The level design in DMC2 is filled with a lot of big open environments, which is in stark contrast with how the levels were designed in the first game. A lot of the time, you’ll be moving around with nothing interesting going on until you encounter an enemy and have to deal with the game’s atrocious camera. It’s abysmal with how it’s laser-focused on the enemies, and you’re forced to fight against the camera when you’re trying to navigate around the area during those encounters. It’s, without a doubt, worse than the camera from the first game. The gameplay is at its worst when you’re forced to do the underwater segments since you barely have any semblance of control while you’re swimming slowly and are forced to awkwardly attack enemies with your devil arms. Despite the changes, the gameplay of DMC2 does not have the technical nuance that made the first game special to play.

In regard to the story, it’s practically almost non-existent. Stuff just happens without any reason or build-up. The main antagonist is a meme, Lucia is boring, and Dante himself is severely depressed.

The least offensive aspect of the game is the soundtrack itself. While I don’t think it is objectively bad, it’s the least memorable out of all the mainline games. 'Parasitic Evil' is a standout track for me personally.

DMC2 simply does not have any of the special sauce that made DMC such a unique game. This game has little to no personality to its name, and I do not recommend it.

[h3][i]DMC3[/i][/h3]
This game is undoubtedly one of Capcom’s GOATs, and it’s objectively the best-designed game in this collection. Itsuno returned to direct this game to make up for the failure of the second game, and he absolutely cooked everything to near perfection with Dante’s Awakening.

Being a prequel to the first game, you play as a young Dante at his new shop who gets invited by an unknown man associated with Dante’s brother to visit Temen-ni-gru. Dante makes his way to the tower to fight his twin brother, Vergil. The premise itself is simple, but there is more to it as you play the game. I really appreciate the added details to the characters and established lore as a long-time fan of the franchise.

The gameplay provided in DMC3 streamlines a lot of what worked well in the previous games and sets the foundation for the rest of the franchise. Dante has access to different Styles that allow him to do many sorts of actions to aid the player. The extended amount of moves you can pull off while alternating between your weapons and Style on the fly is extremely satisfying when pulled off. It is similar to a fighting game in a sense with how many different moves you can dish out at once while also juggling enemies. Level design is mostly linear and is done in a manner that doesn’t pointlessly waste your time. The camera has been adjusted to make it easier to navigate, and you have more control of it.

The soundtrack in particular is fantastic. It’s got the most effort put in, with iconic tracks that are very much loved to this day, like 'Devils Never Cry', 'Taste The Blood' and 'Divine Hate'.

If you’re trying to get into character action games, this is an absolute must-play.

[{"review_text": "Counter-Strike 2: Not an Update, a Rebirth
At first glance, you think — oh, it's just CS:GO with ray tracing and protein shakes. Then you play it. And you realize: nope, this isn’t an update. It’s like your good old AK-47 suddenly developed a sense of smell.

CS2 is still that same adrenaline-fueled classic where one bullet can change the round, but now everything feels tangible. Source 2 didn’t just slap on better graphics — it poured a bucket of raw concrete into the game. You can feel things now: water droplets from explosions, the flicker of your teammate’s shadow around the corner, and smoke that doesn’t just exist — it lives.

Speaking of smoke — it’s no longer a wall. It’s a character. It moves, it breathes, it reacts to grenades like it’s got emotions. I wouldn’t be surprised if it starts streaming on Twitch next year.

The guns? Still the same arsenal, but every reload feels like you’re reloading your soul. The AWP doesn’t just boom anymore — it tears a hole in reality, pauses time, and gently lets you back into the match.

Servers finally hit 128-tick, and that’s like upgrading from smoke signals to quantum teleportation. Every movement is a dance. Every kill? Poetry. The feel is tighter, snappier, and your muscle memory comes back like a loyal dog that never really left.

It’s not perfect — hitboxes sometimes act like confused teenagers, and the UI is a bit extra. Matchmaking still throws you in with people who think the bomb site is a Spotify playlist. But that’s fine. CS2 is a foundation, not a fad. It's here to evolve.

The Verdict:
CS2 isn’t the second chapter. It’s a second life. For the aim gods and the eco warriors. For the smurfs, the noobs, the spray control philosophers. It’s not just a game — it’s the art of control, the sound of chaos, and the silence before the last shot.

As it stands only buy this game for those modes.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 58, "timestamp_created": 1763526662}, {"review_text": "Let me preface by saying: If you are good with ignoring issues in the games you play, then this will easily be one of the best tactical shooters you could every play, but my god, the issues in this game are very difficult to ignore. I want to love this game, I really do, but given this game's development history, I would never recommend ANYONE play it

To be clear: this is not my first time playing the game. I have around 2500-3000 hours across both of my Tarkov accounts. To that, you may ask: Dave, why do you have 2 accounts?

Back in 2020, I built my first PC, and the first game I purchased on it was Tarkov. After putting hours into the game, and loving it, I heard about the "Edge of Darkness" edition. On top of the in-game perks that you get with purchasing it, you were promised to receive all further DLC they add in upcoming updates. The thing about the EoD edition was that it cost 150 fucking dollars. Even to this date, I have never spent more money on a video game, ever. I loved this game, but there were so many issues, and everyone who bought the EoD edition of the game was so excited to see that extra cash for the company be spent on fixing those issues. $150 is a lot of money, and we all thought it a worthwhile investment, because we were naive enough to think that Tarkov was a passion project with a lot of potential. 

We were wrong

Let me talk about some of the problems that the money DIDNT go toward fixing:

1) Server Performance

This was by far the most annoying problem for new Steam players. On the 1.0 launch, there were players who couldnt get past the launcher for fucking DAYS. Not minutes, not hours... DAYS. That is inexcusable for a game like this. If you played the beta, you'll know this happened nearly every wipe day. The beginning of the wipe is usually the most played time for the game, and given that BSG has seen this issue of flooded servers happen about every 6 months on wipe day, youd think that theyd know what kind of hardware they need in order to make servers run properly... Nope. Embarrassing

2) Hardware requirements/game optimization

This is the most pressing problem for casual players. I have a decent PC. It's nothing fancy, but it's good enough to run any AAA game on full graphics at 60 frames at the least. I have never once been able to play on Streets of Tarkov at anything over 40 frames. Ever. On other maps, my frames usually sit around 50-70, dropping and raising for the most random reasons... On top of the horrendous stuttering issues, that are CONSTANT...
The average income in the United States is somewhere between $40-60k. A majority of Americans, Gen-Z and below, are living paycheck to paycheck... In what world do you think the average gamers have the money necessary to build a setup good enough to play this fucking game? It is borderline impossible to run Tarkov on a gaming laptop, unless you have a really fucking good one. What chance do you think a blue-collar worker with a $1000 gaming setup has, fighting sweats at dorms, when he's also having to fight with 30 frames per second? 

3) Cheaters

Cheating is a problem in nearly every game, but I have never seen one as rampant as in Tarkov. A couple years ago, a content creator by the name of "Goat" dropped a video called "The Wiggle that Killed Tarkov" in which he downloaded cheats himself just to try and investigate the cheating problem. The information he gathered in his investigation showed that there was a closeted cheater in 60 PERCENT OF ALL RAIDS that he joined... The video blew up, and what did BSG do to respond? Nothing. Since that video, theyll release updates showing the community "look guys, we've banned this many cheaters in the month of ___" This gives me ZERO hope. Banning cheaters does absolutely nothing to prevent them from coming back. Only anti-cheat software does. 
Speaking of: Recently, pre 1.0, they seemingly released some anti-cheat software, and Nikita boasted before-hand on Twitter saying "preparing somethin special for cheater scum"
What did this software do exactly? It false banned THOUSANDS of accounts. We know this, because Nikita admitted to them being false bans in his pre 1.0 interview with Pestily! 
The cheating situation in Tarkov has never been properly addressed, and because it's so normal and has been for fucking years, so few content creators actually talk about it...

4) Queue times

Tarkov, like any game, has it's exciting moments, and it has it's boring moments. One of the most boring things in video games as a whole, is waiting for a match. Tarkov has by far THE WORST queue times of any multiplayer game I've ever played in my life. The fastest I've ever got into a Tarkov match is maybe 3 minutes, and the average time for me is maybe 5-7 minutes. The longest? Ive waited close to an hour for a match before. That is unacceptable given how many concurrent players this game has had over the last several years. 
One of my worst Tarkov memories: Years ago, I was teaching a friend how to play the game. He had maybe 50 hours at the time, so he was very new. We loaded into Interchange, and we waited 38 fucking minutes for a match. When we FINALLY got into the match, we got ambushed off our spawn on the highway, and he got grenaded within the first minute. He didnt touch the game for another week, and I almost felt like I was personally responsible for wasting his time. 

5) Game-breaking bugs

When you play a game like Call-of-Duty, and you encounter a bug that gets you killed, most people will just say to themselves "that was bull shit" and simply move on with their lives. In Tarkov however, it is a very different story, because often times youve spent literal HOURS of your life working toward using a specific kit, working on a quest, or trying to find a specific item... and when a bug gets you killed, it can be a genuinely brutal feeling. Tarkov, is absolutely LOADED with game-breaking bugs.
Bugs that occur in Tarkov include: 
Your magazines being loaded with "ghost bullets" that dont do anything when shot
Being stuck in a healing or reloading animation that is impossible to get out of
Inventories being bugged causing you to not be able to loot them
A random system error causing you to disconnect from the match
Items bugging when shift-clicking them too quickly into your inventory, causing them to turn into ghost items which arent actually there
Jumping over certain rocks seems to glide your character over that terrain, leaving you stuck in a "falling" animation, and can sometimes throw you off of cliff edges 
Grenades seem to clip on the most RANDOM hitboxes, and will sometimes lag mid-air, causing them to drop at your fucking feet and kill you...
ALL of the ones I just listed have got me killed before, and some of them I know for a fact are still in 1.0. Some of them are more common than others, but damn, theyre all so annoying. BSG has FAR worse problems to address, but bug fixes should be something that costs very little money, so the fact that theyve been present for so long infuriates me.

In conclusion: 

I feel betrayed for supporting this company for so long. The game is still unfinished, nothing about it is new. The interesting things theyve added to 1.0 dont at all compensate for years and years of abuse and broken promises we've endured for the sake of this game. None of the most pressing issues have been addressed, and I feel genuinely horrible for everyone who gave so much money to see this game develop into a playable and finished state, only to be scammed... If you still play Tarkov past the 1.0 release, youre either a masochist, a streamer who relies on the game for money, or you have stockholm syndrome.

Escape from Tarkov is not a game you casually “pick up.” Its a game that confronts you. Coming from years of Call of Duty and only recently transitioning from console to PC gaming, I was struck by how differently Tarkov treats the player. It’s not playful or forgiving, it’s tense, punishing, and, at times, genuinely intimidating. Its one of the few shooters that made me question my own skill, awareness, and decisions. Hearing footsteps or voices from another player can trigger real fear. For the first time, I understood what people meant when they said a game could cause anxiety.

I watched Tarkov evolve over the years. I saw it announced long ago, and only began truly playing within the last 3–4 years. Even without fully dedicating myself to it, I’m glad I experienced the beta and that the game finally reached its official release.

Tarkov’s flaws are clear. Its complex, demanding, and absolutely not for everyone. It began as a small studio project and grew far beyond its original scope, bringing with it technical issues, controversial decisions, and a rocky launch. All of these are legitimate criticisms, and I won’t defend the mistakes.

But at its core, Tarkov remains one of the most challenging and rewarding FPS experiences available. Its not “racist” it’s classist. Those with wealth have a distinct advantage. The game rewards intelligence, preparation, discipline, and the ability to adapt under pressure. Tarkov tries to break you, and once it succeeds, that’s when you finally start to understand and enjoy it.

I cant recommend this game to everyone. But for players looking for a serious, high-stakes shooter, one that pushes your limits, tests your patience, and makes every decision feel meaningful, Tarkov stands alone. The story is present as well, not in the traditional way, but in a way that adds weight to the world if you pay attention.

If you’re considering buying it, ask yourself:
Do you want challenge, tension, and a game that demands everything from you?
If the answer is yes… then:
Welcome to Tarkov

[{"review_text": "I never thought I will be writing a "Not Recommended" review for this game.

As you can see from my playtime, I've poured quite a huge part of my free time into Hunt. That itself proves my fondness to this game.
I started playing right after its early access, back when there was no "1896" in its title. I was drawn into the grim, ruthless nature of the Hunt; everything around you can and will kill you, and you have to make the most of what you have―your equipment, your trait, your position and your knowledge of other enemies' equipment, trait and position. Forming a strategy is a must to at least survive, even though that means you're leaving without bounty. You need to traverse the map carefully, paying attention to the surroundings, and plan your next move deliberately. Failure to do so will result in your (and your partners') death, losing everything you brought in.
Every firearms had something to offer; each gun had its own strengths and weaknesses, so there was no such thing as "trash weapon" nor "superb weapon," meaning that you would always have a chance to topple over enemies, if you know how to play your gun right.
The world and environment is something that no other game would be able to pull off, its occult-esque darkness surrounding the world, which can be found both in-game in the lore book, i.e. the Book of Weapons and the Book of Monsters. The events pre-1896 were on track with its lore and brought interesting seasonal addition into the game in the form of short stories (and some cool narrations along with them).

But right now, after Hunt's 1896 reboot, everything matters no more. They completely removed all the books from the game, so we can't even have a look of the game's lores anytime you want (Crytek did announced that the books will be available on Hunt website, but why ripping them away from the game in the first place?).
Gunfight-wise, they've started to add more and more broken weapons and traits which makes any strategic aspects completely useless. They are now encouraging more fast-paced fights by implementing absurd equipment and buffing up more spammy weapons. They made every gun have all same custom ammo, made every shotgun buffed, made more expensive weapons powerful, and de-penalized being downed with Revive Bolt and Restoration shot. The worst weapon so far is the "Shredder," a crossbow-ish weapon that shoots sawblades semi-auto that ricochet off the walls and home on enemies in proximity. That's the most absurd mechanics I've ever seen in any other shooter games (other than CoD), and it doesn't even fit into the game's original gunplay system in any way. They completely lost touch on what to do with equipment and are only focusing on attracting [i]major audience[/i] by steering away Hunt's core gameplay.

What dove a final nail in the coffin is the recent event, Post Malone's Murder Circus. Before this event, at least themes of each event were always on par with Hunt's originality. But the Murder Circus is all for Post Malone, a real-life celebrity (evident as shown in its title). Almost all weapon skin has a "PM" initials engraved, and there are two Post Malone Hunter skins in the battle pass. If I ever wanted to see a famous musician or actor, I'd go play CoD or Fortnite. I liked Hunt for its own unique atmosphere, not for having a real-life celebrity.

I don't know what to think of Hunt: Showdown anymore. This isn't [i]the[/i] Hunt I used to know. Once a dark, tense and slow-paced game, with an actually fine-balanced equipment, has become nothing but a so-called "Western" run-and-gun trigger-happy shooter. I may come back when my Hunt partners group up for a couple of matches, but I'm not going to actively play this game onwards.

They never responded, so, be better Crytek, you guys fucking suck.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 55, "timestamp_created": 1751998347}, {"review_text": "used to be one of my favorite shooters ever made. unfortunately the ever increasing issues with the game's ui, networking, matchmaking, and bugs makes hunt feel unreliable at best and unapproachable at worst. given the user experience has degraded so much over time with nearly every single update I simply can't recommend it anymore.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1743572137}, {"review_text": "For Clarification:
I want this game to succeed and become better. I have no grudge against the Devs. That is why I give my honest feedback.

I would not recommend to start getting into this game unless you are a real masochist and enjoy dumping hundreds of hours in it to become somewhat decent and learn the ropes.

Recently I am loosing the fun with this game after almost 4.000 Hours because of the direction the game is heading. I am not saying it is wrong or bad in general, it is just not my cup of tea anymore.

- Ingame Voip and Chat not working properly
- UI Functions to equip your hunter are sometimes not working correctly
- Sound Bugs (sometimes a major inconvienience in a game that is designed for great audio)
- Server Performance sometimes randomly goes to hell with rubberbanding out of nowhere and lagging.
- Texture Loading Bugs and Derendering of walls or trees
- Reconnect Feature not working 
- Ingame map bugging and leading to stutters

And so on. Most of this is not the worst thing but in combination in intense situations it becomes very frustrating because this stuff happens often.

The Devs started to improve on communication again which I highly appreciate even though it is by far not as good as it was a few years ago.

The biggest issues that are making me leaving the game more and more are the following:

- The Instaburning meta.

For those who dont know. When you get killed in Hunt, your team mates can pick you up a few times and you loose part of your maximum health for every revive until you are at zero maximum health and red skulled. Then you can not be picked up again (besided when your team has the bounty, the main objective of the game). But even then they have to sacrifice their own health to get you back). When you are downed and people set you on fire, you rapidly loose your maximum health until you are redskulled.

I hated it when they implemented burning downed hunters long ago. But I see from a gamedesign perspective, that they needed some sort of mechanic to handle solos with self revive and stalemates from people that are just hiding and waiting until you leave, to pick up their team mates again. And I think it was fine how it was. But the devs decided not so long ago that it was not enough.

Before you had to bring a firebomb or find a lantern in the world to set hunters on fire. Which was fine because you had to invest ressources and time to burn a downed hunter and you had to move and take a risk because people could shoot you when you had to come close to burn a hunter.

Nowadays you can burn hunters with a million tools and consumables that are easy to restock and to bring and you can safely ignite hunters from behind cover with a flare pistol even from 50 meteres away. No ressources have to be invested, no risk taken. It is nowadays a surprise if you are not instantly getting set on fire even before your body has hit the ground.

And no that is not enough they even cranked up the burn speed by far so that if your mates do not instantly save you or throw a choke bomb (which is basically useless because it got also nerfed) you are out of the game in a very short time. Often enough you are not able to get your mate back because the bounty already left the game.

The official reason for this was they wanted to break up stalemates so people are not camping around dead bodies for hours. The effect is that people are even more camping now because the risk of getting burned is so high and punishing that it further promotes the passive meta, sitting around an waiting for others to make a move to third party them. Which means more stalemates and more boring camping.

Again everyone can play as they want and if people like to camp and sit around it is absolutely their right to do so and play the game this way. But I do not enjoy this at all, that is why the current development towards this gameplay is loosing me as a player.


- Matchmaking

Crytek changed the matchmaking system so that more players are in the six star bracket (the hightest bracket is six stars, most players are around 3-5 Stars). The Skill difference between a high six star player and a low six star players feels way bigger than the difference between 3 and low 5 star. In Six star you have a lot of bush camping snipers and a few shooter gods that are just very very good at the game.

Sometimes you get matches with a mix of 6, 3 and 4 Star Players in a trio that have a 5 Star Rating as a team. If you read through official discord and forums you will see a lot of people screenshoting their Matchmaking Team Compositions and if you are a team of 3 stars or 4 stars, one six star can sometimes be enough to fuck up your whole lobby.

They also built in a more robust system so you do not drop in MMR as fast as you did once. Which is an issue for me because if I get on 6 stars (which happens regularly) I will get my ass handed to me for days before I finally get down to 5 Stars and find somewhat enjoyable matched with people that are on my skill level. I know from the people I play with (most of them I got to know through hunt in the recent years) have the same issue. While this is good to protect newer players from people intentionally dropping in MMR (Which was an issue before), it can also be a big pain for others.

This leads to me stopping to enjoy the game because every round becomes a sweatfest. I started to pick meta weapons and loadouts more often because using fun weapons punishes you way to much if you hit your skill ceiling. Which is a shame. Because playing the same 5 Weapons all the time really burns me out from the game.



- Objectives

I think a lot of people play Hunt for the PvP. The PvE Part is just a motivation for people to get in the game and fight. This leads to a lot of situations where people rather ambush people fighting the bounty team and letting the bounty escape for free to get one or two kills. While in general I think ambushing is a valid tactical move in Hunt, it really annoys me that the motivation to get the tokens are very low.  Quite often the bounty lair is right next to an extract in the corner of the map. So at least 1 or 2 teams are furthest away from the boss and if you get in a fight it is almost impossible to catch up with the bounty. Most of the extracts are designed to heavily favour the people who are trying to extract. Which itself is fine. But even if you run in to block the extract (which kills you a lot of the times you do, to buy some time for your team to catch up) people are despawning right in front of your nose even though you tried to use the quickest way possible to stop them. I think it should not be possible to have an extract exactly at the boss lair.

- Major Bugs
Hunt has some reoccuring bugs that are very annoying and can ruin a good round sometimes. They are battling them more and more which I appreciate but still there are some issues.

-- Explosives and Walls
Explosives and Wall blocking in Hunt are inconsistent. Frag Bombs and frag arrows making you bleed even though you are behind a solid stone wall. Dynamites killing you through solid walls or through a massive ceiling while you are upstairs and it explodes downstairs are super annoying. I do enjoy playing explosives and I am pretty good at using explosives in Hunt if I am allowed to say so myself, but it can be very annoying to throw a dynamite at someones feet and they only get a scratch.

-- Hitboxes

Hitboxes in hunt are pretty whacky sometimes. It could also be a mix of bad server performance/ping and weird hitboxes but the amount of arm hits and shotguns not killing well within their OHK Range is high. Even when you check replays and see the bullet enter a body or a head, the dmg chart shows you only an arm hit or a lower torso hit.

I will update this post when I have time to add a bit more context and maybe some constructive criticism and idead how to resolve some of the issues. Sounds good? No? Okay, lets release it.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 60, "timestamp_created": 1734311583}, {"review_text": "Hunt Showdown used to be a great game. It was challenging, rewarding, and most importantly. Fun. It was the thinking mans FPS, where no matter how bad your gear was, if you out thought or out shot your opponent you could win. 

This still holds true to a degree. However since the 1886 Engine/UI update its been reduced to an okay game. 

The Engine Update has more or less been good. Tons of players have reported issues with the game since then, I was lucky and my AMD based system didn’t suffer anything worse then reaching barely playable frame rates. Overall, this is the only part of the update I don’t believe has damaged the games core identity in any way.

The UI topic has been done to death so I’ll only say that in the hundred odd hours I’ve played since it was released, I still struggle constantly. Its without a doubt a nightmare for new players.

The various weapon changes and balances are however where things start to take a turn for the worse. Hunt has always had weapons that were simply better in every way then other weapons, regulating them to meme loadouts or simply never to be seen in the Bayou. With the addition of special ammo, this only made weapon variety worse, as the good weapons became great, and the great weapons God-tier. This isn’t restricted to PvP weapons either. The weapons that were best used against AI have been heavily nerfed. On the PvP side, tweaks and balances have been implemented to improve the worst affected weapons. Such as certain types of special ammo to be removed from some guns or given to others. On the AI side. Nothing. This was one of the biggest and most divisive updates in Hunts history, and in hindsight was a sign of what was to come with the 1886 update and its changes.

Gameplay changes are what is making most people leave the game currently. The stated goal of these changes from Crytek themselves is make games end quicker. That is it. They want players to enter the server and leave as fast as possible. To this end they increased the burn rate of downed hunters, reduced the effect of the choke bomb, and added more options to burn bodies. They also changed Necromancer, a powerful-ish trait that allows players to revive downed teammates from a distance, to such a state that I have seen it used only a handful of times. Hunt Showdown used to be more then a name, it was a description for the gameplay. You searched for clues or hunted other players down, reaching a compound where you had a showdown that left only one team alive. Now the way the game is played people rush areas of high traffic and force conflict, with the bosses becoming a secondary objective. It’s PvEvP style of gameplay has changed perhaps irreversibly to PvPv(on occasion)E

This all adds up to a far more frustrating game, where small mistakes that already punished you greatly are simply brutal. You can still kill anyone or anything with any of the weapons and tools in the game, you can still out think, out maneuver, and outshoot your enemies. However the frustrations you run into have gotten worse and the enjoyment of fighting AI is now non-existent. 

And this leads me to my biggest concerns about this games future. Its no secret the playerbase is small and tends to shrink more each year by about a hundred or more players. When I started the average daily player count was about 20,000, now its about 12,000. A really good number for the type of game it is. However it seems like with the newest event and its controversial premise that leads me and others to think Crytek might be trying to appeal to a larger player base. Which has historically killed the soul of every game that does it. I don’t want Hunt to lose its soul, but it looks like its heading that way. So if you’re interested in trying this game, alone or with friends, do it sooner rather then later. Crytek has shown they’re willing to meet players half-way on most issues, but not enough to bring back people who have left. Play now before it stops being Hunt and becomes a ever more generic and wider appealing game then it was when it launched. 

I do recommend it still, but you should be forewarned, its a different game then it used to be, and is constantly changing so fast and so much that what makes you fall in love with might change and drive you away in a year or less. 

I'll nearing that point myself, and will see what the next event holds before I make the choice leave or not. Hunt: Showdown 1896 is a joke. A bad one.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1734032648}, {"review_text": "Briefly: I do not recommend buying this game at full price and, honestly, even playing it — although that part is more subjective.

More in detail: this is a game about missed opportunities, which also reflects the history of the developers — once promising innovators, who over the years have lost their advantages and APIs.

It’s worth making a remark right away: I played all my hours exclusively with a friend who kept calling me into it; on my own, I regret every hour spent there after the eightieth, with rare exceptions only because of that friend.

[h3] Players [/h3]
First, an important point: the game is not widely known, the influx of new players is small. After each “major” update (more on that later), the number of players rises by about 50% — from ~20k to ~30k. When servers are divided by region for ping, this makes the pool quite small and closed.

And when we have a small community in one pseudo-hardcore game, we get annoying types you don’t want to meet. One of the main downsides is the unpleasant player base, which sticks to the meta, camps, and spams traps. Sure, that’s a matter of taste, but the game is extremely poor in counterplay options — there are few, if any.

Also, many belong to a rare breed of toxics who, after a match, if you killed them in a way they didn’t like, will pilgrimage to your Steam profile and tell you exactly what they think of your playstyle, you, and your relatives.

[h3] Game [/h3]
The concept isn’t new anymore: it’s a PvPvE extraction shooter. Today that sounds like the most clichéd thing Ubisoft could release. However, once upon a time, Hunt was one of the first in this field.

The game has a unique setting — 19th-century America with a mix of occultism, monsters, and dark magic, a variation on Supernatural. But here we hit problems that, in my opinion, are 100% the developers’ fault — unwillingness to risk, lack of staff or good designers. In fact, the setting isn’t revealed at all.

We have a bunch of weapons, which boil down to 4–5 types: rifles, pistols, shotguns, melee, and unique. They may have modifications — like sawn-off or scoped versions. The differences between them are pretty subjective within the same class and caliber.

The topic of magic isn’t revealed either. Recently we got an FPV drone — a magical beetle for scouting and small suicide damage — as well as a mine detonated with magic.

This season added Tarot cards, but there are two “buts.” In fact, they’re just consumables like heals or antidotes, only with different effects. The only difference is the way you obtain them.

There are also tons of traps — bear traps and tripwires, barbed or poisonous — and they come not by 1, but 2–3 per slot. You have to remove them manually or with a grenade; but grenades still trigger them, so they do their job of blocking paths and alerting others.

The gameplay is moving from one point to another, fighting zombies while searching for the boss and clues. Loop: collect three clues → find the boss → kill it → extract reward → other players attack → kill them or run like a sad weasel → extract → profit???

But there are hidden problems. Ammo is limited, and without resupply (fairly accessible), you may not have enough for two fights with players — let alone the boss and hunters chasing you.

Also, you don’t want to make noise — so suddenly you’re not in a shooter but in a Rambo simulator: sneaking past dogs, coops, branches, old lady Zina, and stabbing zombies with a knife.

Fights with players generally work, but the game is still oppressive. Headshots are one-shot kills from everything, so every time you peek, there’s a ~40% chance you’ll die instantly. Sure, friends can revive you — maybe — but nothing guarantees they won’t die, or you won’t be shot again. After a revive, you STAND UP immediately, even if you were crouched before — like a gopher in an open field.

But the main issue is the futility of it all. Bosses give ~500–800 currency for extraction. Enough for budget builds, but nothing else — only money and XP for hunters and account.

A hunter can take perks, most of which are useless except maybe four. If you hire a non-free hunter for 100, you instantly get 10 perk points to buy key ones.

Leveling the account unlocks gear and perks. At max level, you just get 1000 money per level, removing any money problems. You can reset to zero for prestige, but it gives nothing — only takes money and XP.

So we have no economy and complete futility in doing the main task, which is sometimes unpleasant by itself (like stabbing bosses with knives or shovels).

[h3] Developers [/h3]
The most depressing part is the so-called “game development.” Developers moved to a seasonal model. Each season brings minimal balance tweaks, usually like this:
“We’ve disabled bleed ammo because it’s too strong. Now you must find it on the map.”

There are almost no real number tweaks or weapon changes. “New” weapons are usually modifications. In a good update, we might get one truly new weapon and maybe a map.

Also, developers don’t add new mechanics permanently. They lock them in a season and then remove them.

For example, they added barbed branches. Sounds exciting, right? In practice, it was just a second type of branch: same crunch, but applied bleeding you had to stop. Not genius, not complex, just unpleasant. And after one season, they removed them.

Speaking of magic: in one season (maybe the same), there was a covenant mechanic. You could find spots, poke an object, and join a group. This could change perks and give one unique perk.

One group had a perk to deal damage once. It cast quickly, was convenient, and at least slightly revealed the magic theme.

New season — no covenants, no perk. Now we collect Tarot cards. Likely they’ll remove them too.

So we end up with small, often insignificant changes and mechanics that vanish as fast as they come. But every season they redraw the UI — which changes minimally. At least this time it came out nice — since there’s nothing else left to do. Such a “rich” and “full” experience.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1759147831}, {"review_text": "This game is a detriment to my mental health, its terrible and borderline painful. 10/10 recommend it", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 17, "timestamp_created": 1751776186}, {"review_text": "Developers do not care about player feedback so wasting my time at this point.

- The UI is still terrible. Far worse than it was a few years ago, we've put up with it for long enough now.

The graphics are fine, if weirdly pixelated at times (even with AA cranked up the foliage can look so jagged). Audio is honestly great. Performance is... iffy. I'd get random stuttering and FPS drops (from 60 down to 20 or so) despite having a pretty decent PC (i7 12700k, 32 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 3060). Not often, but I noticed it more on the desert maps for some reason. The game is hard, yes, and you'll die repeatedly to enemies you never even notice. I've played Rising Storm/Red Orchestra before, so it didn't bother me much. Gunplay feels pretty good and snappy, and while movement does feel a bit sluggish, it isn't something I ever found annoying or egregious. Save for the FPS drops, I never noticed any game-breaking bugs either.

A pretty good start, all told. Optimize whatever's causing that stuttering (maybe its the random weather they proudly talked about adding in the desert maps?) and it'd be a decent game with some interesting mechanics going on (I do like the simple logistics and construction system).

The part that's getting the thumbs down is the actual players.

Each server is community-run, meaning that they're all hosted by individual groups shoving VIP benefits in your face if you join their discord/teamspeak/whatever. If you manage to find one that has decent ping (anything under 120 or so), theyre probably full-up with a maxed out queue (but of course, VIP slots to get you in early).

Every time a match starts, people insta-lock the recon squads, and the irony is that nearly every server has a rule against "solo locked recon squads" but I'd regularly see lone-wolf scouts/snipers going off to god-knows-where during matches, keeping the squad locked, and laughing at anyone who tried to call them out for it. Same thing would happen, to a lesser degree, with armor and infantry squads. So you'll get around 4-5 players on your team who just... don't play the objective, don't want teammates, and just run off to weird corners of the map to camp and rack up kills.

The locked infantry squads are even more egregious, because that's what 90% of the players are gonna be in. Nobody wants to actually lead squads, so you sit there on the squad select screen for a good 30 seconds, staring at the one locked infantry squad with some level 100 player sitting in there, and then the moment a public squad opens, it gets eaten up instantly. I'd sometimes join servers where all the public squads are full and the private squads refused to let anyone in, and I'd be forced to sit there waiting -- after waiting in a queue to even join the server! -- to be let into any squad at all.

Sometimes you get nice squad leaders, who communicate and use their mic and do callouts. More often than not, it's dead silent, with zero cohesion as people run around willy-nilly, the leaders maybe remember to put down an outpost/garrison or two, and commanders seem to sit there with a thumb up their butt. The text chat is most likely people getting mad at the SLs/Commander. 

And then you enter servers with stupid level restrictions -- set by the community, mind you. Wanna join the tank crew? Gotta be level 30 first! Finally got into the recon role? Nope, can't pick that class, you need to be level 50. I was on one where everything but rifleman was locked before level 20. And if you try to pick a class you're not high enough level for, or if a squad leader dips for whatever reason, you get this giant popup warning you that you'll be kicked. If earlier you were thinking "well if nobody wants to lead squads, why didn't you?" Well, I'd have to be a higher level first on most of these servers, first!

When you do finally get into a server, find an open squad, and get a role other than the basic rifleman, you then have to deal with god-complex admins and level 150+ players who demand everything be done exactly or they'll yell at you or teamkill you (with zero repercussion). 

Tried my hand at Engineer, went to go build resource nodes in a safe tucked-away corner, and got shot in the head by another Engineer (high level, of course) because "I did it wrong" and when I asked how they said "go look it up" and dismantled what I built. They demanded I swap to another class so I can "learn the game properly before fucking it up". I watched him build the nodes in basically the same spot, but in a slightly different configuration and with barbed wire around it, wasting even more resources. None of the nodes were even threatened the entire game. The server proudly touted its rules for "No Teamkilling! Report any TK to the admins". I did so. They shrugged it off.
