[{"review_text": "Okay, I need people who are looking to buy it to understand one thing - THIS IS NOT A SOULSLIKE. DO NOT BUY IT THINKING THAT COMBAT IS THE CORE PART OF GAMEPLAY!

You have combat here, sure, but combat here is like driving in GTA - a thing to do while you're not doing something else. Hence it is very easy. There are no bonfires, no character level ups, no souls you collect. 
Most of the time you spend solving puzzles and exploring the world. The game is about mystery first and foremost, and you need to understand it before you jump in. 
The world and characters is the main driving force here, you find items, you read documents, you figure out which items go where, you trade items with characters, and in between doing that you might kill an enemy or two.

Game does become a bit harder as you progress, but as long as you don't leave the map you're exploring - enemies do not respawn. If you encounter a pack of 5 enemies and kill 4 of them, after which you're killed, you will respawn and you'll have to defeat only 1 enemy.

It's weird, it's unique, it works incredibly well (aside for rare traversal stutter). Easy recommend.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1757184047}, {"review_text": "I absolutely loved this game. The atmosphere and story are fantastic, and the combat difficulty feels just right, not too easy, not too hard. 
I really enjoyed the focus on investigation, solving puzzles, and piecing things together from documents and enviroment clues. 
The minimalist interface, with only the compass, makes you think like in the old days instead of just following markers like a sheep from point A to B. 
I like the lore and in which way they told it to the player.
The inmersion and history was really great but It would have been nice to see a bit more variety in enemies, but overall I had a great time and highly recommend it.
I want more!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1758016685}, {"review_text": "I haven’t seen an apt portrayal of the reprehensible nature of war and the psychological toll often swept under the rug by most games since Spec Ops: The Line.

This is a fascinating game that feels like a mashup of Death Stranding, Myst, and a touch of Resident Evil-style puzzles. I’m hesitant to call it a souls-like because, although combat is prevalent, it’s not the main focus. However, you can customize settings such as losing items on death or enemy difficulty if you want. The game is very narrative-driven, which some interpret as weak gameplay. However, the mystery and discovery demand a level of curiosity often missing in today’s waypoint-driven games. There’s no “go here and do this” mechanic. Instead, you’re expected to piece together what you need to do. While not exactly groundbreaking, I appreciate the direction this takes the game.

You are encouraged to meander and retrace your steps. This can be frustrating for some and might be seen as a time-waster. This game is not for those people. The gameplay itself is quite solid, though don’t expect a deep variety of enemies. The focus is more on puzzles and curiosity. Dispatching enemies becomes easier over time, and the game doesn’t throw too much at you because it’s designed to complement the puzzles you need to solve. The combat adds a subtle pressure and sense of failure that underpins your investigation of the in-universe events.

The narrative is excellent and resonates well with today’s climate of mindless online vitriol, spite, and other overwhelmingly negative emotions. The game isn’t violent from a combat perspective, but it is narratively. There are scenes and topics that are difficult to stomach. It lays bare the raw flotsam of the human race and explores the consequences of war and hate with a fantastic supernatural twist.

I highly recommend picking this up.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1757008936}, {"review_text": "[h1]Lost and Loving Every Second[/h1]
10/10 – For people who love wandering around like headless chickens and actually enjoy it
Okay, so I bought Hell Is Us right after pre-ordering Lost Soul Aside and immediately regretting that choice like a bad haircut
But this game? No regrets at all. It just tosses you into this gloomy, war-torn mess and basically says, “Good luck, Sherlock, Find your own way.” 
And honestly? I did. Sort of. After walking in circles a lot

[h1]No Map, No Clue, No Problem[/h1]
This game is the king of giving zero help. No maps, no arrows, no glowing lights pointing where to go—just you, your bad sense of direction, and a whole lot of confusion
You’ll wander around like a lost puppy sniffing every corner, hoping you’re not retracing your steps for the hundredth time
SPOILER: You probably are. But that’s half the fun. Or half the headache. Depends on your mood.

[h1]Sadness Everywhere, And I’m Here For It[/h1]
The world looks like someone forgot to turn off the “depressing war movie” filter
It’s dark—but also kinda beautiful in a “wow, this place really hates me” way
If you like your games like your coffee—dark and bitter—this one’s got you covered

[h1]NPCs Who Could Win at The World’s Most Boring Tour Guide Contest[/h1]
Forget friendly chatty people
The NPCs here are more like, “Go over there. Solve that thing. Don’t get killed. Bye.” No emotional backstory, no dramatic speeches
Just blunt directions like your least helpful friend who still somehow gives the best advice
Sometimes they drop puzzle hints, but mostly they sound like they’d rather be anywhere else

[h1]Fighting That’s Actually Fun (Surprise!)[/h1]
The combat is fast, brutal, and really satisfying
The finishers are so savage I laughed and cringed at the same time—like watching a horror movie but with swords
Plus, there’s a big bunch of weapons to choose from, so whether you want to stab, smash, or just mess stuff up, you’re covered

[h1]Puzzles That Make You Question Your Life Choices[/h1]
The puzzles don’t hold your hand
You’ll stare at a weird rock or some random thing for ages thinking, “Is this important or just a rock?” Then suddenly you figure it out and feel like a genius… right before the next puzzle makes you feel dumb again
It’s confusing, annoying, and somehow addictively fun—like trying to assemble furniture without the instructions

[h1]Runs Like a Dream, Unlike My Life[/h1]
Big shoutout to the developers because this game runs smooth
No crashes, no weird bugs, no lag. The only thing breaking here is my brain trying to understand what the heck is going on

[h1]Final Thoughts: I’d Get Lost Here Again in a Heartbeat[/h1]
If you’re into:

Walking around totally lost and loving it
Solving tricky puzzles that make you want to scream
Fighting creepy monsters with brutal weapons
Exploring a sad, broken world that’s basically a big emotional mess

Then Hell Is Us is your perfect nightmare.
10/10. Got lost, got confused, fought monsters, solved puzzles, and had an absolute blast. The story is intruiging, with a lot of care and thought given to both the world building, the aspects of war, and the central mystery. The fact you dont have a map only adds to the mystery, having to piece everything together on your own. Yes the combat isnt the deepest, but thats not why you would play this game, its for the story and the exploration.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1757362658}, {"review_text": "I let some days pass since I beat it to settle my thoughts, and here is the thing, I think it needs a sequel to fully realize its ideas...

First off, performance is great, has great PC features at launch and one of the better launches of the year on the technical side.

Now the game, it starts really strong and at the beginning I thought it was going to be one of my top 10 this year, but the more I played the more I notice that the game it's, at several points, at odds with itself:

- The paying attention part is oversold, its quite easy to know what to do next, it feels condescending at times, except for like 2 puzzles, there is very little brain power needed, and most of them are number codes.
- They cleaned up the UI just to bury the information in convoluted menus (?)
- The combat is like a souls game, yet there are no real boss battles, which is weird to have the combat system of games that thrive on them. There are just "beef up" regular enemies, or groups of enemies as final battles of areas. there just 5 types of enemies and 4 thematic orbs with 3 difficulty tiers...
- Speaking of, difficulty is a joke, and you heal way too much with the nioh-like white ring, I beat it on merciless with my inventory full of medkits and other stuff that was never needed.
- Most of the stuff you pick is either for a fetch quest, puzzle, or useless... I still explore but I got disappointed more often than not, those chest that needed several color and shape coded keys were the worst offenders, takes a lot of time to find the correct ones and the best reward they offer usually are the crystals to close time loops, but several just give you a useless consumable. 

I don't think the game is good as an exploration game and neither as a souls game...
[b] Why recommended then? [/b] 
The world building, visuals and voice acting were enough to carry me, really on those aspects, [b] masterclass. [/b]  They need to figure out what they want it to be gameplay-wise for a sequel tho.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1758918750}, {"review_text": "First of all, if you’re looking for a chill game to play after work, forget it. This isn’t that type of experience. Hell is us is puzzle-driven, and if you play on the harder difficulties, it’s hard. The puzzles don’t hold your hand at all. Sometimes a single voice line, one conversation, a random letter, or even an old artifact might hold the clue you need. If you miss it, you’re stuck. You really have to focus, take notes, or be ready to check YouTube guides. Without that, you’ll get lost fast.
Now about the world: it’s big, and you need patience. You can fast travel between provinces, but that’s it—no cars, no mounts, no quick shortcuts. Most of the time you’re on foot. And you have to be careful, because a wrong step or a fall might mean reloading since the game uses manual saves (think Resident Evil 4 remake style).
The combat? Surprisingly good. Not exactly Souls-like, but definitely inspired. It feels unique, with satisfying weapon variety. You get a drone, four different weapons, and upgrades that unlock special abilities. The downside is the enemy variety—it’s weak. Most enemies look and fight the same, and even though there are a few boss fights, none of them felt truly special.
On the positive side, the world design is amazing. One moment you’re surrounded by bright fields full of flowers, the next you’re in a wasteland straight out of Mad Max, and later you’re exploring a creepy underworld. The story is also a strong point. It’s well-written, with themes of religion, history, and mystery. Is this game a masterpiece? No, but fans of Souls-likes could nevertheless enjoy it a lot. The story is set in the 1990s. Hadea, the fictional country where the story takes place, has been ravaged by civil war, and the surviving factions are still fighting each other. The country is cut off from the rest of the world. Most of the people still living here are suffering from the consequences of the war. The landscape is destroyed, and the civilian population has to find ways to make ends meet. You have to do the same – the game gives you very little help. Hell is Us is deliberately designed so that the game does not take you by the hand. The missing arrow on the missing automap to guide you almost blindly to the next waypoint/quest marker is not an oversight, but has been deliberately omitted. You have to figure out for yourself how to get by in this world. There are also no quest logs. At least you have a compass from the start, and there are tutorials to familiarize you with the game mechanics.

Even though the title suggests that we humans are the worst evil in this world, the story seems to show something quite different. In this land, you encounter supernatural creatures that modern weapons cannot harm. Perhaps humans are to blame for the appearance of these beings? And so Hell is Us soon plays out similarly to a typical Souls-like game. With an ancient sword in hand and a drone above us, we make our way through the nightmarish world to explore the mystery of the monsters' origins (and find our parents). Compared to a real Souls-like game, the battles are easier, but the puzzles are more frequent and the conversations more numerous.

At the beginning, we choose between three difficulty levels – from story mode to nightmare mode. The game then begins with a lengthy introductory sequence that raises more questions than it answers. The actual game then begins as a flashback. We are Rémi, a soldier in a peacekeeping force who illegally invades the civil war-torn country of Hadea. We were born in Hadea, and our parents may still be here. We leave our uniform behind and have (more or less) no weapons with us. We meet a farmer who lives in the basement of his destroyed house; his sons were killed in the war. He gives us a key to open a gate so we can continue on our way. Climbing over the (slightly higher) fence is not possible. That's somehow understandable, but why we can't just climb over all the other knee-high stone walls is not logical. I thought that these 20 cm high, immersion-destroying level boundaries had gone out of fashion since Witcher 1. In any case, we quickly find a seriously injured soldier lying next to an armored personnel carrier. He sends us on our way to a camp to get a medkit for him. When we bring it to him, we receive... an ancient-looking key. We insert the key into a lock in an old rock not far away, whereupon three pillars rise from the ground. We can turn the pillars, which display different symbols, in several directions. The first puzzle... on the walls we see unknown characters – will they bring us closer to the solution?

After solving the first puzzle, we find one thing above all else inside the old building – corpses. Then we encounter the strange creatures for the first time, and after our pistol proves ineffective, we fight them with a sword. A young woman showed us how to use it shortly before she was killed by the strange monsters. We take her sword, her poncho, her drone – she doesn't need any of that stuff anymore. And soon we encounter enemies consisting of two creatures – a walker and a creature that emerges from it, connected by a kind of string. First, take down the walker, then you can hurt the second enemy. And now you're exploring the land where these creatures roam.

You can walk, run, climb ladders, strike, block, dodge – but you can't jump. Stamina is depleted when we perform certain actions and regenerates during quieter phases. However, our health bar does not regenerate on its own; only a medkit can help. Or quickly absorbing energy from enemies, which they regularly lose when we hit them. We can use our drone to distract enemies, and it also translates ancient texts and serves as a flashlight. Additional functions are added with new modules. The drone sits on our shoulder like a parrot, or we can let it fly above us. We talk to NPCs by clicking on conversation topics, and the conversations are voiced. The inventory is quite manageable – two weapons, up to two (additional) items of clothing, up to two relics, and a few consumables. There are also cosmetic items, but nothing compared to all the stuff we carry around in Diablo. We can view our inventory, as well as the information we have collected so far and the status of our drone, on a tablet that we carry with us.

The developers recommend playing the game with a gamepad. The game is saved at manual save points – if you can find any. If you don't find a save point, you can't save and all your progress since the last save is lost. Not very convenient. But it's not quite as bad as it sounds – if you die, you start at the last save point with full energy, and enemies you have already defeated remain dead. Defeated enemies also remain dead despite saving – unless you activate a special mode that revives enemies when you save/die.

[u][b] Conclusion:[/b][/u]
Hell of Us is set in the present day, in a remote country torn apart by civil war – full of ancient secrets. The country is full of terrible monsters – which must be fought with a sword. You explore the country, searching for your parents – but without an automatically generated map. If you like Souls-like battles (with a lower difficulty level), want to solve the occasional puzzle, and feel like getting lost in the vastness of a mysterious world (or exploring the world, depending on how you look at it), Hell of Us is a good alternative to the usual fantasy Souls-like monotony offered by other games. You see, while the game manages to immerse me with its supernatural mystery, [b]often great worldbuilding[/b] and fairly unique civil war themes, the character writing frequently takes me out of it again, with its insistence on having [b]characters self-analyse in a way that’s more appropriate for a history book about the social effects of this particular civil war, rather than a three-dimensional human being living in that exact moment[/b]. Most characters you meet will be more than eager to explain how their hatred of the other ethnic group started and what factors, from propaganda to pogroms, played a part in that development. It’s not always so bad, but when it is, it feels like the writer is speaking through a mouthpiece to explain the (unfortunately very real) mechanisms that lead to sectarian/ethnic violence, rather than a person describing their situation from their own very limited point of view.

One notable early example of the dialogue being so devoid of subtlety that it strains my ability to suspend my disbelief is [spoiler]a woman living in the first village you visit. When you approach her and initiate dialogue, she immediately explains to you that she was part of a lynch mob targeting a family belonging to the other ethnic group. When the military of that ethnic group then started occupying the village and killing its inhabitants, they kept her around to sexually abuse her as “punishment”.[/spoiler] And while that situation feels uncomfortably real, the fact that this character would so openly tell a complete stranger about any of this (with armed hostile soldiers nearby) makes it come off as very artificial. There’s even [spoiler]a soldier in the village who talks about “paying her a visit” once his shift is over[/spoiler], so wouldn’t it have been much more subtle and believable to have the character be more evasive and let the player figure out what’s going on via context clues and remarks from other NPCs? At the very least, [b]it feels very incongruous to have the characters spell everything out for you like this, in a game that otherwise touts itself as a "no handholding" player-driven exploration experience[/b].

I feel like games such as [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/50300][i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i][/url] or even [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/292030][i]The Witcher 3[/i][/url] do a better job of depicting the horrors of war in this regard, simply because characters in these games were written as actual persons who would rather hide their trauma out of a sense of shame or try to conceal their own complicity in the atrocities depicted by the game.

So while [b]I really enjoy Hell is Us for its atmosphere, exploration gameplay, lore and themes[/b], this aspect of [b]the writing is a real fly in the ointment for me[/b]. The game sits comfortably at a 7.5/10 for me. But a VERY GOOD 7.5/10

From the hook, to the environments, to the ambience and monsters. This game is absolutely incredible in these aspect. Shining the absolute brightest in the sound design. As a produced piece of artwork, this game stands tall, as a prime example of what world design, graphical design and sound design should be. But with all these positives, the game unfortunately does have a few shortcomings.

While the enemy design is awesome, the enemy variety holds the game back a lot. There are very few enemy types in the game, which means that after a few hours of combat and exploring a couple zones, you've seen everything. Now, this is remedied a bit by the [spoiler] Haze enemies, which are like emotional manifestations that attach themselves to some enemies. These increase in power as the enemies do. But at the same time, they ALSO increase in complexity. Meaning a Tier 1 Haze is very simple to deal with, but a Tier 3 Haze will require you pay some serious attention, and learn how to fight them properly. Until you get max upgrade weapons, Tier 3 hazers keep you on your toes and ready. However, once you get good equipment and max weapons, then Tier 3 are pushovers, unfortunately. [/spoiler]

Exploration also takes a few hits sometimes. Generally I'm someone with a really good sense of where-the-fuck-am-I, and have no trouble keeping mental maps in my head. However, for anyone who struggles with it, this game is going to feel really bad. I understand you had a design in mind, and you executed it well, to which I applaud. But having an option for someone to point you more precisely in specific directions for story related progress, would be really nice, and open the game to people who like the vibes, but suck at navigating.

Following on the above note, it would be wonderful for future games in this series, to have the option to take pictures with your drone, to then view in your datapad. While I thoroughly enjoyed having to break out the notepad and write clues down myself for some puzzles, I also write like shit. I made it through, but being able to have the visuals, and even further maybe the ability to write simple notes on said pictures, would've been awesome for immersion. And piggybacking off of this: It would also be wonderful if you slowly collected data on the enemies as you fought them, as well as the empowered ones, to learn their strengths, weaknesses, and how to handle them in the best way.

And my final downside for this game, before getting into the good stuff again, is the clue management. I wish the game (or by immersion, the character) would discard clues that have been used to solve puzzles and riddles. Because by the end of the game, I had 3x more clues in my list, than puzzles to solve, and that simply became overwhelming.

But aside from all of that, I still wholeheartedly recommend this game, if you want a very unique experience, with some action RPG involved. The upgrade systems are very interesting, and the various types of abilities, not to mention the wide selection of abilities in each type, make this game really nice to play. Crowd control, brute force, and stunning, that all go together really well between weapons skills, drone skills, and your own relics. learning the extensive lore about the game as well has been a blast. I'm impressed by the amount of lore and background to everything that's happened.

As I said, a VERY GOOD 7,5/10, that could be an easy 9/10. Fully recommended!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1759008058}]

Developer tried to be unique in this matter, but in fact some of the tatoes don't seem to be challenging at all, even on highest Danger 5. Once you unlock Danger 5 by playing consequently each of them, it becomes available for all your characters.

So the game has six difficulty levels, step by step adding more enemies and more types of them, ending on having three random swarms/elites during a run and double boss at the end. You can see it's a game for kids since "completing the game" doesn't require from you beating it with all characters on danger 5, this can be done on baby-easy danger 0.

Finishing a run with a new character gives you new item/weapon that comes up when rolling between waves or at the start of the run. - To add to this, I've found increasing the toughness and amount of the enemies to be extremely useful, and borderline essential to this game. Definitely play with it as you go if you find that you're too OP!

The loading times are great! It is really quick to jump into. The best part is that the game saves your progress when you quit. If you were in the middle of a run, you can quit, and later jump straight back in. This makes the game very accessible, and friendly for people with little time. The travel system and movement is also very fast; travelling back to where you died is actually fun, not a slog like in some other games.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1742407435}, {"review_text": "I was initially inclined to leave a thumbs-down due to the lack of indicators, but hey it's early access (not using it as an excuse), I understand that plans can change, and they clearly have in this case. The game will no longer feature just 6 levels, but rather a significantly larger number, spanning across different biomes. Regarding the absence of indicators, the primary concern stems from the fact that the game currently offers only two playable levels. While it's possible to infer that the lack of a tome suggests no additional levels to unlock, this is not immediately obvious to players. However, I do appreciate the inclusion of a roadmap in the menus, as well as the "unstuck" button—thank you for those additions. It's clear that the developers care about the game's progression, but the overall scope and eventual endpoint remain somewhat unclear. It would be helpful if this were more transparently communicated. 

Visually, the game has a sleek design, and the traversal mechanics, though seemingly basic on the surface, feel fluid and satisfying. The core mechanics include dashes, a weapon throw for teleportation, and occasional grappling points. Combat is fluid and responsive, with dashing as the central feature, offering brief invincibility. Engaging enemies and landing hits gradually regenerates health, taking notes from the philosophy of Doom Eternal, where offense is the best form of defense.

There is a noticeable contrast between the first and second levels. The first is relatively linear and restricted, while the second offers much more exploration, with numerous points of interest and multiple layers to a degree of almost being a closed world in itself. There is loot to be discovered, and a strategic approach—where players complete expeditions to familiarize themselves with the map and gather resources before tackling the primary objective—seems beneficial. However, given that future maps are expected to be more numerous, but not necessarily as long (around two hours in dev's words), the quality of these new levels remains uncertain. While more content is always appreciated, it’s hard to predict whether the added quantity will match the quality of the initial levels.

The game also features elements of an extraction roguelite, not a roguelike (a distinction worth noting). This allows players to cleanse their equipment and retain it permanently. Additionally, equipment upgrades are available, and after reaching a certain tier, players will need to acquire duplicates of the same item to increase its "satiety." At the highest tier, RNG rolls come into play. Players can also level up their character to increase their overall damage output.

The game certainly holds promise, but I’ve witnessed many early access titles used primarily to fund development, a model that doesn't always succeed. While I’m not suggesting that this is the case here, some players may not fully grasp the valid concerns of the community. Being a solo developer is undoubtedly challenging, and I appreciate the developer’s commitment to continuously updating the roadmap and responding to every available feedback. That said, for some, the $20 price tag might feel steep although, with regional pricing and my own access to a free key, I felt my conscience wouldn’t allow me to take a personal hit on that. I’m genuinely invested in seeing where the game’s development goes, and I hope it lives up to its ambitions.

The review will be (kept) updated as the game continues to receive updates.

It's a solid remaster. The visual overhaul breathes new life into these RTS classics while maintaining that distinct Command & Conquer aesthetic. Both Tiberian Dawn and Red Alert plus their expansions are included, giving you plenty of content to work through. There are some rough edges here and there, but nothing that ruins the core experience. The price point feels just right for what you're getting.

The gameplay holds up remarkably well despite its age. You're still building bases, harvesting Tiberium, and commanding armies in that familiar rock-paper-scissors dance of unit counters. The pacing strikes a nice balance between resource management and combat, though you'll spend a good chunk of time waiting for your economy to ramp up. Your units die fast and hit hard, so positioning and timing matter more than raw numbers. It's a satisfying loop of expansion and destruction that keeps you coming back.

The remastered soundtrack by Frank Klepacki is the standout feature. The original compositions were already iconic, and this enhanced version amplifies everything that made them memorable. The music seamlessly shifts between industrial menace and triumphant marches, perfectly matching the on-screen chaos. 

What's genuinely shocking is EA's restraint here. No forced account creation, no always-online DRM, no microtransactions - just a straight remaster that respects the source material. The quality-of-life improvements like unit queuing and improved pathfinding modernize the experience without fundamentally changing it.

Overall, Command & Conquer: Remastered Collection is how remasters should be done - a faithful recreation that enhances rather than replaces.

The GTX 1050 Ti is not stressed much with remaster.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1734905066}, {"review_text": "With the 30th anniversary upon us, I finally decided to give this game a proper write-up. This review may be long, so I'll try to cover the most important parts here in the beginning:

This 25th anniversary collection contains the very first game from 1995 (also known as Command & Conquer: Tiberian Dawn or C&C95) and its prequel, the original Red Alert. Both have fundamentally identical gameplay to the originals, but there are many Quality of Life features, bonus content including Behind the Scenes and Missions exclusive to the console ports, visual overhauls, and audio improvements. If you play this, you must keep in mind that the PC RTS genre was merely 3 or 4 years old when these were released. The gameplay tries to be as faithful as possible, so have an open mind about possibly dated level design.
That being said, this collection is an utter triumph as far as quality remasters go. More importantly, it's a glorious bright spot in the past 15 years of (mostly) neglect this franchise has faced from the holder of its Intellectual Property. EA did the fans right this time. They asked for community input and oversight and involved the Former Westwood Creators. If you're on the fence, this game frequently goes on sale for a bargain.
Please also consider the Ultimate Collection, which includes all 17 major PC releases (RIP Sole Survivor) including the ORIGINAL Win95 compatible versions ONLY of C&C95 and RA1. If you buy that one on sale it's technically less than $1 a game because of expansions. Finally, The Modding Community is excellent for many games in this series. Seriously, Mods revolutionized things for me once I discovered them. The dedication of the community is keeping this franchise alive even with a decade and a half of relative silence.


With that out of the way, I'm going to devote most of the rest of this to C&C95, so I want to quickly mention my thoughts on Red Alert 1. RA1 is probably the more approachable of the two. It has a fantastic competitive scene with a high skill ceiling (mostly on CNCnet). It can be fast-paced, and marks the birth of the Tank Rush. There are a multitude of missions. There is more variety of technologies and unit types, and the two factions are quite distinct. From a singleplayer/casual standpoint, feel free to experiment. I think it probably has one of the more impressive soundtracks in the series too, especially tracks from the Aftermath. (I have other personal favorites, but that's trying to look at it objectively). All-in-all, Westwood took a large step towards solidifying the identity of the series when they released it in 1996, and while it may be challenging, the gameplay holds up pretty well and the package here in the Remastered Collection has wonderful presentation.



Now, on to the main event. Command & Conquer 1 holds a special place in my heart. I am the same age, though I didn't realize how close until a few years ago. I didn't actually play the PC version until I got "The First Decade" collection from 2006. I DID however play the Nintendo 64 Port as a child, and I struggled with it. Most of my experience came as I grew up watching my Dad get wrecked by Kirovs in Red Alert 2 until he finally figured out how to prepare anti-air in time and subsequently defeat hard enemies. He showed me how to surround my base with pillboxes, and thus began my long history of turtling. I also yearned for Yuri's Revenge and Generals, which my cousin had. Naturally, I got a lot better with time, and once I got the First Decade, I was able to catch up on all the other games I'd missed. Nowadays I've become our family's resident LAN game and C&C Mod expert, so this series has remained very important to me. TFD is when I started to play C&C1 for real, and it was a journey that helped me improve in other games too.
So, most people would probably find C&C95's level design to be annoying, cryptic, or punishing. Why? In my opinion, it's a Puzzle game as much as it is an RTS. It quickly gained a reputation for me as "the game where you never have money." You will ALWAYS run out of money unless you farm or make bold moves. I am a shameless turtle, and I like the former method, but there are some impressive ways to humiliate the AI. (Please look up guides from Nyerguds, he loves this game even more than me and he's a pro.) In base-building missions, you need to micromanage your harvester so your Tiberium Field is not consumed. only harvest in diagonal "checkerboard patterns" and the resources will slowly grow back. If you don't, then the field will either be permanently gone or take an absolute eternity to grow back with only a Blossom tree.
When there is no base, or if you're strapped for cash, here's the other fun part about this game. YOU MUST MAKE EVERY UNIT COUNT... most of the time. I went back to the N64 version later, and I distinctly remember the GDI mission where you start with a few grenadiers on the beach taking out the three turrets so your MCV can arrive. I moved to the right and started getting some minigunners and a guard tower, but I didn't have enough money for a weapons factory. Then an early flame tank ate my infantry for breakfast and buildings for lunch. That left an impression on me that every choice I made in that game mattered. You will struggle to find the right strategy for every situation, but when resources are tight and you are put in impossible situations, you will come to appreciate the niche of every unit. You are also rewarded for keeping your units alive through micromanagement. Most of the series will let you slide by with tank spam, and if you're good enough you can probably get away with it here too (or maybe bike/buggy for Nod,) but this game will actually test you. It's the little things too, like the garbage HP and absurd cost of the Bazooka men is offset by excellent ability to take out tanks and guard towers if you can place them at the perfect range, or facing away with Mammoth Tank turrets to maximize the rocket attack. This is a game where the design is wholly different from everything that came after, and while that means it shows its age, C&C95 has solidified itself as one of my favorites in the whole series for the unique flavor it brings to the table.
Aside from gameplay, it was a pioneer in both CD Audio Music and Full-Motion Video in PC games, and has a story which fits the period of the mid-90s well. Most of the characters were simply Westwood Employees on green screen. Joe Kucan is timeless as Kane, but he initially planned to simply direct rather than also star as the villain. The plot is not too exciting if you want a modern drama with twists, turns, and inter-character dialogue, but it does a great job of dropping you into the world and letting you see how war is changing with the proliferation of Tiberium. It's a slow drip-feed of information--you learn things as they develop. The finales are also rather brief and open-ended, leaving the consequences of either Kane and Nod's defeat or their discrediting and humiliation of GDI up in the air. (That is, until Tiberian Sun or the Mod Twisted Insurrection.)

In closing, Command & Conquer 1 may not be for everyone, but as the codifier of the RTS genre, it leaves an indelible legacy on everything that came after. It may be tough, but like most things in life it becomes much more enjoyable when you invest the time to get better at it. You can analyze the subtleties of units, learn their strengths and weaknesses, abuse and cheese the AI, micromanage your units, and do the impossible--even the Covert Ops missions which still give me trouble.
I'm enough of a nerd that I have a 486 DOS PC and installed the REAL original from 1995. (By the way, it's a little slow so it's better to at least have a Pentium) I wholeheartedly hope others will come to appreciate this game for what it is. This Remastered Collection is an excellent way to do so.

[h1] Overview [/h1]
Don’t Starve Together is a multiplayer survival game by Klei Entertainment, building on the success of the original Don’t Starve. Players are thrown into a dark, eerie world filled with challenges and must cooperate (or compete) to survive. The game features a unique art style, intriguing lore, and demanding gameplay mechanics that test creativity and strategy.

[h1] Story and Atmosphere [/h1]
The game’s lore is subtle yet engaging. Players are stranded in the Constant, a mysterious world filled with strange creatures and environmental hazards. The story unfolds through exploration and scattered clues, leaving much to player interpretation. The gothic hand-drawn art style and atmospheric music amplify the eerie, survival-focused tone.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
At its core, the game is about survival—gathering resources, crafting items, and fending off dangers such as hunger, darkness, and hostile creatures. Multiplayer introduces new dynamics, requiring teamwork to split tasks, defend against threats, and manage limited resources. The challenge increases with changing seasons, each bringing unique obstacles like freezing winters or scorching summers.

[h1] Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Unique Art Style: The hand-drawn, Tim Burton-esque visuals stand out.
    [*]Replayability: Randomized worlds and dynamic challenges keep the experience fresh.
    [*]Multiplayer Depth: Cooperative gameplay adds layers of strategy and fun.
    [*]Challenging Yet Rewarding: Success feels earned due to the game’s difficulty.
[/list]

[h1] Cons [/h1]
[list]
    [*]Steep Learning Curve: The lack of hand-holding can overwhelm newcomers.
    [*]Resource Management Pressure: Balancing food, sanity, and health can feel repetitive.
    [*]Team Dependency: Multiplayer can frustrate if teammates are inexperienced or uncooperative.
[/list]

[h1] Final [/h1]
Don’t Starve Together is a creative and challenging survival experience that rewards teamwork and strategy. While it may not suit players seeking a casual experience, fans of survival games will appreciate its depth and charm.

[h1] Score: 87/100i [/h1]", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 17, "timestamp_created": 1735769946}, {"review_text": "The goal of Don't Starve Together is to find and fight all ~ 26 boss monsters, a lot of which can be more or less hidden.

Two of these bosses are considered "final bosses" in the sense that killing them is the big accomplishment of two separate journeys with many different steps, one taking you deep in horribly dangerous underground dungeons and one taking you all around the sea.
After each of these 2 bosses, new content is added in the form of new "post game" world modifications that each gives new bosses, new mechanics, new weapons, armor and technologies to use.

I wanted to start by describing that because DST looks deceptively more simple than it truly is when you first take a look a it, when in truth it actually is quite complex, rich and intricate!



In this game, surviving is tough and difficult and requires you to understand a lot of different specific steps, and understand how many resources are tied together or meant to be exploited in strange and unexpected ways.
At first it feels like learning to stay alive during each of the 4 seasons is the game, and it won't necessarily make you feel like it's super deep because it is actually only step one. It's supposed to be simple and slow! It's possible to survive a year without too much trouble in a kind of baren base with not so much stuff at your disposal, but that is very far from the goal, which is about learning to thrive and accumulate wealth in order to get out there and fight bosses (that won't come to you unless you come to them.)

There are lots of different resources you can take from the world and bring back home, creatures who'se homes you can move, beneficial structures you can acquire, all kinds of things that are meant to saturate you in food, tools, weapons and armors for your many expeditions.

But the game never holds your hand through any of it at all. Learning can be really unclear and counter-intuitive (who would think that butterflies are the most basic and most essential source of food early game, or that you are supposed to relocate pig houses around a pen in order to have a steady supply of armor every full moon? No one, at first!) and every step of the way can make you think "is that it?" just because you may likely fail to see the link between things for a while, or how you are meant to abuse the heck out of them, or how they are just stepping stones towards something bigger.
It's a game that you just won't be able to enjoy if you struggle with challenging yourself. You need to throw yourself out there, be active, be looking to learn and practice survival techniques and get busy trying to do things on a grander scale, or do research about which bosses should be next and how to reach them.
Knowledge is either difficult to acquire on your own or requires you to practice several times to get it right, and then so much better than right. It can be intimidating, which can make you become a bit too passive and invite boredom because you're nowhere near having completed all there is to complete, but you may not understand how to get there, or how to learn.

Nothing research and interacting with the community can't fix though!
I regularily give many tips and explanations to people from a particular discord community server, it's a great vibe.



All in all, I recommend this game with all of my heart with the knowledge that it really may not be for everybody, especially if you tend to be too passive or can't bother with putting too much effort into trying to overcome challenges. 
It's my own favorite survival game out there specifically because it gives survival so much purpose and so many steps, because of how much effort you can put into learning and how rewarding it can be; but it can put some people off.

There's a lot of ways to achieve the same things. Tons of different knowledge, a bunch of different mechanics that you will likely gloss over for a couple hundred hours until you start using them and start realizing "why have I never bothered doing this awesome thing before" (like taming and riding big cows to become the ultimate war machine) 
There's fun in joining random worlds and seeing how you can contribute, fun in starting over and doing things better and quicker or in different order, fun in practicing the same skills because they're tough and require good habits, fun in seeing how everyone's lack of knowledge can create so many shenanigans due to lack of preparation, lack of resources, lack of having made enough structures in time, and fun in modding the game and tweaking the little things along the way.

There's lots to love!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1744153365}, {"review_text": "[h3] Okay guys, I played a little bit... It's time to finally write a review. I promise to be concise. [/h3]
This game is annoyingly obstinate in theme, design, and user interface. It comes packaged with a flimsy combat system, deliberately useless-sounding/actually-useless tools & structures, and a slightly uncanny and weird art style that's honestly something you just have to see for yourself.

[h3] This game is also kind of... hard. Maybe in a bad way. [/h3]
Seriously? Well, this is a positive review. I'll explain. Nothing gets explained to the player, and players basically just have to point and click on random stuff, make some random tools, and either die of darkness, or die of boredom once they've been sitting at a campfire for 8 minutes straight. If they survive longer, then they die of hounds. Live a little longer? Die to insanity. If somehow they make it to Winter... well, you can guess. I don't have any large praise for this game design, as while I look at this learning process fondly now... it's really frustrating at its core to be entirely honest. I was definitely interested in the game a LOT, don't get me wrong. There's no way I could have possibly played as much as I have now and probably more in the future if I didn't enjoy this, but this game is deliberately difficult: accomplished through ignorance and severely punishing mistakes. Y'know, as a solo-player game, I'd leave it at that, but there's more.

[h3] This game was not meant to be played alone. To that end, it is a lot like another game we all know and love. [/h3]
Minecraft. I think it's a lot like Don't Starve -- maybe not in genre -- but in the sense that the way players learn how to play the game is shockingly a bit similar. In Minecraft, not a whole lot is really explained, and I feel like, to a stranger, you can only really explain it as a game where you play with lego blocks and make crappy log cabins... like, forever (sounds boring?). 

Anyways, No One Learned How To Play Minecraft On Their Own. Seriously, how did anyone learn how to build their first nether portal? How did anyone figure out the ending of the game and all of the steps that led up to defeating the ender dragon? We all learned it through each other. Older siblings, friends, school peers, those crappy Minecraft journals at the book faire, ONLINE guides? That's how we learned, and that's how the public understanding of Minecraft became so advanced, for an otherwise obtuse and poorly explained game. 

[h3] That's Don't Starve. [/h3]
Dropping in on public servers, toiling away like a dolt, barely surviving with a few other, dull campers until some Enlightened Soul steps in to your base to actually organize it and show you the ropes of the game. You'd learn about crockpots, iceboxes, you might really get into base-building. Later, you'd learn about all the biomes, find out how to survive the seasons, start exploring the caves, etc. All at the advice of others in public lobbies or on the internet. All of the pitfalls of Don't Starve's deliberately difficult design and the obscure knowledge that players have to learn are all elements that make mentors and collaboration even more valuable. We all taught each other, and while this game did not truly start out as a multiplayer game... 

[b] I think I can at least say that the experience of sharing knowledge, learning the ropes, and tutoring new, acolyte survivors in this stupid, obtuse little survival game was truly valuable in the end. Don't Starve guys. This game provides a familiar survival experience, as you start the game in the middle of a procedurally generated world and must immediately start collecting resources and crafting gear. However, this game is much more punishing than most survival games and you're immediately racing against the clock to make sure you collect things so that you can feed yourself and have enough light to survive the night. This wouldn't necessarily be a problem if it wasn't for the way death works in this game. There are some difficulty options that can be configured to make things easier, but by default, you become a ghost when you die, can only respawn with certain items or objects, and the world will reset if everyone dies and no one respawns within a certain time limit. This means that one unfortunate encounter with a poorly understood enemy can force you to start from scratch, and constant restarts seems to be the intended way to play this game, which I found extremely tedious. Even on easier difficulties, where respawning is much more forgiving and is always available, you can still end up in a state where you're stuck dying at the respawn point over and over because you don't have the necessary items to survive and can't collect them before you perish.

It's worth mentioning that the game is still getting frequent updates, and I think some of the more recent updates have made some progress on making this feel better. The upgrade trees they've been adding for each character are cool, and the compendium they added which has every item and enemy in the game in it makes learning about various things in the game substantially easier. So far this hasn't been able to keep our games from feeling extremely difficult to learn, punishing, and unfair, but hopefully they'll continue to work on making the game easier for beginners and I can one day change this review to a positive one, because I do really want to like this game.

The art style of this game is extremely good, and is very iconic. The game ran very well, and I don't recall running into any major bugs.

[b]TL;DR[/b] This survival game has a fantastic art style, runs well, has a unique world which is fun to explore and experiment in, and is still getting updates after many years. The story is as simple as an IKEA chair manual: a couple on the verge of divorce is magically turned into dolls. To become human again, Cody and May must learn to work together. Sounds adorable until you find yourselves yelling at each other in perfect harmony.

The gameplay is a constant experiment. One level has you shooting nails and swinging on ropes, another has you steering a tiny minecart, or even fighting a talking vacuum cleaner. Yes, an evil vacuum cleaner. Probably the one I forgot to clean for years.

The visuals are bright and vibrant, as if the artists binge-read children’s books while drawing... and maybe took a bit of, let’s say, inspiration from Madagascar. The levels are so diverse that by the end of the game, you might start to suspect they tried to cram EVERY genre into one box. You’ve got platforming, racing, and even a marriage argument simulator.

But the real star of the game is Dr. Hakim, the talking relationship book. With his charisma and lines like "dance like a butterfly, love like a boss," he’s clearly aiming for the title of the most annoyingly wise NPC of the decade.

It Takes Two is a game that reminds you relationships aren’t just about "press a button and it works." It’s therapy, teamwork drills, and absolute chaos wrapped in the most creative storyline I’ve ever seen in a game. If Pixar and your relationship counselor made a baby, this would be it.

Now, I went into this thinking, “How hard could it be?” Turns out... very. There were moments when I was majestically failing at every jump, puzzle, and timing challenge, while my duo (who I’m convinced is part ninja, part Einstein) was flying through it all like a caffeinated squirrel. Of course, fast-forward a few levels, and the tables turned. Suddenly he was the one crashing into walls and dying spectacularly while I was doing aerial stunts like a pro. Balance, I guess.

The game is built for two people—literally. You cannot play solo, and honestly, that’s the charm. You need each other to survive, to progress, and occasionally to scream, “WHAT ARE YOU EVEN DOING?!” It tests your communication skills, your patience, and your ability to not throw your controller when your partner presses the wrong button for the 17th time.

The story? Oh man. Best. Ever. No spoilers here, but imagine a heartfelt, emotional rollercoaster wrapped in hilarious dialogue and breathtakingly unique levels. One moment you’re bouncing on jello, the next you’re fighting squirrels, then suddenly you’re flying a plane made of underpants. It never lets up and never gets boring.

Whether you’re a couple trying to spice up date night, siblings who want to prove who the real favorite is, or best friends who think they’ve seen it all—It Takes Two will challenge you, make you laugh, frustrate you (in the best way), and leave you wanting more.

If you survive it without passive-aggressively muting your mic, you know your bond is real.

I also think the devs love this game because it feels and plays like a passion project to me and they dont try to sell you stuff so no micro transactions which is refreshing too.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1734035863}, {"review_text": "Witchfire – In-Depth Game Review (9/10)
Developer: The Astronauts
Genre: Dark Fantasy, First-Person Shooter, Roguelite
Platform: PC (Early Access)
Score: ★★★★★★★★★☆ (9/10)

Introduction
Witchfire is a dark fantasy shooter from The Astronauts, a team known for their storytelling brilliance in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter and intense gameplay roots in Painkiller. After years in development, the game finally enters Early Access — and it’s absolutely worth the wait.

Blending gritty action with haunting environments and rogue-lite mechanics, Witchfire manages to carve out its own identity in a genre dominated by titans like Doom and Dark Souls. It’s visceral, it’s beautiful, and most importantly — it’s fun.

Gameplay & Combat – 9.5/10
At its core, Witchfire is a high-octane first-person shooter with tight, snappy gunplay. You play as a Vatican-sanctioned witch hunter dropped into a cursed land teeming with eldritch horrors. What sets the combat apart is the hybrid system of firearms and magic: you’re just as deadly with a flintlock rifle as you are with lightning spells or time-manipulating hexes.

Each encounter feels dangerous and deliberate. Enemies are relentless and intelligently designed, ranging from undead soldiers to grotesque monsters powered by witchcraft. Learning their attack patterns and weaknesses is key to survival — a satisfying challenge that rewards precision and experimentation.

Weapons are customizable and varied, each with its own upgrade tree and personality. Combined with different magical perks and passive bonuses, the combat system offers remarkable depth.

World & Atmosphere – 9/10
One of Witchfire’s strongest points is its atmosphere. The world is meticulously crafted, dripping with gothic horror and medieval dread. Environments shift from fog-drenched graveyards to storm-ravaged villages and warped forests, each filled with secrets and danger.

There is no hand-holding. The world tells its story through environmental storytelling, item descriptions, and subtle clues. This design choice creates a sense of mystery and discovery, encouraging exploration and immersion.

The sound design deserves special mention — thunder cracking in the distance, eerie whispers, and satisfying weapon sounds all enhance the tension and immersion.

Progression & Replayability – 8.5/10
Witchfire employs a rogue-lite progression system: death sends you back to your safe zone, but many of your upgrades and gear persist. This creates a compelling loop of exploration, risk, and reward.

Some players may find the grind a bit repetitive, especially during the mid-game. However, the constantly evolving enemy encounters and new abilities keep things from getting stale for too long.

Frequent updates and a clear roadmap from the developers promise even more content, including new biomes, bosses, and lore expansions.

Narrative & Lore – 7.5/10
While Witchfire isn’t heavily story-driven, the bits of lore you uncover are intriguing. The premise — a holy war against witches in a world where religion and magic collide — is compelling. However, much of the story remains vague or hidden, which can be a double-edged sword.

If you're a fan of FromSoftware-style storytelling (like in Dark Souls or Bloodborne), you’ll likely appreciate the cryptic, environmental approach. But those looking for a cinematic, character-driven narrative might be left wanting more.

Visuals & Performance – 9/10
Graphically, Witchfire is stunning. Built on Unreal Engine 4, the game features photogrammetry-based environments that look almost lifelike. Lighting is used masterfully to build mood — flickering candles, shafts of moonlight, and eerie green glows add to the game’s chilling aesthetic.

Performance is solid, even in Early Access, with well-optimized settings and minimal bugs. The UI is clean and minimalistic, keeping you focused on the action.

Pros & Cons
Pros:

Excellent and satisfying combat system

Beautiful, atmospheric world design

Deep customization and progression

Rewarding challenge and skill-based gameplay

Strong sound design and visuals

Cons:

Story is underdeveloped for lore-focused players

Early-game progression can feel grindy

Some repetitiveness in mid-game loop

Might be too challenging for casual players

Final Verdict – 9/10
Witchfire is a bold, brutal, and beautifully crafted shooter that delivers on its promise of dark fantasy mayhem. With a solid combat foundation, haunting world design, and endless potential for expansion, it’s already one of the best indie FPS games in recent years — and it's only in Early Access.

Whether you’re a fan of DOOM-style combat, Dark Souls-like atmosphere, or rogue-lite progression, Witchfire offers a rich and rewarding experience. It’s not perfect, but it comes damn close.

If that's what you're looking for, Witchfire is the game for you.

The game has a simple gameplay loop. You have a lobby area where you can upgrade your characters levels, research new weapons/spells/equipment, manage your buffs, power ups and test weapons etc. Pretty stock standard basic stuff like you'd see in any other game. Eventually you unlock a shop you can buy supplies from as well.

Then you load into a map. There's initially one map you can load into, unlocking more later through gameplay and upgrades.

The maps are designed with a medieval/fantasy theme in mind. Large towers, islands, old style shipwrecks, rocks, mushrooms and herbs everywhere. The game visually looks very stunning but can become overwhelming when you're getting attacked by a lot of monsters (lots of colours/flashes on your screen).

The gameplay. The gunplay feels absolutely phenomenal and a lot of inspiration was taken from Destiny. Guns feel very unique one to the next, each can be upgraded to have very helpful powerups and there isn't one single gun that makes all other guns obsolete. You'll need to change and adapt depending on the situation.

The gameplay loop works in a couple of ways. You either load into a map and kill enemies/collect resources or else you aim to progress in the story/upgrade arc. You can definitely do both at the same time - you just get dropped in then do what you want.

This game is difficult. It is challenging without it being overbearingly punishing. Health is a resource so you cant just face tank every situation. Bosses are well thought out. As far as I'm aware each map has a sort of "raid" that combines the use of puzzles/thinking as well as at often times genuinely hectic gameplay.

The best thing about this game though - it doesn't feel like a job. You're not competing with anyone. You're not going to get left behind because others progress faster than you. It's the perfect game to kill an hour here or there but also is rewarding for longer gaming sessions in terms of advancement and content.

There are a couple of things that I don't like about it though which are things the community is aware of that hopefully do get fixed in the future.

There are issues where randomly but not often frames seem to crash for about 10-15 seconds. The best solution I've found is to just press escape to pause the game until the frame rate sorts itself out then continue. Happens maybe once every couple of hours for me.

Some general gameplay bugs such as some animations not triggering properly, portals spawning on top of loot making it difficult to pick it up after boss encounters. Minor things that are more of an inconvenience rather than game breaking but in Early Access I'll let it slide.

The biggest win for me though - no microtransactions. None. I play a game to have fun, not to have more products sold to me. Please keep it this way devs!

Pirated this first then decided that I wanted to pay them instead as soon as I got to pilot the game", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1753908671}, {"review_text": "I love so much of what we're seeing from this game thus far, but it has some major issues baked pretty deep into its DNA.

The best thing about Witchfire is its premise, it's genuinely a gamechanger. It's a looter-shooter roguelite extraction-shooter amalgamation with free roaming levels, a lot of build customization, and an extremely satisfying core gameplay loop where the hardest challenges that levels have to offer are best done after doing all the easy challenges, but without strictly enforcing that so good players can really show off their skills and builds.

I especially have to give a round of applause to the curse mechanic, where you can effectively bait the witch into launching a curse against you to get a ton of juicy upgrades for a level's raid or boss. It creates unintentional high moments where you get caught off-guard by a curse and need to adapt, it creates intentional high moments where you feel like a mad genius for doing it on purpose and getting richly rewarded for your efforts, it's absolutely brilliant.

Witchfire really is something special, but what I find a bit problematic is that this outstanding high-level gameplay loop is complimented with a much more scrappy low-level gameplay loop, and I mostly don't mean that in a good way.

At the early stages of the game's progression the combat feels like fencing with guns, which is very fun and engaging. The enemies don't overwhelm you with enough projectiles to make sidestepping without dodging unviable, nor are the melee enemies so fast that they have to be dodged away from instead of letting you backpedal and shoot. Your offense is tempered with having highly limited ammo and long spell cooldowns, which plays into the gameplay loop where basic ammo drops become valuable loot.

Then, as the game gets harder, it starts throwing more and more aggressive enemies at you. At first it's knights that lock onto your position and jump at you. Those are actually quite fun since they're the only enemies that do something like this by this point, so they can be fun to dodge then counter.

However, the game ramps this up and up and up to the point where the only enemies that spawn are ones that fire projectiles with aggressive tracking, or launch pillars of silencing lightning that require dodging at the exact correct angle, or fire explosive poison balls that need to be shot out of the air (and by that I mean shot 20 times, not just once), or simply carpet bomb the cramped corridors of the later areas with enough explosives to render positioning almost pointless.

So what do you do? Dodge with perfect timing? Well beyond that being a difficult task in of itself, if even possible when facing off against a horde of 15 enemies, the stamina system has you in a chokehold. Almost every action you can take costs large amounts of stamina including basic stuff like jumping, sprinting, and a particularly baffling choice to make you lose stamina when getting hit, making rallying a bad situation nearly impossible.

The net result is that Witchfire feels like "A Game where You Cannot Defend Yourself". So how do you keep yourself alive in a game where you can't defend yourself? Equip the most laughably overpowered build you can muster, point the camera in the general direction of the enemies, and watch them all blow up before they can get an attack off. In particular the heavy spell Burning Stake almost-literally plays the game for you with its unending barrage of explosions that instantly nukes entire enemy encounters while fully recharging itself in the process. It's not even easy mode by that point, it's peaceful mode.

I want to see Witchfire's endgame (or midgame considering less than half the levels are out) better mimic what the early game manages to achieve by letting players bolster their defense while keeping a lid on their offense. The game as it is now severely lacks any push-and-pull during fights. You either push and instantly win or you pull and instantly lose, barely anything more interesting than that.

If I was making the game I'd probably do something along the lines of:
Make sprinting, single jumping, and taking damage cost no stamina
Make dodging go a shorter distance with more iframes (bit iffy on this one, but the long-distance dodge is very janky)
Remove the slow on losing stamina (the fact you have no stamina should be all the punishment needed)
Make empowered melees have no cooldown but require a chunk of stamina
Make spells have a cooldown in addition to needing charge
Make heavy spells not be able to charge while they're active so chaining them is much harder
Nerf the hell out of Burning Stake and buff Cursed Bell
And then maybe give all light spells multiple charges. That way players can cast a lot of light spells and only a few heavy spells.

I'm not going to pretend this would magically fix everything but I think something to that effect would make Witchfire more "Destiny meets Dark Souls extraction shooter roguelite" and less "Burning Stake 10,000,000 must die" especially since the latter invalidates how much effort the devs put into having enemies with interesting designs and animations.

I'll throw in one quick bonus: The equipment upgrade system isn't awful but it needs work. The game ask you to get hundreds of kills with a single weapon that isn't even maxed out. Already a problem in of itself but everything else you bring to a level can steal its kills. This incentivises you to farm fodder for an hour in the starting level or go to endgame areas and get your ass handed to you while trying to chip away at hordes of tough enemies with the worst gun in your arsenal.

Not a complete dealbreaker, especially when the loot is super cool and rewarding once upgraded, but still extremely tedious and unsatisfying. I think the idea is to get you accustomed to how a weapon works before you get to upgrade it to its full potential, but in practice this just doesn't work at all since upgrading weapons unlocks perks and not straight damage buffs. This means that the weapon at upgrade level 0 or 1 could be unbearable and stupid only for upgrade level 3 to fix everything. 

That's what happened for me with Midas, an assault rifle whose gimmick of overheating as it fires felt obnoxious to use. Then I reached upgrade level 3 and it unlocked a fast, damaging reload while overheated, and now the weapon feels perfect. The same thing goes for the sniper rifle All Seeing Eye, where the core gimmick of poison explosions on headshots doesn't exist until upgrade level 3. To put it all into perspective, both of these weapons each require 315 un-stolen kills to fully upgrade despite their gameplay being gimped before you've done this.

I don't know what specifically the fix for this is, but the devs should at least let us spend currency to bypass the challenge. Doing the challenge just doesn't contribute anything enriching to the experience, and I don't want what the developers have created with these cool weapons to be squandered just because it takes hours of grinding to actually get your collection of weapons ready to use.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1738253544}, {"review_text": "This game is a perfectly accurate simulation of a witch hunt: being that the witch does not actually exist and you instead spend your time systematically eliminating entire populations.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 94, "timestamp_created": 1749479684}, {"review_text": "If you took Destiny 2's gunplay, slapped it into a single player extraction shooter that's challenging but well balanced then added the character loadout/build mechanics from Remnant 2, you would get this game. Thanks to the Dev's, you really have something special here.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1742149064}, {"review_text": "Witchfire is a strange one. I've been looking forward to it ever since it was announced at the game awards in 2017, but I cannot recommend it in it's current state.

Theprimary game loop is divided into two segments, the hub and expeditions. The hub allows you to level up, research new gear, level up said gear and level up the overall world difficulty and progression by researching Gnosis. This loop feels really solid and you always feel like there's something new to do every time you come back to the hub from an expedition.

The expedition is the second segment. An expedition is basically just choosing which level you want to play and you then set out to collect resources you can use in the hub. Levels are fairly small but open and you choose how you want to tackle each challenge in whichever order you want simply by exploring. Encounters and enemy groups are clearly marked on the map and clearing these will yield resources and temporary buffs. Depending on your Gnosis (world progression) you'll be able to see and interact with more hidden stuff in each level, giving you a reason to come back later as well. Witchfire borrows aspects from extraction shooters as well by robbing you of everything you've collected if you die, so sometimes it's not a bad idea to abort early and try again for the main objective some other time.

Movement is smooth and slick, enemies are varied and well designed and the guns look, sound and feel great. The core loop is phenominal, but Withfire also has some massively negative points towards it.

First off, the environments are simply not designed for combat. You always fight in open fields that sometimes have some debris spread around. Every encounter feels the same and it gets repetetive and boring extremely quickly. Areas feel like they are designed to be traversed through rather than fought in. Despite your flexible movement, there's only ever a single plane of elevation, unless you're fighting on the slope of a hill. Enemies also tend to spawn around you for seemingly no reason. Sometimes you'll be alone only to turn around and notice 10 skeleteons following mere meters behind you. Sometimes they'll spawn when you're already fighting a group of enemies, causing what the game clearly marked as a small encounter to become an overwhelming onslaught. And with the environments being so open, there's oftentimes nowhere to hide as you're suddenly surrounded by 30 riflemen shooting at you from all sides.

The problem is only made worse by the fact that you can only dodge while you have stamina, but taking damage also drains your stamina, leaving you open to the next attack, which then leaves you open to the next attack and so on. Most of the game is actually extremely easy until suddenly it snowballs out of nowhere and you suddenly find yourself completely out of options. Doom 2016 and Eternal reward players with more health the more damage they've taken, allowing players to climb back up from the brink of death and continue fighting, but Witchfire does the complete opposite and it's incredibly frustrating.

Lastly, there's no real narrative to be found beyond the intro cutscene, no story to string me along and keep me interested. How about the opposite, stalking your prey and sniping from afar, using careful accuracy to do what others would achieve with a hail of bullets?  Perfect!  There's sniper rifles, bolt action rifles, and spells that will help you do all that and more.
