Hopefully that gives you a ballpark of what performance to expect with your own hardware.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1750916099}, {"review_text": "Witchfire is a really good shooter mired in some weird and contradictory design decisions that make the gameplay more frustrating than enjoyable for me. When the game gets out of its own way, it feels awesome, with very snappy combat and fun powers. The atmosphere is great, and the performance is well optimized, with only occasional dropped frames in some environments. As far as the core gameplay is concerned, it should be a slam dunk.

But then the game gets too “clever” for its own good. Witchfire mixes elements of soulslikes, extraction shooters, roguelites, and traditional RPG leveling, but these elements clash in weird and tedious ways. The need to level up ends up gating you constantly, and it’s really the primary thing that matters in terms of how well you will do in a run (the roguelite in-run ability unlocks are underwhelming and don’t actually make for meaningfully different runs, at least at the levels I’ve reached so far), which makes the game loop come down to just repeating the same couple levels again and again with very little meaningful variation and playing in the most boring way possible to grind resources.

For example, you start the game with very little stamina. Stamina is what helps you dodge enemy attacks. This is important because on the first island, all of the enemies you encounter have attacks that target you without fail (some are slow heat-seeking missiles; others are fast deadeye shots, and others are melee attackers with teleport mechanics). So with your limited stamina, you can only dodge one or two of these attacks before you need to rest behind cover. But the game spawns enemies in groups of 4-6 right next to (often behind) you. If you encounter more than one swordsman at a time, you just die; you can’t run from them and can’t effectively fight them, because the game hasn’t given you tools to do so at the start. What you have to do is spend a while dipping into the level, shooting from cover, finding a bit of gold and witchfire, and leaving so you can level up and unlock more guns. This isn’t a tense experience, so it doesn’t work as an extraction shooter, really. Either you trigger the right mobs and it’s kind of too easy, or you trigger the wrong ones, and you get overwhelmed and die. It’s just kind of a rote experience you have to get through, so that you can level up enough to play the real game.

And you do, and the game starts to feel a bit fun. Then you meet the first boss. His attacks also home in on you, and they have very wide area of effects. So wide that your newly leveled up stamina isn’t leveled up enough for you to be able to dodge them with a single dodge. And every time he hits you, he takes out half your health bar and chunks down your stamina, which makes you less able to dodge. Basically, trying to beat him without leveling your stamina significantly is going to end up with you dying, and since you can only fight him after clearing the entire island, you end up clearing the whole island multiple times, just to lose all the resources in a boss fight that feels cheap and unfair. The smart play is the boring one again–farm some resources, then walk away, multiple times, until you’re leveled up enough.

Meanwhile, many of the game’s mechanics are cryptic and obtuse and can only really be understood via googling, so you often just get killed by things you can’t possibly understand (like a pirate ship that shows up mid bossfight for reasons and kills you by quickly draining a sanity meter you didn’t know you had).


Out of sheer obstinance, I powered through, I leveled up, and I became one of 20% of steam players to actually beat the first boss (that feels like a pretty low percentage to me, and indicative of how many people aren’t enjoying the experience of the early game enough to keep going–it’s the first boss, after all). It felt like I accomplished something, of a sort. And I was starting to learn enough of the game. Maybe it would be more fun-challenging and less punishing-hard now.

I leveled up my gnosis (difficulty) to unlock some more weapons, because item progression is hard-locked by your gnosis level. And one of my next tasks was to explore a crypt. And I’ll just say that the crypt is one of the most frustratingly artificially “hard” level designs I’ve ever encountered in a game. And I realized that it wasn’t a matter of getting past the first cheap boss to unlock the fun game. This is just how the game does difficulty; it wants to be a hard game so badly that it mistakes what makes a lot of hard games fun. I don’t feel challenged by tense encounters; I feel punished by obtuse rulesets, level gates, and odd mechanics. The shooting (because this is a shooter, in the end)--is actually maybe a bit easy, if anything.

I’m sure I’ll get some responses telling me to “git gud” and saying I’m playing the game the wrong way. I’ve seen plenty of such responses to other criticisms of this game, where folks say “It really clicks at about ~30 hours in.” And I know that for some people, Witchfire will be exactly what they want.

For me, it’s too tedious and frustrating in its current state to justify spending that kind of time on it. I don’t want to wait for a game to get enjoyable, googling obscure mechanics and hidden traps and cursing at hard level gates while I slog to level up and unlock the promise of what the game could be.

It’s still early access, so this all might change (I don’t suspect it will significantly, because a lot of the problems, really, are design choices, not implementation flaws, and it’s quite late in early access at this point). I’ll come back and reassess and update my review after it hits 1.0. But until then, I’m done trying to git gud and done waiting for the game to git gud too.

Edit: 
Y'all: my criticism is not that the game is hard (I like hard games): it's that the mechanics it uses to be "hard"  are just grindy roadblocks and cheap gotchas that make the game repetitive and not actually very skill-based.

On its surface, Witchfire promises the combat loop of a Destiny or Doom: an aggressive, movement-heavy shooter where you experiment with loadouts and abilities on the fly and where the challenge comes from adapting to a wide variety of enemy attack patterns. And maybe it becomes that…eventually.

But it starts you with no mobility, no equipment, long cooldowns, and next to no health until you grind through a bunch of levels. It rewards you for playing in a risk-averse way (extracting early is always more rewarding than pushing your luck and losing everything, and getting hit is punishing in unrecoverable ways). So the actual way you play the game for the first 10 hours is to farm the same five mobs on the same 2 levels from a safe difference and extract as soon as things get risky.

If the devs removed the grindy leveling, the extraction-shooter rewards, the insanity mechanic, and the slow-drip level-gated unlock of loot from this game…it might be a lot of fun. But while those things are in there, it's not worth slogging through 10+ hours of a bad game to hopefully unlock a good one.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 25, "timestamp_created": 1754224144}, {"review_text": "Witchfire is a gorgeous, moody game. Everything is dripping with style. The movement is tight and every gun is creative and feels great to use. It's mind-boggling (and disappointing) just how little fun I have when playing it.

[h2]What is an appropriate punishment for taking damage?[/h2]

A well-designed game will comprise a balance of incentives and punishments. You're incentivized to kill enemies through XP drops; you're punished for ignoring enemies when you run yourself into a dead end and have a gaggle of foes on your tail. 

It should go without saying that getting hit is something you want to avoid; you can only do it so many times before it's a game-over, In theory, no further punishment is necessary -- death is its own punishment because it ends your play session and you lose the progress you've been working towards. Surely, then, taking damage should be its own punishment. The Astronauts appear to disagree.

So what happens when you take damage in Witchfire? The first and most immediate effect is that you lose your ability to see [i]sigils[/i], an additional weak point that can be used to immobilize enemies, interrupt attacks, and boost damage. You lose this ability instantly and can only regain it by absorbing witchfire (i.e. killing enemies). You are punished for taking damage by losing access to a powerful ability that could help you turn a bad situation around. [b]The game gets harder temporarily.[/b]

The next thing that happens is that you lose max stamina. Stamina which is used for every action in the game -- shooting, sprinting, jumping, dashing. You now have less leeway. Every action you take must be more considered. You're not able to dodge as often or to shoot for as long. [b]The game gets harder permanently.[/b]

All this pales in comparison to the Calamity mechanic. There's a system in the game, which nobody seems to really understand, where making mistakes (of which "taking damage" seems to be one) will alert The Witch to your presence and she'll cast a curse on you. This curse can take the form of a flying pirate ship that shoots homing balls of energy, or a powerful knight who was actually just an area boss in the previous patch.

Yes, dear reader: taking damage from a boss can trigger the approach of [i]another[/i] boss in addition -- one which will slowly drain your sanity and kill you regardless of your remaining health. [b]The game gets an insane difficulty spike once it already has you on the ropes.[/b]

The developers have explicitly designed the game to work this way. They want you to be at your weakest before the Calamity appears. They think this is fun and that it makes sense in The Lore.

I think I don't care about how much sense it makes. 

I almost never play early access games but I've been looking forward to this since the first teaser trailer back in 2018, and I bought it as soon as it was available on Steam. I've played both major updates and unfortunately the design ethos doesn't feel like it'll ever crystalize into a game I enjoy. Lots of people seem to love it (and will relentlessly tell you "git gud" in response to any feedback, despite the game ostensibly being still in development). I think I've given it enough chances to prove itself to me and will not be playing more.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1754345987}]

[{"review_text": "This game is for a very particular type of person - someone who enjoys both puzzles AND rogue-likes. It's an unusual combination, and I think many of the negative reviews are from either puzzle fans who either don't like or aren't familiar with the way one progresses through a rogue-like game, or from rogue-like fans who find the switch to progressing through puzzles vs combat to be obtuse and frustrating. But if you're someone who actually likes both kinds of games, then you'll REALLY enjoy this, especially as a wonderfully novel and unique experience.

The key to really enjoying the game, I think, is to remember that you progress through your own knowledge. Early on, you'll encounter a note suggesting that you might want to take notes. Please follow that advice. There are a huge number of subtle details that can provide a great deal of information and guidance, and which I'm sure the game would be much more frustrating if you either aren't pay enough attention to notice them, or if you're not writing them down so you forget them later when it turns out to be relevant. 

In particular, the player needs to learn the patterns of how certain rooms are drawn, and I don't just mean the obvious cases where the game spells out that taking a certain action will add a new room to your list of blueprints. There are patterns such as rooms that only appear on the west-most or east-most sides of the house, or the fact that a room, built for the day, will typically not appear as a blueprint option again. There are a huge number of patterns like this, and you need to learn them and use them to your advantage. Or else, yes, this will be a frustrating game. I think many players are treating the game as if the puzzles only exist INSIDE the rooms, but the truth is that most of the puzzles ARE the rooms - you need to puzzle out how to place the rooms to maximize the chances of getting the draws you need. But the game systems and the design of the puzzles themselves seem like they will drive any player to eventually quit in frustration or boredom without completing it (or worse, give up and  get solutions from the internet.) Because I believe that unsatisfying conclusion appears inevitable, I can't recommend it to others.

It's been great being able to bounce ideas off each other, but also caused a lot of fights about note taking being too slow.

Some things I like: This game has a LOT of content. There is some padding due to the RNG nature of the roguelike genre, but so far there have been enough leads on new things that we have rarely had a run where we accomplish nothing. There are permanent upgrades as you get further, and many things can be manipulated. For the most part, the puzzles so far are doable. There's a couple puzzles we found but haven't cracked yet, but I figure we'll find more clues at some point. There is also a pretty engaging story and you get in bits and pieces. I'd love to give this another try if such a feature were implemented, even as an option to toggle on in the accessibility settings.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 33, "timestamp_created": 1763397510}, {"review_text": "Blue Prince came highly recommended by critics and early fans for people who love games like Outer Wilds, Obra Dinn, The Witness, and other knowledge gated games.  It also came recommended by many of those same people suggesting that the roguelike elements are minimal and would be enjoyable even for people who don't really enjoy that genre.  This review is for those people, who came here curious about this game but are unsure about it being a roguelike.  There is absolutely a target audience for this game, and if you are not in it, then this game isn't for you.  I feel somewhat lied to by critics and fans of this game because of that.  I've put about 5 hours into this game but I am done with it for now.  I may come back to it, I may change my overall opinion of it with more time, but the substance of this review will not change as it won't change how bad the opening hours have been.  

I've heard there are 100 hours or more worth of mysteries under the surface of this game, perhaps similar to a game like Void Stranger.  There's a lot of mystery threads and lore to uncover so far which has kept me going, but I will note that many of the rules and game conceits so far do not feel 'organic'.  They are rules that are primarily constructed because this is a game and because the character themselves are playing a game, if that makes sense.  Why do you have to leave the mansion each day?  Because that's what your grandfather said you have to do in order to play his blueprints game for his inheritance.  Nonetheless, this view could change with more time, there could be more organic explanations under the surface.  I can see why someone may assume any fan of knowledge gated games would enjoy this one as there is clearly a lot to uncover. 

The problem is, virtually all progress so far is gated behind RNG.  You need luck for finding individual rooms, you need luck for resources, you need luck for just basic progress where your run doesn't end on a whim because every path forward was met with only dead-end rooms.  You need luck to get the right combo of rooms for some puzzles.  You need luck to have rooms that only show up in certain places to actually show up once you are there.  You can spend run after run after run not fulfilling a key few things that you would have been able to fulfill on earlier runs.  Everything happens through manipulated happenstance as the strategies I can know so far only lightly mitigate the RNG.  

But each run must have new things to learn right?  Roughly half my runs so far do not offer new information as they are just repeats of unchanged rooms I've already been through before.  Other times a couple threads may pop up, but usually nothing that benefits that run, just a theoretical future run.  There are surely more secrets to decode in these rooms, but I wouldn't know, the game's RNG keeps preventing me from learning new clues.  And if there is something I missed and could have figured out?  It's still RNG if I even draw that room again to investigate.  It is exciting to finally have the stars align when you can access somewhere new, but I don't get enough of a buzz from that to overcome the frustration of the much more frequent bad runs.

I'm sure there is some kind of logic and meta knowledge that you unlock/learn about after awhile to cut back on the RNG.  There is some basic strategy to mitigate some of the luck (such as trying to reduce the deck's less desirable cards on dead ends or side paths and saving certain rooms hopefully for later), but such strategies so far still allow for A LOT of RNG, and further strategies would be gated behind either hours upon hours of trial and error to learn what I need, or alternatively deciding to look the information up to save on the hassle which defeats the purpose.  

On the flipside, you could be one of the lucky few and beat this game first run within an hour if the deck happens to line up right.  It almost happened for me, my very first run is still the one I made the most progress in, I built around the antechamber and had all of the needed tools but ran out of steps (this game's version of energy)...I've yet to come close to that far again despite having a couple permanent unlocks added.  That is how RNG dependent this game is so far.  

Lastly, this game perhaps somewhat erroneously requires you to take a lot of notes yourself.  This is chiefly because none of the documents you find are tracked in any way by the game.  Imagine if a game like Outer Wilds didn’t have the ship log, that’s the level of personal notetaking you are going to need to do here, probably primarily with screenshots of everything you come across.  This could have largely been avoided if you could review the documents you’ve seen in a submenu like many other games already provide.

So be warned, if you dislike roguelikes, or even just roguelikes with a heavy amount of RNG, this game is probably not for you.  I would recommend this game to a fan of something like Balatro long before I would recommend it to a puzzle game fan.  It is not for me, it is seemingly not for a fair few other people like me as newer reviews are coming in, and the blind recommendations to all puzzle game fans needs to be curbed.  This is a roguelike first, and likely only becomes the type of puzzle game I like after hours and hours of frustration and investment.  

With all that said, if you like both knowledge gated games AND RNG-heavy roguelikes, then you will likely love this game as the critics and fans have.   Alternatively, if a game like this intrigues you but you dislike roguelikes and/or heavy RNG elements, check out last year's Lorelei and the Laser Eyes instead.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1744396600}, {"review_text": "This is a good game with really clever puzzles, but it is held back by a number of really irritating oversights that can be summed up in one phrase: it does not respect player's time. [{"review_text": "For $15, Escape from Duckov gave me 80 hours of gameplay without a burnout - I completed 100% of the game! I tell you honestly and genuinely, it's the best game I've played in 2025. Nothing else was better value, better quality, or better fun. Seriously.

It's a really fun top-down shooter. The first 10 hours feel like a stealth/survival shooter, and by hour 80 I felt like I was playing Hotline Miami. All of the mechanics surrounding shooting make sense, are fun to explore, and make for a really adrenaline-pumping game that's so satisfying to get good at.

The many forms of progression are extremely addictive. You've got character upgrades, base upgrades, gear upgrades, NPC unlocks, map unlocks, crafting, fishing, exploration, and more. Honestly the closest thing I can compare this game's progression to is Terraria, which should say a lot to those who are a fan.

And it was perfectly challenging and satisfying on the Survivor difficulty for me, but there are several difficulty presets to choose from as well as a custom difficulty that lets you tweak a lot of settings to get things just right. This game really can be enjoyed by anyone.

The developer has played Tarkov and really knows what makes the amazing parts of Tarkov feel so good. You'll progress through this game, collecting loot, upgrading your hideout and enhancing your character as you equip stronger armor and weapons. This allows you to traverse deeper into the maps for even better loot.

This game nails progression more than anything. Upgrade your hideout, then upgrade those modules. Upgrade every aspect of your character, from your carry weight, to your needs of food and water, and even gun statistics like recoil and reload speed. You'll use a huge variety of items to contribute to all of these upgrades, and it really rewards your hoarding and filling up your stash (which you can also upgrade.)

The quests aren't particularly interesting, but that's not why we're here. Just like Tarkov, the quests are a means to experience and rewards. I love how the developer takes a tongue in cheek approach to quests and often recognizes notorious Tarkov quests. 

Clearing enemies and looting them feels fantastic. Some enemies can be quite hard, so it feels great to equip some really good gear and ammo to take them down. There are harder common enemies and even named AI that will absolutely tear you up if you're not ready.

The cute aesthetic is funny at first, but you'll quickly look past it as you get sucked into looting, taking down enemies, and of course upgrading every aspect of your hideout. Don't be fooled and think this is a meme game. Other than Tarkov itself, I don't think another game nails extraction progression better. This game scratches such a great itch for me and I can't praise this game enough.

In short, I was trying to say it sold well with great solo gameplay and by positive word of mouth within its first week without marketing/promotion this side of the gaming market.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 11, "timestamp_created": 1761094005}, {"review_text": "I keep seeing people referring to this game as a "Tarkov Parody", which I personally don't agree with. Sure it has a good amount of parallels to Tarkov, but very few of those transfer to its mechanics or used for comedic effect, hell, the game isn't even particularly trying to be funny for that matter. It's just a very well put together third person, top down extraction based PvE shooter which happens to have a tarkov pun in its name. 

The game loop is very simple: You will start on a bunker where you can craft and take missions. You can leave the bunker at any time, explore, loot, shoot, and come back before dark. As you do so, you will be able to craft upgrades, build more crafting stations, get more missions, and unlock further areas. The beauty of Duckov is not how well it does anything in particular, but how incredibly solid its foundations and core gameplay is, which coupled with its incredibly dense and well paced content, it means it will keep you thoroughly engaged as you discover new areas, fight new enemies, try new weapons and look for the next tchochke you need to improve your base.

In other words, and to be blunt, this is better Zero Sievert.

The game is quite colorful and pretty, almost reminiscent of the Zelda remakes for the Switch, and, for a game in a genre that hypes up being hard and unforgiving, it is actually quite easy... at first. Your character is always an absentminded wander away from a lucky enemy getting a hit too many in, and then you'll be sent back to base, having to go back to wherever you were killed to pick up your gear and *then* extract. It is an expertly designed game that knows exactly how far to push it without becoming obnoxious, and it also allows the player to change the difficulty level at any time during a campaign. You can't get locked into any fail state or run out of money, although with a game that has taken off this hard and that offers mod support from day one, I am sure difficulty fiends will get their fix sooner rather than later.

The gunplay also deserves a mention since it's probably the best example of how it takes the Zero Sievert formula and elevates it with slight wrinkles to add depth and nuance: holding your reticle exactly over enemies will cause critical damage and make your shots go over low cover, firing from right next to an obstacle will protect you from incoming fire while allowing you to shoot past it, and you (and enemies) can even shoot through thin enough materials. Stealth also plays an important role, and if you are careful and make good use of items, you can just sneak around without getting into trouble, great for those inevitable corpse runs.

There are a couple of negatives, such as being unable to track missions, the lack of a loadout system, a weirdly lopsided weapon design due to mostly ARs being *way* too good, and what looks like a seeded RNG that more likely than not will massively favor some kinds of items dropping while absolutely leaving you high and dry with others; but honestly, none of those are anything other than an occasional mild inconvenience (that I'm sure mods will address anyway).

Escape from Duckov doesn't pull any flashy features like procedural generation or terrain deformation, it doesn't have particularly good graphics, or crazy complicated controls, or even a particularly good sound design. The most defining characteristic of every single one of its parts is that "it works". But you know what? In a world where every damn launch is either an Early Access with 2 hours worth of content, an $80 AAA release that can barely reach 40 FPS, or a combination of both, playing a no-nonsense, well designed, well paced, well performing, reasonably priced, finished game is a breath of fresh air. Absolutely GOTY material that deserves the success it's finding.

I do clearly have a yearning for some sort of extraction shooter; I am just not all that competitive anymore. So spending hours in Tarkov, losing my mind, enduring endless fear that someone somewhere will hit me in the head and I crumble like a crouton. But sometimes that's exactly what you need. 

During my search for a Tarkovesque game I found, months ago, a game called Hole. Which filled the void that Tarkov left, without the erasing of all progress upon your inevitable death. Hole is genuinely brilliant, but short and sweet with the Devs moving on to their next game. I also found the demo for Escape from Duckov during that search. 

I spent the next 4 hours, 2200-0200, roaming through Duckov and doing everything I possibly could. And then it was over, and I was devastated but impressed and excited for late October. And then here we are. Escape from Duckov is everything that the beta promised. Which to me was a jovial, and dare I say fun, version of EFT. 

You still start with next to nothing, but it doesn't feel like you are a chicken with its head cut off. You get a pistol and go hunting. For food and equipment, quest items, other ducks, so on. In a world that feels like a PG-13 Tarkov. Things are destroyed, and overturned, and doors are locked. If you have played Tarkov it will feel familiar. As will the quests. Get this, go there and fix that, kill these with X weapon. And the quests are fun. The directions in the quest description makes sense, so you aren't aimlessly running around hoping to God you get lucky and find where you need to be. And a little quest marker pops up when you're fairly close. 

This is also benefited by the fact you have maps, and they don't feel horrible to use. Locations are what you'd expect from a Tarkov-like. But they have depth and charm, along with not being too big that you feel trekking across them is a chore and not too small that you are entirely across the map in moments. There is also persistent change within the maps. Moving a log to open a gate, destroying a wall, building a bridge, making traversal easier while forcing you to explore and not making that null and void as soon as you extract. Duckov takes the blindness that Tarkov thrusts upon you and gives you a pair of glasses that make sure you aren't tripping over everything in front of you. 

Usually, I am a skeptic of isometric games and their gameplay. I wasn't a huge fan of Zero Sievert, but I am a huge fan of this. Movement once again isn't sluggish or tedious. And the gunplay feels shockingly good. It's as simple as point at thing and shoot. But guns have an effective range, and just pointing isn't the extent. Actually aiming at the other ducks makes your life easier and massively ups your damage output. All the guns feel punchy, and sound good. The combat is incredibly fun, and feels adequately refined and rewarding for the kind of game this is. With guns feeling unique enough to use that you are allowed to have a preference and choose your engagements. Finding them isn't impossible, nor is finding ammo. Which does come in different grades that do make a substantial differences. You have different classes of armour, you have different meds to use. You get shot and bleed needing a bandage, you get dehydrated and hungry meaning you need food. All the survival systems that Tarkov has are also here. And done in a way that won't ruin your experience. 

From what I've experienced bosses are always on the map, and don't feel unfairly tuned that you must waste every resource on fighting them. Facing a boss isn't the end of your raid, as long as you survive. And running can be an option. Crafting is an option, and finding the materials by digging in boxes and jackets and garbage bins is just as satisfying as it is in Tarkov. Expanding your base is the main goal, leading to you Escaping Duckov. Meaning there is an end, and progression feels meaningful. And the biggest benefit of a game like this, YOU MOVE AT YOUR OWN PACE. There isn't a chase or feelings of being left behind. You are allowed to be slow, and play a few hours a week, and just not worry about falling behind. 

If you are a person who has an itch for extraction shooters, but not the time to abuse yourself with them, EFD is genuinely perfect. A fully customizable difficulty scale, which allows you to be as brutalized as you'd like. The same mechanics that make Tarkov good but without Sword of Damocles hovering over you in anticipation of a few bad raids and resetting days and days of progress. Gunplay that feels good and weighted, and scales very well. A story that is interesting, and quests that mimic the goofy nature of some of Tarkovs while still feeling unique enough that you aren't doing the same things over and over again. 

Buy this game. Get your Tarkov fix on your own terms. The game oozes care and love and joy. As someone who isn't all for fighting games and completely new to street fighter, I'd strongly recommend this game to anyone who is either: a fan of street fighter, plays almost every game genre even if more than some, or anyone who wants to give it a go. Plus, if you get bored there's always mods.

Gameplay-wise there is two control schemes, being classic and modern. Classic is the original street fighter experience in terms of controls. Two lights, two mediums and two heavys, plus your other button like drive impact, special, etc. Modern caters to players that prefer modern standards of fighting game controls, being one button for light, one for medium, and one for heavy, while most of the other controls remain unchanged, with small exceptions. Classic opens up every possibility for extensive combos, as you have access to everything the game has to offer. Modern slims down possibilities for combos but makes them easier to pull off and let's a new player breathe with less controls to worry about. I would recommend switching to classic if your on modern when you get the hang of the game, but it isn't necessary. All controls are fully customisable, and even allow for double inputs to be allocated to one button. Different presets are available if your sharing or wanna have a different control scheme.

 I don't play online much so I can't give an opinion on it, however I can confirm oceanic servers aren't fucking dead like every odd game that has them.

Story mode, or World Tour, is fun and addictive. Making your own character and getting moves from masters Xenoverse style is super fun. Character customisation is always redoable, and gives you access to extensive customisation. You can equip different fighting styles based on each in-game character, which changes your character's base moveset and animations. You also have the skill-tree which is mainly for buffs to your custom character, things like "Punches do more damage," or "Gives one more meter." Custom characters aren't available to use outside of world tour sadly. I personally would love to use my avatar in training to at least be able to practice chaining my moveset with other character abilities, but the amount of fighting you do in world tour justifies this I suppose. Each character's outfit 2 is unlockable for free in world tour by getting max bond level with them. Otherwise you can spend premium currency to unlock them if grinding isn't for you.

There's 18 available fighters in the base roster with a nice selection of DLC characters and more to come as of this review. Each character has a unique "story mode" so to speak, with a cutscene a the start and one at the end after the boss fight. There's a couple other gamemodes to play in custom battle but I won't get into those.

Graphics are great, i'm able to run them at max with 120fps constantly and its above modern day standards, so it's definitely nice to look at with the exception of occasional angles and positions where the lighting looks absolutely cooked. But that's mainly only in world tour mode.

Overall the game is colourful, cast is great, gameplay is fun, and the price is pretty worth it for a modern-day game. Don't get any ideas, Capcom, but the game could've easily gotten away for being sold at $100 AUD and no fuss would be made. 

Buy it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1752654690}, {"review_text": "Far and away the best experience I've had playing a fighting game. Not perfect, but at least I no longer feel like the ground itself is refusing my architectural dreams.

Some old habits still linger, though. The UI occasionally decides it is done working and clocks out for the day. It especially hates when I move through tutorials too quickly, as if the game takes it personally that I already know what I am doing. During the breeding tutorial, it told me to incubate male dinosaurs, but the entire menu locked up with a condescending yellow highlight around the gender option like I needed help finding it. The option was greyed out. Completely unusable. Restart required. Then in a Japan mission, my park was open but no guests ever arrived. Not a single human soul walked in. Another restart. These issues aren’t game-breaking early on, but they are the kind of annoyances that slowly chip away at your sanity.

The real disaster is pathfinding. Somehow it is even worse than Evolution 2, which is impressive in the most depressing way possible. Rangers and maintenance crews get stuck behind everything: trees, rocks, fences, electric poles, buildings, shadows, oxygen molecules, you name it. A gate closes while they are halfway through, and they simply give up on existence. Then your park collapses because your staff decided to embrace nihilism. The new maintenance outposts are a great idea on paper, but when the workers cannot navigate a straight path, your entire operation ends up held together with duct tape and hope. Evolution 2 let me build dedicated ranger-only roads to help, but Evolution 3 decided that quality-of-life was optional. A simple pathfinding view mode would have saved my blood pressure.

Now onto performance. The game looks incredible, sounds incredible, and absolutely nails the atmosphere. But zoom in too far and the terrain starts to warp like reality is melting. That is minor. The real performance assassin is the Paleo-Medical Facility. Trying to place one of these things dropped my framerate from 80 down to 5–10 FPS instantly, as if the game was performing a ritual sacrifice. Only happens during placement, nowhere else, and I have no explanation for it. Just pure, unfiltered madness.

And object rotation. I don’t know who designed this on controller, but they deserve a strongly worded letter. Rotation is painfully snappy unless you switch to advanced mode, which suddenly makes rotation smooth but disables movement. So you are constantly juggling tools like a clown trying to balance dinner plates. Mouse and keyboard fix that problem, but introduce their own awkwardness. It’s a tradeoff no matter what you use.

With all of that said, Jurassic World Evolution 3 is still a huge step forward in freedom, visuals, and overall creativity. The sandbox mode looks incredible. There’s an overwhelming amount of content, decorations, systems, and tools to experiment with. This is the kind of variety I wish Ubisoft’s Far Cry map editor had instead of whatever half-baked scraps they now pretend is “creative mode.” But despite all the new options, this is still the only building game where my creativity packs up and leaves the moment dinosaurs get involved. I tried recreating The Lost World’s park in Evolution 2, and maybe I’ll try again here, but beyond that, something about dinosaurs just shuts my brain off. I respect the people who build massive, elaborate parks. I won’t be joining them.

One last complaint: blueprint sharing. Just like in Far Cry, people will steal your designs, repost them as their own, and take credit. It is predictable, rude, and annoying every single time it happens.

In the end, Evolution 3 is absolutely worth trying if you love dinosaurs or park builders. It has a ton of content, a ton of charm, and moments of genuine brilliance. But it still lacks the polish needed to become the perfect evolution of the series. If you enjoy The Sims or inZOI, you’ll probably feel right at home here.

That’s all for now. The scientist mechanic from game 2 has been reworked you no longer need to pay an exorbitant sum for your scientists to rest, now they just wait a default of 4 minutes which you can shave down to about a minute wait time to get them back.

Rangers no longer handle repairs the new maintenance buildings ATV's do that now, instead of your park only taking damage from storms or rampaging dinosaurs it will need constant maintenance, meaning if your feel like it you can let your park end up being in a state of disrepair in sandbox, without having to have it hit by storms over and over.

Hybrid carnivores however are still largely killing machines, if anything you would think they added a bit of Jason Voorhees DNA to the genomes.

If your looking for a deep management simulation, your guests are bascially walking scenery, they pay to enter, they spend at park amenities but other than that they just wander around, ride attractions, like in game 1 and 2.

If anything they dumbed down the need to be strategic placing your amenities that game 2 had now it is just fill up the guests needs capacity on your path network, although the positive is you can set up your shopping area, provided it has transport and not need to scatter shops everywhere, rest rooms and shelters however need to be spread out around your path network.

Getting more guests has gone back to the appeal system of game 1 along with meeting specific conditions on each map, eg X number of species anywhere from 10 - 16 species, X number of dinosaurs, X amount of income, X amount of dinosaurs visible, X amount of guest satisfaction etc.. Appeal targets are quite high meaning you can end up with 100 - 200 dinosaurs on some maps.

The dinosaur breeding, they are cute, be aware herbivores will keep breeding until there is around 17 - 20 individuals of each species within a territory, so if your have a lot of species that like each other the popualtion can get quite large if your not paying attention, before the nests block further breeding, so plan your enclosure size accordinly. Keep any eye out for bad traits sure some are passed from the parents but it basically just acts like an automatic hatchery with random traits mixed in.

Where the game shines almost as much as the dinosaurs is the modular building and workshop, if your the creative sort and have the patience you can create some truly impressive stuff, be easier to look on Youtube then have me try to explain it.

If you have terrible imagination and no patience you can download the creations of others to use in your parks instead or just make use of the default buildings, one great thing about the scenery is it can act as cheap indestructable fences, meaning you could make the entire perimiter of the enclosure minus the gate out of scenery stuff, rocks, fencing etc and never need to repair or maintain it you just need to make sure collision is turned on otherwise the dinosaurs will be able to walk right through it, building stuff too close to it can turn off collision causing escapes. If you place a rock over the non gate half of the normal gate it prevents the carnivores from being able to do their smashing the gate open animation keeping them trapped as well as invisible fences.

Most of the crashes I experienced were with the new random island generator, the regular sandbox maps and campaign and challenge maps I rarely ever had a crash.

8.5/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761092021}, {"review_text": "Unfortunately, it took me about 8 hours to realize that this game is falsely advertised. It’s not a simulation — it’s essentially a map or park creation tool sold for $60, with features seemingly designed only to drive social media engagement.

There’s absolutely no economic challenge. The financial balance is unrealistic, boring, and completely breaks immersion.

I was genuinely excited to play a game with over 92% positive reviews, expecting to build a dinosaur park from scratch — earning money through careful planning, designing guest paths and attractions, and experimenting with dinosaur genes to eventually create a sustainable business. I thought I’d be sending out teams to search for fossils, managing risks, and celebrating small wins when luck was on my side.

But the gameplay, challenge level, and immersion all feel like they were designed for a broad mobile game audience.

Let me describe one situation. I really tried to like the game, so I started a new park on a blank map, hard difficulty, and with minimal cash to make things more challenging. Then this happened:

I hired a PhD-level scientist (Level 1) for $50,000, paying a $1,500 wage. He then received an invitation for a 10-minute marketing tour for a park that had literally 5 basic dinosaurs. The result? I instantly earned $3 million, solving all my financial problems with zero effort. Suddenly, hundreds of guests showed up to see those five dinosaurs, spending all their money on soft drinks and listening to the jukebox. I didn’t even need ticket sales — a single drink stand was making more profit than the cost of an entire team of PhD scientists!

Maybe some players are happy with cheap employees, overly generous customers, and random events that throw money at you, but I found it disappointing. :(", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 27, "timestamp_created": 1761209670}, {"review_text": "After having completed the main story with 5 stars I can say that JWE3 is a fairly good game, however it does suffer from many of the issues that most new games suffer from being that it is a bit buggy, however it is still a fairly good game, something I Ignored for a large part of the game but wish I didn't was terraforming, more specifically making pit enclosures for dangerous carnivores as it means you can concentrate all of your security on one specific point of the enclosure because it's physically impossible for them to get out anywhere else, one thing that I don't like is how they moved multiplace from a keybind to having to go into the building you already placed and then clicking duplicate, however that is certainly better than not having it at all. Another thing that I completely misunderstood was baby dinosaurs, oh god are they annoying, if you don't stay on top of their numbers or make sure that they have a lot of space then comfort will become an issue very quickly, I ran into that issue several times, mainly in Nevada, Indonesia and Japan. On the topic of comfort, I dislike how incredibly greedy certain animals are, most especially the Spinosaurus, I swear if you want more than 1 Spino in the same enclosure you need to give it half of the entire map, humble is simply a must have trait for them, and tbf humble is a must have trait for every single dinosaur, especially with how small some of the maps are and how greedy the dinosaurs are. However the biggest improvement JWE3 has above all other JWE games is the level of freedom it provides, and while that freedom can lead to a big of jank here and there the things you can do with it are quite literally limitless, pretty much every single building can be custom designed from the ground up meaning the biggest limitation is your own creativity. JWE3 also steps away from the old 5 star system and instead requires you to reach certain goals for each park instead of having a certain number of dinosaurs and a high enough rating like the previous games, this adds to the difficulty of the campaign and means that you can't really just use the same strategy every single time, along with different parks having increased ratings for specific species, It makes every park a unique experience and you tend to use more unique species than the previous games where you could just slap down a T rex some raptors and a few sauropods and you were done, all of those factors combine together to mean that 5 staring a park takes time and is somewhat difficult, and while in some parks it comes naturally just by making the park better, in others you almost have to go out of your way to 5 star it.

In conclusion Jurassic World Evolution 3 is a logical next step in the JWE franchise and certainly is different from the previous games, and while in certain aspects it can feel a bit not fully fleshed out and a bit clanky and rough around the edges, it certainly makes up for it with all the other features it provides, With a campaign that actually takes time unlike 2 and difficult but still enjoyable challenges even on Jurassic difficulty, JWE3 is a pretty damn good game, 8.5/10

One frustrating way that this shows up is that the timing of enemy attacks makes it hard to deliver most combos. They're easy to dodge, but you have to dodge so often you can't build up to any power attacks, making the combat feel boring and repetitive.

The second major issue is the sudden death / revenge mechanic. When a coop teammate dies, you have to kill a certain number of enemies in a short time period to revive them. I'd expect nothing less from the creators of Dead Cells.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1754635626}, {"review_text": "Windblown is a dynamic and exhilarating roguelike that stands out with its fast-paced combat, vertical level design, and a strong emphasis on cooperative gameplay. Developed by Motion Twin, the game combines precise, rhythmic fighting mechanics with the challenge of navigating a series of floating islands connected by narrow pathways and platforms. It offers an experience that feels both fresh and familiar, especially for players who enjoy titles like Dead Cells but crave something with more vertical exploration and multiplayer options.

At the heart of Windblown lies its combat system, which is quick, fluid, and rewarding. Players control a character equipped with two weapons, blending melee and ranged attacks while chaining combos to unleash powerful special moves known as “Alterattacks.” These combos keep the combat engaging and encourage skillful play, while the “Crystallize” mechanic adds a satisfying layer of flair—when you land enough consecutive hits on tougher enemies, you trigger a dramatic finish that rewards timing and precision. Though some weapons feel more effective in certain environments, the overall combat remains tight and exciting throughout the game.

The game’s world design is equally compelling, with a vertical structure that breaks away from the typical side-scrolling or flat arenas of other roguelikes. You traverse a train of floating islands, moving swiftly between floors with dashes and jumps to find hidden areas, secrets, and tactical positions. Each biome presents its own unique challenges and aesthetics, though some players might notice occasional repetition or unclear platforming sections. Still, the verticality adds a refreshing dimension that deepens exploration and combat strategy.

Progression in Windblown feels meaningful and motivates continued play. Between runs, you collect resources called Cogs that unlock new weapons, abilities, and enhancements at the central hub known as the Ark. During runs, you can acquire temporary boosts and face trials that offer risk-reward decisions to further customize your build. This meta-progression system strikes a good balance—it’s straightforward enough to keep the action flowing but offers enough variety to support different playstyles. However, some may feel that once most upgrades are unlocked, the incentive to keep experimenting lessens slightly.

One of the game’s biggest draws is its seamless drop-in, drop-out cooperative mode. Playing with two or three friends adds a chaotic and rewarding layer of teamwork, where shared healing, loot distribution, and combined tactics make every run feel lively and unpredictable. The social dynamic transforms the usual solo roguelike grind into a shared adventure full of memorable moments. That said, the cooperative experience can sometimes be tense, especially when one player’s defeat affects the whole team’s survival during intense boss fights.

Visually, Windblown embraces a bold, cel-shaded art style that blends whimsical floating islands with a gritty, mechanical aesthetic. The character designs are distinctive, and the animations keep the action clear and readable. Complementing the visuals is a pulsing soundtrack by Danger, whose synth-heavy tunes perfectly match the game’s energetic pace and atmosphere, enhancing both the frantic battles and the quieter moments in the hub world.

While Windblown is polished in many respects, it is still in early access and shows signs of that stage of development. Some players may encounter minor bugs, occasional interface roughness, or balancing issues—especially for solo players, who might find the experience less smooth than in co-op. The learning curve demands quick reflexes and adaptability, which might be daunting for newcomers but rewarding for those who master it.

In summary, Windblown offers a thrilling and distinctive roguelike experience that blends fast, rhythmic combat with vertical exploration and an exceptional multiplayer mode. Its tight mechanics, striking art style, and engaging progression systems make it a standout title in a crowded genre. While it still has room to grow, especially in terms of content variety and polish, Windblown is already a compelling game that promises to deliver even more excitement upon full release. Whether playing alone or with friends, it’s a wild ride worth embarking on.

Overall, very good game but you might want to pace yourself or risk becoming a danger to society.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 62, "timestamp_created": 1739409827}, {"review_text": "If you're looking for a game where you can punch demons in the face, surf on shotgun shells, and headbang to heavy metal while doing it — [b]DOOM[/b] is your new best friend.

Performance? Smoother than a buttered-up chainsaw. Graphics? Totally solid — not mind-blowing, but hey, you’re too busy splattering hellspawn to care.

Now let’s talk about enemies: these suckers are freaky, fun, and full of attitude. Special shoutout to my boy [b]Pinky[/b] — big, angry, and dumb as bricks. Love that guy.

The story’s there if you want it, but let’s be honest: you’re here to smash demons, not read a novel. And the game respects that; You don’t play DOOM for deep thoughts. You play it to turn demons into red mist.

Now the maps? Huge, layered, and loaded with secrets. You’re not just running hallways — you’re leaping across platforms, unlocking hidden rooms, and hunting collectibles. Every level is like a violent puzzle box with blood and metal. There’s even fast travel at the end of every level so you can go back and grab what you missed. Verticality, exploration, and brutal combat arenas — it's all here.

It’s fast. It’s loud. It’s metal.
[b]Highly recommended for anyone who thinks therapy should involve explosions.[/b]", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 16, "timestamp_created": 1749362148}, {"review_text": "After 9 years, what more can I say about this masterpiece that hasn’t already been said?

DOOM (2016) is a masterclass in how to reboot a beloved franchise. The gunplay is incredibly tight, weighty, and satisfying. The introduction of Glory Kills was a brilliant design choice; they’re fast, brutal, and perfectly complement the game’s intense pacing. The gore system hits the sweet spot, reinforcing the fantasy of being an unstoppable demon slayer. id Software absolutely nailed that core experience.

The Mars setting was a smart and effective choice. Most areas are crafted with care, featuring impressive detail and strong atmosphere. I especially enjoyed the inclusion of hidden areas, secrets, and collectibles that reward players for going off the main path. It adds extra engagement without straying from the game's linear structure.

The story is simple and wisely kept in the background, which suits DOOM's tone perfectly. That said, Samuel Hayden stood out as a particularly memorable character. His voice actor, Darin De Paul, delivered a powerful performance that added some unexpected depth. Even though narrative isn’t the focus, the world-building and presentation are excellent.

Enemy design is varied and memorable across the board. The boss fights, while a bit easy even on higher difficulties, are still fun and well-executed. This isn’t meant to be a punishing or methodical game like Dark Souls.it’s all about speed, power, and chaos. I’m genuinely looking forward to trying DOOM: The Dark Ages and seeing how the new parry system plays into that formula.

And then there’s the music. Mick Gordon, you’re an absolute legend. The soundtrack doesn’t just set the tone; it fuels every encounter with raw energy. It’s like a shot of adrenaline that pushes the action into overdrive. I’m not someone who typically listens to music in my free time, but these tracks grabbed my attention from the start. I played them so often my sister decided to learn the main theme on her electric guitar, and hearing her practice it is genuinely awesome.

The only part of the game I didn’t enjoy was the multiplayer. The modes become repetitive quickly, Demon Runes are far too overpowered, and certain weapon combos (like double shotguns) are frustrating to deal with. Cosmetic unlocks require a long and unrewarding grind, which just adds to the frustration. Matchmaking is also an issue outside of peak hours. Since few people play during those times, I often have to switch to North American or Asian servers, and that causes lag and high ping due to the distance. It really takes away from the experience.

Despite that, DOOM (2016) stands as one of the best first-person shooters of its generation. id Software approached this reboot with confidence and respect for the series. I strongly recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed the classic DOOM titles or is simply looking for a fast-paced, high-impact shooter done right. Skip the multiplayer and jump straight into the campaign. You won’t regret it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1753578585}, {"review_text": "At its best, Doom is everything it should be: a single-player campaign that’s just you, your super shotgun, and barely the amount of ammunition required to kill every single demon on Mars. It feels like a Doom game as you desperately try to find health pickups to keep you going, an ever-growing menagerie of demons snapping at your heels. It's exhausting and exciting and a little bit dumb, and when you're into it you're all the way in. At its worst, Doom is a repetitive series of enclosed rooms filled with demons, all of which you must kill to advance, complemented by a derivative and poorly thought-out multiplayer mode.
First impressions wise, Doom strikes all the right notes. The Union Aerospace Corporation's research facility on Mars runs red with the blood of employees who’ve learned a new meaning for the phrase 'wrongful termination,' but that barely matters to the inexplicably mute Doomguy, who shoots anything and everything which moves. Starting with only the pistol encourages you to focus on the diabolically delightful Glory Kill system — shoot your nearest Demon enough that they become staggered and highlighted in blue or orange, and if you press F (or R3 on a PS4 controller) while standing next to them you will rend them asunder. That is to say, you'll tear off their limbs and, in more than a few cases, joyfully beat them with their own appendages.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1735920260}, {"review_text": "I was just a kid in 2016 when I first got my hands on DOOM on the PS4. I probably shouldn’t have been playing it at that age, but I’ll never forget the feeling when that menu screen kicked in with that industrial soundtrack and the Slayer cocked his shotgun without a single word.

Back then, I didn’t fully understand the legacy of DOOM, but I knew right away this was something different from the other shooters I’d seen. There was no cover system, no reload button, no stopping. It was like the game wanted me to keep moving, to never be afraid — just angry. And it felt incredible.

The gameplay loop hooked me hard. The glory kills were like finishing moves from a dream (or a nightmare), and the way the music ramped up when the demons started swarming gave me chills — the good kind. The level design was this perfect mix of chaos and clarity, with secret areas that made me feel smart when I found them, even if they were mostly full of armor and ammo I didn't need because I was already too hyped to slow down.

Looking back now, I realize how smart the game was — how it brought the soul of the original 1993 classic into a modern package without trying to be something it wasn't. The story was there if you wanted it, but it never got in the way of ripping demons apart with a chainsaw or blasting through Hell with a Super Shotgun.

DOOM (2016) wasn’t just a game I played. It was a game that taught me what a shooter could be when it didn’t try to hold your hand. It was raw, loud, fast, and fun — and for a kid growing up in the age of cinematic shooters and online multiplayer grindfests, it was like waking up.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1747563433}, {"review_text": "Trust me bro if you are lonely, feeling lost in life, alone, depressed, just play this game. You play as the Doom Slayer, an ancient warrior awakened to stop a demonic invasion on Mars caused by corporate greed and reckless science. The narrative is minimal but effective, told mostly through brief interactions and environmental clues. It exists to give context, not to interrupt the slaughter.

Combat is the core of DOOM, and it’s perfectly designed. The gameplay loop rewards momentum and decisiveness. Health and ammo are scarce, but you can earn them through “glory kills” and chainsaw executions, forcing you to stay aggressive. Every encounter becomes a violent ballet of movement and timing.

The enemy roster is diverse and deadly. Each demon has unique patterns and weaknesses, demanding quick analysis and constant adaptation. Battles take place in arena-like environments with vertical movement, jump pads, and open space for dynamic positioning. Standing still means death.

Visually, DOOM impresses with sharp detail, clean design, and striking use of color. The environments shift between sterile sci-fi corridors and grotesque hellscapes, both rendered with precision. The performance is smooth, keeping the action seamless and uninterrupted even during chaos.

Mick Gordon’s industrial-metal soundtrack drives the pace of every fight. The heavy guitars and electronic distortion match the tone of pure destruction. The music rises dynamically with combat, amplifying the sense of unstoppable force.

Doom can be best described as  guns, demons, and unrelenting metal. DOOM (2016) doesn’t just recapture the metal spirit of the originals. It rips the soul out of modern FPS design and stomps it into the dirt with a size-13 Praetor Boot. 

[h2]Narrative & World[/h2]

There is a story here — hidden in terminals and environmental hints — and it’s surprisingly self-aware. The game knows its job isn’t to dump exposition; it gives you just enough to frame your rampage through UAC’s Martian hellscape. But what little is there has bite.
Also, the game opens with your character literally throwing a monitor aside mid-cutscene. A statement, and a promise.

[h2] Design & Systems [/h2]

There’s an elegance in how DOOM structures its upgrades and progression. Weapon mods and rune trials act like lite-RPG systems: not enough to bog you down, but enough to let you make meaningful choices about how you play. Do you glory kill for health, chainsaw for ammo, or just go full Berserk and rip your way to enlightenment? The game makes you earn your power — and once you do, it lets you unleash it with wild abandon.

[h2] Sound & Atmosphere [/h2]

The soundtrack deserves its own paragraph. Mick Gordon’s industrial metal score doesn’t just accompany your slaughter — it fuels it. It is the heart of the game.

[h2] Final Thoughts [/h2]

DOOM (2016) isn’t just a reboot — it’s a resurrection. A chainsaw-sputtering, double-jumping, demon-gutting celebration of everything that made the original iconic. It honors its legacy not with nostalgia, but with fury. It doesn't try to evolve the formula into something it’s not — it perfects it.

Even if you come from the world of tactical RPGs and turn-based battles, there’s something undeniably primal here. Something sacred.

Hell didn’t know what hit it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1750916970}, {"review_text": "Fast-paced demon gore ultraviolence extraordinaire. [{"review_text": "I saw this game mentioned in the comments of a video of Sseth about Space Station 13 and wanted to play it ever since then. A few months ago, an old friend of mine and I decided to play it together while reconnecting after a long time.

I like this game because it greatly rewards good communication, realistic planning and wise decisions. The way you cooperate with others has many layers and you can learn a lot about yourself this way.

It was kinda hard to get a solid group going after my friend went back to his other games. I started visiting random private servers. But it can be hard to find a public server with a good host. So I started my own public server. I put in the effort to be a good but serious captain, to motivate earnest people and quickly sort out problematic randoms and to plan forward and keep morale high.

With a good amount of patience and diligent, perpetuous attention, I built a solid server out of the random players who came at different times during the weekend. We now have a Steam groupchat and a Discord server. We recently finished the campaign, too, which I didn't get to do with the old friend nor in singleplayer.

We bonded over all kinds of terrible situations and epic clutches. Every single one of us grew in the process. We got to know each other in our highs and lows and learned how to talk about everything with mercy as well as severity. And above all, we learned to function as a team in all kinds of situations. This is exactly the experience I was hoping for and I am very glad that I took the leap of hosting my own server.

Barotrauma is obviously a very niche game and it is a niche I uniquely enjoy. I believe that cooperative multiplayer games with great freedom and complexity like this one bring out the whole spectrum of human behaviour. That is too much for most people, but I enjoy it because it means freedom and opens up the possibility for exchanges and experiences which would otherwise not be possible.

It does take effort to take the brunt of all the strange, dishonest, sadistic or also just kinda daft and unworkable people, to fairly talk it out with all of them, give everyone their just "trial" while keeping up the energy (and managing a submarine of eight other people at the same time), but it rewards you with friends who will stick around for some really crazy unexpected rounds of Europan madness. It can feel very punishing but also very rewarding.

I haven't really played with any serious mods yet, but there are good community mods which easily add another hundred hours to the normal campaign, new enemies, weapons, pets, all kinds of items, even musical instruments and much more. The community is wacky, but I kinda like it. The memes are funny.

10/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 31, "timestamp_created": 1754080792}, {"review_text": "It’s like the titan sub you saw on the news, but the game.

A Moloch in the deep,
Silent and sleek.
A Basuk it did sink,
In just a blink.

Drugs, guns and hookers but instead of hookers you have aliens trying to kill you. But the drugs are pretty cool.

It’s like Among us meets We Need To Go Deeper.

My wife calls it Space Submarine Sims 4

My wife’s boyfriend says It’s a Death Simulator...

… And maybe a "how to kill your colleague and boss" simulator. 

I'm an experienced domestic terrorist in Barotrauma, so that fits.

Imagine a bunch of idiots that either don't know what they're doing or don't want to do it, in a submarine 4000m deep in the ocean, on a planet where pretty much everything wants to kill you and any mistake can be fatal. Also clowns. 

The best disaster simulation you’ll ever play.

It's an unforgiving 2D Co-op Horror exploration and management game with many ways to die, many ways to survive and many ways to murder anything or anyone you wish… With a submarine editor to make your own ride and mod support to add or remove almost anything you'd want.

But before I go on, let me ask you this…

Have you ever wanted to go on a rampage and slaughter an entire outpost while being so high on several different drugs that you don't feel pain, just to save one guy?
Have you ever ventured too deep into the icy crust of Europa and found something THEY don't want you to know?
Have you ever wanted a pay raise, only for the captain to refuse, so you caused the nuclear reactor to increase the amount of steam produced, causing an explosion?
Have you ever got so high on meth, that you joined a highly controversial and illegal church, that wants to transcend humanity by uniting with a flesh eating parasite?
If you answered yes to any of these questions, then congratulations, Barotrauma IS a game for you!

During the game you walk around this submarine in space and everything and everyone that you aren't directly playing or isn't directly playing you wants to kill you. Disclaimer: Your crew will ABSOLUTELY and WITHOUT HESITATION fire a full on NUCLEAR RAILGUN SHELL at you POINT BLANK, given the opportunity. You need to manage weight, hull strength, cargo space, ammunition, fuel, welding fuel, navigational systems, ship maintenance, and medicine along with having a proper medical practitioner, just to survive transporting f**king 3 clowns to the next station over. You beat the game in campaign mode by killing God with the scraps of bulls**t you've harvested in the course of being a glorified delivery man. You eventually die… In some of the most horrific manners by the hands of ungodly creatures born from the depths of our fears. All the while trying to keep your floating coffin working and armed to hopefully prolongue your nightmare that is life just a little longer. Within an ocean of darkness that hides our fears even inches away from your face.

This is one of the few games where you can do a very simple job (repair everything, keep people healed, etc) and still have a vital role to the mission. It is really satisfying. And then the mudraptors decide they want a hug... 

My wife’s boyfriend has called it a "Drowning simulator" many times. The game is complicated and much of the player skill comes in learning the various systems. Single player it is a submarine and crew management simulator. Multiplayer can be anything from a crew simulator to an RP station or pure clown chaos. There is a tendency for one problem to spiral into many. One example is monster attack and tear holes in your hull, which floods the adjacent rooms, water damages the electrical equipment which cuts power to the pumps.  So you might have to choose between fighting the monsters causing the leaks, fixing the pumps to remove the water, fixing the leaks so more water doesn't come in, or fighting the monsters now boarding your ship! In fact the name "Barotrauma" refers to death by water pressure. This can be very frustrating or exciting as you overcome challenges and survive desperate situations. It is an attitude to gaming made famous by Dark Souls, but with less twitch skill and more cooperation, strategic decisions, and understanding of the game.

The main gameplay loop happens when travelling from one station to another, where you are moving through a passage. You will have to navigate and repair your sub, as well as defend it from aggressive fauna. Each segment is broken into travelling and spending time at a station. At stations you can buy/sell repair and craft items. There are skill trees for each role, and there is an interesting campaign progression based on making sure stations are available late game. 

The average round goes a little something like:

Captain chooses path on map from station. Everyone is ready.

The Captain chose a missions to kill a Hammerhead.

Along the path, you encounter a few smaller monsters that the ships guns handle easily.

You encounter the Hammerhead, it doesn't die immediately and it attacks your vessel.

Here is where it gets fun.

Maybe you quickly repaired your leaking sub and were able to continue.

Maybe someone gets crushed by the water pressure when a room filled too fast and they weren't wearing a suit.

Maybe the navigation console was fried and now you have to drain and repair.

Maybe you weren't able to repair fast enough and you accidentally missed the bottom of the passage and now your sinking towards crush depth in the abyss. Oh and a monster larger than your sub just spawned.

It’s got underwater clown shenanigans, big guns, cool ships, lots of things blowing up and breaking down. Also unspeakable, deep-sea horrors… what the hell are you waiting for?! Have fun.

[{"review_text": "Generally, PWS2 is solid. The innovations added to gameplay and the overall cleaning loop are immaculate, and I feel encouraged to use the entire spectrum of equipment I'm granted as opposed to just climbing the walls like a powerwashing chimpanzee.
I will go over the good and the bad - as good as this game is, there is some things I've noticed that need fixing.

THE GOOD
- Graphical fidelity. Dirt looks muckier than ever, and washing it off looks refreshing, satisfying, and leaves a shine on the proper surfacing, while leaving bright, saturated colors on things that don't shine as much. Cleaning cars is utterly beautiful; the metallic paint on the [spoiler]Car & Trailer[/spoiler] makes me cream.

- New equipment. Oh, hell, this is a livesaver. Scaffolding has a quick top-ladder, the scissor lift is a far better alternative to just jumping and spamming the long nozzle in the first game, and the Swirlforce floor brush can be a genuine lifesaver. Pro tip for the swirler; use the free cam and make circular motions with your mouse as you sweep the floor. It works wonders. Not to mention, the soap rework. Far, far better.

- Ulysses, Bubbles, and Squeak. Call me a Redditor, I don't care. Those 3 cats have my soul. I don't know where they found such good noises for the cats, but they're utterly adorable. Plus, you can pet them all! I have 3 orange beasts of my own, so the PWS LTD. cats remind me of them.

- Maps. The map design is immaculate, and features, yet again, a stunning variety of jobs to complete, from a simple moving van to a roller disco, and even onto [spoiler]the interior of the Ancient Temple you cleaned in the first PWS[/spoiler].

- UI. The menus are easy to navigate, and the overall HuD is nonintrusive and satisfying to look at, with multiple options for convenience and accessibility.

- The gameplay. It's PWS1, but improved. Washers feel more satisfying, spraying down dirty domiciles feels even more liberating, and getting a new washer, or equipment for it feels gratifying, and like you've accomplished something. The buy & sell feature helps with this tenfold.

THE BAD

- Multiplayer. There's no better way to say this. Multiplayer is fucked. Utterly fucked. You can't find lobbies. You can't join lobbies. You can't host lobbies. You can't invite your friends. Rough, rough playtesting for multiplayer was a necessity, and I don't believe it was tested thoroughly enough. I could be wrong, and this could be one of those cases of "this didn't pop up until we dropped the full", and I do hope this is the case, but as it stands, this looks untested. BE MINDFUL. AT THE TIME OF REVIEW, MULTIPLAYER IS BROKEN.

- General miscellaneous issues. Things I have a personal peeve against.
In-job text messages cannot be viewed anywhere, as far as I'm aware. This makes lore hard to follow if you have to tab out of the game during a text message, or if you're too distracted with washing a certain item. The lore is great, so this is a very bad thing.
You can't see the kind of material you're washing off of surfaces. This is an issue, because in the first game, being able to determine what you were blasting, and what your current washer did was a good way to gauge if you needed to either swap your nozzle to something more high-pressure, or outright purchase the next tier of washer. This was most adamant on the Vintage Car, where you had to blast rust off of the Cadillac with the red nozzle. This almost makes progression feel not worth the time and money spent, despite the obvious difference in power if you do compare the blasters.
Harper seems to be attached to your soul or some shit. Considering the other lore of PWS1 and 2, I'm willing to look past it, but the dude sees everything. Is there, like, a bodycam on me? I'm scared of Harper Shaw, man. Game over, man, game over!

That's all I have for now. Overall, I recommend this game wholeheartedly, but ONLY when they fix the multiplayer. Do not get it as is, and let FuturLab know that these issues NEED to be fixed. This game is at a bargain price - $25 USD for almost 45 hours of content - but the broken multiplayer gives it a very bad look.
