Ended up at almost 600hrs of full nights and weekends getting baked aF and blasting greasy Dubstep obsessively Powerwashing to my Mexican gardener souls content. Played the Campaign, bought all the DLCs, played it over and over. So here we are with Powerwash Simulator 2 that goes for the new and improved, bigger and better dynamics of a typical sequel which sometimes works and sometimes doesn't. 

Things I liked... 
-Soap is far more satisfying, unlimited and better here. Altho after the initial wow factor of it I didn't use it all that much since it feels redundant cleaning over the same area 2 times aka soap and rinse.
-Adaptable nozzle... replaced my love for PWS1's Yellow nozzle. This is all you need with an extension and you are golden.
-Multi-stage levels. This kept things cool and fresh. It wasn't overused, but also felt underused and in one case... the Theater job I found it kind of annoying
-Surface Cleaner... man if you angle this at a decent downward angle you can just hold up and move at a solid great pace to completely clean floors. It was satisfying to use and felt like a nice change of pace from completely only using Powerwashers.
-Dirt snipe tool that pops up near the end of the level... I hated this at first but after a few levels i really liked it. Better than constantly having to go to the menu and/or scour a level trying to find highlights. 
-Dirt looked better and the water effects were a step up. But for a sequel I was hoping for some sort of realistic dirt/water physics system which I can understand might be taxing on system resources

Things I didn't care for or like...
-Decorating your base. While I love this idea in games with this feature, it felt pointless here. I only put out 2 pieces of furniture then never touched it again. 
-Abseiling Rig... felt too wonky and annoying to use.
-Massive levels... coming home from work and having a few hours to play. You could spend your entire few free hours of a night cleaning a single level. I can see some people liking this but it made me feel like my time wasn't spent well with a low sense of progress progress. This here really kills the replayability of the campaign. The first game the bigger levels like Skatepark were the perfect length. You could knock a few out and feel like you accomplished more and this is the biggest weakness of this game. Bigger isn't always better. 

The campaign's massive time consuming levels personally are the reason I don't feel invested to replay the Campaign and probably just resort to going back to PWS1 on too tired chill game nights. I also just didn't find myself very interested in many of the levels in this game. Barely any stood out that made me want to replay them. I could still go back and replay that Skatepark and filthy ass bathroom in the first game countless times. It's a mixed bag for me. While I did still have a good time playing this game and there is incredible bang for buck gameplay here. I can't see myself investing crazy amounts of hours on it like I did the first game. 

Overall... it's good and worth a play if you liked the first one.

Don't expect this to convert any players who weren't into it before, but for those of us that enjoyed the original, this feels just as great.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761672106}, {"review_text": "100%'d the base game so dropping a review. just things i noticed. also, great game to play while listening to podcasts.

pros compared to the first game:

Once that is fixed I'll change this to a positive review.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761553925}, {"review_text": "TL;DR - if you enjoyed the later DLCs like Shrek and Alice in Wonderland from the first game, and disliked the fiddly detailed vehicle levels, I can guarantee you'll enjoy your time in Powerwash 2.

I'm most of the way through career mode and I can easily say that this is just like the first game, with some QoL changes and (IMO) better level design.

It feels like they took on the criticisms of some of the original's DLCs and have focused on making larger sprawling "landscape" levels rather than a heap of finicky little detailed vehicles.  FWIW, my favourite DLC from the original is a tie between Alice in Wonderland and Shrek, and my least favourite was the Warhammer DLC.  If you're like me and enjoy the big levels, you'll get a lot of enjoyment from the second installment.

They've added a couple of new powerwashers, including one that specialises in wide flat surfaces which helps speed up the larger levels with lots of walls and that sort of thing.  Soap/cleaning fluid is not longer a consumable, but does seem to have a limited capacity per level.  There's also actual situations where the fluid is almost necessary to get through some of the more persistent grime like rust etc, instead of just blasting through the game using only one nozzle and brute forcing everything.

I haven't really delved into the home base stuff, but I think it's a cute addition and separating currency means that you spend the $$$ you earn on upgrades, and then the points you earn get spent on cosmetic stuff.

I honestly haven't been able to put the game down since it came out because I'm so dang stressed right now, and this is the most cathartic and soothing game for me to wind down with after a hard day.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761550876}, {"review_text": "I have a, quite frankly, obscene amount of hours in the first game, so it was never in doubt that I was picking up the second on release day. Powerwash Simulator is my guilty pleasure. It is my way to switch off my ever chaotic brain and unwind. 
Compared to the first, so far, this is great. It's exactly what I wanted it to be, it's more Powerwashing. 
Performance is excellent, and I do love the newer additions like a home base with things to buy, and the new accessories for cleaning. 
I do still find the mini text boxes with the very loose story of the game to be a little needless. I don't play this for the story, I just want to clean things and get the mini dopamine hit from the dings, thanks. I know some people have been annoyed about the number of DLC for the previous game, but when you also look at the free content that was added over the years, I have zero complaints about throwing a few quid their way every once in a while if it means I keep getting more things to clean!

At the end of the day, you already know if this is the type of game for you or not. It wont be for everyone, many of my friends wouldn't play this if you paid them. But, if you DO like this kind of thing, then this is another exemplary game from a dev team who just know how to make a good game. 

I hoped I would love this as much as the first, and I was not disappointed.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761305509}, {"review_text": "This is my comfort game when I'm sad

Not anyone's priority 
But atleast i can powerwash well enough for a digital fake person to care", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1761620629}, {"review_text": "After 100%ing the game, I wanted to leave a review to let others know what to expect. While I dont believe a game should be broken down into a Pros and Cons list, I feel like this one has to be, especially compared to the previous entry.

Pros:
- New levels are bigger, better, and have fun articulate parts that make them more enjoyable, such as a ride-able roller coaster or the shooting gallery
- Some levels are broken into parts, and so are the timelapses
- Story is much better, with more communication with people, and a continuation from the previous game, with some fun things to discover
- Equipment upgrades feel more worthwhile and substantial
- Old Equipment can be sold, so you can sell all the previous nozzles of one model, and use it to buy the next washer
- More Equipment to buy, and with a third category
- Cosmetics are bought with a Point system, with money help just for the washers
- Soap is now much more powerful, is infinite, and doesn't need to be bought
- Scaffolding now has ladders, and there's a new step ladder, scissor lift, and sometimes a pulley system which makes levels really fun
- I rarely had the issue from the first game where I couldnt fully wash something. The added feature to reset a partially washed object also helped when this very rarely occured

Now onto the regretted cons
Cons:
- First are foremost, the Multiplayer is utterly broken, which absolutely ruins why myself and so many others bought this game in the first place
- You can't rebind your keys???? In 2025???
- Game has some bad performance issues (Im on a 9070XT and 9800X3D). This had led to really bad frame drops when inside menus, and sometimes during levels
- I had 3 full PC crashes while playing; one during a level, one when finishing a level, and one when opening up the store to buy a new washer
- Timelapses can get super compressed, so you can barely see what you did sometimes. Also the bug from the first game where ladders and scaffold is invisible is still here.
- Soap is SUPER OP, to the point where many early levels can be done extremely quickly when you dont have a powerful enough washer
- The last washer can be obtained super early and is also super OP, to the point where you can do 99% of stains with the white nozzle, rendering the Turbo or Triple nozzle useless
- Cosmetic point system has a cap (Edit: this is being removed in a future update) so you constantly get nagged to spend the points
- The texts appear and disappear so quickly that its hard to keep up with the story, and there's nowhere to pause and read all the texts you got like you could in the first game

And to top it off, the final level to the game was so underwhelming. Last game you got to do a GIANT PYRAMID, that took hours to do, required harder nozzles, and had massive revelations about the story so far.
In this game, the final level took me about 40 minutes to do with the white nozzle, with the exception of soap on the very last part, and it finished up with no fun story beat or cool revelations, even though you were getting hyped up about so many things leading up to it.

All in all, this game has alot of flaws, both intentional and unintentional, that Im sure the devs will fix over time. But for now, maybe wait until some of these things are fixed.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761819031}, {"review_text": "two words.

I payed for sequel to the first PWS and i got exactly what i paid for. mechanical improvements from the first game while still maintaining the old games charm and functionality. 10/10 you get what it says you get.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761326923}, {"review_text": "Definitely a worthy sequel. The good:

Its a very faithful adaptation to the first game, while expanding on the world and story. Not to mention you can pet all of the cats (Squeak and Bubbles have my heart). You'll visit places that you did in the first game, and see all of the things you washed then as well. This is really fun in my opinion. I love the change for the soap, not making it a limited resource where you have to pay for more is a great change from the first game, and I find myself using it more. The satisfaction of cleaning a surface after coating in in soap is very nice. I am also a big fan of the adjustable nozzle myself. The ability to create our own space in the home base is fun, and adds another thing that makes the game feel bigger and better than the first game.

The bad:

Most of the issues I have with the game are things I have seen many others bring up. The most glaring thing is that there is no way to change your key binds manually, and are limited to the new key binds and the first games key binds. On top of that, the multiplayer is very buggy. Often times it take up to 10 minutes to get into a lobby with a friend, and then there are bugs, like picking something up and not being able to put it down, lag, and sometimes the game crashes entirely. The game is also very bright, even when turning the brightness down. When you clean a surface the shine of the sun is extremely bright, which can really hurt your eyes, or in my case, give me very bad headaches, even after taking painkillers. The game also often crashes when trying to quit the game, which can cause issues with the cloud saving. My personal biggest issue with the game though, is that the game maps can completely crash the game. The rock climbing map is the biggest one for this, as I had to put all of me settings down to the lowest settings, or turn things off entirely just to get into the map, only to crash every 10-15 minutes just by turning around. This can make the game completely unplayable.

Conclusion:

[{"review_text": "On the 3rd February, 2025, in the newest newsletter Gaijin introduced an auction system where players can bid GJN (Gaijin Coin) on virtually limited tank and jet skins. (1GJN = 1$ basically). It sets out an horrible precedent where in the future they could start selling Rare, removed from the game or OP vehicles for exorbitant prices (As in 70$ jets weren't expensive enough). If this system isn't criticized by the community at large, the rare vehicle scenario might actually happen knowing how greedy Gaijin is. 

Vote with your wallet and remember - Every negative review matters.

EDIT - 07.02.2025:  Today a Gaijin added a response to my review and while I understand some  of the points - I've decided to keep this review around. Game is suffering from a lot of smaller to bigger problems, from weak battle passes, balancing, bugs, grinding, and me (As well as a good chunk of community) doesn't exactly trust the company for a lot of good reasons. There has to be a visible, continuous change for the better for that to change.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1738617810}, {"review_text": "Has the potential to be one of the greatest games of all time but it is ruined by Biblical levels of greed and it's showing less and less signs of improvement with each update. As someone with thousands of hours both on steam and on the game's own launcher, I wholeheartedly urge you to not play this game if you are considering downloading it. 

Gaijin does not care for you, they don't care for their game, they lie, they treat you like a fool and all they care about is your money and they feed you the bare minimum to keep you engaged so that you keep spending more. 

Half of the content of the updates for the past 2 years are vehicles locked behind a paywall with the price tag of a full AAA game per vehicle or they're vehicles that are behind a 3 month minimum hard-locked grind that involves your own activity as well as your fellow squadron (clan) members, however you can simply skip the whole ordeal by forking over real money and you get no benefits like the aforementioned premium vehicles, for roughly the same price, and the vehicle you purchased also comes stock and you have to grind the modules anyway.

Your good performance in a match is not rewarded as your XP is heavily reliant on the length of a match. For example a match where you went crazy and got 12 kills in ground battles, a zone capture and you dropped a nuke without dying and ended the match in 5 minutes, will give you less XP than a match where you died 5 times, got 5-6 kills but it lasted over 20 minutes. 

The game's progression is heavily built around the monetization, the subscription system that flat out increases your rewards as well as the premium vehicles, that in a lot of cases are better than their free counterparts, also do the same. Premium vehicles that go all the way to the highest tier, spitting on the effort and time you put in to grind to that top. Why would you spend months or for some people years grinding for that F-15, F-18, Abrams, Challenger, T-80 etc. when you can just fork over 70 euros and get it instantly?

Gaijin loves advertising their game as realistic which is completely false and countless vehicle characteristics are wrong, some more egregious than others, and whether something will be made to be accurate to what it is in real life is dependent solely if they agree with it or not. You could present the most accurate, unclassified information from the literal manufacturers, government, crews, whatever, but if they do not like it, they will not implement it, state that your source is not good enough or they don't think it's that way as the info states.

The maps are horrible, the game modes outdated and not given attention, the balancing atrocious with vehicles artificially nerfed or buffed, updates will take 3 weeks of test server and still go live completely broken with game breaking bugs or performance issues, some issues never getting fixed or reappearing an update later. In every regard but the core gameplay and feel, it is a complete failure of a product.

Save your money, save your time. Indie games are on the rise and there are products far more deserving of your attention, than this money trap of a grindy game. It is never going to get better and be what it could, it is only going to get worse and the only reason it still holds as many players as it does, is because it holds a monopoly over this genre and no other game competes with it, there is no alternative. The day we do get one, if ever, this game is going to fall off.

In this final segment I want to state that I write this review because I hold...held, a lot of passion for this game, it is a big part of my life and I've met some of the greatest people I know through it. The game's state is incredibly frustrating but at some point you have to face reality and it is time to move on, it's never going to improve. Thank you for your time reading and I hope you'll find something else that'll intrigue you. Peace.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 13, "timestamp_created": 1761091036}, {"review_text": "The planned auction house is a terrible idea.  This game is monetarily predatory enough with battle passes, loot boxes, and the Gaijin Market.  There's already plenty of interesting content that's arbitrarily locked behind these three paywalls.  We do not need a fourth that will end up being even more expensive.  Stop scamming people with this false FOMO nonsense.  There is no scarcity with these items.  They are not limited edition.  They are pixels on a screen and their circulation in the game is based entirely on the developers' whims.  Gaijin, fix some of the fundamental issues your game has before trying to introduce more monetary systems.

Speaking on those issues:

The rate at which you earn silver lions and research points is far too slow.  If you don't buy premium, you might as well not even bother trying this.  God help you if you're trying to get to top tier as a free-to-play player.  You will basically be pulling a second shift every day for months to unlock anything modern.  Even with premium and premium vehicles you're still going to be grinding incessantly.  There's a mechanic in this game called Convertible RP.  You earn it slowly in every battle and are meant to be able to use to unlock anything in a tech tree.  In a sane system, one like their sister game Enlisted, this is something to give back to the players who are willing to waste hours of their life grinding.  It's meant to buffer the tedium that is switching to a new nation.  In Enlisted, this Convertible RP is completely free for the player to use.  At one point they wanted to place a cap on the amount you could store.  The players revolted and the developers, to their credit, actually listened.  In War Thunder, to use Convertible RP you have to spend their premium currency.  The conversion rate?  It's 1 Gold Eagle (the premium currency) per 45 RP.  I have a little over 3.5 million Convertible RP.  It would take me slightly less than 78 thousand GE to use it all.  The largest pack of GE is 25 thousand and it costs $114.  So three of those wouldn't even cover all of my Convertible RP.  The highest rank vehicles (12.0) cost 400 thousand to research.  Ok, you don't want me to complete half a tech tree for free, that's fair.  Then decrease the rate at which Convertible RP is earned if it's free!  Heck, even if you were to make the conversion rate better like 1 GE to 500 RP, I'd be happy.  Give us anything!  Enlisted also has a feature where you can converted their free Convertible RP to silver (the free currency).  The conversion rate is awful but it's at least something!  War Thunder fails to include a similar feature despite being on the market for three times as many years.  

Compression.  Please, for the love of all that is holy, stop compressing based on player stats.  Actually look at how the vehicles perform and balance based off that approach.  If you've added in too many vehicles to do such, stop adding in more vehicles until you balance what you have! Gameplay: 10/10
Dead Cells fluid and responsive combat with featuring various weapons, skills, and power-ups in the fray. Its difficulty is quite high yet fair. Its nature as a roguelike keeps each run fresh even though the punishing difficulty won't appeal to everyone. Parry system in this game is well made, its actually so much satisfying to parry like Sekiro.

Graphics: 8/10
The pixel art is quite amazing, with rich colors and detailed animations. Environments are diverse and atmospheric. This style complements the game's fast pace. Don't really care about graphics actually. Loved the artstyle!!

Sound & Music: (9/10)
The soundtrack is dynamic and immersive, making the game even more intense. From eerie ambient tracks to high-energy battle themes, the music keeps you engaged. The sound effects, like weapon clashes and enemy growls, are crisp and satisfying.

Replayability: (10/10)
Dead Cells is an exemplary game in terms of replayability, thanks to its procedural generation and variety of combat options. Every run feels different, and the progression system offers meaningful upgrades that encourages you to keep coming back. Dungeon generation is actually random always making this game more interesting to play again and again.

Dead Cells is a must-play for fans of challenging action games and roguelikes. Its fast-paced gameplay, beautiful art, and high replay value make it an indie gem.

On PC and PS5 and I’d do it again in a heartbeat. I know it’s on Game Pass, but I don’t care. This game is that good. Easily one of the best gaming experiences I’ve had in years.

Dead Cells isn’t another roguelike; it’s a love letter to the genre and to indie devs themselves. The sheer number of nods and easter eggs tucked away in the game makes every run feel like you’ve stumbled into an inside joke or a secret handshake with the developers. Even watching a gameplay video spoiled the magic for me and turned it off immediately, because I realized the real joy is in the exploration: trying out different outfits, testing weapons, and discovering what wild, unexpected thing happens next.

The combat is pure poetry in motion: fast, fluid, and punishing in all the right ways. The variety of weapons makes it so much fun. The more absurd the better. I don't even like metroidvania's nor pixel art. This game changed that. The pixel art is gorgeous, the animations are buttery smooth, and the soundtrack drives every moment with an energy that makes you push just one run further. The expansions have been excellent, but I wish there were more because this is a world I don’t want to stop returning to.

It's the perfect game for just shutting off your brain after a long day at work. It perfectly blends the roguelike and metroidvania genres, and the weapon and enemy variety is fantastic! I was sad to hear that more Dead Cells updates were planned, only to be canceled so all hands could work on Windblown. That's not to say I'm not looking forward to the finished product of Windblown, as I'm a sucker for roguelikes of all kinds. But as a primarily single-player gamer, I'd gladly pay up for more Dead Cells updates in the future, it's such a phenomenal game and I'd love to see it grow ever more. Updated Review:
I really did not like this game when it initially came out.  It didn't seem to have enough and quite frank the enemy design still turns me off.  Just the way they look.  The gameplay is tight and captures a metroidvania in essence.  You can jump in and out of the game quickly.  Which leads to that "Just one more game" feeling.  The runs get better as you advance into the roguelite elements.  Once acquiring certain permanent upgrades, the game opens up.  

The beginning of the game can really turn people off because it simply doesn't feel good at first, you feel weak and start frail, it's a real gear shift that makes the game seem not fun, but you have to peel a layer off the game first before you can enjoy it.  At least that's what happened with me.

[{"review_text": "Probably the most conflicted review I have ever written. Darkest Dungeon is one of my favorite games of all time, but Darkest Dungeon 2 is an exhausting experience.

What made the first game so enjoyable was its sense of urgency and pacing. It was a thrill to explore a dungeon and leave with your party barely intact, grateful you had survived, or to dominate a run completely with loot to show for your skill. You were in, you were out, and you had a story worth telling.

If you were not in the mood for an intense challenge, you could bring strong gear, keep your torch level high, and do the bare minimum for less loot. If you wanted a desperate fight for valuable materials, you could still optimize your gear but take fewer supplies, keep the torches low, and brace yourself for a run that was both punishing and fun. Either way, it was a short but exhilarating rollercoaster. It had its flaws, but the experience was powerful and rewarding when you played well and made the most of your resources.

In Darkest Dungeon 2, those dynamics are gone. Runs are long and draining, with a fixed and punishing difficulty curve that can ruin you for a single mistake or a misunderstanding of your heroes’ abilities and quirks. All of your favorite characters return, but they feel weakened. Loot is no longer about the thrill of discovery; it is tied to a fixed currency-based progression or repeating the same mini-boss grind in hopes that he has the trinket you need once you reach them. The only way to influence difficulty is to choose a safer route, but you are still locked into the same drawn-out road toward the inevitable defeat that awaits at the final boss, one you are unlikely to survive if you took the safer path that only rewards you with scraps.

Perhaps Red Hook wanted to capture the fatigue of a stagecoach journey through a harsh, oppressive land. But in doing so, they forgot what made the first game exciting. Difficulty and tedium do not have to coexist at the expense of fun.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1754654463}, {"review_text": "Dear Developer,

Please rename the game to Darkest Road, and the Steam rating will go up. The game is fun, but it's just very different from its predecessor.

Warmest regards 🤍", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 38, "timestamp_created": 1734210943}, {"review_text": "After spending over 900 hours immersed in Darkest Dungeon 2, I can confidently say it is a challenging yet rewarding masterpiece. The game strikes a balance between punishing difficulty and the exhilaration that comes with overcoming it. If you're looking for a game that demands strategic thinking, and rewards adaptability, this is it.

Initially, I found the level of randomization in the game—particularly at launch—to be overwhelming. Too often, failure felt like the result of bad luck rather than poor decision-making. However, the developers have worked  to address this issue through a series of updates and balance changes, creating an experience where every loss feels like an opportunity to learn and grow. Today, success in Darkest Dungeon 2 is far more about your strategic choices, your understanding of the game mechanics, and your knowledge of enemy behavior. This shift has made victories feel even more gratifying and defeats less frustrating - most of the time :)

One of the most impressive aspects of the game is how it encourages experimentation.  Every team composition is now viable—a huge improvement from the early days when certain combinations felt sub-optimal. With a bit of understanding of game mechanics and enemy abilities, you can succeed with any group of characters, which has transformed Darkest Dungeon 2 into a sandbox of tactical possibilities.

The journey itself—navigating the game’s haunting, beautifully rendered landscapes—is unforgettable. Every step feels consequential, and every decision matters. Whether you’re managing your team’s stress levels, deciding which encounters to tackle, or weighing the risks of pushing your luck for better rewards, the game constantly challenges your ability to think ahead and adapt on the fly. The tension is relentless, but it’s this very pressure that makes every small victory feel monumental.

Another standout feature of Darkest Dungeon 2 is its community. The game’s fans are incredibly supportive, and the tight-knit nature of the player base fosters a sense of camaraderie that’s rare in today’s gaming landscape. Whether you’re looking for tips, sharing war stories, or just enjoying the creativity of small but dedicated content creators, there’s always something to engage with. The content creators, in particular, deserve praise for consistently producing entertaining and insightful material that enhances the overall experience.

In its current state, Darkest Dungeon 2 has become everything I hoped it would be and more. It’s a game that demands your respect, tests your resolve, and rewards your persistence. While it’s not for the faint of heart, for those willing to embrace its challenges, the payoff is unparalleled. Whether you’re a seasoned veteran or a newcomer, this is a journey worth taking—a journey into madness, perseverance, and triumph. Darkest Dungeon 2 isn’t just a game; it’s an experience, one I’m thrilled to recommend to anyone who dares to face its horrors.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 12, "timestamp_created": 1737146409}, {"review_text": "[h1] YES, IT IS NOT DARKEST DUNGEON 1! [/h1]

However, this game deserves a way higher rating. It is fun, it is well made, it is unique experience.
Unfortunately its main game loop takes away several aspects that Darkest Dungeon 1 players enjoy so much.
This explains the sour ratings for an otherwise highly enjoyable game.

What is different:
Instead of slowly restoring your hamlet, your heroes travel the landscape with a stagecoach.
The expeditions are long and follow a roguelike gameloop. You can choose which regions to travel to and, like in many other roguelike/roguelite titles, select the next waypoint from a choice of 2 or 3 options.

Positives:
1. First off.. the greatest thing about it.. THE SOUNDTRACK. 
Stuart Chatwood filled this game with a bunch of absolute bangers: Sprawl Battle, Traverse the Mountain and Battle of the Mountain - these songs will put you on edge in epic decisive battles, where small mistakes will be even more punished than in the first iteration of the game. Sprawl Battle became my personal most heard song on Spotify.
2. The graphics are great. The pre-move animations add a lot of life and dynamic action in comparison to the more static first Darkest Dungeon. The winddown animations are just beautiful too.
3. The relationships between characters are a fantastic addition. Unluckily, it became a bit too easy to always get good relationships, which often makes the game a lot easier. Unluckily the powered up moves are random and sometimes just useless.
4. The boss fights can be hard if you bring the wrong team comp. To me, these harder fights are very enjoyable. Beating the boss with one man standing basically in the last swing was a very amazing and memorable experience.
5. The token system adds a bit more consistency in your battle plan. For most players, this might be an improvement. I personally enjoyed the randomness of the first part a little more.
6. The reflection shrines tell the stories of the heroes and are really cool.
7. The narrator (June Wayne) delivers once again and the lines slap hard. Yet, most lines feel less iconic than the first part.
8. Less micromanagement.

Negatives:

1. There is no gravitas when failing a run or when a characters dies. You don't lose them. You can just select them again in your next run. This bitter aspect of the first Darkest Dungeon is what made it so thrilling. Here you can basically end a run early with little consequences. Sometimes it is the best course of action to abandon midway and cut your losses.
2. Good team comps are limited. You can't play some goofy stuff anymore like 4 Lepers.
3. Decisions along the way have no impact. You decide on whatever resource you need most in the moment.
4. Many beloved characters are missing in the base game and are trickling in with DLCs. As things are progressing right now, getting the full DD1 roster in the future might cost you another 50-100 bucks.
5. Camping is replaced by the inn, which is less immersive. The fear of ambushes and the little moments of respite inside the dungeons was a great touch.
6. Spending a few hours just to get smacked by a boss or miniboss is pretty bitter. Yes, you can upgrade a bunch of stuff and it was not completely for naught. But the upgrades are whatever.
7. Many paths of the heroes are inferior to other paths and for me there is no reason to play semi-useless builds.
8. Some characters are strong and they play nicely (e.g. Highwayman and Man-At-Arms). Some characters are quite weak like the Runaway.

Conclusion:
It is not Darkest Dungeon 1. It is still a fantastic game. Some gameplay mechanics are better, some are worse.
The DLC money-squeeze is a bit of a turn-off. Especially hiding already designed characters behind a paywall is a huge no-no.

Addendum:
Redhooks EULA agreement is pretty dank: https://store.steampowered.com/eula/262060_eula_0 (Section 5, 14 and 20)
This is a singleplayer game. I am not speedrunning. Why do you want to monitor my RAM?", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1737500374}, {"review_text": "Of course, of course, this isn’t DD1.

The first game had a brutally high entry threshold: it punished you over and over while you desperately tried to save as many of your characters as possible through dark, convoluted mechanics and merciless RNG. Over time, you’d study the system, upgrade your recovery spots and gear so your people could survive longer and be better prepared. You’d start to understand the quirks and weaknesses of every party member. And after weeks... months... years, maybe, just maybe, you would finally beat the game.
In the second game? None of that.

Now DD2 is a pretty standard roguelike across three maps, where the main idea is to throw yourself forward and experiment aggressively. Made it to the furthest inn you could reach? Wrap up the run, gather your candles for meta-progression, and get ready for the next go.

The pros: the game is faster, more accessible, has gorgeous visuals, a genuinely interesting story, and some pretty unique mechanics for its genre.

The cons: well, the pros are also the cons. Now when you lose or someone dies — nothing bad really happens. Just pick that hero again on your next run. There's none of that soul-crushing bitterness from the first game.
Also, forget about fun meme-squads like four Lepers — freedom of choice is officially dead.

Ironically, they put way more effort into fleshing out each "character" this time around than they did in DD1. Which honestly feels pointless, because characters die and respawn endlessly, with only the tiniest shred of permanence.
You're not investing in a hero, no matter what the game tries to tell you — you're investing in a class. The individuality of any given character doesn’t really matter.

Still though — it’s a damn good game. Some mechanics got better, some got worse.

...but after almost 300 hours, I still have one question:
Where the hell are the dungeons?", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 14, "timestamp_created": 1745790430}, {"review_text": "Update
I completed the entire confession. Now I see what I dislike the most, there's no buildup. My team is set at the beginning and I'm only increasing stats with trinkets and trophies. The gameplay is stagnant for the entire run. 

In case of FTL, a great roguelike, you can build your ship into a raid party, missile spammer, asphyxiation machine, drone carrier, beam master, or anything in between. Play style changes as the player wishes and the ship is shaped by the player's choices. Not just FTL, every great roguelikes has great buidups, which DD2 lacks.

Additionally, this game has an exceptionally terrible first impression in terms of gameplay. With all the locked characters, skills, and items, the early game loop is undoubtably the worst I've seen in a  while.

-----------------

The music, graphics, and tokens are great. Everything else is questionable.

DD2 is a flawed roguelike. It somehow managed to scrape off all the good parts of roguelike and Darkest Dungeon, then merged what's left.

I remember devs referring to Slay the Spire in their early development. Looking at how DD1's systems are put into Slay the Spire structure, I don't see why it had to be a roguelike when it killed all the roguelike's fun.

Sts
-quick runs, about 1-2 hours.
-Some control over rng
-various builds, replayability
-Meaningful meta progression
-Improvising and adapting mid-run

DD2 
-A run takes more than 3 hours. Roguelikes in general rely on rng, so bad runs could happen. They minimize the frustration of failure by keeping the game short and snappy. DD2 only took frustration and failure from that sentence. Failures are mandatory in the early game. No matter how good you are, you must grind to get better meta progression and grinding isn't fun in this game. It's like 'you must grind to have fun' instead of 'you could grind for more fun'.

-Combat rngs can be somewhat negated with more knowledge and grind unlocks. I couldnt find ways to counter quirk/disease rngs though.

-Builds lack variety and there's not enough room to experiment. Since almost every growth is random (affinity combo, trinket, quirk), there's not much to plan ahead. 

-DD2 has a lot of progression trees going on, but they all feel insignificant except new skills. Would 5% more death resist help? Certainly. Does it change how I play? NO.

Heroes aren't balanced, some subclasses are useless, the early game openly rewards dumping more playtime over being good at the game, and there's just not enough variance in the game to justify its genre as a roguelike and its price. Candle rewards are full of uninteresting bloats. Why does negative relationship lock skills when switching skills mid-run is the last bit of adaptation left in this game? 

DD2 is squeezing itself into roguelike's clothes and it's chocking itself in the process. I dont mind changing genre but why bleach out all the fun?", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1742076754}, {"review_text": "It's a complete slot machine for the first thirty hours. After that, it becomes a slot machine that you can influence. 

It's dice-rolls on top of dice-rolls on top of dice-rolls and they call it game design, then slap a disclaimer that "oh, it's hard." on top of it to excuse the complete lack of balance.

I have to say I like it _more_ than DD1 -- to this not-too-serious gamer it's been a bit easier for me to get a handle on, advance with, and enjoy. The (not entirely, but more) linear paths make it easier for me to parse what decisions to make, I find combat a bit easier (madness seems to accumulate more reasonably) and on the whole, as a casual gamer that doesn't want to explode my brain every time I fire up a game to relax -- it's a good fit for me.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1751662300}, {"review_text": "combat is much more fun than the first game, requires much more thinking, less randomness, in the first game you'll just randomly miss an attack with a 85% chance to hit and screw you over, in the second game when you hit normally it will 100% hit, if enemies have dodge or you have blind you know exactly what you're in for when you decide to attack, the atmosphere in my opinion is weaker compare to the 1st game, the storytelling is also a little worse, but still an extremely fun game thanks to the much improved combat", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1735542078}, {"review_text": "I'm a huge fan of the darkest dungeon series and thoroughly enjoyed DD1, but I think I have to make it clear:

DO NOT GO INTO THIS GAME EXPECTING A REPEAT OF DARKEST DUNGEON ONE.

Darkest Dungeon 2 is controversial when it comes to being the successor of the first game, but if you can look past that you'll find something fantastic. Darkest Dungeon 2 is more appealing to me because of how easy it is to start a new run. It excels at being easier to jump into than the first game, as runs could take multiple weeks irl in DD1. If you don't have the time or commitment necessary to complete the first game I wholeheartedly recommend Darkest Dungeon 2 in its stead.

RIP Wayne June and thank you for your contributions to this series.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1744070987}, {"review_text": "One of the most significant games to me personally.

Disclaimer: it's nothing like Darkest Dungeon 1, not even close. I am honestly puzzled as to why they called the game "DD2" at all. Whatever minor PR won by this is clearly outweighted by previous game fans' backlash. It's a spinoff at best, both in story and gameplay.

So, why like this game? To me it's mostly themes of the world, the characters, the story. Someone astutely said that there is a Silent Hill vibe (a very different game), because the entire world is build around spiritual torment, and obsession with it. Combined with beautiful immortal voice of Wayne June (who ever lives in our hearts), the games gruelling gameplay becomes more of a meditative experience. You play just to hear another one of his great quotes.

I won't sugarcoat it: this game's triumph is also it's weakness, Wayne carried 90% of it all. Without him this game is pretty much exactly what negative reviews paint it as. Still, visual and sound design, combined with story and again, voice acting come together as something that is bigger than its flaws.

If pure gameplay is what you're here after, then first: bad idea; second: let's talk about that.

Combat wise it's a significantly simplified version of DD1 gameplay. Hits are guaranteed unless specific effects indicate otherwise. Buffs and debuffs no longer stack to same extent as they used to, values are easier to remember. Something to the effect of "15% 25% 50%". There has also been some attempts at innovation, giving some heroes unique buffs and debuffs and the like. For example, Occultist now needs to accumulate and spend Celestial Autism (not real name but idk) tokens to cast his strongest spells. In some cases it's okay, in others it's kind of annoying and you just avoid a character so you don't have to construct your entire party to accomodate for this one character's BS. Generally, I think tactical encounters actually got casualized, it's a strategy layer that gets to people. And yes there are bosses. Those I think might be the worst offenders of tactical layer. Actual run-end bosses are alright, but do be sure to google what they do, because they are gimmicky (more so than in DD1). As for "mini" bosses - completely awful, I am an adamant defender of this game and I hate them. Each "mini" (not really) boss is a ticking clock towards party wipe, and you either hardcounter them throught one "correct" strat or you feel so helpless it's not even funny. End-run bosses are legit much easier.

As for strategic layer, you have a kind of "car in zombie apocalypse" scenario, where you travel down a forking road on a carriage. There are several biomes, each with very specific hazards. At the end of each biome you can restock, replace fallen heroes and choose the next biome (out of 2 available). In every individual map you have a forking highway I mentioned, and you essentially travel from one mini-location to another, by choosing to turn one way or another. And naturally you can't go back, because the protagonist wouldn't be where they were, if they were intelligent. The mini-locations have either prompts, tactical encounters or long-term hazards. Some locations are known beforehand, some are not. Most mid-late biomes are insaaaanely long, taking about 20-30 mins each. Artistically it's interesting, because it really does make you feel fatigued, but in a good way. From a pure gameplay perspective, however... Eh... I mean like I said, this game has a big case of "videogames are art". And if you believe the same, this game will test your conviction.

Oh and the stress system got revamped, it's easier to tell from scratch, rather than what's different. So when heroes' stress is at maximum (it's now 10/10 rather than 100/100 by the way), heroes generally have their health reduced to 10-20% of what it was and relationships with other heroes suffer. There are no longer permanent stress conditions like "abusive" or "masochistic". Although having frequent mental breakdowns does give bad quirks as well as ruin relationships. Speaking of, what is a relationship? It's something they replaced stress buffs/debuffs with. Can be weirdly wholesome, but just difficult as the mechanic that was replaced. It's neither better nor worse than stress conditions, really. It's pretty standard practice and would have been an easy sell to players who wanted more of the same. But these devs don't settle for easy. With DD2 they decided to redo all visuals in 3D, update the combat system, break down the progression structure and build two roguelite modes. 

[quote=The Narrator][h3][i]"What is it, then, that gazes back so intently from the abyss?"[/i][/h3][/quote] 

The new 3D visuals retain the gorgeous art style of the original game and fix its issues: body proportions are much healthier, depth feels better and animation transition make it all look smooth.  

The updated combat system has dropped traditional stats such as Accuracy and Armor, which were responsible for weird RNG spikes like failing three consecutive attacks at 90% accuracy. DD2's battle flow revolves around positive and negative tokens, such as Blind and Guard, which are applied or cancelled by combat actions. The result feels less random and more predictable, which is helpful in a tactical game, but harder to pick up: new players must first learn all tokens. Ditching the permanent progression of the original game, DD2 introduces two roguelite game modes: Confessions and Kingdoms. 

Confessions are gauntlet runs with multiple regions to cross and a different final boss in each of the five difficulty levels. You need to carefully build a party of 4 heroes as opportunities to replace any casualty are very limited.

Kingdoms offer longer runs against one of three factions: the beast clan, the witch coven and the cursed courtiers. This was a fun rant but honestly I am really broken hearted about this game. I felt like this wasn't as well balanced as the first one and was far more likely to land you in a completely irretrievable no-win scenario.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1742246033}, {"review_text": "This is definitely not the DD1 experience.

I was hoping for something similar, maybe even better than DD1 (my mistake, I know) — but this game just isn’t that.
I’ve played for a while now, and at first I was impressed — but then the small details and minor gameplay issues broke my rose-colored glasses.

It may still be a good game for some, but for those who fell in love with DD1, it will likely be a heartbreak in the end.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1761556746}, {"review_text": "This game was not for me. I was looking for a sequel to the wildly successful Darkest Dungeon. This game is not that. It takes an entirely new direction than the first one, which I can appreciate the devs for taking a swing, but for those of you looking to pick up where you left off on the original Darkest Dungeon, you'll need to look elsewhere. I hate that there is only a "yes" or "no" because if you enjoy this game I am happy for you; I just wanted to warn others like me.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1751207466}, {"review_text": "Okay the screen shots already show you what the game is, so lets skip that and get one thing cleared up real quick:  You will see a lot of reviews saying how Darkest Dungeon is "better", and how Darkest Dungeon II is "Not as good" as Darkest Dungeon.  Take that with a LARGE grain of salt. 

Now, if you have never played Darkest Dungeon, yes you will want to play that one first. Reason being it gives you a lot of backstory you need if you want to fully enjoy this game, which provides the backstory to the heroes you had in the first Darkest Dungeons Game. Darkest Dungeon is the main plot and universe building. Darkest Dungeons II is the subtext omnibus that helps complete it if you really want to learn more about the various lives involved and the dark happenings since.  

So, is it not as good as Darkest Dungeon? It is, BUT it is a different type of game play and that is the key thing to know. Don't let the fact the game play changed a good deal confuse you. It is NOT a worse game, but IS a DIFFERENT type of game, set in the same universe with many of the same characters as well as a few new faces and continuing the story in more depth.  It is every bit as enjoyable and i would argue more so for those who are invested in the deeper story telling of a game. 

My advice? Get both. If you have not played Darkest Dungeon, play that first so you have the main plot and stories already down. Once you have done that and IF you enjoyed it, THEN get darkest dungeon II and enjoy the more fully flesh out character arcs and story.  Darkest Dungeon II can be faster than Darkest Dungeon at times, but keep in mind that while both have plenty of mods, Darkest dungeon II also gives you ways to play beyond the main game which are official so you have more variety  as far as full game play goes than in Darkest Dungeon. 

Summary: Both Darkest Dungeon and Darkest Dungeon II have value. They are NOT the same game or game play style, nor are they meant to be, Rather than bringing more of the same with the sequel, they brought a new dish to add more variety and flavor to the Darkest Dungeon Universe. Go in understanding this and you should have absolutely no problem enjoying it for what both games offer.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1755579983}, {"review_text": "I just picked it up again to try out Kingdoms and after just one run, really just after the first couple fights, it reminded me of what pushed me away from this game to begin with. I could not recommend this game less, it is straight up no fun. Every fight is a tedious chore, with no sense of progression. 
Why do enemies have so much, and seemingly unlimited, healing? The player has healing mechanics because they have to fight 10 times in a row, enemies do not have this, they just have to fight once. If they win, the game is over, and if they lose then the next enemies replace them. 
It feels like the only reason they have it is to prolong the fights, and it feels terrible. The game is actively undoing all the progress you are making in the fight. Its like why am I even doing this is the game is just going to immediately undo it.
And if I have just picked up this game and 20min later I am asking myself why I am even doing this, then the game is just not fun.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 9, "timestamp_created": 1742644455}, {"review_text": "Counter to some reviews, I actually enjoy this sequel a lot more than the first game, so YMMV. Props to Red Hook for trying something different.

The relationships system is probably my biggest gripe for how impactful it is for being a two-dimensional mechanic: everyone either hates eachother, or loves eachother, and there's not really any inbetween. Your first impressions of the game will be dramatically warped by this system due to how snowbally it is in either direction. 

Your runs will be made significantly harder or easier depending on how well it's managed.  You must keep everyone below the magic 4/10 stress number to the best of your ability in order to ensure they make only positive connections or else your team will rip itself apart. That's about 90% of the work that goes into managing relationships. Stress begets stress; low stress begets low stress. 

Still, DD to me has always been a combat game first and foremost, and DD2's combat is vastly more polished and balanced.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1751622754}, {"review_text": "Coming from Darkest Dungeon 1, I was very excited to try out the sequel. I was optimistic about the game and cautiously aware of the fact that the core gameplay loop had changed in the sequel, so I tried to keep an open mind, but unfortunately all I can conclude after playing the game myself + reading more about it afterwards is: I don't find it fun. That doesn't mean it's a bad game, it's simply that I don't enjoy it coming from the original.

This review is intended primarily for folks who enjoyed the original Darkest Dungeon, detailing some differences between the original and sequel to help you decide whether the game is worth your purchase.

To start off: the artwork, music, and general atmosphere is fantastic and very reminiscent of the original Darkest Dungeon. The core, turn-based strategy element of combat encounters remains the same and carries a similar, punishing weight to the original. Certain combat mechanics have changed, such as base accuracy not existing (always 100%). In fact, all combat mechanics have largely done away with base values and have been replaced by a new combat status effect system called tokens. I.e instead of a hero having "20 base Dodge" and an ability giving a "+25 Dodge" buff, base dodge is non-existent, and instead an ability can add a "Dodge" token to a character that gives a raw 50% chance to dodge the next attack, or "Dodge+" token that gives raw 75% chance to dodge the next attack. Some new tokens like Combo, Blind, Weak, Vulnerable, etc... exist that will be unfamiliar to players coming from DD1. All tokens are represented by an icon below the health bar, which take some time to learn and get familiarized with, but the information is readily available in a menu by pressing C. I personally think this token system is a shining jewel of DD2. It makes combat modifiers much easier to understand and digest, while avoiding the problem present in late game DD1 of soft requiring accuracy buffing trinkets on all heroes in order to land any attacks on monsters in high level dungeons.

My main gripe with the game is it's near complete removal of linear progression. There's no Hamlet, consequently there are no Hamlet buildings to upgrade, there's no resolve XP or levels on your heroes, trinkets all disappear at the end of mission, money disappears at the end of a mission, there's no upgrading a hero's weapon, there's no upgrading a hero's armor, there's no upgrading a hero's skills (you can upgrade them 1 level during a mission, then they're reset afterwards), there are no heirlooms (because there's nothing to spend them on), stress is reset to 0 at the end of every mission for all characters which completely removes the aspect of end of mission stress management that's so integral to DDI. The game feels like a mini DDI campaign that would normally consist of weeks of meticulous planning, gold and heirloom management, varied roster building, calculated risk taking for trinket hunting,  multiple ups and downs that all play their part in a grand story, all crammed into a 1-2 hour long, rouge like experience. Once you complete that experience, you run it back. If you're someone who enjoyed the long-term planning associated with DD1, just know that that virtually doesn't exist here.

I say "virtually" above because there are some aspects of the game that do persist. E.g new skills can be unlocked for a hero via a "Shrine of Reflection", and those skills will remain unlocked in future runs. These shrines are nodes that will randomly spawn during a mission, and you'll choose one hero to complete a sort of combat mini-game (for some reason? the mini games are trivially easy and more of a chore than a challenge, which contrasts oddly with the typical, high-difficulty identify of Darkest Dungeon) or sometimes simply go through a bit of narration in order to unlock a new skill. The intended narrative aspect here is that the hero is "confronting their past memories" to unlock new skills in their kit, which may be enjoyable for some, but to me feels like an annoying "jump through this hoop" way of getting your hero equipped with the skills you want. It's far different than DD1's take the hero to the guild and spend 800 gold to unlock your desired skill system. While it still allows for full hero skill tree unlocks and consequent skill loadout flexibility in the long run, it takes multiple hours to unlock all skills for a single hero, which puts you 1-dimensional, restricting position of feeling like you should be using the same 4 heroes that you've already spent time unlocking skills for if you want to have a synergistic lineup.

There are some other persistent unlocks, such as relics, stagecoach upgrades, and content from the Altar of Hope, but these are more-so improving the baseline of subsequent runs in simple ways as opposed to giving a true feeling of progressing through the game.

The stagecoach driving system feels very clunky. Navigating left and right across the path feels like an unresponsive, subway surfer esque mechanic randomly inserted into larger game for no apparent reason.

If you're someone coming from DD1, I'd recommend you come into this game with the mindset that this isn't Darkest Dungeon. It's a game with a punishing, turn based strategy combat system similar to DD1 with similar design and atmosphere, but at it's core is a rouge like consisting of multiple 1-2 hour experiences, not one over-arching campaign. The game is largely great when viewed in its own light, just don't expect a general, upgraded version of the original Darkest Dungeon.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764564695}, {"review_text": "i think this game is criminally underrated

it has the most thought out and amazing balancing and system ive ever seen

the themes are so beautiful and greatly delivers on the “making the most of a bad situation”

everything screams inspired from enemies to characters to music to literally everything, I’ll run out of characters if I list it all

top that all off with an entirely free post game alternate game mode which, in my opinion, delivers on some of the themes from the first game even better than the first

i don’t know how they’ll continue without Wayne Jude, RIP. i trust that they’ll do their best to honor his memory and carry on respectfully.

in a way I’m happy Wayne Jude got
to play the role of the Academic instead of the antagonistic Ancestor before his passing, but this might actually be me coping with the loss of a beloved VA.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1755518668}, {"review_text": "DD2 is a strange sequel. Red Hook tried to do things differently, and while I commend them for the attempt, the game is not as good as its predecessor. The new token system and character paths make the combat more engaging and more of a consistent puzzle than ever before! However, the game has far too many RNG-based systems- relationships, trinkets, trophies, and even whether you get mastery points are all based on random chance. It's not so much a game about weighing options and taking risks, and more about trying again and again until the RNG lines up.

I still finished it, though! It's probably a 7 or an 8/10.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1733697046}, {"review_text": "I appreciated the art style, atmosphere, and memorable narrator of the first Darkest Dungeon, but I never fully connected with the gameplay. The steep difficulty and rigid systems kept me from sticking with it. I hesitated before picking up Darkest Dungeon 2, but it surprised me - in a good way. I ended up really enjoying it.

The visuals have improved noticeably. The game uses a 2.5D style that makes characters look like detailed ink drawings in motion. The animation is smoother, the environments are more varied, and when combined with the music, it creates a dark  and engaging mood that pulls you in.

The game is still very difficult, and it tells you that upfront. Trial and error is part of the process. You’ll fail often, but each run teaches you something. It doesn’t explain everything clearly, so figuring things out on your own is expected - and required.

Compared to the original, DD2 adds more systems and mechanics around the core gameplay. The new structure, with its roguelike progression and road trip format, changes how the game flows. It can feel overwhelming at first, especially with a UI that takes time to get used to. Some fans of the first game might not enjoy the added complexity, since DD1 had a simpler and more focused design. But for me, the extra depth made it more interesting. 

Character backstories are split into multiple parts, which makes them harder to follow, but they still add some welcome personality and background. There’s a lot to learn - between skills, relationships, items, and progression - but it becomes manageable over time.

The narrator returns, but his tone is more reserved this time. I missed some of the sharp, memorable lines from the first game. He’s still good, but not quite as impactful.
 
The game runs well on the Steam Deck, though navigating menus with a controller can be a bit awkward. At the time of writing there is an issue on Steam Deck with the controls not responding when waking from sleep or opening menus/overlays. Despite that, I found Darkest Dungeon II more engaging than the first. It builds on the same dark tone but adds new ideas that worked better for me.

Darkest Dungeon II isn’t for everyone. It’s tough, sometimes frustrating, and asks a lot from you. But if you enjoy a grim setting and don’t mind a challenge, give it a try!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1748589093}, {"review_text": "I tried my hardest to like this game, but in the end I just can't.
I guess I'm just wishing for more of the first game.

-The Great Host Fleet", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 189, "timestamp_created": 1748555816}, {"review_text": "A few hours before the time I'm writing this, the region-lock that was enforced on Helldivers 2 was lifted for over 100 countries. That was probably my last remaining gripe with the game. 

The power fantasy of having an entire military arsenal in your pocket is an itch that not many other games scratch for me, but Helldivers 2 definitely does. The last two major updates (Omens of Tyranny and Heart of Democracy) are some of the most fun I've had in a game... ever. It has it's issues but there's SO many things that this game does right in my opinion. I am very excited for what the future of this game holds.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1749846718}, {"review_text": "> Watched Starship troopers before hand
> Watched Terminator before hand 
> Watched Battle: Los Angeles before hand
> Booted up Helldivers 2
> First game I get absolutely curb stomped by a Bile Titan

10/10 would play a third game", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 87, "timestamp_created": 1738402958}, {"review_text": "This is the most addicted I've been to a multiplayer game since Left 4 Dead 2 or GTA during the pandemic. This game is honestly incredible. One of the best PvE Coop games out there, and one of the best communities I've ever seen, and am proud to be a part of.

What keeps me coming back besides the excellent gameplay and awesome metagame is how Helldivers 2 wears its influences on its sleeves very proudly, as it should with how well it's been executed. The world, tone and mechanics that the game has is very reminiscent of (but not limited to): 

1). Starship Troopers (fighting alien bugs on planets far from Earth, the overly bombastic and satirical military tone, the fact that it seems for the massive amount of bugs you fight the only vehicles you get are some walkers, and it's mostly just ground troops thrown into the meat grinder).

2). Terminator (pretty self explanatory, fighting the Automatons gives a very Terminator 1/2 feel even down to the music and overwhelming nature of the Automatons).

3). Halo (Helldivers compared to the ODST's being called the Helljumpers, being dropped from orbit in pods into battle, even the aircraft that extracts you is called the Pelican).

4). Left 4 Dead (Enemies are incredibly satisfying to fight thanks to the feedback similar to how zombies in L4D2 are always fun to blow to pieces, not to mention the very arcade like fun and feel of the game).

5). Star Wars Battlefront 2 (The Galactic Conquest mode in that game is basically how Helldivers 2's metagame sort of plays out, but it's closer to a Dungeon Master that creates community events, defence campaigns of planets, and so much more. It feels like Galactic Conquest in BF2 fully realized, and with more than 1 player). 

6). Warhammer 40K (A universe in constant war with other races, a general bloodhungry atmosphere cultivated by both the in-game characters and the fans referencing the game in memes that scratch that certain itch that can't really be explained by people not in the know but those within the fandoms revel in).

There are likely many other influences that I probably haven't played or can think of off hand that have played a hand in the direction that the developers took to craft. Either way, the game takes these influences and puts its own spin on it that is so original and awesome that it feels truly unique. It truly does feel like one of those perfect fantasy game concepts that you'd put together in your imagination.

Gameplay wise, the shooting and aiming feels very different from any other game. There are no hitscan weapons (lasers notwithstanding), it's all projectiles so leading your shots is necessary, but the game throws a very unique wrinkle into the mix: the aiming reticle is essentially split into 2 pieces: where you want to aim with the mouse, and a second circle where your character is actually aiming. This second reticle has drag and takes into account the direction of the actual gun and recoil from firing or your aim being thrown off by an attack. As a result, unless you are using a armor set with a specific perk on it, you can't whip your aim around all willy nilly, you have to pace and time your aim, which can be difficult under pressure, but adds to the fun challenge of the game.

The other wrinkle of the Gameplay is the use of Strategems, which are basically like killstreaks from COD except you can call them in at any time assuming they aren't under cool-down, or have run out of uses, etc. Airstrikes, orbital strikes, support weapons like different rocket launchers with different functions, support backpacks, automated turrets, even mech suits once you've leveled up enough to unlock them. Having only 4 at a time per player helps to act sort of like a class system without a class system specifically. There is a great variety of them to use, and most to all of them are viable as long as you use them smartly. Punching the codes in also adds to the challenge of trying to do it under pressure especially when completely surrounded, which can lead to accidental team kills, which leads me to the next point.

Team Killing is bound to happen in this game, whether by a bad stratagem throw, overly zealous aiming, even the backpack drones accidentally setting you on fire. TK's are just the name of the game. It adds to the frantic and panicky nature of the game, as doing things under pressure like aiming and trying to punch in codes is tricky and hard to do fast and properly. This can lead to some deaths and the game sometimes feeling like bullshit (which it can be, cough cough random ragdolls cough), but it's for the best to do your best to not get frustrated by them, as honestly most of the time it's funny especially in hindsight, and this game is truly at its best in a semi casual setting. Getting sweaty and mad decreases the fun of the game, especially on the higher difficulties. I recommend sticking to the difficulty that you feel is most fun.

The difficulty and challenge is quite fair up to Difficulty 7 I find. 8-10 is honestly bullshit though, especially if not prepared. It can be fun once in a while to try out the highest difficulty, as it is exhilarating to barely extract alive, but it does end up feeling so stacked against you that you feel forced to rely on the meta Strategems and Weapons, which does limit a fair few off of the table since some of them are just too niche to be viable to survive on those difficulties. I find that personally up to 7 for bugs, and 6 for bots gives the best balance of fun and challenge, and also still allows for most of the weapon and stratagem sandbox to still be viable as long as you don't play dumb.

A coop game is nothing without good coop, and this game has some of the best I've played. Coordinating with your team is great, and this is like one of very few Steam games where players will actually use the in-game voice chat as well as the text chat, and in-game callouts instead of everyone having to hop in a discord server and arrange a whole meetup and whatnot. Any match where at least one person has a mic is infinitely better than a silent one where nobody is speaking, as even just one person can help to coordinate different plans, choose which objectives everyone should be going to and doing, etc. If you're gonna play this game, HAVE A MIC. You will have a much better experience than without, though if you are stuck without one, the in-game callouts are a decent substitute.

Customization is a bit limited, unfortunately. There isn't any options for changing the colours of the armours or weapons yet, though that does seem like something that might be added down the line. There are lots of options for the player cards and titles, emotes at the stats screen and during the game, so that's good at least. Paint jobs for the vehicles are locked behind most of the Premium Warbonds, so that's unfortunate.

My biggest problem with progression is with the Ship Modules, which require Samples that you can find on missions. The requirements for the samples for the Modules is ridiculous, and maxing all of them out takes a long ass time. I still haven't done it in my 77 hours so far. I will do it eventually, but man having to farm commons and super rares takes so long. They really need a way to boost the amount of samples you get, maybe a way to multiply it based on the difficulty of the mission or something.

Overall, there is so much to cover with Helldivers 2 that I can't do it justice in a couple paragraphs (I was 4000 characters over the limit for this review and had to delete several paragraphs just to be able to post it). I highly recommend this game even if you don't have friends to play it with, since this community is one of the best I've ever seen a game foster. It's a great time, whether you wanna be a sweaty meta abusing nerd, or just a casual 2 hour killer with the bois. This game is excellent, and I hope the support continues for a long time.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 16, "timestamp_created": 1733986192}, {"review_text": "This game is slowly turning into a tragedy.
At its core, Helldivers 2 is a fantastic, infinitely replayable, co-op horde shooter where the higher difficulty creates an unrivaled feeling of badassery. During the first year and 3 months or so, it remained as such: a shining example of live service done right. Recently, however, the development of this game has devolved into a series of missed opportunities and baffling issues in balance and performance. 

With recent changes, new enemies and environments have been added that feel like they have not been playtested whatsoever. Absurd difficulty and mission softlocking from bugs with objective equipment have led to the new Into the Unjust content being pulled entirely for rework. This could be passed off if it was the first time new content fell flat from lack of polish. The Incinerator Corps was too difficult and sparked complaints. The illuminate revamp that added fleshmobs and stingrays was criticized on launch for its difficulty, and fleshmobs still receive criticism for their poor balance. The leviathans post Super Earth invasion are widely hated for their ability to infinitely ragdoll divers from the sky and one-shot players on a direct hit, and they require heavy AP like that of the AT emplacement to kill. Add in some high spawnrate magic, and you get the single most hated enemy in all of Helldivers 2. Now we have the new bug missions that were so unfair and broken that they barely lasted a week before the devs had to pull it. 

New enemies lack exploitable and tangible weaknesses and tend to just be upgraded versions of existing enemies that amplify everything annoying about their predecessors. Automaton war striders are just upgraded hulks that spawn just as often, ragdoll you more, and are only really countered by AP explosives. Terminid dragon roaches are just bile titans that fly, making their weakspots much harder to hit, and set you on fire with their bile, killing you instantly. These also spawn faster than they can be killed. The burrowing enemies in new bug missions would kill you instantly with medium armor in an un-reactable time frame. These enemies cross the line from difficult and intimidating to overly-punishing and unfun to fight. War striders are the least offensive of these new units specifically because I like the grenade barrage for how it shakes up the cover-based gameplay.

Alongside this, the weapon balancing seems to enforce an over reliance on anti tank equipment for most situations with alternative playstyles being punished for no good reason. Gunslinger builds took a recent hit where movement heavily effects the sway on your secondary for a few seconds after you stop. This sounds fine on paper, but it suffocates the run-and-gun punch that draws players to gunslinger loadouts behind gunplay that is unsatisfying to play around and destroys the speedy utility of the gunslinger passive. Melee weapons have had their armor penetration downgraded recently, meaning the days of stunning hulks and chargers have ended. Taking down these heavy enemies with melee weapons wasn't easy in the first place, but apparently, it even being possible was too much for Arrowhead. Melee loadouts were a joke in the first place, but with enough tenacity one could succeed with them. Now, any melee weapon, particularly the flag, have been reduced to an unfunny gag that wastes 40 minutes of your time and all of your team's reinforcements. Can you tell I love both these playstyles?

Lastly and most importantly, the performance is inexcusable for a game of this nature and has been a constant and recurring issue since the introduction of the first urban maps. BeamNG Drive, a high detail soft body driving simulator, runs better in VR on high settings than this game does on NVIDIA's recommended optimized settings. With a 5070, I can get a stable 80 fps, and when things get hectic, I'll get as low as 40. ON RECOMMENDED SETTINGS WITH A 5070. My friends on 3060 laptop GPUs can barely play the game at all. Stability has also been severely effected with the most recent content update with constant stuttering and freezing during gameplay. Many players other than myself seem to have issues with recurring crashes as well. Stability and performance are the biggest issues with this game and need to be top priority.
