[{"review_text": "Right, as a lifelong gamer and newbie game developer, this is my first review ever. I felt compelled to write this, not because it's a good or bad game, but because my feelings are so mixed. 

I first bought this game on Xbox and I played it all the way through. I've completed all of the story lines, side quests and challenges. If you're playing this game on a console or the PC version without mods, let me just say this: the highs are highs and the lows are lows. 

Experiencing Hogwarts for the first time on this game truly has you in awe. The problem is that towards the second half of the game, you barely spend any time there. To that end, the map is way bigger than I think anyone anticipated. For people who really love to explore, this is something that you'd enjoy. Personally though, I would've enjoyed having a smaller map with a few big cities as opposed to just Hogsmead. Some of the towns, though they are unique in nature, start to feel a bit copy and pasted with how equally small they all are. Other than that - the quest lines, graphics and mechanics are overall nothing short of awesome. HOWEVER, the game play itself starts to fall off right around the time you begin to learn unforgivable curses.

I found that even on hard mode, enemies were still too easy to defeat. I personally dislike the fact that "dark wizards" don't use unforgivable curses against you. I also dislike that if you do use an unforgivable curse or respond negatively to quests, there's no negative impact or outcome. It's almost kind of like, aside from a cool lock screen animation, what's the point in even using these curses? This is where mods come in.

The problem is that you can only use mods on PC; but thankfully, the game does have a built-in mod manager for PC players. It should also be noted that it's relatively easy to request custom mods from creators because they've made the Hogwarts Legacy Creator Kit in Unreal Engine completely free for anyone to download and use; and as a developer myself, that alone speaks volume about how much the developers want this community to have the experience they desire. 

But to answer the overarching question of "do you recommend this game," my answer is yes and no. If you are a potterhead like I am and are considering buying it on the console, then you'll enjoy it through and through. If you are not though, you're likely to lose interest half-way through; but if you are able to run this on a PC, I ***highly*** recommend doing so with mods that fix the aforementioned issues. Below is my recommendation for mods and why you'd want them based on your gameplay style:

[olist]
[*] Enhanced NPC Schedule is simply a MUST for everyone. It populates Hogwarts with more students that run on a much better in-game schedule that is aligned with classes. So for example, if a class ends, you can see a visible group of students that look like they just got out of class. This is in opposition to just seeing random NPCs in random places. My guess is the reason why this wasn't a thing on the original game is due to limitations on console performance capabilities; because more NPCs, the higher requirement for processing power. But I mean if you have a desktop in general, this won't be an issue. I just think they kept the requirements as minimal as possible so that it made it more accessible to a bigger player base.

[*] Azkaban, Enemies Enhanced, and Enemies Balance are going to be fantastic for those who enjoy a challenging PVP style like I do. Spells enhanced is an honorable mention here, too.
[list]
[*] The Azkaban mod works similar to GTA in the sense of if you do something bad (e.g., use an unforgivable curse in front of a good witch or wizard), you get reported and the authorities chase after you. In this case, aurors spawn all around you and you have to fight your way out. If you get caught, the mod will provide you with options: go to Azkaban where you can attempt to fight your way out, or you can skip that and still respawn from the last check point. 

[*] The Enemies Enhanced allows enemies to also use unforgivable curses; and yes that includes the killing curse, so there's a very real possibility that you can be one-shot by a dark witch or wizard. 

[*] The Enemies Balanced mod makes so the enemy NPCs scale better in terms of gameplay difficulty. If this is your first time playing this game, I would hold off on enabling that until you've found your groove.

[*] Spells Enhanced is a mod that provides you with custom spells. Personally, if it were my first time playing this game, I wouldn't enable this mod until at least the second half of the game. The reason why is because some of those spells are immediately available to you, which makes a lot of the quests easier to complete because you have more spells than you're supposed to. It could also make learning the basic mechanics of the game a tad more confusing than it needs to be.
[/list]

[*] Auto-season, Hogwarts Express Train Plus, House Points, Sleep Mod are strongly recommended for players who desire an immersive experience, with the Curfew mod being an honorable mention. 
[list]
[*] The game doesn't cycle through seasons (e.g., winter, fall, spring, summer) on it's own. It only changes after completing a major quest-line. The auto-season mod makes it so it naturally changes with the in-game clock. The Hogwarts Express train is also pretty rare to see in the original game, but the Hogwarts Express Train Plus mod makes it run on a more frequent schedule. I personally don't know why either of these weren't already a thing, but I don't have to understand I suppose. 

[*] The house point mod is pretty much what you'd expect it to be, it allows for the player to collect house points to win the house cup at the end of each season (so it pairs very well with the auto-season mod). If you complete the weekly quests assigned to you, you gain points. If you respond kindly to relationship (side) quests that take place with other students, you gain points. If you respond negatively to to a student, you lose points (ah finally, a consequence for your actions).

[*] The sleep mod doesn't necessarily require you to sleep at night, but it does make it difficult for you to play the game if you don't. For example, if you don't sleep, you can't sprint. The reason why I like both the house point and sleep mod is because it gives you a reason to continuously go back to Hogwarts on a regular schedule in the second half of the game, in opposition to you're just a random student roaming around in the woods for however long doing whatever; but if that's your preference of game-play, then I'd just suggest only sticking with the auto-season mod.

[*] The curfew mod is an honorable mention because you don't really need it per-say if you have the sleep mod since it basically forces you to sleep at night anyways, BUT the curfew mod itself does make it so if a prefect or professor catches you out of bed at night on school grounds, you'll be sent back to your dormitory with a consequence of paying an in-game fee. The mod does have it's own hotkey menu that can be used to disable it in-game; so if anything it's worth downloading, even if you end up disabling it later.
[/list]

[*] For those who enjoy sandbox building gameplays, get these:
[list]
[*] Bigger Vivarium - increases creature capacity
[*] Rescue Animals - rescue non-magical creatures
[*] Unlock All Conjurations - unlocks all build items
[*] Remove Conjure Budget - removes moonstones as a budget requirement
[*] Conjuration Everywhere - allows room of requirement item conjuration
[*] Remove Conjure Placement Restrictions - allows for items to be stacked on one another, similar to a bb.moveobjects on The Sims.
[/list]
[/olist]

Honorable mentions: Floo Companions, Emote with Any NPC, Character Editor, Cheat Plus, Alohormora Autosolve and Instant Silent Bigger Revelio.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1755624702}, {"review_text": "The biggest problem with Hogwarts Legacy is that after the initial excitement, the game quickly becomes repetitive and empty.

[b]Wasted Potential of Hogwarts: [/b] The castle is gorgeous, but underused. You only spend a few hours inside, classes and professors have only few cutscenes, and there are only three puzzles throughout the entire school. For a game set in Hogwarts,this is wasted potential.

[b]Repetitive Filler Everywhere:[/b] The open world is stuffed with Merlin Trials (95 of them), bandit camps, and countless caves that all look the same. The loot is almost always useless, and minigames that could’ve been fun just repeat endlessly. What starts as discovery turns into chores.

[b]Combat Without Variety:[/b] You’re stuck fighting the same four enemy types (goblins, trolls, spiders, and humans) on repeat. Spells should open up creative strategies, but in reality, the system pushes you toward spamming the same few effective combos. Shields force you into matching colors instead of experimenting. Enemies never actually catch you off guard, and boss fights are just damage sponges with recycled mechanics. The game makes you feel powerful, sure, but not in a satisfying or tactical way more like a button-masher. 

[b]Story and Choices Don’t Matter:[/b] The main story can be summed up in five minutes: you’re the chosen one, and that’s it. Side quests are more interesting than the main quest, but none of your choices matter. Learn unforgivable curses or not nobody cares. House reputation? Doesn’t exist. Freedom is an illusion, because the world never reacts to you.

I HATE WARNER BROTHERS AND I WILL NEVER BUY ONE OF THEIR GAMES AGAIN.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 66, "timestamp_created": 1751339850}, {"review_text": "I almost quit at first.

This game had the chance to be a masterpiece but unfortunately fails short in some departments which make it just good. In fact, there are aspects of it that are pure genius 10/10 while others are really bad.
Rarely have I seen such a gap in quality within the same game.

This developer got ahold of an incredibly powerful, fleshed out IP rich with lore and personality.
And to their credit, they recreated that atmosphere impeccably. The world feels magical, dreamy, cozy, and superbly crafted as a whole. There's a lot of attention to detail that really brings this whole vibe to life.
The music, and even sound effects, which are both excellent help even further when it comes to the mood and ambiance. It is a real pleasure to just wander around, and especially to fly on your broom seamlessly across the gorgeous map. That too was perfectly recreated, you feel a real sense of freedom and liberation.

That said, the masterpiece part of this game comes from the art direction. Few games have had this kind of quality and there are some side missions that blew my mind, particularly one in a haunted basement. It felt like that side level took more effort and creativity than the whole main story put together. I wouldn't want to spoil anything so I shan't go into details. But let's just say it was a work of art. The art direction team is goated.
Visually, the one issue I had was with the face animation tech. That part looks like it's a 20 year old game. Stiff faces with barely any expression, which resets after every line, like the old point & click games.
While that's nothing major, it does hurt the otherwise extremely high standard the rest of the game has set.

The game itself starts off REALLY slow, I was wondering what the heck was going on when 5 hours into it, I was still just going from class to class doing relatively boring quests. I almost quit, But then, about 7hrs in, it picks up steam as Hogwarts opens its doors to the outside.

The main issue I've had with the game was the writing. It is just bad. It's childish and as cringe as it gets.
It was painful having to listen to the conversations most of the time, so much so that I skipped a lot of it.
Now, I do realize Harry Potter are children's books and perhaps the game is meant for a much younger audience, but it is still based on books that are written amazingly well, poignant, funny, witty, engaging. This game has none of that, every conversation is so bland, weak, void of character, even AI would've come up with better.
There is no reason it should be this way, even if small kids are the audience, they are not redacted, they're smarter and sometimes more mature than we old people are.
And I've noticed this is becoming a trend unfortunately. It is so hard to find good writing anymore.

When it comes to combat and gameplay, it's in between the incredible art direction and abysmal writing, it's neither horrible nor is it great, it's just mid. Very easy, same 5-6 enemy types, pretty much the same 3-4 buttons on repeat. The lack of diversity and challenge handicap an otherwise interesting base idea of hitting combos in a timely and reactive manner.

Now the puzzles, which are the vast majority of the game, are even more mediocre, and even simpler. A puzzle will literally consist of you jumping on 3 platforms in a row, or shooting 10 balls without moving from your spot, and you're done. It's mind numbing and that's a real shame too.

Funny story, at one point I encountered what I thought was a really challenging puzzle. Finally!
You're supposed to turn cubes on top of columns until all 3 sides match, a sort of a simplified Rubik's cube.
Only here, one of the cubes was floating above the column,
AHA! I knew exactly what I had to do, I had to first flip it while it was hovering, then slam it down with Descendo. BOOM.
But wait, no that didn't actually work, 15min later I gave up, feeling shame.
Here I was wanting a challenging puzzle and I couldn't solve it, so I looked it up.
Turns out it's a bug, it's not supposed to be floating at all :/

Speaking of, the game has a lot of bugs. Nothing game breaking, but definitely a lot of achievement breaking ones. If you're a completist you're gonna have hell in some cases. From getting stuck in the ground and having to load an old save, to crashes to desktop, to icons not showing up on the map, enemies becoming invisible mid fight so you cant hit them back, to chests not opening, and a ton of others I don't remember.

There's as much good as much as bad about this game. The best way I can summarize this game to you is [b] very repetitive[/b] but also [b] graphically stunning[/b]. It's for both new and diehard Harry Potter fans but it'll exhaust and bore the heck out of you. 

There's far more side content that main content and I didn't complete the main content consecutively so my understanding of the plot may not be that perfect. 

[h1] About Hogwarts Legacy [/h1] 

Embark on a magical journey throughout the wizarding world during the late 19th century, about a century before the years of the Harry Potter series. In Hogwarts Legacy, you'll be playing as a wizard or witch who has been admitted to Hogwarts as a fifth year student - which is very rare, usually no student is admitted to Hogwarts so late. Along the way to Hogwarts for the first time, you're spied on by a man named: "Rookwood" and later on attacked by a goblin named: "Ranrok" who believes you possess something that others don't. After the unfortunate encounter and following your initial arrival to Hogwarts, Hogwarts professors sort you into a house like in the Harry Potter movies and decide to execute a fast-paced education program to teach you everything you're supposed to know from year one to five. At the same time, you embark on an "extracurricular" journey to find out what Rookwood and Ranrok is after and prevent them from getting their hands on it. 

If you want more details, you can read this as well but beware that it contains [b] very major spoilers [/b]:

[spoiler] Throughout the game, you'll learn that you can wield ancient magic that almost nobody else can wield. Centuries back in the past, a little girl named Isidora had her village destroyed. If I recall correctly, her brother died during the destruction. Hogwarts professors wielded ancient magic to restore the village back to normal, undoing its destruction. Some years later, Isidora would grow up to become a Hogwarts professor teaching along with her saviors and she'd learn to wield ancient magic as well. Her father had been silent since her brother's death, so she wanted to find a way to cast a spell to rid  her father's pain. Eventually, Isidora succeeded and decided to store some of her new magic used to cast the spell in Goblin silver (you can consider the silver like a chest or reservoir to store things). Later on, everyone would learn that the magic also makes people emotionless, so her colleague professors urged her to stop using it but Isidora refused so her colleagues killed her by force using the unforgivable curse Avada Kedavra. The colleague professors would then contain the remains of the ancient magic beneath Hogwarts.

Ranrok is after goblin silver. Because of this, he's been researching every goblin reservoir location and drilling inside of them, hoping to acquire the ancient magic for malicious purposes. 

Rookwood is just a partner of Ranroks with mutual interests. Rookwood is being used by Ranrok to find reservoir locations.

It is your job to stop Rookwood and Ranrok! Learn how to wield ancient magic and put an end to Ranrok's intentions before immense power falls into the wrong hands!  [/spoiler] 

[h1] My Review of Hogwarts Legacy [/h1]

I'm writing this after having completed the main story, having gained half of the achievements and having completed 80% of my collection. 

It's a graphically stunning game, it really is, the graphics are what's carrying this game - the map and environment designers really gave their best at creating Hogwarts, Hogmeads and the rest of the world. In fact, I made great use of Photo Mode at times, it's just that beautiful but the repetition is what ultimately ruins the gaming experience. The repetition drew me nuts, the number of repetitive tasks is way beyond the industry average for a RPG game as well. I'm not thrilled to do 100% completion because everything else I need to do are just repetitive tasks. But putting repetition aside, I had fun casting all the spells (especially unforgivable curses), attending classes at Hogwarts, exploring Hogwarts castle and the rest of the open world and defeating enemies. The plot was kind of cliché but I didn't mind. My favorite main mission was the third trial for its unique style and my favorite side mission was all of Sebastian's missions. I didn't like most of the side missions because many of them were saving creatures or items from caves which felt really repetitive and boring after some point because there's too many of such missions.

I found it odd how the team made use of the southeast portion of the World Map but left  the southwest empty. Maybe in the future, more content could be added so that the southwest is put into use. 

I wish we could change the color of gears, that would be such a useful feature. 

[h1] My Pain Points About Hogwarts Legacy [/h1]

1. [b] My ultimate pain point is the repetition. [/b] There are nearly a hundred Merlin trials - which is absurd, and tens of everything else like caves, balloons, goblin outposts, stargazing telescopes, landing platforms, etc. I was so sick and tired of entering caves with spiders. This game is a horrible choice for those with Arachnophobia! [b]My point is, making us do the same thing X times doesn't make it a good game.[/b]

2. Most gear to equip on your avatar are ugly in my honest opinion, and there's not a lot of house-based gear, other than house scarves and some rare robes. 

3. I have maxed out my gear slot and it's still not enough for me to hold my gear. Because of this, I can't hold a bunch of gear that I find appealing. Why not extend the Merlin trial challenges so that it matches with the amount of Merlin trials on the map?

4. There aren't a lot of different puzzles. For example, you could have done a different puzzle for each of the three different lock levels and you could have introduced more ways to complete Merlin trials. 

5. There aren't a lot of different types of enemies. I know that there's multiple species of the same enemy type (for example, there are more than 10 species of spiders) but there aren't a lot of different enemy types. I think it's just Goblins, Ashwinders, Poachers, Trolls, Spiders, Dulongs, Wolves, Infamous Foes, and Inferius. I've never read the Harry Potter books, so my presumption is that the lack of enemy variety is to stay aligned with the books - this might also explain why there are cats but no dogs in the game, but, this is what happens when executed in a game - it causes the player too feel bored of the same enemies. 

6. NPC facial expressions often don't match the NPC dialogue tone - it's really hard to tell if a NPC is happy, angry, afraid etc. just by looking at their faces. I think this has to do with how mouths and eyebrows don't bend. Also, I dislike how NPC facial expressions switch to a serious look once the dialogue is over. I remember somewhere outside but nearby Hogwarts I witnessed a woman crying for losing someone close to her and her face suddenly became normal and serious once the discussion was over - that just seemed unnatural and unsettling to me. 

7. Mission specific issues:

- In the personal shop mission at Hogmeads, playing with the Poltergeist on the foyer side is buggy. Progression takes too long. The time between defeating mannequins and the Poltergeist spawning new mannequins is too long. In the same mission, after talking to Penny later on at the end of the mission, she can clip into a corner of the desk inside of the shop.

- In the castle mission with Onai, the second wall to climb is too high and very hard to climb even with the crate placed, it took me a long time to climb, I don't even remember how I succeeded. I think I glitched to the top. That was a pain. Later on in the same mission, after you land the birds, in a cutscene, Onai's brown highwing clips through her as it flaps its wings.

The game by itself seemed fine for as long as I was able to play.

Following a vague and unexplained account ban by EA — which blocked my access to this single-player game — my account has now been reactivated. I can play again, but EA never explained what “rule” I allegedly broke. Their response simply mentioned “toxic behavior” without any details.

The way the game slowly unveils his past and trauma kept me hooked, and the bond with BD-1? Instant favorite. The world-building, characters, and set pieces all felt so grand and immersive that I didn’t feel left out — instead, I felt pulled in.

The level design reminded me of Metroidvania-style games, with a real sense of reward for backtracking and unlocking new paths.

What’s wild is that by the end of the game, I actually wanted to watch the movies and learn more about this galaxy far, far away. Jedi: Fallen Order didn’t just entertain me — it turned me into a curious fan of a franchise I had ignored for years.

As a person who has never played a Metroidvania up until this point, I grew tired of all the exploring that I had to do and how the game seemingly gives you no direction (except for, of course, telling you how to attack and control your character). However, I'm glad I gave this game a chance, because the gameplay quickly became much more entertaining, showcasing its beautiful art style, difficult (yet fair and rewarding) bosses, an amazing soundtrack, and fun and, well, interesting characters (to say the least).

Oh, and despite how often I got lost exploring and trying to find something to do, I grew (to somewhat) appreciate and understand why people like this aspect of the game, since it gave me more of a chance to admire and observe the different environments/areas of the game.

After playing almost 100 hours of this game, I now might finally have the confidence and the skill to defeat Gruz Mother.

Thank you Team 🍒", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 21, "timestamp_created": 1743869643}, {"review_text": "Back in 2018, I bought Hollow Knight, played it for about two hours, and then let it collect dust in my backlog. At the time, I had no idea what I was missing. Fast forward to 2025, with Silksong looming on the horizon, I decided to revisit the game, and that’s when everything clicked. 

By the time I was done, I had pushed myself all the way to 112% completion, completely hooked from start to finish.

The combat in Hollow Knight feels deceptively simple at first, but the more you play, the more you realize how deep and rewarding it is. The game’s free-flowing movement is addictive, you’re constantly weaving through enemies, dashing, pogoing off the enemies, and chaining together attacks in a way that makes every encounter feel like a dance. And then there’s the progression. As you unlock new abilities, double jump, shadow dash, crystal heart, you gain a new sense of freedom. The map suddenly opens up, and backtracking turns into discovery. It’s here that the game truly shines, blending smooth platforming with exploration in a way that makes you eager to dive deeper into Hallownest.

The bosses are nothing short of phenomenal. They’re challenging but never unfair, with patterns that beg to be studied and mastered. Then there’s the charm system, which might just be one of the smartest mechanics I’ve seen in the genre. Experimenting with different builds keeps the gameplay fresh, and it’s fun to find synergies that completely change how you approach fights or platforming challenges. 

For me, it’s an easy 10/10. Team Cherry has set an incredibly high bar, and Hollow Knight will remain the gold standard for metroidvania games for years to come. If Silksong manages to build on this foundation, we might be looking at another all-time great.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1756688857}, {"review_text": "This is definitely my favorite game of all time. Beautiful game and soundtrack - highly recommend.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1749119541}, {"review_text": "I love this game, which should be evident by my 750 hours playing it. It's difficult, but with practice I'm able to develop strategies to beat the bosses. Learn when and how to dodge, when to make your attacks. Silksong is similar, but ramps up difficult by requiring fast reaction times, which I don't have, possibly because of my age. So, while Silksong has improvements over this original, I think this game is a masterpiece, while Silksong is reducing its target audience at a smaller percentage of gamers that excludes me.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1762548143}, {"review_text": "Ya know, I bought this game so many years ago and played hundreds of hours, and I just never left a review, so here it is.

If you haven't played this game, you need to. Emphasis on need, as this is one of the best games to exist.
The world of Hallownest is one to truly behold, the rich sense of wonder and lore hidden within the world will leave you constantly wanting more. The art direction for the game is visually stunning, and the music is some of the most memorable music in gaming. The boss themes give you a rush and the area themes are whimsical. The NPC's are quite the cast too, leaving you always wanting more.

This game is what other companies strive and wish they could create, but 3 amazing people created Hollow Knight and this will forever be my favorite game of all time, that is, until the long awaited sequel Silksong may take its place, or at least sit on the bench beside it.

Speaking of Silksong, we have all been awaiting this games release date for so many years, but I am glad that tomorrow Team Cherry is finally dropping a trailer and it will give us a proper release date rather than just the second half of 2025.

Thank you Team Cherry for inspiring me to improve on my own art and pursue my passions by creating a masterpiece.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1755707640}, {"review_text": "Hollow Knight was the first time I truly felt like a gamer. Also, the mantis lords were the first combat that showed me how combat could be a dance, truly.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1758839466}, {"review_text": "I'll start this off by saying this game never gets old. What possible virtue hasn't yet been extolled by someone smarter, more dedicated? The game's success is inexplicable, coming out of nowhere and establishing itself as a high watermark of the entire metroidvania genre. It is not unreasonable to rank this game as one of the best of its kind, for sheer artistic merit and razor-sharp gameplay that has kept an audience immersed for almost a decade. A modern classic, and an essential must-play.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1755932421}, {"review_text": "A wildly great game that unfortunately lived up to the hype I got from the fanbase. It’s a fairly open-ended metroidvania which creates awesome experiences into a sense of adventure. It does get bogged down a little from having to retrace your steps a lot, but the highs are crack levels of entertainment. It was Eureka moment after Eureka moment. There are a bashful amount of secrets that pulls a unique immersion in the game. You will find secret passages, different ways to attack enemies, and characters that the devs did not make to be found - but to be discovered. The added content to the game really fleshes it out to the point where it’s difficult to know how much there is. Beating this game the first time shows you nearly every pillar of gameplay, but only a fraction of the bosses and zones. I learned that I took very different routes and used different strategies for most bosses before beating the game compared to others yet it felt like a totally fleshed out experience.

This, in my opinion, is the epitome of a cult classic game. It is so masterfully presented to its audience but hides layers of gameplay and other secrets that could be realistically obtained if someone is willing.

I see why there's such high expectations for the sequel.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1747459355}, {"review_text": "its very silent and creepy makes the game feel so good

Hollow Knight is a game that truly embodies the spirit of adventure and discovery. Its [b]smooth and non-linear gameplay[/b] offers players the freedom to explore at their own pace, uncovering multiple side-quests and hidden paths. Every moment spent in the world of Hallownest feels deliberate, as the game masterfully rewards exploration with meaningful upgrades and utilities like charms, keeping you hooked as you uncover its many secrets.
[h2][b]The worldbuilding:[/b][/h2]
It's one of the game's standout features. Hallownest is a place teeming with history, packed with secrets that not only reward the player mechanically but also deepen their understanding of a kingdom that was once prosperous but has since fallen into ruin. The [b]art style[/b] is breathtakingly unique, conveying an emotional story through its hauntingly beautiful environments and designs. It’s not just a backdrop—it’s part of the narrative, pulling you into the melancholic beauty of the world.
[h2][b]The NPCs:[/b][/h2]
They are memorable and fully fleshed out, each with their own personalities and backstories. They add depth and life to the world, making every interaction meaningful.
[h2][b]The bosses:[/b][/h2]
 Both challenging and diverse, with a wide variety of encounters, including optional fights for those who seek an even greater test of skill.
[h2][b]The Story:[/b][/h2]
Getting lost in Hallownest is more than just a challenge—it’s an adventure. Every corner of the map holds something exciting or rewarding, and the game's design encourages curiosity. The combination of its stunning art style, intricate world, and rewarding exploration makes Hollow Knight a standout title in the Metroidvania genre.
Whether you’re in it for the challenge, the story, or the thrill of exploration, Hollow Knight delivers on all fronts. It’s a game that doesn’t just tell a story—it lets you live it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1737972608}, {"review_text": "At first glance, Hollow Knight might seem slow or even a bit dull — but give it time, and it reveals itself as one of the most captivating and rewarding games ever made. What starts off as a simple platformer quickly transforms into a rich, atmospheric, and emotionally charged journey through the hauntingly beautiful world of Hallownest.

The game hooks you gradually, but once it does, it doesn’t let go. You fall in love with every moment — the somber ruins, the haunted silence, the haunting soundtrack, and above all, the intense, challenging combat. Boss fights are tough but fair, and every victory feels hard-earned and immensely satisfying.

The atmosphere is dense and unforgettable, every area full of secrets and hidden paths. It’s one of those rare games where exploration feels like discovery, and where the more you put in, the more it gives back.

Push through the slow start — you’ll find yourself completely immersed in a masterpiece.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1749213543}, {"review_text": "Hollow Knight is an absolute MASTERPIECE!

Hollow Knight is more than just a side-scrolling adventure—it's an atmospheric, emotionally resonant experience wrapped in layers of combat, exploration, and mystery. It’s not just one of the best indie games ever made—it’s one of the best games of the last decade, period.

Hollow Knight keeps its combat system deceptively simple: you have a nail (essentially a sword), a jump, and eventually a few magic spells. But don’t be fooled—this minimalism allows for incredible depth. Enemies are fast and unpredictable, and boss fights are challenging tests of reaction time, pattern recognition, and precision.

Each victory feels earned, and even basic enemies can be lethal if you let your guard down. The game balances difficulty beautifully—harsh, but fair. And when you finally overcome a tough encounter, the feeling of accomplishment is unforgettable.

Set in the ruined insect kingdom of Hallownest, the world of Hollow Knight is vast, interconnected, and absolutely bursting with secrets. From the forgotten crossroads to the fungal wastes and the haunting City of Tears, every area is distinct—both visually and mechanically. There's no in-game map until you find the cartographer, reinforcing the sense of being truly lost in a crumbling empire.

Exploration is king here. There are hidden paths, breakable walls, and entire zones that many players will miss on their first run. The interconnected nature of the world design rivals Dark Souls, and the non-linear progression means players are constantly rewarded for curiosity and persistence.

Visually, Hollow Knight is breathtaking in its simplicity. Hand-drawn characters and backdrops exude charm and gloom in equal measure. Despite a palette heavy in blues, greys, and shadow, the environments never feel dull—each region has its own emotional tone.

The music by Christopher Larkin is nothing short of masterful—subtle, sorrowful, and sometimes triumphant. It underlines the loneliness and faded grandeur of Hallownest without ever overwhelming the gameplay.

Sound design also plays a key role. From the tinkling footsteps of the Knight to the skittering of bugs in distant tunnels, every audio detail deepens immersion.

Hollow Knight doesn’t hand you a story—it whispers it from beneath the earth. Lore is hidden in dialogue, item descriptions, and environmental storytelling. Themes of sacrifice, decay, and forgotten glory permeate every corner of Hallownest.

Your silent protagonist, the Knight, might seem blank at first, but over time, a moving and tragic tale unfolds—one of lost kingdoms, ancient pacts, and a desperate attempt to hold back an unstoppable infection.

Hollow Knight is a modern classic. It’s a triumph of game design, blending tight combat, breathtaking art, and profound atmosphere into an unforgettable experience. With dozens of hours of content, rich lore, and a true sense of exploration, it stands not only as a high watermark for indie games—but for gaming as a whole.

Pros:
-Deep, satisfying combat
-Massive, beautifully interconnected world
-Gorgeous hand-drawn art and haunting soundtrack
-Rewarding exploration and secrets galore
-Incredible value, especially with all free DLC

Cons:
-Challenging for newcomers to the genre
-Story can be obscure without lore-hunting
-Occasional difficulty spikes may frustrate casual players

Hollow Knight isn’t just a game—it’s a descent into a lost kingdom of melancholy and mystery. A masterpiece that respects your time, intelligence, and curiosity.

[{"review_text": "[UPDATE: After almost 2 months playing, I felt the need to adjust a few things.]

tl;dr: It's very good IF you have the heart for gacha. This is a dupe heavy game (details in the comments).

Honestly, I did not expect this game to be any good. The first time I saw it, a couple of months ago on my discovery queue, I remember thinking "ugh, another gacha trash" and moving on instantly because I prefer to avoid the genre.

But I came across it again last week and was drawn in by the art and the atmosphere before remembering I had already seen it. So I ended up deciding to give it a try, to see how egregious it could be and because I'm a sucker for card games.

There are a few caveats but I gotta say I am positively surprised. I expected way less of it than what it offers. Let me start with the caveats because, y'know, bad news first. That's just basic manners. 

First of all, gacha's gonna gacha. Morimens is surprisingly non-agressive about it and offers a good amount of free resources for you to play with IF you have the patience and the heart for it. If you are prone to gambling addiction, have poor impulse control or little patience for the free resource management, just do yourself a favor and stay clear of it. It has all the trappings of the "gacha genre", which is basically a bazillion of different time gated resources for you to juggle and both character and equipment lotteries. This means the main way to acquire and upgrade both characters and their equipments is through gambling with limited, time gated (or real money gated, if we're being honest), resources. So, yeah, this is potentially very dangerous and can be very damaging.

It is possible to stay free to play. And Morimens seems to be more accomodating in regards to that than others in the genre. But if that is your intention, you have to be smart about how you use each of your resources. There are even guides for it in one of its discord channels (Mythag University) and the community in both discord channels that I frequent is, usually, quite helpful and friendly.

That being said, Morimens is pretty good at what it does. So much so that I decided to spend some money in it  the game just to show my appreciation and support (yeah, they got me, dammit). There's real effort here. The art is beautiful. The music is good and fits the setting very well. The voice acting oozes quality and care. The story is well presented in a visual novel style and, as far as I have read it is well written (mind you, I have partially lost my vision a couple of years back, so I've been skipping some of the story. But I do intend to read it later, it's just that it takes extra effort. But I digress). The animations for the characters and their special moves (here called Exalts) are truly remarkable (or just endearingly goofy. Karen, I'm looking at you!). There are various activities to do and, as far as I can tell, there's almost always an event with good rewards going on.

With all of that out of the way, the core mechanics of the game are pretty good. [h3]This is split into the following: Gacha & Rewards, F2P Friendly, Difficulty, Deckbuilder, Updates, Design & Artwork, Horror Elements, Story & Translation, Steam Version, Anniversary Rewards, TL;DR[/h3]

[b]Gacha & Rewards:[/b] For context, I have played 19 other gacha games and Morimens is the most generous. The amount of rolls you get from the campaign and frequent events is incredible. The pity rates don't require as many pulls compared to other gachas and the devs often give free "reset" vouchers which allows you to reallocate dupe characters into a character of your choice. There's zero materials, currency or characters that you can't earn by playing for free, the [i]only[/i] item locked behind paying is 3 wheel cards which can easily be substituted with another. 

[b]F2P Friendly:[/b] It hurts seeing Morimens called "Pay to Win" because it's simply not. The campaign gives you more than enough rolls to obtain every standard [i]and limited[/i] character-- limited characters are also added to the standard banners over time. If you're familiar with gachas, there is an in-game currency to convert into rolls called Silver Prime, every first clear gives you more! The stats, upgrades and enlightenment are disabled in PVP (the free starting team is actually quite Meta there too) so if luck is on your side and you already have experience with deckbuilders/card-battlers, the PVP mode can give you a massive boost. 
Personally, I have only spent $15 total since playing, this was after 2 months so at that point I didn't even need the upgrades from the monthly pass, I just wanted to try one of the previously mentioned exclusive cards (and after such a heavy time investment, it deserves an extra tip as support) 

[b]Difficulty[/b] I am going to hold your hand when saying this; but if you're really struggling with the stages [i]there is a really powerful revive function[/i], this is completely free to use too! There's "Death Defiance" which prevents death if the value is over 100%, but there's also "Emergency Gnosis" which FULLY restores your health, immune to damage and maxes ultimate energy for your whole team. The only catch is that you must wait 24 hours to recharge emergency revives, however this stacks up to 5 times and can be used multiple times in the same battle. I've played my fair share of "unforgiving" card-battlers and Morimens is easy and very forgiving (did almost every mission under the recommended level), plus the revive function secures your victory, if you do need that extra boost!

[b]Deckbuilder:[/b] I'm a really huge fan of this genre and have played 15 different deckbuilders, I absolutely adore the mechanics introduced here. There's 4 very unique factions with their own dedicated mechanics and aesthetics, you can mix and match any two! This wasn't always the case though and the devs updated every faction to allow them all to work seamlessly together! After you unlock Wheel of Destiny cards and Covenants, this is when careful planning and discovering powerful synergy between characters and gear really comes into play. The PVE gamemode offers a rouge-like experience where you can pickup relics and orisons that modify your stats, mechanics and cards, this is the more traditional "deckbuilding" seen in the genre. Bosses and enemies require different strategies, using a different faction, character or wheel card can make a stage drastically easier-- or similarly turn against you, so you must adapt and plan accordingly! 

[b]Updates:[/b] The devs are [i]incredibly fast[/i] with patches and bug fixes, in the same vein; the size/time to update the game itself is very well optimized and doesn't use much data. The PVP mode is surprisingly balanced and there's not many team comps that you can't win with some extra luck, planning and counters. 

[b]Design & Artwork:[/b] I am ridiculously picky when it comes to character designs and art style, but every aspect is high quality and satisfying to look at! Every character is unique, the lovecraftian horror elements is a massive bonus, while the art style is perfectly consistent and beautiful. Small disclaimer; [spoiler]there is one character that I dislike and think is inappropriate because of how young she is,[/spoiler] but that's only one character out of a massive cast so it's easy to avoid characters you personally don't like-- you can even [i]send them back to the void[/i] if you accidentally pull them! The user interface is clean and quick to understand too, with exact percentages in descriptions for accurate buff increases and auto calculated math on many skills. For example, it will tell you what 30% of the enemy's health is, the final damage after buffs/debuffs and even highlight cards when you can activate the special effect.

[b]Horror Elements:[/b] There's many Lovecraftian and horror tropes that are a delight to encounter, it's [i]refreshing[/i] to have a more mature focused gacha with dark topics that doesn't shy from heartache or angst. That said if you're not a horror fan or sensitive to grim media, you can skip the story and still enjoy the gameplay, which leads to the next point... 

[b]Story & Translation:[/b] Full disclosure that I am not a fan of visual novels in general, I am a chronic skipper for stories told in this format. That said, I have completed both campaigns and read the chapters that were engaging or feature my favorite characters, there have been many times where I've cried! Every character gets their turn in the spotlight and most have a dedicated story mode. Now the elephant in the room; the English translations... Yes, there have been several errors, misfitting words and inconsistencies, but if you can allow some grace for not being the native language, the story is still easy to follow, entertaining and emotional. I have been playing for six months and the translations keep getting better with every update! The card descriptions, story, events, UI, everything, there's [i]constant improvements[/i]. I honestly just appreciate there's an English option at all and it's been clear enough to fully complete the game and memorize every characters' mechanics in both PVE/PVP by heart.

[b]Steam Version:[/b] The mobile version of Morimens is so identical to the steam version that I can't tell which was first and both perform flawlessly. As with any game, your mileage may vary based on device/wifi used, but my phone and laptop runs without any issues, no lag, no glitches, no heating up-- even after playing for 4+ hours straight during events!

[b]Anniversary Rewards:[/b] To end this review, I must emphasize again how generous the rewards are. Currently, with the 1.5 Anniversary Event, you can get 100 free gacha rolls [i]just by logging in[/i]. Free exclusive wheel of destiny card that's given an extra upgrade with each login. A newbie/starter banner which guarantees a character completely free, once per account. A player-wide event mode that allows you to repeatedly challenge a boss up to 20 times each day, which matches your team/level to 60 and you borrow characters from friends to make it even easier. Lastly, four new skins that you can also acquire for free by completing in-game tasks.

[h3][b]TL;DR:[/b] Morimens is the golden standard for what a gacha game should be and brings many unique experiences to the table as a deckbuilder! The first starting setup is strong enough to play through a considerable portion of the game before you need to move on to a different and more complicated team setup. It gives you enough free gacha tokens to provide this setup. Although not a perfect one, it will be much more powerful than the one you start with. 

[h1]Mechanics and Gameplay[/h1]

Every character has an Attack card, a Defense card, and a unique playstyle shown in their other cards that can mesh well with other specific characters, making certain team lineups overwhelmingly powerful when the characters in it play to each others' strengths. The different factions, 'Realms' each have a synergy that isn't a stat bonus, it's an entirely new set of mechanics (except for Chaos) that will greatly influence how and in what order you play the ability cards you're drawn. Chaos provides a massive boost to energy regeneration for both Exalts (ultimate abilities) and Posse/Possess. (a party ability that the Investigator, the persona you make, casts.)

For example, one of the characters, Lily, has an ability card whose damage output scales with a status you gain when taking damage. This card can scale to ridiculous levels with high party hit points. I'm frustrated with myself for not using this character sooner. 

Each Realm's synergy is as follows: Caro gains the Crimson Furnace, which is a source of healing that counterbalances some of the self-destructive effects that some Caro characters have. It also has Embryos, which are cards that do not leave your hand until used. They can be used to charge and empower Exalts. Aeqor allows you to build up and command a roster of Tentacles, who deal additional damage and whose behavior depends on the behavior of the waves they reside within. Ultra, meanwhile, adds an [b]entirely new deck[/b] to your game, which you start drawing from when it becomes full from the effects of the Ultra Realm's playstyle. The complex mechanics behind each character and realm likely explains the somewhat limited roster the game has presently. 

Since the Chaos Realm doesn't have anything as special and complex as the other Realms, it can act as a support for other Realms.

That's just the game mechanics, which blew me away with its depth and deceptive complexity; every playstyle is stunningly easy to use, requiring only that you read the descriptions of abilities and cards, as they contain all of the relevant information to use them effectively. This game also rewards experimentation, teaching you new things about what strategies are effective against specific bosses and enemies. Sometimes, you just need a giant blast of damage, which Helot is excellent at delivering, for the record.

[h1]Lore and Storytelling[/h1]

Moving on from game mechanics, we have the story. The game's artwork really drives home the bleak atmosphere that plagues its locations, with a heavy utilization of unsaturated colors and subtle shading. The piano and violin notes that persist across many soundtracks emphasize the nightmare you are walking through. Bright colors in niche art pieces help convey the elements of surrealism that bleed into the world as a result of the Dissolution's effects, and that of the Awakeners. 

The best part, though, in my opinion, is that this game's narrator only comes to narrate objective scenery not shown well in the artwork. The music and the visuals combine with this objectivity to create varying atmospheres despite how the narration voice doesn't change. It tells its story with dialogue and thoughts from and between characters, leaning more into thoughts at pivotal moments such as the ending of Chapter One. It shows no gore, and yet, the way it reads is gut wrenching. The ending of Chapter One made me cry, and I suspect it will make other players cry, too.

Many things are not explained, and many questions are left unanswered, but the most important ones always have their resolution met. Be it a character's fate, or the incident you're currently following, the twists and turns and surrealist nightmare this game presents leaves you with conflicting senses of fear and hope. A character without clear plot armor could just as easily die as make it through to the next chapter, and the game starts out very quickly by showing how even the characters you have in your party, even you, yourself, are not immune to harm. Sure, you are plot armored, but you are most definitely not [b]safe.[/b] It adds beautifully to the dark atmosphere that permeates almost every scene, and that haunts the few moments of joy in the madness. Its storytelling is brilliant.

[h1]Final Thoughts[/h1]

Its storytelling is brilliant, its complex mechanics are easy to learn and use (for me at least) and it never fails to take you to hell and back, so quietly that you barely notice until the chapter's end is bearing down on you. The way it builds tension makes every chapter feel like an individual story, each tentatively linked to each other through a common denominator. I highly recommend this game to those who appreciate a muted noir, those who appreciate a degree of mystery and madness, and those who take well to deck-based battlers. Highly recommend to strategy lovers", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 15, "timestamp_created": 1735131834}, {"review_text": "**Title: A Cautionary Tale: Lords Mobile is a Pay-to-Win Trap**

Lords Mobile is a quintessential example of a pay-to-win mobile game that has made its way to PC. While this isn't typically the genre I gravitate towards, I wanted to analyze the mechanics of such games in depth. To explain the ridiculous amount of "played" hours listed, it is simply from very often being logged in 24/7 on my phone, by now I have deleted the account.

**Graphics vs. Reality**

First and foremost, the game does not live up to the expectations set by its promotional videos. Instead of the engaging gameplay promised, it primarily consists of a series of mini-games that run automatically after a simple click. Initially, the game is enjoyable; development is rapid, and rewards come in abundance.

**The Hook of Addiction**

The primary goal of Lords Mobile seems to be to hook players into a cycle of addiction. Once someone invests a considerable amount of time or real money, they often find it psychologically challenging to quit. This is where the game slows down, and the push for microtransactions begins. These "micro" payments start at €/$0.99 but can escalate to €/$25, €/$50, or even €/$100 for "boost" packages. Unfortunately, purchasing just one or two of these packs won't make a significant difference. There are players who have spent thousands—rumors even suggest amounts as high as $250,000.

Remaining a free-to-play player means enduring years of grinding to build up your might. Even then, you risk being wiped out in a matter of moments by a pay-to-win player. In the PvP arena, without substantial real-money investments, you will find yourself at a severe disadvantage. It's important to note that this isn't an investment; once you decide to quit, all your progress/money is lost.

**The Role of Free-to-Play Players**

Free-to-play players just serve as bait for pay-to-win players, providing them with easy resources, boosts, and a false sense of superiority that fuels their addiction. 

**Communication Challenges**

Forming and maintaining an international guild is a daunting task, as many players do not speak English, despite the guild language being listed as such. This lack of communication can lead to frustration and hinder the overall experience, making it feel like you're dealing with a group of shy 10-year-olds.

**Final Thoughts**

I could elaborate further, but I encourage you to read the numerous negative reviews—many of which echo my sentiments. Be wary of the "very positive" reviews, as they often appear disingenuous.

**Avoid This Game!**

While it may start off interesting and feature some friendly players, ultimately, Lords Mobile is an addictive money sink designed to exploit its users. 

I understand that Steam does not favor listing games like this, so I question why it remains available. First of all it's something different. One shouldnt buy it expecting to find something like Elden Ring cause it's not. It's fast, it's hectic and it's not about exploring. But that's good. It's something new. It's exactly what they had advertised from the very beginning. And it's tons of fun.

So first the pros:
- Really nice and smooth gameplay loop
- Amazing character design with 8 characters who are totally different from each other but each got their strengths and is viably playable in any comb.
- It's hard. like. hard. But that's fun. You don't insta kill everything, you actually have to learn the nightlords
- Nice builtup of mapdesign, lot's of objectives and events which you're easily getting into after a few runs, knowing where to find things for your class, buffs to get from each area, buffs all over the map to pick up etc.
- each class has their own little quest line which gives class identity and class specific rewards which is nice and adds a little more depth
- you can play a viable bow built which I love a lot after the low bow scaling of Elden Ring
- the music. The ambience. The hub. The nightlord boss designs and fight designs. Damn. Especially the nightlords arena design. pure cinema
- you are able to queue for a random boss or a random variety of selected bosses which I find really nice to smooth out queues
- there are no "this is the to go" built. It's random what you find each run. And I find that to be really refreshing. Of course there are tier lists and stuff but in the end you have to roll with what you get and that adds a lot of built variety each run and a lot of different weapons to be tested
- a lot of old known bosses from each game which is nice (except for you Revenant..) alhtough there seem to be pretty few Dark Souls bosses and way more Elden Ring bosses

Cons:
- It does get a little too repetetive map wise, you know exactly which enemies can spawn in which areas after a few runs which had been advertised with a little more randomness. So it doesnt have as much variety as I had hoped for.
- The random events are pretty damn rare at the moment. So far we had 3 different random events in 26 hours of game time which I find to be a little too low
- The notice you get when the area is starting to closen in is pretty small and you don't have any kind of timer on how much more time you got left until the fire starts moving in.
- It would be nice to see where the end safe zone will be from the start cause it can be a little frustrating to have the safe zone close in to locations which you cleared at the very beginning.
-At the moment it doesn't have cross play which I can understand to be frustrating since it is a multiplayer game
- no Voicechat which makes multiplayer a little hard to communicate although there are ingame pings at least
- no duo mode although they have already talked about adding that and they had straight communication from the very beginning that this was gonna be a 3 player game

So all in all. It's an amazing concept. I am very glad to see them experimenting. It's not perfect but it's a solid and fun start with a lot of potential to improve. I am looking forward to polishes and changes to variety.

I personally feel that the online journalism doom and gloom is overblown. This game is sick, and it's some of the most fun I've had playing a game in a while. I am fairly confident that future updates (duos, more content, possibly hard mode) will only reinforce this sentiment. I think it's an 8-9/10 and easily worth the purchase. With that said, here are my pros/cons:

Pros:
[list]
[*]Combat is excellent. Movesets and fighting styles from various games (poise tanking from DS1, Sekiro perfect parry, Bloodborne mobility, etc.) are all available and feel great. The skills/arts are a super interesting addition. 
[*]The bosses are very fun and beautifully designed. If you're not targeting their elemental weakness (shown before you queue up on an expedition), prepare for it to feel unfair. This mistake is where a lot of "this game is BS" complaints come from.
[*]One of my biggest Elden Ring complaints was that the "open world" format felt empty when 90%+ of consumables/item drops weren't things I would/could use given my build. This is addressed in this game. Holding weapons in your inventory will give you their passive statuses, and almost every consumable is good. I stumble on a variety of decent loot every minute.
[*]The gameplay loop both in/out of expeditions are great. Each character has "remembrances" (questlines) that you can complete. Completing them gives you rewards. This, along with relic customization, gives you meaningful things to work toward even when you don't succeed in a given expedition. Inside expeditions, it's fast-paced (you're making constant decisions based on RNG) and has plenty of high risk/high reward paths that make it exciting. 
[*]Build variety is insane. I've gone bow Raider, colossal Duchess, madness caster, and more (and made it work) using various special relics and run-based drops. Even how you play - which ruins/camps/field bosses you run to in which order - can be dictated by their locations and how you kitted your relics before the game. As you progress, your options will expand.
[*]The OST and visuals are gorgeous. 
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
[*]The game seems to have issues with newer graphics cards. Some of my friends have been crashing constantly. You can rejoin, but you lose a level and need to pick up your runes as if you had died. These hardware compatibility issues need some patching. 
[*]The choice of passive status effects you get after defeating great enemies would benefit from more variety. Some of the options (I'm talking about you, "flask slowly restores hp") are almost strictly bad, and I think there tend to be too few options in general. I think expanding on this would really polish the game's roguelike elements.
[*]The game could use some scalable content. In previous titles, that was NG+. An endless night/hard mode/etc. is something I would like to see. As of right now, you cannot scale the difficulty unless you handicap yourself.
[*]While there is procedural generation that keeps gameplay relatively fresh, there is only one main map. I would love to see new terrains/maps just to mix things up.
[/list]

Let’s get the most important thing out of the way first:
✅ No battle pass
✅ No microtransactions
✅ No Paid BS

Everything is included, and some content is even hidden in a way that many players won’t ever find. I guarantee a ton of people haven’t even unlocked the Revenant class yet. If this were EA, Ubisoft, or Activision, they’d be selling that class for $40.

People complaining about the lack of duo mode? It’s already solved with a mod. And FromSoft isn’t trying to block it. They even let you disable Easy Anti-Cheat and mod the game freely, or just play offline solo. What other multiplayer game lets you do that these days?

This is a rare chance to support a game that isn’t built around greed or FOMO. That alone is worth something.

Now for the real talk:
If you have two friends, this game is a blast. Communicate on Discord, plan your route, take on the night together, it feels like a full campaign co-op experience.
If you have one friend, grab the duo mod and you're still set.
(thanks weszty for reminding me, fromsoft is also planing to add dou to the game)
If you're solo... That’s where things get rough.

Yes, there are good runs with randoms who "get it," and those moments shine. But most of the time, it’s chaos. One guy is running off to fight a level 10 boss solo for no reason while the rest of the team is halfway across the map. You’ll spend more time confused than progressing.

There's no in-game voice chat (Souls tradition), just emotes(gestures), talk items, and pin drops. It works in its own cryptic way, but for random matchmaking, it’s far from ideal.
Luckily, I play with friends now, so this isn't a problem for me anymore. But if you’re going in alone, you really need to love Souls-style gameplay to stick with it.

Gameplay?
Smooth as butter. You’re not supposed to clear the whole map. You choose what to tackle, who to fight, where to go. Make strategic decisions, scale your power, survive the night, and fight the Nightlord.
Some say the night cycle is too fast, but no, it’s perfect. This isn’t a slow, scenic open-world. You need to move, adapt, and level up quickly.

Bosses hard? Of course. It's a Souls-like. They’re supposed to be hard. You’ll get smacked, but it’s fair. There’s a revive system, and if you play smart, aggro, revive, coordinate, you’ll get your fair shot at each fight.

Some folks hate the revive system. They’re wrong. It’s genius. Your attack opportunities are a resource, and spending them to bring a teammate back creates high-stakes moments that feel earned.

First revive: 3-4 hits

Second: 6-7 hits

Third? Let’s just say… good luck.
But characters like Guardian, Executor, Recluse, and especially Revenant can turn the tide and revive the whole squad like heroes.

In conclusion:
If you’ve got a friend or two, get it. You’ll have a hell of a time.
If you’re solo… tread carefully unless you’re a hardcore Souls fan.

I was skeptical before launch, but now I’m fully satisfied with what we got. This is exactly the kind of game I want to support.

The rogue like elements (currently) hold the game back from being as great as it should be. For now let me go over some of the Positive and Negative things about the game.

Positive
---------
+ Honestly the game is fun with friends and (Sometimes) with randoms. 

+ The different characters and play styles they bring.

+ The remembrance Quests are great and worth doing. (The Que is an issue though)

+ The Nightlord / Original bosses (For the most part) are all honestly great additions! The main issue ends up being how you (Practice) them.

+ Fast paced (40+ minute long) sessions for each expedition. 

+ Honestly some pretty epic moments can happen with a good group that I will remember for a good while!

+ The returning bosses from Dark Souls 1,2 and 3 are a fun experience! Tons from Elden Ring of course but seeing the Souls Bosses makes me happy.

+ Not having to worry about how my character is being built stat wise. Some people may not like this and I understand that however with how this game works...that would not do well. It could take much more time than needed for the fact this is a fast paced game.

+ Unlike Elden Ring this game makes playing around with weapons fun. In Elden Ring it can take forever to get something good. In Elden Ring i have to change my build OVER and OVER. In this though I can actually try out things and I love it. As a Souls one trick Great Sword Pony...it has felt refreshing that I could try other things / builds without having to respec a thousand times. Makes me wanna try out some stuff in Elden Ring now.

Negative
-----------
- While playing with friends is amazing and sometimes randoms can be also...more than likely if you play without friends and 2 randoms you will end up with an absolutely terrible group that can make progress close to impossible unless you yourself end up carrying. Which is not always fun.

- 40+ minute long expeditions are fine. However Nightreign has had some pretty bad server issues here and there. If your session gets screwed over you will get nothing at all. You will only have wasted 40 minutes of your life because of something out of your control. Sometimes you may D/C and be able to rejoin but sometimes the game won't let you...and then threatens to penalize you. Which is absurd.

- No Duo is a huge let down for me. Of course Fromsoft plans on adding it but i'm gonna be real. There was no excuse to ship the game without Duo's. Delaying the game would have been the best option. Sometimes you and a friend can do great even if a third player leaves or hold you back but like...being punished by a boss being scaled for three players is still annoying.

- Needs more classes honestly. I love what they have going with them (even if some feel much better than others)

- The 40+ minute run back. You know in Dark Souls / Elden Ring when you die? You remember the corpse run you do getting back to the boss? Those usually were pretty quick...however this game gives you no way of practicing the new bosses in general. You will eventually get used to them but until then enjoy dying learning the boss pattern. Even in solo where things are now easier you will still be punished if you did not (Get good) enough on your first run. It just takes away the fun for a good while.

- Bosses are weak against certain elements however you are not guaranteed a elemental area with a weapon for your class. Which kinda blows. Sure you can use the gems to bring one in yourself but that's not the point.

- The Gems / Relics etc. The randomness factor (Rogue like Game) is...honestly kinda depressing. It's harder to get a good gem in this than it is in Diablo 4. To be fair the recent patch did add an end game vendor that is great but before that it's beyond random. You don't get to take much with you into a run. I wish the game handled each runs start like Dead Cells honestly.

- I do wish there were more returning Souls 1,2 and 3 bosses. 

- The remembrance Que issue and getting into a match sometimes. When this is fixed I will remove this.

- No voice chat or even Chat in general. Would love a RETREAT option or something...Since randoms have issues understanding what is going on sometimes with just a simple ping.

- Plenty of important information is hidden in the Codex in the west wing that I don't understand WHY it's only in the codex. Things plenty of players have missed reading. Like what your ACTUAL abilities ACTUALLY and FULLY do. The weapon scaling stuff + character scaling stuff. Just so much information is only in here and people now of days have a case of the zoomies...speaking of.

- The fact this game is all about the zoomies. I get it. It's not Elden Ring. But still not being able to really explore kinda blows. The Battle Royal death storm / circle I feel still happens too fast / moves faster than needed. I am not saying take it out. Just calibrate it a little more. Heck you can survive in the storm for awhile before it just instantly kills you...which also sucks.

- Please let me quit to the Roundtable Hold without having to go to the title screen if I am playing on Single Player. Thank you...or at least have a restart run option. This won't work in Multiplayer unless a voting system was added. I just want this for Solo.

- Dropping your souls when dying is fine...losing a level on the other hand is stupid and a waste. Why is it a waste? Because when you pick your souls back up you get them back + (Most I think) of your souls from the level loss back as well. Why? Just get rid of the level loss in general. There is no reason for this.

- No animation cancelling is a DISASTER in 2025. Ran out of mana? Heavy Weapon? You are locked into a long animation.

In conclusion
---------------

I know I wrote a ton of negative stuff and still gave this a 7/10 (Above Average) and a positive review. Why? Because I still love this game and I care about it. I give negatives because I want the game to improve. I want to see Fromsoft succeed as I have loved this company since back in the old Armored Core 2 / Otogi / Demon Souls days. I know not every game will be a hit. Not ever game will be perfect. Of course not! I just know the quality that Fromsoft can deliver. I hope they continue to improve the game and maybe even add some more content (That was never intended to be added) overtime. When Fromsoft shows love we show it back. When they improve issues we take notice. This game may have made me angry but I love it. I have 100%ed the achievements and remembrance quests and I still look forward to playing with friends and helping randoms when I can...as long as the randoms put in some effort as well. Thank you for reading my life story of a review. I will add / update this overtime with other thoughts + when content is added. So far as of typing this one Enhanced boss has come out. I defeated it on my first try and it was stressful. I had fun though! I hope everyone else is having fun and hopefully not suffering the disconnection depression much. Because that almost made me quit a few times. Good luck and see you in game! (I apparently hit the word limit! May Edit more later)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1750385392}, {"review_text": "From the very start, I thought this concept was interesting but I was very cautious. I'm very glad that From Software is experimenting and allowing other devs than Miyazaki to direct. I played the network test on PS5 and thought the first couple of runs were atrocious before the game started clicking with me. Still, by the end I only thought it was okay and would be fun for a bit and had lots of worries. Sadly, basically all of those worries weren't properly addressed in the full game.

[h2] Content [/h2]

I did a few runs with randoms but most of my game time was with two other friends. We've managed to beat every boss and I personally was able to complete two character quests in full. There is only one world event that I haven't managed to do yet so a good chunk of the game has been explored. After all of that, I still think that this game fails at being a proper roguelike.

It isn't full of content as I would like and the map itself and POI's in it feel way too repetitive. So much of our routing felt similar and many of our builds ended up being stuff we'd done maybe even in the very previous run. There's not as many bosses in the game as I thought they would have with it being a roguelike. At the end of each run, it feels like we are largely doing chores by following set plans rather than fully catering to things within the match.

[h2] Gameplay [/h2]

It is mainly Elden Ring but with both improvements and worse elements. There's some neat stuff here that I would love the main games to include like how the Ironeye class redefines ranged weapons in this game and how the Recluse has an interesting magic system. Honestly, every class feels unique and largely good, though I haven't tried much of the more magic based characters.

This game feels far more[b] janky [/b]than Elden Ring. The mantling system and being able to climb whatever is nice but feels worse than Sekiro. Sometimes, it just doesn't happen. The super sprint is interesting but the stamina drain is intense and overall stamina in this game feels like a tedious amount. The way some bosses hitboxes end up hitting behind them sometimes feels annoying. All of these things could be improved tremendously and I hope they do so.

The controls are even janky too. It's slightly modified from their prior Souls games. The controls all throughout the series have never been particularly great but some stuff here is silly and easy to mess up like scrolling through items with the down key and up to use. A big part of it is also likely because healing flask isn't a hotbar item in this game.

[h2] Bosses [/h2]

There are a ton of annoying bosses in this game. The day 1 and 2 and field bosses are all things we've seen before from Elden Ring and a bit of Souls. I would have loved more from the latter and was disappointed with the small selection. Still, the slightly modified movesets are interesting but still feel like a let down when there could have been many more.

Nearly half the Nightlord bosses are just outright annoying and even various levels of trash. So many just run away nonstop making things extremely tedious. All play out like raidbosses in an MMO and that's perfectly fine. The highlights include the first boss and more of the final ones that just straight up fight you and offer up many chances to attack instead of running. The worst boss in the game has to be a discount Elden Beast fight. The final boss is quite a treat at least.

We ended up doing the worst bosses first and the first half of my playtime at the time of writing was legitimately one of the most average and even annoying experiences I've had gaming. The final runs helped make up for it.

[h2] Speed [/h2]

This is my biggest complaint about the game. The zone is just a bother and the timer with it. I feel like the game would vastly improve without either of those things or both. There is absolutely no time to just explore, take in the sights, collect your thoughts, and celebrate or riff with friends. It's always go here, ping that, route here, fight this boss, over and over until the run is done. It's just terrible and elevates any grievances with the entire game. Even just a five minute increase to the days might do a whole lot help the matter. I would love to let my fingers off the run and sprint buttons please.

Also, why isn't the clock that's in Elden Ring when you pass time in this game's UI somewhere? It would help indicate the time which would also help figure out better routing. It very well just might help make things not feel so damn chaotic all the time.

[h2] Story [/h2]

This has never been a reason to play From Software games but the character quests offer interesting lore. They're all basically glorified fetch quests though but that didn't detract much from the experience. I would still vastly prefer From Software have good lore and good storytelling rather than just the former.

[h2] Final Thoughts [/h2]

Halfway through this game, I would absolutely not have recommended it but I would have commended it for being a good experiment that all game devs should strive for. I don't mean this exact kind of game but it's important to explore different ideas. We don't want anything to be milked and, despite this being an Elden Ring spinoff, this hardly feels like a cashgrab considering it's a roguelike which is already a niche genre.

By the time the credits rolled after defeating each Nightlord including the amazing final one, I do recommend this game but hope that it will be improved drastically. I think it's an overall okay game with tons of terrible stuff but the highs I felt toward the end feel like they made up for it. Maybe it's just because it's the last thing I felt as credits roll but it really did do a lot for me.

For all the solo players, I hope there's patches to help make the experience better. I hope there's a duo mode added since it's silly that it's only solos and trios. I hope that they fix all the jank in the game. Most of all, I hope they realize how many trash bosses are in here and don't do them again in another game but, then again, we had what felt like a million annoying dragons in Elden Ring so we shall see.

Considering all of these thoughts are from veteran players of these games, I feel like any issues would be made worse for newcomers. The tutorial isn't really that great and the game is just so damn overwhelming no matter what. I have no frame of reference for how this game might be for them but I feel like it won't be good.

From Soft dropping the hardest boss ever: having friends.
