YOU DIED (friendless and alone)

It's 6AM on a Monday. I play with strangers and we beat the Night Lord. Dance and repeat. It's a fast phase Elden Ring, you get all the power ups and rush to the last boss. OG Elden Rign feels more solo, dedicated. Nightreign is Fast Food. Get guns, do the job John Wick style. If your friends are like mine though, it's gonna be a struggle…

Fellow maidenless, 

Nightreign f**king rules. The game is experimental, flawed, but good. I personally don't think it should win GOTY or even get any MP awards at the VGAs this year (and I say this as a massive Fromsoft fan), but I definitely think the game is worth playing if you enjoy Souls games and rogue likes. It’s like Elden Ring Seamless Coop but you don’t have to actually go through the entire open world for an hour between each boss. Every character is well-designed and fun to play. The returning bosses are great and the new Nightlord bosses are some of the best in the series. THEY REMOVED FALL DAMAGE. I see a lot of negativity towards the game. Some of it is fair criticism. But the idea that this is just an asset flip cash grab or the beginning of the end of fromsoft is absurd. If you liked Elden Ring, it’s more Elden Ring, except without all the annoying busywork of Elden Ring, and you can play with your friends or wife’s boyfriend without a mod or the awful souls game co op mechanics.

It's so good. Maybe the hardest game they've put out yet, at least on first pass when solo. It's brutal, but the satisfaction of overcoming a mere single run is enormous. At first, it can feel overwhelming for a solo player, nigh on impossible. Once you've figured out how to manage and coordinate your runs is when the game starts firing on all cylinders. And it's not even a full priced game. You can pick it up for 40$, which at this point, is becoming half the price of a new over budget AAA game.

Nightreign shocked me by having lore and story as well. It has personal quests for each character, that include cutscenes and NPCs around the world's hub in addition to tasks to perform within matches. There are also quite a few endings connected to the remembrances, which are quite fun and interesting to complete. Additionally, there are static set pieces in the game that are added to maps as you progress the game forward, and those include interesting handcrafted level design. They are not as robust as a legacy dungeon, but they are very cool nonetheless. They scratch the itch and include some wild descents and boss fights, all pasted on top of the procedural maps. And lastly, all the original bosses I've encountered so far are fantastic. And each character has brand new move sets (in the form of tactical and ultimate abilities) that are unique to Soulsborne games in general. Oh, and many of the old bosses that are directly reused have new move sets as well. So, even their recycles have had a little bit of dev work.

Honestly, the amount of new development for this game (that isn't even a full-priced game) has impressed me. To each their own, but Nighteign does not remotely resemble shovel ware. It is good and there is fun to be had for sure. But it’s also… a one note game. It does one specific thing and outside of that it is pretty sparse. Which is fine, especially for a budget title, but I have to say I’m pretty underwhelmed with it after beating the final boss in 40 hours. There’s really not much more to the game unless you just love dropping in and doing it all over again. I don’t feel the urge to grind skins or rng for better relics so there’s no real reason to keep playing. Some people will love just playing it over and over which is great but it’s definitely the quickest I’ve put down a fromsoft game. Still, overall it’s a great condensed version of Elden Ring that has you doing all the fun stuff that Elden Ring provides in a frenzy of fighting, looting, and building your character. It’s just a refreshing game in a sea of corporate slop.

These are a few things I think needs to be added/ fixed, but I still think it is a good game", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763842597}, {"review_text": "The previous two games in the series (Thief Simulator 1 & 2) were fun play-at-your-own-pace open-world games, where you burgled, fenced, and upgraded your way to greatness. I was looking forward to a co-op version of those games, but this is a disappointment.

This iteration adds features that seem calculated to increase player frustration.

First, rather than giving you infinite time and 24-hour NPC schedules for each house (so you could pick the perfect time for your burglary of each residence), this game has two gameplay phases: a daytime hideout where you sell goods and a timed (~10 minute) nighttime section where you must commit all your thefts. The earlier games allowed strategizing, whereas this one forces under-equipped early-game players to recklessly enter as many houses as possible in a limited time to meet a new quota system.

Second, you are beholden to a criminal group that bailed you out of jail and the game adds that quota system giving the player 3-day quotas (30 minutes of thieving playtme) to meet dollar amounts of stolen goods. This further reduces the time spent plan heists while incentivizing reckless play, and adds a ticking clock that is at odds with the strategic gameplay of earlier games. And unlike the prior games, which gave you all your earnings, this game leaves you 10% after the crime syndicate takes the rest.

Third, inventory is severely limited. Rather than the backpack (weight-capped) inventory of prior games, this one provides just 5 inventory slots early in the game and some of those slots must be taken up by tools like the prybar or lock pick. This means that needless extra back-and-forth trips to your nighttime item drop point are required. wasting already scarce time.

Finally, all tools now have durability meters, breaking after a fixed of use. Rather than the prior games' breakage mechanic that allowed lock pick breakage only after sustained mistakes at a single lock (careful usage would allow a pick to last for in-game weeks), this game forces players to spend their meager earnings on replacement tools.

You can read the other reviews for an in-depth examination into the quirky AI, repetitive NPC behavior, static locations and props (Save for stuff like codes, notes and mechanic-relevant items), static object physics making it easier to get stuck than to actually maneuver around, and having the Stamina of an underdeveloped child with severe asthma.

The common theme with these "Simulator"-type games is that they're pumped out almost a dime-a-dozen. You can clearly see [i]some[/i] effort has been put into this title to make it better than the previous iterations, but it's still just as patience-testing and grindy as how the original Thief Simulator felt to me.

As I usually say with these types of games; Give it a few years to develop, maybe it won't feel like such a chore to wrangle around with.

[h3]What I Liked[/h3]
[list]
    [*] Voice acting is decent, doesn't overstay its welcome. Even the AI barks - While certainly coming out of their mouths like robots - Isn't bad audio quality.
    [*] The character animations aren't as floaty or jank as previous iterations of Simulator games made by the same people.
    [*] The Skill and Ability system is interesting, with Skill books and Skill boxes. Although, the fact that it's a two-part system that both requires XP gates to gain "Skill Points" in order to make use of the Skill books reeks of artificial progression. Hopefully it'll be tweaked in the future.
    [*] Co-op support, giving the game a higher chance of staying relevant in coming years.
    [*] Varied locations offer a reason to revisit to maximize loot potential.
    [*] Expansive toolsets with various methods to approach "marks".
    [*] One doesn't require a Stethoscope to loot Safes, it just makes them easier. (Why isn't this mechanic used with other tools??) .
    [*] Jumping out of the Safehouse map fence has the Handler play a funny line before the Player gets sniped from a distance, respawning back in-bounds, which I thought was pretty funny and cleaver.
[/list]

[h3]How It's Bad[/h3]
[list]
    [*] Rudimentary NPC AI lends to both predictability in some aspects of their behavior and unpredictability in others. For example, NPCs will sometimes exit on to the street going "Who is there?" when you leave, since they're programmed to "Home in" to triggers (Like if you make too much noise, or are seen). The issue is that these triggers are extraordinarily quick to proc in the beginning due to the Player Character having.. Zero Skills.

Police response is almost immediate, offering VERY little time to compensate. Police [i]also[/i] don't run out of Stamina - [i]YOU[/i] do however - So getting away is a back-and-forth of letting my one-lunged elderly wannabe-thief regain their sweet oxygen while Police or angry Civilians keep hot on my tail.

Police Tazers are instant-kills. Regardless of if Co-op players can revive you with a Medkit, one-hit-kills regardless of Health level don't feel good, fair or balanced. Just because you can also buy a "Vest" to survive one or two doesn't make it better, it's artificial difficulty.

Police flip-flop between knowing [i]exactly[/i] where you are at all times (Likely due to overlap from the beginner Player Skill being zero, and funky behavior by the engine in regards to NPC sightlines and level geometry), or straight-up running past you.

Civilians who notice the Player will call the Police every time without fail, regardless of whether you're actively punching their lights out or smashing their face with a crowbar. There actually is no animation for Civilians calling the police (As far as I've observed), it just happens. There's zero reason to try and stop them from contacting the Police once you're seen.

Civilians follow set paths and activities depending on their AI, however the way they go about this is extraordinarily jarring. NPCs will sometimes be crouching in the middle of rooms, standing in one place occasionally turning around only to stare into nothingness, or immediately change what they're doing to begin moving to another location. There is very little telegraphing from them - If at all - Which makes circumnavigating them a frustrating chore.
    [*] Unless the Players are fulfilling Challenges, money (Credits) are impossible to gain until after one has earned enough past the "Quota", which increases with every subsequent submission. In addition, extra cash achieved through going over quota isn't distributed to the Players until the current amassed amount of stolen goods are "locked in" and submitted, leaving Players with the decision to either turn-in early to get cash to continue heisting, or enter missions without extra tools or supplies.

    [*] You cannot open/close doors with a "Two-handed"/"Heavy" item in your hand, requiring the Player to drop the item to interact. In a rush this easily translates to dropping the item from standing height, alerting every NPC in the house whilst also potentially blocking the door you're trying to exit from.

This is typically why other games have visual indicators for the Player in those situations.
    [*] A static physics engine in regards to level geometry makes objects as small as gnomes, standing circular grills, benches and other props impossible to move, easily creating obstacles that can freeze the Player in their tracks if one attempts to push, maneuver, or otherwise jump around them.
[/list]

The Sacred Cards and Reshef of destruction will forever stand at the very top of most fun games I've ever played, as well as Dungeon Dice Monsters; all 3 included into this collection and along with many more certified hood classics. 

The state of modern Yu-gi-oh saddens me as it feels completely soulless; a stark contrast to the vibes of these games.  Unfortunately we won't be getting these times back in the form of future janky YGO games with original twists to the core formula. But, at least we can play these on Steam now and re-live the good ol' days again. 

And for those who got into Yu-gi-oh later on in time; now's your chance to find out what is lacking in the modern era which these older games have in spades (that modern era of YGO games being, ever since Duel Carnival released on the 3ds basically)

Thanks Digital Eclipse for the big effort! (bought on Switch as well, running great both there and on PC!)

Had they included Forbidden Memories, Duelist of Roses, and Capsule Monster Colosseum, $50 would have been a justifiable price point. But given how dated and grindy these games, I can’t recommend at full price. The biggest issue for me is the oldest games even with a manual do not give you clear instructions how to play.  The first Duel Monsters game for example, fusion is VERY important mechanic for success, but outside of a few examples the manual doesn’t really explain how fusion works at all. You’re at the mercy of ancient internet guides to halfway understand these games.  

The later games in this collection are better, but also unfortunately grindy. I can tell you from experience the online experience with these games will be dead just like all the other collection games that drop because of no crossplay. 

As a diehard Yu-Gi-Oh fan, this was worth it for me for at the price I bought it ($38) because I love these games. For a casual fan, I’d wait for a deep sale and even then only if you’re ready to invest in learning some really dated mechanics for over half of this collection and very grindy games", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 14, "timestamp_created": 1740746383}, {"review_text": "TL;DR: EARLY DAYS COLLECTION is a good game collection that features a mixed bag of games. Some are good, some are great, and some aren't worth playing. I recommend getting this collection when it's on sale, because the $50 MSRP is steep.

First and foremost: The price. It's steep, and I think it's the main thing many people will point to regarding this collection. This collection is good! But the price makes it a tough sell for anyone who isn't the most diehard Yugioh fan. (Specifically the kind to care about a bunch of old Gameboy games)

This collection is genuinely solid. The 4 brand new translations featured are a VERY welcome inclusion. Though it's worth noting that Duel Monsters 1, 2, 3, and 4 are very similar games overall.

The ability to switch game versions from US/EU/JPN is very nice. I appreciate the "Enhancements" menu (basically a selection of cheats) as they make so many of these older games a lot more approachable. Basically every game has a cheat to give you 1-9 copies of every card in the game so you can skip the grind entirely. Some of the games (including The Sacred Cards, Reshef of Destruction, and Duel Monsters 4) have options to have maximum Duelist Level and Deck Capacity, which skips a huge part of the grind in those games (particularly Reshef). It's genuinely very nice to see here.

Technically speaking the collection is solid as well. I've had 0 crashes or issues while playing it and have only experienced 2 instances of slowdown/lag while playing Stairway to the Destined Duel.

To speak on the games themselves for a moment:
- the pixel art in Duel Monsters 1-4 is incredibly charming! I love seeing the pixel art renditions of all the cards since many were redrawn in these games. (It's not like say, Stairway to the Destined Duel, where it uses the official card arts but compressed.)

- Duel Monsters 1 & 2 are fun if you give yourself a head start with some Enhancements. These two games operate like the old Bandai card game and Season 1 of the anime, where high level monsters can be summoned without Tribute. This leads to a power fantasy of being able to summon Blue-Eyes White Dragon, Perfectly Ultimate Great Moth, and Meteor Black Dragon without Tributes on turn 1. Games are incredibly quick as a result, lasting 3-5 turns in my experience.

- Duel Monsters 3 has a unique gimmick of crafting your own cards using Card Parts. The idea is sadly better in theory than in practice since none of them have any effects so you end up crafting the biggest beat sticks that you can. I applaud the effort and wish this could return in a future game.

- Duel Monsters 4 is surprisingly fun. It reminds me of The Sacred Cards. Despite functioning like its predecessors (DM1-3), some of the card inclusions and effects are reminiscent of The Sacred Cards. For example, the Egyptian God Cards are present and are as powerful if not moreso than they are in TSC. [I think this game's version of Ra is the strongest I've seen, letting you revive the monsters in both players' GYs and steal your opponent's monsters in play when activating Ra's effect.] Use an Enhancement to give yourself a head start and you'll have a great time with this trio of games.

- Dungeon Dice Monsters is slow but very interesting. I hope it gets multiplayer in the future because this game is tiresome to play solo due to how RNG heavy it is. With proper dice pools this issue is alleviated however, so I recommend using an Enhancement to skip the grind.

- Destiny Board Traveler is a historically divisive game due to its lack of content. Aside from unlocking new characters (done with secret button commands) and new stages, there's very little replay value. However, I found DBT to be surprisingly fun! Look up the rules ahead of time and you can have a blast. This game is great in short bursts.

- Stairway to the Destined Duel is a solid duel simulator and a personal childhood game of mine. It features one of the most messed up ban lists I can think of (Delinquent Duo, Confiscation, The Forceful Sentry, Raigeki, and Harpie's Feather Duster are all at 1 and Graceful Charity is at 2!). The ending of the game is confusing to trigger but you can ignore it entirely and approach it as a solid duel simulator. It's one of the most solid duel sims in the collection.

- The Sacred Cards is an amazing game that any fan of the anime should play. It retells the story of Battle City with you taking the role of a new character who essentially duels all of Joey's opponents. This game features the same rules as DM1-4 but refines them in a few key ways to make things more enjoyable. The Sacred Cards is in my top 5 favorite Yugioh video games for good reason. I do not recommend using any Enhancements for this game as there's very little grind.

- Reshef of Destruction is in my top 3 favorite Yugioh video games. It's a great sequel that has one major flaw- it's grindy. The creators heard complaints that The Sacred Cards was too easy and they overcorrected, making Reshef of Destruction "harder" by nerfing duel rewards heavily. You'll be dueling 5-10 opponents just to match what you'd get from beating 1 opponent in TSC. This being said, with a few Enhancements turned on, this game is a great time and I highly recommend playing it. (My personal suggestion is to give yourself 1 of every card and Max Duelist Level. You'll still need to grind for Deck Capacity to be able to play with the best cards, but once you have room in your Deck you can play anything you want. This preserves the RPG experience without making it a mind-numbing grind like it is originally.)

[I'll update this in the future as I play more of the games in this collection.]


Some things I hope Konami works on in the future:
- Communication. It would be nice to know what games will be getting online play in the future, how many games will get online play post release, and roughly how long these updates will take to create. It would go a long way in making a lot of us happier with this collection and any future collections they release.

- Price. While I understand the $50 USD asking price ($50 for 14 games is roughly $3.60 per game), I think a lower MSRP would be ideal for targeting the casual Yugioh fan, which I believe is the intended demographic for this game. At $50, Konami is putting this game collection up against titans of the industry like Elden Ring and Baldur's Gate 3! That really scares away a lot of customers. Especially when you start to consider how hard it is to convince friends to get the collection so you can play the games online with them.

- Content at release. As a game collection, EARLY DAYS does a great job in this department. 14 games on day 1 is a very nice offer. However, I'm mostly talking about Online Play functionality with this point. I think 2-3 games should have had Online Play functionality on release day. Online Play is a lot more appealing to the casual Yugioh fan than game translations in my opinion.


I hope Konami makes more collections like this one for Yu-Gi-Oh because it's received a lot of games over the years! A console game collection would be very appreciated (Forbidden Memories, Duelists of the Roses, and Capsule Monster Colosseum! Just imagine) but so would a Tag Force collection (I NEED an official translation for Arc-V Tag Force SPECIAL. It's my favorite Yugioh duel simulator!) and a DS collection. There's even the Power of Chaos trilogy and things like Yugioh BAM, if Konami wants to go down that route!

Game Collections like these are a big deal to people like me who care a lot about games preservation. I think there's a way to preserve video games while the company makes money, and collections like these make that happen. I only hope Konami sees it worthwhile to continue making Yugioh game collections as they have for Castlevania and Metal Gear Solid!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1753628793}, {"review_text": "I hate to say it, because it's a fine collection (a little barebones, and the lack of a turbo function really hurts the more tedious games), but this is a game where you should wait for a sale. 

Pros:
+ Rewind feature is great if you accidentally hit the wrong button
+ Save states make some of the games way more bearable (being able to save before duels in Reshef makes the game much less awful)
+ Some of the games, like the Eternal Duelist Soul, are genuinely fun
+ The AI doesn't "cheat" (have unfair knowledge)
+ The "enhancements" allow you to skip some of the grind if you so wish, which can make Reshef considerably more accessible for people unfamiliar with its crap

Cons:
- The AI is extremely primitive. It was never given rules not to go minus in cards over the worst possible plays imaginable. For example, in the games based on the actual card game rules, it loves to activate Magic Jammer and pitch a card in response to you targeting Magic Jammer for destruction. This is a play no sane human being would make. 

- Almost all of the games lack multiplayer features. Given what I just said above, that can be a huge bummer.

- A lot of the games operate on "Madden Rules." What the heck do I mean by that? Well, they're often just updates of the previous game(s). So while you do technically get a variety of games, that variety is a lot more limited than it sounds.

- Some of the games are REALLY interesting to check out and play ONE game of. I don't mean clearing the game, I mean literally playing ONE match. Destiny Board Traveler, some of the early Game Boy Color games, Monster Capsule, and Dungeon Dice Monsters all feel like extremely weak entries compared to entries such as EDS. Dungeon Dice Monsters in particular is just absurdly tedious. You roll dice for crests to take actions, and you and the AI just stand there blinking at each other until you FINALLY crush it with movement and attack crests.

Decided to wait until I got all the achievements until I wrote a review. I'll write a quick review for each game in the collection along with it's biggest pro and con.

Duel Monsters:
Very reminiscent of the original few anime episodes where they make rules up as they go. 98% of the cards are normal monsters.
Pro: Pixel art is good
Con: basically just the card game 'War' where big number wins and you slam fatter monsters into each other. No tributes, just play Black Skull Dragon with its 3200 atk or Perfectly Ultimate Great Moth with 3500 atk and swing.

Duel Monsters II:
Like Madden in the sense where it's a slightly upgraded version of last year's game. Remember in Duel Kingdom where they added elemental weaknesses? This game now has those.
Pro: They took more effort to balance the game, which can't be said about the first game.
Con: Kuriboh will one shot your Blue Eyes White Dragon due to type chart

Monster Capsule:
The first YGO game in the collection that isn't just 'vanilla YuGiOh'. It's a really awful tactics game. And trust me tactics games are my favorite genre of games but this is one of the worst I've played in many years.
Pro: An attempt was made to call back to the manga where they play more than just card games.
Con: Extremely grindly, long, slow, permadeath to set you back hours, most guides don't go more than halfway through the game. Honestly this is probably the worst game in the collection.

Dark Duel Stories:
Earliest English released YGO game in the collection. Very similar to Duel Monsters II but with better graphics, some censorship, and a weird card combo mechanic that can be used to easily make powerful cards.
Pro: the card combo mechanic is specific to this where you have a suffix and prefix combined to make a unique card.
Con: elemental weaknesses and deck capacity mean you'll be fighting with 300-700 normal monsters for awhile until later in the game.

Duel Monsters 4: Battle of Great Duelists
This game has 3 versions (Yugi, Kaiba, Joey). The Kaiba achievement takes awhile to get but the others can be obtained quickly. Same game, probably really cool back in the day where each had exclusive cards and you could trade with your friends but nowadays they're a bit redundant.
Pro: I bet this game was amazing to play in 2001 with friends and link cables
Con: for achievement hunters, you gotta do 51 duels in each game to get the achievement or you can use cheats to get 2/3 of those achievments.

Dungeon Dice Monsters:
More of a tactics/board game but significantly better than Monster Capsule which came out only a year earlier. Probably the second best game in the collection.
Pro: actually a really fun game in it's own right. Not your standard YGO by any means but a very unique creature collection/tactics game.
Con: since it isn't a vanilla YGO, it lacks a tutorial so you gotta figure things out. Which isn't hard because the collection comes with instruction manuals but thought I'd throw trhat out there.

The Eternal Duelist Soul:
Aside from Falsebound Kingdom, this is my most played YGO game. The oldest vanilla YGO that doesn't use made up anime rules, strictly following the card game rules.
Pro: just duels, nothing else. Play games, win cards.
Con: the harder AI cheats by not attacking your face down cards if they know they can't destroy it.

Duel Monsters 6: Expert
This is the only game in the collection that is strictly in Japanese so I didn't play it much.
Pro: the achievement is easy to obtain with cheats
Con: It's Japanese so I can't read anything and have to rely on card art

The Sacred Cards:
The first YGO "RPG" but they brought back elemental type matchups, deck capacity, and duelist level to add more grinding. The easier of the two.
Pro: this is the most whack game in the collection to speedrun. If you like speedruns, I recommend looking up a vid for this one on YouTube.
Con: kinda obtuse sometimes on where you're supposed to go

Reshef of Destruction:
Oh my double gosh! By far the hardest game in the entire collection. By far the grindiest game in the collection. However, it isn't without merits. An effort was made to write a compelling story and it isn't revolutionary but it's got some neat characterization for otherwise one note characters. A fun game to play with cheats to skip all the grind. It's a direct sequel to Sacred Cards.
Pro: very fun if you use the built-in cheats to supercede the grind and never once did I need to look up what I was supposed to be doing as Ishizu tells you at anytime.
Con: the cursor rapidly goes through all 10 spots on both fields and both graveyards everytime anything happens to check for effects that might need to be triggered. This wasn't in Sacred Cards and wastes a lot of time.

Worldwide Edition: Stairway to the Destined Duel:
I don't know why Duel Monsters 6 is in the collection because this is just the English translation of that game. For the record, you can change the language of any game in the collection except that one so weird that they separated it into two games.
Pro: it's in English
Con: The first part of the game has you fight against random opponents and if you run into Kaiba you will get smoked

World Championship Tournament 2004:
Kinda like Eternal Duelist Soul but not as great. For starters a lot of characters cheat. It has the returned "don't attack face down monsters if I will lose life points" mechanic but also has 'luck' stats which actually allowed characters to use multiple limited cards. Someone like Yugi who has very high luck can run 3 Monster Reborns and 3 Raigeki for example while you're stuck with 1.
Pro: this was the vanilla YGO game in the collection to allow multiplayer, so that's nice.
Con: this is probably the worst singleplayer vanilla YGO game in the collection because of the AI and them running so many limited cards

Destiny Board Traveler:
It's a board game because every franchise needs a board game. And not a good one like Dungeon Dice Monsters
Pro: the achievement is fast
Con: not really my cup of tea but I can appreciate the effort

7 Trials to Glory: World Championship Tournament 2005
This is the cream of the crop in the collection if you were looking to play some vanilla YuGioH this here is your game. You don't get one random card after every duel and thus farm Mako for a specific card, you get money based off how well you did in the duel and use that money to go buy packs that you want to build the deck you want. Then it has the RPG mechanics of walking around the city, talking to people, and finding the many secrets hidden within. The ultimate goal of the game is to win the... 7 tournaments as the title suggest but it was a fun romp regardless.
Pro: best vanilla YuGiOh game in collection hands down
Con: I didn't want to use cheats for this one and the online guides have outright wrong information a lot of the time. For example I wanted to use an Exodia deck and the fandom said "win a tournament" when it really means wins the championship tournament late in the game.

Overall, had a fun time playing the collection and hope we get an "early console collection" including Monster Capsule: Breed and Battle (JP/PS1), Forbidden memories (PS1), Duelist of the Roses (PS2), Falsebound Kingdom (GCN), Power of Chaos Yugi the Destiny (PC), the Dawn of Destiny (Xbox), Power of Chaos: Kaiba the Revenge (PC), Power of Chaos: Joey the Passion (PC), Capsule Monster Coliseum (PS2). [{"review_text": "So, about half a day of playing the game with a friend and I gotta say, I have some notes. Let's get off what I have good to say about the game first.

+ Grounded 2: Exactly what it says on the tin. The game is just that, the sequel to Grounded. If you liked Grounded, you'll like this game. You got a lot of returning elements such as your day-night cycle, survival elements such as base building and eat/drinking, crafting tools from bugs, dealing with bugs in general. Not much to say there, it's definitely Grounded 2.

+ Buggies: Definitely a welcome inclusion. One of my complaints about the original game was the traveling was very sluggish. Setting up Ziplines was a hassle, making them tall enough so it actually went fast was a pain and your only other options were walking or a teleporter, which you couldn't get unless you beat the game 3 times already (which made the travelling problem more pronounced). Buggies solve this by making travelling actually *feel* fast. Just the simple act of giving a speed boost and riding a bug really helps the travelling feel good (even if it's not faster than teleporting or a good zipline) because you actually feel like you're riding an ant really fast. It tricks your brain into being satisfied with the ride, and that goes to show that what's basically "Running but on a Bug" can feel great if you put in the time to make it feel good. The Ant Buggy helps with building, like the game said. I had an issue with it, though, occasionally just walking in front of me when trying to do literally anything. Since you can interact with it, that meant it would cancel whatever I was doing and force me to focus on the bug. It would be nice if it didn't do that, I'm not a big fan of being interrupted while trying to harvest stuffs. 

+ Omni Tool: I wasn't exactly sold on the idea at first, because you can't swing-cancel to break resource nodes like pebbles or clay faster like you could in Grounded because of how the Omnitool works, but I hopped on board because it helps mitigate the storage issues. You no longer need to carry an axe, a shovel, a hammer or a wrench. That's 4 (Technically 3 because who the hell is carrying a wrench all the time) slots in your inventory opened up for other things. That, and it solves the issue of forgetting the tool you need. Now, the Omnitool is a permanent addition to your belt, it's not even in the inventory. You can always dig, bust, or chop. No comments here, it's just an all-around buff.

~ Combat: Everyone and their mother is talking about combat, so I won't waste too much time here. The fact that charge attacks are expanded on and bugs block your attacks now is great, it makes you think a little more about how you'll approach the battle. I will say, bugs block too much. Way too much. Sometimes they'll block, and I'll break their block, and they'll just block immediately again. That, and the only way to break blocks seems to be to charge your attack. Sometimes leads to an issue where you'll charge your attack because the bug just won't stop blocking, but then the bug will start swinging on you like it just gained sentience and figured out your next move. Other times it just leads to these boring fights where the bugs just. Keep blocking. Bugs need to block less, and I think they shouldn't block twice in a row. It would be cool if they had a fakeout to try and trick you into charging, but it definitely feels like the bugs just randomly decide attacks and one of them so happens to be a block. Other than that, the archetypes and combat system as it is vastly improves on the old game. The Rogue playstyle in particular is great, though I've noticed sometimes ambush attacks aren't counted, and it would be nice if bug awareness wasn't so touchy. They notice me sometimes from stupid angles, and sometimes it feels like they just stop pretending to think they don't know where I am. You can't really do a stealthy surprise attack in the game if the enemies can catch you for seemingly no reason, you feel?

+ Content: So many complaints about content, so many people not seeing the bigger picture. The amount of the bugs in the game, as well as the content, is a bit light, yes. But as it is, this is leagues better than even end-of-development Grounded. I feel everyone's so quick to forget that we were hyped for what was basically a thousand reskinned enemies, with 4 of them literally just being ants with a new attack every now and then. The Black Widow, Tiger Mosquito, Termites, Ladybirds...at some point, Grounded stopped adding in new creatures and started adding in reskins, and that was okay. But you could tell burnout and limitations were applying, the devs seemed to be running out of ways to add interesting content into the game near the end of its life. Grounded 2 doesn't have this problem. Granted, it's early access and we haven't seen what the devs plan to add later, but right from the start every enemy feels unique and plays into their own niche. The Wolf Spider looks nothing like it did in the last game, there aren't any variants or reskins (yet). It feels like this is a much more coherent and put together plan, something the devs are actually working hard to make unique and actually feel interesting. This is *actual* content, not the reuse and recycling we got in the Fully Yoked update. With more things on the way, we'll just have to see if Obsidian continues this trend. 

Now, onto some negatives I have about the game.

- Understanding and Readability: On the surface, most of the stuff in Grounded 2 is obvious, and if you played Grounded you won't have any issues. But even as a returning player, some stuff just isn't obvious enough. For instance, I have no idea how to customize the new Hot Pouch. The ability to have your hot pouch instantly select items such as foods and light sources is great and handy. Too bad I couldn't use it, because I couldn't find anywhere in the game to change the slots without overwriting them. Dragging those items to it doesn't work, it just replaces the slot with the item you chose. If you have 30 dried snail jerky, your gnat jerky hot pouch slot doesn't care. And the help section doesn't help either. The information in it is just straight up wrong, the key to bind things to the hot pouch is not the one labeled, even though it confidently states so. Despite what the game suggests in the beginning and in the help menu, there is no obvious way to customize the hot pouch as far as I'm concerned. Another issue is starvation and thirst, or rather the fact that it simply isn't obvious enough. You get one audio cue when you're thirsty / hungry, and that isn't enough when you're fighting for your life or focusing on something else. I need the game to scream at me in some way to tell me to eat, because the icons are just in the corner off to the side and you don't think about them until it's inconvenient. I can't tell you how many times I learned I was close to dying of thirst because I couldn't swing my weapons because I ran out of stamina, an effect that happens when you're thirsty but isn't announced. I shouldn't be made aware that my character needs to drink only in the *middle of combat,* yknow? I could go on, but in general I feel the game needs to be a bit more clear about certain important mechanics, such as not dying or utilizing a system that the game clearly encourages.

I could go on about glitches or issues, but I'm certain Obsidian is aware of a lot of major issues. In the future, I might leave another review if these issues don't get checked or patched, or if there are better things, but as for now I'm mostly satisfied with how Grounded 2 is at its release. It's definitely not finished, nor is it outstanding, but it is promising. And in a sea of game releases that end up being mediocre, I'm glad to say thanks to Grounded 2 for actually living up to my expectations when so many other games got me hyped and fell short,", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 11, "timestamp_created": 1754030548}, {"review_text": "You will get solid 20 hours of game in this early access game, will not recommend it if you played first Grounded and expect at least everything first part gave you, For example Tier 3 weapons and tier 3 resources we had access in Grounded 1.

Please take into consideration a lan option for the future.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1754142360}, {"review_text": "I played Grounded 1 soon after it launched in EA years back, so I was with it from the start; and it was incredible to see it grow and evolve.

And now I'm back at Day 1 with Grounded 2 in EA.

Biggest complaint I'd have for the game, really the only complaint in fact, is the performance - much like a lot of people have been saying. My PC is able to run Grounded 1 no problem, but I've had to really dumb down the graphics in order to get it to run somewhat decently, which admittedly impairs the experience a bit.

That being said, this is again, an Early Access game, and is currently at Day 1 launch; and I have complete faith that the performance issues will be addressed soon.

The positives are numerous.

If you loved 1, you'll love this. It literally feels like coming back to the first game again, but with a new world to explore and new bugs to face off against. They've reused a lot of the same assets from 1, which is perfectly fine with me and seems to me an intelligent move overall. There was nothing wrong with the assets from the first game, and the similarities help to make a fan of the first game feel right at home from the get go.

If you loved having all the individual tools (axe, hammer, shovel), you might be sad to hear that they've done away with those completely in favour of the Omni-tool, which is bound to a single button and will just active accordingly depending on what resource node you're trying to harvest - and you still upgrade it using bug parts.
So the tools lose a bit of their colour there, but the stream-lining of resource gathering is still much appreciated - you don't need to worry about the tools taking up space, don't need to worry about it being left behind since the Omni-tool doesn't use an inventory slot and is always with you. 
It also doesn't have any durability either, so you don't need to worry about maintaining it. So while its a bit of a bummer to see the unique-looking tools get shelved, there's plenty of positives to make-up for it.

Overall, I'd definitely recommend this game, just keep in mind, this is Early Access, there's gonna be issues, and you might need to play on reduced graphics for a decent frame-rate; but these issues are gonna get addressed in time, as with any EA game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1753867973}, {"review_text": "Great game, I hate bugs, this is exposure therapy", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 97, "timestamp_created": 1754877781}, {"review_text": "**EDIT: game is now marked as EA, we did it everyone 🥳 🎊

That’s not a typo. That’s a lifestyle choice. So when Grounded 2 dropped, I put on my tiny armor, grabbed my axe, and dove in like a gnat into a lamp.

Pros:

•	Buggys are hands down the most chaotic and fun addition. You haven’t lived until you’ve launched a leaf-powered death cart off a root ramp and landed in a puddle. I’m not saying I tried to Tokyo Drift under a juice box, but I definitely did... 
•	The new rolling mechanic is pure joy. I can now roll through fights like I’m starring in a backyard (park) remake of The Matrix. Nothing quite matches the satisfaction of perfectly dodging a Scorpion charge and retaliating with a spicy staff spell cast. I don't just fight bugs—I style on them.
•	Base building is a full-time job—and I love it. There are dozens of hours to be had just designing, expanding, and decorating your park empire. 
•	The world is dense, imaginative, and full of secrets. Exploring never gets old. One moment I’m on a peaceful stroll gathering clay, the next I’m being attacked by the worse bug in Grounded - the mosquito. Classic Grounded.

Cons:

•	They removed some bugs... and I’m sad about it. 
•	The frame drops are so frequent I started to wonder if the game is simulating heatstroke. Combine that with the random crashes, and it’s less “smooth experience” and more “accidental speedrun to desktop.” Entering my own base now feels like playing Russian roulette with my GPU / CPU. “Augusta Unreal Engine crash”
•	I get it—it’s early access. But crashing during autosaves, losing progress in co-op, and rubber-banding across the park like a possessed flea? That’s not “early.” That’s “should probably still be in the garage.”
•	Mosquito's are back.
•	And here’s the thing: Microsoft doesn’t need the money. This game, in its current buggy (pun intended) state, should have been $19.99. Charging premium for a game that runs like a tiny potato strapped to a rubber band launcher is just not it. Especially when players are functioning as unpaid QA testers.

Final Verdict:

Grounded 2 is good — packed with charm, creativity, and chaos. Whether you're rolling through combat like a ninja seedling or building the bug-proof base of your dreams, there’s a ridiculous amount of fun to be had here.

But for a game this fun, the technical issues sting. Hard. It's borderline unacceptable for a major studio, even in early access. If you can handle some crashes, minor loss in progress, and frame drops that’ll turn your beast of a PC into a Chromebook trying to run Cyberpunk, it's still worth diving into.

More bugs, more places to explore, more lore & story, more biomes and the park is absolutely MASSIVE! It's worth mentioning the area we have at launch is approx 4 times the size of the backyard in Grounded 1, and It's been reported the the portion of the park we have at release is only about 25% of the total park. That means potentially 16-20x the size of Grounded 1 by the end of Early Access in a few years.

The new bugs in the park are excellent and there are now bug to trigger fears other than arachnaphobia. I forgot people have major issues with scorpions and even more so with cockroaches!

The additions are awesome and while I was on the fence about the mounts, that all changed the first time I breezed through the grass on the back of an ant. Two mounts in the game, one on the way and potentially two more after that.

I enjoyed the story and lore of the first game, and am already engrossed in the story unfolding here in the sequel. Who is that person? Does this circle back to Grounded 1? I have tons of questions & speculation, and that's part of the fun of Early Access, guessing what's next and picking apart every detail.

I am fully aware this is Early Access and lots more to come, and it's not perfect. I crash every few hours, randomly things glitch in the game, etc... but we've already had two hotfixes and have updates on the way. Obsidian was really on the ball w/hotfixes, updates and new content in Grounded 1, so seeing them up the ante here is pretty sweet. The next update is giving us the first major boss encounter Axl, quality of life improvements etc, with a bigger update planned for the end of the year

I've just barely scratched the surface at 50 hours, and even with the limited story progression at this time, there's still tons to keep you occupied.

The sequel feels less like a new adventure and more like a significant regression, and it's clear that the game should have waited until next summer to deliver a more complete experience that justifies its price tag and honors the legacy of its predecessor.

The core issue lies in the game's sparse content. What should be a sequel that builds on the foundation of the first game is stripped away from the player behind future updates. Materials like lint, pinecones, and sour are visible in the world, yet progression is gated by these updates. This leaves players with a handful of new items and enemies while constantly being teased with features that are just gone.

This removal of existing features is baffling. Why take away beloved elements like diverse mushroom sets, the coziness factor and lack of any water elements?  We are given the Orb Weaver buggy after completing current story content, long after it would have been most useful for traversing the world's challenging terrain. This design choice turns a potentially rewarding tool into a consolation prize.

The official roadmap for Grounded 2 only adds to the frustration. It promises the return of these features—Sour 2.0, Coziness, Mushroom sets 2.0, Swimming 2.0, PEEPER 2.0 and ziplines—but spreads them out over the next year. This forces players to wait for what should have been launch-day content. The community is being asked to pay $30-$40 for a game that will only become whole a year down the line, essentially paying to beta-test a product that feels far from finished. You wanted us to test these features, but you didn't even have them prepared for us.  You are forcing us to wait 4-6 months for the feedback you wanted while already giving you our money.

The introduction of buggies, a major new feature, is surprisingly unrewarding. The "taming" process lacks a sense of progression. On top of that I just stumbled upon the eggs while exploring with no sense of what to do with them. You give us Ant bait and Spider bait, I think using these to tame the bugs and then implementing a system with the saddle, friendship levels and new mutations would have added significant depth to the gameplay.

Beyond the buggies, the game suffers from a significant lack of enemy variety. A huge number of foes from Grounded 1 are simply missing, leaving the world feeling empty and less threatening. The list of absent creatures is long and includes:
Black Widows, Roly Polys, Black OX Beetles, Tiger Mosquitoes, Moth, Ticks, Fireflies, Wasps, All Infected Bugs, Termites Antlions, Green Beetles, Ladybirds, Ant Queens, Fire ants, Black ants and any Water Based Bugs.

Furthermore, enemies that are present seem to be scattered randomly, lacking the defined territories that made encounters in the first game so memorable. The limited number of mutations and a lack of collectibles like statues further compound the feeling that this is a stripped-down experience.

[{"review_text": "Ngl after the first round I thought I was gonna refund this within 2h.
Almost 7h later in one go, yeah, this is neat.
It's pretty much a Lethal Company clone but with an LLM mimic feature that actually tries to make sense out of the voice clips it gets per session. When the session starts, it's not really impressive. But the longer you play (without creating a new session/lobby) and the more you yap, the more material it gets to use. Eventually the mimics become quite troublesome plus absolutely hilarious moments are gonna be a thing.

[strike]Though the mimics are already insane strong at times, running straight at you, grabbing and instant killing you...that needs some tweaking. There's little point in having mimics when they could be just blatant monsters that one shot you with no way to escape. Like, even when you KNOW that's a mimic, it oftentimes just doesn't matter because it's just too strong.[/strike]

Update on the mimic balance: They are definitely more common now, but they did nerf them so that they don't outright one shot you if not saved instantly. They'll grab you and will fill up your toxicity by about 75%, then drop you. That fill up happens slower now, too. So unless you're already somewhat full on toxicity, you can actually survive being grabbed without any help. Before they'd quickly fill it up to 100% every time, meaning any small mistake would mean death really.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1762018933}, {"review_text": "Mimesis is built on a genuinely brilliant idea: an AI monster that learns how players talk, mimics our behavior, and blends into the group so naturally that you can’t tell who’s real and who’s fake. On paper, that sounds incredible. But in reality, the game just isn’t polished enough to reach that vision.

The AI doesn’t actually “learn” anything meaningful. Instead of adapting to conversations, it randomly repeats lines players said earlier with zero understanding of context. You’ll be trying to figure out who’s human, and suddenly the monster blurts out a completely unrelated voice line. The movement animations suffer from the same issue—they’re stiff, unnatural, and nowhere near how real players behave—making it far too easy to spot the AI.

Even when you do identify the monster, the game doesn’t reward you for it. In most games, catching the imposter feels like a victory. In Mimesis, being right just gets you killed. The monster walks up, grabs your neck, and instantly one-shots you with no chance to react. There’s no teamwork payoff, no satisfying moment of deduction—just punishment for noticing.

The player controls add even more frustration. The movement system feels extremely limited and clunky. Jumping is unsatisfying, like you’re hitting your head on an invisible ceiling every time. There’s no crouching at all, which removes an entire layer of mobility and immersion. Everything feels rigid, slow, and uncomfortable, making the experience less engaging than it should be.

Mimesis truly has potential. The concept is creative, the atmosphere is intriguing, and the idea of AI deception could be amazing. But right now, the AI behavior, movement system, gameplay balance, and reward structure all need serious refinement before the game can become what it’s aiming for.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1763002540}, {"review_text": "Game is cool but here are somethings the devs NEED to fix ASAP;

1. Bugs related to rejoining and switching players. Disconnected players can't hear mimics, can't see voice chat participants, and may not even see the players themselves. 11/10.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 371, "timestamp_created": 1736279181}, {"review_text": "It started like this: no minimap, no player marker, just a weird map, a compass, and a vague sense of direction. 200 hours later, I still don’t exactly know where I am half the time - but I’ve led squads confidently into ambushes, driven into trees at 100mph and exploded in the most hilarious ways, regularly driven my car around like a lost tourist shouting for the navigator, and somehow had more fun than in any shooter in years. Coming from Squad, HLL, and the BF2:PR days… Reforger feels like chaos, community, and comedy pretending they planned it that way

I don’t usually write reviews as you can see from my profile, but this game deserves one - for the direction it’s heading, the modding scene, and the ridiculous amount of fun it regularly delivers on every play session.

After more than two decades of gaming—from OG Battlefield 2, Project Reality, to newer titles like BF1, BF4, COD: Warzone, Squad, and Hell Let Loose - I can honestly say Arma Reforger has quickly become my favourite strategic-teamwork-big player but small squad FPS. I’ve sunk nearly 200 hours into it in just two months, despite a busy personal and professional life. That should say something.

Early on, I stuck to vanilla for the first couple of weeks, just to get a proper feel for the game. And honestly, it was the right call. No GPS, no map marker, no night vision it all felt a bit punishing at first, but it’s manageable. Eventually, those limitations become part of the immersion. Daytime-only servers help a lot if you’re new. Don't jump into mods before you've spent a good 20-30 hours in vanilla, because you won't go back.

Then I moved over to modded servers - mainly WCS - and that’s when things really clicked. The mods bring variety, polish, and quality-of-life improvements that make the experience smoother and deeper. All the things you expect, map visibility, direction pointers, compass bearings, night vision, the lot. 
The performance has also been solid for me on my mid-ish-spec rig (i7-11700 + 4080 super): crashes are rare, and desync only shows up now and then, usually while in a vehicle or crossing sync zones of some of the larger maps like Everon- but it isn't always there and does not affect the whole server or your gameplay, it's small, brief, and periodic - much less than what I often experiences in Squad with Heli's flying around at times. I'm sure they'll fix it too as it's seemed to improve. Firefights on the ground are smooth and reliable. Solid gun work and feel to everything. 

When things line up, (which is multiple times per 2-3 hour play session and even more if you find a discord group of friends, which you will), people using mics, decent teamwork - the game delivers incredible, unscripted moments. It’s hard to explain, but you know it when it happens: a coordinated push, a perfectly timed flank, or even a chaotic skirmish that somehow works out. It's a great balance between travel time and action on many of the maps - I think that's what really helps keep the magic going constantly.

That said, be prepared to shop around for servers. Some are unmoderated, and I’ve run into the usual nonsense - mic abuse, racism, etc., even on official servers. I nearly walked away from the game at one point because of it. But stick with it. There are excellent servers out there with great communities and regular players. Once you find your spot, it feels like home. For me, that's the official WCS servers.

I’ve essentially retired from Squad and HLL for now. Reforger isn’t a full-on milsim - it’s less rigid, more forgiving - but that’s part of the appeal. Vehicles are a blast to drive. Chaos and comedy happen often. Combat is intense but doesn’t punish you for every mistake. You can usually get back up, heal, and rejoin the fight. It strikes a balance that other tactical shooters haven’t quite managed.

Of course, it’s not perfect. The squad and map systems are confusing and could really use a redesign. The upcoming commander role could be a huge boost for deeper cross team coordination, it's next on the list but it’s not here yet. Comms are limited - more mic channel control would go a long way for those times when you platoon chat is going crazy. You can mute your radio easily, but I haven't found a way to mute just the Platoon chat and not my Squad chat. And the arsenal system is just plain unintuitive until someone explains how to navigate it. (Spoiler: inspecting your weapon is your friend.) 
Thankfully, modded servers remember your loadout, so you only need to suffer through it once per server. Someone dropping you their kit, you picking it up and saving, actually bypasses all of that in seconds anyway. 
Server queue time is the thing, it takes on average 40-60 seconds per player in the queue ahead of you, so you can be queuing to join the most popular servers from anywhere between 10-25minutes - so factor that in, boot the game, join the queue, and deal with a bit of housework or scroll reddit.  The good thing is if you disconnect, you can normally reconnect and skip the queue if done within a few minutes, so crashing isn't as bigger deal as it was a few months back before they fixed this.
Sometimes there is then a queue to join one of the teams if you are picky, normally each server will have a "good team" and a "public team", where it's regular players will gather and join the same team, but I have noticed servers and people starting to rotate teams more between maps, so I think this will balance out.
Finally, there is no way really to track your kills and deaths in game with a score board, you get used to it, even if I do wish they'd add something.

But here’s the thing: none of that stops me from playing. If I were reading this, I’d probably be put off by that list. But in practice, the good far outweighs the bad. And the community - at least in the right places - is full of players who are happy to help you get your bearings, team up, and take on the objective in whatever way you suggest. People are happy to tag along, or for you to tag along with them.

Reforger is already a great game, and it’s clearly on track to become something special. It’s not there yet, but it doesn’t need to be. The foundation is solid, the devs are active, and the modding scene is carrying it in the best possible way.

If you’re after a shooter with strategy, depth, and the kind of moments that can’t be scripted - this is it right now.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 11, "timestamp_created": 1750384469}, {"review_text": "Arma Reforger isn’t just the best shooter I’ve ever played, it’s also the funniest. Clearing bases from 700 meters away makes you feel like a ghost, but what sets this game apart is how ridiculous and unforgettable the moments are.

Like tonight I accidentally became ARMA’s most wanted. I discovered you can climb trees on modded servers, and suddenly I was a leaf-covered menace with a silenced monster of a rifle. For nearly five hours, I terrorised bases, downed helis, stopped cargo runs, and erased squads before they even knew what hit them. At one point they had helicopters sweeping the woods and grenades carpet-bombing the treetops. They came close a few times, but I lived.

The best part came when I eventually had to give myself away (they thought I’d cheated and glitched into a bridge). One guy asked where I was, and I just said, “Look up.” He did, spotted me in the branches, and immediately started laughing. Then he called his squadmates over one by one so they could share the joke. Every reveal was pure comedy—silence, then hysterical laughter. Instead of killing me, they asked for a tutorial. Absolute legends.

And then came peak chaos: my teammate Monster popped out of a bush mid-conversation, scared the life out of them, and we all laughed until we were crying. Finally, one of them asked, “So what now?” I told him, “Back to respawn” Me and Monster then turned around, and bang… that was that.

That’s Arma in a nutshell: one minute you’re public enemy number one with helicopters hunting you, the next you’re laughing with strangers in the woods before getting executed together. I’ll probably never see those players again, but I’ll never forget that night. Chaos, comedy, satisfaction. Genuinely everything I want in a shooter. 11/10 would buy it over and over again.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 37, "timestamp_created": 1757730075}, {"review_text": "The most accessible "milsim" I've played. It takes less than a minute to get into firefights. No more running for 5+ minutes, only to get one-shot by a pixel in the distance. Reforger is a tense and often hilarious action shooter. 

It's got all the pros and none of the cons of Hell Let Loose, Battlefield, CoD, and Squad. It's Arma 3, but actually playable.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 11, "timestamp_created": 1741542350}, {"review_text": "Pros:

Graphics & Performance: The Enfusion engine is a major upgrade. 
Lighting, terrain, and animations are beautiful, and the performance is surprisingly solid for an Arma game (as long as your rig can handle it).

Multiplayer Experience: Playing on Everon with friends is nostalgic and exciting. The dynamic events and role-based teamwork capture the essence of the Arma experience.

I have feedback for this sim.

Pros:
- Physics are exceptional, even though there are flaws. 
- Car behaves realistic, way more authentic than most sims out there.
- Graphics are natural, not the most outstanding but quite good.
- Car basically feels really good in FFB wise, feels numb but it's basically how real life works as well with power steering, most authentic simulator you can so far with that kind of stuff.
- Weight in the car feels great, especially feeling the weight transfer in the car with the FFB is great.
- Some car's sounds are really nice, especially S2000 and Porsche Cup.
- Having selections to different specs/trims of cars is a huge plus, not every sim have that.
- Launch control features and drive modes are nice, dashes are nice as well, again not every sim has that.
- Race car and road car electronics has a difference, huge plus because most sims don't have that, especially AC1.
- Really good foundation for an early access game.

Cons and must be improved as soon as possible:
- Road cars are too fast, too much grip available, GR86 is 6-7 seconds faster than irl in Laguna Seca with road tires. Road tires feel like brand new fresh semi slicks, Hypercar tires are basically slicks, it's better to balance it out, it's too fast.
- SoP effect isn't enough, it feels more like after the initial snap there is more effects into it, and it's the main reason AC1 is easier to catch snaps and feel when the car is going out, easier to drift in game as well. Overall oversteer effect is simply too weak. It's only the M2 that I can feel it properly. (Note that I run 0 damper)
- Front wheels completely lock up if you entire into the gravel in rain.
- Menu for keybinding is much more complicated than usual, rather properties are always shown and FFB in another page.
- Rain feels a bit too forgiving in my opinion, but a bit makes more sense than ACC.
- ABS needs fixing in terms of how the brake locks you up if you turn, it is supposed to increase braking distance not make the car lock up, except the race cars they are made to beat humans. The only cars that work so far are the BMW M2 CS Racing, and slower road cars.
- AI needs complete rework.
- Needs working on online servers, as well like ACC if the servers go down you basically are done.
- Slicks have too much grip in the wet.
- Too extreme level of kerb usage and not enough punishment into it.

Cons and but nothing really:
- Optimization is better after 0.14, still needs a bit of improvement and it's there. So far playable.
- More drive modes for some cars (I think I'm not sure if drive modes even affect the driving performance), but make different drive modes more noticeable in performance.
- Sounds are quite mediocre but nothing really.
- Not enough understeer effect when you are understeering but you can tell it visually.

Stuff that we all like to have:
- PRNDM/S (realistic automatic transmission for some cars) and being able to switch from auto to manual or something like that
- A different tire model with different tire brands, and being able to buy tire sets with different brands.

Side notes:
- In my experience this is more GPU intensive than CPU intensive.
- In my experience my game runs well without upscaling/frame gen. Can be different to your experience. I'm using 1080p with i5-12400F and RTX3060Ti.
- I'm not sure if there is eSports in this sim, but probably the focus isn't that really good.
- I'm not sure if the mods will be available in this game, but don't cry if there isn't mods in this game, because this game doesn't really need mods in the end of the day if this is how it drives.
- Pricing is aggressive, I know but for what it is it can be one of the best sims in sim racing history.

Here are the reasons TO buy it:
- Demo of drive modes and features
- Driving experience very authentic compared to the real thing, superb handling.
- Discount (Duh) or want to buy cheaper now so you can get all the content now for v1.0
- Graphics are quite natural and not over exaggerated
- Porsche Cup fans who like Porsches

- Performance issues in v0.1 (I mean you can still buy it and save it up for a better PC then)
- Issues with triples and VR in v0.1
(I think these will be fixed soon)

PROS:
- At least the system is there, and can be improved.

CONS:
- Too easy to pass 3 stars on all of them except the electric car one.

[{"review_text": "( A.v.A Vet Honest review ) 

Hackers can control your PC from this game!
Please bear with me as i dedicate the last bit of energy to this game before saying goodbye. Very detailed review! 

I got into this game with my cousin back around 2011. Though he had played from around the start. This was way back when we were kids scrambling funds together to add ram to an old DELL Laptop on a dual core just to run 50 FPS. Over the years we have always resorted back to A.v.A and seen the highs and lows of the game. Every "re release" we were there, From being kids staying up late for school waiting for servers to come online, To being adults calling in for work to be there for the A.v.A Dog tag release, As well as the A.v.A global release. We used to have screenshots of us being the first ones on the server a couple times. Point being this game holds alot of sentimental value and holds value to some of my childhood memories. 

A.v.A was a game that was far ahead of its time upon release. It most definitely competed with top FPS titles on PC! Over the years even through the shut downs and IP transfers it always had a really strong competitive scene. ESL picked it up. LAN tournaments and events it was the real deal! My opinion : If managed correctly and updated early on it was on track to easily hold the value and significance of current state counter strike. 

Now lets transition over to the release then the current state of the game. 

After redduck supposedly went bankrupt and shut down the newly released A.v.A Dog Tag which had a good launch until anticheat quit working..( Also same game different name) the IP or "Rights" to A.v.A were auctioned off in court to Neowiz. During this downtime no one knew anything and expected it to be the end of A.v.A. The old A.v.A Dog Tag discord was turned into a HUB for players to stick around and share A.v.A memories. This was until some time later official news came that Neowiz was going to give A.v.A another go! During this time their was a surprising amount of hype for the game! That slowly faded away when the first big red flag met us. Their was almost 0 transparency from the developers and a LOT of time had went by. Also little to no updates to the community instead they reminded the community multiple times "Soon" and that is it! No im not joking.. Throughout the closed betas and a really unbelievable wait for the release they had various shenanigans in discord like "Hey fill out this discord google doc survey and let us know what you feel needs changed and what would make the game better" They had promised to listen tot he community and use the feedback provided. It seemed kinda promising i guess. 

ISSUE #1 - No anti cheat from launch!

Now keep in mind, Me and my cousin were able to binge this game for a few days and relive out our younger days and that felt great, So that is one good thing i can honestly take from this! Upon release it was fun for the first i would say 12 hours.. Then things quickly started to go downhill. The games population peaked at 11,883 players which was HUGE, It is expected for some of the hype to wear off and players simply be like " Eh this isnt my thing " and the population to drop some. But within a little over a month it was hitting a steady 3K.. A major drop! This unfortunately continued to happen until now the 24 Hour peak is around 200.. Here is why. After around 12 hours their was what seemed to be a overload of cheaters they started out kind of rare but as the population was fading the cheaters were showing more and more. Over a few weeks the A.v.A discord was filled with players complaining and arguing with developers and comedic (A.v.A Discord MODS) over the games anticheat. Multiple people had sent videos in discord proving that you can disable anticheat and the game will still run. In other words. This game had 0 Anticheat from the launch and that is a FACT!. Running on 2007 code, You can imagine how many cheaters, And not just the normal Aimbot, ESP cheats. No they will flash your screen. Freeze you in place literally take control of the lobby. It was unplayable.

ISSUE #2 - BUGS

Another major issue was around the time of release, The game was filled with several bugs, and many continued to give the game a chance given it was just released but the bugs seemed to never get fixed. Even when brought to attention to devs! Many players were even getting banned for no reason. I hadn't tested this personally but some were saying you would get banned after a certain amount of reports and that was the games only source of anti cheat! And thats why just natural good players were spamming discord demanding to be unbanned. The same thing happened to me at around 4 weeks in. Keep in mind i had already spent money on several skins, Weapon crates, ETC. I was never able to get the account back even after making tickets in discord and emailing neowiz. Still nothing. Money gone. 

ISSUE #3 - Lack of content on release

Upon release this game felt like it was still in closed beta with how little they gave us, Keep in mind this is after beta tests and alot of time passing with devs making unfulfilled promises. To summarize we could do ( Quick play ) and party up with friends for quick play, Spend money in game and IRL. Buy a few skins and that is ABSOLUTELY IT! Not even custom rooms. Ranked mode. Nothing. The basic necessary features that should have been added to begin with were added way after the games community died out. 

ISSUE #4 - CASH GRAB > Make a good game! 

It reached a point to where me and my friends had just gave up and determined the game was unplayable though we still try and tap back in every now and then to see how its going and run a couple games if we can even find a room of players because yes its THAT DEAD. We still kept up with the game though we had little hopes of it lasting too much longer and its almost scammy how much these devs are pushing skins. You have major issues at stake like 0 anticheat. Players getting banned at random ( Happened to me 3 times total. ) You dont even have custom rooms but hey thanks for pinging the community to announce a brand new BATTLE PASS!!! The devs really done it with this one. Could have made a good game or even released the Aeria version and that would have been better and yeiled more income instead of pushing skins so much its comedy.

A few more things ill add and rant about. This game had major support for a competitive scene. But without custom rooms quick enough the competitive players gave up and left for the most part. The devs were never worried about producing a good game, This was solely to leech off your nostalgic purposes and make a few quick bucks and milking it till its no longer profitable then shutting it down for good. You A.v.A heros who are or used to be discord mods were literal comedy you guys were given a volunteer role and acted like you were lead dev at neowiz. I was banned from the discord for trying to get help and talking to others about how lousy the devs are. Mods were literally banning people for stating the game had no anticheat. Discord mods were treated special and for some time only a discord mod could create a custom room for you or your friends. The active mod dont like you? Yea your not getting a custom room then. Just kinda spamming complaints here. I have been banned on several accounts for nothing as i stated my 1st account had well over $100 spent. No support at all. 

Ill finish with this and heres the real kicker. Im not sure how this game is even allowed on steam due to the cashgrab aspect and how bad the hackers have taken it over. I was playing earlier and i had a hacker take over my PC through the game. First typing in game chat saying it would happen then it actually happened. A chat window appeared on my PC and i turned it off and had to reinstall windows. This has been a nightmare all because i wanted to give this another try.

A.V.A Global has so much potential. I’ve tried other FPS games like CS2, Team Fortress, and Fortnite, but I always find myself coming back here. Why? Because the gunplay is unique — recoil control, burst/tap mechanics, and crosshair placement that reward pure skill. When it works, it feels incredible, and that classic AVA feeling is something no other FPS really delivers.

But the reality is tough:
	•	Servers: NA is completely dead. EU customs might see 3–5 games, but Asia is the only region keeping this game alive. If you’re outside Asia, expect 150–250+ ping.
	•	Hackers: Still at large and ruin matches too often.
	•	Low Power Mode: The devs seem to be running the game just enough to keep it alive — no real push for a competitive scene, no marketing effort, and updates feel like bare minimum maintenance.
	•	Community: Mostly old players returning, with very few new players adapting. Without growth, the game feels like it’s just recycling its veteran base.
	•	Monetization Gap: In A.V.A Global, some skins and guns require real money, while in other versions like KAVA (Korea) or JAVA (Japan) those same items can be bought with in-game Euro — no cash needed. It makes Global feel more pay-to-win and less rewarding for dedicated players.
	•	Uncertainty: Player count has risen a little, but with weak communication and little visible effort from the devs, the future feels like survival, not progress.

My reality: I’ve poured in over 1,500 hours, but my playtime is shrinking because frustration outweighs fun. Still, I keep coming back because the gameplay feels so good — when it clicks, it’s addicting in a way no other FPS matches.

Verdict: A.V.A Global is a flawed gem with unreal potential. If you’re in Asia or don’t mind high ping, it’s worth trying.
