https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3558007462", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1756481258}, {"review_text": "MGS DELTA is a safe, almost a 1:1 remake for sure. But being a game that is also one of a kind (in being overly specific more than anything) and incredibly hard to replicate, I do understand KONAMI. I don't really see how else it could have happened. While 1:1 reconstruction is a merit and an achievement on its own, it's important to note how extraordinarily well MGS3 uses the videogame medium; if it weren't for Kojima et al.'s meticulous attitude, this simply couldn't have been achieved. In other words, if you are indeed the average of the five people you spend your time with, MGS DELTA could not have been achieved without the original team and would have been doomed to mediocrity, even if Konami dared to expand upon the original and even if built in-house.

That is not meant as an excuse, however. I would truly have appreciated it if there were new "small" QoL features, like being able to loot enemies without actually holding them and waiting for the animation, and/or ledge takedowns, etc., that really wouldn't hurt the logic of the game and would help the flow instead. Regardless, the new autosave feature & the addition of records and titles (and limitless saves for FOXHOUND) is very welcome, along with quick camo switch, a damn compass, skippable codec conversations (which also fixes the audio issues from the original), and new, slick animations for Snake.

They could have gone more ambitious, but again, I can't say it wouldn't have hurt the game logic. MGS3 plays level by level, allowing you to memorize and master each section (and abuse it if you will). While the AI is not the greatest (and sometimes outright worse than its HD Collection counterpart) and there are occasionally logic-defying moments, within its own logic, MGS3 works quite precise once you figure things out and deduce how to make them work to your benefit. It can be hard to interpret the cone of vision of the enemies (although I would say it was always more likely to run into that issue in MGS3 compared to its predecessors) and it really boil downs to your camouflage meter (you are able to abuse AT-Camo in lots of situations). 

There's obviously a big difference between experiencing it for the first time and knowing exactly what to do. I found myself in the latter category; however, it really didn't hurt the overall experience as much as I thought it would.

Perhaps I should state that MGS DELTA is also quite easy to trivialize, especially with CQC. A pacifist run (especially on Hard/Extreme) always felt easier than in other "stealthy" stuff like Dishonored, Deus Ex, or Thief. The camos and utilities you find later in the game trivialize it to a large degree; however, I would call that where the fun is. Foxhound (which is essentially a 0-alerts playthrough more than anything else) was always an issue, especially due to camera angles. Now, it's probably the easiest of all MGS entries but is still a decent challenge.

There is some "bad stuff" carried over from the original. One of them is the last sequence with EVA, where she must follow you. If you take a quick detour to clear the area beforehand so she can follow you with ease, you'd be dead wrong. Her AI still gets stun-locked, and she refuses to follow if you steer away for a while. Commanding her can be incredibly stressful in a pacifist run, as by the time she makes her way up to you, enemies would have fucking woken up. However, this is also one of the rarer games where you can say, "I tranquilized her, carried her myself, and kicked her to wake her up."

On the other hand MGS3 was also one of the rarer games where you could say ''I found my way through a cave by spamming flashbang and even smoke grenades''. It's no longer a necessity thanks to how UE5 handles the illumination. I know it's cherry picking but still...

Boss fights are easier in some capacity. I found The Boss's CQC to be easily parriable (as long as you almost insta-click, which works every time). The Fury was the part where optimization (and the excess amount of VFX) did hurt the actual fight; knowing how easy it was, I had to spend much more time trying to figure out where he was, but one could say it's better for providing a challenge since he sets everywhere ablaze. The Pain is most definitely still painful; gotta give him that. I don't mind the removal of stamina drain tactic for The Fear to be insulting, it does make sense. Yet, both bosses and enemies lack proper balance adjustments to align with the new (and improved so to say) gameplay. 

While there are slight visual glitches and frame dips, I was actually able to run it smoothly enough, so I can't partake in the optimization debate. However, there was noticeable ghosting. It has a neat legacy filter (along with some other filters), a photo mode at launch (which is still a surprisingly rare feat), and a new rendition of "Snake Eater" which, unlike the majority I guess, I quite liked. But it shouldn't go without saying that with the tech of 2025, MGS3, especially its presentation, loses context. This is noticeable not only in the cutscenes (which all use the old animations) and I'll use two of the easiest examples I could give: The End's eyes popping out and Snake kissing but also in exaggerated gameplay segments.

As much as I dislike stagnation, I understand the need for preserving a relic of its time, trying to restore it, and serving it to a broader audience. MGS games weren't available on Steam until about 2 years ago and MGS4 is still stuck ONLY on PS3.
There is no point in asking it to run before it can crawl. Besides, remakes are more of a 50/50 thing. You either get a Silent Hill 2 or RE2 (and those are not free of sins either) or... you get RE3 and Rebirth, the latter of which is universally acclaimed but gives you a plethora of reasons to dislike it (or in my case pretty much hate it). If there's a breaking point where I must choose between the two: a brave remake that is its own entity but damned with mediocrity, and a 1:1 remake of what is deemed to be an all-time great, I must choose the latter. It at least doesn't create a time paradox!

Overall, MGS DELTA surely deserves a shot to be experienced by veterans, and it's a strong starting point for newcomers. It really can be tough to talk about MGS without spoiling not only its presentation but also the gameplay (which is essentially what makes the whole experience unforgettable), as you'll notice the bullshit aspects both the story and gameplay have, and how flawlessly MGS executes them like no other game ever could.

Footnote: The price, especially for EU, is egregious. I am skipping that part.

★ ★ ★ ★ ☆

Pros:
- Cool new graphics.
- Camos can be equipped using the d-pad instead of pausing the game
- Improved Gun-handling
- Very faithful to the original story wise
- Original voice cast 
- They bought back Cynthia Harrell to sing a new version of snake eater and it’s REALLY GOOD. She’s still got it. 
- Clearer audio (easier to hear voices over other noises)

Cons:
- Expensive $116-131 AUD.
- Noticeable audio clipping in some cutscenes.
- Some sound effects are way too quiet like knocking on wall surfaces.
- Martial arts system is slower for some reason? Snake's 3 hit combo isn't as fast as in the OG snake eater.
- Cover system is clunkier and frequently results in accidentally being seen because you don't snap to it as quickly as you do in the original.
- Sight-lines are inconsistent, sometimes guards see you too easily to the point where it feels like the game isn't fair, other times they are really stupid.
- Movement has a weird amount of delay which makes turning around really annoying.
- CQC is based on orientation and due to the weird delay in movement, facing the correct direction to perform CQC during combat is inconsistent and annoying. 
- Holding people up with a gun has an inconsistent trigger so you have to spam aiming the gun at someones back to get the holdup to trigger correctly which is really frustrating.
- In the cure screen, you have to re-select/scroll to the same item you previously had selected for each wound rather than keeping an item selected and applying it to each wound. This is really annoying if you have a bunch of leeches or any other specific injury that doesn’t require disinfectant. The disinfectant is always re-selected whenever you look at a different wound. In the original you could select one cure item, apply it to all the wounds then change items. 
- Difficulty hasn't been increased enough to compensate for snake having advanced gun-handling ability being able to headshot a bunch of people and move around at the same time. (Yes even on extreme difficulty)
- AI are less aggressive than the original and play way more cautiously.  
- Performance is pretty bad and there is a lack of configuration options to alleviate this. No option to make foliage less dense or lower shadow res (you just turn them off entirely), or decrease res of particle effects. Low preset completely destroys the art style making the image look really washed out. Makes this release much less accessible for anyone running older or non-recent hardware. (This is a criticism of desktop performance, not just steam deck performance)

Nitpicks (subjective things not everyone will care about, and that’s okay):
- Snake's CQC feels a little too aggressive in this game, he strikes like Batman whereas his strike style felt more controlled in the original. 
- Some of the faces look a little too different for my liking.
- Some areas like the cave after the ocelot fight are too bright which makes the torch and cigarettes useless.
- Choice to use realistic graphics instead of opting for a stylised look decreases the ability for the audience to suspend their disbelief
- While this is subjective, removing the colours of the original game and opting for more 'realistic' lighting greatly detracts from the emotional impact of many of the cutscenes and the  general vibe of many areas. It makes them much less visually interesting to look at. I am aware that there is a 'legacy' filter but even this filter didn't do justice to the cool and warm tones of the original game in my opinion. 

Conclusion: Cool remix of sorts, definitely not a definitive replacement for the original which still holds up really well today. Arrgh!", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 52, "timestamp_created": 1756631578}, {"review_text": "The way Konami bombed my screen crediting Kojima felt more like a legal formality rather than a celebration of his work, but the more I played the more I reflected on how his creative legacy is being handled, the game looks wonderful because it's built on the foundation he created, it just would have been nice to see that acknowledged with a bit more grace.

At first, I was impressed by how this remake honors the original's vision by sacrificing some modern appeal. they offer two playstyles,  some visual filters for nostalgics and a surprising return of the original voice actors and singer, and a full spectrum of difficulties inviting everyone to experience it their way. I liked the fact that it understood its own purpose by being a remake by its very nature, It felt like a respectful preservation effort, focused on refinement rather than innovation, which I believed was the right approach since radical evolution was always Kojima's specialty.

But now I see the critical difference between technical replication and artistic understanding. [{"review_text": "(Hi! The majority of my hours are me sitting in the menu with another game open. I think I really have about 400-500~ real in-game hours.)

This helps, this helps alot. But there is a wrong way and a right way to play kovaaks. Playing the wrong way can really fuck up your aim if you don't realize what you're doing for a long time.

This is what happened to me when I initially purchased this game and started getting into aim training. I initially started around 4 years ago, on and off, but i never really started grinding until last year. I now realize that the 4 years on and off blindly aim training set me back really bad. 

I used to uncontrollably flick left in right whenever i'd get into any aim duel. While this is also a symptom of panicking in-game and not keeping calm, there are mouse movements I sometimes could not (and still can't, to a degree) stop myself from making. It had become instinct. This was because for those four years I thought grinding close fast strafes and scenarios much higher than my skillset would help me.

You will hear people saying "Kovaak's doesn't work" or "Kovaak's ruined my aim" - This is true if you don't know what you're doing. 

It's much more obvious, known, and easier to get into these days, but if you're looking to start aimtraining, a nice google search to start with is: "voltaic kovaaks". Voltaic is an aimer community with lots of resources and information revolving aimtraining and kovaaks. 

Remember to disable your high score bar sometimes
Always listen to music*
Prioritize undershooting
Hold your mouse like you would hold an egg
Track your target with your eyes like you would track the blade of a spinning ceiling fan

dont just try to flick to your target because you're losing score. this is a cope tactic, and one that will ruin your aim. do not worry about your score. worry about how you're training yourself. keep in mind the muscle memory you are teaching yourself. read the descriptions of scenarios if there is one. i had to came back to this review to update it because i found myself making the same mistake again, and i wanted to really get this point across.

*Someone commented about the music thing and it got me thinking (also music is just very important to me). For some people you may find it better not to have something distracting in the way, and I feel that when I listen to some especially disorienting songs. Find an album from an artist you haven't listened to or find a playlist with some new music on soundcloud and listen to them while you play. I still remember the match that got me Radiant—not because it was smooth or easy, but because on the other side was Dasnerth. Yeah, that Dasnerth. The infamous judge rat who makes Bind showers feel like a horror game.

But before I get to that, let me rewind.

🧊 Stuck in Immortal
For months, I hovered around Immortal 2–3. Some games I felt cracked, other games my aim fell apart. Everyone said “just deathmatch more,” but it didn’t stick. My shots felt forced, my flicks were panicky, and any whiff tilted me off the planet.

I thought aim was something you either had or didn’t. Turns out, it’s something you build.

⚙️ Discovering Kovaak’s
One late night, after rage-quitting a loss streak, I downloaded Kovaak’s. At first, it felt useless—tiny dots on screen, my wrist cramped, and my scores were garbage.

But unlike DM, Kovaak’s showed me numbers: accuracy, reaction time, scores going slightly higher each session. Even +1% felt like a win. It was addictive.

I started doing 20–30 minutes a day:

Close-range flick scenarios

Small head-sized target switching

Tracking bots dashing side to side like Jett on caffeine

Over weeks, my crosshair placement got tighter, and my flicks weren’t guesses—they were built into muscle memory.

🐀 The Rank-Up Game vs Dasnerth
Finally, promotion game: Bind. And sure enough, guess who’s on the enemy team? Dasnerth himself, crouched in Hookah, Judge in hand, ready to delete anyone breathing too loudly.

Early rounds were rough—he shut down three B hits single-handedly. My team was already molding in voice.

But this is where the grind paid off. Instead of wide-swinging like usual, I held tighter angles, crosshair stuck right on the head (not the chest). Next B hit, Dasnerth peeks Hookah: I pre-aim, flick—instant headshot. No time to fire the Judge.

The team explodes: “Bro killed Dasnerth?!”
We took site, got the plant, and momentum shifted.

🏆 Radiant 
Final score: 13–10. Match ends, and there it is: Radiant.
No scream, just a quiet grin. The same kid who couldn’t hold Immortal now clipped the scariest Judge demon on the server, all because aim was finally reliable.

✍️ What I Learned
Kovaak’s taught me:

Aim isn’t magic—it’s reps, focus, and data.

Raw aim buys you confidence. Confidence buys you rounds.

Even “unfair” fights like a Judge demon can be won if your crosshair is already there.

If anyone’s stuck thinking aim is luck: it isn’t.
Build it, track it, and one day, you’ll peek showers, see Dasnerth with a Judge… and still one-tap him.

[{"review_text": "It's pretty good, there's a LOT to do and it is fun to play alone or with friends. I like the game quite a bit, but I never enjoy it as much as I do playing with my grandmother, she has thousands of hours in ESO lol", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 29, "timestamp_created": 1737508724}, {"review_text": ""No game subscription required." Unless you want to do even a minimum of crafting. It's kind of insane that such a basic feature is locked behind a subscription - it's not like the game is free-to-play. If you can practice extraordinary meticulousness with your looting and inventory management, and have no desire whatsoever to do any crafting, you can get by without it. But your inventory and bank space can fill up real quick.

Mount speed not being account-wide is awful. No big deal right? Just visit a stable master once a day right? Except each time you visit you can upgrade only one of three stats, and they improve by a meager 1 point each time. Why? I think I know why - because you can buy a pack of 10 "Riding Lessons" on the Crown Store for 1,000 crowns (roughly $10). 18,000 crowns (over $120) to fully max out your riding skills FOR A SINGLE CHARACTER this way.

Oh, and don't you worry. Albeit optional, ESO's got loot crates too! Let's review the financial model:
* Buy the game
* Subscription required to not be hamstringed
* Pay for convenience due to outrageous decisions like locking riding skills to a single character
* Loot crates.

Enough about the unabashed greed on display. The game itself seems to have a healthy population, I never had to wait in a queue for a dungeon or trial terribly long. Quests are unique, the story is... OK. Some dungeons are also pretty unique. Each zone has it's own character but the art design kind of results in them feeling a bit samey, with some exceptions of course. A lot of them have a sense of drabness that I can't quite put my finger on.

Combat is bad. Really bad. Floaty, impactless. Popular meta involves exploiting what I can only imagine was an unintentional flaw in design - animation canceling. Fortunately there are builds (that are also meta but much more niche) that can forgo this exploitation.

When I first started I was really thrown off by my starting stats. Why were they in the thousands already, I'm level 1? Why is my damage in the thousands? It's level-scaling. This has one huge positive - you can go almost anywhere and attempt to tackle almost any content you want. But it has a gigantic negative - character progression feels extremely stagnant.

I tried several classes and while I didn't max them out, they all felt kind of samey. Any class can wear any armor, can wield any weapon. Due to the limited nature of the skill bar, all classes have relatively simplistic skill/spell rotations, with none of them feeling truly unique. I also hate the Champion Points system. The improvement afforded with a single Champion Point is miniscule. You'll feel nearly no difference until you accumulate a significant amount of them. 	I've spent nearly 10,000 hours in The Elder Scrolls Online (ESO), roughly a year of my life in-game. As a veteran player, I love the game's enormous world and the amount of content it offers new players. However, for veteran players deeply invested in the endgame, ESO feels increasingly neglected. While ZeniMax Online Studios has focused on attracting newcomers, the endgame community has been forgotten, as if they no longer mattered. We face persistent issues such as server lag, an easy-to-abuse ban system, and a lack of meaningful content updates.

The New Player Experience:
	For new players, ESO is a treasure trove. The game's massive world, rich lore, and seemingly endless number of questlines provide hundreds of hours worth of engaging content. I always see new players exploring Tamriel, and it's nice to see the game's newbie community grow.

Endgame Woes, Performance, and Optimization:
	For veteran players, the experience is far less satisfying. ZeniMax's focus on new players has come at the expense of endgame quality-of-life improvements. Things that seem simple in the grand scheme of the game have been persistent problems for years. One of the most glaring issues is unplayable in-game lag, particularly in Cyrodiil during high-pop times. This isn't a standard latency issue, but a slideshow-like drop in framerates similar to dropping thousands of cheese wheels in Skyrim or meshing props in Garry's Mod. Even high-end hardware (like an RTX 5090 or AMD 9950 processor) can't overcome this lag. These issues come from poor server hardware, outdated netcode, and a lack of optimization. I got into ESO while unemployed, and I [i]still[/i] didn't feel like I had enough time for it. It was very easy to get caught up in just doing daily quests (of which there are hundreds), and never have time to do anything else (like play the story quests, or roleplay, or PVP, or).

This game isn't super unique, it's quite literally just an MMORPG with Elder Scrolls flair to it, and I don't think I would like it if it wasn't Elder Scrolls, it translates every typical mechanic and trope from MMORPGs and fits it into the Elder Scrolls world very well. Now it might make some people upset that the mechanics of this game aren't the most lore-friendly, being that this game is the only case where we can grow spikes out of our backs, but Nirn [spoiler] canonically isn't real, [/spoiler] I say anything goes.

There are a couple of things that make your character, race, and class, race has some stat effects and its own set of passive skills you can unlock, while classes will give you exclusive skills that are both active and passive. Each class has 3 skill categories, their DPS skills, their Tank skills, and their Support skills. DPS skills do damage, duh, and apply effects onto enemies, Tank skills draw aggro and protect you from damage, and then support skills provide utility to your group, not always just healing, but still mostly healing. Then there are weapon skills which are attacks and passives exclusive to that weapon, and then there are armor skills which are just passive and improve the performance of armor, and then there's a whole load of secondary skills that are unlocked by doing certain activities and are by far the most painful to progress, especially the crafting skills. The combat-related skills can be very fun to progress as you try to figure out your playstyle and optimize your character, but the rest of them are a huge pain, they involve immense repetition and it can get very stale, very quickly, but the payoff is pretty good, having a well-made character is super fun to play with, especially in a group.

Your gear is another very important thing, there are a few ways to obtain weapons and armor: Craft it, find it, receive it as a quest reward or random drop. The gear you're gonna want is gonna belong to sets, which give you stat buffs depending on how many pieces of the set you have equipped, and based on how many stat buffs a set maxes out at, you can get about 2-3 full set bonuses when fully kitted out. You have 2 weapons, 6 armor pieces, and 3 jewelry slots (2 rings and one necklace). Pieces of a set can be obtained two ways, boss drops in dungeons and then crafting, and there is no overlap, specific sets can only be found in dungeons while the others can only be crafted at specific stations in specific parts of Tamriel, some of which require DLCs to access. But it doesn't matter how you end up getting your gear, crafting is very important. Crafting is super simple, you only need two types of items to make it, the item which determines the quality of your gear which just determines the level of your gear and then the style material which is purely cosmetic but you still need one to craft anything, just one style material per item though, so don't worry. In order to craft higher level gear you need the necessary skills unlocked in the crafting category for that specifc type of crafting, there are 7, 4 of them are for gear, the other 3 or for consumables, each takes their own materials (except style materials) and need to be leveled up separately, this can be done by crafting items that belong it that category, disassembling gear, (gear made from other players and gear with bonuses listed for disassembling will give you the most XP for it) and doing writ quests, which require you to craft some specific items for rewards, you get one per crafting category per day. You can also put secondary effects on gear, which require their own items which you find through various means, and the only way to craft gear with these effects is to destroy gear with the effect to research it, which is put on a timer, which is an exponential increase each time you do it, going up to a month, it's really not that fun. The grind for gear is probably one of the most tedious parts about it, it's not hard, just time consuming, use some add-ons if you don't want to be searching forever for crafting materials, Zenimax allows it so it's fine.

The actual gameplay is actually quite fun, you end up getting two weapon slots for double the amount of skills you can use, just push a button to swap weapons and now you have different skills to use, what I often do is have my setup skills on one weapon while all of my attacks are on another. The name of the game is use your skills effectively, most classes have a "spam skill" that you're meant to use repeatedly when you're not using something else, and some classes are built around the spam skill, like the Arcanist, where each time you use the spam skill, you generate something called crux, and some skills consume it, and they get more powerful the more crux it consumes, I really like it and I think it's super fun. The game is most fun when played with a group, dungeons are 4 players, and then Trials are 15, and Trials are my favorite, especially when they're planned well, and it feels super good to win them, its really where the MMORPG magic shines. I also don't recommend playing in first person, it might feel more like Elder Scrolls that way, but you're putting yourself at a disadvantage, you'll be losing a lot of sight that way, and the game seems built around third person despite defaulting to first.

The graphics are much more cartoony than the other Elder Scrolls games, they don't look bad necessarily, Elder Scrolls games never looked that bad when compared to games of the time, but the ESO artstyle is different, and I think it fits well.

The Soundtrack isn't super special, it's mostly just rehashes of old songs from the series, but that doesn't stop it from sounding pretty good, all Orchestral and whatnot.

The writing in this game is pretty balls, it's very clear that story was not a huge concern for Zenimax, at least not in the dialogue, I never bothered listening to it, the stories were never that engaging, some of the story moments can be really cool, be it the bossfights or the end of the main story, but overall it leaves a lot to be desired, I love good stories, games like RDR2 and Cyberpunk 2077 have some of my favorite stories and my ears were wide open and listening to all the dialogue even though the games were dozens of hours long each.

This game is not lacking in content by any means, the base game alone will give you a couple dozen hours, both by doing the main story and going through all of the zone stories, I'd recommend doing a good chunk of the Base Game before deciding on buying any DLCs.

The DLCs in this game are a bit strange, first are the chapters, these are the big DLCs and they add the most content, usually in the form of new classes and mechanics, each chapter comes with a new Trial, a new area to explore, new quests, a new story, etc. After a chapter releases, soon after we get some smaller, follow-up DLC, these will be in the form of zone and dungeon DLCs, zone DLCs add new areas with new quests and story while the Dungeon DLCs add new replayable dungeons to grind for items in, neither Zone or Dungeon DLCs add new mechanics or classes, but these follow-up DLCs are also usually continuations of the Chapter DLC's story, if you care about that at all.

This game's community is a mixed bag, there are the enjoyers, and then the complainers, you'll see the enjoyers actually playing the game and are a part of a guild to do dungeons and trials with and help their fellow players out, while the complainers usually stick to the forums to bitch about whatever complaints they have, and sure, their complaints are valid, but I often see them crapping on people just trying to enjoy the game and asking questions on the forum to get help, stay away from the forums.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1737359488}, {"review_text": "---{ Graphics }---

NFS Most Wanted (2012) is a fun game as long you dont compare it to the original. However it is held down by severe input lag, which I have fortunately been able to fix by a little googling and finding a 4 year old thread with 20 upvotes.... I will share this info in case it is useful for anyone else who want to enjoy the game and to have some more visibility. Thanks to Cryio on Needforspeed subreddit for the fix.

[b] Step 1: [/b] 
Go to Documents > Criterion Games > Need For Speed(TM) Most Wanted > Open config.NFS13Save ini file with notepad

[b] Step 2: [/b]
Disable Vsync by changing VsyncInterval to 0 (VsyncInterval=0)

[b] Step 3: [/b]
Documents > Criterion Games > Need For Speed(TM) Most Wanted > Save > 1004299468619 (could be different for you) and Open controls.NFS13Save ini file with notepad (you might need to open the game first and change some settings for this to show up)

[b] Step 4: [/b]
Lower the right most value of STEERLEFT, STEERRIGHT, ACCELERATE, BRAKE, HANDBRAKE, NITROUS   from 1.00 to 0.10

For eg, in my case it ends up looking like this:
STEERLEFT=0,KEY_A,0.00,0.10
STEERRIGHT=0,KEY_D,0.00,0.10
ACCELERATE=0,KEY_W,0.00,0.10
BRAKE=0,KEY_S,0.00,0.10
HANDBRAKE=0,KEY_SPACE,0.00,0.10

[b] Optional Steps: [/b] 
To disable the horrible screen tearing the game has when disabling vsync, use Borderless gaming app to play in Borderless fullscreen which will eliminate the screen tearing. 

In NVIDIA control panel, set low latency mode for the game as ULTRA 

[b] Original reddit thread link for further reading if needed: [/b] [url=https://www.reddit.com/r/needforspeed/comments/hljwhm/nfs_most_wanted_2012_input_lag_fix_for_pc/] Link [/url]

The story here is absolutely forgettable. You start from the bottom, earn bounty through causing havoc and events, which you can complete to upgrade your car. After about an hour, you can challenge a rival. Beat them in a race, wreck their car to get their car, and repeat another 10-ish times until you're the 'Most Wanted,' an accolade that feels like you just won $2,000 at a casino after putting in $5,000. If you're here for the 2005 story, forget it. There are no names here, let alone significant adversaries to captivate you.

With that said, the game is perfect on the couch. It works with a controller out-of-the-box, and the graphics pass alright for 2024, especially with 4K and ambient-occlusion support. You access cars by finding them parked around the map, and [obligatory BMW M3 reference]. The map is one of my favourites of the NFS franchise: representing what I think is Boston, it contains a freeway spanning the map, an airfield and an airport, spinny-donut-ramp-things, billboards and speed cameras for you to cry about your friends' records, and a park where you can do jumps and bully the police AI. - The simulation is more in-depth than CS1, but it is half-baked because Colossal/Paradox needed more development time for this game. There are a lot of nuanced characteristics which dictate how citizens own houses in the game, for example, but Colossal/Paradox are always tweaking those variables in each patch because of how unprepared it was. 

The CONS of CS2:

Each patch tweaks these variables to make the game better, but the devs are kinda playing a game of whack-a-mole because each change they make has cascading effects. 
- If you have a low-end PC, don't bother running the game. Like I stated in the PROS section, if your PC has some oomph behind it, you can and will be able to build BIG. I also recommend forcing it to run in DirectX 12 - this solved my stuttering.

I am so very glad I solved the performance issues of this game. It's not only one of the very best Star Wars games of all time, but it's also one of the most compelling Star Wars stories of all time, with some of the best Star Wars characters of all time, and definitely the best droid of all time. It's also an amazing refinement of the action adventure genre to the point that Miyazaki himself could learn a thing or two from it.

By the time the credits rolled, no zone was less than 95% explored, and at no point in that exploration did anything feel forced.

Tip = Turn OFF Raytracing to stop it crashing! :)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 24, "timestamp_created": 1745525991}, {"review_text": "WARNING: Before You Buy Star Wars Jedi: Survivor

Jedi: Survivor is a strong follow-up to Fallen Order, and in most ways, a better game. It expands on what worked before—combat, exploration, story—and gives players more freedom, more customization, and more to sink their time into. But like the first game, it’s not without its flaws. If you’re planning to jump in, here’s what you should know.

The story picks up a few years after Fallen Order, with Cal Kestis continuing his fight against the Empire. Without spoiling anything, the narrative feels more mature, and while the stakes are higher, it still keeps a focus on Cal’s personal growth. It avoids leaning too heavily on existing Star Wars characters, which helps it feel like its own story. The worldbuilding is solid, and there’s a good balance between quiet character moments and large-scale set pieces.

Combat is a clear highlight. There are now five lightsaber stances, including dual wield, crossguard, and a saber/blaster combo. This variety lets you adjust your playstyle depending on the fight. It still feels weighty and skill-based like Fallen Order, but it’s a bit smoother and more flexible. Boss fights and tougher enemies can be challenging, but never feel unfair. It rewards timing and patience without being overly punishing.

Exploration is much more open this time. Planets like Koboh are massive and layered, with side areas, hidden upgrades, and plenty of optional content. You’ll unlock mounts and new traversal abilities that make getting around easier, and yes—fast travel is now a thing. You can move between unlocked meditation points, which helps reduce unnecessary backtracking, though you’ll still have to do a bit of it if you're hunting everything down.

If you’re going for 100%, be aware that collectible hunting can feel repetitive. There’s a huge amount of cosmetic items, lore logs, and hidden upgrades. Some are fun to find, others feel like padding. The map is better than the first game’s, but it can still be unclear in vertical areas or tight spaces.

Now the biggest issue: performance. Even after multiple patches, there are still bugs—occasional crashes, texture pop-ins, and frame rate dips. They’re not constant and don’t make the game unplayable, but they can interrupt the experience. If you’re someone who wants everything to run perfectly, these issues might get in the way, especially during more cinematic or intense moments. For most players, it won’t ruin the game—but it’s something to keep in mind.

Enemy AI also varies. Some encounters feel smart and well-paced, while others are let down by odd behavior or enemies getting stuck. Side quests and bounty missions are a mixed bag—some are worthwhile, others feel like filler.

Jedi: Survivor takes what Fallen Order started and pushes it further without losing what made the original great. It’s fun, cinematic, and packed with moments that feel genuinely memorable. It’s not perfect, but it doesn’t need to be to leave an impact. If you’re looking for a solid Star Wars game with strong gameplay and story, this is a good pick.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1750407694}, {"review_text": "Oggdo Bogdo and the Spawn of Oggdo are the actual final bosses of the game. For me, I am enjoying the game on medium to high graphics with zero crashes post patch.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1743787739}, {"review_text": "I'm making this review for the benefit of the upcoming Summer Steam sale, 2025, when I'm sure there'll be a lot of folks thinking about adding STAR WARS Jedi: Survivor to their library.

As a Gen X guy who grew up on Star Wars, whose favourite Star Wars console game was probably Force Unleashed for PS3 and XWing for the old 386DX PC, I'll say that Jedi: Survivor is a fantastic console game with great writing, characters, graphics, and gameplay.

I didn't connect well with this game's predecessor, Jedi: Fallen Order, so I was pretty apprehensive about this one.  I didn't like how I felt FO was too heavy a platformer-puzzle game vs. fighting and maybe being a Jedi?  I don't know, but I didn't connect with it.

This game started to feel like that, stiff, puzzle-y, so I was unsure.  Sticking with the game, however, and as Cal gains more abilities and unlocks new ability trees, the experience truly 'opens up' to allow the player to revisit earlier levels to access what was previously cut off.

From a writing perspective, I'm graciously offered an update to all the plot I didn't see when I chose not to continue playing Fallen Order, and the pieces of the past game mesh nicely with the plot of the current AND ties to the greater STAR WARS canonical past.  There are also very good moments where Cal, now separated from the Jedi order, comes to terms with human emotions without guidance.  It's good, and allows some credence to some of the otherwise more violent choices that Cal makes in his sometimes very agressive combat.

Speaking of combat, it flows well.  The player starts with a basic lightsaber, but in short time they will be given a series of lightsaber stances (like dual wield, or double bladed staff, plus new and older styles), force powers (a variety of interesting ones), and it feels very satisfying to slice through hordes of combat droids with huge swinging arcs of lightsaber combined with force crushing and pushing off high spaces.

Graphics are 2025 standard.  What I mean is that if you have an RTX capable card you'll be rewarded.  Sound is equally impressive if you are one of the select few of us who know that onboard audio controllers suck.  I crank my Edifiers through my SBGC7 and it feels movie-quality.

Play for a few hours and you'll eventually get access to your 'hub' of activity, where you can access stores, do mini games, exercise your right to view your collection of Star Wars trinkets you bought, give yourself a mullet and long handlebar moustache, before going to revisit older levels with your newly-learnt mobility power.

I am a slower player, and I'm about 50 hours in to the game.  I have quite a long way to go.  I have not completed the main plot (although if I'm wrong in my assumption as to where this plot leads I'll be absolutely shocked: if there's a twist incoming I've seen it all along), so the verdict is out on what happens next.   Side note: I used to love how, in Force Unleashed, you could be Starkiller as a Sith with the right skins and powers - I wonder if that's an option for Cal?  I don't think so.  I doubt it.  Cal feels like he's just going to be a good guy. 

I'd be remiss to not mention the humour that runs throughout in this game.  There are so many very well-written characters that are both brand new and based in some of the more contemporary Star Wars canon (like from the Mandalorian, for example). 

Are there those platforming sequences that feel like just a big puzzle?  Yes.  Yes there are.  Cal climbs everywhere - everywhere!  He's constantly jumping from clingable wall to rope to ledge to ceiling to wall run and everything in between.  But thankfully, the most difficult of these sequences are few and far between and when they are present, I'll tell ya, they tend to be visually stunning experiences.

SO.  You have this game on your wishlist and it's on sale for Steam Summer in 2025?  Do you like Star Wars?  Do you like to use a controller?  Do yourself a favour and grab this game.  

I'm confident to say that Jedi Survivor is my new favourite Star Wars game (although playing Starkiller as a Sith was pretty rad)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1750255968}, {"review_text": "Still very buggy at times, crashes for no reason, seems to be a total resource hog.  still fun to play, but can't say I can recommend a game that crashes. Let me just preface that I REALLY love Apex Legends and have played it since launch (Console switch to PC) I have spent GODLY amounts of $$$ into this game because I love it so much. So... Why am I not recommending it? That's because Apex Legends is a shell of the game it once was. a once beloved game by a respected developer turned into a Soulless Cash-grab. Apex legends is the only game I have ever played that made me wish loot-boxes were still the industry norm. With the changes to legends making certain characters OVER OP (Lifeline) to ridiculous metas (Lifeline, Newcastle, MASTIFF.) All the joy of hopping into a match with your friends and playing either quick play or comp have been eviscerated like that cousin you hate. By far the WORST change to happen in Apex is the battlepass changes and the store revamp. Remember when Heirlooms were $128 when a new one was released? well now you can get a CSGO Karambit Knife for $200!!! [{"review_text": "A Unique Blend of MOBA and Battle Royale with Room for Improvement

Eternal Return offers a fresh take on the battle royale genre by combining elements of MOBA gameplay with survival mechanics. Set on the mysterious Lumia Island, players choose from a diverse cast of characters, each with unique abilities and playstyles, to outlast opponents in intense matches.

Gameplay and Mechanics
The game's core mechanics revolve around crafting, combat, and strategy. Players gather resources, craft weapons and items, and engage in battles with other players or AI-controlled creatures. The crafting system is intuitive, allowing for quick upgrades and customization during matches. However, some players have reported issues with unresponsive controls and inconsistent skill usage, which can affect the overall experience .

Visuals and Design
Visually, Eternal Return stands out with its anime-inspired art style. The character designs are detailed, and the environments are well-crafted, providing an immersive experience. The game's aesthetic appeals to fans of anime and adds a unique charm to the battle royale genre.

Community and Matchmaking
One of the game's significant challenges is its player base. Outside of Korea, finding matches can be time-consuming, and the community's activity varies by region. Some players have expressed concerns about the game's balance, particularly regarding certain characters dominating the meta, which can lead to frustration .

Monetization and Progression
Eternal Return is free-to-play, with monetization primarily through cosmetic items and character unlocks. While the game offers a battle pass and seasonal content, some players have found the progression system to be grindy, requiring significant time investment to unlock all content .

Final Thoughts
Eternal Return is an ambitious title that successfully merges elements of MOBA and battle royale genres. Its unique gameplay mechanics and appealing visuals make it a standout in the free-to-play market. However, issues with matchmaking, character balance, and progression may deter some players. For those interested in a strategic and fast-paced battle royale experience, Eternal Return is worth exploring.

Rating: 7/10 – A promising game with areas needing refinement", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 16, "timestamp_created": 1749247863}, {"review_text": "Eternal Return combines MOBA-style combat, survival mechanics, and battle royale intensity into a fast-paced, anime-inspired multiplayer experience. With a growing roster of unique characters, strategic gameplay, and deep item crafting, it’s a game that rewards skill and adaptability.

The Good:
✅ Unique Genre Blend: The mix of MOBA, survival, and battle royale makes for a fresh and exciting experience.
✅ Diverse Character Roster: Each character has distinct skills, playstyles, and abilities, offering deep strategy.
✅ Strategic Gameplay: You must craft gear, manage resources, and adapt to changing zones to survive.
✅ Frequent Updates & New Content: Developers consistently add new characters, balance changes, and events.
✅ Free-to-Play Done Right: No pay-to-win mechanics—progression is based on skill, strategy, and knowledge.

The Bad:
❌ Steep Learning Curve: Mastering crafting, combat, and strategy can be intimidating for new players.
❌ Matchmaking Can Be Hit or Miss: Sometimes unbalanced matches can affect the experience.
❌ Limited Player Base in Some Regions: Finding matches quickly may be an issue in less populated areas.
❌ Solo Play Can Feel Tough: While duos and squads shine, playing solo can feel overwhelming at times.

Final 
If you enjoy strategic battle royales with MOBA mechanics and deep character progression, Eternal Return is a hidden gem worth trying. However, be prepared for a steep learning curve and some matchmaking inconsistencies.

This review is written from the perspective of someone who has played this game for a few years, has been in high ELO in NA the majority of that time, and despite being bad at the game, has played in and among the NA competitive scene from seasons 3-6. 

     Let me start by talking about the things this game does well. This game has a large cast of interesting and diverse characters, and if you enjoy MOBAs, there will be at least one character in the game that you will enjoy. The concept of the game is pretty unique, and the pacing of the game is extremely fast for the genre, which makes it really fun to learn if you are willing to put in the time, and you will finish games where you are severely out-skilled far faster than you would in most other games in the genre. The crafting and looting mechanics are unique and quite enjoyable, though they have taken a bit of a back seat over the years and have been simplified to the point where they are more of a chore than a fun and engaging mechanic. The movement in this game is very fluid, to the point where I constantly complain how slow and clunky the movement in League of Legends feels whenever I go back to playing that game with friends. 

     Now, let's address the current issues with this game. The game, as it stands, has a very bad tutorial, and leaves many new players confused or uninformed about many of the games mechanics and the general flow of the game. While this issue is not unique to this game, and is quite common within the genre, this is a major factor contributing to the low player retention in this game. Most people that randomly download a game to try do not want to join community discord servers and ask players how the game works in order to learn how to play the game. The new player experience in general is quite bad at the moment. They go from bot games that don't really help them improve to immediately being dumped into the same norms lobbies as immortal players that are three stacking because ranked isn't popping yet, partially due to the NA player-base being so small that MMR for norms wont help since only one or two lobbies of norms are popping the majority of the day. Another  major issue this game has is frequent bugs that cause gameplay issues, client crashes, and matchmaking to break. While there has been a massive improvement the past two years, I have noticed a sudden increase in these bugs again recently, and it is concerning since last time this was happening the player count dropped massively and took months to recover. Another major issue is that Nimble Neuron seems to balance around pick rate over performance. Characters that consistently have been extremely strong continue to get buffs despite massively over-performing because they maintain a low pick rate. I'm not going to get into my personal opinions on how the game should be balanced and what characters and classes need to get taken down a peg or be buffed, but Nimble Neuron needs to understand that making a character more and more over tuned to try to get more people to play them is not healthy for the game. This game also needs significantly more promotion in the west, try doing cheap sponsorship campaigns through StreamLabs/Twitch to get a large number of smaller streamers to stream the category and show the game to new audiences, do more art competitions on multiple social media platforms, hire someone to edit clips and compilations from official events and post them on YouTube and TikTok to showcase gameplay to a large potential audience, and I am 100% certain that this game will start to grow significantly in the west. Games need new players constantly because even the most dedicated of fans will burn out or eventually just grow apart from the game, and without new players, the game will eventually die. A larger player-base will help with many issues the game is facing in the west, and I can not stress how much this would help with player retention and the general matchmaking experience in both ranked and norms in the west. 

     Overall, I love this game, and that is why I feel it is important to address the issues with it. Please Nimble Neuron, if you are reading this, consider some of the things I've said. I want this game to grow and be successful, but in order for it to do so, there are many things that need to be  addressed, especially when it comes to the new player experience and your advertising in the west.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1753706939}, {"review_text": "This game is capital D Doomed. By now, everyone remotely interested in this genre has heard of it, given it a shot, and slammed the door on it for one reason or another. And who can blame them? Let’s tally them up: a learning curve that feels more like a wall (yes, skill issue, but come on—it’s practically an ant hill compared to the speedrun simulator it used to be); a sparse player base (outside Korea, it’s a ghost town); balance that’s been broken since day one (mages at the top of the rankings like they own it, which, let’s face it, they do; can you remember a season in which they weren't overwhelming?); and a ranked system so bullshit and easily inflated that high-tier matches outside of Korea feel like an after-school Gold lobby.

This game is pretty generous in term of gifts and rewards, you can get a lot of free cosmetics (  skins , emotes , backgrounds , etc...),

What I like most about this game is the gameplay loop , you can feel your progress in every part of the game :
-Optimising your loadout to allow you to have the best preparation possible (you can always select recommended ones). 
-How fast you complete your items early game .
-Where and how to farm animals optimally .
-Your decision making when it comes to moving on the map , what objective to contest.
-Your skill level , some characters are extremely demanding in terms of clics and awareness .

As you can see from what I previously stated , I totally recommend this game . 
Biggest issue imo is the lack of players in some regions that can make queue time pretty long depending on when you are trying to play , but don't give up , I hope you will be able to see why I love this game .

[{"review_text": "Way too many people sleeping on this game just because 66L exist, despite this game is one of the most feature complete fighting game out there.

Rising has:
- Rollback
- Crossplay
- Free Version
- Tons of cosmetics from the progression system

- Minigames", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1747805457}, {"review_text": "I'll be honest, after playing this game for a full year, GBVSR is sick.

I can't tell how many things GBVSR does well compared to other fighting games of this era and yet, it's not as popular despite all the good things we have in this !  
It really feels like a polished game overall.

- Menus are working well and everything is accessible easily without having to search for decades.

- Good online, rollback, matchmaking, lobbies, no issue ! (It's almost fun to just walk around and talk with people in the lobby)

- Ranked is also working well. (although it has a lot of wifi warriors and AFK players in lower ranks.)

- Lots of different modes outside of online battles. (story, arcade, figure, Grandbruise although there is not enough mini games and not many people to play with, robomi and we are getting survival mode in 2.0 ver !)

- Many Characters, all created with lots of love to the source material. (Vikala even has a JustinWong meme reference) 
Each character has a lot of different color and weapon skins.  

- Balancing is overall pretty great ! We had some busted characters and still have 66L spam but the devs are listening and after playing this game for a full year, I think it was great compared to other games. (and also the fact fighting games are HARD to make and balance.)

- Training mode has a lot of options although I would add a frame meter just like SF6 does. (a mod exist for that at least)

- Lots of different input options and macros available to play exactly like you want !

- A generous FREE version of the game is available and simple controls makes the game easy to access, they are well implemented and don't feel clunky or limited like other fighting games.
I introduced so many friends to fighting games thanks to this game. (some of them still play to this day !)

- You may have heard fighting games have DLC and battle pass issues, but GBVSR let's you buy the DLCs with the in game money !
You need to grind a bit but it won't take you months and months to get what you want. (If you want every DLC though... Good luck lol.) 
For Battle Passes, the content is overall great for those who want them, it's completely optional and the free version is also cool.
I'm not really the type of player who will buy the BPs but none of them made me feel like it was a scam and they now sell you the content of older BPs as DLC if you missed one of them.

Overall, I really like this game because it's one of the rare ones where I just like to hang out in it, play a couple of games, have fun with Grandbruise for a little break and tchat with others.
I traveled in tourneys for this game and I lived so many great things because of it.

The devs are communicating well with the players and creates really fun things for us. (See their April Fools Joke as a reference, it was a fun thing !)
It's useless but they did it anyway, It just feels like they also have fun creating the game and it's just so cool.
We will even get Pop Team Epic crossover for lobby avatars ! Why ? Don't know but it's amusing ! 

Thanks for all the hard work you have done GBVSR Team, Arcsys and Cygames.
I'm genuinely happy with all the content you did and hope the season 2 will be just as fun and exciting as the first one.

Granblue Fantasy Versus is a fighting game made for a gacha game, and Rising is the upgraded version of the original Versus, with rollback netcode and some updates to the formula.

This game has one button specials, for the people who that matters for, though you can do the regular inputs for pretty much no benefit besides comfort. Character movesets are quite unique and frequently come with significant gimmicks that you need to keep in mind, and damage is for the most part on the low to middling range, though TODs and 70%+ combos can be achieved in rare situations or by certain characters with plenty of meter to spare.

There is a block button, though it's not necessary to use besides for its 'Dodge' function, as there is also a universal unblockable option that costs a secondary resource; the punishment for losing which is taking additional damage, and getting hit by this unblockable option, getting hit by supers, or using the 'get off me' button will use this secondary resource. If you lose all of this resource, the high damage combos  get significantly easier and a lot of characters will likely be able to 1 touch you by that point in the round. You'll need to get used to using the block button for the purpose of using the dodge and avoiding that.

It's neat, it's a bit gimmicky, and if you feel like playing Gran and only Gran, you can get the game for free. The Free edition also has a rotation of characters for you to try out each week or every two weeks (i don't remember).

It has an active enough playerbase, rollback netcode, cute avatars in the lobby system, and a decent enough ranking system. The skill floor is low and all characters are easy to pick up and play, because they all share a similar combo structure. Also has a free version that lets you use Gran alongside a rotation of 3 non-DLC characters in all game modes. 

My biggest problem (for mid-level play and up) is that 66l and brave counter kind screw the flow up this game up. 66L centralizes the neutral: it's a plus on block move, long reach, 9 frame startup (8 +1 for dash start-up), whiff punishes,and generally the best answer for many decisions in this game. 66L helps make this game feel super volatile, along with half screen jump scares. Brave counter is a needed mechanic to deal with the strong stagger pressure in this game, but it's very mindless in the state it's in currently. Not enough counters to it, PLUS 6 on block, and gives a hard knockdown on counter-hit. While it markets itself as an accessible game that's very beginner-friendly, that's not to say that it lacks any depth. This has turned out to be one of my favorite types of fighting games, or really just games in general. Fairly low skill floor, insanely high skill ceiling. It won't take long for you get some exceptionally sweaty people to face off against both in ranked and casual matches, but that's where everything Rising provides comes in handy. Everything from its detailed but easy-to-understand character guides and combo lists in training mode, frame data, tutorials for pretty much every single mechanic in the game, it's all here. Technical inputs exist, and in many ways, mashing your face onto your controller as we all do when we start off will get you killed, just as it was in the OG GBVS, but simple inputs make timings much easier to chain your normals into your specials. The addition of the Bravery Points system for raging strikes, raging chains, and how these points also interact with supers and how much damage you deal the less of it your opponents has is a great addition, and more than makes up for the removal of a universal overhead. And the U-versions of your cooldown skills are also a great addition, giving you much more options with your meter outside of just using supers. It also helps that compared to the OG GBVS, you get a TON of meter now. It used to be that filling your meter took basically the entire round, and it was mostly only ever used for supers despite it having other utilities that have since been removed. There's a lot to consider, but none of it ever felt overwhelming, and that's even considering how much faster the pace of Rising is now compared to the first game. Even if Cygames themselves likes to meme on this game being centered around "one button for easy kills" like that hilarious April Fools trailer, the game's far more than that. The addition of dash attacks is currently one of the more controversial things about the game, and I admit, it does feel like 66L is way too good for literally every character, but for the most part, it hasn't felt like the "I Win Button" that a lotta folks seem to frame it.

But all that minutia's for the sweats. I'm a filthy casul, so let's move onto Rising's story mode and some of its other features. Rising does get rid of the old RPG Mode which makes for a leaner experience for its story, though I do miss being able to select basically the entire roster at the end game when I wanna fight certain bosses, and there's no longer the Tower of Babyl for some extra challenge either. It's definitely leaning heavier now on being a visual novel with some occasional cool animated cutscenes and bosses to fight. The additional chapter they added doesn't even have trash mob quests anymore, but I think for its short run time, those weren't necessary, and they weren't the best part of the original story mode anyway. I like that this new chapter just focuses on the most important characters and events, raises the stakes far more than the original did, and just has the VN-style chapters leading into all the different boss fights.

Without spoiling anything, this game now has quite possibly my two favorite bosses in any fighting game, both in terms of how cool I think they are as characters, how satisfying they are to beat up, and most importantly, how they play. A lotta the times, fighting game bosses break the rules in ways that aren't that fun. They go from just standing or floating there, letting you wail on them for a bit, before they do boring things like raise their arms to conjure up some high damage projectile, or even leave the arena to make you fight someone else in the roster. I'm lookin' at you, Kronika. But that's not the case with Rising. The final bosses have actual movesets. Hell, they're playable in ranked for a reason. It's just that they hurt way more, have way more moves that have armor, and have that good ol' Overdrive mechanic. Without the old RPG Mode's elemental weapons and levels to consider, it is much easier to just straight up fight everything now, but the Hard mode for the story bosses is still a decent challenge.

All of this, and you're rewarded with a strange, Skyrealm-shattering tale that somehow kinda still makes sense, despite involving epic Biblical levels of gods and angels fighting each other, parallel universes colliding, some genuine emotional drama, and the mandatory cutesy anime trash. I love it. All this just so we have a proper lore excuse to have the male and female versions of the Granblue Fantasy MC being able to meet and fight each other online, as well as explaining the mirror matches, because this is still a fighting game.

For the most part, everything in Rising is a vast improvement over the original, and with its addition of crossplay on top of rollback, even though I'm already over a year late to this party, I'm still getting a ton of matches daily, there's still lobbies getting full at peak hours, and even when I'm at a losing streak, they've added a lotta other features that take my mind off it. Modes like Grand Bruise, which is the blatant Fall Guys ripoff that's genuinely pretty fun if you're willing to wait a little while to be matched up with several other people, or just the larger, more expansive, and way prettier lobby to wander around in, or the minigames. And my god, that Figure Studio. That's my end game now. It's basically a photo mode that lets you play around with 3D assets ranging from every character in the roster to side characters, to even just world objects. I'm still gonna play online, get salty, try to escape A rank with Vira and B rank with Beatrix, but the end goal now is to get every possible figure so I can take funny screenshots with my favorite waifus in the roster.

I'm glad Granblue Versus got this second chance. Back then all I and a lot of other people wanted was rollback. Now, we got it, and everything else, even a free edition that lets you play ranked as Gran and three other characters that rotate weekly, the first third of the story mode, and any progress you make is carried over when you buy the game. And they're not done. At the time of this review, Sandalphon's out and Galleon just got teased. Issues like a few mfs trying to manipulate ranked got dealt with. There was a recent crossover event with Guilty Gear Strive. Tournaments are still being played. Ilsa's on the horizon. There's never been a better time to jump in. Granblue Fantasy Versus Rising is the perfect game for me, and I think it’s great for anyone who wants to play an anime fighter (or fighting game in general) without being overwhelmed by long combos or high execution requirements.

It plays fast without sacrificing clarity. Even though it uses modern fighting game features like auto-combos and special move shortcuts, it’s not dumbed down at all — there’s still plenty of depth.

[h2] Character Roster [/h2] 
Right now there are 38 playable characters, with one more on the way. (Season 3 hasn’t been announced yet, so we’ll see.) Every character feels distinct, so you can easily find an archetype that fits your playstyle. Some characters even come with extra gimmicks that make them stand out more.

[h2] Online Experience [/h2] 
Matchmaking has been fine for me so far. I’m playing from Indonesia (SEA) with a so-so internet provider, and I can still get stable matches against players from Japan and China. Disclaimer: I use a cable connection — and you should too.

The playerbase is still active enough that you can find online matches without long queue times. And since the game has crossplay, the actual number of players is bigger than what SteamDB shows.

[h2] Single Player Content [/h2]
There's Story Mode, Arcade Mode, and Survival Mode (where you get random power-up bonuses every 5 rounds). That’s already enough for a proper single-player experience.

Is the story only for Granblue Fantasy fans? Not really. Newcomers can still enjoy it because the game includes glossaries and character bios. The cast is lovable enough that you won’t feel alienated or lost.

[h2] Art Style & Soundtrack [/h2]
The art direction is chef’s kiss 🤌 and the soundtrack goes hard. Every character has a theme that fits their personality and vibe, and almost all of them are bangers.

[h2] Price & Monetization [/h2]
I suggest to grab the Deluxe Edition when it’s on sale (usually around 60% off). You’ll get the base game plus Deluxe Character Pass 1, which already unlocks about 87% of the roster. Most of the other DLC aside from Character Pass 2 — are cosmetics only and is purely optional.

There is also seasonal Battle Pass, which also unlocks more cosmetics contents. [b] Do note that with recent updates, some battle pass exclusives item (costumes, weapon skins, exclusive colors) will be sold as separate DLC at later date. [/b] So less FOMO contents I guess?

If you’re still unsure, there’s also a free-to-play version. It limits you to 4 rotating characters and locks most modes outside of online lobbies, but it’s enough to test the waters.

[h2] Overall [/h2]
This game is fun for both casual players and competitive ones. Like I said earlier, every character is charming in their own way, so you’ll definitely find someone to love — whether that’s for their design, gameplay, personality, or the whole package.

[b] Now go give Cygames your money so we can get Season 3! As much enjoyment the rpg mode and single player content that had to offer, I wanted to play with real humans, and at the time, servers were EMPTY (because dumb me purchased the ps4 version), to make matters worse, with a global pandemic, naturally no locals to play this game offline either

These two factors alone made me reconsider my choice for fighting games, and I end up settling up with Guilty Gear Strive , but always wondering, when granblue will received same treatment? 

Well, that thought lasted 3 years, because finally in 2023 we had a proper version of granblue versus with rollback, but it's not technically the same game but more so a 2.0 version of an already existing game, you get 3 new characters, new mechanics, all the previous dlc characters and most important for me, rollback netcode with crossplay!

GBVSR simply put, its mix between street fighter and anime , it has a bigger focus on spacing and footsies, but at the same time borrow things you typically see on anime fighting games like air blocks or rolls, it has a bigger focus on approachability and accessibility making a great fighting game for starters.

With that said, I must put and asterisk, as GBVSR isn't a super popular game like sf6 or tekken 8 and likely you encounter people who might have way more experience playing the game, but for those are unsure about buying, there's a free version that let's you play online with rotating character so give it a try.

As for those who want single player content, I don't think this game will be for you, there's less offline content , and things you can unlock feels more geared towards people who play the game online, if you happened to have already the vanilla game and didn't care for the online portion I think this will be much harder game to justify the money, as for me, it's one of my favourite modern fighting games.

Tldr : Fun gighting game that mix between anime fighter and street fighter , with proper rollback and crossplay, not so much  value added on singleplayer side, so might not be worth it for everyone", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1734897030}]

[{"review_text": "[h1]Confession of a Newbie[/h1]
[hr]                                                                                                                                                                                            [/hr]
I have never been particularly close to the Resident Evil game franchise. I watched all the movies with Milla Jovovich, but I’ve only heard something about the games somewhere, and they never really left a deep impression on me. The hype around the Resident Evil remaster passed me by because it didn’t evoke any nostalgia or positive emotions. As a result, my opinion about the game will be an honest reflection of its core without sugarcoating.
I would like to start with the positive aspects. What really surprised me was the unusual setting of the game. When I first launched RE 2, I thought it would be a game in the style of Dead Space, but how mistaken I was. Naively shooting all my bullets at useless zombies and thinking I no longer needed to conserve ammo because there were no enemies I couldn’t handle, I encountered him… Tyrant. At that moment, my gameplay turned upside down because now I was not the hunter — Mr. X became the hunter. He didn’t react to gunfire in the usual way; instead, he punished even the slightest delay with a brutal death animation. From that moment on, there’s no room for error when he appears — you can’t afford to waste time studying the map, because he’s always nearby. Even if you think you’ve hidden successfully, he mysteriously appears behind your back at the worst moment, scaring you out of your mind. Most likely, my gaming experience was influenced by the fact that I thought I’d be playing a different game — and how awesome that was!
I was definitely pleased with the nice graphics, engine physics, and storyline. But with all due respect, why is the game so short? I understand it’s just a remaster and that we have access to a second storyline, but I still wanted more. Surely those who bought the game at launch were left asking themselves: “Is that it? Was that all? What did I spend my money on?” However, I bought it at a big discount and can’t complain — for its price, it justified every euro spent. Perhaps those are all the cons. With updated graphics, refined gameplay mechanics, and a deep focus on storytelling, this remake is a masterclass in survival horror.[/b]

[h1]A Returning Classic[/h1]
[b]The game offers two intertwined perspectives, showcasing both Leon Kennedy's and Claire Redfield's struggles during the outbreak. Leon's journey highlights his transformation from a rookie cop to a hardened survivor, while Claire’s path focuses on her determination to protect Sherry Birkin, a child caught in the chaos. Both stories are well-developed, offering a sense of depth and emotional connection to the characters.[/b]

[h1]Engaging Multiple Perspective Gameplays[/h1]
[b]The addition of Ada Wong's segments brings a fresh layer of intrigue, as her espionage-themed gameplay contrasts perfectly with the survival horror. Similarly, the Ghost Survivors mode introduces side stories of other characters, exploring what-ifs and adding more replayability to the game.[/b]

[h1]Visuals and Atmosphere[/h1]
[b]Visually, the game is stunning, with the RE Engine delivering atmospheric lighting and grotesque enemy designs. Every encounter with zombies and the relentless Mr. X feels heart-stopping, thanks to impeccable sound design and dynamic music that heightens tension. Sometimes Mr. X comes out of nowhere and that is Scary AF.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Faithful yet innovative retelling of a classic.
[*]Stunning visuals and terrifying atmosphere.
[*]Engaging dual-protagonist campaigns with meaningful storylines.
[*]Replayable content with Ghost Survivors mode.
[*]Intense and satisfying survival horror gameplay.
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Some puzzles may feel repetitive.
[*]Mr. X's relentless pursuit can be frustrating for some players.
[/list]
[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]The Resident Evil 2 Remake is a love letter to fans of the original while being an excellent entry point for newcomers. Prior to RE2 Remake the only RE game that I know like the back of my hand was RE4. I have played it religiously as a kid on my PS2 and that gave me the initial entry to the RE Universe. RE2 Remake was nothing like the previous RE games that I have played but it didn't make me feel like it was distant because some elements that were familiar to me were present. I haven't played all the RE games and I know each one will have similarities and significant differences when it comes to the story, game play etc. This review has been crafted, and is a reflection of my opinion that's been influenced based on what RE games are familiar to me, what I've played, and the capacity of my RE Universe knowledge.

Since RE is mostly about zombies, of course Combat is gonna be a big part of it. 
The combat system present in all the [b]remakes[/b] is streamlined and identical. But this was a breath of fresh air from RE4,RE5, and RE6 which I've previously played. 
Zombies and bosses work differently here unlike the other games where you can potentially purge everyone you see.

RE2 Remake(and to some extension the other remakes) will teach you:
-Resource, and inventory management. 
-Picking your fights
-Learning silly movements and juking zombies as if you're playing Dead by Daylight
-Pathings that you take will either be beneficial or consequential in your run.

Some will say that you can easily see these things being present in the other RE games, fair point. 
But fighting zombies in this game is not as straightforward as you thought so. You have to rely on crits, aim on certain areas, head shots won't guarantee a kill, and you have to double down on them to [u]make sure the undead is actually dead[/u]

The storytelling, shifting thru different characters and world building is insane. This game also allows you to learn more and touch up on stories of characters that would usually be written out or just finished for the plot's sake. In some sense you won't be leaving this game wondering too much about [hr]What happened to this person? Is there more that I can learn about them[/hr]

Overall this game is superb and I would rate it 10/10, it is expected that you might see this game differently because we have varying experiences and knowledge about the RE Universe so not knowing some characters or stories might confuse you and not give you the same effect. Unless you're just like me with the same circumstances.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758655617}, {"review_text": "At the beginning, I felt tempted to play because the graphics are amazing. Then I realized the game is very rich in horror—and it is.
The whole game is dark and has a macabre atmosphere, with blood on the floor and walls, broken windows and doors, storms, jump scares, and tight spaces.
In my first playthrough, I didn't find it too difficult to explore and complete the objectives. Basically, your map is very dynamic and shows if you’ve cleared 100% of a room or if there are still missed items. Because of this, it becomes easy to find and loot items.

In my opinion, the most difficult part of this game isn't getting lost while looking for mission items, but rather managing and saving weapon ammo. In some parts of the game, you’ll face a lot of enemies with very limited ammo. In your first playthrough, you’ll probably often find yourself running out of ammo or having very little left. On your second run, you’ll suffer because the game is sooooooooo miserable when it comes to ammo.

The character gameplay is good but not perfect. It’s very slow, and it’s hard to get past zombies without taking damage. In some scenarios, like the sewers, you’ll struggle a lot if you don’t have enough ammo. The story is pretty amazing—too bad Leon and Claire don’t interact much, unlike in the classic RE.

I understand that RE games don’t focus on combat or killing hordes of zombies. The main focus is survival, saving items and resources and using them at the right time. But, man... The fact that you need to spam bullets just to kill one zombie is frustrating. You save ammo the entire game, and then, when you have 60 bullets, you face three zombies, kill them, and suddenly you’re low on ammo again. I know this is part of the old RE experience, but if we could kill a zombie with seven headshots, fine. But two full clips? That’s just too much.

The boss fights, for me, are very good. They’re challenging, but after finishing the game two or three times, you’ll get the hang of it.

I really recommend this RE. The horror is amazing, and all the character models are incredible, whether it’s the survivors or the zombies. I’ve finished it three times, and it’s worth it.
