RE3R rightfully receives a lot of critics for cutting a lot of content from the OG RE3: Nemesis, but I barely hear people complaining about the fact that RE2R cut almost all the differences the original game had between a playthrough A and B. 

The TLDR review is: Resident Evil 2 (1998) is better. Much better. I would recommend playing the original versions of RE2 and RE3 before (or even instead of) the remakes. You can find them on GOG for a fair price. But I understand most people nowadays may not be inclined to deal with tank controls and PS1 graphics, and, if you are one of those, just enjoy RE2R and RE3R for what they are. 

From now on, the review will have SPOILERS:

In RE2, you run through scenario A with Claire or Leon and then you go through scenario B with the other character (the canon way is Claire A, Leon B by the way). In the 1998 game this will lead you to different boss encounters during each run. 

G-Creature, for example, is always the first boss for scenario A, no matter wich character you chose, and that boss fight is not reutilized in scenario B. The same goes for the giant crocodile: it is the second boss for scenario A, but doesn't appear in scenario B. The final boss fight for scenario A is always the 4th form of Birkin (which is also exclusive to scenario A). In scenario B, the first boss will always be the 1st form of Birkin, you'll have to deal with Mr. X and the final boss is the 5th form of Birkin. All of those encounters exclusive to scenario B.

You can see they made an effort to distinguish scenario A and B. Not only the characters have exclusive weapons, but they also interact with different characters throughout the campaign and have to beat different bosses. By the other hand, in RE2R you'll deal with some bosses in your scenario A and then you'll have to beat the exact same bossfight (same arena, same everything) in scenario B. This happens for the first, second and third encounter with Birkin. It's mind-boggling, really. I cannot believe this game is praised as much as it is when it is a clear downgrade from the original in some aspects. The most outrageous change in my opinion is that Mr. X now appears in both scenarios, and that was a BIG difference in the OG where he just appears in scenario B. It really made that B run feel special.

To be honest, I don't really care that much about the story in RE games... that's not exactly why we like Capcom games, so I would be a little more inclined to ignore these incoherencies in the narrative if the gameplay was good enough, but I don't think it is. I think the atmosphere in RE2R is just fantastic through and through, but from all the over the shoulder games in the numbered series (with Revelations included) that's probably the worst the combat ever felt, no joke, I HATE the combat in this game. Guns feel very underpowered and even if the dismemberment is the best in the franchise (better than RE3R or even RE4R btw), I did not enjoy encountering zombies in this one. The RNG is through the roof, I bet you the original game from 1998 had more reliable patterns than the remake.

I remember entering the cafeteria near the reception of NEST in my first playthrough (on normal difficulty) and putting 7 bullets to the forehead of a zombie for him to finally fall, and I got so pissed I had to load the save to try it again. It took me 1 shot with the exact same weapon, and the zombie's head exploded. My average experience was much more akin to the first encounter with that zombie: a bunch of bullets and nothing happens. Maybe I'm the unluckiest guy in the world with RE2R RNG, that would explain why people love it so much while I would rather replay RE3R any day of the week than it, and it did not get better when I decided to replay the game earlier this year to get all the achievements (and I got them all, by the way). I genuinely think the combat in this game is worse than it was in the original game, so the only thing that was actually improved were the graphics.

I would still recommend, I guess... being one of the worst games in a franchise where most games are GOATed is not exactly the end of the world, but I actually think RE2R is as "bad" as RE6, if not worse. Overall Impression:

Resident Evil 2 (Remake) is not just a re-release of the iconic 1998 game, but a complete reimagining that carefully preserves the spirit of the original while offering modern gameplay and stunning graphics. Capcom has managed to create something more than just a nostalgic trip, but a complete horror experience that can scare and captivate both newcomers and veterans of the series.

Pros:

•  Stunning Graphics and Atmosphere: The RE Engine works wonders. Raccoon City looks grim, dirty, and incredibly detailed. Lighting, sounds, and animation create an unparalleled atmosphere of horror and despair.
•  Improved Gameplay: The classic Resident Evil gameplay has received modern controls, a third-person camera, and an improved combat system. The game has become more dynamic and responsive.
•  Respectful Treatment of the Original: The developers have respectfully treated the original, preserving the main locations, characters, plot points, and puzzles.
•  Two Campaigns for Different Characters: You can play the game as Leon and Claire, each with their own unique storyline, weapons, and skills. This adds replayability.
•  Nemesis - Mr. X: Mr. X is one of the scariest and most memorable enemies in video game history. His relentless pursuit creates constant tension and forces you to look for new ways to retreat.
•  Many Secrets and Easter Eggs: The game is full of secrets, easter eggs, and references to other games in the Resident Evil series, which will delight fans.
•  Excellent Optimization: The game is well optimized and runs smoothly even on mid-range computers.

Cons:

•  Some Plot Changes: Some plot points have been changed or simplified compared to the original, which may disappoint some fans.
•  Monotony of Locations: Despite the excellent graphics, some locations, such as the sewers, may seem monotonous.

Who is this game for:

•  Fans of the Resident Evil series who want to experience a classic game in a modern interpretation.
•  Horror lovers who appreciate atmosphere, tension, and scary moments.
•  Those who are looking for a game with an interesting story, memorable characters, and complex puzzles.

Who is this game NOT for:

•  Those who don't like horror and prefer a more action-oriented approach.
•  Those who don't like games with limited resources and difficult bosses.

Do I recommend this game?

Resident Evil 2 (Remake) is one of the best remakes in video game history. It not only carefully preserves the spirit of the original, but also offers modern gameplay and stunning graphics. If you like horror and haven't played Resident Evil 2 yet, this is a great reason to catch up.

The game looks really promising, but I can't recommend a game that uses an "anti-cheat" that is literally just a RAT virus.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1735850938}, {"review_text": "My Honest Thoughts on the Game

I have a love-hate relationship with this game.

On one hand, it’s visually stunning, has a massive open world, and offers hundreds of hours of grindable content. 

On the other hand, it's also one of the most aggressively pay-to-win games I’ve ever played — and I’ve spent over $1,500 and logged 4,000+ hours, so trust me, I’ve seen it all.

Incredible graphics & character creator — still top-tier most even in 2025

Massive open world with seamless zones and no loading screens

Life skills (fishing, farming, trading, cooking, etc.) are deep and relaxing

Combat is fast and flashy — feels great once you get the hang of it

Classes are unique and constantly rebalanced

Guild content is fun — world bosses, wars, node fights, and events

You can enjoy the game as a free-to-play player (if you're patient)

The Bad (a.k.a. Why I Burned Out):

💰 Horribly Pay-to-Win

The cash shop is predatory, offering enhancement items like memory fragments, cron stones, and costumes that directly impact progression

I’ve spent $1,500+, and almost none of it truly helped

Players with deep wallets will always have the advantage in PvP, life skilling, and rankings

🔄 Endgame Progression is RNG Hell

Gear upgrades are tied to random chance, and failure can wipe weeks of effort

Enhancement is a black hole that’s emotionally and financially draining

🏹 PvP is forced

After level 50, PvP is open-world and mostly unavoidable

Stronger players can grief you for farming in “their” spot

Your only option is to change servers or log off

💀 The Marketplace is limited

No personal trading, fixed prices, and all gear is listed via an auction-like system

Getting rare items depends on luck or nonstop grinding

😵 UI & Systems are overwhelming

New players are bombarded with menus, notifications, and overlapping systems

Even after a tutorial rework, it’s still more of a learning cliff than a curve

!!!! Personal Warning !!!!

I've played over 4,000 hours and spent $1,500+... and I still feel like I barely made progress.

If you're the type of player who:

Likes structured dungeons/raids? ❌ You won’t find much here.

Hates forced PvP? ❌ You're in trouble.

Wants meaningful reward for time spent? ⚠️ You might get frustrated.

⚠️ DO NOT get baited into enhancement addiction.
⚠️ DO NOT spend real money expecting progress.
⚠️ DO NOT trust the memory fragments and gear upgrade bait system.


Despite all this, I still love parts of this game:

The world is stunning

Mount breeding and sailing are actually fun

My time with top guilds was amazing — the community can be great

I recommend trying it free, enjoying the world, and avoiding the cash shop at all costs unless you're 100% fine with spending without return.

✅ Recommended: Yes — for F2P sandbox enjoyers
❌ Not Recommended: If you hate RNG, forced PvP, or paywalls

(UPDATE 2025) 

Not to get confused with earlier Review above this was done a few years ago. 
This is a current update from July 2025.

P2W Depends on the Definition
Some players define P2W strictly: “Can you buy something that gives an unreasonable advantage that cannot be earned by gameplay alone?”

Others view P2W more broadly: “If money gives you any meaningful advantage or skips time investment, it’s P2W.”

There’s agreement that BDO does meet both definitions depending on context.

Pearl Shop → Outfits → Silver → Gear
Players can:

Buy outfits from the Pearl Shop

Sell them for silver

Use that silver to buy high-end gear on the market

This creates a real-money-to-gear path, which is the core P2W mechanic in BDO.

Cron Stones and other enhancement materials are also sold for real money, accelerating gear progression.

There’s a limit on how many outfits you can sell per week (30), capping silver gain.

Outfits are expensive (~$35 USD or more), and outfit-selling alone isn’t fast unless you’re spending thousands or doing it over time.

To buy gear equivalent to top players, you'd need:

~670 outfits

~$23,000 USD

~6 months at max weekly sales

So, P2W is possible but requires massive investment — only viable for the 1%.

Having BIS gear doesn’t make you win automatically:

Combat skill, class knowledge, and experience still matter.

In PvP especially, a highly skilled player with slightly lower gear can still outperform.

P2W can accelerate progress, but it doesn't replace actual gameplay mastery.

Even whales still need to:

Grind for failstacks

Participate in market competition

Deal with RNG on gear enhancement

Buying silver doesn’t eliminate progression frustration or guarantee upgrades due to RNG mechanics.

WoW, FF14, GW2, Albion, etc., are all mentioned as having elements of P2W, especially with:

Boosting services

Token-based real-money-for-gold systems

BDO is considered worse by some due to the direct monetization of power, while others feel it's more sustainable as long as you play consistently.

Yes, BDO is pay-to-win, but:

It’s heavily capped, long-term, and costly.

It still requires time, knowledge, and skill.

It’s not unplayable without paying — but you’ll progress slower, especially in PvP and gear race.

Forced Open World PvP in BDO – Clarified (2025 perspective)

BDO does have open-world PvP, but here are the facts:

⚔️ PvP becomes enabled at level 50. You are automatically PvP-flagged and can be attacked or flagged on.

🛡️ You can avoid it: Stick to Season Servers, Olvia Servers, or use Marni’s Realm (1hr per cooldown, recharges) for private grind zones.

🗺️ PvP is disabled in safe zones (towns, cities) and is rare outside Elvia/Arsha or contested grind spots.

👤 You can stay level 49.9999 forever to avoid PvP entirely (but you’ll be locked out of endgame).

⚠️ Karma system punishes griefers: Killing unflagged players drops karma, making them red (outlaws) — they risk gear downgrade, exp loss, crystal loss.

🔁 Server swapping is fast (5min cooldown), making it easy to escape toxic players.

🔇 Most players now avoid PvP altogether — many grind solo or in Marni zones and rarely see flagged players.

⚖️ PvP is no longer the core of BDO like it once was — guild wars, griefing, and forced duels were all nerfed over time.

🧠 The game originally was designed with sandbox PvP in mind, but over the years, it has leaned more toward PvE accessibility.

✔️ PvP still exists, and technically it's "forced" at level 50+, but in modern BDO, you can completely avoid it with the tools provided.

If you're a solo PvE player: you'll be fine. If you like competitive PvP — Arsha, Node Wars, and Arena of Solare are for you.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1745436462}, {"review_text": "characters look great, its a grind fest, what you grind for? i dunno, number get bigger, yippie, you wanna efficiently grind? leave your pc on and just fish, theres so much focus on just afk fishing, at this point its Idle barbie dress up simulator.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 34, "timestamp_created": 1749847815}, {"review_text": "What happens when you take an game with an incredibly high skill ceiling, deep and complex combat mechanics with very unique class identities (some of which requiring some classes to require thousands of hours to become even decent at) facilitating some of the most intricate and captivating PvP of any game in existence, then proceed to drain all of those unique parts out of the game in favor of mindless, bland, and never-ending PvE.

You do not need all the bloat everywhere to keep people around.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 14, "timestamp_created": 1759029500}, {"review_text": "Oh, bdo...

If you're considering playing this game, you need to understand that the minimum time spent to get your bearings is probably around 80-100 hours.
If you're writing a review and you haven't logged the time, it's not really helpful. However, it is absolutely true that if you don't like complex (and convoluted) games, this game is not for you, period. This game is extremely peculiar, in so many ways. You either enjoy that kind of stuff, or you don't.  

I played a lot some years ago, I lost the account, I rejoined the game a couple months ago, started from scratch. And my brain melted and seized repeatedly, even though I was already familiar with most of the game mechanics from before. Thankfully I joined the right guild, they saved me so much time trying to figure things out or having to look things up.

This is NOT a game for everyone. 

This game is NOT easy, unless all you want to do is relax, pick some flowers, catch some horses, decorate your house, or do fishing or alike. And I know quite a few players like that. They just enjoy the game for the scenery, doing quests, or doing ONLY fishing. It has a very steep learning curve, from the UI through understanding how things work, through constantly doing maths (especially if you choose to do lifeskilling). 

You don't have to engage in PVP. The game has a very rich PVE, and you don't have to do the endless grind to enjoy most of the content. And there is a LOT of content. If you do want to PVP, expect so much grind it will make santa cry. That said, the combat in the game is nothing like you've experienced before, in a good way. It's really, really good and complex.

The graphics, environment, even ambient sounds or sunsets - really amazing. Sunset in the desert, beautiful. City goes quiet, crickets come on, sun goes down, it's really enjoyable, and the different zones offer completely different ecosystems. Character creation, great. Customization, pretty great. Being able to just explore and even get lost (on the open ocean or the desert), great. Unless you're a hardcore player, there is always something to do in the game that's new and interesting. And they also add a lot of content and seasonal events, continuously.

Is it F2P?
Kinda. You can get away with it, but you don't really want to. It is NOT a P2W game. It is however pay for convenience and pay for looking at really pretty things all the time. In-game armor, even some end-game stuff, is terrifying. You will want to spend money on an outfit. However, they're giving away so much stuff these days that you don't need to spend money on that. Not really. The monthly "subscription" is about $15, and you can easily get it on sale for half off or more - worth every penny. I have spent about $80 total and got pretty much everything that's essential to your sanity (including 3 month subscription), and I still have $20 credit left. It would be super-easy to blow a lot of money in the game, they make a lot of cute/adorable pets, outfits, beautiful boat skins and carriages, horse equipment, etc. However, it is not necessary, and you can get a lot of that stuff on the marketplace for in-game money. Anyway, I feel like the $60 I've spent is accurate for the value of purchasing this game.

The bad:
* UI is super clunky and weird, takes time to get used to. It's really weird. Once you figure it out, easy peasy, but it's a steep learning curve.
* Some RNG stuff is really, truly bad & annoying. Not a deal breaker, and they're addressing a lot of that stuff right now. 
* Random weird shit will happen to you, like getting stuck in an alchemy tool, or your horse trips on a boulder and dies. or randomly walks off the cliff on it's own for no reason. It's part of the game, we just LOL at that stuff, like people having fishing chairs on their heads. Yes, after all those years, it's still buggy. To me, it's part of it's charm at this point. Nothing serious has affected me bug-wise, except mixing the main questlines (between LOML and mainland)
* Not doing the quests in order (if you're a new player) is suicide. DO NOT START A NEW CHARACTER ANYWHERE BUT VELIA! It is also imperative to do the MAIN QUESTS first and foremost, and then get distracted with everything else. Main quests are what unlocks a lot of the stuff in the game. I absolutely hate that part (the convoluted code spaghetti that is BDO - they really need to revamp the entire quest system), as I returned and made new char in LOML, which ended up being a massive time sink in trying to figure out what and why things aren't working as they should (progression for example). This is purely based on the gameplay etc. 

TLDR:
BDO is a great concept and a visually beautiful game, built on an outdated engine. This loot grinder MMO has 30 unique classes to choose from, 26 of which have 2 different specializations.  It's mostly a single player PvE experience with a selection of large/small scale pvp content. Find a class that works for you and get to grinding. Better gear = better grinding = more upgrades. PvP on the other hand is an extremely polarizing experience. While classes are fun to play and extremely satisfying to master, the desync and pvp balancing can really make pvp feel unpolished. To top it all off BDO has a RNG % based upgrade system. Love it or hate it, that's what the game has. One day it's punishing you and the next it's giving you a handy. It's not bad when you start off, but gets worse the closer you are to the gear ceiling.  All in all a pretty solid PvE/PvP experience with one of the best combat systems in any MMO. It has the potential to be the best combat-based MMO available, but suffers from performance issues and bugs. 


Character/Gear Progression:
Probably the hottest topic whenever BDO is being discussed. This is a game all about GEAR, not character level. When it comes to combat performance, the gear will provide a vast majority of your stats. Character levels beyond level 62 are pretty much pointless. As long as you have enough skill points(obtained separately from levels) to get all skills for your specialization, 62 is the last level that provides any combat bonuses. From there going forward, it's all about the gear. This gear can be copied to one additional character via the "Tagging" system for a small amount of in-game silver. Allowing you to experience other classes at the full power of your main. 

Basically enhancing works like this:
Every item has a base enhance chance for it's current enhancement level(pretty low %). You add items called "Failstacks" to increase the chance of success(there's a softcap where failstacks beyond a certain point will net little +%).  So essentially there is a "max" % chance an item can be enhanced.

Then there are items call "Cron Stones" that "protect" the enhancement. Cron Stones are the bread and butter for endgame enhancing and can be acquired in game with silver, from events, or via P2W. So there is a cost to protecting your important items. Whether you are a whale or a F2P player, it's still RNG. Although you only Cron Stone certain items. Most items are not worth cron stoning. 

Lastly, is Pity. This is the maximum enhancement attempts you can make on an item before the game feels bad and gives you the enhancement at 100%. Every item in the game has a pity. You pray you don't hit these...but it will happen. They added these about a year ago and thank effin god. Before you could fail forever and it sucked!

There will be a point in your gear progression where buying the upgrades will no longer be available....then you must gamba enhancement levels whether you like to or not. This will be quite a ways down your adventure path, so don't let that be the "make or break" on you trying the game. Just know that's how current end game progression works. At the peak gearscore, expect most enhancements to be <5% or some as little as .6% with adequate failstack applied.

Enhancing is the biggest make or break for people. It's a lot better than it used to be, but still can be pretty disheartening. Thankfully the Pity system ensures you will get the upgrade after x amount of fails.

PvE:
PvE is a pretty enjoyable experience with a long term gearing curve. You will be spending a lot of time PvE'ing in this game as it is your primary source of obtaining money to upgrade your gear. Even if you play this game to PvP, you will be PvE'ing or Lifeskilling to get them upgrades. The better you can PvE the faster you can obtain upgrades. Thus creates the loop of this game - grind to grind better. Once you have enough upgrades you can go to a new zone. Rinse and repeat. If you only play this game to PvE/Lifeskill(which a lot of people do), you can really do the gear upgrades at any pace you would like. Each step is just a chapter in your own book. No reason to rush. Just take it all in and try out all the zones and lifeskills YOU want to do. There's a lot of different options, choose what's fun for you. Freedom of choice in the mid game is what makes this game great. Enjoy this time before your end game progression becomes more linear(for better or for worse). 

PvE Bosses:
This game offers a lot of solo/4man bossing content....unfortunately it's mostly trash. The rewards are good, but the bosses can be frustrating. Dysnc'd instakill moves, buggy mechanics, and some bosses living in immune frames really make bossing one of the low points in this game.

PvP:
This is where the sweat comes from. My personal favorite piece of the game. PvP. 

Capped :
AOS (3v3 arena)
T1 Node Wars (multiple guilds 100+ players)
T2 Node Wars (multiple guilds 100+ players)
T2 Siege (attacker/defender battle over castle 100+ players)

Capped content, as the name suggests, puts limits on your total base stats like Attack Power, Defense Power, Evasion. These are made for all players. Reaching these caps varies on the content. The 3v3 arena for example can be done with no gear! While the T1 and T2 caps give two different gear limits. These requirements are very easy to hit for a new player. T1 caps can be hit within a month and T2 will generally take 2-4 months to acquire. If you only want to do capped PvP content, you really don't need to PvE a whole lot once you reach the caps and have your crystals/artifacts/lightstones squared away. You can just log on to PvP and use the PvP currencies to buy consumables for future PvP. Kind of a nice feature if this is your goal.

Uncapped:
All open world pvp(unorganized 1v1 -> 100+)
Uncapped Node Wars (multiple guilds 100+ players)
Uncapped Siege (attacker/defender battle over castle 100+ players)

Uncapped content the sky is the limit. You are competing with the whales and no-lifers here. This is in my opinion the pinnacle of BDO PvP, but also is the hardest to reach. If you aspire to do this content you will need to invest a lot of time or a lot of money to get to this point. You will be optimizing your silver per hour and AFK lifeskilling while you are not actively grinding. I would say the entry level for uncapped is ~1 year if you grind a few hours a day. If you're a gamer dad playing a couple hours on the weekend and you are not willing to whale, it would probably take you 2-3 years to get to this gearscore. All that being said, this is a gamba upgrade system. You could get MEGA boosted for very little effort....but the likelihood is low. 

PvP is all around extremely satisfying in this game. PvP has unique CC(crowd-control) mechanics, allowing you to CC unprotected opponents.  Learning your classes protections and CCs makes the skill expression S+ for BDO. Although BDO has great diversity in its 56 specialization, the dev has shown that it's near impossible to balance them all. On top of this, the game engine struggles with desync and frame drops in large scale content(100+ people on screen).  Pretty much all serious PvPers need a graphics preset that reduces the games fidelity by 90% to play at decent FPS. You could have a gaming rig made by jesus himself and still get <30 fps in siege...I'm not kidding. 

7/10 (9/10 with an engine update)
+PvE
+PvP(still fun)
+Long term progression
+Gear does not become obsolete like "raid tier" style MMOs
+Looks Great
+Best darn action combat system in any MMO

[{"review_text": "Sins 2 is a good game and is heading in the right direction, so my move against recommendation is more to do with release and marketing practices rather than an indictment of the game itself. TL;DR, I would wait about a year (or even two!) before buying just to let the game settle and for some good mods to come out, currently very difficult in this development environment.

In short, I think Sins 2 released "officially" on Steam far too early, and that a lot of the development that's happened between now and then has been largely remedial, but is marketed to us as "new features."

What's good about Sins 2?

The game generally looks gorgeous, especially zoomed out.

It's somewhat controversial, but I think they made the right call to take out some of the 'mandatory' gameplay aspects by now having resource extractors exact a logistics slots cost; diplomacy's pacts are gone, seeing as they were just strictly better to have than not have; stuff like starbase constructors have been removed in favour of instant placement.

The combat model, with simulated ballistics/missiles and real-time turret tracking and lines of fire, is much more interesting than its predecessor. You get to have those Battlestar Galactica moments of watching flak turrets spin to intercept missiles, with some punching through anyways.

And finally, the game is moving in a good direction overall. It was fun to play on 'release,' and has only gotten more fun since then. The devs are responsive and communicative, there are opt-in betas for most patches, adjustments take community feedback into account.

So what's the problem?

Sins 2 had an official 'release' on Steam last year in August, but the way things have gone since then, it's clear that the game was not ready to officially launch, and the magnitude of certain changes clearly demonstrates that. My understanding is that the official launch coincided with the addition of the third race, Advent, to the game.

I'm going to gloss over the AI art, addressed well elsewhere. What I will say is that the new UI is generally soulless and lifeless compared to the first game, the colours of which, while goofy and animated, made the game feel a lot more vibrant than this sober slate blue we have to stare at everywhere we go.

More importantly, the Advent factions almost immediately had to be reworked because they were poorly differentiated between one another, and their major race feature also had to be significantly rebalanced. This rebalance still isn't done, by the way, and they have plans to further differentiate the two. It's admirable that they're committed to fixing these issues, but it doesn't feel good to invest time into a race that you know is going to change significantly in the coming months.

In the same way, gameflow has changed considerably. In the time from Steam launch, we have gone from a slow early game leaning heavily into capital ship spam and the extinction of mixed fleets, to a fast early game into cap spam with high lethality, then to a system that bottlenecks caps with high lethality (meaning large fleet battles were over in the blink of an eye), to the current 1.41 patch, where we have bottlenecked caps and low lethality, meaning more considered and thoughtful battles -- not to mention the addition of the Population mechanic which has drastically affected the impact of culture on the player's economy and is now non-optional if you want to keep up.

People will say that, yes, of course RTSs go through changes and adjustments throughout development. But these are larger than changes and adjustments, these are gameplay changes through which the devs are trying to nail down what they want Sins 2 to feel like at base -- and that would be fine for a game that is still IN DEVELOPMENT. But Sins 2 is supposed to be finished, and finished games don't tend to have these crises of identity.

As it stands, players are not simply learning a new meta from patch to patch, they are almost getting new takes on the design philosophy underpinning the game with each major update.

So the core flow and feel of the game is not yet stable, though it seems like it's getting there. What else?

One of the early official updates headlined the addition of visual destruction debris when your capital ships, starbases, and titans are destroyed. Really? This seems like a basic element of the visual oeuvre you'd expect to find in a large-scale RTS and should not be a headline of a major patch, and probably should have been there before the game's official release.

Patch notes will also have little gems like updated planet visuals, updated ship visuals, certain audio cues being added. To be clear, these are not pitched as bug fixes or retroactive development updates, they're pitched as new additions to the game. But it's clear that what was being updated was not intended for full release, but was simply a first-pass from the game's development phase. 

Finishing passes to visual and audio which are not bug fixes are a part of development, not an "upgrade" that the customer is receiving for free.

Other updates are borderline. We sometimes get new planet types. Great. Others are "new," but they're just restorations of what existed in the first game, and any returning player might have reasonably expected to find them in Sins 2 on release. So for much of 2024 you would not have found uncolonizable gravity wells like space storms, or at least not as many as are currently in the game now, which, again, is somewhat unbelievable to hear as a returning Sins 1 player.

Finally, many road map updates are padded out with these kinds of "features," essentially finishing passes spun as "updates." More egregious is the promise of a whole new Advent minor faction (these are like city-state factions in Civ) -- which should NOT be a road map update feature but an expected part of the base game. Why? Because the game still lacks that Advent minor faction only because the Advent are the newest race to the game at launch -- they clearly didn't have time to design the corresponding minor faction for the race as well.

I don't want to lose sight of my original thesis -- the game is good, but it released too early. Even their new scenarios DLC did not release with multiplayer functionality -- something they're going to add eventually (it's on the road map!), but it probably should have been considered a basic feature of the package to launch with, not spun as a free upgrade coming down the line eventually.

I want to reiterate that all of the above is fine, expected even, for a game early in its life cycle. But Sins 2 is still at the stage where it would be more appropriate to consider it an Early Access title: one that is probably close to completion, but isn't quite there yet.

If I had paid Early Access pricing to play this version of the game, knowing it would still be under heavy development and balancing, all would be forgiven. BAR, another RTS on a grand scale, is probably just as rough as Sins 2 is, maybe even rougher, and I have no complaints about BAR because they didn't charge me money to beta test for them.

I don't expect free Sins 2. I do expect to receive a finished product if I buy the game at full retail price. Give them another year or two at minimum to work out all the kinks, and you will have at last a complete game.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1745422187}, {"review_text": "This is my favorite 4X Space Strategy game!  They also often get their entire armies stuck in a gravity well, most often a sun for some reason, when their enemy has garrison planet augment that trickles in units one by one. I do think performance is better in long and large games though so that's one positive.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761060158}, {"review_text": "This is somewhat tough, as on paper in a mechanical sense, Sins of a Solar Empire 2 is a GOOD sequel. It follows the design philosophy that a sequel should be more of what you like, but iterated upon. Planet management has a deeper scale to it, fleet compositions are less spammy, and faction differences (Aside from the loyalist/rebel unique techs) are more complex.

Controlling and managing multiple fleets feels more streamlined and less granular without losing complexity, and early game exploration is heavily rewarded. Queuing researches and build orders is easily done and altered. It is a GOOD sequel. If you liked Sins 1, you will like Sins 2. 

However, what is a terrible shame and an absolute travesty is the sheer amount of AI generated images in the game, and something I cannot condone supporting. Especially when the first game had so much charm in it's programmer art and colored concepts.

Once noticed- it's impossible to look past. At first the Balenciaga stare on some of the portraits- then that odd uniform light shading. The constant tilt shift on anything that's supposed to look granular. Odd, in-congruent positioning and posing in images where figures are supposed to be interacting with each other. Figures staring at the camera and screaming. That telltale 'figure standing in front of a bulbous space ship' that doesn't match the design of the rest of the game.

The portraits you select when in the set up lobby have lost all of their unique charm. Sure- there's more of them, but what's the point when they all look vaguely the same? Thirty nearly identical portraits will never be better than 5 filled with personality. Even the in loading screen 'ads' for upcoming DLC's have a clearly AI generated figure within it. (Look at the eyes of the green eyed woman in the paths to power DLC banner.)

The UI is too clean, some of the buttons do not look like buttons. It is serviceable, but lacks the gritty charm the original had. The steam page states that: "This game used AI to help quickly iterate through designs for some UI elements using our own artwork as a baseline. AI is also used to help translate the game."

And this feels like a lie. The UI design does not feel iterative- and the amount of AI images used when you supposedly have an artist on payroll just screams 'We only wanted to pay them for a quarter of the work we wanted done.' 
If you have an artist, you have an artist. And even then, quirky programmer art will always be preferable to soulless AI generations.

One also has to wonder if some of this AI usage affected the visual designs of the ships themselves. Why did the Advent lose nearly all of their nautical theme?
(The hangar defenses- for instance, are now just wedges, rather than evocative of sea shells.)
Why did the Vasari ships lose their insectile appearance?
Why do the turrets on many of the TEC ships look like they were tacked on as an afterthought?

Were these conscious decisions from a person, or- did an AI simply smooth out the edges without understanding why those notions were present?

It's questioning like this that makes it hard to recommend. And the first game was very good, so this one is as well. Now....there are some minor details I do have to complain about. The music in this game is also no where NEAR as good as Sins 1. This is so much true that my favorite mod is the one that changes the music back. And speaking of sound, the sound effects here are also WAY worse than they were in Sins 1. Fleets do not move in nor do they maintain any discernable formation as they move through a gravity well and engage in combat. This was something basic in Sins 1 that just doesnt happen in Sins 2. I wish there were more polish and details that made the world feel more alive and like a story narrative existed with each and every faction. Because the first game had more of these little things. This game does play well and what not, but the atmosphere feels less alive and more robotic, and maybe thats just in line with the trend of ALL modern games lacking that level of polish and attention to detail. 

Now, sins 2 as of this writing currently doesnt have a story campaign, or much of anything that the first game didnt have other than the scenerio battles. The plan however is to release new content and updates over time, by the end of which I'm hoping will differentiate Sins 2 enough to distinguish it from Sins 1. There will be new units and a whole new faction added, which by itself should be quite an exciting prospect. Will this be deemed adequate in the eyes of man and worthy in the eyes of the gods? I sure hope so, but what I KNOW is gonna be the real fire with this game is the inevitable modding community that will bloom in this game. So far there has been a mod adding the Galactic Empire from star wars into the game as a fully playable faction, and my hope is that mods like these will add factions from many fan favorite franchises into the game and we will have a game where we can pit all these factions against each other along with the factions already in Sins 2, which will TRULY create a experience beyond what was possible in Sins 1. As in, they are all equally strong enough that none of them feel particularly too overpowered, although there ARE some arguably overpowered scenerios a couple of them can create. Namely the Vassari Alliance with their titan, and the TEC Enclave with their late game garrisons. Arguably between mid-late game, both factions of Advent can stomp you out real bad too. But overall I would say a good player will win easily with any faction, which tells me, this game is down to skill and game knowledge. Thats as fair as it can be, and I like the current balance. I refuse to pay for additional DLC just to unlock improved game play.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1758940165}, {"review_text": "It is basically Sins of a Solar Empire 1 but updated to look and play much better, though some features of what SoaSE eventually became through expansions and smaller dlc are not present, they, or variants thereupon are on the cards for future updates, so if you enjoyed the original game but want a smoother, more visually striking experience this is great, if however you want a diverse and wide range of mods to enhance your experience beyond what is currently on offer (at the time of writing) stick with SoaSE:Rebellion for the time being.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1740823193}, {"review_text": "I am a long time sins fan, and I really like what Stardock did here. 

A lot of games focus on adding features, but don't take the time to make sure that the game is performant enough to be playable, especially in the late game. Stellaris is an example of this: tremendously fun, but with serious late game slowdowns on large maps.

The problem is that making your game more performant takes time, and means shipping fewer features, at least at first. (units, maps, gameplay mechanics, etc)

With sins 2, they really took the time to make sure that the have a powerful, fast, multi-core game engine, and it shows. My 10 year old computer has never had any drops in performance, and the game looks beautiful. I especially love the animations when weapons fire impact shields.

For fans of sins1 who are into modding, this isn't just sins1 with better graphics. The old sins1 engine was 32 bit, and IIRC, single threaded. There was a very perceptible limit to how many mods you could run, and how many players and ships you could have. The new engine largely removes that limit. You can really go big.

Writing a performant, multi-threaded game engine is a very difficult thing to do well. I expect my camera to go where I clicked our how I clicked, and the options in game here haven't really helped me get over that.  The panel for following planets/ships/fleets is similar to the first game, but not. I used to be able to very, very, easily find out what is on what planet, where, and select it and interact with it without being at the planet. And, you can do that here also, it's just...not the same lol

I have to admit the first game vanilla gameplay was uh, lackluster for me. Too much samey samey, different skin ships per race, which is the reason why most of my incredibly excessive playtime in the first game was modded for various space IP flavored mods.  Here in the sequel, there is a much nicer distinctiveness to gameplay between races that I really appreciate, both in game start up and overall playstyles. Game comes with an integrated third party mod handling instead of using the workshop, which makes sense since the game is available on different stores so it should be useable for all their platforms not just steam, this is absolutely a positive in concept. Sometimes the connection and getting stuff to your computer is a little wonky but overall serviceable. There were many AMAZING mods for the first and it's expansions, and some have started up for the sequel and it's just.....*dreamy sigh*

The computer AI has felt like a work in progress. Sometimes it is okay, sometimes it is just ?? ???? ???? No idea about PvP bc I would rather jump off a cliff than engage with any of that.

It's missing some depth I was used to from the first, but that's not a fair comparison to a much more mature game with two expansions and various DLC. Some things that were in the base game ARE missing though or much more vestigial than I expected them to be(like diplomacy), after dev time and a full year or whatever released before it was on Steam.

There are also some weird choices, design elements I do not agree or like, but are very playable generally. If you need a fun 4X -sort-of-deal in your life, and like watching pretty ships go pew pew at each other, this is probably your jam. Unlike the original, the use of Generative AI to create and prototype the interfaces definitely damaged this game so severely that I cannot in good faith recommend it to anyone. Even fans of SOASE1.

The single most interesting addition is the Orbit mechanic, a feature the original direly needed where-in planets move dynamically along a rail, changing their possible Phase Lane connections. A mod that adds this feature to the original game would basically make this game pointless. An utter waste of potential, the new tech tree is completely noisy beyond reckoning and the interface just... I can't explain it. You will not be able to find the things you need.

SOASE1 had a challenge or three to its scale specific to not always being able to figure out which freaking identical asteroid was under attack. Changes to the Tactical and Logistics slots system have made some differences to the fine balance of your first dozen planets, but this game is at its absolute weakest when player count and planet count starts getting too high. 2v2 or 4-way FFA probably is the best this game gets, the smaller the map the better so-as to force conflict before everyone is running into late-game balance issues.

Like the first game, Advent have substantial global disadvantages, only alleviated through their unique faction mechanic, the second new idea this game had. TEC has the old trade system but it's even less compelling than making a big trade line running across the galaxy, Advent have a spell and psychic power system that makes their starbases and capships stronger, and Vasari have the lamest passive bonus system possible for their faction. These faction systems like the orbit mechanics could be put into the old game, and this game would not need to exist.

There's some new space ships, some utterly unnecessary redesigns of virtually all of the old craft, and broadly speaking the UI damage just utterly destroys the game's once-decent fleet management options. The new Fleet system lets you build a titanic kinda-manageable mass of ships that rally to the node the fleet 'leader' is at (usually a cap ship or titan), but it doesn't let you set something like a Quota per-unit for battles that will come with attrition. As mentioned, the game's later phases are kind of just miserable grinding conflicts and the new neutral faction system honestly just isn't as cool as the old one which let you bumble into neutral planets with defenses to make initial expansion more challenging.

Now it's more like, you wipe out all of the neutral ships and claim your half of the galaxy within 15-30 minutes using a handful of frigates and your free cap ship. You couldn't do that in the past very easily, and that sort of blitz and streamlining steps done throughout contradict the awful menu design and frankly deplorable tech-tree which could have been trimmed to fit on the freaking screen. Just play the original, actual humans designed it, and I frankly don't think that happened with this one.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1760665543}]

   It seems to be all true. 

   But, this is also a Gacha game, so while you may hesitate to get involved with this type of genre (i was) - and not get to experience all that glorious combat and open world content- I'm going to defuse for you the powder keg that is Gacha here with two easy points to keep in mind while playing this game, so you can take advantage of all this game has to offer and also keep your wallet safe.

   *Point number 1. The 'free' part of the game is incredibly vast, on purpose.

    New characters are typically released over a period of 3 weeks. That's a long amount of time they need players to hang around to keep them as potential buyers when the next new character drops. So how do they keep players around? Give them compelling things to do. Story quests, puzzles, bosses, gear hunting, team building, lore and world building all entrenched in some really fun gameplay mechanics. It's all here. When you see the amount of events you have access to participate in when you are an appropriate level, you will know what I mean. The great thing is, everything you do gives you gems that you can throw at the Gacha system if you choose, but that leads me to my next point.

   *Point number 2. In terms of this Gacha system, there are really only two cash cows. 1 is you, and the other is the game world itself.

    If you have fun playing this game, and you mine the gameworld for all its worth in free gems, over the long term you will allow yourself to naturally pull hundreds of times on whatever character banner you want. That's hundreds of dollars worth of what some people may put into the game just to fast track obtaining a character instantly. Will you for sure get the character you try for, after saving up all those gems? No. And that's the true catch. But that catch, unfortunately, is also just a universal truth about what tends to make things more memorable. Does the raid boss in WOW always drop the piece you need? No. But when it does, you may remember that event for life, depending on how hard it was to get. So if you manage to keep the mindset that there is a years worth of game to play for you here for free, and you are not in a rush to get through it, you can have a 1-game-to-rule-them-all situation, and wallet that stays full too.

   So yes. The game is stylish and flashy. The combat is great. The open world, is actually jaw dropping. And the Gacha system is real. Luckily for you the Gacha system can be defeated if you simply remember to just not be in a hurry, accept what life gives you, and enjoy what's in front of you  as you go.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1757011115}, {"review_text": "A Promising Open-World ARPG with Great Potential

The combat system is definitely one of the game’s strongest points — responsive, stylish, and full of combo potential. Each character feels unique, and switching between them mid-combat adds a nice strategic layer. The mobility and traversal mechanics, like wall-running and gliding, make exploration feel fun and rewarding.

However, the game isn’t without its flaws. Some UI elements feel a bit cluttered, and the progression systems can be overwhelming for new players. There are also occasional performance dips and bugs, but nothing game-breaking so far.

The core structure echoes Genshin's open-world exploration and team-based combat, which makes it easy to pick up. But what surprised me was just how much deeper the systems run here.

Combat is where WuWa really sets itself apart. It’s fluid, fast, and far more dynamic, thanks to the addition of Intro/Outro skills that encourage team synergy in a more engaging way. Every switch-in feels impactful, and characters flow together naturally during battle. The parry/dodge system rewards skill expression, giving the whole experience a more action-heavy edge that Genshin lacks.

The Echo system—WuWa’s version of artifacts—feels like a breath of fresh air. Not only do they provide stat boosts, but some grant unique abilities, making builds more flexible and exciting early on. It adds a layer of strategy without the overwhelming RNG grind Genshin veterans are all too familiar with.

Even the starter team surprised me. Unlike Genshin’s initial roster, which often feels underpowered until you invest heavily, WuWa’s starting characters are well-rounded, satisfying to play, and synergize well together. It’s a much smoother onboarding experience.

In short, Wuthering Waves captures the best parts of Genshin while introducing bold new mechanics that make it feel fresh, rewarding, and a bit more hardcore. If you loved Genshin’s world but wished the combat had more bite and depth, WuWa might be exactly what you’re looking for.

TLDR: it pretty much beats Genshin in every single aspect in my opinion, except for music.

Here are the specific things for those who are considering jumping ship from Genshin:
1. Teleportation to important events as a new player do not require manual teleportation unlock. It doesn't try to waste your time with forced "map exploration".
2. Character gacha is more lenient (80 rolls for pity at 50/50), Weapon gacha is guaranteed at 80. Soft pity is noticeable once you are at 50+ rolls.
3. Daily stamina (the thing you use to consume for time-locked grinding) has a bank for regeneration overflow. Most dungeons also give you the option of x2 consumption without the need to craft any items (one grinding run counts twice if you spend double stamina). It's completely free and a built-in feature without you having to do anything extra.
4. Echos (artifact eqivalent) can drop from normal enemies at top rarities. Also after a certain point, all echo drops are 5 star at 100% chance. You will never have those useless purple artifacts in Genshin.
5. Open world items collection for character limit breaks are entirely guided by the UI. It shows you exactly where things are and they require far fewer in quantity than Genshin. One day's collection run can get you through most of what you want to do (though I think Genshin more recently implemented something similar?).
6. Combat is more action based and character controls are actually important. You can solo your favorite character if you truly want to. No character is truly a backstage "support" in Genshin whose only purpose is to give buffs.
7. Manual input and enemy reading determines combat, not superficial knowledge checks about elemental reactions like in Genshin. It's not like Genshin's 4-character braindead swap circles for elemental reactions (splash, swap, splash, swap, splash, swap, boom ad nauseam).
8. Dialogues can be skipped entirely.
9. Daily mission is just 1 and it covers most of your daily reward. It's very time friendly. It usually involves talking to 1-2 NPC or killing 1-3 enemies. Symbolic and respects your time.
10. Climbing has the "running" option.
11. Normal running doesn't consume stamina. No open-world stamina annoyance.
12. Quest markers are far more accurate than in Genshin.
13. Your character can literally fly like a jet plane in addition to the usual Genshin gliding, giving you Z-axis. It gives you more creative ways to access the map without wasting your time.
14. As a new player, you will mostly get a 5 star character you want because there are several guaranteed banners exclusively for new players, some characters are not even supposed to be available on your current banners. I started off with a past-event character I really like that isn't on the current event banner exclusive to me as a new player. You get that for weapons as well.
15. Additionally there are fixed common pool 5 star characters that appear in new player events. The freedom of selection is fairly high so you are pretty much guaranteed a full team of 5 stars within your first few days.
16. Enemy drops do not require manual pickup.
17. Chests on the map can be clearly detected by the UI once you unlock the features.
18. There is no weekday rotation for any kind of farming. All farming is available at all times.
19. Characters are built VERY differently from each other. Button smashing wouldn't do you any good. You actually have to learn the input and combos.
20. Built in guides and recommendations from the game client itself (though I think Genshin added this as well). It also has character-specific tutorial to walk you through the specific mechanics and input/combos.

Now for the more opinion based comments:
1. The music is inferior to that of Genshin, mostly because they lack distinct melodies and feel truly like "generic video game background noises".
2. The character designs are superior to Genshin, but I understand this depends on your demographic. There are far fewer childish characters here and most look and act sexy/handsome/mature. And I don't mean lolis. I am mostly talking about characters who act and look one dimensional like a Disney character regardless of body type. Plenty of those in Genshin.
3. The story is less childish. This isn't a fault of Genshin as Genshin still targets children for a lot of its contents. This one has far less silliness even in side quests. There are not that many sanitized optional contents with cringeworthy pixar/disney style side character plots with all sunshine and rainbows that torture adult players.
4. The main character speaks and is part of the story. The silly and childish "banter" is a lot more toned down than the MC+Paimon combo in Genshin. It is far less aggravating.
5. Cooking so far seems entirely optional as it wasn't required by any quest I encountered. I prefer this to the heavy-handed push for cooking in Genshin.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1759431049}, {"review_text": "A gacha game that feels more like an actual game than a gacha. [h2]7/10 [/h2]

[h3]Opening [/h3]

Since the release of Genshin Impact in 2020, the work has been troubled by controversy. Although it is far ahead in terms of commercial revenue and has a player base that cannot be understated, its reputation among players has always been remarkably polarized due to factors such as its excessive borrowing from well-known games like The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and its slightly crazy community. In any case, the success of it is unquestionable. Genshin Impact's outstanding commercial performance and revelation of the massive potential market and audience for ARPG mobile games have attracted countless followers and imitators of its model. Wuthering Waves is one of them. While using a more profound oriental culture as the game background, Wuthering Waves excels in combat, art style, and main storyline. However, its highly repetitive battles, monotonous open world exploration, lackluster side storylines, and mediocre gacha bonuses have also become its undeniable shortcomings.

[h3]Strength [/h3]

Wuthering Wave's art level and graphics are indeed among the best in similar mobile games. The more refined scenes, character modeling, and support for ray tracing allow players to fully immerse themselves in this mysterious world, abundant in oriental charm. The top-notch music and excellent dubbing further enhance the immersive experience. As a game driven by plot and quests, Wuthering Waves has a significant amount of text, a grand world view, and intricate forces. The main storyline is the most orthodox shōnen style, gradually reaching its climax after act VIII of the first chapter, with breakthroughs in plot presentation, performance effects, and BOSS design. The game's plot, graphics, and gameplay are constantly being optimized and adjusted compared to the closed beta and public beta versions, which shows that the developer team listens to players' suggestions and feedback.

As a game with open world exploration as its core gameplay, the monster levels here will be dynamically adjusted according to the player's progress, and mechanisms such as grappling, gliding, and climbing are also very beneficial to the player's map exploration. It is also characterized by elements of puzzles and other mini-games, the overall difficulty is noticeably low as well. Wuthering Waves provides players with an unexpectedly refreshing and hearty combat experience, with greatly high character flexibility and mobility, team battles of up to three, and cooperative mechanisms such as intro and outro skills, as well as easily triggered parry and dodge counter-attack designs, which make the combat highly operational and enjoyable to watch. Only heavy attacks and dodging will consume stamina, and the player's attack frequency will not be affected. Echoes that can be absorbed like Pokémon and transform briefly during battle also add a lot of variables to the battles. The energy in the game is mainly used to obtain currency, skills, as well as weapon upgrade materials, and echoes. Among similar games that pursue grinding, the daily pressure of Wuthering Waves is relatively light. The game also supports cooperative exploration up to three players. In terms of character strength, the protagonist provided by the game is well-equipped to complete all game content, including high-difficulty levels. If non-paying players are willing to invest time, they can also get a good gaming experience.

[h3]Weakness [/h3]

As a story-driven game, Wuthering Waves has an extremely long text volume. The plot in the early stage is relatively straightforward. Some side quests and exploration quests closely related to the later exploration are profoundly unengaging and make the player drowsy. Players may trigger the plot content of multiple tasks simultaneously, and the task tracing design also has serious loopholes, and will often replace the currently tracing tasks. The protagonist only has plot voices in highly infrequent situations, and the overly passive plot advancement seriously damages the viewing experience. Wuthering Waves's portrayal of the characters is clustered in a specific version and mission. Many characters have no news after that, and all the completed missions and cutscene CGs in the game cannot be reviewed for now. In addition, the game will experience a brief black screen loading when switching between certain scenes, and characters will often appear to be clipped through the model, stuck in the model, and in other situations that substantially affect the gaming experience, especially when climbing.

The gameplay of Wuthering Waves can certainly bring a lot of fun and freshness to players at the beginning, but as the process continues, the high repetitiveness of combat and world exploration, which are the main content, can easily make players feel bored. In medium and high difficulty challenges, players are frequently required to follow a fixed character and team action combo sequence to maximize damage, and overly dazzling battle scenes often affect operations. Farming for the echoes and their sub-stats is the main point of character enforcement throughout this game, but this process is quite long and highly random. Though various gameplay and mechanics are integrated into the open world exploration, they all lack in-depth content, and the excessive number of puzzle elements is rather convoluted. The rewards gained from exploration are far from enough compared to the time and effort committed by players. As a gacha game, the bonuses of Wuthering Waves can only be said to be average. The gacha resources that players can obtain after entering the game are severely constrained. After the initial grinding, players will inevitably have to go through a long dead period because the character's level cap is tightly bound to the account level. Compared to Genshin Impact, this one primarily targets males in terms of player groups or operational tendencies. The small proportion of female players is one of the biggest differences between this one and Genshin Impact. The game's pool has a guaranteed size of 80/160 and a 0.8% drop rate. It is divided into a character and a weapon pool, and its design is rather malignant.

[h3]Conclusion [/h3]

Though Wuthering Waves seemed relatively immature when it was first launched, after a year of operation, the game has gradually matured, and both its player base and revenue have become stable. Overall, the current Wuthering Waves is by no means as useless as some have disparaged it, but it is also far from being perfect, as its loyal fans claimed. It can only be said to be average, with obvious advantages and disadvantages, and a very clear target audience. This game is quite rich in content, but it is extremely time-consuming. The rigid link between character level and play time also means that players can only slowly savor the game content. Since daily grinding stress is generally low, the ability to tolerate highly repetitive combat and open world exploration will be the key to determining whether players can stay.

Since players cannot re-experience completed quests for now, it is recommended that players who plan to play for a long time try not to skip the main quest and the companion quests plot, both of which are key to shaping the game world and characters. Also, cause the combat of Wuthering Waves still has certain requirements on the player's operation, it is recommended to use a controller or play it on PC for mobile players. It is also worth mentioning that Wuthering Waves is quite friendly for returning players, so to some extent, it can be regarded as a game that can be freely picked up and put down at will.

Warframe has gone from troubled start up to live service dark horse to diminished prospect to finally, the premier frontrunner in the PVE-FPS sphere. Should you play it? Yeah, probably.

When you ask 'what's Warframe like?' most Warframe players say 'just play it it's free'. Any sane person sees that as a red flag, and in any other game it is a red flag. League of Legends is free, and 'just play it it's free' is a one way ticket to regret. Warframe isn't figuratively free, it is genuinely free. It is the most functional free to play economy outside of Guild Wars 2. 

[h3]Wait. Economy?[/h3]

Yeah. Trading is in the game. It's unobtrusive, it's easy to get in and out without too much hastle, it's optional, and it gives pure free to play players access to Platinum, the premium currency. If you like Tarkov but think BSG don't know what theyre doing, give this a shot.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1757990146}, {"review_text": "one of the better free to play games out there, proper little boredom killer, literally just arcade tarkov for the casual players", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1759228128}, {"review_text": "I have played this game extensively in their own native version before Steam's launch for a couple hundreds of hours. 

It is a game which i generally recommend to the hardcore extraction fps fans. It is not a classical online fps like CoD or BF; it is much more similar to games like Escape from Tarkov and Gray Zone Warfare.

Arena Breakout Infinite (ABI) as an extraction shooter has a much softer learning curve than Tarkov, known by everyone who's into this subgenre and i'm writing it both as a warning and as a feature.

The scope of the game is to safely extract from the map with as much loot as possible while also possibly complete a few missions to reach the season's endgoal and thus rewards. 

Nothing gets reset or wiped, not until now atleast, since i've logged in after 3 months and found all of my belongings and hard earned cash in my cache as long as the cosmetic rewards i've grinded for.

Dissimilarly to it's competitors, ABI has a ranking system which can be enabled or disabled depending on the type of map and game mode you queue up for.

It has different and more approachable modes for every kind of survivor, such as maps where only Solos can enter, or modes where you don't lose your gear (but you can't extract it either, meaning every loot you find is automatically converted to cash, with a lower ratio).

The ranked system is pretty nice, however, the last rank (Legend) requires an abnormal amount of points to reach compared to all the other ranks before it. I've attempted to reach it on the last season, however i ceased the grind while realizing i had to win 3 or 4 matches to compensate about 1 single loss. 

Anyway nothing prevents you from playing lower risk, lower rewards modes and i think it's a genuine way to separate the "for fun" players to the "ultra hardcore" ones.

One thing i really, really DO NOT LIKE is the tiers assigned to the bullets. It is true that you should be rewarded if you decide to spend 1 million Koen for 1 mag, but it's also true it's frustrating to be melted like butter in max heavy armor by them. This is a common and valid issue i have with these types of games which i'd change. I prefer rock>paper>scissor style of equip rather than Tiers.

Anyway, all in all ABI has much quality of life, lots of customization, great gunplay and complexity, all while staying Free to Play and not at all demanding you to spend any amount of money to enjoy. The completionists will surely consider spending some money for even greater quality of life (such as expanded safe boxes) and cosmetics but i have to say i never felt forced to do so.

Recommended.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1758034074}]

It has its flaws which will be addressed below but lets start with clearing up some misconceptions/outdated information regarding the game. The most obvious deterrent for potential new players to even install the game is that it requires HVCI to be turned off. While this was true when Windows 11 was new, this requirement was removed via an update several months later. HVCI is no longer required to be turned off as of this review and all other reviews that mentioned this issue are either outdated or just trolling. Next, there are claims that the game is infested with hackers (some reviews claim up to 90% of players are hacking). This is completely false. I have spent over 3k hours in the game and the number of people that were hacking/using some exploit can be counted on one hand. There definitely are players who still use hacks/find exploits but they are a small fraction of the playerbase (the same can be said with any other BR). The devs also publish weekly banned players lists to remove hackers and keep such behaviour in check.

With the misconceptions out of the way, lets move on to the negatives. First of all, the playerbase in the West (NA/EU servers) is tiny compared to Asia (SEA/AS servers). If you play on SEA/AS servers, kindly skip to the next paragraph as matchmaking is not an issue. For NA/EU servers, most new players will only be playing against bots (and winning most matches) in ranked mode until Solar. Assuming that they have the patience to reach Solar, newbies will then be placed in lobbies with top server players and proceed to be obliterated by them. Such matchmaking is understandably frustrating for new players as the learning curve can seem too steep. This is the point where newbies quit because they are demolished by veterans almost every match past Solar rank. Personally, I have also experienced this when I was new to the game so all I can say to new players is: Stay patient & "Get Good". Participate in custom lobbies to learn Neutral/combos/movement tech and you will be able to put up a fight against good players eventually. 

Another negative is the abysmal server disconnects during games, especially in crowded areas/endgame fights. These can vary in severity from being mildly annoying to causing the match to be lost. These glitches can happen quite often too, sometimes a few times during every match on bad days. You will experience screen stutters in mild cases, to seeing the screen buffer icon while the screen freezes and tries to reconnect to servers in worse cases. There is also the less common but potentially game breaking bug where you are sent back to the login screen during a match if you use certain hero skills, such as Tianhai's combo breaker F skill. As of writing this, the hero skill bug seems to be fixed but I will update this review if it happens again.

Finally, I shall address positives after all that doom and gloom. From all the previous points mentioned, you may think that all the drawbacks outweigh the positives, but I beg to differ. This is hands down the most unique BR available. Its depth of combat and movement mechanics is unmatched by any other modern game of its genre. Fights against real players are satisfying regardless of outcome once you have learnt the basics of Neutral/True Combos/Scalerushing. In a world where most if not all new games try to make you feel like a champion, this game constantly reminds you of your shortcomings in skill. You will lose way more than you win until you "get good". You will need to earn your wins which in turn feel much more fulfilling. I would also like to mention that there is a PvE mode called Showdown which is similar to Souls-like games and an extraction mode called Rift Traversal for those looking for something other than the BR. I highly recommend trying Showdown if the BR/PvP is not your cup of tea as boss fights there are just as challenging and fulfilling at the highest difficulty.

In conclusion, Naraka stands out as a unique melee-based BR experience in a sea of shooter BRs. 
Is it perfect? No.
Does it have technical issues? Yes. Sometimes.
Is it challenging but fulfilling to learn and improve? Absolutely.
Is it fun? Hell yea.
More importantly, is it worth your time? Find out for yourself. 
Naraka: Bladepoint is free to play and available across PC, XBox & PlayStation.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764248120}, {"review_text": "This may change later, but for right now, this game is friggin awesome!

This game is really great and everyone should give it at least a try.

[b] What you must know from the get-go is that this game is full of RNG mechanics. Skill still matters most, but the RNG factor plays a big part in how everything is going to go in your runs.
You will have to decide if this is your thing or not. I assure you, in case you are not used to this genre, in the very beginning when you're still learning how to do everything, you will 100% get very frustrated at times.
I suppose that was the intention of the developers. [/b]

I am one of those players that didn't have experience at all in Roguelikes. I knew what they are and how they function, but I didn't play any of them properly at all.

What I can tell is that although I got irritated often early on, I got used to the game mechanics, and once I got used to them, I was completely unbothered by them.
Don't get me wrong, I still have my opinion that Isaac could have been a lot better, but not everyone will see it the way I view it.
Others will say that all of those inconveniences make Isaac what it is today and why it's this popular and beloved.
So at the end of everything, my opinion is my opinion, you will have to decide for yourself.

[h2] Content & Replay Value: [/h2]

There’s a vast amount of content here - truly, a lot. The more you complete the game, the larger the pool of items, monsters, bosses, and floor levels gets.

Players are given an incentive to keep playing, provided they want to challenge themselves a bit, as the game consistently rewards the time and effort invested.

I can’t speak to how difficult it is to achieve 100% completion, as that wasn’t my goal, I prefer to explore other games as well, not only focus entirely only on one. However, it’s clear there’s a substantial amount to unlock and accomplish for those who are completionists.

I haven’t looked into it in depth, but I hope the achievements aren’t tied to extremely rare or arbitrary events that make them frustrating to earn.

In short, if you’re looking for a game with near-endless replayability, The Binding of Isaac is certainly one of those titles.

[h2] Combat System & Bosses: [/h2]

Once more, it's in your judgment whether it is good or not.

Personally, I don't mind it; it's not even a discussion of liking it or disliking it. I think it gets the job done; it's what it's supposed to do, and it's not bad.

I've played the entire thing on hard, and I didn't think it was all that hard at the end of everything.
It was fine.

What I will say, though, is don’t get discouraged if you can’t beat the levels for one reason or another. A decent number of people can be pretentious snobs, and they love calling others bad just because they don’t have the same level of experience. What they don’t realize is they’re just gatekeepers, preventing new players from enjoying the same things they love about the game.
I’d suggest these folks try out new genres of games they’re not used to, instead of just sticking to the ones that are easier to pick up, or already in their comfort zone - let’s see how they handle that.

[h2] What I'm not fond of: [/h2]

I repeat, by the end of it, I was unbothered by the design of the game because I got used to it, but that doesn't mean it didn't affect my enjoyment in the early parts.

The RNG was too much for me. It was either a fun run or complete torment, depending on how boring the items I received were. That made everything feel lame and slow. I didn’t like how you could finish an entire floor without getting any reward from it, especially since the items you did receive were either useless or actually made things worse.

Questions started popping into my mind: why am I doing this if there's no proper reward? Just a chance at one, and strictly that.

I believe it could have been balanced better. Not everything needs to be left up to chance. I do agree that some RNG adds a lot of replay value, but at the same time, it can turn the experience into a bit of a circus. And without mods, you don’t even know what the items are doing. You have to suffer through it to learn. That’s what the devs wanted, I guess. It’s their game. I can’t change what they view as good if they have a certain vision.

For me, I preferred having challenges on floors, something where you have to fight to evolve your stats like speed, damage, health, and so on. Not getting 100 items that all basically do the same thing. It’s not too interesting to get a 0.3 movement speed buff item as your reward.

Yes, I know, those fun items can make it too easy to win. So balance them in such a way where they’re not broken. I’ll take fun and interesting over everything else in this environment.

Co-op is already hard to balance, since you can beat the game effortlessly with multiple people.

They make sure RNG is always present, no matter how much depth you have in your Isaac game knowledge or how well you know what every item does. You’ll still have floors where the items are shown with a question mark, meaning you don’t know what you’re picking up.

Once again, it’s like they’re trying to make it a potential pain in the butt if you decide to take a chance on those question mark items.
You either pick them up and risk it, or skip them, which, again, basically means no reward for you. No chance at fun, if you catch my drift.


[b] I can go on with the discussion of the game, but I don't want to make this review too lengthy. [/b]

Are Isaac's traumas supposed to be jokes, or are they meant to be taken seriously though?

In one of his memories, he looks at the clouds, and the cloud gives him the middle finger, which makes him start crying.

In another, you see Isaac having a nightmare of him having a nightmare of him having a nightmare.

They’re jokes, aren’t they?

At first, everything is pretty confusing, but once everything comes together, there isn't much that compares to it in my opinion.

One of Isaac's strengths stems from what causes this initial confusion. There are HUNDREDS of items and dozens of bosses.
