After years of playing it on and off (about 6 years I think), I finally got it done. 
I feel like there's so much for me to say but at the same time my brain's like "I'm done with it dude, go away" lol. 

The Binding of Isaac is *THE* rogue-like, I wanna say it's the game a majority of people think of when you mention rogue-likes. The amount of replayability this game offers with it's randomly generated rooms and floors, hundreds of items that'll help or hinder you depending on what you have, a variety of bosses and secrets, and dozens of ways to play via unlockable characters and items makes it seem truly endless. 
 
Gameplay starting off might be a bit slow and can test your patience a lot of the time when starting a run, but the fun of runs comes from the snowballing effect after you've collected a few items and wind up being an amalgamation of tear effects and stat-ups. Item synergies and which item works best with others will be the key factor in your runs to wind up being practically untouchable by the end, or surviving by the skin of your teeth. Whether the items found are in a basement, cave or wherever else Isaac winds up in, the way Isaac looks changes with each item too. I've taken a few pictures of Isaac looking like an absolutely distinguished gentleman, or sometimes a void of a creature manifested from multiple pieces of a dead cat, a hooded cloak and a doctor mask (which made him look like a hooded cat doctor it was cute actually lol). Over the course of your time with the game you'll definitely come to despise certain items and gasp in happiness to see others (Guppy's Paw/Bozo my beloved).

Difficulty can be rough sometimes, especially considering it's a rogue-like, so best prepare for unfamiliar enemies, weird rooms and sometimes straight up bad luck messing up your runs. You can have the ability to win a good portion of runs if you're patient enough and are good at dodging projectiles, but sometimes it's best to restart for better luck. If runs aren't going so well, don't feel bad to take a break either 'cause I've taken weeks up to month long breaks and come back to an easy win more than a few times. It's probably why it took me this long to get around to 100%ing this game lol.

When it comes to DLC's, base game is fine if you wanna give it a shot, but Afterbirth & Afterbirth+ I think are necessary if you want Steam Workshop support and want access to the 'External Item Descriptions' mod, which saves you a ton of time by telling you what an item does in-game (unless you're me and don't mind having a wiki/Platinum God open to figure out what an item does lol).

Storywise, you get the intro. After that, you're off, and what little glimpses are shown make a big difference as to how you yourself render the story in your head. For what little story there is, personally, I'm glad about how it all wrapped up with the most recent DLC, Repentance. Really amazing community as well.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1764783170}, {"review_text": "I didn’t need to buy this again because I already owned the game and all its content outside of Steam, but I wanted to show my support for ArenaNet and the developers.

Whether you’re a new player or a returning veteran, now is a fantastic time to experience Guild Wars, especially with the current price offering great value. It remains one of the best MMORPGs ever made. However keep in mind, Guild Wars is very different from Guild Wars 2.

Why Guild Wars is worth playing:

Three full campaigns in one package - Prophecies, Factions, and Nightfall (Eye of the North is separate) give hours of rich story, challenging missions, and memorable environments for a great price.

Engaging and helpful community - Both new and veteran players are generally welcoming, making it easy to get into group missions, PvP, or just learning the mechanics.

Two decades of documentation - The Guild Wars Wiki (not the fandom one) is an incredible resource for quests, strategies, lore, and item details.

Timeless gameplay mechanics - Skill-based combat, strategic party composition, and challenging PvE encounters make the game rewarding even today.

Beautiful and varied world design - Each campaign has distinct regions, environments, and music that still hold up remarkably well.

PvP and PvE content - From epic story missions to competitive arena matches, Guild Wars caters to multiple playstyles.

No monthly fee - The original Guild Wars model still shines for players who enjoy an MMO experience without recurring costs.

Looking Forward

I hope the developers consider adding new content in the future - new campaigns, missions, or quality-of-life updates would be amazing. Even after all these years, Guild Wars has the potential to continue.

Verdict:

Guild Wars has aged gracefully and still offers hours of engaging gameplay. Whether you’re exploring the rich lore for the first time or revisiting old favorites, the combination of strong story, community, and timeless mechanics makes this game a must-play for anyone interested in MMORPGs.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1764785287}, {"review_text": "Bought the game again to support ArenaNet. Now I just need to figure out what I was doing 20 years ago on these characters.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 26, "timestamp_created": 1764789537}, {"review_text": "🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟 20-Year Veteran Review – A Perfect Reforging of a Legend


I’ve been playing Guild Wars since the original launch nearly 20 years ago, with over 20,000 hours across all campaigns. I’ve lived through every meta, every balance patch, every speedclear era, and every community wave this game has ever had.
Guild Wars Reforged isn’t just a remaster!  it genuinely feels like coming home, but everything is polished, modernized, and smoother without losing its soul.

The original combat system is still here: fast, tactical, skill-based, and punishing if you don’t think. But now it runs like silk. The revamped visuals keep the classic style without turning it into some generic modern MMO. The QoL updates alone feel like ArenaNet finally granting every wish veteran players whispered for years.

Running through Ascalon, Kaineng, the Desolation… it all hits incredibly hard emotionally. The nostalgia is real, but Reforged adds enough new features and improvements that it feels fresh again, not just recycled.

What impressed me most:

The original atmosphere is 100% intact

Hero AI improvements are insane better than 15 years ago when they slightly changed AI combat system

Classic builds still work, but new options open up creativity again e.g. current Meta

Towns feel alive with players like in 2005

Performance and load times are still good

The community vibes are just like the old days – helpful, funny, chaotic, depends.


After 20k hours, I honestly didn’t think Guild Wars could surprise me anymore.
I was wrong. 20th Anniversary gave us what we needed.

If you loved the original, this is the version we always dreamed of.
If you’re new, this is the best way to experience one of the greatest MMOs ever made.

Massive respect to ArenaNet. This is how you honor a legacy.

In game player count at the time of reforged release has hit nearly 40k. 
(During a weekday at 1pm EST)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764787488}, {"review_text": "Here is my initial review after 10 hours of playtime (which I know isn't much for an MMO):

This is my first time playing this game (never played GW2 either). I did play many other MMO's in the past including WoW, OSRS, Eve Online, Everquest, SWTOR, New World and many others.

The game itself is not a true MMORPG as the world is not truly open but zones connected via loading screens which are instanced so you cannot run into another player in the world. You get to see and meet other players in hubs around the world though where you can group up with them or join guilds to then venture into the world together to do missions.

The game is clearly showing it's age and that it came out at a time when the WoW formula hadn't been adapted yet by every MMO. There are no mounts, you character cannot jump, movement feels wonky. It's missing many QoL features from modern MMO's. And yet, I'm enjoying it.

Perhaps specifically because it does not feel like a WoW clone. It feels unique in it's own sense similar as what draws players to OSRS. Seeing dozens and dozens of players in player hubs still makes it feel alive and like an MMO, even if I know I won't see those players (unless I group up) in the game world (or zones). 

What I'm really digging so far and what feels very unique in this genre is the way classes (called professions in Guild Wars) work in this game. You get to pick your main class at the beginning and can later (soon actually) pick a second class. You will only learn some of the abilities of the second class though. There are dozens of potential abilities (as far as I found out) for any of the classes that you can eventually learn. Your hotbar is limited to 8 abilities at a time though. This combination of dual class system and abilities seem to allow for an insane amount of varity in playstyles. There is no paladin class? No problem, create a warrior and take monk as second class which has many healing abilities and you got yourself a paladin type of class. 

There seem to be no profession (crafting) skills as far as I can see. However you there are traders/crafter NPC's that require specific materials and they can then craft specific gear for you.

All in all the game feels like taking me back to the early 2000's when the WoW formula wasn't established yet and where every new MMO would use the exact same formula. So it feels refreshingly different and fun to learn how the game works compared to modern MMO's where you already know how they work because they are just copying WoW which in the mid/late 2000's turned out to be the winning formula in this genre. 

I would recommend this game to anyone who likes oldschool online games, a game that sometimes feels like an MMORPG but isn't really. I wouldn't suggest it to anyone who strictly likes the WoW formula exclusively that is used in modern MMO's and who expects modern MMO features.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1764916142}, {"review_text": "Don’t let the small (current 32h) of gameplay fool you, I have around 10 000 hours into this game via the original launcher.

This game has one of the best replay value on the market. Probably my best game story experience since I play video games. 
Even years later, you’ll find new stuff to do. 

Completed campaign? Alright, gear up your heroes with the best armors and skills bar you can do, that’s done? Explore the 3 huge maps designed carefully with stunnings views (desert, winter, post-apocalyptic, jungle, asian themed in one of these, and meet the vast list of npc and quests they have to give you to make progress in an instanced open world, absolutely beautiful map designs. Do PvP, done with pvp? Do Guild versus Guild to earn your guild a coloured outline! Done with GvG? Complete your Hall Of Monument for GW2, completed that? Grind the titles, done with titles? Get all the skills and pets available. Also done with that? Trade stuff between players to find the best weapon stats/ skin you can afford in one of the 3 main cities (Lion Arch, Keineng, Kamadan). You just learned that there’s actually been a time that some weapons actually droped with special stats and requirements before being ‘’nerfed’’ so they don’t drop anymore withing that time specs, but not removed from player’s inventory , so there’s still the possibility to find it somehow if the player’s willing to sell it to you for the right price! I mean, there’s ton of stuff to collect at some point from mini-pets, crazy rare weapons and shields! 

That game, is just the most complete one, most fun to come back, most fun to enjoy with friends! You’ll never find a complete, balanced skills list like the one this game has to offer. Make YOUR own build, try it , fix its flaws, make it better! Figure out if the market (ectos or armbraces) is going up or down and make fortune selling stuffs you droped while playing or obtain from a bargain to other players!

Your hero name will at somepoint be known by a huge community that still plays even to this date!

The best part? They still update it from time to time and add some stuff even since its predecessor (Guild Wars 2) came up in 2012. I have bought many copies, storage extensions etc just to support the devs that are still maintening this game, it’s a pure gem.

Honestly, I’ve been playing since 2005 and it’s the only game I actually keep replaying casually. I always find stuff to do or search in the trade chat channel. 

Be a master of the Fissure Of Woe or Underworld by going there with henchmans, friends, or alone choosing between normal mode and hard mode for a better chance to drop rare weapons!

This game just feels organic, no fancy infusions, no overdesigned armors or weapons. Just pure style with knives, fur, metal or even, chainmail. Theres bunch of armors and professions you can mix and match to your style! You can even dye your armor parts and weapons! Need to show what’s the plan to your friend ehile playing? Draw it on the mini map and it will show them instantly! You can even play almost like a top-down game or like a 3rd person game using either your keyboard or by clicking where you want to go with your pc mouse.

Guild Wars is my #1 PC game of all time, no questions asked, it’s an absolute masterpiece, and worth playing even to this date. The amount of contain is just crazy, it even has halloween , christmas events, new year events and more!

Only game I give 100/100 and even tho i’d put 110/100.

- Rooted combat. It will take some getting used to.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1765048744}, {"review_text": "They should have added new optional servers for Reforged.

This isn't how the original game even was. And it isn't fun playing an MMO that is only kept interesting if you don't interact with the other players and the greater economy. That defeats the purpose of it being an MMO.

Please rate this up so ArenaNet knows we want optional fresh servers.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 19, "timestamp_created": 1764878563}, {"review_text": "A classic and one of the early pioneers of the multiplayer RPG format. This game isn't like a traditional MMORPG. If you were expecting something like Gw2 or WoW, its not close. The multiplayer system is more like PoE where the player hubs are shared (towns, cities, hamlets, etc). While the explorable world, dungeons, missions; those are all instanced unique to your character. You can play with other players or add NPCs called henchmen to your party that act as NPC players. The next step are "Hero NPCs" which are more advanced customizable henchmen. Reminds me almost of a CRPG with how you handle grouping with heroes. The game is very narrative driven. Combat is tab target. The skill system has a significant amount of depth. You choose a primary class at character creation, this class cannot be changed. However, you eventually choose a secondary class. So you can be two classes at once. There's about 1,400 abilities between all the abilities. So the amount of builds you can play are endless. There's a significant amount of PvE and PvP content. Especially once you reach level 20. A significant amount of story to play through between the 3 campaigns that come with Reforged + Eye of the North DLC + bonus missions DLC. You can also unlock skins/titles in Gw2 by playing Gw1 through the hall of monuments system (make sure your Gw1 and Gw2 accounts are on the same platform. You can't link say a Gw2 account on the stand alone client to a Gw1 steam account). 

Such a very fun, unique game. Nothing else like it on the market. Graphics/animations are dated since the game is from 2005. But still very fun.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764824244}, {"review_text": "Just for clarity: at the time of release, "Reforged" is a relatively small update to the original game. If you already owned Guild Wars previously, simply log in using your existing account and you can play it.

The main selling points of the Reforged patch are:
- Steam Deck and gamepad support
- They used to have a bazillion different packs for sale, but it's more straightforward now: Reforged includes the original trilogy of Prophecies, Factions, Nightfall. Eye of the North is still a DLC sold separately.
- The technical updates include: support for higher resolutions, skill icons updated to higher res, better antialiasing/bloom. Nice small things, but nothing major.

---

As for the game: it's still a great game, now sold for really cheap. Easy to suggest giving it a try, even if you're only interested in a single-player experience. There really aren't many games that play like GW, due to the whole thing with NPCs that you build, gear up and sometimes micromanage while playing.

GW often comes up in conversations about MMOs and I won't argue against it, but I think "cooperative RPG" is a good term just to set expectations. You can see other players in the towns, but the "open world" zones are instanced, so you won't run into other players when exploring.

You can invite people in the town, and then go play any content with those players. Unless actively playing with friends, you will spend vast majority of your playtime playing with a group of NPCs, as you won't really group up with randoms just to do some standard quests.

Many people, including my self, primarily just play this game almost as if it's a single-player game. For me a major motivation in progression is to optimize my group of NPC heroes. The only reason I'm in a guild is to chat with people, I rarely group up with anyone.

At the very top end of the game there are a handful of quite difficult dungeons that were made for player groups, but with optimal NPC group, even those can be soloed (there's guides made for all of them).

---

...but just to be clear, if you want to play with players, you can find groups for most of the challenging parts of the game (and even for easier exploration stuff). There are active guilds out there, and the game is currently more active than it's been in a decade (at least at the time of writing).", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1764841675}, {"review_text": "The best PvP in games like this till today: GvG, a miracle for me that no one has copied that so far.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1764836376}, {"review_text": "Good Game, Jeremy Soule's music is iconic (bring him back for GW3).

I'll update my review when they fix this but for now I'm sad because I just want to play the game and have the ability to purchase items for the GW store.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1765079061}, {"review_text": "Guild wars - моя ММО всех времен.
Не то чтобы я в неё много наиграл - /age говорит, что я провёл в ней 942 часа за последние 234 месяца.
И вот в течение этих 20 лет я нет-нет, да и возвращался в неё.

Это игра, благодаря которой я ещё в школе получил возможность практиковать английский язык с реальными людьми.
Это игра с великолепной атмосферой приключения.
Это игра с самым безумным билдостроением в жанре.

Если открыть по ней вики, то можно увидеть список из 3500 (три тысячи пятьсот) скилов.
Разумеется не все они рождены равными, но эксперименты с кнопками это то, что может дать много приятных часов (всего с собой можно иметь до 8 скиллов - поэтому синергия очень важна).
За 20 лет игра, разумеется, была "решена" - и есть мета билды (нынче я такое и юзаю).

Но это не особо важно, т.к. основа игры - это партийное pve (хотя есть и pvp, возможно с выходом рефоржа оно оживёт).
Контент расчитан на группы от 2 до 8 персон. Собрав такую пати и настроив билды в хабе - выходишь в инстанс на локацию (что-то аля PoE). 
И прелесть в том, что даже малая популяция не становится для неё проблемой - т.к. со временем набираешь себе команду нпц, у которых можешь настроить как скилы, так и шмотьё.

Минусы в том, что это очень олсдкульная игра.

Rather than reinventing the game from the ground up, ArenaNet approaches Reforged as a restoration—polishing, refining, and enhancing the experience without disturbing its fundamental identity. From the moment the game loads, those who once adventured through Tyria will recognize the familiar atmosphere, but now with a clarity and sharpness that better reflects modern hardware standards. Reforged feels like returning to a cherished world after years away, only to find it lovingly cleaned, repaired, and illuminated with new light.

The visual improvements are among the most immediately striking upgrades. Textures appear sharper, lighting is richer, and subtle effects like ambient occlusion and improved shadows help breathe new life into environments that were already memorable for their artistry. Skill icons, interface elements, and character details have been updated to preserve the original aesthetic while making everything clearer and more readable on high-resolution displays. The 3D audio overhaul contributes even more to the sense of immersion, giving zones richer environmental soundscapes and adding a layer of atmospheric nuance that was previously absent. Instead of altering the world itself, these enhancements amplify the beauty and tone of Guild Wars as players always imagined it, rather than how it was limited by mid-2000s hardware.

Quality-of-life improvements further bridge the gap between old and new. Modernized UI scaling, a smoother quest-tracking system, enhanced navigation tools, and complete controller support—including compatibility with portable devices like the Steam Deck—make Reforged feel far more accessible without simplifying any part of the original gameplay structure. The addition of official support for modern hardware configurations also removes longstanding barriers that returning fans may have faced, making the game easier to launch, configure, and enjoy. These refinements allow players to engage comfortably with Guild Wars in a way that aligns with contemporary expectations while fully retaining the original systems that defined its gameplay.

One of Reforged’s major strengths lies in its content model. The package consolidates the full trilogy—Prophecies, Factions, and Nightfall—into a unified experience, making it easier than ever for new players to explore the vast narrative arc of the original game. This approach honors the original buy-once, play-forever philosophy that helped set Guild Wars apart from other MMOs of its time. Players who already owned the classic campaigns receive Reforged at no additional cost, ensuring that the decades-long community can step back into Tyria without barriers. For newcomers, the complete collection creates a cohesive entry point that presents the entire Guild Wars storyline in its most polished form.

Gameplay remains true to the original design. Guild Wars Reforged does not attempt to reshape its instanced mission structure or its distinctive skill-based combat system, both of which were foundational to its identity. Missions still unfold as carefully crafted scenarios rather than open-world zones, and the combat still relies heavily on tactical skill bar design, party synergy, and strategic execution. This fidelity to the source material is refreshing; rather than diluting what made the game special, Reforged preserves the tight, thoughtful systems that differentiated Guild Wars from the MMOs that dominated its era. At the same time, this adherence may feel dated for players accustomed to modern sandbox worlds, but fans of strategic, instance-based RPG storytelling will find the experience just as compelling as it ever was.

The enthusiasm surrounding the release demonstrates the enduring affection players hold for Guild Wars. Reports of server congestion following launch highlight a resurgence of interest, suggesting that both nostalgia and curiosity have drawn substantial numbers of players into the reforged world. This renewed attention opens the door for a revitalized community—one made up of veterans revisiting old memories and newcomers discovering Tyria for the first time. Reforged is more than a technical update; it becomes a shared event, a bridge between eras of MMO play, and a way of preserving a piece of gaming history for future audiences.

Guild Wars® Reforged ultimately succeeds because it understands what made the original powerful and does not try to overwrite it. Instead, it enhances the experience in ways that respect its legacy while removing the friction points that once made the classic difficult for modern players to revisit. The result is a revival that feels authentic, elegant, and thoughtfully crafted. For longtime fans, it is an invitation to return home with fresh eyes; for new players, it is perhaps the best opportunity yet to explore a landmark MMO in its most accessible and visually appealing form. In both spirit and execution, Reforged stands as a testament to how a classic game can be renewed without losing the essence that made it endure.

Brings me back to the golden days.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1764784388}, {"review_text": "The Guild Wars Trilogy (now updated and named reforged) is possibly the greatest blend of co-op RPG with MMO elements ever created. Originally released in 2005, most components here have really held up through time especially compared to it's competition. The reforged update made small tweaks to modernize the game, like gamepad support (with that noticeably better movement control when using WASD on keyboard as the game was largely click to move focused during development), further render distance, improved lighting with SSAO, and HD bloom. The team responsible for this update also found original UI elements that were uncompressed and replaced the old compressed assets that didn't scale well on modern displays. 

What I have always liked about this game
- Classes - A lot of them, with instantly recognizable class identity/design behind all of them.

- Duel Class - You can choose a secondary class, to really customize your experience - you get nearly all of the second classes tool kit as well it isn't watered down.

- Skills - being limited to 8 skills keeps the game complex and engaging enough, but it's the hundreds of skills you have to choose from that really sets this game apart. Their exists optimal meta builds but you can really build your own playstyle here for better or worse. limiting the skills you can use to 8 brings a unique way to do class customization that is so much more impactful than passive talent trees of it's contemporaries. There is also a system of stealing "Elite" skills from different enemies throughout the game, a really cool system I have not seen elsewhere.

- Visuals - in 2005 this was like magic especially for a game in the MMO genre, it almost appeared photo-realistic at that time. In 2025 I appreciate the art style still, it never was photo-realistic as my rose tinted glasses would have me think, but instead more of renaissance painting stretched across polygons that really creates something special that the 2000s era of gaming had - and that is the creativity of working within your limitations. 

- UI - the UI has since launch been seen as one of the greats. Without needing to be strapped together by addons, or waiting 15 years for a re-vamp, every element of the UI has been able to be repositioned or re-sized since launch in 2005. It's simple, and not gaudy, it's withstood the test of time and the newly added controller support is just awesome for using a mobile PC to play. They also added a quest tracker without needing to keep the quest panel open which was a great add.

- Story - Guildwars has always been unique in that, people treat it like an MMO but it's really a co-op RPG with multiple campaigns to play. Well these campaigns are considered some of the greatest in RPG history, but as an MMO these blew everything out of the water at the time. Cutscenes, voice acting, a coherent story from start to finish. There is even in the first campaign a zone (Prophecies) that becomes inaccessible early on into the game. This zone holds a solid 10 hours of content that you could accidentally miss, it was unafraid to do knew experimental things. You can start from any campaign on any character at any time. Back when the game was new, you didn't even need to own Guild Wars, as Guildwars Factions and Guild War Nightfall were considered base games and not expansion packs. Eye of the North is the only expansion pack for Guildwars - this was another thoughtful way to handle expanding a game while acquiring new players, retaining old ones, and not ruining what was made before.

- Sound - zones have distinct sound effects through them, which helped greatly with immersion, I could sit in Shing Jea monastery all day and listen to the different bells and windchimes. Spells, and different areas of feedback in the game have instantly recognizable sound design to them - You will now when someone is using a curse, heal, or elemental magic fast. 

- Music - Jeremey Soule has composed Guild Wars since day 1, you may recognize him from The Elder Scrolls, Guildwars 2, WoW, Neverwinter Nights, Company of Heroes, 40k Dawn of War, or Star Wars KOTR. Point is he is a legend, and I believe that Guild Wars was his greatest work ever. I'm torn between the soundtrack for Prophecies and Factions, giving the edge to Factions as that was my first experience in Guildwars and the soundtrack to Cantha really is meditative. 

The World/PvE - Guildwars is not an open world game, in 2005 MMOs as a giant continuous open world where not really existent. However, it is also not a traditional MMO in that every zone is separated by portals yet always online connected to other players. It uses cities and outposts as player hubs with channels in between them to link players together during downtime to trade, communicate, and group up. Your group get's it's own instance every time it leaves one of these safe zones. This allows for a game world that almost always feels like you are in a dungeon group with real senses of danger. As far as endgame PvE this mostly materializes as collectibles, titles, filling the Hall of Monuments for Guild Wars 2, and rare item hunting for perfect stats. Dungeons were added in Eye of the North, and before that were things like Urgoz which may be considered a boss raid. The endgame on PvE is a bit lighter in GW1, but that's part of the design philosophy of not being a traditional MMO but more cooperative RPG. 

PVP - Player vs Player content, is the highlight of the game. The very name of the game is a massive feature, you can do guild wars between enemy guilds, where your guild hall (think of it as a private zone your guild can buy and lightly customize) turns into a battleground that you fight enemy guilds in. Players outside of the guilds can tune in and watch these battles in real-time and watch recordings! In Factions campaign, you may choose Kurzick or Luxon and partake in non-competitive PVP more like a battleground between these factions. Guilds within each faction also war of control of zones in Cantha. However one of the biggest features is the ability to create PVP only characters, so you don't have to play every single class in the campaign side of the game and level them to experience high-end PVP, there is still a progression system in needing to unlock skills via playing and access to the best gear, but you get to skip the grind if PVP is your goal. 

TL:DR
I love this game, it does have it's flaws and parts that are dated (Lack of Jump) but it's a unique game that really has never been replicated. This is an instant buy for anyone who wants to play the first game coming from Guild Wars 2, MMO vets who missed out on it back in the day, or fans of Older RPGs. The reason for that is simple, it's one of the few fighting games I've played that is easy to both understand and pick up and play. My biggest issue with other games of this genre is that while their systems have great depth, to reach that depth you have to cross multiple barriers before you can begin having fun, and one of them is the input combinations. I simply don't care for the obsession of other games for making me do God of War quick time events for even the most basic moves, it ruins the fun for me. Not the case here, everything from specials to supers is simple and straightforward; a Quarter-Circle + a Button, that's it. There's no BS, to hoops to jump through, just an open invitation to learn the systems at play. This makes a world of difference in being able to enjoy the game, it allows you to focus on learning the neutral, playing mind-games, bettering your defense, learning advanced combos, practicing team-synergy, creating set-ups and mix-ups, all without having to worry about whether or not my hand will be able to pull off the move I want to use. For this, it's one of few competitive games where I've been able to have fun right off the bat, while improving my skills constantly too.

This is all without mentioning how gorgeous the presentation of the game is, doing true justice to the show's artsyle, looking 2D while being 3D with many techniques like frame timing, model manipulation, smears, impact frames, and more

Some were clunky, others were flashy but shallow. But DRAGON BALL FighterZ? This was the first time I felt like I was watching the anime and playing it at the same time—and somehow, it all worked.

The first thing that hits you—besides a Goku beam to the face—is the absolutely jaw-dropping art style. Arc System Works captured the look of the show perfectly, blending crisp 2D-style animation with 3D models in a way that feels straight out of the series.

Every attack, every transformation, every beam clash feels handcrafted to ignite that nostalgic fire. And those cinematic finishers? Yeah, watching Goku launch a Spirit Bomb or Frieza destroy a planet never gets old.

I expected fan service. What I didn’t expect was a tight, competitive fighter underneath the flashy anime exterior.

The 3v3 tag system adds depth and team synergy, but it’s also surprisingly accessible. Even as someone who’s not a fighting game pro, I could pull off cool-looking combos and feel powerful. At the same time, I’ve seen high-level players turn matches into surgical battles of reflexes and mind games.

You can button-mash if you want, but FighterZ rewards practice and smart play. It walks the tightrope between entry-level fun and esports-level depth, and somehow doesn’t fall off.

The base roster is packed with series favorites—Goku (obviously), Vegeta, Frieza, Cell, Majin Buu, Gohan, and more. And with DLC, you get characters from Dragon Ball Super like Jiren, Kefla, and UI Goku, plus wildcards like Broly (Z and Super).

Each character plays uniquely, with different assists, supers, and mechanics. Whether I wanted to crush with Android 16’s grabs or zone with Beerus’s unpredictable orbs, there was always someone fun to try.

And let’s be real—hearing the Japanese voice actors (or English dub, if that’s your thing) in the middle of a mid-air battle just makes it hit that much harder.

The story mode is... okay. It’s mostly a “what-if” scenario involving Android 21 (an original character), mind control, and a lot of map-based movement. It’s not as gripping as the anime arcs, but it’s fun for lore and unlocks.

Arcade mode, training, ranked and casual online matches, and replay features round out the experience. The online netcode was spotty at launch, but improved over time—though the community still wishes for rollback netcode universally.

DRAGON BALL FighterZ is the most stylish, most polished, and most faithful Dragon Ball game ever made—and one of the best fighting games of the past decade. Whether you're a die-hard DBZ fan, a casual gamer, or a seasoned fighter, there's something here to dig into.

It's not just a love letter to the series—it's a full-powered Kamehameha blast of adrenaline, competition, and style.

As thrilling to watch as it is to play. A Super Saiyan-tier fighter.
Fast. Flashy. Deep. Fun. DRAGON BALL FighterZ nails it all.

🕹️ Hours Played: 1000+ | Platform: Steam | Played with controller 🎮

After over a decade of waiting and a detour into the reboot territory (DmC), Devil May Cry 5 roared back onto the scene in 2019—and it was worth every second. This game isn’t just a return to form for the franchise, it’s the definitive evolution of what Devil May Cry was always meant to be: brutally stylish, emotionally impactful, and technically masterful.

⚔️ Gameplay – 10/10
Let’s get this out of the way: DMC5 is arguably the best action combat system ever made. Period.
You get to play as three completely different characters:

Nero – Back with his Red Queen sword and Blue Rose revolver, but now rocking Devil Breakers, a collection of prosthetic arms with unique powers (grapple, time stop, explosive punches, and more). He’s more versatile than ever.

V – A brand new character who commands three demon familiars (Griffon, Shadow, Nightmare) to do the fighting while he stays out of harm’s way. A completely different kind of gameplay—tactical, poetic, and risky.

Dante – The king returns with all his iconic style-switching madness, multiple melee weapons (Rebellion, Sparda, Balrog, Cavaliere, Devil Sword Dante...) and a deep arsenal of guns (Ebony & Ivory, Coyote-A, Kalina Ann x2, and the absurd Dr. Faust). There’s nothing else like him in gaming. SSS rank or go home.

The combat depth is absurd. You can juggle enemies mid-air for minutes, style-cancel attacks, experiment with hundreds of combo routes, and still feel like you’ve only scratched the surface.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3517936514

🔥 Performance & Visuals – 10/10
The RE Engine shines here. DMC5 looks jaw-droppingly beautiful without sacrificing performance. Fluid 60 FPS gameplay (even on mid-range rigs), crisp animations, realistic lighting, and expressive facial detail. Each environment, from ruined cities to demonic hellscapes, is dripping with mood and style.

It’s one of the best optimized PC ports Capcom has ever released.

🎵 Music & Sound Design – 10/10
Every character has a dynamic battle theme that builds as you fight better.

“Devil Trigger” for Nero is an adrenaline bomb.

“Crimson Cloud” for V is eerie, poetic, and deadly.

“Subhuman” and later “Bury the Light” for Dante and Vergil are metal masterpieces.

Sound effects are razor-sharp. Every sword slash, gunshot, and explosion is punchy. Voice acting is top-tier, especially Johnny Yong Bosch as Nero and Reuben Langdon's iconic Dante performance.

🧠 Story – 8.5/10
Surprisingly heartfelt. The story picks up years after DMC4, revolving around a mysterious demon king named Urizen and the secrets behind V’s identity. We get to see Nero’s growth, Dante’s pain and duty, and even Vergil’s long-awaited return.

While it’s still a bit campy and full of one-liners (as it should be), there’s emotional weight here—especially in the Dante/Vergil arc. The ending is bittersweet perfection.

🔁 Replayability – 10/10
With multiple difficulties (Human, Devil Hunter, Son of Sparda, Dante Must Die, Heaven or Hell, Hell and Hell), secret missions, S-rank challenges, hidden blue/red orbs, and three completely unique playstyles, DMC5 begs to be replayed.

Add Bloody Palace mode, where you climb floor after floor of enemies with increasing difficulty, and the Vergil DLC (where you can play as him in the full campaign and BP), and you have a game with infinite replay value.

📌 Pros:
✅ Deep, rewarding combat for all skill levels
✅ Gorgeous graphics and animation
✅ Flawless controller support & PC performance
✅ Incredible soundtrack
✅ Three main characters, all uniquely fun
✅ Vergil is playable (DLC or SE)
✅ Bloody Palace & multiple difficulty tiers
✅ Fan-service that actually respects the lore

⚠️ Cons:
❌ V’s playstyle can feel passive for some players
❌ The game ends leaving you desperately wanting more
❌ Level design is good, but not as varied or interactive as DMC3/4

📝 Final Verdict: 9.5/10
Devil May Cry 5 is a love letter to the fans, a masterclass in action game design, and one of Capcom’s crowning achievements. Whether you're a series veteran or a newcomer, you’ll find an experience that’s equal parts challenging, stylish, and unforgettable. This isn’t just about killing demons—it’s about doing it with flair.

The game-play is fun. The story is stupid but charming and silly in its own way because of how self aware it is. The combat is easy to pick up and hard to master, with so much variety in combos, unlocks and characters providing a ton of skill expression. The optimisation of this game is so unbelievably smooth, you'd think capcom had to do a demonic blood pact with virgil himself to make this RE engine as good as it is.

What impressed me the most though is how phenomenal the cut scenes were. The amount of detail put into the characters, the environments and the designs are truly top of the line for this genre (and any game really). This game genuinely has some of the best cinematic choreography and directing I’ve seen. It is incredibly impressive and hats off to the talented and passionate people behind this game. They clearly put their hearts into it, and it shows.

My only nitpick with this game is how the level design hasn’t evolved much since the previous entries. This franchise has always  had very linear design that boils down to: move forward, kill everything and repeat until the credits roll. I was hoping DMC 5 would have innovated or changed this formula at least a little but it hasn't. 

Furthermore, the environments in this game aren’t that varied as they are exclusively made up of two locations, London and the demon realm. they do vary slightly in color but overall look and feel the same. This makes all the levels feel repetitive and undiscernible from each other. 

It’s a real shame too considering how impressive the art direction of this game is. Having more variety in locations would have been such a great way for the art team to flex their talent and creativity. These issues are minor nitpicks though, and they did not take away from the overall experience, especially when compared to everything this game does right.

This game slaps like no tomorrow and it’s a must play for any fan of hack n slash games. As a big DMC fan, this game has hands down the best gameplay and boss fights out of all of them and they make for an endlessly replayable experience.
 
And because of that, I recommend DMC 5 to longtime fans of the franchise and newcomers alike.

The gameplay rewards dedication, and you can pull off stunningly stylish combos if you put in the effort, but accepts casualness so you don't fall behind if you struggle with it. The story is delivered non-linearly through a mix of gameplay and short cutscenes, and although context from previous games certainly helps, you can go into this game with very little working knowledge and get by just fine. All the characters have distinct personalities, identities, and roles within the story, and each has their own play style. I’ve been a Borderlands fan for years. The chaos, the humor, the endless loot grind... it’s always been about fun first, never too serious. But Borderlands 4? It feels like Gearbox got dazzled by Unreal Engine 5, slapped on a $70 price tag, and forgot the part where the game is supposed to actually run..

[b] Randy Pitchford said fans should have “realistic expectations.” But if “realistic expectations” means paying $70 for a stutter ridden mess that crashes every few minutes and wrapped in Denuvo DRM that tanks performance even further, then no thanks. That’s not realism, that’s laziness dressed up as ambition. [/b]

The stutters are constant, the crashes are brutal, and it feels like the game fights you harder than the bosses do. Every firefight turns into a slideshow, every new area feels like a gamble whether the game will hold together or not. For a series built on fast, frantic chaos, it’s painful when the biggest challenge is just keeping the game from breaking...

[h3] Unreal Engine 5 Looks Pretty, But Plays Ugly [/h3]

On paper, Borderlands 4 looks gorgeous. Unreal Engine 5’s lighting, reflections, and seamless world transitions give it a scale and detail the franchise never had before. But the moment you actually play, the shine fades. Stutters, frame drops, and bizarre loading hiccups pop up constantly. Even top-tier GPUs like the RTX 4080 and 5080 are struggling to keep 60FPS in 4K with DLSS on, and if the cutting edge hardware can’t do it, what chance do the average players have? 

Gamers on Twitter couldn’t even crack 60fps at 1080p with an RTX 3070, a card that’s miles above the so called minimum requirements. That’s not just a hiccup, that’s proof the system requirements are complete nonsense. And Gearbox basically shrugged, warning that if you don’t meet their next-gen minimums, the game might be unplayable. 

Imagine being told that before you even buy it. It’s not honesty, it’s them admitting they knew it was broken, but also knew people would still pay anyway.

[h3] Pricing Feels Like a Joke We’re Not In On [/h3]

And then there’s the price. $70 for the base game is steep already, but $100 for Deluxe and $130 for Super Deluxe? Come on. For a game this unstable, it feels like paying premium for early access to a beta test. [b]  Randy Pitchford’s comment about real fans supporting the price was honestly insulting. Fans aren’t ATMs. We want to support the game, not bankroll optimization patches. It’s insane how devs keep shipping games with game-breaking bugs like it’s normal. These aren’t tiny glitches/bugs, they’re constant crashes and stutters, and they want full price for this mess? [/b]

[h3] What’s Still Great [/h3]

I won’t pretend Borderlands 4 is all bad. In fact, underneath the mess, it might be the best Borderlands since 2. The humor lands, the gunplay is as addictive as ever, and the new mechanics have real potential to take the series forward. The tragedy is that none of it matters when the game can’t stay stable long enough for you to enjoy it. Every stutter, every crash, every performance hiccup turns what could have been the return of peak Borderlands into an expensive tech demo. And that’s what stings the most, there’s a damn good game here, maybe even a great one, but it’s buried under technical failures and a price tag that feels like a cruel joke.

[h3] Final Thoughts [/h3]

Borderlands 4 should’ve been a victory lap. The full power of Unreal Engine 5, a fanbase that stuck around through every spin-off and cash grab and this is what we get? A broken, stutter-filled mess hidden behind Denuvo and a $70 paywall. Gearbox didn’t just drop the ball, they spiked it into the dirt and told us to clap anyway.

The cruel part? This is actually the best Borderlands since 2. The writing hits, the gunplay is fire, and the world begs to be explored. But none of that matters when you can’t play for more than ten minutes without a hitch, a crash, or your frames falling off a cliff. It’s like locking a gourmet meal behind a glass case and handing us a plastic fork.

Randy Pitchford told us to have realistic expectations... 
Fine. Here’s mine: I expect a $70 game not to run like a beta test. I expect a studio with Gearbox’s legacy not to let DRM strangle its own players. I expect respect. Instead, we got excuses.

Unless Gearbox pulls its head out of its own hype machine, Borderlands 4 could kill the franchise. First the garbage and total joke of a movie, now this broken mess, they’re turning a legacy into a joke.

In a lot of ways I think Borderlands 4 is like Borderlands 3 in that mechanically the gameplay is fundamentally better but everything else is kind of a mixed bag. Just being able to mantle ledges and slide while running in Borderlands 3 felt amazing, now in BL4 your vault hunter can glide, air dash, double jump, use a whip to yeet things to yourself or to launch yourself around the map and even climb along walls. The moment-to-moment gameplay in BL4 is so much more kinetic and fun than any other entry in the series.

Farming specific bosses is so much better now in BL4, there's a Mad Moxxi cutout in front of boss arenas where you can pay to respawn the boss. And there's a portal back to the front of the arena after you beat the boss. Gone are the days of running through a zone, getting to a boss arena, dropping down, deleting it, not getting the drop you need, quitting out to the main menu, reloading and trying it again and again.

Gun manufacturers can now have licensed components of other manufacturers as a modifier. For example a Vladof SMG can have a Maliwan underbarrel, so you get two elemental damage types you can switch between. Grenades, mini-guns and rocket launchers are now classified as ordinance equipment which just regenerate a limited set of ammunition rather being expendable ammunition like every other weapon and sort of frees up one equipment slot. Take like 70% of the campaign you got in older Borderlands games, take those linear gameplay sections that used to dot a zone and replace them with boring, repeatable openworld activities. [h2]Recommendation: Recommended[/h2]

[h3]What I Liked (Pros):[/h3]
+ Movement and gunplay are phenomenal, grapple hooking, gliding, sliding, and chaining it all together feels buttery smooth. It’s easily the best-feeling Borderlands game to date. Even spawning your vehicle and riding through the open world feels awesome, fast, responsive, and reminiscent of Destiny’s Sparrow in the best way.
+ Open world and sandbox design are a huge win. The verticality, traversal options, and sheer scale make exploration genuinely fun.
+ Skyboxes are jaw-dropping, especially in the second half of the game. The celestial vistas in zones like Dominion and Terminus Range are unforgettable, [spoiler] especially the moment you ride the sky lift into orbit, and the haunting beauty of the area where you find Lilith. [/spoiler] Those visuals were next-level.
+ Gun customization is wild. Mixing and matching manufacturer parts creates an insane amount of weapon variants to chase, it’s loot heaven.
+ Customization is excellent. Tons of skins and colour options for your character, guns, vehicle, and Echo (your little personal robot). Unlocking them through challenges and mission completions feels earned and rewarding.
+ Side quests are surprisingly excellent. There’s a ton of them, and most feel meaningful. Some even outshine the main missions. Standouts include:
Escape Room – A puzzle-heavy mission that rewards observation and lateral thinking.
Meat Is Murder – A twisted culinary mystery in The Fadefields.
Vend of the Line – A noir-style investigation in Carcadia Burn.
Abduction Injunction – Alien conspiracy meets bureaucratic chaos.
No Place Like Home – Emotional and eerie, set in a shifting dreamscape.
Claptrap’s Contractual Crisis – Classic humour and surprisingly heartfelt moments.
+ Story is solid. It’s second only to Borderlands 2, and let’s be honest, nothing’s ever going to top Handsome Jack.
+ Villains like Calous and Vile Lictor are far more memorable than the main antagonist, Timekeeper. They steal the show.
+ Faction design is a big step up. The Outbounders and Electi are way more interesting than anything we got in Borderlands 3.
+ Boss mechanics are genuinely impressive. Some fights rival Destiny 2 in complexity, it’s not just “stand on a plate.” You’ve got multi-phase encounters, environmental hazards, and puzzle-like mechanics that keep you on your toes. It’s a huge step forward for the series.
+ No in-game shop. No microtransactions, no premium cosmetics, everything is earned through gameplay. It’s refreshing and makes progression feel meaningful.

[h3]What I Didn’t Like (Cons):[/h3]
- Performance issues crop up way too often, especially in high-density combat zones and open-world traversal. For how the game looks, which, yes, is a visual step up from Borderlands 3, it still shouldn’t be running at 40–60 FPS. It’s a cel-shaded game, and the frame drops are brutal. Spawning your vehicle and riding through the open world causes massive dips, especially after long rides.
- Endgame content is thin. Once the story wraps, there’s not much to keep you grinding beyond loot.
- Timekeeper is forgettable. As the main villain, they’re overshadowed by stronger side antagonists.
- UI and inventory management still feels clunky, especially when sorting through hundreds of weapon variants.
- Multi-character progression is a mess. You can boost a new character to level 30, sure, but everything else? You’re stuck redoing the same grind. Map fog doesn’t carry over, so you have to re-explore every zone. Gun manufacturer challenges and faction reputation, none of it is account-wide. It’s exhausting. If you want to experiment with builds, the game punishes you for it.

[h3]Wishlist – Things I’d Love to See Added:[/h3]
[list]
[*] Endgame Raids or Dungeons – High-level co-op challenges with unique loot and mechanics would give players a reason to stick around. 
[*] Performance Optimization – The game should run better without relying on AI upscaling tools like DLSS or whatever Randy suggested — especially since those features are only available on 4000-series GPUs and above. A cel-shaded Borderlands game shouldn’t need cutting-edge hardware to maintain stable frames. 
[*] Expanded Faction Systems – Reputation, perks, and faction-specific gear could deepen engagement. 
[*] More Traversal Challenges – Parkour puzzles or time trials using the movement system would be a great addition. 
[*] Account-Wide Progression – Map fog, challenges, and reputation should carry across characters. Let us grind once, not five times.
[/list]

[h3]Achievements:[/h3]
Most achievements are pretty manageable and can be earned just by playing through the game and exploring thoroughly. There’s a bit of grind if you’re going for 100%, but nothing outrageous, except for one: getting all Vault Hunters to level 50 and unlocking their vehicles. That one takes serious time.

There are also two missable achievements to watch out for:
[list]
[*] All Things Vend – Can be missed if you don’t follow the correct steps during the “Vend of the Line” side mission.
[*] Rift Incompatible – Requires interacting with Oddman’s frozen body at the end of “Exit Through the Rift Shop.” You only get one shot at it — no replay.
[/list]
And yes, difficulty-based achievements exist. Reaching Ultimate Vault Hunter Rank 5 (UVH5) is one of them. It’s tied to post-game progression and requires pushing through increasingly tough enemies and bosses. It’s not brutal, but it’s definitely a challenge. The grindy ones are listed below.
[list]
[*] Catch-A-Ride - Collect all personal vehicles, to get these you will need to reach level 50 on all vault hunters.
[*] Area of Expertise - Complete any Gear Challenge category.
[*] Grassroots Campaigner - Complete all side missions.
[*] Brand Equity - Complete any Manufacturer Challenge category.
[/list]
The rest of the list is pretty chill, you’ll knock out most of them naturally as you complete zones, finish missions, and collect along the way.

[h3]Memorable Quotes:[/h3]
[list]
[*]“Well if it isn’t my favorite…… it’s you”
[*]What? Oh, yeah! Followed the safety manual for flinging people over the void to the letter, I did!
[*]"wait, why am I buying your shite"
[*]"Tips welcome - money, not advice."
[*]"You'll never get me plucky arms!"
[*]"You keep talkin' to me - you know I'm a HOLOGRAM, right?"
[*]"Oh, what a mighty Vault Hunter! ...and you're here too."
[*]"One man's junk is another man's... junk. But hey - CREDITS!"
[/list]

[h3]Final Thoughts:[/h3]
Borderlands 4 is the most mechanically refined game in the series. The movement system alone, with its grapple, glide, and slide, makes traversal and combat just feels really fun. It’s the first time I’ve felt truly free in a Borderlands game, and the open world complements that beautifully.

The story doesn’t quite reach the heights of Borderlands 2, but it’s close. Timekeeper is a weak link, but Calous and Vile Lictor more than make up for it. The factions are richer, the world more alive, and the side quests are genuinely some of the best content in the game.

Performance issues and a lacklustre endgame hold it back from perfection, but the core experience is so strong it’s easy to forgive. That said, the multi-character grind is a real buzzkill. If they want players to experiment with builds and alts, they’ve got to make that process smoother. Right now, it feels like punishment for wanting to try something new.

Still, Borderlands 4 proves the franchise has evolved in all the right ways. If they build on this foundation, the next entry could be legendary.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 23, "timestamp_created": 1763548270}, {"review_text": "The best borderlands has been in a long time.

[b]The Forest[/b] was a really pleasant surprise, i went expecting a survival game with horror elements, but received a lore more than that. There's actually a lot to explore, mysteries to solve and, of course, the survival horror aspect is there, and it is very well done.

Though I have to say, I think the Singleplayer mode is the definitive experience for this game. From the moment you step into the game, you're immersed in a beautifully crafted world filled with mystery, danger, and adventure. The AI and enemy design are top-notch, and the constant feeling of unease makes every moment in the game exciting. Multiplayer is a blast with friends, and there’s always something new to explore. The way the game balances exploration, combat, and crafting is perfect!

If you're a fan of survival games, this is a must-play. 10/10 would recommend!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1743766329}, {"review_text": "I started the game thinking, "I'll chop down some trees and build a house," but three days later, while trying to diplomacy with tribes in the forest, an eight-armed mutant jumped out at me.
I think sitting by the fire at night wondering, "I wonder if that sound is the wind, or a naked creature watching me?" is the epitome of The Forest experience.
The building system is really solid, but let's be honest—in Sons of the Forest, we cut the wood more precisely, more like an engineer. Here, while trying to build a house, I often accidentally throw a log into my friend's face.
Descending into the caves is a whole other level of torture. Your flashlight battery dies, your torch goes out, and then you panic in the dark with nothing but clicks and clicks.
The story, however, turned out to be much darker than I expected. I went in thinking, "I'll find my child," and ended up forgetting my sanity somewhere in the forest.

In short, The Forest is more like a "group therapy with a nature walk" than a survival game.
You're scared, you laugh, and eventually you wonder, "Why did I build this house next to a cave?" You ask yourself. I would recommend getting it on a sale (usually around 4-5 euro).", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1733795373}, {"review_text": "best horror survival game is steam highly recommended play sons of the forest afterwords", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1750235529}, {"review_text": "It's a really good game about cannibals and if you like survival crafting games you should definitely play this.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1753115172}, {"review_text": "The Forest is a rare charm of a game which is a bit rough around the edges and has its fair share of bugs, but you can tell it is the love child of a developer with a vision rather than a heartless AAA project with a hundred contrasting ideas. The game itself take an interesting turn on the survival genre, forcing players to put quiet a fair amount of effort and experiment on different ways to survive against the cannibals.

The player learns the game incrementally, discovering different ways to use tools, different locations, buildings, and structures. Woven into the survival is the ‘story’ which is played out through a serious of dungeon like caves, caverns, and experiences. Nothing feels ‘tacked on’ and the survival/story elements work together seamlessly, even if the game only ‘truly’ opens up once the player learns the game. It manages to successfully pull off the typical rather steep but rewarding learning curve rarely seen in newer games. There’s a sense of accomplishment after finding a helpful item in a cave, beating the first mutant or creating the first base that can fend off cannibals without much personal input.

Some might be worried when they see what looks like a default Unity Engine launcher from the start, but after getting in the game I often found myself forgetting that I was in the Unity Engine. There are certainly some improvements to be made to the game, but in 3 years I think the game has come pretty far and I’ll be excited to see what else the developers choose to add to this game.

It’s hard to really target who the forest really appeals too. It’s got quiet a few elements built into one. There’s times it feels like a horror game, other times a survival/crafting games, sometimes a strategy game and now and again a dungeon crawler type RPG. I wouldn’t say there’s “Something for everyone” but If any 4 of those appeal, then it’s certainly worth a try.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1737163485}, {"review_text": "I’ll admit it: I bought The Forest one night after a few too many beers. I played it for a bit and honestly thought, “What the heck is this? Trees, sticks, and weird cannibals?” The only thing I liked at the time was how it looked — and, oddly enough, chopping wood. There was something oddly satisfying about building your own little cabin in the middle of nowhere.

But everything else? It felt boring and just... weird. I expected more from an older game that so many people seemed to love. I thought it would blow me away — instead, it gently poked me with a stick and ran off.

Fast forward a bit: I gave it another shot... and, to my surprise, it wasn’t half bad.

Sure, it’s not mind-blowing. The story starts off strong, then vanishes like a neighbor who went out for cigarettes, only to reappear at the end carrying a suitcase full of emotional baggage. But as a survival game? It’s genuinely solid. Building shelters, crafting bone weapons, setting up traps — it’s all weirdly satisfying once you get into the rhythm. Just be careful not to spend too much time min-maxing every structure, or you’ll end up a spreadsheet hermit in the woods.

Yes, you fight cannibals — and yes, you might end up eating them. Survival karma at its finest.

In the end, The Forest tricked me in the best way possible. I went from thinking it was garbage to obsessing over finishing my luxury log mansion. It’s not a perfect 10/10, but it’s far from trash. I’d give it a solid 7 out of 10. If you’re in the mood for a bit of wilderness nostalgia and casual cannibal chaos, it’s absolutely worth diving in.

P.S. Play it with friends. It turns into a chaotic comedy show in the woods — highly recommended.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1751653574}, {"review_text": "The plane crashed, child was stolen, attacked by locals, then committed cannibalism. I highly recommend the game, especially when you've got friends to play it with.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1753833274}, {"review_text": "Someone gifted me this game a loooong time ago. Truth be told, I was too scared of the caves whenever I played it. I don't think I made it (probably) 50 paces into any of the caves.

The thing is, if you don't go into the caves, you don't advance the story. Sure, you can craft, scavenge, and fight to survive all you want, but you aren't advancing the story. I say that to show that my high playtime was mainly just base building and surviving.

Until recently, for the first time in years, I booted it up co-op with my buddy who is more brave than me, Together, we conquered The Forest. After all those years it was still just as unsettling (moreso when seeing what was inside the caves) and still JANKY. So janky. But, a lot of fun despite it all.

The story is vague, it's there, but easy to miss. It's a lot of fun but I really recommend playing co-op.

Oh, I got one complaint but it's a big spoiler, so here goes: [spoiler]The ending is a choice. One of those choices does not officially end the game nor does it give you the Survive The Forest - Finish Game achievement. Well, if you choose that one, you are able to pop the achievement and roll credits by using console commands (you can use the The Forest Wiki as a guide, if needed). An ending that locks you out of rolling credits is just mean.[/spoiler]

All in all, it goes on sale cheap and is a lot of fun. It's vague. It's JANKY. It's fun. But, it's even more fun playing co-op.

Fastest campaign ever finished in any total war games LOL

10/10 will try setting another personal record of fastest defeat again", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 23, "timestamp_created": 1758796266}, {"review_text": "TL;DR: One of the best mostly-historical TW games, a little confusing to get into for series veterans, lots of small changes add up to a brilliant package.

3K does a lot of small things different to the other Total Wars, but in aggregate they add up to a lot of good changes that deepens the strategy required to succeed. It was a little confusing on my first go through, but I don't know to what degree that's me with my well-walked expectations of TW games or the games on-boarding design.

As a long-time fan and player of the TW series, it can be easy to get a little fed up of the formula. Most of the time; All resources are condensed into "income", every army has 1 leader and about 19 units (no limits on the types), diplomacy is very basic, family tree/court mechanics come and go and don't amount to much. 3K changes a lot in a lot of small ways, and it helps it feel fresh again.

When learning the ropes of this one I was always surprised with an new feature, like how generals/agents can establish positive or negative relationships with each other and how this effects who can be posted where and how. Generals can only have 6 troops attached, but multiple generals can be in one army. Military Supplies are separate to unit upkeep, and add meaningful complexity to army logistics.

My main negative for this game, and its not anyone's fault really, is that the map is a bit repetitive. China is a MASSIVE landmass with a lot of different climates and features, but at the end of the day you have plains, mountains, rivers and forests, and that's it. The ocean may as well not exist, and the jungles and dense mountain regions are at the very edge and don't come up much. Going from TW:W3 that has every natural and un-natural climate to fight in, its hard not to feel a little bored in this aspect.

I think the dev's could have also done a little better with introducing players to the context and history of this entry. A lot of people outside Asia are only vaguely familiar with the 3K history and stories, and with all these factions and named characters its very easy to lose your place and have no idea what you're doing. Why should you pick Cao Cao over Liu Bei? Unique unit/building or faction mechanics aside, not a clue.

Also, its a Sega game, so there's piles of DLC ranging from utter trash to almost essential. Devs, thank you for everything and keep creating, no matter what other comments may tell you!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1749600605}, {"review_text": "Should you play this game ? Is this the best total war to choose ? The answer is yes.
I’ve been asking myself the same question 2 months ago, as I wanted to play a new total war (last one was probably Attila and Warhammer 2).
And thanks god I made this choice.
This the most refined total war game out there and clearly hundred time better than Warhammer III that is receiving plenty of DLCs. I love fantasy, and I also tried WHIII, but this game is overrated, and I was deeply disappointed. Any player that ever touched Three Kingdoms can tell: this is pure diamond.

You may hesitate since it’s ancient China and you may not be familiar with this era. I was totally ignorant about this period, and I was so into the game that I started to be interested to the lore (it’s so cool).

GOOD POINTS

First, this game is beautiful, in many ways:
-	Interface is great
-	Construction buildings look cool when you click a commandery 
-	Character artworks are very nice 
-	Map looks awesome, there are a lot of visual and sound details when you zoom in
-	Battles look so great, nice screenshots to take 

Second point, there are plenty of interesting mechanics:
-	Many faction leaders have special buildings, capacities, attributes and units that can be very cool, unique, and enjoyable, making every game different in its own way
-	Despite some weird and rare cases, diplomacy is overall very nice, lot of possibilities, and AI is doing fine 
-	Characters have a LOT of distinct attributes that affect their administrative, battle and campaign skills, so there are plenty of possibilities (Stats, capacity tree, items, traits, roles)
-	To complete the previous point, you can even give special titles to your characters, which is very cool and boost them as well (example: General who gives tranquillity to the north, orator, etc). 
-	Court, relationships and administration is interesting, and scales as you rank up. At some point, you can regularly choose special events/boost for your faction.
-	There is a spy system that is cool and give plenty of possibilities (such as your spy becoming the faction leader of the faction he was sent in)
-	Research tree is fine and allow a lot of different possible choices that are decent
-	Your goal is to be emperor. If the original emperor is still governing, an additional imperial system exists and affect slightly your faction (ex: you can be marked as imperial enemy by the emperor)
-	 Food and money are balanced and never seemed frustrating
-	There are actually a ton of little mechanics that are cool, but I won’t detail it here (resources, assignments, seasons, faction leader tendencies in diplomacy, satisfaction, xp and weapon, rank scaling possibilities, unique features, etc)

There are a lot of things to consider, and even with +300h I’m pretty sure I’m missing some stuff to optimize everything. It can be overwhelming at start but keep it up and you will have a blast.

 About battles: 
-	Best battles in the entire franchise in term of gameplay
-	Units are reactive, the interface is easy to understand and managing unit is pleasant
-	Units are not randomly stopping to do what you asked them (it happens for me in WHIII and ruin the game really)
-	You can burn stuff like forest, and can be game breaker
-	Generals are cool as they have special abilities, and if you don’t like this kind of gameplay, you can just change the game mode, so your general is just a unit as in total war Attila (and other historical title I believe) 
-	I said it already, but it’s so good looking

About units:
-	There are some very cool units, with some elite units that are unlocked by research (every branch has its specialized unit), or by being emperor for example
