[{"review_text": "Here's what you need to know from someone who has actually been playing the game and not judging a surprisingly complex and fun book by its cover:

GOOD:

- Simple but hard to master combat system that rewards skill over stats and hides a SUPRISING amount of depth with physics, projectile travel time, armor angling, etc.

- Satisfying gameplay loop that rewards you well for engaging in any part of the sandbox you want to play in.

- Rare case of a game placing emphasis on PVP in a way that is accessible and rewarding instead of punishing pvpers and forcing pvp onto those who don't want it via reasonable bonuses to loot and xp for pvp flagging.

- Ship builds are reminiscent of EVE and offer nice ways to specialize your ship and lean into a playstyle that suits you in combat.

- Lots of sandbox opportunities for any group size; and a very interesting end game pvp system revolving around big guild fights to control port cities (similar to territories in Albion Online, but with a player cap for both sides in the fight to avoid imbalance)


NOT THAT GOOD:

- it DOES have monetization; and while ALMOST everything besides cosmetics are earnable in game, it does allow you to effectively buy progress via materials for real money and has a few sidegrade premium ships you can only get via a classic gacha lootbox. NOTE: the premium ships are genuinely fine and balanced, and are mostly just reworked versions of existing ships. There are also caps in most of the lower tier zones preventing high tier ships from sailing into those waters; this prevents heavily uneven fights from occurring or having to compete with someone's credit card before you can earn what they bought.

Regardless, i understand that this is a big issue for some and it cant be left unmentioned.

- For many this will be a pro, but this IS a sandbox game and ultimately the gameplay loop and fun is what YOU make of it and ultimately comes back around to collect lots of stuff via the many avenues offered so you can make cool new stuff and go do it bigger and  better next trip. For many, this can be repetitive if not invested in the sandbox overall.

- If you are expecting to be handheld and spoon fed all the mechanics through a nice tutorial; then this game will turn you away pretty quick if you aren't willing to do some legwork yourself in learning; and good luck finding a guide for this game lol. The tutorial is serviceable, but skips on some of the finer mechanics like workshop crafting intricacies, the depth combat is hiding, world events, etc. The game is selling itself short by not showing how much is going on under the hood in its earliest hours and most players will not learn these things until many hours in through trial and error if they make it there.


THE OBSCURE:

So if you are still reading, you may have seen other reviewers saying stuff like "oh this game is 9 years old" and yapping on about no wipes occurring and strange stuff with servers overrun by veterans. here's what the deal is:

- Game seems to have been a super niche Russian game for at least 3 years and some change. The earliest reference I can find of this game ANYWHERE is early 2022. Maybe i'm the fool, but it doesn't seem to be 9 years old.

- There are 3 servers and they DO NOT SHARE PROGRESS.. RU server is the original server and probably the one polluted with veterans. EU server started with the demo released in mid October and DID NOT WIPE before the release, with a small handful getting effectively a week or two headstart, this is not a very big deal IMO, but worth noting. Lastly, NA server released with the steam release making it just under a week old at the time of this review. 

EU by far seems to be more popular than NA server; and as a side note i play from east coast NA and somehow get 60 ping to the EU server and 0 problems with latency or lag of any kind. Truly some black magic in those servers.



THE FINALE / TL:DR:

Really good nautical sandbox game with a little bit of something for everyone if you dont mind the grind and enjoy the gameplay loop. There is some pay for progress features that are mildly lame, but the game is designed with pvp in mind and prevents you from buying power to abuse people who didn't. Everyone is effectively on the same playing field regardless, so don't let the weird reviewers throwing random **** out there trick you into believing its a massive garbage fire with nothing but p2w lame stuff. 

This game is a hidden gem with tons of realized and unrealized potential; that is only ever so slightly tainted by microtransactions in a way that is ALMOST perfectly fine and IS ultimately balanced quite fairly and simply. Download it and just try it for yourself, its free and 1 gig, form your own opinion if mine isn't enough.






P.S. The game name and front facing advertising is horrible and just SOUNDS and LOOKS like shovelware. Mix that with the somewhat generic trailers and I genuinely almost wrote it off immediately thinking it would be some horrible world of warships knockoff or something. Boy was i pleasantly shocked, but plz devs, do better for yourself and stop showing this hidden gem off like a a generic cash grab looking game when its really one of the most fun sandbox mmos ive played in years.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1761614863}, {"review_text": "As someone who played this game before it even released on steam and had several hundred hours on their old account, I really wish I could recommend this game. And I almost want to, because at its core it is a brilliant game, one of the best age of sail games out there right now and what *could* have been a shining beacon in a very small genre of mostly failed titles. 

However, over the course of its development this game has undergone a non-insignificant amount of shadow changes that make things intentionally harder for F2P players. All without so much as being mentioned in patch notes or in the discord server. Things like making battle marks infinitely slower to get with arena changes that initially seem positive, adding ways to get volcanic ore passively but locking it behind a pay wall, nerfing personal island production rates, and most recently, nerfing event currency drop rates. The holiday events have traditionally always been great opportunities for F2P players to obtain rare or otherwise paid items with relative ease as long as they don't mind grinding a little. But only two days into the first ever event since the game released on steam they make drop rates for event currency roughly 50-70% worse than they have always been, making it yet again more efficient to simply swipe your credit card and frankly infuriating for those of us who don't spend money on the game. 

As always, they assume we simply won't notice these changes, as with the amount of new players joining each month the players who remember how things were before are less and less likely to be heard. This combined with sneaky wording in official comments makes it almost impossible to really stop these changes that are so obviously motivated by greed. 

During the last event for instance, the event menu stated that completing a certain amount of challenges would award either 14 days of premium subscription, or 200 coins (premium currency.) I, like a lot of people acquired the minimum amount of premium in order to get the coin reward only to not receive the coins at all, and be given the extra premium subscription instead. When I opened a support ticket I was told that the coins would only be awarded provided you had at least a month of premium subscription, which costs over double the coin reward anyways. This was not stated anywhere on the event page, nowhere in game, and nowhere in the discord server. I pointed this out. After weeks of back and forth, as they take that long to reply to anything in their support tickets, I was told that it was not their fault that they completely omitted this information and that they could not award any of us the actual reward we were EXPLICITLY promised. They then closed the ticket and that was that. Now, with this new event they have the exact same reward promised, but now a tooltip appears when you hover over that specific section that states the actual parameters of the reward, and that you need at least a month of premium to be awarded it. 

All of this says, to me at least, that they A) could have easily made this information available last event before people spent money, B) only want to make this information as clear as they absolutely have to in order to not be called out for their lies, else they'd make it apparent in the actual main body of the text rather than just appearing when you hover over it, and C) remember the problem they faced last event several months ago and instead of compensating the people they screwed over and lied to, are simply covering their tracks so they can't be held accountable for it this time.

In short, while I love the game itself, the combined effort of changes made without patch notes or other clarification that very clearly, *intentionally* make things harder for F2P players, a lack of account migration to the EU and NA servers from the RU server even for people who spent hundreds of pounds, and utterly terrible communication from the developers means that this game is slowly travelling in a direction I adamantly refuse to monetarily or vocally support, and can only advise against supporting to other people. Maybe in time things will change, but for now I can only see this game heading in the same direction as other immense failures in the genre like, for instance, Naval Action. Funnily enough, a lot of the original players were people who transferred from Naval Action for the exact same reasons I am writing this, and most of them have either abandoned this game as with NA, or are like me, trying and failing to hold out hope that this time it'll be different.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1761996105}, {"review_text": "The imbalance gets worse since most veteran players (mostly from Russia) had early access and dominate the seas, leaving new players hopelessly behind. In short, while I love the game itself, the combined effort of changes made without patch notes or other clarification that very clearly, *intentionally* make things harder for F2P players, a lack of account migration to the EU and NA servers from the RU server even for people who spent hundreds of pounds, and utterly terrible communication from the developers means that this game is slowly travelling in a direction I adamantly refuse to monetarily or vocally support, and can only advise against supporting to other people. And to this, I've been playing a variety of Russian, or combloc MMOs for close to two decades now (in addition to the other games I play that is). I have several hundred hours before this released on steam.

And this game is about the epitome of what I've seen from Russian developers.

1. Pay to Win. Pretty simple. You spend money, you can get extremely powerful ships and items that can only be earned with thousands of hours of effort otherwise. You spend money, you get bonuses to damage, speed, etc on your ship that no one else can get without paying. You spend money, and a player with 10 minutes in the game, can get top tier endgame tech tree ships.

2. Balance. I've learned repeatedly that apparently the Russian market doesn't care about balance. They cheer for unbalanced things, especially when they're paid for. I've seen this nonstop with every Russian game I've played. From Stalcraft, to World of Tanks/World of Warships (specifically what Lesta, the Russian spinoff had done with their titles since separating), Game-Labs (Naval Action, ultimate admiral, ultimate general), Mailru (armored warfare), so on and so forth. And while extremely overpowered premium items would see significant backlash from EU and NA servers and communities in those games, the RU players would cheer for it. Clearly this is a cultural divide that I can only speculate on coming from behavior evolved to survive under the soviet union. And unfortunately Russian devs all seem to replicate this.

3. They're never wrong. They get called out by the community? Even have the russian playerbase mad at them? Well clearly the players just don't know better, and the developer is going to do whatever they want regardless of backlash. See the list of developers above to find other devs that act like this.

4. identity crisis. None of these russian games can figure out what they want to be when they grow up. World of tanks is 15 years old and it still doesn't know what it wants to be. They all simultaneously try to cater to casual pvp, pve, and competitive players. And they end up failing at pretty much all of it, sacrificing the gameplay of each category to help another category, while that category is sacrificed for the first two. The closest comparison to World of Sea Battle is going to be Stalcraft. Basically the entire game is pvp and full of griefers. The devs tried to stop this by having level, or tier based zoning. But both games sell OP low level items/ships in their stores, so you get griefers who reroll to a new character, and then just buy those OP premium items and late unlocks, continuing the grief the real low levels. So the protection for casuals is hampered by their desire to make everything competitive. But everything can't be competitive when you're gating off lower levels unless you reroll. And you want to do pve only? Prepare to be extremely nerfed in your progression and basically restricted from playing the game in both this and Stalcraft. Finally, both this and Stalcraft have an extremely limited late game. Last I looked on this game's map, 3 clans owned basically the entire competitive map, and every capturable port. Stalcraft is the same, 2-3 clans will own the entire competitive map. This is in stark difference to most competitive clan games, even world of tanks, where you'll see dozens of clans on the map at once - and unlike here and stalcraft, even if you don't make it on the map, a clan can still earn competitive currency at a lower rate for their attempt to get on the map. Both this and Stalcraft have made the clan vs. clan scene so ultra-competitive, and so "sink or swim", that now 99% of clans don't even engage with the content in either game. When you have hundreds to thousands of active player clans in your game, and only 4 or 5 active participate in your competitive end game? You're a failure with game design.

5. Lack of scaling. Without instancing their global map, this game will never be able to grow to a good size. But honestly I don't think they'll ever have to worry about that, because the playerbase will never even fill up a single map. See point 3.

6. Finally, displaying just outright contempt for your community. First and foremost, I came to this game because I wanted them to make it better, and I wanted to bring in an English speaking audience for them to grow with. And what did I get for it? The devs kicked us off the official discord server for the game that previously had full English news and announcements, as well as a good number of multi-lingual russian players who would interact with the English community. They kicked us off, and stuck us into a dedicated English server that is effectively dead. An English server where they stopped bothering to translate news and announcements for us, until sometimes days or WEEKS after posting the news to the russian discord, if they posted it at all. My effort to grow the English playerbase in this game was rewarded with a slap in my face. Oh, and they reduced how much in-game content they bothered localizing to English too around then. And now, as the English playerbase in the game, that has been SO ISOLATED and barely hanging on, wants to transfer off the Russian server, to the European server so we can actually play the game with other people who speak the same language as us? The devs tell us, "no, we don't feel like offering server transfers, so if you want to be with other English speakers, you better restart with a new account and pay us money again to get all the stuff you bought and worked for back". - Effectively, their PROFIT MODEL right now is screwing over the English players who supported them for years. And after going back and forth for the year before steam release, saying "oh we'll allow transfers", to "oh we won't allow it for balance reasons", they all of a sudden make up a lie, and claim its "not technically possible to allow transfers, but we'll consider it in the future". - Just like how Wargaming allowed tons of server transfers in World of Tanks, then all of a sudden one day went "oh geez its not technically possible to do server transfers. We'd love to do it but it just isn't possible. Pretend those earlier transfers never existed because they contradict the lie we're telling you now" - So many Russian devs seem to LOVE to make up their blatantly obvious lies because they think it'll go over better than saying "oh we don't feel like it because we want to make you pay for the same premium items and boosts twice"

Normally that'd be fine, but each repeated playthrough leading up to the credits felt really dry when I discovered a single strategy and was rarely given much challenge in executing it (go for one symbol, make sure that symbol has a higher base chance of showing up and have token + golden modifiers on it). A lot of the game boils down to building that up with whatever items you come across, and any attempt the game throws at to raise the challenge rarely pushed me to try something different.

I think a lot of this stems from the actual slot machine being a pretty flat design - one that has a specific set of rules for scoring, and the only thing items do is react to certain outcomes or increase the likelihood of certain ones, but not how you actually interface with the machine, or how the machine even scores. There's no ways to make symbols match each other, no overarching goal when playing the machine (believe it or not, some slot machines actually have "mechanics" in them that happen based on chance rolls), and no way to change the patterns it can choose to track. For this reason, a lot of the items end up doing very similar things, and once you see multiple variants of the "same" item show up, it's hard not to feel like the game already has run out of new ideas on how to keep things fresh before it even technically "ends", which is not great!

You can breeze through this in like, two sittings, and never find much compelling reasons to play again. In some ways, I appreciate that as someone with not a lot of time. The memory cards are potentially a great incentive to keep you playing, as they offer various modifiers that can completely alter how you play.

However, the only way to unlock memory cards is to go into a new deadline with enough money to already complete it. Which is extremely RNG dependent of you having an amazing run early. There's also no way to unlock specific cards, it's yet-again more RNG. So if there's one you really want, you're stuck grinding and crossing your fingers over and over again.

But the worst part? The cards are single use. You can select a memory card, lose on the first deadline through no fault of your own because the slot machine refused to give you enough money, and now that memory card is unusable. Gone forever, until you get lucky enough to find it again.

Outside of that, the RNG is just very annoying at times. As stated before, losing on the very first deadline is more common than you'd expect. Unlike Balatro, where you can choose what hand you play and can plan around which cards still remain in your deck, the odds of discarding and drawing what you need for a certain play, understanding what hands will give you enough chips to clear the blind and move on. CloverPit is literally just pushing a button. No interaction, not much planning. You can tweak the odds, give yourself more rolls, synergize trinkets so they alter the odds even more. But outside of the active-item trinkets, you do nothing other than "pull the lever and hope for the best." In Balatro, you can add 3 more of a card to your deck and reliably slap down five of a kinds every single blind. In CloverPit, I can have 60% chance to manifest cherries, and over the course of 11 spins I see exclusively 3-pattern cherries at best and a single jackpot for diamonds. And since I'm building for cherries, that jackpot is actually worthless beyond the third deadline. Not saying it happens frequently, but the fact that it can just... Happen. Feels immensely unsatisfying.

It feels like some junk food auto-battler "number go up" perversion on Balatro. -in general a little bit too low of feeling of control on how u start runs. picking cards feels a bit of a waste often as u cant anticipate or control how it goes. wanted to do 666 runs multiple times but game didnt let me. often felt like the game controls how i need to play instead of me how i want to gamble. multiplyed with the above strength of a few strats it can pigeonhole", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1759096234}, {"review_text": "Despite it's attempts at replayability, Clover Pit really felt a bit lacking for me in some of the areas where it needed to really shine. Personally, I believe that the game really fails to hit the target variability most roguelites need you to get hooked on. Please note that from the time of writing, I have beaten the game, but not gotten into all item unlocks nor memory card completion.

The first and heaviest issue that I had was items. I beat the entire game, drawer keys to the door, from only one leading synergy: Gold + Picture. Every symbol has a gold item and picture item associated with it, where the former adds a modifier that permanently boosts the value of that symbol and the latter makes the respective symbol show up more often when activated. I could not find a single other strategy that worked as well as this, so my gameplay loop turned from actually experimenting with other items to constantly resetting in search of the synergy before the third deadline, and then adding other stuff that helped it. I really think that there could be a bit of item tweaking to make other synergies with the potential to lead a setup like gold-photo can.

Secondly, Memory Cards, to me, were a waste of time. Memory cards show up in the middle of the gameplay, where you open a pack of three if you can skip a full deadline with excess money from the last. These are the "Challenge Runs" of the game, varying gameplay substantially to have players make a new strategy to beat the run. However, they are not permanent. You consume these cards as you collect them, in order to attempt their respective challenge. If you lose all of them, you need to get more. Now, I think that this is just to deter players from restarting repeatedly until they get a good first-deadline setup, but this really could have been done in another way, especially given that the cards have their own rarity system... I don't think anyone wants to open pack after pack hoping for a legendary-rarity challenge run.

On this topic, the actual card effects are kind of uninteresting. There are one or two cards that affect end-of-round items drastically, and that was a bit of a cool challenge, but like I said, I could only attempt each one twice because they were consumable, and I didn't collect too many from the packs. Others were just small tweaks to the shop, or tickets, interest, small mechanics like that. One card simply doubles the card packs you get when meeting the requirement for getting a Memory Card pack; a memory card for getting more memory cards. Even the two legendary cards I could manage to collect felt a bit bland. For game-changing runs, they really don't do a lot of game-changing.

Some other small things I didn't like were the lack of music (save for the little tracks you could play off Discs A-C), the randomly-generated parts of Jimbo (Though I do love the Balatro reference, I could never seem to find him with a particularly beneficial group of effects), and the semi-uselessness of the drawers (I'm aware they get you corpse parts and can hold items, but... well, I never really needed four of them).

Of course, I still want to say that this is a very good game and you should still play it if you don't care about any of this. 10/10. The ultimate build a house to get laid simulator.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 229, "timestamp_created": 1755743986}, {"review_text": "A medieval game that forgot what made the medieval world exciting

Medieval Dynasty sets the stage for something grand — building a dynasty from nothing, surviving the harsh realities of medieval life, growing a village, starting a family. But once you've pushed through the grind and made your little settlement thrive... you're left wondering: Now what?

1. No Real Endgame — Just Emptiness
You spend hours — maybe 40 or more — slowly crafting a stable economy, assigning workers, managing resources. And then? Nothing. No new threats. No advanced tech. No social or political complexity. The game just coasts. You’re not building toward anything — just keeping the lights on.
What kind of dynasty has no legacy? No evolution?

2. Where’s the Medieval Part?
No wars. No armies. No lords or factions. No ability to build a castle, a watchtower, or even defend your people from anything real.
What is a medieval world without conflict, ambition, or danger?
You’re stuck micromanaging farming output while your villagers walk around with dead eyes. It’s peaceful — sure — but the kind of peace that becomes boredom.

3. The Building Cap Is a Creativity Killer
You’d think the joy of village-building would come from scaling your town into a bustling hub, but the game stops you in your tracks with a hard cap on how many buildings you can place. Worse yet, you have to save building slots just in case your villagers have children, otherwise they’ll grow up with nowhere to live.
Why does a game about growth punish you for growing?

4. Multiplayer Feels Pointless
You can play with friends — and for a while, it’s fun. You help each other survive, build some homes, hunt together. But once you automate your systems, the purpose vanishes. There's nothing left to do together. No shared goals. No projects. No enemies.
What’s the point of building a world together if the world doesn’t push back?

5. A Flat, Empty World
The map is big, but static. No dynamic events, no rival settlements, no evolving narrative. The NPCs are lifeless, the quests are cookie-cutter chores, and nothing feels like it matters. You can build a village, yes — but the world outside that village never changes, never notices you.

Final Thoughts
Medieval Dynasty has every opportunity to become something remarkable — a true medieval life sim with ambition and weight. But, for now, instead of growing into a legacy, it stalls out in maintenance mode. It’s a sandbox that doesn’t let you build castles. A dynasty without conflict. A medieval world without the things that made it legendary.
Where’s the struggle for power? The danger? The glory? The ambition?
Without those things, all that’s left is chores in the woods.

Still Holding Out Hope
This is a negative review — for now. The moment these issues are addressed — more late-game content, higher building caps, real conflict or goals — this could easily become one of the best simulation games out there. It already has the bones of greatness.

And honestly? Despite its flaws, it’s still one of my favorite games... until it gets boring. I always get excited when a friend wants to start a new village. Designing the early stages, managing the first winter — it feels fresh every time. It has the bones of a great game, but I don't foresee a future where it becomes the amazing game it could be, which is honestly just sad.

To its credit: the environments are beautiful, and exploration is fun. The early-game grind doesn't feel too bad, although you do have to cut down a whole lot of trees (which will only regrow if you leave their ugly stumps laying around). The multiplayer is fun, and although multiplayer survival/building is a somewhat over-saturated market, Medieval Dynasty does feel like it stands out due to the environments and the fun of multiplayer combat.

Unfortunately, the economy, building, and NPC character interactions fall flat. For a game that advertises itself as a "dynasty" building game, you'd think there would be more detailed interactions with your spouse and other villagers, or even with your child who will inherit your dynasty. There are no rewards for being friends with other villagers, and the only upside to being on good terms with your spouse is the threat of them leaving and taking your child with them if you displease them. It's also annoying that you have to balance male and female NPCs, as only opposite gendered characters can live in the same house. The building system could use a lot of work; all buildings are presets, and although you have to go wall-by-wall and build each piece, you can only customize the materials of the residential buildings. There are only three tiers of building, locked behind leveling up your skills. Additionally, crafting becomes endlessly frustrating as you realize that every single tool, clothing, or decorative furniture piece not only has to be unlocked by getting to the correct skill level, but also costs money to unlock. The economy does not have any sort of supply/demand system, so while you have to scrape together coin in the beginning, once you get going, money is only limited by the amount the NPCs have to give you, which feels unsatisfying.

The developer also explicitly prohibits modding, which, in my opinion, has hampered their game. With the recent reveal of the new DLC, it has also become clear that they are choosing to prioritize a low-effort cash-grab over actually improving their game in a meaningful way.

Overall, I had high hopes when I bought this game, and it was fun for the first 20-30 hours. However, taking into consideration the flaws mentioned above combined with the developer's attitude, I would only recommend you purchase it if heavily discounted.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1749964014}, {"review_text": "its ok...one of my biggest pet peeves and immersive breaking feature was the bandits you kill dont have ANY lootable armor or weapons.  fully clad armor, high end swords, and axes just left on the ground for *someone else* to pick up i guess. HUGE undersight. just kinda seems like its for nothing, like why bother?", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1751075186}, {"review_text": "The game isn't that bad, but it's core mechanic, namely settlement management, is just barely there. It's all about micromanagement and cannot be played in any other way. Practically speaking, the micromanagement IS the core mechanic. It's entirely impossible to make the village fully self-sustained, and if anyone would claim "But I have my village self-sustained" I would ask: "for how many years?"
Because in the best case, if you played this game in Excel, accurately balancing production, and your only interaction with the village would be selling final products and paying taxes, the village would still eventually starve on intermediate resource or overfill your storage with them. So you HAVE to fine tune pretty much everything again every time there's a new villager or someone raise their skill, or mood is changed, because everything will throw out your balance out of the window.
And because there's no tools to regulate the local economy whatsoever, all you can do is micromanage your settlement all the time, throw villagers from one place to another, change production rate in vain hope you get it right, buy whatever you're missing, sell excesses. You're not developing your colony, you're getting more things to micro-manage and keeping it on manual life support.
That's the core mechanic of the game, as interesting as that.

Now, if developers would read this, few things that they absolutely have to implement:

* Production limits. That's absolute must have. Imagine a landlord in real life seeing his smith making 1000th axe, while there's no sickles because all resources goes to axes, and farmers are loafing around in autumn and everyone is starving. And all the landlord could do is ask his smith nicely to produce less axes and more sickles. Just so that all resources would now go to sickle production and none to pickaxes, so now miners can't get copper and smith and farmers and miners are loafing around, and whole village is starving. What SHOULD happen is the landlord getting a biggest trunk there is and piking that smith on it and telling the next smith to make only one or two axes or sickles or pickaxes or whatever ONLY WHEN THERE'S NO LEFT.

* Seasonal workers. Those farmers do nothing for the whole year except two-four days - to sew and to harvest. Yeah, there's carrot and wheat that can be sown in winter or autumn, but this still does not add up and generally you don't sew fields just to keep your farmers busy, you do it to maximize overall productivity of the village when it's necessary. You might not need that many carrots. So what should have is an option to reassign farmers to other workplaces, so they can make things during winter or summer, instead of spitting in the sky.

* Overhaul of production system in general. Just do it like in literally every other colony management game. Throw out that abomination of +/- % of production and replace it with orders. So the use scenario is following: player opens the building, adds a production assignment and selects assignment completion options: "make n", "make until n", "make forever". The same with seasons, so assignments change with seasons. Or, alternatively, add seasons to assignment options, like "make until n when it's winter"

* Finally, and optionally, and instead of seasonal workers, a new labor system, where buildings optionally might have specifically assigned workers, but otherwise anyone can do the job, as long as there's one. For some buildings, like smithy, job assignment might be compulsory, but for others, like farms or barns - no, as they should not require skilled labor.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 11, "timestamp_created": 1738559513}, {"review_text": "Simply majestic title-- I have never so quickly poured 150 hours into a game.

Everything about this screams that the devs want us to have fun - from perfectly paced build progression to narrative quests to quality of life mechanics that I now can't live without. 

Everytime I thought "Oh it'd be super fun if X,Y,Z", MD had already thought of that and was lined up to give it to me. When I became super attached to my little town, having watched it evolve over a hundred hours of gameplay, I thought "it'd be nice to get a little map tag for it!" and bam - MD already had something in place for me.

[h2] Introduction [/h2]

[i]Medieval Dynasty[/i], developed by Render Cube, is a survival RPG that immerses players in the Middle Ages. Set in a medieval world full of opportunities, you start with nothing and work to build a thriving dynasty from the ground up. The game combines resource management, farming, hunting, and building mechanics with a strong focus on survival. Over time, you can grow your settlement, manage its inhabitants, and even expand your family legacy.

[h2] Graphics and Visuals [/h2]

[✔️] 🌳 Stunning Environments: Medieval Dynasty offers a beautiful open world with lush forests, rolling hills, and detailed villages. The game's natural beauty and realistic landscapes add depth to the experience.
[✔️] 🌅 Day-Night Cycle: The transition from day to night is visually striking, with sunsets and sunrises that enhance the atmosphere of the medieval world.

[h2] Gameplay and Mechanics [/h2]

[✔️] 🏰 Village Building: One of the main features of Medieval Dynasty is the ability to construct and manage a village. You gather resources, assign villagers to different roles, and ensure the survival and prosperity of your settlement.
[✔️] 🚜 Resource Management: Balancing food, building materials, and other resources is key to expanding your village. The management system feels rewarding and keeps you engaged as you try to optimize your village’s growth.
[✔️] 🦌 Hunting and Gathering: The game offers a variety of ways to collect resources, from hunting wild animals to gathering herbs. This creates a sense of immersion and provides practical ways to sustain your people.

[h2] Story and Narrative [/h2]

[✔️] 📜 Personal Legacy: The game's narrative centers around your character’s journey to create a lasting legacy. While the plot isn’t complex, the personal story of survival and prosperity is compelling.
[✔️] 🌾 Character Relationships: Your interactions with NPCs are important as you can build relationships, recruit villagers, and even start a family, adding an emotional layer to the gameplay.

[h2] Audio and Sound Design [/h2]

[✔️] 🎶 Calm Soundtrack: The soundtrack is soothing and matches the game's pace. The gentle melodies complement the tranquil atmosphere of village life and exploration.
[✔️] 🔊 Realistic Sound Effects: From the sounds of chopping wood to the rustle of leaves, the sound design immerses you in the medieval environment. The ambient noises in nature enhance the overall experience.

[h2] Content and Replayability [/h2]

[✔️] 🔄 Dynamic Growth: The game's open-world nature and village-building mechanics offer a lot of replayability. As your dynasty grows, you can try new approaches to resource management and expansion.
[✔️] 🌍 Exploration: The map is vast, and there’s plenty to explore. You’ll uncover different locations, interact with new NPCs, and find hidden treasures that keep you coming back.

[h2] Pros and Highlights [/h2]

[✔️] 🏰 Village Management: The focus on building and managing a settlement is both challenging and rewarding.

I played Sengoku Dynasty, which was garbage. I gave this game a shot hoping to see improvements, and there are some.

Positives

-The game and landscape look beautiful, and the music sets the vibe nicely.
-Compared to Sengoku, there’s more content and story. You actually get a somewhat fleshed out backstory and character arc with purpose.
-The UI has improved. Being able to sort and filter inventory is very well done.
-Voice acting is limited but solid, and the random NPC lines add immersion.
-Wildlife diversity is impressive.
-Gathering feels smoother being able to simply hold E while walking instead of tapping a thousand times.
-Options to toggle crouch, run and auto run are much appreciated.

Not So Positives

-The aesthetics are medieval, but the written dialogue feels modern, with corny humor that just doesn’t fit.
-Some crafting logic is off. An entire log for a single wooden spear? Needing a loom to make any sort of cordage for a bow? 
-Building and crafting progression is frustrating: you unlock a structure but can’t craft anything useful from it right away.
-In single player, time doesn’t advance in menus (skills, tech, etc.), but it does during long, drawn out dialogue. I started talking to an NPC at midday, tried to read it all for the story sake, and by the time I finished it was dusk in game.
-Vanilla Seasons are very short (3 days) and can be modified, yet everything—movement, melee swings—feels bogged down, like running through mud. Playing at 5x speed with WeMod felt far more natural.
-Food spoilage is inconsistent. Raw meat apparently lasts longer than cooked. I grilled food, went to bed with it at 100%, woke up with it at 50% queue the "what year is it" meme
-Tutorials are half baked. Example: “Build a rabbit trap.” Ok… how? Where? Of course it’s under Decorations in the pinwheel menu.  Also forcefully limited to stunt progression and advanced.  You're literally limited to how many traps you can build.  I have never seen this in a survival game before.  It seems like a lazy way to drag the game out.


Final Thoughts

There's no one thing that's horrible with this game it's a myriad of small things that could be better.  I wish Steam had a neutral rating. There are definite improvements since Sengoku Dynasty, but would I recommend it to my friends who play survival games like Abiotic Factor, 7D2D, Project Zomboid, and Rimworld with me? Unfortunately, no. It may click for some, but to me it’s too much grind and pain for too little payoff.

I tried to play vanilla for half a day, then switched to modded, and I'm not compelled to continue.

edit: Cripes I had no idea this game is older than Sengoku - if that's the case they took a step backwards with that game for sure!

I'll revisit in the future to see if anything has improved.

So don't beat yourself up if you're super lost and everyone is yelling at you over game chat. Just mute the salty people and report them if they TK. Trust me there are a lot of people in the game that will back you up and want to help, so don't let one bad experience make you quit the game for good.

There are a LOT of maps to learn and a lot of small details in every one. It's going to take the average person until your siege level is at LEAST 50 before you really start recognizing map layouts and details on all maps - including room orientation, call outs, soft wall, hard wall, what should be reinforced in each site, common paths of travel, etc.. And then probably until 75 until you're actually comfortable with most maps and operators. I'll give 15% to your own gun skills, 20% to team work and communication (call outs call outs call outs, people. Don't be that guy that just looks at memes after dying. Unless it's casual.), and 15% to your knowledge of the operators and ability to utilize their gadgets.

More tips:
-There are a lot of Diamond/Plat smurfs in newcomer that like to make new accounts and s*** on actual new players because it makes them feel good for some reason, so you're better off playing quick match.
-To learn maps faster, make your own custom games and run around in them.
-When you die, make sure you watch the replay so you know what cheeky angle the enemy was holding and then don't do what you did next time, or use it to your advantage when you switch sides.
-If you're not on cams, watch teammates. Look at the places they check as they sweep rooms. Watch the paths they take. Look at how they engage in gun fights and how they rotate around the map.

[h1] The Rise and Fall of Rainbow Six Siege [/h1]

I first played R6 in 2017 on my PS4. It was my first realistic tactical FPS and I was completely hooked by the unique gameplay loop and mechanics. I witnessed what was in my opinion the rise (2016-2021), downfall, and funeral of the R6 I knew and loved playing.

[h2] When Everything Started Going Wrong [/h2]

The beginning of the end was when the Ubisoft split the R6 devs to create this new game called R6 Extraction. To give some context, there was a limited time mode called Outbreak during operation Chimera where it was like R6 and COD Zombies had a baby. It was pretty fun while it lasted and it was well received by the community, but poopisoft decided to make it a separate paid game that expanded on it. Content creators given early access to that game had some pretty negative things to say about the game and same thing goes for when it was released for the public. While all this was happening, R6 started losing its soul and gained so much downhill momentum that even the original developers couldn't recover the losses. The quality and quantity of the content dropped significantly and below are some examples:
[list]
    [*] [b] One operator per season [/b] with recycled guns (we used to get two operators with new weapons and a new, not reworked, map)
    [*] [b] New gun/s every 2-3 seasons [/b] instead of with every operator release
    [*] [b] Map reworks nobody asked for [/b] that the commmunity either hates or bans constantly in ranked
    [*] [b] The original recruit removed [/b], one of the last pieces of original content that made the game fun 
[/list]
The list goes on but this review is already going to be very long.

[h2] What Made Siege Special is Gone [/h2]

The developers listened too much to crying pros instead of preserving what made the game fun. The game took a turn and started sacrificing realism and tacticalness for balancing sake:
[list]
    [*] [b] Caveira's old pistol [/b]- reworked, not as fun anymore
    [*] [b] Ash and Jager ACOGs [/b]- removed (R4-C acog is back but it was gone for a very long time and it is not the same as it was before)
    [*] [b] 2-second timer before detection when going outside as a defender [/b]- removed, apparently attackers know the exact and precise location of your character's head the moment your toe touches the outside of a building
    [*] [b] Widespread ACOG availability [/b]- stripped away and replaced with 1.5x scopes that in my opinion, didn't change much and did not address the root of the problem they were trying to solve and arguably made it worse
    [*] [b] Valkyrie cams being placeable outside [/b]- removed
    [*] [b] Zofia's withstand ability [/b]- banished (okay so this one was actually unfair and turned the tides on one pro-league round, but it was moving toward an interesting idea of operator-specific passives unique to their lore that I would have liked)
[/list]

[h3] The Fortnite-ification of Siege [/h3]

The game gave off mobile game and fortnite vibes with how beginner friendly and arcadey it felt after some changes. No shade to mobile games and fortnite as I enjoy them too, but what makes them enjoyable is not something that R6 should also implement, but unfortunately did which ruined the immersion and realism:
[list]
    [*] [b] Mobile game-like UI [/b] that destroyed immersion and I aesthetically didn't like
    [*] [b] Enemy outlines [/b] where there used to be none
    [*] [b] Free base game operators [/b] (you used to have to earn them)
    [*] [b] Free attachments [/b] (another thing you had to work for)
    [*] [b] Battle passes [/b] locking cosmetics behind a paywall for a game I already bought. Free games like fortnite or apex legends make most of their money through cosmetics but for a paid game like R6, just put new free content in the bag bro
    [*] [b] Ridiculous skins [/b] that shatter any sense of tactical realism. Don't get me wrong I love the april fools cosmetics but it has gone out of hand with the new paragon skins that look like they came straight out of valorant.
[/list]

[h3] What I Miss Most [/h3]
  
[list]
    [*] [b] Night maps and old graphics [/b] that felt atmospheric
    [*] [b] Plane map and other classics [/b] are unplayable. The Plane map is not even in the casual map-pool and only in custom game. The new House and Hereford Base map is too different from the old map to call it a rework.
    [*] [b] Situations mode and Original Terrorist Hunt [/b]- situations were a nice and challenging way to learn the ropes of the game and introduces the player to the lore of the game. It also used to be a way to play old maps that were reworked.
    [*] [b] Recruit Rushing [/b] 
    [*] [b] The lighting, old recoil, and slow-paced tactical gameplay [/b] (could be a skill issue because everyone sucked back then and didnt treat this game like COD search and destroy)
    [*] [b] Realistic Operator trailers [/b] when you first unlock them
[/list]

[h2] Sound is Horrendous [/h2]

For a tactical shooter that makes you heavily rely on sound to locate enemies, it is pretty unreliable and makes you question whether you suck, need a new headset, or the sound design sucks (its this one btw). Im pretty sure my hair loss is due to me pulling my hair everytime I die to an enemy which sounded like they were coming from the opposite direction.

[h2] Cheating Epidemic [/h2]

From 2021 to 2024 was when I started mainly playing on PC and cheating was absolutely rampant. While it's somewhat under control now (Im not entirely sure as I dont play much ranked nowadays but I hear its gotten better), it felt like poopisoft was prioritizing other stuff instead of their anti-cheat. Don't even get me started on xim and MnK users in console controller only lobbies.

[h1] The Final Nail: Operation Siege X [/h1]

They hyped this as "a new era of siege" that they'd have been working on for years, the "biggest transformation" claiming to make siege great again by improving graphics, developing core elements resulting in more tactical gameplay, and new ways to play. New ways to play? meta was still the same with same objectives and standard approach to each objective from both sides. Felt stale and bland. I immediately realized this IS what siege is now, it is definitely not for veterans who remember what made this game special. Since they advertised this as the "new era of siege", I slowly came to the realization that the siege I fell in love with a long time ago is dead and will never come back and this new siege is what the developers intend to expand on in the coming of years. 

I immediately uninstalled. It just wasn't fun anymore.

[h2] For New Players [/h2]

If you're looking for a tactical, realistic FPS experience, you're about 7 years too late. The closest I've gotten to that original R6 adrenaline rush was from playing Escape from Tarkov and Arena Breakout: Infinite.

[h3] The Verdict [/h3]

Rainbow Six Siege 2016-2020 was a tactical masterpiece. Rainbow Six Siege 2025 is a hollow, arcadey, and cash-grabbing shell giving you the bare minimum while wearing the corpse of that masterpiece as a skin.

The game I loved is dead. This review is its eulogy.

[b] Save your money and find another game and company that respects both your time and energy [/b]

This game definitely feels special.

I was gifted this game in 2013 by a friend of mine, a friend who expected me to have as many hours of enjoyment with it as he did back then. And while I haven't even come close to the amount of playtime he had even back then (if I recall correctly, he was at around 4000 hours already), I still had a lot of fun with this game.

I'm writing this review now, after over 10 years having the game, since I've finally, properly finished it. And yes, while at first Terraria might look just like a 2D sandbox game (I even thought it looked like 2D Minecraft when I first saw the game), it's much more than that. When starting the game, after creating your character and your world, you're thrown into it without much of an idea about what to do. There's a guide who'll give you helpful tips, the most important as you start being that you need shelter. And from there, it begins.

Gameplay starts simple: you'll have a few tools with which to chop wood, mine for resources, eventually getting a sword to fight monsters. You'll create a humble house, start crafting better equipment, and start exploring. As you go, you'll meet new NPCs who might join you in your base if you build them a proper home. However, you'll also attract the attention of certain powerful creatures. And that's where the main gameplay loop lies: the progression. You'll fight a boss, get access to new, more powerful items, fight another boss, and so on and so forth. Along the way, there might be invasions, events in which you have to defend your base and so on. As you explore, you'll find new enemies, and as you kill the bosses, more dangerous creatures will appear. Honestly, the game has loads of content.

Graphically speaking, well, it has a simple 2D style, but it's still a beautiful game. While the market might feel saturated these days with 2D pixel style games, this one was one of the pioneers, and its simplistic style keeps the main draw of the game front and center: the gameplay. Even then, there's a lot variety in terms of areas you'll explore, equipment and NPCs you'll find, both in terms of allies and enemies; if anything, I'd say the 2D style made the art team behind this game go out of their way to give loads of variety. The soundtrack is also excellent, with specific tracks for each event and biome you might encounter, including some for biome variations as well.

Honestly, I think it's a great game, and the previous two paragraphs, I think don't do it justice. While I don't want this review to go longer, in fear of reaching the character limit, I'll say this; at the moment I'm writing this review, I've had nearly 12 years with the game. I lost my first save when my laptop's HDD failed back in the day, but when I got a new one, I went back to the game, to start again from scratch. I didn't even touch Hardmode until last year, as I was too afraid of the harder enemies and bosses, but since I did it, I've been playing the game daily until the moment of writing this review. On October 17th, 2025, I beat the game for the first time. A bit of a spoiler, yes, the game has an ending, but one that I think is worth mentioning because of the following, which is a comment I made on a thread about finished games:

375 hours I have with my character. 375 hours of fear, sweat, anxiety. But also 375 hours of discovery, of wonder and amazement. I'd be lying if I said I didn't get emotional when I finally beat the final boss for the first time and the credits started rolling. It's been one hell of a journey.

--------------------

So, with that paragraph above, if it's not enough of a recommendation, what would be? You should definitely get this game, especially given how cheap it is. It has a dedicated dev team behind, who haven't stopped making updates since the game released. It's always one "final update", and personally, I hope this game keeps getting a final update for as long as I live. At its core, Terraria is a game about exploring a massive world, gathering resources, and facing off against waves of increasingly bizarre enemies. But once you dip your toes into the modding scene, the world expands to infinite proportions. Calamity Mod is the be-all-end-all expansion that turns your Terraria world into a living nightmare of epic bosses, new biomes, insane loot, and a whole new level of difficulty. Want to battle gods, summon ancient celestial entities, and break your controller over insanely tough bosses? Calamity’s got you.

Without mods, Terraria is already addictive enough with its endless crafting, treasure hunting, and massive bosses. But with Calamity, you're not just fighting the regular Eye of Cthulhu—you’re fighting Calamitas, Supreme Calamitas, Providence, the Profaned Goddess, and a whole army of high-level bosses that will make you question your life choices. And don’t even get me started on the massive post-Moon Lord content—if you thought you had completed the game, think again.

Mods in general expand Terraria into a whole new world. The Thorium Mod, Spirit Mod, and Tremor Mod all add unique biomes, bosses, and mechanics, making the game feel fresh even after hundreds of hours. New weapons? You got 'em. New events? Check. Even cosmetic mods can make the game look prettier, or add weird stuff like making your character a floating pancake.

One of the coolest things about Terraria with mods is that it’s still very much its own game. Mods like Calamity don’t just add a bunch of content—they integrate seamlessly into the core game. You won’t feel like you’re playing a completely different game; it’s more like you’ve opened a Pandora’s box of insanity. It’s got all the classic Terraria charm—digging, building, crafting—but amped up to 11, with new dimensions to explore, terrifying bosses, and new mechanics to wrap your head around.

And multiplayer? Chaos, pure chaos. You and your friends can team up to fight the crazy new bosses, explore newly crafted worlds, and argue over who gets the best loot.

In short, if you’ve been playing Terraria without mods—good for you, you’re in for a solid time. But if you’ve never experienced Calamity, prepare to lose weeks of your life fighting, dying, crafting... and then dying again. It’s a whole new game that never stops surprising you.

- Not much to do after killing the last boss", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1739005800}, {"review_text": "Terraria, developed and published by Re-Logic, is a masterpiece of creative freedom, exploration, and survival that has evolved far beyond its humble beginnings. At first glance, it may look like a simple two-dimensional sandbox, but underneath its pixelated surface lies an endlessly complex and rewarding experience. The game begins with you dropped into a procedurally generated world, armed with nothing more than a few basic tools. From there, Terraria gives no explicit direction—it trusts the player to explore, experiment, and learn its systems through curiosity and perseverance. The lack of hand-holding may seem daunting at first, but it is precisely this freedom that fuels its long-term allure. The first time you dig into the earth, face nightfall, or stumble upon a cavern of glowing crystals, the sense of discovery feels deeply personal, as if you’ve uncovered secrets meant only for you.

What makes Terraria so remarkable is its balance between creativity and challenge. Unlike many sandbox games that focus purely on construction or resource gathering, Terraria is driven equally by exploration, combat, and progression. Every new ore, material, or biome you uncover leads naturally to crafting better gear, building more elaborate structures, and ultimately facing more formidable foes. Boss battles are the beating heart of this loop—each encounter is a thrilling test of preparation and adaptability. The sense of progression is palpable: you begin by fending off slimes and zombies with rudimentary weapons, but before long you’re soaring through the air in enchanted armor, fighting colossal mechanical gods and demonic monstrosities. The steady rhythm of exploration and conquest, coupled with the satisfaction of crafting new tools and unlocking new powers, creates an addictive gameplay flow that keeps players returning for hundreds of hours.

Terraria’s world-building is equally impressive. Its biomes—ranging from verdant forests to eerie crimson wastelands, from underground jungles to shimmering celestial realms—feel distinct and alive. Each area has its own atmosphere, enemies, resources, and secrets waiting to be discovered. The day-night cycle and dynamic weather add another layer of immersion, transforming the same landscapes into different experiences depending on the time and conditions. Despite its retro pixel art style, the game achieves an incredible sense of depth and beauty through color, lighting, and sound. The soundtrack, composed by Scott Lloyd Shelly, is an unforgettable accompaniment to the adventure, shifting from soothing melodies during calm exploration to intense orchestral tracks in boss battles. Every note enhances the rhythm of play, reinforcing Terraria’s emotional core—the wonder of exploration balanced against the tension of survival.

The creativity the game encourages is another of its enduring strengths. The building system is deep yet intuitive, allowing players to construct anything from humble cottages to sprawling castles, intricate machinery, and entire cities for non-playable characters to inhabit. This freedom has fueled a passionate community of builders who continue to push the limits of what’s possible within the game’s framework. Beyond building, Terraria’s crafting system is vast, featuring hundreds of materials and recipes that support multiple playstyles—melee, ranged, magic, and summoner builds all feel distinct and viable. Every new discovery in crafting or construction feeds directly into progression, ensuring that creativity and advancement remain intertwined.

The sheer volume of content in Terraria is staggering. What began as a modest indie project has grown over the years into a game bursting with depth. Its numerous free updates have added new bosses, items, biomes, events, and even entire post-game expansions, culminating in what the developers call the “final” version. This continued support over more than a decade has made Terraria one of the most complete and polished games in the genre. Each update has respected the game’s roots while expanding its horizons, ensuring that returning players always have something new to experience. The inclusion of Expert and Master Modes offers higher difficulty for those seeking a challenge, while the Journey Mode provides powerful creative tools for those who wish to experiment freely. This adaptability has made Terraria accessible to all types of players, from casual builders to hardcore adventurers.

Multiplayer further enhances the experience. Playing Terraria with friends transforms the adventure into a cooperative odyssey, where exploration and discovery become shared triumphs. Building together, tackling bosses as a team, and coordinating different roles in combat create some of the game’s most memorable moments. The blend of cooperation and chaos brings out the best in its design, allowing players to divide responsibilities—one building defenses, another crafting weapons, another exploring the depths—and watching how those efforts converge toward survival and victory.

While Terraria’s complexity and lack of early guidance can be intimidating to newcomers, its open-ended nature ensures that patience is rewarded. The learning curve, once overcome, becomes part of the game’s charm. Every small breakthrough—crafting a new weapon, finding a hidden biome, defeating a new boss—feels earned through genuine effort and discovery. The game’s minimal storytelling allows players to create their own narratives through their actions, turning each world into a personal legend of exploration and triumph.

In the end, Terraria is a timeless achievement in game design. It combines the endless creativity of a sandbox with the structure and thrill of a traditional adventure. Few games manage to capture both freedom and focus so elegantly. Its world feels infinite, its systems endlessly rewarding, and its sense of discovery as strong today as it was at release. Terraria is not just a game—it’s a world that grows with its players, a universe of infinite possibility crafted from the simplest pixels and the grandest imagination. It stands as one of the most beloved and enduring indie games ever made, a testament to how creativity, passion, and player freedom can come together to create something truly extraordinary.

New season dropped and they made every character into a braindead easy mix up machine without a single buff to defense, from the start of tekken 8 players where vocal about the prominess of easy mix ups and the glaring nerfs to defense compared to past tekken games and yet they do a huge patch with lots of new moves that enphasis on every aspect the players disliked about the game.

No one litterally no one asked for these changes, even new players never asked for more offense in a game that clearly lacks defensive options and is easy to mash button and win like in most Tekken games.

Tekken especially with competetive Tekken 7 scene garnered a reputation of a game that has solid focus on fundamental skill such as movement, neutral and defense and seeing how Tekken 8 nerfed all this aspects is sad, even the tournament views are worse for T8 compared to T7 for how homoginized the characters are and streamlined the gameplay is with new systems.

But i still had hope since things could change for the better. however devs turning a deaf ear on their community that was extremly vocal about all te negative aspects of the game which made the experience worse just to double down on what everyone hates for some fabricated notion that "it's good for new players" is incomprehensible when people loved Tekken 7 which was massively succesful for a fighting game.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 18, "timestamp_created": 1743476294}, {"review_text": "I do not recommend Tekken 8 season 2 for these reasons.

-The developers do not understand the characters they design. They see that the character has strengths and weaknesses and continue to not let them have this weakness. Instead, they homogenize the character to be like the others making them overtuned. This was a big issue in Season 1 that made 70% of the roster oppressive. And the game is suppose to favor the aggressor, but it favored the aggressor too much to the point where it will look like a one player game sometimes. There is very little counterplay to these characters.
=Season 2 did not address these things, they only made minor defensive changes like being able to side step from crouch and side step buffer. But that is not enough as they decided to buff almost everyone while giving them major/minor nerfs. However, this isn't the only thing that makes it bad. They also killed character identities like Law's WS4 CH DSS not being a thing anymore, Zafina stances, Feng Wei snake dash block, etc. They gave characters like Dragunov some more identity which is cool, but no character should have their identity being killed or overtuned. All they did was buff the weaknesses of each character instead of just letting them have this weakness and just buff their strength instead. But the developers do not understand their character designs.
-The developers also did not address any of the dumb tracking some of the moves have like the heat bursts. Yes, some of the Heat bursts like Bryans still track even though they aren't suppose to.

Also removing CH Ki charge is the worse change I've ever seen. No one complained about it and people liked it.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 12, "timestamp_created": 1743511036}, {"review_text": "To make a non fighting game player understand the most recent changes. Imagining CounterStrike becoming more like Call of Duty.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 65, "timestamp_created": 1745003710}, {"review_text": "To preface this - it's currently the launch of season 2 of Tekken 8.
I like Tekken, I've played Tekken since Tekken 2. I've played every Tekken game to date.
I like this franchise so much that I've spent energy following it and playing it over the course of my life. 
This game is quite possibly the worst Tekken game I have ever played. I would consider Death by Degrees to be more true to form to Tekken's formula and aesthetic than this game. 

You can see right now I have hundreds of hours in this game, you might be asking why? If you don't like it - why spend so much time. Here's why - I have desperately tried to cling onto the idea that if I played enough/ranked up enough it would suddenly click. I've also always liked Tekken and didn't want to drop a franchise I've historically enjoyed so I thought I was missing something. 
I wasn't and that point has been proven now.

Tekken 8 was given out to players initially as a review copy without a battle pass addition.
Once official release came around a battle pass was added to bypass the review phase.
This battle pass and each one afterwards till now contains items which were normally obtained in Tekken games through in-game currency obtained from Online Matches or Arcade mode or even other party modes added in previous games such as Tekken Bowling or Tekken Volleyball. 
However with Tekken 8 this was a unwelcome surprise and now it requires real world money.

This is why Tekken 8 now has a asterisk with the message "This product has experienced one or more periods of off-topic review activity". 
This is not one of those times.

With the launch of season 2 they emphasised that the updates would favour defence options a bit more.
Currently plus frames are rampant with many moves or heat activations which leave no room at all for you to retaliate and certain characters are utterly broken. I don't mean overpowered either but they have them too.

Paul can currently do f,1+2 into while standing 3 and it will bypass the guarding system and hit every time.
To go even further, he can press 2 after that unblockable ws,3 and if you're at the wall, you just got wall splat.
Which will possibly lead to you losing the match because you anticipated the move coming and blocked like a normal sane individual (You shouldn't have done that).

There is a plethora of similar issues with the game right now.
There are many reasons the game is in the state that it is in but it comes to who's currently in charge.
This narrows down to Kouhei Ikeda now being game director and Harada becoming an adviser.
All "heat" on this issue is directed towards Harada who is sun setting his time with Tekken.
All positive notes to take from T8 will be accredited to Ikeda's work on the game.
All drawbacks will be learned from for the next game hopefully but ultimately it's Ikeda's series now.
Many Soul Calibur developers have transitioned to Tekkens development. 
That is the state of Tekken 8's development right now.

There is a bunch of issues why the game is not good right now:
Too many plus frames.
No actual defensive options.
Terrible Heat mechanic.
Many moves hitting off axis.
Combo damage is incredibly high.
Too many stance transitions (Everyone is Lei now apparently).
Stock/State Power ups.
Chip Damage.

The aesthetic of the previous games' are also lost entirely.
T4 still holds the bar for the best with so little to show for it.
They only needed a hint of flashy stuff or ridiculous concepts in Tekken.
If you look at Clive you can see that's been thrown out the window.

What's also really disappointing is that a lot of players have tried putting the thought into peoples head that previous Tekken games were worse and they don't have the stomach to actually say the series got worse.

It's a really funny twist of fate that Tekken Tag Tournament 2 didn't kill Tekken but Tekken 8 - their most lavish and expensive title to date is doing a better job than Tag 2 ever did.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 16, "timestamp_created": 1743526867}, {"review_text": ""For Season 2, we'd like to focus on defense in terms of the lateral aspects of a 3d fighting game." 

Followed by the developers spending over two hours without mentioning any defensive changes and only focusing on more BS 50/50 casino gameplay is hilarious. 

Oh right, some genius decided that you should be punished for breaking a throw correctly and take chip damage. 

Would not recommend anyone purchasing this game until they actually improve defense/movement to counteract the constant aggression.


[b]EDIT:[/b] Just wanted to add some extra feedback in case the developers become truthful when it comes to taking feedback.

1. Remove Chip Damage completely: Its a garbage mechanic and makes being on the receiving end of heat even more frustrating because even if you block the mix-ups correctly you're still punished enough to where you'll often lose 40% of your life bar from just chip damage and be put in range to where the next mix up will kill you.

2. Buff Movement: Backdash needs to be buffed to bait and create whiffs otherwise Tekken turns into everyone just constant throwing out hitboxes without thinking knowing that at worst they will hit on block and often times be plus still. Sidesteps need tuning to be more reliable since they can fail even if using them in the same situation as one in which they've succeeded previously.

3. Fix Phantom hitboxes/Nerf range of moves/Increase whiff recovery/Nerf homing moves/Remove string realignment/Make moves more linear GLOBALLY: All of these changes will also help with the problem above. People would play a lot slower in neutral which builds tension, makes a defensive more viable and allows there to be more neutral interactions instead of each player trying to bulldoze their way into constantly being in close range forcing a guessing game.

4.Severely nerf heat: I would love to just remove it completely but its already built into the core Tekken system. Instead just make it so that heat is something you have to earn in a game and make it so that once you activate it the meter never stops going down.

Remove the ability to regenerate heat from moves/stances. Nerf Heat smashes across the board so that they don't cause stage interactions or wall splat. 

5.Lower the plus frames on moves across the board, +5 is crazy for heat dash considering its not even something you have to earn to be able to do when you have heat active. There are also too many high reward moves that are also +6 on block or higher... Why?

6. Remove guard breaks from the game. They are just way too powerful and mentally taxing to deal with. Guard breaks also often lead to wall splats or wall blasts which makes them low risk for too high of a reward.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 37, "timestamp_created": 1742884406}, {"review_text": "I have played every single Tekken since the very first one, each one thousands of hours, and by far the worst one of them all is Tekken 8. Sure, it looks good, has very good production value etc, but outside of all that - the actual game itself, it is just bad and I am tired of pretending that it is not. Bandai Namco likes to gaslight the player base - it wasn't bad netcode, it was YOUR bad internet. It is not bad game, it is YOUR skill issue etc, while in fact - it is the game.
Everything is for the offense. Skill ceiling is destroyed, there is nothing to lab anymore, since everything follows, moves, tracks, is plus and launchers. Everything is a 25 second combo, everything takes you to the wall and all walls sticks like a fly paper. Everything auto corrects, so at this point this game might as well just be fully AI, no need for any player, because essentially you are just watching cut scenes and not really playing. So many long animations that interrupt the flow. Even basic knockdowns have built in followups into guaranteed oki, that cannot be avoided. Risk-reward is like 9 to 1 in favor of the attacker. All defensive tools are removed or nerfed, so you just have to guess. Tekken 8 is a casino, where you just have to be lucky. Never has there been a Tekken game where max rank is filled with player with 0 knowledge about the  game, movement, later movement, ducking etc, because you can just keep mashing since plus, plus, plus, mid, mid, launcher, launcher, no execution. This game is hell on training wheel and a perfect example when 12-year olds design a game thinking "lets give everyone everything with no drawbacks", so it will be fun fun fun.
If this game frustrated you - don't worry, the problem is not you, but the game. It punishes skill, time and patience, rewards recklessness and fast brain dead rewards. Utterly disgusting and sad remnant of a franchise that used to be the best fighting game in history.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 18, "timestamp_created": 1759366571}, {"review_text": "Welcome to Gambling 8, where everyone’s got 50/50 moves.
