(Yes, I'm writing this after an unholy loss streak. Let me cope.)", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1743864017}, {"review_text": "After 30 years of playing Tekken, I have never been as disappointed as I am with Tekken 8 – Season 2. This patch is a complete disaster that destroys the very essence of the game.

A chaotic gameplay experience
The developers have completely shattered the game’s balance by making offense far too powerful. The game has turned into a mindless rushdown fest where defense, once a core pillar of the series, has become unnecessarily difficult. Reacting now requires an absurd mix of inhuman reflexes, encyclopedic knowledge, and lightning-fast analysis. Even worse, the game has become a never-ending lottery, a simple rock-paper-scissors match where luck outweighs technical skill. Every interaction feels like a gamble, making the experience frustrating and unbearable.

A disastrous development direction
The decision to bring in SoulCalibur developers was a fatal mistake. Tekken is not SoulCalibur, and trying to force mechanics from a completely different game into Tekken’s system betrays the very DNA of the franchise. Harada and his team seem to have lost sight of what made Tekken a true fighting game masterpiece.

An outrageous price tag
As if things weren’t bad enough, Bandai Namco is charging €40 for this mess! This price is absolutely ridiculous for a patch that turns Tekken into a game of pure luck. At this rate, I’d rather spend my money at the slot machines at the carnival—at least there, I know I’m gambling from the start.

An ultimatum for Tekken
If this patch isn’t fixed soon, I’m done with Tekken. This is no longer the game I’ve known and loved for three decades. In its current state, it’s unplayable and no longer worth my time.

Bandai Namco, fix this before it’s too late!", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1743588131}, {"review_text": "Game's fantastic but having Eddy & Heihachi in a dlc in a game I already paid 70 euro is more than funny.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 17, "timestamp_created": 1763737493}, {"review_text": "i have played a lot of this game and a lot of tekken in general. I am uninstalling today for good. 

tekken has always had a lot of knowledge checks, and thats okay. one of the best parts about tekken is getting bodied by a character's flowchart, hitting the lab, figuring out the options, and then beating it next time.

that being said, the game's new design concept with hyper focus on aggression/oppression has created a bunch of situations where the ONLY option for defense is guess block, and if you guess wrong you die. this is not an overstatement. there are way way too many plus frame set ups in this game. if you can predict what an opponent is going to do, you should have the option to avoid by movement, defense, or choice offense. but since there are so many plus frame set ups ON TOP of heat which gives plus frames, the meta has devolved into heat engager-mix up-oppression-chip with plus frames-heat smash-wall mix up. 

It's not that defense has no reward, but the amount of knowledge/execution it takes to play defense properly vs spamming offense makes this game super frustrating. I am a defensive player and i always loved tekken because of how many options there were for counterplay against aggro opponents. But if i am defending a character who is in heat and attacking me, it is not worth the risk to make a defensive read. its better to just sit there and eat the chip and hope i land a heat engager and can do the same thing back. THIS IS BORING. 

I made it to tekken god with my main and blue ranks with a handful of other characters. i'm nowhere near GoD and recognize that there is a lot more I could learn to play better. I am not blaming the game for my lack of skill or practice. I just don't think the amount of effort i need to put in for match-up specific defense is worth it in tekken 8 like it was in the older games. Defensively this is the hardest fighting game i've ever played and offensively it's the easiest. when i stopped trying to play defensive and just focused on steam-rolling i climbed way higher and enjoyed it much less. the identities of the characters have all been replaced with rushdown mix up. 

maybe i'll check out season 2 but i can't see the game changing much since this is the direction they went with. sad to finally say goodbye but it's been toxic for a long time and i am not happy playing it anymore. wish they had made it different.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1733870829}, {"review_text": "i've got ultimate edition since last year and it does not include season 2 content, anyone who buys the exact same edition for the exact same price gets twice the dlc content for free, my fav fighting franchise scammed me.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1755197937}, {"review_text": "I am a lifelong Tekken player and I cannot, in good conscience, support this entrance in the series. This review is not a summation of everyone's gripes, just mine. I spent a lot of money on this game. I spent a lot of hours pretending to enjoy this game. I tried to get others I know to get this game. In return, I am made to look like a fool for caring deeply about a franchise that has been in the background of my entire life. When people ask what's going on with it, I can't really explain it. With everything Bamco's done *from the beginning* with this game, it's unraveled a lot of my connection with this franchise. Story, lore, characters, music, everything. Tekken's just another dumping ground for advertisement slop, desensitizing gameplay, broken multiplayer, and a mind-numbingly bad story mode. I am left only asking one question: Why? 

I once had a dream of competing in Tekken. This was finally going to be the one I'd play more than casually. I had put it off for years until this entry. As I write, I realize maybe the simple answer is to just let go of the game entirely. The fruit has more than soured on the vine. Why keep giving this attention it so clearly does not deserve nor even accept? I know I am not the only one contending with these feelings. I'm just expressing my own and I'm finding there's simply not enough words. 

I cannot, especially as a Deluxe Edition owner, recommend this game. Take the time you'd spend playing this game and go pick up a martial art. You'll feel much better about yourself.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1750711326}, {"review_text": "This review is written after the v2.03.01 update with the early access release of Fahkumram.

This patch shows the developers have now tripled down on the game's direction, aggression. The skill floor for beginner players has been lowered with heat burst, heat smash, chip damage, unblockables, improved lows, armor moves, homing throws, low risk high reward strings, realigning strings, infinite range weapons, safer/fewer getup options, and rage art. Mechanically difficult options have been made easier or replaced with simpler moves, lowering the skill ceiling for intermediate to advanced players. Professional level players have been affected too but they sit above the ceiling at mastery of the game. They can still be the best, but the removal of depth only removes enjoyment from the game. Everybody can now do the highest damage combo with ease. Combo variety is gone, the best damage and wall carry is accessible to all. Single hit pokes and fast counter hit moves have been being selectively nerfed to encourage the use of big moves. Defensive movement is a non-option with far advancing moves, bigger hit boxes, forced 50/50 sequences, and weaker movement. Too many situations come down to a raw guess. Option selects are almost nonexistent, because characters have been given new coverage moves to their move list from Tekken 7 or added in the season 2 patch. The devs refuse to delete these moves or at least make them terrible. Weakness and character identity has been patched out. Online cheating has gone unanswered, and the best solution was a spreadsheet of Twitter reports. These problem have existed since the launch of Tekken 8 and have not been addressed to a satisfactory extent. The developers have had plenty of time to listen to the community which they pretend to be close to and improve the game, but they would rather appease to the greatest common factor in the hopes of greater player retention.

Bandai Namco has gotten what they wanted. A game for the spectators and casuals. Fast-paced rushdown fights with little neutral or spacing, where your best option is to be the first one swinging. Infinite stages have been removed and tournament rules changed on stage selection to discourage defense and make sure all stages are shown. Matches are now flashy particle effects, lengthy combos with cinematics for flare, and the combo and damage counters to let the audience know that was a big combo. There is a lower time investment to pick up the game and feel like you're good at it by flying up the meaningless online ranks, just enough to get the cash cows into the Tekken Shop to buy the uninspired battle pass and costumes while selling Unreal Engine default shapes and assets from previous games. Bandai Namco has taken the momentum from the success of Tekken 7 and turned it into a game that demands less, provides less, and respects less of the community that made it great.

I know casuals don't want a hard game, but there were better alternatives than to turn Tekken into a party game. Investments should have been made on secondary game modes for casual players. Expand on Arcade Quest, why can I finish a visual novel and a couple bot battles in an afternoon? Why not have modifiers, character leveling, a continued story? Bring in extra features to Tekken ball. Train your ghost. Where is tournament mode? Why is Tekken Force one level in the story? Give character episodes that mean something and advance their story. Add in all the cool cinematics and super moves there. Leave online matches for those that want to make the investment and don't ruin it for those that have already invested.

This game had the legacy and potential to be the best fighting game ever, but now it's a disappointment.

Positives:
[list]
[*]Roster is good.
[*]Graphics are good.
[*]Story mode is good.
[*]More story expansions like Unforgotten Echoes should be done.
[*]Fight lounge and Arcade Quest are great for new players to become familiar with the game.
[*]Tekken Ball is fun.
[*]Music is good.
[*]Jukebox is great.
[*]Practice and match queue mode settings and UI display tools are great.
[*]My Replay is great, replay takeover is an amazing tool.
[*]Customization is good.
[/list]", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1751948881}, {"review_text": "I was promised a defensive-focused update for season 2 and that did not come at all. Seems dishonest and they tried to buff everyone to appease everyone.

Perhaps we treated Tag 2 too harshly", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1743475933}, {"review_text": "The game is in a very rough state. Here's the good and the bad.

The good:

More fluent gameplay, more responsive controls, new mechanics make the game feel fresh and new, yet still feeling very similar and helping players that have legacy skill with Tekken. Roster is good, characters feel nice, look nice, play nice. Great visuals, great stages, nice new moves, and they add more moves every season. Game was sort of tuned in terms of notations and input to make complex and difficult moves become easier for all, for example some Just Frame moves are not that strict as it used to, and most command grabs got rid of the old "know the button" character specific inputs, and instead all characters now have the uf1+2 input for command grabs. Heat mode is good, and helps in comebacks and cool combos. Makes it look impressive. A bit of a dumbed down version of Tekken compared to older titles.

The bad:

The game *IS* a dumbed down version of Tekken. Lots of moves and new mechanics make the game very imbalanced, and some characters just have better moves that others, and are now easier to perform. Why play my old favourite character (Lee Chaolan) who has very difficult gameplay and difficult inputs and demanding playstyle while I can simply pick another character that does the same, with less effort? It feels unfair and silly. The Tekken Store is a joke, it makes you pay for cosmetics by paying extra money, while you already paid money for it. The Tekken gold coins you get from the game are essentially useless, even more so that it was in Tekken 7. Online play is trash, ranked games have no satisfying rewards when winning, and losing hurts a lot more that winning feels good. Lots of intentional disconnects make the experience worse, cheaters even more. Frequent game disconnects for no reason while it wasnt your fault at all, and yet STILL you get punished by the game, letting you know that if you leave frequent matches, you'll get a penalty. Game is too dumbed down, thus making learning the game mean nothing, since new players and moderate players can spam powerful moves at you (and with the help of Special Mode, which is TOURNAMENT OK), and make winning a match a tedious and tiring process. New season's changes and modifications made the game very awful, and the price tag for the new season pass is basically half the game's FULL PRICE (40€).

Utterly absurd, you can try joining the party and try not taking the game seriously, because I cannot. But you won't have a nice time. Wait for a discount on the game and the season passes, and check again. It's a fun game at some times, but most of the times, I want to break my desk in half. MAN I LOVE THIS GAME.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 24, "timestamp_created": 1761240609}, {"review_text": "[h1] Tekken doesn't know, what Tekken is anymore [/h1] [i] (don't get this twisted and think T7 is some holy grail, because this started with S3 of that game or towards the end of S2, if you want to be specific) [/i]

[b] Bamco, have to be, one of the the most incompetent publishers (and devs!?) I have ever seen! The community (mostly high level tournament players) are literally telling them what's wrong with the game, improvement suggestions and so on. BUT they ignore all that and give us the worst built Tekken ever! Bamco in general have never treated their Tekken fans well.

At this point, I honestly believe, they are making these changes on purpose to push out legacy players. They don't want players like knee, Arslan and other top players dictating the game. They want legacy players in general, gone.

So, I actually liked this game on release. S1 was really fun and the devs, were making changes in the right direction. Then for S2 it went the complete opposite direction (or how they intended the game to be on release) and they basically nuked the game. [/b]

[h2] General overview [/h2]

[*] If you're new to Tekken, you'll probably have fun regardless. Just press buttons, experiment and enjoy.

[*]Get this out the way first - in game store with in game currency (tekken coins) that you purchase with real money. Now I don't mind cosmetic packs being sold, except the PUBLISHERS (Bamco) have this unethical way of selling cosmetic items. The new stuff made for T8 look nice, the older ported stuff look off, lazy. The way it's sold is predatory; first it's handled outside of Steam, what happens if servers go down, like what is this transaction tied to? Second, packs are sold separately (male/female). Third, the amount of Tekken coins purchased, with how much stuff cost, encourages you to buy more coins, you always have coins left over,  from purchases, you can't just buy two things, you will need to buy more coins, with again coins left over and repeat the cycle. 

[*]Story - average, cliche, anime story, with some hype moments and video graphic cut scenes that look nice. But, why a mass genocide murderer is forgiven?...Because he believes in his heart! It is peak anime story telling.

[*]Graphics/art style - Easily the best looking Tekken game, with nice looking effects (but too much). My review is being written as of Day 3 of Season 2.

[h2] Network and PC performance [/h2]
When the game released on PC it still had performance and network issues that were reported in the network test. As a user with a custom build machine that is tuned well and can play all the latest games on highest settings Tekken 8 still has performance issues at times. Every time I am on the character select screen the game will become slightly choppy when swapping and selecting characters. The game can sometimes crash on PC. Users that played Tekken 7 on PC will remember if you would alt tab there was a chance the game would crash. This is still on ongoing issue with Tekken 8.

Regarding net code issues, it still feels like Tekken 7 season 4. I am not a developer so I do not know what can be done to improve the net code but it is sad to see a fighting game release in the year that it did (2024) and have such poor net code when other titles like street fighter 6 and guilty gear strive have phenomenal roll back net code.


[h2] Presentation + content [/h2]
The costume redesigns the characters received are a warm welcome and do a lot for the returning cast. The music and stages in the game are brilliant. Tekken 8 honestly has one of my favourite soundtracks in the series. I was really looking forward to the story mode as I was invested in seeing what happened after the ending of Tekken 7. The story mode was brilliant and is easily my favourite one iv played in a fighting game. Hopefully we can see a big follow up during a DLC release for Tekken 8.

Customisation is cool and I hope it continues to see free updates over time. The jukebox features is something I always wanted for PC users so it's nice to see us finally get it after missing out on it being a PS4 exclusive for Tekken 7.

I do wish there was more game modes available to play. For example having Team battle come back from the older entries would be really fun for offline play with friends or online in private lobbies.

[h2] Gameplay [/h2]
This entry is very rewarding for aggressive play. The new heat system promotes players to stay on the offensive rather than  using movement and blocking to counter play their opponent.  With the new chip system you are punished for blocking and trying to play slowly to get into a better position. This is a huge change in the direction from the previous entry (Tekken 7) where you could use that games movement system to block and take your time to get out of situations. Since Tekken Tag tournament 1 (1999) players have been using movement (Korean back dash cancelling + sidestepping) to avoid these guessing situations and create whiff opportunities however with Tekken 8 having nerfed movement  (With season 2 they have buffed side steps which is nice but back dash cancelling still feels horrible) you will find yourself at times being forced to guess on a 50/50.  I think some of the hit effects are too much. When Clive activates heat and starts doing through his moves it really takes away from the fight and is too distracting.
 
Every member of the roster got some new tools coming into Tekken 8.  Characters have new single hit and combo strings to change how their game play looks and feels. Some users may find characters play vastly different than their previous entries (Jack-8) is a great example of this.

I think it is important that characters feel unique and have clear defined strengths and weaknesses. I am unsure what approach the developer team are taking with Tekken 8. But it feels to me that characters are starting to feel similar and lose their identity which is a first for a series that has so many unique and interesting characters. Take King for example. Does he need to have the best counter hit string in the game (DF+2,1) which you can hit confirm for a full combo? This does not make sense to me. As a wrestler type character he should be more focused on doing big single hits and using his cool chain throws. 

There are currently 14 characters in the game with the guard break mechanic (Bryan, Clive, Devil Jin, Feng, Heihachi, jack, Kuma, Lidia, Panda, Paul, Reina, Shaheen, Steve, Yoshimitsu) which will break through your block and guarantee a follow up vs you.  In Tekkn 7 only two characters had this functionality (Lidia and Fahkumram) with Bryan also has a unique version of this mechanic since Tekken 3 (Taunt). Seeing it become such a normal part of the game really has made it no longer feel special. 

With the latest update to the game (Season 2) we were expecting the developers to tone down how aggressive the game is and show us what defensive options they were working on. Since the latest patch characters across the board have become even stronger and more oppressive. Chip damage is still a massive issue and heat lasts for too long when activated.  There are also currently some game breaking bugs from characters such as jack and Paul that have new moves that seem to have slipped past testing and are causing interactions that were not intended. It being only day 3 of season 2 more bugs could be found in the coming days/weeks. Hopefully we get an emergency patch to fix them.

[h2] Closing thoughts [/h2]

I am not sure what the future holds for the game.  

I feel like Bandai Namco have been developing Tekken 8 to be enjoyable for the user on the attack without thinking how does it feel to be the user on the defending side.  Just because being on the offensive feels good doesn't mean being on the defending side has to feel bad. But with the core systems in place for Tekken 8 that is exactly how the game feels. From speaking with casual and pro players it does not seem that either group is happy with the direction the game is going. 

I think the developers have lost sight of what made Tekken so much fun. It wasn't big flashy hit effects, over powered moves, characters having no defined weaknesses.

[list]
[*] It was the unique characters and their specifics strengths.
[*] It was seeing someone put years into a character and mastering what their specific game plan was and aspiring to be that great.
[*] It was being a new player and seeing a clip of someone moving around the screen fast thinking "Wow how are they moving like that??".
[*] It was the people who took the time out of their day to host online and offline events just for people to show up and play their favourite fighting game.
[*] It was seeing people coming together from different countries to compete and change their lives
[/list]

[b] It was the community.[/b]

And right now it feels like the developers are no longer listening to the community.

You can do as many collaborations and have as many guest characters as you want. If no one is around to play the game who will purchase the future dlcs you make?

I am lucky enough that I have a healthy offline scene of cool people who play for fun and want to improve. I hope the developers can open up a bit more with the community and maybe reach out for more feedback on future patches or ideas they have.  Everybody who purchased Tekken 8 loves the series. We just want to see it go in a different direction than the current one.

All the best

As someone who came into Tekken 8 fresh — no prior Tekken experience, just raw curiosity and the willingness to grind — I’ve dropped over 600 hours into this game. I wanted to love it. And for a while, I did.

Season 1 felt rough, no doubt. The mechanics were flashy, Heat System felt like a gamble, and damage was through the roof. But at least there was some learning curve, some level of commitment required to climb the ladder. Even when the balancing was questionable, wins still felt like they were earned.

Season 2, though? Somehow worse.
The balancing is completely off the rails. The game is now so “beginner-friendly” that it actively rewards button mashing. I get that fighting games need to attract new players, but we’ve gone from helping newcomers to handing them the keys to the kingdom. You can mash your way up the ranks now. It happens. I’ve seen it. I’ve played against it. And worst of all? It works.

Characters like Hwoarang and Anna are absolutely cracked, able to overwhelm with relentless pressure and flowcharts that are way too safe. There’s no risk vs reward when you're rewarded for just pressing buttons faster than your opponent can think. Bryan’s damage output is ridiculous, and it’s getting to the point where one clean read turns into a 70% health swing. That’s not rewarding skill — that’s just bloated numbers on top of unbalanced mechanics.

I’m not complaining because I’m bad. I’ve stuck with this game longer than any other fighter. I’ve practiced, labbed, watched high-level play, and fought through the grind. I’ve earned my frustration. And it’s frustrating to see the game I dedicated myself to turn into something where neutral, spacing, and decision-making are losing value in favor of autopilot offense and spam-heavy strategies.

Accessibility shouldn't mean brainless.
You should still need to learn how to play neutral, how to whiff punish, how to condition, how to block under pressure. But in its current state, Tekken 8 feels like it’s punishing players for thinking, and rewarding those who just go full throttle and pray.

There’s still potential. The core of Tekken is amazing — legacy mechanics, mind games, matchup knowledge. But the current direction? It’s not sustainable for serious players. If this is what Tekken 9 will look like too, I might be out.

after this battle, it open up more offensive item & skill that really make the game more enjoyable.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 23, "timestamp_created": 1735461213}, {"review_text": "You smoke space cat opium to heal yourself. ‘Nough said.

It's like if Silksong had actually released.

My wife’s boyfriend on the other hand says it’s 2D Sekiro but with even deeper combat.

This is a game that speaks to me in ways no other Metroidvania since Hollow Knight has... Nine Sols is a masterpiece. Really one of the best Metroidvanias I've ever played. It's near or equal to Hollow Knight in terms of quality. The combat is fantastic and the boss fights are very well done. The story is interesting and the characters are memorable. The environments and visuals are fantastic, though they can be a bit gory so not as suitable for a younger audience like Hollow Knight is. I'd say overall it's pretty much the same quality as Hollow Knight and I even enjoyed it a bit more. HK has better exploration with some nicer, less streamlined secrets to discover but Nine Sols blows it out of the water combat and story-wise. 

Like most people, I got into the game because it has a lot of Hollow Knight DNA, but the game is quite different from HK. It is definitely more Sekiro inspired gameplay wise. The biggest difference is that Nine Sols has a very strong focus on story, more so than any Metroidvania. I would say it is Hollow Knight inspired but leans more toward Ori or Cave Story regarding its narrative. Nine Sols has a tonally consistent, and well delivered story that takes itself seriously, unlike Iconoclasts which tries and fails miserably to be both dark and funny/quirky. Nine Sols had more characters that I actually really cared for compared to HK, which made me more invested in the story, but that's also extremely subjective. Personally, the Sci-fi Eastern Philosophy of Nine Sols was more novel and interesting to me than the 'Dark Souls but bugs' of Hollow Knight. And that's not a dis to HK either, as I love that theme/atmosphere/trope. 

I loved Yi's character so much because there are so many layers to everything he's doing. He's such an emotionally clueless hypocrite, but he's also incredibly intelligent, and despite everything, he never quite slips into being unlikeably evil. I loved that your dialogue options in the game underline this, you are often given two questionable options that help to colour in his personality. I also think there’s a good amount of dialogue at the start, but beyond that it proceeds like a normal game telling its story. The dialogue also develops the characters in a way I haven’t really connected with in other games. Shuanshuan is one of the best kids in any game I’ve played.

I also like how DOWN TO EARTH the story of Nine Sols is. Most of the Metrodvania that try to present a deeper story tend to make the story-telling as complicated/ as confusing as most of the Soul series, for example, Blasphemous and many imitation of Souls-like Metrodvania games.
Those games may have a good setting, but the way they tell their story is so convoluted/confusing to the point most people stop caring about it. Nine Sols and Ender Lillie are some of the few exceptions which tells a coherent, relatable and touchy story. One does not require an extended exposition to understand the culture, the drama is what pulls everything in. The last dialogue "When the curtain falls, none of us are really at fault" encapsulates the philosophical attitude of Taoism entirely. There were so many layers to each of the 9 souls, it gave me the desire to research into them even after completing the game. I have been changed entirely along with my perspectives towards Taoism.

I have seen a few people get turned off by having to read text bubbles for the story but sorry this is a huge mismatch in expectations. Like playing a story focused game like Mass Effect and ending up getting Kingdoms of Amalur instead; or if you go to the theater expecting a fun marvel style action but ended up watching Logan. So when trying the game, do consider engaging with its story as all other mechanics (exploration, combat, etc.) are there to support the narrative, not the other way around like most Metroidvania. It has a really compelling story for a Metroidvania, which is extremely rare in this genre. The game has a Story Mode too with adjustable difficulty settings, and the game length is not too long but not too short. Many people would know the burnout after playing HK or Elden Ring. On the other hand, Nine Sols respects players time, and the ending is so good it made me feel sad that it was all over.

Now while there's a lot to love about Nine Sols, the bosses were what made the game a stand out experience for me. Some of the boss fights in this game are absolute masterclasses in design. The level and consistency of boss quality was among the highest I've encountered in a game. That final boss in particular was probably the best 2D boss I've ever fought and the last boss in general was probably my favourite boss in general since Isshin. The final boss is just so perfectly executed I can't even comprehend. It's Consort Radhan type of difficulty, but much more fair overall. It's so good and so hard it gives you stockholm syndrome and makes you wanna replay the fight despite it taking HOURS to beat initially. The experience of overcoming the final boss is going to stay with me for a long time.

The combat is some of the best Metroidvania combat l've seen in a long time, it's difficult and so satisfying to pull off. The game is ridiculously hard. You have to LOVE parrying. So if you’re a platinum Sekiro-loving bastard like myself you’re in for a great time. Now it’s difficult, but also f**king amazing. When you lock in to a boss fight, it’s like a dance. The controls and movement are a little different from Hollow Knight, and there’s definitely an adjustment period while you get the parry down, but once you do it’s SO satisfying and you move through the game BEAUTIFULLY.  

I cannot imagine playing a Metroidvania without a parry System now. This is so incredibly executed that I would dare to say this really improves and innovates the Metroidvania formula. The Boss Fights are an exciting dance of striking, dodging and parrying. Rarely the game is intransparent and it felt like every death taught me something. I loved that it makes me react to the fight coming to me, rather than getting to choose when to engage. I loved that I have multiple options for dealing with every incoming attack. I loved that I don't even have the option to sit back and cheese it out with a ranged attack. It's a wonderful experience and unlike a lot of other games I've played. Yes, it's difficult, but I found that learning to use the game's systems effectively was equally rewarding. 

Now to clarify when people talk about "parrying" its more a deflect than a parry. If you ever played Sekiro, you know the difference. I only say this because I HATE parrying. I DESPISE parrying. I do NOT TOUCH the parry button on souls-likes and that almost made me miss out on the f**king master piece that Sekiro is. Years later, coming into Nine Sols was a breeze but old me would've flinched away from it when hearing about "parry based combat". If you like Metroidvanias and challenging/rhythmic combat, give this game a try, even if you're not a fan of parrying it’s absolutely worth it.

Game is phenomenal and I would highly recommend it to anyone who likes Metroidvania games with a good difficulty. Can even play storymode if your skills are not up to par. I enjoyed this game more than Hollow Knight. I know that may be blasphemous, but that’s how high it ranks for me. Really absolute banger of a game, If the year it came out wasn't so packed it would have definitely had a shot at some real heavy hitter awards, maybe even GOTY.

Nine Sols is what happens when a developer truly understands the balance between mechanical depth and raw, distilled gameplay. It’s not bloated with systems—it refines a handful of tools and demands you master them. Attack, charged slash, parry, counter, talisman, and bow. That’s it. And that’s all you need.

Where other games offer experimentation, Nine Sols offers discipline. It doesn’t hold your hand, nor does it rely on overcomplexity to inflate its difficulty. You learn, you fail, and you return—not to try a different build, but to perfect your execution. There’s something beautiful about that.

The peril of enemies and the risk they carry contain the potential for your most powerful technique—the Talisman Explosion. It makes you feel like an actual anime character, absolutely decimating an enemy by using a gentle hand; pressuring foes for attacks, coming out unscathed, and using the energy obtained to pulverize anything foolish enough to cross your path. It’s one of many ways the game rewards patience, precision, and an unflinching approach to combat.

This isn’t a game of exchanging blows, politely waiting your turn—it’s a violent dance, and you’re learning to master the rhythm.

The world is equal parts mysterious and oppressive, the art style deliberate and striking. Enemies don’t feel like fodder; even minor encounters demand attention and finesse. Bosses are a test of will and reflex—no luck, just skill.

If you're looking for a game that makes every mechanic feel intentional, every movement meaningful, and every success truly earned, Nine Sols delivers that experience tenfold. I've played a lot of really good Metroidvanias: Hollow Knight, Guacamelee, Ori, and many of the Metroids/Castlevanias. So let me just say that Nine Sols is one of the finest entries in the genre. 

This game features the typical utility gated exploration and platforming that's seen across all Metroidvania games, but what sets Nine Sols apart from the others is its strong focus on combat, and boy does it do an exceptional job at it.

Your primary weapon is a 3 hit-combo sword and an explosive talisman that can require some finesse to detonate in boss encounters. On top of that, you will also need to get the hang of the 2.5 different types of parries. If it sounds very hard, don't worry, progression in this game is done well enough that by the end of the game, you'll start feeling like Daigo Umehara.

And on top of your arsenal of abilities, the design of mobs and bosses, who all have their own unique abilities and attack patterns, is incredibly well polished. Most enemies can bring you from 100 to 0 in a few hits, but I never really felt like anything was particular cheap. 

For instance, a certain boss in this game took me 6 hours ([i]I was quite sleepy to be fair[/i]) to beat. But after beating it the first time, I immediately managed to beat it again on a subsequent attempt. This is why I say that the combat isn't cheap, because once things "click", you'll beat bosses with relative ease, and it is VERY satisfying when that happens.

[b]But make no mistake, this game absolutely falls within the category of "Cuphead-Megaman-Dead Cells" category of difficult games and definitely isn't for everyone.[/b] For reference, 85% of players beat the "tutorial" boss, but that number dropped sharply to 61% for beating the first real boss of the game.

A special mention also goes to the game's story. I was genuinely surprised by how well the various mysteries gradually unraveled and brought everything together for one epic conclusion. I daresay the story is written even better than Holllow Knight, which I found to be pretty convoluted.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Nine Sols is a combat heavy Metroidvania that is incredibly well polished and virtually flawless. The combat, level design, story, and OST is terrific. My only minor criticism is I wished cutscenes/dialogue and the end credits were skippable, but otherwise, I believe the developers achieved everything they wanted to achieve and more. [b]9.5/10[/b]", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1748431710}, {"review_text": "[h2][i]Nine Sols - The Tao of Parry[/i][/h2]
Nine Sols delivers such a refined experience that it’s hard to compare it to anything else. Calling itself [b]“Taopunk,”[/b] it blends a cyberpunk world with Taoist philosophy and martial arts combat. It’s a hybrid that pulls together several genres I love, wrapping them in a beautiful hand-drawn art style, incredible gameplay, and an equally powerful soundtrack.

[hr][/hr]
[b]🔹[u]Story[/u] :[/b]

The storytelling in Nine Sols completely surprised me. Yi’s journey was already enjoyable, but finishing the game with the bad ending pushed me to look up how to unlock the true one and when I did, the game blew me away all over again (like it hadn’t already done that fifty times before).

It concludes properly, with no dangling threads, while also giving meaningful closure to the NPCs you meet along the way. The interactions feel refreshingly human, and the world-building adds more and more layers the further you progress. It’s one of those rare games where I actually felt connected to the characters.

[hr][/hr]
[b]🔹[u]Gameplay[/u] :[/b]

The art direction combines 2D visuals with 3D backdrops, creating a unique and immersive presentation. Structurally, it’s far more linear than a traditional Metroidvania, so if you’re expecting a Hollow Knight style experience, you may be disappointed. There’s little backtracking, and exploration is fairly light.

Abilities are unlocked as you progress, while most skills are purchased through vendors. I approached Nine Sols as its own experience instead of comparing it, and I’m glad I did because it constantly surprised me. Just when I thought I’d seen it all, it presented another bold idea that left me in awe.

Every stage and boss fight has its own theme and mechanics, keeping the experience fresh. The game length feels just right, and the achievements add a lot of value (though some are missable, so check a guide if you’re aiming for 100%). The upgrade/power-up system, which balances exploration and money gathering, also felt very rewarding.

[hr][/hr]
[b]🔹[u]Combat[/u] :[/b]

Combat is heavily parry focused, and that’s the heart of the game. A well-timed parry completely negates damage, while regular blocking chips away at your health (which you can later recover). If you don’t enjoy parry-heavy systems, this game may not click with you but if you do, it’s incredibly satisfying.

Enemy variety is decent, though I wish there were a few more types. The bosses, however, are perfectly balanced in number and difficulty. Each one is fair but challenging, with the final boss being the ultimate test. It took me hours to learn its patterns, but when I finally beat it, my love for the game turned into obsession.

[hr][/hr]
[b]🔹[u]Performance[/u] :[/b]

I played Nine Sols on a Steam Deck OLED at high settings, running perfectly at 90 FPS with no stutters or dips. Battery life is excellent too, especially if you cap it to a 10W TDP. This is easily one of the smoothest, most polished experiences I’ve had.

[hr][/hr]
[b]🔹[u]Final Thoughts[/u] :[/b]

Nine Sols is one of those rare games that holds your attention from start to finish, rewarding you with every step. With its deep storytelling, satisfying combat, stunning art direction, and flawless performance, it’s easily one of my favorite games in recent memory.

Art style - it is very lovely. I love games which come after cartoony/unique artstyle (and not chase this "realism" trend), because this is what make them so nice to look at. But god damn, scenes being such grim and cruel at times, despite being in hand drawn art style.

Story - can't say im deep into stories, but i would lie if i wasn't touched by it. The world in Nine Sols is neverending nightmare, with cruel events, with immoral choices done by all characters (and only one character being innocent, you will know them when you see them). And whole story revolves around "You lost it all when you tried to see too far" (attempt to defy nature and find a way to achieve immortality), and "proper" main story ending is about not saving Solarians, but to become a good person and die with dignity. What a way to end your own species. But aside from main point of story, around which game events revolve, it also tells us a story of Solarian race themselves. Also like the way we get a hint at that Lear and Yi know each-other through spacetime, and they actually made kind of time loop (present Yi somehow teaches past Lear, and past Lear teaches present Yi, without Yi's teachings (whatever how that happened) Fangshi Guild might have never succeeded in past, and likewise Yi would have not succeeded at present without Lear's teachings).

Regarding difficulty of game, i wouldn't say that final boss is hard (and in general, game is overall "hard", but when it comes to relative difficulty, i found that easiest boss would definitely be Jiequan because of simple attack set and everything being in single beat), she is just kind of annoying to get used to. Personally, i had  most issues with first phase (way too slow attacks), but once first phase got manageable, second phase and third phase were much easier to master relative to first phase, because her attacks become more rhythmic. Also, you probably want Swift Descend jade for third phase, because after screen-wide slash attacks you would definitely want to be on ground as soon as possible to perform unbounded counter.

If you love "live - fight - die - repeat" style of games, especially Souls-like, and don't mind it being 2D platformer, then you would definitely love this game, the combat in Nine Sols feels truly fluent compared to HK.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1756638777}, {"review_text": "After spending almost 34 hours in Nine Sols and finishing the game for the first time, I can confirm this game is a masterpiece. With near perfect art, gameplay and writing, Nine Sols is one of if not my favorite game of all time. Overall, I had a one of a kind experience with this game and would love to see a DLC or sequel soon!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1746504825}, {"review_text": "phenomenal game great story excellent combat

Would highly recommend as a fan of hollow knight, katana zero, and ori", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1756265865}, {"review_text": "Great game. It's mostly compared to Hollow Knight and Sekiro, and these are fair comparisons, though I don't know if it's quite as good as either of those games. While movement often feels much like Hollow Knight on a basic level, it's never as fleshed out or interesting. Combat of extremely well done and mechanically is probably a little better than Hollow Knight, but it's not as creative or in terms of enemy design and attack variety. The whole game's level design pales in comparison to other really high quality metroidvanias, but that's not a dealbreaker. As for Sekiro, Nine Sols's combat is based on a similar premise but generally less well executed. While in Sekiro dealing damage to enemies is generally incidental, in Nine Sols it's usually your primary method of defeating them. Parries are super important, but they're mostly about avoiding damage than about dealing it. This is what I think Sekiro does much better - the posture mechanic is brilliant because every attack you successfully deflect not only helps you, but also hurts your opponent. There's a "jade" (basically a charm from Hollow Knight) that allows your parries to do internal damage, but this isn't until the midgame, is optional, comes at the expense of other jades, and even still isn't a real substitute for the posture mechanic. What was so satisfying about posture is that you'd open an enemy up to be killed instantly by a single deathblow - internal damage is usually just a small bonus of chip damage. It can add up over time, but it's not as singularly powerful as posture in Sekiro. 

The art and music are all nice, but not quite as memorable as some other games. The story is quite good but I admit there was a lot of talking that I didn't care about. It could have been a lot more succinct, if you ask me. That said, I really enjoyed this game. The vibes are cool and some of the boss fights (especially the last one) have some of the best design I've ever encountered in a game. I think the difficulty is a little overstated, to be totally honest - there's very little in this game that feels unfair and with practice even the toughest attacks become trivial to avoid. That's a sign of really good game design in my mind. 

Anyway, definite recommend for fans of either metroidvanias or soulslikes.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1748819750}, {"review_text": "Okay... this... might be one of the best games I've ever played hands down... mechanics: amazing, Animation: spectacular, Story: INSANE. PLAY THIS GAME", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1759435738}, {"review_text": "The hardest souls-like game I ever played. The final boss on true form destroyed me. I enjoyed every drop of blood and pain.
Amazing game. After you get used to the 2 different mechanics: charged parry and talisman charge the game becomes easier.

Lovely story with multiple layers.

Just play it, at least enjoy it in story mode.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1741202589}, {"review_text": "Usually I don't like metroidvanias that much due to some issues that are still present in this game, but this game in particular is a masterpiece. Description says it's a 2d Sekiro-like, and that isn't too far off, but various mechanics make the combat so much more faster paced and challenging in its own right, while it also has a lower difficulty mode if you only wish to go through the story - and the story is so fantastic I'd recommend not spoiling yourself. The bosses are fantastic, with the last 4 or 5 bosses being some of the best designed bosses I've ever fought. The story, art, gameplay, design, music, everything is near perfect. Highly recommend playing through the entire game and taking the time to do all the little extra things, it's worth it and it's worth even reading the little lore things you pick up or look at. It adds to the atmosphere to the game.

First let's talk about a few things I disliked - the problem with metroidvanias is not exactly knowing the "correct" path. This causes a lot of backtracking, especially if there's no 'quality of life' pointing to where exactly things you've missed are. In particular the early game can become a bit tedious due to the lack of traversal, but this solves itself by mid game. Some options are locked behind story, while something like sprinting is locked in the skill tree. These problems I had did dampen my enjoyment early on, but I'm glad I stuck to it and by mid game I was thoroughly enjoying the game.

The story was extremely well executed, giving you enough to interest you in the world but not enough to fully piece together. Some things were obvious of course, but there was enough mystery to possibly keep you second guessing. It isn't an uncommon story, but it was told beautifully and expertly while staying profound to its core. 

Everything from the combat to the designs and atmosphere were so cohesive and well done. Sometimes to a fault, where animations and things kind of felt a bit slow and tedious at times. The combat mechanics keep building as you go along in the story, being so mechanically tight while also thematically stylish. And the bosses aren't pushovers either, the final boss in particular is definitely worthy of being final boss material on Standard difficulty. When you get the mechanics down and respond properly to enemy attacks, it's extremely satisfying not unlike conquering the hardest souls-like bosses. Standard difficulty for me had just the right amount of challenge, and again the lower difficulty is still there for those not looking for that kind of challenge. One of the best games I've played.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1745190306}, {"review_text": "Personally my Game of the Year for 2024. It's the peak of combat, it feels like this game is so ready to satisfy hardcore Hollow Knight and Blasphemous player for another memorable epic combat. The story is no slouch either.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1743431342}]

[{"review_text": "To the devs. If you're reading this, do NOT give up on this game. Bought it for myself as a Christmas gift and now I can't put it down. It feels like a real game, it feels fun, and you can feel the passion that went into it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1736702787}, {"review_text": "as of 24/12/2024, i have seen some adverts from a game called "king of Avalon," on youtube using footage of this game. however i cannot report it and i suspect that the footage is being used without consent. i do not know how to contact the devs about this.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 36, "timestamp_created": 1735082306}, {"review_text": "Normally don't write reviews but seeing the recent ones are mixed felt obligated to chip in.

I myself have spent hundreds of hours in this game, albeit in custom difficulty modes. Customization is good here; I've crafted a difficulty scenario where I am not being mercilessly attacked nor having my territory taken, but fighting the AI Lord is still a challenge. That being said...

The level of depth in the Burgage plots alone is what drew me to this game. It's Banished but with real upgrades that mean something. You can build burgage plots that are just big enough for a backyard, and plan that entire family around becoming a tailor/butcher/brewer etc. to boost your economy and resource production. The fact that at level 1 these plots can be made MASSIVE and turned into a vegetable field (Or Orchard!) while simultaneously housing up to 2 families is amazing!! It allows such a wide variety of strange and natural shapes to exist within your town, and can help keep village designs from turning into grids.

The learning curve here is similar to every colony sim IMO, you just kinda have to face smash the first few colonies until you understand how to quickly setup the things necessary for a taxable village, then mercenaries and retinue can be aquired to fight the bandits and prepare for later combat with the AI Lord. The difficulty here is that if the AI Lord is "aggressive" he will be able to claim your starting territory before you can get any troops gathered, and it's kinda game over from there. Changing that setting alone will make the game much more playable. I recommend playing with just bandits for a bit to get the feel for quickly getting troops together.

The graphics are amazing, and among the best I've seen in a colony sim. The villagers hammer and saw on structures and individual beams and walls get added on as the construction goes on, which is an incredible touch. Animation of the villagers is good from afar or up close. On the larger villages (50+ level three burgage plots) you can get some chugging, but that could also be my dated CPU.

All in all this is one of my favorite colony sims I've ever played, and I eagerly await the updates. From the begining this has been a very small team, but they've always done great work and listened to the community. I get the feeling that some of the updates they are working on are more challenging than the last, but I have faith that this game will be carried through to it's potential!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1757641286}, {"review_text": "I don't think the reviews saying the developer has been on "radio silence" are particularly fair. They've communicated pretty well throughout as far as I'm concerned. I think some people have quite unrealistic expectations and that's led to disappointment.

Personally I have enjoyed the game a lot since launch and I've felt very excited to play again each time there's been a new update. Did the last major take longer than expected? Yes. Did I put it down and play other things while I waited? Yes. Was any of that a problem? No.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 9, "timestamp_created": 1759458087}, {"review_text": "Alright, so I have a love/hate relationship with this game. Its a fun game and if you wanna spend alot of time developing a nice city and doing all that then this is great for you. But somethings to be aware of:

- The economy is ****EXTREMELY**** broken. You could be selling swords, spears, helmets, boots, cloaks, veggies, beer, dyes, charcoal, wool, linen, wooden parts and both types of shields. But if you need Barley & grain it'll sink your regional wealth. Which in turn bankrupts you. So basically if you cant build a town that is 100% self sustaining then you may as well quit and start over. 
- The enemy will spawn directly into your town. Wether it be bandits or the opposing Lord. Sometimes they'll spawn other places but majority of the time they are going to spawn from off map, directly into your region. So prepare to have your town completely wiped several times a game. 

- When the off map Lord decides to attack, don't just assume you won because you won the first battle. Give it about 60 seconds and he will spawn a completely new and fresh army to attack you with. So you could of spent ridiculous amounts of money mainlining a standing army of your own, supplementing it with mercenaries, and it'll likely not be enough. So get ready to lose. Also understand that you will never have a retinue as large as his. He will have around 30+ and max you can get is like 24. Plus have several bands of mercenaries with him. Which again, will all re spawn fresh and ready to go.

- If you have mercenaries spawned on the map be prepared for your carts/oxen to get caught in them. So keep an eye on them or it'll cause a clog. 

- Resource distribution is wild in this game. A house directly next to a fully stocked market might get the resources from it. Maybe. But one a few blocks down the road will definitely get them. 

- Keep an eye on production. If you don't set limits on what your specialists make then they're going to drain every last resource you have and its not physically possible to keep up. 

- Lately unassigned workers have been disappearing. Why? who knows. You'll have 10 unassigned families and they will all disappear. 

- The villagers are MASSIVE drunks. Your most valuable resource in the entire game is ale. Everything comes to a screeching halt without it. You cant upgrade buildings. You cant get perk points. You'll lose. But again you cant really import it because it'll bankrupt you. So good luck.

- DON'T BOTHER WITH APIARIES. They are worthless and a massive waste of time. Streamers say they're great but they're lying. You get maybe 3 honey a month from them. Which is instantly gone and you don't see a benefit from it because its burnt through so fast. So do yourself a favor and pick a different perk. It doesn't matter how many you place down or how many families you assign. You re only getting a max of 3. Period. End of story. 

- Also don't bother getting the hunter traps or double meat perks. They don't work either. You cant physically produce enough meat to sustain a villages wants. So forget it altogether and focus on veggies, berries and apples. Maybe if you're lucky you might get good farm land and can grow some wheat and barley. But don't count on it. Farmers will consistently not plow half a field or wont plant most of it. I've found it best to make small .3 size plots for farming. But the problems still persist regardless of how many farmers, oxen and time you devote to it. 

For all of its flaws it is a fun game. Sometimes you'll do alright and somehow survive long enough to complete a map. But odds are you wont. Get comfortable with the idea of spending hours, even days, working on one really awesome town. Then it's going to be levels by bandits and the rival lord will take it over and then you'll have to start all over. For a single developer its a very beautiful game and has some seriously solid bones. But obvious being in early access its gonna have issues. Apparently there's a complete rework being made so maybe soon all of these issues wont even be a thing anymore. Fingers crossed cause I do enjoy it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1754748413}, {"review_text": "the solo developer took 10 months to develop an update that doubles the content in the game and hire team members, and the games reviews fell into mixed in that time period.

anyways the game is best-in-class for colony management and medieval combat.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1759423986}, {"review_text": "[h3][b]A Flawed Gem with Immense Potential[/b]
[/h3]I wanna start off by saying—I love this game. With all its imperfections, things that need repolishing, or straight-up reworking, Manor Lords is still fun. I’ve spent over 50 hours in under three weeks. It hooked me fast, even if that excitement slowly faded over time.

[table]
[tr]
[th][b]Pros [/b]: [/th] 
[th][b]Cons [/b]: [/th] 
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][b]Great graphics and art style[/b]. It's genuinely one of the better-looking city builders out there.[/td]
[td][b]Slow updates[/b]. This is the main issue. The game has been sitting in Early Access limbo. I looked at it six months ago, and honestly? Not much has changed. Yes, the dev released a preview for an upcoming update—and it looks promising—but until it drops, I have to call it like it is: the game lacks innovation right now.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][b]Flexible building system[/b]. The modular housing and placement freedom are a joy to work with.[/td]
[td][b]Bugs that won't go away[/b]. I haven’t had as many issues as some others, but I’ve still seen families disappearing, or burgage plots refusing to build despite having all the materials and workers ready.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][b]Trading system has potential[/b]. Imports/exports work well enough, but the packing station (used to trade between your own regions) is basically useless right now.[/td]
[td][b]Micromanagement gets tedious[/b]. There’s no way to manage multiple buildings of the same type in bulk. Setting work areas for each logging camp or forester one-by-one gets old fast. Also, each new region starts from scratch with its own progression tree, which kills the pace. If I’ve built up one region, I should be able to transfer that momentum.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td][b]Helpful tooltips[/b]. Most buildings have a "?" icon that explains their purpose and requirements. Super handy when you’re learning the ropes.[/td]
[td][b]Optimization is rough[/b]. Could be on my end, but I’m running an RTX 3060 and i5-10500, and this game runs worse than Cyberpunk or RDR2. Even on medium settings I get frame drops, and x12 speed turns the game into a slideshow.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

A lot of people have pointed out the €40 price tag—and honestly, I get it. For an Early Access title, it is [i]steep[/i]. I managed to get a key for just under €20, and I don’t regret it one bit. At that price, there’s more than enough content to justify the purchase. At €40? Not quite yet. Manor Lords is far from polished—but even so, I still recommend it. With the right updates and some much-needed refinement, it has the potential to become something [b]truly special[/b].", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1744804840}, {"review_text": "It would be great to add a court system for villagers who commit crimes. And we can decide what punishment to give. So, prisons and gallows can be built near the settlement. Also, people living in the settlement can be happy or disappointed according to our decision. Because, if we decide to kill criminals for every crime, society may lose trust in justice and therefore there may be a decrease in happiness.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1742480019}, {"review_text": "I've clocked thousands of hours in Cities Skylines (and predecessors) and Civilization (and predecessors) so my reviewing expertise is mainly in quality as a sim builder and medieval sandbox.

Manor Lords is very representative entry in the gaming landscape over the last decade--tiny teams of indie developers producing games that clean the clocks of AAA studios. We are in a very weird era of underbaked, obviously bad, insanely expensive games from major studios that violate basic rules of game design. And next to those, we're getting staggeringly impressive games like Valheim. 

Based on how enjoyable the last (checks notes) 84 hours have been, Manor Lords will be a staggering achievement when it's finished.

The core mechanics of Manor Lords are fleshed out, the rest is less than half done--but it's already more fun and gives more hours of playtime than most of the AAA games out right now. Electronic Arts would release this as finished for $50 and charge $50 for every improvement.

Perhaps the thing I find the most striking about the game is that you can shove your buildings pretty close together, at whatever angle you want, and roads can go anywhere you want, and plopping feels natural. If you're a city builder then you know that you normally have to mod your game to give yourself any real building freedom--Manor Lords bakes it in. As someone who has plopped down (checks notes) tens of thousands of little roads and buildings in Cities Skylines and Planet Coaster, I appreciate a developer who makes plopping down roads and buildings easy. Tool-tip style buttons let you tweak number of buildings. (I hope for the addition of an option to turn off collision entirely, along with the other conventional toggles you'd find in a sim cheat menu.)

The choices in gameplay are great. The balance is currently incomplete (as of March 2025), but all the paths to medieval success are different in style and weird and fun for their own reasons; each path shapes the town (literally!) in its own way. Right now the math is not mathing for breeding sheep, but just plopping them them down for aesthetic reasons alone feels enjoyable, and I look forward to building around pastures.

Battles are fun. I don't fully understand the strategy yet, but I look forward to them when they happen, which says a lot, since I'm a city builder person and have no experience with any grand battle games. Literally none. So if you don't either, don't worry about it, you'll be fine. The mercenary mechanics are great, as is the retinue system, as is the equipping the citizens system, which really connects the city you build with the army you make. It's really just very inspired, which is kind of hilarious, in that... the game literally just cloned historical accuracy. 

If this game is remembered for anything, it will be for correctly deciding which pieces of historical accuracy to keep (answer: the fun ones).

Unless the developer were to make an incredible error in judgement, unlikely given the game's quality to this point, I assume the game will be made easily moddable when it's finished. Manor Lords has the same quality that The Sims and Cities Skylines do, which is their inherent appeal as a platform for expansion. I could see how modders would expand on elements like pastures, or trading, or resources, for a mini Stardew Valley situation for those who wanted it. And of course, modders can do what game developers can't, which is provide an infinite source of building skins for maximalist realism.

As of 3/15/2025, core features are missing due to the early access status. The castle building system is very much in progress, the UI is sparse in terms of allowing you to do things like find buildings and trade routes, and diplomacy systems and other enemy AI components are missing.

If you like builders or medieval sandboxes, and are relying on such things to give yourself some sense of control in an out of control world, you can go ahead and buy Manor Lords now. If you need a game to be finished before you buy it, then wait until it's done (or buy now if you want to be a patron). Quite a few game components are yet to be added or have the balance to make them functional.

As far as the political statement of the game--that's why the game is worth reviewing now and releasing in early access. Much of the world's recent tumult and fiction has been idealizing benevolent monarchies--framed in both liberal ideals of Bridgerton to right wing technocratic autocracy in post 2024 politics. Manor Lords engages the brutal rules of survival and the savage violence of the medieval era, its expendable mercenary war economy, the equivalent autonomy of computer variables and medieval peasants. You play through the costs and whys of those systems, and watch your people get pillaged with not much imagination required to guess what actually happens to civilians in war. 

Twenty years ago, an ostensibly apolitical, historically accurate game about medieval times wouldn't have registered much as a statement, but it certainly does now. 9/10, with it on track to ding several "of all time" lists when it's finished.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1742069957}, {"review_text": "When I first bought Manor Lords, I had an amazing time — the initial hours were genuinely fun and immersive. However, after just a few hours, the lack of content became apparent, and the game quickly started to feel empty. I decided to take a break, hoping that with time, new updates would bring fresh content and improvements.

After nearly a year away, I came back… and sadly, almost nothing has changed. The game still suffers from the same content shortage and becomes repetitive far too quickly. Even worse, I encountered bugs that prevented me from continuing my saved game, which was incredibly frustrating.

Manor Lords has massive potential — the foundation is there for something truly great. But at this moment, I cannot recommend buying it. I sincerely hope the developers start releasing meaningful updates that add actual content and fix critical issues, but right now, it doesn’t seem like such updates are anywhere on the horizon. It’s a shame, because so much potential is being wasted.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1755091170}, {"review_text": "I really want to love this game, and I think there is a strong core / framework / foundation for the city-building, but unfortunately everything outside of that feels woefully shallow and/or unfinished. That's understandable in an EA title, but even in the newest beta update (which I understand is mostly refactoring/reorganizing) these kinds of core issues aren't addressed to any degree. 

In short, the good/great:

- Great city-building mechanics
- Interesting resource allocation, management and progression
- Very cool building tile system and specifically the use of core burghs/houses which can upgrade several levels or be specialized
- Interesting new perk and environment system which looks promising, but only available through a single perk (for now)
- The scale and building animations are great

The bad:

- Diplomacy is non-existent and shouldn't even be in the game in it's current state
- The UI is clunky at best. It desperately needs an update for things like the Help pages, where tabbed content doesn't have any kind of logical organization and you can't search, only to find in many cases extremely vague and curt descriptions some of which end with where this resource comes from but don't bother stating what it's used for and what you do with it (like Wax).
- Population management becomes a chore and there's no menu that lists out all the families in a town and lets you unassign at will, instead forcing you to meticulously point-and-click search through buildings to see where spare families might be. This becomes very unwieldy once you reach 40+ families.
- Family assignment to buildings is too simplistic, and inevitably causes you to babysit buildings like farmhouses where workers are only relevant for 6/12 months of the year. Since you can't assign a family to multiple roles with any kind of priority/seasonal system (farm until harvest, plow/sow, then go chop wood during winter instead of sitting around doing nothing for the next 9 months) you have to heavily micro-manage.
- Resource nodes are too scattershot and random in the region-system of the game. As of the beta you're guaranteed to at least get stone and food, but if you don't have rich iron, clay, or etc, you have no way to gain these except trading, where fees are exorbitant and trickle even with 4 traders on horses is very slow.

Unfortunately I could go on and on with more and more nitpicks, and it feels like this is yet another case of an indie game with fantastic potential that is simply trying to cram too many mechanics into itself instead of having a more concentrated and focused core gameplay loop. Maybe this will change in the future with the newer team and all this refactoring and promise of smaller more consistent updates, but as of now, it struggles under the weight of it's own ambition.

I'm giving it a Recommended, but a very tentative one. There's a lot of potential here from someone clearly very talented, and it's a smart idea to get a team together, but the game desperately needs entire sections of itself (almost every aspect of the in-game UI, diplomacy, etc) overhauled or replaced because it feels and very obviously is placeholder content.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1759648591}, {"review_text": "Well, I really like the game and its design, but it's been out for over a year now and still hasn't seen any major updates. Most of the features are currently unavailable, and there just isn't much to do after about 25-30 hours of play. Updates are coming out painfully slow and unfortunately, I'm worried people might forget about this game soon. I really wish I could give it a thumbs up, but right now, I wouldn't recommend it. Maybe I'll change that later.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 15, "timestamp_created": 1750961990}, {"review_text": "Game is an enjoyable city builder, but there has not been an update in 7 months, apparently the dev is working on a 'major update' but I'd hold off on buying it until the update cycle becomes more regular and transparent as at the moment this is a very early access game and at this pace will remain so for a while (if it doesn't wind up being abandoned...), risk of EA sure but that is why I cannot recommend it at this point", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1755687977}, {"review_text": "Millennial Game Reviewer Extraordinaire

[h1]🎮 Manor Lords – 6/10 (Potential for 8+)[/h1]

[h2]TL;DR[/h2]
[b]✅ A promising medieval strategy game with a unique blend of city-building and real-time tactics.[/b]
[b]❌ Currently lacking polish, with some features still in need of refinement and updates coming slower than a knight on horseback.[/b]

[h2]What Works[/h2]
[list]

A very strange design choice to make only a select plot with perfect fertility instead of spreading it out more.

Villagers seem to have issues with field rotation on season change. They will be plowing fallow fields after harvest and only after hitting the new month switch to the fields that should be plowed. This happens every single cycle and wastes a lot of time. Sometimes they can't even finish in time before winter comes and are then behind on produce, when they could just have started earlier.

Another farming related issue is the pathing for the plow on the ox. It becomes totally useless if the plot isn't a perfect square. As soon as it has more than 4 corners or is at an angle, the farmer will go over the already plowed part continuously, wasting a lot of time and energy. They also don't seem to know how to work two oxen at the same field. If you have two assigned oxen to your farmhouse, they still only use one on the field. This makes the ox vastly inferior to having 10 families plow by hand, which is over 4 times faster and their pathing much much better. I know that lowering workforce required is the best option, but if I can still feed my villagers with a good amount of food to spare, I don’t mind overworking 10 families to death.

There are also a lot of other smaller issues like, villagers getting stuck when time is sped up and villagers trying to cross the rivers instead of using the bridges and more.

[h3]What I would like [/h3]
It is a really fun game but it is also a bittersweet experience if you are looking for something more realistic and hardcore.

The whole dynamic city flow, if you can call it that, is one of the reasons I got this and when the biggest issues are fixed and most important features added, I hope these virtual citizens will have more ways to make a visual impact on their surroundings. Like creating new roads or paths on the ground decided by where they typically like to cut corners and such would be great. It would also be cool if villagers could build certain things on their own.

Another thing I really hope to see is a huge overhaul to sickness and diseases. Having different poxes and plagues enter your city and halve your population would be really fun and make it both more realistic and challenging. It would of course have to have visual representation as well, like doors marked with white crosses and dead people in the streets, so it isn't just a numbers thing. At the same time being able to hire physicians and such to decrease the chance of it spreading and cure people faster would fit perfectly. Since farming is a big thing in this game, a time relevant fungal infection from contaminated grains like Saint Anthony's Fire would fit really well.

At last, other things I hope to see added are blueprints and Steam Workshop. I bet this game would have a lot of cool mods if the Workshop was available.

Since a lot of resources are very scarce, it would be great to have a way to protect a specific resource that you really don't want bandits to get their hands on. Maybe by assigning a family to protect.

A proper night cycle would be nice. There currently is a visual night cycle that can be toggled in the settings, but it really just is visual. So a proper night cycle would be great. Night is scary and could fit well into boosting taverns, but also crime levels if and when that gets added.

[h3]Closure [/h3]
I haven't had much time to play with combat yet, as I have spent all my time learning how to keep my cities healthy and alive. But I will come back later once I have more experience and the game has had more updates.

I love this game and I, as many others, see huge potential in it, but it still leaves a lot to be desired and the question is if the time and dedication is there for this game to see its true potential.
