I have a large library and a lot of experience from the genre and will say this one definitely scratches an itch no other game does. 

First of all, it is the first game I've played that features both realistic graphics and a good system for irregular buildings. At least the villagers' homes and the farm fields and roads you are allowed to shape them by yourself by setting out the four corners of the plot. Because the fences and borders align to roads and other buildings, this is the best game I've played in terms of giving you medieval villages that actually look fairly lifelike instead of some square grid suburb where the houses happen to have thatched roofs. The music is highly fitting and it definitely adds a new level of realism that you actually see the villagers using oxen to drag logs and carry planks over their shoulders when building something, and resources often have to be worked in several steps. (E.g most games would go grain -> bread in a single step, Manor Lords goes grain -> flour -> bread, and to make shoes it goes hides -> leather -> shoes, and so on). 

The game is still noticeably in early access, but is being actively worked on. It is always a difficult balancing act for devs to choose between launching new features to show what they have in store for players in the future, and fixing bugs and smoothing out existing systems. The game has been mostly solo developed by a guy named Greg for many years, but is getting more and more help to see this through from his publisher Hooded Horse, which has seen many of my favorite games through to the finishing line. The scope of the devs ambitions is huge though, and he may well have to scale them back in the future. 

It feels unfair to criticize a game in EA, but it does have some quirks you should be aware of. It is NOT an action-packed game focused around military conquest. It is more of a satisfying kind of organic development over time where you meet the needs of the village as it grows. As is, you only get a handful of development points to unlock new technologies, and each village has it's own technology tree with no shared knowledge between them. This is partially by design, as the goal is to have several cooperating villages in your barony rather than one totally self-sufficient megacity, and the resources on the map will totally change your strategy. However, it feels pretty silly that your tame sheep don't breed at all unless you unlock that technology (I am fairly certain the sheep know how to do that without having it explained to them), but the sheep aren't that expensive to buy so unlocking that technology would be a huge waste. I guess I'm stuck buying new asexual sheep when I need to expand the flock? 

My main contention so far is the trade system, but I expect it will be fixed. Trade prices are static and heavily slanted to your disadvantage. The export prices of pretty much everything is very low, and if you lack some crucial resource the import price is truly punishing and most of your total wealth will be spent importing that thing. Whereas in a real economy (both historic and current) it would be possible to earn money by importing a raw material and refining it into something more valuable, as Manor Lords currently works, this is impossible as even the most valuable exports sell for 6-12 gold while even the cheapest raw materials cost 10-12, e.g importing raw iron ore and exporting finished swords would land you at a considerable loss. Pros: The base gameplay is super fun and addictive for a competitive game. The best and honestly the only other good thing about this game is the community. It's full of dedicated and cool people (despite some occasional drama) and honestly it had great potential... Keyword "had".
Cons: This game is practically dead. The devs have abandoned all sort of support on it. Not even a single person is working on it. If you disconnect for a second your single player game locks up an exits to main menu.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1739673350}, {"review_text": "I loved this game. I really did. It was great to play the first few months. 

That being said...

I have noticed recently a lot of the player base have been dropping off daily like flies. The game was just released in September for purchase. And by February it was already basically given up on. The game has completely plummeted and ran its course. The developers have pretty much given up on the game. They have completely removed all daily and weekly challenges from the game. Earlier this year, they dumped the entire content they had in mind for future seasonal events and season passes into the in-game item shop. Not only that but they did away with the season passes turning it into one big permanent pass, which has no real rewards past reaching level 300. Unless you want to count the gold currency which is obtained from each 1+ level gain. The thing is, I've reached level 300 and also purchased every item available for purchase via the shop. So I'm really not sure what the purpose of gaining any form of currency in game would be when its basically useless to me and many other players. 

Don't get me wrong... 

The game can be really fun to play. If you can get past the 30 minute (or longer) queue you may get stuck with. That also depends on what role you wish to fulfill. In my case, it was often "beater", which seemed to have the longest queue times. While you can play with NPCs its still not quite the same. Of course you can change the level ranging from casual (easiest difficulty level) to championship (hardest difficulty level). Championship still doesn't compare to some of the competitive player base out there for the game. While championship may help you prepare for those kinds of players its still not the same. And it doesn't have the same feeling as if you were playing other real players. There's a few tricks and such you can do that even the NPCs don't do that you wouldn't be prepared to face otherwise.

I feel that if the developers are going to basically toss aside this game that so many players once loved they should at least make it available for offline play. I don't see a point in forcing online play and checking people's internet connections when it takes as long  to queue up as it does. I myself have already uninstalled the game and have no real reason to continue playing it. But for those who still play and asking for offline play I feel that it needs to be considered to make things right for the people who still play and love this game.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1746942139}, {"review_text": "TL;DR: Online multiplayer is painfully sweaty, playing the bots in career mode is quite delightful

I wish there was a "I recommend this with a huge grain of salt" option

Mechanics wise, I think this game is a lot of fun. There is a learning curve on every role that I think is fun, reminds me kind of of Rocket League in some ways (I have about 1400+ hours in rocket league).

This game was not marketed like, at all. So because of that, there is a rather small player base, the bulk of which have been playing the crap out of it and are hyper competitive. Playing online is infuriating and makes me not want to play. 

BUT the career mode is nice because I can just play the game at whatever difficulty I want and not worry about some unemployed sweat lord twitch streamer thrashing my sh*t. If you want fun, just don't play online. It's truly and utterly horrible. 

I normally hate playing bots, but the highest difficulty bots are actually quite difficult and make for a nice challenge if you want one! It even resulted in my friend yelling at me mid match out of frustration! 10/10

The cosmetics are cute and fun, and no microtransactions!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1737766084}, {"review_text": "This game really makes you FEEL like Harry Potters broom.

My wife’s boyfriend says that as soon as he hears the word “Quidditch”, he thinks about me and my other grown ass friends who play in parks pretending we are on brooms flying around.

It’s like Blitzball from FFX with online.

It's the Rocket League of the Wizarding world!

This game is similar to Star Wars Squadrons in the way that it’s a really good game for what it is, but gets next to no content because it's not a cash grab for investors.

This is the Harry Potter game of my dreams

I think Quidditch Champions has an amazing foundation and the structure is just made to be built up overtime. The game is actually pretty deep and has a high skill ceiling in pvp. People always complain about something they can't do better. This game is amazing and in my opinion I don't care that it wasn't a part of Hogwarts Legacy for the simple fact that Quidditch has always been its own game.

I can confidently say it is one of my favorite games to play. The fast-paced action, strategic gameplay, and the thrill of competing in the wizarding world’s most iconic sport make it a truly unique experience. The rule changes were all about game balance and the rules work well for what the game is. The controls for the flying take getting used to. You feel like a toddler learning to walk at first. But after about 10 games you'll have the hang of it. Then it's a blast to be doing drifts and dodging bludgeons. Yet, it saddens me to see that the game isn’t doing as popular as I’d like. 

The problem I think it’s a very niche type of game, it’s a sports game and specifically a sports game for people that both like these games and are part of the Harry Potter/Quidditch fan base, which just makes it less marketable than a game like FIFA. It's definitely a good game though if you like quidditch and sports games. The gameplay can go deeper than what it seems but it takes practice and can be pretty difficult. It’s a lot more fun than I expected it to be, though they had to change some of the rules to turn it into an actual playable game. It has all of the usual quidditch roles, like seeker, beater, chaser, and keeper, and each is quite unique compared to the others.

I understand the upset fans who wanted it to be a 1:1 interpretation of the lore accurate Quidditch but I see why they made the changes. Having 2 beaters would almost always result in 1 person camping whoever has the quaffle and the other camping the keeper or seeker. There is even an actual Quidditch league (Quadball), in real life, with the exact same rules as in Quidditch Champions. That's where Quidditch Champions got the rules and such. Truth is Quidditch's actual rules are silly and would not work in a real sport. It's fine when it's fiction and it all just works because the plot says so. But it doesn't work when it's a multiplayer game that depends on people actually wanting to play in the various roles. It can basically be summed up in J.K. Rowling being good at creating a world people love, but not being great at game design. 

Like I said, the game can be challenging at first and has an easy to learn, hard to master learning curve. In my case at first the game was kicking my butt, it took some getting used to before I finally got the hang of it. Now I'm crushing it. You just have to persevere and the game becomes quite addictive. I only wish it was a little more impressive graphically, but everything else is fantastic. Some games the beaters are so good and the seekers are bumping each other so much that there's only enough time for one snitch. As the seeker you can only catch the snitch if you're ahead of the other seeker, even if the other seeker has 100% snitch meter, so playing through an actual neck and neck race with the seekers bumping each other for a chance to win the game just feels incredibly authentic to quidditch and it's incredible what they were able to accomplish.

Overall I love this game. The AI is challenging on full difficulty without being unbeatable which is fun. Online is fun. I think the game is great, and I can’t understand everyone hating on it. I feel like anyone who is hating on it has some very small minute reason or is stuck in the past with the old quidditch games which quite honestly were trash in comparison. I’ve played prisoner of azkaban, goblet of fire, and quidditch world cup. I still think this quidditch is better than all of them. It’s not perfect  or without faults, but I would take this quidditch over any other. Overall, the game is exactly what I wanted a qudditch game to be. And at the end of the day it has what I miss most about video games. It's just plain fun. Like Blitzball in FFX fun. I could and have played for hours. Give it a chance. 

And for the rest of you muggles… you can keep your damn Rocket League!

[{"review_text": "I struggle, again and again, with The Outer Worlds 2. 

It's a game I dearly want to like, even love, and there are aspects of it I find worthy of praise. Momentary glimpses of good writing in twists and barbs that aren't immediately blunted by being overwrought. It is absolutely better than the first Outer Worlds, and yet, in the question of whether it's worth your time and dollar, I again find myself giving a rather pointed no.

The modern Obsidian is too obsessed with being funny. It's been felt in nearly all their games of recent years; sometimes it hits, but most of the time, it absolutely doesn't. The original Fallout games absolutely had black humor, as did New Vegas, but these were lightening touches on decidedly macabre worlds; the purpose of humor was to prevent you from taking everything so seriously *all* the time, not to rob the setting of gravitas, or its characters of the compliment of sentience. In The Outer Worlds 2, just like its predecessor, the only description I can muster for the setting and most of its cast is 'ridiculous.' There is no logical belief I can conjure for how these organizations work in the short term, let alone the long term.

It is popular, now more than ever, to critique capitalism and fascism, but Outer Worlds 2 welds its writing so deeply into satire that little point can be made aside from the obvious. Capitalists are obsessed with advancement. Fascists are deaf to logic and reason that goes against the state. Why? How do these systems interact? What appeal do they have that draws people in? What about them gives rise to conviction that they're the right way to live life?

People might think it strange that I'm beggaring sociopolitical discourse from a video game, but Obsidian has done it before, and better than pretty much anyone else, in New Vegas. People have argued for years about the pros and cons for each major faction in that game, because the setting grounds and establishes each overarching belief as reasonable. The Outer Worlds 2 would turn 99% of Caesar's Legion hostile, and make the NCR completely, irrationally irreverent to its citizenry, while Mr. House rambles in scientific sermons in a tower that's painted like the Sistine Chapel. 

Aside from the writing, the world wandering falls eerily, confusingly flat for me. Once more an aspect that was done so much better in New Vegas; there was next to nothing I stumbled on in my time with this game, I just wandered between block to block on the map. Enemies don't wander or interact with each other. They are preset in scripted encounters that only serve to make the world feel more artificial. This was the same design direction that guided Avowed, and it's one of the pieces that I feel most severely harms the moment to moment experience.

It's not my belief that The Outer Worlds 2 is awful, but in many of the things I want from a RPG, it comes out to below average. There are parts of roleplaying, and a fun enough shooting sandbox, but without writing that grips me, it all feels meaningless. I would rather go play a better RPG, or a more dedicated shooter. Not everyone will feel this way, and I respect that, but with the resources Obsidian has, it's a wonder to me that they've left all their ambition behind in the comfort of producing consistent mediocre content. It feels completely alien to the studio I once cherished, and it is with this release that I must at last acknowledge that the change seems irreversible. Worse, in my mind, they seem convinced that this direction is for the better.

The RPG mechanics are miles better than TOW1, and honestly even FNV.

You actually have to choose specializations in your skills. You CANNOT be a jack of all trades, and you cannot max every skill so that you pass every skillcheck, especially late game skillchecks which require really high points in specific skills

THAT BEING SAID, there are also traits (and even flaws and backgrounds) which come up in speech often. So even if you can't pass a skillcheck, sometimes you can just use your lucky trait, or dumb/sickly flaw, or your background as an ex convict or professor or whatever to pass those checks instead. 

So yeah. Hot take but it's better than FNV in this area.

----------------

I like space. I like sci-fi. I like space sci-fi. If you don't like these things.. well why are you even considering this game lol.

I liked the charm of TOW1 but it felt like the areas were way too small, uninteresting, or just otherwise streamlined. This game is a complete upgrade on all of those aspects.

- in-game lore texts are bad, most of them read like ChatGPT generated filler texts with no relevant information or interesting story telling, just bland (e.g. no comparison to texts on vault terminals you may remember from Fallout 3/4)
- most dialogue is of the category "long and rambunctious sentences with little real value to your current mission", you could go with skipping all dialogue and just read up the journal, much less hassle
- character progression in TOW1 was limited and simple, but in TOW2 it's even more simplified and runs out of steam quickly, e.g. playing a gunslinger there are not even enough good gun perks to pick up to level 30 - just lazy design
- loot progression does not exists, not even near the simple tier 1 to tier 3 system that was in TOW1 - as I said I used a pistol at start then switched over to the unique sniper rifle like 1/3 in the story. - companions are mostly bland and one-dimensional, Marisol was somewhat better written and a little more deep, but if you expect anything near Mass Effect 1/2 companions you wont find it here, I'm afraid (a 2007 game with waaaaaay smaller dev team, mind you) but much much better writers it seems

- step to close to a gas cloud and die

So I did not and do not care a single bit about Obsidian's pedigree in relation to that series. I did, however, complete the first Outer Worlds (w/ all DLC) and the base game for Avowed. So I can speak to what the dev is currently putting out, and how this second Outer Worlds game compares to the first.

We good? Good. Onto the spoiler free, useful stuff!

[h2] -- The Good -- [/h2]
I just finished my play through. I did what side-quests I came across, and didn't go out of my way to 100% the game. If you played the first game, you know that Outer Worlds (OW) has a very particular sense of humor. It's still here, but it has been refined in a way I found more enjoyable. The setting, atmosphere, and story paint a much more consistent picture of Arcadia, and the well-written NPC dialogue doesn't have to be as wacky and quirky to paint the picture instead. Note the use of the word "as". It is still very humorous, but it flows a lot better than in the first game. 

The writing: On the whole is extremely good. And I was worried it wouldn't be, going into it. Lots of different options for dialogue, and the choices felt meaningful. I maxed out the speech skill, so I got to enjoy all of the ways to verbally tie people in knots. And the choices tangled together in strange, fun ways that I couldn't have anticipated. The world felt very reactive to me. And unlike recent games I have played, I am actually wanting to play this game again in a few months or a year. I want to go a different build, and will probably go for an anti-corporate run!

Combat: Fighting is very fun, flowing well and punishing me for not adapting to the situations more often than not! I jumped between a couple of different load outs in the first half of the game, and enjoyed all of them. Running and gunning with light weapons felt incredible. Pulling out a hard hitting machine gun made me feel like a slow moving terminator. And the triple barrel shot gun makes you feel like a god early on. All in all, amazingly fun and I was always wanting to get into the next fight.

Performance: I had to upgrade my rig recently (thanks Microsoft, have a middle finger salute), so I am running an extremely high end, all AMD set-up. Besides a few very minor graphics bugs, such as grass floating off of the ground in a single, small area, I encountered basically no bugs. NPC path finding bugged once, but reloading a save from 30 seconds earlier fixed it. 

[h2]-- The Mid -- [/h2]
Factions: They matter, but also don't. Certain narrative paths will be opened or closed based on how much you are helping or murdering a given group. It's really not hard to get them to like you, though. It didn't really bother me, but I was also trying to go for a "friendship and flowers" first run. It mattered for maybe four main story beat, and never again.

Companions: I actually quite enjoyed all of the human companions. The robot one is blander, but that felt right. All of their stories were intriguing, and I was surprised that several of them were companions! I did grow to care about each of them differently, and wanted to try and get the best out come for all of them. They were reactive, had funny additions to situations, and I loaded a save more than once to make sure a specific one was present for an event that felt important to them. However, something was missing. Maybe it was how their stories were spread out to favor the back half of the game? But regardless, each companion's arc felt like it ended with a wet blanket of "I think I have resolved my issues and have changed. Thank you, player! You made all the difference!." It didn't ruin the experience, but I feel like the writers were so close and just dropped it at the end.

Flaws / Perks: Putting these together, because I was thoroughly whelmed by them in the first game. Flaws actually are worth considering in OW2. A boon for a bane. I think it takes a dozen hours of playing before you'll understand if a flaw is fun for your build, or ruinous to it. Great for extra play-throughs! The perks are a lot more fun, but also weirdly vague as to how they might work in the world. And there are no re-specs! The perks feel like a guide to potential builds, and they are quite versatile in what they cover.

[h2]-- The Poor -- [/h2]
Environments: On the whole, they are functionally fine and pretty to look at. Even gorgeous at times! The art style does feel very Avowed. Fantastical and very colorful, especially with compared to the human-made parts. It's a style, I feel neutral about that. The map DESIGN, however feels off. Maybe it's how all of the points of interest are spaced out, maybe its how I felt a compulsion to open the map every few minutes to make sure I was filling it in? [{"review_text": "As a long-time Sims player, I was always optimistic about InZoi after seeing it's initial reveal trailer, and I have to say it has really impressed me. If you love the life simulation genre but have felt frustrated with The Sims 4’s endless DLC model and limitations, InZoi is absolutely worth checking out.

Right off the bat, the level of customization is fantastic. The character creator is incredibly detailed, allowing for more realistic and unique Zois right from the start. The graphics are also a huge step up from The Sims 4, with smoother animations and a more natural look.

One of the biggest wins for InZoi is its open-ended gameplay. Instead of being locked into rigid, pre-designed interactions, it feels like you have more organic ways to develop relationships, careers, and daily life. The open world is also a huge improvement over The Sims' instanced neighborhoods. You are free to explore seamlessly without loading screens breaking immersion, making the world feel more alive and connected. You are also in direct control of your Zoi, able to walk and run using traditional controls, rather than being locked to the "click here to move" system, which is still present for those who want it.

On top of that, the developer actually listens to the community. After backlash about Denuvo being in the game, it was removed before launch, showing a real pro-gamer mindset. The dev has also stated that he wants InZoi to be highly moddable, which is a huge plus for anyone who loves community-driven content. Unlike EA’s approach of locking features behind expensive DLC, the creator seems focused on giving players real freedom and customization options.

It is still early and there is room to grow, but the foundation here is solid. If you have been craving a life sim that moves the genre forward and actually respects its players, InZoi is absolutely worth keeping an eye on.

Edit: For some reason people are claiming that I am either a paid reviewer, used ChatGPT to write this, or my account is a "bot". We joked, we hugged, we were engaged within an hour of our first date and then I got a text while I was asleep informing me that she died. 10/10 No Notes.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6157, "timestamp_created": 1743142418}, {"review_text": "I really, really want to like inZOI, but I have very mixed feelings about it…

On the surface, the game looks fantastic - the graphics are great, and the character designer is impressive. I had lots of fun playing with it and creating characters, but the gameplay itself is incredibly bare-bones, even for Early Access. Skills feel totally meaningless, and the world lacks depth. For example, you can just stand in one spot watering the same tomato plant all day to max out gardening. Cooking only lets you prepare a single portion at a time, followed by washing a single plate, which makes everything feel slow and artificial. There’s no real depth or immersion behind these mechanics. Again—I know it’s Early Access, but the systems don’t seem well thought out at all.

Beyond the gameplay, I’m seriously concerned with how the game is being managed. Despite being just launched into Early Access, DLC has already been mentioned multiple times, which is unsettling when the core game itself is still so underdeveloped. There are also predatory tactics in place, like FOMO-driven events and exclusive rewards only for streamers, leaving regular players out. The "Play Together" event is especially bad—it’s essentially a referral campaign where you have to convince others to buy the game just to get a cat costume, and even that doesn’t work properly. Krafton has been slow to acknowledge or fix these issues, frustrating a lot of players.

This kind of approach might be expected in mobile games, but for a single-player PC game in Early Access, it’s just wrong. If you’re on the fence about buying inZOI, I’d recommend waiting to see if it improves and reveals it's identity. Right now, Krafton is not making a great first impression.

Edit after the latest update:

The new patch added a holiday island themed city and some new farm-sim like skills like in theory improved gardening (you can plant in soil and have some farming tools) and mining. Sadly, even with these features, the gameplay is still shallow as hell and I feel like it didn't bring anything to the game at all. Many mobile games are honestly more engaging than this. The cities feel empty and dead. Zois just run around and change outfits with no logic, instead of following a career or doing something interesting. If you go to the market or a restaurant the space looks somewhat busy but no one interacts or sits down to eat.

When you move in a custom family they just seem to stay at home behind locked gates and never leave. Romances are broken. You can marry someone in five minutes, or you get constant refusals and negative outcomes no matter what you do, even when characters seem perfectly compatible. Professional relationships also feel pointless. They exist as a category, but I have not seen any clear gameplay benefit to building them beyond having a label and unlocking some more shallow interactions that just differ in label alone. Players online also seem to say the same thing, that these systems are undercooked and offer no real reason to engage with them.

The new skills look nice at first but they are just as shallow and repetitive as the rest of the systems in game. On top of that the visual quality has gone down. Textures were reduced and now look messy or blurry even on high settings. A lot of players have noticed this and think it is because Krafton is trying to optimise for weaker machines, but it ends up making the game look much worse for high end PCs.

Surveys from players seem to show the same picture. The main problems are a lack of simulation depth and very awkward social interactions. There are also bugs, like remarriage when children are involved causing whole family members to vanish. No surprise then that the player base has dropped by more than 80% since launch.

Krafton says they will release a roadmap and fix things, but at the moment inZOI feels like a beautiful shell with very little inside. For now IMHO 6/10 with a huge emphasis on the future.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 23, "timestamp_created": 1755588102}, {"review_text": "A lot of the positive reviews for this game are based on the POTENTIAL it has. Meaning that little to no people like the game for what it actually is at the moment. So, don't be fooled by the ratings. 

This game has three things going for it. 

1. The character creator. I think a lot of people have a lot of fun and spent a lot of time on this. I did too. 

2. The graphics. The world is quite beautiful to look at

3. The player-made content. There are a lot of nice Zois, clothes, furniture and more made by players. 

The downside is that it has literally nothing else. There's simply nothing to play for. The world is pretty, but there's nothing that urges you to explore. The tiny events that brings your Zoi to different locations are nothing special. You go to places to talk/eat, nothing you can't already do in your own home. 

The daily routine is just wake-up, go to work, eat, maybe wash your hands occasionally since hygiene doesn't really drop much. 

The relationship part is also quite shallow since they progress very quickly. You can get to BFF with most NPC during your first encounter with them. The texts received on the phone are also quite pointless because you don't actually pick from options that might/might not make them feel negatively by accident like you might in a Dating Sim. You just pick the first one everytime. 

One of the more annoying things of the game for me was the chatting. It's the KEY feature of the game at this point, so that's really a turn off. But, for a game that wants you to interact with other NPCs, it makes it really annoying. For starters, when I invite multiple people to hangout, I could never talk to more than one at the same time, making it dumb because when three people sit together, one will always be left out at any given time. Another thing is that the Zois might want to keep moving when the conversation moves from one topic to the other. So, you'll get a scenario where 2 Zois talk on the sofa for 10 secs, get up and talk while standing for 10 secs, then go to the sofa again, then maybe one would be seated and the other would be standing.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 31, "timestamp_created": 1745454014}, {"review_text": "So far it's a great foundation for a true "Sims successor". I won't be going into performance issues and bugs because it just came out of early access so go figure. But there are fundamental features missing from the game which I feel contributes to the game's barebones feeling, specifically the inZOI interactions with one another and everything.

[h2] The Good [/h2]
[b]1)[/b] You're able to walk around the town a la Sims 3. This plus the shoulder view feels really immersive.
[b]2)[/b] AI features which lets you create custom items, ability describe how the inzois should act and even create custom emotes via videos or gifs
[b]3) [/b]  You're finally to actually commit a proper crime like driving a car to run over people. So creating criminal or evil sims isn't just petty theft, burglary or grand theft auto. Hopefully we get to see more crimes we can commit.
[b] 4) [/b]  Characters designs and creation looks gorgeous, it's like having cosmetics mods installed from the get go
[b] 5) [/b]  The Karma system is promising though a bit tedious to use. It allows your zois to affect the town in a dynamic way. 
[b] 6 [/b] The devs actually removed that POS DENUVO from the game after fan feedback. That itself is a huge plus for me to the devs.

[h2] The bad [/h2]

[b] 1) [/b] Character interaction between each others feels disjointed. You can't just ask a sim whether they want to hang out by the couch together, go to a park, or do activities together. It's almost always through menus and not the Zoi actually interacting with each other.
[b] 2) [/b] Speaking 'synthetic' Zoi interactions, dates feels overall pointless since there's not interaction features that let's you do thing together. 
[b] 3) [/b] Characters boost their relationships extremely fast, like faster than the Sims which makes the progression and challenge of socialising feel unfulfilling
[b] 4) [/b] Zois age way too fast, I'm only 3 weeks in and my Zois dad who started of as an Adult died within 3 weeks. Old man didn't even live to see winter.
[b] 5) [/b] Not a lot of activities to do in town. Even the hotspots shown on map lack much activities to do there. Your choices are either buy food from kiosk or street food, buy lottery, browse the shelves for merch, go surfing alone, go rollercoasters alone
[b] 6) [/b] Woohoo animation feels like a placeholder. Your zois lie down in their bed wearing their everydays, a giant ass bright red heart pops up and you can clearly see your zois lying straight on their backs staring at the ceiling.
[b] 7) [/b] Zois will always try to pick a fight with their family/housemates even if they have good relationships and good karma. So a good natured zoi can out of nowhere destroy his/her relationships within the span of a half a day because of the relationship change speed.

Overall while the game got great potential but I cannot recommend it in this current early state, there's many basic features which I feel should have been polished before entering early access. Because right now Zoi interactions doesn't feel organic and there's little activity to be done aside from just going to work or running people over with your cars. So if the devs are reading this:

[b] 1) [/b] Give more options for the players to use the Zois to do things with other Zoi using dialogue. Having to call over  other Zois using the menu doesn't feel immersive
[b] 2) [/b] Have more fun activities that gives fun rewards for playing them
[b] 3) [/b] Give us the option to manipulate a ZOI's lifespan, they die too fast
[b] 4) [/b] Reduce the speed of ZOIs gaining relationships, maybe give dates or hangouts a bigger boost to relationship instead of just talking. Also incentivise using group mechanics
[b] 5) [/b] Reduce the tendencies of ZOI actively seeking out to destroy their relationships. 
[b] 6) [/b] A better woohoo animation would be great, right now it looks cheap.
[b] 7) [/b] Being able to try for a baby outside of marriage would also be great to have
[b] 8) [/b] Give us more criminal activities for evil ZOI playthroughs like mugging, kidnapping or even murder. It would go so well with the city's karma system.

I hope inZOI work on making zoi to zoi interactions more organic and believable instead of relying of menus to call over only for zoi to just stand there and do nothing. But seeing as how inZOI devs listened to the fanbase and removed DENUVO, I've no doubt that they're willing to listen to their players and add more features that brings ZOIs to life.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 19, "timestamp_created": 1743317901}, {"review_text": "Buy two copies of Schedule 1, if you want to have a good time.

If inZOI pulls off being successful then there's literally no reason for another Sims.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 589, "timestamp_created": 1743120411}, {"review_text": "Yes, the game is still an early access, but as things stands now, I really recommend you wait for the final product before you purchase it. As a +20 years The Sims player, I don't want to compare this game to The Sims because it is clear that they are two different games, and I hope it stays that way. But as they both fall in the life simulator category, I will use The Sims as an example for some features.  I will now share with you the pro and cons I have experienced in the game:

Pros:

Stunning graphics - the graphics is far beyond any life simulator I have seen. Details such as cities, environment, buildings, are super good

Super detailed characters - The Inzoi's are highly customizable, and they are super realistic. You can customize things such as legs and arms hair, and differently from The Sims, they don't have that idiotic smile (or they don't randomly smile every two step they make, which I adored in this game. The inzoi look different from one to the other, unlike The Sims (still they all look like photomodels, which can be solved in the future maybe?). Also hands and especially feet are highly detailed. In the Sims I had to install mods to get detailed feet, as they looked horrendous and unrealistic.

WASD control - This is one of the main features that I love about this game. You can directly control your character, as it makes it more immersive

Ability to take control of any other Izoi's - You can take control of any Inzoi you see

Realisticism - Inzoi's remove their shoes when they get inside (if the option is enabled), they go to their wardrobe and change in their pajama's before they get to bed. Kids wear their school bags when going to school

Almost no loadings - The city is completely open world, without any loading breaks. Your Inzoi will either use a car, a subway, or a bus to travel long distances, with absolutely no loading screen (and if there's any at all, it only lasts a few seconds)

- Use of AI to customize poses and clothes


Now it is time to list the cons

- Many actions don't last long enough, such as watching TV, sitting on the sofa, playing with the ball etc. and its really frustrating, as I have to repeat the action many times over. No matter what, the Inzois get bored super quickly and interrupt any action they are currently doing after just a few seconds. Also they don't sleep a full night, once the energy bar is full, they will randomly wake in the middle of the night.

- They are completely still while sleeping, like statues. They never change position, even in a whole 12 hours sleep session, the just lie on their back, wich I find extremely unrealistics.

- Kids while in bed, have half their face covered. As cute it may seem, I find it a bit unrealistic as they could just position themeselves a bit higher on the pillow without the needing of suffocating themselves with the blankets

- There is LITERALLY NOTHING for children to do. You can play with a swing or with a few park toys, but besides that and a few toys that your Inzoi will only use for five seconds, there's nothing that children can do. I tried to take mine to the beach and play with the sand, but there's no option for that. You can't dig a hole, you cand build a sand castle, nothing. The same applies with water, you cannot dive underwater, you cannot splash it to other Inzois, you can only swim as a way to move back to the shore. 

- There are only a few mother/father son/daughter interractions. You can't cuddle your children while on the sofa, can't hug them, can't cheek kiss them, can't help with homework, basically parents can only speak to them, making it so cold and empty. Add more interactions, even physical, between parents and their children.

-The game is blank in general, and I don't understand how some people can spend hundreds of hours on it when this game at its current state feels empty in every possible way. You go out in the streets and then what? NPC's are braindead, there are almost no ambience sounds (such as traffic, or general city sounds), actions are super limited

And to end this review, I will report some bugs I've encountered

- When children ask for food, the adult Inzoi will sometimes place the food on top of the wardrobe, making it inaccessible for them (if you click on eat, nothing happens and you have to enter build mode and trash it)

- Other Inzois in the street have delayed spawn and will randomply spawn from a few meters in front of you breaking realism

- General animation bugs such as Inzois eating with nothing in their hands while the food is on the table or anywhere else

I will also leave some suggestions if the developers will ever read this:

Make it so that children and even adults can play with sand when at the beach, make it like something that you can interact with instead of just a different texture with different sounds.

- As stated above, make it so interactions between parents and their children are less cold and more realistic, such as hugging or cuddling, or even watching movies togheter

- Make it so that when a child leaves the house, it is accompanied by an adult that follows him (father, mother, older brother). It is not very realistic to see a child Inzoi wander around the city, take the subway, and just go to places like he is an adult

-Make other things customizable, such as lenght of the Inzois neck, types of hands, types of feet, both hands nail shape, and toe nail shape, ears shape, and make the mouths more customizable. Also I hope you will add the option to adjust height. 

This is all for now. I will come back to this game in a year and check how it evolved. This game hes the high potential to be the best life simulator ever made, but it all depends to the developers, and what they decide to do with it.

After all this, I want to leave a thump up because I believe in the project, and because I don't want to put it in the trash bin being an early access game. But only buy it if you are willing to accept all those things, otherwise wait one or two years and see how things evolved and then make your decision.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1760720088}, {"review_text": "I used to love The Sims, no doubt,

So far, I do not recommend this game and for several reasons:

[h2]#1 NOTHING TO DO[/h2]

I fully realize that some stickler is going to drive-by this review and either laugh because of this or leave a nasty comment, but it IS the truth.  Besides going to work, cleaning your house, and interacting with other sims in pointless socials, there is nothing else to do in the game - literally.

You can go to the beach and socialize.  You can go to a volleyball court and socialize.  You can socialize, but there is nothing else to do. 

Can you swim or tan at the beach?  No.
Can you play a game of volleyball?  No.

[h2]#2 YOU'LL CLEAN MORE THAN ANYTHING ELSE[/h2]

It's seriously broken.  After a few in-game days, everything gets dirty within an in-game hour after you clean it:  Your clothes, your house, etc.  If you make the mistake of saving a clothing loadout while one of the loadouts are dirty, all of your clothes will be dirty, FOREVER until you completely delete every loadout and re-dress them.

[h2]#3 THEY SAID THERE WOULD BE NO RABBIT HOLES[/h2]

Yet, everything is a rabbit hole.  This game was specifically hyped at being a sim that you could go explore and see your characters working.  That was not true.  There is no more than 1 usable/editable building/lot per "region".  Everything else is a rabbit hole or entirely decorative.   Many of the houses and buildings you will find will be impossible to build or even interact with because they're simply not really there.

[h2]#4 THEY SAID I COULD WALK TO WORK[/h2]

Notice how I said "regions" above?  No matter what it is you do, it will happen outside of your home's region which means you get a load screen whether you walk, drive, etc.  You cannot simply joy-ride around town.  And when you go to work?  You simply walk outside your house, and disappear in front of a taxi. I personally think yes, because the creative systems are really very good, and you can have a lot of fun with them. Overall though I am disappointed in the where the game is now (vs where I hoped it would be), this current version actually seems to have less features than previous builds, which also creates more questions than answers.

It's a tough call, because it does have so much potential, but that's the thing about potential... you don't actually know how well its going to work out. It's an investment, a hope, a gamble.

I would tread very carefully about purchasing inZOI and I recommend if you do to really try to get into the game ASAP (don't spend two hours in the character creator) and see what you think of the game play before you are unable to make a return.

This could someday be the real Sims killer, but it has got a long, long, long way to go first.

You fired up Steam, saw the words “grand strategy,” and thought you were about to play a nice little game of Risk with knights and castles. No. You’re not ready. Nothing can prepare you for the generational hellscape of betrayal, incest, witchcraft, and passive-aggressive Pope drama you’re about to unleash.

This isn't a strategy game. This is a medieval chaos simulator, duct-taped to a family tree that looks like it was drawn by a spider on meth. You don’t play a character—you play their entire bloodline, across centuries of bad decisions, aggressive inbreeding, and mysterious “hunting accidents.”

You start off with a decent ruler. Charismatic. Just. Beloved by their vassals. Naturally, they die choking on a chicken leg during a feast. You’re now playing as their 6-year-old heir who’s terrified of birds, has a lisp, and is somehow already an alcoholic.

From here, it’s a slow-motion dynastic car crash. Your vassals hate you. Your siblings are plotting against you. Your aunt is trying to seduce your husband. Your court physician keeps suggesting “leech therapy” for everything, including syphilis, cancer, and a stubbed toe.

And yet... you love it.

The actual gameplay? It’s a paradox of emotions. One moment you're reforming the kingdom’s laws, carefully arranging alliances through strategic marriages. The next, your rival queen has called you a “naked coward” during a feast, and you're now plotting her murder with your court jester and a bag of bees.

Stress mechanics? Amazing. Every time you go against your character’s nature—say, executing a heretic when you’re compassionate—you gain stress. Enough stress, and you start snapping like a medieval rubber band. This means your noble ruler could spiral into full-blown depression because someone insulted their embroidery skills.

You’ll spend hours trying to create a pure bloodline of genius warrior-poets, only to realize your heir is an obese lunatic who believes he's literally descended from a bear. Oh, and he's married his first cousin. Twice.

Wars? You can fight them. But why do that when you can simply marry someone with a claim to the kingdom, murder half their family, and “inherit” it in what historians will politely call “a series of unfortunate events”?

Also, let’s talk about religion. You can literally invent your own. You can create a faith that encourages cannibalism, nudity, and human sacrifice, and then demand everyone take it seriously. The Pope hates you. You love it. You are the Pope now.

Multiplayer? Oh yes. Want to play with friends? Prepare to witness the absolute worst sides of humanity. One friend will seduce your spouse, another will excommunicate you, and a third will “accidentally” press a claim on your kingdom and burn your capital down. The good news? You can stab all of them. It’s the CK3 way.

Final Verdict:
Crusader Kings III is not a game. It’s a medieval family drama written by a drunk raccoon with a PhD in backstabbing and no understanding of genetics. It’s confusing, ridiculous, and often downright cursed—but once you start, you can’t stop. It’s digital crack for history nerds with god complexes.

10/10. Would marry my sister to a lunatic duke, steal his title, imprison her for “treason,” and then die of stress while possessed by demons again.

[b]Honestly, this is one of the best games I’ve ever played.[/b] The blend of strategy and RPG elements keeps me coming back. Achievements require real thought—despite occasional RNG. The game is frequently updated, and the recent addition of automated armies is a huge quality-of-life improvement.

That said, [b]there are a few flaws I hope the developers address:[/b]

[b]DLC Overload:[/b] Updates often coincide with expensive DLC releases. While I don’t mind paying for gameplay content (far better than gacha mechanics, in my opinion), many DLCs include modifiers that make the game too easy, letting you steamroll opponents and lose the challenge.

[b]Lack of Late-Game Challenge:[/b] Early and mid-game are exciting, especially when you’re strategizing to defeat larger neighbors. But once your empire snowballs, the game becomes too easy. Rebel factions are the only real threats, and they’re easily managed with mechanics like feasts and funerals. Late-game domination often devolves into a repetitive loop of declaring war, sieging, and enforcing demands.

[b]Late-Game Lag and Population Bloat:[/b] The late game isn’t just repetitive—it’s also plagued by performance issues. Exponential character population growth causes severe lag, especially on high speeds. Developers seem reluctant to implement population control after backlash to mechanics like plagues, which could thin out characters. As a result, to contract the bubonic plague required actively exposing my character, hurting immersion. Or the dev can fix it with a better solution: optimizing the game. Reaching the 1453 end date becomes a test of patience due to lag.

[b]Future Performance Concerns:[/b] With the addition of Asia—a historically populous region—these performance issues may worsen. I’d recommend caution before investing in this expansion.

[b]Annoying Pop-Ups:[/b] While the game’s pop-ups tell great stories, they become tedious in late-game empires. Constant prompts to name dynasty members, handle common events (e.g., dealing with plagues), or address minor court scandals disrupt the flow. Automating repetitive decisions would be a welcome improvement.

[u][b]TL;DR - My 100% Subjective Review:[/b][/u] An amazing blend of grand strategy and RPG elements with frequent updates. An excellent game that plays different every time I start a new game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1756120843}, {"review_text": "I honestly have mixed feelings about CK3. I'd give it a recommendation of "maybe" if that was an option.

 PROS:

If you're new to Paradox grand strategy games and looking for a game to test the waters with, then this is a great start. The game works well out of the box without any of the DLC's, unlike say, EU4. It's built on a 64-bit engine, So it runs fairly well on modern systems and has a greater headroom to work with. Unlike some of the older 32-bit titles from Paradox which are, or already have, reached their limits in what can be achieved with the engine. The graphics have gotten a nice up lift from CK2 with the introduction of 3D character models. The world map is pleasant to look at and is provides information in an easy to read format.

 The UI is significantly more approachable to newcomers and flows generally well. Embedding pop out tool tips as part of the UI design was brilliant and makes the on boarding process for new players significantly better (Less tabbing out to look at a Wiki or having to watch a 2 hour Youtube video, shout out to Quill18!) as there is a tool tip for practically every major and minor gameplay mechanic and concept. The base game mechanics are fairly simple and presented in a way that makes it easy to wrap your head around them, in part due to the aforementioned plentiful tool-tips. Your greatest difficulty and source of frustration as a new player starting out will be dealing with succession. Otherwise the rest of the mechanics are rarely punishing if you make a mistake. Which makes finding yourself in a run ending scenario rare. While the starting dates are historical and have historical figures, the game does not rely on railroading the player (In comparison to HOI4 and to a lesser extent EU4) and plays more like a sandbox and facilitates free form play. There are some historical events which are tied to a start date, but otherwise you are free to set your own goals and achieve them at your own pace, no matter how silly or absurd they are.

 The game has Steam Workshop support built in, which makes browsing, installing, and playing mods a breeze. The mod scene is lively and has some of the best total conversion mods you'll find in any Paradox title. For example you have, A Game of Thrones, Princes of Darkness, Elder Kings 2, After The End, Realms in Exile, The Fallen Eagle, Shogunate, Godherja the Dying World, and many more. Seriously go check them out, extremely impressive work from the community! You could spend all your playtime on total conversion mods and never touch the base game. 

CONS:

 However, if you are a veteran of Paradox titles, have experience with other strategy games, and have a functional prefrontal cortex then you might want to skip this one since it will leave you bored to tears and unsatisfied with how little tension and complete lack of push back on the player the game offers. The mechanics, while easy to get an initial grasp of, are extremely surface level and offer very little in the way of actual depth and have not evolved since the launch of the game back in 2020. After a few runs you'll be able to consistently get most random nobody counts up to the title of emperor in one life time. And now with the DLC, you can do it even easier and quicker with random lowborn nobody wanderers! The AI is laughable stupid, passive, and an easy push over once you start snow balling in the slightest. You will quickly surpass the AI, even on the new poorly implemented hard modes.

 You'll quickly learn that the man-at-arms and knight system is horrendously broken in combination with the overwhelming amount of positive modifiers the game likes to dish out like candy and how easy it is to modifier stack WITHOUT MIN-MAXING. Warfare is a mindless point and click adventure of stack wiping the AI repeatedly and waiting for sieges to tick over (PARADOX WHY IS WAR SCORE FROM BATTLES STILL CAPPED AT 50%??????). Your options for peace deals are STILL LIMITED TO "Surrender, White Peace, Enforce Demands" peace deals have not been expanded on since release (You still need 100% War Score to Enforce Demands lol). Realm politics and vassal management feel completely binary, as vassals will either be in complete open revolt, or they are complacent and passive, with no in between the two states. Diplomacy is on the level of, actually no, it's worse than the diplomacy systems you'd find on offer in a Civilization game. Most characters lack agency, members of your court and family will either be sitting around doing nothing and waiting to die of old age, committing adultery, or trying to murder random nobodies, and that's about it. The game STILL lacks variety in events. You will quickly see them repeat and won't even bother to read them. You'll even see some events repeat multiple times in a single rulers life. Events are all mostly inconsequential, uninteresting, and have an air of "Le Reddit" tone to the writing. The economy, economic buildings, and economic scaling are completely FUBAR.

 The developers "shotgun" approach to DLC will leave you frustrated as random portions of the map get a smattering of random content that varies in quality (Some okay, some bad, some lmao what were they thinking) and is usually poorly integrated with the base game and the other DLC's, which ends up making each DLC feel completely isolated. DLC has also recently been suffering from A LOT of power creep (Looking at you, Khans of the Steppe). It's been 5 years and a majority of the base game mechanics STILL need major expansions or complete reworks.

 CK3 is suffering from an identity crisis. The developers need to finally decide if this is a character driven RPG, Grand Strategy Game, or a FUNCTIONAL mix of both. Because right now the two different systems are at odds and undermine each other. It want's to be a character driven RPG, yet you lack many interesting, memorable, and unique ways to interact with the world and it's people. It's people lack agency and are too static. It lacks drama, stakes, and memorable stories. When is the last time that a character's name stuck with you because you were invested in their life? Their toils? Their ambition? Their betrayal? Their rise and downfall? When is the last time you saw a truly interesting and larger than life character? Why does it feel like the dynamics of family drama are completely absent. The world lacks the flavour and immersion needed to be an interesting and believable medieval setting and it's character system of interactions and personalities is lacking, which all in all creates a boring space to role play in.

 It's systems lack the depth, complexity, and challenge to be an engaging grand strategy title. Your conquest and victories feel hollow as there is no challenge from the AI and there are no difficult systems to master. There are no difficult goals to archive, only tedious ones. There are no catastrophic failures and setbacks, only minor annoyances. There are no wars to be won with a risky gamble. There is no long term planning to sit and think about. There are no political or regional complexities to exploit to undermine your enemies. No complex schemes to put into motion. You will quickly reach a point where each session feels like you are no longer growing and getting better, and that you just turn your brain off to play.

 CK3 in it's current state is frustrating because I believe it has the potential to be greater than the sum of it's parts and be a truly timeless classic in the genre. But right now it feels as if there are two different development teams working on this game who have wildly different philosophies and goals. And rather than work together on a unified vision and create something truly unique they continue to undermine each other and waste the game's potential.

TL;DR
If you're new to Paradox and curious, get the base game on sale. Stronghold crusader: Definitive Edition is a castle-builder/colony sim RTS developed by Firefly Studios in 2002. The game relased another "extreme version in 2008, and later in 20012 firefly released an HD version of both games.

For those new to the stronghold franchise: The main gimmick about this game is that your way towards building most units or getting the most out of your economy is to manage a production chain and managing the town's logistics and your lord's reputation, all while building walls and defending them against waves of enemy units, and building forces of your own to take down your opponents castles.

This version of Stronghold Crusader is built from the ground up with unity engine, it is enhanced with new graphics and with remastered sounds and music. The game combines all elements from its old installments - From the main game's 50 level trail and from Warchest with its extra AI opponents and new 30 level trail which utilises these said opponents, and the optional "Extreme", which adds it's extra game mode that turns the game into a medieval supreme commander (Meaning, you have up to ten thousand units instead of the 1000 max) and having access to power ups. 

Along with all the old features, new gameplay elements are also added to this version, such as a whole new recruitment building with 8 new units themed around the Beduin, larger maps, workshop support and 4 new AI lords: Two Arabic (centered around the new units) and Two European ones. Each of them come with their own flavor, castle layouts, attack patterns and unit groups . Some bugs that plagued the old games have been fixed, while the game introduces new bugs (not unexpected) and has still left some exploits that abuse the AI to great effects.

And also, settlements with Arabic lords now have their own versions of temples instead of having christian churches, which is cool as hell.

New content updates, both free and DLC are promised down the road - economic campaign, new skirmish trails (both co-op and singleplayer), more AI Lords are planned in the near future. 

The networking can be horrible sometimes (EDIT AFTER VERSION 1.05. They have fixed quite a few desynchronization issues, networking has a ways to go, but it is a LOT better now), multiplayer PVP feels unbalanced as there's a large disparity in unit abilities and general usability, the UI feels smaller and as stated before, some old bugs that are reminiscent of the old days can be frustrating or can cheese the game with ease, but overall: The game feels great, looks great and definitely plays great. Unlike some other remasters, this is far from just a cash grab and it feels that firefly has put their love and attention into crafting this beautiful game. With some polish, it might just be my personal 10/10.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1755295561}, {"review_text": "+ look and feel (polished OG stronghold with quality of life features)

Same goes to other things, like Moat diggers randomly stop digging moats near trees or archers keep on shooting in front of a target instead of shooting their target.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 9, "timestamp_created": 1762580508}, {"review_text": "DISAPPOINTING.

The game introduces some QoL improvements, such as auto-trading, units no longer disappearing after getting stuck in the ruined keep monument, some buildings can be constructed even if civilians are in the build area and shields can no longer be used on walls or towers (it was OP). However, it still retains bugs that have existed for over 23 years:

1. Bugs That Still Persist:

1.1) Workers still sometimes get stuck at the bonfire. Peasants can enter buildings from all sides, but if their default and current side of entering gets blocked, they still disappear, respawn and enter the building from another accessible side. Nothing dynamic here.
1.2) The stone depot at the quarry is still placed in inefficient locations due to a lack of space. It should be a rotatable building, with the stone depot shown before construction begins. Additionally, oxen should be able to be assigned to specific stone depots, so they don’t travel long distances to another quarry.
1.3) The reaction time of gates is still poor, requiring constant player intervention. This was fixed many years ago by the unofficial community patch (UCP) in the HD version.
1.4) AI lords still place their quarries inefficiently, particularly with oxen.
1.5) AI lords continue to build farm buildings too close to the player's base, sometimes even behind their castle or scattered across the entire map.
1.6) Ballistas still prefer to attack moving targets instead of siege weapons. Each siege weapon must be targeted individually.
1.7) Ballistas sometimes fail to hit stationary targets, often undershooting.
1.8) The “improved” AI still places attacking armies (especially siege weapons) within range of the player's archers on towers, making attacks even more ridiculous.
1.9) Even the smallest damage from a ram or close-range units can cause drawbridges to be removed.
1.91) Placed moats are still not shown permanently. Good luck digging out a moat while building walls on a larger scale.

2. New Issues:

2.1) [Mostly Fixed] A lot of ghost units remain on the battlefield, including corpses, common units, and even ghost units in a faded state.
2.2) Some of the “improved” AI is worse than it was 23 years ago. AI lords hoard massive amounts of gold (+100,000 gold with about 80 units) without doing anything. Attacks rarely happen. I noticed this primarly in skirmishes. 
2.3) The “improved” AI still doesn't attack strategically with all units at once, instead sending small groups. The points 1.8, 2.2, and 2.3 were handled much better by the UCP.
2.4) Pathfinding remains poor in many situations, especially with closed gates. Assassins’ pathfinding is particularly bad when climbing walls.
2.5) Lancers remain the most useless unit, still not running by default (unlike in the unofficial community patch). Slaves have been nerfed and can no longer run. [Note: slaves can now run—wow.] When clicking on moving horse archers, their running animation stops for a moment, which looks terrible and even nerfs their effectiveness.
2.6) The new art style may be subjective, but many of the new animations are poorly done (especially for new units). The new javelin unit is especially cringe-worthy, and some of the assassins' movement animations are also terrible.
2.7) [Now Fixed] Fire ballistas are now bugged, as they can’t overshoot buildings or walls. The shooting animation plays, but no shot is actually fired. Their death animation is still bugged.
2.8) AI's Mangoles only shoot at buildings or siege weapons anymore. A huge army running up to them? Yep, not shooting those.. 

Other Issues:

The two new Bedouin AI lords are also unappealing, both in terms of dialogue and gameplay. Many older pictures seem to have been upscaled by AI, and the new menu looks like it was ported from a mobile game.




Bigger Update After Playing Most of the New "Sands of Time" Missions:

While the original Stronghold: Definitive Edition from last year failed to capture the true core of the game (castle-building), instead delivering missions focused on reaching flags with limited troops, Crusader: Definitive Edition fails in a similar way, but with a different approach. In the +25 missions I played, I NEVER built a proper castle. The goal in these missions is always to quickly kill the enemy lords, with no real benefit from reaching the highest, if any, rank. I finished every mission with only two types of units: horse archers and assassins. Much wow, such fun.

In most missions, you're so low on economy that you can't even build castles (even if you wanted to), forcing you to cheese the game by placing your stockpile next to quarries, iron, or farmland to drastically improve efficiency. This forces you to rely on a mobile army—horse archers and assassins—for protection.

This is their second Definitive Edition, and both have failed to deliver what players want: building an economy and a castle. A hilarious failure.

AI and Gameplay Issues:

After playing these missions, I want to highlight how bad the AI has become (which is my main dealbreaker with the game). The AI is completely braindead and doesn't react to anything the player does. For experienced StarCraft or Age of Empires players, this game (and even the franchise) must feel like a bad joke.

More in Depth:

AI Build-up: The more starting resources the AI has, the better. They build their castle, recruit units, and once they reach a certain point, they attack the player. Every map, every match, it’s the same static scheme.

If their starting resources are low, you can immediately rush them. Build horse archers and kill off their archers. That's it. Their close-range units will sit in the castle and wait to die to arrows. While doing this, you also erase their economy, and there's nothing the AI can do. You can just finish them off later.

If they do manage to attack, you can still ambush them with archers, and they won’t react. They’ll follow the same waypoints with no disruption (minor stops for archers shooting back happen occasionally). What happens when hills or rocks block their siege weapons' path? They'll shoot at those rocks/hills because the AI is that stupid.

Unit Behavior: In default mode, close-range units just stand there like trees. No reaction to anything. Most AI units are set to this behavior. For example, you can shoot the enemy king with archers and force him out of the keep. Then, you send your close-range units up to the keep for an easy kill. Most of the enemy’s troops won’t leave the keep and will just watch their king die. It’s that stupid.

Conclusion:
Improving unit behavior would be a minor fix. The entire AI system needs a fundamental overhaul to become more dynamic. Unfortunately, this seems too complicated for Firefly. We’re stuck with this trainwreck forever.




Final Thoughts:

In short, there are some bright spots, such as the new units offering a fresh style of play, co-op mode, and the automatic trading feature providing a significant advantage. But these can't distract from the overall flow of the game at this point.

The extreme stupidity of the AI lords, along with the numerous small problems, really spoil the enjoyment of the game. All in all, the HD version with the unofficial community patch remains the better alternative for veterans, as long as the fundamentals do not improve.

After the original (2002), Crusader Extreme (2008), and the HD version (2013), the game is now on its fourth version, yet it still hasn’t managed to solve all its problems. Some issues may hopefully be addressed over time, but the new graphic style—with its strange animations—will remain. Yes, there are some QoL improvements: auto-trading, builders no longer moonwalking to siege weapons, and a few stubborn bugs finally laid to rest. But for every step forward, the game seems to take two awkward steps back usually into a bonfire where a worker is permanently stuck.

The AI, supposedly improved, is often laughably worse. Lords now sit in their shiny new castles hoarding gold like medieval crypto bros, refusing to launch actual attacks. And when they do, their tactics still make you wonder if they’re trying to win... or auditioning for a blooper reel.

Pathfinding? Still tragic. Ballistas? Still drunk. Lancers? Still jogging like they're on a casual Sunday walk (unless you mod them). And the new javelin unit? Well… let's just say it's not winning any popularity contests in the barracks.

Graphically, it’s subjective. Some might like the updated look, but many models feel AI-upscaled and lack the charm of the pixelated grit we grew up with. The new UI gives off mobile game vibes — and not in a good way.

There are some bright spots: the co-op mode is fun, and the few new units and content do add a hint of freshness. But none of it really sticks. It’s like putting a fresh coat of paint on a castle with structural damage looks okay from afar, but step inside and you’ll still fall through the same broken floorboards.

Verdict? At this price, it doesn’t justify the title of “Definitive Edition.” If you’re a veteran, stick with the HD version and the community patch. Unacceptable.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1760182471}, {"review_text": "The actual gameplay, world building, and design are all fantastic. Great metroidvania that doesnt tread much new water, but does the classic things really well. If you liked the first one, or hollow knight, youll enjoy this.

However, the reason I can not give this game a positive review, is due to the DLC existing. Despite not paying for the DLC, the walls blocked off by getting a sword in that DLC are still present in the game. From past experiences in games like this, I would assume I just need some upgrade I havent found yet and continued to look.

I finally caved after 6 hours of looking all around the map for every secret, and looked up the answer. Turns out, the answer is to pay an additional 12 dollars and there is no in game hints that this is blocked by the DLC. This is extremely frustrating as I would prefer the game to have a pop up saying "this is blocked off dont look here" or not existing at all. 

Long story short, if the base game had a map without the DLC present, I would have 0 beef with this game.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1744049625}, {"review_text": "Blasphemous 2 looks absolutely gorgeous. The design for the characters, bosses and NPCs, as well the general horror-religion vibe are incredibly evocative and engaging. The gameplay, however, feels like a considerable downgrade from the original. The abilities feel like they've been rehashed from other metroidvanias, and some of the later boss fights are just unimaginative (some pretty unfair attacks, or just bullet-hell-like patterns that are plain repetitive). But the worst sin this game has committed is to display areas that are only accessible via DLC in the main game. I lost hours trying to figure out how to get past them, and when I couldn't I looked up Reddit threads only to find out there was no way to get past those areas unless I shelled out some more cash in a poorly-reviewed DLC pack. Either make it clear those obstacles are part of the DLC or don't display them at all - do not waste a player's time. Bad, bad design.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1748049592}, {"review_text": "A Metroidvania style game where you need a DLC to unlock all doors is unacceptable period.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1761779024}, {"review_text": "Wish I could recommend this game but locking the true ending behind collectibles that are bugged and not fixing the bug for two years makes it really hard to recommend.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1741865606}, {"review_text": "While technically a better game, the first game is a far, FAR superior work of art.
I mean this one is aight, but dont play it shortly after finishing the first one, trust me.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1759073697}, {"review_text": "Everything aside from the gameplay, Blasphemous 1 does better.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1753522392}, {"review_text": "So, I'd like to preface this recommendation by saying the way the devs handled implementing the paid dlc into the game is stupid and frustrating. It ruined any momentum I had at getting 100%. What happens is, you'll come across thin thorn walls and no utility to pass them if you're playing the base game with no dlc installed. As someone who doesn't check guides unless really lost I had no in-game indication that a paid dlc weapon was needed to pass them. Literal pay walls… in a 'vania. JFC! Quite frustrating I had to find this out by a web search. The Game Kitchen needs to address this :)

Anyhoo, the base game is pretty darn good! The bread and butter here is the superb art and sound direction. If you're in it for moody music and locales, and wtf visuals, you're in for a treat! Best in genre in that regard.

The gameplay is solid and tight but not going to blow your mind. I did like having three weapons to swap between (though I only really used two) and movement and strikes felt good. Quite competent. 

Boss fights were challenging enough and should satisfy any un-jaded gamer. Same for level/map design, which is thankfully clearer in direction than the previous game. There's a story I think, but like the first game, it's all mumbo jumbo religious words reminiscent of the stuff I heard in Catholic grade school as a kid. Sets the mood just fine.

Shame that dlc issue soured me on an otherwise great base game. Come for the amazing art and sound, stay for the solid gameplay.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1742458010}, {"review_text": "In game where exploration, discovering secrets and figuring out how to reach certain areas, visibly adding DLC areas to the base game that aren't accessible without purchasing the DLC is a shitty thing to do. There's also the Steam achievements for the DLC even though I don't own the DLC so I can't get all achievements if I don't pay for the DLC. Truely a scummy move.

Very questionable design choices mostly around boss fights and the guilt system. When you die, you accumulate guilt on your fervor bar like in the first game but for some reason, retrieving your guilt fragments doesn't always take off the guilt from your fervor bar. There's already not a lot of them and the later ones are just unfun with one in particular that has projectile attacks you cant dodge/dash through making it more frustrating than challenging.

However, once you go back to the earlier areas, you realize that you can now double jump and dash across pits where once you had to wait for a moving platform. All of this is to say that Blasphemous 2 might be one of the most fulfilling experiences in this regard.

The blessing is that you will get to revisit every area (except for the last ones, which you already had every ability upon entering), and during these romps you will be able to tear through and grab item after item. Blasphemous 2 has... none of that. The 3-way weapon puzzles are clever in design but very gamey. There is no rug pull of expectations for design, no clever twist, nothing compelling in content or surprise. The bosses are all just two archetype -- Some Dude W. The NPC sidequests and special ending quest really just feel arbitrary. I feel like the writers of the last game aren't present here or didnt know what was needed to make a compelling sequel because the story just doesn't exist here. I beat most first try but then, for whatever reason, they give those specific bosses more demanding movesets. Eviterno is the 2nd to last boss and took a few tries and then... the last boss was laughably easy and his story dialogue and endings A & B just felt so bad. Why was it so weird? Its not my fault surely. But maybe I got lax with how easy the rest of the game was, with how Veredicto was the best weapon and taught you you never needed to parry, how I wasnt encouraged to be precise like I was in the first game. But then the item upgrade pacing is also super mid-to-back loaded, and then the backloading immediately disappoints and sours itself by all that endloading being LEVEL UP POINTS. Not even cool gear! You waited all this time to keep me from my reward and the reward is less grinding I dont need for non-primary weapons. Less. Grinding. Ugh. Also some of the powers dont work so great. Timefreeze powers can reveal that hitboxes appear before graphic animations. You can softlock after certain bosses if they kill you post victory with a lingering projectile.
