Yeah it needed some quality of life to smooth out the backtracking, yeah it got a lot of post-launch loving that Blas2 doesn't have yet and some it didnt need. They DID do better about those things. Even the art's way more polished. But Blas1 had WAY better pacing, better story, better design, better flow. Blas1 is the better quality gem even if Blas2 is less rough around the edges.

So sure, you can play this game, but you should probably play Blasphemous 1 instead if you haven't.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1735468252}, {"review_text": "Blasphemous 2 is basically my wish granted. I was disappointed by the first, which still is artistically and musically incredible but a clunky ass annoying metroidvania to play. The sequel takes the fine chisel and some oil and focuses chiefly on tweaking the basic game feel and greasing the numerous gears which used to grind before. And they succeeded: the result is a far snappier game, which is satisfying to control and more fun to actually play.

It's kind of a shame that for all the polishing, this is pretty much a basic ass metroidvania. Plus, for all the intriguing imagery that's still very unique in the gaming world, the way the concept is used narratively is laughably bad, bordering on ridiculous.

The Penitent One returns after centuries or whatever from the events of the first game and must travel to prevent the birth of a God baby from a giant heart in the sky. Understandable, I've had Tuesdays like that, this makes sense. The whole plot is basically an excuse to send you to kill some bosses to collect MacGuffins in order to enter the big bad's lair. And look, I get it, it's a classic structure dating back to Super Metroid in the genre, but it's so unbelievably repetitive here. You defeat the first three main bosses and get a nigh identical cutscene each time, then in the latter part of the game you defeat five other bosses to release some bloody doves or whatever and you get the same dialogue for each one. It's by design, based on the refrains for the various psalms and hymns of Catholicism, but due to the writing and how rigidly the game is structured it's so boring and annoying.

The writing style doubled down on Blasphemous 1's haughty edgy "Berserk and religion" theme and it's even more ridiculous here. Every single line of text is so pompous and meandering and makes absolutely zero sense. I'm pretty convinced that some of the names and concepts in the game are just random keyboard garbles. Yeah, religious mythology is often obscure and symbolic but this game is just silly in terms of narrative conveyance.

Luckily, for all the nonsense on the writing level, the artistry is absolutely spectacular once again, with rich architectures, opulent decorations and very inspired designs (some highlights: one boss is basically the reliquiary containint the purported skull of Mary Magdalene, while another is a choir of countless interchangeable faces as a personification of the Synod). All of this conveyed through a sublime pixel art that has few rivals in the indie 2d world. The attention to detail and the sheer love for Spanish and Catholic culture and imagery are awe-inspiring, and it's this artistry that makes exploring the world fun despite the writing nonsense, in conjunction with another masterful soundtrack by maestro Carlos Viola, who is an absolute treasure. The animated cutscenes don't really fit with the overall style, but whatever, it wasn't a big deal for me. 

The game proper is much improved, give or take some leftover rough edges. There are three weapons to choose from, each with their own skill tree and unique mechanics, plus a specific function during exploration and puzzle solving. The balance is wonky, as I feel like the censer is the best weapon no contest, but the variety is commendable. Rosary beads return, with utility and defensive passive buffs, though the latter feel pretty inconsequential as far as I've seen. The game kept claiming they some beads buffed some resistances "significantly", but I do not think that word means what they think it means. Prayers (basically magic) are back, divided between verses (quick Castlevania subweapons like spells) and prayers proper (big slow magic spells that are stronger, sometimes ludicrously so). Finally, you have altarpieces, very cool equippables that allow for a build of sorts and can have hidden synergistic bonuses when paired correctly. So the system has evolved from the prequel in a way that makes sense and is more rewarding. The controls are so much better: jumping and moving around feel more fluid (so platforming is way briskier), dodging is more smoothly integrated with the basic moveset, and the weapons are satisfying to use, making combat feel more punchy and fun. It's basically all they needed to improve on this front, and while some wonky hitboxes and stiffness remain, in places, this is quite the glow up.

I feel like such an assh0le to this series I swear, but I can see a potential that is just not realized. One half of the theming (art) is incredible, and I just wish the other half could catch up with it. This game is a fantastic improvement over the first game. While I thoroughly enjoyed it, I do think the ending could have been more satisfying.

First and foremost: Catholics might find the game's themes unsettling. It delves into the corruption of religious institutions, and you’ll encounter enemies such as cardinals in flying chairs, saints with bloody skeletal hands, and numerous bosses tied to religious symbolism. However, your character is not an atheist - save points are located at shrines, your mission is to purify the corruption.

At the start you choose between three weapons: twin daggers, a sword or a flail. After experimenting I opted for the flail due to its extended range and ability to knock enemies back. The game has plenty of secrets and loot to discover, and in the first town I discovered a big bell that revealed new platforms, thinking it was a default mechanic. Later I learned that only the flail could interact with the bell - This is one of the game’s unique features: each weapon has a special ability to interact with the environment, and you will need to collect all 3 (and upgrade them) to finish the game. The daggers allow you to dash through mirror walls, while the sword lets you break fragile floors. Some puzzles and challenges require quick thinking and fast execution, adding much complexity to the gameplay so get prepared.

The battles are tough. I can’t say I loved them but considering the first game, I’d say devs have already lowered the difficulty, and I still recall the difficulty of facing the big armored soldier on the bridge and the final boss. I’m not a fan of souls-like games but the rich environment kept me engaged and motivated to push through the challenges. My favorite scene has to be that long corridor connecting two different areas, which strongly resembles the Mosque-Cathedral in Cordoba, Spain. There’s also a scene with a man breastfeeding a baby, which is almost identical to a painting in the Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid. It’s clear that the developers paid close attention to real-life locations and works of art, that adds a lot of charm to the game. Kudos to the devs.

Also I must point out, the most frustrating elements is the game map. While it shows you locations of rooms, it doesn't always make clear how they are connected. I found myself lost on multiple occasions, at a point I almost gave up and eventually, I realized I needed to enter a specific room from a higher point rather than the rooms directly adjacent. Since the map itself resembles a maze, devs seem to recognize this by allowing player to place icons. However, the icons are not always helpful because sometimes, I'm not sure how to remind myself when I can’t pass a room as the icons don’t provide enough clarity. While I enjoyed the gameplay, getting stuck like this was frustrating, and a hint system would have been a great addition.

Lastly, the game features two possible endings. However, unless you have the patience to uncover all the secrets, you’ll likely only reach the regular ending, which is underwhelming. It’s reminiscent of games like Animal Well, where an Easter egg ending awaits, but in this case, the alternate ending didn’t feel as rewarding.

All things considered, I still recommend this game. It’s a fantastic experience.

[{"review_text": "Game so good some people tried to copy it making some indie game called Dark Souls or smth like that i don't really know.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 357, "timestamp_created": 1764389619}, {"review_text": "Disclaimer: I've played this game before and wanted to show my support by buying the steam release and future replays.

I found myself wandering through a world of nightmares masked by dreams, enveloped in love, lust, sin and insanity.

Ever since I was a child, I've been infatuated by fairy tales. From Disney adaptations to eventually reading Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and its sequel and some of the Grimms' Fairy Tales when I got a little older. It definitely had an impact on my creativity and lead to my habit of day dreaming. There's something so whimsical and innocent about them that layers over the top of the more graphic and mature history lying on the underside. Twisting that whimsy and innocence into something grotesque, horrifying, and almost unrecognizable can create very powerful interpretations of the original work and themes. I've always had a thing for dark fairy tales and that's whats led me to Black Souls. I won't really be writing about how this spoke to and impacted me personally but I wanted to write about some of the things I thought it did really well.

Black Souls II crafted a grimdark world in which I could easily lose hours and days into exploring and unraveling. Toro's world building has been a joy to see evolve. After finishing Black Souls 1, I went back and played Red Hood's Woods. A short 3 hour precursor to the Black Souls series and despite the spotty translation, had an interesting spin on the Red Riding Hood fairy tale but was lacking on the RPG side. Definitely check it out if you're thinking about diving into the series (both games have some callbacks and references for the fans), very creatively inspiring too. BSII expands on emphasizing the exploration, ramping up the freedom, multiple paths lie in wait for you, even before the first boss. Charming and unique cast of core and side characters to meet and fall in love with, beautiful set pieces to discover, rich lore to immerse yourself in and piece together. There’s so much to love about the world of Black Souls II. BSII takes joy in making you uncomfortable, refusing to conform in its approach to storytelling and presentation, unabashedly itself (something I really admire). Incredibly fun to go into blind and lose yourself down the rabbit hole of madness.

There's always something new to see, something around every corner, something you didn't see your last cycle. A perfect example of ludonarrative harmony, BSII incentivizes replaying through cycles to get almost entirely different playthroughs of the same game. Ever inching closer to the goal only to find yourself right back at the start as the curtains rise once again, questioning your actions as you begin to explore again. Bosses you might've fought your first playthrough all of a sudden become new characters for you to interact with on a new cycle. Scenes you would've otherwise missed out on become available as you learn and understand the mechanics of Wonderland as well as the layout to be able to progress in the story. The addition of the Chaos Dungeon is brilliant, providing an area to endlessly explore and grind for OP items, spells, weapons and of course, SOULS, giving it immense replayability. Plenty of H-Scenes to collect too, indulge as you wish.

BSII fleshes out the RPG mechanics of the previous games. Translating the Souls experience to Turn-Based RPG perfectly while still keeping their own originality in mechanics. Extremely addicting and adrenaline inducing, I've never wanted to spend my every waking moment playing with a combat system before this game. Allowing for almost endless customization, changing builds for different bosses becomes borderline puzzle solving. Learning how to switch between weapons and when to time each switch becomes mandatory. DLC3 puts everything into the difficulty, requiring a deeper understanding of the games mechanics, its not something you can brute force your way through like after your first couple of cycles. Some of the most fun I've had interacting with RPG mechanics since Xenogears back in 2023. Every fight is tense and brutal, barely surviving by the hairs on my back. I'd love to replay BSII for a difficulty 9 playthrough in the future.

I fell in love with Toro's art style almost immediately when I started BS1 but its here in BSII where his style takes a huge step in evolution. Possibly one of my favorites, invoking a very raw, grimy and horrifying feeling, keeping that same amateurish style of sketching in-tacked, while still only increasing in talent and progress. From what Toro has shown of Red Dead Hood so far, he's only improving in his art style as he continues to create.

SPOILERS FOR DLC3 AHEAD
Please skip over if you haven't played it yet

Black Souls II looks deeper into the relationship of Lewis Carroll and the Liddell family, specifically his relationship with Alice. Something very striking I took away was the memories you collect and the ADV Visual Novel section close to the end of DLC3, Grimm dreams about memories of the Liddell family, as the days progress in the dream it slowly descends into a psychological horror centered around the Liddell family. When Grimm wakes from the dream he states that it was a nightmare. My interpretation of these scenes is criticism of Lewis Carroll, the person, and the actions and behavior he took and made around the Liddell family. Spinning theories about why the Liddell family distanced themselves from him (possible indecency or marriage proposal to Alice on his part, we will never know) into an HP Lovecraft influenced tragedy provides for an incredible meta-narrative of falling into the abyss of regret, guilt, dread, defilement, and what it means to struggle as Grimm pushes forward in his mechanical stage play of descent to the tune of the gods.

Black Souls II is an ambitious project brimming with passion. Putting heart and soul into creating and developing these ideas. Toro’s genius and brilliance shine from start to finish, a one of a kind experience, creatively invigorating monumental release for indie games and love letter to the original works and influences. Thank you Toro, Eeny, meeny, miny, moe? and the translation team. Incredibly excited to play Red Dead Hood whenever it and a translation release.

If you want to truly understand what’s happening in Black Souls 2, it’s worth reading the original Alice books and learning a bit about Lewis Carroll’s life. The game borrows not only characters and imagery from Alice in Wonderland and Through the Looking-Glass, but also their deeper themes: identity distortion, dream logic, wordplay, and the unsettling tension between innocence and madness. Carroll’s own style—playful, symbolic, and subtly disturbing—shapes the tone of the entire game world. Knowing the source material helps you catch hidden references, understand character motivations, and see how Black Souls 2 twists familiar scenes into something darker. In short, Carroll’s works act as the foundation that makes the game’s storytelling richer, stranger, and more meaningful.

Lovecraftian mythology also plays a major role in Black Souls 2. The game builds on the central Lovecraftian idea that humans cannot truly understand the Ancient Ones who shape reality from the shadows. Their motives, forms, and logic lie far beyond human comprehension, creating a constant sense of dread and awe. This influence appears in the game’s cosmic atmosphere, in the characters who lose themselves to forbidden knowledge, and in the themes of identity dissolving before something vast and unknowable.  Maybe it suggests that a hint of madness and a willingness to think beyond all familiar limits are sometimes necessary to glimpse the truth.

[h1] A Harsh Sequel RPG Where Your Choices Alter a Wonderland Sinking Into Madness [/h1]
The setting is a Wonderland filled with corruption and madness, and a system that alters the world’s “SEN value” (essentially functioning like SAN) based on your actions exists throughout the entire game. The highly open field is accessible from the early stages, and each exploration of forests, towers, deep seas, and ruined cities—each reminiscent of various fairy tales—gradually reveals the story’s background.

The heroines you meet in each region have strong personalities, and choices such as saving, abandoning, or killing them directly shape the story. The impression of the narrative changes entirely depending on what you see and what you fail to see, making the weight of choice constantly present within the structure.

Combat uses an ATB system and is designed with a high difficulty level that requires builds combining contracts, rings, and magic. Enemies show no mercy with both firepower and status ailments, and many attacks have first-strike kill characteristics, but since equipment and strategies can be reconstructed to break through, the trial-and-error process itself becomes the core of progression.

Furthermore, when the aforementioned SEN value drops, effects such as text corruption, silence, and the intrusion of aberrations progress in stages, causing the world itself to collapse in response to your choices. Coupled with an anime-style presentation that blends fairy-tale beauty with pathological darkness, it left me with a strong sense of immersion and an enduring aftertaste as a dark horror fantasy.

But then the monetization hits. Hard.

Hosting a multiplayer server requires buying credits through a third-party app, and the cost is ridiculous. You’ll pay as much for a single hour of hosting as you would for an entire month in something like ACC. Because of it, you can barely find online races. Most lobbies are either locked or have frustrating restrictions like being limited to one car class.

On top of that, the EA launch is already leaning into a flood of DLCs, making the whole thing feel like a cash grab rather than a passion project.

There’s a genuinely great sim here but it’s being suffocated by a greedy and short-sighted business model. Unless they change direction fast, Le Mans Ultimate will go down as a wasted opportunity.

Make a good game, charge a fair price, don't gouge your customers under the guise of choice.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1751639256}, {"review_text": "It's a shame, theres so many things that arent great about the game that the things which are good about it are overshadowed, LMU could be a great simracer i could frequent a lot, but i end up growing frustrated every time i play, here's why;

## The Good
The online multiplayer works decently well. I’ve only gotten disconnected once in my entire time playing, and I could reconnect immediately. No major lag spikes or other issues to speak of. How your rank and safety rating change is explained in the post-game summary, which makes improving your racing relatively easy.    

The sounds are good. Cars sound authentic, and while some cars are a lot louder than others in the cockpit, it’s not a dealbreaker. The audio is immersive and well done.   

The FFB is decent, though maybe a bit overtuned in my experience. Curbs are extremely obvious, and so is locking or sliding. What the car is doing is pretty clear from the feedback alone.   

Graphics are serviceable and look up to date. There are some points I’ll touch on later, but overall, the visuals hold up with other games like LMU.

## The Bad
The tyre model is, in my experience, utterly terrible. Grip loss is hard to understand. Overdriving your tyres in any way makes your grip vanish completely. Locking your brakes is a guaranteed spin. Wheel-spinning out of corners usually ends in one too. Even compared to other games on the same engine, I don’t have nearly as many problems with the tyres as in LMU. I hate it, and I really hope that the developers will work on improving these tyres.

Flashing your brights is way too effective. Even with high beams being enabled by default, flashing your lights overpowers all other lights on track. Meaning someone 100 meters back can make the entire track in front of you flash, It’s completely unrealistic.

Also, flashing lights don’t seem to respect walls. If someone spams their flashers on a track with tight sections, you’ll see the flashes through walls. It’s hugely distracting and very annoying. 

## The Ugly
The game’s pricing structure is unclear at best and almost deceptive at worst. You end up paying over double the price just to get all the content they offer. Plus, there’s subscription nonsense in the game that isn’t visible on the store page before you buy. The developers basically want to charge you multiple times for content and features.

The RaceControl Pro and Pro+ subscriptions aren’t clearly explained before purchase. You’re led to believe you’re buying a complete game, but in reality, you’re only getting a fraction of it.

## The Summary
Despite decent audio, stable online play, and decent visuals, the game’s core systems, especially tire physics and lighting at night, are broken in ways that destroy my enjoyment of the game, combined with a misleading monetization model these issues make it impossible to recommend at full price, or any price, really.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1761742137}, {"review_text": "Pros:

This game is no where near finished and they are already out for wallets.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1736561962}, {"review_text": "If there’s one thing Le Mans Ultimate nails, it’s the feeling of driving. The first time you sit in the cockpit of a Prototype or GT machine and push it through a lap of Le Mans or Spa, the game impresses. The physics feel robust, with a strong focus on the quirks of endurance racing machinery, things like tire warm-up, brake wear, and fuel strategy play a significant role. Compared to a normal road car, these machines feel heavy yet razor sharp, and that sense of “fighting but mastering” the car is incredibly rewarding. The force feedback is also strong, giving you constant communication about what the car is doing under you. In that sense, Le Mans Ultimate delivers what sim racers often want most: authenticity and immersion when you’re behind the wheel.

Visually and aurally, the game does well too. The cars are beautifully modeled, with liveries that reflect the real-world grid, and the tracks feel accurate and alive. The soundscape contributes massively to immersion; gear whines, tire scrubbing, and the roar of engines all come together to make you feel like you’re in the middle of an endurance event. It’s not the absolute best-looking sim on the market, but it’s polished enough that, combined with the driving model, the immersion is very high.

That said, everything surrounding the actual act of driving feels underdeveloped. Even after the “1.0” release, Le Mans Ultimate is still a barebones package in terms of features. The single-player experience is limited to setting up your own custom race weekends. There’s no real career mode, no championship progression, no driver management, no sense of building a long-term journey. Once you’ve run a few custom races, there’s very little incentive to keep returning unless you’re purely motivated by hotlapping or experimenting with different cars. For players who enjoy structured offline modes, this is a huge missed opportunity.

Online racing, meanwhile, is a mixed bag. When it works, and when you find respectful players, it’s fantastic,; multiclass racing in particular offers moments of real tension and excitement as you manage traffic and strategy. But in public lobbies, the standards of driving often fall apart. Far too many players dive into corners without awareness, push others off track, or deliberately crash. It’s not unusual to have an otherwise great race ruined by someone using the game like an arcade racer rather than a simulation. There are also occasional server issues, from connection drops to stability problems, which can compound the frustration. In practice, this means that unless you’re part of a private league or community, the online experience can feel inconsistent at best, and actively discouraging at worst.

The monetization model makes things even harder to swallow. Many basic features that would normally be part of the base game, such as proper race reporting, custom liveries, and the ability to organize or run teams, are locked behind the RaceControl Pro or Pro+ subscription. That means that even after purchasing the game, you’re being asked to pay again if you want access to tools that are fairly standard in other sims. On top of that, the DLC strategy feels overpriced, especially since the old season pass model (which gave access to everything in a single purchase) has been removed. Instead, you’re left piecing together content car by car, track by track, which quickly adds up. For a title that is already relatively barebones in features, the decision to put so much behind paywalls doesn’t sit well.

This is the main contradiction of Le Mans Ultimate: it offers one of the best driving experiences available in sim racing today, but the structure around it feels half-finished and monetized in all the wrong ways. The core engine is strong, the cars, the tracks, the physics, but the rest of the package feels like it’s still in early access rather than a finished “1.0” release. And while the developers may continue to add features and polish over time, the current state of the game leaves a lot of players wondering whether the investment is justified.

To put it simply: if you’re a hardcore sim enthusiast, especially one with an interest in endurance racing, the driving alone makes this game worth trying. The authenticity, the feel of the cars, and the immersion of running multiclass races are all top-tier. But if you’re a more casual player, or someone who values career modes, offline depth, or fair monetization, Le Mans Ultimate is going to feel frustratingly shallow.

For me, this is a 7 or 8/10 game right now. The driving earns it that score, it’s genuinely that good, but the missing features, expensive DLCs, and the decision to lock basic tools behind a subscription drag it down. If the developers commit to fleshing out the single-player side, rethinking the monetization, and improving online stability, Le Mans Ultimate could easily climb to a 9 or even a 10 in the future. But as it stands, it’s a fantastic simulator trapped in a disappointing wrapper.

How do you even review The Witcher 3 in 2025? 

Everyone knows what it is and what it's not. 

Regardless, I played the game fully (Main game + ALL DLCs) for the first time now. It was an excellent experience. It took me around 130 hours, all sidecontent included, on the Death March! difficulty.

I was expecting it to feel "old" in some ways, but I was gladly proven wrong quickly. The game looks amazing to this date, maybe due to the "next gen update" from 2022. The game looked and sounded great - maybe not as detailed as some newer games, but the art style carried and the design of the rather grim world of The Witcher still feels unmatched to this day. Death March! added some challenge and in some cases I used oils and bombs to further fight the various enemies and bosses. The best part about the combat was the variety of enemies. The Witcher 3 is full of very different creatures - man or monster - and a lot of different bosses (Witcher contracts mainly) that kept the game fresh throughout. Some recent games I've played had little in the variety department (Dragon Age: The Veilguard) which in those games made combat extremely repetetive. 

Looking past the combat, the game felt fresh due to it's amazing narrative. The story is gripping and every bit of the world feels alive and interesting. It's rare that a game's sidequests have as good or better storylines than the main objective, but the Witcher 3 has that in droves. [b]And this is what the Witcher 3 does best. [/b] The stories. The Wticher, while very action-heavy, is an RPG. There are multiple endings, choices to be made that aren't cut and dry and therefore offer interesting stories to tell. I can't help but compare that approach to the genre again to my recently played games. The Witcher 3 did it better 10 years ago.

-thank you, CD PROJEKT RED for creating and developing such a masterpiece with love and faith", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1747672906}, {"review_text": "[h1]The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — A Love Letter After 100% Completion[/h1]  
[i]"Evil is evil. Lesser, greater, middling... makes no difference."[/i]  
But this game? It’s greatness. Plain and simple.

I’ve played a lot of games. Some stick for a while. Others leave.  
But [i]The Witcher 3[/i]? It stays. It lingers. Like a scent of lilac and gooseberries in a world that forgot how to smell.

[h2]Death March is Not Just a Challenge — It’s a Philosophy[/h2]  
If you enter Death March expecting to button-mash, you're already dead.  
This is a game that [b]demands preparation[/b]. Every fight is a contract, and every monster a puzzle.  
The [i]Bestiary[/i] isn’t just lore — it’s your survival manual.

Reading up before a fight, coating your blade with the right oil, choosing the proper sign — this is what makes you a Witcher.  
A real one. Not just some dude with two swords.

[h2]The Bloody Baron: Where Side Quests Outshine Main Stories[/h2]  
This quest broke me.  
No villains. No heroes. Just people.  
It starts with a drunken brute and ends in tragedy, sorrow, and that deep, uncomfortable place where morality gets blurred.

This isn't a side quest. This is [i]the benchmark[/i] for narrative design in gaming.  
When a game makes you question your choices long after the credits roll, you know it’s something special.

[h2]Triss vs Yennefer — The Veteran’s Choice[/h2]  
If you’ve read the books, you know.  
Triss may be sweet, but she [b]lied[/b] to Geralt. Took advantage of him during his amnesia.

Yennefer? She’s stormy, complicated, volatile — but she’s [i]real[/i]. She’s destiny. She’s the one who would burn kingdoms to save Ciri.  
This isn’t a dating sim. This is [i]his[/i] story. And choosing Yen just feels right.  
(Also, that Djinn quest? Pure magic.)

[h2]Combat That Respects Your Intelligence[/h2]  
The Witcher 3 isn’t [i]Dark Souls[/i] — but it respects the same rules:

- If you fail, it’s on you.  
- You didn’t prepare.  
- You didn’t read.  
- You didn’t [i]think like a Witcher[/i].

Start treating each fight like a hunt instead of a brawl, and the game transforms.

[h2]Gwent — A Side Activity That Becomes a Lifestyle[/h2]  
What starts as a simple tavern minigame becomes a full-blown addiction.  
You’ll chase rare cards across continents, defeat legendary players, and build a deck more dangerous than most final bosses.  
Gwent isn’t just a diversion — it’s [i]its own game[/i] with depth and brilliance.

[h2]DLCs That Put AAA Expansions to Shame[/h2]

[b]Hearts of Stone[/b]  
A tale of deals with devils, riddles, reflections, and unforgettable villains.  
Gaunter O’Dimm isn’t loud — he whispers. He lingers. He haunts you.

[b]Blood and Wine[/b]  
The perfect epilogue.  
Toussaint is a painting — beautiful, yet hiding something dark beneath.  
It’s not just more Witcher. It’s the ending Geralt [i]deserved[/i].

(*Pro tip:* Don’t play these on Death March unless you really, really hate yourself. Enjoy them. You’ve earned it.)

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]  
The Witcher 3 isn’t just a masterpiece. It’s [i]the standard[/i].  
A world of monsters and men, of love and destiny, of choices that never feel clean.

Once it ends, you don’t walk away.  
You leave a piece of yourself behind — in the swamps of Velen, the streets of Novigrad, the peaks of Skellige, and the golden sunsets of Toussaint.

[{"review_text": "Right off the bat: This is a Gacha game. If you don't know what that is, for whatever reason, you should look it up and make sure that's something you're okay with/ ready for before dipping your toes in. 

That said, while this is DEFINITELY an expensive game to play if you want, say, a lot of characters or support cards, it's actually shockingly fine to play without spending any money whatsoever. As long as you're interested in the core gameplay loop, and don't care much about leaderboards or "pvp," you can have a crazy amount of fun with this game for absolutely 0 dollars. 

That in mind, what exactly is the gameplay like in Umamusume? 

Well, it's basically a combination of a stats-building trainer game, mixed with a roguelite shell, with a decent amount of visual novel elements. Think of it as a really really light version of something like... Princess Maker, or honestly any other game where you choose options to "train" a subject, with the goal of hitting certain stat breakpoints to push past events, and clear challenges. That said, it's important to note that if you're not super into min-maxing and very numbers-focused gameplay, there really isn't that much here. 

If you've watched videos you've undoubtedly seen the horse girls actually racing, and while those sequences are VERY well produced, and extremely entertaining to watch, there's actually no gameplay there. Once the race is locked in, you literally do nothing, except probably cheer or curse at your horsegirl. Now, that's not really a con for me, I actually think the balance between the option-based RNG stat building and the races is -extremely- well done, but if you're looking for a game where you actually race... this 'aint it.

In regard to the visual novel aspect, each horesegirl has a few chapters of a story you can watch, after you've trained them up a bit, and a few more as you increase your friendship with them. There's also some main-story segments, that are significantly longer and have higher production value. These are -almost- entirely VN, although there are a couple races here and there, and honestly... they're quite well written; very entertaining to go through. Sure, you kinda have to care about the horsegirls to really get much out of them, but it's honestly hard not to. 

Finally, there's a... shockingly deep system for "legacies," that is to say raising up horsegirls to effectively be "parents" for future horsegirls. This is where most of the grind comes in, as far as I can tell, and while the likelihood of building up good "parents" early on is incredibly slim, it gives the game a lot of replay value, and rewards game knowledge/ time investment. 

With all this in mind, some key questions: 

Is Umamusume fun? 
Yes, absolutely. It's honestly extremely addictive, but luckily in about 30 hours of play I've never felt compelled to pay money, and this is coming from someone who literally has a mild gambling addiction, so much so I refuse to even go near a casino. 

Is Umamusume Pay to Win?
Yes, Absolutely. If you pay the big bucks, you will 100% have a massive advantage over even the most clever and well-researched players. 

Does that matter?
Not really! At least not now. The PVP aspect currently is really lite, and you get rewards regardless of whether you win or lose. Similarly, while the scenario mode will definitely go SMOOTHER if you spend loads of cash, you can easily clear any of the scenarios, multiple times, and build really good legacies without spending anything. It'll just take longer, and you'll be more at the mercy of RNG.

Will I like Umamusume?
If you like cute anime girls with aspirations of glory, racing anime, stats-focused training game, or the absolute despair of watching your racer just barely miss first place, this game is probably for you. 

Umamusume is like candy that tastes better if you pay for it, sure, but not better enough that it hurts the experience to just devour it for free.

At first glance, even if you have no preconceived notion about the Japanese anime artstyle or the weird concept of the world presented, it makes no sense how such a game could hold so many people hostage, that is until you start playing it. 
The characters may look generic from the outside and the gameplay like some afk slob, but once you engage with the game you find yourself lost and hours go by like with the best 'one more turn' Civ games.

Here is what makes the game special:
First of all, all the horses and their storylines are based on (and named after) real race horses and developers took the saying 'you can't write a script like this' to heart. Why would you need to create some rivalries, comeback stories and weird escapades? Just use the funnest, weirdest and most unique stories reality gave to us and extrapolate the story out of the already existing history of these horses!
This idea is actually brilliant, because the writers don't have to come up with some contrived story, they can just interpret what these horses would be like given their history and behaviour, and you somehow end up with a fascinating cast of characters.
The gameplay is also of a rare kind (the last time I remember playing that style of game was, that also has a cult following, 'Long live the Queen') where you guide your chosen horse through a career, by deciding on the training schedules and skills it learns on the way. This gets surprisingly deep, as each horse may have different targets (also based on the real careers), and RNGjesus can always throw a spanner into even the best of plans. And if even that wasn't enough, there is more, because at the end you gain 'sparks' that actually upgrade your horse as parents for the next generation of attempted careers, leading to a satisfying loop of rogue like grinding in a strategy veneer. 
Also, it has to be said that the animation of the races and the expressiveness of the models during the story segments is extremely fluid, making it fun just to watch these girls move!

There are a few more negative things to say about the game regarding the monetization.
Overall the game is extremely free to play friendly, you can experience everything the game has to offer, without spending as much as a cent, BUT the game has a PvP mode that is 100% catered to 'whales' (aka big spenders), with a similar price tag to EAs ultimate team 'professionals' that could have you spend 5 digits (~10000€/$ for the first year alone was roughly calculated) to keep up with the meta!
But all that said, if you don't have the itch to be the absolute top of the foodchain when it comes to PvP, you don't have to spend a dime, which leads to a weird dynamic where a player can either play completely as free 2 play or as a massive spender, but there is no reasonable in between as there is no real point in spending small amounts.

Overall, the game is extremely fun and addicting, and as long as you don't plan on spending a lot of money you don't need to spend any money at all and can still experience everything the game has to offer.

For achievements already completed on phone, you can open the mission menu when playing on steam to trigger the steam achievement pop up.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1754825777}, {"review_text": "[h2]Part training sim, part visual novel, part roguelite, [i]Umamusume[/i] successfully merges a myriad of game genres to create an incredibly unique and engaging experience[/h2]

[h3] Highlights [/h3]
✅ Endearing cast of characters & touching storylines
✅ Incredibly addicting and surprisingly in-depth gameplay loop
✅ Stellar 3D art & animation
✅ Amazing voice acting
✅ Pleasant and uplifting soundtrack

[h3] Flaws [/h3]
⛔ UI/UX could use a few improvements
⛔ Poor scaling at higher resolutions
⛔ Lack of in-game explanations of gameplay mechanics

[h3] Verdict: 85/100 [/h3]
[i]Umamusume[/i] has been an absolute blast to play and has just about consumed my life since its launch on the 26th. The game is incredibly ambitious in its scope and yet it somehow manages to be spectacular in each thing it sets out to do: not only is it a fantastic raising/training sim with a great core gameplay loop and satisfying rogue-like elements, but it's also a fantastic visual novel experience with amazing visuals, great voice acting and a truly wonderful cast of characters.

I really can't stress enough how much I enjoy this game and I think this game will have staying power because 1) the characters are all so freaking well written -- it's truly amazing how the game gets you to care for each girl as you complete careers with them; 2) there's so much story content that's unique to each girl that is well written with just the right amount of tension, relationship building and goal setting; and 3) the core gameplay loop has so much depth from carefully planning out your support deck for each girl to carefully managing the stat raising and events in each career. I really can't wait to see what the next few updates have in store for us.

The game is fantastic, but it also has room for some improvements, mainly in its technical department. For starters, the UI feels cluttered at times and there's a [i]lot[/i] of menus within menus in this game, which makes for a rather cumbersome experience at times. The game also severely lacks game setting options that you'd come to expect with a PC release: you're only given the option to set the graphics to 'standard' or 'basic' and there's no resolution scaling options whatsoever, so the text and backgrounds can get quite pixelated at higher resolutions. On another note, the game doesn't provide enough information about [i]really[/i] important gameplay mechanics so you'll need to do quite a bit of research outside of the game if you want to understand some of its foundational mechanics.

Ultimately, despite a few gripes regarding its UI, the absence of game settings and the lack of proper tutorials and explanations, I would wholeheartedly recommend giving this game a shot. It has a lot of heart and passion clearly put into it and it's just been such a fun experience. [{"review_text": "The Ultimate Time-Gated Time Sink.

Great setting, pretty good gameplay. This is not a traditional 'action-adventure rpg'. This is like a single-player MMO. The setting is beautiful and there's lots of exploration. And, it's free.

However here's what you need to know before investing your time.

Progression is time-gated. You can only level your character so many times before needing to 'breakthrough' to the next tier. These breakthroughs are time gated. The first couple are once a day. But at level 40, I now have to wait two days before I can 'breakthrough' and level again. All xp gained in the meantime is 'stored' until your next breakthrough. The bigger problem is that many quests, the ability to progress 'the story' and move to different areas, are dependent on your level.

EDIT: I'm seeing from a lot of people that the time-gates are a temporary part of the season, I hope this is true.

Now lets talk about the Wuxia gameplay elements. The cinematics in this game are cool. And the combat system is alright -everything looks cool, but it requires more thumbs if you're playing with controller. The gameplay is nowhere near as simple as the previews make it look. As for the 'flying kung fu' that fans love... it's not available until you've explored most of a given map.... which is self-defeating to say the least. It's also extremely janky and you can't really control it, just basically which general direction you want to go. There are other less overt 'Lightness' skills like wall striding, running fast, running across water, etc. However, for most quests you can't use any of these skills. All the Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon stuff seems to be for exploration only. It's extremely jarring and immersion-breaking when you're exploring the world and all of the sudden you're grounded to bunny hops because you found yourself in a quest area.

The last thing you need to know, is that this game is tucked inside a menu simulator. There are menus within menus within menus. There is an enormous amount of tracked challenges, collectibles, resources, skills, talents, shops, events, etc to unlock. This thing is a lot like an MMO. I started having flashbacks to Warframe with the ungodly amount of resources and various things to 'level up'. You have to level up your character, your gear, your martial arts, your mystic ways, inner ways, harmony, your profession, your profession's skills, and no I'm not even kidding -even your gear slots. The main reason this is billed as an rpg is because there is a singular story arc specific to your character.

But hey, it's free. The game is beautiful. The boss fights and cinematics are cool. I nearly shed a tear during the Velvet Shade's Revelry Hall cinematic. The game shoots itself in the foot on a few things, but I'm enjoying it. It's loads of free content that's obviously kept me entertained many hours.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 35, "timestamp_created": 1763418724}, {"review_text": "I saw an egg in my inventory. A F2P RPG with no P2W sounds way too good in 2025, so I expected another forgettable game, but it honestly surprised me in a good way.

The F2P model is very clean. Everything you can buy is cosmetic and the battle pass is also purely cosmetic. There’s no P2W at all, which is still rare these days. The only thing some people might consider “P2W” are the mounts you can buy in the cash shop, since they gather resources for you, but honestly the impact is very small, so it feels more like a QoL feature than anything else.

The first thing you need to know is that this is not an MMO, even if it has an “MMO mode” with world bosses, dungeons, GvG and online activities. The core of the game is an open world RPG with lots of systems, minigames and small interactions everywhere. There’s also a co-op mode, but this one is only for exploring, doing side missions and other activities together. The main story is singleplayer.

The combat feels good, dynamic and fluid. You combine two weapons and play classic archetypes like tank, melee DPS, ranged DPS or even healer. There’s no upgrade system based on probabilities. You simply get the materials and level up your gear in a consistent way. You also have mystical abilities on top of your weapon skills, plus a talent tree, although it’s a simple one.

For PvP you get a 1v1 arena, a 50-player battleroyale-style mode, duels and GvG.

One interesting feature is the AI chat system, which lets you gain friendship with NPCs. It’s pretty basic, don’t expect deep conversations, but it’s well integrated and helps you unlock tasks and extra rewards. Some NPCs can give you items if you listen to what they say and help them, even though they don’t have markers or indicators. It adds a nice sense of discovery.

There are also a lot of activities: the jar game, dialectic duels, musical minigames, puzzles and many small things that make the world feel alive. You can play most of these with friends. On the first day I played a card game similar to “liar’s dice” with several friends. We had a good laugh and even leveled up a couple of times.

The game can run on both DirectX 11 and DirectX 12, but it’s clearly better on 12, with frame generation and more consistent visuals. So make sure to select the right option on Steam when you launch the game. (A small window appears when you click play, so it’s easy to find.)

It also has tutorials for almost everything. Each system, mechanic and feature is explained, so it’s hard to get lost even with the amount of things the game offers.

The biggest issue when you start is the number of menus and different currencies you get. Even though the menus unlock progressively, the first hours can be a bit confusing, but you get used to it after playing for a while. Some translations are also a bit rough and need to be polished, but it’s not a big deal.

In short, Where Winds Meet is a F2P RPG that really surprises. It offers a world full of activities, fun combat and an online mode that, while not a real MMO, adds variety without making things complicated. If you enjoy RPGs with tons of things to do and no pressure to spend money, give it a try. Being an RPG the game is expansive with many hours of content to explore. Although there is your standard increase in exp to level you, there are additional ways to customise your character and their traits, through playing various minigames or completing exploration tasks. Your character essentially becomes what they do, which feels like the very essence of roleplaying. Additionally,, interactions with NPCs include interactions with individualised chatbots for each NPC this harkens back to the days of MUDs where you were able to freely enter info and receive responses. The story itself is phenomenal and ranges from the absurd (rabid geese, kung-fu chickens), to tragic (a love never spoken for an entire lifetime, past losses) and sometimes switches between these abruptly to keep the audience engaged and lighten or tone down the mood to create moments of contrast. Combat is incredible for a wuxia game. Co-op includes running through Outposts killing mobs until the boss arrives ,specific Boss fights with fleshed out mechanics that rely on awareness and co-operation between team mates. I can barely scratch the surface in this short review. 
The multiple mini games are fun and offer a variety so if becoming frustrated in one area, ,hope over to another activity for a bit, ,these games also allow you to level them up such as levelling healing skills, or dialogue cards for the argument minigame. 

There are issues here though, most likely browsing other reviews youll see complaints over the menu complexity ,which is a large issue,, once you have started to figure them out there are some neat tricks to quickly jump around, and the map also is quite complex but once youve figured out the way to set waypoints and track items it becomes a lot easier... it is ridiculous that this can take so many hours of play to figure out.

As a free game (that so far is not P2W) and only really raking in cash from cosmetics, I'd advise anyone to download this, it has the best elements of exploration, combat and social, and offers something for everyone. Just be aware you may need to invest time in learning... menus!

Not only are you fighting the predators actively trying to eat you, you are also fighting yourself cause your damn sluggish cat can sometimes have the dexterity of a lobotomized squirrel.
This game somehow managed to have both the most beautiful scenery and world i have seen yet at the same time i came across the most horrifyingly put-together amalgamations of human imagination which make up the ecosystem of this game
The AI of the creatures in this game can be best described as a dude given 12 beers, LSD and car keys. The creatures genuinely do the stupidest shit and somehow manage to get away with it purely because you wouldn't expect them to be THAT DUMB. The amount of times I have found myself dying laughing at a creature falling out of the sky for no apparent reason, or crashing out because those same creatures falling out of the sky managed to somehow land directly on top of me, pluck me off a perfectly good pole and run off with my dead body is incredible.

This game can be your greatest friend, or your worst nightmare. The world and lore are much deeper than you would expect from a game about a silly slugcat with lanky arms. Explore freely and you will eventually find what you're looking for; there are tons of different pathways and routes around the map. The game will start off confusing at first, but you will get the hang of it pretty quick.

easy 11/10, and i haven't even started the dlc yet. Its so scary but genuinely so fun, i have this love-hate relationship with this game, and its amazing.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 19, "timestamp_created": 1734408737}, {"review_text": "[h1] This game is amazing. But it's not for everyone. [/h1]
[h2]This is not a review, this is a warning.[/h2]

If you are looking for a fun game that is easy to pick up, don't play this game.
This game is meant for people who have patience and are willing to put up with esoteric controls and vague goals.

But if you put up with it and wade through all the obtuse controls and vagueness, you will find that this game is a gem not usually talked about. The story is incredible and the environments look amazing.
The ecology is incredible as well and the world feels alive.

And after some more time, the controls will feel buttery smooth and everything will be clear in hindsight. You'll be able to understand how the game works through careful observation and experimentation.

If you need help, there's wonderful people over in the Rain World discord that are willing to help and guide you through the game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762918193}, {"review_text": "Rain World is a masterpiece. I am not using this word lightly, this game has undoubtedly been a huge influence on my life.

Anyway, onto the game itself.
In Rain World, you play as a small animal - a wet and pathetic little otter thing called a slugcat - surviving in the ruins of an alien world. This is a world of derelict structures and burgeoning ecosystems, a world that is dead and yet so very alive. The line between ruin and nature is blurred into insignificance, as new life grows from a heap of decay. Rain World's beautiful pre-rendered environments convey the experience of a small, nimble animal extremely well. Cities are shown not through living spaces but basements, alleyways and storm drains. Pipes and rusted rebar scaffolds are not background objects but core geometry features of level design. Rain World thus has a wonderfully fresh take on ruined environments.

The gameplay itself is wonderfully unorthodox. While it takes some of the bare bones of a metroidvania, its progression is almost incomparable. The slugcat does not gather upgrades, and has every ability from the start. Instead, Rain World's progression is based on exploration and knowledge alone.

Rain World's story is one of the best I have ever seen. I can't really elaborate, as it's best experienced yourself. I could say a lot about it, but nothing that does it justice.

So overall: pretty nice game. you should play it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1748795208}, {"review_text": "-Evil level design

I never realised it, but the game was an exact representation of what i was going though. Trying and trying again, against all odds. How rewarding it feels, it wants to make me cry. I’m not saying that Rain World saved my life, but it sure made it feel like a story. And the last theme: “Deep Light” means so much to me. [b]and then there's the visual style[/b]", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1751885031}, {"review_text": "i’ve never really had any talent with games. i have poor coordination and shit reaction time, and it always takes me excessive amounts of time to get used to a game. as a result the number of games i have played is pretty low and i tend to sit on the same games for a really long time. i also pretty much never play games blind because i have so little skill that i get stuck and lose all motivation to play. this is what happened to me with rain world, as i initially tried to play it completely blind and (stupidly) expected it to be similar to hollow knight as the person who recommended the game to me did so based on me saying i liked HK. unfortunately they are not even the same genre of game lmao. so i gave up five hours into RW and didn’t ever make it out of outskirts. i acknowledged that the game does what it intends to do extremely successfully, and i thought it was a really cool game, but i didn’t think i’d ever come back to it. 

fast forward to december 2024, a year and a half later. i see a random video about rain world lizards on my youtube feed. i watch it because i am bored. there is lore tidbits. i watch a lore video. oops! the lore is really really cool! and i am a big sucker for lore. so knowing that i am never going to play this game again, i shamelessly spoil the entire game and the dlc for myself, and god Damn is this game cool. i won’t stick spoilers in here but holy heck. i fell in love with the story and the characters and even the lizards, and i finally decided to try the game out again on the easy mode. i did not go in expecting to have fun, and i didn’t for the first few hours. but something kept dragging me back, and at some point i realized i had started to enjoy playing the game, too. i beat the easy mode, played the normal mode, and played the dlc, and today i beat the vanilla game’s hard mode. i’ve only got the final campaign of the dlc left to complete, and it’s already clear to me that this game is going to be one of my all time favorites.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1737457028}, {"review_text": "This is a knowledge based game. You are thrown into a massive, complicated world with its own rules, but given very little guidance on what to do or where to go. You don't unlock anything, you don't get any upgrades or skills. The way you are at the start is how you will be for pretty much the rest of the game (...unless?), and the entire world is open to you from the beginning, without any hard barriers preventing you from going anywhere you want.

Progress comes from the expectation that the player "studies" the game through careful observation of the environment or just trial and error. The skill ceiling is ridiculously high and the process of learning Rain World's rules can at times be very difficult and requires you to experiment, die and backtrack a lot. Rain World's lore is one of grand scale: The story feels epic, ancient and tragic. This game is designed with so much detail, life and layered complexity that you can't help but be fascinated by it, and this desire to understand drives your urge to keep going and see what happens.

Rain World is pretty much a "hard simulation" of what survival in the real wilderness would feel like, taken to its rawest, most extreme form. It does an excellent job of selling this feeling of isolation, high-stakes danger and being just a tiny insignificant part of a much grander world. Overcoming its challenges and learning its secrets are rewarding on a deeply personal level that I haven't felt in any other game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1735028497}, {"review_text": "This game is not for the weak. My first three hours were apprehensive and exciting unlike anything I've ever played before, and I love games that withhold context and force the player to deeply think. But it quickly deteriorated into mundanity for three main reasons: the visuals and sounds of most areas are homogeneous (never mind that the music didn't often function properly), threats quickly became nonthreatening since most are introduced in the first few areas, and the vaguely telegraphed objectives had me discover almost the entire map across ~50 hours before I advanced the story even once. I think these are all legitimate justifications for my frustration, and even if my 76-hour playthrough is abnormally long for one playthrough, this could've easily been avoided because I don't actually think any of these problems were mistakes. Despite my frustration, I always suspected that this game was special, and I'm happy that I had the patience to discover a few key sequences in this game that commanded my attention more than nearly anything I've ever seen. The soundtrack, graphics (that are somehow merely pixel art), style, and presentation are near-perfect. It's also refreshing to see the game succeed at the authentic Lovecraftian approach (not the lazy 'giant flesh blob with lots of teeth' approach that most people think is Lovecraftian) by fully admitting that it can't represent the divine, the afterlife, or infinity. I genuinely mean all of that, yet in doing some research, I realized that this game wasn't designed around any of it (and therefore players like me). Nearly everything I dislike about this game was a choice, not a lack of skill. It was designed to be an intentionally difficult (and sometimes unfair) ecological simulation, and I think it does this exceedingly well. I can only fairly say that I'm disappointed that an incredibly rich world is communicated mostly through intentionally unfair gameplay. This excessively shrouds the story in mystery for its own sake, and isn't conducive for facilitating an emotional connection with it, but a few key moments still make Rain World one of the most beautiful games I've ever seen, and it's very obvious to me why it's so loved.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1754861279}, {"review_text": "You will go from loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game to loving this game to hating this game", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 46, "timestamp_created": 1759278130}, {"review_text": "If you thought Silksong and Hollow Knight didn't have enough difficult enemies and RNG, this game is for you.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 11, "timestamp_created": 1761173852}, {"review_text": "The Souls like of the ecosystem simulations…
 
Rain World doesn’t care for you, the world doesn’t care if you are there or not, it just exists, persists and lives on, like it has before you, and how it will after you are long gone. You aren’t a great hero to save the land, or the main character everyone looks up too, you are just a tiny part in this world, a cogwheel in the circle of life, an animal trying to survive and make sense of its existence and purpose or, most often, food for other animals, which are stronger than you. 
Are you pray or the hunter? Ultimately, you can be both, but be aware, there is always a bigger fish, and it isn’t you little Slugcat. 
  
[u][b]Story[/b][/u]    
Even if I wanted too, I couldn’t tell you, this world makes sense in some way, and there is an interesting and complex story, but finding out about it is a big part of the game, you have to like indirect, confusing, puzzle like story telling to enjoy the way Rain Worlds shares it secrets and what is even going on. 
   
[u][b]Gameplay[/b][/u]   
Rain World is probably the most complex and detailed ecosystem simulation ever made. Every animal/insect/plant in this world has its own AI to a ridiculous level, with movement patters, different behaviors depending on the environment, other animals, fights, hunting strategies etc. Friendly/hostile interactions with every other creature, infighting…
It is like you would imagine a real ecosystem to work.
And on top, your own characters, the Slugcat has its own very complex, and physic  based movement system. 

And you are in the midst of all of this, as the little, very tasty Slugcat that you are, in a world where mostly everything wants to make you its next meal. 
You explore this world either on your own, or with a small guide that shows you the way in a very vague manner, but beside that, you are on your own, you hunt, eat, and evolve, but this system isn’t permanent. You need to eat, or you will starve, and based on countless other action, you can get points in different traits. And if you die, which you will a lot, you go down by one evolution. The game wants you to find out, there is no explanation to it. Certain areas are gated off by, well, literal gates that require you to achieve a certain evolution level to pass. 
As safe points, you need to find hibernation spots, and when you die, you go from there. But these serve several purposes, most of all, the world runs on a rain cycle. Each time it rains, you need to hibernate or you will die, so it is a constant balancing act of exploring, trying to get somewhere, hunting, not becoming food and keeping on eye on the rain timer, and you will die at times without being able to save yourself. Rain World isn’t fair, sometimes things happen and there is nothing you can do about it...
   
[u][b]Graphic and Audio[/b][/u]
I really love the 2D pixel art style of the game, the world looks amazing and the devs really captured the post-apocalyptic vibe they went for. Everything is in ruins, and overgrown and in some state of decay. 
I also can’t say anything bad about the audio side of the game, the world and living beings in it sounds nice, the soundtrack is pumping when it wants you to be on your toes or sometimes is just chill and relaxing.   
  
[u][b]Tech[/b][/u]  
I had no issues so far in my entire playtime, no stutters no crashes or anything. 
  
[u][b]Pros & Cons /tl;dr[/b][/u]
+amazing world and world building
+an ecosystem simulation you can not find anywhere else
+unique enemy behaviors and movement system
+great post-apocalyptic vibe and atmosphere 
+Unique characters progression system

-The game is unfair sometimes, which is by design, but needs to be mentioned
-You need frustration resistance
-Story is a puzzle (no minus for me, but I can see it being an issue for some)
-lack of direction / getting lost
-Absolutely no explanations for anything
   
[u][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/u]  
Rain World makes it really hard to recommend or not recommend it. The game is absolutely unique in so many aspects and its whole own experience. 
If you look for somethings different, and are willing to put the time in and bite through the frustration and at times unfair design you will encounter, then Rain World is truly a unique adventure, you will either look fondly upon or curse every bite of it, there really is no in between I feel.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1753202104}, {"review_text": "tl;dr
Rain World is a hellish game filled with lots of trial and error and will challenge your patience regularly. Yet those who persevere will discover perhaps the most unique and engaging exploration game out there.

[h1]Full Review[/h1]
I found this game through my wife’s obsession with its lore. I tried it out and quickly became frustrated with its difficulty, but it sat at the back of my mind until I played again. I still got frustrated, but I was doing better. And still I repeated this process. Now, 100+ hours in, the game still manages to annoy me sometimes…and yet there’s nothing quite like the feeling of curiosity and adventure it gives. That’s what keeps bringing me back to Rain World.

Gameplay:
Rain World has a high learning curve. You are tossed into the game after a brief cutscene, taught the basic mechanics of controls, eating food to survive, and finding shelter from the titular rain before the end of each cycle. After that, there’s next to no instruction, and you’re left to wander around and figure everything else out yourself.
One of the most curious features in Rain World that you’ll quickly notice is the other nonplayer creatures. Rather than being traditional video game enemies and whatnot, they behave more like animals in an environment simulation, traveling around the region and doing things on their own accord. Some are passive toward you, while others become aggressive and need to be foiled in order for you to survive.
Which leads to another key point: your character is small, weak, and delicious, and your abilities are limited. Besides the low-damage spears you can find scattered around, there’s very few consistent methods to fight back against dangerous creatures. As such, you instead must learn how to outsmart, outplay, and outmaneuver anything that wants to eat or kill you. Along with survival, platforming skills and devious wit become imperative for progression. This is where a lot of the unfairness comes into play, as during some cycles it will just feel like everything is working against you. It can work the opposite way as well, however, as random situations or thinking outside the box can lead to unexpected solutions for moving forward. Such a fascinatingly random environment is both this game’s biggest annoyance, and greatest reward.

Story:
Rather than a traditional linear story, Rain World is more of an anthology of its own ingame world, told through the small and comparatively insignificant struggles of each character’s campaign. Even then, little of that lore is given to you directly, but rather must be gleaned from piecing together environmental clues or dialogue from ancient beings. This form of storytelling fits well with the game, making you once again feel like just a small critter in a world that lives on, with or without you. Those who can figure out Rain World’s lore will find it unique and fascinating. Don’t worry, I won’t spoil any of it!

Visuals:
This is another section where Rain World stands out from other games. The graphics are clearly pixelated yet highly detailed, playing well to the visual storytelling I mentioned earlier. Each creature, including yourself, is actually procedurally-animated, causing them to move even more lifelike…usually. Sometimes the procedural animation can glitch and create some humorous results, haha. Even still, the graphics and procedural animation in particular are often a wonderous sight to behold.

Music:
I’m normally not good at saying much for this section but holy hecc does Rain World leave an impression here. The soundtrack is absolutely a perfect match for this game. Much of the music almost feels diegetic as you explore, and the dynamic threat music for whenever danger is nearby fits the riskiness of each encounter.
But what sticks out in particular to me is the main theme. Along with the title screen version, it plays in three other variants throughout your adventure. It’s such a simple tune, yet the more I’ve learned about Rain World’s lore, the more I feel it perfectly encapsulates the game world’s themes and condition. It is hauntingly beautiful, and almost nostalgic in a way. Very few soundtracks can get me emotional in the same way.

Replay Value:
Although the game’s world stays the same for each given campaign, the high randomness factor and generally nonlinear exploration make Rain World a great game to play over and over. Many secrets lay hidden throughout each campaign, and even without, there’s plenty of fun to be had in challenging yourself to different completion methods or scores.

In conclusion, Rain World is a highly unique exploration game experience that is really worth a look. Thanks to its high learning curve, this game unfortunately might not be for everyone, especially if you get frustrated easily. But those who are looking to try something new, and are willing to use a bit of patience, will find this game unforgettable.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1737344803}, {"review_text": "Super complicated and fun game, everyone says to avoid spoilers at all costs and figure things out on your own, but if you aren't having fun playing anymore I would 100% recommend looking for help.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1757268314}, {"review_text": "Game unlike any other.

this is a survival game, and as fun as this game appears at a glance, the only reward you get for overcoming adversity is more survival.  there aren't any real enemies, just a series of ridiculous animals like you, living in a world controlled by forces outside of their understanding.
