[{"review_text": "The best Party Pack in consistency since Pack 7, but distinctly lacks a heavy-hitter title that Packs 8 and 9 both had.
[b]Doominate[/b] is a fun supplement title to Quiplash, tasking players to take something nice and "ruin" it in comedic ways, with each round having a twist on that formula, but it doesn't have as much staying power as the iconic comedy writing games.
[b]Hear Say[/b] has you make random sounds or speeches, and surprisingly is a great time for being just that, though works far better over call than in-person. There isn't really any other game that uses sound in the way Hear Say does, so it is the main game I see myself going back to the most.
[b]Cookie Haus[/b] is a simple four-round cookie drawing game, pretty enjoyable though nowhere near the peak of Jackbox's drawing games. It's cozy, but doesn't have the hype of Champ'd Up.
[b]Susceptives[/b] is a really fun social deduction game, the survey question base to find out who the criminal is works wonders for the social aspect, but it leans way too much in the favor of the innocents, especially if you aren't at the maximum player count.
[b]Legends of Trivia[/b] is the only true dud, the RPG setting isn’t used to the fullest and largely just feels like a background for the trivia; three worlds to clear also makes it way too short, although the individual games can drag on by themselves.

I did recieve this product for free, but I was planning on buying it Day One after having played Early Access had I not gotten a free key.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761211047}, {"review_text": "Now that I've played all games with multiple play groups, I think I can safely say this is one of Jackbox's strongest packs in years, if not their best pack to date. The tldr is that every game is fun and polished for those who already enjoy said game genres, and its presentation is absolutely lovely. Lemme get into pack specifics (keep in mind I've exclusively played with friends online via Discord calls):

[b]Doominate[/b]: While it's not The Best Jackbox writing game, it's really up there. Takes its concept and makes it very fun, its paced perfectly, and has just the right amount of user prompt creation to keep it fresh. Absolutely agree with those who have comparing it to Survive the Internet. Having multiple prompts visible at a time is a godsend QOL choice, and I really hope Jackbox writing games going further keep this change. Love the presentation and my millennial friend groups loved the 90's/early 00's cultural references.

[b]Hear Say[/b]: Easily the most divisive game of this pack in my groups of shyer/more awkward players. Very impressed with how well this worked in a Discord call, just muting for noise making and unmuting when presenting. Those who like presenting games will enjoy the unique concept I feel, especially when the sounds are being presented with prerecorded footage, and even those going against prompt will get a few good laughs for themselves and others. The minigames feel a bit redundant but I'm sure folks who like the vocal concept won't mind. Keep in mind this WILL test both your comfort levels in presenting/performance and also your throat; for those who enjoy foley and have noisy objects here and there, you'll have your chances to use stuff like instruments or objects if you want to get creative.

 [b]Cookie Haus[/b]: Again, while it's not necessarily The best Jackbox art game, it's a strong showing for its genre!! Mostly in presentation; the cookie decorating concept is cute, its drawing system is stand out and fun, and its color selection and array of stickers and sprinkles keep the core of the game (drawing) fresh. I find it's game cycle a bit lackluster - basically prompt > prompt > fill in the blank > redraw - and I can see the cycle being a reason some would find it feeling stale quicker than the other games in the pack. I think updates to have an optional cycle shuffle and maybe some more cookie shapes would help it stay fresher longer.

[b]Suspectives[/b]: Easily the best game in the pack for really familiar friends. Normally I'm not one for hidden identity games, but the added layer of a "get to know your players" game in there makes it fun and enjoyable for someone like me as well. While you could play it more straightforward (viewing survey answers, deliberating on those who fit the answer, and then interrogation periods), my friend group that is already familiar with each other played it much laxer/sillier and we really got into "detective" roles while asking our friends to elaborate on the few traits we didn't already know. Lots of laughs to be had for familiar groups 

[b]Legends of Trivia[/b]: As someone who loves Jackbox trivia games, I tend to find they're pretty offputting for those who aren't as confident in their trivia skills. That said, making a collaborative trivia game was a crazy inspired decision. Even those who aren't fans of trivia were willing to try it and had fun! All my friend groups are big on TTRPGs, and really enjoyed the fantasy RPG elements as well as the presentation elements (art, character design, music, ect). The only criticisms my multiple groups had were having one or two categories that they did not enjoy (the image questions and hidden questions for example), which thankfully the multiple routes with multiple mode options make easy to avoid for game groups. 

Overall, I really adore this pack!! Maybe it's still in its honeymoon phase but I can see at least a couple of games in this pack being as tried and true timeless games for my friend groups as much as games like Job Job and TMP have been.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761971785}, {"review_text": "As a longtime Jackbox fan who wasn't super enamored with the last 2 packs, 11 is just what I'm looking for. If you've fallen off the Jackbox bandwagon, definitely give this one a shot!
A brief overview of the games:

Doominate - Going to be honest, I wasn't expecting this one to be as funny as it was, but it really had my friends laughing! I'm a Quiplash fan and I thought this wasn't going to be as good, but even people who usually struggle with Quiplash liked this one because the prompts made it a bit more structured.

Cookie Haus - Loads of great moments with this one too. The googly eyes, sprinkles, and depth you can get with the frosting made for some great creations. Only problem we had with this one was that some of our phones really struggled to keep up with the cookie decorating--not sure if it's because the cookie decorating technology is more sophisticated than something like Drawful, or a launch-day server issue. But the game itself was loads of fun.

Hearsay - The absolute star of the pack for us. Our friend group loves to make dumb noises and do silly voices, so this one was nonstop laughs.

Legends of Trivia - A great concept that was also a lot of fun. My only criticism is that at times it seemed pretty slow-paced, but a lot of the slowness was because of the tutorial elements (which were necessary and helpful). I'm excited to revisit this one and see if that speeds it up. There might be settings that help make it a bit faster, too, that I've missed. But it was a nice twist that the trivia was co-op, and I definitely see myself revisiting this with my more trivia-focused friends.

Suspectives - Another big standout from this pack. Truth be told, I'm a big fan of hidden role games, but I haven't always loved the ones Jackbox has put out--except this one! The survey format makes it easy to understand and also turns it into a game of how well your friends know you in real life, not just your tells, while being friendly for remote groups (unlike the somewhat similar Fakin' It).

Overall, a really excellent pack. Looking forward to playing more of it!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761304524}, {"review_text": "Another great entry in the series. A slam dunk for 4 of the 5 games

Doominate:

The latest of the "not quite quiplash" games that are getting really numerous in Jackbox. However, unlike most of the time Doominate does bring some stuff to the table that the OG doesn't. For one the format is quite different instead going for the angle with your submissions are modifying something existing to make it worse or better. And the second one is that it's much more personalized since everyone is choosing 1 of the things on top of it placing an emphasis to input stuff yourself. A solid 8/10

Hear Say: 

So this unironically a contender for the best Jackbox game period. One of only 2 sound based games in the series at that, and considering the other is the aggressively mediocre Ear Wax, Hear Say doesn't have much competition to worry about. Essentially each round you record a set of sounds via muting yourself (yes, this wins the distinction for being not the only first game to use the microphone, but also the first game to straight up not work in person); then once they're all recorded you vote on which is the funniest. Repeat for 3 rounds. Additionally, there are videos that play after a sound is chosen which put your sounds into a new visual context to hilarious results, and a pre round mini game that uses volume as an input. Both of these can be turned off which is really good because the mini games control awful and would be dragging it down if not for that. But this is consistently one of the funniest games, if not THE funniest game jackbox has come out with. A 9.5/10

Suspectives: 

A social deduction game from Jackbox... Off to a great start... Jokes aside this is the one people of their own accord asked to play again immediately. And it's pretty good tbh. Here you get asked a bunch of questions at the beginning of the game, then these questions are revealed one by one to everyone. You have to try to figure out whose lying and which of these things are what person would say. If all you care about in jackbox is the socialization and nothing else I can see an argument for being the best game in general. I am not one of those people, but I'd still be willing to put at a 9/10

Cookie Haus: 

A drawing game with the worst controls known to man and not that great of a concept to begin with. Jackbox has had 2 drawing games released prior with great drawing tools now in Tee KO 2 and Champ'd Up. So why Cookie Haus has such dog shit controls is beyond me. Sprinkles? Aren't a brush instead just dropping a set amount in an area. Undo/Eraser? Eraser isn't here and the undo button only lets you use it once. That nice feature that made line art easy to do while still coloring like a normal actual digital drawing? Sorry, but not here at all. Baffling decisions all around. Even worse, for some reason the cookies are 3d models (despite them always facing front....), and that model is what appears on the website. This causes some of the worst lag known to man for no good upside. Add that to the fact the only humor this game produces is creating bits that won't die in the interim and uh you have a game that's the only dud here

Legends of Trivia:

Oh boy where do we start with this one. For starters this is NOT a game centered around creating a dnd campaign on the fly. I know it has a art style that is based on dnd but it's completely removed from it otherwise. That would be a fire idea for a jackbox game and they should come back to that but it's irrelevant. Rather it's the 4th attempt at trying to make a normal game within the confines of jackbox, and between it, Dodo Re Mi, and Bomb Corp; Legends of Trivia is the only one I can honestly say people have specifically asked for it on multiple occasions now. 

In Legends of Trivia's case, it's actually a rogue like. A pretty good one as well actually. Essentially every attack is a trivia question, if you get it right you attack. In its current state, true failure isn't really possible instead opting for a score method. Every campaign has a set number of paths and what those hold, and there 5 or so questions right now, more on these points later. 

This has two undeniable strengths, it functions even in small groups and people don't need to be actively talking to contribute. A lot of people act like you always have a full party if you're playing jackbox, and it always involves the most sociable people. But if you're actually playing with friends you knew prior that isn't always in the cards, since you know, schedules. So the fact this game completely functions with a party of 3 or 2 does matter a lot to me in particular. And because of the nature of game being cooperative, that means 2 can be yapping while the socially awkward people in the back just sit back. I know that's a strange compliment, but I do think games like this are important. Not everyone I'm playing with is comfortable with being 100% out there. Jackbox isn't a series just catering to socialites, and that should be always remembered before complaining that it's not all about the discussion angle. Now of course, when you do have 5 or 6 players that are all socialites who feel the need to make every second filled with sound, you get a nice recreation of what everyone wanting to be the main character in a co op game looks like. And while this has happened once now in actual testing, this same pack has Hear Say, Doominate, and Suspectives. That situation is more than covered for in this pack, so it's hardly a loss and I'll always support games that fill niches that no other jackbox game can.

Now don't get it twisted Legends Of Trivia has a lot problems and WOULD benefit from a sequel, but none of the complaints I hear are good arguments. Really it's just a ton of fine tuning to make the true rogue like on jackbox experience. Like making death cost more and more every time you die, running out of gold and dying means a failed run. Campaigns that vary in length, not fixed campaigns, new items and events. That kind of thing. All in all I'd say for now an 8.5 out of 10 (tho it's closer to 7 if it wasn't being bumped by it's a niche that isn't replaceable)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761590183}, {"review_text": "As someone who has 6 of the other Jackbox games and play them quite frequently. I never write reviews for Jackbox packs but I feel I have to for this one because it's THAT good.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761453893}, {"review_text": "really really great pack, the 2 year cycle is def better than 1 year, also has some of my favorite narrators, they have so much character

best to worst:

suspectives) amazing social deduction game, everything gameplay wise it is perfect no notes, i feel like it couldve had a grittier aesthetic but i can enjoy the goofier style
my group loved it so much we went through every single survey question rip :(

hear say) incredible no notes, my only gripe is that the intermission games dont work at all unless youre in a completely soundproof room with a high end mic, but you can turn them off which is how my group plays

cookie haus) great drawing game, the way the frosting stacks on eachother is super creative looks great & very fun, unfortuntely the game is not optimized very well so everyone lags rly bad, constant freezing for half the ppl, even crashing for some

doominate) rly good quiplash clone, i LOVE that you get to make your own prompts for r2 which carry into r3 which makes infinite replayability

knights of trivia) good concept but feels very unfinished
co op trivia is very fun & the different types of monsters being each version of how the co op works is very creative, the game looks rly nice & alot of care was put into aesthetic
each character isnt different enough to warrant strategy, my groups been softlocked twice now if you use the instant attack potion at certain times in battle, my biggest gripe is that after you defeat a world boss the game just cuts to black end credits, no cutscene no congrats its very jarring & feels disappointing, multiple ppl went "...thats it??" after getting treated to a black screen for defeating the hardest boss

side note PLEASE add the ability for the game owner to kick ppl, idk why this has never been implemented, having to remake the whole lobby bc 1 person went afk or 1 persons mic doesnt work for hear say is so tedious", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763618499}, {"review_text": "Huge change from the previous pack. In pack 10 by the third game I wanted to refund it, I was laughing the whole time with this pack.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761366102}, {"review_text": "This might be the best pack they've made (though it REALLY depends on how many players you have)

Doominate is like quiplash but you have a chance to make it even funnier
Hear Say is actually really funny if you have enough people (especially over discord were you can mute in-between rounds)
Cookie haus is a game that can go very south very quickly depending on your group (but that's what makes it enjoyable)
Suspectives is probably the best social deduction game they've ever made, my group played like 6 rounds in a row, it MAKES the pack.
Legends of Trivia is fun but only if you like trivia, otherwise it just kinda turns into a slog, also don't worry the turn based elements are very light if you were concerned it might be a bit overwhelming

So yeah this pack is fantastic i think, sure it is slightly more expensive but you really feel the polish in this one so i think it's worth it. 10/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761384178}, {"review_text": "So just for context of my taste, I think packs 6, 7, and 8 are peak Jackbox, and 9 was a big ole disappointment, and I didn't even touch 10 based on reviews. And as a 6-8 fan, I think this pack is a return to form, finally introducing non-sequel games that are both creative and fun in ways we haven't seen in a while.

Hearsay is the stand-out for sure, adding a completely new aspect to Jackbox that's both fresh and hilarious. Just a pro-tip (for in-person Jackbox parties) is that it's most fun when people can very quickly spread out (in our house, some people snuck to the kitchen, some to the basement, and one even went outside to the chilly yard). This way, there is no audio interference, which becomes a big problem if all 6-8 people sit in the same room making sounds. Also, the mini-games are finnicky and not fun, but I only just found out you can turn them off.

The runner-ups for me are Suspectives and Doominate. Doominate is a fun humor-based Quiplash-esque that doesn't change the game, but is one of the more fun ones in a while. It lends itself quite quickly to what feels like effortless humor, which I think is the best metric for how fun these types of games get.
Suspectives is a social deduction game that suffers only from one flaw, which is its unclear instructions on when you're supposed to be honest and when you're supposed to be lying We settled on what works, which is to require honesty but allow vagueness in the survey round, and then allow lying in the interrogation rounds. I think that's how it's supposed to work but we had to figure it out ourselves.

Legends of Trivia we haven't tried enough to figure out if it's a hit or miss yet. It's ambitious, which I appreciate, but it feels a little too confusing for non-gamers, too slow for people just after the trivia, and having too little stakes for people who do want it to be a roguelike experience. Your mileage may vary.

In the meantime, Cookie Haus is trash. I don't know why they made it. It's literally a drawing game with more artificial constraints than ever, unnecessary 3D graphics that are always shown flat anyway, slow unfunny dialogue in between rounds, and worst controls in any drawing game that I can remember.

Cookie Haus is an easy skip, but the rest are great fun. It may be the first pack I got at full price and don't regret it whatsoever. Grab it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1762137883}, {"review_text": "I find in some of the jackbox packs that only one game is fun, in this pack I love every game! Great job!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761202047}, {"review_text": "The Jackbox Party Pack 11 is honestly one of my top favorite packs and it's right up there among my favorites such as 3 and 7.

Doominate is a brilliant joke-writing game where you take something completely innocent and ruin it. First round is ruining something they give you and the second round is writing a couple things you love and having others ruin it for you. Then the third one is a brilliant twist in then having to unruin it. Very fun game and definitely quite replayable.

Hear Say was the game I was the most skeptical on initially but it has since become one of my favorites. Very hilarious and I do think it works best over streams so people can deafen their mics on PC while playing on their phone so you can be surprised by the sounds they did make. But I'm sure it's fine for people in the same room as well. Of course, since Hear Say is a game where the players make the sounds, it is best played with players you trust but it's still a very entertaining game. I do think the intermissions are the weakest aspect of the game so I also appreciate the setting by Jackbox to skip those to keep the action of the game better paced.

Cookie Haus is another one of my favorites and this is coming from someone who isn't even the biggest fan of drawing. But the drawing tools are easy to use and it's fun to create some pretty cursed cookies. It's head-to-head playstyle is similar to Champ'd Up more-or-less but still stands on its own.

Suspectives is the social deception game of the pack and basically, it is a harder version of Fakin' It (though honestly more in the vein of something like Clue) and may take players a couple playings to get the hang of. But it's a favorite of mine and I do prefer it over something like Weapons Drawn. A cool feature Jackbox did was have a setting to set the prompts to either Strangers or Friends and it's set to Strangers by default. So the game is very much playable with people you aren't as familiar with. It also is viable on streams. It is easier with VC (or being in the same room) since you do interrogate players but not mandatory since you can use text chat for this as well. One key is to make sure you answer the survey questions honestly as you can because you may end up being innocent and if you are chosen to be the criminal, well then, then you can lie however you want then to keep from being caught.

Legends of Trivia is already another one of my favorites and has the brilliant concept of blending RPG elements with trivia and is a lot of fun working together with other players to defeat the monsters/bosses. It's the other game in the pack where having VC or being in the same room makes things easier but sharing answers in chat also works. My only thing with the game is that I wish there was more content but this is a great, experimental game from Jackbox and it's definitely one they could and should expand on in the future.

Overall, I don't think any of the games are weak entries and again the pack is right up there with 3 and 7 for me as the best ones from Jackbox as a whole.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761242950}, {"review_text": "Hear Say is hands down the most hilarious game mode I've ever played.
That, Doominate and Legends of Trivia is worth", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761470863}, {"review_text": "literally just buy this for hearsay its the best non sequel jackbox game they have released since TeeKO", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761694720}, {"review_text": "Genuinely one of the best party packs to date. I think the only party packs I may prefer (by a slim margin) are party packs 3 and 7.

DOOMINATE gives off a similar vibe to the adaptable, intuitive goofiness of Quiplash, but with the format of "ruining" a scenario, and then in another round, "re-saving" that scenario after it's been ruined. Laughs all around, no lack of inspiration, reasonable scoring metric: Great game that I foresee being a staple of our friendslop game nights for years to come.

LEGENDS OF TRIVIA is far and away the weakest link. I say this as someone who enjoys trivia, fantasy aesthetic, and cooperative games ... so it's difficult to pinpoint what all is wrong with it. Conceptually it's brilliant — the idea of a cooperative trivia game from the same folks who brought you the very unhinged, hyper-competitive TRIVIA MURDER PARTY is an excellent one. But in execution, it feels like a chore to play. Every moment you're not actively playing — which is often — is excessively drawn out. Between the narrator's bardic antics that aren't terribly funny, the overlong tutorial, the overlong battle animations that are the same animations over and over again ... it just felt like I was spending maybe 10% of the actual playtime solving trivia problems with my friends. If this game were heavily streamlined, it might be better.

COOKIE HAUS is another drawing game. It's neither this developer's worst drawing game, nor their best — because let's be honest, Tee K.O. and Champ'd Up are hysterical thanks to the hype factor. However, I did find the prompts nice and varied — there's plenty on offer to get inspired!

SUSPECTIVES was a solid social deduction game. It's certainly not more of "the usual" a la Among Us or Mafia. Fair warning, you and your friends may find the first round a little baffling ... but by round two, everyone should fully understand how the game works and it will come to life. I definitely foresee us revisiting this one from time to time.

HEAR SAY is surprisingly hilarious. This one has gotten the loudest laughs out of my group, for sure. It's worth keeping in mind that my friend group is full of quirky musicians and theater kids, though — your mileage may vary based on the personalities of your friends. I will say this: HEAR SAY is probably best-suited for remote games. We played via Discord, and the ability to mute ourselves while we recorded our goofy antics made the result a whole lot funnier and surprising. So, HEAR SAY might struggle to be as funny in-person.

All in all, while LEGENDS OF TRIVIA is a disappointment and COOKIE HAUS is fairly mid, the other three games are EXCELLENT. I highly recommend!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761513370}, {"review_text": "Hands down the best Jackbox Party Pack. None-the-less, playable games that drag a bit, but they definitely beat their last three Jackbox Party Packs including The Naughty Pack.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761272220}, {"review_text": "November: They added more content!!

Release: Very good Pack that I've played so far. I haven't played Suspectives yet as our group was 3, but everything else has been very good.

With all Jackbox Party Packs, the fun you get out of these really depends on the people you're playing with, and the mechanics of each individual game.

Doominate is less free-form than its predecessors, Break the Internet, Quiplash and even Joke Boat. However, the prompts and form actually are pretty fun. For fans of those earlier games, this one fits in there as a very good prompted writing game.

Hear Say was the one I thought would be a dud, similar to how I view Earwax, Lie Swatter, Wordspud and Zeeple Dome. These are all games that groups I've been in may have tried once, but immediately didn't see any way to have fun with them. Hear Say is actually very good! It's kind of difficult being in the same room as people making the noises you'll eventually hear again, the way they're presented is surprisingly funny. This was actually one my group of 3 returned to the most.

Cookie Haus is very similar to Tee K.O. and Champ'd Up because it's pitting two drawings against each other, but actually interesting in its limitation of cookie shapes and toppings. 

Legends of Trivia is a trivia game with an RPG-wrapper. The additional mechanics of the RPG aren't interesting, but it's trivia and that still works with my friend group. It takes a little too long to get to the questions, and begs the question of why we don't just play a pub trivia game on Youtube.

Overall, it's a very good Jackbox Party Pack with each one seemingly unique enough to not just be a sequel, and not experimental enough to be too weird and frustrating.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1762719227}, {"review_text": "every game is a winner. played with a large group and everyone had a different game as their favourite. would HAPPILY boot up this party pack to play any of the games by themselves.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761560462}, {"review_text": "After a rocky few releases, Jackbox is back at the top of their game. Very fun and clever games this time around, my favorite so far is Hear Say.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1762025173}, {"review_text": "One of the best party packs I've bought. Not one game is forgettable. I have played every Jackbox pack, and this one takes the good parts about the modern packs and brings them back to a time when all of the packs were good.

It's VERY open-ended, which from my experience means extremely group-dependent. With the right group, it could be really fun. With the wrong group, it just falls flat.

Hear Say: Jackbox really needs more audio games because they tend to be underrated bangers. This one is no different, and in fact might be better than Earwax. My major hang-up is that it would be difficult to play in-person, and is a little complicated to play over Discord. Still, very fun.

Cookie Haus: Kind of just the prototypical drawing game. It's alright, but it doesn't stand out, and I would be more likely to choose several other drawing games first.

No joke, it's a whole new kind of funny, no joke, godam!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763790609}, {"review_text": "Not a single miss in this pack! After how disappointing and messy 10 was (though Dodo Re Mi & Fixytext are still all-timers), this was a huge pleasant surprise. My group was expecting the same launch-weekend bugginess and instability that 10 suffered from, but there was none of that; the whole pack worked flawlessly. As a whole, the art and writing is immaculate; the game tries and succeeds to be funny in its presentation and writing. Our first time through we were laughing at the hosts almost as much as ourselves. Also, the music is stellar across the board. We sat and listened to every ending theme as we played, and I'm considering picking up the soundtrack.

Before I get into the nitty-gritty of the games, I also want to call attention to how streamlined they've made everything. For most of the games, you can start inputting before the explainers finish running, so there's way less waiting if you already know what to do. The VIP also gets a quick-switch menu in the browser client so you can quickly go between games in the pack with minimal fuss without needing the host to do it. There's so many things that have been done to reduce the little points of friction like that and I really appreciate the attention given there. Now, as for the games themselves:

Doominate is one of the two bests of this pack IMO, and is my group's overall favorite. The game starts really solid, but the third-round twist of fixing what was ruined in the second rounds is really what puts it over the top. It's a natural evolution of the goals set forward by Survive the Internet and Quiplash and it works so, so well. It's definitely going in our regular game rotation.

I was skeptical of Hear Say at first, but it's tied with Doominate as the best of the pack. Hear Say rewards creativity; if you've got a desk with a ton of stuff on it, and you're clever, you can do some really effective foley work depending on the prompt, and if you're playing at your computer and quick about it you can use your phone as well. I laughed the hardest I've laughed all year watching someone open the door to carolers only for the Crazy Bus theme to start blasting. I also really appreciate that the end screen lets you watch all of the previous clips, but I do wish we could do the same for the final round, too. 

Cookie Haus is the one I was looking forward to the most. It's cute and cozy and, for a competitive drawing game, actually quite forgiving! It's really fun to work with the different cookie shapes, and all the tools are good and useful, and I quite like the detail in how the fondant gets visibly layered when you're drawing over an existing cookie. Cookie Haus isn't quite blow-your-socks-off compared to the other two, but it's still one of the best drawing games in the Jackbox library and I'm looking forward to playing it again. Also, several people in my group have a crush on the host. 

The closest thing that this pack had to a dud is probably Suspectives, but I'll be honest and say upfront that our group probably just wasn't ready for what it asked us to do. I sure wasn't ready to be the guilty party right away, at least. As far as social deduction games go, it's quite open-ended outside of the bare facts about the players it presents. I like the idea, in theory, of interrogating a friend over the minor details of something, and I think that alone has huge comedic potential depending on the people you play with, but I was so NOT ready to play interrogator and as such bungled that segment completely. I think it's definitely got potential and we're going to give it another shot next weekend. 

My group mostly dislikes trivia outside of a couple of trivia freaks, which is why it's so surprising that Legends of Trivia is as fun as it is. The whole thing being cooperative means that you don't really feel left out if you don't know something. All the art is cute and the writing is funny, even if the attack animations start to feel like they take forever; especially when finishing a boss and doing a segment of supposedly fast-paced questions, it felt sometimes like we spent more time watching the same attack animations play out than actually playing the game. We stopped after doing a world, but there's three worlds total; the aforementioned trivia freaks could probably spend a whole night blowing through this game. As it stands for me, the host, I don't think I'll play it again, but I still appreciate that it exists. 

All in all, excellent work. The individual-led cabal-style production this pack had really paid off and produced five tight and engaging experiences. Seriously, it's the first Party Pack that hasn't had a single miss. It's also the first pack that felt worth $30.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761587481}, {"review_text": "[h3][b]TL;DR: This is the team's most well rounded pack in years; If you've fallen off from the series, Pack 11 might be the game worth jumping back into.[/b][/h3]

[i]anyways here's the individual reviews:[/i]

[b][u]Doominate:[/u][/b]
A Quiplash clone but a competent one. The idea is that 2 players will get something like: [b]"A BRAND NEW 4K TV!"[/b] and then have to [i]'ruin it'[/i] with something like: [b]"-but it only plays Adam Sandler films."[/b] From there everyone votes for who submitted the better response in typical Quiplash fashion. Transitions feel a bit bloated as every single prompt will play angel choir while it shows you the prompt, only to show you the prompt [i]again[/i]... for every single prompt; This won't replace Job Job or Quiplash for us, but Doominate is still solid all the same. [b]3.5/5[/b]

[b][u]Hear Say:[/u][/b]
This was the one game we were all certain was going to be the dud of the pack; It's a game that has players make a stupid sound, and then everyone votes for who recorded the best one. Seemingly a weak premise but jokes on us, because this ended up becoming one of our favorites- with many of us considering it the best in the pack. Where the magic lies is in the TV segment. Basically it will take the winning sound and play it over a corresponding video clip; The intrigue of seeing how the game will apply the dumb sound your friend made to some random stock footage is surprisingly what makes the entire experience. [b]4/5[/b]

[b][u]Cookie Haus:[/u][/b]
A drawing [strike](decorating?)[/strike] game where you're give a prompt like [i]"Weird Undiscovered Animal"[/i] and then have to make a cookie that represents that. Players then vote for which they prefer so there's still a competitive angle despite this otherwise being one of the team's more casual games. About the only misstep is the final round; You're asked to redo a cookie that someone had already submitted which just results in covering frosting with more frosting as a way to override what's already there- it feels a bit sloppy and doesn't really fit the context of the game. It's otherwise a surprisingly very quickly paced with 4 round games often being shy of 20 minutes- and the unusual approach to the drawing tools makes for a game that will likely even appeal to those who don't play drawing games. [b]4/5[/b]

[h2]
[/h2]
[b][u]Suspectives:[/u][/b]
An alright social deduction game that could’ve been so much more. You all answer a series of questions like [i]“has social media made your life better?”[/i] and then question to question it will show you the answer of the culprit who is 1 of 8 people playing. The idea is that you want to look at all the answers, and figure out who in your group would've answered all the questions like what you're seeing. Between the final written answer that is completely unique per each player, and 2 lie detectors that will straight up reveal how someone answered a question- it’s just [i]WAYYYY [/i]too easy to catch the culprit. More settings like limiting lie detectors or only receiving questions with a small number of responses could redeem this one. Cool concept and still fun; But these sort of games are always best with people you know well; However if you know your group well, things are too unbalanced. [b]3/5[/b]

[b][u]Legends of Trivia:[/u][/b]
A DnD inspired trivia game where you fight monsters by answering trivia correctly. Characters have different stats, there are shops where you can buy hints or free attacks- Such a fantastic concept but not much is done with the premise. There's not many decisions to be made outside the trivia itself, you constantly have way too much money and can only hold 2 items so anytime you visit a shop you fill both slots without fail; And the cooperative stuff rarely amounts to much beyond 1 person telling the rest of the group what the answer is to a question. Not to mention there's only 3 levels, so you can realistically complete this whole thing in an hour. As a DnD game it's unfortunately shallow, and as a trivia game it's poorly paced. [b]2/5[/b]

[h3]While no game in this pack is necessarily a run-away hit I'll be obsessing over for the foreseeable future- not a single inclusion here is [i]"bad"[/i] and I can easily see myself coming back to nearly every game with the only exception being [i]Legends of Trivia[/i]. As a stand alone purchase, Pack 11 is a good pack to get because there's great variety, and stuff like Doominate or Cookie Haus are practically proven formulas [i](since they are so similar to past fan favorites)[/i]. If you've enjoyed any of the previous packs, then 11 if confidently a safe buy.[/h3]", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761263459}, {"review_text": "massive step up from the last couple of years. plays it a little safe in some regards but i think it's kind of the exact thing jackbox needed to do right now. looking forward to the future (please give us a new you dont know jack i beg of you).

doominate - a good writing game that shares aspects of quiplash and survive the internet but manages to stand on its own, very impressive all things considered. probably the most solid overall

hear say - a surprisingly good time (over discord, in real life, dont bother) but many on my group wished for more playback options after recording. personally i think if that was available it would make my dumbass perfectionist friends (also me) redo their sounds until the very end of the timer but maybe that's just me. the option would be nice.

cookie haus - the prompts are relatively open ended and the wonky cookie shapes are great for inspiration. the drawing tools themselves are fun and definitely unique. too many of my friends want "relationships" with the host of this one (one is too many). probably my favorite as of right now

suspectives - my group didnt get this one at first and it make me go a little crazy because i watched the 2 left thumbs overview and kinda knew what was happening. will only get better with replays. probably my favorite game aesthetically.

legends of trivia - do not play this one with a stupid baby group that doesnt like trivia, i had 2 of said stupid babies and they did nothing but complain the entire time and call this the worst jackbox game ever. that soured the experience quite a bit but as such i only got 1 playthrough of the first location, with time this will probably end up being at the very least my second favorite. do not listen to the stupid babies, if you enjoy any of the trivia games you will at least appreciate this one", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761491161}, {"review_text": "I wanted to like this pack as it seems pretty neat, but there are a lot of flaws that became apparent when playing.

It is a carefully balanced clockwork mechanism of counters and synergies, but then some abilities let you move so fast and some weapons deal so much damage that "balance" doesn't even seem to be the word you'd wanna describe it with anymore. At the same time, some guns are so laughably inefficient at any range, that you can't help but think that there's something wrong with you whenever someone survives four point-blank shotgun shots to the midsection.

The game has that new-age competitive shooter sensibility, where the only pixel of your reticle that matters might as well be the one in the middle of your screen, and only if you're not in the middle of swaying, suffering from post-reload fatigue, your index finger's ligaments have rested sufficiently and you've achieved ideal stillness against the crashing waves of time and tide. Which is to say, I have never played a game that has so much faff involved with the usually simple act of pointing and shooting. Ideally, if the number that represents my current ammo is above zero, I have placed my cursor on the enemy, and I have pressed my mouse button - the shot will go exactly where it has been pointed. But in this new age of realism, it will go wherever the virtual barrel of my gun was point at for the three frames of animation that occur as the simulated sway of character movement and recoil affect the hairs on my moustache. Everything aims like a railgun, and all the other modes of targeting might as well be secondary.

Then, in the immediate next round, you'll barely fire a shot, spending all your time healing, taking some walls down because you'd like a more open-plan, placing traps, rotating turrets around, rearranging the furniture, moving some barrels around, and somehow win through sheer strength of interior decor.

Eventually, you'll stop and wonder who this game is for: Is it the speed-junkie teenager, who has just taken his entire prescription in one final gulp in order to put to practice all 2000 hours of beginner guides, watched over a femtosecond of real time at 1,358,892,119x speed, in which his neural pathways will chart a course through the three-dimensional space of holes in walls, broken ceilings, and dematerialized surfaces in order to secure one singular kill, rupturing his pre-frontal cortex as he narrowly escapes by turning invisible, only to walk into his own team's mines?

Is it for the guy who hasn't missed a single shot in the last twenty years of playing hardcore first-person shooter games, who suffers cardiac arrest the moment someone even mentions the words "skill-based matchmaking"?

Is it for the phlegmatic cantaimforshit guy in the back of the room, who is too busy building a zen garden out of barrels, turrets and loose chairs, who is still too engrossed in duct-taping their turret, and three different mines onto a throwable gas tank to notice that the fight has moved on to a completely different section of the map?

The truth is, it's kind of for all of them, and they all can't stand each other's guts. It's kind of a unique problem to have. If nothing else, it speaks to the originality and variety of the experience the game provides.

There's game-modes for people who want to be competitive and really show off how good they can train their aim, how precisely they can coordinate with their team, how many angles and power positions they can exploit. There are also modes for people who'd just wanna try and blow some people and buildings up, while trying to play for an objective, with little to no consequence on other players' experience. All the ones with unlimited respawn tokens are good in my opinion. That and the seasonal progression for the quickplay modes and the World Tour give you points even if you lose, and don't rank down ever, so it's all win-win.

The rewards you get for engaging in all of this range from being generous and creative to a recolour of a weapon that you don't even own and tacky street/tech/sportswear kitsch. There's at least five different progression tracks, all with their individual currencies, points, and rewards - the kind of thing that'd make a Korean MMO blush. I personally couldn't care less, but the good thing is that everything requires play to get. There's no way to buy the new weapons without sitting down and getting some matches in. It gives you a functional goal to work towards to at the very least, unless you're one of those people interested in that ultra rare green bucket hat that they keep dangling in front of you.

As of the latest season, they even let you disable hearing all the post-season-2 music tracks that would have you think the game has lost its attitude, and added Team Deathmatch into the already rich selection of game-modes to choose from. These are both good things, and have managed to sway my heart into getting back into this mess of a game. Limbus Company is a shadow continuation of the popular trilogy that began with Lobotomy Corporation, which released some time ago. That first title was created by only a small handful of developers, and even now, despite being in a stronger position than before, Project Moon is still a relatively small indie studio. Many of the negative reviews overlook this background and act as if review bombing couldn’t damage the studio’s reputation.

They gave us a gacha game, but this time it wasn't your typical Genshin give us your money and you MIGHT play the game type of experience. Limbus Company is generous, to the point where it is almost pointless to buy the in-game currency, which is the main income for gacha games. Back to sleep time gn everyone.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 56, "timestamp_created": 1758761352}, {"review_text": "good game but jihoon PLEASE grow a spine and go through with your nerfs, tell your playerbase to fuck off if you have to", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 35, "timestamp_created": 1748263372}, {"review_text": "Great characters and amazing story. only problem is that the characters arent kissing every 10 minutes", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 178, "timestamp_created": 1750597742}, {"review_text": "From time to time, I fall into the pit of gacha gaming, as horrible as that sounds. I’ve played my fair share of them, and still do, but usually drop most of them at some point. Right now, there’s only two that have a tight hold on me: Arknights, and Limbus Company.

I started this game because I heard they would collaborate with Arknights, and solely because of that… and oh boy, I wasn’t prepared for what I was getting into.

Let’s set aside the glaring elephant in the room (the gacha) for now, and focus on what really grabbed my attention: the setting.

To begin with, Limbus Company is the third game in a series. To my knowledge, it all started with Lobotomy Corporation (a SCP-esque management game), and continued with Library of Ruina (a deck-building roguelike). All three of them share the same universe, as a continuous timeline.

The stage is set in a dystopian, corporate-driven world… Which just sounds great, doesn’t it? Despite how it actually sounds, it’s what really drew me in as I began learning more about it.

Our playground is ‘The City’: an urban complex comprised of twenty-six districts, each of them ruled by a ‘Wing’ (the most powerful corporations around). The very concept of these corporations is really fun, as each of them have their own ‘Singularity’; a piece of technology unique to each of them, and so important that it’s pretty much the very backbone of their influence over a district.

Add to that Fixer Agencies (mercenary offices, so to speak), with their own rankings and distinct beliefs or creeds, Abnormalities (monstrous entities, manifestations of the human mind), or the mysterious Head (the ones at the top, overseeing The City with apparent omnipresency) and you have a pretty intriguingly built world.

As for the story itself, we play as Dante, the amnesiac, clock-shaped-head manager of the LCB (Limbus Company Bus), and we’re accompanied by a, huh, merry band of twelve misfits labeled as the ‘Sinners’ (each of them based on a literary work, by the way!)

This is one of the key aspects that, for me, separate Limbus Company from other gacha games, and one that keeps me really invested in the plot. 

Contrary to other games, where the new, shiny unit gets to be the focus of the story for a bit and then completely vanishes, in Limbus Company things are a bit different. 

Here, the twelve Sinners are the only playable characters, and the game keeps them both prevalent and relevant. What you pull (gacha) for is Identities: alter ego and ‘possibilities’ from different worlds, and their EGO (basically, ultimate moves). Since the cast is so ‘reduced’ (despite being twelve, bear with me), I could really get attached to them. 

Each Canto (chapter) focuses on one of the Sinners, going through something related to them, such as their past. Seeing their character development, or the interactions between them, is what drives me to keep tagging alongside them. It helps a lot that each of the Sinners has their own personality, background, and goals, as they’re very well developed thanks to their prevalence.

As for the gameplay, it’s… an acquired taste? The story sections are all reading, like a visual novel, but the combat is an interesting mix of turn-based and strategy with a bit of luck, and despite looking very simple, it can get deep real fast. 

It has various mechanics to be mindful of, like the speed of your Sinners and their enemies, their sanity, and other things I would have a lot of trouble explaining. Basically, you deploy your units and select all the skills they’ll use on your turn, using them to ‘clash’ against your enemies’ skills in a round of dice-rolling.

I prefer to not confuse anyone with my poor explanations, so I’ll end it at that. Still, it can get very fun! …And sometimes, hard.

On a more technical aspect, the art direction is also really good at setting the ambience. Bloody corridors, dark backstreets; it all sets the mood so well. Add to that the sound effects… I simply love it. 

The character designs are top-notch, and a high plus for suit lovers (no comment). The music itself is perfect, with tracks from the band MILI for the opening and most of the Canto boss fights. These songs even loop or change depending on the fight’s paces and all, it’s great. There’s also voice acting (though only Korean), and it’s actually really good!

So now then, let’s talk about the dreaded gacha. What I can say is that it’s not THAT bad, but hear me out. 

While other gacha games have a ‘sparking system’ (basically, pulling accumulates a currency you can exchange for the character, or things along those lines), Limbus also has a shard system.

This system allows you to collect shards of each Sinner to exchange for their different Identities or EGO, and it’s a currency you get by acquiring duplicate Identities on the gacha… or by farming the Mirror Dungeon! (a rogue-like-ish mode). 

This means you can pretty much get almost, ALMOST, every Identity or EGO for free just by playing. It does take grinding, and it depends on how much time you’re willing to spend (and buying the $11 battle pass increases the shard acquisition), but not many games give players an option like this to begin with.

All in all, I think it’s a phenomenal story with endearing, cool characters, an intriguing, yet dark world, and tons of rewarding moments. It helps a lot that the game had two other previous entries as a foothold, so the world-building only expands upon that, and does it expand geez.

There’s many other things I haven’t mentioned, like Walpurgis night and so on, but I think that’s enough for now. 

Despite being a gacha, I can’t recommend it enough. [{"review_text": "Named my newspaper, The Washington Post so I could give out political bribes, sway elections, and do PR for criminal cover-ups just like the real Jeff Bezos.

Now lemme just take off my clown nose for a sec to genuinely say, this really is a fun and engaging management sim, 8.5/10. I tip my newies cap off to the devs.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 145, "timestamp_created": 1763491301}, {"review_text": "Some games get everything just right - the game, narrative and visual design is fantastic, the balance is fair, the progression is exciting, the customisation is really fun. You will name your staff and get invested in their careers, cheering their victories or cursing their failures. You will assemble a solid collection of articles for your reputable paper or chuck every half-assed report together in haste for your despicable tabloid. Whatever you decide to do, however you play, pressing that "Print" button and watching your paper go through the printing machine will never, ever get old.

I played a bunch of this during EA, and I can't quite express the pleasure it was to go through this game, knowing I would be back time and time again. Because there is nothing quite like it, it is filled with soul, deliberate and thoughtful design, a sense of time and place. An easy recommend for any management/tycoon-game lovers out there.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763426064}, {"review_text": "Good game. Its a little stressful but in the good way where it makes you forget everything except for the game", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761955847}, {"review_text": "Since Early Access, I've enjoyed playing News Tower.
It's a fun blend of office management and strategy.

you create a news paper by sending out reporters to cover the news. Then when it's ready, send it to the production line for print.  Once that's done, you sort out which articles make the front page.
Each news article has it's own unique set of icons. Each one acts like a daisy chain if paired with other like articles.  So you can make your front page all about Crime for a bonus, more so if you have matching side news like if it's dealing in scandal, gossip, or whatever.

The interface has a fun way of feeling weighted. Like the HUD is as much a part of your newspaper assembly line.

The bgm is soothing with a energetic tempo and relaxing vibe as you work your news empire.

Overall, I will say this game's a buy.
It's fun, simple, casual and engaging.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763512828}, {"review_text": "It's easy to make a management/simulation game with military units, resource units or buildings, but to make it with an abstract concept like managing a newspaper requires a certain genius and they totally pulled it off. The gameplay is engaging, the choices are meaningful, there are always multiple factors to consider, progression is perfect, upgrades are fun, balance is almost perfect.

Feedback List:
* A good story should be better than simple advertisement, to get a story to 1000$ you need 1 gold (400), 1 silver (200), 3 bronze (300) and 3 quality stars (120) or a combo. There is no way to beat a 1500, 2000, 2500, or 3000 advertisement. Therefore you basically always should put advertisements in the multiplier slots, which does not feel good. I should have to carefully think if a story or ad is better. If I have an awesome story, I should be benefitting from putting it as a headliner.
* Editors should have more to do
* Prestige also should have a chance to add a quality star. If it is just speed, I can also get speed by hiring more people.
* Quality stars should be able to go to 6
* Reporters on photography desk should still be able to use their 2 other reporter skills
* You should not be able to keep news from getting old by deliberately slowing them down to not finish before Sunday -> news should get old based on creation date, not finishing date
* 1 pixel of comfort is as good as 100 comfort, this should not be the case -> 1 pixel comfort should be 50% concentration, 100 comfort should be 100% concentration or something -> low concentration should also give more negative tags that the editor can fix
* It's a bit lame that you can circumvent protestors by dragging reporters over them
* It should be possible to have i.e. 2 scandal tags on a story (major scandal) if one tags is standard and the other was added via trait
* There should be an end-game use for influence when you have unlocked everything, like spending influence to get more sales, better ads or better hires.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1746679142}, {"review_text": "This game is incredibly polished, cute, delightful, and absolutely full of heart... while ALSO being a ruthlessly challenging management simulator that gave me (a person with thousands of hours in business, management, and logistics simulators) a sincere challenge at times. So far, as I enter into the midgame on my initial difficulty playthrough, I've been really taken aback by how many new mechanics are integrated (quite gracefully) which naturally add to that sense of ever-increasing difficulty. With that said, I'm not sure how much of the total challenge is intentional, as I think some mechanics definitely take a second to figure out, and the tutorial (while delightful) does leave some to be desired. But honestly, I am mostly stunned and delighted by this absolute GEM of a game. What a treat!! :)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763543416}, {"review_text": "While this game is initially fun, it becomes quickly apparent that this is indeed not a simulation game that lets you build a Newspaper Empire in the 30s, but rather a 2D-Version of a "Two Point Museum/Hospital/Campus" with Newspaper as its topic.

What I mean by this is the fact that just about every mechanic in this game is more or less a minigame with little to no impact, giving the game the depth of a puddle the janitor leaves when mopping the floor.

There are good ideas in this game, such as "conquering" areas of the city to widen the area where you sell well and gain subscriptions, yet this is not based on the quality of your paper for example, but simply whethere you print a few topics they like to read about. On the matter of quality: It simply does not exist. You can even just print old news, and while this will give you a penalty to sales, you'll still sell.

Another good idea would have been the direction of your paper, giving you the option of being more informative or more sensational. The big issue here is: It truly does not matter. The only influence this has is once again to feed a minigame that gives you certain bonuses if you are particularely this or that this week.

And here comes my biggest issue with the game: It is so episodical it hurts. Whatever you did last week has basically no influence on your reception for this week, or at most, for one week. Opportunities for Ads arise based on the topics you printed the week before. But instead of being able to establish yourself as, say, a conservative economy paper and having a steady audience in this area, also gaining steadily Ads to print for this target market, you'll only gain Ads for the following week if you printed a lot of one topic the previous week, and even if you do not print anything of said topic in the week you print the Ad. Totally ridicolous.

To summarize: The game may scratch an itch if you like arcade-y minigames, but fully fails in terms of a strategic simulation that requires any kind of planing or offers any kind of realism.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763724469}, {"review_text": "I really didn't want to give this a thumbs down. Honestly it's fun and the first 5 hours of gameplay were a blast. But it became stale FAST. 

Here's how I think the game can be improved:
1) Add competing publishers so we have big picture goals - e.g. to become the number 1 tabloid newspaper in Manhattan
2) More sandbox please! Let us take down the Mafia with news stories, or have an antagonistic mayor who is out to shut your business down and it's your job to make sure the newspaper's clout outweighs the mayor's (depending on who you side with, of course)
3) Have a credibility meter where you can embellish stories for a quick buck but over time this diminishes your reputation

Basically, the gameplay loop, while fun, is trivial. The game badly needs more difficulty, deeper thinking, strategy and sandbox elements. Game's still in EA so there's hope.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1748623097}, {"review_text": "This game is an unexpected gem.  

Positive (negative below):

I generally gravitate towards management games with a city builder/ colony survival theme, but this game caught my interest and- I am seriously hooked!  The management aspect is what you'd expect, a game that sometimes has you starting over and questioning your previous choices while you grow, expand and learn. The cartoon style isn't my normal thing but the design is just kind of perfect for the game. The music is good, the story line and mechanics are a fresh concept.  If you like management/tycoon sort of games, definitely add this little keeper to your library.  


A little Negative:

***Update after full play through*** - I will note that it felt like it ended prematurely.  When you start you are given a world map and it lead me to believe that I had goals on each continent to complete before reaching end game/ more bosses so to say like the 3 in the beginning.  I managed to complete the entire game without leaving the state ( a bit of a let down I'll say). I do see that there is an endless mode, but it's really just a sandbox with no rewarding play. Like a 'Oxygen Not Included' but less detrimental.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1763514015}, {"review_text": "Game News Tower has potential, but the execution feels like an early-access project that never grew up. The UI is non-intuitive, cluttered, and far more complicated than it needs to be. For a game built around managing employees, it’s baffling that there’s no simple way to view an employee’s job history or see what tasks they’ve previously failed at. Without that, it’s almost impossible to identify underperformers, which defeats the entire purpose of a management simulator.

Hiring and replacing employees is just as frustrating. There’s no convenient way to compare stats between current staff and new applicants, forcing constant back-and-forth between tabs and data tables. It’s an awful user experience that slows down gameplay rather than supporting it.

Despite being “released,” the game still feels like early access. I really wanted to like it—the trailer sold me—but after playing, I genuinely wish I had refunded it while I had the chance.

The tutorial also feels unnecessary in most steps, and even when I tried to turn it off—and it claimed I was off-rails—it kept hammering me with pop-up windows. I couldn’t find any way to disable it entirely, which only added to the frustration.

Buyer beware despite looking good on a surface this game is just a drag and drop simulator in it's core.

Adding, after giving it a second try:
The faction system leaves you with almost no real freedom. Deadlines become absurd when the required story only drops on a Friday (and believe me it drops on Thu or Fri more than you wish it did), making it harder to meet than a corporate project sprint in real life. The paper system is also completely unreliable—your inventory might show 400+ units, yet only a fraction actually exists on racks, making it impossible to plan production since your main resource just vanishes into thin air. And finally, the employee behavior is nonsensical; aside from reporters, everyone else seems to live at the office 24/7 like they’re camping under their desks, like Elon Tusk (All characters and events in this text— even those based on real people — are entirely fictional).

Devs, please take notes from games like RimWorld, Factorio, Oxygen Not Included, and many others. Those titles have hundreds of times more mechanics, stats, and data tables than News Tower — yet they still manage to deliver cleaner, more intuitive, more user-friendly UI designs than what we have here.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1763614165}, {"review_text": "Easily the best game I've played in some time.  Great design, great depth, very fun to play... it really does put you in the seat of a newspaper publisher walking the line.  You can print libelous trash to appease the sensationalists, or factual news to keep readers informed.  You can print lies to make the mafia happy, or puff pieces about how great the mayor is.  Every week I watch the Sunday clock wind down hoping my reporters and typesetters will get their work done in time to hit the press.

Excellent game.  Please make more like this,", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1751253226}, {"review_text": "This is how you run an early access campaign. It's more employee-management than anything, and you don't really have any control over the "newspaper" part of the game aside from the bare minimum of placing them in the paper and hitting weekly goals you've selected.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1756873746}, {"review_text": "This game joins the rich tradition of games that made their UI significantly worse for the 1.0 release. If you already own the game you can have a fun time switching back and forth between the legacy version the official release noting all the ways the game is worse now. The build menu is smaller and organized in a bizarre fashion that makes items appear twice in the same menu tab. The font was changed to a tiny block script that's impossible to read and also completely destroys the old fashioned vibe the game used to have. If you don't own the game... continue that happy state.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1763627155}, {"review_text": "In [b]News Tower[b], players take on the role of a newspaper publisher in 1930s New York City. The game combines elements of strategy and management as you build and operate your newspaper empire. Starting with a modest office, you hire reporters, assign them to various beats—such as Sports, Crime, Society, Economy, Entertainment, and Politics—and manage the production and distribution of your newspaper. The game challenges players to balance journalistic integrity with business interests, often presenting moral dilemmas, such as choosing between truthful reporting and yielding to external pressures from entities like the Mafia or political figures .

The game captures the essence of 1930s New York with its art deco visuals and jazz-infused soundtrack, providing a nostalgic and atmospheric experience. Players must manage various aspects of newspaper production, including reporter assignments, article editing, and layout design, all while responding to weekly events and reader interests. The game presents ethical decisions that impact your newspaper's reputation and relationships with different factions, adding depth to the management mechanics. Beyond assigning tasks, players must also ensure the well-being of their staff, addressing issues like workplace comfort and satisfaction to maintain productivity.

The more you play, the more things you'll unlock, meaning you'll never run out of ideas on what to do next. For now, employees didn't have the ability to upgrade skills (except for items that do so) and have not been as independent, but it is expected that this will all work normally in the full release. Rather, the Early Access version will contain one part of the main campaign (up to 6 hours of gameplay), Sandbox mode that allows you to create your newspaper the way you want, 100+ objects to build from printers to luxury decorative items, 24 types of jobs, more than 1000 news to report on.

[b]News Tower[b] offers a compelling blend of historical context, strategic management, and ethical decision-making. While still in Early Access, its strong foundation and positive reception suggest a promising future for players interested in unique simulation experiences.

There is some minor RNG that can screw up some planning, but it's BARELY even a speed bump in the majority of cases.

The amount of customization and "flavoring" as to how you style your own paper (the supposed thing that this game is about) is incredibly limited in it's ability to actually CHANGE what you are doing and that is the *biggest flaw* of this game for me - nothing really changes. I don't mind it, but this feels like a lot of wasted potential for something more.

Which would be fine enough, if the 'faction system' and the idea of 'picking what stories to publish' was more fleshed out and not just  - "you can pick this story and get more money, or don't pick this story and get money elsewhere". 

As pointed out in some of the positive reviews, there's not a lot of overall choices to do as a player, and you end up in the same loop that is relatively easy enough, which in turn makes the game super boring.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1739997937}, {"review_text": "TLDR: It's wildly addicting with many possible directions you can take your company in. Highly recommend, even at full price. Even for an EA (early access) game, I strongly feel confident this game will continue to do well in the future.

**Reviewed on EA version 0.18.605.r**

News Tower is a business sim set in the 1930s of a fledgling Newspaper business that you (per typical cliché) inherit from said family member (which always happens to be some uncle). Your task is to make money and grow your business and release breaking news stories across NYC. 

At the end of the main storyline (which took me roughly 25hrs), you get a score based off certain factors such as but not limited to; most sold units, combos, tower height, unlockables, etc. This feature mimics a score system similar to Game Dev Tycoon in a good way; giving you an opportunity to replay again and with the knowledge you earned while playing and get a better score.

The gameplay is absolutely addicting. As you grow your business, you will have to work to access to other technologies such as photo imagines, maps, illustrators, and much more. There is plenty to do that will keep you engaged. The stories that you have sent your reporters to gather, some are based off real events that has happened such as the election of FDR, the great depression, and Babe Ruth’s journey with the NY Giants. And as those stories release with your weekly newspaper, you gain more subscribers who always buy your paper; whether it’s more informational, sensational, or moderate overall.

Graphics: Absolutely stunning, I really enjoy the art style the devs went with. It’s a very clean design similar to Fallout Shelter, for example. The texts/fonts are very fitting. The maps are nicely made. All of this while having such INCREDIBLY low system requirements; only needing a Intel Core i3 6100 & a 1GB discrete GPU is crazy, that’s 10 year old hardware! That’s Skylake and Maxwell era technologies!

Music/Audio; Very fitting for the era. It feels like it goes with the theme well, it’s not music that I would get sick of hearing while playing for hours on end; its enjoyable. Every click and sound effect is unique and satisfying. 

Moving onto somethings that need improvements, none of which are game breaking, just annoyances:

-	Sometimes, employees get stuck at either a door or an elevator, and they seem to pile up for no reason. A simple save->main menu->reload will fix it. However, sometimes I wouldn’t notice it happening for a while; if you have multiple floors and you’re not looking, it can set you back.

Another game where I would love a 'mixed' option on whether I would recommend it. News Tower does a lot of things right and has a lot of things where it encourages you to keep going just one more week, which very quickly turns into hours. But it also does a lot wrong and becomes very frustrating to play.

First what it does right. It's a great idea and concept for a game. The news, sending out reporters and picking what news is important for you to run and what you should drop is great. There are varied stories and multiple playstyles are possible, allowing you to run news the way you want to. There are factions with their own things going on and a lot of interesting challenges on what they want you to print. As the main gameplay loop, this is great. It makes me want to play more!

But then we get to what it does poorly. The default tower is too small. There is no space to place everything you need to run your newspaper, even without placing largely cosmetic things like plants and coat racks. At first, my skepticism was a bit high due to the fact that it isn’t exactly developed by Kunos, but Supernova Games Studios instead, a company I had never heard of until the announcement. I was worried they got the license only to surf on the franchise’s massive reputation and deliver something quite underwhelming. 

Skepticism aside, I’ve always been a huge rally fan, so - locked and loaded with the possibility to refund within two hours of gameplay -, I decided to give it a go. To be fair, I was no longer as skeptical as before because some creators had the opportunity to try it in advance, and the feedback was overwhelmingly positive regarding the key aspects, which further influenced my decision to proceed and hope for the best.

I realized the game was released at 11:57 my time, and I was loading into a stage by 12:05. The first rally of choice could be no different from Wales (the 11km one). By 12:08, I was already in a ditch with my car completely ruined. The most surprising part is how quickly I managed to get everything configured (I didn’t really have to assign anything; my Logitech G29 worked from the get-go), which is always good to see. The driving experience in AC Rally is nothing short of spectacular: the weight transfer on corners, feeling the gravel sticking to the rear tires as you step on the gas, the barely useful brakes that send you flying into a ditch - everything feels authentic and natural, as it should be.

Despite being an Unreal Engine 5 title, which generally correlates with poor performance and slightly washed-out visuals, AC Rally is one of the exceptions to the rule, boasting jaw-dropping visuals across both vehicles and environments. Surely enough, the fact that the stages are laser-scanned definitely helps, but you can tell they have paid great attention to trackside (stageside?) detail, vegetation (it’s impressively pretty and very distinct, with a massive difference between the two locations at hand), and the overall ambiance is very convincing. As for performance, I’m achieving around 60 to 80 fps on the Ultra preset in 1440p (32 GB RAM, Ryzen 7 9800X3D, RTX 3080 10 GB), which isn’t too shabby considering my GPU is five years old. I was actually very impressed that it ran as well as it did.

It is essential to keep expectations in check, though: this is an early access title, and there are only ten cars and two locations, each with two unique variants (and multiple layouts); therefore, do not expect hundreds of hours of content just yet. Granted, it’s under active development, and the developers will surely add new features as time goes by. However, as of now, the option roster is very limited, and the low price point reflects that.
