This one concerned me at first, so close after Assetto Corsa Evo, another Assetto Corsa game? Another EARLY ACCESS Assetto Corsa Game? If you have any grey matter left in your head, this should be ringing alarm bells, and for good reason.

Assetto Corsa Rally feels like what DiRT Rally 2 should've improved, packed into a small, neat little tech demo.

# The Good
Most of the game is part of this category, so let me just start: 
The Physics are great, although i personally feel like the car suspension is too bumpy on almost all cars, the tyres feel great, cars move how they should move, differentials behave exactly as i imagine them to, it's incredible how quickly you feel at home in your car.

The Graphics are spectacular, although performance is "Okay", the game looks the part, colour grading, car models, trackside objects, trees, everything looks spectacular, nothing more needs to be said, just look at the screenshots on the store page.

The cars look and feel authentic, slow cars feel slow, fast cars feel fast, it seems every car also has their engine bay and trunk modelled, which is a massive upgrade compared to AC Evos half-assed ports of ACC Cars.

## The Bad
As with all Early Access Kunos releases so far, this one lacks in content as well, although not nearly as bad as the release of AC Evo, with only 2 locations (with each around 8 or so variations), it does get old fairly quick, hopefully Supernova Games can keep up the pace and add more stages in the near future.

As with the track list, so the car list is very limited, pretty much every decade of rally is currently represented with at least one car.

## The Ugly
Force Feedback just isn't quite there yet, a lot of users, me included, feel like the FFB stiffens up in places where it doesn't feel like it makes sense, and its either too sloppy or much too harsh, there is also not much in the way of Force Feedback Settings, or Controls Settings at all, playing on a controller is a waste of 20 bucks.

Having spent countless hours with Richard Burns Rally, which I still regard as the gold standard for realistic rally simulations, my expectations were naturally high.

At this early stage, it’s clear that the game has strong potential, but it currently falls short in a few key areas. The most noticeable issue, in my experience, is the lack of proper side grip. The car dynamics don’t yet convey the natural balance and feedback you’d expect when driving on loose surfaces. Suspension and tire physics, in particular, need further refinement to deliver the authentic feel that real rally drivers are looking for.

That said, there’s a lot to appreciate. The sound design is excellent, capturing the essence of modern rally cars with impressive depth and clarity. Visually, the game is stunning — the environments, lighting, and car models are all top-tier.

In summary, this is a title with immense promise, but it’s not quite ready to satisfy those seeking a truly realistic rally experience. I would recommend waiting for a few major updates that address the physics before fully committing.

I’ll continue to play and follow the game’s development closely, and I’m confident that with the right improvements, it could become one of the best rally simulations on the market. For now, though, it remains a work in progress.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SMALL EDIT ( 11-14-2025)


After reading through the comments, it seems that some people have formed opinions about me as a person and about why I gave the game a thumbs-down in my review.

The reasoning behind my thumbs-down was simply to make the developers aware of my concerns. With so many positive reviews already posted, I wanted my perspective to stand out rather than just follow the “wave.”

I never said the game is terrible or that people shouldn’t buy it. What I did say was that the points I raised were meant as constructive criticism — not something bad, but aspects I personally would have liked to see handled differently. If others feel differently, that’s completely fine, but this is what I want, nothing more.

Regarding my rally driving background, it seems some people misunderstood or didn’t read carefully. I’m not claiming to be the fastest driver in Sweden or the best out there, but I have had significant success in my class from 2021 to 2024. The 2025 season has not been my year so far, and I’ve struggled to adapt to a new car.

I hope this clears things up. It was never my intention to hate on the game if that’s how someone interpreted it — quite the opposite. And yes, I used ChatGPT to help clean up my review so it would be easier for everyone to understand.

And certainly not to put myself on a pedestal in any way.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

DETAILED EDIT  (11-18-2025)


In my earlier impressions, I highlighted that the game had strong potential but lacked the side grip, suspension behavior, and overall feedback needed to truly satisfy players searching for realistic rally physics. I want to expand on those initial thoughts and provide a more detailed review.

First, the game excels in several areas. The graphics are outstanding especially during night stages, where the way light interacts with the road and surrounding environment creates a level of immersion that few racing titles achieve. Combined with the replay system and its varied camera angles, the presentation sets a new technical standard.

The audio design is equally impressive. With a proper audio setup, the engine notes, environmental effects, and overall soundscape deliver genuine goosebumps. Even through regular headphones, the quality stands out. That said, I still miss certain mechanical details, such as the characteristic bite of straight-cut gears during aggressive downshifts.

Another strong point is the ability to adjust road conditions beyond simply “wet” or “dry.” Options such as optimal or green surface states add valuable realism for players who want a more authentic rally experience.

However, the core driving experience still needs work, particularly on gravel. Suspension, tire, and braking physics don’t yet provide the confidence and predictability you expect from a proper rally simulation. Situations where you must slow to unrealistic speeds just to keep the rear from stepping out highlight that the car balance still requires refinement. The cockpit and hood camera also feel too rigid, lacking the natural movement that should follow the car’s dynamics, even after adjusting available settings.

The default car setups have similar issues. While personal preference always plays a role, the baseline should be solid enough that players don’t feel forced to overhaul half the setup just to achieve drivability.

Finally, the pacenotes need greater consistency. At times they feel late or mismatched from corner to corner, even when set to the earliest call-out option.

These points are not complaints born from negativity! They come from someone who sees the game’s enormous potential. I want to emphasize, as I did before, that this is my personal perspective based on real rally experience and thousands of hours in simulations. And despite the flaws, I still believe the game is absolutely worth purchasing, especially at a discount, because its foundation is extremely promising and the development team clearly cares about quality.

With the right improvements to gravel physics, camera behavior, default setups, and pacenotes, this title could evolve into one of the strongest rally experiences on the market. I remain optimistic  and I look forward to giving it a thumbs-up once those key areas reach the level the rest of the game already demonstrates.

I would like to add that these are my opinions. If you don't think the same, that's fine, I mostly just want to share my opinion and give constructive criticism. Epic rally game, well worth in EA but also hyped for what new cars and stages they add.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1763489272}, {"review_text": "After nearly 500 hours with DiRT Rally 2.0, and getting bored after just a few dozen hours with other rally games, only about 3 hours with Assetto Corsa Rally were enough for me to realize — this is what I’ve been waiting for since DiRT Rally 2.0.

I bought it instantly when I saw the name Assetto Corsa Rally, because I’d already spent over 100 hours with the original Assetto Corsa almost a decade ago.

Graphics are stunningly realistic. The cars are incredibly detailed — even the mirrors are meticulously crafted and functional. The rally stages are full of curves, bumps, and uneven terrain that look so real it feels like the developers literally scanned an entire stage from real life. The color grading and lighting are superb, creating an atmosphere that feels alive.

Sound design is another highlight: the roar of the engine, the crunch of gravel, the rain hitting the roof, the muffled cheering of the crowd — everything is rich and detailed.

Physics are phenomenal. I’m extremely satisfied with how the car moves, how it interacts with the surface, and the overall driving feel on gravel, wet roads, and asphalt. I use a Logitech G923, and it works beautifully here.

Watching replays is pure joy — they look like real rally footage. The way the car slides by, the grass and trees reacting to the airflow — it’s breathtaking. One thing that really impressed me is how hard it is to recover once the car starts sliding or losing traction, just like in real rally videos. This game rewards drivers who understand car behavior and punishes careless driving — casual players may find it brutal at first, but veterans will love it.

Driver and co-driver animations are surprisingly well done, reacting naturally to bumps, slides, and impacts. Even the crowd NPCs are impressive — they actually follow your car with their heads as it passes, unlike many other rally games where spectators look like frozen mannequins. The small details, like NPCs standing on the track and running away as your car approaches, are straight out of real-life rally footage — incredibly immersive.

I love watching replays after each stage, and the developers didn’t disappoint. The visuals are sharp and clean, with excellent lighting, realistic car movement, and believable interaction with the environment, spectators, GoPro-style camera angles, and dynamic weather — all of it looks great to excellent.

Performance is also solid. I can play smoothly on High settings without using DLSS or FSR, which is very satisfying.

There’s still room for improvement to make this the ultimate rally simulator.

Input customization: I really hope the full release includes proper input configuration. It would be great to have presets for popular steering wheels. As a serious sim racer, I don’t use a gamepad — my wheel is recognized, but I can’t map functional buttons for in-game menus, so I have to use the keyboard and mouse for adjustments.

NPC details: The crowd looks great, but it’s a bit funny that many NPCs holding phones have static lock screens instead of camera views. It’s not a big deal, but maybe darkening or blurring those screens would look more natural, especially in low light or night stages.


Overall, for someone who has spent countless hours in sim racing, this is the best rally experience after DiRT Rally 2.0 — in visuals, sound, and driving physics. With just a few small improvements, it could become truly legendary.

If the developers release DLCs in the future, I’ll buy them without hesitation.

I don’t even know where to begin with MLB Rivals, but let’s start with the absolute worst part: the menus. Who designed these? A team of people who have never played a video game before? Everything is cluttered, laggy, and confusing as hell. It’s like they actively went out of their way to make navigating the game as frustrating as possible.

Want to check your roster? Get ready to click through five different screens just to get there. Want to upgrade a player? Hope you enjoy waiting for unnecessary animations and load times. And don’t even get me started on the UI design—everything looks like a cheap mobile cash grab rather than an actual, well-thought-out sports game.

Oh, and the lag? Scrolling through menus feels like dragging a rock through the mud. Button presses don’t always register, and half the time, I have to back out and reload just to get where I need to go. This isn’t some small indie project—we’re talking about an MLB-licensed game! [{"review_text": "I do appreciate the efforts of the developers to fix the issues with the game. I just finished another attempt at  playing and again I became frustrated with the forced age transition. The age transition is is the major problem; Cities revert to towns wasting time and effort, forcing the change of civilizations and leaders disrupts the continuity you claim to have fixed, being unable to stop the relentless religious conversions, having to redistribute resources, and many other issues...

I am 69 years old and a long time player/lover of this game.  I honestly believe the only way to salvage what to me is a major disappointment is to allow players to disable the "age" transition aspect of Civ 7.  Like many others I am going back to the older versions until this is remedied, and I will no longer purchase any future versions of the Civ series.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 27, "timestamp_created": 1757725818}, {"review_text": "I've played every Civ since the first one. This game has the chance be great - maybe in a few months with updates and mods, but right now, it's not great. It has some fatal flaws. 

The game doesn't lack features - it is FULL of mechanics and depth - but the game is set up in such a way that prevents you from fully enjoying all these mechanics and depth.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------

THE POSITIVES:
1) The city growth system is really smart and fun. I absolutely love how they removed workers and changed it into a system where you pick tiles to improve when your city grows. Same with specialists - they are very powerful and important additions to the city. I overall really like the quarters system.

2) Commanders are cool and very powerful. Units are no longer upgraded but their air, land, or fleet commanders are. This adds a very powerful unit that can "load" units into it for transport and also provides buffs. The commanders are very powerful and carry over through ages, so they add a new unit that is important to protect through the whole game. Fantastic.

3) Related to both combat and the growth mechanic is how cities are captured. Now, you have to capture not just the city center but also all urban quarters of the city to capture it. This is a really interesting idea because you can now imagine massive armies fighting through mega-cities. Imagine a city with quarters on both sides of a river. Your army capture the city on one side, but the river gives the defender a line of defense. Interesting dilemma that adds a lot of depth.

4) The town/city dynamic is SUCH A SMART IDEA - I can now build settlements without making them full cities if I want to just control certain resources, chokepoints, etc. And the towns can be used to support cities by specialization that spreads their food, science, production, etc to the full fledged cities. I am loving this mechanic because it lets you mix and match playing tall and wide. You can play tall in a few key cities and have your "wide" empire of towns support the cities. 

5) Definitely has the "one more turn..." feel!!

6) The AI used air power!! The AI seems perfectly serviceable. Definitely not perfect but absolutely playable and a reasonable base to build on.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

THE NEGATIVES:
1) This is HUGE. Any Civ game that doesn't let me play an infinite number of turns isn't a Civ game. The game just ends at the end of the modern age. No one more turn option. This is a deal breaker for me.  Whatever else, please fix this!

2) The ages system is clearly meant to make it so the human player can't just win by the renaissance or whatever. They want to perhaps handicap the human player to an extent so the whole game is engaging. And there's some merit to this. I am finding the late game enjoyable in a way because it's challenging. BUT - THIS IS HUGE  - the system is so abrupt that you're not playing a whole Civ game. You're playing three separate mini-games that are connected by the cities you own. I simply can't believe FIraxis chose to do this, but for example - your military units CHANGE LOCATION when an age transitions. So if you're in a war, too bad - units move. You can't research techs from an age after the transition to the next or choose to finish a prior age wonder. This is a flaw that really affects the gameplay.

3) I agree that the UI is barebones. And there are small annoyances - for example, if the AI offers me a city, I can't look at the map to see where it is because if I close the negotiation screen, it counts as rejecting the offer. There is just an overall lack of information, and things feel like a blackbox. 

4 The modern age ends with battleships and tanks. I am guessing they're adding more ages/units with future DLCs, but the game doesn't really run to the present. No helicopters, missile destroyers, etc

5) Overbuilding seems cool - but how do I know what I'm losing? It's not clear what the effects of removing prior age buildings is.

6) Pacing seems a bit off. I am going to play a game with extended age length to see if that helps.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

NEUTRAL - these are things where I am withholding judgement for now and these could be positives or negatives long-term:
1) Leader attributes, ideology, civics, religion - these mechanics feel... incomplete? I cannot articulate my issues here. There's depth here (the leader attributes have a lot of impact for example) but I'm having a hard time immersing myself in them. Religion is extremely barebones. I put this as neutral because it could just be me and it's likely these will be expanded in the future.

2) No great people? This feels very incomplete, and the mechanic it's replaced with is really unclear (I was playing China and this mechanic basically disappeared after ancient age??). Again, this could be a me problem.

3) Trade...this grants you powerful resources that give yields. I think I like this but ... there's no trade screen unless I have a merchant, so I can't see my trade overview? Maybe I'm wrong, but I don't think so, and it goes back to the UI not giving enough info. Also, no companies! You have factories, but they don't function like companies as far as I can tell but I'll need to play more with it. I hope companies come back.

4) There is now no more resource requirement to build certain units. For example, everyone can build tanks - but if you own oil, your tanks add attack points. I am unsure how I feel about this. I really like the strategic dilemma of needing to capture resources in Civ VI to build a modern army/buildings, so I do miss that part. I can see the arguments for and against, so I put this in neutral. Maybe the effects of owning the resource need to be more powerful/impactful? So owning oil would make your tanks much better, not just a little better, and owning rubber makes them even better.

5) The decoupling of the leader and civilization means I am playing a game where Confucius is currently leading the United States of America in the Modern Age. I go back and forth on this mechanic. I have no problem with the idea of a culture "evolving" from an ancient one to modern (i.e., Norman to French) - but the total decoupling of the leader from the Civ does take out some historical immersion. Overall I think this is a mechanic the community just needs to play more with to get a sense of. I am holding judgement right now. But it's not a dealbreaker from me, and I could imagine enjoying the game with this mechanic remaining the same. 

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Overall, I bought the $140 ($130 plus $10 tax) Founders Edition because it's Civ and I always buy the full version of Civ - but this isn't quite the game I was hoping for. It has a lot of potential to grow, and the city growth mechanics (where workers are removed) and city/town dichotomy are fantastic changes that Firaxis should be applauded for. And the combat changes - the commanders and the idea of all city quarters needing to be captured - add so much depth.

And that's a theme of the game - it DOES have depth. This isn't a game without features - it has SO many features. The problem is you can't fully enjoy them because of the abrupt age transitions and the inability to play endlessly (no "just one more turn..."). 

I personally think the best solution to this problem would be to let the player decide when to move to the next age - for example, let's say I want to build a few more treasure fleets in the exploration age before moving to the modern. Why does the game force me into the modern age - why can't I stay in the exploration and leave at my pace?

Firaxis, you have a fantastic base of a game with so many features and so much depth! Now please let me play it at my pace without railroading me through the ages!", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1739048093}, {"review_text": "Buyer Beware - Locked out of game play by 2k's FairPlay System.

I purchased the £119.99 deluxe edition version of the game when it came out on Steam with full intent to play it fairly. No cheats, no mods, just the based game and the DLC content. However, i was and have been since launch, locked out of launching the game due to 2K's FairPlay enforcement system, which flagged my PC simply because i had unrelated modding tools installed (used for other games). I never modded Civ VII in any way or had plans to.

This restriction was not disclosed at the time of purchase, and 2K's support confirmed that unless i removed the modding software (even though it wasn't used in conjunction with Civ VII) they wouldn't let my play the game i legally purchased. 2K refused to escalate the issue and i was initially denied a refund due to an automated policy by Steam. 

After weeks of persistence and failed launch attempts (the time was flagged as 'playtime'), i was eventually granted a steam wallet refund - only after explaining that i never have actually gotten to access the game. 

This is more than a technical issue, this is an invasion of digital autonomy. I believe it is completely unacceptable for a game publisher to dictate what software you're allowed to keep on your personal PC, especially when it has nothing to do with the game in question. 

If you have modding software or game tools on your PC for any reason, you may be blocked from launching Civ VII at all. Proceed with caution. This kind of behaviour from a publisher sets a dangerous precedent. 

In its current state, i cannot in good conscious recommend this game to anyone who values digital autonomy and due to the extreme lack of support from 2K. Steam, on the other hand, gets a big tick from me for being helpful and easy to deal with.

This change homogenizes the play experience, eliminating the thrill of racing ahead (or clawing your way back from behind) and turns progression into a slow, bureaucratic drip-feed of underwhelming milestones.

Even the aesthetic and mechanical transitions between eras feel muted. Units, city visuals, and technologies evolve with all the drama of a patch update. There’s little sense that your civilization is growing, changing, or even reacting to the times. The game wants to present a smoother, more balanced curve—but in doing so, it sacrifices the very soul of Civ: the joy of historical transformation.

[h1] Lack of Identity and Depth [/h1]
This era flattening ties into a broader problem with Civ VII: a loss of identity. The game strips back or over-simplifies many systems that used to define your playstyle and strategic thinking. Technologies and civics have been streamlined to the point of blandness. Unique units and buildings feel like cosmetic swaps rather than defining traits. And while the UI is slicker and more modern, it's also worryingly sterile, removing the character and charm that made each Civ feel alive.

The developers seemed intent on making Civ VII more "accessible," but in doing so, they’ve diluted the sense of agency and discovery that made each run in previous games feel like your own historical saga.

[h1] Final Verdict [/h1]
Sid Meier’s Civilization VII is not a disaster, but it’s a profound disappointment. The series that once championed dynamic progression, asymmetrical competition, and rich historical flavor has settled into a bland, feature-thin iteration that feels like it's treading water. The era system, in particular, is emblematic of the game’s broader failings: a misguided attempt at innovation that strips away the magic of watching your civilization rise from humble beginnings to global dominance.

[h1] TL:DR [/h1]
Fans deserved better. Here’s hoping Civ VIII, if it ever arrives, remembers that history is supposed to be [i] epic. [/i]", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1753349408}, {"review_text": "Civilization VII: A Disappointing Departure from the Norm
This review is based on my experience with the current state of Civilization VII, and unfortunately, it feels like a significant departure from the deep, intricate experiences the series is known for.

Core Gameplay Lacking Depth
Frankly, this game feels nothing like a Civ game. It is significantly slim in terms of technology, culture, and religious advancements. Instead of the carefully crafted, multi-layered strategy we've come to expect, Civ VII plays more like a short builder without real depth. It leans far more toward an action-focused strategy builder than the beautifully carved, expansive game we all miss. The fact there are only 3 eras is disappointing and makes the technology gameplay way too strong, especially in the modern era. The first planes just completely take over the game.

Unbalanced and Clunky Mechanics
I was very grateful that Humankind offered some competition in this genre, pushing the Civ team to make some adjustments, particularly to the warfare. However, a major issue I ran into involves the new era progression system.

One specific mechanic I truly disliked was tied to the era transition. After you progress to a new era, you can spend your achieved points on certain improvements. Within this menu is the option to transfer your capital city to another one. This transfer looks like an immense, unbalanced bonus if you figure out the precise effect.

Normally, upon advancing, all your cities are reduced to settlements, and you only maintain your capital as a full city. However, transferring your capital means:
1. Your previous capital stays a city
2. The selected city becomes the new capital city

This effectively grants you one additional starting city for the new era, which is a huge boost you have to figure out by yourself. It's a mechanic that feels completely unintuitive and breaks the balance of the transition.Another bug, in my opinion, is that if you annex a city, you have to choose between keeping the city and destroying it. So far, so good, but I was not successful in giving back a city to the original nation it belonged to. That way I increased my number of cities way too quickly and ended up with +10 cities over the normal cap. However, the negative effects were too small or not noticeable, which is bad balancing in my opinion.

Final Verdict:
Civilization VII is currently a shallow, action-oriented strategy game that lacks the intricate depth and polish expected of a flagship title in this franchise. This game takes away a lot of your freedom of choice that Civ players are used to, and it is sad.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1759666414}, {"review_text": "It's like the devs took a long look at the venerated 34-year history of the Civilization series and asked themselves, "Yeah, but how can we make it more like Clash of Clans?" Thus, Civ(s) 7 was born.  

Let's be clear; this game is not Civ.  I've played the series since Civ 3 and there has never been a bad Civ game. Any game that has people playing it for 30+ years doesn't need to be changed.  Updated? Sure. Enhanced? Sure.  Changed into another game entirely? Absolutely not.  

Despite the early negative reviews, I bought this on release day because the bad reviews had to be trolling, right?  I mean, there's no such thing as a bad Civ game, right? The game is not called "Civs" (plural), it's "Civ" (singular).  The fact that your Civ(s) leader also seems randomly assigned doesn't help either.  It is jarring and disengaging to have Ben Franklin lead the Normans in diplomatic negotiations against Harriet Tubman who's representing the Qing Dynasty. Again, this handicaps the basic concept of what Civ has historically been.  Those who explore, discover, negotiate, and conquer are rewarded and reap the benefits of their efforts as the game continues.  In Civ(s) 7, the player is actively penalized for this.  How else would you describe the fact of arbitrarily losing any military unit not tied down to a commander, losing city-state allies with whom you've cultivated a relationship, losing production capacity for all but one of your settlements, losing all diplomatic ties with the other civilizations, and having to start back at basically square one ? Now, if you'll excuse me, I'm going to go re-install Civ 6.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 16, "timestamp_created": 1742870179}, {"review_text": "After spending 40 hours on Civilization VII, playing several games, and winning four of them, I can confidently say one thing: I am disappointed.

[h2]UI: A Major Step Back[/h2]
The user interface is one of the worst aspects of the game. It’s overly simplistic, unintuitive, and a clear downgrade from previous entries. In a strategy game where clear information is crucial, this poor design choice is hard to justify.

[h2]The Era System and Its Unsettling Soft-Reset[/h2]
One of the most controversial changes is the introduction of the three-era system, which forces a soft-reset between eras. This completely disrupts the natural flow of the game and takes away the sense of progression that has always been a core part of the series. Instead of adding strategic depth, it feels like an artificial mechanic designed to extend playtime without real substance.

[h2]Playable Characters and Civilizations: A Cash Grab in Disguise?[/h2]
The selection of civilizations and leaders at launch is underwhelming. It’s clear that many iconic factions have been deliberately left out, most likely to be sold later as DLC. This growing trend of excessive monetization in AAA games is frustrating, and Civ VII is no exception.

Now 4/10. Was 5/10.
So, I'm one of the old crew that played civ 1 on an 8086 back in the 90s. Played Civ 4 on PS1. Played civ 6 on PC, bought all the DLCs. This game........... I don't like it. I'm already going back to Civ6, or even Millennia. Even the base Civ 6 portable/handheld experience is better than this. I literally just spent the holiday weekend playing civ 6 on my Iphone as Tomyris and had a better experience.

Civ 7 is buggy. Holy crap is it buggy. Vulkan flat out crashes to desktop repeatedly. It is almost unplayable. DX12 has all sorts of flashing and flickering issues in the UI. Yes, all my graphics drivers are updated. Radeon Vega 56 eGPU. Windows 10.

The scenery is lush and beautiful. It is absolutely gorgeous. No expense was spared on the graphics. I love looking at it. Unfortunately, the UI is terrible. It's like they just didn't even try to play test before release. Even a couple starts on a decent monitor with a couple different manufacturers' GPUs would have revealed these issues. Very disappointing.

The amount of civs available in each age is worse than Civ 1. Beyond disappointing. But this is what happens when you lock 2/3 of them behind the "Ages" mechanic.

Talking about Ages: My first time after the age changed and I found out that I literally lost units because "reasons", made me rage. WTLF?! Don't take my units because mechanics! Terrible design. Rise and Fall was my least liked feature in Civ6, and Firaxis chose to make it the core of the game in Civ 7. No. Just no. Do not take things from me or alter the game state without justification. And it is completely out of my control. I am literally penalized for no reason. All alliances and wars canceled?! And now I am required to swap to another entirely different civ, with different bonuses? NO! I can see what Firaxis were trying to accomplish here. But it just doesn't work. This is not Civilization.

The core concept from Civ 1 onwards was that we pick a civilization and play as them. Yes, we have a leader. Having specific bonuses attached to that leader that follows them while changing the civ was an interesting idea. But in practice it breaks the game. Swapping leaders would have been more realistic and acceptable. Many long-existing civs have had multiple leaders. Why not that?

BTW, Napoleon rocks. +1 movement on all military units forever, and culture on killing a unit? Yes, plz. He is better than Simon Bolivar from Civ6.

What I liked. Commanders. What a great mechanic! I love commanders. They both simply and amplify gameplay. Moving all the experience from the units to the commander is ingenious. Who ever thought this up needs to be promoted.

What I would change:
Reconnect ages/civs. The disconnect from age-to-age is game-breaking. Let me play the same civ! It's fine to give us the option to swap, similar to how we could swap governments in Civ6. Thanks Spain, France, England, Portugal, etc. But you get the point. It wasn't like one day the entire Egpytian people rose up and and declared "We are now German!"

As things stand now, I can't recommend this game. It's just not Civilization at its core. The state of the game is mediocre at best. I don't regret buying it, but I'm glad I didn't spend more on any fancy stuff either. I will not be buying any of the dlcs or expansions until the major issues (glitchy UI and age disconnect) are fixed. I'd rather play civ 6 or even Millenia.

Stay away from this game. Firaxis should be ashamed of what they've done. if you like rogue-lites and ARPGs this is a must try and fortunately theres a free demo, just be aware that your progress there doesnt carry over to the actual game. highly recommended.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1737029355}, {"review_text": "Heroes of Hammerwatch II is a generational leap from Heroes of Hammerwatch, the roguelite action RPG that accompanied the more traditional ARPG format Hammerwatch. Taking the best features of HoH and adding smart improvements makes this an easy recommendation, and while I would easily recommend both games I'll focus on what's new here.  

The equipment system offers some flexibility in weaponry and builds, letting you experiment with a selection (though not an incredibly robust one) of different weapon and armor types. Try playing a rogue wearing light armor with a wand, or a wizard with a sword and shield and heavy armor, or a warrior with a bow and medium armor- while it might not be optimal, the flexibility is neat. Weapons and armor can be a good way to build up across multiple runs, giving bonuses to an array of stats and sometimes even special effects that can open up opportunities for a specific playstyle. It's not so overpowering that it feels like you're hitting a win button, but it is significant enough to really feel like progression, while not being so convoluted or deep that it becomes unapproachable without a theorycrafting guide. Later in the game, upgrading item levels and enchanting gear to change effects or increase rarity can be useful as well, though not required to do well.

Redone classes with additional customization offers more complexity to the gameplay loop. HoH had classes that had one attack, three skills, and two passives. HoH2 has similar, with weapons that have either one or two attacks depending on how many hands they occupy (both of which count as weapon skills, benefiting from your weapon power- including some very powerful staff attacks for casters), classes which have two active and two passive skills, and then on top of that a choice from three class specializations (unlocked at level 10) for each class that add two additional skills, one active and one passive that can transform your playstyle signficantly. Additionally, each run gives the chance to unlock temporary but transformative skill upgrades that allow you to leverage a class or specialization's playstyle in a particular way- regain health when using your melee attacks as Warlock to become a powerful caster tank, or become a demolitionist rogue who can drop grenades when you dodge away from enemies. These can even be used to transform a class's playstyle, like turning sorcerer's lightning crowd control shotgun style attack "Discharge" into a more precise ice cone that can easily destroy bosses at the expense of AoE capability.

Trinkets have been reexamined and a lot of them now either scale better into the later game (including the highly repeatable NG+ cycle) or are generally more valuable to begin with. Many of the "filler" trinkets in HoH that became annoying and could ruin runs because of their comparatively low value are gone, while most classics returned. Adjustments made to some trinkets seem to be balanced well in my experience. While I've sometimes been disappointed to get certain trinkets because of what a specific run needed, there aren't many I find myself disliking entirely and I am very strongly opinionated about trinkets.

Additionally, the graphics have been made much more granular, with a smaller pixel size than the original HoH. While there are a few graphical bugs at this time like flickering on specific floor textures or the occasional mistake with an errant tile or detail, there is some beautiful pixel art and the game looks spectacular. Importantly, it's also much more readable and easy to understand in busy situations, which is great when a bunch of particle effects are flying about.

If you enjoyed the original game, I can easily recommend this one. And, if you didn't play the first, I'd recommend this to you too if the combination of top down action RPGs and robust meta progression appeals to you, as I really haven't played anything quite like HoH/HoH2 in the action RPG scene.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1737103476}, {"review_text": "[i]Heroes of Hammerwatch II[/i] is a massive improvement on the original game. The game is significantly less of a grind this time around, and the primary progression resource in the first game, is split into multiple resources here allowing you to make improvements to your town essentially every run. The environments feel fresher, and transition to one another in a more natural way - they're also slightly smaller making the repetition of running through them less taxing. I never played co-op in the first game, but loved it here and made great memories with some friends. Overall, I had a great time and it would probably be my game of the year so far (I haven't played much, but also this is great).

That being said, it is still missing some positive features the first game had, and struggles in some ways. You still receive permanent stats to all your characters for leveling up each class, but the Rogue's bonus of decreased trap damage feels pretty worthless. If you're a good player you're already avoiding the traps, or can spend gold to disable them; evasion chance, critical chance, resource gain, etc. all would've had more impact. A missing feature is the ability to make your runs more challenging for the potential of increased resources, items, larger maps, stronger enemies, and other modifiers. Taking shortcuts throughout runs doesn't provide enough in the way of items - running through all the environments hunting out secret rooms feels like the necessary strategy if you're going for the win. Lastly, the scaling still feels wonky once you get deeper into NG+ runs; the number of viable strategies decreases significantly, and the level cap feels like it could be adjusted for a smoother experience through the first NG+ runs.

Overall, [i]Heroes of Hammerwatch II[/i] is a wonderful game. Improvements to the meta progression system make progress come significantly faster, and the increased detail to the environments give the game much more life. I've played [i]Heroes of Hammerwatch II[/i] less than I played it's predecessor, but feel that I experienced more, and had much more fun in that time, there's no longer a wall you run into where progress becomes a slow grind. It thrives as a co-op experience, and stays mostly true to what made the original great. There are improvements they can make, and I hope they continue to improve the base game before selling any DLC. Regardless, I've had a great time with [i]Heroes of Hammerwatch II[/i], it's been my favorite 2025 release thus far.

[b]Highly Recommended[/b]

After 50+ hours and multiple NG+ runs, I’m torn. This game has fantastic bones—tight combat, satisfying progression, and a killer retro aesthetic that hooks you fast. But it also feels like it’s stuck halfway between Early Access and a full release.

The Good:

Addictive core loop. Swapping classes, upgrading the town, and chasing trinket sets kept me glued for days.

Co-op is a blast. The revive/penalty system encourages teamwork without punishing casual play.

Nostalgia done right. It’s like Gauntlet meets Diablo with a roguelite twist, and that works.

The Rough Spots:

Balance whiplash. Trash mobs hit harder than bosses, and one biome’s silence/disarm spam feels unfair, not fun.

Unfinished vibes. Red dust/gold ore with no purpose? Missing set bonuses due to ultra-rare epic drops? It screams cut content.

NG+ lacks depth. After the first clear, it’s just "enemies hit harder" with no new mechanics or goals.

Verdict: Worth $20? Absolutely—I got my hours in. But with better balancing, more polish, and post-game love, this could be a 10/10. As-is, it’s a great foundation begging for updates. Recommend with caveats.

Why this works:

Balanced tone: Criticizes fairly while celebrating strengths—no ranting, just constructive feedback.

Specifics + humor: Calls out oddities (red dust) and contrasts highs/lows, making it relatable.

Clear verdict: Helps players decide while nudging devs toward fixes.

[{"review_text": "I bought Sekiro to relax after work. Now my neighbors know every curse word in three languages, my controller has trust issues, and I’ve achieved a kind of spiritual enlightenment that only comes from being repeatedly stabbed by a seven-foot monkey with a sword.

This game will break you, rebuild you, then break you again—like a violent personal trainer who only accepts your tears as payment. But when you finally parry that boss after the 437th attempt, the dopamine hits harder than any FromSoftware backstab.

Gorgeous world? Check. Swordplay tighter than my grip on the last healing gourd? Double check. Story that whispers “you’re not worthy” while secretly making you a shinobi legend? Triple check.

Buy it. Suffer. Transcend.
—10/10 would die to a chicken again.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 156, "timestamp_created": 1757969653}, {"review_text": ""A brutal, beautiful journey through feudal Japan that rewards patience, skill, and perseverance."

Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice is not your typical FromSoftware game, even though it shares the studio's signature difficulty and atmospheric storytelling. Unlike the Soulsborne titles, Sekiro leans heavily into action and precise combat rather than RPG elements. There are no stats to grind—just your own skill to sharpen.

The swordplay is incredibly tight and satisfying. Every encounter feels like a deadly duel where posture, timing, and reflexes matter more than raw damage. Boss fights are intense and memorable, and the learning curve is steep but fair. Death is part of the process—each failure teaches something new.

The game world is stunningly crafted, with gorgeous, varied environments inspired by late 1500s Japan. The level design encourages exploration, and the verticality introduced by the grappling hook adds a fresh dynamic to movement and combat.

I came into the souls-like genre relatively late, starting with Lies of P (9/10) and later The First Berserker: Khazan (9.5/10). Both taught me patience and respect for the genre while proving that even a brutal challenge can be beautiful.
When I began Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, I felt I was stepping into something legendary. It was also my first completed game from the masters at FromSoftware, which made the whole experience feel even more meaningful.

It’s clear that the game comes from the PS4/XONE era, yet its visual direction, lighting and artistic style completely transcend its age.
The cutscenes are captivating, the characters and story pull you in right away, and the atmosphere is soaked in unmistakable Japanese spirit. Among Japanese games from that era, Sekiro’s story stands out as one of the best — powerful, symbolic and full of moments that stay with you long after the credits roll.
I fully understand why Sekiro is considered a “holy grail” among action games.
And yet, I can’t shake the feeling that it’s slightly overrated. Not in terms of quality, but in how uncompromisingly some fans worship it without acknowledging its extremes.

Pros
• Stunning environments and art direction. The fusion of feudal Japan and spiritual mysticism works beautifully, and every location feels like a painting.
• Outstanding cinematic presentation. A film-like rhythm, attention to detail and characters that truly leave a mark.
• Unique combat system. The parry-based rhythm and posture mechanics are demanding but brilliantly designed and deeply satisfying.
• Excellent PC optimization. Smooth performance, fast loading times and virtually no bugs.
• Immense sense of reward. Defeating a boss that once felt impossible is pure adrenaline and relief.

Cons
• Extreme difficulty and frustration. Not everyone has the patience for repeated boss fights; sometimes it feels more like a test of endurance than fun.
• Limited RPG flexibility. There’s little room for experimentation; success relies entirely on skill and reflexes.
• Certain mechanics punish the player too harshly, like the Dragonrot system or the unforgiving XP economy.
• Pacing issues. Some sections feel repetitive or less inspired compared to the game’s best moments.
• Intriguing yet cryptic story. It’s engaging, but much of it remains unclear without diving into external lore.
• Traversal mechanics like grappling, jumping, swimming and diving feel more like add-ons than natural gameplay elements. They’re used only superficially and make the world feel more linear than it initially appears.

Reflection
Playing Sekiro today, after modern titles like Lies of P and Khazan, feels different. The genre has evolved — technically, stylistically and in how it respects player choice.
Khazan, for instance, carries Sekiro’s DNA but refines it further, offering multiple difficulty options and smoother pacing.
Players who once viewed Sekiro as an untouchable pinnacle might benefit from revisiting it today — not to diminish its greatness, but to see how much the genre has grown since 2019.

Conclusion
Sekiro is like a master duel — sometimes unfair, sometimes brilliant. It’s not a game you simply play; it’s one you endure, learn from and ultimately overcome. When you finally do, it leaves behind a strange calm after the storm.
Not all of its design choices worked for me; some, like the grappling, swimming and diving, might have benefited from a simpler and more focused approach. Still, its true strength lies in the fact that even years later, it stays with you.

I might return to Sekiro someday. It offers multiple endings and a New Game+ mode, and there’s something about its world that keeps calling you back. But for now, this is how it felt after my first journey through its storms and victories.
For me personally, it’s a game I admire more than I love — and maybe that’s exactly what makes it special.

When I first started this game, I really wasn't feeling it. Having played many other games with heavy parry mechanics, I just didn't understand why every enemy kept blocking my attacks, and waiting to parry every enemy for counterattacks felt very tedious. It also didn't help that just about every section of the map was packed with enemies that would swarm me as soon as one got alerted to my presence. I didn't find the game "hard" per se; I beat every one of the early bosses I encountered on the first try, but I found the overall gameplay very tedious.

I was about to call it quits, until I beat a certain [spoiler]Genichiro[/spoiler] boss, that I finally understood the game and its core combat mechanic: posture.

See, what got me confused is that Sekiro kept getting described as a "parry game". And while parrying is somewhat of an important mechanic in this game, Sekiro should be more accurately described as an "aggression game". This is because that unlike other parry focused games out there, Sekiro isn't really about the patient dance of parrying and counterattacking.
Really, it's more about hacking away at enemies and consistently applying pressure due to the posture mechanic. Because guess what, it doesn't matter if your enemies block your attacks; your goal for 95% of encounters is to overwhelm your enemies with enough attacks to allow you to land that insta-kill deathblow.

And it is AMAZING how much you can get away with by simply tapping the attack button. Oh no, you opponent is about to hit you with an unblockable attack? Well, just thwack them in the face with your sword and they get interrupted (disclaimer: does not work every time). It was pretty funny realising that instead of waiting for enemies to attack, I could simply continuously attack, parry counterattacks every 2-3 hits, and then just keep repeating the same process.

Also, dodging was often times a lot more efficient than parrying, because several bosses would straight up not finish their combo if you dodged to get behind them. This is most obvious with the much hated [spoiler]Demon of Hatred[/spoiler] boss, which is trivialised by merely getting behind him, and jumping every now and then.

The second most important thing that I learned the hard way, was just how much [b]stealth[/b] is important in this game. Sekiro absolutely SUCKS at dealing with more than one enemy at a time; it doesn't even matter what sort of grunt you're dealing with- face more than one enemy at a time and you end up dying very quickly. 
So once I actually started playing like a ninja- crouching and luring away enemies for backstabs, exploring the world became a lot more tolerable and even enjoyable.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Can take awhile to get used to, but once the posture mechanic "clicks", along with adopting a stealth approach to exploration, Sekiro can become a very satisfying experience. I have never played another game like Sekiro, and I probably never will again. I hated it for the first ten hours. I would install it, play a few hours, get stonewalled by a boss, quit for months, then try again. One holiday, I forced myself to push through. Sekiro will teach you more about yourself, patience, determination, and persistence than any other game I have found. You do not really level up your character so much as level up yourself. Everyone should do at least one playthrough and experience what it means to master something. As the game teaches you, hesitation is defeat.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Good[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Combat that is its own genre.[/b] The posture system makes every fight a duel of nerve. You are aiming to break posture for a deathblow while deflecting strings at the precise tempo. It feels closer to a rhythm game than a brawler once it clicks, and the flow state is very real.
[*][b]Vitality versus posture is a clean conversation.[/b] Chip vitality to slow posture recovery, then keep the pressure. The rules are readable and fair, which is why you can feel yourself improving.
[*][b]Telegraphing you can trust.[/b] Audio tells, spark showers, and enemy cadence all train you. Hanbei’s practice arena is an honest classroom. When you die, you know what you missed.
[*][b]Mikiri Counter is an all-timer.[/b] Learning when to Mikiri, when to jump, and when to backstep is the heart of the dance.
[*][b]Characters and story land.[/b] A mythical Sengoku tale about duty, bonds, and the cost of immortality. It is very Japanese in delivery, with honor and obligation baked into the choices.
[*][b]The Shinobi Prosthetic is a real toolkit.[/b] It is a fun gimmick that also enables problem-solving. You can cheese some nuisances if you are disciplined about timing. If you are sloppy, you die. That tradeoff is the point.
[*][b]Deaths feel owned.[/b] Almost every failure is because you did or did not do something. The edge it forces you to walk produces some of the most satisfying wins you can have in games.
[*][b]Traversal and level design reward aggression and curiosity.[/b] Grapple lines, vertical routes, and stealth angles let you set the pace between duels and pick your entries.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Bad[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]The swamp quota is alive and well.[/b] Another FromSoftware toxic zone because of course there is.
[*][b]This is a sword game, period.[/b] There is no real build variety beyond prosthetic loadouts and a few passives. If you want multiple viable archetypes, play Elden Ring. Here you have one solution. Get good at it.
[*][b]Late-game pacing can grind you down.[/b] A few stretches near the end feel like nuisances more than tests, with long jogs back to the lesson if you whiff.
[*][b]Camera and lock-on in tight spaces.[/b] Beasts in corners and multi-enemy encounters can make the camera your third opponent.
[*][b]Miniboss repetition pads time.[/b] Variants of spear elites, ogres, and monks reappear with small tweaks. Knowledge helps, but it still reads as reuse.
[*][b]Spirit Emblem economy adds friction.[/b] Burning through emblems to use tools can turn experimentation into resource management busywork until you learn when each tool is worth it.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Ugly[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Quest design is opaque even by From standards.[/b] Two endings are effectively hidden, and you will likely need a guide to make them fire. FromSoftware remains committed to making NPC logic feel like solving a crossword without the clues.
[*][b]Collectibles are a chore to track.[/b] Prayer Beads, Gourd Seeds, and treasure carp scales are scattered in ways that sometimes feel punishing to collect. Expect to keep a guide open if you want a full clear.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Notes and Tips (No Spoilers)[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Learn the counters early.[/b] Mikiri for thrusts and jump for sweeps are the whole game. Drill them until they are reflexes.
[*][b]Use the right tool, not every tool.[/b] Some prosthetics hard-counter certain enemy families. Others are traps if you spam them. Treat them as a scalpel, not a crutch.
[*][b]Sugars and items matter.[/b] Damage, posture, and terror mitigation consumables are not optional on first-clear walls. Bring them.
[*][b]Collectibles sanity.[/b] If you care about 100 percent, keep a short checklist for beads, seeds, and scales so you do not backtrack the whole map at the end.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
Sekiro is a test of you as much as it is of your character. It will make you angry, then it will make you better, and then it will make you unstoppable. If you want multiple viable builds and flexible difficulty, this is not that game. If you want a pure, surgical duel system with the cleanest parry loop in the business, nothing else feels like Sekiro.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761380707}, {"review_text": "Stick with it and don't give up, you'll experience a first class story, soundtrack and gameplay, wield your own katana to your heart's content!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1746755735}, {"review_text": "Folding screen monkeys hardest boss

[h1] Gameplay & Mechanics [/h1]
The combat system in the game is like a lot of RPGs, you slash and deflect attacks. You can engage onto enemies by either sneaking up on them or going head on against them, although it is a bit difficult whenever there are multiple enemies coming from all directions. It is a matter of knowing attack patterns and expecting when they will land to time the deflect perfectly.

The difficulty is really great, the game starts off pretty difficult due the lack of prosthetics tools/buff items you have at you disposal which they can be beneficial or necessary to beat certain bosses/mini bosses. You can vary the difficulty of the game by giving Kuro his "Kuro's Charm" (Added chip damage for when you block attacks, forcing you to adapt into deflecting attacks more often, increased enemy vitality and posture, increased vitality and damage taken and status effects build up roughly 40% faster. But with an added XP boost for skill points and increased gain of sen, the in game currency) back to him and/or utilize the "Demon Bell" (Pretty much the same deal as giving Kuro's charm back with an added increase of loot drop chance) [spoiler] which can be found up the hill from the Shugendo Sculptors Idol, right before fighting the Armored Warrior through a barred door [/spoiler] . Note that not having Kuro's Charm and having the Demon Bell, the disadvantages will stack. The difficulty cannot be changes unless you start a new playthrough with a new save or NG+ (Except for the Demon Bell).

The more you play, the stronger you get. Pretty much the spiel of majority of RPG games; you get more health, more posture, multiple resurrections, increased attack power, more prosthetic tools/items are your disposal, more skills/combat arts and more healing items.

[h1] Graphics & Visuals [/h1]
The visuals and graphics of this game are [b] STUNNING [/b]. The environment and the combat arts VFX are so well made.

The UI is minimalistic, showing your health bar, how many resurrections you have, your current prosthetic tool, current quick item, how many Spirit Emblems you have, enemy vitality and posture, boss/mini boss vitality, posture and how many phases they have.

[h1] Pacing & Story [/h1]
The game fairly long, taking 20-30 hours on their first playthrough or 50-100 hours just to 100% the game by unlocking every single achievement this game has to offer.

The story is amazing, the pacing is very well done. Nothing much more to say about it there.
There are 4 endings present in the game.

The side quests are available in the game, most of them are necessary to earn certain achievements and others are pretty much useless. They usually reward you some useful goodies or story related items. You don't need to do them all for 100% achievements. But if you want to do them just for the thrill of it, go for it!

[h1] Personal Take [/h1]
For me it was kind of annoying needing to find all of the prayer beads and gourd seeds to max out vitality/posture and my healing gourd but oh well. [spoiler] Oh and the headless ape is a pain in the ass to fight against, hated every second of fighting them. [/spoiler]

The combat is really fun and with the added combinations you can do with prosthetic tools really makes it more fun.

[h1] OVERALL RATING 10/10 [/h1]

Learn to listen to your fucking community, ask your neighbor Arrowhead how they do it, they're certainly not saints but oh boy are they are miles better than you.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 57, "timestamp_created": 1749469543}, {"review_text": "Darktide is my favorite co-op game of all time. That comes with the huge caveat that I never was really into co-op games.

There are three aspects that make Darktide a winner in my opinion. 1. Easy to get into a public game without having to hear annoying voice chat. 2. Extremely good and tight controls 3. A huge variability of characters, skills, and weapon combinations.

There are two things about it that may be annoying initially but they end up being key parts of why Darktide ends up being enjoyable for me. One, the characters talk all the time. I had read that the developers had lots of dialogue and I didn't really understand what that meant until I got really into the game. Second, there are no individual scores/rankings. While there are mods to see stats privately, this ends up being freeing and may even help cooperation since players don't end up chasing scores/rank.

Honestly, when I first tried Darktide, I had no idea that it was a co-op game. After the prologue I figured I'd try a couple of missions and then quit. Once the inevitable annoying voice chats came on, I decreased the voice volume, until eventually turning them off completely. This is where the talking characters come in. The characters call out resources and you can mark targets so there's no need to yap about it. If you're the kind of player that likes to talk with team mates, strategizing and/or shooting the feces, then this is probably not a positive. But for someone who just wants a public game without annoying chatter, it's a complete game changer.

From the get go, the characters seem really scrawny and this ends up being part of the charm here. I spend a lot of time in Japan each year and the characters here are as far away as you can get from the cute teenage characters in most Japanese games. In fact, my main character Elke is a middle aged woman with a dueling sword and revolver.

Darktide also has great aesthetics with beautiful environments. It takes the over the top parody world of Warhammer 40k and makes it more interesting than I ever remember it being. The voice acting is great and there is some fantastic situational music.

It's got interesting character ability trees, unique weapons, and weapon variants. Not all of them are winners of course, and some are obvious fillers, but there is enough there to customize to any play style with a lot of variety. Each weapon has perks, blessings and sometimes weapon variants (marks). A lot of this used to be random, but now they're all adjustable so you're not beholden to the RNG gods. I'm not a fan of automatic weapons and in fact I hate nothing more than bullet sponges, so the aforementioned Elke offers precise one shot with the revolver and one poke with the dueling sword. Oh and did I mention I don't like slow characters? Elke is lightning fast. She's also a bit of a glass cannon and requires a bit of precision. Even so, the hitboxes are a mile wide so sometimes just shooting in the general direction is good enough. There's a lot of melee combat options as well and sometimes just continuously smashing heretics with a hammer or club can be quite cathartic. With the new Arbitrator class, I have a precision range weapon and smashy smashy melee one. In fact, Darktide can generally be both relaxing and intense.

The negative? The game used to crash A LOT. You couldn't go a day without it crashing. The list of possible reasons from the developer was a mile long. It's MUCH better now. It crashes much less, plus there is an option to go back to the game in progress after the crash. Crashing isn't a big deal anymore IMO.

I never meant to put 760+ hours into Darktide, but it just happened. Most games are fun and easy to get into and last 30 to 40 minutes. There is a range of difficulties, with "Auric" maelstrom at the upper end of casual play and then a "Havok" mode for those looking for more of a challenge (where losing has some mild consequences). I find "Auric" maelstrom to be the sweet spot for me. Darktide has an amazing way of making you feel that you accomplished an impossible mission, even though it really wasn't. Most games are fun but on average 1 out 10 are heart pounding squee. I blinked, and suddenly it’s 3 AM, my base has tripwires, I’m hoarding mushrooms like a feral raccoon, and I’m emotionally bonded to a rifle I named “Susan.”

This game?
Absolutely unhinged in the best way. It’s like Fallout, The Forest, and Stranger Things had a weird little apocalypse baby—and somehow it works. The world is rotting and glowing and horrifying and BEAUTIFUL. And I? I’m thriving. Screaming, but thriving.

✔️ Base building? Addictive.
✔️ Crafting? Endless.
✔️ Combat? Chunky, chaotic, and so satisfying.
✔️ Lore? Creepy as hell, and I need answers NOW.
✔️ Monsters? I love them. I fear them. I run from them and come back with a flamethrower.

Even the bugs feel like part of the chaos. I shouldn’t love this game this much—but it scratched an itch I didn’t even know I had.

10/10 — I’ve joined a cult, and it’s this game.

Come back to edit for one of the events: 

Once Human – Nalcott Survival Review (Manibus Vision Permanent Server)

I’ve been exploring Nalcott for 11 days, bearing witness to both its beauty and brutality. The world feels alive, vibrant in its details and full of moments that genuinely pull you into its mystery. Every corner seems to whisper a story, and I’ve done my best to help shape it into something thriving and alive.

But I need to be honest: the Lunar Event has started to turn excitement into frustration. The Lord of the Night seems to appear far too often, sometimes what feels like every thirty minutes, interrupting exploration, crafting, and any real progression. When that event triggers, it doesn’t feel like a challenge; it feels like punishment.

The copy of yourself that spawns during the event is over-tuned and nearly impossible to defeat solo, especially for players who aren’t fully geared. At level 35, I should be able to handle level 19 mobs, yet even with steel AP arrows, I’m barely scratching them. By the time the event’s chaos unfolds, my HP is already low, and one unlucky hit can end it all in a single shot.

Being forced into participation rather than given a chance to prepare or opt out makes it worse. It gets to the point where I’m barricaded in my base, just waiting it out, which kills the pacing and fun of the game. And when multiple Lords of the Night trigger back-to-back...it’s pure burnout.

Still, I stay because of the community. The people I play with on Server Y0222 make the experience worth enduring. There’s something special about a world that can frustrate you to no end, but also bring together a group of players who refuse to give up.

Verdict:

[/list]

[u]What is not so great[/u]

[list]

I had pretty much closed out 2025 for FMV games already, but a huge surprise landed in November: Mandate Of Heaven is the best Chinese historical drama FMV I’ve ever played.

You play as the king’s second son, locked in a struggle for the throne, and you follow his whole life through wars, battles, and political intrigue as he fights to shape his own fate.

It’s a fantastic concept for an FMV, and it’s executed extremely well.

Special mention to the sheer number of hours of content and the game’s cinematography, which manages to blend third-person and first-person shots in a really satisfying way.

⏱️ Playtime
First playthrough: ~9 hours

🎧 Technical Highlights

🎵 Soundtrack – Excellent and fits every scene. The menu theme and the tracks used throughout the game are really catchy.

🎬 Cinematography – Stunning. Every scene was shot in real, beautiful locations. Direction, shot composition, and costumes are top-notch. Nothing feels out of place. The region where it was filmed is gorgeous.

👥 Characters – Fantastic. The performances are great, and there’s a large cast of characters in the game; it works perfectly.

🌍 Localization – Very good and easy to understand, but there is one issue: the time-jump/title cards are not translated, so you still don’t know what’s being written there, and also when a new character is introduced on screen.

If you’re on a tight budget and love FMV games and historical stories, Mandate Of Heaven is the one to buy.
💸 Worth every penny. Highly recommended!

Rather than relying on sprawling open-world systems, it leans into the structure of an interactive historical drama, positioning players as the Second Prince of a fractured Southern regime. From the very beginning, the game establishes a tone of political tension and looming crisis, framing the protagonist as someone caught between personal comfort and national obligation. The northern territories have fallen, the empire has grown decadent, and the question of whether the protagonist will restore the dynasty or allow it to crumble becomes the emotional and thematic spine of the journey. It is less about predetermined destiny and more about how choices—large and small—carve the future.

What immediately distinguishes Mandate of Heaven from traditional strategy RPGs is its interactive cinematic presentation. Live-action performances, stylized set pieces, and carefully staged dialogue scenes replace the usual animated cutscenes, giving the experience a theatrical, character-focused sensibility. The approach allows the narrative to emphasize human emotion over battlefield spectacle, pulling the player into court debates, confidential meetings, betrayals, alliances, and moral dilemmas with a sense of closeness that few strategy titles attempt. The branching decision system encourages reflection rather than instinctive button-pressing, because every response—whether diplomatic, defiant, compassionate, or ruthless—visibly alters relationships, political standing, and long-term narrative outcomes. The game is built to be replayed, not for mechanical mastery, but to explore how different philosophies of leadership reshape the empire.

Despite its cinematic framing, Mandate of Heaven does not abandon gameplay. Strategic planning, military management, and state governance emerge between story segments, allowing the player to witness the practical consequences of their choices. Instead of overwhelming the player with micromanagement, the systems are streamlined to maintain narrative flow. The focus remains on decision-making—choosing which territories to prioritize, which advisors to trust, whether to pursue aggressive expansion or careful diplomacy. The result is a strategy experience that feels accessible yet weighty, not driven by statistics but by the moral and political identity the player constructs. The design invites players to imagine themselves as rulers navigating complex cultural, familial, and national expectations rather than tacticians pushing armies across maps.

Visually, the game’s reliance on live-action and realistic presentation gives it a distinct artistic identity. Costumes, architecture, and environmental composition reinforce a setting inspired by historical dynastic China, with enough stylization to avoid strict historical reenactment. The atmosphere feels grounded, dignified, and immersive, carried by expressive performances and deliberate cinematography. Audio design further strengthens the tone—measured dialogue delivery, restrained musical scoring, and environmental cues create tension without resorting to melodrama. While the scope and budget of an indie studio are visible at times, the sincerity of the production outweighs minor imperfections, and the stylistic cohesion gives the game a personality not easily confused with larger, more conventional projects.

Where Mandate of Heaven excels most, however, is in how carefully it handles consequence. Many narrative games advertise branching choices, but the results often feel cosmetic. Here, decisions genuinely redirect political fate, character arcs, and even the philosophical direction of the state. Endings vary significantly, reflecting different legacies—prosperity, collapse, exile, authoritarianism, reluctant peace, corrupted victory, or noble failure. This range transforms the game into a meditation on leadership, reminding players that ambition, compassion, pride, and compromise all carry costs. The writing respects the intelligence of the audience, refusing to portray any decision path as universally correct. Instead, it invites introspection about responsibility, sacrifice, and what truly grants someone the “mandate” to rule.

Of course, the game’s strengths also hint at who it may not appeal to. Players expecting constant combat, large tactical maps, or complex mechanical systems may find the gameplay lighter than anticipated. Its interactive film format requires patience—reading expressions, absorbing dialogue, and considering outcomes. Technical limitations, occasional pacing inconsistencies, or branching paths that vary in refinement may also remind players that this is an indie production reaching beyond typical boundaries. But these qualities feel less like flaws and more like natural trade-offs in service of its narrative ambition.

Mandate of Heaven ultimately succeeds because it understands the appeal of power not as domination, but as responsibility. It invites players to step into a dynasty on the brink, surrounded by flawed humans, uncertain futures, and competing visions of salvation. It delivers a cinematic role-playing experience where storytelling, atmosphere, and consequence carry more weight than spectacle or mechanical complexity. For players who value narrative agency, political intrigue, grounded emotional stakes, and replayability driven by ethical curiosity, it offers one of the most engaging and distinctive interactive dramas in recent memory. It may not aim to please everyone, but for those receptive to its approach, it feels more like inhabiting a legend than simply playing a game.
