[{"review_text": "Just like PoE1, GGG again fails to understand that their top 2% of players aren't the right indicator of game balance.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 16, "timestamp_created": 1749469633}, {"review_text": "truly awesome game! I'm 42 and this game really brings back the feeling I got when I first played Diablo 2. The dark grim atmosphere, the difficulty, the beautiful voice acting and subtle feeling of dread! Truly an honor to be alive to play this game!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 25, "timestamp_created": 1733685589}, {"review_text": "This review is for those with experience playing Path of Exile 2; new players are encouraged to play the game to develop their own opinions.

To be clear, Path of Exile 2 has the potential to evolve into something great… the greatest ARPG ever in fact. Even small design shifts like the introduction of a dodge roll have added substantial tactical depth to the gameplay. But despite these improvements, the game’s publicly stated design philosophy is increasingly at odds with the actual gameplay experience. 

GGG has repeatedly insisted that PoE2 is meant to be slower and more deliberate. That’s a fine vision; but in reality, endgame mapping and enemy speed blatantly contradict this claim. The pace remains just as frenetic as it was in PoE1 and there’s just as much onscreen effects which can make it exceedingly challenging at times to even know what’s going on. If the intent was to slow things down, then loot distribution should have been adjusted to match. It hasn't been. On the contrary, this current iteration has made currency even more scarce, doubling down on grind without commensurate reward. The trade system? Still a disaster, faithfully carried over from PoE1 with all its archaic inefficiencies.

GGG seems unwilling to internalize a lesson that should be fundamental by now: punishing gameplay is not the same as challenging gameplay. Many systems are saturated with negative modifiers that drain momentum and morale rather than inspire mastery. Nowhere is this more obvious than in end game mapping, where stacking mods can paradoxically make a map less playable due to sheer mechanical overkill. Several mods outright mean that if you luck into the wrong map suffix you will automatically be throwing that map in the trash (I’m looking at you temporal chains).

Yes, the game is in early access, but GGG seems to have misunderstood what early access is for. It’s supposed to be a testing ground, a sandbox for players to explore systems, theorycraft, and search for broken interactions. In a  game that’s loot dependent, that requires access to resources. Instead, loot is miserly. I constantly run over 100% magic find and still see abysmal returns. Divines are rare. Exalts bizarrely drop more often than Chaos, Regals, or Alchemy orbs. Orbs of Annulment or Chance? Nearly mythical (I say this after playing for over 420+ hours).

Crafting is nonexistent in any meaningful form as the entire system has been reduced to pure gambling. The tools are there and were shown to work in PoE1, but in PoE2 there’s no actual semi-deterministic crafting so experimentation dies on the vine. 

Defense stats in PoE2 remain deeply imbalanced. Armor is still underwhelming, scaling poorly in the face of high incoming damage. Evasion is serviceable. Meanwhile, energy shield continues to dominate across most content. This persistent asymmetry undermines build diversity and reinforces a stagnant meta. This is further exacerbated by the aforementioned lack of currency and crafting, which often leaves players stuck if they’re not wealthy enough to regear their characters in a different manner.

The Trial of the Sekhema is one of the more baffling screwups in the game. The central mechanic, an “honor” meter that diminishes when you’re hit, actively punishes entire archetypes of play. Builds that rely on taking damage as part of their identity such as anything melee related, thorns-based, armor-heavy, or self-damage synergies, are effectively penalized for functioning as intended. The concept of "honor" in combat might make sense thematically, but from a gameplay perspective it's incoherent. “Oh but honor isn’t an issue if you stack honor resist”, ok, stacking “honor resist” is a lazy workaround, not a solution. “Well you can do the Trials of Chaos then”, sure, let’s talk about the ToC.

The Trials of Chaos continue the trend of stacking punishment under the guise of difficulty. Layer upon layer of negative modifiers are applied to both the player and the environment, creating scenarios where success often feels less like a result of skill and more like surviving Jonathan’s spite. Once again, the issue isn’t that the trials are difficult, it’s that GGG confuses misery with difficulty. These trials don't challenge a player's decision-making or adaptability so much as test their tolerance for suffering. Some of the modifiers will 100% of the time be a death sentence, which is ridiculous for a game mode that demands you run a gauntlet.
To reiterate: punishing gameplay is not the same as challenging gameplay. And until GGG takes that distinction seriously, much of the game's potential will remain unrealized beneath the weight of its own contradictions.

And then there’s the death penalty: a flat 10% XP loss. It’s an outdated design relic that punishes players disproportionately, especially in a game this unstable. The optimization is rough; CPU usage spikes inexplicably, screens freeze, and enemies with invisible on-death effects can wipe you before you even register the threat. The game already limits player through currency scarcity and map restrictions, why stack another misery mechanic on top of it all? Literally nearly every one of my high level deaths has been due to the game freaking out and freezing for a split second at the most inopportune times. This is the mechanic that makes me rage quit. This is the mechanic that makes me put the game down and leave it for extended periods of time. This is the mechanic which makes me rethink spending money on stash tabs, cosmetics, mystery boxes, etc.

Let me be absolutely clear here: the XP penalty is not just frustrating, it’s demoralizing. It actively discourages continued play and reveal a fundamental disrespect for player time. Once you hit the late 80s or early 90s in level, even fully juiced maps roll several levels below your character level, making XP grinding a slog. Combine that with PC performance issues and what you’re left with is a bad experience. And yes, I can already hear the diehard fanbase trotting out the same tired defense: “There have to be consequences, otherwise people will just spam content and they won’t learn how to get good.” Sorry, but no. That argument falls apart under the most basic scrutiny. Players can’t spam the same content; maps are gated behind RNG & limited runs. The system itself is already self-limiting. You don’t need an additional punitive XP penalty to “preserve challenge”; you need a well-balanced game that respects player time and rewards effort instead of eroding it in a hot instant.

Things I would like to see:
• Campaign Skip After Completion
Once a player has completed the campaign, they should be allowed to skip it on subsequent characters. 
• Make the Remaining Campaign Choices Reversible
In both Act 3’s, characters are forced to make two decisions regarding stats that are currently permanent. This design is incoherent, especially given that ascendancy choices can now be changed freely. Please allow these decisions to be changed as well (Let Doryani be the interface to make the changes).
• League Character Imports
The requirement to re-run the campaign for each new league or character is, again, tedious. A solution could involve importing characters back into a new league; either starting fresh at level 1 or with a baseline (e.g., level 60 with 500k gold and access to early maps). 
• PoE1 Atlas Skill Tree
The Atlas passive tree in PoE1 was amazing. The current iteration in PoE2 is by comparison a poor imitation. Bring back that depth!
• Boots: movespeed is necessary, so make it an implicit
• An Actual Early Access Philosophy: Treat the current state as a live experiment, not a soft launch. Be generous with currency, unique’s, and loot bases (hell let Ketzuli have another few tabs that just sell white bases), focus on testing systems rather than preserving some arbitrary economy that can easily be reset or wiped.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 29, "timestamp_created": 1746161089}, {"review_text": "I did not like PoE1. Got very overwhelmed with the skill tree and had to watch a bunch of explainations on YT to understand anything.
PoE2 is MUCH more accessible and fun. Bosses are clean. Maps, environments, and abilities look great. Skill tree is much easier. 
This game is great if you are a normal functioning human with a job and don't have to spend 4 hours to know wtf everything does. 9/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 39, "timestamp_created": 1734411214}, {"review_text": "I'm nearing the end of Act2 and I am loving this game. Why? The game balances weapon builds by allowing 100 points to allocated. Upgraded weapons can go over 100 points, therefor in general, upgraded weapons are better than custom self-made ones.

Use a website such as battlefinity.gg to compare stats such as TTK or damage drop over distance.
The most important stat (after dps) is precision. NOT CONTROL.

5. KV9, USG-90, UMG (good early game smgs, replace them when you find something better from above)
666. Any sniper is good to have but i pref M210 or Mini Scout

SL9 + M210

It definitely holds the most potential of all the current in-development RTS games and I wish it to keep going and improve and maybe one day reach that potential. It has a huge amount of content (single, and multiplayer) and is so much more engaging to play than its  most direct comparisons (e.g. Men Of War, COH) and indeed all other wee-men RTS games. The campaign missions are varied and fun. Its an absolute adrenaline rush for me,  So many battlefield like moments occur at that level", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1753754233}, {"review_text": "“Good, [strike] bad[/strike] and ugly"

As someone who enjoys playing the Men of War series, Call to Arms: Gates of Hell – Ostfront immediately felt familiar. It’s a real-time tactics game set on the Eastern Front of World War II – gritty, grounded, and utterly relentless. You command squads of infantry, tanks, artillery, and everything in between in brutal and historically grounded battles.

What makes this game shine for me is its authenticity and attention to detail. The visuals, the sound design, the pacing – it all comes together to recreate the look and feel of warfare in a way that’s hard to match. The units behave like real soldiers, the armor feels weighty and vulnerable at the same time, and each engagement feels personal and intense. The penetration and damage model are spot on.

As a self-declared historical nerd, I adore the sheer variety of equipment. Whether I’m fielding early-war Panzer Is or later beasts like the Tiger I and II, the game constantly feeds my need for historically accurate gear. The same goes for the Soviets – T-26s, KV-1s, and the mighty IS-series make appearances in all their brutal, riveted glory.

One of my favorite aspects is the dynamic campaign mode. It's not just battle after battle – there's an economy to manage, a tech tree to develop, and meaningful strategic decisions to make between missions. It adds depth and consequence to every victory (or defeat), and scratches that long-term strategy itch without getting in the way of the core combat.

I still remember one battle where my defenses were holding just fine – until a Soviet KV-1 rumbled onto the field. My 50mm PaK AT gun couldn’t even scratch it. It was like watching history unfold – just like in real life, the KV heavy tank series was a shock for the Germans early in the war, a machine that could shrug off nearly all early AT weapons. I was forced to scramble, reallocate units, call artillery, bait it into a minefield – whatever I could do. It was a desperate, cinematic moment that ended in victory, and I swear I had a wide grin on my face afterwards. Moments like that are why I play these games.

Now… let’s talk about the ugly. Because yes – the UI. It's bad. No – ugly. The interface feels like a relic. It’s like someone dropped a toolbox on the screen and said “good luck.” It takes time to get used to, and even after that, it feels like a major missed opportunity. A cleaner, more streamlined UI would be most welcome.

Still, despite the interface struggles, Gates of Hell – Ostfront delivers one of the most immersive, satisfying, and historically rich RTS experiences I’ve had in years. If you’re into WW2 tactics and love games that reward positioning, timing, and authenticity – this one's for you.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1754395539}, {"review_text": "this game made me realize how stupid I've been for spending 800 hrs on Company of Heroes 2, desperately trying to "patch" the game with "realism" mod such as Wikinger n Spearhead, when this exist all along.

The game runs relatively well considering whats going on during regular gameplay, its far less jank than its predecessors and the development team consistently delivers quality updates, hotfixes, etc. These people have a good understanding of what they're working with, being comprised mostly of modders. 

My only real complaints with the game are some of the lingering AI jank (pathing and general behaviour lacking all common sense) and the fact that the game is only going to match MOWAS 2 in terms of sheer content if you opt to buy all the DLC, which gets expensive fast. I still think the DLC is reasonably priced considering the effort that goes into the extensive research, accurate modelling and general design put into everything (some of the missions in some DLCs do not reflect this though in my opinion) but its definitely something you need to consider with how barren the base game can feel. Workshop support is good as the game retains that healthy modding scene that the other games have seen, and its generally a fun time. But even though I personally continue to play it, objectively I just can't recommend this game when after 3 years we have:

- occasional synchronization issues in multiplayer/coop, when one player sees different things to another
- tanks sometimes teleporting/instarotating in multiplayer/coop
- very minor things like fences or some trees eating tank shells completely
- visibility/battlefield readability issues ignored even though I came up with multiple mockups
- random hard to diagnose performance degradations (especially at game start)
- a feeling that networking is even worse than in MoW:AS2
- pathfinding being stupid, causing stuff like people getting out of trenches for no reason at all when ordered to go to another part of the trench and getting killed
- a lot of other small but annoying issues, like inventory contents occasionally vanishing, bugging out, soldier AI being stupid, shells flying in whatever direction etc.


That isn't even mentioning things like Soviet SPGs not having the switchable indirect fire mode that was apparently promised ages ago, and missing armor mechanics that make certain matchups biased, like Panther upper glacis being able to tank endless amount of early IS-2 shots at distance and not giving a damn, even though the armor would've cracked IRL already (and the devs also won't do anything about it). Sometimes, it feels like GoH's engine has more broken things than fixed things compared to the iteration of engine in MoW:AS2, which makes playing a frustrating experience, if you're not a hardcore historism fan.

I was reporting many of the things above that make the experience frustrating, but I feel like my feedback is mostly neglected, so I stopped doing that mostly.

I really want to love this game because I like the idea of a more realistic MoW:AS2, but currently it feels like basic playability is neglected. You can't make up basic playability issues with accuracy to details and a lot of contents. I honestly regret my decision to spend so much money on copies of this game when this is the experience I get after all this time.

I only recommend to buy the base game at discounts and see for yourself if you enjoy or get frustrated. + Textures
+ ANIMATIONS (They're so much better omg)

[h2]Why I'm so frustrated[/h2]

The game gets ruined by an [b]immense amount of AI spamming[/b] in some missions. It gets to the point where it's literally unplayable. Strategy doesn't matter when the enemy gets infinite units, as the game just turns into a meatgrinder where you focus on endlessly killing AI tanks and hoping yours survive.

To make things even worse, sometimes your own AI just picks a weird path and runs straight into the enemy for no reason. So you're fighting an enemy that's a perfect micromanager, while also trying to stop your own guys from getting themselves killed like idiots. It's frustrating as hell.

And when the AI starts spamming, the performance starts to show some cracks. It all just becomes a huge, laggy mess.

[h1]Final verdict[/h1]

Basically a hit-and-miss game.

[b]BUY THIS FOR CO-OP[/b], if your friend has enough money to buy all the same DLCs.

The Katyusha rocket launches deliver a thunderous crescendo that echoes the terror of the battlefield, maintaining an atmosphere of unrelenting tension. These elements transform routine maneuvers into pulse-quickening events; even subtle cues, like the crunch of boots on frost-covered ground, draw you deeper into the simulation.

At its core, the gameplay delivers unparalleled depth. With an expansive array of historically accurate units, from rudimentary early-war equipment to formidable late-game assets, you can customize forces with granular control over loadouts and formations. Campaigns present evolving challenges that demand adaptive strategies, the AI responds with intelligent aggression yet allows for masterful counterplays, and co-op multiplayer fosters coordinated operations of remarkable scale.
One highlight is commanding the Tiger tank, a behemoth that instills an overwhelming sense of dominance. As it rumbles across the battlefield to seize a contested zone, its guttural engine roar shakes your teeth, underscoring its unstoppable presence. Disposing of enemy armor with a single, precise shot to the hull feels profoundly satisfying—nothing else on the field seems capable of challenging it, turning advances into exhilarating displays of superiority.

Equally captivating is unlocking the artillery barrage, a spectacle that elevates the strategic layer to cinematic heights. The anticipation builds as you call in a strike on a stubborn enemy position, eyes fixed on the sky, willing that perfect shell to land true. When it does, the devastation unfolds in breathtaking fashion: troops ragdoll violently from direct hits or convulse from the concussive force of nearby blasts, scattering debris and morale in equal measure.

If there's a minor drawback, it's that Gates of Hell has redefined expectations for WW2 RTS titles to such an extent that returning to others feels diminished by comparison—their shallower mechanics pale against this benchmark of excellence. Yet this speaks volumes about its quality.

[{"review_text": "Path of Exile rewards curiosity in a way few action RPGs manage. The early acts feel familiar at first, but the moment you start experimenting with support gems and the passive tree, the game opens into a giant sandbox of ideas. A single skill can become a completely different tool depending on how you route your passives and which supports you pair with it. I went from glass cannon mapper to tanky boss hunter without rerolling, simply by rethinking links and a few key passives. That sense of agency never really fades.

The league model is the engine that keeps it fresh. New mechanics arrive regularly, but the knowledge you build carries forward, so coming back never feels like a reset. Endgame mapping is where the design really clicks. Atlas choices, crafting decisions, and bossing routes layer together, and you can feel the impact of your planning in your drops and in your fights. There is a lot to learn, no question. The community tools are excellent, a good loot filter turns noise into signal, and the game gives you room to grow at your own pace. Monetization stays in the background. Stash space is the clear quality of life buy, cosmetics are optional, and nothing leans on pressure tactics.

If you enjoy theorycrafting, tinkering, and the satisfaction of seeing an idea turn into a build that melts a map you once tiptoed through, this is a long term home. Give it a weekend, and it has a way of taking over your evenings.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1761529584}, {"review_text": "You'll hear that you can only play this with a guide. Be rational, please.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1738438795}, {"review_text": "This is a weird genre to review, as it's a loot based arpg that also seems to have co-operative / social mmo-lite elements included. One way or the other it's designed to suck up as many hours of your time as is humanly possible, whether that's the grind to level up in the single-player content, or the end-game content that seems nigh on impossible without another players assistance.

The fundamentals are quite enjoyable and there is a fair bit of depth to its mechanics. The only problem is that by the time you get to the point where you can really start experimenting, well, you'll have finished the most meaningful story content and along the way have encountered some horrendous difficulty spikes that put a blight on the enjoyment to be had.

You can't "get gud" with this type of game, only understand its systems better, and hope to get lucky with the random drops. As it isn't a reflex-driven action game like Dark Souls, but is instead one where you load up with the best spells / armour / weapons and then mindlessly obliterate enemies whilst most of the time you can hardly even see what's going on due to all the special effects.

Every time you level up, or upgrade your gear, it gets "better" to play, but at the same time devolves when it comes to the action. You're either going to get one-shotted by something that will takes ages grinding to be able to overcome, or you'll cut through mobs like a hot knife through melted butter. 

Come a certain stage of development this is the default response. It's either ridiculously easy, or insanely hard, and both to my mind are the kind of poor design (or not, if you like this kind of thing) that sums up the genre.  Yes, you have to think when setting up your gear, but in the heat of battle it's just spamming attacks and anyone will do (even when an enemy is supposedly resistant to its effects, if you're high enough in power they will die to anything)

So it can be fun and thoughtful as you min / max your loot, and the action is visceral with its graphics, sounds and feel. Up to a point it's enjoyable, but then the difficulty spikes for bosses, and the somewhat clumsy general game-play that accompanies them, take off a lot of the shine. 

The narrative is...there...and it's...okaaaaaay, I suppose. Even though it seems like its made up of several different stories bodged together (which it is, given that this was developed over years of early access) and none of the characters or plot-points are especially interesting, or original. 

There's enough here to be reasonably satisfying, right up until the time where it gets tedious trying to do the end-game content. I want to address anyone who has ever thought Path of Exile LOOKED potentially really fun or interesting, but found it too intimidating or dense and ultimately decided against playing it.

Path of Exile has a long and storied history of being "overly complicated" and you hear so many memes, jokes, but also serious advice about how you "NEED to follow a build guide" to enjoy this game, how you NEED outside tools and resources like loot filters and how if you don't go do hours of research and watch guide videos and read a Leaguestart Build Guide on Maxroll.gg before even installing the game you're going to have a bad time and not understand anything.

THIS IS ALL 100% FALSE. 

Or, at the very least, HEAVILY over-exaggerated. 

Is Path of Exile a complex game with a lot of interlocking systems that take time to learn and understand? 
Yes.

Does Path of Exile do a good job tutorializing these systems adequately within the game itself?
Not really.

But - crucially - is a robust understanding of these systems necessary to try the game out and enjoy it?
NO.

Path of Exile is no more or less complex than any other isometric RPG out there - I would easily compare the first-time playthrough of POE to something like Divinity: Original Sin, Pillars of Eternity, or one of Owlcat's Pathfinder games in terms of system complexity - although certainly not in narrative design. Path of Exile's strength is certainly *not* in its narrative but that's not a bad thing!

So if you are an RPG enjoyer, if you enjoyed the MECHANICAL COMPLEXITY of the above or similar games and want to try something more real-time, action-combat focused - PLEASE DO YOURSELF A FAVOR, IGNORE EVERYONE TELLING YOU THAT YOU NEED A BUILD GUIDE AND A LOOT FILTER AND THIS AND THAT AND THIS OTHER THING AND JUST PLAY THE GAME. 

The campaign of Path of Exile, the first time you play through it, assuming you're not trying to speedrun it for some reason and you take your time to just enjoy the game for what it is, will last you somewhere between 20 and 35 hours. 

For FREE. 

And it's GREAT. 

As long as you have a *baseline understanding* of how RPGs work, how to generally understand things like stats from your passive skill tree and items, and you put in SOME amount of effort to actually engage with the *basic* systems the game presents to you like the skill gem system, you can 100% beat the campaign without any sort of build guide as long as you're not just allocating your passive skill points by essentially throwing darts and hoping for the best. 

You don't even need to "decide" what kind of "build" you're going for, really, until you're done with the first two Acts of the game. You have plenty of time to experiment with the variety of different skills in the game, because Path of Exile's variety MOSTLY comes from its Skill Gem system - something you can easily experiment with and swap around freely in the early game with little to no opportunity cost. Even in the later stages of the campaign you can still experiment and play around with swapping skills - it might take a bit *more* effort than in the early stages of the game, but as long as you're not trying to swap to something that's the polar opposite of what you've been doing for the last 15 hours, you'll be fine.

So - pick a class that seems to have a power fantasy you enjoy. Do you like throwing lightning bolts and fireballs? Play the Witch or the Templar. Do you like being a sneaky, stealthy ninja or assassin? Play the Shadow. Like killing enemies from a whole screen away with a bow? Play the Ranger. Do you like being a jack-of-all-trades of martial combat, able to use any weapon to a reasonable degree? Play the Duelist. 

Do you like bonking things really hard with a big hammer/mace/insert other two-handed big weapon here? Play the Marauder. 

Then, when you see the passive skill tree for the first time, *don't panic*. It seems VERY intimidating at first - but I promise you, it isn't. The reason the passive tree is so big is because it's the SAME TREE for EVERY CLASS - each class just *starts* somewhere different. So zoom in to *your class's* section of the passive tree, and just take a look at what the class has easy access to. You don't need to make any decisions yet - just take a look and start feeling it out. For now, all you need to do is start putting your skill points on a path to things that give you stuff that will serve you well on any sort of build - for example, it's NEVER a bad idea to path towards more Life with your passive skill points until you've filled out the two or three clusters of Life skills closest to your starting location in the tree.

By the time you start running out of "generalist" passive skills, hopefully you'll have settled on a skill that feels fun and good - and you can start investing your precious skill points into passives that are a bit more specialized. Don't just abandon investing in things like Life and Resistances - but you can start really "building" your character a bit here!

That's it. As long as you have some semblance of a *plan* for your character - like you should in any RPG - you won't screw up your "build" to the point where you can't even beat the campaign. In fact, the problem will usually be your gear - something that can *definitely* be fixed. If you feel like your damage is too low, if you're dying too much, checking and upgrading your gear will fix 90+% of your problems. A good rule of thumb is to always prioritize gear that has high Life and at least one Elemental Resistance stat - except on your weapon, where you want high damage. A pair of gloves that only has two stats, but those stats are +70 Life and +26% Fire Res, are better than a pair of gloves that has 5 stats but only +10 Life and no resists.

By the time you beat the campaign and reach the endgame, with maps and the Atlas Tree and Crafting and Pinnacle Bosses and all that - the parts of the game that DO need a build guide, that DO need a more robust understanding of its more complex systems - you will already have had 20+ hours of a fun RPG experience to inform you if the game is something you enjoy enough to be *worth* all the legwork.

So - do yourself a favor. If POE looks fun, or interesting, and you've always *wanted* to try it - but everything *surrounding it* sounds really intimidating? 

Try it anyway. 

You might not like it. You might get halfway through Act 3 and feel like the game still isn't meshing with you, and you're not having fun. That's okay! At least you can say you tried! 

You might only play through the campaign once or twice and have a good time, but then move on to other games. That's great!

Creating your build is unintuitive too. With the way the skill gem system works, ideally you only want one or two damaging skills, while the rest of your gems go to utility or support. Skills aren't tied to classes, so the first step to finding out what you like to play is picking a skill (most of which you won't know about until later in the campaign). Then you work your way backwards and find nodes on the passive tree that compliment your damage skill, then you finally choose your class based on what direction of the tree you're trying to reach toward. It feels like you have to fully level a character and study the tree before you can start to get an idea of what you want to play.

Basically I think the game is horrible to play blind and a huge time investment, but can be great fun if you don't mind following build guides.

EDIT: Since posting this, I've logged another 60 hours or so. The game finally started becoming fun when I stopped listening to veterans' suggestions and just played at my own pace. They put such an emphasis on the campaign being the "tutorial" and the endgame being when the game actually starts that I thought I was missing out, but the campaign is a significant part of the experience.

If you play blind, the best advice I've found to succeed is:
[list]
[*] Focus mostly on a single damage type.
[*] Every act will have a decent difficulty spike.
[*] Remember to put points into maximum life and defenses (300 health per act is a good rule of thumb).
[*] Focus mostly on one type of base defense but make sure to layer it (if you go mostly evasion, you'll eventually get hit, so you need something else to survive that hit).
[*] Keep your resistances as close to the max of 75% as you can (most easily achieved with crafting a suffix onto each of your gear pieces--hold Alt to see item details).
[*] Links on gear are incredibly important. Use orbs to upgrade basic whites to yellows if they have good sockets and links. Put your main damage gem in one socket and put nothing but supports in the adjacent sockets.
[/list]

What finally made the game click for me was when I let go of being attached to my characters and realized that every decision is meant to be meaningful. If a build didn't work out or became boring, I just started a new character with my newfound knowledge. It was such a satisfying moment when I finally felt my builds becoming stronger with each new iteration.

I still think the game is awful to play blind because they don't explain much of anything to you. And playing through the acts can be repetitive, so I wish they let you level through randomized maps. But aside from how unwelcoming the game is, this is basically what I've been looking for in an ARPG. Not a braindead easy game where you press buttons and the screen blows up. And not a game where you have to complete the campaign on 3 separate difficulties just to get to the fun part. PoE is actually challenging right from the get-go.

But Infinite? Nah. They cut the game in half, slapped a $60 price tag on the campaign, and then turned multiplayer into some predatory free-to-play battle pass scheme. They shoved armor coatings, color palettes, and even basic-ass helmets behind paywalls. Shit that we used to unlock through playing the damn game is now locked away unless you open your wallet. And if you did pay for the campaign? Congrats, you get absolutely nothing extra in multiplayer — you’re basically on the same footing as some free-to-play tourist.

It’s insulting. We didn’t just buy Halo Infinite, we funded their excuse to gut the series and chase live-service trends. And the cherry on top? They drip-feed content at a snail’s pace, while charging more for cosmetic bundles than old Halo map packs used to cost.

I’ve been playing Halo since Halo 3 back in 2007, so this series means a lot to me. Even though I enjoyed Halo Infinite early on especially around Season 3 and the Spirit of Fire operation I can’t help but feel disappointed with where this game has gone. The newest operation, “Operation: Infinite,” is finally releasing some coatings that were in the game files since launch but were never available unless you paid absurd prices in the shop or waited for them to show up in an operation pass.

Remember when 343 said they had a 10-year plan for this game? That fell apart almost immediately. At launch, Infinite felt fresh fun gameplay, fluid movement, and a lot of promise. But after 2,000 hours, you start to see all the cracks.

Ever since the so-called “network update” about a year ago, the experience for me as a PC player has been steadily going downhill. Anything above 80 ping and the game becomes borderline unplayable constant blanks, heavy aim, broken hit registration, grenades disappearing midair, and rockets that simply don’t fire or explode. The gun-play feels great mechanically, but the networking and desync completely ruin it.

343 has had control of the Halo franchise for over a decade now, and after three mainline games, it still feels like they’ve learned nothing. “One step forward, three steps back” should honestly be their company slogan at this point. Infinite nails the fundamentals the art direction feels closer to Bungie’s golden era, your Spartan feels agile and grounded, and movement is crisp like Halo 2 and Halo 3 not the hyper-speed, twitchy mess of Halo 4 and 5. The insider flight tests were amazing, the community feedback was overwhelmingly positive, and everyone was saying, “Halo is back.” Then the game actually launched… and it was the exact opposite of what we were promised.
The live service model is a desperate cash grab. Six years of development, over a hundred developers, and half a billion dollars yet Halo Infinite still has less content than most $40 indie shooters. They marketed it as “free to play,” but still charged $60 for the campaign which itself launched incomplete, lacking mission replay, co-op, or proper progression for months.

They promised “Halo Reach-level customization” and delivered a system where 85% of all cosmetics are locked behind paywalls or FOMO-limited event passes. You either grind through uninspired event challenges or pay up. And even then, the shop prices are ridiculous.

There’s just no motivation to play anymore. I only log in when there’s an operation or limited-time event, just to grab cosmetics I’ll probably never use. And even during those, I end up frustrated desync, heavy aim, disappearing grenades, and constant blank shots make matches infuriating. Playing on keyboard and mouse feels awful; aim feels sluggish and inconsistent, as if my Spartan is wading through quicksand.

The population drop tells the story: from millions at launch to under 7k daily players. For a franchise as legendary as Halo, that’s depressing. It’s a shell of what it used to be.

Honestly, they should’ve just delayed the game another two years instead of rushing out a half-finished product to meet deadlines. 343 has had 12 years to prove they can carry Halo’s legacy and every time, they fall short. Infinite had everything going for it nostalgia, hype, solid mechanics but they still managed to fumble it beyond belief.

And now with the recent reveal of Halo: Campaign Evolved (the new remaster), it’s clear no one at 343 or Halo Studios knows what they’re doing. Instead of fixing core gameplay issues or restoring community trust, they’re chasing remasters and marketing gimmicks. At this point, I just want a solid Halo multiplayer experience again something that respects the players, plays smoothly on PC, and doesn’t nickel-and-dime you at every corner. Until then, I’m done. Honestly, if you want to play a good Halo game, go play the Master Chief Collection. It’s far more enjoyable, the customization actually feels rewarding, and Halo: Reach is still alive and well with players who genuinely love the series. MCC feels like Halo. But now I just need level 100 in a battle pass for an armor effect. Worse yet, the grind is absolutely horrible. Weekly challenges can be done in a day and your performance when playing has next to no effect on your exp. It just feels hollow. 

Moreover, the game really doesn't bring anything new to the table. It's a return to form after Halo 5 basically turning Halo on its head, but past that... I mean the vehicles are red? The weapon sandbox on release was honestly a near deal breaker for me at the time, they all just felt so lackluster, especially the new weapons excluding a couple key highlights. It's been rounded out since then, but that brings this facet of the game 0, instead of in the negatives. Previous games, however, brought something new and impactful to the game since Halo 3. ODST brought Firefight, Reach with Invasion, 4 with Spartan Ops, and 5 with Warzone. Infinite? Well... Invasion is back... And Infection... Both in inferior forms... But most of the highlights, including the aforementioned, are built on the shoulders of skilled, passionate, creative... Uncompensated Forge creators. Thought I was gonna say something positive? Wish I could.

So, well, where does that leave us? A solid foundation with an enjoyable gameplay loop but nothing built on said foundation and nothing to actually keep you playing. I wish I could say that the game will get better with time and it'll fulfill the massive potential that it has, but come on. Still, for all the nickel-and-diming, the game underneath is one hell of a return to form. Every gunfight feels like classic Halo. Every vehicle is an invitation to cause problems on purpose. Every moment reminds you why this series was legendary in the first place.

[b]TL;DR:[/b]

Developed by Two Point Studios and published by SEGA, the game invites players to build and manage a healthcare empire from the ground up, diagnosing bizarre fictional illnesses, hiring eccentric staff, and balancing the fine line between patient care and profit. With its charming art style, witty writing, and surprisingly deep gameplay systems, Two Point Hospital manages to be both lighthearted and engaging, appealing to casual players and simulation veterans alike.

At its core, Two Point Hospital is about constructing functional, efficient hospitals across a series of increasingly challenging scenarios. Each new level presents a unique location with distinct objectives, environmental hazards, and patient populations. Players must design and organize treatment rooms, GP offices, diagnostic labs, and staff facilities in a way that maximizes patient throughput while keeping morale high and finances stable. The building interface is intuitive and flexible, allowing players to place and decorate rooms freely, tweak layouts to optimize workflow, and respond quickly to the changing needs of the hospital.

One of the most distinctive features of Two Point Hospital is its delightfully absurd sense of humor. Illnesses range from “Light-Headedness” (where patients literally have light bulbs for heads) to “Mock Star” (a Freddie Mercury impersonation disorder), each with comically themed treatments and animations. The visual gags, tongue-in-cheek dialogue, and frequent radio announcements filled with dry British wit give the game a unique personality that sets it apart from more serious or sterile management sims. Despite the satirical approach, the game does a commendable job of capturing the core elements of hospital management—triage, patient flow, staffing issues, and budget constraints—without ever feeling grim or overwhelming.

Staff management is a major pillar of gameplay, and it’s far more nuanced than it first appears. Each staff member has unique skills, personalities, and quirks that affect their job performance, morale, and even how much chaos they introduce into your hospital. The game also introduces a number of systems to keep things interesting as your hospitals grow. This metagame progression gives players a sense of continuity and long-term achievement beyond just completing individual levels.

Visually, Two Point Hospital uses a clean, cartoonish art style that balances functionality with charm. Managing your hospital's resources, balancing staff morale, and keeping up with patient demand can get tricky. You'll need to be strategic when it comes to building your layout and prioritizing research to unlock new treatments.

The game does a good job of gradually ramping up the difficulty as you progress through different hospitals, ensuring you always have new challenges to overcome. Some missions can feel a bit repetitive, especially with the more intricate hospital layouts, but the rewards for solving these complex puzzles are rewarding.
Performance and Stability:

On Steam, Two Point Hospital runs smoothly with no major performance issues. The game's system requirements are reasonable, and it's optimized for both high-end and mid-range PCs. Load times are quick, and there are few bugs or crashes to speak of, making for a generally pleasant gaming experience.
Final Thoughts:

Two Point Hospital is an incredibly fun and quirky simulation game that offers hours of entertainment. Its mix of light-hearted humor, strategic depth, and charming art style makes it an easy recommendation for anyone who loves management sims. The game does have some repetitive elements, and the challenge can sometimes feel like a bit of a grind, but the overall package is solid.

Whether you're a veteran of the genre or new to hospital management, Two Point Hospital delivers a unique and enjoyable experience. Highly recommended for simulation fans, though those looking for a serious or realistic experience may want to look elsewhere.

Pros:

    Fun and humorous premise
    Charming visuals and sound design
    Addictive gameplay loop with strategic depth
    Smooth performance on Steam

Cons:

    Can feel repetitive at times
    Some levels can be grindy or frustrating

In this game, you are the administrator and your purpose is to run an efficient hospital and meet the requirements to earn a star and move on to the next challenge. Having played both Theme Hospital and this game, I appreciate that the world map provides a sense of place as well as context to where you are going to be sent to next. The DLCs stretch where you go. From the frozen mountains, to the tropics and even through time and space, there is plenty to do. More on those later.

The game’s graphics, gameplay and quality of life features are steps above Theme Hospital in many significant ways, especially thanks to some update patches. With only a few minor niggles when it comes to pathfinding or assigning jobs to your staff, running a hospital is a smooth process and you are not punished for changing your mind about room layouts or even changing its location. That is not to say that it is easy, and in fact the best feature to manage patient flow is to make treatment prices the max cost while telling diagnosis rooms to fast-track treatment, so that doctors are freed up to work on incoming patients, while earning as much money as possible.

As a small aside, the hospital that is run like a nationalised service in the base game, is considered one of the most difficult. This is simply because it is the only one where you don’t get paid for treating patients...nothing like real life at all!

It is quite easy to get into a comfortably flow with this game while listening to podcasts, and with the ability to save room layouts to be loaded later, the game is designed to be highly entertaining with a mix of deadpan humour and ridiculous diseases and cultural references.

[{"review_text": "⚠️ Background:
This is a review of the 4.0 overhaul. It maybe belongs on the Biogenesis expansion page, but requires spending £20 to put it there. I followed the development of this release very closely. I read all the diaries. Dev forum comments. Watched the streams. Followed discord dev messages.

📜Review:
4.0 ("Phoenix") left the game in a grim place. Biogenesis itself seems excellent and was clearly QA tested - the expansion team did very well! ...But they have been caught in the custodians' crossfire - catching flak for things that aren't the expansions' fault.

[olist]
[*][b]The primary objective[/b] of 4.0 was to resolve Stellaris' performance issues (pops now, and a fleet patch coming later for that half of the problem). Understand that performance is a promise the developers have made before, particularly with 2.0 and 2.2. And after both of those patches Stellaris ended up with worse sim speed and lower frames. Whatever gains the studio made were lost with scope creep and new ideas. Eladrin and his modern team knew this history. So to promise the same thing again in 2025 demonstrated real confidence. The result? Oh dear. 4.0 performance is not better than 3.14. In fact it's not even on par. In fact it's [b]considerably worse[/b]! Unbelievable.

[*]Before Christmas PDX polled the community on a number of exciting reworks and improvements to various game systems. Long awaited features. High potential areas. Internal politics. Espionage improvements. Warfare resolution. Fleets. [b]Immediately after[/b] christmas they announced 4.0: Affecting nothing listed and instead shipping a rework to the planet GUI [i]for a third time[/i] which was already fundamentally sound and had no one asking for changes. Time wasting.

[*]Around New Year PDX reflected on the fact that 2024 had been a messy year with lots of very large DLCs that didn’t have the time for quality they should have. They reassured the community that they would scale back for 2025. Give things more quality control. Breathing room. [b]Immediately after[/b] (a matter of days!) they announced 3 massive DLC's for 2025, non negotiable launch dates, 4.0 squeezed in the middle and the busiest year to date.

[*]The new “District Specialisation” system is convoluted. It doesn't reduce clicking and it doesn't help the AI. Have fun guessing which buildings go where. Have fun with dry and flavour-less "x support" specialisations.  The change nullifies the past half-decade of AI and planetary automation improvements. The rework had nothing to do with the new performance-relating pop changes and [b]was not necessary[/b]. When asked multiple times why it was being enacted PDX were unable to give more than two or three meaningful applications in the entire game.

When asked to add new districts in 4.0 (e.g. research districts), a hotly requested feature that would have been quick to implement and has all the same benefits as their bloated rework, the Phoenix team explained that they too loved the idea! It's what started this whole thing! But what concerned them was GUI space. So instead they enacted this massive time sink of an overhaul, with all the implementation, bug fixing, and balance costs (still ongoing), that allow you to [i]customise[/i] a district. This is staggeringly poor decision making because:

[list]
[*]UI space is not an issue for additional districts! Even with 10-20 district types. The selection area can be made scroll-able, and once the first is built it can be pinned to the top of the list. In 99% of situations the player never has to scroll again. This is perfectly usable. District expansion mods are extremely popular and have been for years. They are “solving” an issue that doesn’t exist.
[*]The only reason the planet GUI is limited is because it must conform to 720p (or 800p) resolutions. When asked to relax the limit here in 2025, by both the community and his own UX designer, Eladrin has said no.
[*]The 4.0 planet rework hasn’t produced a more useable GUI regardless! Just as with performance, 4.0 delivers a worse experience. Myriad stats, buttons and options are now buried in secondary tabs and nested menus when they used to be on the main screen. Yes, you read that correctly. This rework started by quibbling over a little district scrolling and now instead half the planet GUI tools are buried behind multiple clicks. (Update: As of 4.1 some of this has been resolved. Personally I am OK with the interface now.)
[/list]
[/olist]

On three personal notes, there are some more subjective elements I loathe about 4.0:
[olist]
[*]The unnecessarily massive numbers. 1000's of pops and jobs. Stellaris used to be elegant. 1 food for 1 pop. Now it's messy and tedious to parse. These off-putting numbers are so bloated they couldn't fit into the UI when first shown and the tool-tips look [i]ridiculous[/i]. The studio argued this was necessary because they felt fractional pops wouldn’t make sense. When of course they do. They also argued that reading lots of decimal zeroes/integers on pops would read poorly, so we get inflated zeros on [u]every[/u] planetary management mechanic! Baffling.

[*]Trade as a resource is a half baked idea trying to do too many things. It’s logistics, shipping, galactic credit and wealth stockpiling all in one. As with many custodian initiatives (such as paying "unity" for leaders) the story considerations were not made. Then there are energy-credits. For the purposes of all the dialogue, stories and events already in the game that’s still the only currency. It’s an obvious half measure, but the team didn’t want to comb through all the files.

[*]Civilians are poorly implemented. They muddy the waters with unemployment. They spam relentless warning notifications that players are being asked to ignore (resolved in 4.1). They have broken the slavery mechanic. They conflict with empire role-play. They are fuzzy to develop/manage, and so far in practice they're basically just power creep.
[/olist]

These are all examples of sloppy, flat-out badly designed systems. The custodians, whose remit was to [i]support the DLCs[/i] and provide fixes, have ironically driven a bulldozer through Biogenesis with poor quality work. And while certain elements of 4.0 (like the currently broken AI, balance and bugs) may be resolved in upcoming patches, the wonky aspects I've reviewed here are permanent. Stellaris is stuck like this now. Forever.

Not recommended.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1747654359}, {"review_text": "Stellaris is my first real experience with Paradox, and on a larger scale, 4X games in general. I literally don't realize where the hours go when I'm playing it. Extremely deep and detailed mechanics make Stellaris insanely replayable. You'll never run out of ideas to do in a playthrough.

At the time of writing this review I've played the game for 75 hours and I still haven't seen the infamous end-game crisis. Hell, I don't even know how the game ends and someone wins. That's how insanely big it is. I just keep restarting my games in favor of implementing a better idea, only for it to fail even more miserably :D

Be warned though, you'll have to give it time, maybe watch a few tutorials as well. So the barrier to entry, on a complexity level alone, is already high. And is made even higher with Paradox's business model for the game and its DLCs. You simply don't want to spend that much money on a single game. I get that. So if you do decide to give Stellaris a shot, I'd recommend picking up the Starter Edition and then expanding your collection with each discount sale (Stellaris goes on sale a lot) if you enjoy it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1733449676}, {"review_text": "TLDR; Stellaris is incredibly fun and allows for many playstyles and an unrivaled amount of customization, but don't get it if you don't have the patience or if you aren't prepared to shell out quite a bit of money (or wait for sales).


I just reached 1000 hours in this game so I thought I would write a review finally. I will probably have to change it soon though since tomorrow is the release of the 4.0 update.

Stellaris is a very fun game to play on your own or with other people (if you can ever get someone to play with you) and I would absolutely recommend it. That being said there are a few things. Stellaris is not a game for people who like completing a match in half an hour, which makes sense because it's a strategy game. You can play it for like half an hour at a time but a full game of Stellaris can take days to finish if you have it on the default time settings. Also the DLC scheme is a little annoying. The base game is really not worth paying 50$ for if you aren't going to buy at least a few DLC over time. I would recommend waiting for a sale to buy it since you need at least like 3 of the DLC for it to be enjoyable long term.

Now that I've gotten the bad out of the way there are a lot of great things about the game:

1. Replayability: Replayability in a game is really important and Stellaris has a lot of it. Every time you play the galaxy is completely different with different events, systems, planets, and empires. Even if you played the exact same empire every time your experience between two games would be fairly different. 

2. Customization: my favorite part of Stellaris is how customizable it is. I went into the game expecting it to be like a lot of strategy games with a few empires you can play as. The game is way different and allows you to completely create your empire from scratch; including your species, your government type and ideals, your origin which can drastically change your playstyle, and the look of your units and flag and stuff. In one playthrough you can play as a peaceful race of bird-people with psionic powers, and in another you can play as a collective of mass murdering machines who kill everything that breathes. 

3. Appeal to different playstyles: Stellaris is a game that can be fun for very different people with different wants out of a game. If you are interested in being a peaceful nation of diplomats there are very in-depth mechanics that deal with diplomacy. If you like trade and capitalism then there you can do a lot of that. If you like playing strategy games just to murder everyone then you can be a purifier and go total war on everyone with the in-depth war mechanics. 

4. Mechanics: the mechanics of Stellaris are very original in a lot of ways. The tech "tree" is more random and has a lot of mechanics dedicated to getting research of different types and specializing leaders to get the techs you want. The tradition tree mechanic gives you cool ways to customize the ideals of your nation and get different bonuses depending on how you want to play. You also get ascension perks for completing them which give you interesting new mechanics or massive bonuses. The game doesn't do turns or grids but instead uses an interconnected web of systems that ships can move about freely, and has everything happen in real time instead of being turn-based. I could go on and on about all the interesting and original mechanics but basically its very good and fun.

Basically Stellaris is a must have for anyone who likes any kind of strategy or roleplay, but requires a bit of a monetary investment.


If you have decided to get the game then this is the part where I give unsoliscited advice on which DLCs to get (you're gonna need a few). These are my top 10. 

1. Utopia: 
Basically everyone says to get Utopia first. This is for good reason because without it you basically aren't playing stellaris. 

2. Machine age:
Machine age is a massive addition to stellaris. The DLC adds machine empires (as an alternative to synthetic dawn). It adds the cybernetic and synthetic ascensions which are super good. It adds a new megastructure that produces some minerals (arc furnace), 3 new fun origins, and a new Crisis path that allows you to leave the universe for a better one while annihilating the old one and anyone who stands in your path.

3. Federations:
Federations is important not just because of the mechanics, but also because of the origins. Federations adds the most origins of any DLC (8) and almost all of them are fun. It also adds federations (duh) which allows you to become allied with other empires and get useful bonuses. 


4. Megacorp:
some people don't like megacorp (they are wrong) but personally it is my favorite way to play. Megacorp adds a few great things. It adds Ecuminopolis worlds which are worlds that are encased in a massive city, it adds a bunch of megastructures, it adds the caravaneers which are like space vegas, and finally it adds Megacorps. Megacorps are a style of government where you are governed by a massive company.  This is THE DLC for trade empires and is a must have if you like money.

5. Overlord:
Overlord is a great DLC if you like conquering and war because it expands the vassal system. Even if you don't like war this is a good DLC to get because it adds the conclaves. The conclaves are independant groups that help you in different ways. 

6. Paragons:

Sadly, Paradox have done what they always do. They simply do not know when to stop. Effectively the overdevelop the game in order to milk as much money as possible from their player base. As it stands today after years upon years of tinkering and meddling by the devs we're left with yet another impenetrable grand strategy game that makes it difficult to come back to after any reasonable time away. To my assessment, Stellaris has undergone so many changes that there could have been three separate titles created from the effort. Literally, we could have had Stellaris 1, 2, and 3 by now. 

What once could have been a timeless classic has now been altered and tweaked into a shape that's near unrecognisable. These alterations have effectively taken a classic genre defining game into a forgettable and somewhat irrelevant title.

I do then seriously believe that Paradox need to learn when to say that enough is enough. What fueled this apathy was the constant release of DLCs that further fueled my lack of interest in this game. Not only was the game overhauled to my mind, it locked some of those overhauls in a paywall, or segmented interesting features in what seemed like DLC on DLC. I can play the space Civ5-Like update from 2018 (at least to me it reminded me of Civ5 for some odd reason).

This is such an annoying attitude because its utterly clear they do not extensively playtest their main updates and just release semi developed milestones and then frantically update dump over the next couple weaks to even a few months.

all in all, i dont recommend this game, at least until it hits a period of stability. Small maps are too quick and boring. large maps, especially from mods are a blast, though get super slow and once an update drops and nukes your save, you will ragequit.

A pretty good survival game with fun building, survival mechanics, traps, helper NPCs, etc. Decent combat, with maybe a bit too much power given to the players, and a story that didn't pan out very well. A decent survival game with some good things going for it, though not as strong as it's predecessor where it counts. 7/10

The good:
The visuals are much better and the level design felt more rich. The forests feel properly dense and good to navigate. The new building system is better to work, allowing for much more specific manual control to let you engage in more nuanced construction. The inclusion of friendly NPCs was a welcome addition and it worked fairly well. The game ran well with fairly high settings and I played through the whole game with 2 friends and we never suffered a networking or connectivity issue.

I've never done SWAT at my Department, but for most situations involving things that require a tactical unit, we have the tools usually necessary to go in as patrol officers and I'm very much impressed by the realism here.  The scenarios and situations introduced are legitimate scenarios that SWAT teams and police will unfortunately encounter. So many police games either too over-the-top, use of force isn't scrutinized, and probable cause and other legal terms aren't recognized, but this game really seemed to get it right. There's too many cop games that have no idea how law enforcement actually works, but in this case, the dev team must've had good help behind the scenes from real world law enforcement. Thanks for not shying away from the more "triggering" scenarios, because even though they might be triggering, it's just the real world and what cops have to see and deal with in their line of work.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 42, "timestamp_created": 1734629954}, {"review_text": "I am a sucker for milsim games. I've played anything from DCS, Operation Flashpoint, Arma, Hell Let Loose, etc. so when I saw a SWAT game that looked pretty realistic, and from the many clips I saw on social media, I just had to give it a try.

Since most combat simulations revolve around the military, seeing a law enforcement game pull that level of realism immediately had my attention. Now, don't take it from me, I cannot speak on if it's truly 1:1 with reality. I've never served in the military or law enforcement to any capacity, but this game really immerses you. Looking back to relatively recent history all the way back to 50 years ago, this game definitely shares elements of the worst case scenarios and most intense law enforcement clashes in history. So basing it off historical events, this game comes pretty close.

As for immersion in-game, as a well traveled simulation player, this game has it all. For starters, the customization of pretty much everything is amazing. You can't customize character's body features outside of tattoos which is nice. I hate spending 20+ minutes designing characters only to look like an ogre. But you can customize your kit from the weapons you carry, what's on those weapons, the ammo type, grenades, armor type and coverage if any task oriented gear like shields, mirrors, and, well, you get the picture. But not only can you do this for your character, in single-player, you go in with a squad of 5 (including yourself) and you can customize just as much with your squad as you do yourself to suit the mission with the ability to save loadouts so you don't have to spend 30 minutes in pre-mission decking your team out. The AI all around is also insane. Your team will issue orders to civilians and suspects, will detain everyone they come across and bag evidence along the way with or without orders if it's safe enough to do so. The civilians will do dumb things that may make it seem like they're a threat when it's just a phone they're reaching for. "Dead" suspects may not be so dead. I played a mission where I shot a guy and he collapsed but I pushed passed him to clear the connecting room so I wouldn't get shot trying to arrest someone and the "dead" guy was just faking it. He waited until I stepped over him, stood up, and stabbed in the back. They'll also flee if they can and run circles around you until you run into each other again.

Speaking of single-player, not only do you deploy with a squad, you are given a command tab that allows you to control your team any way you see fit. Want to breach a door? Go right ahead, but HOW is the question. Want breaching charges? Maybe a shotgun to blow the lock? Maybe simplicity is bliss and you just want to kick the door in, flash and clear. Those are just a few examples with several more options available depending on how you kitted your team. For the most part, your AI teammates are competent and watch your back, follow your commands to a tee, and will even continue clearing buildings if no further commands are given. Some of the best, non-scripted friendly AI I've ever seen in a game. I've only had a few instances where they didn't do what they were supposed to do which I feel has something to do with their stress levels... yes, as team leader, you have to choose who you take on missions and manage stress levels... it is THAT in-depth.

As for multiplayer, you lose your AI squad but that's kind of the point. You NEED to work as a team with your friends if you want to survive, let alone win. It's all the same missions but with the added difficulty of usually fewer numbers and human error. Generally, the AI doesn't mistake civilians for threats and visa versa.

Controls... ah yes, what most new simulation players fear. I am happy to say this is the least complicated sim game I've ever come across. You have a key for quick commands and a key for the command menu. Weapons are universally the same as far as aim and shoot, however you have a key for attachments (one for zoom if applicable and one for light/laser if applicable). You have two different aiming methods which you can switch between whenever: sights and canted. You have hot keys for grenades and the previously mentioned quick command which will change depending on what you're looking at. Movement is universally the same, WASD+QE, a key for crouch, and a key for, what I call "free-lean," where you can crouch low to check underneath various objects and peer around corners with a little bit more flexibility. The rest of your gear is, by default, your numbers. Any item box with an arrow means you can use your wheel to select exactly what you want if multiple items are under the same category (ie. grenades, less lethal, etc.). Best part, the keybindings are customizable to suit every player.

Story. Well, it's complicated. There technically is a story however it's not as linear and black and white as, say, Call of Duty. There are missions that are connected to each other via evidence you come across and underlying clues to bigger elements. But like the daily life as law enforcement, each mission is different and not every case is connected.

Character development... non existent. In fact, there are only a few parts where anyone shows any form of emotion. Otherwise, all eyes are forward and all anyone is worried about is completing the mission.

Themes... well this is the most sensitive part. I'm a rational person and usually don't get mad at elements of a video game... however... there are some pretty rage inducing parts of the game simply because of the fact a lot of this has happened under similar circumstances. This is obviously not a game for kids, but there are some adults that may find this game VERY disturbing, or even upsetting. However, no matter what you come across and see, just know, the developers did an amazing job at not glorifying or encouraging anything. The game is very dark and parts were clearly meant to invoke an angry response to emphasize the tragedies and how horrific and close to home some of it is.

DLC and future updates. My favorite part and, what I'd assume, many more are concerned with. The devs are continuously working to improve and add to the game. As of this post, they recently just released their new Dark Waters DLC with new missions and weapons. The DLC is just as action packed as the main game but with even less story than there already was. Still fun nonetheless. From what I can tell though, the weapons are part of the updates which is free. The only extras you're paying for is missions. Great flexibility for players who want new gear but don't want to pay a large price for more content than they're looking for.

Cons... My least favorite part. For starters, you don't have a save feature. This game runs on auto save which only happens when you change your kit or upon completion of a mission. If you leave mid mission, it negatively impacts the morale of your squad and may cause them to quit as well as you having to restart that mission from the beginning. Any special perks they had are then gone and you'll have to hire replacements which may or may not have the same perks. It's just a luck of the draw. The missions can be rather long too depending on how meticulous and methodical you choose to be. The longest mission took me about 15 minutes to complete just running and gunning. Playing it methodically took me about an hour. Each mission is vastly different with maps being all sizes which will greatly vary mission time. To me this isn't an issue, but this is not a game I'd play if I'm on a time crunch. Lastly, no game is perfect. This game does occasionally bug out a little.

If you've made it this far, this game is obviously spiked your interest and I greatly appreciate your time. It may be a long review but there are too many games where it's just people praising or complaining about the game and not giving people a chance to understand what they're buying.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 10, "timestamp_created": 1736225750}, {"review_text": "1. bring non-lethal 'beanbag' shotgun to mission

This is like being asked to write your good friend a reference and then spend your entire time shitting on him...

Ready or Not is, at its heart, a fantastic game which captures the moral challenges of being a SWAT officer. Your enemies aren't necessarily inherently evil, and the game pushes you to make tough choices, like letting Voll live so he can tell a judge about his grotesque habits. It’s a game, much like SWAT 4 that kicks you in the throat when you’re not expecting it and I am only happy I got to experience that BEFORE the recent updates.

I’ll address the censorship first, as it’s the hot topic. I have to say I didn’t mind being told that I was no longer able to decapitate corpses – that’s not something I’ve messed on with since Soldier of Fortune 2 and whilst I thought it took away from the tone, I wasn’t totally against the covering of nudity – I just thought it was a stupid decision that I could live with. 

What gets me though is the reskin of valley of the dolls the console lot have to put up with (Completely ruins the moral strain, the mood, setting – everything on one of the most challenging and compelling maps of the game) and, I think moreover, the changing of the girl in the spider.

The girl not moving changes a situation from seeing that you need to clear this hellhole out as quickly as possible so she can get the immediate medical attention she requires, to her just being another victim – someone who can be passed by. It’s still shocking of course, but the original convulsions amplified the depravity and the desperation of the scenario – now it falls flat of being truly impactful. 

We’ve also seen a massive graphics downgrade – which I can only assume (not a game dev) is to make the game run better on the consoles hardware (because if not then why the fu.. would you do that to your own game?!?) 

I can look past the fact that I lost ALL of my progress with this update – all the unlocked cosmetics etc – but when trying to go through every level and S rank them (again – I might add) some missions have completely level busting issues with suspects getting stuck in the crawl spaces making an S rank unattainable. I know they are aware of this and are working on it – but I came back to a game I love that was in a MUCH better state than this and its been heartbreaking. 

I want to believe that this is just a rough patch, and that perhaps through either modders or sense we will see some of the old animations (the new arrest animation is just... odd – do I need to check everyone for dandruff?), and a return to better graphics. But it is with a heavy heart, despite the positive new additions in free levels and weapons – that, on PC at least – or console if you’ve played it before – I cannot recommend one of my previously favourite tactical shooters. 

Void – on the incredibly slim, next to zero chance you stumble on this rant and make it this far… Either run 2 versions, or tell us the red lines given to you by the console companies, so we can work together to determine what is and what is not okay to cut or change completely. 

Thank you for reading and sorry for the wall of text!", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 33, "timestamp_created": 1753481799}, {"review_text": "Ready or Not is a tactical shooter game in the style of Sierra's former SWAT 3 & 4 games.

You can select all of your equipment before a mission, including many details regarding its appearance. However, new equipment is only unlocked after successfully completing missions at a certain rank.

The missions can be difficult at first, but you'll remember the difficult points by repeating them. To get to grips with all the details of a mission, it's recommended to play it in single-player first, where you can also plan the entire tactical approach of the task force.

Overall, it's SWAT 5, even if the mission presentation could have been a bit more atmospheric, with short intro videos, for example, but it's still a definite recommendation.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1746130434}, {"review_text": "This is an extremely painful review for me to make.
The game itself is great; a more grounded shooter where your main goal is to defuse situations and only kill if out of options. Less gore and nudity is already stupid enough as is, but it does include changing the girl in Twisted Nerve from convulsing due to drug overdose to just sleeping all soundly unaware of the gunshots taking place, and to change the eponymous basement room in Valley of the Dolls, replacing pictures of the main suspect's daughter with just plastic dolls. Keep my $120, because I have a feeling you will not be making it long in the gaming industry.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 11, "timestamp_created": 1760355578}, {"review_text": "To the developers of Ready or Not,

We, your dedicated player base, write this with heavy hearts and a profound sense of disappointment. Ready or Not was once a beacon in the tactical shooter genre, a game that not only challenged us with its demanding gameplay but also resonated with its unflinching portrayal of the moral complexities faced by SWAT officers. It captured the gritty realism and difficult choices reminiscent of classics like SWAT 4, pushing players to confront uncomfortable truths and make split-second decisions with significant consequences. The "Valley of the Dolls" map, once a masterclass in atmosphere and moral strain, has been rendered a shadow of its former self, and crucial narrative moments, like the altered "girl in the spider" scenario, now fall flat, robbed of their original visceral power.

The persistent issue of LOD pop-in, always a concern, has been exacerbated to unacceptable levels, even on maximum settings, with world models visibly degrading just feet away. This visual regression feels like a betrayal of the PC experience we were promised.

We feel as though we have paid for a superior PC experience, only to have it compromised and delivered as a lesser console port. This is not a minor setback; it is a fundamental degradation of the game we loved. We implore you, VOID, to acknowledge the depth of this disappointment. We urge you to consider reverting the detrimental changes, particularly to the AI and graphics, or to provide transparency regarding the specific constraints you are facing. Our hope is that you will address these issues with the urgency they deserve, restoring Ready or Not to its former glory and respecting the investment and passion of your player base.

We sincerely hope this message resonates and prompts the necessary actions to restore Ready or Not to its former acclaimed state. until that time im sorry but i cannot recommend this game.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 31, "timestamp_created": 1756697042}, {"review_text": "good game you get to kill child predators and terrorists 10/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 64, "timestamp_created": 1763305273}, {"review_text": "Since the console update dropped, figured I’d circle back and update this review.
