Give us to option to toggle crossplay, which will allow us to enable or disable censored content.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 67, "timestamp_created": 1751352539}, {"review_text": "I haven't lived my whole shooter career in the realistic milsim subgenre. Instead, like many, my infancy in FPS games was spent on games like Call of Duty, Medal of Honor, eventually Battlefield when I thought I was more mature but was still a little baby. Now that I've grown, I find myself searching near endlessly for something that can contrast the dopamine tube-feeding of modern arcade shooters: a thinking man's shooter, a drip feed of the good stuff. I played more complex games like Arma and eventually DayZ. The type of games that mandate a 100% keyboard and where the expectation was to spend 20 real honest-to-god minutes(of which you have a limited amount, as a reminder) traveling to a hillside you'll get one tapped or shelled to death on in 5. Solid games, definitely an occasional play. But perhaps a little too much thinking for constant play.

Then I find games like this. Ready or Not is something I didn't grab for some time despite it being on my radar. The reason? Copaganda. I was worried this was a game that, while fun to play, would be busting its ass to glaze the cops. And, I mean, there is a lot of sympathy here. However, its all showcased in a way that layers the good with the bad. It shows that being a cop is hard, which can be true. Especially if you have one of the actually stressful jobs, the ones that are pretty self evidently necessary. It provides complex situations that are sometimes fundamentally rooted in evil and sometimes entirely in the grey. You get to hunt down King Pedo, but then you have to apprehend some young men for selling weapons to pay for their mom's cancer treatments. It rewards a playstyle that, while immensely harder, leaves the most evil among us tied up, demoralized, wheezing as their diaphrams reset from a half ounce of plastic denting in their thorax at 300ft/s, and at the mercy of the American Justice system. A fate worse than death, some say. So, the subject matter is complicated and multifaceted enough to not only get a pass from me, but actually engage and interest me. 

As you can see, I've played a lot of this game. I've S ranked every mission, went through a perfect ironman run to get the biggest cosmetic flex in the game. Jesus wept, for there were no more lands to conquer. AND YET, I keep playing. An impressive number of maps, insane level of detail and random elements of missions keep me coming back. And I have friends who make the experience fun and interesting each time. Unlike many I seem to stumble across, it seems we are capable of basic language skills and self control. When we are locked in, stacked up and keeping each other informed, it feels like a dance. Choreographed movements in perfect unison. We all know where grenades need to go, where enemies are standing and what their status is, what flanks are safe to gain dominance of a room. When you've put time into this and start to feel the flow state, its one of the most satisfying gameplay experiences you'll have. You aren't slide cancelling and crouch spamming your way through a gunfight. There isn't even a sprint button. You're listening, waiting, following procedures, employing real cqc tactics, vetting hostiles vs civilians as fast as you can, holding angles. Thinking. 

Its good. Good enough for me to sit down and write this for like 40 minutes because I really feel its an injustice to give this thing a "concise" review when I feel as strongly toward it as I do. The best shooter I've played in years, perhaps thus far. Its got some problematic bugs, including ones that have bungled S rank runs like unarrestable suspects and teleporting jihadists. Speaking of, some imagery and subject matter might be too much for some. There are some real reflections of humanities darkest modern moments in here, and it doesn't pull punches. But more often than not, its a stressful, intense, incredibly engaging experience in the best way. Solo is great, coop is fantastic with friends and a very mixed bag with randys, but very funny if little else. If you're looking for a shooter that respects you, pick this up.

[b]Ready or Not[/b] is not your average first-person shooter—it’s a brutal, slow-burning tactical experience that feels more like a high-stress job than a game. And I absolutely loved it.

You play as a SWAT team leader in the fictional (and deeply cursed) city of Los Sueños, responding to some of the most intense scenarios imaginable—hostage crises, active shooters, bomb threats, and downright terrifying cult hideouts. [b]The game pulls no punches[/b]: [u]every step, every breach, and every decision can mean life or death[/u], not just for your squad, but for terrified civilians and twitchy suspects who may or may not be concealing a weapon behind their back.

What makes it so compelling is also what makes it so frustrating—in a good way. [b]This is not a game you can breeze through[/b]. It demands discipline, communication (especially in co-op), and a serious respect for the rules of engagement. You can’t just shoot on sight. You have to give commands, restrain suspects, and clear every room like it’s hiding the final boss. Sometimes you’ll spend 30 minutes clearing a level only to fail because a suspect pulled a gun while surrendering or a teammate forgot to check behind a door. And you’ll love it anyway.

[i]Visually, it’s dark, gritty, and immersive[/i]. The lighting and sound design do a fantastic job at ratcheting up tension, especially in cramped hallways or abandoned homes where shadows seem to move and every creak makes you panic. It's not a horror game, but it might as well be when a suspect bursts out of a closet during a routine sweep.

[b]Is it challenging? Absolutely[/b]. [b]Unforgiving? Constantly[/b]. But that’s what makes every successful mission feel earned. There’s something incredibly satisfying about clearing a map with zero civilian casualties and perfect teamwork—it’s like winning an Olympic gold medal in stress management.

The AI still needs work, and bugs crop up here and there, but the devs are active, the updates are meaningful, and the game just keeps getting better. [b]Ready or Not is still growing, but what’s here is already a masterclass in tactical FPS design[/b].

If you're looking for a game that respects your intelligence, punishes your mistakes, and makes you feel like a real operator (while also occasionally making you scream in fear or rage), then [b]Ready or Not is absolutely worth the dive[/b]. Just don’t forget to mirror under the doors. Sometimes, when I play this, I have to hold back tears because I remember that although this is just a game, some of the missions you will play have actually happened or are happening right now in some part of the world. 

Unless you live under a rock, you know there's a mission where you’re taking down the leader of a CP (child corn) organization, and the details in that mission are some of the most brutal and disturbing things I’ve ever seen. In the basement of that mission, there is a section of the ground that had been dug up, uncovering barrels (see image link 1), and if you put the context clues together, the child victims are k worded and placed into those barrels. If you continue in the mission you come into a red room where they’ve placed printouts of CP (child corn) and on the wall of that same are is what appeared to be a bookshelf, but looking closer at it its a shelf full of DVD cases labeled with a name and a single or double digit number (see image links 2 and 3) . Frankly, you can only imagine whats on there. 

Sometimes while playing a mission, I have to force myself not to shoot the suspects after they’ve given up. I mean, it’s a game where you’ll spend 15 minutes trying to complete it to unlock the next mission. The game itself is something that cannot be topped. The detail, the realism, that gut-punching feeling of “this is happening somewhere in the world right now and you can’t do anything about it.” 

I can say right now that I’ve never played a game where I truly had to stop for a second and take a breather regarding what I just saw. I’ve heard some people say, “Its not worse than no russian,” and it’s such a crazy thing to say. Looking at the missions and the detail, no game tops this.

No Man’s Sky is the kind of game where you log in to “just explore for 20 minutes” and suddenly it’s 3 AM, you’ve cataloged five alien species, built a base on a floating island, and accidentally adopted a space squid as your best friend.

Since launch, the devs have turned this game into something truly special. Every update feels like opening a surprise gift, and the sheer scale of the universe means there’s always another breathtaking planet just over the horizon.

The combination of exploration, base-building, and starship tinkering is endlessly satisfying, and the community is surprisingly kind for a game where you can literally vaporize each other with laser beams.

If you’ve ever wanted to wander the stars, discover worlds no one else has ever seen, and occasionally get chased by space police for “accidentally” mining too much, this game is for you.

Hello Games you have my unwavering respect. Just go buy it folks.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1751701785}, {"review_text": "From Zero to Hero, the game!
No Man’s Sky is a space exploration game with an endless galaxy to explore, right at the tip of your fingers. And it is truly endless, millions of star system, trillions of planets, and probably much much more. If you dream like Anakin that you will be the first one to visit them all, you probably won’t succeed but it is the right spirit!
   
[u][b]Story[/b][/u]   
There is one, and it isn’t bad, but I personally just followed it as a small guidance through the galaxy, so I have to admit that I can’t say too much about it. Something with very ancient aliens and an A.I. !
   
[u][b]Gameplay[/b][/u]   
The basic gameplay loop revolves around collecting resources, to survive, and upgrade your suit, tools and ship over time, to be able to explore more dangerous planets, and make further jumps between Star System, but there is much much more.
Of course there is the main quest and countless side missions you will encounter, but to list some of other actives. 
→ Spaceship part hunting and building your own
→ Bounty Missions / Collecting missions / Delivers (pretty much busy work yep)
→ Base Building on any planet
→ Learning alien languages
→ Completing your different collections
→ Find and explore lost spaceships 
→ Manage your own fleet
And so, so much more. 
  
[u][b]Tech[/b][/u]  
It’s honestly still impressive how Hello Games managed to pull off the smooth transition between Space and planets, no loading screens, just going for it. 
For landing on space stations and jumps between star systems you have a short loading time, but they are disguised by docking animations and an well designed faster than light jump animation. 
    
[u][b]Pros & Cons /tl;dr[/b][/u]
+An endless galaxy with endless planets, missions, space stations etc.
+tons of gameplay systems that work well together and give a lot of variety and things you can do
+Spaaaaaace
+True feeling of freedom of exploration
  
-They didn’t design a trillions Planets by hand of course, so at some point you will explore bioms and planets you visited before, but that shouldn’t be a surprise
-Personally I found the start a bit tedious
-Learning the alien languages is more of a chore than fun
-At some point things just repeat itself, but that is expected, so only a half con
    
[u][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/u]   
From one of the worst game releases to one of the best space exploration games made, No Man’s Sky truly has a remarkable journey behind it.
If you enjoy exploration and don’t mind some repetition, you will have a good time with the game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1750591409}, {"review_text": "Message to Star Citizen players.
You have to try this game, NMS is years ahead in terms of game mechanics and playabilty compared to Star Citizen.
I backed Star Citizen in 2013, spending a total of just over $4000 USD, I stopped playing SC in 3.18 as the game changes, loss of lead team designers and just the feeling I was being ripped off had grown too great.

I put off playing No Mans Sky because I thought it looked too kiddie, too cartoony ... how wrong I was.
No Mans Sky is everything a Star Citizen backer would want. The missions are great, the main story mission chains are excellent. The exploration is 10/10, your name will forever be labeled with any new system you discover, and there are literally thousands upon thousands.
*No loading screens, 
*Seamless space to planet landings.
*Docking, finding and repairing crashed/lost ships, both terrestrial and alien .
*Research for blue prints , ship building
*Base building
*Amazing underwater exploration ( this was mind blowing )
*Tamable creatures, breeding, genetics, breed rare versions
*Piracy, freighters, smuggling, boarding and on and on and on.
*Community events
I am 160+ hours in and playing every day

No Mans Sky absolutely blows Star Citizen out of the water and then kicks it all the way down the road, then beats it again with a stick.
Star Citizen is going no where, Squadron 42 is a scam, come and play No Mans Sky , you will not regret it", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 44, "timestamp_created": 1758686167}, {"review_text": "A new update just significantly overhauled the world again after another significant update last year.
If you were staying away because of the reputation it had at launch, it might be time to give it a go. It's 60% off at the time of writing. 

Yes, this game is kinda just "walk around and scan rocks" but I also spent 600+ hours looking for cool ships, the perfect planet, the perfect star destroyer, decorating bases, becoming a trade lord, kitting out my starship to shred pirates in half a second, etc. Over that period of time the game has updated like half a dozen times in significant ways, expanding the amount of things you can do in this simulated universe. I might be jinxing it by saying this, but I hope this game continues to grow over the years.

I just thought I'd drop a positive review just in case anyone was on the fence about it. I don't regret the time I spent on this game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1738163272}, {"review_text": "I'm going to be honest. I play this on easy mode. You can play this as a tough survival game where most of the worlds are out to get you. I don't. I joke that its my bird watching game, I fly around and discover the fauna on new worlds. And I find it incredibly relaxing and zen. My life is stressful enough, I appreciate that this game ISN'T. But good to note that it can be for you folks who like a challenge. 

I also really enjoy the world building. The three races are interesting, as are their history and nuances, and I like that you need to learn the language. I guessed the rough strokes of the story, but the details keep me invested and guessing, and they might still throw me a curve ball! This many hours in and I'm still finding little details and learning things I didn't know before.

PS, has anyone else seen the tiny rock guy who's not technically a discoverable creature in the same way the titan worms aren't? He looks like a normal rock till you try and use the mining laser and then he pops up on little legs and runs away. I've only found him once and I love him!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1753291454}, {"review_text": "As a survival game I feel that it is still lacking in some areas; there is not much incentive to take part in any of the building, farming or automation aspects of the game, they can be avoided entirely with little to no impact on the experience, combat is not great with only a couple enemy types that you will ever encounter and a lot of the planets/flora/fauna sort of blend together. 

Despite these "flaws", this has become one of my favourite games and the story is an incredible experience that I wish I could play through again for the first time, this is clearly where most of the focus has been placed and it has so much character and creativity, I loved the feeling of being lost in this seemingly infinite universe with no idea how you got there and working to find answers to all the questions you are presented with at the beginning of the game. 

I played this game on PS4 in 2016 and, as with pretty much everyone else who played at that time, I left feeling disappointed, but it has come such an incredibly long way that it barely resembles the game I played back then, the continued support from the devs with regular (FREE) high-quality updates has, in my mind, erased any bad blood from the initial launch and I hope they keep this momentum going into Light No Fire.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1747064815}, {"review_text": "Having put 235 hours into this game at the time of my review, I can safely say I more than got bang for my buck. This game respects your time so much and on so many levels... 

Want to fight Sentinels? No problem. Don't have time to fight them the next day? You can disable hostile creatures in the settings. Fights become too easy? You can turn all creatures to hostile and make it so you take more damage. You can turn on item destroy on death, item drop on death (only one grave though, so if you die twice items are gone - don't fall asleep like I did!), or you can not lose anything on death at all.

I recently finished the Aquarius redux in a night - starting off, I didn't want to waste time getting supplies for life support, shield strength, etc... so I just turned them off. Oh my goodness how much more enjoyable the expedition became because I could focus on just enjoying the journey! Currently doing The Cursed expedition and left my normal settings on, and it's been a blast. 

The fact that in 200+ hours I have yet to get bored, have yet to finish the story (because you can play any way you want... You can just jump around and explore / build like I have been with zero detriment!), and still enjoy all aspects of this game. I highly recommend this if you are a casual dad trying to live his best free-time low stress gaming life, and doubly so if you have a Steam Deck - *all* of my hours have been logged on my Deck without a single issue, and the Sleep function coupled with this game is an absolute win.

The only thing is I wish there were some other stuff to do, but it is a sandbox game so you write your own story.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 8, "timestamp_created": 1756036241}, {"review_text": "Alright, its been almost 8 years of penance from Sean Murray and the team at Hello Games, I think at this point they've earned this. 

I was one of the disaffected poor bastards that preordered the ORIGINAL version of No Man's Sky on the PS4 fully expecting a game that, well, basically expecting what the game is today. Obviously, that did not happen. 

It was brutal, because that was the first time that I had experienced genuine false expectations and an awful, buggy, horrific launch of a game. A few years later KH3 would happen and despite having waited since I was a literal child to play that game, NMS had already prepped me that things might not be as amazing as they seem in the trailers. 

I was so frustrated that I brought my copy of NMS back in the next week to Gamestop and wanted to trade it in, but because there were so many people like myself they said they would accept a "swap" at my local store for a game that was out or coming out, so I used my NMS pain to preorder Persona 5, which ended up being a blast. (A great game if you have 100 hours to spare, as a senior in HS back then, I had nothing but time). 

Fast forward to a few years ago, I keep hearing rumblings that No Man's Sky is... good? Infinite planets, alien ecologies, interstellar dogfights, deep lore, and multiplayer adventures. What players got, initially, was a lonely, shallow space sim that felt more like a tech demo than a finished game. Fast forward to today, and No Man’s Sky has become one of the most remarkable comeback stories in gaming history.

Hello Games didn’t just patch the holes—they rebuilt the starship mid-flight.

At its core, No Man’s Sky is a procedurally generated space exploration game. You travel between planets, gather resources, upgrade your gear, build bases, fight pirates, discover alien life, and trade across the galaxy. What’s incredible is the scale—there are over 18 quintillion planets, each with its own ecosystem and terrain, generated by complex algorithms.

Initially, this scale felt empty. Now, thanks to years of updates, it feels alive.

The introduction of base-building, freighter fleets, co-op multiplayer, living ships, story-driven missions, and even VR support has turned the game into a sprawling sandbox. Whether you’re role-playing as a space trucker, a biologist cataloging alien creatures, or a pirate lord terrorizing trade routes, the galaxy feels like it’s finally yours to shape.

No Man’s Sky has a unique, vibrant art style that draws heavily from 1970s sci-fi pulp covers. Planets can be serene, horrifying, or outright bizarre—neon fungi forests, frozen deserts, and floating rock islands abound. The game doesn’t chase realism; it aims for wonder.

That said, the visuals can occasionally feel repetitive, especially after dozens of planets. Some textures are still a bit rough, and creature animations can be wonky. But considering the sheer scope and procedural complexity, it’s often jaw-dropping.

What makes No Man’s Sky special is its sense of solitude. Unlike most games, it’s not afraid to let you be alone with your thoughts. You’ll spend hours mining minerals, jetpacking across alien landscapes, or simply flying through space while synth-heavy music pulses softly in the background.

It can feel like a space-age nature walk—until you stumble upon a derelict freighter haunted by corrupted AI or get ambushed by Sentinel drones.

The game’s loop—gather, upgrade, explore, repeat—takes time to click. But once you’ve built your first planetary base or discovered an uncharted paradise planet, the hook sinks in deep. The grind is real, but rarely feels punishing. The latest updates have also added better tutorials and quality-of-life features that ease new players into the galaxy’s rhythm.

Despite its transformation, No Man’s Sky still suffers from some long-standing quirks. Inventory management can be a pain, menus aren’t always intuitive, and the sheer amount of content can be overwhelming. Performance hiccups can pop up, especially on older hardware or during multiplayer.

Also, while the narrative has grown deeper with the Atlas Rises and Echoes updates, it still can’t compete with more tightly scripted RPGs in terms of emotional storytelling.

No Man’s Sky today is not the game it once was—it’s better, bigger, and infinitely more interesting. It’s a testament to what a small, passionate team can do when they commit to their vision and their community. What was once a cautionary tale of overhype has become a shining beacon of perseverance and transformation.

Best Served With: A sense of wonder, a good pair of headphones, and no plans for the weekend.

As for the current state of the game, I don’t really have any complaints. Playing solo, the game runs really well. Gameplay-wise, the amount of content in the current version is huge. You can explore, build bases, fight, fish, and even build your own ships now. It *is* beautiful and unique. Just the possibility to land anywhere on a planet, explore, then take off to another planet or another system is fantastic. They all look strange, switching between funny wonderlands and hostile Dune-like deserts. The world is simple huge: you can get on planets that no player has visited before.

The obvious and expected drawback of this vastness is the emptiness of the game. There are resources, bases, enemies, wrecks everywhere but they all feel the same. You can land anywhere on a given planet, but it will be the same everywhere: the biome will be identical between poles and equator. Same for the day/night cycles that won't change. Exploring a planet is then without interest past the few kilometers around your landpoint.

Crafting: you collect all the time the same resources again and again (and it takes quite some time) to recharge your tools, and craft different object (tool upgrades, ship upgrades etc). But you also collect tons of items here and there. After 60h I have dozens and dozens of items that I don't even know whether they are useful. My inventory can't stop getting full of I-don't-know-what, which is very frustrating. And I can't sell it because it will be useful and hard to get in the future...

You can have an admiral ship and send hired bots to different missions. It consists in: choosing the mission, choosing the team, ensuring they have sufficient skill and fuel, and wait. When they get back you earn money, items, and you have to hop on the ships to repair them by yourself. It is not very rewarding or entertaining.

There are automatically generated missions that all look the same since there are automatically generated. The main mission itself feels like a seconday mission. I don't know where the story leads me and I'm not even curious at this point. None of the characters are interesting, none of the worlds you have to visit in the storyline are particularly interesting either (not anymore than any in the game). Sometimes you get to choose a line during a dialogue and I never felt it had a consequence.

It is marvelous in some way, but I feel like I tried to explore emptiness during 60h. It also feels like I still have 60h of procedural content to explore, and I just don't want it.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 22, "timestamp_created": 1736289960}, {"review_text": "No Man's Sky is an ambitious, decently fun game about exploring over 18 quintillion semi-unique very large prodcedurally generated planets and doing other fun stuff in space like stealing money, smuggling, fighting, building, farming, hunting, and the like.
It's a very wide and rather shallow game in that the gameplay loop gets a bit old if you do the same things (mine, craft, build, repeat) but there's actually a lot of cool misson-type content and the sheer scale of the game is genuinley awe-inspiring.
The developers (Hello Games) have more than repented of the game's rocky launch nearly a decade ago, and they give free and interesting updates all the time.
I don't know if you should buy this game for $60, but for $30 on sale it's a great investment.
Also, there's such cool events as encounters with a massive space worm in the void that I saw a month ago which is hyper-rare, exploring creepy abandoned spaceships, and unearthing the story's lore.
If you're into linear story games and get bored in a sandboxy vibe. this probably is not for you, but it's a very fun, original vibe that feels kinda like "Minecraft in Space with Better Graphics".
Thanks for reading this, hopefully you are better informed on your purchase!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763421210}]

[{"review_text": "Disclaimer : Played through the game solo only and reached the end in 60h.

I don't think i've ever seen a game that blend genres that well. As so many pointed out, it's Half Life 1 aesthetics meets Subnautica survival mechanics and the SCP universe. It's immersive, highly customisable and highly addictive. Just one more supply run, one more base to build, one more minute (hour ?) exploring this giant interconnected facility you find yourself stranded in.
I'd recommend going blind, as the horror of the unknown and wonder of discovery is what hooked me in right from the start, then kept me locked in for those wonderfull 60h.

To me, Abiotic Factor is to survivals what Baldur's gate 3 is to CRPG, or Elden Ring to souls-like : It's the new gold standard against which any future survival will be compared to from now on. It is THAT good.
I can't recommend this game enough.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1755247606}, {"review_text": "this game permanently broke my perspective on open world survival craft games. the bar is now so high that everything else feels half-baked, and i'm posting this while the game is not in full release.

if you want a game that is visibly a labor of love, with mechanics and design that will feel modern and retro at once, as well as a really rewarding grind progression with carefully thought-out project zomboid style skill system, this is it. it's perfect for couples - one goes out exploring for resources, other focuses on cooking, crafting and base-building. me and my boyfriend would come back home from work and would dive back into the game. worth the price, no item in this game is useless, every component has multiple crafting purposes. replayability potential is massive.

easy example of gamers-for-gamers dev behaviour - if you die, the bag with your leftover items doesn't spawn right where you died (which would mean full loot loss if you fell into the void), but at the nearest easily accessible spot on the map, as if certain areas of the game were excluded from death bag spawn. buy it for full price if you can afford to.

EDIT: after the newest dark energy update, the content we have been provided with is absolutely massive, at least 20 more hours of gameplay to fully take on the new maps and items. devs keep adding QoL items that are commonly requested. i made a new save just for solo play last night and i feel like i fell back in love - quest design contributes to this freshness.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1736603459}, {"review_text": "fun solo, could be even better with friends, unfortunately i have no friends..", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 109, "timestamp_created": 1738709836}, {"review_text": "This is one of the best games I've played in the last five years, I have only one thing to say to the developers of this wonderful game. Buff the pizza, I beg of you, on my life. Just please make the pizza better. We spent 28 hours on a fresh save, to get pizza, and it was so mid, that I'm have a religious crisis. Please buff the pizza, or I might not be able to find my way to heaven, thank you", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 172, "timestamp_created": 1743824109}, {"review_text": "I wasn’t sure if I wanted to write a review for this. I played it in early access but decided to wait for the full release and now here we are

This is one of the most surprising indie hits in recent memory. On paper, it looks and also feels like “Half-Life meets survival horror with a splash of SCP weirdness,” but in practice it stands out as its own thing. you play as a scientist in the GATE Cascade Research Facility on the day everything goes wrong. Instead of being the Gordon Freeman type, you’re just another researcher forced to improvise, survive, and escape as the world collapses around you. 

The atmosphere is fantastic. While it naturally invites Half-Life comparisons, each part of the facility feels distinct and imaginative, and the way areas connect recalls the level design of a souls game or a 3D metroidvania. Discovering a new route or better yet, stumbling into one of the many portal worlds never ever stops being exciting. Those portals in particular are wild, They can give a very surrealist feeling that keep the game’s environments fresh. 

The monster design is excellent too. Some are standard soldiers or recognizable alien exors, but others are massive, unique, and downright creepy. The Leyak and Krasue especially got under my skin at first; they pop out of nowhere and look terrifying, making me jump more than once. Then you have larger threats like the Reaper, which ratchet up the tension and make every trek through a new area feel dangerous.

Gameplay is a mixed bag, but mostly in a fun way. progression feels rewarding, with tons of systems like food and sleep mechanics to crafting that lets you turn staplers into weapons and drag filing cabinets around to build a base. There’s a playful creativity here, I took a skill that locks my guns (Fear-of violence) so I didn't experience higher-tierd weaponry. From my limited playtime the gunplay is janky and traditional firearms often feel weaker than your “science weapons” or even throwables. Survival elements are handled well; power sources are scattered around the map, encouraging you to settle wherever you like, and while the main map doesn’t respawn, there are special areas with regenerating loot to keep you stocked without forcing constant recycling.

The tone is lighter and occasionally humorous, with some toilet jokes and janky voice acting that oddly fits the 1990s vibe the devs seem to be going for. The worldbuilding itself is amazing, with some plot holes and underdeveloped characters, yet reading emails and the environmental story-telling says a lot about what's happening and it never gets in the way of the gameplay. Secrets and odd little tales pepper the world, making exploration feel rewarding beyond simple survival.

The game isn’t without flaws. Some systems feel half-baked (field batteries, useless weapon redundancies, and underwhelming farming), multiplayer can get grindy, and the final boss did not fit the gameplay loop. Still, these drawbacks don’t stop the overall experience from being engrossing.

Ultimately, Abiotic Factor is one of the best story-driven survival games of its kind. It blends Subnautica’s survival-craft, Half-Life’s sense of setting, SCP’s strangeness, Bioshock's RPG flavor, and the interconnectivity and map designs of Dark Souls, all while giving you the freedom to tinker, hoard, and carve out your own survival story. It might not be perfect, but for an indie title, it comes remarkably close to being GOTY material.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1756986798}, {"review_text": "I've grown genuinely bored of open world survival crafting games, wandering around a forest collecting sticks and stones for the first majority of game-play. Abiotic Factor puts you in a unique setting that is perfectly complimented by its graphic design. 
No more sticks and stones; you're a scientist. With each new recipe you unlock, you feel more and more like Tony Stark stuck in his cave, using the bare minimum to fashion some great technology. Using pens for ammunition or turning old electronics into high-tech teleporters, it feels like anything is possible. The crafting is designed to be both creative and entertaining.

In many ways, this game makes you feel like a child again. The graphics feel almost nostalgic, yet even with 80 hours under my belt before the most recent update, it felt like I was far from discovering everything. 
Each new hallway, office, laboratory, and multiverse portal you discover brings about such a sense of  childlike wander and excitement; its almost addicting. I've fully dedicated work-shift long sessions just to prepare for new areas and explore.

The characters you meet in the game act as simple guides, but each of them feels whimsical and full of personality. Their voice acting adds so much to the overall mood of the game and I feel like the NPCs themselves set up an amazing foundation for the most core aspect of the game.
Multiplayer.
Trust me, this game is so much more with a friend or few. My friend group fell into the role of "goofy posh scientists" very quickly. Proximity chat is utilised perfectly alongside walkie-talkies and pagers, and the animations of player-characters make the funny moments happen without even trying. 

Have you ever questioned why so many survival games allow you to feast without ever seeing a single loo? No?
Well, now you do. Your friends better remember where the toilets are and keep each other safe when the situation gets dire. There is nothing more memorable than someone spectacularly shitting themselves in the middle of battle in the Containment Sector. 

You're still a scientist though, so worry not. You can at least turn that humiliation into soil. There's your food problem solved!
Even making it to the toilet isn't boring, because then you're awarded with a POOPING MINI-GAME.

Who'd have thought of that?

This is a game made by goofy people for goofy people, and it is evident with every step that the developers are having as much fun as we are.

My rump is sat, and I'm about to spend the rest of the day fighting aliens and breaching the multiverse to effectively shit on my friend's bed. How will YOU benefit science this weekend, hmm?", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1739107062}, {"review_text": "what happens when half-life 1, scp: containment breach, valheim, and project zomboid have a nasty orgy. that's the love child that this game is.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 32, "timestamp_created": 1754211824}, {"review_text": "Let me say, as someone who has a small amount of playtime with this game...

Deep Field cooked with this one. Abiotic Factor is everything I could ever want out of a facility survival game. Interesting tech, fascinating enemies, and a compelling world and story if you look deep enough.

And the base building... Want an armory to rival the US military? Make it. A kitchen that would make Gordon Ramsay blush? Get out there and craft it. A dinner spread, a greenhouse, a deranged poop shack? It's all yours if you have the eye for it.

Abiotic Factor has been a time sink for me, and I don't regret it. I'm happy to say that I was able to see it grow and change. It started as a product that had my attention; now it has my heart. Buy it please. Buy it and enjoy this fantastic science man game.

One the greatest bangers to be released, can't wait for the extra content.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1753467936}, {"review_text": "[h2]Reviewed on Dark Energy Update[/h2]
In the saturated market of the survival-crafting genre, Abiotic Factor manages to bring out something new and actually fun.

[h2]Graphics:[/h2]
Faithful recreation of the original Half-Life style, enhanced with a modern lighting engine. Very charming.

[h2]Gameplay / Progression[/h2]
In terms of progression, this game is pretty similar to Terraria. You go on an adventure, find new types of resources/loot to make weapons, armor, base upgrades, and unlock new areas. The devs clearly put a lot of thought behind balancing items. Acquiring higher-tier items doesn't immediately make your older ones obsolete. Items in this game are treated as situational tools; for example, a random recipe from earlier in the game can be very effective against late-game enemies. The game also encourages you to explore every nook and cranny and rewards you with a lot of surprises.

[h2]Performance[/h2]
It's not that bad but your frames tends to drop when making base with a lot of stuff/ lightings.

[h2]BUGS[/h2]
A lot of them are related to vehicle, be gentle with them and you should be find.

[h2]THIS GAME HAS SOUL[/h2]
It's full of random details that aren't necessary for gameplay but make the world feel more alive. For example: All office chairs are non-static objects, and you can scoot around on them. Ingesting toxic food and then vomiting on your friend gives them the "filthy" status effect.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1744644089}, {"review_text": "I haven't reviewed a game in 5 years, but I genuinely feel I'd be doing this game a disservice if I didn't support it with a review. Abiotic Factor is undoubtedly one of the best survival crafting titles of the decade, and it's understandable why many reviews are claiming it to be on par with genre-defining games like Subnautica. Deep Field Games has clearly poured so much passion into this project, and whoever is scouting titles over at Playstack is on a generational run - snatching up Balatro & Abiotic Factor in less than 2 years is insane.

You'll immediately notice a major difference with Abiotic compared to the average survival game in that the entire world is contained indoors. Rather than grinding for generic ingredients in typical biomes, you instead must scavenge the limited resources within the abandoned facility and base up in the previously inhabited environment. The result is an experience you can't really find elsewhere, where you're strategising what areas of the facility to occupy depending on their unique differences and available resources. Since your base requires electricity, you'll need to hook it up to the facility power grid. When the facility goes offline at night, so does your base, making the dark atmosphere of the world twice as eerie. Last I felt this unsettled by a game's atmosphere was way, way back playing Tremulous as a child. No other game, besides Abiotic, has captured this feeling for me since - really impressive!

I was initially nervous about two things when starting out on Abiotic. One was where to place my base; I was nervous that I'd have to pack up and move my base as I progress. Fortunately, the map design is extremely well thought out. You'll pass locked doors and gates that feel like they're just part of the scenery, then later discover they loop around to new sectors that you have just discovered. The world feels huge yet accessible, giving you plenty of options for traversing around. The only downside is the static map, which doesn't really help much in the way of navigation, but you do quickly get a feel for the layout of the sectors.

The second concern I had was about the facility's limited resources. Fortunately, without spoiling anything, the game does offer solutions to this and ties it gracefully to the lore. If you've played the game before, you'll know what I'm talking about. I'd love to write a whole section on some of Abiotic's amazing, thought-out game and world design surrounding its resource gathering but it's always best to experience it fresh without spoilers. One thing is for certain - you'll be pleasantly surprised at how much content is in this game. Just when you think you're reaching the end, you'll discover a whole new sector full of new items, enemies, mechanics and challenges, and then that'll happen again countless times over while consistently keeping things fresh and exciting each time... it's just absolutely brilliant.

Unfortunately, it's difficult to talk about the best parts of the game without spoiling the first-time experience. So, if you're a fan of the survival crafting genre, I implore you to stop reading reviews and try out Abiotic Factor for yourself!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1753269634}, {"review_text": "I just realised I never wrote a review for Abiotic Factor. It's kind of hard. The game is utterly insane. It's brilliant and crazy, just like most of the scientists and science in it. It's half-life, but it's also survival builder. It's a stealth FPS, but it's also tactical melee bash. It's a lore-based storytelling adventure, and it's also complete nonsense.

11/10. More, please.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1754346558}, {"review_text": "Abiotic Factor is Half-Life if, instead of Gordon Freeman, you played as a Scientist instead.

That obvious inspiration aside, it is a mechanically deep entertaining experience. Abiotic Factor is a Survival game. You have to scavenge for resources, and food and water as you make your way through the facility. Along the way, you can bring furniture and other items with you to fortify "safe" locations to make bases. You also have Skills, that are leveled up as you use them, like in the early Elder Scrolls games. For example, crouching near enemies without being noticed will increase your sneak skill, and successfully cooking raw meat will increase your cooking skill.

Progress is slow at the start, as you  really rely on breaking down basically everything around you to craft basic things, but as you make more and more progress, this grind becomes shorter and shorter. The early game, which includes the Cafeteria and The Office Sector, doesn't really have much of a variety of resources, so you will be relying on the Makeshift Spear, and whatever armor you can find or craft, and when you can finally make a keypad hacker, the standard handgun, but once you reach Manufacturing West, the game really opens up, throwing new materials and items at you in droves.

Along with the GATE Facility, there are also "portal worlds". Much like XEN in Half-Life, Abiotic Factor has numerous alien worlds you can explore by finding and fixing portal equipment. These range from bizarre dream like alien worlds, to a world that is literally just Silent Hill, with infinite Fog. You can build bases in these worlds, and leave them at any time to go back to the facility, adding even more depth to the Open World.

This game is good fun, and the challenge of the enemies makes stealth actually viable. One of the more interesting things the game does is, any resource can basically be part of a crafting recipe, and the first time you pick up a new resource, your character will think of a unique way of using that resource. This will show new crafting recipe ideas in your recipe tree, which, to actually be able to use them, you need to solve a recipe puzzle, i.e., dragging and dropping the correct resource to creating the crafting recipe.

You cannot "lose" these puzzles, and they just exist to show you what you will eventually use for said recipe, but it's fun, and makes learning recipes more engaging than just leveling up and suddenly being able to know how to create something.


Abiotic Factor is overall, one of the more interesting survival open world games out there. It also supports coop, as is a genre staple, so really, this game is well worth it's price. Highly Recommended.


July 22ND, 2025 - 1.0 Full Release Update

I have had nothing but enjoyment from my time with Abiotic Factor, and 1.0 has added even more amounts of content.

At the time of my review, I had just gotten to Reactors, which was the full amount of content up until 1.0. As of this update, I'm still in Reactors, however, there is a huge amount of new content that has been added. All of the Skills have been raised to Level 20, adding more depth to the skill system, and adding more tiers of bonus upgrades you can get as you increase them.

One of the new things I have seen, is an entity called "The Moving Box". I am assuming this creature spawns randomly in a radius around you while you're moving about the facility, and anything you put inside of it, you can take out later when he spawns again. That is just a guess at this point however.

Biggest inclusion is another crafting bench, the "Enhancement Bench". Before 1.0, weapons were mostly static, with melee, projectile, and firearm options. However, the only real upgrade you could give the firearms was a flashlight attached to the Security Pistol. Now, this Enhancement Bench allows you to upgrade vast amounts of all types of things. Deployables, Weapons, Tools, etc. I am very happy with this inclusion, so much to the point that I enjoyed going all the way back to one of my starting bases to get the required materials to make it! There are LOADS of recipes for this thing, and the amount of different useable weapons it as added is awesome!

Having said that, however, the Reactors portion of the game is def the weakest point in the game so far. All of the GATEKEEPER type enemies are just absolutely annoying to fight against. You have floating psychics that just eat damage forever, literal Juggernauts with miniguns, and high flying silent assassin type enemies. Reactors is the first place you see these enemies, and you'd expect them to ramp up, but no. As soon as you enter the wasteland portion of Reactors, almost every other corner you turn around will be more GATEKeeper enemies.

Cloud reactor is a good example lmfao. They throw 6 of the psychic type enemies in a row, which have high health pools, and are immune to plasma damage, making two firearm upgrades useless against them. Other than the shit enemy balancing in Reactors, every other sector has been greatly enjoyable so far.

I am not at the newly added story content as of writing, but, the review remains the same. This is one of the most enjoyable and deeply rich Survival Crafting games I've played, and it def belongs in your library.

August 3rd, 2025 - FINAL REVIEW

I have completed the base story content, and like the rest of the review, this game is fantastic.
Reactors is def the "Xen" of this game. You will be increasingly out of resources, unless you spend time either resource farming, or, bring friends. Pushing through it, however, the end game content, was surprisingly enjoyable.

The Praetorium is a human enemy Gauntlet. After that, you finally reach Residence Sector, which, understandably, is the game's biggest challenge. I will not spoilt what Residence Sector ends on, but I will say, it once again, drags on quite a long time. I *honestly* didn’t expect this game to grab me the way it did. Both me and my husband started it thinking we’d just mess around for a bit, it'd probably be this 'generic-but twist-game' and boy we were happy to say we we're wrong! because then suddenly.. it was 80+ hours later! aand we were still finding new things to laugh at, get lost in, and get spooked by. (and killed, unfortunately)

As a couple.. we tend to finish games pretty quickly (we ensure games we purchase will give us enough content to factor in their price) ..As we get hyperfocused until we beat them; but this one kept us going non-stop and eager for more. See you’re actually constantly rewarded for exploring. (Wow!!)

The storyline is simple enough to “be there” without becoming that annoying, overstuffed “here’s the lore dump, now wait five minutes while an NPC shares their life story” kind of thing (But if you want ALL the lore, it's hidden away, and fun to find and read through - it's not even that long to read!).

Best thing is.. it’s not linear at all.
You can (and probably will) miss things.. even exciting ones.. and you don’t *need* to visit every location to finish the game. <3

I love that the developers clearly put so much effort into making every area worth seeing, and fun to explore and navigate too. The thrill for us of stepping into a new zone never wore off, is was always a huge "Woahh, come over here; look at this!!).

And as a bonus the enemies aren’t just lazy re-skins either; they’re all unique! with their own strategies to counter and consider. And don't forget when daylight falls.. there’s a genuine fear factor that stays with you the whole way through, mixed with some wonderfully weird and wacky enemy designs.

This game rewards you for being innovative, even encouraging you to “cheese” your way to objectives (basically, thinking outside the box!). And you’re never just progressing in a straight line; you can go wherever you want, whenever you want. (So if you want to be a loot goblin, go-ahead! you'll love it! if you just want to go kill some things, do it! If you want to explore and find the lore, and hidden doors, caches, and secret places, you can do that too!)

I utterly love the nostalgia in the art style, and I also love that this game doesn’t hold your hand. So you *will* get lost, you *will* get confused, but *when* you figure it out, you get that “Ohhhh!” moment that makes you fall in love with it even more. (And trust me, I always get lost; so a tip from me - get the employee tracker ASAP if you're co-op with someone else!) <3

I’m so very grateful the developers made this fully playable online or via LAN co-op. LAN is my personal favourite, and is so rarely thought of now'days.

The variety of weapons and armour is fantastic! I wish I could say more, but I promise I'm not going to spoil a thing for any possibly buyers. <3 <3

After a short break from finishing, my husband and I are already planning a re-run on the Apocalyptic difficulty (Just for fun). And we NEVER do that with other games, which shows you how 'special' this one is to us.

10/10 Once you dive in, and start getting a grip; you won't regret it!

How to describe this criminally unrecognized indie gem? Not an easy task by any means, but here's my best try: take Half Life 1, Arkane Studio's Prey 2017, Resident Evil and ARK: Survival Evolved and shove them into a mad science mecha-hybridizer. These are not pieces you'd think would naturally fit together, and yet somehow they just do. The result is a glorious Frankenstein's monster that works and plays unlike anything else on the market: a bona-fide first-person/immersive-sim/coop-survival-crafting/survival-horror/metroidvania/RPG!

Abiotic Factor's biggest asset is probably it's level design. Intricate does not even begin to describe it; in the true signature of masterful, Soulsborne-tier world design, the research facility you're trapped in isn't huge, but it FEELS absolutely enormous, and you will relish exploring every inch of it. Each sector is it's own distinct, sprawling environment, with unique enemies, resources and navigation challenges. The devs make excellent use of their game's central premise (essentially, a Resonance Cascade at an SCP containment site), creating a cohesive and believable environment that I was never less than eager to learn about. Nothing is lazy or repetitive, and there's oodles of fascinating and brilliantly-written lore you can find that expands on this engrossing original universe.

Notably, despite the abundantly compelling narrative, this game is also--refreshingly--very systems-driven. Abiotic Factor borrows heavily from the Immersive Sim genre, and that genre's most vital and enduring lesson is this: the most effective and reliable way to create player immersion is to make it clear to the player that this world has [b]Rules[/b], and if you do not [i]pay attention and learn them[/i], [b]you will get screwed![/b] Entirely aside from the personal admiration I have for the devs for choosing to put more video game in their video game, this systemic focus serves the gameplay tremendously. You really do have to learn and engage with the world on it's own terms, and it's always satisfying to devise a solution to or discover a way to circumvent a problematic situation using the ample suite of tools the game provides you. After all, you are a scientist; ingenuity's kinda your thing. Although this game doesn't have a Gloo Gun or versatile Typhon powers, it does have a robust building system.

I could go on. 

Suffice to say that Abiotic Factor has impressed me in more ways than I can readily describe. Not only does each component work great on it's own, everything dovetails together beautifully into a whole greater than the sum of it's parts. Please believe me when I say you are doing yourself a disservice if you do not at least try to play this game. If any of it's above-mentioned inspirations have compelled you at all, especially if you've enjoyed more than one of them, you owe it to yourself to give Abiotic Factor a look. You might just fall in love with it like I and (as of the time of this writing) over 18,000 other Steam users already have.

[{"review_text": "Enshrouded, as an Early Access title, does some things well and some not so well, but it is all subject to change. We'll see how things go over the next few years. Overall, it's fun enough, and the developers have been very forthcoming with game additions and are also very open and responsive to player feedback. This game does Early Access right.

Pros:
-Gorgeous visuals
-Gorgeous world, procedurally-generated and then lovingly populated with hand-crafted locations
-Incredible, detailed and interesting dungeons to delve through, filled with puzzles and environment hazards
-Beautiful, if inconsistent, armor and weapon designs, which are fun to collect.
-A fairly robust building system, with benefits to decorating and constructing a base that you then populate with craftspeople and villagers
-Simple, but satisfying combat
-A leveling system that revolves around perks instead of stat increases (though you can still boost your stats from the perk tree)
-Dedicated cosmetic slots for your armor, with options to hide both your headgear and your gloves
-Fully cosmetic clothing sets to find behind exploration and bosses
-A food-based buff system, wherein the food you eat increases your stats and stat regeneration
-Lots of lore to discover through characters, locales, obelisks and books throughout the world
-Highly customizable game settings, including the ability to turn off weapon and tool durability or turn on starvation mechanics

Cons:
-The bonuses from armor and weapons are largely pointless, or too small to make much of a difference. Some are even entirely pointless, such as one set that offers a small 10-20% bonus to unarmed damage, with unarmed attacks dealing only 8 damage to enemies (when your mace is doing over 400 per swing, and swings faster than your fists)
-There are tons of weapons, but there are very little differences between weapons of the same class: All one-handed weapons use the same three-swing combo, regardless of what the weapon actually is, and even legendary items don't have anything to differentiate them outside of their raw damage and visuals
-The few weapons with "unique" effects are things like 5% lifesteal, 1 point of health regen, or some bonus critical chance and damage. None of the weapons are build-defining or unique in any meaningful way. For example, the "Dragon Sword", found only one hidden place and tied to a piece of esoteric lore found in your travels, just adds a flat +7 fire damage... Five times in a row. The Dragon Sword is a weapon with nothing going for it except minuscule damage bonuses that don't even interact with your perks.
-Extremely linear item and location progression: New areas are blocked off by "Deadly Shroud," a gas that simply kills you if you haven't leveled up your base enough yet (using the heads of bosses and regional materials). Essentially, your ability to explore the "open world" aspect of the game is heavily restricted by boss progression.
-Heavily reused enemies with very limited attack variety
-The magic system is bland, being exclusively ranged elemental attacks and two healing spells. There is no utility magic to speak of, outside of a single knockback spell
-The perks you gain from leveling are very restrictive in what they affect, very strictly confining their offerings to their respective stat tree (Strength, Intelligence, Dexterity) with very little overlap
-Every quest is a fetch or kill quest with some lore sprinkled around it. "Skyrim quest" is how I would describe them: Talk to a person, go to a place, get a thing, repeat until you run out of quests", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1737240401}, {"review_text": "I love this game, I just wish the 6 friends who forced me to buy it for $30 didn't stop playing it after 2 hours.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 112, "timestamp_created": 1752445584}, {"review_text": "🛡️ Enshrouded – 100+ Hours Later, Here’s Where It Stands (June 23, 2025)

[h3]What Works For Me[/h3]
✅ [b]Building.[/b] Once you get the hang of it, building is amazing.  The assets are gorgeous and plentiful, and you have incredible freedom and flexibility to build everything from spooky cellars to hobbit holes to towering castles either brick-by-brick or wall-by-wall.  The auto-snap is decent, but you can also turn it off and rotate [i]anything[/i] however you want on any axis.  The more I experiment with building and decorating, the more I love it; I'm currently working on a tavern... which somehow turned into an entire town with a farmer's market.  I don't know. 

✅ [b]NPCs[/b].  You unlock new NPCs as you progress, and each one has new craftables, skills, and quests. They're not particularly interesting or special, but they live in and wander around your base, and complain endlessly if you don't at least make them a bed.  It's such a great reason to build more, and it makes your creations feel more alive. 

✅ [b]Sandbox Settings.[/b]  The vanilla game is well-balanced and accessible for casual survival vets (I recommend turning starvation on, though), but you can also fully customize each world to fit your play style.  Similar to [i][url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/108600/Project_Zomboid/?curator_clanid=45365863]Project Zomboid[/url][/i], you can turn this into the coziest crafting game or truly punishing survival. 

✅ [b]World Design.[/b]  Embervale is [i]huge[/i], and every inch was hand-crafted with love and care.  I love exploring the diverse biomes and appreciating the little details… before smashing them for resources.

✅ [b]Characters ≠ Worlds.[/b]  Your characters, their inventories, and some quests are not tied to a particular world, so you can hop from one game to another with abandon.  This lets you train up a new character for an old save, experiment with new builds, or funnel resources into your building save while also keeping things fair; your character gains XP but does not gain extra skill points by completing the same tasks in multiple worlds. 

✅ [b]Top Tier Early Access.[/b]  [i]Enshrouded[/i] launched into EA with more content than many full games, and continues to add more with every update.  The devs communicate well and deliver so consistently that I didn't even question their ambitious 2025 goals.

[h3]What Doesn't Work For Me[/h3]
❎ [b]Character Customization.[/b]  While the character models have improved since launch, customization options are limited and the female character is still quite buggy (some gear swaps in a male body type or the older, broader-shouldered female body).  I typically cover her in gear as early as possible, but as someone more on the petite side who loves a good character creator, I'd appreciate more diverse options and body types.

Enshrouded is an incredible open-world survival game that offers a deep and immersive experience, whether you're playing solo or with friends. From its breathtaking visuals to its intricate gameplay mechanics, this game has a lot to offer for fans of the genre.

[b][u]The Highlights:[/u][/b]

✅ Stunning Visuals & Atmosphere – The world of Enshrouded is beautifully designed, with diverse biomes, atmospheric lighting, and an incredible sense of scale. Every location feels unique and rewarding to explore.

✅ Immersive Sound Design – From the ambient sounds of nature to the clashing of weapons in battle, the audio design adds depth and immersion to the world.

✅ In-Depth Skill Tree – Whether you prefer melee combat, ranged attacks, or magic, the game offers a well-designed skill tree that allows for diverse playstyles and progression.

✅ Massive World with More to Come – The world map is already huge, and with more content planned, exploration remains an exciting and rewarding experience.

✅ Detailed Building System – The base-building mechanics are robust, allowing players to create anything from simple shelters to elaborate fortresses. The level of customization makes for a truly personal experience.

✅ Plenty of Combat Variety – With numerous build options and a wide range of enemies and creatures, combat always feels fresh and engaging.

✅ NPCs That Expand Gameplay – As you progress, NPCs unlock new options for crafting, builds, and other mechanics, making settlements feel alive and purposeful.

✅ Fun & Rewarding Multiplayer – Playing with friends is a blast, and cooperative exploration and building make for an unforgettable experience.

[b][u]The Downsides:[/u][/b]

❌ Multiplayer Performance Issues – Some stuttering and lag can occur, especially on GPortal servers. Hopefully, future updates will improve stability.

❌ Quest Progression Bugs – Transferring items between worlds can sometimes cause quest progress to become desynchronized, which can be frustrating.

❌ Solo Play Can Feel Overwhelming – With so much to do, single players might find the game a bit daunting, though the challenge can also be part of the appeal.

❌ No Water Yet – The game currently lacks water, but the developers have confirmed it’s in the works.

❌ Storage Organization Could Be Better – A minor issue, but the lack of item labels can make organizing chests a bit of a hassle.

[b][u]Final Verdict[/u][/b]

Enshrouded is an excellent choice for fans of open-world survival games, especially if you have friends to play with. The game continues to receive updates with frequent content additions, and its early access price is fair for what it offers. While there are some minor technical issues, the overall experience is incredibly fun and rewarding.

Its Yugioh but Speed format. What does that mean? To spare you the nerd talk, basically duels wont be more than 20-30 mins of the player doing one thing and a dozen other things on top of that, in other words, the duels will last less than 20 mins. 

For the Yugioh fan, this game is a huge fanservice to all YGO series from the OG or as it's known in Japan, Duel Monsters, my favorite like 5Ds, all the way to SEVENS and GO RUSH with their own summoning method called Rush Duels, separate from the other series. I prefer this over Master Duel, not that I hate it but when I just want to go through a quick duel, play as my favorite characters be it Yusei (5Ds), Declan (ARC-V), Yugo (ARC-V) to Varis (VRAINS) and use decks built around their respective archetypes. 

Oh yeah, its a gacha game.... well if you ever opened a pack of cards then you should know the rates. Although the in-game currency which is Gems is fairly generous and there's ways to earn like leveling up characters to doing the events, even online PVP. You can also use money and honestly it isn't so bad compared to waifu/husbando gacha games where their rates are bad to skins being $20-60. 

Fairly certain I dont need to say that I recommend it cuz feels like everyone and their momma might have it on their phones but yeah.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1747290397}, {"review_text": "Duel Links, In my opinion, is a good Yu Gi Oh game and is miles better than Master Duel for a bunch of reasons: 

1) The game is fast paced. With Speed Duels, you have 3 monster and 4 spell/trap zones instead of the traditional 5 monster and 6 spell and trap zones. Less cards are needed to create a deck meaning instead of making your traditional 40 minimum/60 maximum deck, you have a 20 minimum/30 maximum deck. This means matches are quicker (for the most part, if it isn't PVP) and you will most likely have a better hand given the deck chemistry. Also instead of 8,000 life points, both players start with 4,000 and there is no main phase 2. 

2) It is aesthetically more pleasing than Master Duel. Instead of Master Duel giving certain monsters in certain archetypes a slight GIF summoning animation from their card art, Duel Links actually gives you full 3D model summoning animations of certain Ace monsters for each character (and call outs for specific monsters they use).  The menus are very clean and concise and believe it or not, the card art actually is in higher definition and resolution than it is Master Duel. 

3) The game is F2P friendly. Duel links is more generous with rewards than Master Duel. They both use gems but it's much more abundant here as gems are given out during the launch of card boxes that come out periodically (2 weeks - a Month) [Master duels does not do this. You have to grind it out via PVP or solo mode, it sucks], during events and as level up rewards for each character. You can get mostly get what you want whether it's pre-made decks, cosmetics, specific card bundles or just to roll for more cards in the boxes with either enough time and level grinding.

4) The Meta is closely monitored here by the devs. You will notice the ban list is drastically different here than the current TGC or Master duel (Because Speed duels have less rules and whatnot and cards are released at regular intervals frequently here. I get it, its a complete headache.) Particularly in each update, after a PVP season, the developers actually look into some of the most popular or abused cards online and will either limit or ban cards that flat out break the game with the current Speed duel rules .Some cards are flat out nerfed and some effects are actually omitted at times to keep the game more fair and playable which is concerning if you remember cards differently in the physical or yu gi oh video games (Which to be fair, they should just add a mode where you play with the original effects of monsters/spells/traps.)

5) The game is more character oriented. Typically in master duel, Konami usually encouraged people to "Frankenstein" archetypes together to make really bullsh*t decks that abused special summoning or severely limited players to do things for a means of victory. This game, However, introduces skills for characters. These skills serve as a means of dominating the battlefield or a comeback mechanic if you are in a tight bind. These skills can be acquired through events or achievements and they are pretty good but have restrictions upon use to make it more fair PVP or otherwise (For Example: Every 1.500 LP lost you get to draw a random spell or trap, Gain 1500 life points in the beginning of the duel but start off with one less card, etc). Some skills are more associated with the archetype that characters play while others are more general skills. Thats not to say you are restricted to just playing whatever character archetype because Konami recently made an update where you can get more skills if you play with various archetypes several times. You have the choice of using these skills or not but you have the freedom to play as you see fit. Don't worry, Skills are balanced as well to avoid any abuse or Meta abundancy.

These are all the positive points that I have accumulated over the time I have played this game.

The only real negatives of this are probably just certain cards not being included in the archetypes you love and of course, encountering PVP matches with people using Troll cards/decks (You know the ones. Parasite Paracide, Lava Golem, Needle bug nest, Crackdown, Kiteroid, Man Eating Mimicking Bug, Cyberse, etc). But hey, at least you don't have to wait a thousand years for a dude to play one card, or fill their field, chain by chain. Thankfully, you only have 200 seconds of time instead of the 300 seconds plus bonus time in Master Duel.

Wrapping things up,  If you want a fun, quick match and play a more balanced version of Yu Gi Oh with several twists that has a ton of fan service, events and references to the shows/manga, pick it up and give it a try. As a Veteran Yu Gi Oh fan, you'll be pleased.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1735089314}, {"review_text": "It can be fun if you're a fan of the Yu-Gi-Oh anime, but the monetization is awful. This game desperately needs a way to craft cards.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1756819472}, {"review_text": "If your life is anything like mine (Phone always low on storage, tablet and computer are basically dinos, or You just need something that runs well on worse devices) or you just want to see how the characters from the anime interact together in a mostly solo experience, Duel Links is your answer.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1738867144}, {"review_text": "I've played this game more that I would like to believe and admit, but I can't in good faith recommend this to any player seeking enjoying Yu-gi-oh unless you really, and I mean REALLY want to play for the anime aspect of it. The game itself is functional, and it can be a lot of fun, only if you're willing to spend hours and hours of your life unlocking stuff and grinding for the cards.
The best parts of this game are the fantastic music and the anime characters that thanks to the amazing voice acting (will depend if you like Japanese or English dubs) makes you feel that you're playing a duel of the anime. The summoning animation of the monsters are also quite cool most of the time. 
The fun aspect of the game is heavily dependent by the current meta game, some metas are a lot of fun, others makes you question what on earth was Konami thinking.
The game is divided into 2 formats currently, Speed Duels and Rush Duels, both share the same currency, so if you're a free to play player you will have to decide what format you like the most because there's no way to keep up with both. Worse part is that if you want the free resources the game offers to you through events, you'll have to play both formats. Or if you're not free to play but only like one of the formats, you'll have to wait sometimes up to a month before the format you're playing gets new cards and content.
The new player experience is horribly dated, the tutorial still forces you to open the first box released that has no usable card. You at least can get a deck through the invite friend campaign, but that's about it, you still need lots of different cards to complete the mission stages so you can unlock basic features like the card trader, or other worlds. Unlocking characters is a nightmare if you don't have a particular ticket, and affording cards from the card trader as a new player feels impossible. The game gives you the equivalent of 5000 gems to start, but that amount will most likely get you nothing good. Even if you go the route of buying a newly released structure deck with money, you'll still need other cards from sometimes multiple boxes just to keep up with the meta game (this applies for both speed and rush duels). 
Leveling up characters take forever and it is necessary to access skills and key cards. Suppose you want to play "speedroids", you need to 1) unlock arc-v world. 2)reach stage 6 in that world. 3)either complete the missions that allow you to unlock the character Yugo or use a Character ticket on him. 4) level up the character to the max level. 5) get the cards for his deck from 2 different boxes (not including staple cards), that process alone can take you easily 2 to 4 days of gameplay. And worst, if the character you wanted to play was from an event and you missed it, you are out of luck until the re-run event or until the character gets added to the gate, which can take up to 3 months.
The game is very expensive, with konami finding any way to get you to buy overpriced digital cardboard, sometimes locking important cards behind paywalls like the selection boxes. For the amount you're going to spend to open 30 packs you can buy like 2 to 3 fully featured games. The worst part is that there's a lot of fear of missing out aspects to the game, like the events I mentioned before or that special boxes are only available during a particular period.

TD;DR: The game is good and can be a lot of fun, but the grindy aspect, awful new player experience and the expensive monetization of the game and lack of real crafting, makes it impossible to recommend to new players, you're better off trying out Master Duel first, which is much more accessible to new players (excluding its complexity)", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1753376340}, {"review_text": "an alright mobile version of the classic yu gi oh game everyone knows.

Duel Links – A Nostalgic Duel Back to Childhood

I’ve been playing Yu-Gi-Oh! Duel Links since its early days, and wow, it really takes me back! The thrill of drawing the perfect card, setting up combos, and hearing the iconic voice lines from classic characters—it’s like reliving my childhood duels all over again.

The excitement of outsmarting an opponent with a well-timed trap or summoning a powerful monster at the perfect moment never gets old.

If you haven’t tried it yet, I highly recommend giving it a shot! Find your favorite archetype, build your dream deck, and jump into the dueling arena. It’s a game that brings back childhood memories while keeping the competitive spirit alive. Let’s Duel!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1742491268}, {"review_text": "Whether you're a veteran duelist or just someone who shouted "It's time to d-d-d-duel!" in the early 2000s, Duel Links hits the nostalgia button hard.

The animations, voice lines from the anime, and the iconic cards?Pure serotonin. And the fast-paced format (Speed Duels) makes it super easy to jump in and out without needing a PhD in card effects.

It's surprisingly generous for F2P players too – you can build solid decks without spending a dime if you're smart with your gems. Plus, new characters and events keep things fresh.

🔥 Easy to learn, satisfying to master, and it makes you feel like Seto Kaiba on a caffeine rush.

Highly recommended if you're even slightly into Yu-Gi-Oh!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1752584801}, {"review_text": "It starts innocently. "Oh, cool," you think, "I'll summon Dark Magician and relive my childhood." You lie to yourself, saying you'll stay free-to-play. But then you see it. That one Ultra Rare card that will complete your deck. You start grinding gems. You do the loaner deck challenges. You level up characters you hate. In sum, while Yu-Gi-Oh!
