For quite some time, I have been avoiding BG3 completely. Of course, the huge popularity and high appraisal of this game didn't pass me, yet I didn't have much interest in it. I can't explain why exactly. Maybe I wasn't in the mood for turn-based combat. Maybe I was "afraid" of the sheer size of this game and didn't want to commit too much time to it. Maybe I was a dumbass trying to be "not like everyone" and not play what was popular.

Time passed, one of my friends got a gaming PC, and we started to think about what games we could play together. We were looking through what Steam could offer us, and nothing interesting popped out, except for BG3. Suddenly, I thought, "Well, if I didn't play this game myself, we could try coop, I guess". And after that short thought, the month of non-stop BG3 gameplay started for us both. I just lived in the mode of "I hope the end of my work day comes faster, so I can play BG3 with my friend". 

Despite not having the best-in-class graphics, the game still looks very good. As always, creativity and designers/artists can bring a lot to the table without taxing players with immense hardware requirements. I liked how characters look, how armor and weapons look, spell effects etc. The locations and landscapes were stunning.

The sound design was good for my limited knowledge and taste. The musical score is amazing, magical even. As always, after beating a game with good OST, I went straight to a streaming service just to listen to said OST on repeat. I only wish the music was more "present" during the gameplay and more frequently "took the stage".

Overall, I liked the gameplay, even though I can't really critique it, because I didn't play many of the similar games; Only Divinity Original Sin comes to mind. My friend and I played on Tactician difficulty, and even with our subpar, non-optimized builds, we managed to beat the game (I know, I don't have the achievement, yes, we briefly dropped difficulty for the fight with Apostle of Myrkul, but then switched back to Tactician and stayed on it to the end). The combat is interesting and engaging, with a lot of combos and possibilities. There are only so many classes and mechanics we experienced and explored in our 100+ hour playthrough. If you get stuck and think that the fight you faced is impossible to win, it's most probably not. Don't be afraid to experiment, study your enemies, and don't hesitate to use potions, scrolls, environment etc. The game provides all these things to make your life easier (except for explosive kegs abuse, that one doesn't count as fair play). Of course, there were a couple of annoying things, like characters missing their shots/hits in the most comical manner ever, characters not having enough mobility etc., but all of these come from the fact that our builds weren't the best, us not using all the mechanics and items, plus it's just the nature of the games with the dice. Even with a 99% probability of hitting the enemy, you can still miss (and it's right, because that is how probability works). You just need to get used to it.

Exploring the maps was interesting. As I mentioned, the locations were really well done, in my opinion. The only gripes I got with exploration were episodes of camera freaking out in buildings with several floors, and those ladders, which can be used only by one character at a given time.

Also, as in every other self-respecting RPG, you can fight with your words in this game. I will remember for a long time how my friend who had high charisma just verbally un-alived that sick doctor in Act 2 in the hospital.

And now for the most interesting part - the story and characters. I will never get tired of realizing how important good and interesting characters are. At first, I was kinda afraid that the writing part of this game would not be that good, because in my mind it was like that - "it's built upon D&D, in D&D people create new stories/characters every time, i.e. characters may not be as defined, the game may be 'faceless' etc.". I can't explain why I had something like that in mind, and thank God I was wrong. I absolutely love the characters in this game. Yes, maybe they are stereotypical here and there, but I don't really care. They were interesting to me, I wanted to listen to their dialogue, do their quests, I worried about them, so on and so forth. For me personally, it's one of the most interesting parts of such games - to see the stories of your companions unfold, taking part in it, helping them, building relationships with them, having their unique input about different situations and such. It's amazing. I liked how the majority of your companions' stories unfold throughout the course of the entire game, gradually giving you new story bits. The voice actors did an outstanding job in bringing said characters to life. Worth saying that not only companions are done well, but the majority of the NPCs. And of course, I enjoyed my romance with Shadowheart. It was really nice, how it slowly progresses together with her story and such. Also, that celebration at the very end of the game, when Withers gathers all of your companions - you can clearly see that the developers knew what they were doing, and they too understand the importance of our companions and how players can get attached to them.

I think the story was good. We played the "good" route, and maybe it wasn't as deep and fresh, but it felt fulfilling. I enjoyed my journey, truly. Sidequests were very interesting to do.

In my profile you can see how much I was glazing The Witcher 3 in my latest Steam review, and now I think I shouldn't have done it. Don't get me wrong, I like CDPR work a lot, but that review was written under strong emotions. I think that BG3 offers much more, and other game developers should take notes. Baldur's Gate 3 is packed with content, has amazing art design and music, good stories and lovely characters, a lot of interactivity in its world, variety in both gameplay and narrative. Add to all of this the countless number of mods and good replay value, and you get a game that can be played for hundreds and thousands of hours. I am already planning a new playthrough with mods, where I will recruit every companion (we didn't get Wyll and Minthara), try different classes etc. From a story perspective, I will probably make the same choices and romance Shadowheart again and again, but you can do things differently. And this is the beauty of this game - the player's freedom to shape their story in whatever way they want.

This game doesn't really need any recommendations, everyone has heard about it and knows that it's worth playing. Playing this game with a good friend of mine was a truly special experience, living through all these adventures together - it was amazing. BG3 easily became one of my favorite games ever.

Also, I should just point out one bit. In my country, the game costs like 20–30 dollars, which is basically a steal. I don't know how Ukrainian gamers earned such generosity, but thank you devs. Add to this the fact that the game has full Ukrainian text localization, which is rare on its own, and even more rare for a game of such a scale with so many text lines - I can't be grateful enough. It means a lot.

It’s hard to overstate how magical [i]Stardew Valley[/i] really is. It starts as a simple farming game, but quickly blossoms into one of the most emotionally rich, comforting, and addictively satisfying games ever made. Whether you’re fishing at 8 a.m. in a pixelated fog, giving someone their favorite birthday gift, or just planting beans while rain taps gently in the background, [i]Stardew [/i]has this almost sacred ability to slow time down and remind you that life can be soft, quiet, and meaningful. And it was made by one person. That still blows my mind.

🌱 [b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] A slow, beautiful life on your terms. Whether you want to farm, fish, mine, romance, decorate, or just walk around petting your animals, [i]Stardew [/i]lets you play at your own pace. There’s no pressure. You can optimize for gold and rare crops, or you can just vibe and grow turnips while chatting with Shane about how bad life used to be. It’s your little world.

[*] One of the best farming loops ever created. There’s something endlessly satisfying about planting seeds, watering them, harvesting them, then reinvesting in even more complex crops or artisan goods. The loop is tight, clean, and deeply rewarding. It scratches that perfect simulation itch.

[*] A cast of characters that feel real. The people of Pelican Town aren’t perfect. Some are prickly, some are shy, some are struggling. And over time, you see them change. You hear their pasts, uncover their trauma, celebrate their birthdays, and maybe even fall in love. Even characters I disliked at first grew on me, because they’re written like real people, not just game mechanics.

[*] Gorgeous pixel art and serene music. The visuals are simple, but warm and expressive. Every season has its own palette and charm. And the soundtrack? It’s iconic. Peaceful, nostalgic, and instantly grounding. Every track feels like a warm mug of something sweet.

[*] The best version of “daily tasks” you’ll ever find. Watering plants, checking the coop, upgrading tools, remembering villagers’ schedules—it sounds like work, but it feels like love. The rhythm of a [i]Stardew [/i]day is cozy, not stressful. You do what you can. You go to bed when you're ready. It’s a reminder that routine can be a gift, not a grind.

[*] Freedom to play however you want. There’s no "wrong" way to play. Want to marry Emily and become a wine magnate? Go for it. Want to live alone, max out the Community Center, and raise cows? [*] Mines, combat, and mysteries. Beyond the surface-level farming sim is a full-on dungeon crawler with weapons, gear upgrades, and secrets to uncover. 

[*] Incredible post-launch support. ConcernedApe has continued to update the game for free for years. New festivals, dialogue, late-game systems, and even co-op? He didn’t have to do that, but he did, and it shows how much love is poured into this game.

[*] It’s multiplayer now and still feels magical. Whether you're building a farm with your partner, tending animals with friends, or just running around gifting villagers together, multiplayer doesn’t break the game’s peaceful energy. It amplifies it.

[*] It stays with you. Long after you put it down, you’ll remember your favorite spouse, your cat’s name, the layout of your first farm, or that one perfect autumn day when you found a prismatic shard and felt like a god.

A place I came back to when life felt overwhelming, when I needed a break, or when I just wanted to remember that slow, quiet progress still counts. On the surface, it’s a farming sim. But underneath, it’s about connection — to land, to people, to yourself. There’s a stillness to it, a sense of rhythm, like exhaling after holding your breath too long.

It’s hard to describe how powerful that first spring feels. Clearing out your tiny patch of land, planting seeds, waiting. And then — one morning — something grows. Not much, just a few sprouts. It trusts you to find your own way, and that’s rare. There's a kindness in its design that makes it feel more like coming home than completing objectives.

I think the reason Stardew Valley means so much to me is that it showed me progress doesn’t have to be loud or flashy. You can build something beautiful out of small routines, slow days, and a lot of patience. It reminded me to appreciate little victories — a good harvest, a rainy day, a new heart in someone’s dialogue. I didn’t just escape into Stardew — I learned from it. [{"review_text": "After getting 100% in this game, it’s about time I leave my honest review of Constance.

This game gave me mixed feelings throughout the whole time I was playing it, mainly a lack of polish. I will note my issues with the game below:

-Bosses feel too bare bones and unrememberable, they feel more like fighting a regular enemy with a long HP bar as they do not have a lot of attack variety and the game tends to stall out fights by making bosses invulnerable which feels more uninteresting as the attack varieties are very repetitive. What I personally love in metroidvanias is the strong engagement with the boss where both the player and the boss can fight at the same time rather than dodge a long repetitive attack, stagger the boss and deal most of its health, repeat.

-Parkour chase segment, the respawns could use a rework as instances such as falling into the void can teleport the player directly into an instant death zone, this segment got rather gritting as this was a frequent occurrence and the same cutscene to initiate the segment was forced to play every time.


[strike] -From a 100% completion perspective, exploring feels like a chore, running through the rooms over and over until the final collectable has been found, backtracking rooms feels very tedious as the general map layout is very strange with its lack of shortcuts and rooms not really giving much of an impression. As the map in this game is fairly vague, something that could improve exploration without feeling tiresome to those dedicated to 100% the game could be some indicators that and individual room has had all of its secrets and collectables discovered such as changing the colour of the room on the map. The game does have a feature that shows an entire areas percent, but this still leads to a whole chunk of the map to backtrack. [/strike] There is now a feature that shows the completion of individual rooms, thanks for the change.❤️

-Need for more animations, do not get me wrong, this game has a lot of lovely animations, though there are several moments where it feels like the main character is missing an animation and it really stands out. these include no animation for leaving a lift, there is no proper turn right to left animation in cutscenes, which is a funny one as it does exist in gameplay. fluid stand up animations suddenly snap to a static talk idle animation where the weapon just shows out of thin air, etc. Of course this does not make the game unplayable, just touching up on these would help with immersion. 

-NPC conversations, this one is a more minor pick, there is instances where the final repeat text does not line up with the games progression such as the shop keeper saying he is out of stock, find more of his brothers to get more despite already finding all of his brothers and bought every item that exists to buy.

-Most quests feel too vague, it felt more like the objectives would be found out of pure chance rather than figuring it out through the hints, more structured hints would have been appreciated.

This was a big list of my personal issues with the game, do I find this a bad game? no. I actually think the game was pretty good, just not strong enough for me to recommend it. I would feel bad leaving the game on a fully negative note so here are a few things I did like:

-This arts style is very pretty, the art feels consistent and polished. there are a few animation issues but for the most part they are very fluid and visually pleasing. 

-This game has a lovely OST, there may not be a lot of themes in this game but the themes are not the kind to grow tired of, they are very relaxing and fit their dedicated environments really well.

-The story was simple, but the nice kind, it may be relatable to some people.

Overall, I think that Constance is a chill low difficulty metroidvania, it may be worth trying if you are a big metroidvania fan but want to play something more casual to take a break from difficult games. And maybe who knows? the game has not been out long since this review so some issues could have been adjusted to enhance peoples gameplay experiences. I do believe the devs still did a really good job, its just those extra tasty toppings on the cake that is missing.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1764206753}, {"review_text": "Before anything else, I want to be clear, Constance isn’t a bad game. There’s definitely a vision here, and the devs clearly have potential. But my experience was very mixed. A lot of the time I felt more frustrated than anything and honestly there is a lot to be desired, the whole time playing I just could not help but feel that there was something missing. 

To sum up a few major dissatisfactory points, as other reviews have mentioned:

-[b] Exploration is a chore [/b]
The map looks cool but it does not help much. It's practically useless. I have no way of knowing where I may have missed an item, backtracking is not fun and there is a noticeable lack of shortcuts between rooms, some of the platforming was just plain bad, and the level design itself could use some improvement. 

-[b] The quests are bad.  [/b]
They are way too vague and don’t even give you a direction to go in. Any objective that I made progress with honestly happened by pure coincidence as I was exploring.

-[b] The bosses are conceptually interesting, but weakly executed. [/b]
No boss was particularly difficult, just tedious and most of them just have the same 2-3 moves repeated and stalling for time. Going through the carnival fighting the jester and manipulator both twice, then fighting the main boss of the area. I just wanted to stop playing by the time I got through that boss rush of an area. The bosses were not fun at all.

-[b] The healing system is not good [/b]
Having to find breakable objects around the map in order to heal just a little bit of my health is not great. I understand wanting to try something different instead of going the usual estus flask route, but sometimes the systems that are already in place are what work the best. 

-[b] The NPCs are very dull, unmemorable, and the dialogue is boring. [/b]

-[b] The story was quite lackluster, too much so for me. [/b]

-[b] The game is way too short. [/b]
I did not rush and yet I completed the story in just under 6 hours with 64% completion.

On the positive side, 
I really like the art style and atmosphere of the game, I believe that this is something they excelled in and honestly is what captured my interest in the first place

Overall, I don’t think Constance is a bad game. I did have some fun with it, but there just isn’t enough here for me to recommend it to someone. There is something here, but it needs a lot of refinement. I wish the devs the best in their future endeavors.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1764296479}, {"review_text": "It's a bit like if [b]Silksong[/b] or [b]Biomorph[/b] had 6 biomes and under 10 hours of content.  [b]Constance[/b] is quite the disappointment, it feels like it ought to be 5x bigger than it is.

Colourful and fun otherwise, but that was a big pill for me to swallow.  There are many short metroidvanias that feel complete for what they are: [b]Islets[/b], [b]Moonlight Pulse[/b] etc, but I didn't feel that way about [b]Constance[/b].  It felt like the devs called it quits and threw in the final boss long before finishing making the game.  This may or may not be true to what actually happened, but most importantly, that's how this product feels to me.  

I felt somewhat similarly about [b]Bo: Path of the Teal Lotus[/b], but here it's even more egregious.  Some games like these set you up to expect and feel that you're playing something grand in scale due to the pacing and then you hit a point where you realise that it's almost over which collides with what you were feeling a minute before: that it had only just begun.

The wall jump takes getting used too, it felt pretty awkward at first.  It also requires you to press the dash button rather than the jump one, which goes against what we've all been trained to press in that situation.

Some platforming sections are actually very difficult, requiring a lot of different inputs that need to be done correctly and quickly.  Most rooms aren't like this but when you hit a place with the tricky platforming it can be reminiscent of the challenge sometimes thrown up in games like [b]Lone Fungus[/b] or [b]Aeterna Noctis[/b].  Because the game doesn't go consistently hard like this, or entirely limit its hard platforming to optional segments, at times it felt like the game had a bit of an identity crisis, difficulty-wise.

The game lets you take screenshots for its map marker system, but you have a limited number of them and if you run out that can be very annoying.  Whilst exploring you can aquire more film to take more pictures, but limiting your film so strictly in this way only serves to self inflict a quality of life problem that shouldn't exist.  

While I do think screenshots are a nicer version of map markers, I don't like when devs replace having a well marked map by having the players do it all by themselves.  One way that system can fail the player is if they explore part of a room and then enter a new one.  The map will show the room you were in, fully mapped but with no markings, and it is very easy to never think to revisit it for 100%.  This is less of a problem in games that have more detailed maps, that don't fully map a room for you when you enter it.  

Speaking of the map; rooms just display as squares or shapes, similar to [b]Ender Lilies[/b] in that it doesn't show any useful detail of the rooms geometry.

I'm leaving this a positive rec, because for the most part I enjoyed [b]Constance[/b] despite its shortcommings.  That doesn't change that it was lackluster and a disappointment though. 
 There's actually a real temptation to leave a negative rec, just to put my foot down on releasing what feels like 1/5 of a metroidvania (and at a full length price point!).", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1764148107}, {"review_text": "Don't compare it to Hollow Knight or Silksong — it's not a soulslike and the scope is intentionally smaller. It's no Ori or PoP: The Lost Crown either.

But it [i]is[/i] a little metroidvania gem! Think more along the lines of Islets, Guacamelee, SteamWorld Dig, The Messenger or Haiku. The [i]"your backlog won't judge you for picking this"[/i] tier.

Constance shines with its unique setting about a paintress confronting her inner self. The world is beautiful, the controls are tight, and the focus leans much more toward platforming than combat.

A top-tier Steam Deck game... especially if you enjoy looking artistic while falling into pits.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764080715}, {"review_text": "Tbh, the background design and game-play are the one I decided to buy and play, it made me feel so chill and relaxing somehow even fighting against the boss. The most interesting feature in this game is snapshot, it's good way to remind what I pinned before. 

Sadly, the story is shorter than I thought. As all the comments I've read so far, NPC stories are unmemorable, true; dialogue is boring, true (but i love main char reaction ^^).

Anyway, this is first time this studio build this kind of Metroidvania game so I wanna give them a thumb up! Hopefully it's a motivation for them to make a greater DLC/ game in the future!

I still love the game btw ;)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764427520}, {"review_text": "I'm enjoying the game so far, it's beautiful, well-made, and you can see that the developers put in a lot of effort to deliver the best result. Gameplay is good(maybe add pogo, just saying :D) and the story is even better. It takes a lot of sensitivity to deal with topics like this in games

Edit: It has pogo yaaaay >.<", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1764246206}, {"review_text": "Constance is a platform, exploration, combat game within a connected world of multiple distinct areas. This is not a metroidvania game. The world is not designed to encourage the player to rediscover older areas with new abilities. Rather my playthrough consisted mostly of exploring an area before going to the next with few occasions where I had to go through older rooms. This structure is fine by itself, but don’t approach the game with the idea that you are going to play a metroidvania.

Constance falls within the category of short games (8 hours to reach the end for me). While short, these types of small games can still offer a lot. The good games from this category compensate for their length by clever ideas, new gameplay mechanics frequently renewed across the game and overall a sense of very good ideas packed within a short playtime. Constance is none of that. It is too academic to float above the rest of games.

The way the character plays and moves is too classic, it doesn’t have its own identity. I have seen the same gameplay mechanics in other games already. The movement and the platform is just fine. I would have liked to see more original platform sequences. Constance is deliberately not a hard game, which would be fine if the level design had several good ideas (like a mario game) and I wouldn’t say Constance satisfies this criterion. 

The overall world lacks coherence and direction. The characters and the enemies design feel a bit random at times, as well as the story. The environments are whatever. However I will say that the graphics are pretty, this is probably the strongest point of this game.

Overall I wouldn’t say Constance is a bad game. I didn’t have moments of frustration or boredom. The pace of the game is good (as long as you don’t try to backtrack for everything) and the game feels somewhat polished in terms of animation and graphics. But the gameplay is usually my main criterion for deciding if a game is worth recommending and it lacks in that area.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1764420799}, {"review_text": "The game has a lot of potential but the boss fights and level design really pushed me to leave this review. Most boss combat in this game put you through a fixed-sequence "fight" where it feels like a repetitive trial-and-error more than a challenge.

- This is not about difficulty because the boss does the same thing every single time. It just pushes you into memorizing the entire combo until a new one appears with zero window to react, forcing you to try again and again.
- In many boss fights, the choice of VFX make attacks and hitboxes extremely hard to see. One boss only has semi transparent attacks that I believe is a dash/dodge QTE rather than an actual hitbox. It feels like the visuals is contradicting the gameplay.

The level design besides the first area feels uninspired, almost like just an arrangement of assets, not intricate designs that showcase the wonderful platforming mechanics.
- Many design choices in this game feels counterintuitive, however, the movement, art and music are all amazing. I hope the devs can improve this as I truly believe the game can be great <3", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1764047978}, {"review_text": "It’s a short but very well-made Metroidvania
with beautiful level design and art, accompanied by very satisfying gameplay, Highly recommended 

I escaped Silksong’s sickness and decay and came here.. feeling mentally at peace!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1764000408}, {"review_text": "I came into this game with a lot of hope. It's very pretty, the paint abilities flowed well, and the use of color seemed bright and deliberate. However, the game itself is intensely barebones. Combat is brainless with no attempt to marry momentum into the swings. Enemy placement and variety is haphazard. The bosses have extremely simple patterns but to compensate they do large amounts of damage, and healing is only through environmental objects so there's none of the resource management of estus flasks or the risk/reward of Hollow Knight's soul system. The paint system is novel but is extremely limiting unless you play incredibly slowly, as it lands in a sour spot between a stamina bar and an MP bar. Use too many special attacks and you can't dash, which is a real shame if they were to make several platforming segments and boss fights around doing both of those things repeatedly in short order. There's also a real fondness for having the player make blind jumps into hazards without any way to predict where they'll land once that hazard is cleared.

Mechanics aside, what really killed the game for me was the story. I understand that being an artist is a high-pressure industry, but I came here to find hidden rooms and double jump on platforms. I did not come here to click through slack messages and move files around in a hamfistedly frustrating cutscene. Combined with how the insufferably twee dialogue already had me on edge (any story that starts with the narrator as a character heckling the protagonist is a hack job, you're lighting the fourth wall on fire for kindling) and I'm done. I will give them props for them making me dislike the personality of a character with no written dialogue, that counts for something.

EDIT: Forgot to mention, if this game looked good but you want something both better written, longer, and actually fun to play, please try Chicory.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 13, "timestamp_created": 1764020258}, {"review_text": "So, first of all, HUGE SUPPORT FOR A SMALL STUDIO THAT MADE SOMETHING REALLY COOL AND BEAUTIFUL. I am 100% not regreting buying it and I will keep an eye out. Now...

I'm 6 hours in and I feel like I'm about halfway through, and I don't think I'll keep going. The game is beautiful, the story is cool, the movement is fun and feels nice. But the game seems to be fighting itself so much in some moments, and the exploration and the fights don't hit the mark. I'm going to just list it out so I explain myself, if the devs see it I wish you all the luck in the world with this and future projects! I really don't want this to feel like I'm shitting on the game and the devs - this is me writing a review purely out of appreciation and just trying to give some feedback, since for a game of this size I feel like someone might actually see it. This game has some FREAKING AWESOME ARTWORK, good music, cool ideas, cool mechanics. Everyone, enjoy the game if you get it!

- the bosses all feel the same, or better to say have the same problems; they feel like and are just predetermined cycles going one after another. The difficult part is just doing all of the moves in order and remembering it. Nothing reacts to you. Once you try the fight a few times, it just keeps going in circles, and all the difficulty comes from remembering the sequence. Some of them have fun mechanics, all of them have problems - pogoing up to a boss is cool af, but when you try to start your climb and the window to jump up to a ballon is so tight that you just pogo into its oncoming hitbox and get damaged, it sucks. Also, too many fights are "cant hit me while I do my shit. After that, I'll stand still for 10 seconds and do nothing so you can just spam attack - then we will do it again". 

- exploration is not fun. Movement is good, but you find almost nothing. No cool worldbuilding places, no items, no upgrades. I cleared 3 areas almost fully and I found 3 almost useless inspirations, 1 inspiration that should be a core gameplay thing (the dash doesn't damage you one), 1 piece of heart which I need 3 of to get anything out of, 1 piece of paint which I need 4 of to get anything out of. Thats it. No dopamine hits, no wonder, nothing. And the common enemies are boring or freaking awful. They are either 3 hit go left to right type, or OH I DO THIS, YOU ARE GONNA F**CKING HATE IT type.

- I went through 3 areas and didn't find the healing thing. If my bud wasn't playing at the same time, would have thought it doesn't exist. For a thing that important, I really, really shouldn't be able to miss it, especially when I really tried to explore every given path. Imagine if hollow knight (which this game takes clear inspiration for) just puts healing as a non-main-path find-it item? Many people would never finish that game.

- The death mechanic is useless. When in bossfights, its literally the choice between "do you want to die and restart the fight" or "do you wanna restart the fight, but it gets harder". Like, what? And okay, then it should work for exploration. Nope, because it doesn't just make everything tougher, it also makes it so you cant dodge through them, making traversal an absolute nightmare.

- Its too linear progression wise for a metroidvania. Thats it, that simple.

So, with all of this, I'm left with exploration that doesn't award me, boss fights that don't keep me on my toes and are often janky, enemies that are just boring or make me pull my hair out, and, I'm sorry, the story is cool and fun, but its just not nearly good enough to pull the whole game and keep me playing... atleast not from what I've seen so far.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764107256}, {"review_text": "I really loved playing through this game and I consider it one of the best metroidvanias of 2025. With a conscious message about burnout and challenging bosses and platforming, it is the best of both worlds. Seriously, play Constance.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1764009344}, {"review_text": "I played the demo at Games Ground Berlin, and I'm so glad that I went; otherwise, I would have missed this wonderful piece of a game. The music, the art, the feeling, the juice—it was all wonderful. If you're a fan of Metroidvanias, I highly recommend you give it a try!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1763998047}, {"review_text": "This game does all the thing I love about Hollow Knight and gets rid of all the things I don't like about Hollow Knight. 

Movement and combat is super fun and rewarding. The game is definitely challenging, but feels fair and is not incredibly punishing. Probably the most fun I've had with a metroidvania since Ori and the Blind Forest.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1764295515}, {"review_text": "[h1]A good game with wasted potential[/h1]
Finally beat the game's main plot at a little over 7 hours with some side exploration mixed in. If you're a completionist I can easily see you taking another 2-3 hours doing some sidequests but due to the way they're structured where you can't immediately beat them without some other obscure thing that isn't immediately obvious, i didn't feel like it. 

My original thoughts on the game on the first hour was that it was good, an 8/10. Having now finished the game, I think I'm going to bump down my review to a 7.5/10 where I still think it's enjoyable, I still think it's worth your money for a specific group of people, but I can't help but feel this game's original plan was bigger and they were forced to cut back due to scope creep or huge ambitions that they couldn't fulfill in a reasonable time. 

Some things to note while you consider the game:

[b]1. The elephant in the room:[/b] the game has some inspiration from Hollow Knight among other titles. And since Silksong just came out a few months back for a similar price point, my guess is if you have to choose either, that will be the better purchase (see point 2 below). Constance is a beautifully animated 2D action platformer that delivers far more mechanical depth than I expected. Beneath its emotional narrative and paint-splashed world is a genuinely skill-based experience that rewards precision, practice, and mastery.

The movement is snappy, the dodge-focused combat feels great, and new paintbrush abilities consistently shake up both traversal and boss strategy. Every boss fight is memorable. Not just visually, but mechanically, and the carnival section in particular is a highlight. There’s no filler here; the game challenges you through tight encounters and smart level layouts, not waves of enemies.

Exploration has meaningful rewards like health upgrades and paint expansions, though the limited capability of fast travel makes backtracking a bit tedious. Still, the pacing overall is strong, and the finale is a perfect test of everything you’ve learned.

The art and animation are fantastic, the soundtrack is nearly perfect, and the world, while thematically broad in its mental-health focus, is atmospheric and well-realized.

If you love Hollow Knight, Celeste, or any mechanically driven indie platformer, Constance will be a delight!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1763997865}, {"review_text": "I preface this by saying that I haven't finish the game yet, but I'm not that far from it, from my savefile I'm at 60% completion for 6hours of gameplay more or less. Also I usualy don't rate game, and don't realy like letting my negative opinions known, but this one's just very frustrating.
I realy try to like the game, and I can't deny that it clearly have its qualities, obviousely the art direction, the music is nice too tho maybe less remarquable IMO.
But it also have some  glaring issues that just drain my enjoyment, lots of smaller issue here and there that aren't that detrimental to the experience by themself, but stack up to be just anooying enough together, things like the traversal not being that fun, the fealing that there's not realy a lots of reasons to backtrack once you obtained a power-up from another zone, the map just feeling very bad in general, the mouvements being a bit too cluncky, and the lack of fast travel with wouldn't be as bad without the previousely mentioned issues related to traversal.
This one may just be me but the story realy doesn't engage me in the slightest so I would apreciate a skip bouton for these long and uninteresting dialogues. I won't complain about the "real world memory sections" cause I think they were made to be tidious on purpose, wich I respect, but doesn't mean I enjoyed them still, but I don't think the whole game being almost as tidious at times was on purpose.
I'll also add that the brush just feel like a gimmik for the "art theme", none of the power-up raly tie to it in any way, wich is a shame cause its realy not the possibilities that are lacking.
As I said, lots of small things that aren't dealbraking on their own.

But then there's the last and main issue, it being the boss designs (gameplay wise, visualy they are immaculate), there is just too much waiting and doing nothing, the bosses for the most part aren't very engaging.

Writting this review I had a realization so I place it here before the more spoilery reasons I hate certain bosses: My issue with these bosses is that they are designed like they would have been for a game with no combat, like a Mario game, where you wait around dodging a few things, and punish the boss, repeat 3 times...
But Constance gives you 2 attack boutons, 2 dashes one of wich also deals damage, a pogo, and more, but you can't even use most of these options on most bosses.

Bunch of spoiler for some specific bosses ahead.

The worst offender IMO is the Jester (but it apply to almost all the cast), where it takes a whole 1min-1min30 of dodging unengaging attack patterns before you even have the chance of damaging it, and that it, if you don't F-up your opportunity wich in the fist few attemp you're likely to depending on the pattern the RNG use for this one. same if you don't damage it enough to 2 cicles it, just 1more minute and a half to wait... and that's only if you understand that you have to hit 3 black cards even tho they come one by one and there's no feedback with the first 2 to indicate that it does anything, wich IMO is a terrible design. 

The manipulator second fight was probably the only tolerable one of the 4 preceding the boss of the circus, or it would be, if the first 3 fight didn't condition you to not even try to attack the boss... this whole section realy is that bad.

And the Jester only is the worst offender for me because I manage to skip the tornado phase of the last boss of the circus by damage-tanking it and spaming stupidly, reseting the fight if he ever activated that tornado phase du to how boring and OVERTLY long for no reason it was... I realy didn't want to deal with that shit. And I enjoyed that fight because of the way I played it, but it shouldn't take skiping half the fight for me to enjoy it...

Fortunaly not all bosses where as bad, the 2 bosses in the sewer and one in the observatory (the one that shoot lasers) where the highlight of the game for me, the sewer knights for exemple also had a moment where he's invincible but it's short enough to not overstay its welcome unlike every other bosses that have that mechanic. Contrary to the other bosses I didn't mind having to deal with a 3rd cycle of these ones (wich sound like a low bar, because it is, but I enjoyed these ones).", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764460971}, {"review_text": "Do you like beautiful hand-drawn animation? I played the demos and game in expecting a pretty good metroidvania, but what I've seen so far has really been something special. The focus on movement and puzzle solving over the more traditional combat challenges I usually see in metroidvanias helps it stand out a lot, and the story segments between bosses felt surprisingly effective to me. Як резюме: це непогана гра, з хорошим потенціалом (який нажаль розробники не до кінця розкрили) і яскравим впізнаваним візуалом, якщо розробники не зупиняться на досягнутому то їх наступний проект точно стане ще цікавішим та успішнішим!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764973599}, {"review_text": "It's a fun, cute game with a great art style, but at times I'm not sure it knows what it wants to be. There's a bit of a weird mix of 'delayed' combat with the bosses but then you have some real fast-paced and fairly challenging platforming sections that take a bit to get used to. Still, I think it's unfair to compare it to Silksong which is an (or, the) absolute giant of the genre.

[b]Pros[/b]
- I love the art, I love the vibe of the world, I personally love all the animations too.
- It's fun. That's hard to quantify, but ultimately it's why I'm giving it a positive review - I had fun going through the game. It isn't the top of its class in what makes a good metroidvania (up there for art though!), but it's not the bottom of the barrel either.
- I thought the inspiration system was a creative take on the usual skill/trait/charm system

[b]Neutral[/b]
- It's a relatively short game but that's ok for me. Haven't quite hit 100% on my first playthrough and I'm close to 12.5 hours.

[b]Criticisms[/b]
- Map does not have much detail and is a bit like the first Ender Lillies game, [b]but the dev has already said they're improving this in the next patch!  [/b] We shouldn't settle for maps like this in 2025 tbh. [strike]Game completion is based on region completion % which is based on room completion %, but currently there is no room completion % ingame, so it's a pain to find what you're missing. [/strike] [b] Fixed with latest patch![/b]
- The boss fights aren't particularly memorable, and follow a pattern uncommon in metroidvanias I've played - a phase where you're vulnerable and the boss is near invulnerable followed by a vulnerable/staggered/knockdown phase where you can beat on them unchallenged. - Without any spoilers, once you're up to the part of the game where you have to collect the 4 tears, in hindsight, it feels like you're at a disadvantage if you don't go a certain direction first to get a certain upgrade. - Maybe I just failed at exploring in this game, but I felt like I got most of my paint/health upgrades + several important/useful inspirations after I'd already beaten the majority of the main story.

Hopefully it all works out, would love for the game to succeed.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1760904272}, {"review_text": "So here are my thoughts on the game as a World of Warcraft Mythic Plus veteran and Mythic Raider.

The game on the whole is legitimately everything I've ever wanted in a game. I play WoW specifically for the two end games I previously mentioned. I don't really care for much else WoW has to offer. I do those things in WoW so I can go raid and do mythic plus because it is required of me. This game is playable out the box. I legitimately love this game. I don't really do steam reviews and I have 14k hours on some games. But I went out of my way to make this one because I genuinely love what this game is and I want to to be successful and get an even bigger following. I want this game to do well and pioneer this sub genre of game type (they're called MODAs multiplayer online dungeon adventures). I do want to note however to compare it to WoW in it's entirety as I've seen a lot of people do, is unfair. It's not an MMORPG. There is no questing (thank god) or any of that nonsense. It's just pure dungeon grind. That's it. It's as if someone just took the mythic plus game mode and made it into it's own thing with an automated dungeon finder.

I want to touch on pros and cons now starting with the pros:

1. This game as mentioned is playable out the box. No addons or mods needed. Has a built in dps meter and boss cooldown timers and everything.The UI is editable.
2. The graphics are made so even a toaster oven could run it, which increases accessibility and reach for players
3. The tutorial is actually pretty well flushed out in my opinion. It covers all the basics you really need to know as far as combat goes in only a few minutes. It teaches you what interrupts are etc. from a tank perspective. I just wish they had a healer version as well to show dispels but this is in early access so I'm giving it grace. They even show you how to mark your interrupts so you don't overlap kicks.
4. When you fail to time a dungeon the worst thing that happens is you get less rating. There is no such thing as "key depletion" or any of that nonsense. You still get all the loot you would have as if you timed it. Whereas in mythic plus you could do like 8 dungeons and not get squat for it. And after you get the loot you just queue and try again. 
5. Account progression is very alt friendly. Once you clear your first capstone and progress into the next league anything from the previous league is open and available on the vendor as a quick way to gear alts. Though each character does have to still progress through each league. 
6. There is incentive to do quickplay here. Quickplay in this game is literally just an interactive training dummy. Once you get the hang of your class there really is no reason to do it. EXCEPT if you want to buy the chests that have the mats to reforge gear you need to do quickplay. So new players don't get screwed over once vets have moved past that. Therefore keeping the loop healthy. 
7. Because of the worst thing happening if you don't time is getting less rating and still keeping all the loot you get less leavers and people are more willing to finish a dungeon unlike mythic plus where a group would just disband with people angry. Here it's so far been far more chill. 

All that being said I want to be objective and not just glaze the whole post and list out some cons:

1. There is no way to queue for a specific dungeon if you're not a premade four stack. I feel like there needs to be a way to queue for specific dungeons and levels you'd like without having to be in a four stack. Someone once joked that having friends is a competitve advantage and it really does show here. If you're playing solo like me (unless you're playing a tank or healer and get instant queues) you get thrown into queue based off of your item level and your dungeon rating. But sometimes especially if you're a the point that you're ready to tackle the capstone that dungeon doesn't show up on the list of 3 RNG'd dungeons that people can vote on. So then you're at the mercy of the system to hopefully get the capstone and hope that you can complete it in time. Perhaps the devs did it this way to not split the population too hard for the sake of queue times but if players feel like their progression is being cucked by RNG then it can be a turn off for them. Something for the devs to consider. Either allow us to select specific dungeons to queue or give us a looking for group tool. I'd rather the former over the latter since this game is literally designed to fix the problems the WoW group finder tool has. This is probably my biggest gripe with the game thus far. 
2. Make reporting mean something. I'm not sure if it does or doesn't at the moment. For all I know it's an automated system and nothing happens but I want to see people who leave on first pull like in mythic plus actually get some sort of penalty. Tanks because they can get fast queue times will sometimes do that even in this game. And I don't want it to make the players bitter and turn away from the game.
3. There is no incentive to roll non dps roles outside of avoiding long queue times. This isn't necessarily a huge issue but it can only help dps queue times offering incentives like WoW's call to arms or in Overwatch there were incentives put in place to push more players to tank or heal which will only help smooth things out for those who are experiencing longer than ideal queue times (myself included at times in the day). Maybe a bit more gold or supplies as a reward? (rewards are account bound)
4. There is not a huge dispersion of players in multiple ranks which offsets queue times for specific ranks. Or so it feels. Contender queue times were actually pretty nice. Rarely more than five minutes long at most. Once hitting adept it feels like people are either past adept or not in adept yet. Therefore the queue times can be pretty gross especially during specific times of the day. I've seen times as long as 25 minutes. However the game just came out, it's in early access so I'm giving grace that will sort itself out.
5. Honestly what is left of my complaints are more just nit picky things that I'm sure are in place due to early access. Like not being able to drag and drop spells and other quality of life things. Or cheaper visuals.

Overall to wrap up my thoughts. I think this game is amazing and has huge potential. I usually take a long time to decide if I want to buy a game since money is tight but with this I had no hesitation. I want this game to do well. While there are some pretty hefty cons that should be taken seriously I'm sure the devs are working to sort those out as soon as possible since they were pretty quick to nip the server issues in the bud. Quicker than Blizzard would have on launch day for sure. I want this game to do well and create a new staple of gaming genre and pioneer it's way into the gaming industry. That being said, I do not regret my $25 I spent. Even if the longevity isn't there I had my fair share of fun that has made the amount of time I have played well worth the money. The more people that support the game the more likely we'll see that longevity we all want. Best dungeon crawler I've played yet. I'd rate it an 8/10 and hope it only goes up from here :)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1761041593}, {"review_text": "Prepare for 20,000 hour WoW virgins to flame you and rage quit.

Here's how it works: You queue up and get matched with 3 random players (1 tank, 1 healer, 2 DPS). Like every MMO dungeon finder, DPS queues are oversaturated, so you're waiting 10-15 minutes just to pop.

[{"review_text": "I started Factorio as a mere man. A fool. A weak, pathetic human who thought "I'll just play for an hour." That was 4 days ago. My body is in ruins, my mind sharper than ever. I have eliminated all inefficient thoughts. My blood pressure fluctuates in perfect sync with my main bus throughput. The factory must grow.

"it’s just a game."

 WRONG.

 It is a way of life. Do you think a beaver calls dam-building a game? Do you think an ant optimizes for fun? No. It is war, it is survival. And every second wasted is a lost potential space science pack.

The police came after neighbors reported "mechanical whirring" from my apartment. I explained that my copper smelting arrays required better output. They called me "unstable." Fools. They are blind to the inefficiency all around them.

I tried to return to work. My boss asked for an urgent report. I set up an automated Excel system to generate real-time charts. He said he just needed a PDF. I informed him that the conversion was in a later stage of the production chain. My coworkers tried to make small talk at lunch. They asked about my family. I replied that family unit production was currently outside my scope. I have lost all capacity for normal human interaction.

I no longer dream of love, friends, or companionship. I dream of belts. I dream of robots. I dream of perfect, fluid efficiency.

If an Amazon logistics manager saw my factory, he would fall to his knees and weep — tears of admiration, terror, and unworthiness. His entire career, his vast warehouses, his so-called "efficiency" would seem like the crude fumblings of a caveman smashing rocks together.

Now I am an optimization algorithm wrapped in human skin. A transhumanist entity, devoid of inefficiency. My heartbeat syncs with production ticks, my thoughts run in parallel processing. Emotions? Redundant. Rest? A bottleneck. The only metric that matters is output.

The Factory Must Expand.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 208, "timestamp_created": 1749084100}, {"review_text": "You know that game you bought years ago on a whim, played once, and then completely forgot about?
Then one day, you hit a rough patch in life and you're just looking for a little escape.
And suddenly, you remember that game, Factorio.
"Let’s give it another try," you think.
Just for a bit. Build some factories. Automate some stuff.
A weekend, at most.
That was 8 months ago.

It starts simple. Mining some iron. Automating the steam engines. Getting red and green science.
Then black science. Killing biters to expand.
Then comes oil.
Oil was threatening my intelligence, pounding at my confidence. But with some help from my favourite Polish Factorio player, I managed to stay on top.

And then came trains.
I like trains. Trains should be fun, right?
Right?

[b]Wrong.[/b]
The fact that “Factorio Train Tutorial - Absolute Basics” is an 86 minute video should tell you enough.
After hours of watching tutorials on train signals, I finally got my train network functioning. [i]Barely.[/i]

Then, just when I felt the final sciences were within reach, I learned about this thing called ratios.
And whatever the definition of “ratio” is… I quickly realised that whatever I’d been building was not it.

So I did what any sane person would do:
I built thousands of construction robots and tore down everything I had created so far, just to rebuild it. In ratio.
That little detour ended up taking over 40 in game hours.

At this point, I haven’t left my house in days. I’ve spent more time inputting numbers into a ratio calculator than I’ve spent sleeping.
My family is starting to worry about my obsession with Factorio, but they don’t understand.
I can stop anytime I want.
I just have to fix this little bottleneck first.

At this point, I don’t know what life is anymore without hearing Trupen talk about oil processing, or Nilaus explain city blocks.
And yet, I’ve never felt more in control. Every problem is solvable. Everything is automated. Every part of the factory… works.
[i]Sort of.[/i]

Eventually, I launched the rocket. The “end” of the game.
I watched it soar into the sky. The culmination of countless hours of planning, designing, and rebuilding.

I sit back. Take a deep breath.
Maybe now, I can finally take a break.

I close the game. I feel at peace.

That's definitely how I felt when I first decided to give this game a shot when Space Age dropped near the end of 2024. However, I quickly realized how wrong that initial assumption was from my end.

The most daunting thing about booting up Factorio for the first time turns out to be its hotkeys and its sprawling tech tree. In terms of its hotkeys, it's much like any graphic design software where initially some hotkeys seem so unbelievably specific its almost absurd. After some time with the game (in my case, 400 hours in and I'm still picking up new hotkey tricks) you'll probably end up surprised with how naturally you've adapted to their use. So, no rush there.

The tech tree, if you stare at it long enough when you start your first world, might seem a little nauseating. Your mind may spiral a bit trying to understand how you'll prepare to make components, or plan to use structures, that are hours of gameplay down the line from the start. It may help to look at the tech tree as a series of courses that the game will serve you during your playtime instead. The game is gating you, presenting you with a challenge at each step. "How do I stop needing to manually feed all my furnaces and get more smelted products?", "How do I keep up with my demand for gears and circuits?", "How can I improve my power supply and access to distant resources?".

This series of compartmentalized challenges is how this game ropes you in. All of those videos and images you've seen of crazy mega-bases and efficient train networks aren't gated behind some genetic predisposition to being talented at Factorio. Rather, they are the result of approaching each of these small, bite sized challenges the game presents you with as you progress through its tech tree. Before you know it, you'll be producing answers to questions this game asks you that you weren't even aware were a possibility 20 hours prior. The pieces will keep falling into place for you over and over and over again, and after 400 hours playing this game, they haven't stopped for me.

If you let it, Factorio will take you on a journey of endless problem solving, where the problems you solve only grow more complex and where your answers only become more elegant and clever. It comes highly recommended from me, it is one of the most rewarding and fascinating games I have played in my life.

The biggest negative I could assign Factorio is how its post-endgame content functions. With space age especially, what drove me in this game was rounding out and perfecting my main base, along with discovering and conquering new planets and optimizing them as I went along. However, at a certain point, as the tech tree begins to fizzle out into repeatable researches, the end game content simply becomes a game of pushing your production values higher.

This works for some people, but doesn't work for me (at least, not yet). And from what I've seen of the modding community, there are countless ways to customize the game's content to mitigate this issue. I don't think its necessarily a bad thing, how vanilla Factorio concludes, it's just not for me.

I'd very quickly like to endorse a game that does address this issue for me, which is Dyson Sphere Program. While not yet finished, the core gameplay loop is nearly as robust as Factorio's, and I have a far greater desire to engage with that game's endgame than I do with Factorio's. I would highly recommend both of these titles, and I am excited to return to DSP at their next update and see how my experience with Factorio will change how I approach problem solving in that title.

All in all, the unique fervor surrounding this game is definitely earned, and I will spend the rest of my life scratching the itch that Factorio gave me.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1739215523}, {"review_text": "No need to explain what the game is about, the trailer does a fantastic job for that.

This game is a classic.

A zombie invasion is happening, chaos is everywhere and how do you defend against it? With Plants, of course!

This is a Tower Defence game that is exactly what the name implies, you help your definitely sane friend Crazy Dave, by collecting sun and using multiple Plants to defeat a variety of Zombies. 

It doesn't matter if it's on the lawn, backyard or even the roof, or if it's day, night or with fog, or even if they're inside vases. The Zombies are coming, and you better be ready to get set and plant your Peashooters and Sunflowers to victory!

Anyways, let's get to the pros and cons.

Pros:

- Almost every level gives you something new to play with, maybe it's a Plant, a new Minigame, or the ability to access Dave's shop. Thanks to that, it keeps you engaged throughout the whole experience.

- Several minigames that changes how you would normally play, there's even one that allows you to play as the Zombies instead.

- The Soundtrack is fantastic, every music fits the area and more instruments are added if there's a lot of Zombies on the screen. My personal favorites are Crazy Dave (the main theme), Ultimate Battle, Grace the Roof, Zen Garden, Brainiac Maniac, and Zombies on your Lawn.

- The Artstyle is gorgeous, all the Plants look cute and charming, even a flower pot has eyes and a face. As for the Zombies, despite them usually being depicted as scary in games, they look goofy and simple in this one.

Cons:

- The game is way too easy, most Zombies are barely a threat, the lawnmowers can also defeat any Zombies on an entire lane. Even something like a Balloon Zombie, which can fly, gets affected by it. The game is so easy in fact, that it can be completed without ever using Sunflowers and Sun-Shrooms. Some of the plants are also way too powerful, speaking of which...

- Overpowered Plants.

> Puff-Shroom is a 0 cost Plant, yes, a free Plant, that attacks similarly to a Peashooter, with the only downsides being that it doesn't have a lot of range and it doesn't work on daytime. This Plant single handedly turn night levels into a joke since you can just spam it.

> Ice-Shroom freezes most Zombie types on screen for several seconds. After the freeze is gone, the zombies are still chilled.

> Doom-Shroom is just a better Cherry Bomb, having more range than it, with the only downside being that of preventing you from planting in that tile for several seconds.

> Cattail, a slightly more expensive Repeater that can hit zombies on any lane, and also counters Balloon Zombies.

> Starfruit is a slightly more expensive Peashooter that shoots in five directions at once, spam it and you win.

> Winter-Melon does high damage, has splash damage and slows Zombies down, insane.

> Gloom-Shroom is a close ranged Plant that attacks in all directions and demolishes anything that gets close to it.

And on the opposite end of the spectrum we have...

- Super niche or very weak Plants. 

> Chomper takes forever to finish eating a Zombie, understandable if it's on a tanky one, but it takes the same amount of time regardless if it was a Browncoat or Zomboni.

> Plantern is designed to counter fog and nothing else, this plant feels like a Quality of Life feature more than anything else.

> Cactus is made to counter Balloon Zombies and that's it. If that zombie isn't in the level, then Cactus is just a more expensive Peashooter with the same stats.

> Blover defeats Balloon Zombies and temporarily gets rid of fog, does nothing else. Same problem that Cactus has.

> Hypno-Shroom hypnotizes a zombie to fight for you, cool effect but the only Zombie worth doing that is Football Zombies, more problematic ones are immune to this plant. Better off just using Jalapeno.

> Split Pea is supposed to counter Digger Zombies but it lacks the firepower to do so, outside of that it's just a more expensive Peashooter.

> Umbrella-Leaf counters Catapult and Bungee Zombies and does nothing else.

> Gold Magnet just collects coins for you, pretty much just a Quality of Life.

> Marigold produces coins, that's it. Should have just been exclusive to Zen Garden.

> Sea-Shroom is a slower recharging Puff-Shroom that can only be used on water and during night time. 

> And other plants that only do one thing, such as Grave Buster, Coffee Bean, Flower Pot and Lily Pad.

Combining both the really strong and weak plants leads into..

- Bad replayability. The game is fun to play through the Adventure mode, but after that there's not much reason to do it again. Crazy Dave does force you to use some random Plants in the loadout if you go into Adventure again, and levels are longer than normal with problematic zombies showing up more often, but that's about it. Game also suffers from being really slow to play, a button to increase the game speed would have been appreciated.

In Conclusion:

Despite all that, my final score is a 8/10, pretty solid game with only a few issues here and there.

This is a classic that stood the test of time. Sad to see how this franchise is in such a sad and deplorable shape nowadays, at least this game still works like a time capsule of the good times we had back then.

🌱Happy birthday of 16 years.🌱

Plants vs. Zombies is a game fueled by nostalgia for me. I still remember getting it on a USB back in high school from one of my seniors after watching him finish some of the final levels. I can't even tell you how many times I then went on to finish the game. It’s a classic for sure, but I’m not sure it’s aged as gracefully as I’d hoped.

Still, there’s a reason it’s so iconic.

The silly but charming design holds up. The quirky plants and goofy zombies give it that distinct personality that makes it so memorable. The gameplay offers plenty of plants and maps to experiment with, though I’ll admit it felt a bit repetitive at times. Certain plants are just so strong that there’s little incentive to mix things up or try out less optimal plants. If you see that as a fun challenge, though, then there shouldn’t be any issues for you whatsoever, and you'll likely get a lot more enjoyment out of this game than most.

That said, the game has a decent amount of content beyond the main campaign. The minigames and puzzle missions are fun distractions if you’re looking for more, but the campaign itself is short, simple, and sweet. And the ending? “There’s a Zombie on Your Lawn” is an absolute masterpiece.

I don’t have any major complaints about Plants vs. Zombies. It’s still a fun and wholesome trip down memory lane, and that’s enough for me.

Would recommend picking it up if you’re slightly curious, but just be mindful it definitely shows its age. The game doesn't do a lot in relation to modern-day standards, but it's a fun throwback.

[h3][b]Personal Overall Experience: Okay - 5/10[/b][/h3]", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1736404867}]

However, Ghost of Tsushima is more than a masterpiece. It’s is ART.

The combat system in Ghost of Tsushima has got to be the smoothest of any game I have ever played. No hiccups, no jittery movements. Every button and action used smoothly transitions from one to the next and honestly it’s just amazing. 

The game direction is the best I have ever seen. No stupid marker on the screen in your face. No UI for the most part of travelling. The game uses the wind to guide you through Tsushima and Iki Island. It adds a level of immersion I hadn’t ever thought possible in a game.

The game itself is beautiful. Everywhere you go in this game and in any weather looks fantastic that a screenshot from anywhere anytime can look like PURE CINEMA. The trees, the grass, the sun as it sheds its light on everything just looks… wow!

Throughout my gameplay of this game I have encountered only two bugs. On Iki island there was a rock and you could see a few pixel gap where you could see through the world. But honestly it is super easy to miss. The other was a fault of my personal settings so I won’t include it.

The story is one that hits home for me. Balancing what is right and what is not and of one’s own honour. It is amazing. Literally goosebumps whenever I play or watch the game. I bought Ghost of Tsushima in a real tough time in my life and had no spoilers and thus NO REGRETS.

The music is on another level. I’ve never really stepped into the Japanese genre of music before and this game has it dialled up to 100x. The music gives goosebumps every time, it matches the feel and the action the game is going for at every turn. It is hard to put into words how good it is. How AMAZING it is!

Japanese culture is somewhat inaccurate as the whole Honour theme wasn’t prevalent until 200 years after the Mongolians attempted to invade the mainland after conquering Tsushima and Iki. But their faith, their traditions, the way the armour looks and how many times you hit an enemy with your katana to kill them is really realistic. As blades back then were too thin to cause real damage.

This has changed my opinion on games and is officially my favourite game of All Time!

Just a moment ago you might have been fumbling and tripping in real life, but now you are Jin Sakai, cutting down Mongols like it’s nothing, as if you've been training with a bamboo sword under a waterfall your whole life. The game is stunning, cinematic, and almost a spiritual experience... unless you take into consideration the fact that you stop during a fight to pet a fox. 

The Director’s Cut is essentially the same game, but with an amplified effect of everything, more island, more narrative, more wind dramatically blowing through your cape as you contemplate honor and trauma. The Iki Island expansion is Jin’s journey in therapy, which is cleverly disguised as a side quest. It is aesthetically pleasing and tragic at the same time, and sometimes it can be the “my dad didn’t hug me enough” energy. 

The visuals are worth discussing. This game doesn’t have graphics, it has art. Every single frame could be a piece of art that people museum it and they silently say “wow, the composition.” You might find yourself in the middle of a fight and suddenly stopping to take pictures because the sunset is just too beautiful. While you’re technically supposed to be saving Japan, you are here instead, like a feudal times influencer, adjusting filters and focal depth. 

The fight? Exquisitely sharp. It’s a combination of ballet and murder. Each stunt and every sword strike is real and believable. You’ll transition from button, mashing panic to perfect timely parry that will make you say “yes” quietly to yourself at 2 a.m. They even have a standoff mode where you can basically act as the main character of every cool samurai movie you’ve ever seen, with the difference that you are the one who doesn’t fail and misses. 

Also, the dual, audio Japanese voice acting? The best. If you opt to play in English, that’s ok but playing in Japanese and with Kurosawa mode on is an absolute vibe. Black and white, film grain, wind that is blowing dramaticaly, it really gives you the feeling that you are watching a masterpiece from the 1950s, except without the smell of the film burning. 

The Director’s Cut is not a major overhaul of the game, but a kind of a mirror polish. Emotionally, the weight comes from Iki Island and a handful of new gadgets, and on PS5, ‘blink and it’s done’ would be a pretty accurate description of the load times. It’s essentially the same game, only smoother, prettier, and slightly sadder in a good way. 

Essentially, Ghost of Tsushima: Director’s Cut is the result of art, combat and open, world design teaming up to form a boy band. It’s gorgeous, emotional, and at times, silly, in the way that only a game that lets you write haikus about death next to a waterfall can be. 

Play it. Then play it again. And don’t forget to pet every single fox, they really deserve it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1760839628}, {"review_text": "This game stands shoulder to shoulder with giants like The Witcher 3 and Red Dead Redemption 2. If I had to nitpick, the second act’s main story and side quests dip in quality compared to the blockbuster first act. Thankfully, things improve again toward the finale, which feels simple yet natural. Also, jumping straight into the Iki Island DLC was probably a mistake, because I started to feel some burnout.

This game deserves more recognition. Hard to believe Ghost of Tsushima lost Game of the Year to The Last of Us Part II with all its controversie, but I guess that’s subjective.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1761494914}, {"review_text": "Ah yes, the Japanese Assassin's Creed Ubisoft wishes it had made.

Just how the Spider-man games make you FEEL like Spiderman this game really makes you FEEL like a Samurai. 

After playing Ghost of Tsushima, I decided to start taking Kendo, laido, and Kenjutsu classes. I will admit, it was stupid to get into a martial art after playing a video game. However, I realise that this is something I should have started doing a while ago. I really enjoy it and it has helped me a lot in defending myself from my wife’s boyfriend!

It seems to be what the newer Assassin's Creed games were trying to do, it's just executed with more integrity. I first played the game during the pandemic and it was the perfect game for me during lockdown. I would just wander the countryside and take in the scenery. I would chase foxes to their shrine, and wear different outfits depending on my mood. I would zone out to the ambient shakuhachi flutes, and bang my head to the taiko drums. I would compose haiku under the stars, and perfect my showdown stances. The whole game felt organic and natural. When I finished the game, living there in that little hut, with all the trophies, I indulged in the memories of each one, like having a glass of wine with an old friend. It was bittersweet but fulfilling, and I still remember it fondly.

When I originally played it in 2020, I felt it was my favorite game of that decade. Have yet to play a game in the last 2 years I love more. Those touches were MAGICAL for the first hours. The first time I wrote a haiku was an experience that made me reevaluate how I view video games. The whole thing was like I was playing one of my beloved Samurai movies. I would get excited when I saw the Fox dens, since it meant there was a chance I could pet one.(love giving animals scratches in games) The stoic characters felt authentic to the the type of old school Samurai movies they were seemingly inspired from. And having the guiding wind to help you to your objectives was a very nice touch and really innovative way to get rid of quest markers. The mythical tales are excellent, and so are the duels that come with the quests. This is where the game really shines, as it is able to combine the best of the great visuals and good combat into memorable segments.

The game sure has several of the open world tropes that studios are apparently tied to these days, But it’s a lot less bloated than the recent AC games. To me it felt like the perfect size and length to play through and not get bored toward the end. And to me it kinda feels how AC would feel if they took the time to make their games well. Ghost of Tsushima has a level of care built into it that Ubisoft games don't. There's no micro transactions. All cosmetics are unlocked through gameplay. The UI is minimalist. Both combat and stealth are equally viable and fun. It's a well built game. The combat, the scenery and visuals, and just kinda the way everything feels is just better. In AC I would always be rushing from A to B trying to get the traveling over with. In Tsushima I’m always just slowly walking my horse place to place, looking around, soaking everything in and just vibing.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

The graphics are absolutely gorgeous and the world is filled with a variety of biomes - from tall grasslands, to dense rainforests, swampy wetlands and snowy mountains. Every shot is screenshot-worthy and you will never get bored of the scenery. At times, I chose to ignore the fast-travel option because I wanted to enjoy the beautiful landscapes more. 

The world is made more immersive by the lack of UI and the use of its unique wind mechanic as its navigation system. However, the game does suffer from the repetitiveness of its map activities like most open-world games do. But what Ghost of Tsushima does really well in this aspect compared to others is that they actually offer great rewards in the form of permanent buffs e.g. maximum health boost, resolve increase & new skills. Hence, you never feel like you’re wasting your time doing these activities despite the sheer amount of them, as the rewards for completing them are things which will benefit you in all future combat encounters. 

Speaking of combat, initially it may seem shallow and difficult, but as you start to gain more resolve and skills, it opens a lot more and becomes much more manageable and fun. The combat never dulls as there are always different builds and playstyles you can switch to, whether that be stealth, direct frontal attacks, range or standoff duels. The stealth in this game is satisfying good and the swordplay, most importantly, is tight and responsive. Each hit feels like your character has weight on him, making you feel like a real samurai.

As for the story, the main plot itself isn't that deep and is pretty straight-forward, but the excellent writing and the cinema-like presentation elevates it to a level where you will be kept engaged to it. The game will question your morality a lot, especially in regards to your honor. However, you don't really get to have a say on that as the game lack choices that you can make (there's only two in the entire game – one at the end of the main story and the other in a side quest in the DLC). The DLC is a must-play since it offers a very introspective look on Jin's character, further exploring his backstory and growth and making him much more likeable.
