The moment it was announced for PC, I knew I had to experience it, no matter the hurdles. Unfortunately, the game was region-blocked in many countries, and I even went as far as changing my country just to purchase it. Now that I’ve finally played it, I can confidently say that the wait and effort were worth it, this game is an artistic triumph.[/b]

[h1]A Breathtaking Journey Through Feudal Japan[/h1]
[b]Set during the Mongol invasion of Tsushima in 1274, the game follows Jin Sakai, a samurai torn between honor and survival, as he defends his homeland from an overwhelming enemy. From the very first scene, Ghost of Tsushima captivates with its stunning visuals, epic narrative, and atmospheric soundtrack. The game brings feudal Japan to life with unparalleled beauty, from serene forests and golden fields to violent battlefields and peaceful shrines.[/b]

[h1]Engaging Narrative and Character Development[/h1]
[b]The story of Jin Sakai is one of honor, sacrifice, and personal struggle. As Jin transitions from a traditional samurai to the stealthy "Ghost," his journey explores themes of loyalty, morality, and what it truly means to protect one’s people. The supporting cast is equally memorable, with characters like Lady Masako, Yuna, and Sensei Ishikawa each bringing emotional depth and compelling subplots.
The narrative strikes a perfect balance between personal storytelling and epic historical drama, keeping you engaged from start to finish.[/b]

[h1]Fluid Combat and Playstyle Freedom[/h1]
[b]The combat in Ghost of Tsushima is nothing short of spectacular. Whether you prefer the honorable approach of facing enemies head-on with your katana or the stealthier path of the Ghost, the game offers fluid, satisfying mechanics for both.
The samurai duels are cinematic and thrilling, requiring precision and patience, while the stealth mechanics allow you to creatively outsmart your foes. Coupled with Jin’s customizable gear, skills, and stances, the gameplay remains fresh and exciting throughout the adventure.[/b]

[h1]Exploration: A Living Work of Art[/h1]
[b]Few games make exploration feel as rewarding as Ghost of Tsushima. Instead of overwhelming the player with cluttered HUDs or waypoints, the game uses natural elements like wind, birds, and foxes to guide you, creating an immersive experience that encourages curiosity.
From uncovering hidden shrines to composing haikus at scenic locations, every moment of exploration feels meaningful. The island of Tsushima itself is a character, and its beauty is a constant source of awe.[/b]

[h1]Director's Cut: Iki Island and Beyond[/h1]
[b]The Director's Cut adds the Iki Island expansion, which deepens the narrative and explores Jin’s past. Iki Island offers new gameplay mechanics, unique enemies, and stunning landscapes that complement the main game. It’s a fantastic addition that elevates an already outstanding experience.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Breathtaking visuals: Tsushima is one of the most beautiful open worlds ever created.
[*]Engaging combat: A perfect blend of samurai precision and stealth tactics.
[*]Immersive exploration: Natural guidance systems make exploration intuitive and rewarding.
[*]Rich narrative: A story that balances epic drama with personal stakes.
[*]Memorable characters: Supporting characters have depth and compelling arcs.
[*]Cultural authenticity: The game is a respectful and loving homage to Japanese culture and history.
[*]Director's Cut additions: Iki Island expansion offers more gameplay and narrative depth.
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Region blocking: Sadly, the game is region-blocked in many countries, making it inaccessible for a large portion of the fanbase. This is disappointing for a title of such high demand.
[*]Repetitive side activities: Some side quests and activities can feel a bit repetitive after a while.
[*]PC optimization quirks: While the game looks stunning, occasional performance hiccups on PC may disrupt immersion.
[/list]
[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]Ghost of Tsushima: Director's Cut is a masterpiece that excels in nearly every aspect, from its stunning visuals and immersive world to its engaging story and refined gameplay. It’s a love letter to Japanese culture and samurai cinema, offering an experience that feels both authentic and cinematic.

[{"review_text": "After around 100 hours in Blue Protocol, I have several thoughts that I feel need to be considered. This game is trying to strike a balance between popular MMOs like WoW, FF14, GW2, and ESO and, most notably, the Hoyoverse games. In some ways I do think that it succeeds in making a "Hoyoverse MMO", but in other ways, it has a lot to improve. 

Graphics Quality: 8/10. I think that the quality is good, though there are some instances even on high graphics where NPCs' teeth don't load in during cutscenes and such.

Sound/Music Quality: 7/10. Like the graphics, I think the quality is perfectly fine, though I do think that the generic battle theme is highly repetitive and could have been a bit less of something that I'd rather mute and play my own music over after several hours.

Story: 3/10. Way too fast-paced. I won't go into spoilers, but the story for this game moves at 100 miles an hour, to the point that most "important" character moments for the cast of NPCs fall flat because we've only known them for five minutes. I think that the developers focused way too hard on having a story that they could reasonably deliver during the opening hype for the game. If you didn't keep up the story with the small daily chunks they timegated off during the first two weeks of the game, I think a playthrough of the first arc could maybe be only 6 hours long, with you only being familiar with the main villain for 1.5-2 hours of that. The characters also, in medias res, act like major things have happened in-universe in the span of you doing a 2 minute puzzle. I genuinely wonder if there were plans for there to be like 30-50% more quest content and they just cut it for some reason or another. 

Localization: Tied to story. My GOD the locatlization in this game is ROUGH. Most of the localization is fine, if not a little awkward, but some of them are just atrocious. I think one of the text boxes I found with placeholder "Type Here" text just said "Please". PLEASE have someone go over the text before it gets shipped.

Quality Assurance: 6/10. Not great. I learned that apparently dialogue in the game is built in HTML since I noticed one of the lines of dialogue had a ? instead of a > to line break. Some sentences are missing spaces between words, it's not uncommon to randomly disconnect at times, and I noticed a sound bug in one of the high-level areas where the sound randomly starts and stops. This game REALLY needed another month or two of QA testing before release.

Class Design: 9/10. I actually really like the classes in this game and look forward to any future releases they may put out. While most of them have clear analogues to other MMOs (Frost Mage being WoW frost mage, Wind Knight being FFXIV Dragoon, etc.), I don't think that's a bad thing. They're aesthetics that people are familiar with and already like. Also, THIS GAME GIVES YOU TIPS AND USE CASES FOR YOUR INDIVIDUAL CLASS ABILITIES! How have the other big MMOs not done this yet? Massive props from me.

Fight Design: 9/10. The Master difficulty fights aren't out yet, but I've been pleasantly surprised with what I've seen so far in the "casual" content. AoE dodges, add phases, rot passes from FFXIV, and more. If the high-end combat was more accessible to the average player, I'd give this a 10/10. 

Economy: 2/10. Garbage-tier. There are approximately 8 different currencies to keep track of, each with their own weekly/monthly lockouts, and two of them are just "unbound/f2p" versions, with one being presented as the "general currency" and the other being the "freemium". Ironically, for the purposes that you need them for, the "general currency" feels like the most you want and is harder to obtain in meaningful amounts. In other MMOs, you'd just supplement this by using crafting and gathering to make things to sell and vendor mob drops. THERE IS NO VENDOR TO SELL SURPLUS MOB DROPS. YOU WILL BE STUCK WITH THEM FOREVER. I'll get into crafting and gathering next, but the game systems have essentially culminated in the classes needing massive amounts of the "general currency" to progress your character, but not having enough to actually do anything for it. This is probably my biggest complaint in the entire game aside from the crafting and gathering.

Crafting / Gathering: 1/10. This game has a stamina system for crafting and gathering. It's shared between all of the "life skills", so you have to pick and choose what you want to do every day. If you don't use stamina, you gain 1/40 of the exp you would have if you used stamina. This is honestly just not acceptable. Other MMOs have tried to do this and it hasn't really worked out. This needs to not be a thing. What happens if you have a raid group that needs food and "serums", but you're capped on your stamina or don't have enough to make what you need? You can see many of the positive reviews already; the game is fun, bouncy, and when things pop off, it's very satisfying.

There are several notable flaws in the title, though, that you will run into if you play for an extended period of grind. These criticisms aren't meant to say the game is bad or anything, far from it, but no game is perfect and there's plenty to improve upon. I really like this game and want to see it become the best it can be.

- You will hit a wall. The game will become fairly grindy after some hours of play. You expect this out of survivorslike titles usually, but the wall doesn't feel very good in this game.
- You will, very often, die within the first 3-5 minutes of a run just due to bad RNG. Even with the option to turn unwanted items off, and getting things like Skips and Banishes, these still /consume/ your current level-up opportunity which means no power boost, and needing more exp to make that up will ensure you rapidly fall behind and become too weak to kill enemies for exp in the first place.
- The lack of manual aiming hurts the game once you get used to the flow of gameplay. This is a common feature in many survivorslikes for a reason; relying entirely on the game to decide what to hit is good for accessibility, but can become a massive pain point. You can and will die to the targeting system targeting random enemies, and it stings a little when you know you could have gotten out of an encounter if your character would just target the dang enemy on your tail. While the recent "Nearest Enemy" tweak helps to alleviate this, it still isn't as good as manual aiming.
- I'm still in the Forest and Desert. I see there's a castle level in the trailer, but apparently it's unreleased in the full game. You might find yourself sick of the same scenery after a while; I don't like desert levels, so being stuck in the same two levels is getting tiring at my point in the game. I'm sure the game will get updated to have more levels though.

All my criticisms aside, this is a genuinely good game. I think with proper QOL updates and maybe some balance tweaks, it could be even better. If you don't mind the occasional frustration and are willing to take a lot of breaks to prevent the burnout from getting to you, this is absolutely worth a pick-up.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1758415044}, {"review_text": "The kind of game you can use to actively avoid engaging in critical real life responsibilities.

Rating: 11 / 10

Alright, forget your $70 AAA disappointments. Forget buggy messes, pointless stories, and games that demand a $2,000 graphics card.

MEGABONK IS HERE. AND IT IS A BANGER.

I went in expecting a cheap laugh. I've come out 30 hours later, sleep-deprived, seeing glowing XP gems when I close my eyes, and my life has been fundamentally changed. This game has a "Very Positive" rating on Steam for a reason: it's one of the most addictive substances legally sold.

What Even Is This?

Imagine Vampire Survivors. Now, give it a 3D engine, a physics-defying jump button, a hit of 1990s-era graphics, and a truly stupid sense of humor.

You are dumped into an arena. Hordes of enemies appear. You run. You jump. You slide. And you automatically "bonk" everything in sight. You grab loot, you level up, and you create builds so absurdly overpowered that the game engine starts to sweat.

The "Just One More Run" Addiction

This game's core loop is so perfectly tuned it should be studied by scientists.

    10:45 PM: "Whoa, I unlocked 'Monke' who can climb walls. And I just got an item that makes my axes orbit me. Okay, one more run to try this out."

    1:30 AM: "My build is insane. I have 70 items. I'm shooting 4,000 projectiles a second. The screen is just a solid wall of damage numbers. I am a god. I cannot be stopped."

    1:32 AM: A boss looks at me sideways. I die instantly.

    1:33 AM: "THAT WAS BULLS**T. JUST. ONE. MORE. RUN."

This is it. This is the whole game. It's perfect.

Why It's Better Than Everything Else

This game puts $100-million-dollar titles to shame.

    It Costs 10 Bucks: That's less than a single, ugly horse armor skin in Diablo. For that price, you get 20+ characters, 70+ items, and endless replayability.

    It Runs on a Toaster: The system requirements on Steam literally list "potato" for the processor and "no" for the graphics card. And it's still more fun than games that require a quantum computer.

    The Builds are STUPID (in a good way): This isn't about tiny 5% stat increases. This is about finding combinations that break the game. You can become an unkillable, screen-clearing demigod, and the game wants you to.

    No Bugs, Only Features: Unlike some games we've discussed, if you suddenly clip through the map and fly into the sky, it just feels like part of the "bonk" experience.

Conclusion:

This game is an absolute, 11/10, life-ruining masterpiece. It's pure, uncut, chaotic fun. It asks for nothing and gives you everything. Stop reading this. Go spend the 10 bucks. If you've played V:S, you know what this game is going  to be. Rolling loot, upgrading items, unlocks between runs. Seemingly the only novelty is the third dimension. Movement is fittingly complex. Bunnyhops to maintain momentum, sliding down cliffs, using enemy knockback as a boost. Its no Tribes- but it has the juice. All of these options can be invested in and built towards with lategame movement builds getting very fun and zoomy.

In this you get full trilogy, all DLCs included with enhanced graphics. And there is no series like this one, from the very beginning it really feels like it was meant to be a three part story.
For the whole series I must say it looks good, soundtrack fits what is going on the screen, story is amazing, the characters are very well written, sidequests are interesting and I enjoyed gameplay. And what is most important: YOUR CHOICES MATTERS! Feels good beeing able to shape your character your way.
As for the cons, I encountered few minor bugs and I don't like some changes they made across the titles.
It's kinda hard to talk about whole trilogy so I'd like to say few words about each part.

[h1] Mass Effect 1 [/h1]

As befits the first part, we are introduced to the main character and the world in which the action takes place. We get to know some of the lore and we meet our most important companions. This game is a great beginning to something really big that comes later. That's how series start should look like.
This game has the best RPG elements in whole series imo. There are plenty of abilities for each class and companions and there is a lot of equipement you can find. There are different type of armors, good amount of weapons and addons to them, you can also find different types of ammunition. Not only that, there are different levels of each item so you can find upgraded one with your character levels up. So it's important to look for a loot and bring on a mission someone who can hack/bypass locked containers or terminals.

Only issue I have to deal with is that EA launcher only allows for one instance, so make sure that you don't log back into EA on your PC while the game is running on your Deck, or vice versa.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1745652895}, {"review_text": "Mass Effect Legendary Edition is like digging up an old sci-fi trilogy you loved, polishing it to a cinematic shine, and realizing, “Oh yeah… this series still slaps harder than a krogan in a bad mood.”

You play as Commander Shepard, humanity’s most stressed-out space marine, juggling galaxy-wide extinction, alien politics, and the very real threat of punching reporters. Across three games, you build your squad, fly the Normandy, and make choices that range from “save the galaxy” to “hook up with your hot space coworker.”

The remaster modernizes textures, lighting, and character models, especially in ME1, which now feels more like a game and less like a nostalgia tax. Combat’s smoother, load times are faster, and yes, the Mako is still a clumsy space cow, but slightly less painful now.

What makes this trilogy timeless isn’t just the action—it’s the storytelling. Each companion feels like a real person: from Garrus and his calibrations to Tali’s tragic loyalty, to Wrex being Wrex. Your decisions carry across all three games, leading to dramatically different outcomes. You feel the weight of every choice, even if most of them involve space bureaucracy, interspecies romance, or telling someone to “stand down.”

Is it perfect? No. ME3’s ending still sparks debate, and some faces in the remaster still give off “mannequin in distress” energy. But taken as a whole, this is one of the greatest sci-fi sagas in gaming, now polished and bundled together like a care package from the Citadel.

I'm Commander Wingers and I recommend this game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1744825487}, {"review_text": "[h1] The brightest star in the action RPG firmament [/h1]

I’m ashamed to admit that I’m one of those people who never played Mass Effect before the Legendary Edition came out. When you’re young(er), other genres appeal more to your tastes, I was into RTSs, hack and slash games and the occasional RPG, so a story rich, choice driven, decision and consequence type of game, even with some RPG elements, didn’t seem like the kind of thing I wanted to immerse myself in or “waste time” with.
I’m no stranger to BioWare’s work, I’m a fan of Dragon Age, SWTOR, and even today I still play Neverwinter Nights, but for some reason Mass Effect never piqued my interest.

I was so wrong…

I can’t speak for the legacy versions of Mass Effect, but with the Legendary Edition (LE), all I can say is that this feels like the way to play it, or rather, the way it was meant to be experienced all along. The original trilogy released between 2007 and 2012, built fully on Unreal Engine 3 with all its capacities and limitations, and in 2021 LE arrived still running on UE3 but with a plethora of upgrades in lighting, textures, QoL, models, shaders, performance and so on.
So let’s get one thing straight, LE is, in the true sense of the word, a deep and thorough remaster, not a remake.

Regarding graphics, by today’s standards, even with the upgrades, it has aged, and the limitations of UE3 do show. Even so, it’s still a beautiful game to experience. Starting with Mass Effect 1, you notice that some mostly interior locations are almost identical to one another, the only thing that changes is the colour palette and textures, and the lack of asset variety is evident. This aspect is mitigated in Mass Effect 2, and further improved in Mass Effect 3.
But overall, even with these “downsides” and I put it in quotes because I don’t consider it one, but some people might, the visuals are enjoyable and credible, and the simple touch of using Mass Effect 3’s character models and details as the base for all three games was brilliant, visually consolidating the entire story and making the trilogy feel more cohesive.

This is, of course, a matter of opinion. Even with LE, it’s still a four year old upgrade of an eighteen year old game, but I would rather play something with dated or old school graphics that keeps me entertained and immersed than a game with nearly lifelike visuals that feels void of emotion and purpose. And nowadays there’s no shortage of titles that chase graphical fidelity but fail to connect or captivate the player.

In the sound department, the cast of voice actors is blessed with legends like Lance Henriksen, Keith David, Steve Blum, Seth Green and Raphael Sbarge, among many others, and all of them deliver performances that bring characters to life with such feeling, gravitas and emotion that very few games possess.
As for the soundtrack, Sam Hulick and Jack Wall did an incredible job dressing the galaxy with music that ranges from ethereal and ambient while exploring to synth and hard techno when wandering around places like Afterlife or Purgatory, and even some truly epic scores for when you do epic things. No spoilers.

Gameplay wise, I often feel like I’m playing three completely different games from ME1 to ME3. You see concepts evolving, features being added or removed, systems being streamlined. For example, in ME1 you had to manage inventory and equip companions one by one through lockers, something later improved in ME2 and ME3 where you equip as needed right before missions. The only management becomes choosing which upgrades to use and which armour pieces look best on your Shepard.
Another thing is movement and motion. From ME1 to ME3, you will notice a lot of differences, especially during firefights. Duck, cover, flank, you’ll need all of that.
Oh, and starting from ME2, don’t bother looking for a walk toggle. There isn’t one.

One of the most memorable aspects of Mass Effect is the depth and richness of its universe, the races, cultures, values, beliefs and traditions. From some of these races come your companions, characters larger than life with their own stories and fears that you uncover along the way. The narrative you find yourself in is intricate, full of twists and revelations, and your companions grow with you. No doubt you’ll feel closer to some characters than others, but trust me, take the time to know them all. You’ll be amazed by the complexity and roundness of their personalities and stories.

Now for some advice: ME1 > Liara and ME2 and ME3 > Tali.

To finish this review, and to sum up my shame, I’m reviewing this jewel of a trilogy in 2025, meaning I’m 18 years late. But I genuinely feel this deserves a review, even a late one, for all the laughs, tears, wholesome moments, intricate narrative, memorable characters and the masterpiece of a story it gave me.
If I could go back in time and meet my younger self, I’d kick him so hard for skipping this that he’d still feel it today. No matter what I write, I’ll never do justice to the masterpiece this trilogy is. You have to play it to feel it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1763419678}, {"review_text": "I defeated the reapers, I punched the reaper king, there was no little ghost boy, that was a dream.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1757451646}, {"review_text": "ME1: The game is and feels dated, but in a retro, enjoyable way where it’s not a broken mess, but an actual enjoyable game. It’s got some decent rudimentary gameplay, and the guns felt kind of samey, with the biggest difference being stat checking between them, making for a rather boring selection. The more unique ammo system that relies upon a heat meter instead of having to grovel to pick up ammo felt nice and refreshing, and I was sad to see it go in later versions of the game, where in turn they overload you with ammo laying around to the point you might as well have an unlimited amount.

The story feels like it’s solid and self-contained, and even if you were to only play ME1, you’d have a well-rounded story experience.

Main story missions are good and paced well, but there is not much side content, and the planet exploration feels kind of hollow and didn’t appeal to me much.

Overall, a solid game that holds up surprisingly well and, in its simplicity, can be very enjoyable. 

ME2: Simply speaking, ME2 is the best in the series, hands down. It expands upon ME1’s story brilliantly. It has great character development, where ME1 had something left to be desired, a stronger narrative, and decisions to be made that feel more impacting and meaningful. Side missions actually felt somewhat worth doing.

The guns feel more distinct and less like a stat sheet, though I lament the upgrade system, which feels shallow and cumbersome, especially the resource collection from planetary probing. I also do not prefer the use of ammo in comparison to ME1, due to it not egging you on to actually use your full armory like the previous system, but I found it not to be a hindrance all in all.

The new and reworked ship feels much more lived in, as you talk to the characters within and unlock all the areas inside it. The graphics for the game actually look remarkable and, at some points, looked very modern, to the point it made it feel like remaking it really boosted it to modern standards. The levels themselves hold up to this standard, making me enjoy the care put in.

Honestly, definitely worth it and my favourite game in the trilogy.

ME3: Mass Effect 3 follows up on Mass Effect 2 by really hammering down on the choices you made, making you face the consequences and the decisions that come with them, once again making for an enjoyable and gripping plot. There is less time spent bonding with characters, and not a lot of extra depth is achieved. The new characters that are introduced honestly feel like filler.

The main story missions are great, but I felt there was a definite lack of sideline stories, and of the ones I did encounter, one of them felt terribly out of pace with the story and is foisted upon you and unskippable, making for some annoyance.

The guns for the game feel good, and it feels worthwhile switching them out for different enemies or damage types, but I disliked the over-availability of ammo to the point of it littering every nook and cranny. The collection method for them and the modifiers feels fun, having them strewn throughout the levels, making it rewarding to explore more and making you pay more attention to the nicely detailed levels.

I did, however, find the armour options for the game lacking and would have liked to see more.

ME3 has a great story and rounds off the series nicely. It would have been far better with a little more content and better controls, but it just falls slightly short of great.

Following the trend of multiplayer task-based horror games, Backrooms: Escape Together has you play as a scientist exploring the depths of the Backrooms, and attempting to escape from them while avoiding the horrors that exist within. 

With numerous levels, and multiple ways to escape, not to mention decent graphics and good sound design, BET is more than than the sum of it's parts. 

It's punishing, but the difficulty spikes from level to level seem a little unpredictable, and I think that's almost the point - the game structures itself as a hellscape where attempting to predict what happens next is - even if you're familiar with Backrooms lore, a futile endeavour. 

I played with two people across two playthroughs, one which lasted barely fifteen minutes, one which lasted roughly 3 hours. With my other friend, we surged through it and realized how addictive, albeit challenging the game was. Every environment came to life as soon as the monsters came into view, and there was still that tension when there were seemingly empty levels.

I recommend the game only in the context of its €13 price. To be honest, I’m also disappointed—if the price were higher, I wouldn’t recommend it. That might sound controversial, but hear me out (Minor spoilers below).

EDIT: I will play more to discover everything. I won't remove anything from the initial review for now, just add here some updates:
- I was super wrong about the basement, I found 2 extra stuff down there, it's worth to discover it! :)

A bit of context:
I played the demo back then, and in the full game I’ve done one complete playthrough (unlocked a single ending). I’ll play more to unlock other endings and see if there are hidden major features I’ve missed. I didn't encountered any bugs, especially gamebreaking ones. Patches may also improve things over time. This review is just my subjective opinion—I could be wrong on some details, so feel free to correct me. 

Price and Value:
This is a small indie game priced at €13, and I think that’s fair—even though I criticize it a lot. Compared to a movie ticket, you get similar value: 1–2 hours per playthrough, and more if you chase multiple endings or want to meet every character. Indie games are about innovation and unique ideas, and I respect the devs for trying something different. I’m happy to support projects like this, even if the execution isn’t perfect.

The Positives:
- Legendary art style. Weird in the best way—unique and memorable.
- Excellent soundtrack. Fits the visuals perfectly and adds to the unsettling atmosphere (Please release it individually).
- Fantastic premise. An apocalyptic event, humanlike “visitors,” and paranoia-driven decisions reminiscent of The Thing.
- Immersive storytelling. News on TV, radio interviews, and glimpses through the window all make the world feel grounded and personal.
- The checking system is engaging. You can examine people’s eyes, ears, hands, armpits, etc. No single clue is fully reliable, so you’re encouraged to check multiple traits. Limited action points add tension—you can’t fully check everyone in a single day, so choices matter. I especially enjoyed the “grey area” moments—like when someone claimed they hadn’t slept well, their eyes were red, and they insisted it was just exhaustion. Do you believe them or not? Those decisions made the paranoia real.

The Saving System:
Many people complained about saving, and I understand why. Getting softlocked or losing progress after a crash is frustrating. The system could definitely be better.
That said, a full run is only 1–2 hours. You can buy kombucha for extra saves, and personally I didn’t need more than that. Still, it’s fair to say sometimes real life happens and you need to quit unexpectedly, so more flexible saving would be a nice quality-of-life improvement.

My personal problems:
Managing people feels shallow. You can’t stay alone (otherwise a serial killer gets you), but the feds also randomly take people away. This constant shuffling means you can’t build real bonds with characters.
For example, I tried to keep the neighbor’s little girl safe, but a hazmat-suited guy took her away at random. That made it feel like individuals didn’t really matter, and the game devolved into a half-baked management system where you just keep somebody around, not somebody you care about or somebody that being useful somehow.
Even when people stick around, conversation options dry up quickly. They rarely affect each other beyond an occasional request to kick someone out. So, generally speaking, once you’re sure someone is human and have talked with them a few times, there’s literally nothing else you can do with them. That’s somewhat understandable given the constant turnover, but it’s still disappointing.

Missed Opportunities:
I expected either deeper story/interaction or stronger management mechanics. Some ideas that could have added depth:
- special in-house events
- daily tasks for survivors
- cleaning up dead bodies or burning them to avoid infections or other issues like people being mad about the smell, etc.
- more usable items
- more stuff to interact with, similiar to the phone, TV, radio
- more converstation options
- a rapport/relationship system
- sorting out resources like food/water/etc
- roommate compatibility (or conflict)
- voting on potential decisions
- sidequests or minigames with risks/rewards
- more options to use the phone, TV, radio, would be cool to interact more with other people from different places, sharing information, perhaps trading stuff with them, etc.
- betrayal, conflicts, or alliances
- It would have also been interesting if people could turn on each other—if a human disliked someone, they might actually kill others. Then you could investigate the dead body and question others to figure out who the culprit was, and whether they were human or a visitor.

Please keep in mind that these are mainly just vague ideas, but any of these, even partially would have added more depth.

Beyond that, several teased elements go nowhere:
- In the demo, the basement was not an option. The trailer teased it, so I expected new mechanics or secrets. In the full game, the basement is basically useless gameplay-wise. Why?
Same for household items. You can interact with the curtain in your room, the cross on the wall, or the storage box (“open if you miss me” from your father)… but they don’t really lead anywhere. 
Beers exist, but drinking them just wastes the action points. Why not use them alternatively to build rapport, unlock hidden dialogue, or test how visitors react to alcohol? Especially when at least one of my guests mentioned it that he likes beer and I should share some with him?

In my personal opinion there are so many missed opportunities for deeper lore, mechanics, and interactions. One of the other reviewer said it in a kinda fitting way, I quote: "The game is presented as a puzzle, but it's just slots."
At the same time, I want to note that this is a criticism, but not in a malicious way. Considering the size of the development team and their budget, I understand that some of these ideas may have been beyond what was realistically achievable.

Final words:
But at the end of the day, this is just my personal take. Let’s be real—it’s essentially a somewhat interactive visual novel for €13–15. For that price, it’s a fair value. So yes, I do recommend it—just go in with tempered expectations. It’s not a bad game at all; it simply had the potential to be much more, and that’s where my disappointment comes from. I remember seeing demos of it a year ago and being very interested in it. That said, there are some significant issues that prevent this game from being great. 

- The gameplay loop lies in the fact that there are only a handful of characters that are always human and always visitors. This is great because you can't just solve who is who and carry that knowledge across playthroughs. The problem is that the dialogue tree at the door is static no matter if they are visitor or human. This makes pulling decisions based on dialogue entirely arbitrary and removes player agency. The fix is to include 3 responses that hint at being human, and 3 responses that hint at being visitor at the very end of the dialogue tree. By putting it at the end you prevent players from being shocked at completely different options and depending on where you place the clue players may not even access it every time. 

- If adding that much content is too much, we should also be given maybe 2 energy at night so we can check for signs before people come through the door. 

- Sometimes the balance can be a bit wonky. For example, I've had multiple playthroughs where I had 4 people at the end of a night, one dies during the day, I know which is the visitor and shoot them, then that night the first knock is FEMA taking two people away followed by The Intruder which leads to an automatic loss. There are some mitigating factors such as being able to feed the cat to prevent a murder, but it also seems like the cat will disappear during the day randomly. 

- I think you can really enrich the player experience by offering unlockable roles or professions for your main character that give you one special ability. I won’t lie: the first impression of this game is magnificent. The eerie atmosphere, the grotesque character designs, and the mysterious story instantly draw you in. It’s an intense and memorable experience… the first time you play it. Unfortunately, after that initial run, everything falls apart.

-Zero Replay Value-
The game tries to sell the idea that each playthrough is different because the visitors at your door each night are random. But in reality, it’s always the same NPCs, with the exact same lines and behaviors. Some will always be human, some will always be visitors, and some can be either one or the other without any clear indication. This turns every replay into a repetitive grind of skipping through already-seen dialogue that adds nothing new.

On top of that, key events always happen on the same nights. This means “replayability” quickly becomes nothing more than skipping through text until you reach the same moments you’ve already experienced.

-RNG Over Design-
The game relies almost entirely on luck. The AFAE agent, who appears on certain nights, takes away an NPC completely at random—even the one whose storyline you were following. This forces you to restart and replay several times, hoping luck is on your side so you can actually finish that character’s arc.

The visitors themselves always have the same dialogue and appearances. They can be “good” or “bad” at random, but the game gives you no clues to figure this out. As a result, your choices are meaningless. Worse yet, visitors can never kill you. They only kill other NPCs, and this has zero impact on the narrative. Nobody reacts—not the other NPCs, not your character. This makes the game a constant cycle of skipping days until some specific event happens, since what goes on in your house doesn’t really matter at any point in the game.

-Endings That Don’t Matter-
The game offers multiple endings, but most of them don’t actually depend on how you play. Two endings are tied to “completing” all the nights, and the only factor is how many humans or visitors are left at the end. The rest are tied to specific NPCs showing up randomly, which means you may have to replay several times just to see them.

Instead of encouraging strategy or meaningful choices, the game devolves into a clicker where you skip repeated dialogue night after night, waiting for RNG to let you see something new.

-Bugs and Technical Issues-
As if the design flaws weren’t enough, the game is riddled with bugs. In my experience, loading a save often broke the game: black screens, endings not triggering despite meeting all requirements, or the door viewer reticle permanently stuck on screen. These technical issues make an already frustrating game even worse.

-Conclusion-
In the end, this is a game with a brilliant start, capable of delivering 1–2 hours of tense, atmospheric gameplay. But after that, it turns into a repetitive, luck-based mess plagued with technical problems.

The potential was there: with a tighter, single-playthrough narrative, more complex characters, and better-structured events, it could have been an unforgettable game. But in its current state, it’s not worth the $15 price tag. This is a game with a fantastic first impression… and nothing more.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 18, "timestamp_created": 1758713721}, {"review_text": ""No, I'm not a human" is one of the most interesting games I have ever played in my life. I've never watched so many YouTube videos about a game's lore. I want to know everything about it.
The first playthrough is an experience everyone should have. You learn about people's stories, you are scared of the half naked visitor, you question whether or not you can trust FEMA and you don't know what the cat is for and what’s going on. Eventually, you achieve one of the game's many endings, each of which requires different approaches and choices which I love.

However the main problem of this game is the gameplay.
Don't get me wrong: I love this game. As I mentioned, I love its lore and story, I want to discover the truth about the visitors and I've followed the game since the demo came out and I still watch videos nowadays. I still recommend that everyone buy and play it at least once.
But after the first playthrough the game loses all of its mystery and horror. You can speedrun every dialogue interaction because guests repeat the same text regardless of whether they are human or a visitor. You end up rushing or avoiding the game mechanics because you know how the game works. I want to offer few suggestions to the developers, hoping they read my useless review xD.

1) While adding more guests for the upcoming update is fine, all guests should have more dialogue options depending on their true identity. It would be more interesting if another game challenge was figuring out who is who based on contradictions and lies in their conversation. Imagine realizing a guest is a visitor because they accidentally contradict something they said, allowing us to not be forced to physically check them for signs and use more our head. This could be maybe the game hard difficulty if it will ever be done.

2) To increase replayability and make the game interesting again, the game needs two new gamemodes. The first one is a fully randomised run. Imagine if FEMA, the half naked visitor and the vigilante come to the house randomly. This would create a constant sense of worry for the amount of guests you have and you have to make sure you don’t have any signs either. Also any guest could be a visitor, forcing us to engage with the game mechanics every time unlike in the main story where we all know now who is always a human or a visitor. Another gamemode could be an endless / survival one. It would work similarly to the Randomizer one but would simply not end and we could have leaderboards for people surviving most days. While the current game is random in few aspects, these modes would fix the main problem of knowing what happens every time after the first playthrough.

3) If a sequel is made, or in a major future update, please consider adding a guest conflict mechanic. Right now, guests only have problems with others only if another guest is in their designated spot. But what if they start fighting each other over food / resources or for any other reason? What if even the human guests begin killing each other due to their conflict or because they think someone is a visitor? This would make the player worry more about who they are housing and turn the atmosphere of the game even more tense.

4) There are many videos of people who have found all the ways to identify a visitor (it works 100%). While this is amazing for achievement hunters like me, for a better gameplay for everyone, which I care about, I suggest adding more randomized elements that complicate the identification process and make it truly random each time. This would prevent players from being able to "cheat", forcing us to use our head and guts rather than outside knowledge even though we could simply ignore these videos and play the game normally unless you have an amazing memory.

5) The cat feeding mechanic is too strong. Being able to get two cans of food and being able to order more every three days means you can’t "protect" your guests from any visitor for just 1 day. We should get only one can of food or be unable to order the same thing twice in a row. Or maybe introduce a currency system which does not allow us to buy whatever we want everytime?

In conclusion, the first playthrough is amazing and a must experience, but that's where the enjoyment ended for me and many other players. Once you play the game once, the next playthroughs become repetitive. I can see many players dropping the game unless they are aiming for achievements or all endings. I probably forgot some suggestions, but the five listed earlier are the most important for improving the gameplay in my opinion.
Can't wait to see what comes next. Good job, developers!

I miss him..", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 17, "timestamp_created": 1759446706}, {"review_text": "I wanted to like this game, but the best way I can describe it is missed opportunity.

This game got amazing sales due to amazing demo, as the final version is worse than the demo. It became a glorified minesweeper game with very specific paths for weird endings and a lot of side content that has nothing to do with the supposedly main theme of the game.

The game has a very interesting premise: people show up to your door and you need to decide whether to let them in or not. Some are Humans, some are Visitors, and you need to figure out which is which.

The game takes place in 14 days with a day & night cycle. During the day you investigate guests to see who is Visitor and who is not. During the Night people come at the door and you decide who to take in or not. It's a game about distrust and paranoia. Sounds interesting? unfortunately that's where the interesting part stops.

You would normally expect to have some text clues, stories don't fit, kind of signs that they are visitors. Instead, all visitors are RNG with the only difference being different symptoms when examinated. You can skip 100% of the chat and would make 0% difference in determining who is visitor or not. It's just a mini-game of [i]"check the teeths, hands, eyes"[/i].

The developers could have expanded this concept. Instead, they did not. That's all there is to the main part of the game.

Afterwards, they only added [i]"side quests"[/i]. You have a radio for extra information, you can call to different numbers for extra information and items. There is a lady with a cat and the cat will be very important later, there is a vigilante that if you show even 1 visitor sign he will shoot you, there is a cult. The developers are doing everything in their power to move the game from its original premise.

They completely ruined it gameplay-wise.

Lore-wise, the Visitors and people of the world are not all that interesting. Once you read the 1 story a person has to tell that's it. And as I said previously you can ignore the conversation with them as Human/Visitor is pure RNG, their story will be the same.

Visitors are resources to manage, not threats. Even if you get a Visitor in your house, you can kill him with a shotgun and that's it. But the devs aren't going to bother with fleshing out the base game, they will probably add another ending with a very weird path with a mushroom man. Oh wait, they did.

Here is how to play: let people in randomly, check for signs, kill them if visitor, take a weird path if you want a weird ending. That's it. It's a shallow game. They add things like phone adding more narrative to the game to distract players from the shallowness of the main dish. In the same way you would put a lot of spices on a bad meat to cover up the fact the meat itself is bad.

There are also counter-intuitive stuffs in the game:
- Guests say the same lines of dialogue regardless whether they are visitor or human. There is no way to catch someone lying or contradicting himself and because of that they are a visitor.
- Cannot check guests for visitor signs at the door. Even as dialogue options.
- During the day you can: TV, Radio, Phone, Feed Cat, Guests. All aside from Guests are meaningless distractions that you must take into account only if you want one of the weird endings.
- Once you check a visitor for signs, you can either (1) listen to their excuse (2) shoot them. But you cannot listen to their excuse and then shoot them because it's not convincing. [i](listening to the excuse is useless anyway as the dialogue is the same regardless whether they are visitors or humans)[/i]
- Visitors/Humans just stand there during the day, there is no making food or whatever, you don't make food, they don't make food, no interaction or urgency or paranoia beyond playing a glorified Minesweeper game.
- The radio is a bit of an annoying feature where you look for signal, especially on repeat playthroughs.
- The phone is basically tons of lore + ForRest where you can order items every other day.
- Energy, the way you get/lose energy is dumb. You begin with 2 Energy, then you gain 1 or lose 1 depending whether you let in a human or visitor. The quote unquote "logic" is that you sleep better at night without visitors in the house, but this logic forgot that you won't know who the visitors are and the whole point of the game is to find out. At the same time, you have no way of knowing who is human/visitor from the door, so it's literally a coin toss.

In conclusion, this full version doesn't deliver on the demo's promising concept, nor does it meaningfully expand the ways you can interact with characters. The only thing added was extra noise mechanics. The endings added in the full game also disappoint, offering little aside from vague vibes.

Risk of Rain 2's primary verbs are the same as its predecessor: search and fight. You search for items that make you better at searching and fighting, search for the teleporter to proceed, and fight enemies to remove threats and make money. What spices this up is how enemies power scale over time, so you're incentivized to search and fight quickly as to not let the enemies outscale you in offense and defense. With this basic setup there's an elegant interplay between the systems: movement items make you better at searching and evading damage; damage items make you kill faster; defense items mean you have less downtime in combat. There's also utility items that help you search or make money. You have to find a balance between these priorities. Gaining this understanding of how the game works, and then finding your ideal balance, is part of the game's fun.

On every level there are three phases of gameplay: 1. Fight and search for items and the teleporter, 2. Fight the boss and charge the teleporter, and 3. The first phase challenges you to fight and search simultaneously, and make a call on when to start the teleporter based on your incomplete information about what items you might buy and your confidence in the boss fight. If you activate early, you risk being underpowered for the boss; if you do it late, you might gain more money than you can spend on the map, meaning the excess money (i.e. time spent) was wasted. The second phase is a pure combat test, and the third is mostly a test of your searching ability. These phases generally provide moderate, high, and low levels of tension respectively, giving the game a good flow.

You know why? Because Souls games are all about having a steep learning curve. The insane difficulty is meant to challenge you. There is absolutely no hand-holding, no quest markers, nothing. You get a tutorial on how to do basic things then you get thrown into the frying pan. This game is not easy, Dark Souls became its own genre for a reason. You WILL die, hundreds of times. You will want to quit. You will be frustrated with the mechanics, and the combat, and you will feel like quitting. But you will feel the need to come back, to complete it, to finally beat that ONE annoying boss. And after 50, 100, or even 1000 failed attempts you will finally beat it, and the feeling of accomplishment will be like nothing you've ever experienced. Because you earned it, you took your time, you trained, you practiced your moves, and in the end you won. You can respawn an infinite number of times, the only way you can lose is if you give up.
And that's the poetic beauty of Dark Souls. You decide when you lose. You decide how hard you're going to make it for yourself. Not with a regular difficulty slider, but through hard work, dedication, and summoning a bunch of Sunbros who are better fighters than you are to beat up the big mean hard bosses for you.

Good luck for everyone who find it interesting.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1762161886}, {"review_text": "The Fire Keeper reacts to your gestures. 10/10 and best FromSoftware game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1760514689}, {"review_text": "This game stands as the grand finale of FromSoftware’s legendary trilogy, a melancholic swan song that perfectly encapsulates the series’ themes of decay, futility, and fleeting embers of hope. It is, in many ways, a love letter to long-time fans, tying together lore threads that have dangled since the original Dark Souls. However, while the narrative and atmosphere reach impressive heights, the game’s approach to build variety feels like a step back, especially when compared to the sprawling arsenal of Dark Souls 2.
On a technical and artistic level, Dark Souls 3 is a masterclass in world design. Lothric’s interconnected, ruined beauty is a haunting sight, echoing the best of the first game’s level design philosophy while improving upon it with smoother traversal and verticality. The lore is rich, weaving in references to past games in a way that feels reverent rather than redundant. Gwyn’s legacy, the Undead Curse, and the ever-repeating cycle of fire and dark all find resolution here, bringing a sense of finality that Dark Souls 2 never fully embraced.
However, where Dark Souls 3 falters is in its gameplay variety. Compared to the sheer level of options in Dark Souls 2, which boasted an almost overwhelming number of weapons and builds, Dark Souls 3 feels streamlined to the point of limitation. The removal of power stance mechanics, the reduced dual-wielding options, and the emphasis on a faster-paced, aggressive combat style cater more to a specific meta rather than the ‘choose your own playstyle’ philosophy that defined the series. While the introduction of Weapon Arts offers some variety, they often feel underwhelming compared to the adaptability and unique movesets from previous entries.
Magic builds also suffer from this streamlining. The separation of FP from individual spell casts allows for more sustained magic use, but the nerfs to spell damage and the overall slower casting times make them feel underpowered, especially in PvP. Meanwhile, faith builds—once a cornerstone of versatility—are left with little to stand on outside of buffs and healing.
Despite these limitations, Dark Souls 3 still provides an immensely satisfying challenge. The boss fights, from the relentless Nameless King to the poetic tragedy of the Soul of Cinder, rank among the best in the series. The combat is more fluid than ever, encouraging a mix of aggression and careful stamina management. While the game may not offer the sheer experimental sandbox that Dark Souls 2 did, it refines what it does have to near perfection.
Ultimately, Dark Souls 3 is a worthy send-off for the series, closing the loop in a way that respects its past while pushing forward into a bleak yet beautiful unknown. It may not offer the same level of build variety as its predecessor, but as a final journey through the dying embers of this world, it remains unforgettable.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1743734921}, {"review_text": "What a game! Also, better with friends too", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1758533370}, {"review_text": "Warhammer: Vermintide 2 is a brutal, fast-paced, and highly satisfying co-op experience. As someone who loves both action and the Warhammer universe, this game hits all the right notes. It combines intense combat, a rich fantasy setting, and cooperative gameplay in a way that keeps you coming back for more.

The game's combat is visceral and relentless. Whether you’re cleaving through hordes of Skaven or facing off against the Chaos warriors, each swing of your weapon feels impactful. The weight of each character’s unique playstyle—from the tanky dwarf with his powerful hammer to the agile elf with her bow—is felt in every fight, and there’s a real sense of progression as you level up and unlock new abilities. The satisfaction of chaining kills and coordinating with your teammates in the heat of battle is unmatched.

The setting, of course, is fantastic for fans of Warhammer. The grimdark world is beautifully realized, and the environments are both detailed and atmospheric. You’ll traverse through ruins, forests, and desolate villages, all while facing waves of enemies in a truly immersive experience. The soundtrack adds to the intensity, creating a sense of urgency during combat and providing a fitting backdrop for the game’s dark tone.

What sets Vermintide 2 apart is its emphasis on teamwork. This isn’t a game you can breeze through alone—cooperation is key. Whether you’re coordinating attacks, defending an objective, or reviving fallen teammates, the success of your mission relies on the collective effort. It’s that sense of camaraderie that makes Vermintide 2 stand out in the crowded co-op genre.

The game does have a few issues, though. The difficulty can feel punishing at times, especially when facing the harder challenges. It can be frustrating to get wiped out by a single wave of enemies or to fail an objective just because of one mistake. Also, while the loot system and progression are solid, there’s a bit of grind required to get the best gear.

Overall, Warhammer: Vermintide 2 delivers an incredible cooperative action experience with a real sense of reward. If you enjoy intense combat, tactical gameplay, and teaming up with friends to fight back a relentless horde, this is a must-play. It’s a chaotic, thrilling ride through the Warhammer universe that leaves you wanting more.

For whatever reason, Fatshark decided to add some stuff like Versus mode (which for sure can be fun for some ppl) and therefore broke the game to a level where I decided to write this review after over 1150 hours.

The base game (co-op mode) is what its about, which a lot of veterans (and also new players) play since years due to its challenges, varied encounters, great heroes (and careers), the atmosphere and of course the style of a great Warhammer game.

But as said earlier, whatever they changed ruined the game experience for me and prbly others as well due to feedback i read in the chat of game sessions. As an example I met a guy a few days back which came back after over a year to the game. And i typed how wonky the game became because of some stupid sh** that happened (more following) and he just said: "right?" so that he wondered the same what it became.

The desync and behaviour of some attacks and foes have became so ridiculous, that you just can make jokes or memes of it. Enemies rubber banding around corners, Monsters throw you out of the map (through terrain), stuff that you usually really know how to do (attack patterns, dodges and what so ever) became feel random and wonky.
Beside of the disaster of the new "Anti Cheat" they integrated because of Versus which caused just more problems like random connection losses, ages for ppl to join games, crashes, mod incompatibility and so on.
Just a side note, the player base is still looks the same since years, no difference if Versus mode or not.
Also to mention, that widely reported bugs which are in the base game for years don't get fixed...

I mean, if the game would become harder or whatsoever, that would be fine. But all the mentioned things make it just frustrating to continue play the game on higher difficulties.
If you die or whole team wipes because of mistakes, that's fine. We almost always make fun of it and easy can admit when mistakes happen. But when a party wipes because of the mentioned behaviour, it just makes you want to uninstall the game honestly and wait until Fatshark sorts their things.

Due to the way they work (like over a year for a weapon pack) or the Darktide situation, where stuff still not in the game since launch (around 3 years) which was promised, I don't have much hope.

It is just sad that they broke a game which worked and was fun as mentioned and had a solid player base over almost 7 years.
So yea, that was what ruined it for me after 1150 hours.

This is a co-op action game with a focus on first-person melee. It shares Left 4 Dead's structure but trades gunplay for finely-tuned melee combat. Each of the five characters has three careers (with more available via DLC), offering unique playstyles and weapons. The balance between ranged and melee, plus the depth of its dodging, blocking, and crowd control mechanics, keeps combat engaging and skill-based.

[h1] Content & Progression [/h1]

The base game includes a solid selection of maps, enemy types, and loot. Some maps and careers are locked behind DLC, but you can play DLC maps if the host owns them. The loot system revolves around increasing your power level, with weapon traits offering gameplay variety rather than raw upgrades. Unlocking higher difficulties and refining builds gives meaningful progression without forcing a meta.

[h1] Atmosphere & Design [/h1]

Levels are well-designed, with excellent environmental storytelling and hidden collectibles. Characters are well-voiced, and their banter adds depth without overstaying its welcome. The Warhammer setting is fully embraced, and the tone is consistent—grim but often darkly humorous.

[h1] Community & Teamplay [/h1]

Vermintide thrives on teamwork. Most players are helpful and cooperative, but solo queuing does occasionally bring the typical rush-ahead-and-blame-everyone type. The game rewards team play over lone-wolf behavior, especially on higher difficulties. Public lobbies are usually reliable, and the matchmaking is fast.

[h1] Support & Longevity [/h1]

The core gameplay remains strong years after launch. Content releases are slow and inconsistent. Some seasonal content is time-locked unnecessarily. Still, the few major updates that do land often improve or expand the game in meaningful ways. Cosmetics have taken the front seat for monetization, while major new features are rare.

[h1] Final Verdict [/h1]

If the combat clicks with you, there’s a lot to enjoy here. It’s deep, satisfying, and distinct in a genre full of shallow co-op shooters. While long-term support is uneven, the existing content offers more than enough to justify the experience—especially with friends.

—The Ember Archives

If you're looking for a more in-depth review then check out other reviews, since this is mainly my personal opinion, but a quick comparison for the game would be: think L4D2, but more dense hordes and way more melee oriented. If you didn't like the melee in L4D2, don't worry - L4D2's melee doesn't feel nearly as good Vermintide 2's, and Vermintide's has a lot of depth to it between different weapons, their weapon combos, their special attacks, etc.

The game can be frustrating at the start. Enemies always seem to find a way to sneak up behind you and hit you, and it feels like it's just that over and over. Not only that, some specials can be really annoying. Hookrats? Oh, you mean the guys that hook you from a mile away, and from what feels like behind walls? (Alright, they really do hook you from behind walls sometimes)

As you play the game more, you'll gain situational awareness. Hordes become less threatening, you learn to constantly be checking behind you for the stragglers that try and sneak up behind you, and you really start to get a feel for the game. Things that were threatening at the start of the game become fun to deal with. 

That hookrat I mentioned before? Now you know to listen for the little jingle (if you'll call it that) of the skulls and try and keep track of where it is. It's going to be trying to get closer to either you or your teammates, and you learn to prepare for it. You learn the timings for when they throw out their hook and when to dodge it, and it eventually becomes second nature.

Still having trouble with the game? Check out some Steam guides written by members of the community. There are players that write extremely detailed and helpful guides that you can use to improve. Chances are you'll learn something from reading them. Did you know medkits cleanse not only your wound, but also another player's wound? I only learned that after 150+ hours of playing the game. Woops.

Fatshark has also recently improved on the progression system to make it less annoying/grindy, and while it's definitely not perfect it is still improving. I imagine they'll eventually tweak it to a point where people don't have many complaints, even if it takes them a bit of time.

Is the price too steep for you? Add the game to your wishlist and wait. Fatshark very frequently put the game on sale, and for very significant discounts. At the time of writing the game is currently on sale for $2.99 USD. If you're worried about why the price is so low, no - it's not because they rake you over the coals with microtransactions or DLC. The base game itself is enough to play and enjoy for many, many hours.

If you starting enjoying the game and feel like grabbing some DLC - which often goes on sale as well - awesome. You can pick up some extra campaigns (sets of new maps), but what's better is the fact that only the host has to have the DLC for you to play those new maps. You could buy the DLC and share it with your friends, or your friend can buy the DLC and share it with you. Something to keep in mind with this is that while you can share the maps with your friends, they CANNOT use or obtain the weapons from the DLC to use with their careers.

One notoriously crappy thing that Fatshark did is lock the Cataclysm difficulty behind a DLC. I wasn't around when the DLC initially dropped, but I've heard many players that were around when it was released complain about it. Poor balancing with the Beastmen, mediocre and now-dead game mode (Weaves), and only one map that was also overtuned. 

They've improved on this. They are in the process of changing the game to allow the host to share the Cataclysm difficulty with others, similar to how they have it set up with other DLC, provided they have the prerequisites to play Cataclysm (killed all the Lords on Legend). The Beastmen are, without a doubt, the most annoying faction by far, but they're also in a lot more tolerable of a state than what they were in at release. They've also nerfed Dark Omens (the new map), and made it less overwhelming for players.

There's a lot more to cover about Vermintide 2 (Chaos Wastes, etc.), but I'll leave that to others that are better at detailing the game and writing about it than I am.

To call Dark Souls merely a game is a disservice. It is an experience, an ordeal, and for many, an awakening. Playing Dark Souls Remastered is not just about rekindling a classic—it is about revisiting the foundation of a trilogy that fundamentally changed how I interpret storytelling in video games. It is a reminder that not all tales need to be told in upfront exposition, nor should every journey be neatly plotted by quest markers. In an era where games like Skyrim sought to guide the player's hand, Dark Souls did the opposite: it let us stumble, fall, and carve our own meaning from the abyss.

 [h2]A World Told in Whispers, Not Shouts [/h2]
What makes Dark Souls so profound is its refusal to speak too loudly. Lordran is a land of hushed myths, decaying grandeur, and cryptic figures who offer guidance just as often as they deceive. Its story is not delivered through cutscenes or a journal of dictated objectives but through ruins, item descriptions, and the silent suffering of those who still cling to existence. There is no exposition-laden Jarl to welcome you, no noble guild waiting to anoint you as a chosen hero. Instead, Dark Souls looks at you with hollowed eyes and asks, Why are you here? What are you willing to endure?
This storytelling philosophy—where meaning is not handed to the player but uncovered—resonates deeply with Nietzschean existentialism. Dark Souls forces players to find their own purpose amidst the decay. There is no singular right way to interpret the game’s narrative, just as there is no absolute meaning in an uncaring universe. The First Flame will always fade, and the gods are not eternal. To persist is to impose meaning onto a world that has none.
 [h2]The Strength of a Community-Built Mythos [/h2]
Unlike Skyrim, where every story is spelled out for you, Dark Souls thrives on ambiguity, and in doing so, it fosters something far greater: a living, breathing myth shaped by its community. It is in the shared experience of piecing together fragmented lore that the game’s narrative finds its fullest form. Players dissect every item description, theorize on the nature of Manus and the Abyss, debate whether Gwyn was a hero or a coward. It is a game where knowledge is just as much a reward as victory over a boss, where every new theory reshapes our understanding of the world.
This communal storytelling turns Dark Souls into something transcendent. It is no longer just a personal journey but a collective endeavor, an eternal cycle of discovery and reinterpretation. In this way, it mirrors how real myths survive—through countless voices passing them down, each altering the tale with new meaning.
 [h2]A Lesson in Perseverance and Interpretation [/h2]
Returning to Dark Souls Remastered in the wake of the series’ legacy only reinforces what was already apparent in 2011: this game is a monument to the power of interactive storytelling. The feeling of finally besting Ornstein and Smough, the dread of descending into the Tomb of the Giants, the quiet, sorrowful notes of Gwyn, Lord of Cinder’s theme—these are not just moments of gameplay, but moments of personal revelation. They are tests of will, framed within a narrative that allows players to define their own understanding of struggle and triumph.
To play Dark Souls is to wrestle with the abyss and emerge changed. It is a game that does not tell you what to feel but allows you to discover meaning in your own perseverance. It is, in the end, a testament to the idea that the most profound stories are not the ones told to us—but the ones we carve out of the darkness ourselves.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1743735373}, {"review_text": "The game that created a new genre.

Dark Souls isn’t just a game — it’s an experience. Specifically, the experience of being repeatedly and unapologetically bullied by medieval architecture, undead warriors, and the very concept of hope.

You don’t play Dark Souls. You survive it. Barely. Then you die. Then you survive a bit more. Then you roll off a cliff because your fat-fingered dodge was two pixels off. Classic.

The story? Oh, it's there. Somewhere. Probably scribbled on a wall behind a hidden wall behind another hidden wall guarded by a depressed dragon. Every NPC speaks in riddles, metaphors, or what sounds like Shakespeare having an existential breakdown. Meanwhile, you’re standing there in a rusty bucket-helmet, covered in regret and moss.

Combat is tight, rewarding, and feels great — for the five seconds before a 12-foot skeleton dropkicks you into the sun. Boss fights are majestic duels where you die in 0.3 seconds, whisper “okay, fair,” and queue up to die again.

And let’s talk about mimics. Remember how other games reward curiosity? Not here. In Dark Souls, opening the wrong chest gets you eaten alive by a demonic tongue monster. Trust no one. Especially furniture.

The game’s world design is stunning in a “look how beautiful this place is, shame it wants me dead” sort of way. You’ll traverse haunted castles, poison swamps, and hell dimensions… all while questioning your life choices and the sanity of the developers.

Final Verdict: 9/10
Lost one point because I screamed at a goat demon so loud my neighbor asked if I was okay. I wasn't. I’m still not.

Recommended for people who think “fun” is overrated and want to feel something. Anything.

I never liked Souls games. As a matter of fact, I was afraid of them. I knew of the hardship and difficulty people used to talk about it in the internet, through memes and articles. This is coming from someone who grew up playing First Person Shooters and Platform Adventure games. Until I got the chance to play the Devil May Cry Series. Years went by and I saw Fromsoftware's proclaimed game [b] ELDEN RING [/b] getting a DLC. It peaked my curiosity so I caved in and bought the main game with the DLC. To my Surprise, Elden Ring has become one of my favorite games of all time. Thanks to Elden Ring, I wanted to expand and try out Fromsoft's other titles such as [b] Sekiro Shadows Die Twice [/b] ,[b] King's Field 1-3 [/b]. Then, I decided to try out Dark Souls Remastered. Where it all began.

Dark Souls atmosphere really made it unique and interesting. Fromsoft's environment storytelling is phenomenal in this game. Dark Souls world is grim, desolate, brutal, lonely. The atmosphere is heavy and defeating. While Elden Ring sure feels courageous and uplifting with its godly battles. Dark Souls, in the other hand, immerses you in a realm that appears old, heavy, and ruthless. Right from the initial moments, you are met with a feeling of solitude. This is not a world where individuals guide you. It’s an adventure in a deteriorating realm brimming with concealed stories, enigmatic NPCs, and an atmosphere of unavoidable downfall. You get to experience these themes and emotions through the game's many places. From Undead Asylum, Depth, Undead Burg, New Londo Ruins, Catacombs. Even beautiful but eerie looking places such as Darkroot Garden, The Duke's Archives, Anor Lando, and many others.

I completed 100% of Dark Souls a while ago, and looking back, it’s easily one of the best RPGs I’ve ever played. When I first tried it, I gave up after Blighttown, but coming back six months later completely changed my perspective. The constant deaths, learning from mistakes, and slow but steady progress are what make it so rewarding. Maybe it sounds funny, but this game didn’t just shape me as a gamer - it shaped me as a person too.

Combat is deliberate and punishing. Some bosses can be clunky and frustrating, turning fights into a real struggle, but the standout battles, like Ornstein and Smough, Artorias the Abysswalker or Manus - are unforgettable. That duo fight (O&S), especially back in 2011 was incredible - managing two completely different threats at once was a brilliant test of skill and strategy. These moments make everything else worth it.

The world of Lordran is essentially a metroidvania, interconnected and full of shortcuts, secrets, and hidden paths. Exploration feels meaningful, and even after over hundred of hours, there’s always something new to discover. The second half of the game feels a bit rushed and less inspired than the first; some areas reuse enemies and bosses, which reduces the sense of uniqueness and discovery. That said, the game has incredible re-playability - the range of builds, challenges, and ways to approach combat feels endless, and it cleverly breaks the sense of linearity most RPGs have. 

The DLC is outstanding, adding some of the best areas and boss fights in the game.

The story and world are steeped in darkness. Lordran isn’t just a setting - it’s a place where decay, despair, and fading light are part of every step you take. Piecing the story together yourself through items, dialogue, and environmental storytelling makes the sense of looming, almost oppressive darkness even more impactful. Every player who wants to truly feel like a gamer should play the Souls series - don’t make excuses about difficulty or not being skilled enough, just dive in.

Overall, Dark Souls is challenging, immersive, and incredibly rewarding. It’s one of the best RPGs ever, a game that teaches patience, skill, and persistence, and offers some of the most memorable experiences in gaming.

Elements of the game work marvelously, most notably, the cinematics. Between the repetitive game play loop that doesn't really go anywhere and the grind for minimal rewards, the game loses its luster quickly.

The story is serviceable, but unfinished. Blizzard has opted for a continual story with limited resolutions to keep people paying for expansions. The main issue here is that quantity has taken priority over quality, which means you have loads of quests, most of which aren't memorable. In fact, you'll likely start skipping most of them. A few side quests do have their charms, but because the reward system is so banal, it's only worth it to get the progression bonuses. It is unlikely the lore will suck you as you'll feel mostly separate from it.

As for the progression system, it has its up and downs. You will go from feeling really powerful to utterly worthless if you switch to a different Torment too early. This wouldn't be so bad if the torment run you left weren't mind numbingly easy. And the drop rate is a bit absurd. While I appreciate a truly random feel to the drops, it does seem stacked against the player to try to challenge themselves. Most of the time, you can get better drops mass running easy mode than taking a risk against enemies that are challenging, but dropping the same garbage.

Then there are the instant kill mechanics, which I personally don't like. They're not used often enough to get the player to build up an understanding of them in general, but rather, just some single event situation to overcome and be done with it. I don't hold this against the developers entirely, but it does feel like a lazy way to make a game harder without doing much to the rest of the game to compensate for it. Sure, you can grind away the difficult bosses to learn their moves, but that grind only translates to those specific bosses. They don't really translate to anywhere else in the game. It can also make hardcore frustrating to all, but the most dedicated fans of the game.

Lastly: the shop. The shop is just plain bad. Not conceptually, in the sense of buying skins (but even that seems silly to me), but the overall cost per skin. Not only does Blizzard have a manipulative transaction scheme to get players to not think about the actual cost, the cost of each skin is priced in such away to pressure people into buying more so they don't "waste" left over platinum. Had they simply left it a straight currency cost and/or battle pass option, I'd be less bothered  by it. But the limited choices, the lack of a color wheel, and the manipulative pricing, it's just a regular slap in the face. And that's not even counting the regular slaps coming in the form of lazy Season design.

Bottom line: is it fun? Sure. I had a lot of fun, but it felt like empty fun. Not mindless fun. I have great mindless fun with Vampire Survivors, but empty fun. There's so much potential to Diablo 4 that was limited for unnecessary monetization options and focus on streamlined eye candy in lieu of a power fantasy with an interesting story. 

I think you'll have a better time in general with a different aRPG, unless you got a couple of friends who want to play. It's definitely more fun with other people, but even that is contingent on each individuals time investment potential.
