So let me break it down, both from the perspective of someone coming in new to the franchise, and a vet Diablo player. 

Story - (4/5 for newcomers, 1.5/5 for vets) - Blizzard probably assumes no one currently gaming played Diablo 1 and 2. Otherwise, they wouldn't have copied the plot ending of D1 and part of D2 into D4. As it is, the game has a limited and recurring cast of baddies, and a plot that repeats the Hero/Mysterious Wanderer's endgame (albeit with a different outcome) is bound to feel jaded. 

For newcomers, though, the biggest question is why this game is called Diablo. There is no Diablo in the picture (so far) and instead we get Lilith and Mephisto. Otherwise, the story is decent. Lilith comes across as perhaps the most morally ambiguous antagonist, which makes lack of any meaningful decisions in the game makes the game feel like something out of Sunday School. You can probably predict the ending of the story halfway through the game, with only minor variations dragged in. That said, if you don't use your brain too much, the game has a fairly engaging storyline IF you joined the bandwagon with D3 or this is your first Diablo game. 

Graphics (4/5 for all) - It's a point and click game so breathtaking details are probably not what anyone expects. They're a climb up from D3, and that is probably all that matters. Max settings at 4K don't really demand a beast of a GPU, though you'll need a fairly beefy CPU for those Infernal Hordes waves when there are dozens of enemies on screen. Effects have been improved, and the transitions are also better. Together with some excellent background scores, they provide excellent atmosphere. 

Gameplay (2.5/5 for newcomers, NA for vets) - Those unfamiliar with point and click games would probably have some difficulty persuading their wrists to click hundreds of times per gaming session. Beyond that though, the gameplay is, well, classic Diablo. Nothing much has been changed since D3, or even D2 for that matter, in terms of core gameplay mechanics. You choose a class, and depending on it, you have some core mechanics that you have to repeat time and again with better and better gear to take down more and more powerful enemies. The skill trees are simpler than POE/2, but they can be daunting at first. My advice would be to use your common sense to build your first seasonal toon, and then go for build guides in the endgame. 

The endgame used to be a long slog to Level 100 after Level 50. That has been replaced by the more familiar (and comfortable) Level 60 + 300 Paragon levels. Most players don't manage to go beyond Paragon 250 in any season, as it takes an insane amount of xp. But by that time, you should have filled up everything on your skill tree and paragon board (a kinda extended skill tree) to make you truly badass. 

The gear system is even more complicated than in D3, with lots of percentages, ranges, this effect procs on that, etc. etc. It takes a while to figure out, but these days, that's your lot if you go into any major RPG. Overall, returning players won't feel too overwhelmed, since the expansion has now added back mercenaries and runes to complete everything you got in D3. 

Finally, the difficulty system has been made even more convoluted, and not necessarily for the better. Normal is very easy, Hard is easy, expert is hard, penitent is very hard, and then you have the torment difficulties where difficulty rises exponentially. The goal is to get better gear, hone your stats and push the pit till you unlock the next difficulty. Reach the highest one, and you're facing tormented bosses that can drop mythic items. Collect mythic items to complete your gear journey and then melt everything on the map that has a red health bar over it. 

Next season, rinse and repeat. 

Conclusion - Diablo continues to do what it has done for the past decade - churn out what was a decent story once, and keep making variations of it as if the scriptwriters were asked to work on half pay. At the same time, the game remains engaging and the progression feels meaningful. Once you're at the peak though, it just feels good to let off steam after a long day at work by melting metric tonnes of infernals. Not everyone will want to "just let off steam," and it will get boring for some after a season or two. [{"review_text": "I'm not generally a person who plays games for the difficulty. I like a challenge, but for me, the main draw to any single-player game is the story. If the difficulty prevents me from experiencing the narrative, I'm not going to enjoy it.

I have played through Lies of P probably three or four times now.

There's something about this world the developers created, something that keeps making me want to come back, even though I've experienced nearly everything there is to see in this game.

The gameplay is incredibly fun, the characters are engaging, the music is phenomenal, and the twist on the Pinocchio story is beyond interesting. It's gripping.

I cannot wait for the DLC to release just so I have a chance to experience something new in this world.

[h2]Overview[/h2]
Lies of P is honestly a fantastic game and a great way to get into Souls-like games not made by FromSoftware. Everything from the design, enemy variety, and music to the storyline feels polished and enjoyable. Major credit goes to the developers for making a beautiful game that runs smoothly, especially when many new games struggle with optimization.

[h2]Pros[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Polished world design[/b] with great atmosphere and attention to detail
[*][b]Impressive enemy variety[/b] with good distribution throughout levels
[*][b]Weapon customization system[/b] that actually impacts gameplay
[*][b]Beautiful visuals[/b] and consistently smooth performance
[*][b]Top-tier music[/b] and sound design
[*][b]Endgame bosses[/b] are exciting and skill-based
[*][b]Exploration and side quests[/b] are rewarding and meaningful
[/list]

[h2]Cons[/h2]
[list]
[*]Platforming sections feel frustrating and out of place
[*]Early boss patterns can feel off due to delayed and unpredictable attacks
[*]A few enemy reskins, though they come with new move sets
[*]Parry window is tight and can be difficult for new players
[/list]

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
The gameplay feels great whether you prefer parrying or dodging, but the game does encourage you to learn both. Weapon customization is a highlight. You can take weapons apart and mix handles and blades from different weapons. This isn’t just for looks. It actually changes how the weapon performs, making fights interesting and varied.

[h2]World & Level Design / Enemy Variety[/h2]
The world in Lies of P looks amazing and is packed with details, making exploring really enjoyable. Enemy variety is also impressive, even if a few are reused with new moves. This keeps things feeling fresh.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3454510657

Exploration is rewarding, especially because side quests often impact the ending you get. My only complaint is the platforming sections, which feel out of place in this type of game. It’s frustrating when ranged enemies push you off edges, forcing you to repeat sections again and again.

[h2]Boss Battles[/h2]
Bosses in Lies of P range from decent to really challenging, especially towards the end. Late-game bosses remind me a lot of Sekiro because they heavily rely on precise parrying. However, early bosses tend to use delayed and unpredictable attacks, making fights feel less rhythmic. Fortunately, bosses get much better later on. They're faster, fairer, and more satisfying to beat.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3453831674

[h2]Visuals & Atmosphere[/h2]
The game looks great and runs smoothly. Little details like the rain and the atmosphere in Hotel Krat really stand out. The whole aesthetic feels carefully crafted, and I don’t have any real complaints here.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3450429950

[h2]Music[/h2]
The music in Lies of P deserves special mention because it's genuinely amazing. Boss music, background themes, and especially the tracks you unlock for Hotel Krat are all fantastic. The soundtrack perfectly matches the game’s tone and makes the whole experience better.

[h2]Story[/h2]
Without spoiling anything, the story is engaging and offers multiple endings based on your choices. I recommend going in blind to fully enjoy uncovering the story yourself. It’s definitely worth it.

[h2]Should You Play If You Liked Sekiro?[/h2]
If you loved Sekiro, you might enjoy Lies of P, but don’t expect exactly the same experience. Parrying is important here too, but the timing is tighter and you'll often switch between parrying and dodging. It’s different enough to be its own unique game and definitely worth checking out.

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]
Overall, Lies of P is an excellent game that does almost everything right. From its visuals and gameplay to the music and storytelling, it's a solid experience. Despite minor frustrations, it’s a rewarding game that’s definitely worth your time.

Long story short, this game has a really snappy combat system and a super cool aesthetic and storyline.  It is a really good example of the modern soulslike genre, and I would recommend it to anyone who is into those kinds of games.

So first off and most obvious, the art and story teams are on point.  Lies of P is a reimaginging of the story of Pinocchio.  They managed to take that source material and keep it whimsical as well as make it dark and tense.  They did little things that really link it up.  For example, a lot of the humans in the game are wearing animal masks, you will be given the opportunity to lie frequently, and a cricket does talk to you.  They are not just following the story of Pinocchio, but no spoilers from me.

The combat system in this game is more guard and parry heavy than dodge heavy.  That means in combat you won't be dodge rolling around as much in this game as you would in a lot of other soulslikes.  Which gives it a more "stand your ground" feel, which I personally prefer.  I feel like I am dancing with the enemies more this way.

There are a couple of things that this game does differently that I really appreciated.  Firstly, when you run out of flasks in this game you will be able to build another charge of it back up by attacking successfully.  You can do this as many times as you like as long as you don't die; even in boss fights.  It gets you to push a little bit further in the levels and use your last flask early during bossfights; which I liked.  Secondly, the normal weapon system is neat.  Every non-special weapon can be broken into a handle and a head.  Each of those has a unique Fable attack associated with it, which is sort of a magic attack.  Also, damage is linked to the head of the weapon (which can be upgraded) while the handle is linked to weapon scaling and moveset.  That lets you have a lot of customization on the moveset you want to have moreso than many other games I've played.  

People seem to like to compare this game to Bloodborne, Sekiro, and Lords of the Fallen.  Bloodborne I have not played, so no comment there.  The Sekiro comparison is likely due to the focus on guarding and parrying correctly.  I played Sekiro last year and while I think the variety of combat is higher in Lies of P, the depth of combat is higher in Sekiro.  P is not as difficult as Sekiro either.  The Lords of the Fallen comparison is a bit more of an Apples:Oranges comparison, they are just different things.  I think they came out about the same time which is the main reason people compare them.  I played LotF a few months ago (in 2025) using a parry heavy build, so my perspective is that LotF is not really meant to be played that way.  It is more of a traditional dodging-style soulslike slow combat experience.  I do think that when both P and LotF launched P was probably hands down better; but they have continuously updated LotF since launch and not P.  In 2025, I think that LotF has more to offer in the base game than Lies of P; though Lies of P is still great.

As for criticisms, there is a weapon sharpening/durability system in the game that I didn't like.  You need to keep your weapon sharp in order to use it, so sometimes you will need to stop and sharpen it as you play. 99% of the time this doesn't come up, but every time it does it is annoying (and it is in a boss fight).  Secondly the when you parry an attack, get hit, or sometimes hit someone else you will get knocked back. The story is captivating and filled with intrigue. Set in a dark and twisted version of a Belle Époque-inspired world, Lies of P takes you through a beautifully detailed city plagued by madness and destruction. The narrative, centered around Pinocchio’s journey to find Geppetto, is fascinating, and it keeps you hooked from start to finish. The environment itself is immersive, with every corner hiding secrets and mysteries to uncover.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3479131338

[h1]Combat:[/h1]
The combat in Lies of P is a perfect blend of difficulty and satisfaction. It draws clear inspiration from Dark Souls, but it doesn’t just copy what’s been done before. There’s a real weight to every swing of your weapon, and the strategic depth required to overcome enemies is immense. The weapon crafting system is an excellent addition, letting you customize your gear to suit your playstyle, whether you prefer fast, agile attacks or heavy, powerful strikes.

[h1]Customization:[/h1]
The amount of customization available is remarkable. From your character's appearance to the weapons and abilities you use in battle, Lies of P gives you numerous ways to make the game your own. Whether you’re optimizing for a particular playstyle or just experimenting with different combinations, the freedom here is something special.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3479131430

[h1]Difficulty & Replayability:[/h1]
This game is challenging – in all the right ways. There’s a sense of satisfaction that comes with defeating a tough boss after multiple attempts. The game’s difficulty isn’t just about punishing the player; it’s about rewarding skill, patience, and learning from your mistakes. With multiple endings and secrets hidden throughout, Lies of P has great replay value.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
In a market flooded with Soulslike games, Lies of P not only stands out, it thrives. It takes what we love about the genre and makes it its own with a fascinating story, brutal combat, and an unforgettable atmosphere. If you’re a fan of the genre, this game is a must-play. If you’re new to Soulslike games, Lies of P is a perfect introduction. You’ll be hooked before you even realize it. Highly recommended!

Looking forward to the recently announced prequel DLC.

Once I become familiar with the play, it became my favorite game.  It is so much fun to fight the big bugs on a team with them. Connecting with them this way is so precious. Also, this is the most entertaining way to maintain brain plasticity that I've discovered so far.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1761243766}, {"review_text": "[h1] Okay, I kind of feel the need to write this review simply because it's my most played game on Steam. [/h1]

I understand that my point of view and playtime of Deep Rock Galactic aren't the norm, but seeing as how I love this game and have a lot to say about it, I think it's worth exploring those opinions and thoughts.

DRG, at its core, is a class-based co-op shooter set in procedurally generated caves. Your goal in every mission is to collect resources by mining ores and shooting a lot, and I mean A LOT of bugs. There are four classes to choose from, each having their own weapons, movement abilities, and most importantly, role and "job" in the team. You can level up your class by collecting upgrade materials in missions, used to add buffs to weapons and movement tools. 

Now on the whole, that is about as brief of a summary I can give without going into the minutiae of Deep Rock Galactic. There are a LOT of other details about the gameplay loop, class perks, Overclocks, and the roles and quirks of the classes themselves. However, if you would like the joy of learning and experience all of that on your own and wouldn't like to read my thesis on DRG, then you can stop reading and take my recommendation and pull the trigger on purchasing the game. 

For those still interested in reading, strap in.

To give some context on how and why I'm writing the rest of this review, I'll start with how I began playing DRG and why I continue to play it. This was my comfort game during the s**tshow that was the year 2020. My friends and I picked up the game to help us through the trying time, and we were hooked. Fast forward five years, and I am the only one of my original friend group who has over 200 hours in the game or plays it today. As their interest waned in the game, I played more and more with randoms in public lobbies, which led me to play with people in the official Discord server, where I met some really great people and became friends with a lot of them.

I say all of that because a lot of multiplayer or co-op games rely on, and indeed assume, that you are playing with friends or at least people who make the game entertaining in its own right. I have never held a belief that a game which is "more fun with friends" is a good thing in and of itself. Technically, ANYTHING is more fun with friends. A s**t game is more fun with friends. It doesn't mean the game itself is worth playing. 

Deep Rock Galactic, on the other hand, allows for fun to be had regardless of whether you're with a group of close buddies or complete strangers. A lot of that is due to the amount of agency and player autonomy each person has in the group. There aren't any keycards or similar that require two or more people to simultaneously engage with. There aren't specific enemies that require elite military-like coordination in order to take down. Each player and class has, to varying degrees, a manner to handle any and all situations the game throws at you. Obviously, certain classes and playstyles have their strengths and weaknesses, and good teamwork is always desirable, but there's not really any reliance on teammates outside of picking up downed players. DRG walks a very fine tightrope of giving each individual freedom to act autonomously, while also giving you an important role in the group context. Which brings us to the classes:

As said, there are four classes to choose from: Driller, Engineer, Gunner, and Scout. Each have their own niche and role in the group:

Driller's main role in the group is twofold. His primary weapons, with his starter weapon being a flamethrower, allows him to clean up trash and low priority enemies, as well as give debuffs to tankier targets. His movement ability, the drill hands, allows him to tunnel through terrain very quickly and efficiently. He is often seen at the front of the group, making pathways for his teammates and clearing out a spot to fight with both his drills and C4. 

Engineer is probably the hardest to describe succinctly. In lower difficulties and lower bug density environments, he struggles to find a particular role outside of securing holds and points of interest. This is due to his main tool, his automatic turrets, being stationary and moving them around, placing them, and then building them, especially during moments of chaos, can be troublesome. He is also the least ammo efficient class, owing to him having to pick and choose a lot of "fight or flight" moments. However, when the difficulty is raised and larger swarms are part of the mission, he really shines. His aforementioned turrets can help pick off low health enemies, his primaries are all servicable "get off me" weapons, and two of his three secondaries are quite amazing at killing large groups of enemies very quickly (Sorry PGL, hope you get the love you deserve someday <3). His movement tool, the platform gun, allows for you to place "shelves" into walls allowing for players to climb and scale up terrain very easily. It also has a lot of hidden tech that I don't really need to get into here, and is largely the most slept-on portion of his kit. 

Gunner, in contrast, is very easy to describe. He presses LMB, and holds it until he needs to stop pressing it, either when he runs out of bullets or things to shoot. His primaries are all large and in charge, ranging from the standard minigun to a Flak-cannon to a guided missile launcher, all of which pack a punch. He's also the class with the highest degree of survivability, owing to his insane DPS (Best defense is a good offense), and his bubble shield. His shield can be used offensively, thrown into an unexplored room to clean it out, or defensively, such as reviving a teammate and giving them some breathing room or holding a position. He makes up for all of this by having, in my opinion, the worst and most situational movement tool: The zipline. Slow, dangerous, makes you a target for flying enemies, and capable of falling off of it make it very risky to use it any other way except downhill. 

Last but certainly not least is Scout. As his name suggests, his job is indeed to scout out rooms and light them with his flare gun. I may not have mentioned it yet, but this game is incredibly reliant on light, as the caves can range from dim and atmospheric to pitch black nothingness. He also has access to a grappling hook, which is less Spiderman and more "Look at a wall and get pulled toward it". This leads to a natural progression of logic that Scout is more often than not the resource bag of the team, owing to his ability to reach high up ores and objectives. As for his guns, they are best used to pick off important targets, such as highly disruptive enemies, or enemies that are out of reach of the less accurate guns the other classes might have equipped. 

This seems like a very comprehensive description of what these classes do, but I'm leaving out a lot of synergies and interplay that they have with each other (Volatile Bullets + Flamethrower, Sludge Pump + Fire Bolts, etc). I would go into more details such as Overclocks, perks, difficulties, enemy varieties, and fun little distractions in the Hub area, but I have found out that there is a character limit on Steam reviews... so...

I cannot recommend Deep Rock Galactic enough. It's so fun I spent an hour and a half thinking of things to put into this review, ran out of space, and am now trying to summarize in what little space I have left. Just buy it and give it a shot. It's worth your money and time. It's a blast and I'm still playing five years later.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1749570941}, {"review_text": "This game literally made me quit most PVP cause of how good it is.

The Drillers who carry a brick of C4 and blow up literally everything including teammates when they feel threatened. most of the time themselves.

The maniacs who turn every Liquid Morkite mission into a rollercoaster ride.

The rookies who join high difficulty lobbies with sky-high confidence, only to fall down every five seconds, forcing you to babysit them like a full-time nanny.

And countless other weird, wonderful personalities that make each run unpredictable.

On the weapons side, every build makes you feel like you are playing a new game. I’ve got almost 3000 hours in this game, and I’m still finding new combinations. Wanna be a vampire? Wanna be a maniac ice wizard instead? Throw on the Ice Spear overclock and start throwing massive ice spikes to everything that moves and deal shit ton of damage. And to everyone who says “Scout is just support, can’t deal with crowds” nah uh . Stick Cryo Minelets on zhukov, pair it with Aggressive Venting for the Plasma Carbine, and suddenly you’re outkilling Engineers. Speaking of Engineers, you don’t even need to move to deal with those ugly aracnids: cover the ground around you with platforms, electrify them with Micro Conductor overclock (one of the stubby smgs overclock), drop some turrets, unleash your flying buttplugs (yeah, those little shredder guys), and watch the bugs fry while you just sip your beer.
As Gunner, equip Cluster Charge, find yourself a jetboot if you are lucky, and boom you’re basically a B-52 bomber dropping hundreds of tiny clusters on everything below. Pure chaos. Absolute joy.

The caves? Beautiful. Genuinely gorgeous. But after enough hours like a thousand, you kinda start predicting the formations, which is my only tiny complaint. I’d love to see new ones in the next updates but still they’re hypnotic. Every cave feels magical. Go in not just to kill bugs, but to explore and you’ll see what I mean.

The music and atmosphere? straight up brainwashes you. Like, you’re not just playing a game anymore you’re living in Hoxxes and i mean it i would sell my soul to a space mining company like drg.

The community? Honestly feels like we’re all sharing the same single brain cell. And thats perfect. You’ll have some of the dumbest and funniest moments of your life.

And the true heart of the game: the Space Rig.
Dance until you pass out from drinking with buddies. Play Prop Hunt (yes, there’s literally a beer that lets you do that). Kick barrels around, play Jetty Boot, the in-game Flappy Bird game, Or my personal favorite: fill your afk teammate’s quarters with barrels until they come back to find a surprise barrel-apocalypse waiting for them.
I swear I’ve spent at least 500–600 hours in the Rig alone. Which other game lets you have that much fun without even actually playing the game?

Long story short: every cent you spend on this game is worth it. You’re gonna have fun 100%.

If you’ve ever wanted to go on chaotic space mining missions with your friends while fending off alien bugs and yelling “ROCK AND STONE!” every five minutes, this is your calling.

The core gameplay is simple but endlessly fun: you’re a dwarf in space, you mine valuable materials, you fight off waves of hostile creatures, and you GTFO before it all collapses. But it’s how the game feels that makes it special. Each class plays differently and contributes in unique ways, so whether you’re drilling through rock, setting up turrets, lighting up the cave, or ziplining across a chasm, you always feel useful — and the teamwork is real.

The environments are fully destructible and randomly generated, which keeps things fresh. Sometimes you’re zipping through caves like a pro, and other times you’re lost, surrounded, and yelling for your engineer to PLEASE set up a platform. It’s tense, hilarious, and incredibly satisfying all at once.

And now — the devs. Ghost Ship Games is one of the best dev teams in the industry, period.
They didn’t just launch a great game and walk away — they’ve been updating Deep Rock Galactic consistently with free content, new missions, weapons, cosmetics, seasonal events, and quality-of-life changes that actually matter. They listen to feedback, engage with the community, and have built a game that keeps getting better without nickel-and-diming the players.

It’s not just a good co-op game — it’s one of the best.
Whether you’re dropping in solo with your trusty drone, or teaming up with a full squad to shout nonsense while digging your way to glory, DRG delivers every single time. It’s fun, it’s polished, it’s generous, and it has one of the most wholesome, chill communities you’ll find in online gaming.

Four dwarf classes—Gunner, Engineer, Scout, Driller—slot together like clockwork: minigun suppression, turret crossfire, grappling-hook scouting, and drill-dozer shortcuts all feeding into one smooth mineral-grinding machine. The environments are fully destructible, the caves are procedural, and the moment you carve a bespoke tunnel to out-flank a Dreadnought you feel like a subterranean genius.

Weapons and gadget upgrades arrive in an almost Borderlands-style gush of overclocks and cosmetics, but the balance is tight enough that a fresh recruit packing a stock shotgun can still hold the line beside a veteran with a radioactive autocannon. Seasonal updates keep the sandbox mutating: 2024’s Season 05 ‘Drilling Deeper’ dropped new Rockpox corruption events and a terraforming drill escort, and March’s S05.09 patch continued the tweak-fest with balance passes and fresh assignment rewards.

The headlamp-lit spectacle is matched by audio that roars and clatters with industrial heft—pickaxes crunch, glyphid armour splinters, and HoPoRo’s synth soundtrack pumps just hard enough to raise a dwarven eyebrow without drowning squad chatter. After 36 hours in Deep Rock Galactic, I’m convinced that being a space-faring, beer-drinking, bug-slaying dwarf is my true calling. This game perfectly combines teamwork, exploration, and explosions into a package so fun that I’m surprised it hasn’t been outlawed.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Gameplay – Chaotic Co-Op Goodness[/h2]
The gameplay is an absolute blast—literally. Whether you’re mining rare minerals or fending off waves of horrifying alien bugs, every mission feels unique and exciting. The classes are perfectly balanced for co-op, with each dwarf bringing a critical piece of the puzzle.

Want to shoot bugs in the face? Pick the Gunner. Prefer to light up dark caves? Go Scout. Need to build a highway to nowhere? That’s Driller. And then there’s Engineer, who… well, builds turrets and just looks cool.

It’s teamwork at its finest, though you’ll still argue over who didn’t deposit their minerals in the mule.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]World – Dark, Beautiful, and Alive[/h2]
The procedurally generated caves are a masterpiece. They’re dark, eerie, and filled with hidden treasures (and sometimes death traps). No two missions feel the same, and the dynamic environments keep you constantly on your toes.

Oh, and the bugs? Terrifying. Watching a swarm charge at you while you’re screaming for help is as thrilling as it is horrifying.

[h2]Highlights – What Stands Out[/h2]

✔️ Perfectly designed co-op gameplay with diverse classes.
✔️ Procedurally generated caves that keep things fresh.
✔️ An arsenal of ridiculous, satisfying weapons.
✔️ Incredible atmosphere enhanced by the game’s lighting and sound design.
✔️ The ability to drink beer in a space dwarf bar—what more could you want?

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Cons – Minor Nitpicks[/h2]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts – Rock and Stone Forever[/h2]
Deep Rock Galactic is a game that thrives on teamwork, humor, and pure, unfiltered chaos. It’s a love letter to co-op gaming, wrapped in an explosive, bug-slaying bow. Whether you’re navigating treacherous caves or singing drinking songs at the space bar, every moment in this game is a joy.

If you’re looking for a game where you can shout “Rock and Stone!” with your friends while mining for riches and fending off alien horrors, then this is the game for you. Trust me—you won’t regret picking up that pickaxe.

[b][u]Recommended[/u][/b] for anyone who loves cooperative chaos, dwarven shenanigans, and yelling “Rock and Stone!” at their screen!

Long-time player here that has played for 334days since the start of the game opening up to the Asia community on steam back in season 1 of the PVP season. Been maintaining my black hole rank (Upper Tier player rank title) every season since S4 and also a strong supporter of the game. The below review is to try to provide my views on some aspects regarding the game experience so far.

Starward is mainly a live service game with gacha where players select female characters to fight it out in 2-on-2 battles in an arena online. There are also 1 V 1 player mode and arcade mode but those are not the main modes of the game. For players that are familiar with the “Gundam VS” series, you will find yourself quite at home with the gameplay aspects as a lot of it has taken inspiration or were brought over from there. 

Gameplay:
With a constantly expanding character roster of unique characters since the game started. Experience a myriad of playstyles with 42 unique characters (as of this review date), each with their own unique gameplay, strengths and weaknesses. Characters can range from low cost to high cost, from close range to far range, with various skill ceilings and difficulty to use. 

A player online experience will depend on how skilled the player is at using their controlled character and their ability to make quick decisions to create a favorable situation with your partner to beat the opposing team. No 2 games are the same as the choices that the player makes provides endless possibilities to how the outcome turns out, making it a unique experience that can end in different ways. It being a live PVP environment means the partner you get and the opposing team can change in the next game with your ally before becoming your enemy.

Gacha currency economy and gacha system:
Unlike some games, newly released characters (exception of collaboration characters due to IP rights) will enter the available pool of a permanent custom select gacha banner after 2 updates from their initial release (approx. 6weeks equiv 2 big update cycle later) where one can choose the previous limited character release to be the target guaranteed character. One can also choose the 100% rate up banner pool instead if one does not want to deal with the 50% gamble when hitting the hard pity of 70rolls. However, on the 50% banner, if you were to roll out the non-rate up before hitting pity or hitting the pity, your next SSR character is guaranteed to be the rate up character of your choice or the current banner. 

There are 3 currencies for the type of gacha tickets that can be used to roll the banners. Being standard ticket, advanced ticket and rerun ticket. Each can only be used on their respective gacha pools with the advanced ticket being able to use on both the limited banner and the rerun banner (custom select gacha pool). Dupes of characters that are obtained during rolling will be converted into “talent upgrade” items and also another currency “star essence” that can be used to purchase items such as more gacha tickets or a limited character copy themselves. For dupes of the “burst” from characters, it will be converted to “star dust” that can be used to purchase “burst” of characters you own, more gacha tickets (limited to X times a month), or even character shards of characters that can used to redeem additional limited character copies.

The player gacha free currency economy is more on the generous side, with a daily income minimum of about (130 -195) star crystals through clearing the daily requirements. With additional 100 weekly through collecting on their support tracking site. You also can redeem from a ranking reward box every week depending on how high you have achieved (about 400crystals from the lowest competitive rank of Superstar 3 reward box). This nets you about 1410crystals which is almost a 10pull worth (1600crystals). With the free currency you get through playing every week, you can redeem SSR dupe item or up to additional 15 standard rolls and 15 advanced ticket rolls every 3weeks(every character update). So every character update, a f2p can accumulate almost a pity worth.  There are also at least 150rolls worth of standard banner tickets you can obtain through the free PVE modes.

Character dupes:
Dupes of a character are used to upgrade their talent that provides upgrades on their kit like additional ammo, new cancel route or new weapon. It does not affect the core gameplay of a character, and players are able to try out the character in a trial room at max upgrades against an AI opponent. The gacha is not the only way to get dupes for a character, one can obtain random character shards x2 from various sets of daily character shard packs which are free (like pack 1 features 4 characters, pack 2 another 4 etc). collect 60 shards and u get to redeem a character dupe free. For the standard banner characters, you can get 100 character tickets every day, with an additional 3000 every 3 weeks update, so just through saving 5400, you can buy out enough char shards of any standard SSR character of your choice. SSR dupe upgrade item are also obtainable as a f2p through the season shop (free currency through playing) and exchanging 12000 character tickets for another copy, these items reset every version update (approx. 63days) so even f2p can max dupe a limited SSR character with enough time.

Matchmaking:
As the pool of players available to match with are dependent on various factors such as the region selected (up to 3 can be selected at any time), and the current attained rank of the player (even in casual matches). One can easily identify whether facing a AI bot or player when seeing the wifi icon next to the player name during a match. Generally players just starting out will find issues facing the same people or bots constantly, just raising your rank will make it easier to get games. The game will not match people of too different rank against one another. You should easily reach the rank most suited to you if you have a net positive win rate, even against bots or players. Noone wants to keep losing every game constantly for 10rounds straight against too strong enemies.

Other points:
Constant updates – every 3 weeks a new character releases with balance adjustments made to characters depending on their performance during the season. Teaser videos before every major version update on the upcoming characters.
Strong developer support and loyal community – Developers sponsor prizes for community hosted tournaments that are informed to them. Join a community (JP, SEA, NA, TH, KR, HK etc) to find other players to play with to enhance your game experience in a custom room with them or learn from them. More content creators on social media have been joining the community with live gameplay and guides.
Dedicated developers – they have come a long way since the game started. Already announcing collaborations with figure making companies, IP like Frame Arm Girls, and hardcore mecha. More server regions have opened up like the North American, Japan and Singapore regions to accommodate players to have better latency during games. Tournament hosting support and spectator modes are being worked on to provide better support for community events.

Conclusion:
Now is a good time to join the Starward community since it is the first anniversary, plenty of freebies and interesting collaboration with Frame Arm Girls. I don't think this game is pay to win either, sometimes the new character is broken (but that happens in street fighter, smash, tekken, kof, mortal kombat, and guilty gear all the time.) but if your playing for daily rewards and not spending resources on upgrades until you have 90+ (I'd recommend 200) pulls ready for the new characters, you'll have more than enough to get the whole roster, expect to unlock everyone in a month or two (it only takes 90 pulls per character, and you can target old characters whenever) but only expect to upgrade your main fourish characters, and the base roster that they use to pad out banner pulls. Anyway tl;dr spend money wisely, do your dailies and the gacha isn't a real problem, the whole roster is accessible within 90 pulls so you can get who you want too and also everyone, game is fun, it's an actual fighting game where your more likely to get outplayed than outgunned and if the new character is running roughshot they're probably working on patching them but it might take a few tries (seems like a small dev team.), worst case scenario the higher ranks have character bans so you can just perma-ban them, solid game, definitely play the tutorial gundam versus kinda does it's own thing, none of the traditional nor platform fighting game rules apply, and actually learning the rules is fundamental to winning, mashing doesn't work.

[{"review_text": "After playing Ark: Survival Evolved and buying into the hope that Ark: Survival Ascended would be a true upgrade, I can say without hesitation: no, it is not better. In fact, it’s significantly worse.

We were led to believe this “upgrade” would bring improved graphics and quality-of-life enhancements—that was the whole reason many of us were willing to buy the same game again. We wanted to support the developers and enjoy a better-looking, smoother experience.

Instead, what we got was a game that still suffers from the same bugs as ASE, along with a whole slew of new ones. And to make matters worse, the only way to get ASA running at a remotely playable level is by turning down the graphics so far that it ends up looking just like ASE did years ago.

Wildcard Studios and Snail Games seem more interested in chasing quick cash than creating a quality, lasting experience. If they have long-term goals, they clearly have no intention of following through.

To anyone considering buying this game: let me be honest—the concept is incredible, and the game could be amazing. But the execution and technical work simply aren't there. Unless there's a major change in leadership or ownership, this game will never reach its full potential.

Save your money, your sanity, and your time. Play one of the many other games out there that actually run well, play well, and respect your investment.

If the day ever comes that Snail Games or Wildcard lose the rights to the IP, there might be hope. Until then—do yourself a favor and steer clear.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 33, "timestamp_created": 1749155640}, {"review_text": "Instead of constantly releasing new expansions and DLCs that are exclusively “pay to win”, developers should rather focus on optimizing the game itself to bring new or old players back to play and thereby generate profit.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1750687317}, {"review_text": "I Love This Game. I DESPISE Its Developers.

I've sunk thousands of hours into ARK: Survival Evolved, across PC, console, even mobile. I've built empires, tamed titans, fought tooth and claw through its brutal world. This game is, without a doubt, my favorite game of all time.

But Studio Wildcard? They're the worst developers in the industry. Bar none.
I cannot express enough how much I loathe them for what they’ve done, and continue to do to this absolute gem of a game.

Let’s start with the obvious: 
This game runs like complete dogshit. Always has. Always will. High-end PC? Crashes. Console? Melts. Xbox Series X and PS5 choke on it. ASA was supposed to be a fresh start. What we got was a $60 tech demo wrapped in Unreal Engine 5 lighting with all the same bugs that have been there for nearly a decade. Memory leaks, rubberbanding, insane loading times, desync, dinos glitching through the floors.

how is this STILL happening?

Oh, and let's not forget their glorious marketing strategy:

-Kill the original game.
-Force people onto a new version.
-Charge them full price for the same maps, same content.
-Split the community AGAIN, and leave console players in the dirt.
-leave the game in an unplayable state and start pumping out micro-transactions 

It’s not just a money grab. It’s predatory. And they know it.

Wildcard doesn’t fix things. They patch over things. Then they break ten more. They promise transparency, then go silent for weeks. Roadmaps? Lies. Timelines? Bullshit. The entire launch cycle of ASA was a masterclass in incompetence and PR bullshit. “We’re rebuilding it from the ground up!” No. You slapped new lighting on old unworkable code and called it a day.

And yet they still have the nerve to push paid DLC and cosmetics, when the core experience still barely works. It’s insulting. This isn't a small indie dev trying their best, this is a company that knows their game is broken and monetizes the hell out of it anyway. How can they ask us to pre-pay for content when the base game is borderline unplayable??

Modders do more for ARK than Wildcard ever has. The community carries this game on its back while the devs laugh all the way to the bank. They've weaponized nostalgia and community loyalty to milk us dry, all while shipping out broken updates and delayed content with the same tired “sorry for the inconvenience” routine.

And I still play it. I hate myself for playing it. I hate them for making something so brilliant and treating it like garbage. Imagine if this game had competent devs behind it. Imagine if it actually worked.

But we’ll never get that. Not while Wildcard’s in charge.

ARK is a masterpiece buried under a landfill of developer greed, laziness, and outright disrespect.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 21, "timestamp_created": 1752444522}, {"review_text": "Having about 500 hours in ASE and 265 in ASA, I can't believe how bad it has become.  The game used to be great with tons of mods by the community that kept you coming back.  I've lost all trust in the team responsible for the games direction.  Now it's just a revolving door of money grabs.  Ark never needed power rangers or ninja turtles or paid mods for every other dinosaur you run into, or content blocked behind pay walls.  What made Ark great was the community behind ASE and modding it. I do recommend but with caveats. Wait for a sale if you're not interested in Official Server Play. The only benefit to buying full price at this point is early access to materials as they drop (and thus official servers for early land claim) or supporting the developers if you're really into them.

[h2] Long Version [/h2]

I would give this game not really a thumbs up but not really a thumbs down and there's several reasons that go into this. I've played both ARK Survival Evolved and ARK: Survival Ascended enough time that I feel able to give this sort of review at this point. 

[b] Let's start with the Good: [/b]
[list]
[*] Unreal Engine 5.5 is the current engine of the game as of this review. (I may update this in the future but unlikely.) It has resulted in a gorgeous game visually. 
[*] The developers are releasing all of the maps and content that were originally DLC (paid and free) for ARK SE as free updates to ARK SA, meaning for the box price you are getting everything that came with ARK Survival Evolved (eventually, they have just dropped Ragnarok as of this review, with Gen 1/2, Fjordur, Crystal Isles, and Valguero still to come among a few others.
[*] There is new content being added to ASA that is not going to be added to ASE, including new gameplay benefits, creatures, and cross-platform mod support. 
[*] Development is active, with a pretty active community and a healthy unofficial community as well. 
[*] Crossplatform mods also give rise to Premium mods, are very easy to install from within the game and tend to work... most of the time, with some whitelisted to work on Official Servers!
[*] The developers do maintain an active official network where those who can't afford to rent their own servers or prefer to play with others outside of SP can do so. 
[/list]

[b] Now to the Bad: [/b]
[list]
[*] There are still bugs present in the base game that have existed since ASE, the reasons for these vary, but while some has been fixed not all of it has. If you were hoping for a less buggy game I'm afraid that classic ARK jank is still present. 
[*] The game has been optimized repeatedly since it's initial early access release, but it is still pretty hard on older rigs. I would recommend making sure you have updated hardware. 
[*] No Steam Deck support due to the aforementioned hardware requirements. You can get it to run, it just won't run well. 
[*] MTX. You can call it DLC and it functionally is, but $5 here, $5 there, that's a microtransaction and there's a significant number of them.  
[*] The arrival of crossplatform mods has also meant the arrival of premium mods that you also pay for. This isn't really a sticking point for me, as I love supporting passionate individuals but it is a turnoff to some, especially with many premium mods starting at $5 USD for varying quality.
[*] Though the Official Network is fairly healthy, the developers have begun a pattern of sunsetting inactive official servers, potentially leading to progress loss for those who don't manage to get their characters off onto a different official server. They do kindly offer the saves themselves so you can play with them on SP or load them onto a personal server cluster, but this has been a point of contention for the community. 
[*] The additional DLC that provides gameplay changes as well as unique creatures to tame can be pretty expensive.

Overall I have been a longtime ark fan even if I wasn't around for the 'beta' days. I enjoy the game but I fully admit that it's not a game for everyone. It can be buggy, and if you play on officials (and even then) it can be extremely unforgiving when something bugs out, or you lose progress etc due to server troubles. 

The game has gotten better from its initial release, but that doesn't mean its perfect and as of writing this review it is still in early access and adding yet more content at a pretty blistering pace while translating over older content from ARK SE. As far as the promised content goes, I do believe that promise is being kept pretty admirably but for a lot of other people I fully understand the anger regarding the costs.

It is worth emphasizing that the exorbitant cost of this game is all in optional content that has come across as Pay-to-Win because the creatures involved are very powerful, but locked behind these DLC Passes. If you are someone who thrives in PvP and were hoping for fair fighting grounds, I'd argue this game is not for you unless you have $$$. 

Even among PvErs though, the game is costly if you want some of the really cool critters. This is why I recommend purchasing on a sale if you really want to get into it with all the bells and whistles. to me it's not worth the value that I myself have paid out over time so far. 

As of this writing, total cost to enjoy this game at full price with all new things: (rounded to nearest whole dollar)
Base Cost: $45
Bob's Tall Tales: $30
Fantastic Tames Pyromane: $5
Fantastic Tames Dreadmare: $5
Fantastic Tames Drakeling: $5 (after LC release)
Partner Map Astraeos: $15 (The only map where Maeguanas, a reptilian version of the Maewing that was released as an early access baby trough spawn naturally. Otherwise an optional community map developed by a modder working along with WC as a partner.) 
Lost Colony Expansion Pass (currently w/Veilwyn and Drakeling): $30 USD (Drakeling will be sold separately after LC releases and Veilwyn is only temporarily available until the LC map releases which is its otherwise exclusive spawn.)

There is additional optional content released by WC in regards to cosmetics, one which is available on Steam STore, the other which I've seen on their internal Overwolf Premium Mod offering: 
- Power Rangers Official Cosmetics: $10-20 USD total (not super positive on this one, I feel like the price changed for it.) 
- Official ARK Show Cosmetics: $15 USD

Without these cosmetics and just the main creature DLC though you are still looking at $135 USD just to keep up with their pace of releases and have access to genuinely GAMECHANGING mechanics and devices. Things like a gestation incubator, the ability to tame Pyromanes or Dreadmares or Armadoggos etc, all of which naturally spawn on the otherwise free base maps, the ability to use special mechanics like the shovel from bob's tall tales to hunt for treasure and dig it up. Or even the ability to access new lore notes related to the expansions. 

To be perfectly clear there is plenty of reason to be upset at this level of gameplay being locked behind additional paywalls, but this content also goes several steps BEYOND what was initially promised with ASA, which was simply bringing ARK SE forward in terms of technology and engine. They have accomplished that portion, and as a company need to continue funding development so to an extent I understand it. However it leaves a bad taste in the mouth of many players, myself included when we go beyond the occasional $5  release and announce more 20+ USD expansions. I love the game and I'll still support it at the end of the day, but I won't say the anger is unjustified to an extent.

[b] Overall my verdict is that if you're new to ark, then starting here is a great point, because you won't really have much background context or even nostalgia to be furious over. If not though, then maybe wait for a sale.[/b] It will save you a lot of money in the long run, and unless you're competing for early fight rights or land on the Official Network it genuinely does you no harm. 

There's a healthy unofficial server community that caters to a vast array of interests and time availabilities so I'm positive  you will find someone or someplace to hang out, and if you're a Single PLayer then there's already a vast amount of content available to you before the DLCs that you can chew on until you're ready to purchase.

I should’ve stopped then. I couldn’t then. I cannot now. Every time I try to quit, a free Dart Monkey whispers sweet nothings in my ear: “Just one more medal.” The Banana Farm is thriving. The Glue Gunner is vibing. My social life? Gone. My sleep schedule? Irrelevant. But my defenses? [i]Immaculate[/i].

This isn’t just a tower defense game. It's a commitment. A vow to never let a single bloon live to see the other side of the screen.

My friends ask what I’ve been up to lately. I tell them I’ve become spiritually one with the Super Monkey. They've stopped asking.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 223, "timestamp_created": 1750081990}, {"review_text": "This is a game that has monkeys and the monkey pop balloons and its fun cause the balloons pop when the monkeys pop them.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 65, "timestamp_created": 1761701820}, {"review_text": "I bought this game thinking it would be a casual little tower defense experience. You know—place a monkey, pop some balloons, sip some coffee, move on with my day. What actually happened is that I am now 347 hours deep into debating whether a monkey with a crossbow is superior to a monkey in a helicopter with an Apache gunship.

The balloons aren’t even threatening me in real life, but somehow they’ve infiltrated my dreams. I wake up at 3 a.m. sweating, whispering “round 63…” while my wife asks if I’m okay. No. I am not okay. These balloons don’t play fair. They come in ceramics, camos, regrows, leads, and then suddenly a purple one shows up like it owns the place. Why does purple make my entire strategy useless? Who decided this?

And don’t get me started on Paragons. I spent three days farming enough money to summon one, and when I finally did, it felt like unlocking God himself, except God was a giant dart-throwing monkey with glowing eyes. Watching balloons melt under its power gave me more satisfaction than my last five birthdays combined.

The worst part? My bank account. I bought this game for like $7. Since then, I’ve purchased every hero skin, every cosmetic, and I’m seriously considering buying that banana farmer just because my clicking finger hurts. I now measure real-life purchases in terms of how many Banana Farms I could build with that money. “Should I buy lunch today?” No, that’s a whole marketplace upgrade, are you insane?

My social life is gone. My boss asked why I’ve been late to work three days in a row. I told him “round 98 fortified BADs” and he just nodded like he understood.

In conclusion:
	•	10/10 monkeys.
	•	0/10 balloons.
	•	Would sacrifice friendships, relationships, and possibly my sanity again.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 74, "timestamp_created": 1757813714}, {"review_text": "Maybe the greatest Tower Defense game ever made. Aside from maps there are community maps, events, boss events, races, so much content to go through and it never gets boring. It can also be played casually and it is really a great "background" game while you're listening to a podcast, music, or doing something on a 2nd monitor. 

Since it's release in late 2018 this game gets frequent updates, balance patches, new towers, heroes... It's seriously laughable how cheap it is compared to what it offers. Do yourself a favour and give this magnificent gem a chance. You will probably get addicted.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1742332963}, {"review_text": "this game changed my life. i got a girlfriend, payed off my car, bought a house, lost 45 pounds, my dick grew 5 inches all because i installed and played this game...", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 90, "timestamp_created": 1761105400}, {"review_text": "Let me review the game based on what I didn’t like — because that’s more fun.

The worst thing about BTD6 is that you have no idea what the actual stats of towers are. Pierce, damage, bonus damage vs. certain bloons — none of that is shown. Upgrades often just say “increases attack speed” without telling you if it’s 10%, 50%, or 2%. You’re left guessing from the animation. You could argue they want the game to feel less technical, but an option for advanced stats would fix this easily. Some upgrades are even worse, saying things like “bloons will fear you” with no explanation of what that actually means.

You also don’t know which bloons spawn on which rounds unless you memorize them. If you want real info, you basically have to open the wiki.

Each map has way too many “easy” challenges, forcing you to replay them several times if you want a black border (all challenges + CHIMPS without retrying). It’d be nice if we could do multiple challenges at once, especially the easier ones, to speed things up. Personally, I would have preferred if CHIMPS was balanced with Monkey Knowledge for more progression, but it’s fine as is.

The game can flood you with abilities, many of which aren’t explained well, leading to a messy UI with 20+ buttons. The Tech Bot helps automate abilities but costs monkey money and space; there really should be a built-in auto-cast option, similar to what the DLC game mode does.

As a live service, BTD6 has added tons of content — but much of it feels unnecessary. Bosses and Paragons are cool, but they don’t add much outside their specific modes. Paragons are trial-and-error, since you don’t know the degree before buying them, and thresholds are extremely important. Because of their cost, you mostly end up using the same few Paragons while ignoring the rest. Some are only used when the “good” ones are disabled, which feels artificial. Honestly, Paragons and bosses could have been the foundation of a future BTD7, instead of being bolted onto 6.

The in-game purchases also leave a bad taste. They’re not really worth it (which is good and bad), but just having a store in what is mostly a single-player game feels off. You earn a lot of monkey money, but I don’t like spending it — it feels bad. Instant monkeys are similar: they feel cheesy to use, so you hoard them instead of playing with them.

Biggest reason I still recommend BTD6: you quickly know if the game is for you. If you don’t enjoy the first hour, you won’t enjoy your 50th. There are maps that are either easy or maps that can be very difficult to beat, depending on the difficulty chosen, but it is all part of the fun of this game.

This is definitely a must game to buy for any tower defense and strategy players, and not to mention, it has co-op you can play with either random people or friends, which is even more fun.

[{"review_text": "Raft is simply one of the most charming survival games I’ve played. Simply standing on my raft as it floats over the waves through an endless body of water is truly relaxing. There’s also a great sense of pride and achievement that comes with seeing what I’ve built every time I load into the game. It’s an easy recommendation for survival fans that may have been holding off on jumping into early access, as well as those just learning about the game for the first time.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1747143988}, {"review_text": "This game is awesome. I used it as a tool to help me quit smoking, (no joke) because it just makes time fly. Hours feel like minutes, days feel like hours. Plus its fun and the art style is cool. 9/10 ★★★★★★★★★✩", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 9, "timestamp_created": 1751220217}, {"review_text": "I like this game because I do nothing and sit in the boat while my friends beat the game", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 67, "timestamp_created": 1754813385}, {"review_text": "It’s a game about a Cuban guy on his journey to Florida.

Ah yes, Waterworld The Game.

Builder games always hook me.  I become strangely addicted (Subnautica being my favorite).  Raft is not any different.  I loved all aspects of it. I just wish I had friends that liked games like this instead of being humiliated by having to play this with my wife’s boyfriend. 

It's more of a "the voyage itself, not the end" kind of game. I love it. Great game to destress to. It's both so mellow and engaging, and occasionally "DAMN YOU, YOU F'ING SHARK". It's complete zen playing this game. When it's calm, it is a very relaxing game. Great with a friend. Terrific solo. The game is notorious for "I'm just gonna play for 20 mins..... what do you mean it's 2am?!" The only video game that actually calms you down and changes your mood, absolutely worth it.

The first hour or so is a bit rough. You need to focus pretty hard on survival very quickly while you're still feeling out the mechanics of the game, which I do feel is kind of poor design. If you don't push hard and fast it's easy to get stuck in a loop of barely surviving without being able to expand, and not knowing what upgrades to focus on when you're starting out compounds the problem. It also tends to follow the philosophy of giving you a really bad, inefficient kit at the start to make you more appreciate the upgrades later on. Whether that's good design or not is up for debate, but it does work. 

The fun in the game though is finding the solutions to make that survival loop a little bit easier. Stressful in the beginning to manage your resources and staying alive and not starving, but the learning curve is quick. Don't waste too much time building a monstrous ship. Keep it simple. Focus on piloting your raft, getting a mast and using the currents and wind to get around until you find the.. something to start story mode. Story progression is linear, and it’s nothing special, but it’s exactly interesting enough to feel a sense of progression. 

What I loved most about the game was gradually honing the raft that I built into a cleaner and more efficient machine. I liked to find artistic ways to incorporate all my necessary fixtures into a usable space. I really enjoyed making a compact raft with as little wasted space as possible while still feeling like a real, livable space. And that’s something I really liked about Raft specifically over most other base-building survival-type games is just how central the raft itself is. 

A lot of the time in a survival game you can just sort of take off into the wilderness and survive on what you can find, or make a series of small camps along your way, or even just uproot your whole camp and take it with you wherever you need to go. In Raft, your base is all you have, and that forces you to really focus on making it as good as it can be. It's both your camp and your mode of transport, and without it you're completely helpless. It really feels like a part of your character, not least because you construct the entire thing yourself from virtually nothing, even the very ground it's built on. It's got a similar appeal in that way to things like Skyblock in Minecraft.

When it comes down to it, I have a fondness for sailing games and I appreciated the zen-state gameplay that comes eventually as you develop and refine your survival system. I loved the high amounts of customization that you can go into designing your raft, and I liked creating fancy designs in creative mode. I think the art style is just the right amount of cartoonish to be overall pleasant while keeping threats feeling threatening.

I could keep rambling but I think I've said my piece. The game opens up a lot more once you establish a basic survival equilibrium and have the resources to experiment. You can go in, spend hours creating and building, or blow through the story. I think it’s my favorite feel-good game out there, very chill, and incredibly fun. If you have a friend or your wife has a boyfriend like me, play it in co-op, because sharing the fun is always worth it. Definitely worth the price.

Finally, my best friend and I have finished this amazing game. I’ve wanted to complete it ever since the alpha versions came out, when there was only the raft and some floating debris around us. That concept of collecting trash from the water and building your own raft was what initially hooked me.

We only decided to buy the game this year, but we don’t regret a single minute of it, we had such a great time surviving and building our big ship. The game was so engaging that our sessions often lasted over five hours.

[b]I highly recommend buying it![/b]", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1761433086}, {"review_text": "Raft is a fun and cozy survival game that turns a tiny wooden raft into your own floating adventure.

You begin stranded on a tiny raft with nothing but a hook, surrounded by open ocean. From there, it’s all about collecting floating junk, expanding your raft, crafting gear, and fending off a very persistent shark. It’s simple at first, but quickly turns into a full-on ocean adventure.

Co-op is where Raft really shines. I've played the game with my boyfriend and we divided up tasks. 
He build our raft into a floating palace and crafted everything else we needed to survive, while I took care of our needs by gathering supplies and making dinner. 
Exploring islands, diving for resources, and surviving the ocean felt way more fun with both of us working side by side. 
The co-op is smooth and easy, and honestly, it's the perfect game for a cozy gaming session together.

The story is a cool addition too. Finding abandoned outposts and learning what happened to the world gives you a reason to sail beyond your comfort zone. The islands and underwater areas are fun to explore and packed with useful resources.

Overall, I really enjoyed my time in Raft.

There isn't a reason to farm an immense amount of resources especially if you're trying to complete the story. the amount of food and water you have to drink is more tedious than anything. there were multiple craft-able items that we just didn't bother using like almost any item involving titanium because by the time you get titanium, the game is almost finished. I'm recommending the game though just because i think its a game that can be worth the time to play with a friend or two for the one time. and since the game isn't crazy expensive i don't think you'll see yourself saying you wasted your money.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1736714060}, {"review_text": "I mean, I guess the game is fun, I've got a lot of time in it (don't take my playtime literally, I leave games alt-tabbed quite often) just playing with the raft, but frankly it has to be said: this game is scientifically engineered to be an infinite treadmill of annoying BS. In most survival games, you unlock better technology and it helps you survive those elements easier so you can move on to other things. All the technology you have just unlocks a new stream of busywork. 

I mean, you make glass bottles to carry crafted drinks, but after you drink them, the bottle is destroyed. Same with meals, when your clay bowl is destroyed. Why? What is the point? Well it's to force you to endure some BS to get more glass for more bottles. All but I think ONE of the recipes are designed to require ingredients that you can't just grow on your raft. You "can", but all crops except three will eventually run out of seeds and it's back to busywork to get more seeds, especially Strawberries which require you to go to one specific location. There's multiple ingredients that you literally cannot grow at all. You need specific fish for some recipes, but you can't control what fish you get, so you have to fish randomly, but everything wears down quickly, so it's back to more treadmill BS to craft more fishing poles which require materials from islands...

And lastly, the final crime, the really good equipment that finally begins to reduce the busywork, you unlock on the final island, which means the game is over and there's no point anymore. You even unlock engine controls that let you 'drop anchor', but you can't drop the anchor without the upgraded anchor and you get the upgraded anchor on the last island. So for no reason, there's more busywork, requiring you to manually drop the anchor.

This treadmill is probably fine in coop but solo? You just run around endlessly doing pointless errands. You need more fuel? Fuel requires honey (FOR SOME REASON???). Honey can't just come from a beehive, no, you need glass bottles, which you don't get back, so there's MORE BUSYWORK.

Just to underscore the ridiculous busywork one last time: you can craft pipes, and pumps, and things that require electricity. You even have to build a radio system, which lays down wires to the antennas. But you know what you can't craft? ACTUAL ELECTRICAL WIRES. So that means everything runs off of batteries. Batteries run flat very fast. Batteries require fuel to charge (meaning you need more honey so more busywork), or you get the windmill on the second to last island. But at no point can you just connect the windmill to the electrical systems and bypass batteries. Note that you don't need any resources for the windmills, and batteries don't degrade... it literally is just PURE BUSYWORK to make the player run all over the raft constantly swapping fresh batteries with old batteries.
Literally imagine playing Satisfactory but you can only use biofuel generators, requiring you to manually constantly get more biomass to manually feed in to them. That's what this is.

Why did it have to be this way? I don't understand the enormous positive reviews when the gameplay loop is literally intended to be anti-fun and force you to constantly do menial chores. There's no explanation for much of this except to waste your time. How can anyone give a game a positive score that is literally intended to waste your time to the fullest extent possible?", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 34, "timestamp_created": 1749969340}, {"review_text": "Incredibly fair price - surprisingly fun.

For a small survival game, Raft does the job well. The premise is simple: You are on a raft. You need to survive.

Where it differs from other survival games is that you are mostly restricted to your raft. Debris floats endlessly by your raft and you need to capture that debris to build up your floating base.

As you progress, visiting random islands and their reefs is essential to stock up on other resources. And there is actually a story quest line to follow, which will reward you with progressively better raft parts [i](the ability to steer/turn the raft, engines, fuel, controls, larger storage)[/i]

Oh, and there's a shark - apparently named Bruce - who likes to chomp chunks of your raft off, and is ever-circling, waiting for you to dare take a dip in the big blue. If you're especially cruel and playing multiplayer, it is possible to nudge your team member into the sea, too.

For a small game, it does initially feel huge. The conditions are harsh, and you'll spend a lot of time re-arranging, perfecting your raft to become the base of your dreams (and more importantly, needs)

A huge amount of fun has been had for a game that takes up only 6.65GB space. This is one I'll certainly re-visit over and over again. :)

Certainly recommended.

My only gripes:

- [b]No character creation[/b]. You get a choice of two (a male, a female) at the start, and unlock four more characters as you progress. None of them appealed to me, personally. You can change the colour palette of what they're wearing.
- [b]Just as your raft gets awesome, there's no more story.[/b] You've got top tier storage, you can operate your entire raft (river boat, ship, galleon, cruise liner, etc) from one spot. You're drowning in resources... but then there's nothing to do with it?

Suggestions for the developers:

Being very aware the game is 'done', this is only a wish list:
