Crabs-like is the greatest genre to exist, I love you Kril.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1737254086}, {"review_text": "[h1]This game is the Dark Souls of 3D Platformers[/h1]
And I mean that literally, from the way the combat works to the difficulty and several mechanics being very similar to what you'll find in various FromSoft titles. But this game has a sea of original ideas of its own to set itself apart from others in the genre.

For one thing, there's a bit more of a focus on platforming in this game compared to other Souls games. You can swim in mid-air for a short time kind of like Yoshi's flutter jump, and thanks to the drop shadows that always appear right below you, I rarely had issues lining up my jumps properly. The grappling hook you get very early on also unlocks more platforming opportunities and is used very effectively with the level design. It all works well and is very enjoyable, with some surprisingly tough platforming challenges towards the end.

This is also one of the very few 3D platformers to actually have good combat. Unlike many other games in the genre where you can just spam the attack button over and over making it feel mindless, you won't get very far if you try to do so in this game. Similar to Souls games, knowing the best timing to dodge, block or strike requires paying attention to the enemy attack patterns then reacting accordingly. Each enemy type has different attacks that keep you on your toes, constantly evolving as the game progresses and remains interesting from beginning to end.

The combat isn't without its issues, however. The camera can be rather problematic sometimes, occasionally obscuring the view of the enemy you're targeting, leading to me getting hit when I can't even see them. I've also had times where enemy AI gets confused and doesn't really try to attack as they should, leading to me getting some very easy hits on them when I shouldn't. Fortunately, these issues don't happen too often and aren't bad enough to ruin the experience.

Scattered throughout the ocean are various shells you can wear. Simply equipping one will drastically reduce damage taken, but each one also comes with their own skills you can activate with an Umami charge. You can hide in a shell to protect yourself from damage, which goes to the shell instead, but will break after taking too much damage so you may be better off dodging if you can. Parrying is possible by leaving your shell just as the enemy hits, but can be very tough to time so I usually don't bother unless I do so by accident.

The game looks very nice. I loved the ocean setting this game uses and is full of its own personality. Characters are expressive and well animated, each environment feels unique, and the real time cutscenes, when they do show up, are entertaining to watch while also having voice acting that usually gets the job done. What I certainly wasn't expecting, however, was a short mini-documentary of sorts about aquatic ocean life when I booted this game for the first time, yet it still somehow fits into this game's narrative perfectly.

True to the Dark Souls series, this game is tough. Enemies hit hard and you'll die very quickly if you don't "get good" at combat. Microplastics, which are this game's Souls or Runes, can be used to level up at Moon Snail Shells, which are this game's Bonfires or Sites of Grace, but you'll drop every single one on death. You can go back to collect them at the spot you died at, but you'll lose them for good if you die again before doing so. Although punishing, it's never unforgiving, and it helps that dying at a boss will respawn you right before the boss, allowing you to try again quickly without having to go all the way back.

If you do find this game too difficult at any point, however, there are assist options that allow you to reduce damage taken and/or increase damage dealt. There are settings to disable losing Microplastics, as well as giving you a gun to shoot enemies with if you find melee combat too frustrating. However, I "got good" and was able to beat the entire game without them, and I'm glad I did as it made conquering every single challenge feel like a satisfying accomplishment, which I would've felt deprived of had I resorted to changing these settings to make it easier on myself.

For the game's asking price, you're getting a good amount of content as well. The main story can be finished at around 20-30 hours depending on how much you explore and how good you are at the game. New Game Plus becomes available after finishing the game which increases enemy damage drastically and changes enemy layouts, with much stronger foes appearing early on where they did not on your first run, but to make up for this, your shells, levels and most items will carry over. An overall nice way to provide replay value for the more experienced players looking to get even more out of it.

At the time of writing this review, my experience with the genre is very limited. The only other Souls game I have played is Elden Ring, and only for a few hours before getting absolutely destroyed by it. I don't know how this game's difficulty compares to that or other Souls games, but if you want a gateway game to get into the genre, this is a good place to start with. Mechanics are much more simple and not so overwhelming, there's a good amount of platforming and exploration to break up the combat, while also maintaining the difficulty the genre is well known for.

Other than the occasional camera hiccups I mentioned earlier, this game runs really well on my computer with very few glitches, short load times and at 60FPS with very few performance issues even when running on the highest graphics settings. I haven't tried running this game on Steam Deck yet, but for those who have one and want to play this on the go, I have heard it runs fine on that as well.

Not only is this overall an easy game for me to recommend to anyone that's never played a Souls game before and want to get into the genre for the first time, but the unique game mechanics, art style and setting also makes this worth playing even for Souls veterans. It regularly goes on sale, but has enough content to make it worth buying at full price unlike many AAA releases nowadays. It's also gotten me interested in checking out the Dark Souls series of games that inspired this someday in the future, and perhaps giving Elden Ring another chance.

If you do pick this game up but don't end up liking it in the end - just remember that One Crab's Trash is [b]Another Crab's Treasure![/b]", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1756255972}, {"review_text": "In this game, you fight crabs, the camera and the physics engine to reclaim your shell.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1761203522}, {"review_text": "Really fun take on a Soulslike with some Metroidvania vibes. Rating: 9/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1752403548}, {"review_text": "[h1]The Reluctant Forksman[/h1]
TL;DR: A surprisingly well-crafted game that is everything you could want in an indie soulslike. A little easy for the genre, but features creative combat and platforming systems, great comedy writing, and a story that is more touching than a goofy game about crabs has any right to be.[hr][/hr]
I’m wary of trying out new soulslike franchises, especially when they aren’t from a tested studio like From Software. There’s a fine line between challenging and frustrating, and the slightest bit of jank can be a real turnoff in a genre that demands precision. Despite that, [i]Another Crab’s Treasure[/i] got enough affection from people whose opinions I respect that I opted to wade in. What I found was a genuinely funny and enjoyable game that has a few fresh ideas and punches well above its weight.

In [i]Another Crab’s Treasure[/i] you step into the role of Kril, a true hermit of a hermit crab; he lives in a tidepool on the beach, does largely nothing, has no friends, and is perfectly content. He is ushered into utter turmoil after his shell is repossessed to cover back taxes, and he must brave the sea bed in his quest to recover his home. It’s a goofy setup for a story that is unexpectedly grounded, seeing our hero leave his comfort zone to broaden his horizons and find value in things he had previously scarcely considered. Not only relatable, the tale is woven throughout with humor that lands fairly consistently, as well a fair number of groan-worthy marine life puns.

On his odyssey to reclaim his shell, Kril will be forced to take up the fork in self-defense. The melee combat is pretty standard for the genre, but well enough crafted not to feel frustrating except in a few rare situations where footing can be an issue. There are a few variations, like releasing block at the moment of impact to parry, but the real USP comes in the form of shells. Kril can protect himself with a wide variety of found objects, from soda cans to skulls. These have different stats and weights, but the stroke of genius is that different shells enable different spells, and they have their own durability. It’s not uncommon to find yourself scrambling to jump into a new shell in the middle of a boss fight after yours has soaked a few hits. It’s a fun way to tie systems together, and encourages you to try moves you might not otherwise engage with. By the end of the game you’ll probably have a favorite shell, and you can insure it so you always respawn with it, but collecting the different options and trying out the various moves was a lot of fun.

Exploration is a little more lively than most soulslikes, with 3D-platforming eventually bolstered by swimming, climbing, and a grappling hook. Areas start fairly basic and ramp up to some truly impressive levels, ranging from electrified mining rigs to pitch-black abyssal plains. The environs shape the combat, and as mentioned above, this can lead to some slightly wonky encounters, but that is very rare and seemed to happen most in the first handful of levels. The art direction is cartoonish, and fits the tone and humor of the game beautifully. When the surroundings turn inevitably bleak (this [b]is[/b] a soulslike, after all), the loss of light and saturated colors serve to reinforce the severity of the crisis and the depths of Kril’s alienation. This degree of attention to detail is not something I’d expect from a first-time developer, and it’s both impressive and refreshing.

It’s an overused phrase, but this game is a true indie gem, and well worth your time and money if you enjoy the genre. Even if you haven’t in the past, there’s a decent chance you’ll have fun here, and if you get too frustrated, Kril can always bring a gun to any fight and win in one shot. The game’s systems, plot, art direction, humor, and level design have all clearly benefited from a lot of love, are so much better than anticipated, and leave me excited to see what this team puts together in the future.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1739983545}, {"review_text": "By Cod, what a game! Solid Return, But Not a Return to the Old Glory of Dying Light 1 [/h1]

Dying Light: The Beast brings back Kyle Crane and delivers many of the things fans enjoyed about the franchise. On release, it runs surprisingly well on PC. That said, there are also notable design decisions that hold it back, especially for players who loved the complexity and depth of the first game.

[h2] What Works Well [/h2]

Performance & Technical Stability: In my testing, the game holds a steady 60+ FPS at 4K with DLSS or upscaling enabled (no frame generation). It rarely drops in less-demanding scenes, and I didn’t encounter major crashes or instability.

Visuals: Lighting, shadows, ambient occlusion, and general environmental detail are strong. The game looks good, particularly in well-lit areas and during the day. While there is some “noise” in lower-resolution ray tracing effects but it never feels so bad that it breaks immersion.

Movement & Parkour: The core mobility is satisfying. Crane moves well, jumps, climbs, and navigates the world decently well. The "Beast mode" addition gives some new dimension to combat and traversal, which helps freshen up the formula.

Story Elements: Seeing Kyle Crane return and moving toward a conclusion to his arc is one of the more compelling narrative hooks. So far the plot seems engaging and seems to deliver on what many fans hoped for in seeing Crane’s journey.

[h2] What Falls Short / What Could Be Better [/h2]

Grappling & Combat Interruptions: One frustration I repeatedly ran into is zombies being able to grab or interrupt you in ways that feel unfair. Such as being grabbed/grappled mid-air during a drop kick, or losing on momentum / or an attack when you expect an animation to complete but the zombie grabs you and overpowers you mid swing for no reason. Techland noticed.

Kyle Freakin’ Crane Is Back
That’s right.
THE Kyle Crane. The man who dropkicked zombies off rooftops and dropkicked his way into our hearts

This is Crane’s story, and we’re back in it.

I’m Only 5 hours in btw

Already better than Dying Light 2. By a mile.

Should You Buy It?
If Dying Light 2 left a bitter taste in your mouth…
If you’ve been waiting for a proper sequel since 2015…
If your soul still cries out for Kyle Crane and parkour‑based violence…
Then yes.
Buy this game. Immediately.

Kyle Crane is back. After years of torture at the hands of the comically clichéd Baron, Kyle escapes with the help from a rogue scientist named Olivia. The only way he can beat the Baron is to kill super-mutated Chimeras and inject their blood to gain beastly powers, and Olivia will help locate them as the story progresses. Perhaps the only good part of Kyle’s return is how often he voices the player’s own thoughts. How many Chimeras are there to kill? How many towers need climbing? Major characters vanish from the world after they’ve served a purpose. So most quests are dull and some of the writing is awful. Not once but twice did survivors insist that the Baron is the real monster, just after Kyle decapitated his 500th walking corpse. The story is repetitive too, framed around hunting chimeras and doing similar tasks for survivor groups.

Quest activities are not great either. Too often you are sent to a location to climb a long and linear path of ledges. This was bad the first time and continued to be the worst part of quests. When you do get to a destination, you probably won’t find what you are looking for either. All Kyle seems to be doing is running fetch tasks and plugging in cables. 

Fortunately the zombie killing and gore is still good. Ribs are shattered, legs get severed, torsos become separated, and rotten flesh is torn off the bone. What does get a good run are the countless pickup trucks that scatter the landscape. Unless you want to wait for the cold death of the universe, they become the default method of travel. This review is also post hotfix 1.2.1 which addressed 2 major bugs

[h1]What is Dying Light: The Beast[/h1]

Dying Light: The Beast is an open world zombie action game that mixes parkour platforming with melee and ranged combat. Dying Light: The Beast also uses RPG mechanics for a leveling system. This game was originally planned to be a DLC for Dying Light 2, but after some consideration from Techland, the DLC was shelved and reworked into a whole new... well... a whole new Beast. Sorry. Could not resist that one. So the DLC turned into a completely standalone expansion... or full game...  whichever side of that coin you're on. And don't let the price fool you. While it is priced at just shy ($59.99 at time of writing) of the standard USD for a current AAA game ($69.99 at time of writing), it's a big game. But is it an expansion? Is it a full game? Given how it came to be I could see how some would think it's an expansion. But it definitely feels like a completely full game. At the end of the day though, does it really matter? DLC, standalone expansion, full game? None of that should really have an impact on one's enjoyment of the product. The game should speak for itself on that. 


[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

If you've played the other 2 Dying Light games then you know mostly what to expect here. The Beast takes the better aspect of DL1 and 2 and incorporates them here while adding some new mechanics with the beast mode. But for the most part things will be super familiar. Dying Light the beast takes place in Castor Woods, which was once a tourist hotspot, and now a hotspot for the infected. The open world map has a bunch of different locations to including parks, a tourist town loaded to the brim with climbable buildings, a power plant, major factory, and much more. The different sections will house different levels of threats and warn you before entering the area if you are underleveled but does not restrict you. So you are never really gated from exploring the outside parts of the map as long as you are skilled enough. 

Combat is your mix of melee and ranged with certain weapons having durability (with limited repairs) as well as upgrades and mods. And outside of combat you have a mix of various missions broken down into the typical "big bad" arc, chimera hunting missions, and tons of side missions. all which are crucial for gaining XP. 

The game has your typical day night cycle which is common in most open world games. And while the night time may be a little tense for some with the decresed visibility and the increased threats (such as volatiles), it's best not to avoid it when possible as you can get increased XP for missions and kills. And leveling up is important as it makes going to new zones easier, and allows for new skills to be obtained. 

Mobility in Dying Light: The Beast is largely the same as other Dying Light games. You can run, hop, climb buildings, and more. There are trucks you can find scattered about to reach destinations quicker (with limited fuel), a grappling hook you can get later in the game, and more. Using mobility is essential to this type of game, for while it's really fun to fight zombies, there are situations where you really want to avoid them. Especially at nighttime as you might come across the volatile which are extremely hard to fight and will chase you until you can reach a safe zone. 

The Beast mode is the main new addition to the game. Beast mode is triggered when your rage meter is full, and basically makes the character pretty much overpowered for a limited duration, which primarily starts out with them having increased strength allow them to rip and shred through zombies with ease, even refilling their health with kills. As you level this up though you gain new abilities including offensive and mobility types. One of the best things though is that you will even be able to level up to points where you have more control on when to use the beast mode, and even being able to initiate it before the meter is even full. So at first it is limited, but later on you can use it a lot more. And it comes in super handy in the more tough encounters. 


[h1]Audio[/h1]

It's great! You don't have a constant blast of loud music, except in certain situations. Most of the time the music is very subtle and more audible parts are well spaced out to give you more opportunity to focus on the ambient sounds of the world which are important to know your surroundings, especially at night time. You'll hear zombies growling nearby, or maybe the occasional gunfire or other survivors (friend or foe?) talking in the distance, as well as other natural sounds of the environment. Occasionally the music will ramp up to more audible levels and change in some instances, like when zombies are on the attack, boss fights, or getting chased by the occasional volatile! There's nothing really to complain about here. It's well mixed and it sounds great! 

[h1]Performance check[/h1]

Dying Light: The Beast uses Techland's own in-house engine called the C-Engine (rebranded Chrome Engine) Chrome Engine has been around for over 20 years. Don't worry. While Chrome Engine has been around for over 2 decades, it has been rebuilt several times and the current version, now know as C-Engine, is great. So far from my own experience and what I have seen from others the game is extremely well optimized. However there are some noticeable omissions at release that hopefully will be addressed and fixed soon. For right now the game only has settings that go to high. There is no very high or ultra. Now this could be intentional and left this way permanently, or it could be leaving room for the game to get a slight graphic bump later on as new increased graphic setting ceilings are added. Also missing was the announced ray tracing feature. And since this was mentioned before game release I am certain it will be added later on. For those who want a more optimal experience the game does also support upscalers including DLSS, FSR and XeSS. There is also frame generation, but honestly unless your computer is really struggling the frame generation is almost certainly unneeded as I said the game is already well optimized and hitting an FPS of 60 or above should be easy for a lot of people. At the highest settings with DLSS Quality on my own system I was getting around 80-90 FPS with a newer GPU (4070ti) and an older CPU (i7-9700KF) and 32GB of Ram. The game recommends you have at least 16GB of ram, and this checks as the game by itself actually pulls in around just shy of 8GB of RAM by itself. With max settings also Dedicated VRAM was pulling a little over 7GB. 

The game also has native support for Ultrawide as tested with my own 3440x1440 monitor. The caveat on ultrawide for some though may be the placement of the UI. Luckily it is not stretched, but instead places the UI in a 16:9 orientation on the screen. I personally did not find this to be an issue, and others may also prefer this as the UI readouts will be easier to set your eyes on. But your preference may differ. There are some mods available for those that would rather have the edges of the UI fixed to the corners of the screen instead. 

[h1]Closing[/h1]

While the beast is more of the same, this is not a bad thing. It offers up the same familiar fun of the previous games with a slight new addition of the beast abilities. The game is extremely well optimized and an all around blast to play.

I'll first start by stating that I am mostly an ambivalent fan of the franchise. Zombie games ruled the landscape of 2012-2016, and Dying Light was the only exception that added anything to the stale formula that had grown old, stale and safe. The parkour, the grappling hook, Be The Zombie, and all of the other unique and special things made me both love and dislike the game. Until today, I would say DL was a great game for the time (Albeit, with its issues of the story, and the following, but that's for the past.)

10 years later, and the rather unexceptional release of DL2, we have finally arrived at Dying Light: The Beast, and with Crane back, it was the signal for a return to form for the franchise, with new mechanics, and a hopefully revamped story... Or so it was to be.

[h3] So how is it? [/h3]
Good-ish. Once again, Techland hit some marks, missed (this time a lot), and missed some hits so far off the mark you can't even score it. 

[h2] On the World (The Map) [/h2]
DL is a franchise that lives and dies through the parkour and movement mechanics. DL:TB does not compliment this at all. In fact, it's rather mediocre, sometimes even just bad. The Slums and Old Town of Harran perfectly complimented the mechanics of the first game, there was enough both to run, sprint, vault, wall run, ledge, perch, and climb on, without flat fields of nothing (until you reached Old Town, and even these were minor.) In TB, half of the map is literal countryside/suburbish areas. Only the Old Town of this game compliments the mechanics this franchise is best known for. Flat open fields of nothing but grass, hills, sometimes roads, a highway, and the occasional house or small building is not. This isn't as much of a problem by the first few hours of gameplay, but as soon as you get out of the Old Town and the quests of Town Hall and explore the rest of the map you realize that Techland has adopted the Ubisoft Open World model of dropping a few keypoints of interest/places to do quests in, and the rest of the world simply serves as the mandatary form of wasting your time by either having to run (or drive) your way hundreds of kilometers off in Narnia to do one specific thing of a quest, or to pick up one item. This is especially bad the second you start doing the quests for the Exiled, where they have you walk from the northernmost point of the map all the way down south for some quests. It's just clearly padding, and doesn't fit the style of the franchise whatsoever. On top of this, despite how big the map looks in the in game overlay, you'll soon realize that it's just split four ways into the Mountains/hills side of the South, the West of this games Old Town, the North of an industrial center, and the East of random homes, suburbs, and small forests. The rest of the map is unused, and just there to force you to do side missions, or hunt for specific trophies/mementos. It felt underwhelming, weak, and worst of all, just an excuse to extend the games low 16 hour campaign into more playtime. 

[h2] On the Gameplay (and The Beast) [/h2]
Expect the standard DL formula. Find random weapons from the environment, from dead guys, or from quests, use them till they break, fix em, or find a new shinier weapon to replace that weapon, or a blueprint that becomes your main weapon. Nothing of this was changed. I didn't mind this in DL, and I don't mind it either in TB, but if you were a person that hated that gimmick, then don't expect anything mindblowing here. You still have to hit a zombie a couple times, dash back to regen stamina, use a bandage, and all that, at least until you get legendary weapons, where the zombies mostly become pushovers that you can kill in two or three swings, and the tension of getting swarmed is gone. However, the gore and the actual feeling of getting that hit on the zombies is incredible. The gore is Dead Island 2 tier of good, maybe even better. You can knock off parts of skulls, mandibles, break bones clearly, rip intestines, etc. It is fantastically done, very satisfying to fight enemies. Missions are mostly the same. Talk to a person, said person bosses you around, Crane does it, walk 100km to go get to said item, walk back 100km to give back said item. Still busy work, and still nothing special. As for the elephant in the room, the Beast System is nothing revolutionary, but certainly something that helps the old combat being far more enjoyable. Crane essentially tweaks out, pulls his two guns, and punches zombies/tears them in half, and against some enemies (like the dudes with the rebar hammers, or the Charger guys) you get unique and special executions to finally put the pin cushions down. The main problem is that not enough was done to make unleashing the beast more than anything of an assistance (and against bosses, a crutch). Unleashing the Beast forces you into Melee, which in difficulties like Brutal, means you can easily die in one or two hits (such as fighting some bosses of this game, the Chimeras). While this would be an awesome power fantasy, it dies the second you realize you get nothing more than punching, a ground slam, or jumping up high and slamming back down(You can also charge run, but this doesn't do much, and you can also kick, but the kick is the same generic animation with more damage). You can use the environment against the world, but you can only lift rocks/engine blocks. This was honestly the biggest mood killer for me because it would have been awesome for Crane to be able to lift up zombies, toss them like rag dolls, or even just using said zombie as a weapon, or lifting cars, fridges, desks, etc. Limiting this to two things really kills the power fantasy when Demolishers can break the floor to launch rocks at you, and you can only really throw grandmas porch rocks in response or punch him until you can do the execution. You can also scream, but this does really nothing but force a few generic zombies to stand in place. Greatly missed opportunities.

[h2] On the Skilltree (and movement)[/h2]
Another of the games major L's is undeniably in the skill tree. The Level Cap in TB is 15, and while this wouldn't be a bad thing on its own, it is, when we compare what skills we get here versus in DL or even DL2. In TB, Crane kept almost all of his parkour abilities( Except being able to slide kick). The skills you have to unlock the rest of his movement (Vault Kicking, Rolling after dropping, the Dropkick) are all things that have been seen a thousand times already (and you even start with some, like Wall Running). In fact, for some reason, despite being "The Beast" Crane is rather slow and sluggish, (especially in Ledge Jumping, where you sometimes snap into a random ledge, or get richocheted up in the sky). The skill tree itself also clearly seems to be half done. Getting a blueprint for a flamethrower? Grenade Launcher? Grenades? Really? This by far has the smallest skill tree in the 3 games, and certainly the least rich one. It is probably unironically faster to just sprint normally than it is to waste your time trying to climb up unto rooftops and trying to lower yourself constantly from there. In terms of the Parkour, I would say this is the weakest of the three. DL2 had Aiden be a motorcycle, gliding, dashing, running everywhere. DL1 had you unable to even run without wasting stamina, forcing you to think where to go, where to run up to, and where to avoid enemies. In TB, you do it to explore, or to get away from volatiles. 

[h2] On the Story [/h2]
TLDR, because I'm running out of characters, The Baron is an TEMU version of Albert Wesker. Betrayals happen out of circumstance, not conviction. The fact that Crane can beat Volatiles with his bare hands and shoes, letting some twink belittle him is just character assassination in the worst form.

[h2] Conclusion [/h2]

I was overall mostly satisfied with the game. A lot changed, a lot could be better. Get it on a sale. 6/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1763968074}, {"review_text": "Having finished Dying Light 3 with 100% completion and all achievements unlocked, I can finally share the full picture of the world revealed in this installment.

To my surprise, the return of the car was completely pointless here. In the first game, it made sense: massive open fields, speed, freedom, fun. Here? Narrow streets, trees everywhere, and good luck turning without hitting something. 

The second thing that hit me right away was the missing glider. Man, in the second game, that thing was a revelation. Combined with the grappling hook and other mechanics, you could become a true parkour legend, a master of movement and air. The glider let you zip back to places you’d already explored, skipping tedious runs, making exploration fast and fun. Losing it in this third game was a huge loss for me.

Subway could’ve helped. Like in Dying Light 2, one click and boom — instant travel. Sure, running around is fun at first — it even helps you explore — but after a while, you just want a faster way to reach specific spots. Subway solved that perfectly back then.

Compared to the previous entries, Dying Light 3 feels noticeably simplified. In the first game, players could level up all the way to Legend level 250, in the second — even to 300. Here? You hit the ceiling at level 15. It feels like your character’s growth got cut off halfway through the gym membership. On top of that, side quests are few and far between — barely enough to fill a weekend. The tougher parkour challenges that once made Dying Light stand out are also gone.

In that sense, Dying Light 3 feels like a “lite” version of itself — streamlined, trimmed down, maybe even a bit too neat. Still, to be fair, on other hands it might actually enjoy that. Less grind, fewer distractions, more straight-to-the-point zombie smashing.

And yet, playing this game, you get the feeling that you’re experiencing both the first and the second parts at once. And despite the shortcomings mentioned above, it somehow preserved the beloved combat mechanics, skill progression, and overall spirit of the series. 

I can’t skip over the combat system and gameplay — they don’t just replicate what came before but evolve it with fresh touches like the Beast Power ability and those brutally satisfying finishers. It looks and feels downright awesome. And exploring the world and leveling up your character? That’s pure Dying Light 2 at its finest — lovely, fluid, and endlessly satisfying. That’s what keeps the game feeling alive and exciting.

And of course, playing as Kyle Crane again with the original voice acting? Absolute joy. Sure, the game’s a little different, but that doesn’t make it bad. In fact, Dying Light 3 feels like a graceful continuation of the series, seamlessly blending the soul of the first two games into one captivating whole. And it gives a fresh, unique experience that’s totally worth it enjoying from start to finish.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758222138}, {"review_text": "Much closer to DL1 in gameplay and tone - great so far", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1758568061}]

I do enjoy them, though. If you are a total scrub/noob/casual that's simply happy to be at the party, then this one's for you.

FF: COTW is actually really good. The art style is great, it runs perfectly, and it's easy enough to get into without having to lab for hours on end just to be able to beat the AI. Coming from SF6 - it's most direct competitor - I would say this game serves the hardcore FGC a bit more than SF, but not by much. In some ways, mostly related to structure and design focus, it's certainly more for serious players. Comparing the two, COTW is stripped back and focused, with one great example being the single player RPG mode. 

In SF6, World Tour is like this whole pseudo-open world game with random NPC's, food vendors, etc. Episodes of Southtown reminds me of older, classic FG campaigns, like Soul Calibur etc.  The dialogue is text based and the entire focus is on fights. There is no running around, you literally just choose the next battle you want to participate in. That doesn't mean it isn't fun, though. It gets right to the point, and I can see how some people actually prefer this style to World Tour in SF6.  For casuals, I'd say this mode really shines at teaching you the most natural way possible how to play and win. You start off with total jobbers who are easy to beat by spamming throws and specials, and it ramps up at a steady and manageable pace from there. It is infinitely more interesting and engaging than combo tutorials and way less anxiety than online matches.  In this way, I think Episodes of Southtown is perfect. 

In terms of mechanics, the move set is surprisingly deep; the defense options are nutty, for instance. Considering it's ostensibly a 4 button game (there's a REV button so sort of 5), it takes a little variety away from attacks but gives you more depth in other areas that overall change up the game enough that it doesn't feel like a SF6 side story. It's its own game, but similar enough that you should be able to transition from one to the other no problem. Similar to SF6's Drive Gauge/Burnout system, there is a REV system here, but it works in reverse. Instead of actions depleting the gauge, they build up until you overheat. The ways both of these systems work are very similar overall, though, and of of course your super gauges build and are used like you'd expect, too. 

For casuals, one thing I'd point out is that spacing feels tighter in COTW. Throws, crouching heavy kicks, etc, feel like they need to be closer to land when compared to SF6. This is dependent on the character, of course, so I am talking about overall feel.  I also noticed more attacks that penetrate block, like overheads, and there's also some attacks that have what we Dark Souls guys would call poise. Luckily most I've seen are slow super heavy attacks that you can throw them out of if you're mindful, but if you try to trade or hit them out of it, it won't work.  This is the kind of stuff that makes you stop and think more during a fight, which is why I think it leans more into a hardcore fanbase, but just a bit. In SF6, there is so much you can do in terms of pressure that you can win a lot of matches by just being relentless. This game has a little more strategy imo. 

There's been a lot of crossover between the SF and FF franchises as of late, which I think is a good thing. Fighting games are niche for the most part, so bringing everyone together is an important part of sustainability. There's a lot of high level players out there, and I love watching their matches even if I could never hope to play at their level. I'm just glad these franchises are coming back in a big way and am super, super satisfied with City of the Wolves. It plays great, it's very engaging in all modes, and the pricing structure so far is reasonable and fair compared to SF6. You get more content with SF6, for sure, but at the end of the day, I imagine there are a lot of players who don't need that content anyways. City of the Wolves is a mechanically strong and uncompromising fighting game that will reward the committed but offers little to onboard, entertain, or retain those outside the hardcore competitive scene. If SNK sticks the landing with DLC and ongoing support, this could very well become a competitive staple.

But as it stands today, it’s not for everyone and it probably never really tried to be.

Full Review:
City of the Wolves is a good fighting game for players who thrive in tournament-level environments or just like to grind ranked. In many ways, it delivers exactly what a specific segment of the FGC has been asking for: a high skill ceiling, powerful defensive mechanics, no universal "neutral skip" options like Drive Rush, and clear, consistent match outcomes that reflect skill gaps between players.

If SNK supports the game with consistent high-quality DLC characters for the promised three seasons alongside meaningful balance updates, City of the Wolves could become a tournament favorite. If you're a competitive-minded player, or tired of SF6/Tekken 8, and you're willing to lab out the JD/HD system, this game may be exactly what you're looking for.

That said, for casual, beginner, or even some intermediate players, I think City of the Wolves asks too much and gives back too little for its $60 price tag. The game bombards you with systems, and JD and HD in particular can be major hurdle. Especially once you layer in JD&HD cancels, and frame 0 supers. It does little to teach or ease players into its mechanics, which may alienate anyone not already embedded in the competitive mindset or willing to adopt it.

The roster is a mixed bag. Unless you're a die-hard Fatal Fury (MotW in particular) fan, or you're content treating characters as "functions" rather than personalities (as I suspect many players are), the cast may feel underwhelming if you were expecting more "colorful" characters like the ones from KOF or SF6.

I don’t personally value single-player content in fighting games, but to echo the general sentiment: Arcade Mode is enjoyable if you're invested in Fatal Fury lore and want to see these characters' arcs concluded. EoST is a neat concept, but it's ultimately barebones and repetitive.

As for the marketing, between celebrity guests and flashy sponsorships, there was a disconnect somewhere. The developers set out to create a focused, niche love letter to Fatal Fury, a heartfelt sendoff for a beloved franchise. Meanwhile, the marketing tried to sell it as a mainstream, earth-shattering franchise revival which it simply isn’t.

City of the Wolves is a mechanically polished, high-commitment fighter that offers deep rewards for the dedicated. But it builds no bridges for anyone outside that mindset, and even less for those just starting out. It’s a game that knows exactly what it is, and for better or worse, refuses to compromise.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1747762158}, {"review_text": "fun game, but honestly, not worth the buy. small, niche community that is not friendly to new players online. unless you wanna get one-and-doned and teabagged constantly, just don't even waste your time or money and enjoy your day elsewhere.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 17, "timestamp_created": 1749683496}, {"review_text": "Ahhhh, I hesitated and hesitated. [/th][/table]

Is this game a masterpiece? No, but it is still one of the premier fighting games on Steam. One of the most successful Japanese 1v1 fighting game series has finally received a sequel after 26 years. But well, the big fighting game series are immortal - even if they sometimes take longer breaks, a new installment will always be released to continue the franchise. Whether it's Tekken, Mortal Kombat, Street Fighter, Soulcalibur, Guilty Gear, Dead or Alive or King of Fighters - a new part is always released at some point. This was also the case with Fatal Fury, even if it took 26 years. Fatal Fury was one of the major fighting series on the luxury NEO GEO console, the priceless home console of the 90s that brought arcade quality into the living room for its well-heeled customers. The NEO GEO console was known above all for its fighting games - over a third of the 150 games released were from this genre. This included the Fatal Fury series, of which a total of eight games were released for the NEO GEO between 1991 and 1999. The last installment was the fantastic Garou: Mark of the Wolves (SNK, 1999). And now comes the next installment, Fatal Fury: City of the Wolves, allegedly financed with money from Saudi Arabia, produced and published by SNK (the manufacturer of the NEO GEO), just as it was back then.

Although it is set in the same universe as the older games in the series, it is of course not necessary for you to know the old games. In fighting games, the background story is usually not that important anyway. Although there is usually one, sometimes elaborated in great detail (or even made into a movie), in essence there are always two fighters facing each other and hitting each other until the loser's energy bar is depleted. What sounds very primitive is actually a fine art - especially in the good games of the genre. There is a lot to consider and learn here, from the countless different attacks and defense moves to the right timing and, of course, the combos. There is also the REV system - where you can perform additional actions under certain conditions as long as the REV meter is not overheated.

The heart of the game is of course the online mode - in addition to casual fights, there are also ranked fights that affect your online ranking. The rollback netcode ensures a smooth online experience, and battles can also take place across platforms (but can be turned off). There is also a “Clone” mode, where you fight against an opponent created by artificial intelligence based on your own online battles - so you are effectively fighting against a clone of yourself.

In Episodes of South Town (EOST) you play through a story - you choose a character and explore the town almost like in a role-playing game. You choose where to go next, can find hidden locations, talk to other characters, watch your character rise in rank and get better, there are even additional improvements to find - and also fight various enemies. You can see the approximate strength of your opponents before the fight (and any unusual details of the fight). If you lose, you can try each fight an infinite number of times. All in all, an interesting way to get to know your character and prepare yourself for the tough online battles.

You can currently choose between 16 fighters. More are scheduled to be added via DLC in the coming months. You can currently only buy the game in the Special Edition - this already includes Season Pass 1 with the five additional fighters planned until early 2026. In addition to the actual game with online mode, offline mode and the new EOST story mode, Fatal Fury: City of Wolves also offers a few extras. For example, a jukebox where you can put together and listen to your favorite songs, or an overview of the short films with the background story that have already been unlocked. Graphics are also unlocked during the course of the game and can be viewed in a separate overview. In another menu, you can customize your fighter's graphics to your liking - by changing the color of his various items of clothing.

The controls on the PC work great with the gamepad, whereby exotic devices - such as my beloved Stadia controller (with Bluetooth) - are also perfectly supported.

[u][b] Conclusion:[/b][/u]
A fighting game that appeals to both casual and competitive gamers. It's fun to fight your way through the story and explore South Town in single-player mode. It's also fun to sit on the couch with your family in local 2-player mode and try out a few new moves while chatting about the day's events. It's less fun to be beaten down by a stranger in a matter of seconds in online mode without even having the chance to fight back. Damn, some players are really good! The game has only just been released, hasn't it? Well, practice makes perfect, I'll specialize in May now and then we'll see if I can win a fight or two online!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1750180400}, {"review_text": "I waited a quarter of a century for a new Fatal Fury game only for established characters to get sidelined for street fighter characters, a real life dive grass player and some random dj that is friends with SNK's current owners. Guest characters just come off as cheap marketing and makes it look like you don't have faith in your own character, history or brand. 

Maybe I'll pick the game up in a few years when the whole thing hits 75-80% off. The game could be the greatest fighting game every, but jamming in real celebrities into the game devalues the game as a whole.

I assumed this would just be a run of the mill survival craft game, but I was wrong. This is more like a blend of Stardew Valley, Core Keeper and Rim World. Gameplay is a mashup of Rimworld's colony control and camera placement with Terraria's progression and gameplay style. Progression and combat are reasonably challenging, with mercy mechanics to help bypass bottlenecks where skill and gear alone aren't getting the job done. Necesse does a great job at hitting all the normal things of this genre and does it well. I tried Terraria multiple times but never got into it. I always thought the 2D vertical design was dumb and it kept me out of immersing in the game. Necesse is absolutely everything I hoped Terraria would be when I first got it, plus the Rimworld elementa are a very nice element. This is up there with my other favorite games. The QoL features are amazing and the devs listen to the community and roll out fixes as quickly as possible.

There’s a lot of content. Multiple island types, randomized cave generation, NPC’s, bosses, mobs. Not to mention the whole settlement mechanic: assigning workstations/storage, being able to assign specific items/categories to said storages, building the houses and farms, assigning what to craft and how often they can craft it, etc. If you’re dedicated enough, even if you’re not making the town look nice like I am, it’s quite a timesink. 

The beauty of this game is, you play how you want. The missions are just there to help you know where to go next but you can do whatever your little heart desires. I know easier said than done but try not to over think things! All things come in abundance!! It’s not like some games where there’s a small chance to get something and then you will never see it again. Ya know? Everything can be obtained as many times as you want! As long as you explore and visit different islands, you’re golden. 

The developer (there’s only one guy working on the game) pumps out a decent-sized often so there’s always something to expect. I’d say the game is very polished, obviously there’ll be some things that’d be better, I certainly noticed some things, but you’ll get used to it. I really think it could reach Terraria levels if it reaches a certain point of popularity where the developers can start upping their output and just go wild with content. W game, 8.5/10, would recommend.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 17, "timestamp_created": 1758646309}, {"review_text": "It's about the journey, not the destination. The ultra late-game of Necesse is characterized by an endless stream of boss fights against bosses you've already fought, just with boosted stats (barring a handful of new bosses in unique zones who then become part of the repeat-with-boosted-stats roster). I may or may not see the game through to the final boss, because the reward at this stage is just boosted stats on my own equipment.

But that doesn't put me off of recommending it. It just feels like I've hit the "infinite mode" at the end of the game (though I know it's not infinite, I'd estimate the ultra lategame provides about as much gameplay as the rest of the game put together, but missing a lot of the variety).

All the reviews compare this game favorably to other popular games, I'll try to give some details on why those favorable comparisons get drawn. It's in the little details. Like the forge, operating the same as a furnace in minecraft or other games, has two slots by default for smelting. It only smelts one thing at a time, but it smelts the higher-tier ore into bars first, then smelts the lower-tier ore, and it has two output slots so it can go automatically. This prevents you having the "wall of furnaces" so common in this kind of game, in my wife and I's MP game, we've gotten to the end of the game using two forges the whole way through. It lets you build a smithy that actually looks like a smithy.

And that's another great thing about the game. The decorations. They really let you dress up your base so it feels lived-in. Characters' mood is improved by having a well-decorated bedroom, and your mages enchanting chances are better if they're happier, so you're rewarded for decorating. And it's easy to do, too! Slap down a table and a couple of chairs, craft a decoration for on the table, a few potted plants, and you've got a lively looking bedroom in a few seconds.

A caveat: We play on Adventure (the second-easiest) difficulty, with item drop on death and food spoilage turned off. Neither of us is a big fan of padding playtime with increased difficulty. And at least for us, this is the perfect difficulty. We still die occasionally in fights, but we never get stuck. So my advice if you're reading reviews and put off by some of them mentioning hard bosses: You can change the difficulty midgame, and have nothing to prove to anyone, just tune the difficulty to where you feel comfortable. There aren't even achievements related to difficulty.

Another great thing to mention is how easy it is to feed your settlers. I'll remind you again: We play with food spoilage turned off, so I'm unfamiliar with how the icebox works, but compared to Rimworld, where the primary difficulty with large bases lies in reliably feeding your colonists, some quick back of the envelope math is all it took to have an infinite food supply going. We have about 45 settlers in our settlement, and I planted 40 of each crop once we had them all available (conveniently, the storage boxes show "x unknown items" in the categories, so I knew how many types of seeds there were before we had access to them and could prepare the farmland ahead of time), we had 40 settlers at the time. Settlers automatically replant crops when they harvest them, and every settler is capable of farming and equally competent at it, so combined with a few cooking stations (each workstation can only hold 10 automatic recipes for settlers to craft, which annoyed me when I first ran into it but then I realized naturally makes your base look larger when it [i]should[/i] look larger), we have our settlers automatically crafting every variety of "gourmet" quality food. Even before we had the high-tier cooking crafting table, feeding our colonists was never an issue. Nothing is wasted in this game, if you break a blueberry bush, you get a blueberry bush sapling, 100% of the time. So just relocate some blueberry bushes near your housing in the early game and your settlers will be contentedly eating "simple" quality blueberries all day until you can sort out your production lines.

I saw a negative review that mentioned the settlement storage settings were confusing. I'm biased coming from 100s of hours of Rimworld, but I found it all fairly intuitive. The kinds of problems you run into with the storage are the same you run into with rimworld, you set a list of allowed things and a priority for the container, so if you forget about a chest on the other side of your base that allows the same things as the one you're looking at, you might be scratching your head wondering where the stuff you're looking for is. But this same system has copy/paste so you can delete a storage and remake it with the same settings instantly if you find a new container you like the aesthetic of more, and you can set a limit to how many stacks of each item are in a container, preventing a "drops" storage from filling up with 10000 bones. In the midgame, you unlock a shipping container you can send your colonists on trading missions to sell the contents of, and this is also an option for "settlement storage" that you can buy extra copies of. [h1] So, what is Necesse? [/h1] 

Well, if Terraria and Minecraft had a baby... and if Stardew Valley and Rimworld had a second baby... and then, by some chance, if THOSE two babies met, and one thing led to another - what would emerge is the utterly charming gem that is Necesse. 

In short, Necesse feels like somebody tastefully put Terraria sprites in a Stardew Valley world, with Stardew-style farm management and Rimworld-Lite™ colony management + building, with endless procedural world exploration.

Necesse seems to have taken its inspiration from all the best qualities of the spiritual predecessors mentioned above, and yet nothing feels out of place or particularly tedious. You can tell just about every aspect of the game was designed with the player in mind. 

What if you like the appearance of wood walls over stone? 
No big deal, they appear to function the same - build however you like. 

What if you're one of those players who wants the game to hate your guts? 
No problem - there are many settings you can tweak your liking to make your time playing as merciless as possible. 

Whether a filthy casual or a glutton for punishment, there's options for just about any player in Necesse.

Even in early access, it's been [b]a wonderful experience that I cannot recommend enough,[/b] as a grizzled veteran of these sorts of titles. 

Most other similar titles feel at least somewhat contrived to me in one way or another, but Necesse is truly something special in the making. 

[h1] Automation/Management, you say? [/h1]
[h2](+ Thoughts on Intuitive Design) [/h2]

Games with management systems walk a fine line between ease of use, technical complexity/depth, and tedium. 

Necesse's automation system, while not the most intuitive at first, is simple enough to understand without needing a tutorial, while retaining depth. By contrast, it's nowhere as overwhelming/byzantine as Rimworld's.

I've only had to look up a few things in my playthrough (only to realize I just hadn't recruited a specific settler type that lets me automate collecting a certain resource).

While it could be more intuitive from an interface/UI standpoint (early access, remember) Necesse's management system feels accessible enough for casual players, and deep enough for those who enjoy in-depth colony management with granular control over how things go in their settlement. 

Rimworld almost requires granularity. Kenshi suffers without it. Necesse purrs along and simply benefits from it - if that's your preference.

For context, Rimworld is one of my favorite games ever, along with Kenshi... but I did have to research quite a bit to understand the systems and their quirks/nuances for both games - Rimworld, primarily due to its technicality, complexity, and granularity... and Kenshi, due to, well... what I'd call an "endearing lack of polish requiring players to get creative." 

Haven't had to really do that with Necesse so far, from a UI standpoint, which has been a breath of fresh air. 

Maybe I'm crazy, but when I play a game, I prefer to spend more time [i]playing the game[/i] than looking up [i]how to play the game.[/i]

[h1] Thoughtful Design Choices and Player-Centric QoL Features [/h1]

I play on Normal with default settings, as I'm still on my first playthrough. Every time I've felt like I might consider stepping up the difficulty, I get slapped by something and have to go retrieve my inventory, which feels like the perfect balance to me.

To the previous point, I did savescum a lot in both Rimworld and Kenshi to keep the experience enjoyable for me and not overly punishing. However, games that autosave too often can enable overt savescumming, which can be a boon for very punishing games/bugs, but can also become a slippery slope of cheese in some games, causing you to miss out on half of the experience if abused. 

Necesse does keep save backups, should you run into issues of any kind. I'm not sure if there's a native way to save more frequently than once every in-game day, but that design choice feels like a balanced compromise to make big mistakes fixable without taking away from the wins/losses of experiencing the game in full.

I've only savescummed Necesse after fumbling my Deck and banishing a settler by mistake, or learning I shouldn't keep dynamite in my hotbar while at my base... but after the lulz of discovering I should never trust a lever out in the wild, it was more worthwhile to go to retrieve my stuff than to reset that day's progress and re-explore those areas. This keeps me engaged in the gameplay loop, but also keeps settlement mishaps easy to fix, since I tend to pass more days at my base than out in the mines - so less progress is lost if I need to restore. Fair compromise.

There are countless other little technical QoL features that give the impression of truly thoughtful design, some of which I imagine could have only come from a developer having been in such a situation themselves - looking up where their autosaves are stored locally after a save corrupted, renaming a main character or world through save editing, etc. 

There is even a dark mode UI window in the settings, and plenty of other customization options to refine your visual UI experience to your preferences. The settings menu is well worth a gander once you're acquainted with the game and understand what the settings refer to.

[h1] The Soundtrack [/h1]

The soundtrack has some [b]bona fide bangers,[/b] and without spoilers, the integrated ability to collect specific tracks in-world and set them up in "playlists" however you like (whether in settlement or exploring) really keeps the experience feeling fresh.

"Murky Mire" for in settlement, for something chill and vibey.

[h1] Early Access/Bugs [/h1]

On the point about Early Access - I have only come across very minor bugs so far, myself. They were very intuitive to find workarounds for, without having to give it a Goog. 

For example, on a specific repeat dialogue window, I wasn't able to re-select the same choice again. So I'd have to move the dialogue selection to the second choice and back again, in order for me to select the first choice. Stuff like that - very minor and hardly an inconvenience.

It has the exploration of both games, the crazy dungeon madness and bosses of Terraria, and the digging and ore discovery of Minecraft. Similar to Stardew in its [b]gameplay[/b], Necesse offers a little variation to the series with the option of playing with friends. Where Minecraft has pre-built villages, Necesse gets the player to make everything from the ground up. In short, a pretty solid game with replayability.

Necesse has pretty decent [b]gameplay[/b] for similar games of its genre. Navigating the [b]controls[/b] and menus are a little funky at first, but after getting used to the [b]control[/b] systems the game starts to flow quite nicely for the player. BothFor example, one of the main items the player will use is torches. Torches have been assigned as a hotkey on both the controller and keyboard. Both methods of control work fine depending on what the player prefers. The game can be a little wonky sometimes when trying to build, especially juggling the twin-stick shooter scheme incorporated into the game, as both the building and shooting/fighting can be relatively the same when trying to perform the action. It does take a little getting used to and when the player does, defending, attacking, and even building become easier and easier. The essential premise of the game is exploring above ground (and even travelling to different island biomes) and exploring caves underneath. Caves underneath provide most of the resources the player will need to further their progress in the game.

Cave formations are seed generated (as all the parts of the maps are) and feel well balanced in enemies, ore, sections, and treasures. The starting map is a good difficulty and offers a chance for players to get a good foundation in all areas (creating a settlement, crafting items, recruiting other NPCs to join). The dungeon itself is sort of difficult without the right equipment, but as I moved on to other lands and other dungeons I quickly realized I'm going to have to start equipping myself better (in addition to taking NPCs that joined my settlement to fight alongside me). The settlement feature in this game is absolutely amazing. Where Minecraft and Terraria players build from the ground up, there are some parts of the map that already exist or villages that already exist. Necesse sort of has that, but the player is designing it all. This means houses, common areas, walkways, farms, husbandry, recruitment of new villagers... all of it! This is what sort of makes the game unique in its own sense as the player is sort of building their own NPC village (like Minecraft), but unlike a seed generator, the player makes ALL of it! This paired with the ability to have some automation in the game adds value to the player's time, allowing them to go off and explore or establish new settlements.

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] resemble that of Stardew's, but has some unique animations and shaders of its own. Music generally switches or adapts to the particular environment (or map) and isn't overpowering or overwhelming (actually pleasant to listen to). The required sounds are all there in the game and can sometimes become a little annoying (imagine mining in Minecraft, holding down the left button, and hearing that "clang" sound over and over again). Both domains were given proper attention to deliver a pretty good game.

Overall, the game is really well done for an Indie type game. It can be overwhelming, sometimes it can be underwhelming, but for the most part its quite fun. The fact its also coop/multiplayer also makes the game that much more appealing. If there was a split-screen option - I feel that would attract a lot more players to try it out. Family sharing is there but I haven't had the chance to try it out. By the time the story ends, you won't remember any of it, and trust me, that is for the best.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 11, "timestamp_created": 1744960058}, {"review_text": "I'm an old-school MK fan, ever since Mk2 on Sega I've been playing every game in the series. With Mk1, looking at its release quality and the predatory monetization practices they implemented soon after, I decided to wait a while and only recently picked it up on sale.

The game looks gorgeous, I kinda enjoyed the story mode (not the DLC part though, it's horrible beyond any words), I like the roster, I don't mind the grind and the customization system is fine by me. But no matter what I do I just can't have fun with this game at all, which is pretty sad and frustrating. And the issues this time are not so much on the surface, so it took me a while to figure it out why it feels so bad to play MK1 for me.

[b]I came to a conclusion that the game is just... too hardcore for me, and not in a fun way[/b]. With thousands of online matches in MKX and MK11, I just can't get a grasp on this one, and most importantly I don't want to cause it doesn't feel rewarding.

All the mechanics that currently piled up in the game, and the way they're implemented, and all the long-standing issues, they all together smothering me as a player from all sides. It's like I'm mostly fighting against the game rather than my opponents. I mean, how in such a dynamic game am I supposed keep in mind:
[list]
[*][b]Cameo moves and their shitty delayed inputs
[*][b]Move enhancements
[*][b]Fatal blows
[*][b]Cameo fatal blows
[*][b]Desperate moves
[*][b]Perfect blocks and upward blocks
[*][b]Extra-mechanics of every character on the roster [/b](stances, cancels, trap-setups, portals, you name it)
[/list]

All of this + remembering your regular combo strings and specials.
All of this + your attack won't hit cause the game has no actual hit/hurt boxes and uses cheap solution in form of polygon mesh collision instead.
All of this + sloppy online connection.
All of this + some stings in combos don't schedule for no clear reason and require absurdly precise input timings after the character recovery.
All of this + bdf/bfd/dbf... specials that are difficult to pull off consistently. 


[b]NOW AT WHAT POINT CAN I ACTUALLY FOCUS ON JUST PLAYING AND ENJOYING THE GAME?[/b]


When between all that cognitive load do I have a window to actually think about my opponent's actions, about my or their mix-ups, about zoning, and everything else that fighting games are about? How many hundreds of hours do I need to learn all of the above on the muscle memory level and switch my mind to something that is actually fun in the game?

And then I'm comparing this to previous games, MKX and MK11, where it took just a fragment of these efforts to consistently pull off beautiful satisfying combos that involve several different specials and basic attacks.

I remember how I used to main Erran Black and there was a not so hard string that includes almost all the character gimmicks - shooting, acid, rifle butt strikes, slides. Or MK11 Geras string that I used to spam online that had bed of spikes, time freeze and sand portal in it - all you wanna see from your boi.

Now in MK1 it feels like you have to do twice the effort, and the string you get would be something like "punches combo, legs combo, one special that basically looks and feels like a normal attack, more punches, same special". Make it twice as long by slapping a cameo extender after learning its unintuitive timing by heart.


It just doesn't feel worth it to learn all of it to start having fun, not for me at least.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1761682800}, {"review_text": "I'll start by saying that I really wanted to like this game but just couldn't. Invasions sucks. Krypt should be a staple in all MK games.

As a long-time fan of the series, I have played every Mortal Kombat game that has been released on PC. I have over 1,000 hours in MK11, and I bought this one right after its release.

Bringing back characters that weren't in the previous installment of the game like Ermac, Ashrah, Li Mei or Havik was a great idea, the graphics are really decent and the gameplay would be fine too, however, a few key changes make the game drastically lose its value.

Firstly, the Kameo characters – I understand the idea behind this, but it completely doesn't fit the Mortal Kombat playstyle. I often found myself completely ignoring the existence of these characterss, both solo and ranked, despite the advantages they offer. From what I understand, the game was originally intended to be Injustice 3, which didn't happen for reasons unknown to me. While this idea could have worked in Injustice, here it's a completely unnecessary addition that poorly justifies the lack of more iconic characters like Kano, Sonya, or Goro.

Secondly, there's a lack of any solo play content. In the previous installment, we had the Crypt and Towers of Time, which easily sufficed for hours of gameplay. There was grinding, that's true, but it was rewarded with cosmetic items. In MK11, we could customize our weapons, masks, and even our character's intro/outro, which provided a unique customization for every player. In this game, everything was hidden behind greedy monetization, with time-based called "Invasion" events that were incredibly boring with stupid and frustrating puzzles and the rewards were maybe one unique skin, while the rest were recolors of the base skins. Overall, compared to MK11, this installment feels completely neutered. Even MK10 had more to offer.

The final issue is the discontinuation of support for the game after the release of the first and last DLC, which was unsustainably expensive for its content, leading the studio to complain that the add-on sold poorly.

I hope the next Mortal Kombat will be more thoughtful.
