[{"review_text": "This game requires 3rd-party DRM and anti-cheat: XIGNCODE 3, though not enforced by the new policy, I believe it should still be disclosed on the store page for transparency reasons.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1750596477}, {"review_text": "Fun game, however it's overshadowed by the fact this is an always online title. Meaning once they axe the servers, goodbye to all your DLCs and game! 

Literally no reason for it to be this way.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1743285478}, {"review_text": "[h2] One critical flaw... [h2]
Don't get me wrong, the game is great. One of the best if not the best rhytm game I've recently played, but there's one single HUGE mistake devs made... Whole game is always online. You can't play even a simple singleplayer track without the internet connection. I understand that implementing a DRM in a game is a good way of dealing with piracy, but it shouldn't have a place in games like DJ MAX.

All of the older games in the series got killed by "always online" mechanic, and surely, one day, Respect V will face the same fate.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1749224930}, {"review_text": "DJMAX RESPECT V is a fantastic starting point for anyone new to VSRGs, especially those who prefer to play with a controller, the original charting was made with a DualShock4 in mind as this game is essentially an enhanced version of the original PS4 version, therefore the diversity of majority of patterns are limited to what the DualShock4 and a pair of thumbs are capable of, for better or worse.

The game offers a solid variety of difficulty in charts, great for easing a new player into higher difficulties, each of the 100+ songs typically has 3 different difficulties with a 4th, made specifically in mind for keyboards, that is, in each of the four game modes of 4b 5b 6b & 8b., this is some outstanding value if you buy the base game when it goes on sales for 80% off, you are getting over 1000+ charts, and even more with DLC, although I wouldn't particularly recommend it.

DJMAX RESPECT PS4 was my first VSRG, I played it for over 400+ hours, watched myself improve every day, bought every DLC up to V EXT 3, played damn near every chart on 4b & 6b, spent hours competing for top scores on the leaderboards...
But the PS4 version has many, many critical problems that I will not get into here, what matters is this versions gameplay is superior in almost every way.

However I am deeply concerned with the direction the company in charge of this game is taking it in.

Firstly they have large;y abandoned their PlayStation playerbase, bringing DJMAX RESPECT V solely to XBOX and Steam and REMOVED critical features such as the fast/slow indicator and delay offset options from the original PS4 game entirely.

This game has implemented online only DRM and could in theory at any point revoke any ability to play the game and it's content from it's users just as they have done in the past to their older games as well as not allowing you to play offline or when servers are down (PS4 version doesn't have this problem btw)

The sheer amount of DLC, Battlepasses, micro-transactions this version has is astounding, it breaks my heart even thinking of buying anything other than the base game when they could and inevitably will pull the plug in the future (I'm also personally not buying anything twice lol)

I love DJMAX, I even play the PSP games but THIS DJMAX worries me dearly, I can't justify spending a cent more than I already have on the PS4 version, especially so when there are FREE alternatives here on PC such as Quaver and Osu! Mania. This game does not guarantee you'll own it in the next decade, it'has been turned into another scummy live service.

TLDR Good for learning VSRGs, only buy at 80% off, beware DRM, microtransactions, immense quantity of paywalled content and the inevitable death of the live service likely leading to you having wasted your money, which the company has a record of\ doing just that. Play Quaver and Osu! Mania.

I don't recommend opting for the PS4 version instead, it has far too many issues.

We can only hope that the DRM is removed when support is dropped buuttt with their track record.. I doubt it.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1747670011}, {"review_text": "71 GB for a rhythm game is absolute madness but it's a good rhythm game fun songs", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1747826212}, {"review_text": "for those who wonder why there were so many negative reviews for a while: there was a certain song out there that caused a major uproar in the country this game was made in, and the producers planned to include the track in the V Liberty 3 pack, without knowing the potential consequenses, 2 days after the trailer, they decided to ban it and replace it with a completely different track, a remix of 1 of the Base game songs to be precise. there's still nothing that can be done about the fact they made a mistake, so for now the June 2025 ratings will still stay very low until they decided to change their responses again like i did. negativity over, here's the actual review:

i think it goes without saying that this is 1 of the best rhythm games on steam, and it was 1 of my main interests when starting on that platform. you can play about 200 different songs in the base game alone, and with all packs released so far, the total hits at around 700, which will soon be 720. i've owned the game since August 2020, and i've improved my rhythm skills by a lot during these 5 years. more about that later.

the game has massive sales which occur quite often. these sales make almost all packs 4/5 times as cheap, resulting in the Deluxe Edition costing almost less then the base-game without sale! the sales are weaker with the newer packs, which only get 15% for the newest pack, 35% for the 2nd newest, 50% for the third and 65% for 4th. but that's still more than most recent games, so they're good deals nontheless. with the full sales, you can buy every pack for around 150 euros, which is a much better deal than most other rhythm games!

if you want to know which packs to buy: Trilogy gives the highest Tracks to Cash ratio and is rather cheap, but most tracks miss a few charts. Clazziquai is ideal for if you want to start out on 8B mode having very easy charts. the Technika packs each feature great music and special charts in mission mode. the Black Square pack isn't as reccomended from the Legacy packs but can still be very enjoyable. Portable 3 features the exclusive Remix charts which are very fun to play, even if they are tough. Emotional Sense let's you practice the songs normally exclusive to the mission mode, but is actually unnecesary for 100%!  just about every pack in the deluxe edition gives brandnew tracks which are of high quality. save the collabs for last as they aren't that important; but if a pack gives songs you love to play, feel free to buy them!

there are lots of gameplay videos of this game out there, and there's a guide / checklist for all the achievements, but in order to 100% the game you must own every pack minus the Gear packs, and perform some nigh-impossible feats, including clearing some missions that seem quite unreasonable, but for 60% the achievements aren't too hard to get.

as for my skill level... when i started out i had trouble clearing charts of level 8, and i was very proud of myself when i finally managed to pass an SC pattern or a level 12 chart. in 2021 my skill increased a bit, with me being able to clear a few level 14 charts & clearing multiple Technika exclusive charts. 2022 the scale got redesigned, and with the help of tier lists, i could pass a few normal scale level 15 charts. 2023 my ability in this game generally improved a lot, being able to pass charts of SC9 (at the time, comparable to new SC6) and eventually SC10 as well. 2024, before the 2.0 update which completely rehauled the level system, i've been clearing normalscale level 13 charts left and right, and was able to clear a few SC12 charts on 4B mode, as well as SC9 on 5B and 6B, and SC6/7 on 8B.

with the scaleback the 2.0 update caused, i'm still able to clear almost every SC9 chart (and half of SC10) on 4B, 60% of SC8 on 5B, a few SC9 charts on 6B, and most ~SC5 charts on 8B. so i'm ironically better with SC then Normalscale on 8B! my DJpower generally stays at around 7.8K for 4B, 7K for 5B, 7.2K for 6B, 6K for 8B. since i'm still getting better at the game, my power remains at fairly equal value, but i'm afraid that after a few more packs, i can't hit Pro DJ anymore on 5B mode & High Class on 4B... oh well, i don't have to be the master in this game!

the main issue this game has is that it's massive like you might realize. if you plan to buy it, make sure to spend about an hour doing other fun activities, so that the game can download at it's own pace.

and for those who are wondering why there's potential unsafe content, don't worry too much about it. it's primarily the 13th season that caused the issue, which focused on swimsuits; and Lena had... some "issues" during that season. no wardrobe malfunction, but she had quite a revealing swimsuit, which apparently triggered the unsafe alarm.

all in all an excellent rhythm game that i highly suggest to most people that played rhythm games in the past! it you can save at least 100GB of room on your console, that is.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1749815388}, {"review_text": "This is no doubt the most impressive rhythm game on Steam, so I can definitely recommend it for people who really like this genre. Hope you're looking forward to being unable to play every time they do server maintenance.  And if that wasn't bad enough, just look at what happened to previous djmax games, almost none of them are playable anymore due to the same thing.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1745300939}, {"review_text": "Note- The game is currently being review bombed over inconsequential streamer drama. Ignore it, nothing about it matters unless you're a terminally online Korean.

It's a pretty phenomenal rhythm game with a massive catalog. The price tag is not as daunting as it initially seems, if you shop around for sales you can get everything very cheap. I got the game and every non collaboration dlc for like $70. If you're wondering what dlcs to get, you want V extensions 1-5, and V liberty 1-2 (and presumably 1-5 later). After that you want Portable 3, classiquai, black square, trilogy, emotional sense, and all the technikas. This covers the main expansions and the songs from older games. The collaboration packs can be safely ignored if you're not interested in the games they're from.

The music itself is notably a bit better than most rhythm games. There's a pretty good amount of variety here, so you'll find something you like. There's some songs I don't care for, some that are fine, and some that are stuck in my head on a daily basis. In addition, every single song has a custom music video. Sometimes these are kinda lame (or a bit too anime for my tastes), but they're often very cool, or at least odd enough to be intriguing. It's a very neat addition to the standard formula and beats the digital bands you'd get in games like guitar hero.

This game uses keysounds, which is also pretty cool. Essentially, various noises during songs are directly controlled by your keystrokes. If you don't hit the key then it won't play at all, and you can be early or late. Some people don't like this, but I think the majority (including myself) think it's a nice feature. It makes you feel like you're actually contributing to the song.

There are some negatives, but not anything terrible. The biggest one is that the game is always online, for basically no reason. The devs are VERY concerned about piracy, though this is actually a bit less extreme than they've been in the past. Previous games required a usb key to play the game. Yes, seriously. Obviously this is unreasonable and bad, and you should be aware that if they ever decide to abandon the game's servers without making an offline mode then the game will become unplayable. I'm willing to take that risk, but you should know what you're getting into before making a decision.

I'm also not a big fan of the constant focus on anime waifus. Just not really my thing, and that's down to personal taste. That said, some songs I would be a bit embarassed if somebody was looking over my shoulder while I was playing them. Take that as you will.

The game's size is a bit big. It's understandable considering all of the videos and audio, but wow 70gb is massive for a rhythm game.

Overall, I see this game fulfilling all my rhythm game needs for the next few years at least. If you're a fan of the genre or looking to get started with it, I'd suggest picking it up.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1749790151}, {"review_text": "Amazing rhythm game! For one thing, I have no idea how any human being in any year in the current century releases a rhythm game which does not have accurate and system-wide audio offset syncing. For some reason rhythm games are the only genre where, because for some reason the discrepancy between audio output and visual synchronization cannot be optimized out, it has to be either detected, or, worse, manually programmed in by the player. Nothing makes me instantly hate my experience with a rhythm game more than playing the first song, realizing how off-sync it is, and then learning that instead of some kind of handy detection algorithm or input sensor to calibrate my offeset, I have to manually tweak a number by hand and then test it, basically cooking a steak by estimating in degrees until it's burnt or raw at the end.

It needs to be clarified: there IS one offset sync detector in the game, and it works for the judgement window just fine--but it does NOT work for the actual tracking of objects on screen, which means, in addition to having to compensate for the visual desync regardless of going through the detection process, if you leave audible keystrokes on, they will be so off-beat your performance will demonstrably suffer as your ears and hands try continuously to reconcile the discrepancy.

This is rhythm game 101, and it was solved over 15 years ago by the most basic implementations of this genre on PC hardware. Even if this aspect of the interface was somehow tolerable, all visual adjustment options are either entirely cosmetic or relegated purely to lane position and speed. You do not get a note-size value, you do not get an option to change the lane orientation to highway or moving up, and a stupid amount of the playefield is taken up by a useless arcade pad simulation which robs you of already valuable screenspace in a game where the default speeds won't uncluster groups enough, and the max speeds will rocket notes down to the fake arcade pad too fast to react. This is, again, rhythm game 101, and it has been solved, but not implemented in this game in any fashion.

I could stop there and I think I have to for my sanity's sake, because no amount of good songs or good charting could ever make up for these fundamental system level flaws... but then you get to the actual songs, and 75% of them are either instantly forgettable electronica or j-pop hybrids with a tempo more suited to elevator music than a rhythm game. The charts compensate for this a bit by rapidly switching lines of instrumentation, but I couldn't discern the immediate association between my inputs and which tracks I was hearing, if they were affected at all... so switching instrumentation tracks was often just a pure guess. And what's the unique feature this game adds in its most basic gameplay model, which constitutes it's ENORMOUS 66 gigabyte install footprint? Animated backgrounds. Animated backgrounds that are just as functional for gameplay as the animated backgrounds were in Dance Dance Revolution, except instead of individually tailored sequences that are toned down in terms of their graphical impact so as not to overload the player with visual noise, these are often animated music videos or excerpts from similar, meaning they'll demand your visual attention even if you want to focus on the notes instead. You can, of course, turn them off, but then what on earth am I wasting 60GB of hard-drive space for? 

The last straw is the DLC. Even picking this game up on sale, even grabbing the DLC at an 80% discount if you do, they are outrageously overpriced, basically equalling out to $1-2 per song in a pack of about 20 songs. Maybe that's the going rate for rhythm game DLC at this point, but there are an infinite amount of free ones with better features, more usable system interfaces, less space wasted on pointless background animations, and limitless song libraries due to the nature of them being free in the first place.

This game is not bad--it is terrible. It is beyond terrible--it is not functional as a basic gameplay model within its genre. It is borderline theft, and the only reason I'm glad I finally bought it after years of debating is so I can definitely say it is not worth a purchase in any universe, multiverse, or meta-verse which exists, will exist, or ever has existed.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1735431149}, {"review_text": "DJMax Respect V: Finally, a rhythm game that lets me fail stylishly to Korean/Japanese bangers at 300 BPM while questioning all my life choices.

I binged OT 1&2 before this game came out because i was anticipating the enjoyment i would have for this game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1764889429}, {"review_text": "[b]From Zero to... Well, About Eighty Hours Later[/b]

Look, I'm not saying Octopath Traveler 0 consumed my life, but I definitely forgot what sunlight looks like and my houseplants have staged an intervention.

[b]The Good Stuff:[/b]

This is what happens when Square Enix takes their mobile game, strips out all the gacha nonsense (thank the pixel gods), and asks "what if we made this "actually good"?" The result? A legitimate 80-100 hour JRPG that somehow justifies every minute.

Let's talk about the elephant in the room: [b]EIGHT-PERSON PARTY BATTLES[/b]. Not four. EIGHT. Split between front and back rows with completely different tactical roles. The front row dishes out pain while the back row recovers HP and SP every turn, and you can swap them mid-combat. It's like the previous games' combat system got a tactical depth upgrade and suddenly became the most engaging turn-based system I've touched in years. Breaking enemy shields with your front line while your back row batteries up for massive Boosted attacks? "Chef's kiss". This isn't just an improvement—it's a complete game-changer that makes every fight feel like you're conducting an orchestra of violence.

Character customization is here for the first time in the series, which is great because I finally got to create a protagonist who looks appropriately dead inside after their hometown gets torched in the opening. Speaking of which, the story actually *coheres* this time instead of being eight separate tales awkwardly duct-taped together. Your town burns down, bad guys need punching, revenge needs serving—simple, effective, emotionally devastating.

The HD-2D art style remains absolutely gorgeous. It's like someone took my childhood SNES memories, ran them through a modern graphics card, and added depth-of-field blur just to make me cry.

[b]The "It's Complicated" Stuff:[/b]

Town building is here and it's... fine? It's like someone said "what if Stardew Valley, but make it medieval trauma recovery?" You'll rebuild your hometown brick by brick while hunting down the jerks who burned it down. Does it feel slightly weird to pause your revenge quest to arrange crop fields? Yes. Will you do it anyway because those stat bonuses are too good to ignore? Also yes.

Random encounters remain as prevalent as ever (series veterans know what they signed up for). The combat is so good that I don't mind, but if you bounced off the previous games because of the encounter rate, nothing's changed here. You will fight. A lot.

[b]The Reality Check:[/b]

The middle section drags like you're walking through molasses. The prologue slaps, the finale delivers, but hours 40-60? That's when you'll question your life choices. Power through it. The payoff is worth it.

With 30+ recruitable characters, some inevitably feel like glorified stat sticks. You'll have your core crew and then... everyone else who shows up for a side quest then ghosts you harder than that Tinder match from 2023.

[b]Bottom Line:[/b]

Octopath Traveler 0 is a 100-hour commitment to beautiful sadness and tactical excellence. It's comfort food for JRPG fans who miss when Square Enix made games that respected their time by *not* respecting their time at all. The town building is whatever, the random encounters are excessive, and yes, you will occasionally wonder if this could have been a 60-hour game.

But then you'll pull off a perfect Break chain into a Boost-powered ultimate ability while Yasunori Nishiki's soundtrack swells dramatically in the background, and you'll remember why you play JRPGs in the first place.

[b]Recommended if:[/b] You have 100 hours to spare, you're emotionally prepared for pixel-art trauma, and you think "town management during a revenge quest" sounds like reasonable multitasking.

[b]Not recommended if:[/b] You value your free time, hate random encounters, or think 80 hours is "too long" for a game. (It is. I played it anyway. Send help.)

[b]Final Score:[/b] "Started from zero, now we're several existential crises deep" out of 10.

The game isn't bad at all, it's fun and filled with content, but it is a step back in budget investement.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1764933787}, {"review_text": "This is a fairly early review but I've gotten into the main gameplay loop (and have played the other Octopath games) and I can say that I am really enjoying it. 

All of my playtime so far has been on the Steamdeck. It runs very well at the default settings and  battery life has been fine (It seems like I'd get around 3 hours) even at 60 FPS so capping it to 30 would likely result in battery life that is longer than my attention span but I haven't required that so I'm keeping it at 60 FPS for now. Some people have mentioned low quality audio issues but I haven't noticed them, possibly because I am playing on a handheld with small speakers. The only issue I have run into is that occasionally during a cut scene I will get a very brief audio crackle but this is very sporadic and hasn't really bothered me.

For those who have played Octopath games, you'll like this if you liked the other games and you won't like this if you didn't like the others. The main change is that you have a single protagonist and then 30+ recruit-able characters to fill out an 8 person party. The main protagonist is completely customize-able and the others have a set job that can then be upgraded and refined a bit but only the protagonist can completely change jobs.

For those who haven't played an Octopath game this is essentially a more old-school take on the JRPG formula that is heavily influenced by pen and paper RPGs. You build out a party where each member has a job/class and that composition influences how you approach combat and also opens up path actions that allow you to interact with NPCs that you meet along the way. This could be anything from haggling, picking fights, stealing, or just opening up new dialogue options depending on your abilities. It is really a nice approach that leads to a more open ended gameplay experience instead of being on rails as has been more common  in JRPGs.  There is a "main story" still but even that has branching paths and then these branching paths have a large variety of side quests so the game word really feels a lot more like a pen and paper RPG without being totally open ended/open world. It is a nice compromise in my opinion.

Combat is turn based and similar to the bravely default games where you can stock up extra actions and then strategically take big turns or just boost to stun an enemy by attacking its weak points to stop it from taking its turn. Add to this the strategy of back row of characters and it is a very engaging system that builds nicely on the past two entries in the series.

Music is solid fantasy fare and I've already caught myself humming along to some of the tracks. I'll probably end up picking up the soundtrack at some point if they put it on Steam (not having it available on any modern game seems like giving up free money, very strange decision).

If I had to list complaints, I would say that graphically, the game feels like a step back from Octopath 2. It still has the same general HD 2D look that this series pioneered but there are some pretty low quality texture (I have these set to high in the settings) and occasionally there will be something extremely low poly in the background to the point that it looks distractingly out of place when you notice it. The look really reminds me of a PSP game in places  due to some of the low quality textures and I have to assume this is an artifact of this game starting life as a mobile game that was likely designed to run on a potato. It doesn't ruin the game or anything but some times I'll run across a texture straight out of the late 2000s and it does take me out of the experience a bit. I sort of hope some of these will get patched out but I'm not holding my breath.

All the things I wanted from COTC, like adding fan and book as weapons, allowing the job classes to remain distinct from the previous mainline entry (Octopath 2 did an OK job with this concept but Octopath 0 has continued that approach), and kind of simplifying the UI are all here.  This is not the same as Octopath 2 and that's a good thing, if people are expecting the big single player RPG it's still here, it's just that some of 2's bells and whistles are not here in return for various aspects that helped COTC stand out from 1 and 2.

Now, does all the above make the game good?  I'm less than 4 hours in, so it's probably too early to tell.  So far, I'm enjoying my time, but I am also someone who has loved each Octopath game in its own way even though COTC's gacha was absolute trash and this game mercifully lacks that "feature."  Unfortunately, even if you've pre-ordered the game, it does not look like you can recreate a character like Sophia from COTC as your MC.  But that makes sense, it would be self-sabotaging of them to make this game too similar to COTC after all.

Maybe this means COTC will eventually go away and we'll have this game to make up for that?  Maybe this means future games will also feature fan and book weapons and thus make various classes have slightly better coverage but subsequently make the game just that much more complex?  We're going to have to see.

The things they added to this game help it seem just that much more similar to the other entries.  In that, Square Enix didn't just make a gacha-less port of Champions of the Continent and call it a day.  In an age of remakes and remasters where the devs half-ass things, it's refreshing seeing that bare minimum effort.

Is that asking for too little?  Yes.  Maybe you're the kind of person who refunds right before 2 hours or feels that games shouldn't be this expensive in general. I played Octopath Traveller 2 for ~200 hours across 3 playthroughs. This game is just not landing for me. The story in OT2 had separate tales for each character, each building towards a larger, mysterious narrative. It was dark, foreboding and engaging. Granted, some characters like Agnea were kind of asinine to the plot, but it all felt like it was leading towards something larger and that kept me hooked. 

In Octopath Traveller Zero, there appears to only be 3 narratives (unless you count the skeleton system of base building as a narrative path, which I don't), which is 3 villains with magic rings. These are the most generic, cartoon-level villains you can imagine. 

One has a ring of power, who laughs maniacally and kills his own soldiers for no reason. 
One has a ring of wealth who laughs maniacally and kills her own subjects for no reason. 
One has a ring of fame, who - you guessed it - laughs maniacally and kills their own servants for no reason.

There's no back story, no real plot, just, hey look these 3 INSANE SERIAL KILLERS are bad, you should go fight them. Bland, dull, unengaging, AI-level slop. 

Power guy burns down your village in the first 5 minutes, so there's some motive to go after him, but I don't see any real incentive for you story-wise to even pursue the other two. Other than the intro scene (which from a character's point of view was never seen), these 3 goofballs might as well have nothing to do with each other. They never interact with each other again. 

Which leads me on to my next point - the stories are 2 acts shorter. If you got used to the 5 story arcs for each character in OT2 (40 total), think again buster. These ones conclude after 3 acts per arc. So that's 9 acts total. Barely any time to flesh out the characters. Which I suppose is a blessing given that all 3 of them are completely ridiculous, over-the-top psychopaths with zero nuance. 

Okay but is the gameplay any good? Well, not really. The town mechanics have the same systems as OT2 - haggle, recruit, duel, etc. Nothing new, just more of the same. Except now it's tied to your power, wealth and fame levels, which is kind of worse. 

The main character doesn't talk. I didn't think this would bother me much (given I grew up in the era of FF7, Star Ocean 2, etc), but having a mute main character while everyone else can talk takes me out of the scenes. I don't feel like I'm part of the story, I feel like a camera man following around the people that are. 

For each person you recruit, you might get a short mini-quest to recruit them, but that's it. If you were hoping for any character development AT ALL for your party members, you're going to be disappointed. There's also this weird thing where for some scenes, the characters have no audible dialogue. Then in the next scene, they suddenly have audible dialogue. Either have them talk or don't. 

The combat systems are rehashed from OT2. They didn't even bother to add anything new. No new classes or abilities. In fact they dumbed down a lot of skills and made them worse - for example changing poison effects to be a "chance" instead of guaranteed. And it feels like a 20% chance. So you can't build around it like you could in OT2. The main strategy now is break bar, then physical attack. It's brainless. 

Also the way they've added the skills, by making some skills specific to certain characters, I thought was a weird direction to go in and makes the game quite limiting in what you can do. For example, if your main character is an apothecary, you won't have the same skills as the apothecary you can recruit. I made the mistake of making my MC a hunter, because I saw the other hunter you recruit got an ability that lets them heal after battle. But the same skill didn't appear for me after levelling. 

The concept of adding skills to compensate this is great, but the execution here is awful. You have to unlock slots to add the skills, and these cost a LOT of job points, which you also need to spend on job skills. So, do you want more skills from your class, or the ability to add more skills through another system? Because these will be competing for the same points. If these were two separate point systems, it wouldn't be as bad. But having to choose/sacrifice one for another is wack. 

Okay so the story and gameplay are lame, but is the combat fun? No. Not at all. Every single random battle is now brainlessly easy. You don't need to break anything. Just boost, attack and it will die instantly. Boss fights are the only ones that don't die in one hit, but then the new system of 8 party members makes this too easy. Damn, the boss just hit me for 50% of my health! Oh well, to the backrow you go, where you're completely safe and passively heal HP and SP. It also means you have way more opportunities to chip away at the break bar compared to OT2. And the break bars here have like 6+ weaknesses. Most of the time, they're weak to swords, axes and bows. So you often have access to all 4 rows of party members all hitting the boss for 4x the same weakness every turn with boost. You look at their bar at 16 and initially go daaamn, then realize you can break it in one turn. YAWN. 

My advice to the devs is - if you're going to implement 8 party member battles then have them all out at the same time, and build the mechanics and bosses around that. Then it's new, and purpose built. Here it just seems to be added because fvck it, why not. Nothing feels thought out. 

The more I play, the less engaged I am. It's more of the same, but it's not the same. It's watered down and mind-numbing in every aspect compared to OT2. I could forgive if one area was weaker, but it's every area. I'm forcing myself to continue playing at this point.

Palworld has been incredibly entertaining for someone like me who is constantly looking for good survival games. Many games leave a lot to be desired when it comes to inventory management, base building and accessibility for people who want to play with different settings.

Palworld has a ton of potential to be a game capable of nailing all 3, from the simplistic design and gameplay that feeds very well into the survival aspect, to the many settings allowing you to adjust grind and pace of the experience. Endgame consists of perfecting your favorite pals, amassing a ton of loot and fighting difficult Raid bosses. That being said, there are still some very unpleasant experiences waiting to be had.

- Endgame Raids are tuned for groups and min-maxed pals. Expect to spend weeks breeding and perfecting stats/IV's/Traits on a specific meta pal for that Raid boss just to be able to beat them alone. Newest raid bosses/Oil rigs are difficulty sponges, add more damage and health. Oil rigs alone are very unrewarding with drop chances for legendary weapons being abnormally low, and loot from oil rig enemies is pathetic so most people end up rushing through them. It's pretty bad.

- No options for speeding up breeding/altering RNG of traits being transferred. Breeding is a HUGE part of palworlds progression, and while you can technically complete all bosses without breeding, it is very hard to do so and most End-Game bosses demand you have at least a maxed souls/IV's pal team at level cap. Breeding can take days to get what you want and its all up to RNG.

- Base building is very unpolished. Expect frequent frustration as you have difficulty placing down items as they find random invisible objects underground preventing you from building there. You cannot multi-build, have fun placing 20 pillars down individually every 3 tiles away to create solid support for structures if you hate the clunkiness and uncertainty of building on ground. No Cross hatching or triangle pieces either, enjoy making a square fort in a circular radius of your base.

- Nintendo. Probably affecting this game in the most negative way possible. Due to a lawsuit that nintendo threw at palworld, many features are currently at risk, or have been removed. You can no longer release your pals by throwing them out due to nintendo patenting the throwing mechanic, making releasing your pals very clunky. Thankfully palworld was able to fix it up to be much more tolerable. So far nintendo has been a huge roadblock for palworld over petty jealousy of being very successful with mechanics that pokemon uses. Instead of letting palworld flourish into an amazing game, they are trying to burry it in the dirt and prevent anyone from switching to a pokemon alternative. My combat strategy?  Pure, unadulterated pandemonium! I release my Pals, yell some words of encouragement (mostly incoherently), and hope for the best.  It's less strategy and more controlled chaos, but hey, it works more often than you'd think!

The Steam Version Sadly Has a Few Issues Though [/h1]

[h3] Actual Review (No Spoilers) [/h3]
I completed this game on the Wii years ago, and a second completion was still fun as ever. The Lego games as a whole are so charming and instant nostalgia machines. I’m unsure if it’s specifically the steam version, but I did notice quite a few differences, particularly with audio, but there are some other changes made from the original two games as well.

The biggest difference/issue is a lot of bugged SFX. Episodes 1-3 in particular have some missing or changed SFX in and out of cutscenes. Episodes 4-6 are much better, but some cutscenes still have broken or straight up muted audio. Again, not sure if this is steam specific.

The other noticeable changes are all gameplay/character related (rip Yoda hoverchair) but due to the various changes some levels have, these are most likely intentional. Albeit slightly annoying. At the end of the day though, these are mostly minor nitpicks. The game as a whole still is a blast.

These older Lego games have such great characterization and physical comedy due to no voice acting. Definitely the best part of the games. The gameplay itself eventually boils down to turning off your brain and running around interacting with everything, but that’s not really a knock on the game due to it being marketed as a kids game.

The time trial and challenge modes are probably where most of the replayability lies. Optimizing your strats to get high scores is still satisfying as ever. Whether solo or co-op, this game continues to be timeless. 9/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1753034432}, {"review_text": "Never gets old trying to 100% (minus the spaceship missions, those blow lol)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1756137540}, {"review_text": "Stunningly functional port of a childhood classic, co-op works well and the gameplay is the same jank I remember from the Gamecube, 10/10.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1751048992}, {"review_text": "I played this on my cousin's Wii back in like 2011-2012 and we had hella fun killing each other. Story: 5/10

Not much to tell—the game has minimal dialogue since it primarily focuses on crafting, mining, fishing, and grinding for materials. The Core at the center is the only source of guidance, providing objectives and occasionally offering some background story and clues about past events.

Gameplay: 9/10

The gameplay feels like a mix of Stardew Valley and Terraria. The game features Health, Mana, and Hunger mechanics.

Hunger affects max HP, but it's not too punishing when it reaches 0%, unlike other survival games.

Health can be upgraded in various ways, such as wearing armor or consuming rare items that permanently increase max HP.

Mana can be frustrating early on as it depletes quickly. However, its regeneration is fair even without a mage-focused build, and it becomes more manageable with dedicated armor or a build centered around magic and mana regeneration.

Combat feels smooth and accessible, offering a variety of builds and playstyles, whether you prefer ranged attacks, melee, magic, summons, explosives, or a combination. In my opinion, melee and ranged weapons feel overpowered from early to end-game due to their high damage and consistency.

The skill tree takes considerable time to fully max out. It levels up similarly to Skyrim—the more you perform an action, the more proficient you become in that skill. Reaching certain skill levels unlocks passive abilities that contribute to character builds. However, you can't acquire every perk even at max level, as you have a limited number of points to allocate, likely for balancing reasons.

Crafting is straightforward and enjoyable, with a vast array of items to create, including base structures, weapons, tools, and other necessities.

Item drops are well-balanced, with specific drop rates for each item. Some rare items may require respawning bosses multiple times to obtain.

Cooking is one of the game’s best features. There are no restrictions on combinations, and with over 100 ingredients, you can create unique food buffs that enhance combat and activities like mining or exploration.

Farming is decent but could be improved. While there are plenty of seeds available, the yield per harvest is quite low—typically just two seeds per crop. Even after maxing out the Gardening skill, seed drops still feel RNG-dependent.

Fishing is straightforward and serves as the primary method for acquiring fish-based ingredients. Many of the best food buffs in the game come from fish-based meals.

Animal Husbandry is poorly implemented and could use improvements. Some cattle species do not respawn in their designated biomes, while others are overpopulated and scattered across different regions. Breeding is also slow, making it difficult to farm meat efficiently. Additionally, animal drops feel underwhelming—milk cannot be used in cooking, wool can be found in chests, and overall, it's not worth the effort.

The map design is great and simple. The overworld is circular, with the player spawning at the center. There are seven main biomes and six sub-biomes, providing plenty to explore. Fast travel options become available from early to mid-game, making navigation more convenient.

Difficulty: 6/10

The game isn't too difficult as long as you prepare properly before fighting bosses. Food buffs and potions provide significant advantages. Every weapon type can be viable against bosses with the right build and buffs. Boss patterns are predictable if you pay attention, making the fights enjoyable rather than frustrating.

My Verdict: 8/10

This is a fantastic RPG sandbox adventure game! If you enjoy Stardew Valley, Minecraft, or Terraria, it's well worth the price and provides a complete satisfying experience without DLCs. As someone who was wowed by the first few hours of the game, I really cannot express how disappointed I am with the experience after a few more hours.

Core Keeper is a cave exploration game that is centered around progression by upgrading your gear and defeating bosses, pretty similarly to Terraria! The game also allows you to flex your creative muscles with some building mechanics, and even has NPCs that you can have move in as well!

Let's start with the good:
The game is visually stunning! The art style perfectly suits it in every way! I found myself eager to explore the beautiful caverns and see all of the diverse biomes where you find all kinds of fantastical creatures! It really is a joy to load up the game as a new player and explore what the early stages of the game has to offer visually!

The music is also incredible! I routinely found myself in awe in the early stages when I would find a new biome and the music would change. It inspired all kinds of feelings of whimsical adventuring/caving. 
(Side Note: I can tell the developers have musical backgrounds by the fact they also put musical puzzles in the game, so it makes sense the music is really good!)

The enemy and boss design is cool! I like the different types of enemies, and I've found many of them to be unique and interesting! (I do wish there were more though)

Unfortunately, that's where the strengths of the game end for me, and the laundry list of problems begin to start.

Mechanics in General:
Core Keeper has several mechanics, and nearly all of them feel unfinished to me. Skill progression is hit or miss, combat is limited for reasons I'll discuss later, building doesn't feel as fleshed out as it could be, the villagers seem relatively uninteresting to me, and the class system really struggles for a major reason I'll discuss later.

Grind, Grind, and Grind some more:
If you love mindless grinding, this is the game for you.
I cannot believe that I am 7 hours into the game, and I'm still grinding for a singular piece of gear to complete the set for my specific class of choice (Mage). The reason for this is that the acquisition of armor and weapons (outside of a very few select sets, mainly the ore armors) is entirely tied to loot tables on enemies or in the environment. After feeling lost for a few hours, I finally took a look over at the wiki to see what I was missing, and as it turns out, I wasn't missing anything! The game has NO way of crafting gear for ANY of the classes.
This might not be so bad, as long as the drop chances are at least pretty forgiving, right? Well, unfortunately, the EARLIEST set of mage gear has a >5% drop rate from every instance you can acquire it from with the exception of a BOSS FIGHT.
I understand that in games like Terraria (A game I quite like), there are some frustrating instances where you have to grind for gear, but for the gear that is essential to progression for your main classes, most of the gear is relatively achievable within a short time frame. I have spent HOURS searching for the FIRST SET of gear for my class of choice.
Also remember, that the drop rate per enemy is equal for each set of armor, meaning that you might find 10 hats and 5 chest pieces, but no pants for instance. Don't even get me started on the weapons. -_-
I would appreciate if, even if the gear is not entirely craftable, there was some way to swap two pieces of gear for one. For instance, maybe I could swap my leggings and chest piece for a hat, or hat and leggings for a chest piece, or some sort of mechanic that minimizes the grind a bit, but alas, there is no mechanic present.

Continuing on the trend of grinding:
In my short time playing the game I can already see how inbalanced progression is among certain skills compared to others. 
Running levels up incredibly fast for something that you do literally all the time in game, but combat skills level up FAR TOO slow for the amount of time you spend doing them relatively. I'm not saying it has to be one to one, but a slightly less grindy balance for earlier levels of these skills would be nice.
Speaking of skills:
The Skill trees feel underwhelming and boring. You spend all of this time shooting magic or your bow at people, and your reward for levelling FIVE levels is (+2% Crit Chance). Come on now. I understand the minor stat boosts for things such as mining and running, but the actual combat skills?

General Takeaways
I've spent a lot of time griping about my largest concerns, so I'll summarize the rest with this:

Similar to Terraria, the game just tosses you in and expects you to figure this s*** out. While Terraria has taken some steps to minimize this, I HIGHLY RECOMMEND consulting the Wiki for this game if you feel lost.

Several other mechanics feel unfinished.
- The Main Biomes don't feel unique to explore. They feel like identical areas but with slightly higher or lower tier ores and a coat of paint.
- There are SO MANY crafting stations, and many of them allow you to craft random assortments of blocks that vary in terms of usefulness. This is particularly frustrating because there are so many cool ideas here, and it feels like the devs either didn't want or didn't have the time to expand on them and make them meaningful.

This is my first ever written review for a game, so sorry if it's a bit scatterbrained, but I found myself needing to get some of my frustrations off of my chest, and potentially bring awareness to some problems that the game has that aren't apparent right away.

[{"review_text": "This game has a ton of potential. MADFINGER, if you're reading this, please look further below for some more direct feedback.

For experienced players of games like Escape From Tarkov, Arena Breakout Infinite, etc, many aspects of the game will be intuitive. Inventory management, weapon customization, equipment slots (with some additions/changes, like being able to wear a tactical belt) will be quite familiar.

The real draw for this game, in my opinion, is the more free-form style of gameplay in place of "raids". You don't have any raid timer, ever. You aren't restricted by timers or boundaries pretty much at all. You can go where you want, when you want. That is extremely cool to have in a game like this.
I think people underestimate the importance of immersion in the extraction shooter genre (which this game effectively falls within, just in a pretty unique kind of way). Games like Tarkov are successful in part because they build such a convincing world. This game does much the same, just with a very different tone. The fact that you can just "live" in this world without restrictions really creates a special feeling that's hard to describe.

Somewhat on the topic of making comparisons with Tarkov, something I really enjoyed about this game (mostly) is the amount of direction they give you with the tasks. I have completed all but 1 or 2 tasks so far (up to the introduction of Ban Pa, in other words: leaving the starter town) without needing any wikis or anything of the sort. I just read what they told me to do and figured it out on my own. WAY easier to follow directions (for most of the tasks) than Tarkov. I'm unsure if this is due to a language barrier issue or just a different approach in design, but either way it was a refreshing boost in immersion to not have to constantly rely on wikis for basic info.


Criticisms/feedback for MADFINGER:

1. -- The game is extremely unclear with VERY important rules involving death and item retrieval. There are very important specific rules in place that the player must know in order to competently approach retrieving their items after death (because yes, after you die, you're still in the same server and you can go back to attempt retrieving your items). i.e. you have 1 hour before your body despawns, and you can ONLY retrieve your MOST RECENT body's items. If you die 2+ times then you can only loot your most recent body. All others will be marked as "old loot", for some reason. This limitation can be completely circumvented by simply being in a squad with other players and having them take the items off your body and throw them on the ground, making the whole feature kinda pointless except for the fact that it puts solo players at a further disadvantage in a pretty arbitrary and immersion-breaking way. The wording is confusing as well. Since it says "old" I thought that it was based on a timer. I needed another player to explain it to me before I realized that dying a second time caused it.

My personal take here? Just remove the "old loot" thing that gets applied after multiple deaths entirely. This only serves to make the experience more frustrating for solos, especially new ones getting bullied by more experienced players/squads.

2. -- The ammunition and armor systems are very confusing. I get almost zero sense of progression when I find anything new, because there's no clear system for what's better/worse. Even a simple instructional chart or something to decipher what I'm looking at would be nice. A huge part of the progression and motivation for players in a looting-based game is to give a clear "Ah HA!" moment when the player finds something good or unlocks the ability to purchase good gear/ammo of their own. Currently, I only get this feeling with guns, and absolutely nothing else. So far, I have almost zero understanding of how any of the armor or ammunition types work. The most clear thing I've seen so far was a description for ammo describing it as sub-sonic, but with the greatly reduced muzzle velocity, I can only assume that it's less effective in SOME other way, I just don't know what's affected. Penetration? Damage? Bullet drop when shooting at a distance? Absolutely no idea what's affected or how it relates with anyone's armor, and more importantly, I don't have any idea HOW MUCH any of those things might be affected. Someone gave me a plate carrier and told me "that's the best one in the game" and the only difference I could find that particularly stood out was the addition of a little "+" next to the armor class, and I have no idea what that means.

3. -- I really like the design choice of having the "marked as aggressor" status placed on players with varying duration depending on the severity of their friendly fire. However, I think that the game is currently overly harsh in cases of immediate defense.
Example: I was walking into hostile territory with 1 teammate by my side. From behind, someone opened fire at us at about 30 meters out, hitting and wounding my teammate and continuing to open fire into his body, and within ~2 seconds, I swiveled around and gunned down the aggressor, who turned out to be a confused ally who mistook us for the enemies that were a little further ahead. When I shot him, I quickly landed a fatal blow, killing him in defense of my teammate with absolutely zero chance to react. I was given 57 minutes of aggressor status for that, even though I literally saved someone's life while the dude was mid-fire, full auto. While I understand that it is not good to encourage "revenge friendly fire", I think there's a line that needs to be drawn when you're quite literally saving the life of an innocent teammate in defense of a rogue ally, regardless if that ally is intentionally acting out or not. Everyone involved was cool with each other there, no heated emotions or anything, and everyone involved agreed that it was unfair for me to get ~1hr with the aggressor status.


Anyway, thanks for reading. There's way more good and bad I could say about the game, but overall I've found it to be a unique and enjoyable experience, so I recommend the game. I just hope that concerns like these are taken seriously and addressed. I'll likely update my review with coming updates to the game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1747439774}, {"review_text": "Let me start off by saying I want this game to succeed more than anyone, and why I opted for the supporter edition, It's the open world tactical fps game I've always wanted. A hybrid of Ghost Recon and Tarkov, that reaches that itch that the latter can't. However there are some extreme disappointments that has me worried for the success and future of the game.


The AI is one of the main things besides poor optimization that just ruins the fun for me, I could write a novel about all the issues with the AI but I'll just list a few of the main ones. 

[olist]
    [*]I can't count the number of times I've died and amount of gear I've lost to AI pulling off 200 yard, hip-firing 1 taps. It's just ridiculous and it needs to be addressed ASAP.

    [*]Another thing is the AI's detection capabilities, being the main game ruiner for me; there's absolutely no reason while I'm shooting at AI suppressed, within foliage, from 200 yards away the AI should be able to turn 180 degrees, know my exact position and return fire pin-point accurate fire (again off the hip).

    [*]Goes with the previous point, but the AI's ability to see through foliage is insane. If I can't see them, they shouldn't be able to see me.
[/olist]


As far as optimization, the main issue I've encountered as well as others are spiking CPU temps. There doesn't seem to be any specific event that causes it, as my PC has hit thermal protection and crashed several times (Ryzen 5900x with an AIO) causing complete gear losses. It does seem to happen more frequently around helicopters, but has happened everywhere.


The vendor levels/rep and items they sell needs to be re-evaluated. Two things don't make sense to me.
[olist]
    [*]Why am I being tasked to go to locations where the AI is wearing III+ Armor and firing M855, when I only have reliable access to FMJ and at best IIIA armor? That's just a recipe for not a fun time. Also the fact that a bunch of good ammo is just not sold by vendors anymore. What happened to M855A1/M856A1 and BP/PP?
    [*]Since this update is based around night vision, I find the decision odd why the best night vision not offered by any vendor (same for AK308). This is an early access, so I'd figure being able to reliably test and experience content in the game is paramount. For a full release I see item rarity/scarcity, but in a test version?
[/olist]


The final thing I'd like to mention is the time frame of major updates, I was very disheartened when the road-map released to see content bearing updates were only scheduled on a semi-annual basis, is that a joke? Before night-ops I had stopped playing for a good 4-5 months as the content had just dried up. No new features, no new weapons or gear to play with, no new quests. Is this what I can expect from the game? Playing for a bit, getting bored, and having to wait 6 months for a new update? Why can't we have minor content bearing updates more often? Having past game development experience, and vast amounts of modding experience; I know it is not a big task or ask for a large studio to pump out some new weapons, gear, or quests within the minor patches to keep the player base alive and interested. I also seriously hope you're joking about not implementing vehicles into the game, that would be just a downright suicidal development choice and I hope to not expect that from this studio... I won't go into the hundreds of quality of life suggestions I have.

For now until some of these rather game breaking issues get addressed, and the devs can step up and show they're committed to maintaining their player base by delivering new content in a reasonable manner, and not just farming funding and posting employee interviews that (just being honest here) no one cares about while the game turns into vaporware; I'd say save your money, and keep an eye on the reviews.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 17, "timestamp_created": 1735022986}, {"review_text": "Great game. This game does not require a crazy amount of time in game to learn, it's fairly easy to pick up and start playing and be moderately good in. I love the aspect that you can choose to play more mission oriented with vendor tasks than how Tarkov does it. 

Some negative reviews are founded, this is what I agree with: the AI can be stupid quick to headshot you from very far away, the game is demanding and frame rate can drop at times, and a lot of the world seems to be fairly empty vegetation.

Mostly, all of these negative points are overcome through gameplay. For example, you quickly learn how to engage the AI to not get killed really easily. Adjusting graphics settings depending on your set up. The cities and towns are so well designed and full of exploration and exciting gunfights. 

My only real complaint is to have a slightly more well rounded library of firearms to choose from. Adding something like a 20in AR option to clone an M16 type rifle would be neat to see.

This game has a very important place in gaming. You can choose whether or not you want PVE or PVP. While there are factions, you can change factions without too much hassle (within limits). Unlike games like ABI or Tarkov, Gray Zone doesn't have a forced extraction timer (which I love. I hate timers). The game, while it does have issues because it is STILL IN DEVELOPMENT, is worth playing. You can play at your own pace and be fine if you just play smart. There are developer updates coming soon that should improve the game for many people. The second of which SHOULD give some needed QOL.

Please do not listen to the majority of negative reviews.

1) While you do die in the game (its a combat game, duh) you have 1 chance to regain your lost items. I have died dozens of times and never permanently lost my gear in the last 2 weeks or so.

2) Performance issues. The game is in development, and that causes some performance dips. Let the devs do their thing. I have a EVGA 3080TI GPU, and I run around 45 - 60+ frames ( I am locked from higher frames due to my monitor refresh rate of 60HZ). I do get frame dips, but that is to be expected from a game being heavily developed.

3) While the AI do have some aimbot specifics that are insanely agrivating, you can work around it by paying attention to your environment. If you want to see 2 people that know how to play the game perfectly fine, look up on twitch Jarh3ad_TV and Credard. You will see how the game plays without relying on stupid negative reviews.

4) Some people have claimed that the "DLC's" in the game are a scam. They are not. The DLC's support the developers making the game. They can't build the game properly without income. The DLC editions to the game give you higher stash, some cosmetic items, lots of medical supplies, and few other things. Obviously, if you go out and die and do not get your body back, your items are gone. GO OUT AND GET MORE ITEMS. It's not difficult, especially if I can do it solo with my PTSD and rage issues coupled with my eyesight problems. The phrase "geht gud" here applies perfectly.

5) The game is quite playable as is. The above mentioned streamers have played by selling all of their gear and starting with just a knife. Played with only sniper rifles, or not silenced weapons. I have seen Jar3ead_TV play and entire storyline run with NO SCOPE (not even iron sights). Jar3ad_TV and Credard are among the game experts (there are others, I just do not know them right now). Listen to them. Not the neggative reviews.

This game is entirely what you make of it. If you are unsure, watch people play it live, ask questions, etc. Please do not trash this game simply to trash it. This game is not meant to be COD, its not meant to be Battlefield, or Tarkov. It is meant to be its own game, and it works very well.

Let me give you a run down.

Pros:
+ If you love Magic, this is a very accessible way to play it.
+ Many formats to choose from.
+ Robust collection of cards covering many sets.
+ Interesting digital-only formats and cards where the cards have been rebalanced or are exclusive to the format.
+ Offers drafting. Always a plus.
+ Honestly very nice looking. Smooth interface, control feels nice, boards are pretty. Has vanity pets, that's always cool.
+ A game with rules enforcement takes away some of the brainpower needed to play, allowing you to focus more on plays instead of trigger orders. Option to go full control anyways, useful for bluffing and other things.

Cons:
- EXTREMELY F2P unfriendly. Like, holy moly they charge a ton of real money for packs and do not hand out a lot of F2P currency.
- They release sets at break-neck speed. It's often hard to settle into a meta without spending money.

The game is very good for MTG players. Great, even. I do recommend it. But the cons it does have are glaring. Much like real MTG, this game will cost you an arm and a leg for cards if you want to keep up with other players. It's unfortunate because it bills itself as F2P but ends up being somewhat P2W. Not necessarily 100% P2W, of course. Having a large collection never guarantees you'll win. Especially if you suck. But it sure helps a lot.

There's also some serious FOMO with the cosmetics and a paid season pass. Never good but them's the breaks. That's F2P for you.

Hate people who just try to timer you out there really needs to a penalty for doing so. like an hour matchmake penalty its total bs that you can just wait someone out with no consequences", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1748375097}, {"review_text": "Magic: The Gathering has held some of my favorite memories of a trading card in my adult life. Yu-Gi-Oh and Pokemon have nostalgia factors, but MTG was the first card game I remember taking seriously. Magic's limited formats (draft, sealed, etc.) are some of the best ways to play with cardboard that exist today, and no matter how hard I try to stay away, there always seems to be someone in my life that wants me to get back in. I have loved Magic for many years, and even though their new direction since Hasbro took the reins has ultimately left me searching for another TCG, I will always come back to draft or play a quick game with friends. 

That being said, Arena is the worst way you could play Magic. 

There are many positives to Arena from both a practical perspective and a gameplay perspective. Being able to play Magic at pretty much any time of day from your PC or phone is wonderful. There are season rankings, multiple formats to choose from (often with their own tournaments/festivals with prizes), and most of it is fairly intuitive. It does a good job of usually having something for you to do. You don't have to bother with the more obtuse parts of TCGs. No fiddling with dice to mark counters or changes to attack/toughness, no need for sleeves/deck boxes/storage containers for all of your cars, most of the minor inconveniences have been smoothed out and you can get to playing the game with moderate ease. The tutorial does a good job at introducing you to the mechanics of the games without overwhelming you. The visuals are generally smooth, the way they have visualized The Chain, mana pools, and various other things is appealing. 

The artists deserve respect for formatting, modeling, coding, designing, and creating a functional, sleek simulator. 

Onto the negative, which centers almost entirely around monetization. 

MTGA is free, and I absolutely hate free games. Not only because that usually opens the game up to exceptionally predatory mechanics (more on this in a bit), but you also now have people who would LOVE to tell you how "Well, they need to make money somehow." Any critique you give towards a freemium game's monetization is twisted to make you sound like a child asking your guardian why they have to go to work instead of playing with you. Yet, I'd still like to talk about it as someone who is exceptionally susceptible to these tactics. 

Every predatory form of monetization is here. Daily quests, weekly quests, a battle pass, daily sales in the shop, a functionally worthless in-game currency alongside a necessary (and expensive) in-game currency, in-game currency bundles that arbitrarily have money reduced from its price, and more. Most festivals/events have a Coin (in-game currency that cannot be purchased directly) and Gem (in-game currency that can be purchased) entry, with Coin or Gem prizes, and each festival/event has a different threshold you have to cross to get a return on your entry fee. Obviously, the easier it is to enter an event, the better you have to do to make a return on your entry fee, let alone profit. 

The main grind for Gems, the actual useful currency, is as follows:
1) Build the cheapest meta Standard deck you can find.
2) Win games of any PVP format, or complete enough quests, to get enough coins for the BO1 Standard event.
3) Go at least 5-X to convert those Coins into Gems. 
4) Use the Gems to enter better events or limited events and go at least 4-X to continue having currency.
5) Repeat

This may sound fairly straightforward, but it is functionally the ONLY efficient way to earn gems. Don't like standard? Too bad. Wasted your wildcards building a deck you thought would work against the meta only to get knocked out first match of the event? Too bad. Finally got enough gems to do a draft, only for you to also get knocked out after your first three matches? Too bad, back to standard. 

Everything costs so much money. The battle pass is 20 dollars, they routinely add cosmetics and cards that will also cost you 20 dollars or more, with even basic profile images running you 5-10 dollars. You could easily spend hundreds of dollars on junk without knowing it, and everything in the game is just BEGGING you to give in and buy gems. 

Of course, Magic can be an expensive game in paper, too. Decks can easily enter the hundreds, even in standard, and drafts usually cost anywhere between 20-40 dollars. However, in paper, you own cards that can be sold or traded. Often, you will win packs that could contain even more cards that can be sold or traded. I think the primary focus of a TCG should be being fun, but right after that is pricing and accessibility. Money is, sadly, the blood that pumps through our system's veins. It is what determines our ability to live, to eat, to survive. As long as this is true, and as long as money is something that is not guaranteed to us, every thing that costs money inevitably is assessed for value. Paper Magic allows me to potentially recoup some of my money spent, and makes that initial investment easier to swallow (even if I have my own gripes with paper Magic). 

In Arena, all of your cards are functionally PNGs. You do technically own them insofar as they exist in your collection, but there is no way to convert that back to real world money (outside of selling your account, which is a ban-worthy offense). Also, there is no meaningful way to exchange Rares or Mythics for other cards of the same rarity, meaning that you can do all this work just for cards that are unplayable. They will sit in your collection, unplayed and unused, for the rest of time. So, every dollar you put into Arena is money just vanishes. Hope the events you play with those gems go well, because that $20 feels the same in Hasbro's wallet whether you win or lose. 

I understand that to many, these may seem like privileged wants and needs. You can literally play the game for free, and you can just go play in paper if you want. Why does it matter? Who cares? 

Hasbro makes hundreds of millions of dollars off of us every year. They drain every cent from Magic's player base and frankly, will sacrifice anything they think will lead to short term gain. I have no interest in pretending like this is a project funded by a small indie company who works on this when they're not working their other job. Arena could be such an incredible simulator that could exist to uplift Magic, to find new ways of connecting players and fulfilling the promise of "The Gathering" while being affordable. Elestrals Clash is a great example, and while their monetization is always gross in its own way, you have access to every card in the game as soon as you open the client. No, Arena does not want to find a healthy balance between gameplay and monetization. It exists to fine the exact amount they are forced to provide so that a brand-loyal player base, or a new player who doesn't know any better, continues to funnel money into the pockets of rich people who could not care less about "the heart of Magic." 

Buy a booster box and draft with your friends. Go to a commander night at your locals. Print out a cube and drag 7 other strangers to a card store to play it. Connect with your community and find the reason that people love Magic.

[h2].[/h2]
[hr][/hr]

[h2]2. Get Used to Seeing the Message "Waiting for the Server..."[/h2]
This message will haunt you. It appears for almost every single click you make, so you might as well accept it as part of the experience.

Stay strong, and know that for every timeout they burn, you’ll receive one in return. However, if your opponent has an instant or any other sneaky trick, you’ll also get to enjoy timeouts in your own turn. Every. Single. Phase.

[{"review_text": "I finally played Fable for the very first time and my journey through Fable Anniversary was instantly memorable, showing me how special this franchise is.

I sat down to play Fable Anniversary on my Steam Deck, confident that I was playing the very best version of this classic RPG. After overcoming the initial pains of playing an older, inaccessible title, I quickly found myself falling in love with the world of Fable and its charming, unique blend of serious plotlines and humorous writing. In some ways, Fable feels more like an RPG than many modern RPGs in that I always felt like I was in control of the Hero's destiny.

Fable Anniversary is an expanded and remastered version of the 2005's Xbox 360 Fable: The Lost Chapters, which in turn is an expanded re-release of the first Fable from 2004 on the original Xbox. Released in 2014, Fable Anniversary brought vastly improved visual fidelity, superior performance and load speeds, overhauled controls and UI, and plenty of Achievements to entice new and returning players. It's a great remaster of a game that was 10 years old at the time, but even Fable Anniversary is now over nine years old.

As I said, I played the game on my Steam Deck, which means my experience was even better than those who may have played Fable Anniversary around its initial release. Upscaled to 4K HDR, with FPS Boost bringing me 60 smooth frames per second, the first Fable has never looked or played better than it does on the latest current-gen Xbox consoles or handheld device. Still, no number of facelifts short of a complete remake can fix fundamental game design, meaning it took me a few hours of easing into Fable Anniversary before it really clicked.

Fable is still a product of its time, and that means everything from exploring its world to battling its enemy lacks the fluidity and seamlessness of more modern games. Everything feels just a little clunky and awkward, and it's clear that the scope of the first Fable game was inherently limited by the capabilities of the hardware on which it launched. Fable Anniversary also lacks in-depth accessibility options, with even subtitles being compromised.

As I'm hard of hearing and have auditory processing issues, subtitles are necessary whenever I play any game or watch any media. Fable's subtitles, however, lack customization and strangely only apply to in-game cinematics, meaning I frankly lost a lot of casual NPC conversations and non-cinematic story moments. Beyond these issues, though, I found a game that I wholeheartedly loved, to the point where I genuinely could scarcely stop playing until I finished the entire game over the course of two-three days.

The story of Fable is a simple one: you're the Hero, orphaned at a young age by a brutal bandit raid and raised to be a powerful, productive member of the Guild. As a part of the Guild, you explore the world, taking on quests for various people, establishing a name for yourself as either an evil plight on the land or a pure-hearted savior. To this end, every major decision in Fable is very black and white — you either choose the good path or the bad path, and the consequences of each choice are fairly obvious.

In this way, Fable may confuse players used to more recent RPGs. There's no character creator here, not even as much as a gender slider or a way to choose your name; the Hero is who he is, and that's all there is to it. Yes, you can alter his hair, get tattoos, and change his body build through rigorous exercise or excessive eating, but you're never expected to put yourself into the world of Fable. You're also never confronted with an endless array of vague, questionably meaningful decisions. Instead, Fable asks not that you role-play as a character of your creation but instead control the destiny of a nameless Hero inexplicably involved in the fate of the entire world.

It's the ways in which you can control that destiny where Fable's magic lies. For one, you can romance almost anyone in Fable's world; you can flirt with all the men, women, and people of Fable wherever you go, have people fall in love with you, and marry them. Fable has plenty of stats to inform how many spouses you have, what your sexuality is, how many times you've been divorced, and even how many times you've, ah, gone to bed with other people. If you want to be truly evil, you can attempt to romance everyone in a town and ruin all their collective lives.

You can invest in real estate, including buying and furnishing homes for yourself or renting out to tenants for some passive income. If homeowners or shopkeepers "mysteriously" pass away or disappear, their properties go on the market and can also be purchased. Yes, you can own pretty much everything in Fable, as long as you're willing to reduce the population a tad. It's ridiculous.

Fable also features a healthy number of Expressions that can be used to interact with the people of Albion. From positive affirmations and pleasant manners to spiteful insults and silly dances, there are plenty of ways to elicit reactions out of NPCs. Your Expressions are influenced by your Hero's alignment (how good and evil they are) and how well-known they are. They can be necessary for finding secrets, completing quests, and generally being a part of Fable's world.

There are so many small ways you can influence Fable, despite its modest scale, that makes you feel like you have control. Many of these ways actually make little to no difference to the game's story and are simply ways to have fun amidst all the chaos and seriousness. Fable isn't afraid to be delightfully silly, and it gives the game a wonderful charm that's just absent in many "AAA" modern RPGs — which often insist on being serious and dramatic to the point of exhaustion.

Modern games look and play better than any previous generation of gaming, and developers are becoming more creative and ambitious than ever before. Why is it, then, that Fable Anniversary is lingering in my thoughts so much longer than other modern RPGs? What is it about this 20-year-old classic that remains so fun after all this time?

Many modern RPGs are filled with vast open-worlds and countless quests, discoveries, choices, and ways to personalize your experience, but they also focus unerringly on the completion. It's all about getting things done, all the time. Complete the next quest, unlock the next level, beat the next boss — RPGs are always giving you another thing to keep you occupied, and it's always so aggressively serious. Fable has plenty of serious moments, but it's also filled with minute details that don't matter at all. They're just there because someone, somewhere, will love them.

Video games are constantly striving to become bigger and bolder than what came before, but this incessant push for more often results in games forgetting that there's value in a simple moment of humanity, or in the option to be ridiculous. Making vulgar gestures at a door that won't open, farting to ward off a common bully, posing heroically in front of a gaggle of love-addled fans, and combating the forces of darkness with a frying pan and a chicken hat are all things you can do in Fable Anniversary.

This charm is absent in so many games nowadays despite the mind-boggling technological advancements, and it's likely a large part of why Hi-Fi RUSH is such an incredible journey from beginning to end. Elden Ring is also a great example of this, with its community messages offering a potent, often hilarious contrast to the dark and morbid atmosphere of its world.

Fable Anniversary Edition is an amazing work of fantasy, with a unique atmosphere, a great sense of humor and fun, and an unforgettable world. There are some elements that really show the game is twenty years old now, but on the whole it holds up as well today as it did in 2004. This is a game to fall in love with, and if you haven’t played it yet, I hope you’ll give it a try.
