[{"review_text": "They stay so true to the original game that even the sudden FPS drops when transitioning to a new location are faithfully recreated.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1456, "timestamp_created": 1745497098}, {"review_text": "I remember the first time I played Oblivion.
It was December 26th, 2006. I was thirteen, my soul hungry for wonder, my heart still unaware of the weight nostalgia can carry.
That day, my mother gave me a Christmas gift.
A simple disc. A green case for my old Xbox 360.
But it wasn’t just a game.
It was the beginning of something.
It was Oblivion.

I installed it, turned on the console... and it was as if the real world disappeared.
I spent every hour of that day lost in Cyrodiil.
Snowy mountains, mysterious woods, ruins caught halfway between dream and nightmare.
I wasn’t playing it—I was living it.

And then… so many runs. So many new characters, new choices, restarts just for the sheer joy of starting over.
I knew every trick, every shortcut, every glitch.
And without any guide—when the internet was still a slow, rare whisper—I achieved 100% completion.
It was my world.
It was home.

Every now and then, my mother would sit beside me.
She’d watch the screen in silence.
She came from Donkey Kong 3, so to her, this was like glimpsing the future.
I still remember that one time... I handed her the controller, let her fight in the Arena.
She lost. She laughed.
She wasn’t made for that world, but... she liked being there.
She liked seeing me in it.
It was my refuge.
It was our small bridge.

And now, 19 years later, I go back.
The world has changed. I have changed. I’m 31 now.
And she… she’s no longer here.

And yet, playing the remaster feels like... like opening a window into the past.
The graphics are new, but the heart remains untouched.
Every tree, every sound, every line of dialogue speaks in a language only the soul remembers.
It’s the voice of childhood.
It’s the whisper of my mother laughing once more after losing that Arena fight.

Oblivion is not just a game.
It’s a time machine.
It’s a second chance to touch, even for a moment, what we thought was lost.

And as the sun rises over Cyrodiil, I remain there.
Fingers on the keyboard...
And a tear I cannot tell—if it’s sorrow or gratitude.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 72, "timestamp_created": 1745400811}, {"review_text": "I have never written a review on Steam before, but I feel compelled to do so for this game.

In 2008, seventeen years ago, my mom took me to a GameStop after a rather grueling orthodontist appointment. I was allowed to pick out a game to buy. I wasn’t sure what to get, but the associate working there gave me a recommendation: a relatively recent game packed full of fantastical adventure, a game where you could go anywhere and do anything. I wish I could thank that associate for what he gave me, because, of course, that game was Oblivion.

It’s hard to put into words just how important Oblivion is to me. It was my first "real" game as a kid and truly what made me fall in love with video games as an art form. Beyond that, I credit it for sparking my lifelong love of fantasy and medieval settings. Maybe it sounds weird or a little cringe, but Oblivion is foundational to who I am today.

As time marched on and gaming standards evolved, Oblivion aged and not gracefully (even worse than Morrowind, in my opinion). I found it harder and harder to go back to it. I tried to replay it several times but kept bouncing off. The years had worn heavily on this beloved game from my childhood. At times, I even wondered if I could still confidently say I [i]liked[/i] Oblivion, since I found it so difficult to revisit. Was it all just nostalgia?

This remaster has given Oblivion back to me.
It fixes all the issues that made me bounce off the game so many times before. It's no longer an early-2000s 3D bloomfest, it looks gorgeous. It no longer feels like you’re floating through the world, smacking enemies with a pool noodle; now, you feel [i]present[/i], tangibly part of the world. The punishing min-maxing system is gone; you can actually play the builds you want to play.
And the incredible part is: it fixes all of this without changing what the game fundamentally [i]is[/i].
If you played this version without ever touching the 2006 original, I wouldn't consider your experience "less than." This [i]is[/i] Oblivion, through and through.

This remaster has validated my feelings about Oblivion. I [i]do[/i] still love this game to death. It had just aged so poorly that I struggled to enjoy it. That’s no longer an issue, because this remaster has brought all of that magic back to me.

2025 hasn’t been a great year for me so far. I've been in a pretty unhappy place for most of it.
As corny as it might sound, this game has honestly given me a lot of happiness. Beyond just playing it, I’ve had so much fun talking about it with other people. The whole rollout, the leaks, the reveal stream, the shadowdrop, is something I think will go down as one of my favorite memories ever.

It’s clear this game was made by people who loved Oblivion as much as I did, and that love shines through in every facet. To me, this remaster is more than just a fresh coat of paint on a 20-year-old RPG. It's a reminder, at least in part, of how I became who I am today.

Oblivion Remastered really does mean the world to me, and I’m so excited to spend several hundred more hours in Cyrodiil.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 39, "timestamp_created": 1745872203}, {"review_text": "It's still Oblivion. THIS is how you do a remaster. This is EXACTLY how you do a remaster.

People have asked me if they need to play the OG before playing this. The answer is they do not. You run until your lungs burn, and still — it’s behind you. Not hunting for food. Not for revenge. Just… to end you.

Walls collapse. Creatures claw through the dark. Streets become labyrinths of debris and blood. You keep moving, not because you’re brave, but because stopping means becoming part of the rubble.

Weapons buy you seconds, not safety. Choices feel like coin flips made in fire. And through it all, that sound returns: those steps, like a countdown you can’t reset.

With that being said, this is still a very good game. A very good game that is tragically bogged down by its short length, it’s re-used assets and locations from the previous game, and by a failure to innovate or bring anything new to the franchise. It’s because of this, compounded by it’s hefty price tag, that despite how good it is in its short run time, it still manages to dissapoint.

Starting with the good, this game has incredibly gorgeous visuals and the detail in the environments and characters are truly jaw-dropping. The facial features of the characters were especially impressive as every gesture, emotion and muscle is captured so well and it really elevates the characters and the story. The combat is very snappy and the feedback you feel when you shoot or dodge is very satisfying. There’s a healthy variety of enemies that keep you on your toes from fear, and the combat sequences are impressive.
 
More importantly than anything though, RE3 has that classic resident evil horror atmosphere that we all know and have come to love. Eerie, somber and gory level design that are still filled with so much detail and color. Environments filled with small claustrophobic dark hallways and corridors that make you feel trapped in closed spaces with horrific undead. Skin crawling horror music that plays as you push forward knowing you will have to earn every room you enter. It is incredible horror and it’s what made Resident Evil a one of a kind franchise. This is all present in RE3 and it is an incredible thing to experience as always.

All of this, ofcourse, is overshadowed by its very short run time of 5 hours. it’s re-used locations from the previous game that wear out their novelty very quickly. its disappointing rework of the nemesis villain that feels forgettable and fails to leave an impression on you like the original. This failure to innovate, when mixed with a hefty price tag, results in a game that feels lazy and incomplete for a full standalone title. For this level of scale and content, this game should’ve been a DLC/expansion to RE2, not a fully priced title.

At full price, I just cannot recommend this game. It just does not offer anything new or fresh enough to justify its price tag, especially compared to it’s predecessor RE2. 

But it’s still Resident evil man, and holy hell do I love Resident evil. Like yes it's got all these flaws but it's still Resident evil. It's still got all the hallmarks that makes this franchise so beloved and so good. 

And that’s why, even though it was disappointing compared to the other games, I still recommend Resident Evil 3.

On deep sale that is.

At least Jill and Carlos are kinda cool. get it when its 5 dollars.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1753467663}, {"review_text": "Resident Evil 3 takes a more action oriented approach compared to its predecessor, much like the original Resident Evil 3: Nemesis did within the classic trilogy. However, even among those older titles, Nemesis was arguably the weakest entry, and unfortunately, this modern remake doesn't manage to elevate its source material in a meaningful way. In fact, it not only falls short as a remake but also struggles to uphold the identity of a Resident Evil game.

Like the Resident Evil 2 Remake, it's not a one to one recreation. It is more like a reimagining with considerable creative liberties, not all of which work in its favor. While some of the original's core ideas are still present, they have been altered in ways that make the game feel more like a cinematic action thriller than a survival horror game. There's a clear emphasis on cutscenes, dialogue, and scripted moments, which gives the game a more "movie like" quality but at the expense of player agency and atmospheric tension.

Visually, there's little to complain about. The RE Engine continues to impress, with highly detailed environments, excellent character models, and realistic facial animations. Zombies, although largely recycled from Resident Evil 2, still look convincing. From a technical standpoint, the game is well produced. But gameplaywise it moves the game further away from its survival horror roots.

Nemesis, the big bad thing you already see on the covers, should have been a standout feature. In the original, his encounters were tense, unpredictable, and often dynamic. Here, he is reduced to a mostly scripted presence. His initial appearance in the city streets is arguably the highlight of the game one of the few moments that captures the chaotic energy of the original. But subsequent encounters are heavily controlled and lack tension. His mutations are less grotesque and feel disconnected from the biological horror that once made him terrifying. Instead of evolving in response to the player's actions, his transformations now follow a fixed, cinematic path, turning him into a quadruped like creature that's visually odd rather than intimidating. It's strange, with the Tyrant from Resident Evil 2, they've already introduced an enemy into the series who has somehow evolved from the original. But here, it really seems to be the case that Nemesis is even better in the original than he is in the remake.

Also Carlos, a side character from the original, plays a much larger role in the remake. His expanded sections include new locations and extended gameplay time sometimes even replacing segments originally played with Jill. While his improved presence could have added depth, these sections often feel more like a generic third person shooter. Armed with an assault rifle and abundant ammunition, Carlos storms through waves of zombies, holding out against dozens of them in a sequence that feels more like a scripted shooter scenario than a survival horror game. It was similar in the original, but here they could go on a different road, instead of making everything more over the top.

Equally disappointing is the removal or truncation of key areas from the original. The clock tower and parts of the factory are missing entirely, and some of the game's characters are introduced so briefly that they leave no lasting impression. The Mercenaries mode has also been cut, and puzzles once a staple of the series have been either removed or simplified to such a degree that they no longer offer any meaningful challenge. You get Resident Evil Resistence instead, a stand alone multiplayer game nobody asked for.

Unfortunately, combat often feels unsatisfying. Zombies are unusually durable, absorbing bullets unpredictably. The game doesn't encourage careful aiming or offer consistent feedback for well placed shots. Critical hits seem to occur at random rather than as a reward for skill. Boss fights are similarly unengaging, typically resolved by unloading the most powerful weapons until the enemy collapses. There's little strategy involved, and these encounters rarely evolve beyond their visual spectacle. The new dodge roll require also less precise timing and makes them far more forgiving and with full control over aiming and movement, there's little reason to flee one of the core survival instincts that the older games used to evoke. While this makes the game more accessible, it also reduces the sense of vulnerability that once defined the series

[h2]GAMEPLAY OVERVIEW:[/h2] 3R picks up the story of Jill Valentine after the events of the first game. Jill is now trying to escape from a virus-infested Raccoon City. Nemesis arriving early in the game.

This remake retains the shift from the fixed-camera perspective of the original RE2/3 to the over-the-shoulder perspective of 2R, making it easy to navigate the streets and buildings of the infected city. The player starts as Jill, transitions to Carlos for several segments mid-game, then back to Jill. The two characters have slightly different move sets and available weapons.

For each character, zombies and other foes litter the way forward. Just as in the remake of the second game, these walking corpses are quite durable, soaking up multiple headshots from starter weapons. They are also surprisingly fast, shambling toward the player with deceptive leisure, only to lunge and cover the final stretch between themselves and the player in the blink of an eye, so stay alert. Old enemies from previous games make appearances, along with some new ones. The action is gloriously gruesome, with exploding heads and sprays of blood. Player deaths are equally horrific. 3R definitely earns its "Mature" rating, so keep the young ones away.

Puzzles were a hallmark of the early RE games and while there are a handful in 3R, I found this game's riddles laughably easy. This game definitely shifts away from that aspect to a more action-oriented experience. There are some new environmental wrinkles added, such as mobile power carts, which spray an arc of electricity when shot, stunning all enemies in range for a few seconds. The player can use these to slip past large groups without using ammo, though save for the end of several prolonged bouts of combat, I never felt a lack of bullets or healing items while playing on Standard. Resource management is usually an staple in survival horror but I never felt the pinch in 3R. Supply status wasn't much of an issue as long as I picked my fights and ran when I could.

One new feature in 3R is the dodge mechanic. It's a little tricky to get the timing down but once you've done so, it's a very effective method of avoiding damage—and honestly, it's essential for the boss fights, so I recommend a player practice early until they are comfortable with it.

With the exception of one fight against waves of zombies, the boss fights in 3R are against Nemesis in some form or the other. Unlike the original RE3, where Nemesis could appear and attack the player at random, in this version, encounters with Nemesis are fixed occurrences at specific points of the journey. Players can opt to fight him but since Nemesis is a bullet sponge who can't be permanently disabled before the game's end, running is usually the better option. There are several mandatory fights against the hulking menace but those encounters are marked by hallmarks of the genre—wide-open arena-like spaces littered with ammo and healing items—so the player should see these encounters coming. After mastering the dodge timing, I found these fights more tedious than anything.

My real issue with 3R is its incredibly short length. I died a lot, explored every nook and cranny I could find, repeated several segments to get the exact outcome I wanted, and still finished in under eight hours. Replay value is minimal; unlike 2R, there is only one real route here and any subsequent playthroughs will proceed along the exact same path. 

The story and gameplay are adequate but there just isn't enough of either on offer. 3R's controls and interface are much like 2R and (aside from the dodge) doesn't innovate much new ... which would be fine, if 3R had retained the bulk of the story and events from its original version, and clocked in at a 25-hour-plus playthrough. But since it doesn't, it's hard for me to do more than give it a slim thumbs up. RE fans will likely enjoy 3R for what it is—and just as likely be left dissatisfied and hungry for more. I did, and was.

[h2]STORY / WORLDBUILDING:[/h2] This story takes place around the same time as the events of 2R, though the two tales don't intersect. More of Umbrella's experiments and dastardly deeds are uncovered as the player progresses, and the narrative is consistent with the lore of previous games. On the other hand, the 3R setting is a bit light. This remake uses multiple locations and tile sets from 2R. At the risk of repeating myself, this probably wouldn't matter if 3R was a longer game but as it stands, such reuse feels like a lazy corner-cutting shortcut. The fact that 3R slashed so much interesting story and so many locations from the original RE3, like the Clock Tower, Raccoon City Park, and Factory, and the boss fight with the Gravedigger, for example. This reduction in length and content only exacerbates the impression that this game could have easily been a DLC to 2R.

[h2]TECHNICAL ASPECTS:[/h2] Like 2R, 3R is a visual and aural feast. Environments are rendered in fine detail and character animations were fluid on my ten-year old rig. The sound design is excellent. In the early areas, ambient noise alerts the player to nearby threats, by both volume and direction, and fills the background with the sounds of a city falling apart. This is in marked contrast to later scenes, where the silence itself becomes almost oppressive and adds to the tension. Voice acting and dialogue for the main characters is generally pretty good, and far better than the original. In terms of presentation, the game excels.

I didn't have any errors or glitches and the game felt perfectly stable. Steam achievements are generally accessible, though maxing out requires finding all collectibles and speed running the hardest difficulty.

[h2]FINAL SCORE: 6.5/10[/h2]

Up vote this people so devs maybe notice it!  We all be much happier with this change.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1764949103}, {"review_text": "[h1] THIS IS NOT A SURVIVAL GAME [119hrs on the Demo] [/h1]

[h2] It's not? So what is it? (and why do you have 119hrs on a demo...) [/h2]

- This game feels more like an "Adventurer's Tycoon-lite". In my personal experience, the game does a really good job at capturing the essence and feeling of what it would actually be like to be an adventurer in the world of Cloudheim, while also adding in the idea of being a traveling merchant as well.
- (Oi, NoodleCat kept updating the Demo & there was a lot to digest lmao)

- A quick note on the player progression, speaking upon how strong you get over time, if you're familiar with "Crackdown" or even "Risk of Rain 2", the game goes from simple fights to you being an all out Beast of a Unit lmao. With how silly the combat is, you're bound to have a great time with using all the weapons and primarily skills that this game has to offer. You can either have skills that force push enemies 100ft, use your hammer to golf swing enemies 100ft, or straight up box with all hand to hand combat and body slam mofos xD

[h2] Is there any survival elements like hunger & such? [/h2]
- No, there isn't. You are able to adventure, beat stuff up, and be a crackhead all you want without stopping [strike] at least until you use too much mana and you're walking at the speed of you reading this while a goblins are trying to kill you [/strike].

[h2] Well what about crafting? Is there crafting? [/h2]
- Yes, but it's extremely streamlined. Instead of crafting a pickaxe to mine ores, you can just roll through them or smack em once lmao. This is great for those that enjoy keeping up your momentum while adventuring. Once you get your materials smelted, all you do is put down 3 ingots and boom, you have your weapon crafted. This applies to everything else that is crafted as well. Making potions? You put down 3 of the same herbs and boom, it will start it's crafting process.

[h2] Okay, so if it's not a Survival Game, what is the gameplay loop like? [/h2]

[h3] Cloudheim / Odin's Shell [/h3]
- This is your home base. The Objective here is to "Upgrade your Shop Level". You do this by "Selling" items that you no longer want, rather than the traditional system of simply discarding items or tossing them off a cliff, lava, or wherever else lol.

- With each Shop Level, you're able to buy more Stations to upgrade your home base (more smelters, gardening areas, etc etc), including various decorations to spruce up how your home base looks.

- Keep in mind that this game DOES NOT have traditional building. This means that you will not be building walls, floors, etc. There is a Tavern that you can unlock, to which you can then decorate however you please.

[h3] Bifrost [/h3]
- The Bifrost is the World Gate that you will be using to travel to whichever Island you'd like to set your adventure on. While adventuring, you have the entire island to explore, find secret chests, fight field bosses, do separate instance dungeons, level up, collect materials, do Quests, etc.

- A huge part to this game is that there is NO ITEM MANAGEMENT in the sense of worrying about carrying too much stuff and being forced to have to go back home. All items gathered while adventuring are automatically sent back home. So while adventuring, fighting, etc, you will only be gathering gathering materials, in addition to occasionally getting new accessories to equip. As it currently stands, you will not be getting "Loot" such as armor (there's no armor in the game) and weapons. You do all your loot crafting and gathering back at home.

[h3] Alright, well am I still able to play casually, similar to Survival Games? [/h3]
- Of course! The game does an extremely good job at allowing the most casual of casual gamers boot up the game and enjoy playing at the pace they'd like to play at. If you're a slow gamer, it's all the better for you as you will be able to take your time and really take in all that the game has to offer. There's even World Settings to adjust not only the Difficulty of the enemies, but also the amount of damage you take, in addition to both how much Mastery Progression you earn whilst leveling up and how much of a stat upgrade you get per level.

[h3] My Overall Opinion on the game [/h3]
- I personally love the game. Having put over 900+ hrs into Craftopia, I stuck with that game for a longggg while in hopes that it would eventually get better beyond what it's been. I have since then dropped Craftopia, but now Cloudheim has very easily filled that spot.

- I enjoy my good vibes and in general, games that just make me feel good. This game does just that. I'm able to toss on my music and just vibe. I'm also someone that enjoys a good challenge (my favorite Hack n' Slash series being Ninja Gaiden) alongside good progression. Starting this game on the hardest difficulty + taking the maximum amount of damage was a great time. As I compared this game to crackdown earlier, as you progress, you'll eventually be wiping the floor with everything which feels really good and well earned.

- Do I recommend this game? For sure. If you're looking for a good vibe game, then this can cater to a large audience of gamers. If you're looking for a Survival Game, especially if you thought this would be like Valheim (based off of the name), then I'd say to at least give it a shot, but not beating around the bush, it's probably not the game you're looking for, although it can still be fun and cater somewhat to Survival Enthusiast.

[h3] Valid Critiques [/h3]
- The Multiplayer System is the BIGGEST issue for a lot of people. Currently, you are NOT able to carry over your own personal progress to the worlds of other players. What this means is that if you have done 7872hrs worth of farming & would love to use your Super UwU Big Melon Anime Woman Slayer Great Sword with +68 Enchant, then you can't lmao. You'll be sharing whatever progress the host has done.
- ADDITIONALLY, you are NOT able to explore on your own. If the Host is taking 2787hrs to figure out how to make a Training Sword, well, you better go play with the jelly cows or something lmao. Unfortunately, you aren't able to go out and terrorize the local orc life while the host stays at the base doing whatever.

--------------------------------------------------------------

Right now probably a solid 7/10 with some of the usual early access suspects like unpolished UI etc. but can probably shape up to be a nice 8-9/10 later.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1764948662}, {"review_text": "Character unlocks are gated behind either a paywall or an oppressive grind that takes forever, and with how little content the game has right now, by the time you unlock the character you actually want to play, there's no game left to actually play as that character.

Character progression is tied to the hosts save file, so you can only play with the same person hosting ever unless you want to regrind over and over again.

Game is always online through the developers servers, even if you want alone/solo. If the game isn't profitable enough and goes down, you don't get to play it anymore. If the devs push some horrible update that changes the game entirely or adds monetization, you don't get to downpatch or refuse it. 

I like literally everything else about this game, like a lot, it was so close to being perfect and they hit three really negative points and the developers and their community are extremely against any sort of feedback.

Response to dev post:

Characters are purely cosmetic, and while some are locked behind progression, but only when you are halfway through a class, not at the end of the game.
  --Characters being cosmetic doesn't change anything, you still have to play dozens of hours to unlock who you want to play as. If you want to be a specific ethnicity/gender/character then you will have to grind many hours to unlock them first. If they wanted to tie skins behind unlocking, sure, thats fine and fun, but they tied whole characters to this.

Character progression is tied to a host save file, but if you unlock a character in one game, your cosmetic will travel to the next world you play in. So if you unlock a character in one save, you can use it in another.
  --But nothing else comes with you, which is what everyone is complaining about. This is a very grindy game. And if you aren't ONLY playing with the same host, then you will star over again.

The game is not always online through our servers, it is peer-to-peer hosted for this very reason - we also hate when games turn off servers and you can't play. We wanted to avoid this, so we went with peer-to-peer hosting.
 --This is just rewording what I said. It's a peer2peer connection as in it still uses your friend's or your ibandwith, but requires a connection to the developers servers in order to function. That means you can't play this game while travelling on your deck or laptop for example (unless you have wifi where you're travelling). It's a bit boring to play alone, and it's a shame the snowy location isn't unlocked right away.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1765017757}, {"review_text": "I wish I there was a neutral option. I was leaning positive before, but because of something I ran into today, I am leaning slightly more towards not recommending it.

The game is pretty decent, It looks good, combat feels alright though a bit hectic, however this hecticness  is part of their advertisement so that was to be expected. The movement outside combat can be a bit janky. where you have to jump on jump pads (air currents) in the air but you can barely move whilst in the air and a second jump might move you way further than intended.

- Classes and Characters
The game has 4 different classes and quite a few different characters you can play as, Characters however do not affect your gameplay besides unlocking skins for said character by playing it.

You level your class by "Mastering"a weapon or skill of said class, you do this by getting enough experience whilst having it equipped you can also level up a weapon itself to make it stronger, however since you need to swap out weapons to a new one when you mastered that specific one you tend to end up swapping back to a weaker weapon quite often. luckily you can hold 2 weapons as this mechanic does not really promote using a weapon you like and leveling it up.

The mastery mechanic kind of baffles me as well, as you master a new weapon/skill you get a mastery point to spend in your class.. however, there is only one line of things to put points in, so unless the Devs are intending to make a fleshed out skill tree I am not entirely sure why we even have to manually spend the point as  there is only one thing to spend it on.
I will say the look of the mastery resembles a season pass (the Tribes of Midgard one specifically in my opinion) It just shows the icon for the next unlock on a horizontal slider.

- Combat
Combat is a bit hectic and fast paced, Enemies show a charge meter on the floor for their attacks/direction which sometimes gets obscured by the environment, or gets really cluttery if there are a lot of enemies.
There is no lock on but there is a slight autoaim which is nice, but can also be a hinderance, unintentionally making you attack an enemy that is either doing an ability or is near an object that causes a slight knockback/stun.
(There is a shield slam ability, that when done without enemies, just slams the floor right infront of you, but if there is an enemy, it will do a slight jump towards them and then slams the floor. This&the autoaim made me jump to an enemy doing a spinning attack instead of an enemy right infront of me, and get knocked back/stunned)

You can equip, 2 weapons, which come with ( so far I've only seen)class specific abilities, and 2 seperate abilities.
Next to a lasso to grapple enemies and move or reveal treasure in specified spots. A kick and a dodge(roll) these 3 can be interchanged with similar abilities when unlocked.
Besides having an active ability, weapons also seem to be casting certain abilities when doing Jump attacks, which is not mentioned anywhere nor could I find any information on this, It does however seem to be weapon type specific. (Every hammer and shield combo seems to do a warcry as jump attack(yes.. warcry) . where every sword and shield combination does the Shield slam attack. these are however also abilities that can be equiped by the player themselves, or be the weapons active ability seperately of the jump attack)

You also play in third person which works on when traversing the map, but during combat can become a hinderance, especially in dungeons. As the Dungeons aren't as open and thus sometimes during a fight your camera angle means you can't see anything that's going on, there is one particular one where the boss room has a fairly compact structure you're fighting in/around, however due to the design your camera will be obscured more often than not, making it hard to see what is going on, This combined with this boss setting out slowing AOE's and there being a lot of enemies around, makes it a pain to deal with.

- The hub
The game is designed around one central home base/hub where you build a bit of your base, crafting benches and gather some basic materials that respawn, and from there you go to instanced area's to explore and fight and do missions, these Instanced area's are quite big So you won't be having loading screens that often.

In the hub, you have a square area (and supposedly you can build a premade home to place certain things in?) Where you can place your workbenches/upgrade buildings etc. 
They look really nice, but they don't fit well together, most of these are premade houses(?) for a tiny species called Blin. Where you can either drop in materials to have it automatically craft something, or add more Blin to get specific upgrades for said building.
Because of the sheer amount and them and being premade, it can easily start looking like a complete mess, and none of them really compliment eachother (this is all in my opinion).

Weapons for a class come in some variety you can craft them at your forge. Where weapons made of the same material, will either upgrade your existing one, or can get sold at your Hub's store.
Item storage/crafting works a little(tiny) bit like Astroneer, you drop your items on open slots, visible on the workbench and then it crafts automatically.
So you drop ingots in your forge on the side depending on what class weapon you want and when it has enough of a certain ingot(/combination ingots?) it will start crafting. However if you are dropping more than it can hold, it will move over to slots on one of the other classes sides automatticaly and might start crafting those.

You can build a store. Which is a building with a bell you use to open/close said store. 
When open random NPC's will start running around your base, either looking at items you placed to sell on tables. or waiting around for other services. 
There is no price setting for the player(at least not that I could find). The price it shows when you place an item to sells seems to not always be what it sells for.

This entire mechanic feels redundant and out of place as you put this fairly big store counter/building in the same area as your crafting workbenches with no fitting decor around it. and all it does is slowly/automatically sell your unwanted items to random NPC's that have nothing to do with your game. and there is no player interaction with it besides putting down the items you want to get rid off.

Now the part that made me lean to not recommend it.
Whilst doing a dungeon, I ended up in the final puzzle room, which.. I coulnd't figure out, this dungeon had a similar looking puzzle in it earlier where I had to lure and defeat enemies into a certain area to progress. However, this area though looking quite the same, with a similar indicated area.. had no enemies.. and nothing else to interact with. 
I did However see a waterfall, and thought that maybe there is something behind it.. and OH THERE WAS.. a very easy to jump up path (by the looks of not intended for it to be) that brought me to the top of the area.. out of bounds, clearly not meant for players to access. 
I thought well,. maybe they just let you get up here but no further and there will be an invisible wall... there wasn't  I could just walk over the top of the map, towards the final room of the dungeon. jump in through a gap in the ceiling.

I am by no means someone who  tries to find their way out of bounds, or unintended shortcuts.. so that I got up here without any effort.. or really realising I was getting out of the map makes me feel like they did barely any tests where people did unexpected things.

If this WAS intended Then I'd say they did a horrible job at the map design on that part as it was just a white void and parts of the map below, 
There is more to say, but this has to be the Limit of my review, The game can be fun, but needs qutie a bit of polishing.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1765007064}, {"review_text": "The game's art and gameplay is quite fun. Being true to its marketing material (Master the chaos), the combat is indeed chaotic. It has received many changes and improvements up to this EA release and I think the current iteration is in a good spot although I still feel like something is off.

Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare set a new benchmark for first-person shooters when it launched, redefining the genre with its modern military setting and intense pacing. The game departed from its World War II roots to present a fast-paced, high-stakes narrative grounded in contemporary conflict. With its expertly designed missions and cinematic presentation, it quickly established itself as a standout title in the series. The sense of urgency and realism it offers remains impactful even years after its release.
The story follows a gripping narrative centered around global terrorism and military intervention, featuring perspectives from multiple characters across various factions. This approach offers a layered and immersive storytelling experience, moving players through war-torn environments and covert operations. Memorable missions such as “All Ghillied Up” showcase not only technical ingenuity but also emotional depth. The narrative structure successfully keeps players engaged through its tense pacing and dramatic twists.
Gameplay in Modern Warfare is tight, responsive, and highly refined, delivering a balance between cinematic spectacle and strategic combat. The combination of on-rails sequences, tactical objectives, and large-scale battles ensures a dynamic experience. Multiplayer mode became a defining element, introducing the now-iconic progression system with perks, killstreaks, and customizable loadouts. Its addictiveness and replayability set a new standard for competitive online shooters.
Visually, the game was a technical marvel for its time, utilizing realistic lighting, detailed character models, and immersive environments. The attention to visual fidelity helped ground the experience in a believable modern warfare setting. Effects such as smoke, fire, and debris added intensity to every combat encounter. The art direction and animations contributed to a polished and authentic look that supported the game’s tone.
Overall, Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare delivers an exceptional blend of storytelling, gameplay, and visual execution. Its influence on the FPS genre is undeniable, thanks to its innovative design choices and gripping presentation. From its emotionally charged narrative to its groundbreaking multiplayer mechanics, it stands as a milestone in gaming history. This title remains a prime example of how to elevate a franchise while pushing industry standards.
Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare gets an 8/10.

While the 2007 original was revolutionary in its time, revisiting it today highlights limitations that the reboot successfully overcomes with modern technology, stronger narrative direction, and far more polished gameplay systems.

The biggest weakness of the 2007 version is its simplistic and outdated gameplay mechanics. Movement is stiff, sprinting is limited, weapon handling lacks nuance, and shooting does not have the realistic recoil, weight, or sound depth that define the reboot. Compared to the reboot’s fluid animations, tactical sprint, weapon mounting, and highly detailed gun models, COD4 feels basic and almost arcade-like. The reboot provides a level of immersion and responsiveness that the 2007 game simply cannot match.

Multiplayer, once praised as groundbreaking, now feels barebones and unbalanced compared to the reboot. The original’s perk system is limited and easily exploited, killstreaks are basic and repetitive, map design heavily favors certain playstyles, and customization is extremely minimal. Meanwhile, the 2019 reboot features a deeper weapon progression system, extensive Gunsmith customization, richer sound cues, and far more refined balancing. Returning to COD4’s small selection of weapons and predictable class setups makes the experience feel shallow rather than nostalgic.

Visually, the difference is even more dramatic. COD4’s graphics once impressive now look flat, washed out, and lacking detail. Character animations are stiff, environments feel static, and lighting is basic. The reboot’s advanced engine brings cinematic realism, dynamic shadows, modern textures, volumetric smoke, and stunning environmental detail. The contrast makes COD4 look not just dated, but almost unrecognizable compared to today's standards.

The campaign, while iconic, also suffers when judged against the reboot’s storytelling and presentation. COD4 relies on fast pacing and memorable set pieces, but the character development is thin and the narrative lacks emotional depth. The reboot offers richer writing, grounded performances, morally complex scenarios, and a more mature tone. Missions feel more immersive and have greater narrative weight, making COD4’s story seem straightforward and less impactful in comparison.

Overall, while Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare (2007) deserves respect as a classic, it struggles to compete with the Modern Warfare (2019) reboot in gameplay, graphics, storytelling, and technical polish. The reboot not only modernizes the formula but elevates it to a level of immersion and quality the original cannot approach. Viewed today, COD4 feels outdated, limited, and overshadowed by the reboot’s far more sophisticated and engaging design.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1765004278}, {"review_text": "Despite being nearly 20 years old, it's the same old Call of Duty you know and love(?). Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. It's still the same CoD4 that you remember. The same campaign with its memorable (though overshadowed by MW2 and 3's campaigns.) The same multiplayer with atrocious perks that are rage-inducing to deal with. The same few good maps surrounded by absolutely stinkers. The same guns that mostly sucked except for a few that everyone used. The same lack of interesting camos except for the red and blue tiger ones. The same old everything... Except Prestige, since that wasn't in this PC port for some absurd reason. Yay, even less of a reason to keep up with a multiplayer experience from 2007.

Do I hate this game? Absolutely not. CoD4 was a very important game to me, as it came out during a very bad time in my life. My very late adolescence was terrible--worse than most people's, but this hunk of golden age multiplayer from the aughts, was there for me alongside several other decent releases from that year. But I'm not gonna go off about that, you're here for a review about CoD4.

The campaign is your usual Call of Duty stuff: Overly linear missions with frustratingly boring combat encounters, and those juicy bits of story that keep you going. Cool set-pieces, cool weapons, and some real cool characters. We love you forever, Captain John Price.

Multiplayer is just as you remember: Frustrating, chaotic, toxic, and absolutely replayable. There's not a day that goes by without yours truly remembering some absurd, insipid moment from playing this game. Getting a taste of Martyrdom, Juggernaut, Last Stand, and the most infamous weapons, and of course, the Godforsaken sniper culture that was born here. Those crazy killstreaks with a bizarre class setup you experimented with for laughs one day, or just having a really hot match that made you look real good in front of a bunch strangers over the internet. I personally remember a great match on Ambush, in which I went 45 and 3 with the Mini-Uzi, and then scavenging other players' weapons until that score limit was reached.

CoD4 is a beautifully simplistic game, that while not the best aged multiplayer experience out there, pretty much appealed to everyone. Now whether that was a good thing, is really up to you; I understand that Call of Duty isn't particularly liked by many a gamer due to its negative impacts on the FPS market and gaming industry, but I'm not here to discuss that.

Do I recommend Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare in 2025? No.
Now, now. I understand that I just talked positively enough about this game earlier, but I have to be honest and admit that this game is just too barebones by a lot of peoples' standards, even later CoD game standards. There's only a handful of good perks that don't make you come off as a cheap dork, most of the maps just turn into spawn-camp, vantage point camping, grenade spamming, nightmares. While I praised the chaotic nature of this game's multiplayer earlier, I don't really think most people with actual lives are looking to do crazy arcanic rituals, just to have a decent match without overly cheap BS.

You will find that the statement: "If you can't beat them, join them," rings incredibly true with this funny game.

I'm not an overly crude 17 year old anymore, I can't just sit down and trash talk people in this, while abusing obnoxious class setups and acting like I'm a king. And as much as I miss those days, I can't find the magic with this game anymore, but I can keep the memories and nostalgia, and as should you.

Overall: Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare is a solid 6.8/10. Nothing is perfect, and CoD4 reflects this perfectly. An above-average experience with a lot of nostalgia and genius game design that appealed to everyone, despite the M rating and disdain for where it took the FPS scene. And while I said "no," as a recommendation earlier, I still ask that you interact with this before just taking my opinion at face value, and moving on. If a future update brings a sick fog horn to my boat, I will then see this as a 10/10 experience.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1762568230}, {"review_text": "Another one of those moments where I wish Steam had a "Neutral" review option.

TL;DR is I'll give this one a tentative yes in its current state because I love the worldbuilding, the aesthetics and the gameplay loop itself is very solid, but it's also probably a decent idea to wait a bit to see what the devs end up cooking up here. I would say if you're unsure, play the demo, as-is currently it's a very accurate reflection of what you'll be doing for most of the game *after* the demo. If you like the demo, you'll like the game as well, just be prepared for some buginess and bad performance, as the demo area is probably the most solid section of the game (the demo is the same as where you start in the game).

---

First off, in my opinion as the game is, 30 Euros is simply not a reasonable price for what's at offer currently. I think starting off at 20 or even 15 is more reasonable for its current early access state, and I can see it being worth 30 down the line with a lot more content and polish applied. I'm running this on a 4080 Super with a 9800x3D, and on medium settings WITH DLSS on Balanced mode (because Performance mode introduces hideous artifacting), I still get a very unstable 70ish FPS at best, with *massive* frame variance and frame drops constantly, especially in the  bigger areas of the game where I'm lucky to reach a stable 40/50 FPS. That might sound decent, but keep in mind that I have a top of the line GPU and CPU and am barely scratching above 60 *with* DLSS and medium settings, I suspect that on weaker machines it runs very poorly. While it's a pretty game for sure, 90% of what you see is small static buildings sitting in the middle of an ocean, so the game really should be a lot more performant and stable.

Aside from performance, while I love the resource gathering loop, it also has an abysmal combat system that you can't avoid. The combat is floaty, with animations that feel like placeholders for the most part, terrible enemy hitboxes and just in general it doesn't feel fun or engaging in any way, it's just a frustrating part of the game that's forced on you. The guns are extremely unsatisfying and clunky to use, the melee is you spamming the C button over and over again and hoping that one of the hits land, and just in general I feel it detracts from the game more than it adds. The loop is basically you see a swarm of 50 little creatures that will scale the tallest structures in the game just to float around in an awkward way and do 1 damage to you as you spam away at them while holding the C button. It's SUPER janky and simply not fun.

IMO the devs need to move away from the combat, because I'm worried that what they'll do is focus a lot more effort into the combat instead of improving other parts of the game that are much cooler and could really make the game stand out among the crowd of other games like it.

What they should be focusing on is the resource gathering & logistical side of the game. They have a system that has the potential to really shine here, where you have a bunch of different resources you can gather and feed machines with through flexible cables that you can run up walls and around corners etc. It's a genuinely REALLY cool and fun system to engage with, all they need to do here is introduce more mechanics surrounding the cable/pipe management and introduce some automation for the player to setup. More intricate machines with more complex inputs.

I'd also love to see more ship-related content. Let us upgrade the engines, customize how the ship looks, add decorations to the ship, add new decks and superstructures, entirely new ships you can unlock from exploring, let us build on-shore infrastructure for the ships, let us use cranes to load/unload a bunch of stuff at once etc. What's there currently is nice, but they could do so much more with the ship gameplay and I'm excited to see what they end up doing with it in the end.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1762511421}, {"review_text": "The Last Caretaker is a visually impressive survival experience with a strong atmosphere. The graphics are genuinely stunning, and the core gameplay loop scratches that classic survival itch nicely. Exploring, gathering, and managing resources feels solid, and the story—when you do come across it—adds a layer of intrigue and mystery to the world.

However, performance is a clear weak point right now. The game seems heavily CPU-bound, and it runs hot. It feels like it may be using AVX instructions or otherwise pushing the processor harder than expected. Even on capable hardware, the framerate can dip and the system load is noticeable. Also enemies are a bit of a mixed bag. Feels a bit rushed and copy pasted. Red, Green or Blue Alien starfish that spawns litte critters. Also the resource management is serviceable,  as in , it could use some QoL love. Like show contents of chests while hovering over them, since you will end op with loads of to the brim  stuffed chests.

- Satisfying survival mechanics
- Story adds depth (if/when encountered)

The lighting effects are lovely and really help mark explored areas clealy.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1763922953}, {"review_text": "The last caretaker is a game about a robot well after the end of the world trying to restore humanity. It is a lonely, yet beautiful trek across a flooded world with only your ship and the long dead voices of those in the logs to accompany you. With each step of the journey, each shattered companion you find discarded on the ground, it can quickly start to feel like the journey is hopeless. That even if you succeed, it may amount to nothing.

And yet, I find that I cannot help but continue. I cannot help but want to restore this broken world. To ensure the success of humanity among the stars. And so I restore island after island, rid them of their infestations, fight tooth and nail, and fix everything I can find that needs fixing. 

It is a deeply satisfying journey to undertake, and very few games have this sense of absolute scale, where you can arrive in a place, realize the incredible amount of work that must be done, and simply shrug and begin work on your megaproject. When you do get a place set up to peak efficiency, the feeling is amazing, and then you pack up and head to the next place to restore that as well.

Without spoiling too much on the specifics of your journey and the turns that it takes, there are moments of genuine tension, wonderful depth in the details, and surprise along the way. I do not in any way regret my journey with The Last Caretaker, and if you give it a chance, I very much doubt you will either. Don't take my word for it, look at the discussions. (for reference, I do not in fact have a potato PC. Mine's mid-high tier).

Most of the game is fine, and honestly plays quite well. However, combat is one of the major problems. In theory with how it's designed (and the rare occasion it's not a total crapshow) it actually works well for the most part, but projectile weapons will, for each shot, either crash the game, crash [i]your computer[/i] if you're unlucky, or make the game freeze up for a period of time.

Storms, while neat and bringing some functionality for wind turbines, will also bring your PC to a crawl every single time lightning strikes. The game will also sometimes randomly slow down without any apparent reason.

Aside from performance the game can also be a little confusing as to how to proceed or handle things at times. Now, I don't expect (or want) handholding, but I also shouldn't have to look around in the discussions to figure some things out or to clarify something.

I grew up with the anime, and it felt great to finally field the Digimon I watched on TV. First thing I did was chase Patamon so I could build toward Seraphimon; childhood dream unlocked.

Combat is classic turn-based: easy to learn, but on Hard it can be punishing in a good way. Turn order, buffs/debuffs, and smart team comps really matter. The quick battle option for weaker encounters is a nice quality-of-life touch.

One heads-up: the personality system can be confusing. If you’re trying to hit the exact personalities for DNA Digivolutions, you’ll probably want a guide and a bit of DigiFarm tinkering. It’s not a deal-breaker, just opaque at first.

The story has a good length and a couple of great plot twists. Pacing drags here and there, but the payoffs land. Main story plus all side quests took me about 58 hours.

What I liked most: the battles and the sheer freedom in digivolution. With 400+ Digimon to chase, it’s easy to lose track of time.

If you like turn-based JRPGs and Digimon, I recommend it. It’s nostalgia done right, with enough depth to keep veterans engaged.

Hi, I wasn't expecting my little meme post to get this much attention. It's not my intent to spread misinformation or deceive people on the fence about buying the game.

Whether it was made with or partially with Unreal Engine 5, I could not get a straight answer from google. But per the comment discussion, it seems that I jumped the gun while looking for a quick answer. I do not believe the game was made with Unreal Engine 5 or previous iterations at this time.

I have experienced so far; 

0 crashes
0 stuttering
0 frame drops during cutscenes or gameplay.

So it is well optimized and runs smoothly. 

Second, I compared the game to Shin Megami Tensei. After a few hours of trying the new systems it's clearly not a 1:1 copy (I can't talk to hostile Digimon mid combat, at least so far.) 

But I can sacrifice hundreds if not thousands for Yen, so that's pretty demonic. 

It is clear to me that they took heavy inspiration from the recent ATLAS hits to make this game, and that's totally ok! It still maintains enough fresh ideas and creativity to not feel like a lazy cash grab! 

My only major criticism is the DLC and micro-transactions. Way too many, especially for a game marketed towards children who don't know better. The NPC in the Theater who takes you straight to the store page to buy DLC is inexcusably greedy. 

With all of that said, so far, I give this game an easy 9/10. Not perfect, might be too easy even on the first available highest difficulty, but that's ok! It's fun! As a fan of this franchise since I was a kid, (I'll remember watching episodes with my brother on Saturday Mornings forever.) I've been with Digimon when it struggled to compete with Pokemon, and I'm happy to celebrate it when it finally has the attention and momenta it deserves. 

Might be too short, might be too easy. Please tone down the micro-transactions.

Lastly, I didn't know that reviews disabled comments by default. I welcome civil discourse and debate on the state of our hobby and Digimon is no exception, so please go wild in the comments. I find myself struggling to put it down and I cannot say that for a lot of games now a days!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1760132099}, {"review_text": "You've probably seen a lot of praise for this game and how it's the best Digimon game ever made - and that's absolutely true, but I'm gonna let you in on a little secret: it's still "mid".

It's a good game, but not great. I've played all previous instalments of Digimon World/Story, and the best way to describe Time Stranger would be 'half baked'. For every positive selling point, there is a glaring asterisk can't be ignored.

- Trailers show a beautiful open world of vast environments - but in reality they're cleverly disguised linear mazes. All of it.

- Over 450 digimon to discover and train - but in reality they are all the same and every Digimon can reach 9999 stats in every stat. Forget team building, there's no differentiation between them. Fast bird? Nah, the turd Digimon can also reach 9999 speed.

- Build your own pocket dimension where you train your Digimon - customise your own world with different terrain and trophies - except it's has zero effect on gameplay. Train your fire Digimon in the middle of the ocean? No problem.

- Exciting 3 v 3 battles - but there's no variety in techniques. The vast majority of techniques are elemental recolors. At least with Pokemon, fire can burn, electric can paralyse, ice can freeze. Here, they all just do the same thing in different colors. There are status effects like 'sleep' and 'paralyse', but...

- Challenging boss fights - except bosses are immune to status effects, rendering any strategy other than buffing and sweeping obsolete. How this was carried over from CyberSleuth blows my mind.

- There's a card game mini game (I loved the one from World 3) - except it's brain dead simple and seems like a lazy afterthought.

So why is this a recommend? Honestly, it's the IP. Unlocking and collecting new Digimon is still fun. But that also means if you stripped out the Digimon, this would just be another mediocre Megami Tensei/Persona clone. And it hurts to say this because Digimon fans have been eagerly waiting over two decades for a game that is both fun to play and can be recommended to a non fans.

But this ain't it, chief. Visuals and story are strong points, but the core gameplay just isn't there yet.

Even if your not a digimon fan, if you enjoy turn based combat rpgs this is the game for you.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1760681869}, {"review_text": "Alright, so I’ve been playing Digimon Story: Time Stranger for a while now, and honestly? It’s pretty dang fun. It’s not perfect, but if you like classic turn-based monster battlers with some nostalgia mixed in, you’ll probably have a good time here.

Gameplay:
The gameplay is solid — your standard rock-paper-scissors elemental system that’s easy to pick up but still has some nice depth once you start building different teams. It’s got that satisfying rhythm of scanning, evolving, and swapping Digimon around to find what works best. Combat’s quick, flashy, and just plain fun.

Graphics & Animations:
The visuals are great. Everything looks clean and colorful, and the animations are super smooth. They really nailed the look and vibe of Digimon here — it feels modern without losing the classic charm. Watching your Digimon pull off their attacks or digivolve never gets old.

Digimon Variety:
There’s a good amount of Digimon to choose from — way more than I expected, actually. You can build a lot of different teams and strategies. A few missing ones feel kinda unnecessary (like, why leave out that one?), but overall it’s a solid roster.

Story:
Now, this is where things drop a bit. The story’s fine — not bad, not great — but your character feels completely irrelevant. You’re just... there. The operator does all the talking (and is voiced, by the way, even if your own character isn’t), and it really makes you wonder why your protagonist exists at all. It ends up feeling like The Inori & Aegiomon Show while you just walk around like a ghost.

Digifarm:
The Digifarm is kind of a mixed bag. The space itself is nice and useful for raising Digimon passively, but the actual management is tedious. You can’t check digivolutions for Digimon currently in the farm without removing them first, which gets old fast. And feeding them? Ugh. Watching the same little eating animation fifty times in a row just to raise bond is painful. A “feed multiple” button would fix this instantly.

Character & World Building:
Pretty much nonexistent. The world feels rushed, and there’s barely any side development outside the main story dialogue. You don’t get much sense of who these people are or why you should care.

Overall:
Despite the issues, I’m still having a great time. The gameplay loop, visuals, and Digimon roster carry the game hard. If you’re a Digimon fan or just enjoy monster-collecting RPGs, it’s definitely worth a playthrough. Just don’t expect deep storytelling or much personality from your main character.

TL;DR:
✔️ Fun, classic combat
✔️ Great animations and visuals
✔️ Tons of Digimon
❌ Soulless protagonist
❌ Weak world-building
❌ Digifarm needs quality-of-life updates

Still, for what it is — it’s a good time. 👍", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1759725250}, {"review_text": "Some ppl announced they'd be review bombing the game because of the delayed release download. Now you might argue that the pricing shouldn’t matter in a review, and that you are rather interested in knowing whether this game is good or not. What you are willing to pay for it is your business alone. Fair enough I guess.

[h3] Things to be enthusiastic about [/h3]
The game has a lot of positive surprises in it. The story may start slowly, but after the first third of its runtime the tension and mystery picks up a lot. It is genuinely a gripping and emotional story with a great main cast and some very positive side characters. Some twists you’ll probably see coming but others will catch you by surprise. Be prepared for the story to feature mature and fairly dark themes such as war and how it affects the population of humans and digimon alike. Don’t worry though, it manages that without feeling overly oppressive or depressive. 

Every digimon has a unique special attack animation, sometimes even more than one which is awesome. And there are all these little details on top of that, which show how much love has been put into this game. For instance every time you use an item in fight on one of your digimon, they happily emote to that. It is really cute and a nice touch. Speaking of the battle system, it has a lot of (semi-deep) tactical options and things you’ll need to manage. The latter boss fights are a delight and you have some great challenges as end-game-content.

[h3] Things that are good and bad at the same time [/h3]
The game has some rather mixed choices in its game design and narration. While the story does get much better later on, the first 20-25 hours are uneventful and at times even somewhat painful to get through. It doesn’t help that most of the human characters are kinda one-dimensional and not all that interesting unlike the great digimon cast for both friends and foes alike. That is a bit of a pity.

Similarly, the battles are great and disappointing at the same time. Yes, I mentioned fun boss fights and I really did like them. Well, mostly the second half of them because the first were almost trivial despite choosing the „hard“ difficulty. However, the real issue are the mob battles. With one exception none of the regular fights were challenging at all. They felt like copy paste filler in between boss fights, which is a shame considering that this is what you’ll do the majority of the game. I acknowledge that this is sadly quite prevalent especially in RPGs. Games like Baldur’s Gate 3 and Clair Obscur showed that this doesn’t need to be the case though.

[h3] The game’s serious flaw [/h3]
If you want to pinpoint the biggest issue of the game with a bit of an edgy comment, it would look something like this: „You’ve most likely already played this game even if you’ve never spend a single minute in it.“ What do I mean with that? This is referencing the real antagonist of Digimon Story Time Stranger: the game and level design. 

If you have played any of the two Cyber Sleuth games, then you’ve basically played this game with less quality-of-life features. In fact, this is also true if you’ve played any linear turn-based RPG from the PS2 era onwards. You have small linear maps with copy paste mob enemies and (very short) loading screens when you move to the next location and of course also a fine selection of fetch-side-quests (go from a to b and fight c) over and over again… Some call this „not pushing the boundaries of the genre“, others will see this as yet another attempt at the classical but overdone turn based RPG-formula with basically zero innovation. 

If that doesn’t bother you and if you really like turn based RPGs, then you probably will have a good, perhaps even great time with the game. If you’re looking for something fresh and unique, you’ll find next to nothing here.

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]
Overall I did have fun with Digimon Story Time Strange and it does have some undeniable strengths. However, it is also very formulaic with a heavily dated map and quest design. You’ll have to decide whether that is a deal-breaker to you or not.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 19, "timestamp_created": 1761082164}, {"review_text": "Actual day one price is $147.96 if you buy all the content they removed and sold separately. 
The $119.99 price they're charging for the "ultimate edition" doesn't include everything.
The greed has to stop. Even 10/10 games shouldn't cost this much.
The video game market is due for a crash. Wait for a sale.

Instead, I'll give you MY experience as a first-time Digimon player. I hadn't even watched any of the movies or anime/TV Shows before picking it up. Just going in blind.

I have absolutely enjoyed ever bit of the 90+ hours I've gotten in the game, and will never understand the claims that the base ($70 USD) is not worth it. I do understand in some countries it might be a higher price, which I know complicates things for some. If you're in that boat, I get it. Even for those who just can't afford it without saving, I do get it... but you're inability to afford it does not make a game unworthy of a particular price tag.

This has been one of the BEST, of not THE best, $70 (USD) game I have gotten in a couple of years, if not longer.

I don't understand why people want collision on NPCs when there is absolutely NOTHING to gain from it. In fact, I foresee the vast majority of players getting PO'd over it if it were the case, because they would almost CONSTANTLY just be obstacles blocking your path. The game will intentionally force you into a certain path if it doesn't want you running through a crowd of NPCs. 

I also want to note that the Demo doesn't do the game's graphical design any justice. I see people put the game down before they even get started because their surroundings are "bland", when they haven't even gotten past the tutorial/Demo area yet, or made it to Iliad -- where you spend a very large portion of the game.

I see Time Stranger's design being more "anime-style", where they pick and choose where to put full detailing. You're not going to get the best details in an area you're not going to spend much time in, or that most players literally wouldn't be paying attention to. There are people complaining that the FLOOR of all things is boring when they are in an abandoned, charred building and underground/sewer tunnels. Of course it isn't going to be all that interesting to look at.

But once you start getting into other areas, and especially once you get to Iliad, you really get to experience the best of the best in terms of design. The places where it actually matters, where they expect players will spend longer periods of time there. The Digimon also, ofc, have amazing detailing to them, which make sense given we spend so much time looking at them. It would be a travesty to leave them with little detail. I also noticed small details about our player character and other NPCs we talk to, such as actual breathing animations (which most games ignore) and a shakiness to an NPC who explains their nervousness and excitement. I hadn't really expected those sorts of detailing, so was amazing when I noticed (esp the breathing animations).

Pokemon Legends Z-A is the same price as Time Stranger, yet more people seem to believe it is worth that price. Let me break down why that doesn't make sense to me, for people to then believe Time Stranger isn't worth the same price as Z-A:

- It's graphics aren't really any better, especially when compared to areas of Iliad.

- You're stuck in a single city (vs Time Stranger's 9+ uniquely designed areas, not including the alternative designs of some zones for different points in the story)

- You can't explore most (if any) buildings (vs the multiple buildings/rooms you can enter, explore, and even pick up side missions, play the card game, or get item drops)

- Pokemon Legends Z-A is the same "copy+paste" every Pokemon game is. It might be a little different with how you're not battling gym trainers for badge, and it's nice to see more story/lore coming into play... but it's still ultimately the same things. You're still just a young Pokemon Trainer going out and battling other trainers/Pokemon for the soul purpose of being one of the best trainers out there and getting Mega Evolutions...

- Vs Digimon's very clear lore/plot/story. Yes, you'll be battling other Digimon on the way, but it's because of genuine conflict. You aren't just using it as a way to make your own team stronger. Your Digimon aren't even "yours" in the same sense of Pokemon. They are your friends, your allies. They are here to help you, not be your pet who just does your bidding. They have their own culture, society, and conflict that we are involved in. There is so much more depth. /// I've also learned, ofc, that all Digimon games are fairly (if not entirely) different from each other, with different plots/stories, goals, and even variations of mechanics. 


Time Stranger certainly isn't the most detailed $70 game I've gotten, but given the genre, I never expected it to be. It has been an amazing ride playing Time Stranger. Over 90 hours, and such a big portion of that time was spent running circles in the Demo area or later zones to grind conversions, enhancements, and general leveling (which also makes the claims you can't grind in the game really weird to me). I haven't gotten burnt out from it, and don't see myself slowing down any time soon. The only reason I've at least taken less time to grind is because my Digimon are so leveled they are just sponging the damage even big bosses should be doing. It's kinda made me feel like I ruined the experience for myself a tad bit, with it almost feeling too easy despite me being on Hard mode. So I'm really excited to finish the story and then be able to do NG+ or the other, harder, game modes. 

As a new player, I'm also pretty excited for the DLC, simply bc it'd be an extension to the same story/lore, rather than them just moving on to a different game, which I assume would have its own plot line (based off people telling me all the games are different). Time Stranger is very much of those games that is kinda meant to be a great starting point for newbie Digimon fans, which I can say it does very well. I could do without the hand-holding the Operator (and maybe some NPCs) do, I get it. Digimon is still popular with younger audiences. I haven't played many JRPGs, but I think I was told this is pretty common for these games anyways. 

The game has definitely made me more interested in Digimon, getting me out of Art Block to do a poster of some of the earliest Digimon I saw and watching one of the old Digimon movies. I need to watch some of the anime and what not, but I will when I've got more downtime, lol. 

It's been a tear-jerker in some cases, and it was certainly a great choice for them to release the Prelude video (I don't even know how to explain it without minor spoilers). 

This game is the first time in AGES where I have seriously buckled down and gotten into the mechanics. I normally get bored with it and with turned-based combat... but no.. oh no, not with Time Stranger. 

No one is going to be able to convince me it isn't worth the $70 USD when plenty of other games with the same price tag have been absolute flops that end up collecting dust and I never actually get my money's worth-- not even $1/hour of gameplay, bc I just lose interest and never touch it again. Meanwhile, I've gone over that $1/hour mark easily, without even completing the story yet, and still having the drive to want to do it again when I compete it for the first time.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1761484325}, {"review_text": "Finally!
