EN: This game has a dark secret that not many know, which can hinder an optimized and dedicated low-spender, where even a free to play player can be better. 
In this game there is the arena, where you can battle players to "get pictures" of their equipment to fill a scrapbook, the higher the % complition of the scrapbook, the more % EXP you get for your quests and thus the faster you progress. After each arena battle, you must wait 10 minutes or spend 1 cash currency to skip the wait. It turns out, people playing the game on a phone can watch an ad to skip the wait time and they can do this around 50 times a day (this is separate from the 10 minutes cooldown and it ticks down independantly). 
So far so "good", since all f2p games do this. However, a smartphone is not equal a smartphone, since the more valuable your data is (the more you use your phone for different non S&F activities) the more ads you get. So if you have a work phone that only has an authentificator and you use it for nothing else, you'll get around 3 ads/skips a day, if you have a phone that you basically spend your whole life on, you can get 250+ ads a day. Yes, you can only do 50 arena skips a day, but the other ads will give you 3 lucky coins per ad which you can the use to spin a wheel that gives very good additional rewards. So, as a player who spends let's say 15 EUR (more if you pay on Steam) for the 2 starter packs, you'll be significantly weaker than someone f2p who has a valuable phone and gets 250+ ads a day. 
As a test, I was doing arena every 10 minutes for the last 3 days while awake from the new server start, and barely reached lvl 36, someone who had 250+ ads daily got to lvl 51 and got way better stats and items from the additional goodies from the lucky coins.
You'll of course ask now, do I have proof, and yes I do, I had 3 smartphones in front of me today, one S&F account, one phone provider, one internet provider (using the wi-fi). My work phone that I only use for 2-factor and has nothing on it gets exactly 3 ads, another phone from a family member, that is a side-phone and used occasionally, had +/- 30 ads, a phone that is being used the whole time with a lot of apps, network activity and so on, had 250+ ads and I stopped the experiment since they seemed to never run out. And I can confirm, all the ads on all 3 smartphones were the same.
TL:DR If you like wasting your whole day to do an arena fight every 10 minutes and thus optimize your game, and in the end see, you are at the bottom of a f2p guild since everyone else watched ads like crazy and made you realize you wasted 3 days optimizing, go ahead and play. 
If you hate being discriminated for havign a "not-so-valuable-data on your phone" and everyone else will be better than you, even free-to-play, then this is definitely not the game for you. Keep away.
If you want to play F2P or low pay to play or even go full pay to play, make sure you have a phone with a lot of valuable data on it or else you will be at a big disadvantage..
I don't know what total playtime Steam is showing, but I have probably over 10k hours, playing since when there were only 4 classes (currently there are 11)

DE: Dieses Spiel hat ein dukles Geheimins, dass wenige kennen, welches einen optimierten und dedizierten spieler hindern kann, sogar F2P Spieler können besser sien. 
In dieses Spiel gibt es die Arena wo man andere Spieler bekämpfen kann und deren "Bilder der Ausrüstung" sammeln kann um ein Sammelalbum zu vervollständigen, wo je höher die % Füllung ist, desto mehr Erfahrungspunkte kiregt man von Aufgaben und desto schlenner kann man voranschreiten. Nach jedem Arenakampf muss man 10 Minuten warten oder ein "Cash-Währung" ausgeben um das Warten zu überspringen. Es stellt sich heraus, dass Leute, welche das Spiel auf ihrem Smartphone spielen, können Werbung schauen um die Wartezeit ebenso zu überspringen and das kann man ca. 50 Mal am Tag machen (das ist separat von den 10 Minuten Abklingzeit, welches unabhängig heruntertickt). 
Soweit so "gut", da alle F2P Spiele das tun. Aber, ein Smartphone ist nicht gleich ein Smartphone, da je wertvoller eure Daten ist (je mehr ihr das Smartphone für andere non-S&F Sachen verwendet), desto mehr Werbung kriegt ihr. Wenn man ein Arbeitssmartphone hat, welches nur ein Authentifikator hat und man verwendet es für nichts anderes, wird man so 3 Werbungen / Arena Überspringungen pro Tag haben. Wenn man ei nSmartphone hat ,wo man sein ganzes Leben damit verbracht hat, aknn man mehr als 250 Werbungen pro Tag kriegen. Ja, man kann nur 50 Mal Arena pro Tag überspringen, aber die anderen Werbungen werden 3 Lucky Coins pro Werbung geben, welche dazu verwendet werden, am Glücksrad zu drehen und gute Zusatzbelohnungen zu erhalten. Sagen wir mal, als Spieler, welcher 15 EUR (mehr, wenn man auf Steam spielt) für die 2 Startpackete ausgibt, wird man deutlich schwächer als jemand sein, der kostenlos spielt und ein wertvolleres Smartphone welches 250+ Werbungen am Tag erhält sein. 
Als Test, ich habe die Arena jede 10 Minuten für die letzten 3 Tage seid neuen Serverstart gemacht wo ich wach war, und habe knapp Stufe 36 erriecht; jemand, der 250+ Werbungen pro Tag erhält hat Stufe 51 aufgrund der Arena-Skips erriecht und hatte viel bessere Ausrüstung und Werte von den zusätzlichen Lucky Coins.
Ihr werdet nun bestimmt nach Beweisen fragen, diese habe ich selbstverständlich, ich hatte 3 Smartphones heute vor mir, selbes S&F Konto, selber Telefonanbieter, selber Internetanbieter (und verwendete das selbe Wi-Fi). Mein Arbeitssmartphone, welcher ich nur für 2-Factor-Verifizierung verwende und nicht anderes hatte genau 3 Werbungen, ein anderer Smartphone von Verwandten, welches ein neben Smartphone ist und nur gelegentlich verwendet wird, hatte +/- 30 Werbungen, ein Smartphone, welches die ganze Zeit verwendet wurde mit viele Anwendungen, Netzwerkaktivität usw., hatte 250+ Werbungen und ich habe dieses Experiment beendet, da es scheinte, dass die Werbungen nie aufhörte. Ich kann auch bestätigen, sämtliche Werbungen auf alle 3 Smartphones waren identisch.
Langes schreiben, kurzer Sinn: Wenn ihr es liebt, euren ganzen Tag zu verschwenden, indem ihr optimal jede 10 Minuten einen Arenakampf zu machen und schlussendlich ganz unten in eine F2P Gilde zu sein, da jeder andere wie verrückt Werbung schauen kann, und dann zu realisieren, dass ihr 3 Tage mit optimierungen verschwendet habt und doch was besseres machen stattdessen machen könntet und es stört euch nicht, dann könnt ihr das Spiel gerne spielen. 
Falls ihr es hasst, diskriminiert zu werden, weil ihr ein "nicht-so-wertvolles Smartphone" habt und jeder andere besser sein wird als ihr, sogar die kostenlosen Spieler, ist das definitiv nicht das Spiel für euch. Haltet euch bloss fern vom Spiel.
Falls ihr gratis oder wenig zahlend oder voll pay to win spielen wollt, stellt unbedingt sicher, ihr habt ein Smartphone mit wertvolle Daten, sonst werdet ihr einen rieseigen Nachteil haben.

Shakes and Fidget starts with an appealing premise — a humorous take on classic RPG tropes wrapped in a quirky cartoon art style. At first glance, it seems like a fun casual browser/mobile game where you can dive into dungeon crawling, character building, and PvP battles with a lighthearted tone. Unfortunately, after spending a fair amount of time with it, the experience quickly reveals itself as a slog masked by shallow mechanics and excessive grind.

The core gameplay loop revolves around sending your character on automated quests or dungeons, waiting for timers to expire, and then repeating the process ad nauseam. While the humor and art style provide some charm, the gameplay itself becomes stale almost immediately. There’s little skill or strategy involved beyond clicking buttons at the right time, and the progression system heavily relies on repetitive grinding rather than rewarding exploration or clever decision-making.

The PvP system, which could have added depth and excitement, feels unbalanced and frustrating. Matchmaking often pits you against opponents far stronger or weaker, resulting in matches that feel either unfair or meaningless. The reliance on gear upgrades — which are frequently locked behind RNG-heavy loot boxes or premium currency — pushes the game further into pay-to-win territory, souring the experience for free-to-play players.

Moreover, the interface and menus feel cluttered and dated, with little quality-of-life improvements to streamline the experience. Notifications and timers bombard you constantly, turning what could be a casual diversion into a chore that demands constant attention to avoid falling behind.

Steam forces me to cut every review in half every time I want to praise or criticize a game, so I'll try to be as brief as possible, although this games deserves at least an essay on how great it is.

[h3] Story [/h3]

One of the greatest improvements I've seen. KCD1's story was decent, but it was mostly just... there. It did what was necessary, provided what was needed and wasn't filled with logical errors and stupid discrepancies. It wasn't something to write home about though. But now? Now we have a proper great story to rival and surpass many other of my beloved games. Absolutely no spoilers here though. You have to experience it for yourself. [h3] Role-playing [/h3]

Another greatly improved aspect. There are so many ways to finish [i] most [/i] quests that even giving one as an example would eat all the space I have here. But there are also soooo many details and non-obvious ways to finish most of the quests, it honestly stunned me, and it still does. It looks as if the developers thought of almost everything, so if you use your imagination and deviate from the given objective while using logic, more often than not you will find that Warhorse have thought of that, and such things can even influence dialogues during this and further quests. NPCs remember what you did, they comment on it, they comment on what you do, how you act, how you're dressed, are you smelly or drunk, etc. TES games had things like that, but they pale in comparison honestly.

[h3] Music [/h3]

Another great improvement. KCD1's was decent. KCD2's is great.

[h3] Combat [/h3]

You guessed it, another big upgrade. It's smooth, it's not frustrating, it's easy. Honestly, too easy for my taste. Master Strike once again solves everything. Maybe Hardcore will fix it, but I didn't like KCD1's Hardcore, so I'm not holding my breath. But even like that it's still highly enjoyable, and you [i] can [/i] lose if you're too cocky. Also, only swords have Master Strike now, so that's something. Turning off indicators is a fun way to make things more spicy, but I had to use a mod for that.

[h3] Open world [/h3]

Yep. Again. Another big step-up. Just riding through the forest is interesting in this game, and this is the greatest praise I can think of. Games like Witcher or Bethesda games rely heavily on POIs such as caves, castles, monster lairs, etc. Almost none of that here. Does this make exploration boring? It doesn't. Because so many space that would be empty in any other game is filled with random encounters (the best I've seen in games so far too) and neat little discoveries that are also sometimes referenced by NPCs, but play no real role in quests.

I took some wine for myself and left. 10-15 hours later I was tasked with tracking down some bandits, and one NPC said that I can find them near said wagon. This will be even cooler when Hardcore is released, because such landmarks will help you find things when you can't see your position on the map. [h3] Interface [/h3]

Here, it's also uniquely stylish and authentic. It was also improved from a practical point of view, you can access your horse's inventory from the same place as you own, for example. 

[h3] Graphics [/h3]

It's at least as beautiful as RDR2 (kinda sad that a 2018 game is the one I'm comparing this one to, as most new games are far laggier, and at the same time far-far uglier and technically inferior to RDR2).

[h3] Issues [/h3]

Surprisingly, almost none. I had a few bugs, but 95% of them were visual. No broken quests. The only big issue was when I needed to chase an NPC, but didn't have the best horse, so I had to try ~20-30 times before I actually caught up with him. Other than that, the game has some minor issues, but that's all they are. Minor and negligible.

I'd also like to point out that realism in this game is not that tedious. Many people criticized RDR2 for such things, but I honestly think that RDR2 is more tedious than KCD2 in this regard. Don't like to rely on them to make the game playable, but it's not like that. The game is fully playable for a casual player, far more than KCD1 was. It's just extremely easy to install mods, so just know that you have that option.

[h3] Summary [/h3]

This is a great game, and one of the greatest RPGs I've played in a long while. It may not be for everyone, and that's a good thing. More games should be "not for everyone". This is what AAA games are supposed to be. What every miserable small indie company like ubisoft wishes to have. The Bad:

Archery - If you enjoyed using bows in KCD1, prepare for disappointment. Archery has been massively downgraded. It feels clunky, imprecise, and practically useless. The game clearly pushes you toward crossbows or, worse, those awful pistols.
No Theresa - This is a huge loss. Theresa was the heart and soul of the first game, yet here she's only briefly mentioned. While characters like Katherine and Rosa are great, none of them fill the void she left.

The Good:
Visuals - If you thought KCD1 looked great, KCD2 blows it out of the water. The environmental detail is stunning-no game does trees, foliage, and landscapes quite like this one. The world feels alive, and the lighting is breathtaking. Watching the sunrise paint the hills in golden hues is a sight to behold. The game picks up where the first left off, but with more weight behind your choices and more momentum in the story. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3428058980

Its not a fantasy epic with dragons and magic. Its a boots-on-the-ground, blood-under-your-nails kind of adventure. The kind where a screwing up a sword fight feels like it has dire consequences. I'd say that this open world doesn't need fireballs to feel alive. The air feels heavy with belief and tradition. Fields stretch into the distance, villages hum with the sounds of everyday life, and roadside shrines mark forgotten prayers. Everything feels touched by something bigger than you, like the presence of God and Kings are baked into the dirt and stone. Life moves around you, peasants go to work, guards rotate shifts, taverns get rowdy at night. Its not just a map to explore. It feels like a living, breathing place. Every detail pulls you deeper. The music swells quietly in the background, building tension without ever being too loud about it. The way the world looks and sounds creates a rhythm that's easy to fall into. NPCs dont orbit around you, they've got their own shit going on. People talk about whats happening in town, remember your past decisions, and treat you like someone with a reputation, good or bad.

At first, I was completely hooked. The story had me locked in from the beginning, it felt human, personal, and worth investing in. But I have to admit that after 50 hours, things started to blur. Some quests repeated familiar beats. Dialogue scenes dragged. I started skipping lines, which felt like okay maybe I've been at it too long, or maybe just something changed. Only 30 hours earlier I still was hanging onto every word spoken. It didnt ruin the game, but the shine dulled a bit with similar fetch quests.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3422888939

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 deserves your time and attention. Its rare to find a game that cares this much about getting the world right, where swords are heavy, towns feel real, and your actions carry weight. This isnt a game for rushing through. Its something to live in for a while. And when it clicks, it really clicks. I'll give it a break for now though and continue Henry's adventure in a while!

Blitz is essentially a more accessible, scaled-down version of World of Tanks, originally designed for mobile but now available on PC. Matches are 7v7, maps are smaller, and games are faster. It’s still tactical, but more arcade than simulator.
🔥 What It Does Well:
+ Fast Matches
Games usually last 5–7 minutes. No long slogs or camping matches — it’s ideal if you want something tactical but don’t have a full hour to play.
+ Large Tank Variety
Hundreds of tanks from WW2 to early Cold War era, across several nations. Every vehicle class feels unique: heavies absorb damage, lights scout and flank, TDs hit like trucks from cover. There's definitely a tank for your playstyle.
+ Easy to Learn, Hard to Master
The gameplay loop is simple on the surface, but angling, map awareness, weak spot targeting, and team positioning all play a big role. There’s a lot of depth once you start digging in.
😬 What Holds It Back
Simplified Mechanics vs. Classic WoT
If you’re coming from World of Tanks PC, Blitz will feel stripped down. No crews, no complex module damage, fewer consumables, and more arcade physics. It’s good for casual play, but may feel too shallow for sim-focused players.
Premium Economy + Power Creep
The grind slows a lot at higher tiers, especially if you don’t have premium time. And while the devs have gotten better, power creep is still a thing — some premium tanks can definitely give players an edge. You can play free, but it’s a grindy experience unless you’re okay with mid-tier gameplay.
Matchmaking Can Be Wild
Since it's 7v7, one bad player can really swing a game. You’ll run into unbalanced teams, especially in mid-tiers. No ranked system or MMR that actually balances teams well.
Clunky transitions, awkward shop layout, and a ton of flashy offers in your face.
Final Thoughts:
World of Tanks Blitz on PC is surprisingly good if you’re looking for quick, tactical matches without the heavier grind or commitment of full-blown World of Tanks. It plays well with mouse and keyboard, looks decent, and has a fun core loop.

That said, it’s not without its flaws. The monetization, matchmaking, and balance issues can be frustrating — especially at higher tiers. But if you’re okay sticking to Tiers V–VII and playing casually, it’s one of the better free-to-play shooters out there.

[{"review_text": "10/10, would return to the depths… but I question what I’ve awakened. [b]Works eerily well on Steam Deck btw[/b]

Dredge is like if [u]a fishing sim and a Lovecraftian horror game had a baby[/u], and it turned out to be both surprisingly relaxing and deeply unsettling. On the surface, you’re just a fisherman cruising around catching fish, upgrading your boat and living your best sea life. But beneath the waves something... [i]otherworldly[/i] is stirring and trust me, it’s not just the fish.

The fishing itself is straightforward. You cast your line by steering your boat to fishing spots marked on the map, and then you use a minigame mechanic to reel in your catch. Depending on the fish, the minigame changes in difficulty, with some requiring quicker reflexes and others just patience. It’s peaceful at first, but the deeper you go, the more you realize you're not just catching cod—you’re glimpsing ancient, eldritch horrors that should not be. The game lures you in with the chill vibes of upgrading your boat and collecting fish but before you know it, you're uncovering bizarre, unspeakable things beneath the waves. Imagine going from “Oh, this is fun!” to “What in the name of is [i]that thing[/i]?!” 

And you’re not just fishing for fun — there’s a whole eerie narrative unfolding as you explore strange islands and try to make sense of... well, whatever is going on. It’s as if the ocean is calling you like a siren song from the deep, pulling you toward madness. The deeper you venture, the more you realize that you might not be at the top of the food chain anymore—and the true horrors that lurk beneath the surface might not even be of this world.

- I would suggest getting the DLCs when they are on sale if you want more of the strange, unsettling world that Dredge creates.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1741074849}, {"review_text": "I wish I could play this for the first time again. If you're worried about it being too spooky, as someone who really dislikes scary games - I played Dredge twice. While there are dark elements, theres no jumpscares and you can tell when things are changing because of the soundtrack. Definitely don't pass on it!

10/10", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1754656376}, {"review_text": "I don't really like horror games in general. Slasher horror is way too camp for my tastes, and psychological horror gets under my skin in an unpleasant way.

So it's great that Dredge really isn't a horror game. I went into it expecting it to be, but what I found instead was an extremely chill, extremely relaxing, satisfying progression and exploration-focused fishing sim where the game pushes back against you enough to keep things interesting, wearing horror as a cosplay.

I think a lot of what it does is brilliant. In many open-ended farming sim style games (Yes, I am comparing Dredge to Starview Valley), it's pretty easy to feel aimless after a while. The fact that Dredge has a main plot, different biomes to explore, each with their own quest, and a relatively concise runtime keeps it feeling like it's moving at a jog, while many of its contemporaries are on a languid stroll.

Another comparison to draw is the day/night cycle in Dredge -- in most open-sims, it's a bookend, encouraging you to optimize your time, and forcing the 'return' in the explore-gather-return game loop. In Dredge, it's not so hard a deadline. Yes, staying out all night is probably a death sentence, but it's an interesting death, full of whispers one can cover their ears against, and rocks that one can veer from. Many activities demand the night, and it often becomes a source of tension instead of a wall; racing back through the dark with safety just in the distance, if only you are skilled enough to make it, if only you weren't so greedy as to stay up so late.

In short, if you have any love for open-ended sim-style games, but always thought they lacked an impetus or an edge, give Dredge a shot. And if you're like me and generally put-off by horror games, don't fret -- it's a very fun, gnarly set dressing hung atop a pleasant, compelling game that stands well on its own.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1737151157}, {"review_text": "Very good game. What slowed me down (in a good way) was how strongly the opening atmosphere pulled me in—the sense of the unknown, and fear of venturing too far too soon. I spent several in-game days fishing and selling basic catches just to slowly upgrade my boat so I’d feel brave enough to leave the starting area.

Once the world opens up, the real fun begins. The map isn’t as huge as it first appears, but each island cluster brings something new—different dangers, new fish species, and fresh mechanics that are introduced naturally as the story progresses.

At first, I thought Dredge would be another one of those cozy upgrade-loop games you can play while listening to a podcast. But the music and sound design are so good that I never felt the urge to turn them off or tune out. The soundtrack is calming, the ocean sounds—wind, rain, waves—are immersive, and even the fishing and dredging sound effects are satisfying. Fish aberration design is also top-notch.

I decided not to go for 100% completion since requirements are a bit much. Instead, I focused on what felt like a natural checklist to get the most out of the story and world. I did enough side content to fill in the lore, but skipped the grind.

Highly recommended if you enjoy atmospheric exploration, a touch of horror, and smart, satisfying gameplay progression.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1747155195}, {"review_text": "I think Dredge's biggest problem is that it doesn't know if it wants to be a chill fishing game with lovecraftian elements or a more horror based game where you have to deal with huge sea monsters.

It tries to do both and I don't think they really mesh well together.

I do recommend Dredge as it is a fun game, just feels a bit unfocused.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1744983231}, {"review_text": "TLDR: A fantastic fishing game that mixes suspenseful themes, time-of-day mechanics, and relaxing 'farming'.  Coupled with a rewarding upgrade tree and gorgeous visuals, Dredge is an unforgettably fantastic game.

Pros:
- At its core, the fishing is simple, fun, and rewarding.  The game gives you an encyclopedia to easily keep track of what you have or haven't caught.
- Simple yet satisfying upgrades allow you to catch better fish and explore further
- A fun map to explore; albeit somewhat limited in detail
- A captivating Lovecraft-ian story that'll keep you motivated until the game's conclusion
- Somehow, the entire experience is less than 1GB in size and looks gorgeous

Cons:
- Can be a bit grindy when looking for aberrated fish 
- Menus could've been more streamlined. Hotkeys for boat abilities, for example
- Upgrade tree and map both could've been larger... hoping for a sequel!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1746072671}, {"review_text": "Pretty sure I was born just so I could play this game

Best thing that has ever happened to me .
Thank you for your work", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 16, "timestamp_created": 1759679845}, {"review_text": "It starts off extremely promising: a weird lagoon, a small town, strange fish in the water, a lighthouse guiding your ship through dark waters. But instead of crafting an experience and telling a story, someone was thinking in terms of cookie-cutter gameplay loops and genre tropes. You must play the same fishing minigame in order to plough through an upgrade tree and go through a sequence of one-dimensional fetch quests until you are treated to a [i]very[/i] basic, almost comically bare-bones genre cliche of a "revelation." What a brutally shallow experience this was.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1740394151}, {"review_text": "DREDGE is one of those games that feels relaxing at first, you’re just a fisherman, out on calm waters, catching a few fish and minding your business. Then, a few hours in, you realize the ocean hates you, your fish have teeth they shouldn’t have, and maybe that fog isn’t just fog.

It’s a perfect mix of cozy and creepy. You’re managing your boat, upgrading gear, and exploring small islands full of suspiciously quiet locals. The days are peaceful, the nights… not so much. The game doesn’t throw jump scares at you, but the atmosphere does all the work, it’s unsettling in the best way.

There’s also this weirdly satisfying rhythm to it. You’re upgrading your boat, exploring strange islands, and pretending the locals aren’t clearly hiding eldritch secrets.

If you like cozy games but wish they had a bit more unease and mystery, DREDGE nails that balance. It’s chill, eerie, and just the right amount of weird.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1759805545}, {"review_text": "24 hours of play. A piece of a life, a day. Sacrificed to the depths. A message to spread, for others now.

Ah so, the game is fun, and charming. There are blemishes like inventory management and swapping between inventories, no hot key for quick management, etc. It's a design choice though, slowing the game down a bit for the sake of a more ponderous pacing. The game oozes atmosphere, but I'll admit I used a guide to power through it so what was charming didn't become tedious. Despite that I found myself wishing for MORE, not that there wasn't enough for what I paid for. I simply HUNGER.

It really scratches an itch that Sunless Sea and sky left. I hope they make another game in this setting.

If any devs read this, there are a few bits of low hanging fruit that I'd actually pay for: Iron rig tier 5 hull dev tree. It'd be fun to get the two last engine slots so we can run twin engine stacks, and maybe a few other small convenience upgrade items. The end tier fishing pole would be nice as a statless container that simply amalgamates all the rods stuck inside, encouraging its use. The Rock Slab fishing rewards feel like a missed opportunity, as many are replaced with superior items quickly, a short quest to fuse them into some sort of unified horror would be neat, perhaps a permanent upgrade for the dredge action.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1742531870}, {"review_text": "Dredge is a solid cozy game that lets you really take it at your own pace. Packed into a very unique, just a bit repettivie experience, this one was fun to chase achievements in and to explore the world on your own :3", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1744048305}, {"review_text": "A "cozy" game in horror theme.
While fishing is the main theme, it's like a 4/10 in terms of how engaging it is.

What makes this game stand out is inventory Tetris (with finite inventory size), exploration, ship upgrades and effectively the puzzle of finding the right spots to fish for specific fish. None of those are super massive or complex, but they are perfect for the scope of the game. The dark setting helps it from getting boring.

I wouldn't recommend the DLCs (they add more of the same, but are required for achievements), but if you're planning on getting them, get them right away. They are made to be played during main game, and not after it.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1755206552}, {"review_text": "The idea of a fishing game with elements of Lovecraftian horror is an interesting one, and Dredge makes good use of it for the first few hours. The cozy atmosphere and music are immediately arresting, and the mysterious narrative hooks and art style make for an intriguing introduction.

Once the novelty wears off, Dredge quickly settles into going through the motions of checklist gaming. After the first couple areas, you've essentially seen everything the game has to offer, and most of the progression entails optimizing tasks that aren't particularly demanding to begin with. The main threats at hand are nightfall and the leviathans that occupy the different areas, but both of these pose minor inconveniences at best and hardly live up to the mythology the game presents. The various tasks you're given are equally formulaic and rarely require much thought or intrigue to get through. These problems are compounded with the addition of DLC which add more padding to a game that doesn't need it.

Ultimately I think the fundamentals of Dredge are solid, and it's worth picking up the base game and spending a few lazy evenings with it. There are a few interesting story beats that crop up, and pulling a new horror out of the water never ceases to be satisfying. But once you hang up your captain's hat, I wouldn't expect much of this largely frictionless experience to stick with you in the long run.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763506232}]

F1 25, on the other hand, is getting praised for having a better handling model, LIDAR scanned tracks and is better looking. Now, one of the main reasons for the game looking a lot better than last year's game is the fact that they dropped support for old gen consoles (PS4/XB1), since it was those consoles holding the F1 games back when it came to graphics. People were also complaining about only having 5 LIDAR scanned tracks in the game (Melbourne, Suzuka, Miami, Bahrain and Imola) but Codemasters and EA have said that all 24 tracks HAVE been LIDAR scanned, but it takes a lot of time to fully implement them into the games, so whilst it may not be much, this proves that they have been LIDAR scanning the tracks. Now, I am going to talk about all the modes in this year's game.

Braking Point 3: This is the 3rd chapter of the Braking Point story mode first introduced in F1 2021. *SPOILERS AHEAD, IF YOU DON'T LIKE THEM, THEN PLEASE SKIP THIS PART* Konnersport are in a battle for both the Driver's and Constructor's Championships, but there are many twists and turns during their journey for the title. Such as team owner Davidoff Butler dying (Butler Global bought Konnersport prior to BP3), Casper Akkerman getting sacked as team principal, Andreo Konner returning etc. In some chapters, you can choose to play as either Callie Mayer or Aiden Jackson. You can also do this for the final chapter. In the final chapter, both Callie and Aiden are in a fight for the Driver's Championship. For me, I decided to have Aiden win the title because he was in Braking Point since the very first chapter in F1 2021. Callie's good, but people were kinda not happy with her during her introduction in Braking Point 2 back in F1 23. Aiden's the OG, alongside Casper and Devon. Even though Butler was first introduced in F1 2019, but I'm talking about Braking Point specifically.

My Team: This mode has gotten a HUGE overhaul and update ever since it's introduction in F1 2020, instead of being a owner/driver of your own F1 team, you are playing the role of a team owner, where you have to sign drivers, manage your upgrades, finances etc. In addition to managing your own F1 team, you can also choose to manage either Braking Point's Konnersport or the F1 movie's APXGP team. Before the race weekend starts, you can choose which one of your 2 driver's you want to race as for this weekend. This allows you to make your own scenarios. You can either treat both of your drivers equally, or you can do a Hamilton/Bottas, Verstappen/Perez, Vettel/Webber, Schumacher/Barrichello etc. type situation where one driver gets all the fame and spotlight while the other is just a wingman. If you choose to manage your own F1 team, you can also choose if you want to have iconic drivers or not. I know that it was also available in the other games, but now, the other teams can sign the iconic drivers to race for them, whereas in the other games, only YOU could sign them. It seems to have taken a bit of inspiration from Frontier's F1 Manager series, which I heard is now discontinued.

Driver Career: Driver Career was heavily focused on in last year's game, whereas My Team is the main focus for this year. So I think it's the same this year as well, and all the updates from F1 24 should be there as well. It should also have the update from this year's game where the AI teams can also sign the iconic drivers.

Challenge Career: I think it's the same thing from F1 24 as well, which is just a shortened version of Driver Career focused on a specific driver, with rewards for completing it. 

F1: The Movie: This mode has a bunch of scenarios focusing on scenes from the upcoming F1 movie which is coming out in theatres this June. People find this mode to be quite gimmicky, but for me, I think it's quite decent. It functions similarly to the Scenario Mode from F1 2012-14. 

F1 World: This mode is still identical when it was first introduced in F1 23, with the fanzones introduced in F1 24 which is just to compete for bragging rights. Furniture and supercars are still gone and have been gone since F1 24, in case someone decides to complain.

Podium Pass: The Podium Pass is still 50 levels long and contains cosmetics and F1 World resources. And like I explained in my F1 24 review, they brought back the option to buy Podium Pass levels, which I deemed to be a little bit controversial. However, the price of unlocking the VIP pass and buying the levels has been increased. The previous price for the VIP pass was 9,000 Pitcoins, whereas in this game it was increased to 10,000. Buying the levels in last year's game was 200 Pitcoins, while in this year's game, it's 400.

Now, I would highly appreciate NOT having people going to this review's comments section and spam shit such as ''Ea EmPlOyEe DeTeCtEd, Ea ShIlL, eA bOt etc.'' DON'T. If you do want to comment on this review, please keep it orderly and civil. No flame wars. 

I have been hearing people saying that this could be the last Codemasters F1 game, since they are saying that Codemasters is in the final year of it's contract with F1, should they choose not to renew. But considering that EA acquired Codemasters in 2021 for $1,2 billion, who would even try to match that? I don't think that F1 is gonna look for another developer, so I think that Codemasters and EA are gonna sign a new deal with them.

One last thing before I end this review, like I said in my F1 24 review, after the EA acquisition, the F1 Game Development Team was split into 2 teams. Team A works on the odd number games (2021, 23, 25), while Team B works on the even number games (22, 24). The odd number games have been doing better than the even number games, yes. People are also expecting the even number games to be just as, if not better, than the odd number games, but we haven't seen that yet. So, what I suggest is to not have very high hopes for the even number games, but you can have high hopes for the odd number games. That should balance things out. And if you have anything you would like to add to this review, please let me know in the comments. Thank you for reading this review till the very end!

I mean, forget the upgraded physics engine, improved tire models, or broadcast-style presentation – let’s talk about the real headline: Lance Stroll has managed to crash in every single race. Six out of six. Consistency is key in Formula 1, and this game absolutely nails it.

In Bahrain, he clipped the wall in Sector 3 during a perfectly calm out-lap. In Jeddah, he drove straight into the back of a Haas under safety car. At Melbourne, he managed to take out himself and his teammate while weaving on the formation lap. I didn’t even know that was programmed into the game – that's how far they’ve pushed the envelope of realism this year.

It’s like the devs captured the exact essence of every awkward, miscalculated divebomb, every oversteer correction that becomes an overcorrection, every inexplicable lock-up from real-world Stroll moments – and rendered them lovingly in 4K.

But it’s not just the crashes. The detail is immaculate. After each DNF, Stroll appears in the post-race paddock interview looking confused, muttering something about “not seeing the car” or “having damage from Lap 1,” even when he clearly did it to himself on a straight. Chef’s kiss.

I tried switching teams, turning off damage, tweaking AI behavior – didn’t matter. He found new and creative ways to bin it. Monaco? He crashed in the pit lane. Silverstone? He drove into the safety car. Spa? He spun under a yellow flag without touching the throttle.

It’s gotten to the point where I no longer play to win the championship – I play to find out how Stroll will crash next. It’s like a mini-game within the game. A beautiful, tragic ballet of carbon fiber and bad judgment.

And honestly? I love it. It adds a new layer of immersion. When I see a yellow flag on lap 1, I don’t even need the engineer to say it – I just mutter to myself, “That’s Stroll.” And 99% of the time, I’m right.

So thank you, Codemasters, for crafting such an authentic experience. You didn’t just simulate Formula 1. You simulated the drama, the chaos, and most importantly – the Stroll moments we all love (or love to cringe at).

The handling actually feels like something I can trust.
In F1 24 I always felt like I was driving on glass, just waiting to spin the moment I touched the throttle. In F1 25, the cars finally behave like… cars. They’ve got grip, weight, and balance. I can push harder into corners, fight for traction on exits, and not feel like the game is actively plotting my death. Tyre wear also feels way more fair — when I ruin my softs in 5 laps, I know it’s because I drove like an idiot, not because the game wanted me to suffer. Oh, and also, they improved the AI a LOT so now they make mistakes, spin out and stuff like that which is really cool.

The tracks are gorgeous — and brutally accurate.
With the new LiDAR scanning, places like Suzuka and Imola are so detailed it feels like the game is actively bullying me for every tiny mistake. Suzuka’s esses punish every lazy input, and Imola has bumps that make you think twice about pushing flat out. Bahrain at night looks absolutely beautiful, Miami FINALLY feels alive, (even though i still hate it) and I swear I hit kerbs I’ve seen on TV.

My Team 2.0 makes you feel like Toto Wolff
Running my own team feels deeper and more important this year. Decisions about staff, sponsors, and R&D actually matter, and I constantly find myself agonizing over which upgrades to invest in. Do I spend on aero or facilities? Either way, it always feels like I don’t have enough money, which, honestly, makes it feel authentic. (Especially if you build your team from the ground up with reduced cash and resource points. which i recommend very much) I love it, even though it also stresses me out like crazy sometimes.

It’s still kind of “F1 24.5.”
Don’t get me wrong, the improvements are great, but this doesn’t feel like a completely new game. It’s more like the best possible version of last year’s title. If you sunk a ton of hours into F1 24, parts of this will feel familiar, just shinier and prettier. (and with much better handling)

The bugs are there, waiting.
I’ve had commentary randomly cut out mid-sentence, a few animations glitching and some menus loading slower than an Aston Martin pit stop. Nothing broke the game for me, but it’s enough to make you sigh and say, “Yep, it’s still an EA release.”

For me, F1 25 is the best the series has ever been. The handling alone makes it worth playing, and the improved tracks plus the deeper My Team mode kept me hooked way longer than I expected. It’s not perfect — it’s definitely more of an evolution than a revolution — but I’m genuinely having fun with it.

(Yes, I know there are guides in the community hub, but I like figuring it out for myself.)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1735338362}, {"review_text": "[H1]So what's it about?[/H1]
TW:WH1 is a mix of Civilization and the Heroes of Might & Magic series: a strategy game in a fantasy world. You pick a scenario or a large campaign and then you can pick which faction you want to represent. Each faction plays different: there is a lot of variation in units, buildings but also in diplomacy, objectives and research. Most of the game is run from a map setting like civilization but battles are massive and go beyond what you have ever seen outside of the Total War series. You can zoom out or go down to the individual troop while everything plays in real time. Battles are chaotic at first but as you progress you learn better tactics and which units work best together.

You can collect artifacts and level up your lords (the person that is leading your army) so they become more powerful and give advantages to the troops. The map is divided in provinces and when you conquer all settlements in one province you get additional benefits. Interestingly enough you can’t just control everything: for example as a human faction you are not able to take control of a dwarf city you can you only loot or raze the city. Then there are quests and minor objectives that each give some bonuses. 

It may sound complicated but as you start to play you will notice that the in game tutorial does a good explaining the basics. You may have to restart one or two times before you get it but it is very enjoyable. It's one of those games that you tell yourself: I really need to sleep, ok one more turn to do A, B and C... and suddenly it's two hours later and you don't even realise it. The first time you play the campaign it may take 20 hours or so, but as there is a lot of replayability which all the different factions, quests and events you can easily spend hundreds of hours. I found one of the largest challenges is that you become too greedy and spread yourself too thin - the CPU will wait for that moment and then you lose a lot. Finding the right balance between building your economy, upgrading your armies and conquering the land is key to success.

Besides the main campaign there are two additional scenarios and there are Quest Battles (about 20 - 30; some heroes have up to seven different Quest battles others have about two). 

[H1]The good[/H1]
Just one more turn... it's been a while since I experience this. It's a really good game. 

The game still looks fantastic. The sounds effect and the voice acting are great. 

You can zoom all the way in onto individual units or zoom out for a birds eye view. This is done really well.

The map is huge and there is a lot of variety. I also like the in-game events and that the AI will not give up and continue to fight to the bitter end or decides to give up and wants to become part of your empire all depending on how you treat them and who you are. 

It's great that diplomacy and trading play a large role; it adds more character to the different factions.

There are so many achievements - great for people that like to earn them :-). 

By purchasing TW:WH and the DLC you are able to bring these over to TW:WH2 & TW:WH3. It's a nice touch and I wish other developers would do the same. 

I really enjoyed the differences between the races: it's not just different troops or buildings, the research trees vary greatly, tactics differ and even how to engage or not engage can make a huge difference between the races.

[H1]The not so good[/H1]
If you want to play with more than the basic faction you will have to buy DLCs. While not necessary if you're not interested - in the end you will probably buy them. However, the game is great and it got a lot of support of the devs. 

I experienced minor slow downs at the biggest battles - likely a limitation of the engine. 

Don't start with this game if you have an important week at work or school. All you will think of is playing TW:WH :-).

I found that the late game suffers in the same way when you play Civilization on a large or larger map: there are too many heroes, too many cities, too much micro management and I got bored managing the cities. You can play a race that is nomadic and that kept my interest longer but the end game is not so good. It's also a pity that it takes so long to get the interesting L5 troops - there are ways around this like using the Steam Workshop but it's a pity the vanilla game doesn't offer like a custom mode where you can start with all the units unlocked from the start.

It's a pity you can't apply the tactics of scorched earth to your own cities.

I wish we could build more defensive structures on the map or road etc similar like you can in Civilization.

It would have been cool to be able to have different formations for your troops or at least to be able to rotate your troops into a specific direction other than forwards at the beginning of the battle.

I wish you could instruct the heroes to auto cast spells and enhancements during combat.

It would be better to have an auto level function - especially when you have a lot of heroes there’s a lot of micro management.

[H1]Bugs and glitches[/H1]
In general I had a bug and glitch free experience. Some minor issues are:

I experienced one bug during the tutorial where the AI would not move and the game didn't freeze but just didn't move forward to the next AI. A restart fixed that. 

Sometimes the game zooms on a hero in the map while you are actually controlling a different one. Clicking on their name fixes it.

[H1]The DLCs[/H1]
There are 13 DLCs of which six are free. Some add new factions that you can play as, new heroes, a bloodpack (which should be free), quests, items etc. None is required but if you're a fan I would recommend to get these on one of the many sales. 

TW:WH1 is in itself a huge DLC for TW:WH2 & TW:WH3 

[H1]Summary[/H1]
A strategy game that takes all the good from Civilization, HOMM and then adds more of its own to it. There is a lot to discover and the game still looks great. It's largely bug free and the DLCs add more replayability to the game. What is there not to like?

[H1]Should you buy it?[/H1]
If you're in deep strategy games in a fantasy world then I strongly recommend TW:WH. My recommendation doesn't come without caveats so tl;dr the game is great and is worth playing.

My personal gripes. Some are just my opinion but others seriously need to be changed for the sake of the games benefit.

- KB&M controls does not have an option to direct attacks to mouse cursor. Targeting in multi mob fights is frustrating more then difficult
- Fast travel points not connected to each other but only to the last one you touch negates the point of it entirely. It causes more backtracking then needed. I want to go through the zones because I want to not because I'm forced to
- Not respawning at your nearest whisper (fast travel point) on death but on the last one you touched is criminal
- Parrying is the coolest thing you can do but this game hates you for trying it. You're not aptly rewarded for parrying enough to justify it leading to path of least resistance
- Giving every other enemy at the start firebombs that have INSANE tracking is a hell of an onboarding choice but there's only one other mob later on that uses an aoe projectile and it's a slow moving fireball. 
- Food being tied to healing is a choice. While I can understand the rpg element to it the friction in other parts of the game can't be denied. It takes early inventory space, it stops players engaging in the actual content to have to restock supplies and food becomes redundant as health gain is more accessible later on. This needs another look into because the idea is sound but the reality is not fluid
- Repair cost, in the same vain as food, causes friction. The idea is sound but when learning/fighting a boss having to go back and repair your gear takes you out of the combat. Overall, the game has a really unique aestethic that drew me in. The gameplay feels akin to Dark Souls in it's flow of careful combat, smart positioning, and long intense battles. I've crushed Elden Ring a few times and the format has grown on me over the years.

However, there are a lot of things this game does that simply doesn't feel "fair", which is quite a turn off. 

1. Enemies flying out with an attack from off screen/around a corner that has not provided vision. I understand the cheeky sneak attack move in ER when you charge too fast in a room. It just feels cheap in this game.

2. Enemy tracking. Quite frankly, it feels sort of like bullshit at times. Again, I understand following the flow of delayed attacks to really test your timing, but an enemy rotating midair just feels flat out wrong. Maybe a boss, but just a random halberd enemy is not fun. It's purely for punishment. It feels even worse when you see it with projectiles. If I hear a crossbow or see a grenade thrown, it is pure instinct to use that moment to move. Yet, it's so frequently a direct hit. It feels unfair. It does not feel rewarding when I'm successful either, which is the strange part. Something about the timing and tracking is simply not right.

3. Parrying/enemy speed. I put these together because the rate of attacks makes the entire combat flow feel so overwhelming. Parrying is not very forgiving (at least with some weapons), which is usually when dodging or proper movement can help. Yet some of these enemies dive so far and move so fast that parrying feels like the only option, which doesn't allow the play to play their way. It's either build for fast dodges or become a master at parrying. Not friendly. Not fun. 

Not to relate it to Dark Souls too much, but enemy movement is the prime opportunity for repositioning. To move around them and attack. Yet, the swings have massive arcs with little forgiveness. If you get hit, expect a follow up or two before you can react with a dodge or parry. 

Things need adjustment. I hope the upcoming update addresses some of these because as of now it's far too much of a slog than a good time.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 12, "timestamp_created": 1742343642}, {"review_text": "After the update, I no longer understand when I'm supposed to enjoy the game.

Secondly, fire him if he refuses to host such a stream. His refusal would confirm that he neither plays nor intends to play this game.

Before the latest patch, it was a complex and engaging game with its own intricacies and varied combat mechanics depending on the weapon and skills used.

REPEAT FOUR TIMES."

[{"review_text": "As you can see from some reviews some people will just cry that a game is a copy of a game that came before it. Yes Anno is still Anno...obviously. Somehow this surprises people. It's also about a 20 second wait for the Ubi launcher the first time you launch the game so these complaints not recommending the game are a bit nonsensical to me. Heres a list of good changes imo. There's a surprising amount

-This is a step up graphically. Anno 1800 looked great, this just adds a bit more weather and atmosphere. The building models and maps are more detailed but things like character models are a significant upgrade. 

-Performance has mostly been a locked 60 with high/very high, raytraced shadows, and DLSS on balanced/quality. I run a 4080 with a R7 9700x and 32gb DDR5 @ stock speeds. I have a 35 inch 3440x1440p monitor so I was very happy with this. When I turned raytracing off and unlocked the frame rate I was getting 100fps in my small town. There was way too much screen tearing without it locked though so I went back. 

-They introduce the game mechanics quite a bit better this time around. New players will have an easier time with this. Small things like game tips popping up in a silent visible notification on the top left of the screen instead of most games where tutorial tips are literally forced on you and often pause the game. This allows some learning at your own pace if you're new.

-This has a much more fleshed out combat and military system which was needed. Actual ground combat was a welcome surprise. I'm excited to be able to play a military RTS, city builder, and logistics simulator all in one game. There's actual varied mechanics to the individual ships and units which is cool to see. 

- You can now build more unique cities. The ability to build curved roads and rotate buildings at a 45 degree angle adds quite a bit to the variety surprisingly. 

- I didn't think I would care for yet another historical  setting but thay manage to make their take on the roman era interesting. I do hope the next title is something completely different though. I'm salavating at the idea of a 1950's Soviet/US era or something that's a fresh take for the series. 

-This launched with more standalone items compared to 1800 if I'm remembering correctly. Decently cool statues and ornaments. 

-This developer is great with UI and this game improved on the already good UI in the previous game

-Added a religion mechanic with varied interesting options

-The story is halfway intriguing so far, which was not expected. I saw some negative reviews that called it "woke" which is just hysterical/sad to me. 

-They've kept some quality of life stuff introduced as dlc in the previous game.  

-Added a research progression tree with three main varied subcategories that will allow rushing certain builds/playstyles which gives you a much more varied playthrough if you want to start fresh. This tree impressed me because it determines pretty impactful changes that can alter a playthrough.

-They added a brush tool that allows you to brush over buildings to change the look of them which adds to the city building element even more. 

Overall, I think this is in an excellent spot. It adds meaningful and welcome changes to the formula without removing core elements that make Anno the series it is. They're doing a lot with this game and I'm looking forward to seeing what they can do with it in the coming years.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 16, "timestamp_created": 1763012790}, {"review_text": "Initial thoughts are this game is exactly what most Anno fans will want, same gameplay as before but with tones of new and additional features that still keep it feeling fresh.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 13, "timestamp_created": 1762993240}, {"review_text": "- they cut the campaign's 3rd act and beyond to get this game out before the holidays. it ends awkwardly & suddenly despite earlier laying out potential plot lines, this confused players. is the story truly over or will it continue in a patch? not really sure

-there are a few criticisms with the interface such as missing bits of info that are tucked away in the statistics screen but could've been more openly displayed. i shouldn't have to use the copy/eyedropper tool to bring up icons of the same building type. sometimes you dont get alerts for important events like fires, you only come to realize there was a fire when they tell you that ruins are ready to be rebuilt. anno 1800's quest tracker is better. anno 1800's diplomacy screen is better.

- performance suffers compared to Anno 1800 because they've added raytracing and perhaps not enough optimization. with my hardware (9800X3D, 5080) i expect the default top-down view to stay at refresh rate fps (120), sometimes it does not, you can use upscaling to improve this but it will add ghosting & artifacts. it does look prettier than Anno 1800.

I guess that the format really isn't suited for a 2600 word essay. 

I’ll give you the intro and outro and maybe I’ll upload a detailed review on Youtube. 

Anno 117 makes a great first impression. The new mechanics are meaningful and feel like a genuine step forward for the franchise. The graphics and overall presentation are amazing and the game as a whole feels like the next logical step for the franchise. 

Why the negative score then? Is it because of the extensive use of AI? Or maybe because of Ubisoft connect? No. While both of these are serious issues, by far the biggest problem with Anno 117 is that it launched in an unfinished state. With its terribly rushed campaign, braindead computer players, dozens of UI bugs and severe balancing problems, some parts of the game feel like a finished product, while others feel like they haven’t left alpha. 

...

Anno 117 has the bones of a truly [i]great[/i] game, but is unfinished and in my opinion needs at least 6 more months of work to fix its core mechanics. I very much doubt that the developer will delay working on the DLCs in order to fix the main game. Anno 117 is playable and most of the time it’s even enjoyable, but built up frustration from the multitude of bugs and lack of balancing left me disappointed. 

I grew up with this franchise and it breaks my heart to think that this may well turn into another case where corporate greed has killed a beloved franchise. I really hope that the developers get their act together and it doesn’t come to that.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1763292035}, {"review_text": "For fans of city-builders, the year 117 CE represents the Roman Empire at its absolute height, and Anno 117 embraces this setting with confidence. The presentation is one of the game’s brightest strengths. The tiers have different complexities and distinct personalities, with the Patricians standing out as particularly demanding and even a bit mean, which adds rich flavor to the social hierarchy. The Mediterranean-inspired soundtrack brings the landscape to life and blends naturally into the experience. The addition of hybrid tiers in Albion feels smart and refreshing, and the UI is clean, readable, and well matched to the era. At its best, the game feels like it could become a new Caesar IV or CivCity: Rome, something fans have wanted for years.

Unfortunately, the illusion cracks the deeper you go. The storyline, while never the main attraction in an Anno game, is extremely rushed and contributes little to the overall experience. The use of AI-generated backgrounds without proper review is disappointing, especially at the game’s price point. Gameplay systems also show signs of uneven development. Diagonal building is awkward and fights against a pathing system that can’t decide between linear or diagonal logic. Clicking on objects often becomes a struggle, and setting up trade routes feels unnecessarily fiddly.

Military development is another weak link. Armies move slowly and require too many residents to produce high-quality units. Specialists and area-of-effect mechanics behave unpredictably, sometimes shifting with minor population changes even when all needs are fully met. Performance issues cap things off: late-game cities introduce lag, forcing players to drop settings like ray tracing and cap their FPS just to keep everything stable.

Overall, Anno 117 boasts a beautiful Roman setting and several promising ideas, but the experience feels rushed and lacks the polish expected of a major release. With time, updates, and DLC, it may still grow into the grand Roman Empire simulator many hoped for, but right now it falls short of its full potential.

Pros:

-Gorgeous Roman Empire setting at its historical peak
-Expressive, demanding tiers with distinct personalities, both charming and captivating
-Mediterranean-style soundtrack that enhances the atmosphere
-Clean, era-appropriate UI
-Clever hybrid tiers in Albion
-Strong potential as a spiritual successor to Caesar IV/CivCity: Rome

Cons:

-Storyline is rushed and thin
-Price does not reflect the level of polish
-AI-generated backgrounds lack proper review
-Clunky diagonal building and inconsistent pathing
-Frustrating click detection, especially for trade routes
-Slow, population-heavy military production
-Specialists and AoE mechanics behave inconsistently
-Noticeable end-game performance issues", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1763391269}, {"review_text": "Anno 117 is a [b]wonderful game[/b], currently held back by technical issues, the use of AI-generated art, and a truncated campaign. Gameplay-wise, Anno 117 compares to Anno 1800 much like 1800 compared to earlier installments.

It offers a fresh variety of gameplay options, both large and small. My favorite is how production buildings now affect nearby population in different ways; the greater variety of Albion pops is a close second. The game looks gorgeous even on my fairly old PC — although, for some reason, I had to roll back my NVIDIA driver to get stable FPS.

If I compare release-day Anno 117 to release-day Anno 1800, 117 comes out on top. It’s better in almost every way. I still recommend playing 1800 (especially with some essential DLC) — that game is fantastic. But please give 117 a chance too. It’s worth every minute.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 9, "timestamp_created": 1763502038}, {"review_text": "I'm confining this opinion to the custom game because, frankly, I have no interest in the campaign, in war, or in the drab, rainy celtic swamp.
I wanted to be able to play a game like Caesar 3, with better graphics, and the option to play peaceful; >>PAX<< Romana.

So far I've played one custom game this way, and honestly it's great. It looks *fantastic*, and is highly customizable, so playing peaceful is an option. Compared to Caesar 3, some of the simulations are a bit simplistic, but I don't mind too much, especially since the QoL features makes it a breeze to play mostly.

I'm missing C3's trading with other NPC-owned provinces, but overall it works. It's a bit annoying that you DO have to play both provinces (celtic and roman) in the same game, if you want access to *all* goods, instead of being able to trade for the raw materials and make it. You wont be able to build just one city either.
To get all the raw resources out of a province, you will have to settle several islands and set up trade routes between those, to access all the items. And you trade in absolute numbers, so no simple "sharing" of resources between islands.
So the old idea of having just one massive map to build a massive sprawling city on, doesn't seem possible. You can have a fairly large city, but nothing like C3, so be prepared to manage several outposts seperate from your major city (or make several major cities).
Not crazy about the forced island gameplay.

I wanted a relaxing Roman city builder that evoked the feeling of playing C3, but with gorgeous visuals and some QoL. I absolutely got that, and so far I'm really enjoying myself.


(PS: German and French audio, but no Italian? Really? Come on)", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1763109036}, {"review_text": "Unfortunately, I don’t think Anno117will keep a high review score as more time passes. The first few hours and initial supply chains are fun and satisfying, but the game drops off hard past that once you realize it’s all window dressing around a bare-bones, AI-generated shell of its predecessor.

I’m a longtime Anno fan since 1404, i have a minor in Roman History (just for fun, not for marketability), and I even made my own custom Risk board game based in the Roman Empire in the year 117, coincidentally enough. So you can imagine that i was SOOO excited for Anno 117. However, it feels altogether stripped bare of the features, complexity, and secondary systems that made Anno 1800 such a masterpiece. There are no Museums or zoos for collecting rare items and beautifying your cities, no Expeditions for fun little story beats (some people didn’t care for these but I LOVED THEM and was terribly disappointed they left them out of 117), no Electricity (obviously) or comparable system that makes you rethink your layout, a severely hamstringed Specialists system, a clunky and unintuitive console-friendly UI, and an infuriating combination of DRM and launchers — though i give that last one a pass since 1800 has the same problem. In exchange for those losses you get ground military units and diagonal roads that are barely usable.

It feels to me like 117 was designed to have as pretty of a facade as possible, but relegated the core systems and endgame to the background while entirely abandoned the art and story and humanity that made 1800 so endearing and “comfy”.

For example, the AI loading screens and art. In 1800, loading screens showed gorgeous concept art of slice-of-life snaps within the world. These were a joy to see between screens because they showed the dedication and multi-discipline effort that went into making the game. In 1800 you could really feel how these drawings, the elegant UI, the solid underlying gameplay, the orchestral soundtrack, and the well-written short-story-esque Expeditions came together as a fusion of all these forms of artistry to make a product that truly felt like a piece of art in and of itself.

In 117 these drawings are replaced by AI-generated hodgepodges of vaguely Roman stuff only tangentially relevant to the gameplay and setting. There are no expeditions, and the story writing that is there in the campaign reads like it was written by an early version of ChatGPT. Importantly, the Steam page disclaimer about the existence of this AI was added only days before its release, which is seriously scummy imo.

Ultimately I’m a little bit heartbroken, as silly as that sounds. I had utmost faith after 1800 and it’s DLC in this team, even preordering the gold edition and taking off the day to play — something I NEVER do (for good reason, clearly). But after 1hr50m of game time i decided to refund Anno 117; I had been more than happy to support the team that brought me so many hours of joy in Anno 1800, but it’s clear to me now that those artists and writers have been replaced by auto-generated AI slop. So don't buy this for the campaign. Game has great bones, better bones than 1800 did. So it could become an all timer but right now outside of some nice quality of life features its not as good as 1800.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1763202617}, {"review_text": "Since I see a lot of negative comments here, I would like to offer some insight from someone who has never played Anno before.

I think it's a shame that there are so many negative reviews because of minor aspects. I'm not a big fan of Ubisoft or AAA titles, but I think it's important to recognize good games. Even though people here call themselves Anno veterans, it doesn't feel like they're real gamers.

It's a shame that more and more negative reviews are being posted without evaluating the game as a whole, just because one thing is negative.


Gameplay:
- The gameplay is a lot of fun and feels very fluid throughout.
- It feels intuitive and it's easy for a newcomer to immerse themselves in this game world.
- The building feels complex, but also logical and coherent.

Music:
- The music is very beautiful, fitting, and gives a Roman feel, and can be listened to for long periods of time.

Campaign:
- For a solo game that I expect to be endless, I also get a campaign, which is no longer the norm today. The campaign is okay, there are better ones, but it's fine as an introduction.

General:
I like how the advisors are portrayed, giving me useful tips. It also looks nice and feels like a living world.


Negatives:
There are still some bugs and unsatisfactory elements, such as the fact that when I select multiple buildings, I can only rotate them at a 90° angle instead of 45°.
The multiplayer desync.
1-year pass – this is an outdated model.

But all in all, I think it's a very good game with a lot of fun and replay value. Don't be intimidated by the negative reviews.
-----------------------------------------------------

What follows is a descent into a surreal realm filled with forgotten memories, warped characters, and the ruins of morality itself. From a gameplay standpoint, Black Souls uses the familiar structure of an RPG Maker title but pushes it far beyond the simplicity of its peers. The world of Black Souls is a grotesque reflection of fairy-tale logic. Its environments are painted in muted colors, their beauty rotting beneath layers of decay and melancholy. Castles crumble into fog, forests hum with the echoes of distant cries, and the roads twist endlessly like dreams you can’t wake from. Beneath its horror, the game speaks to ideas of identity, guilt, and the loss of humanity. Despite its brilliance, Black Souls is not an experience for everyone. Its mature content, disturbing imagery, and deliberate lack of clarity can alienate players looking for traditional structure or comfort. [h1]Dark fairy-tale and cruel choices — a Dark Souls-respect[/h1]
At first glance it looks fairy-tale-like, but it forces cruel choices; a narrative-focused Dark Souls-respect H-JRPG.

You awaken as a nameless undead in a fog-enshrouded country, explore interconnected terrain, and repeat life-and-death gambits in ATB-leaning combat. On death there is a system to recover "souls" at the location, and coupled with the feature that all NPCs are killable, you play within a distinctive worldview. The contrast between unique cute anime artwork and unsettling presentation creates a sense that sharpens tension during play.

To list the key points briefly — high-freedom exploration, ATB combat where parry and timing matter, soul recovery that carries the risk of abandoning hubs, branching where NPC life or death changes the story, over 20 fairy-tale–motif heroines, multiple endings and New Game+ elements…that about sums it up.

Be warned: there are ethically heavy depictions and irreversible choices. The difficulty, which demands learning, is at the core of the enjoyment (cheat items exist, so the difficulty can be lowered).

Ext."whole content".

一見童話的な見た目だが残酷な選択を突きつける、語り重視のダクソリスペクトのH-JRPG。

+ an epic soundtrack that impeccably puts you in the right mood, whether you're absorbing the atmosphere with "walk in the woods", or driving through explosions left and right with Halo's iconic main theme. + epic combat with the covenant. The enemy AI was revolutionary for its day and remains so to this day. Enemies will go in and out of cover to regenerate their shield and outflank you. The only reason I have 26 is because my online leagues converted to it, unfortunately.

Single player hasn't been improved since 23. This "Draft Combine"/"Improved" Dev Lab don't bring any further strategy to the game. Just some cosmetic things that probably took, like, a week to implement. 

OOTP is now just an IP that was sold out in order to be a pay to win shell with Perfect Team. The devs for this are lazy, egotistical,  and actively censor any criticism of the game on social platforms. 

The only reason to buy this game is if your online league requires it or you like paying full price for a pay to win mobile game....on the PC.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 3, "timestamp_created": 1748821970}, {"review_text": "I play OOTP every day, but I cannot recommend this game any longer. Don't let the fact that I have tons of hours mislead you... it’s more a reflection of habit and addiction. If I didn’t get the game for free as part of the beta team, I honestly wouldn’t be buying it.

Perfect Team is a financial success, but creatively, it’s the biggest misstep the franchise has made. It shifted focus and resources away from the core game. After all these years, can anyone really say the offline experience has improved dramatically? Many longtime players would argue it has regressed.

I could write a 10,000-word essay on all of its issues, but here are some highlights in no particular order:

- OOTP is poorly optimized for 2025. A single save file can balloon into hundreds of thousands of files, creating a massive burden for backups, syncing, and long-term storage. In short, cloud saves are just not feasible.

- The in-game 3D remains frustrating. Animations are rough, results aren’t physics-based, and the follow-ball feature is disorienting. After more than a decade of development, I still stick with 2D because 3D is just not good.

- Game mechanics are bloated and inaccessible. Concepts like traditional player creation modifiers, sabermetric modifiers, league totals, and league total modifiers are scattered and unintuitive, especially for new users.

- Online leagues are outdated. There’s no official server support, so commissioners must know how to set up their own server or pay someone to do it. More importantly, there are no anti-cheat tools. Commissioners can view or edit ratings, and concerns about this are often brushed off. A simple player editor lock would go a long way to improve online league transparency and integrity.

- Documentation and support remain major weaknesses. Bug reports frequently go unanswered, and there’s no official manual to help players understand how the game’s many systems interact. It’s trial and error, even for veterans.

- The community wiki helps, but it’s often outdated or too vague. Developers have been hesitant to explain how core mechanics actually function, citing a desire to preserve mystery. In practice, this just makes the game harder to understand and harder to teach.

- The game often feels unpolished at launch. While there is some internal testing, the bulk of beta testing is handled by unpaid volunteers like myself, most of whom have full-time jobs and other commitments. As a result, the testing window before release is inconsistent, and many issues simply don’t surface until after launch.

Despite everything, I keep coming back to OOTP because no other game offers this level of control over a baseball organization. The depth of strategy, both on the field and in roster building, is still unmatched. Even when the mechanics frustrate and confuse me, the foundation of the game is strong enough to keep me engaged.

Customization is another huge draw. Whether I want to replay a historical season, build a completely fictional universe, or run a modern league with my own twist, OOTP gives me the tools to do it. Few games offer this kind of creative freedom.

I’ve also built a lot of familiarity with the game over the years. I know how to work around most of its limitations, and at this point, it feels more like a sandbox than a traditional game.

Most importantly, running an online league is still fun. The stories, rivalries, and personalities that emerge from human interaction are what bring OOTP to life. The software might frustrate me, but the online league experience is what keeps me coming back.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1746574196}, {"review_text": "You can feel the Com2us in this version. "Commissioner Mode" (God Mode) lets you change anything and everything in your leagues to the way you want it to be.

The biggest difference between the two is that great couch co-op aside, there are surprisingly deep builds that change each run, and every run route is different, with variable mid bosses and some common end bosses on each "stage".  You might go from one run of being a distance special attack spammer that can reload special attacks without having to punch someone to the next run being an aerial combo king that does elemental damage, to the next run being someone who can basically turn people you grab and throw into magical grenades that do area damage- and this is all one out of four characters with unique movesets.  

My only gripe is I wish it was four player, but then, I also recognize that the devs clearly put a lot of time into balancing the game for two players, and I could totally see some of the tight game play / focus on dodge and parries / development of ridiculous builds being compromised by adding more players in.

There is a bit more repetition in the map so far that may turn people off for a roguelite meant to be played many times, but branching path options, hidden secrets and enemy variety help it to feel like less of a repetitive slog.
