I love this game. I really do. The community and the devs are unparalleled in the current gaming industry. However, I cannot recommend this game. Everything I say here is in no way blaming the JMods for the game they run.

Recently, Jagex was sold by their previous (venture capital) owners, and acquired by a new (venture capital) corporation. Since this acquisition about 11 months ago as of the time I'm writing this, there have been several questionable choices that have been made that weren't ever really a problem in the past. These include consistently rushed updates that release bugged (or outright broken), which is not something that has ever been such a serious problem before this last year. Sure, occasionally there was something that was missed and was broken as a result, but it wasn't as normal as it is today. 
The other major thing that has come of this, was a pretty significant price increase 5 months ago. This game now costs nearly as much as a game like World of Warcraft. You can still only have one character per account, so if you want an alt, you have to pay a full extra subscription to play it. We also don't have a dedicated customer support. The best we get is billing support KIND OF, a chat bot with roughly 9 total returns which are usually unhelpful, and you can @ the JagexSupport account on Twitter and they MIGHT respond.

This is all well and good, but why am I writing about this now? That price hike was 5 months ago... Recently, some players (myself included) have gotten a survey in their emails about further monetization and price increases. Again, it has only been FIVE MONTHS since the last price increase. 

These price increases include: 
[list]
[*]Paying the amount we paid two price increases ago for a subscription, but you will have in-game ads with no specificity where they will interrupt you, and you have to pay MORE on top of another sub for a second character ($10.99 but a second character would be $12.49).
[*]Paying the amount we paid two price increases ago for a subscription, but the auto-log out timer is shortened by an undefined amount, when afk training methods are a big appeal for a lot of players. Late game grinds in OSRS make the game become basically a second monitor idle game while you work or play something else. And you have to pay EVEN MORE than the last one for another character ($10.99, but a second character would be $13.99).
[*]A mobile-only subscription for the previous price before the recent hike ($12.49). While when this price was still current and in the current state, you could/can freely switch between mobile and PC at any time as long as the same account isn't already logged in.

And finally, the big one:
[*]A staggering $32 per month (a 228% increase in price), or $350 per year, for 8 characters (unclear if you can multilog, but unlikely), "enhanced" player support (again, we don't have a dedicated customer support so pay us extra for a basic facet of online games), and "Specialized" member worlds, whatever that means,
[/list]
This is all not to mention that there are, indeed, two versions of Runescape. Old School Runescape and Runescape 3. Currently, one subscription pays for both games, but you can't multilog between them. So if you're logged in on OSRS, you can't log into that account on RS3. This subscription change wants to split the two games' subscriptions, but keep the same account restrictions. So you'd be paying twice as much to not be able to play both games at the same time.

Again, the developers are almost 100% certainly NOT to blame for this. In fact, the changes feel a little too absurdist and antithetical to the game that they have built and the community they understand. It almost feels like they're trying to make an example for the new investors to just let them do their job because they understand the playerbase. 
OSRS players are in a pretty unique position for this, as a large majority of them were alienated from the original Runescape when bad updates from investor ideas (including microtransactions and buyable-with-cash experience, which is a big no-no for the spirit of the game) pushed them away. So we're literally seeing this happen again in front of our eyes, except we all know for a fact that OSRS players are ready and willing to quit when things go bad.

Hopefully, this is all just a show for the investors and we never hear about this again. But for now, with this being a very real possibility, I cannot recommend this game. If and when they run these ideas back, I will remove this review.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1737048491}, {"review_text": "I have put lots of time on the game over the years ever since it was just 'RuneScape', and have many, many fond memories of the game and its world. I remember when EoC hit and my abyssal whip became worthless. I remember the release of the mobile beta for members-only and hurriedly dropping down the money for a new membership to be there. Completing Dragon Slayer and Monkey Madness for the first time, getting my first set of adamant armor 'trimmed' for free and never seeing it again... there is truly nothing else like this game the first time you experience it. Yes, the game is grindy, but its well-known for it and it can actually be quite enjoyable. You're not locked into any one play-style; everything the game offers is open to you to attempt and do what you like the most.

At least, in theory. For a game titled 'Old School Runescape', perhaps the only thing truly old-school about it these days is the aesthetic and the existence of the long grind. The game has actually modernized quite a bit, and brought with it a ton of quality of life changes that certainly make the game easier to play and more digestible for a modern audience, or for those who are learning the game for the first time. However, I feel that the modernization has crept past QoL and into content, for better and for worse. I don't play often enough these days to understand the state of '2025' OSRS, but that's also the issue I have with the game. And I must emphasize it is *my* issue with the game. New art doesn't exactly match the stuff from 2007, the emphasis on deep understanding of tick manipulation, prayer flicks, and the like to be able to attempt content past 'mid-game', the complete re-working of skills to include much more active focus on the game: for me it has turned what was once a somewhat mindless 'do stuff in a fantasy world' game into a 'I must optimize the path forward as much as possible' game. It can be argued that this is more so due to the culture that has surrounded the game and the desire for as much efficiency as possible, but most of the original content has been abandoned by players in favor of simply better content for grinding out skills. It can really make some areas of the game feel empty and desolate despite the active community the game still maintains.

All of this whining is to simply say, the game is no longer for me from a content and thematic perspective. I didn't realize what it was that I missed until I revisited what the game was like in Classic and 2004, and its the charm and simplicity of the game from those times that I just don't get here anymore. And sure the game is very rough in some parts in those versions of the game, but at the same time I felt more connected to the world itself in the short time I spent in those versions. This is also nothing to say of the rising price of the game, and for someone like me who has become disenfranchised with the game's current state, there is little value I get in return for the membership now. It’s a feeling—a portal to simpler times, pixelated dreams, and unforgettable adventures. Having played RuneScape since before the release of RS2, I’ve seen the game grow, evolve, and sometimes stray a little too far from what made it magical in the first place. That’s why OSRS is more than a re-release. It’s a love letter to every player who wandered through Lumbridge with nothing but a bronze sword and curiosity in their heart.

From the iconic chime of leveling up, to the timeless soundtracks (looking at you, Autumn Voyage), OSRS wraps its players in a warm blanket of nostalgia and challenge. It’s a game that doesn’t hold your hand, but it does reward patience, effort, and a bit of Google searching. It teaches you things no modern MMO dares to: how to fail, how to grind, how to find joy in simplicity.

And yet—this isn’t just a museum piece. Thanks to the passionate Jagex team and its incredibly active community, OSRS has grown into something much greater than a nostalgic relic. With player polling, the game has taken on a truly democratic form. Updates don’t happen unless the community votes them in. It’s like watching your childhood game evolve with you, not around you.

Let’s talk RuneLite—the game-changer (pun fully intended). While my in-game time may not reflect my countless hours (cries in maxed main), RuneLite is the definitive way to experience OSRS. From XP trackers and boss timers to clue scroll helpers and GPU enhancements, it’s the unofficial companion that feels so essential, it might as well be canon. RuneLite doesn’t ruin the purity of the game—it enhances it while staying true to its soul.

So here’s to OSRS. A game I grew up with. A game I grew up in. And a game that, to this day, continues to grow alongside me. 10/10 will play till the end of days.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1745527427}, {"review_text": "False ban for RWT for 10 years old account with 2.5-3k hours of gameplay. [h1]My Opinion After ~8 Hours of Playtime[/h1]

The gameplay concept is great and I'm having fun, especially in co-op. Building cars from found parts and constantly driving forward is entertaining. But unfortunately, there's also a lot of criticism to be made.

[h3]Driving Physics:[/h3]
The driving feels very arcadey — which I don't mind — but sometimes it’s a bit floaty. It depends on the car and engine. Some are very slow, others are pretty fast. I personally prefer the faster ones. But you can easily spin out of control. For example, I had a bug where I was towing a trailer, lost grip, spun in circles, and the trailer just flew away. Later, it randomly dropped from the sky in front of me. No idea if that was intentional or just a weird glitch.

[h3]Combat & Zombies:[/h3]
Let’s be honest, there’s no real combat system. You either punch aimlessly until the zombies fall over, or you shoot — but shooting doesn't feel satisfying either. There’s no impact, no feedback, and zombies don't react properly. They're just default assets with no animation, gore, or dismemberment. Guns like the AK have 30 bullets, and you can’t even combine ammo. You have to drop empty weapons and pick up new ones. It’s frustrating and lazy design. If you can't implement a decent combat system, just leave it out entirely.

[h3]Technical Aspects:[/h3]
Performance is mostly stable, apart from the occasional hiccup during quicksaves. Loading times are surprisingly long. The game has plenty of bugs — items flying away, ladders letting you fly into the sky if held, and more. While the core mechanics work, the overall feel is amateurish. For €25, I expect better quality. Right now, I'd say it's worth €10–15 max.

[h3]Graphics & World Design:[/h3]
The visuals are acceptable but far from pretty. Most things are just store-bought assets placed into the world without adjustment. There’s no real art style. The world feels lifeless — you and maybe your co-op partner are the only beings around. I'd love to see more: AI cars on the road, meaningful intersections, actual locations to discover, and handcrafted environments instead of repetitive filler.

[h3]Sound & Music:[/h3]
Engine sounds are okay, especially bigger engines later on. The music on the radio is surprisingly good and copyright-free, which is great for content creators. Bonus points for the in-game radio hosts who talk directly to players — that's a fun and creative touch. However, there's barely any ambient noise, and many audio clips are weirdly in French while others are in English. That inconsistency is distracting.

[h3]AI & NPCs:[/h3]
Not much to say. There are no real NPCs besides zombies, which I already covered. So this point can be skipped.

[h3]Innovation & Early Access:[/h3]
Is the game innovative? Kinda. The idea of endless road-travel with car-building is fun — and better executed than similar games. The developer is actively working on the game and releasing updates regularly. There’s a roadmap, but it's vague and not super informative.

[h3]Conclusion:[/h3]
The core gameplay idea is great and definitely enjoyable — especially for a few hours. But the game currently lacks depth, surprise, and variety. You’ve seen everything pretty quickly, and that kills long-term motivation. What it desperately needs:
– Branching roads
– More AI life
– Unique, well-designed places
– Real combat feedback
– More surprises to keep exploration exciting

[h1]Ganz cool – aber extrem viel Luft nach oben[/h1]

Spielzeit zum Zeitpunkt der Review: ca. 8 Stunden (Koop mit Freund) 

Ich habe das Spiel jetzt etwa acht Stunden gespielt – größtenteils im Koop – und muss sagen: Ich hatte meinen Spaß, auch wenn es technisch und spielerisch an vielen Ecken noch sehr roh ist. Es ist halt ein Early-Access-Spiel, das merkt man, aber das Grundkonzept funktioniert. Trotzdem gibt’s einiges zu kritisieren:

[h3]Gameplay & Fahrgefühl:[/h3]
Das Fahren ist sehr arcadig – nicht realistisch, aber okay. Einige Autos fahren sich lahm, andere wiederum ganz spaßig. Das Tuning und Umbauen während der Fahrt ist überraschend motivierend. Es ist irgendwie cool, dass man mitten im Fahren sein Auto verbessern oder umbauen kann.

[h3]Zombies & Kampf:[/h3]
Der schwächste Punkt. Die Zombies sind einfach nur da. Keine gute Animation, keine Wirkung beim Kämpfen – man prügelt sie halt einfach um. Waffen gibt’s zwar, aber mit komischem System: Wenn die Munition leer ist, kann man sie einfach nicht nachladen. Wegwerfen, neue finden. Das wirkt unfertig.

[h3]Technik:[/h3]
Viele Bugs: fliegende Objekte, Leitern, die wie Jetpacks funktionieren, Anhänger verschwinden – vieles ist unfertig. Die Performance ist okay, aber die Ladezeiten sind lang, und das Spiel friert manchmal beim Speichern kurz ein. Für 25 € fühlt sich das noch zu unausgereift an.

[h3]Grafik & Immersion:[/h3]
Die Grafik ist akzeptabel, aber nichts Besonderes. Viele Elemente sind einfach nur fertige Assets, ohne eigenen Stil. Die Welt wirkt leblos. Kein Verkehr, keine NPCs außer Zombies, keine richtigen Orte. Man fährt nur eine Straße entlang. Das war’s.

[h3]Sound & Musik:[/h3]
Motorensounds sind okay. Nichts Besonderes, aber auch nicht schlimm. Die Musik im Radio ist überraschend gut und vor allem copyrightfrei – ein echtes Plus. Die Radiomoderatoren reden sogar über das Spiel und geben Infos – sehr charmant gemacht. Aber: Viele Texte und Ansagen sind auf Französisch, andere auf Englisch – wirkt unausgereift.

[h3]KI:[/h3]
Gibt’s nicht wirklich. Zombies rennen einfach nur auf dich zu. Keine Tiefe, keine Abwechslung. Kann man sich sparen.

[h3]Besonderheiten:[/h3]
Das Konzept, immer einer Straße zu folgen und unterwegs zu looten, ist grundsätzlich cool – aber eben auch schnell ausgelutscht. Es gab schon andere Spiele mit ähnlichem Konzept, dieses hier macht es nur etwas besser.

[h3]Early Access & Entwicklung:[/h3]
Positiv: Der Entwickler ist aktiv und bringt Updates. Die Roadmap ist aber sehr vage und nicht besonders informativ.

[h3]Fazit:[/h3]
Das Spiel hat Potenzial und macht in der richtigen Stimmung echt Spaß – vor allem im Koop. Aber es fehlt an Tiefe, Überraschungen und einem eigenen Stil. I never wrote a review for this game because I'm a big Armored Core fan and I knew I would be biased, but let me tell you why you, someone who has never played an Armored Core game should buy and play this game.

If you games for the STORY: The game has multiple endings based on which missions you choose to play. When you go on to new game+, more options are unlocked, keeping the story fresh and you play it additional times. 

If you play for ACTION: The game is fairly fast paced and based on your loadout. I think if you want fast paced gameplay, you can certainly get that out of these missions. You can also play slower and more strategically, it's all based on your build.

If you play for STRATEGY: The amount of customisation you can do with your build is amazing and unrivalled imo. There's no way to max every possible stat, and I believe it's possible to build a viable AC based on any stat in the game (Within the single player campaign, multiplayer has some balance issues). I honestly spend a lot of time building and tuning concept AC's. 

If you play for CUSTOMISATION: The decal and emblem editor are unmatched. There are not micro-transactions for anything. Painting your AC and adding decals is always a pleasure. There's a lot of tools to learn for more in-depth customisation. It's easy to use, but to get the most out of it, you might even want a tutorial! In a good way! 

So, I do suggest buying this game. I don't think you'll regret it. There's a community of players who love the game online if you manage to get stuck.

As an emerging fan of the mecha genre I found this game around the time I started getting into gundam and I didn't have any expectations going in besides the fact it was a fromsoft game (bosses with second phases). Needless to say i was blown away with what this game delivered. My most played mecha game (and favorite game) is Titanfall 2 and this gave me a whole new perspective on what the mecha genre is and can be if done right. I believe Armored Core 6 to be the gold standard in terms of mecha movement and combat and i am eager to try its previous installments. The games story is rich and came with unexpected moral dilemmas that I've lost sleep over, constantly muttering dialogue lines under my breath every now and again. The characters involved are exceptionally made and the 3 endings means you get to see almost every character from a different angle, both for better or for worse (I still think rusty is the true unsung hero of this story). Every single component of this game works and weaves together to give the player an unforgettable experience, whether its spending hours customizing your AC to make the coolest looking mech, or maybe its simply spending a little extra time in a mission to listen to its music or dialogue lines, or maybe its getting overly emotional at the boss you've spent a consecutive 2 hours on, there's always something this game can give you. 

MUSIC: 
The amount of emotion these tracks can bring is unprecedented, specifically for the missions where you need to make a choice between 2 evils, or pushing down the path you've chosen, far beyond the point of no return. The games soundtrack is a mix of gritty ambiance to more orchestral synths that really drive home the feeling of mechanized battle. It is very rare to hear more organic instruments, for example the guitar, which i think further reinforces the feeling of dehumanization on the battlefield. TL;DR at the bottom. Spoilers are 'spoilers' (dialogue lines).

A few weeks ago, I randomly remembered that AC6 exists, so I bought it when it went on sale... and I've got to say, it's probably one of the better games I've played, and one of the few that I've actually strongly felt for since I played Titanfall 2's campaign (way back in 2016). The gameplay is fast, the fights are cinematic, and even though you never see any of these characters' faces, some of them really stick with you - [spoiler]«You found your purpose...didn't you, buddy?!»[/spoiler]

Most other reviews seem to talk about combat and buildcraft and you've probably read some of those before reaching this, so I wanted to take this opportunity to instead discuss (without spoilers) the story and, namely, how I interpreted the main character.

Raven is a character that fits an archetype you don't see often. He[?]'s not troubled, regretful, or even independent - but he's [i]free[/i], and the game hints at this for much of its course. A victim of circumstance that has the blessing of free will, to pick the path that he takes, without being shackled by the thought of 'what if'. The exact type of person that you would want making the decisions that Raven is posed. It's for this reason that I think all of the endings in the game are equally 'correct', as much as people say there's a 'good' and 'bad' ending. For a game to convey this without Raven having a singular line of dialogue and simply the option to choose where he goes (through action) makes him, in a way, remarkably genuine... and remarkably different. He's the best fit for the position he's put in - Raven isn't here to be a hero, his only agenda is his own agenda. He's been given a mission, and he'll see it through to the end, even if he doesn't truly know what it is yet. But what purpose he seeks out and what sacrifices are justified are decisions that he must make himself, and it's ultimately that which changes Rubicon forever.

Maybe I'm overanalyzing a little bit (or making him seem more 'Willard-esque' than he really is), but that's my spoiler-free, summarised interpretation of the main character, and how the ability to choose is probably one of the game's main themes. I did the 'bad' ending first; I was perfectly immersed the whole way through. I felt like Raven, I related to him. Going into the final boss fight, I had this unshakeable feeling that I can't really put into words, like I've just made a difficult, terrible decision that, as sorry as I am, it simply had to be this way. With that, the boss' taunting lines throughout the ensuing fight actually felt significant. The later game really tried to iron this feeling in - I won't reveal how or why, since I'd say that's part of the experience. I wish I could play through that entire ending for the first time again (with no deaths, preferably 😅). All three endings are incredibly fun, but that was by far my favourite.

This is [i]really[/i] high praise from me, because I generally don't write reviews for games, even ones that I've liked. But this was just different. My only true gripe with the game is that the soundtrack felt... [i]lacklustre.[/i] It's not bad, but it's not good either - it's kind of just there, in the background, and you never really take notice of it. There's one fight in the game (that already had a lot of emotional weight for me) where it really kicks off, and that remains the most memorable out of all of them. I haven't played previous AC games, but from what I hear their soundtracks are significantly better and way more in line with what AC6 really needed. Don't consider that a dealbreaker, though, because I'm honestly just nitpicking.

Hopefully this is enough to have informed your £49.99 (or £29.99 if you're reading this during a sale). I would've still been happy if I'd paid full price for this. Amazing experience. [spoiler]«Farewell, Buddy. Things will change-- but I'll remember you.»[/spoiler]

Great Soundtrack.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 20, "timestamp_created": 1749682730}, {"review_text": "I am nearing the end of my playthrough of Stellar Blade on the PC platform and this is truly the definitive way to play Stellar Blade.

I played the entire game nearly, mod free and theres alot to cover in this game so lets go over it all with pros and cons.

Pros:

Graphics - The game is stunning visually especially on the PC platform. I played the game in 4k resolution with maximum FPS and it was a fluid experience. Very few hiccups involved in the game (I think i only experienced one in Eidos 7 that was a odd super slowdown and I had to reset the game) but aside from that the game has ran with zero issues beautifully. The entire game is stunning to look at, from the characters to the main city to the enemies to the areas you get to explore, all of it comes together nicely to give you a great visual experience.

Sound - This game has FANTASTIC sound and music. It is truly top tier. Every song that plays fits the moment, every boss battle song gets you hyped. Every ambient song / sound gets you set in the setting your currently in and matches perfectly. This has some of the best sound design in gaming and it truly shows. Even the combat sounds (the perfect parry / dodges) sound amazing. It is truly the best. 

Combat - The combat is alot of fun in this game. People would compare it to souls, but they would be wrong. This is more compared to DMC, a true hack and slash with some updated mechanics that only souls players would call similiar. The game truly shines in its combo system allowing you to experiment with combinations that may or may not risk eve due to animation lock depending on how fast you are. There is a ton of skills to utilize to fit pretty much any playstyle. 

Level Design - The games level design is really solid. The way there are little nooks and crannies you need to find, secret entrances, shortcuts etc. Its all done very well especially for this studios first attempt at a game like this. 

Skill Tree / Skills - There is so much in this game. between your standard combo moves, then your beta combo moves and then eventually your burst combo moves. Then you have super mode..I wont say what its called for spoilers..and then combinations you can do only when you perfect parry or dodge. You WILL remain busy with this game for a long time finding what works best for you. I caught myself changing up my combat style throughout the game to adjust for new skills i found more interesting. Its overall great.

Voice Acting - The voice acting in this game is top tier. Even the English voice acting is pretty dam good. There is no assassins creed soulless "Shitake" nonsense here, you will find genuine good voice acting that fit the characters being played on screen. 

Customization - This one should be pretty obvious. The insane amount of customization available to eve is ridiculous. Between over 100 outfits and then you have hairstyles, earring accessories, face masks / glasses. There so much to find here its insanity. You will probably end up playing around customizing eve for a while all through the game.

Gear system - The gear system in the game is pretty good. It is more positive than negative for me. It definitely could be more interesting / better, maybe more so like first berserker khazan but it functions, it has customization and thought to it and you will be min maxing a lot here. 

Value - This game has immense value in todays world where 80$ is the standard price. This game is being sold for far below that and the main game offers a TON to do. There was some content I missed during my first play through but there is brand new content unlockable in new game + and it keeps giving you reasons to play. Overall this game adds a ton of value for the price asked. 

Lets talk cons:

Denuvo - At the time of review, the game features denuvo. Alot of people hate this because performance takes a hit. My rig is overpowered so I tend to power through this, but its unfair for those who don't have that. Even on my rig, i experience (not often) random lag spikes for odd reasons that can only be contributed to either bad optimization (I doubt it here) or denuvo. Regardless its there and people should know. 

Animation Lock - The animation lock in this game can be really bad. If you play way too aggressive or combo too hard into a long animation combo, you will be locked hard and unable to defend yourself at all even when the damage has already been done because your busy waiting for the animation to end. Smart play style will overcome this but the game has some of the hardest animation lock ive seen in games like this or similiar.

Lack Of Quality Of Life Features - So the game features certain things like a entire secret area for example that is tied to the affinity of a main character and the only way to know your progress with this character is by doing side missions waiting for it to pop up...no other character is like this. You can see a 1/3 meter every time you talk to them but this one character there's nothing. It may not seem like a big deal but considering an entire AREA of the game is tied to this status..the player should have atleast a decent way of knowing instead of "waiting for it to pop up again". Thats insane. If you progress in the story too fast without paying attention you can literally miss an entire massive area of the game just because the entire affinity is kept secret. I dont know it just seems like weird design. 

Stiff Parkour - The games parkour system is extremely stiff, clunky and downright ridiculous sometimes. If you are sprinting and you run into a edge, she has a 50/50 chance of grabbing it and if she does grab it and brings herself up the cliff she will sprint off into the distance uncontrollably for a second or so potentially killing herself. The parkour needs to be smoother. The swimming needs to be smoother. The movement in general can definitely be smoother and not so stiff. It drags the experience down.

Overall Stellar Blade proves people with a solid hack and slash experience that will keep players engaged for a long time with NG+ Optional features, extra bosses and a boss rush mode and achievement farming / item hunting. Players after completing this will be looking forward to the already announced Sequel supposedly hitting in 2027.

Can't say what was it though.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 85, "timestamp_created": 1754786623}, {"review_text": "[h2]A Stunning Action RPG with Fluid Combat and Engaging Customization[/h2]

I’ve had a blast playing Stellar Blade! The combat is absolutely top-notch - fluid, dynamic, and incredibly satisfying. It really pulls you into the action, and chaining together combos feels so rewarding. The skill customization for Eve is a standout, allowing for tons of variety in playstyles. I loved experimenting with different skills and finding combos that suited my preferences. The combat system really makes this game shine (and of course the outfits).

The world-building is also solid, even though I wish we could've explored it a bit more. What we do see is gorgeous, and I was always excited to discover new areas. The side characters are interesting, but I do wish some of them were fleshed out a bit more. In fact, the Director mentioned that they had to cut quite a bit of content, including more character development for Eve. It’s a shame, as we could’ve seen more of Eve’s personal growth (the Director mentioned things like her first time trying on human clothes or the start of her collection of cans - small moments that would’ve made her character feel even more relatable and nuanced).

One of the highlights of the game is definitely the collectibles you can find scattered throughout the world. From various outfits that Eve can wear (which are both stylish and unlockable after certain milestones) to small trinkets such as earings, there’s a lot to keep you engaged. The outfits in particular are a treat - finding them and customizing Eve’s appearance adds an extra layer of fun and personalization. It's a nice touch that keeps the exploration feeling rewarding and fresh, especially as you progress through the game.

The side missions are where the game loses a bit of steam. Quite a lot of them are just fetch quests or “kill X number of enemies” objectives (don't even get me started on the photo challenges), which can feel repetitive. However, they don’t detract too much from the overall experience, especially when the main game is so engaging. That being said not all of them are designed that way. And some of them even let you explore newly unlocked areas in previously explored locations.

The story is good, though it can be predictable at times. That said, I still found it enjoyable and it kept me invested throughout.

There’s also some replayability built into Stellar Blade. The New Game+ and New Game++ modes unlock after completing the game each time, and they’re necessary to access some of the outfits (mostly recolors) and new skills. It’s great for players who want to dive deeper into the game, unlock everything, and experiment with different builds and gear. The extra playthroughs definitely extend the lifespan of the game and give you more incentive to return once the main story is wrapped up.

All in all, Stellar Blade is a great action RPG with incredible combat and a solid, if sometimes predictable, story. Despite a few underdeveloped side characters and the lost potential in Eve’s deeper development, I highly recommend it for anyone who enjoys fast-paced combat and character customization!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 6, "timestamp_created": 1750517137}, {"review_text": "its a good game but we need to get rid of Denuvo... it lowers the game performance a lot", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 18, "timestamp_created": 1757250087}, {"review_text": "This game made me very happy.

In short, this is a great game with deep flaws; in long, the rest of this review.

To start, the gameplay was the biggest hook for me from the earliest reveals and trailers and it didn't disappoint... mostly. Combat is incredibly fast paced and mostly feels really great; but this is just the start of a few creeping slip-ups the game makes. Sometimes, some attacks don't combo into each other super well, giving brief periods where Eve can't attack and is instead just stuck in a one second buffer period. It's not a big deal but it's absolutely noticable, as is the lack of skills in the game. Typically this type of game has a big variety of different skills for you to use but Stellar Blade only has eight, four of each type and only about four total worth actually using; not counting the skills in your Ultimate state because that's temporary. [h3]Soundtrack [/h3]
Easily one of the best gaming OSTs I’ve heard in a while since Nier. It doesn’t stick to just one vibe but instead, it offers a wide variety of genres and styles, all blended and executed seamlessly into the game. [h3]Combat[/h3]
The combat in Stellar Blade is absolutely [i] stellar[/i]. It's one of the game’s strongest aspects. From the flashy animations and responsive controls to the satisfying sound design, it feels incredibly rewarding to execute combos, parries, counters, and dodges. Intimidated by these kinds of action games?  So was I.

I honestly bought the game mostly blind because I wanted to support the developer and the game.  I really had no idea what I was getting into, though.  I don't usually play this type of game, with fast reactions and parrying and combos.  I've seen a lot of people saying that it is "worse than this game" or "better than this one" but at the end of the day, I have no idea because I never played those other games either.  I can only judge this game on what I have played of it so far.

I'm about 6 hours in, and I'm really having a lot of fun.  It's been a tough time though getting used to it!  I am playing on normal difficulty, and I just beat the first major boss I guess, Gigas.  I struggled quite a bit early in the game to understand how to parry and attack.  I had to really focus on teaching myself not to button mash.  I even watched a YouTube tips video on how to approach combat, and that helped.  

Once combat started to click, I really found it quite rewarding.  I was surprised at how much I've enjoyed it.  I still think I struggle a bit but it felt really good to take down the boss, and honestly sometimes I even now impress myself with how efficiently I take down some of the enemies that plagued me just a few game hours ago.  Feeling yourself progress as a player is kind of exhilirating, and this game has just the right amount of challenge for me to feel like it has been a tough but rewarding and fun experience.
One of my favorite factors in this game though is the lack of punishment for failure.  I die quite a bit, or at least I used to... and you really don't suffer because of it.  Unlike some other games where every death you lose something important, this game prefers to just reset you and let you try again.  It lets you focus on the game play, on your fight strategy.  Want to try a different approach?  Go ahead.  If you fail and die, it's just a retry.  I love that about this game.  Punishment is something I don't value in a game, and is part of the reason I have always avoided the souls-like titles... but this game really doesn't punish you.  It just asks you to practice more, and try a bit harder.  I love that, and it's probably the single most important factor in my willingness to put the time in to improve.  And I've really taken to it!

Obviously the visuals in the game are great.  Not just talking about Eve, though she is visually great... but the rest of the game looks fantastic.  I really enjoyed the opening sequence with everything crashing down.  There have been some really great vistas and areas I've gone through so far.

It's one of those once-in-a-lifetime games that rarely come along. The music is Nier-ish but has its own unique identity. I highly recommend this game if you enjoy compelling stories, engaging gameplay, and exceptional music. It was so good that I had to 100% it.

[u]Positives[/u]
+ The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard in a game. It perfectly captures the atmosphere wherever you go. It's become something I listen to at work.

+ The graphics are high quality, with no stutters or jitters on my computer, likely due to frame generation. Personally, I don't like relying on frame generation, but it runs better than many games I've played.

+ The animations are gorgeous. The art direction of this game is truly something else.

+ The combat has a lot of depth with various combos you can perform. Parrying feels smooth, though dodging can be a bit iffy (unless you know the bosses' attack patterns). Some may disagree with this point, but after playing it three times, I found you can get skilled enough to completely shut down bosses with well-timed skills and burst skills. There’s a lot of depth if you explore it. The combat is the closest to Sekiro’s since parrying, stamina, and break bars are significant elements.

+ The dungeon (level) design is some of the best I've seen. Every dungeon is engaging and unique, with stunning visuals, puzzles, and music. My favorite is [spoiler]Eidos 9 Flooded Commercial Sector[/spoiler] due to the recurring motifs that appear later in the game.

+ Dungeon bosses & challenge mode. They’re amazing, unique, and fun to fight. [spoiler]Scarlet from the Nikke DLC and the 'normal' ending bosses[/spoiler] were my favorites.

+ Collectibles are a great side activity. Collecting sweet cans comes with funny animations and sounds. I love it.

+ Nikke DLC. It features one of the best and most satisfying boss fights I've experienced in a video game. It took me a few attempts. The minigames were really fun and added more depth to the open areas. Also, PINK HAIR—need I say more?

+ Costumes. They add so much replayability to the game, as there are new ones for all three playthroughs. They're all unique, besides a few reskins, and make customizing EVE a fun experience.

[u]Mixed/Neutral[/u]
+- Voice acting. I personally don’t like the English voice actors, as I feel they don’t fit the characters. I played all three playthroughs in Japanese, which, in my opinion, suits every character perfectly.

+- Side quests. There are A LOT of side quests. Some are excellent, while others are fetch quests. I enjoyed all of them, but if you lack the patience or time, I recommend focusing on the important ones (they usually involve characters with many cutscenes). Do not miss them, as they provide invaluable story moments.

+- Open areas. For this review, I won’t name them, but I feel the first open area has more depth than the second. The music in both is brilliant, keeping you engaged, and the puzzles are fun. The second area felt emptier, which makes sense given its context.

+- Open area bosses. I love the bosses in this game, but many in the open-world areas are reskins with a few new skills. I would’ve preferred more variety, but it’s not a huge deal.

+- The story can feel basic at times, but the payoff is great (I loved it near the end). Most of the story is conveyed through data logs (similar to Dark Souls). A second playthrough felt rewarding since I could view it from a different perspective with those notes as a guide.

I can’t think of any major negatives. I truly enjoyed the game, and I’m definitely buying Stellar Blade 2 when it releases. Rating: Not Recommended
After 15 years of adventuring in Gielinor, RuneScape has lost much of the magic that made it a beloved MMO. Once a vibrant world of grinding, community, and exploration, it now feels like a shadow of its former self, plagued by developer disconnect, a broken economy, and outdated content.
The game’s core issue is its shift toward monetization over player satisfaction. Jagex frequently releases powerful content—think overpowered gear or skilling methods—only to nerf it later with flimsy excuses like “game balance.” These changes feel like bait-and-switch tactics, eroding trust. The in-game economy is a mess, with hyperinflation making high-end items (like partyhats or top-tier weapons) cost billions of gold, unattainable for most without real money. Bonds, items bought with cash and sold for in-game gold, fuel a pay-to-win vibe. Want that shiny gear or a 99 skill? Grinding hundreds of hours competes with dropping $8 for a bond worth ~70M gold. It’s disheartening for players who value effort.
Minigames, once a highlight, are dead. Castle Wars, Stealing Creation, and others sit abandoned, their rewards irrelevant compared to modern bossing or skilling. Jagex’s focus on new content leaves these relics untouched, and even their revival attempts (like spotlights) fall flat. The community is still passionate, but many feel ignored, with feedback on forums or social media rarely translating to meaningful change.
There’s still fun to be had—solo PvM like Araxxor or skilling for personal goals can scratch the itch—but the grind feels hollow when real money shortcuts dominate. Old School RuneScape (OSRS) might be a better bet for fans of the classic vibe, with a more player-driven approach, but RS3 struggles to balance nostalgia and modern demands.
Pros:
Deep lore and a vast world.
Solo content like bossing can be engaging.
Active community despite the issues.
Cons:
Hyperinflated economy makes goals feel unreachable.
Pay-to-win bonds undermine grinding.
Dead minigames and neglected content.
Nerfs and developer decisions feel arbitrary.
If you’re new, RuneScape might charm you briefly, but long-term players will likely find it a frustrating shell of its glory days. I’d recommend exploring OSRS or other MMOs like Final Fantasy XIV instead.
Playtime: Thousands of hours over 15 years
Would I recommend? No, unless you’re nostalgic and willing to overlook major flaws.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1745865736}, {"review_text": "I have about 10,000 hours in RuneScape and if you like:

Cheers.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 24, "timestamp_created": 1749444907}, {"review_text": "I'm going to try to describe the game and also translate the hate you'll read about the game, to give you an idea of what to expect from my point of view.

The game is massive. There is a tremendous amount of content. You'll hear old-time players constantly refer to "dead content". In some cases, it's true. In many cases, it's only true for those who have played literally all the content already and have no concept of reality for a new player.

You'll probably hear complaints about how the game is barely updated, and how updates "suck" compared to the past.
First, the game is updated less often than it used to be updated. It still gets new content every month at a minimum. Many players will say "Well THIS new content isn't REAL content" because it doesn't match the content those players wish existed.

If you like lore, the game's pretty packed with it. There are a decent number of quests. While most MMOs have thousands of quests that consist of "Kill 10 wolves." Runescape does not. Runescape uses its quests for stories. Some of those stories are exceptionally well made.

Runescape does not use a class system like some MMOs. It has many different skills, some of which are used for combat.

Runescape is definitely a "grinding" game. If you don't want to grind XP, you may not enjoy it.


The game could definitely use some more work. The company that operates the game, Jagex, has definitely had several problems. There is a lot of outdated content in the game that could use a fresh coat of paint at the very least. Very little of this will affect your gameplay as a new player.

Also, one mechanic that Runescape is lacking: multiple characters. Runescape has a one character = one account setup. You cannot create multiple characters per single membership. The only exception to this is that you can have one character in the modern "Runescape 3" game, and one character in "Old School Runescape", which is an alternative version of Runescape based on how the game played around 2007 (it IS still updated and maintained, it's not just an unsupported relic).

Your one character can do everything in the game, but if you like to roll multiple characters, you'll have to pay the membership fee for each character.


NOW I'll talk about the big bad boogeyman that you'll be hearing about from probably every single reviewer, the subreddit, the steam forums, the Runescape site's forums, that one random guy you know that knows everything, and that other random guy you know that knows nothing:

The game has both a monthly membership and micro-transactions.

The micro-transactions may be considered "aggressive". They range from cosmetics to small in-game XP bonuses. They are only pay-to-win in the sense that you can pay literally thousands of dollars to *not* play the game. Otherwise, they're not pay-to-win. For the most part, most of the outrage you'll see about them is simply that they exist.

Some of the outrage about micro-transactions is justified. Jagex has made some bad decisions and some of the micro-transactions are just terrible.
However, a massive amount of the outrage is generated by people who have played Runescape for over a decade, desperately miss the game they once had, and believe that literally anything and everything different is going to kill Runescape.

In short, the chances of the micro-transactions negatively affecting you are slim. If you've played literally any other MMO, or just about any game released in the last decade, you probably won't notice anything out of the ordinary. If that's a bad thing to you, fair enough.


My final recommendations:

If you get addicted to games easily, run away... or don't. You don't escape, you just take breaks.
Frankly, do not go to the Runescape subreddit. There are some good posts, and you might see some good information about the game. For the most part though, the only people left that browse the subreddit regularly are the most die-hard "fans" that hate-play Runescape, latch onto anything and everything bad the company does, and spam about how micro-transactions are ruining the game. Oh, also several people that won't hesitate to tell you constantly how "This is why I quit playing years ago" . It's also the type of subreddit that makes up roughly 0.01% of the playerbase, but unironically believes it accurately represents the will of the average players.

Just try the game out, and form your own opinion. Even I'm biased. It's impossible to play the game for literal years without being biased.

I'm so incredibly excited Jagex has made this decision, and I'm so excited to see where the future brings Jagex as a company, and my childhood game, now that it's future seems so  much brighter, and not so soul shatteringly bleak.

The MTX just gets worse and worse. This game continues to be a warning sign for exactly how greed ruins games. 
The most amusing part being that "Old School Runescape" still exists and it's like viewing the same game in different timelines. RS3 showing what happens when a team stops actually caring about their players and OSRS showing what can happen when you put the fun and enjoyment of your players above all else.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1737946169}, {"review_text": "Man if you look past the MTX and actually play this game the same way it was, you'll have a great time. I played the OG back in 2006-2009 and haven’t played it since returning in December of 2024. 

This game is very different to OSRS, it has a lot of QOL over the former but at its core it's the same game, think of it this way. 

OSRS  = A snapshot, a time capsule of when the game was at its peak years ago.

Runescape/3 = Continuation and modernisation of that time capsule. Whether you love it or hate it, you'll have to decide for yourself.

This is a true sandbox MMO, you can go and do anything you want, there's simply no right or wrong. Want to do farming and raise dragons? No problem. Want to focus on combat and bossing? Also no problem. Want to do skilling purely? Also no problem, there's like 20 skills you can level, each one will have its use at one point or another. 

There's no forced PVP in Wildy and various areas like there used to be, you also don't lose all your items when you die, you just reclaim them from Death at a small cost. 

Quests are also done really well, what might feel like a slog can actually drag you into something goofy such as fighting a guy that “cant be beaten by any man” so naturally you change your gender to a woman and smack him up. Quests generally serve as means of progress and opening the game systems up for you, a ton of really important stuff and gear, passives, upgrades are locked behind quests, which are in turn locked behind skill requirements, so it creates a natural progression as you play A particularly excellent quest series involves you renovating a fort which will then take part in a battle and serve as a really great skilling hub that will have money making potential. 

Community stood the test of time, in the same way stand users are naturally attracted to one another in Jojo so is Runescape and absolute fkn weirdos. That being said, the community is friendly and helpful ,if you ask a question in one of the popular places like Fort or Grand Exchange, you will more than likely receive more than help such as items or even money to help out in whatever it is. 

The population numbers are also fairly healthy. Don’t look at steam charts because the majority of the players are on the standalone Jagex Launcher. There are approximately 30k daily players so the game is not dying and there is an active players base for most activities in the game, this of course highly depends on the world you are in. 

Free to Play is free and you get access to maybe 15-25% of the actual content in the game, consider F2P a trial. If you enjoy the game you will eventually want to expand into a membership as most of the useful skills and content are locked behind members. You can make money that pays for membership but it will be extremely tedious and time consuming. Most people tend to go into membership, do high level PVM, merching, trading and then paying for membership that way. I met countless players that had enough wealth to have multiple years worth of membership. That being said, it is possible however it requires a time investment, patience and it isn’t easy. 

PvM is excellent as is bossing. You will quite often die a lot, even with best in slot gear, equipment and various other things. Even with max stats, you cannot face roll your way through bosses, sure there are ways and setups to make bosses easier, you are still required to have a brain and learn the mechanics. I have seen countless people swipe for the best gear in the game only to get pathetically wiped at some of the easiest bosses in the game. This is a fairly complicated game at the end of the day and you will have to put time in and learn. Bosses such as Zuk can be particularly devastating to new players but with practice become a cake walk that still requires a good amount of focus and attention. Don’t expect amazing drops right away though, gear and decent loot drops in this game are really rare, you can expect to kill a boss upwards of 200+ times and still not receive any gear 1/200 being generous lol. That’s just how it is, but nothing beats the satisfaction and right of flexing you get for getting all the drops on a boss and a respective title. You attain the rite of flexing in that regard and you’ll also be making fat stacks of money. Certain pieces of gear can go for 500m+. 

Skilling is fun but that depends who you ask. A lot of skills are not active, so you can easily AFK them and only click on your screen every couple of minutes, this means you can comfortably watch YouTube or a friends discord stream on the side whilst the game plays itself. There are many ways to make skilling more fun or active such as items or quest upgrades that make certain actions faster etc. A lot of skills also complement each other, whereas others such as Dungeoneering are a redundant, repulsive time waste that serves no purpose and should be reworked. 

Overall performance in this game is awful and Jagex should focus on optimising this game next, it doesn’t look amazing but it can, which leads me to another issue. The graphics are super inconsistent. You can have an area like fort that looks fantastic. Meanwhile God Wars 1 looks like its stuck in a time capsule from 2010. Stuttering and frame drops in almost every area as you traverse the world, thankfully it does not impact important bossing encounters as they are in enclosed areas but it's extremely jarring to see as you run through the world. 

In general it looks like Jagex is actively trying to listen to its community and is implementing stuff, however decade old bugs still plague the game so it's a bit of a mixed bag. The recent MTX changes and experiments definitely look better than trying to charge people more for membership which is already fairly expensive but worth it over aids like Netflix in my opinion. 

Overall the game is good especially if you are thinking of playing it. It's extremely time consuming if you want to do everything so do keep that in mind. The content that is already there is good but locked behind membership.The game is riddled with MTX but it can simply be ignored for the most part because even if you swipe to get best gear, you will still need a functional brain to use it. The main hindrance at least in my eyes will be the MTX, performance and lack of art direction in certain areas, because the game is so massive I am guessing it's difficult to be consistent. Call of Duty: Black Ops III was a game that had it's peak for a very long time until it got abandoned by its playerbase... If we are talking about the Multiplayer.

You had a very advanced arcade 'n shoot mechanic that worked flawlessly and was satisfying each time you used it to kill the opposite player, the graphics were really ahead of its time back in 2015, literally beating Battlefield 4 at that time and the overall gameplay was just a blast. A lot of clips were made and legends were born that year... until... everything just came to an end. 

Now when you try to boot up the game on its own, trying to hope to get a match, you would literally risk yourself getting DDosed and even hacked on your System by another player and the only way you would be able to bypass this problem is through a tool called "T7", which did work but the hassle needing to get a specific software just to keep playing this game and STILL getting cheaters almost each round was basically just not worth it anymore. 

So if you want to get this game to play the regular multiplayer, I would not only say that it's not worth it but also it's advised that you don't do that.

The devs and the publishers literally just abandoned this game like they would nowadays almost each year.

[h2]So why is it that I'm giving this game a thumbs up?[/h2]

The answer is very simple, [b]Zombies[/b].

They have left us with a very huge gift that made this game still be an absolute hit, and that is Steam Workshop support! You read it right, this game literally has [b]Workshop support[/b] that you can use to simply download any modded content and play it as much as you want and the best thing is that it can also work on Linux! (As a proud steam deck user myself, this is indeed a welcoming surprise)

From all the Zombies that I have experienced in the series, this by far is the best that you can still get, especially because of the workshop support. The gameplay is just smooth, the vanilla content for zombies is also massive, the graphics make things pop up even in today's standard and most importantly, the game is just very well optimized. As I mentioned above, you could literally play this game on the steam deck with around 50-60 FPS on intense waves if you wanted to. And with being able to do modded stuff, if you would be out on a trip for weeks your content could be enough for even MONTHS.

[h2] Is the campaign also worth it?[/h2]

People also asked about the singleplayer and what I thought of it myself, and I must say, it wasn't as bad as people made it out to be. The story itself was actually good and you could have a good time through it, of course it was getting a bit confusing, especially on later scenarios, but if you would follow the plot, it can still be a pleasing trip. Compared to previous Black Ops titles though, this felt least fleshed out on the main character.
The main plot of the story however can still go deep and can come with it's own meaning towards the player, in fact when I played the series myself, I actually felt closest to this game's story telling than the others.

If you already got the game for the Zombies, I think you should also at least try out the campaign too.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1752536716}, {"review_text": "Hours Played: 900+ (not even counting console hours, heheheh)

It had ended with me throwing my hands up in surrender after suffering a team wipe twice, almost in a row, first from the Shambler, and then later to Vvulf. Despite that, I resolved to one day come back and finish this damn game.

And 7 years later, I come crawling back with gritted teeth and bloodied fingers, triumphantly better than ever before. My days of being 'Not Very Good' was over. I was now 'Eh, Acceptable.' And that was enough to fulfill a goal that was more than half a decade old by that point. On Default Difficulty, even! 

(I will not try it in Higher Difficulties. I know my limits. Confidence is an insidious killer, and all that.)

Anyway, all that was to say, very dramatically, that I've finally finished it. Wonderful game. I absolutely love the sound effects and, of course, the narrator. It all really sets the Lovecraftian vibe the game was going for. While I was playfully complaining about the difficulty earlier, I didn't actually hate it. Struggling to be better, to improve, to overcome said difficulties made the victories all the more sweet. From what I understand, the game was purposely designed like that. It's supposed to be hard. Honestly, not sure why it's taken me this long to make a review of this game. I'm kind of nearly 10 years too late (Oh my fuck-ing god it's been almost ten years jesus christ) but since the Autumn Sale is here a lot of people may be checking this game out so I need to pump out the propaganda.

I'll start with a brief overview of the pros and cons of the game for those who just want a quick review, and then go into detail afterwards. 

Pros:

-Phenomenal Turn-Based Gameplay. Simple but so damn good.

-Incredible Art Direction and Character Design. Hauntingly beautiful.

-Amazing Atmosphere, and Narration. Seriously...Wayne June's performance elevates this game to another level.

-Challenging yet Rewarding. Loot is always exciting to find and earn.

-Stress Concept is Unique and Helps it Stand Out

-Perfect Music. Ambiance and Combat themes capture what they need to amazingly.

-Great Modding Scene....if you ignore the gooners (Seriously why for this game in specific is it so bad?)

Cons:

-Difficulty Can Be A Turnoff. Easier difficulty modes exist, but characters WILL die in this game.

-Idk man I'm struggling to come up with any uhhhh stress act outs are kind of annoying and the crimson curse can be too ig

Now for the detailed review.  Where to even begin? The game-play is multifaceted yet easy to understand. This game is called a Rouge-like...but I don't think that's entirely accurate. Sure, dungeons are randomized but your heroes retain their upgrades, trinkets and skills. Progression is much more permanent in this game, with your dungeon delving allowing the estate to grow and grant you new bonuses, shops and better heroes for the future challenges. The game-play loop in very simple terms is to expand your estate and set out on ever more dangerous expeditions with your heroes in order to eventually take on The Darkest Dungeon.

Speaking of, let's talk heroes. There are several different classes in this game- each sporting 8 unique skills. The characters excel in different positions but can be played in many different ways. The back-line healer? Yeah, she can beat the shit out of people in the front ranks too. It makes understanding each one very rewarding and fun. The skills themselves are easy to understand but can also expand into many complex and powerful setups and strategies. Want a team that stacks DoT? Maybe on that applies a mark to one enemy and guns it down? There's a lot of variation here. Your party is still human, though, and are vulnerable to the stress of the expedition.

This game's big calling card is the stress system. It's extremely memorable, and much simpler to understand than it sounds. In short, you can just consider it as a second health-bar with lower stakes. Certain attacks will deal stress damage, which causes a hero's stress to increase. If it gets too high, they will face a resolve check. 75% of the time they will fall into madness, and gain a random affliction. These afflictions can make characters act out against your commands and even hurt their allies. It can admittedly be frustrating to deal with, so managing your stress is important. Many hero skills, trinkets and prioritization of killing stress-causing enemies can make this easier to deal with, thankfully. If a character's stress bar fills out again, they'll suffer a heart attack which can leave them only one hit away from death.

25% of the time, however, your character will become virtuous during a resolve check. Unlike afflictions, these make your character much stronger and even de-stress the rest of your team and themselves. It's very satisfying to dread having a character reach a resolve check in a hard fight, only for them to emerge virtuous and end up saving the entire party. Careful, though, because this game is not afraid to remind you of just how mortal a man really is.

If you're as brain rotted and mentally ill as me, you may know what a Pokemon Nuzlocke is. The game works very similarly to that. if you're normal, then its simply just that characters die permanently. Your favorite Crusader or Leper can be killed forever- barring a very rare event which allows you to bring one character back. This creates real, palpable stakes to each adventure and allows you to develop attachment to your favorite digital freak. I love Darkest Dungeon 2 as well, but this one of the things this game just does better than it. For some, though, this may be a turnoff. Pouring investment and emotional favoritism into your Grave Robber only for her to die brutally to a monster that looks like a deflated testicle? Not for everyone, sadly.

Moving onto the artistic side, this game is hauntingly beautiful in so many different ways. The art, music, voice-work and story are dark, grungy and desolate but are so enrapturing and sometimes even motivational. Sure, 90% of the game is about humanity's corruption and eventual inescapable demise...but god does it feel good to crit and enemy or kill a boss. Each victory feels earned and like one step has been made closer to the end of the corruption.

 This is in no small part helped by the phenomenal narration by Wayne June, who has sadly passed away. In this game, he plays the role of your ancestor and constantly drops lore of the world and comments about your campaign. It sets the mood so perfectly and even bleeds into the game-play. This game has crunch to it- scoring a critical hit makes the game zoom in, and sparks a powerful voice line from your ancestor. Even non-critical hits will have voice lines that make the moment feel powerful and memorable. I think it's at its best when your character's stress breaks- only for them to remain resolute and virtuous. Hearing the narrator cry "Many fall in the face of chaos, but not this one. Not today!" as your beloved little gremlin Plague Doctor scores back after back crit? Yeah, this is cocaine for pathetic white boys like me.

The cons really are hard to pinpoint for me. Yes, the challenge can be frustrating. A badly timed crit can wipe an entire party of invested heroes and you'll want to just shut off the PC right there. It's always worth trying again, though, because as desolate as the game may feel sometimes, there are always more heroes waiting in the stagecoach. There is always hope of rising back up from the ashes and using the estate you've built to raise a new army and take vengeance for your fallen friends. 

The odds are stacked against you, and the game wants you to feel the crushing burden of failure. The game may not be for you and that's okay. If you're willing, though, then there's always a path forward. This game is one of the best uses of video games as a medium to create art I've ever seen. Because you aren't just being told to feel despair, you're actively experiencing it. You don't have to look for the meaning, because it's what you make of it. You'll fall, and you will rise up again. The message of the game is hope- to keep trying no matter how many heroes die or how many expeditions result in disaster, because eventually you will succeed...

Darkest Dungeon has a fun party management system that is well designed and the heart and soul of the game.  Do you select your ranged skills for your Highwayman so he can be in position 3?  Or do you take his pos 1/2 skills and play more of a high risk high reward style of play up front?  Do you put your jester in the back making him a buffing character?  Or do you put him further forward so you can apply bleed and be more of a DPS character?  It allows you to make a lot of different parties in different ways, and as you play you learn what combo's works best for each situation, and which ones you prefer to play.  

The enemies also have positions that work differently for each enemy type, and some of your characters will let you manipulate the positions of your enemies to mess them up or put them in a position for one of your other characters to pummel them into the dirt. That being said, I can see why it wouldn't be the case for everyone else. I tend to keep my reviews from brief to slightly detailed on this platform, but [i]Darkest Dungeon[/i] is such a unique journey that truly resonated with me. I think it's probably for the best to lay out the full picture; especially if you've just got yourself the game, or are wondering if it would be wise buying it during a sale. So allow me to set the stage, in a structured way, to show you what truly is awaiting you in this wretched land. 

[i]"You remember our venerable house, opulent and imperial..."[/i]

[b][u] The Good [/u][/b] 

[i]Presentation[/i]
One of the strongest point of [i]Darkest Dungeon[/i] from the very start, and a reason why it personally stuck so much with me, is how original and defined in [u]presentation & concept it truly is[/u]. The game is set in the Gothic era, but it also inspires itself a lot from Lovecraftian Horror and it fully takes advantage of it. From the first cinematic, the game engulfs you in mystery, and does it with very few words. To be honest, I sometime let it fully play when booting up the game after a long time, or when I feel like fully immersing myself in my ancestor's delirium. 

[u]The visuals[/u], like the title suggests, are very dim and unsaturated. The atmosphere is dark and unwelcoming, even the neighbouring Hamlet that's now decrepit is devoid-ed of any colours. Grotesque black strokes of ink shape the outlines of everything: The [i]UI[/i]s, the menus, the texts' typeface, the buildings, the various collectable objects and more so of every characters. That being said, that plays it to its favour as it fully ties in to the story and how atrocious the situation is: it sets the stage and raises the stake on how depressing the world truly has gone into.

While we are talking graphics, the next logical thing would be to address the [u]monster and enemy design[/u]. To make fairly brief, they are nothing short of amazing and well thought-out. Many monsters have standard ghastly look as you begin : classic skeletons, to wild dogs and madmen. As you progress the game and ramp up in mission difficulties however, they get even more ghoulish. Bosses are the true stars in design though, and should be as they are centre-piece to the story and they all have a unique grotesque, Lovecraftian design to show it.       

As for [u]the music and overall sound design[/u], the tone is gloomy, sometime unnervingly silent while traversing the many dungeons' halls, other time thrilling when engaging in combat. My favourite piece however, is the [i]"The Hamlet"[/i], the track that plays when visiting the main hub - the Hamlet. I think that Stuart Chatwood, the composer, really did something special there. This track is very intriguing to me as it tethers between drops of hopeful and depressive tones. I think they've really nailed in creating a soothing yet unsettling atmosphere.

The jewel of sound design though, inevitably goes to [u]the narration of the game[/u], performed by talented and late [b]Wayne June[/b] (May he rest in peace), that is present throughout every player choice, every discovery and at every return to the Hamlet, after previous expeditions. Something about the cadence of the words and his deep gravelling voice just tie in perfectly with the writing, and it hitches the right spot in my psyche. I sometimes catch myself quoting him out loud during the day, or when playing other games. His overall performance like his character's nightmares was otherworldly and he is sorely missed.   

[b][u] The more challenging [/u][/b] 

[i]"And now the true test... hold fast, or expire?."[/i]

The gameplay loop on the surface is simple : 

Recruit heroes, gather them in an handcrafted party tailored to certain needs via each individual skills (Heroes that benefit from debuffs, status effects, against certain enemy type, etc), and level up their Resolve by exploring procedurely generated dungeons and vanquishing the evil and sometime bosses roaming within them. Gather, in a restrained inventory, loot throughout the expeditions such as gold to buy the various services the town offers like skill and arsenal upgrades, or other valuable trinkets and heirloom to upgrade town buildings; thus improving the efficiency of said services. Rinse and repeat until your roster is strong enough to face the Darkest Dungeon.

The real gripe with a lot of players, especially the new ones is [u]the learning curve and overall investment [/u] of time required to fully enjoy the game. Heroes that end up dying is a very punishing experience during the expeditions as it drastically lowers the chances of successful runs, and it can also set you back a lot in the beginning when resources are finite. A roster that does not perish instantly though can slowly succumb to stress, which adds in a ton of unwanted parameters, and can be the difference between victory and defeat. The real challenge then is to carefully avoid stressing your party during expeditions as it can lead to members skipping their turn, stressing other heroes or worse, succumbing to heart attacks. I've had my fair share of failed excursions from a single recruit that managed to raise panic in the entire party, leading to a full team wipe. Though this is hard at first, you definitely can and should learn from failure, i.e. what stresses your recruits and how to stop it. This accumulated experience makes each run smoother and all the more satisfying when victorious.

Some will say that a game should be fully enjoyable from the get go, and I do respect this opinion, which is why I understand if these same people end up putting the game down for a while, if not forever. Truth be told, I had a previous 60 hour run that sat idle for a good year when I came back to the game. [i]Darkest Dungeon[/i] is a very complicated game to get into, even at standard difficulty. A good tip is to leave the wiki opened and gather as much information / strategies as possible. This will smooth out the experience.  

My recommendations : 
- Upgrade gears and skills first, as they improve your heroes' base stats, and make them deadlier and harder to hit in more difficult dungeons.
- DO NOT activate the Crimson Court and Colour of Madness DLCs as they increase the game difficulty drastically in the beginning, since they implement various, deadlier monsters that can spawn in standard regions. 
- Start with the standard vanilla experience with maybe new hero class unlocked, and activate Districts and other DLCs as you progress and gain confidence.
- Take your time, open the Wiki, seek resources
- Most of all: have fun and be patient, be mindful, be prepared

[h3]TL;DR:[/h3]  
[i]Darkest Dungeon[/i] is a dark and excellent turned-based combat RPG, especially for those who'll be patient enough to learn its core principles and let the game open itself to them. Its presentation, visuals, music and overall atmosphere are uniquely ghoulish and adequate to the setting. The gameplay loop itself while sometime frustrating after losing a hero, failing missions or because of what seems to be random factors, is a perfect proof of a steep, and unforgiving learning curve; it also tie in perfectly with the setting of an unforgiving story. This is probably the most discouraging aspect of the game though, as it can sometimes be a heavy grind and is also why it could potentially be a bad choice for some. Though for those who are looking for a new kind of challenge, a lengthy investment, who'll want to spend it theory crafting and learning the many systems will find an intriguing story, a satisfying loop of scrounging dungeons, gathering resources and obliterating the monstrous opposition, and overall a uniquely phenomenal game.
