So, what we have now is the original game with a few tweaks to utilize some modern rig features. Mostly though, this is the game we all remember. And for those new to the game, its accessibility is one of its strongest features.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3590247833

John Marsten is simultaneously a simple and yet complicated character. Some of this is defined by strong writing and some of it is defined by subpar writing. And actually, this is I think where memories of the game don't match the modern-day experience. I don't think I really noticed his almost bi-polar character development back in the day, but it did stand out while playing it recently. John the side quester is a thoughtful and often charming soul. John the main quester is kind of an ass. It's a bit of a jarring personality juxtaposition that can be difficult to reconcile, even though it's designed to illustrate the gravity of his personal situation. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3599341309

That said, the characters in general are generally written well enough to either give you an emotional attachment or at least provide some moments of laughter and brevity in what it more or less a dark tale. And if you ever make it to the epilogue, it's a cool way to wrap up the Marsten story, allowing you to guide the outcome somewhat. Personally, I enjoy the side stories more than the main story, but things do get spicy in the main story as you progress.

As far as the gameplay is concerned, I think it takes a bit of getting used to. Controls that were commonplace back in the day are no longer typically the way they are default mapped in games today. That said, you get used to them pretty quickly. The gunplay is tight as you could want, and the slow down mechanic is always fun. Horseback riding is definitely wonky, but overall, it's aight. 

Quest design can be cumbersome. Again, we're seeing things that were normal back in the day, which have been tired and played out ever since it became ubiquitously known as Ubi open world design. Bases to conquer, tons of things to fetch for the helpless citizens of New Austin and Mexico. That sort of thing. It's okay, but it does start to feel like a lot of filler pretty quickly. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3587742702

Graphics are mildly washed, but they still look pretty decent even now. Sound design OTOH is top tier, and the voice acting is pretty memorable even where the actors flubbed a bit. Somehow, it's charming regardless. And there is no denying that the dialogue, outside of angry John, is nicely done. Angry John is passable, but as mentioned, there's a bit of a disconnect between John's divergent personality traits, lol.

Anyway, it's cool that Rockstar finally did what people had been asking for and gave us a version of RDR that is playable on modern systems, and I'm appreciative of that. Does it hold up perfectly in this era of gaming? Maybe not. Are its issues more glaring today? Yes. But it does hold up well enough and is an engaging experience all things said. I would be hesitant to spend $50 on this. It's not even close to being on par with RDR2 in quality. But had on sale for +/- $30, it feels like a must play to me. Especially if you missed the PS3 era.

[b]I will note here that a Rockstar Social Club membership is required to play this. I don't love this requirement, but it is what it is.[/b]

+ The music and environments capture the (spaghetti) Western tone well. You've got your guitar strums and bells, and the cacti and coyotes in the desert.

- Sometimes it feels like the characters don't react like they should react to the events in the story. It's as if there are holes in the story, and the characters do a lot of talking off screen. Example: [spoiler] there's a mission where the player has to go to a family's house to take the daughter to a different location. Once the mission is completed, the player can then immediately return to the house to accept a different mission. However, the house has been burnt in the meantime, and the characters don't acknowledge this at all. [/spoiler] I get the feeling that the game was intended to be played in short bursts. Playing in long sessions (like I've done) exposes the choppy narrative. If you've ever binge-watched an episodic TV show, you know what I mean.
- A lot of the time, doing main story missions will result in John asking about the things he needs, only for the other characters to respond with "all in due time", or something similar. This means the story doesn't always feel like it's advancing, and the missions are just there to make the game longer.

The Ugly:
* Acquiring new guns is done in an odd fashion. Sometimes a character gives you a new gun just like that. One time during a gunfight I noticed my rifle was different than the one I had used before, and I had no idea when I had picked up the new rifle.
* At some point, there's no reason to continue skinning animals for money, as the main missions give enough. This doesn't happen particularly late, either.
* John does favours for many characters in exchange for information and resources. He sometimes repeatedly threatens them when they're slow to cooperate, but never follows up with his threats, or does anything, really. There's a lot of "or else" type bickering from John.

[{"review_text": "Basically Medieval Dynasty, but more dangerous. Instead of bandits being a rare and random thing you might have the misfortune to run into, at least the beginning of the game (where I still am) largely revolves around eliminating the many camps of bandits who are terrorizing the region. But other than that, it's still a game of playing as a Medieval peasant who walks around picking up sticks and rocks and edible things to try to survive and build a settlement. Whereas the devs of Medieval Dynasty have been hinting at some kind of mystery to be solved in the Oxbow but never got around to delivering, Bellwright is very plot-driven. Whereas the whole objective in Medieval Dynasty is just to have a kid (not that hard, and the game plateaus after that), Bellwright also has you arriving as a homeless orphan unraveling a history of a crime against a loved one, but leads to you liberating villages and commanding an army. Bit more exciting than just hunting the same bear once every season.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 5, "timestamp_created": 1764302036}, {"review_text": "Bellwright is close to being the perfect blend between a medieval life simulation and a deep management strategy game.

You begin your journey as a humble, broken farmer. Every resource is precious, and early gameplay involves a lot of manual collection. But over time, you start recruiting villagers, expanding your settlement, and learning to delegate. As the game progresses, it evolves from a survival experience to a full-fledged management simulator.

You’ll spend a significant amount of time optimizing villager roles, setting up efficient resource chains, and assigning jobs. Simultaneously, you’ll train and upgrade your people to defend against increasingly dangerous bandit raids. Eventually, the game transitions into a conquest phase, where you lead your own well-equipped militia to reclaim the land, command troops in dynamic, simulation-based combat, and loot valuable resources.

Pros:

    A satisfying progression from survival to strategy.

    NPC automation and village management are well implemented. (npc inventory manager UI need to improve) 

    The combat system, while not revolutionary, adds a fun layer to the gameplay loop.

    The open-ended gameplay lets you lean into a SimCity-like builder or a Kingdom Come: Deliverance style adventure, depending on your mood.

Cons:

    The map is vast, but progression doesn’t fully take advantage of its size. Much of the late-game content can be unlocked without ever needing to explore the southern regions.

    Quests and village development are highly repetitive. Each new settlement follows almost the same gameplay loop, which can feel tedious after unlocking Tier 3 buildings and upgrades.

    The game lacks incentives for long-term exploration. Once you’ve optimized one town, there’s little reason to start over elsewhere.

    Village defense mechanics are basic and could benefit from more complexity and urgency.

Conclusion:
Bellwright is highly addictive and filled with potential. However, its current structure leads to a repetitive late game. If the developers were to condense the map by about 30–40%, introduce stronger town defense mechanics, and diversify the village-building experience, Bellwright could easily go from a good game to a great one.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 1, "timestamp_created": 1747613416}, {"review_text": "While the developers' past of abandoning Early Access games should give you a pause when you're about to purchase another early access game by this developer, I'm giving this a thumbs up because even if it is abandoned as it is right now, I feel it's still worth the price. Still, I'm hoping that this time they will be able to get it through to the finish line and provide a more polished and bug-free game.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1748783703}, {"review_text": "I love this game, I've played it for many hours and still have yet to complete the game because I'm sick in the head and love the grind.

How to play this game successfully:

1.  Stamina makes life easier: There are three food slots, each food item with a health/stamina modifier.  Make sure you eat foods that add some health and more stamina early on.  This will make your life far easier.  Cooked foods are better than raw, smoked foods are better than campfire cooked, and eventually complex dishes are the best as you progress.  

2.  Add fast travel posts everywhere.  This makes the game MUCH better to navigate, obviously.  Start out on a journey down an unknown road with 2 logs, 2 stones and 5 sticks every time so you have at hand the crafting materials necessary to put down a fast travel post.

3.  Do not hire beggars.  They suck and can never be good.  Complete a few quests in each town, acquire friend status, then hire as many "white shirts" as possible.  These are the best early game villagers you can acquire before you liberate a village.  You may want to hire a beggar early on to mine copper at a separate outpost or something, but that concludes their worth.  

3.  HIre a lot of people.  The more you have, the easier your life will be.

4.  Open your settlement menu from anywhere and tell assign tasks to your various buildings.  You don't need to be standing in your village to get your villagers to do tasks.  

5.  Farming is key.  First farm should be hemp and flax combo; no other items.  You will need tons of both throughout the game but especially early on.  Wheat is the next one.

6.  Late early to beginning mid-game goal should be to take over the Wheat Farm.  Once that is done you can set up a separate outpost with a couple people assigned here to continually hand harvest the wheat field.  Build a couple of the storages and a thresher.  Have one person making straw, the other picking wheat.  All you have to do then is go here periodically to collect what you need.

7.  Don't research every single thing.  It takes a lot of materials and time; and most of the items are useless an hour later because you've opened up better things.  This mainly pertains to weapons and armor.  Some you just will never use or need.  Look at the research tree and plan for the things you want.

8.  Use a bow.  Swordfighting is fun against 1 or 2 opponents, but any more than that its extremely difficult to be effective.  Proper use of the bow can have you single-handedly taking out small and medium and even some large NPC bases with relative ease.

9.  Save your Elder Coins.  Do quests until you have to use these coins to put you over the edge in certain villages to speed up the gameplay.

10.  Think you have too many resources?  You don't.  Build more storage and keep your villagers cutting down trees, picking up sticks and tending to your farm.  Make planks.  Make many planks.  Make lots of thatch.  

11.  Farms and the Forrester seem to take the most villagers to be make them successful.  Whenever you put down a farm, add 2-3 more villagers.  Same for the Forrester.  Build a storage which only allows the materials necessary for a Forrester by the Forrester i.e. Tree Seeds; Tree Saplings and Mud.  These types of things will make them do their job more quickly and free them up for other tasks.  

If you have any questions on anything else within the game, please feel free to ask in the comments I'll be happy to help.  

To the Devs: Great job so far.  A special game I randomly found one day.  Appreciate your hard work.

The few reviews which are negative have failed at doing the above, or haven't put the amount of time to realize there is a strategy to playing this game successfully.

The one negative I have?  Peat.  It is in precarious areas and is often not in enough supply.  It is by far the most annoying resource to acquire. I've put in over 100 hours and felt that itch to play every day for the first time in a while. It's been a blast.

The game is a combination of Mount and Blade style combat, coop PvE - open-world impact, and "colony sim".

I grew up playing RTS and grand strategy games and generally love open-world/survival. This captures much of the best of both. 

Progression feels time-consuming and also meaningful - watching your city evolve from mud huts to a flourishing super-town to dominate the region is huge. The new mechanics for liberating towns, building within them to boost their productivity and population, and raising armies to fight against the enemy strongholds/camps is incredibly fun and rewarding.

There is so much opportunity for this game to grow it's content - it's still very early on. I can imagine this game being a top-tier game in it's genre. Hopefully the developers have the resources to continue focusing on it for some time.

Most fun elements.

1. Combat and killing bandits/attacking enemy camps is some of the most fun I've had in a while. Loot feels rewarding, combat is satisfying, and you feel like you're having an impact on the world.
2. Progression feels meaningful. Unlocking new "tech tiers" hugely upgrades your power, and expanding your town feels rewarding and impactful on the game world.
3. Village liberation is super fun and feels like you're changing the shape of the world, slowly taking back the game map from the enemy. There's lots of opportunity for you to trade, interact, and build up these allied towns.

Biggest Gripes

1. Lots of UI improvements are needed. Navigating menus and the management elements (especially late game) can be incredibly monotonous and frustrating. For example once you get several outposts, the default menu that pops up is always your home city. This is incredibly frustrating as you have to constantly navigate back to the outpost you want to manage. These are easy fixes. Also there are no sorting functions for villagers. Want to find the ones with the highest strength? Can't sort. Have to monotonously go through the entire list. I had to write down names so I would be able to find them.

2. Management overall is pretty obtuse and it's hard to tell how to increase your town's efficiency. Villagers have a "priority 1-9" number for each task they can do, or you can disable that task for them. So if I have village set to 1 farming, 2 harvest, and 3 smelting. Does that mean they spend a certain % of their time on 1 vs 2? Does it mean they wont move onto 2 unless 1 is "100% complete?" There is also 1-9 priority on buildings. How does that mesh with the villager priorities? Is it better to have a villager focus on one task or several? How do I know how efficient my town currently is? Finding your way through this system is trial-and-error, lots of google searches, and still landing in a place where you have no idea how efficient you are.

3. There are still a lot of "earflick" issues - for example  a coop player logging out stays in game (kinda cool) but if they dont log in again they cannot be moved or removed from the game (super not cool). We had our town square occupied by 2 players and couldn't build there because they're permanently standing there "afk". Lots of villager pathing issues, getting stuck, not working on tasks when they seemingly should. The army management/squads feature still looks half implemented and doesnt really function in an effectives way. This is all normal early access stuff but there is a lot to clean up here.

Overall I'm elated that a group of my friends and I were able to put 100 hours into this game and feel satisfied the entire time with never more than an earflick here or there. The game is shaping up super well and it's going to continue to be great over the next 18 months. These guys are doing great work and deserve your support. In some areas it is very, very rough around the edges. Building is a pain, especially once you hit tier 2, moving buildings and resources is a big headache. Transferring resources to a new town is an enormous chore.

Moving your units long distances is also a massive headache to the degree I often just ran around on my own. Bandit spawning mechanics feel very rushed and sloppy. They just magically spawn in units and buildings, they ought to need resources and time just like the player.

Combat is janky, one vs one is fine, but as soon as you are up against multiple opponents the combat falls apart. Melee units don't attack at a sensible range for their weapon, they'll sprint towards you like feral zombies (even if wearing full plate armour) until they are literally nose to nose like they want to give you a big hug.

The bad (very bad)

Squad/Army management is abysmal. It's an absolute nightmare to control your units and unless you arrange them into formations manually they will get slaughtered by the enemy (even your toughest max stats warriors). The last straw for me on this playthrough was I ordered my archers to refill their ammo from an arrow basket (they inexplicably don't do this without you telling them to) and they all ran to a nearby warehouse and got undressed. I wish I was joking.

Whereas somehow your own archers are useless, they will plink away all your expensive ammo and hit nothing but terrain.

More than that though your units always feel very underpowered regardless of their stats. Left alone they will always lose to raider parties. With the support this game garners, despite being 13 years old, it is still considered one of the best simulators out there. The community also plays a huge role in all the updates that are provided, which keeps the game enjoyable for years to come. There is no need to worry about dying like in an FPS game because it is a very peaceful game, which makes it one of the most enjoyable and relaxing games to play on the steam market.

The graphics in this game are superb; going around Europe and experiencing the varied topography is one of the things that makes this game so addictive. There's a variety of trucks that you can pick from and many hundreds of ways you can customize them, you can construct your own empire or handle the toughest of heavy hauls with the most fierce V8s or the finest I6s. This simulation game has no competition unlike other games and that makes this game very unique, this game and its wonderful community deserves 5 stars.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 90, "timestamp_created": 1736423610}, {"review_text": "My father played this game a lot, sim games was generally his thing a lot of the times. Unfortunately he passed away back in 2021. I had bought this game a couple months after he passed away. I wished I had gotten it sooner because this game is such a chill game to have.

At the time of writing this, SCS has most of Europe either made or is making. The base game is pretty good on its own however nowadays it is very evident that in order to really enjoy ETS 2, you're going to have to pay a little bit more for some regions but you can piecemeal your purchases whenever the DLCs come onto sale.

The gameplay is relatively basic, you pick up a trailer, drive to the destination, and then drop it off. That in itself can be very boring to some but I think with the amount of points of interest, it may give some life to your journey. The devs do lean on the beauty of Europe and the different landscapes it has to offer so much so that they even allow you to stop your truck in a spot and take in a view they think is interesting.

Though this game does tend to make you want to listen to a video, podcast, music, or whatever but you're literally driving so if you like driving IRL then this game could be for you if you want to not have so much stress IRL worrying about a million things.

The game gives me a silly itch that I never thought I sometimes need, I suppose my father was onto something when he played this game.

TL;DR Good chill game but basic gameplay at its core.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1749862994}, {"review_text": "Euro Truck Simulator 2 is the go-to game for fans of truck simulation, offering a realistic, immersive experience of life on the road. From driving across beautiful European landscapes to managing your own trucking business, this game allows you to step into the shoes of a trucker in a way few others do.

The Good:
✅ Incredibly Detailed World: The game features realistic cities, highways, and landscapes, providing an immersive driving experience that captures the beauty of Europe.
✅ Deep Customization Options: From truck modifications to managing your fleet, the game offers a ton of options to personalize your experience.
✅ Relaxing Yet Engaging Gameplay: While the pacing is slow, it provides a calming, zen-like experience of driving and managing a trucking empire.
✅ Realistic Driving Mechanics: The driving feels authentic, with a focus on realistic physics and handling, making long-haul journeys satisfying.
✅ Active Modding Community: The modding community constantly creates new content, including trucks, maps, and other additions to keep things fresh.
✅ Frequent Updates & DLCs: The game consistently receives updates and downloadable content (DLC) that expand the map and introduce new features.

The Bad:
❌ Repetitive Gameplay: The core gameplay loop can feel monotonous after a while, especially if you're not a fan of slow-paced, methodical gameplay.
❌ Initial Learning Curve: New players may feel overwhelmed by the controls and the complexity of managing a trucking business.
❌ Limited Action: For players looking for action-packed or fast-paced gameplay, this is not the game for you. It’s all about long, leisurely drives.
❌ Minor Technical Issues: Occasionally, bugs and glitches can disrupt the immersion, especially in certain DLCs or mods.

Final
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a phenomenal simulation game for those who appreciate realism, attention to detail, and the art of long-distance trucking. It’s not a fast-paced action game, but rather a calming and deeply immersive experience for players who want to relax and enjoy the drive. With its detailed world, customization, and steady stream of content, it’s a must-play for simulation fans.

Detailed environments, (delightful) long distances to drive and the building of your own trucking-empire are but a few facets of this surprising game!", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 2, "timestamp_created": 1747144153}, {"review_text": "So I kept hearing about the game  and for the life of me I just could not figure out why someone would enjoy it.

Its just driving trucks, I mean for truck nuts I get it, but the game has gotten recognition from so many people over the years that It couldnt just be people whose heartbeat raises when they see a big rig, right?

I saw the game on sale and thought why not, its super cheap, I havent used my wheel in a long time, lets see if I can find any enjoyment in it. The fact that Ive been hungry for any sort of a real traffic simulator certainly helped.

It takes a couple of minutes to set up if youre using a wheel but once thats done, you just choose your job and start driving across Europe.

Even though the game is a sim, its quite forgiving and aproachable for new players, after a couple hours I actually wished the game was a lot more strict with its traffic violation system.

Once I got into the "rhytm" of the game, I couldnt put it down. Ive put in 15 hours in 3 days.

The game has a ton of dlc which are all fairly priced and judging by other players feedback, absolutely worth it.

But even the base game has enough roads to keep you busy for probably atleast 150 hours until you explore most of them.

Im not always into roleplaying in games but when I do enjoy it, I know Im playing a good one. So I try to drive within the speed limit, use my indicators, try my best not to get too much in the way of AI drivers, etc. and its just so relaxing. I love driving through the bigger cities and seeing their landmarks, tune into the local radio to get a taste of the language and I constantly take screenshots during sunsets. For a 2013 release, the game looks pretty darn good at times.

What drives me forward now is progression, I cant wait to buy more trucks, hire more employees, get bigger trailers and start paying of my bank loans and make decent money.

I know most people think its not the type of game they would enjoy, I thought so too, for 9 years, until I gave it a fair try and discovered what Ive been missing.

One last thing thats absolutely great are mods. Theyre super easy to install, most of them are on the steam workshop so its a matter of two clicks, some of the bigger ones require you to drop a file in a folder, thats it. The game captures the rhythm of the road perfectly, from navigating Lisbon’s cramped streets to cruising Norway’s endless highways. Running a virtual trucking company, upgrading rigs, and meeting tight delivery deadlines mirror the real-world grind I’ve lived, where every load keeps the bank from calling. It’s an odd kind of comfort, letting me relive the job without the sore back or the sting of diesel prices.
The game’s long hauls nail the solitude of driving, where I’d usually have a cig in my gob to stay alert. In ETS2, as I steer my Volvo through a foggy Polish night, I can almost smell the tobacco that was my constant companion on those runs. Smoking isn’t part of the sim, but the quiet moments at fuel stops or border crossings bring back the ritual of lighting up, exhaling, and planning the next leg. It’s a subtle connection that makes the virtual cab feel like my old, smoke-stained Freightliner.
My drinking, whiskey and gin mostly, shattered everything that mattered. I chose the bottle over my wife, Evelyn, and our boys, David and Stuart, and they walked away, leaving a void no paycheck could fill. ETS2 is a refuge, where I can focus on a perfect trailer park or an efficient route without the fog of last night’s liquor. The game’s fatigue system hits like those mornings when my hands shook on the wheel, but here, I can pause and stay sharp, pouring my energy into a clean run instead of another drink.
ETS2 is a gem for anyone who knows the hum of the highway, flaws and all. With DLCs adding new regions and cargo, it evolves like the industry itself. Whether you’re a driver or just curious, it delivers depth and a strange calm. I give it a 9 out of 10; it’s the closest I get to piecing things together without a tab. Unfortunately, I have to choose between "[b]Recommended[/b]" and "[b]Not Recommended[/b]," and that's tough because my experience with this game was a mix bag of enjoyment but it also boring me to death.

Mafia 3 is a huge departure from Mafia 1 and 2. Those games had that signature "Mafia feel", you were deeply embedded in the mob, experiencing a gripping and linear, story-driven experience that captured the old-school gangster vibe. Mafia 3? Not so much. While you have ties to the mob, you’re not part of it in the same way. Instead, the game shifts gears and leans heavily toward an open-world, GTA-style/Ubisoft formula. This game isn’t inherently bad, but it does cause the game to lose part of what made the Mafia series so unique. The story is really good imo! It’s dark, gritty, and unforgettable! One of the strongest aspects of this game.

Unfortunately, the gameplay is a hufe let down. The missions are painfully repetitive. Taking over districts quickly becomes a chore. You’ll find yourself doing the same types of objectives over and over, and it drags the experience down. Combine that with frequent crashes! I had to restart the game multiple times just to get it running and it can be frustrating.

In the end, [b]Mafia 3 is a good game, but it’s not a good Mafia game[/b]. If you go in expecting something like Mafia 1 or 2, you might be disappointed. But if you give it a chance as its own thing, there’s some enjoyment to be found. Go to place A, talk to a guy, go to place B, kill a few guys, go back to place A, talk to the dude, Mission complete", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 4, "timestamp_created": 1752881728}, {"review_text": "I mostly wanted to post this to inform on how to get Mafia III into a more playable state. This game is infamous for the technical state it was left in, with numerous minor and major bugs plus crashes galore no matter how good your hardware is. It's also pretty notorious amongst achievement hunters due to counter-based achievements failing to retain your progress once you close the game, resulting in a frustrating to downright impossible 100% experience unless you are incredibly lucky. So after spending some time researching and implementing fixes, this is what I would recommend if you plan on trying this game out:

- Follow the below guide to revert your game back to Patch 1.09, including preventing the game's access to the internet. This should fix every counter based achievement and reduce the frequency that you'll have a crash.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3489276236
- Play the game in windowed mode for additional stability.
- There will be a mission where you have to enter a boxing ring and be pat down by security before you can enter. Lock the game to 30fps briefly to ensure this interaction plays out properly, else the game will soft lock. You can revert back to a higher frame rate after this.

This by no means makes the game perfect. There will be visual glitches, dialogue which does not play, and a myriad of other random issues. But after playing the game through once on the latest patch and the remainder of my 100% journey on Patch 1.09, I found the earlier version of Mafia III to be far more playable, and allowed me to achieve everything the game had to offer in two playthroughs.

Whether this will make you enjoy the game itself is a different story. It is a major departure from both previous Mafia games due to its open world structure and completely different approach to tackling the Mafia subject matter. I really enjoyed the atmosphere of the world, helped by the visual variety of New Bordeaux, and the excellent soundtrack, boasting many popular and lesser-known tracks of the 60s era. I also loved its storytelling and characters, with fantastic performances across the board and a unique documentary-style framing to the whole ordeal that makes every cutscene a super interesting watch. And while its activities may be repetitive, and its open world activities too safe for their own good, the great weapon sounds and feedback, alongside the brutal melee kills, was more than enough to keep me coming back to experience its combat.

I genuinely believe that with a bit of trimming of the open world fat, and abundant time spent to fix the game up to a polished state, Mafia III would be revered to the point of moving out of the mixed Steam and critical reception it will likely be forever left in. So if you've played the other two Mafia games and are curious whether's it's worth trying the third, I'd recommend enacting the above fixes and give it a go; I was pleasantly surprised by how much I ended up liking this, and maybe you will feel the same as well.

Yes, it's an open world game, yes, it's a [i]Mafia[/i] game, so you know what you can expect (an involved story of crime and revenge with lots of characters, punctuated by action missions) but this is incredibly, almost unplayably tedious. Every single mission boils down to "drive over here, shoot 20 dudes with the two weapons you've got, press button to complete mission, repeat" with the occasional flash-forward cutscene afterwards that advances the story about every three such missions. The game makes a big deal about how your goal is taking over the city by unlocking crime bosses to work for you and give them rackets to run, but this is an utterly sterile affair where they just occasionally generate cash and maybe want you to do a few missions where, you've guessed it, you shoot 20 dudes and press the button to complete the mission.

It wouldn't be so bad if maybe there were fun side activities to do, but there aren't -- collectibles is all you get, and these are signposted on the map (but, to be fair, only after you've first collected things to unlock the markers that show you where to collect things, so it's almost like gameplay!) Driving is the usual nonsense where your most impressive accomplishment is going from A to B in a straight line without swerving too much. Don't worry about obeying traffic rules though -- despite the game making a big deal about police attention, they'll let you drive any which way. God help you if they're actually on you for a reported crime, though, as they're utterly relentless and it's really faster and more convenient to just respawn than trying to shake them if you didn't manage to get away from the scene fast enough to begin with.

The best I can say for the fighting is that the AI tries to flank you (tries being the operative word). Stealth is an option, but it's a complete joke -- press key to distract one enemy (always just one), wait for them to come in range, knock out, repeat. Pretty soon you'll have a nice pile of enemies stacked in your corner, and there's always room for some more. You can pick up bodies to drop them out of sight, but if there's ever a need for this I haven't found it, as enemies won't do anything but puzzle over their dead comrades to give you an opportunity to whack them as well. Beyond using stealth to get a foothold in the area, it's arguably less tedious to just go in guns blazing. Enemies drop weapons and ammo aplenty and the only penalty for dying is the classic GTA model of "lose some cash and respawn right outside", so you can bang your head against the wall as often as you like. If murdering clueless mooks by the dozens is all you're here for, this game has you covered.

Even the setting can't save the game. The environs look nice enough and the '60s soundtrack has some certified bangers, but there's nothing to see or do anywhere in most areas until the story mission unlocks that populates them with a big bunch of enemies to slaughter. You can enter shops and rob them for utterly meager amounts of cash and that's about all interaction you get beyond that, which has to be one of the most pointless and petty opportunities for crime I've ever seen in a game that showers you with money. I guess the lesson here is that [i]some[/i] crime pays and you should be mindful of which. Oh, and I guess you can drive a boat instead of a car in some areas, so, uh, well that's different, I guess. Rounding out this dreary package are lots of graphics and physics glitches, none game-breaking for me but still distracting, and the performance is undeniably bad, being saved for me only because I have a 7900 XTX -- and even with that getting 60 FPS on an "unlocked' framerate is the best it can manage. The game looks pretty good, but not good enough to justify that.

Maybe this is one of those games that picks up after 20 hours and then builds to some kind of amazing climax with tons of mechanics that unlock excruciatingly slowly, but I want more out of a game than just busywork, and [i]Mafia III[/i] just doesn't offer enough to convince me it's worth investing more time in, given all the other games I could be playing instead. - Visceral combat. Both you and enemies go down fast, making for some intense gunplay, kills aren't always clean too, with enemies lying wounded, begging for their lives or groaning, emphasising the brutality, though for you you do get adrenaline shots you can use to recover from near-death and buff your health back, but that only goes a little towards making you less squishy until you get late game upgrades for it.
- Memorable setting and story. A Southern US city with French influence, diverse range of gangs (Hillbillies, KKK, Mafiosi, Haitians, Irish), and easily hateable racist scumbags trying to hold back the march of the civil rights era, and a narrative told in several formats, the 60s, which acts as your character's present, and flashforwards in some cutscenes to 2 different forms, a 1970s Senate hearing and a 2010s documentary, speaking about your crime spree in past tense with the characters reflecting on it, those characters are certainly interesting too, both friends and enemies, well voice acted with excellently mocapped cutscenes. Plus the radio music rules.
- Sit Down system. Mafia 3 is all about conquering the city, the basic gameplay loop is this, you have 9 districts to take over by killing their bosses, each district has its boss (representing the whole district) and 2 underlings (representing its 2 rackets/businesses), the first 3 districts are automatically assigned to your 3 different ally gangs, but after that you get to decide who gets what, earning cash and unique perks from the allies you provide for, each offering 4 district’s worth of perks and 3 district's worth of loyalty missions which add a little extra story at the end of the chain. First you can decide rackets individually, but once you kill the boss you assign the district as a whole, giving all of its rackets to your chosen ally. Each ally always wants the turf, but their hunger for it will be impacted by 2 things, whether you already gave them rackets in that turf, and their overall loyalty (based on if you give them turfs previously, or did post-turf loyalty missions for them), you can keep them all happy and make lots of cash together if you play your cards right, but if you don't they'll ditch you and become a problem to be dealt with and a hole in your wallet. The only real flaw it has is there’s no real reason to assign any rackets to a boss you don’t plan to give the turf to, as it just pisses them off with no benefits, making that choice basically irrelevant.
- Quality DLCs. The DLC missions, included free in this edition, are great fun with proper plotlines and unique missions, best played in between waves of district conquering to break up their monotony.
- Smoother controls driving. Taking an even further step in this direction from M2 the driving is fast and it’s easy to make turns, making for really nice cruising round the city that only really is lost if you pick a really shit vehicle or it gets so shot to bits you don’t have any tires left to cruise with. On foot it’s easier to snap in and out of cover too.

Cons
- Repetitive gameplay loop. To draw out a district boss you have to kill their underlings and to draw out the underlings you have to meddle with their rackets, you do that by doing assassinations, interrogations (just a takedown where you hold instead of press the button), thefts, property destruction and the occasional hostage rescue, these get very repetitive very fast. That gets added to once districts are taken over, where you have delivery jobs to do to increase their income and the loyalty missions (which include more collectathons and assassination jobs), although those are at least optional. These generic, repetitive, plot lite, bite sized jobs make up the vast majority of missions, with only the Prologue, District Bosses*, Finale and DLC content including unique encounters.
- Wonky takedown system. Takedowns can either be lethal or non lethal, but rather than being 2 different keybinds or a press/hold distinction, lethality has to be toggled in the options menu, underling bosses can also only be spared if you do the arbitrary extra step of wiretapping their area, otherwise Lincoln will automatically kill them.
- Occasional tanky enemies. In general combat is fast paced, but some enemies have artificially buffed health, being able to take dozens of Tommy Gun rounds to the chest with nothing but a generic shirt on and still turn round and blast you as you reload, not fun. This becomes a non issue around half way through the game, when upgrades to your health restoring Adrenaline make you the tanky one.
- Lacking interactivity. Except for car shops all of the game's stores can't be bought from, with resources instead handled through mobile dealers you can call, although those dealers make for great convenience the lack of stores, makes the city feel pretty barren of things to do. You just have the car dealerships, mission content, planting wiretaps and robbery, a step down from M2.
- Mission bugs. Sometimes missions don't appear when they're supposed to, forcing a restart to get them to appear, and sometimes icons for them can show up on the map when they're not actually available, leading you towards red herrings.
- Lacking faction variety. The early game gives the impression you’ll be up against a variety of factions, introducing the Haitians and Dixie Mafia as early rivals, but in reality almost the whole game has you fighting against the Mafia, with the Haitians joining you and Dixie only appearing in filler missions after the prologue. Though you do face the KKK styled Southern Union in select other encounters.
- Loss of collectivity. In M1 you were part of a gang, very frequently working with other mobsters like Paulie and Sam as well as regular goons, in 2 you swapped from family to family but were constantly with your buddy Joe and sometimes others like Henry and Tony, in 3 there’s almost none of that except for the prologue, where you work with several allies to rob the Federal Reserve. After that Lincoln has people in a support role like the 3 allied gang bosses and their associates, plus his spook ally Donovan, but the actual dirty work is done by him on his own, even though it’s his crime family. His own gang he was part of before, the Black Mob, is also completely forgotten about after the prologue. A nearly entirely one man war, Rambo style, is a departure from the series that just makes the immersion harder to maintain.
- Simplified police system. Cops don’t try to arrest you anymore, they either ignore your shit or shoot, and they don’t enforce most traffic laws unlike M1 and 2 where they’d try to fine or arrest you for speeding or running red lights, I don’t mind not being harassed by that given how much driving there is to do, but the option would be cool, especially for this setting where these racist cops would pull you over for any little thing irl, they also don't remember you/your vehicle’s look after being wanted.
- Outfit choice not respected. Because most cutscenes are pre-rendered, Lincoln will always appear in cutscenes in his veteran jacket, rather than what you chose to wear.

*District Bosses are usually 1 mission, but the last set of bosses have 2 missions, having you take down an accomplice of theirs too

For much of my first 9 hours with the game (where I conquered the first 3 districts) I really hated it, drained by its constant repetition, but after playing one of the DLCs, getting a breather, when I came back to the main game I found I wasn’t bothered as much, since the combat and driving is a solid core, in the end enjoying the game despite its faults, especially since more weapon and vehicle unlocks sped up those repetitive rackets, letting me get to the more substantial parts faster.

The fact that they barely bothered to include proper missions really keeps it down, leaving it as just good, rather than truly great, but on balance, I’d say it's worth a play.", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 0, "timestamp_created": 1761952008}, {"review_text": "This is not the Mafia story based games we have all fallen in love with.

There are 2 ways to play this game and either way you're going to be upset. Either you play vanilla and the achievements don't work 100%, or you downgrade and accept your fate with any bugs along the way.

I chose the later and had to close my eyes and pray quite a few times.

On 1.09, I had cutscenes freeze and only play audio (I could skip and resume gameplay, or restart and fix it all together). Then I had to restart a mission because a story trigger didn't appear. Other times I would exit a car and the radio would keep playing, even if I triggered a conversation. Much later, while playing a DLC, I got a crash during a loading screen after completing a mission and my save got corrupted, but I was able to recover (thankfully the game creates 3 save files you can copy and rename, or you'll have to make manual saves of your AppData along the way). 

So, curb your expectations and roll up your sleeves, there's musclin' to be done.

Disrupt rackets, flip/clip informants, draw out the lieutenants, and slay the head cheese. Build a gang, keep everyone happy, or let there only be one. Steal a police car and feed a body (even yours!) to a gator. The usual criminal stuff.

You'll need 2 playthroughs for everything, if you plan it right the second will be way quicker. You need to save quite a bit of money, and you'll also need to spend a lot too, so plan ahead, synchronize your DLC's with your story progression, and you should be golden. I did 2 DLC's with the first playthrough, and the other DLC with my second. Don't get stuck after the game with nothing to do but idle and let the game cycle bring in another kickback, just because you bought something you didn't need and still need to upgrade the bar or your weed stand!

The city isn't too big so traveling and hitting all your targets felt within reach. You can definitely knock out a good chunk in plenty of time. I watched hella movies and tv.

Sadly, there's not really that much variety in how you achieve your goals. At first I was sneaky, but after however many knockouts I got, I just ran past everyone before they could react, then shoot my target and get the hell outta there. The police will mostly leave you alone if it's just you versus the other gangs. The police also seem like they have no idea how to use a shortcut or drive down an alley. Enemies in general just kind of stand there waiting for you to pop them. Checks notes: "Difficulty: Easy." Ah.

"Tell me about his rackets." ... "Man with a gun!"
Witness is calling the police.

To be fair, the only really cool parts of the story was the Ferris Wheel and the gambling ship. Either I wasn't interested or wasn't following closely (probably I just missed everything because nothing was playing!), but it was all sort of... forgettable. The action was sort of dull, and yeah, I kept thinking the graphics looked blurry. I liked the Stones Unturned DLC, the cult one was alright, and Faster, Baby was fine. Still, I weathered the storm and the game served its purpose of driving and shooting, a couple of screen grabs with subtitles on, and another gold star.

The dev's probably didn't intend for so many people to actually get onto it right away, and, sense this was promoted in the DBZ Game Hour plus, the fact that it's basically season 0/Season 1. The netcode would probably need finetuning after all.

I personally get tired of the constant fighting games from Dragon Ball's end; Arena-Fighter's get stale personally from time to time as someone who's played the Budokai games/Tenkaichi and the like. So, seeing them actually try expirementing is actually something I'm intrigued to see where it'll go on from here.

The balancing of the games rather intresting from someone who's looking at it from a competitve standpoint and the like. I'm at a pretty decent level; level 23 and haven't been using my points for anything stupid. I know they'll be unlocked through quest's and the like more than likely. So, i'm not really complaining about that any.

The gameplay is intuitive and crisp- not wanting to overwhelm your fanbase, many of people wouldn't have them right away unless if they played the beta. However, winning isn't mandatory. It's to teach the player's how to play and slowly work regarding their Divine Card's + Companions. The first one's you get Companion wise are actually really good for newbies to actually end up using actually. The character's you get access to are really easy to pick up and learn- I admittedly used Goku for my first round, and was able to keep up to the rest by actively learning how to utilize his kit mid-play. I personally main Bojack/Trunks/Baby/Kid Gohan, and they all have distinctive playstyles. You can pretty much find whatever character's that suit your playstyle from how varied they are.

The gameplay loop is based around you leveling up and going after the GoD's when the Zeno's give you a proper chance to do so- however, Bosses spawn and you have to balance taking out the GoD's and the Bosses. The Bosses as of current are Nappa/Ribrriane (or however she's spelled)/Android 16/Jaco all are. The Divine Draw system actively makes the matches have a bit of RNG to end up deciding what to do, however, this can make your strategy more and more concise the more you figure out what to do.

As a example; Cloud-Cover? Go into the cloud's and sneakly land a max Gekshin Burst to take down a God's health a large bit and gain a kill. That's a play that I tend to do.

The character-roster is a consistent, flexible and allows for a multitude of options for the player's to go behind. To give a example, Goku is a consistent good mobility option with pretty reliable DPS. Vegeta is a consistently good tank that needs a ton of skill to learn. Krillin can be annoying and stun people rather consistently via Solar-Flare, making them a rather easy target for the player or their team. Buu is a rather great option for debuffing/healing and much, much, more.

I've been playing this with my hubby, so, I know full well how annoying it is to have bad teammates. However, it feels so nice to synergize together. Synergy in games like this would be nice, however, I understand that alot of MOBA's don't give you access to VC- Pokemon Unite to give a example, however, alot of people seem to be wanting this be compared to like League. There is a gacha system after all and a bit of microtransactions that aren't mandatory, but, the reason makes honest sense to me. It's a free game, the dev's would probably want some money to flow back into their accounts for making something like this admittedly, Pokemon Unite was somewhat similar but more P2W in that aspect from what I can personally tell. This isn't. It just get's a bit slower by the latter half of 20-30 around that aspect! But, you need to have patience.

If the dev's end up reading this; I'd reccomend adding Voice-chat as a potential option for those who actually desire to do so in their settings. This would actively make communication and coordination to be more effecient, making for a more strategic gameplay loop between multiple of player's. Due to the foe getting this as well, this would be akin to playing LoL like the fanbase would actually be wanting from what I can tell from a multitude of reviews.

However;

Overall, I do reccomend this game personally as of the current. The issues are easily passable, the game just came out and is starting small. The playerbase may continuously rise depenent on what the dev's do, after all. The gameplay is crisp and the dev's are actively cracking down on the issues rather consistently. It's a enjoyable romp with you, and your friend's too. It isn't too competitve nor too casual. The game is consistently balanced/exciting and pretty well structured as well. I've unlocked over-half of the current character's as a F2P player too, which, you should be able to as well. The monetization isn't even predatory like some other MOBA's/Gacha games out there, you can get capsules to do the summons completely freely which is definitely a bonus within my own eyes. It's just a option at the end of the day and it's presented as such. From my current win-loss ratio showed in the Battle history is 15 wins and 5 losses throughout today and yesterday. So, I'm proud of that!

🔹 REALITY: a cute logic game with zero challenge.

🔶 Is this seat taken? (ITST?) is a logic game about arranging anthropomorphic shapes according to their needs/requests. One might be noisy, another needs silence, so don't put them together. The plot follows Nat starting her acting career, and serves as a link for the setting of levels.

🔸 The game is structured around 5 cities, 4 unique and 1 repeat, but they only affect the backstory and aren't really represented visually in the levels. Each city has 5-6 levels/scenarios, plus one extra unlockable, that are quite varied in general, from a bus to a cinema, a concert or a classroom.

🔸 Each level consists on 4-5 rounds of arranging 'people', with some shapes remaining in the level, while others leave for new ones to arrive. Once everyone is sitting (also standing or laying down), the game will lets us know if someone is unhappy, but it also lets us ignore that and move on.

🔸 The difficulty is low but the worst is that its curve is flat. I expected a challenge or a twist in the game mechanics at some point, but it never came. The way you solve levels at the beginning is the same as at the end, the only difference is the shapes' requests depending on the setting.

🔸 ITST? is beautiful, fun and better played casually. It's a puzzle game for non-puzzle players: those inexperienced, wanting to be initiated or seeking to spend some time on a game that doesn't demand too much thinking.

🙂+
😄+ art
😍+

Is This Seat Taken? is about working out seating arrangements for people, in cinemas, restaurants, trains, cabs, football games, dance etc.  People are represented by shapes like triangle, square, circle, rhombus etc. Some people are sensitive to smell, some don't like loud noises, others want to be alone or want to sleep. What the game does well: its puzzle mechanic. I found it fun balancing the shapes' preferences. It doesn't overstay its welcome, yet it's not too short. The special levels, especially the New York First Dates one, were my favorites. It felt cohesive and unhindered by the game’s core mechanics. The game does well at smaller, self-contained bits like that.

Now, what needs improvement? Someone already mentioned this, and it bears repeating: a reset button. I often found myself putting people and objects back by hand when I wanted to try a new arrangement. I noticed difficulty spikes in a few levels that felt forced in the game’s flow. It's one thing if this was touted as a crazy hard puzzler, and everything had the same level of brain power, but I didn’t get that impression.

That said, I had an issue with the plot. I wasn't expecting anything mind-blowing, and this clearly wasn’t the game’s primary focus. It's a cozy puzzler, not Cube Escape. I found myself rolling my eyes at some of the dialogue writing with the main characters. I’m not familiar with this developer or if they've made games previously, so I don’t think it’d be fair of me to say “oh, it feels written by AI" - but it *was* my initial reaction. Is This Seat Taken? feels like a soft puzzle picnic: easygoing, pretty, and a bit repetitive after just one bite.

You play as a considerate little critter trying to help other passengers find the perfect spot without triggering anyone’s inner drama queen. And honestly? The cuteness of it all is the main event. The art is straight-up adorable, the characters have charming little interactions, and the whole vibe is warm and approachable.

Controls are simple, colors are gentle on the eyes, and there’s a neat little difficulty slider (“complaint level”) if you want to spice things up. The tutorial's quick, and the environments are varied enough to stay visually fresh.

But make no mistake: this one’s for cozy casuals only. If you’re here to flex your logic muscles, you might get bored before your seat even reclines. The puzzles in the first map were very easy (like, “solved before I blinked” easy). And while the overall aesthetic is inviting, things already feels a little samey after one map.

Still, I do recommend it for players who love light puzzle experiences with a wholesome wrapper. It’s the kind of game I’d sip tea with, not compete in.

I’ll update once I’ve played more than the first map, but for now: cute, calm, and not particularly clever. Definitely worth a look, just maybe on sale.

UPDATE: Took 4.5 hours to complete, and everything from my previous review still stands.
Still the same charming, quirky ride I talked about before (just now with an official 100% playtime stamp).

[{"review_text": "13-year-old me had endless time to beat Gothic II every possible way.

34-year-old me is lucky to squeeze in 1–2 hours of gaming per day on a good week.
But I finally found a game that scratches that old itch… even if the journey now comes in tiny, hard-won slices of free time. Cheers Older-GAMERS. Lets dig in

**********************************

5 Hours In - Difficulty: Grayshaft

Called in sick today and finally sat down with the game. Here’s the short version, straight from my own eyes.

The game definitely needs a lot more polishing, but it’s also not a game for everyone. Not everyone will give it enough time to show what it’s actually trying to deliver.

But when it clicks?
The Gothic atmosphere is absolutely there. The exploration is rewarding, the world is much bigger than expected, and yes, you’ll get lost a couple of times, but that’s part of the learning curve.

Combat is challenging but manageable, and it becomes smoother as your stats improve.

BUT... 


------>       I’ve decided to wait for a few patches before I dig deeper.     <-------


Things that break the experience for me right now:

• Most city NPCs are non-functional.
You can’t talk to them, can’t hit them, can’t interact with them. Feels like cardboard stand-ins.

• Some NPCs vanish after their quest/dialogue.
Even if they’re useless, why remove them? In Gothic I knew every NPC by heart, that familiarity mattered.

• Loot density is wildly inconsistent.
Some areas drown you in items, others feel like the developers forgot to place anything.

• Can’t interact with objects while sneaking/crouching.

• Crime system is harsh and needs revamping
I’m wanted across the entire kingdom because I stole.. a carrot at the Woodcutters camp. And I didn’t even get comforted for it. In Gothic it was obvious when you were trespassing or stealing. Here? Not so much.

• Resting/sitting/other animations can’t be interrupted.
You’re forced to watch the whole thing like a medieval Netflix loading screen.

• Opening letters/books kicks you out of your inventory.
Everything in the Quest Items tab looks the same, so you end up hunting for things you haven’t used yet. Highlight new items maybe?


• Following NPCs around is painful.
They walk at their own pace, ignoring yours. A follow-speed match or a follow option would fix so much frustration.



***********************************

LATEST UPDATE

7 Hours In - Difficulty: Grayshaft

People are getting annoyed by these things and after 7 hours, I’m right there with them.
I come from a less spoiled generation, the kind that powered through jank because the magic underneath was worth it.

And I do see something magical beneath this game… but right now it’s buried under too many rough edges. I tried to push through, but I just can’t ignore them anymore.
Maybe I’ve become a little spoiled too.

That’s why I’m putting it on pause.

With a few good patches, this could turn into something truly special, the spark is there, it just needs room to breathe. 

Developers, I believe in you <3", "voted_up": true, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 18, "timestamp_created": 1764024568}, {"review_text": "I really wanted to like this game. It’s the kind of game where you can feel the passion the devs had for the project, but unfortunately I can’t recommend it.
So for you who’s unsure whether you should buy it or not, here’s my quick take:

Don’t buy this game yet. Save your money and come back in six months or a year. The game was released, but it’s not complete. In its current state it will give you a few hours of fun and some open-world challenge (a challenge that sometimes borders on unfair when it comes to combat difficulty, but with enough patience you can push through).

The more time you spend dealing with the game’s broken mechanics, the more frustrating it becomes. You’ll see it’s missing a lot of basic QoL features and is full of pointless mechanics made to “feel realistic and hardcore,” but that in reality only waste your time and artificially stretch gameplay hours. And that’s without even mentioning the bugs and the horrible performance.

I don’t fully regret buying it, but if I could refund it and buy it again after some patches — assuming they ever come — I definitely would. Once again, the essence/sauce/idea behind the game is incredible! Exploring the open world is immersive. You'll have fun, but you'll inevitably get frustrated.

With the hope that the game improves, below I’m leaving a list of suggestions and changes this game really needs, and I hope the devs actually see it. These are harsh and realistic criticisms, but they’re for the good of the game, because I genuinely see potential here if some of these things get revisited.

Alright then, let’s get into it:

1 – The getting-up animation is excessively slow. Nobody stands up like that, especially in combat. Idk if you’ve ever been punched in the face but, unless you got knocked out, you’ll stand up reaaaal quick. In real life nobody wants to be caught in a vulnerable position during a life-or-death situation. And I’m not even starting on the mechanics that make you trip over branches and puddles… jesus bro… who had that idea? The mechanic itself isn’t even that bad, but the time it takes to stand up is just insane.

2 – Add the option to refuse quests. Example: Roach, the NPC in the slums — once I understood what his quest was, I didn’t want to do it, but my character automatically accepted it just because I talked to him. Let us decline quests, or at least abandon them after accepting. Yeah, I can just ignore it for the rest of the game, I know — but being able to actually abandon it would be nice.

3 – Why can’t I sleep in random camp beds or in beds in bandit camps after clearing them? Even with a risk of ambush, it should still be possible, especially considering the game includes basic survival skills.

4 – There’s no way to store your torch or pick it back up from the ground. Why can’t I just extinguish it and keep it?? Or at least grab it after dropping it?? Jumping from a slightly high place makes the torch fall out of your hand automatically, which feels unrealistic. Even if it fell, you should be able to pick it up again.

5 – Enemies aggro without actually seeing you, or just because another enemy aggroed. Idk why this happens — maybe the enemies’ vision cones are too big and they can see way too far — but I aggroed one zombie and literally the whole zombie camp came running toward me.

6 – The game needs more camera options, like a shoulder camera and proper FOV settings. There’s already a Nexus mod doing this within two days of release, so it should just be implemented officially.

7 – Add the option to pause during dialogues. Simple and necessary.

8 – Please fix the stealing system — this is a big one:

• You can’t steal while crouched, which makes zero sense. Why does crouching even exist if you can’t do the most basic thing with it?
• Items marked with the “steal” tag should show in red or at least have a red outline. This is basic QoL, especially with such a broken punishment system.
• The detection system is bad. I stole from an empty room in the mercenary hall and still got caught. All NPCs in the room were sleeping, but somehow they saw me stealing a sword and a carrot, and a guard miles away sprinted to stop me… come on.
• The punishment system seriously needs work. Add jail or something. Right now the only option is paying, and if you can’t pay a level 30 guard just tries to kill you. Paying wouldn’t be an issue, but the price they ask for stealing an apple is ridiculous. I had 1000 gold and it still wasn’t enough to pay for my “crimes.” I had to reload hours back because I didn’t have a closer save.

9 – The weapon sharpening system is extremely garbage. Sorry, but it’s unintuitive and not fun. Conceptually it makes sense, but in practice it’s fucking horrible. Just change it to anything else and it will automatically be better.

10 – At the city entrance in Act 1 you only have one real option: pay or… pay. At least add an Insight or Intimidation option. There’s no nuance, just the illusion of choice. And if you try to confront them… well, enjoy trying to solo two level 30 guards at low level.

11 – The city of Greyshaft has a lot of problems… but one thing no one seems to mention is the complete lack of ambient sound. It feels extremely odd. It’s super underwhelming because you just came from an outskirts adventure full of birds, monsters, footsteps on grass, NPC banter, tons of interactable characters… and then you enter a city that’s dead silent. Combine that with no map, identical NPCs, horrible journal directions, and the place ends up feeling like a student project. I’m not asking for Novigrad-level detail, but some polish would be appreciated.

12 – Lots of people talk about this already, so I won’t go too deep, but… we are a cartographer and we don’t even think about making a map in our own journal or on a piece of paper with charcoal?? Like WTF. I’m an illustrator — when I’m out, I keep a sketchbook to draw dumb shit anywhere I go. Idk why we don’t have a map after 2–3 hours of gameplay. This would literally be one of the first things a cartographer would do. This is a poor design choice.", "voted_up": false, "votes_helpful": 0, "votes_funny": 7, "timestamp_created": 1764266351}, {"review_text": "I'm so torn! TL:DR

All a great start! However this isn't the real world where you can just ask for directions from any rando or read the signs or use a paper map. Instead, I guess they expect us to memorize this entire city's layout, even though it’s not laid out in a navigable manner, a non GPS paper style map you fill out would be great here, especially considering the protagonist's profession. Quests rarely have any sort of intuitive solvability and that's not helped by the number of bugs. It’s chaotic, it’s challenging, and it can be downright frustrating. But it’s also incredibly rewarding, and that’s what has kept me coming back.

The taming system is what hooked me from the start. No other game I've played lets you bond with creatures in the way ARK does. Whether it’s your very first Parasaur or that hard-earned high-level Rex you tracked for what felt like forever, every tame feels meaningful. 

I’ve always loved the progression in this game. Starting out with nothing but a stone pick in your hand and slowly working your way up to full Tek gear and a powerful dino army… there's nothing quite like it. I enjoy games where effort pays off, and ARK delivers with its grind, farming, and patience-rewarding gameplay.

The soundtrack is genuinely beautiful. The music captures the wonder and danger of each environment in a way that sticks with you long after you log off.

That said, I do think it’s a shame that ARK: Evolved has been left behind in favor of ARK: Ascended. While Ascended might offer visual upgrades, I’m sticking with Evolved. It’s the version that I, and many others, built our memories in, and I still wholeheartedly recommend it to new players who want that original, raw survival experience.

Is it perfect? Definitely not. You’ll run into bugs, crashes, and the occasional rage-quit moment. But that’s just part of ARK’s charm. It may not be the most polished game, but it has heart.
